title: Aare
sentence_0: This article is about a river in Switzerland.
sentence_1: For other uses, see [[Aare_(given_name)|Aare (given name)]], [[Aare_(surname)|Aare (surname)]], and [[Aar_(disambiguation)|Aar (disambiguation)]].

table.value: [[Lütschine|Lütschine]] (Lake Brienz), [[Kander_(Switzerland)|Kander]] (Lake Thun), [[Gürbe|Gürbe]], [[Sarine|Saane/La Sarine]], Zihl/La Thielle (Lakes of Neuchatel and Bienne), [[Suze_(river)|La Suze]] (Lake of Bienne), Dünnern

sentence_2: The Aare (German: [[Standard_German|[ˈaːrə]]) or Aar (German: [[Standard_German|[aːɐ̯]] (listen)) is a [[Tributary|tributary]] of the [[High_Rhine|High Rhine]] and the longest [[River|river]] that both rises and ends entirely within [[Switzerland|Switzerland]].
sentence_3: Its total length from its source to its junction with the [[Rhine|Rhine]] comprises about 295 kilometres (183 mi), during which distance it descends 1,565 m (5,135 ft), draining an area of 17,779 km (6,865 sq mi), almost entirely within Switzerland, and accounting for close to half the area of the country, including all of [[Central_Switzerland|Central Switzerland]].
sentence_4: There are more than 40 [[Hydroelectric_plant|hydroelectric plants]] along the course of the Aare.
sentence_5: The [[Hydronymy|river's name]] dates to at least the [[La_Tène_period|La Tène period]], and it is attested as Nantaror "Aare valley" in the [[Berne_zinc_tablet|Berne zinc tablet]].
sentence_6: The name was Latinized as Arula/Arola/Araris.
sentence_7: The Aare rises in the great [[Aargletschers|Aargletschers]] (Aare Glaciers) of the [[Bernese_Alps|Bernese Alps]], in the [[Canton_of_Bern|canton of Bern]] and west of the [[Grimsel_Pass|Grimsel Pass]].
sentence_8: The [[Finsteraarhorn|Finsteraargletscher]] and [[Lauteraarhorn|Lauteraargletscher]] come together to form the Unteraargletscher (Lower Aar Glacier), which is the main source of water for the [[Grimselsee|Grimselsee]] (Lake of Grimsel).
sentence_9: The [[Oberaargletscher|Oberaargletscher]] (Upper Aar Glacier) feeds the [[Oberaarsee|Oberaarsee]], which also flows into the Grimselsee.
sentence_10: The Aare leaves the Grimselsee just to the east to the Grimsel Hospiz, below the [[Grimsel_Pass|Grimsel Pass]], and then flows northwest through the [[Haslital|Haslital]], forming on the way the magnificent Handegg Waterfall, 46 m (151 ft), past [[Guttannen|Guttannen]].
sentence_11: Right after [[Innertkirchen|Innertkirchen]] it is joined by its first major tributary, the Gamderwasser.
sentence_12: Less than 1 kilometre (0.62 mi) later the river carves through a [[Limestone|limestone]] ridge in the [[Aare_Gorge|Aare Gorge]] ([[German_language|German]]: Aareschlucht).
sentence_13: It is here that the Aare proves itself to be more than just a river, as it attracts thousands of tourists annually to the causeways through the gorge.
sentence_14: A little past [[Meiringen|Meiringen]], near [[Brienz|Brienz]], the river expands into [[Lake_Brienz|Lake Brienz]].
sentence_15: Near the west end of the lake it indirectly receives its first important [[Tributary|tributary]], the [[Lütschine|Lütschine]], by the Lake of Brienz.
sentence_16: It then runs across the swampy plain of the Bödeli (Swiss German diminutive for ground) between [[Interlaken|Interlaken]] and [[Unterseen|Unterseen]] before flowing into [[Lake_Thun|Lake Thun]].
sentence_17: Near the west end of Lake Thun, the river indirectly receives the waters of the [[Kander_(Switzerland)|Kander]], which has just been joined by the [[Simme|Simme]], by the Lake of Thun.
sentence_18: Lake Thun marks the head of navigation.
sentence_19: On flowing out of the lake it passes through [[Thun|Thun]], and then flows through the city of [[Bern|Bern]], passing beneath [[List_of_Aare_bridges_in_Bern|eighteen bridges]] and around the steeply-flanked peninsula on which the [[Old_City_of_Berne|Old City of Berne]] is located.
sentence_20: The river soon changes its northwesterly flow for a due westerly direction, but after receiving the [[Sarine|Saane or La Sarine]] it turns north until it nears [[Aarberg|Aarberg]].
sentence_21: There, in one of the major Swiss engineering feats of the 19th century, the Jura water correction, the river, which had previously rendered the countryside north of Bern a [[Swampland|swampland]] through frequent flooding, was diverted by the Aare-Hagneck Canal into the [[Lac_de_Bienne|Lac de Bienne]].
sentence_22: From the upper end of the lake, at [[Nidau|Nidau]], the river issues through the Nidau-Büren Canal, also called the Aare Canal, and then runs east to [[Büren,_Solothurn|Büren]].
sentence_23: The lake absorbs huge amounts of eroded gravel and snowmelt that the river brings from the Alps, and the former swamps have become fruitful plains: they are known as the "vegetable garden of Switzerland".
sentence_24: From here the Aare flows northeast for a long distance, past the ambassador town [[Solothurn|Solothurn]] (below which the Grosse [[Emme_(river)|Emme]] flows in on the right), [[Aarburg|Aarburg]] (where it is joined by the [[Wigger_(river)|Wigger]]), [[Olten|Olten]], [[Aarau|Aarau]], near which is the junction with the Suhre, and Wildegg, where the Seetal [[Aabach_(Seetal)|Aabach]] falls in on the right.
sentence_25: A short distance further, below [[Brugg|Brugg]] it receives first the [[Reuss_(river)|Reuss]], its major tributary, and shortly afterwards the [[Limmat|Limmat]], its second strongest tributary.
sentence_26: It now turns to north, and soon becomes itself a tributary of the [[Rhine|Rhine]], which it even surpasses in volume when the two rivers unite downstream from [[Koblenz,_Switzerland|Koblenz (Switzerland)]], opposite [[Waldshut-Tiengen|Waldshut]] in Germany.
sentence_27: The Rhine, in turn, empties into the [[North_Sea|North Sea]] after crossing into the [[Netherlands|Netherlands]].

title: ACF Fiorentina
sentence_0: ACF Fiorentina, commonly referred to as Fiorentina ([[Italian|[fjorenˈtiːna]]), is an Italian professional [[Association_football|football]] [[List_of_football_clubs_in_Italy|club]] based in [[Florence|Florence]], [[Tuscany|Tuscany]], Italy.
sentence_1: Founded by a merger in August 1926, and refounded in August 2002 following bankruptcy, Fiorentina have played at the top level of Italian football for the majority of their existence; only four clubs have played in more [[Serie_A|Serie A]] seasons.
sentence_2: Fiorentina has won two [[List_of_Italian_football_champions|Italian Championships]], in [[1955–56_Serie_A|1955–56]] and again in [[1968–69_Serie_A|1968–69]], as well as six [[Coppa_Italia|Coppa Italia]] trophies and one [[Supercoppa_Italiana|Supercoppa Italiana]].
sentence_3: On the [[UEFA|European stage]], Fiorentina won the [[UEFA_Cup_Winners'_Cup|UEFA Cup Winners' Cup]] in [[1960–61_European_Cup_Winners'_Cup|1960–61]] and lost the final one year later.
sentence_4: They finished runners-up in the [[1956–57_European_Cup|1956–57 European Cup]], losing against [[Real_Madrid_C.F.|Real Madrid]], and also came close to winning the 1989–90 UEFA Cup, finishing as runners-up against [[Juventus_F.C.|Juventus]] after losing the first leg in [[Turin|Turin]] and drawing in the second one in [[Avellino|Avellino]].
sentence_5: Fiorentina is one of the fifteen European teams that played the finals in all three major continental competitions: the Champions League (1956–1957, the first Italian team to reach the final in the top continental competition), the UEFA Cup Winners (1960–1961 and 1961–1962) and the UEFA Cup (1989–1990).
sentence_6: Since 1931, the club have played at the [[Stadio_Artemio_Franchi|Stadio Artemio Franchi]], which currently has a capacity of 43,147.
sentence_7: The stadium has used several names over the years and has undergone several renovations.
sentence_8: Fiorentina are known widely by the nickname Viola, a reference to their distinctive purple colours.
sentence_9: Further information: History of ACF Fiorentina
sentence_10: Associazione Calcio Fiorentina was founded in the autumn of 1926 by local noble and [[National_Fascist_Party|National Fascist Party]] member Luigi Ridolfi, who initiated the merger of two older Florentine clubs, [[C.S._Firenze|CS Firenze]] and [[P.G._Libertas|PG Libertas]].
sentence_11: The aim of the merger was to give Florence a strong club to rival those of the more dominant [[Italian_Football_Championship|Italian Football Championship]] sides of the time from Northwest Italy.
sentence_12: Also influential was the cultural revival and rediscovery of Calcio Fiorentino, an ancestor of modern football that was played by members of the [[Medici|Medici]] family.
sentence_13: After a rough start and three seasons in lower leagues, Fiorentina reached the Serie A in 1931.
sentence_14: That same year saw the opening of the new stadium, originally named after Giovanni Berta, a prominent fascist, but now known as [[Stadio_Artemio_Franchi|Stadio Artemio Franchi]].
sentence_15: At the time, the stadium was a masterpiece of engineering, and its inauguration was monumental.
sentence_16: To be able to compete with the best teams in Italy, Fiorentina strengthened their team with some new players, notably the Uruguayan [[Pedro_Petrone|Pedro Petrone]], nicknamed el Artillero.
sentence_17: Despite enjoying a good season and finishing in fourth place, Fiorentina were relegated the following year, although they would return quickly to Serie A.
sentence_18: In 1941, they won their first [[Coppa_Italia|Coppa Italia]], but the team were unable to build on their success during the 1940s due to World War II and other troubles.
sentence_19: In 1950, Fiorentina started to achieve consistent top-five finishes in the domestic league.
sentence_20: The team consisted of great players such as well-known goalkeeper [[Giuliano_Sarti|Giuliano Sarti]], Sergio Cervato, Francesco Rosella, [[Guido_Gratton|Guido Gratton]], [[Giuseppe_Chiappella|Giuseppe Chiappella]] and Aldo Scaramucci but above all, the attacking duo of Brazilian [[Júlio_Botelho|Julinho]] and Argentinian [[Miguel_Montuori|Miguel Montuori]].
sentence_21: This team won Fiorentina's first [[Scudetto|scudetto]] (Italian championship) in [[1955–56_Serie_A|1955–56]], 12 points ahead of second-place [[A.C._Milan|Milan]].
sentence_22: Milan beat Fiorentina to top spot the following year, but more significantly Fiorentina became the first Italian team to play in a [[UEFA_Champions_League|European Cup]] final, when a disputed penalty led to a 2–0 defeat at the hands of [[Alfredo_Di_Stéfano|Alfredo Di Stéfano]]'s [[Real_Madrid_C.F.|Real Madrid]].
sentence_23: Fiorentina were runners-up again in the three subsequent seasons.
sentence_24: In the [[1960–61_Serie_A|1960–61 season]], the club won the Coppa Italia again and was also successful in Europe, winning the first [[Cup_Winners'_Cup|Cup Winners' Cup]] against Scottish side [[Rangers_F.C.|Rangers]].
sentence_25: After several years of runner-up finishes, Fiorentina dropped away slightly in the 1960s, bouncing from fourth to sixth place, although the club won the Coppa Italia and the [[Mitropa_Cup|Mitropa Cup]] in 1966.
sentence_26: While the 1960s did result in some trophies and good [[Serie_A|Serie A]] finishes for Fiorentina, nobody believed that the club could challenge for the title.
sentence_27: The [[1968–69_Serie_A|1968–69 season]] started with Milan as frontrunners, but on matchday 7, they lost to [[Bologna_F.C._1909|Bologna]] and were overtaken by [[Gigi_Riva|Gigi Riva]]'s [[Cagliari_Calcio|Cagliari]].
sentence_28: Fiorentina, after an unimpressive start, then moved to the top of the Serie A, but the first half of their season finished with a 2–2 draw against [[A.S._Varese_1910|Varese]], leaving Cagliari as outright league leader.
sentence_29: The second half of the season was a three-way battle between the three contending teams, Milan, Cagliari and Fiorentina.
sentence_30: Milan fell away, instead focusing their efforts on the European Cup, and it seemed that Cagliari would retain top spot.
sentence_31: After Cagliari lost against [[Juventus_F.C.|Juventus]], however, Fiorentina took over at the top.
sentence_32: The team then won all of their remaining matches, beating rivals Juve in [[Turin|Turin]] on the penultimate matchday to seal their second, and last, national title.
sentence_33: In the European Cup competition the following year, Fiorentina had some good results, including a win in the [[Soviet_Union|Soviet Union]] against [[FC_Dynamo_Kyiv|Dynamo Kyiv]], but they were eventually knocked out in the quarter-finals after a 3–0 defeat in [[Glasgow|Glasgow]] to [[Celtic_F.C.|Celtic]].
sentence_34: Viola players began the 1970s decade with Scudetto sewed on their breast, but the period was not especially fruitful for the team.
sentence_35: After a fifth-place finish in 1971, they finished in mid-table almost every year, even flirting with relegation in 1972 and 1978.
sentence_36: The Viola did win the [[Anglo-Italian_League_Cup|Anglo-Italian League Cup]] in 1974 and won the Coppa Italia again in 1975.
sentence_37: The team consisted of young talents like [[Vincenzo_Guerini_(footballer)|Vincenzo Guerini]] and Moreno Roggi, who had the misfortune to suffer bad injuries, and above all [[Giancarlo_Antognoni|Giancarlo Antognoni]], who would later become an idol to Fiorentina's fans.
sentence_38: The young average age of the players led to the team being called Fiorentina Ye-Ye.
sentence_39: In 1980, Fiorentina was bought by Flavio Pontello, who came from a rich house-building family.
sentence_40: He quickly changed the team's anthem and logo, leading to some complaints by the fans, but he started to bring in high-quality players such as [[Francesco_Graziani|Francesco Graziani]] and Eraldo Pecci from [[Torino_F.C.|Torino]]; [[Daniel_Bertoni|Daniel Bertoni]] from [[Sevilla_FC|Sevilla]]; [[Daniele_Massaro|Daniele Massaro]] from [[A.C._Monza_Brianza_1912|Monza]]; and a young [[Pietro_Vierchowod|Pietro Vierchowod]] from [[Calcio_Como|Como]].
sentence_41: The team was built around Giancarlo Antognoni, and in [[1981–82_Serie_A|1982]], Fiorentina were involved in an exciting duel with rivals Juventus.
sentence_42: After a bad injury to Antognoni, the league title was decided on the final day of the season when Fiorentina were denied a goal against Cagliari and were unable to win.
sentence_43: Juventus won the title with a disputed penalty and the rivalry between the two teams erupted.
sentence_44: The following years were strange for Fiorentina, who vacillated between high finishes and relegation battles.
sentence_45: Fiorentina also bought two interesting players, El Puntero [[Ramón_Díaz|Ramón Díaz]] and, most significantly, the young [[Roberto_Baggio|Roberto Baggio]].
sentence_46: In 1990, Fiorentina fought to avoid relegation right up until the final day of the season, but did reach the [[UEFA_Europa_League|UEFA Cup]] final, where they again faced Juventus.
sentence_47: The Turin team won the trophy, but Fiorentina's tifosi once again had real cause for complaint: the second leg of the final was played in [[Avellino|Avellino]] (Fiorentina's home ground was suspended), a city with many Juventus fans, and emerging star Roberto Baggio was sold to the rival team on the day of the final.
sentence_48: Pontello, suffering from economic difficulties, was selling all the players and was forced to leave the club after serious riots in Florence's streets.
sentence_49: The club was then acquired by the famous filmmaker Mario Cecchi Gori.

section_5.value: Cecchi Gori era: from Champions League to bankruptcy

sentence_50: The first season under Cecchi Gori's ownership was one of stabilisation, after which the new chairman started to sign some good players like [[Brian_Laudrup|Brian Laudrup]], [[Stefan_Effenberg|Stefan Effenberg]], [[Francesco_Baiano|Francesco Baiano]] and, most importantly, [[Gabriel_Batistuta|Gabriel Batistuta]], who became an iconic player for the team during the 1990s.
sentence_51: In 1993, however, Cecchi Gori died and was succeeded as chairman by his son, Vittorio.
sentence_52: Despite a good start to the season, Cecchi Gori fired the coach, [[Luigi_Radice|Luigi Radice]], after a defeat against [[Atalanta_B.C.|Atalanta]], and replaced him with [[Aldo_Agroppi|Aldo Agroppi]].
sentence_53: The results were dreadful: Fiorentina fell into the bottom half of the standings and were relegated on the last day of the season.
sentence_54: [[Claudio_Ranieri|Claudio Ranieri]] was brought in as coach for the 1993–94 season, and that year, Fiorentina dominated [[Serie_B|Serie B]], Italy's second division.
sentence_55: Upon their return to Serie A, Ranieri put together a good team centred around new top scorer Batistuta, signing the young talent [[Rui_Costa|Rui Costa]] from [[S.L._Benfica|Benfica]] and the new world champion Brazilian defender [[Márcio_Roberto_dos_Santos|Márcio Santos]].
sentence_56: The former became an idol to Fiorentina fans, while the second disappointed and was sold after only a season.
sentence_57: The Viola finished the season in tenth place.
sentence_58: The following season, Cecchi Gori bought other important players, namely Swedish midfielder [[Stefan_Schwarz|Stefan Schwarz]].
sentence_59: The club again proved its mettle in cup competitions, winning the Coppa Italia against Atalanta and finishing joint-third in Serie A.
sentence_60: In the summer, Fiorentina became the first non-national champions to win the [[Supercoppa_Italiana|Supercoppa Italiana]], defeating Milan 2–1 at the [[San_Siro|San Siro]].
sentence_61: Fiorentina's 1995–96 season was disappointing in the league, but they did reach the [[Cup_Winners'_Cup|Cup Winners' Cup]] semi-final by beating [[AF_Gloria_Bistrița|Gloria Bistrița]], Sparta Prague and Benfica.
sentence_62: The team lost the semi-final to the eventual winner of the competition, [[FC_Barcelona|Barcelona]] (away 1–1; home 0–2).
sentence_63: The season's main signings were [[Luís_Oliveira|Luís Oliveira]] and Andrei Kanchelskis, the latter of whom suffered from many injuries.
sentence_64: At the end of the season, Ranieri left Fiorentina for Valencia in Spain, with Cecchi Gori appointing [[Alberto_Malesani|Alberto Malesani]] as his replacement.
sentence_65: Fiorentina played well but struggled against smaller teams, although they did manage to qualify for the UEFA Cup.
sentence_66: Malesani left Fiorentina after only a season and was succeeded by [[Giovanni_Trapattoni|Giovanni Trapattoni]].
sentence_67: With Trapattoni's expert guidance and Batistuta's goals, Fiorentina challenged for the title in [[1998–99_Serie_A|1998–99]] but finished the season in third, earning them qualification for the [[UEFA_Champions_League|Champions League]].
sentence_68: The following year was disappointing in Serie A, but Viola played some historical matches in the Champions League, beating [[Arsenal_F.C.|Arsenal]] 1–0 at the old [[Wembley_Stadium_(1923)|Wembley Stadium]] and [[Manchester_United_F.C.|Manchester United]] 2–0 in Florence.
sentence_69: They were ultimately eliminated in the second group stage.
sentence_70: At the end of the season, Trapattoni left the club and was replaced by Turkish coach [[Fatih_Terim|Fatih Terim]].
sentence_71: More significantly, however, Batistuta was sold to [[A.S._Roma|Roma]], who eventually won the title the following year.
sentence_72: Fiorentina played well in [[2000–01_Serie_A|2000–01]] and stayed in the top half of Serie A, despite the resignation of Terim and the arrival of [[Roberto_Mancini|Roberto Mancini]].
sentence_73: They also won the Coppa Italia for the sixth and last time.
sentence_74: The year 2001 heralded major changes for Fiorentina, as the terrible state of the club's finances was revealed: they were unable to pay wages and had debts of around US$50 million.
sentence_75: The club's owner, Vittorio Cecchi Gori, was able to raise some more money, but this soon proved to be insufficient to sustain the club.
sentence_76: Fiorentina were relegated at the end of the [[2001–02_Serie_A|2001–02 season]] and went into judicially-controlled administration in June 2002.
sentence_77: This form of bankruptcy (sports companies cannot exactly fail in this way in Italy, but they can suffer a similar procedure) meant that the club was refused a place in Serie B for the [[2002–03_Serie_A|2002–03 season]], and as a result effectively ceased to exist.

section_6.value: Della Valle era: from the fourth tier to European competitions in the 2000s and 2010s

sentence_78: The club was promptly re-established in August 2002 as Associazione Calcio Fiorentina e Florentia Viola with shoe and leather entrepreneur Diego Della Valle as new owner and the club was admitted into Serie C2, the fourth tier of Italian football.
sentence_79: The only player to remain at the club in its new incarnation was Angelo Di Livio, whose commitment to the club's cause further endeared him to the fans.
sentence_80: Helped by Di Livio and 30-goal striker Christian Riganò, the club won its Serie C2 group with considerable ease, which would normally have led to a promotion to Serie C1.
sentence_81: Due to the bizarre [[Calcio_Catania#Decline_and_revival|Caso Catania]] (Catania Case), however, the club skipped Serie C1 and was admitted into Serie B, something that was only made possible by the Italian Football Federation (FIGC)'s decision to resolve the [[Calcio_Catania|Catania]] situation by increasing the number of teams in Serie B from 20 to 24 and promoting Fiorentina for "sports merits."
sentence_82: In the 2003 off-season, the club also bought back the right to use the Fiorentina name and the famous shirt design, and re-incorporated itself as ACF Fiorentina.
sentence_83: The club finished the [[2003–04_Serie_B|2003–04 season]] in sixth place and won the [[Playoffs#Association_football|playoff]] against [[Perugia_Calcio|Perugia]] to return to top-flight football.
sentence_84: In their first season back in Serie A, however, the club struggled to avoid relegation, only securing survival on the last day of the season on head-to-head record against [[Bologna_F.C._1909|Bologna]] and [[Parma_F.C.|Parma]].
sentence_85: In 2005, Della Valle decided to appoint [[Pantaleo_Corvino|Pantaleo Corvino]] as new sports director, followed by the appointment of [[Cesare_Prandelli|Cesare Prandelli]] as head coach in [[2005–06_Serie_A|the following season]].
sentence_86: The club made several signings during the summer transfer market, most notably [[Luca_Toni|Luca Toni]] and [[Sébastien_Frey|Sébastien Frey]].
sentence_87: This drastic move earned them a fourth-place finish with 74 points and a Champions League qualifying round ticket.
sentence_88: Toni scored 31 goals in 38 appearances, the first player to pass the 30-goal mark since [[Antonio_Valentin_Angelillo|Antonio Valentin Angelillo]] in the [[1958–59_Serie_A|1958–59 season]], for which he was awarded the [[European_Golden_Boot|European Golden Boot]].
sentence_89: On 14 July 2006, however, Fiorentina were relegated to Serie B due to their involvement in the 2006 Serie A match fixing scandal and given a 12-point penalty.
sentence_90: The team was reinstated to the Serie A on appeal, but with a 19-point penalty for the [[2006–07_Serie_A|2006–07 season]].
sentence_91: The team's [[2006–07_UEFA_Champions_League|2006–07 Champions League]] place was also revoked.
sentence_92: After the start of the season, Fiorentina's penalisation was reduced from 19 points to 15 on appeal to the Italian courts.
sentence_93: In spite of this penalty, they managed to secure a place in the UEFA Cup.
sentence_94: Despite Toni's departure to [[FC_Bayern_Munich|Bayern Munich]], Fiorentina had a strong start to the [[2007–08_Serie_A|2007–08 season]] and were tipped by [[Italy_national_football_team|Italian national team]] head coach [[Marcello_Lippi|Marcello Lippi]], among others, as a surprise challenger for the [[Scudetto|Scudetto]], and although this form tailed off towards the middle of the season, the Viola managed to qualify for the Champions League.
sentence_95: In Europe, the club reached the semi-final of the [[2007–08_UEFA_Cup|UEFA Cup]], where they were ultimately defeated by Rangers on penalties.
sentence_96: The [[2008–09_Serie_A|2008–09 season]] continued this success, a fourth-place finish assuring Fiorentina's spot in [[2009–10_UEFA_Champions_League|2010's Champions League playoffs]].
sentence_97: Their European campaign was also similar to that of the previous run, relegated to the [[2008–09_UEFA_Cup|2008–09 UEFA Cup]] and were eliminated by [[AFC_Ajax|Ajax]] in the end.
sentence_98: In the [[2009–10_Serie_A|2009–10 season]], Fiorentina started their domestic campaign strongly before steadily losing momentum and slipped to mid-table positions at the latter half of the season.
sentence_99: In Europe, the team proved to be a surprise dark horse: after losing their first away fixture against [[Olympique_Lyonnais|Lyon]], they staged a comeback with a five-match streak by winning all their remaining matches (including defeating [[Liverpool_F.C.|Liverpool]] home and away).
sentence_100: The Viola qualified as group champions, but eventually succumbed to Bayern Munich due to the [[Away_goals_rule|away goals rule]].
sentence_101: This was controversial due to a mistaken refereeing decision by [[Tom_Henning_Øvrebø|Tom Henning Øvrebø]], who allowed a clearly offside goal for Bayern in the first leg.
sentence_102: Bayern eventually finished the tournament as runners-up, making a deep run all the way to the [[2010_UEFA_Champions_League_Final|final]].
sentence_103: The incident called into attention the possible implementation of video replays in football.
sentence_104: Despite a good European run and reaching the semi-finals in the Coppa Italia, Fiorentina failed to qualify for Europe.
sentence_105: During this period, on 24 September 2009, Andrea Della Valle resigned from his position as chairman of Fiorentina, and announced all duties would be temporarily transferred to Mario Cognini, Fiorentina's vice-president until a permanent position could be filled.
sentence_106: In June 2010, the Viola bid farewell to long-time manager Cesare Prandelli, by then the longest-serving coach in the team's history, who was departing to coach the Italian national team.
sentence_107: Catania manager [[Siniša_Mihajlović|Siniša Mihajlović]] was appointed to replace him.
sentence_108: The club spent much of the early [[2010–11_Serie_A|2010–11 season]] in last place, but their form improved and Fiorentina ultimately finished ninth.
sentence_109: Following a 1–0 defeat to [[A.C._Chievo_Verona|Chievo]] in November 2011, Mihajlović was sacked and replaced by [[Delio_Rossi|Delio Rossi]].
sentence_110: After a brief period of improvements, the Viola were again fighting relegation, prompting the sacking of Sporting Director [[Pantaleo_Corvino|Pantaleo Corvino]] in early 2012 following a 0–5 home defeat to Juventus.
sentence_111: Their bid for survival was kept alive by a number of upset victories away from home, notably at Roma and Milan.
sentence_112: During a home game against Novara, trailing 0–2 within half an hour, manager Rossi decided to substitute midfielder [[Adem_Ljajić|Adem Ljajić]] early.
sentence_113: Ljajić sarcastically applauded him in frustration, whereupon Rossi retaliated by physical assaulting his player, an action that ultimately prompted his termination by the club.
sentence_114: His replacement, caretaker manager [[Vincenzo_Guerini_(footballer)|Vincenzo Guerini]], then guided the team away from the relegation zone to a 13th-place finish to end the turbulent year.
sentence_115: To engineer a resurrection of the club after the disappointing season, the Della Valle family invested heavily in the middle of 2012, buying 17 new players and appointing [[Vincenzo_Montella|Vincenzo Montella]] as head coach.
sentence_116: The team began the season well, finishing the calendar year in joint third place and eventually finishing the [[2012–13_Serie_A|2012–13 season]] in fourth, enough for a position in the [[2013–14_UEFA_Europa_League|2013–14 Europa League]].
sentence_117: The club lost fan favourite [[Stevan_Jovetić|Stevan Jovetić]] during the middle of 2013, selling him to English Premier League club [[Manchester_City_F.C.|Manchester City]] for a €30 million transfer fee.
sentence_118: They also sold Adem Ljajić to Roma and [[Alessio_Cerci|Alessio Cerci]] to Torino, using the funds to bring in [[Mario_Gómez|Mario Gómez]], [[Josip_Iličić|Josip Iličić]] and [[Ante_Rebić|Ante Rebić]], among others.
sentence_119: During the season, Fiorentina topped their Europa League group, moving on to the round of 32 to face Danish side [[Esbjerg_fB|Esbjerg fB]], which Fiorentina defeated 4–2 on aggregate.
sentence_120: In the following round of 16, however, they then lost to Italian rivals Juventus 2–1 on aggregate, ousting Fiorentina from the competition.
sentence_121: At the end of the season, the team finished fourth again in the league, and also finishing the year as Coppa Italia runners-up after losing 3–1 to Napoli in the final.
sentence_122: In 2014–15, during the 2015 winter transfer window, the team club sold star winger [[Juan_Cuadrado|Juan Cuadrado]] to [[Chelsea_F.C.|Chelsea]] for €30 million but were able to secure the loan of [[Mohamed_Salah|Mohamed Salah]] in exchange, who was a revelation in the second half of the season.
sentence_123: Their [[2014–15_UEFA_Europa_League|2014–15 Europa League campaign]] saw them progress to the semi-finals, where they were knocked-out by Spanish side [[Sevilla_FC|Sevilla]], the eventual champions.
sentence_124: In the [[2014–15_Serie_A|2014–15 domestic season]], Fiorentina once again finished fourth, thus qualifying for the [[2015–16_UEFA_Europa_League|2015–16 Europa League]].
sentence_125: In June 2015, [[Vincenzo_Montella|Vincenzo Montella]] was sacked as manager after the club grew impatient with the coaches inability to prove his commitment to the club, and was replaced by [[Paulo_Sousa|Paulo Sousa]], who lasted until June 2017 and the appointment of [[Stefano_Pioli|Stefano Pioli]].
sentence_126: Club captain [[Davide_Astori|Davide Astori]] died suddenly at the age of 31 in March 2018.
sentence_127: Astori had suffered a [[Cardiac_arrest|cardiac arrest]] while in a hotel room before an away game.
sentence_128: The club subsequently retired Astori's kit number, 13.
sentence_129: Fiorentina suffered during the [[2018–19_Serie_A|2018–19 Serie A]] campaign and ended the season on a 14 match winless streak, finishing in 16th place with only 41 points, 3 points from the relegation zone.
sentence_130: On 9 April 2019, Pioli resigned as manager and was replaced by Montella
sentence_131: On 6 June 2019, the club was sold to Italian-American billionaire [[Rocco_Commisso|Rocco Commisso]] for around 160 million euros.
sentence_132: The sale marked the end of the Della Valle family's seventeen-year association with the club.
sentence_133: [[Vincenzo_Montella|Vincenzo Montella]] was confirmed as coach for the first season of the new era despite the team's poor end to the previous campaign, which saw them finish only three points clear of the relegation zone.
sentence_134: Fiorentina continued their struggles from the previous year, spending the majority of the season in lower midtable.
sentence_135: Montella was sacked on 21 December after a 7 match winless run which left the club in 15th place, and was replaced by [[Giuseppe_Iachini|Giuseppe Iachini]].

sentence_146: Fiorentina have had many managers and head coaches throughout their history.
sentence_147: Below is a chronological list from the club's foundation in 1926 to the present day.
sentence_148: The official emblem of the city of [[Florence|Florence]], a red fleur-de-lis on a white field, has been pivotal in the all-round symbolism of the club.
sentence_149: Over the course of the club's history, they have had several badge changes, all of which incorporated Florence's fleur-de-lis in some way.
sentence_150: The first one was nothing more than the city's coat of arms, a white shield with the red fleur-de-lis inside.
sentence_151: It was soon changed to a very stylised fleur-de-lis, always red, and sometimes even without the white field.
sentence_152: The most common symbol, adopted for about 20 years, had been a white [[Lozenge|lozenge]] with the flower inside.
sentence_153: During the season they were Italian champions, the lozenge disappeared and the flower was overlapped with the [[Scudetto|scudetto]].
sentence_154: The logo introduced by owner Flavio Pontello in 1980 was particularly distinct, consisting of one-half of the city of Florence's emblem and one-half of the letter "F", for Fiorentina.
sentence_155: People disliked it when it was introduced, believing it was a commercial decision and, above all, because the symbol bore more of a resemblance to a [[Halberd|halberd]] than a fleur-de-lis.
sentence_156: Today's logo is a kite shaped double [[Lozenge|lozenge]] bordered in gold.
sentence_157: The outer lozenge has a purple background with the letters "AC" in white and the letter "F" in red, standing for the club's name.
sentence_158: The inner lozenge is white with a gold border and the red fleur-de-lis of Florence.
sentence_159: This logo had been in use from 1992 to 2002, but after the financial crisis and resurrection of the club the new one couldn't use the same logo.
sentence_160: Florence's comune instead granted Florentia Viola use of the stylised coat of arms used in other city documents.
sentence_161: Diego Della Valle acquired the current logo the following year in a judicial auction for a fee of €2.5 million, making it the most expensive logo in Italian football.
sentence_162: When Fiorentina was founded in 1926, the players wore red and white halved shirts derived from the colour of the city emblem.
sentence_163: The more well-known and highly distinctive purple kit was adopted in 1928 and has been used ever since, giving rise to the nickname La Viola ("The Purple (team)").
sentence_164: Tradition has it that Fiorentina got their purple kit by mistake after an accident washing the old red and white coloured kits in the river.
sentence_165: The away kit has always been predominantly white, sometimes with purple and red elements, sometimes all-white.
sentence_166: The shorts had been purple when the home kit was with white shorts.
sentence_167: Fiorentina's third kit was first worn in the 1995–96 season and it was all-red with purple borders and two [[Lily|lilies]] on the shoulders.
sentence_168: The red shirt has been the most worn 3rd shirt by Fiorentina, although they also wore rare yellow shirts ('97–'98, '99–'00 and '10–'11) and a sterling version, mostly in the [[Coppa_Italia|Coppa Italia]], in 2000–01.
sentence_169: For the 2017–18 season and the first time in its history, the club used five kits during the season, composing of one home kit (all-purple) and four away kits, each one representing one historic quartiere of the city of [[Florence|Florence]]: all-blue (Santa Croce), all-white (Santo Spirito), all-green (San Giovanni) and all-red (Santa Maria Novella).

sentence_183: A.C. Fiorentina S.p.A. was unable to register for 2002–03 Serie B due to financial difficulties, and then the sports title was transferred to a new company thanks to [[Article_52_of_N.O.I.F.|Article 52 of N.O.I.F.]], while the old company was liquidated.
sentence_184: At that time the club was heavily relying on windfall profit from selling players, especially in pure player swap or cash plus player swap that potentially increased the cost by the increase in amortisation of player contracts (an [[Intangible_asset|intangible assets]]).
sentence_185: For example, [[Marco_Rossi_(footballer,_born_1978)|Marco Rossi]] joined Fiorentina for 17 billion lire in 2000, but at the same time [[Lorenzo_Collacchioni|Lorenzo Collacchioni]] moved to [[U.S._Salernitana_1919|Salernitana]] for 1 billion lire, meaning the club had a player profit of 997 million lire and extra 1 billion lire to be amortised in 5-years.
sentence_186: In 1999, Emiliano Bigica also swapped with [[Giuseppe_Taglialatela|Giuseppe Taglialatela]], which the latter was valued for 10 billion lire.
sentence_187: The operating income (excluding windfall profit from players trading) of 2000–01 season was minus 113,271,475,933 [[Italian_lira|Italian lire]] (minus €58,499,835).
sentence_188: It was only boosted by the sales of [[Francesco_Toldo|Francesco Toldo]] and [[Rui_Costa|Rui Costa]] in June 2001 (a profit of 134.883 billion lire; €69.661 million).
sentence_189: However, it was alleged they were to transfer to Parma for a reported 140 million lire.
sentence_190: The two players eventually joined Inter Milan and A.C. Milan in 2001–02 financial year instead, for undisclosed fees.
sentence_191: Failing to have financial support from the owner Vittorio Cecchi Gori, the club was forced to windup due to its huge imbalance in operating income.
sentence_192: Since re-established in 2002, ACF Fiorentina S.p.A. are yet to self-sustain to keep the team in top division as well as in European competitions.
sentence_193: In the 2005 financial year, which cover the [[2004–05_Serie_A|first Serie A season]], the club made a net loss of €9,159,356, followed by a net loss of €19,519,789.
sentence_194: In 2006 ([[2005–06_Serie_A|2005–06 Serie A]] and [[2006–07_Serie_A|2006–07 Serie A]]), Fiorentina heavily invested on players, meaning the amortisation of intangible asset (the player contract) had increased from €17.7 million to €24 million.
sentence_195: However the club suffered from the 2006 Italian football scandal, which meant the club did not qualify for Europe.
sentence_196: In 2007 Fiorentina almost broke-even, with a net loss of just €3,704,953.
sentence_197: In the 2007 financial year the TV revenue increased after they qualified to the [[2007–08_UEFA_Cup|2007–08 UEFA Cup]].
sentence_198: Despite qualifying to the [[2008–09_UEFA_Champions_League|2008–09 UEFA Champions League]], Fiorentina made a net loss of €9,179,484 in 2008 financial year after the increase in TV revenue was outweighed by the increase in wage.
sentence_199: In the 2009 financial year, Fiorentina made a net profit of €4,442,803, largely due to the profit on selling players (€33,631,489 from players such as [[Felipe_Melo|Felipe Melo]], [[Giampaolo_Pazzini|Giampaolo Pazzini]] and [[Zdravko_Kuzmanović|Zdravko Kuzmanović]]; increased from about €3.5 million in 2008).
sentence_200: However it was also offset by the write-down of selling players (€6,062,545, from players such as [[Manuel_da_Costa_(footballer,_born_1986)|Manuel da Costa]], [[Arturo_Lupoli|Arturo Lupoli]] and [[Davide_Carcuro|Davide Carcuro]]).
sentence_201: After the club failed to qualify to Europe at the end of [[2009–10_Serie_A|2009–10 Serie A]], as well as lack of player profit, Fiorentina turnover was decreased from €140,040,713 in 2009 to just €79,854,928, despite the wage bill also falling, la Viola still made a net loss of €9,604,353.
sentence_202: In the 2011 financial year, the turnover slipped to €67,076,953, as the club's lack of capital gains from selling players and 2010 financial year still included the instalments from UEFA for participating [[2009–10_UEFA_Europa_League|2009–10 UEFA Europa League]].
sentence_203: Furthermore, the gate income had dropped from €11,070,385 to €7,541,260.
sentence_204: The wage bill did not fall much and in reverse the amortisation of transfer fee had sightly increased due to new signings.
sentence_205: La Viola had savings in other costs but counter-weighted by huge €11,747,668 write-down for departed players, due to D'Agostino, Frey and Mutu, but the former would counter-weight by co-ownership financial income, which all made the operating cost remained high as worse as last year.
sentence_206: Moreover, in 2010 the result was boosted by acquiring the asset from subsidiary (related to AC Fiorentina) and the re-valuation of its value in separate balance sheet.
sentence_207: If deducting that income (€14,737,855), 2010 financial year was net loss 24,342,208 and 2011 result was worse with €8,131,876 only in separate balance sheet.
sentence_208: In 2012, the club benefited from the sales of [[Matija_Nastasić|Matija Nastasić]] and [[Valon_Behrami|Valon Behrami]], followed by [[Stevan_Jovetić|Stevan Jovetić]] and [[Adem_Ljajić|Adem Ljajić]] in 2013.
sentence_209: In 2014, due to €28.4 million drop from the windfall profit of selling players, the club recorded their worst financial results since re-foundation, despite the fact the club maintained the same level of windfall profit, the result was still worse than in 2013.
sentence_210: Moreover, Fiorentina also revealed that the club had a relevant football net income of minus €19.5 million in the first assessment period of UEFA Financial Fair Play Regulations in the 2013–14 season (in May 2014).
sentence_211: (aggregate of 2012 and 2013 results), which within the limit of minus €45 million, as well as minus €25.5 million in assessment period 2014–15 (aggregate of 2012, 2013 and 2014 results).
sentence_212: However, as the limit was reduced to minus €30 million in assessment period 2015–16, 2016–17 and 2017–18 season, the club had to achieve a relevant net income of positive €5.6 million in 2015 financial year.
sentence_213: La Viola sold [[Juan_Cuadrado|Juan Cuadrado]] to Chelsea in January 2015 for €30 million fee, to make the club eligible to 2016–17 edition of UEFA competitions.

sentence_2: Brazil (Portuguese: Brasil; Brazilian Portuguese: [[Portuguese|[bɾaˈziw]]), officially the Federative Republic of Brazil (Portuguese: República Federativa do Brasil), is the largest country in both South America and [[Latin_America|Latin America]].
sentence_3: At 8.5 million square kilometers (3.2 million square miles) and with over 211 million people, Brazil is the world's [[List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_area|fifth-largest country by area]] and the [[List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_population|sixth most populous]].
sentence_4: Its capital is [[Brasília|Brasília]], and [[List_of_cities_in_Brazil_by_population|its most populous city]] is [[São_Paulo|São Paulo]].
sentence_5: The federation is composed of the union of the 26 [[States_of_Brazil|states]] and the [[Federal_District_(Brazil)|Federal District]].
sentence_6: It is the largest country to have Portuguese as an [[List_of_territorial_entities_where_Portuguese_is_an_official_language|official language]] and the only one in the [[Americas|Americas]]; it is also one of the most multicultural and ethnically diverse nations, due to over a century of mass [[Immigration_to_Brazil|immigration from around the world]]; as well as the most populous [[Catholic_Church_by_country|Roman Catholic-majority country.]]
sentence_7: Bounded by the Atlantic Ocean on the east, Brazil has a [[Coastline_of_Brazil|coastline]] of 7,491 kilometers (4,655 mi).
sentence_8: It borders all other countries in South America except [[Ecuador|Ecuador]] and [[Chile|Chile]] and covers 47.3% of the continent's land area.
sentence_9: Its [[Amazon_basin|Amazon basin]] includes a [[Amazon_rainforest|vast tropical forest]], home to diverse [[Wildlife_of_Brazil|wildlife]], a variety of [[Environment_of_Brazil|ecological systems]], and extensive natural resources spanning numerous [[Protected_areas_of_Brazil|protected habitats]].
sentence_10: This unique environmental heritage makes Brazil one of 17 [[Megadiverse_countries|megadiverse countries]], and is the subject of significant global interest and debate regarding deforestation and environmental protection.
sentence_11: Brazil was inhabited by [[Indigenous_peoples_in_Brazil|numerous tribal nations]] prior to the landing in 1500 of explorer [[Pedro_Álvares_Cabral|Pedro Álvares Cabral]], who claimed the area for the [[Portuguese_Empire|Portuguese Empire]].
sentence_12: Brazil remained a [[Colonial_Brazil|Portuguese colony]] until 1808 when the capital of the empire was [[Transfer_of_the_Portuguese_court_to_Brazil|transferred from Lisbon to Rio de Janeiro]].
sentence_13: In 1815, the colony was elevated to the rank of kingdom upon the formation of the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves.
sentence_14: [[Independence_of_Brazil|Independence]] was achieved in 1822 with the creation of the [[Empire_of_Brazil|Empire of Brazil]], a unitary state governed under a constitutional monarchy and a parliamentary system.
sentence_15: The ratification of the first constitution in 1824 led to the formation of a bicameral legislature, now called the [[National_Congress_of_Brazil|National Congress]].
sentence_16: The country [[Proclamation_of_the_Republic_(Brazil)|became a presidential republic]] in 1889 following a military [[Coup_d'état|coup d'état]].
sentence_17: An authoritarian military junta came to power [[1964_Brazilian_coup_d'état|in 1964]] and ruled until 1985, after which civilian governance resumed.
sentence_18: Brazil's current [[Constitution_of_Brazil|constitution]], formulated in 1988, defines it as a [[Democracy|democratic]] [[Federal_republic|federal republic]].
sentence_19: Due to its rich culture and history, the country ranks [[List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Brazil|thirteenth in the world]] by number of [[UNESCO|UNESCO]] [[World_Heritage_Site|World Heritage Sites]].
sentence_20: Brazil is classified as an upper-middle income economy by the [[World_Bank|World Bank]] and a newly industrialized country, with [[List_of_countries_by_total_wealth|the largest share of global wealth]] in Latin America.
sentence_21: It is considered an advanced [[Emerging_market|emerging economy]], having the ninth largest GDP in the world by [[List_of_countries_by_GDP_(nominal)|nominal]], and eighth by [[List_of_countries_by_GDP_(PPP)|PPP]] measures.
sentence_22: It is one of the world's major breadbaskets, being the largest [[Coffee_production_in_Brazil|producer of coffee]] for the last 150 years.
sentence_23: Brazil is a [[Regional_power|regional power]] and sometimes considered a [[Great_power|great]] or a [[Middle_power|middle power]] in [[International_relations|international affairs]].
sentence_24: On account of its international recognition and influence, the country is subsequently classified as an [[Emerging_power|emerging power]] and a [[Potential_superpowers|potential superpower]] by several analysts.
sentence_25: Brazil is a founding member of the [[United_Nations|United Nations]], the [[G20|G20]], [[BRICS|BRICS]], [[Mercosur|Mercosul]], [[Organization_of_American_States|Organization of American States]], [[Organization_of_Ibero-American_States|Organization of Ibero-American States]] and the [[Community_of_Portuguese_Language_Countries|Community of Portuguese Language Countries]].
sentence_26: Main article: [[Name_of_Brazil|Name of Brazil]]
sentence_27: The word "Brazil" likely comes from the Portuguese word for brazilwood, a tree that once grew plentifully along the Brazilian coast.
sentence_28: In Portuguese, brazilwood is called pau-brasil, with the word brasil commonly given the etymology "red like an ember", formed from brasa ("ember") and the suffix -il (from -iculum or -ilium).
sentence_29: As brazilwood produces a deep red dye, it was highly valued by the European textile industry and was the earliest commercially exploited product from Brazil.
sentence_30: Throughout the 16th century, massive amounts of brazilwood were harvested by [[Indigenous_peoples_in_Brazil|indigenous peoples]] (mostly Tupi) along the Brazilian coast, who sold the timber to European traders (mostly Portuguese, but also French) in return for assorted European consumer goods.
sentence_31: The official Portuguese name of the land, in original Portuguese records, was the "Land of the Holy Cross" (Terra da Santa Cruz), but European sailors and merchants commonly called it simply the "Land of Brazil" (Terra do Brasil) because of the brazilwood trade.
sentence_32: The popular appellation eclipsed and eventually supplanted the official Portuguese name.
sentence_33: Some early sailors called it the "Land of Parrots".
sentence_34: In the [[Guarani_language|Guarani language]], an official language of Paraguay, Brazil is called "Pindorama".
sentence_35: This was the name the indigenous population gave to the region, meaning "land of the palm trees".
sentence_36: Main articles: [[History_of_Brazil|History of Brazil]] and [[Timeline_of_Brazilian_history|Timeline of Brazilian history]]
sentence_37: Some of the earliest human remains found in the [[Americas|Americas]], [[Luzia_Woman|Luzia Woman]], were found in the area of [[Pedro_Leopoldo|Pedro Leopoldo]], [[Minas_Gerais|Minas Gerais]] and provide evidence of human habitation going back at least 11,000 years.
sentence_38: The earliest [[Pottery|pottery]] ever found in the Western Hemisphere was excavated in the [[Amazon_basin|Amazon basin]] of Brazil and [[Radiocarbon_dating|radiocarbon dated]] to 8,000 years ago (6000 BC).
sentence_39: The pottery was found near [[Santarém,_Pará|Santarém]] and provides evidence that the tropical forest region supported a complex prehistoric culture.
sentence_40: The [[Marajoara_culture|Marajoara culture]] flourished on [[Marajó|Marajó]] in the Amazon delta from 400 CE to 1400 CE, developing sophisticated pottery, [[Social_stratification|social stratification]], large populations, [[Mound_building|mound building]], and complex social formations such as chiefdoms.
sentence_41: Around the time of the Portuguese arrival, the territory of current day Brazil had an estimated indigenous population of 7 million people, mostly semi-nomadic, who subsisted on hunting, fishing, gathering, and migrant agriculture.
sentence_42: The indigenous population of Brazil comprised several large indigenous ethnic groups (e.g. the Tupis, [[Guaraní_people|Guaranis]], [[Gê_peoples|Gês]] and [[Arawak_peoples|Arawaks]]).
sentence_43: The Tupí people were subdivided into the [[Tupiniquim_people|Tupiniquins]] and [[Tupinambá_people|Tupinambás]], and there were also many subdivisions of the other groups.
sentence_44: Before the arrival of the Europeans, the boundaries between these groups and their subgroups were marked by wars that arose from differences in culture, language and moral beliefs.
sentence_45: These wars also involved large-scale military actions on land and water, with [[Cannibalism|cannibalistic]] rituals on [[Prisoner_of_war|prisoners of war]].
sentence_46: While heredity had some weight, leadership status was more subdued over time, than allocated in succession ceremonies and conventions.
sentence_47: [[Slavery|Slavery]] among the Indians had a different meaning than it had for Europeans, since it originated from a diverse socioeconomic organization, in which asymmetries were translated into [[Kinship|kinship]] relations.
sentence_48: Main articles: [[Colonial_Brazil|Colonial Brazil]], War of the Emboabas, and Inconfidência Mineira
sentence_49: The land now called Brazil was claimed for the [[Portuguese_Empire|Portuguese Empire]] on 22 April 1500, with the arrival of the Portuguese fleet commanded by [[Pedro_Álvares_Cabral|Pedro Álvares Cabral]].
sentence_50: The Portuguese encountered indigenous peoples divided into several tribes, most of whom spoke languages of the [[Tupi–Guarani|Tupi–Guarani]] family, and fought among themselves.
sentence_51: Though the first settlement was founded in 1532, [[Colonization|colonization]] effectively began in 1534, when King [[John_III_of_Portugal|John III of Portugal]] divided the territory into the fifteen private and autonomous Captaincy Colonies of Brazil.
sentence_52: However, the decentralized and unorganized tendencies of the captaincy colonies proved problematic, and in 1549 the Portuguese king restructured them into the [[Governorate_General_of_Brazil|Governorate General of Brazil]] in the city of [[Salvador,_Bahia|Salvador]], which became the capital of a single and centralized Portuguese colony in South America.
sentence_53: In the first two centuries of colonization, Indigenous and European groups lived in constant war, establishing opportunistic alliances in order to gain advantages against each other.
sentence_54: By the mid-16th century, [[Sugar#Sugarcane|cane sugar]] had become Brazil's most important export, and slaves purchased in [[Sub-Saharan_Africa|Sub-Saharan Africa]], in the [[Slavery_in_Africa#Atlantic_slave_trade|slave market of Western Africa]] (not only those from Portuguese allies of their colonies in [[Portuguese_Angola|Angola]] and Mozambique), had become its largest import, to cope with [[Plantation_economy|plantations]] of sugarcane, due to increasing international demand for Brazilian sugar.
sentence_55: Portuguese Brazil received more than 2.8 million slaves from Africa between the years of 1500 to 1800.
sentence_56: By the end of the 17th century, sugarcane exports began to decline, and the discovery of gold by [[Bandeirantes|bandeirantes]] in the 1690s would become the new backbone of the colony's economy, fostering a [[Brazilian_Gold_Rush|Brazilian Gold Rush]] which attracted thousands of new [[Settler_colonialism|settlers]] to Brazil from Portugal and all Portuguese colonies around the world.
sentence_57: This increased level of immigration in turn caused some conflicts between newcomers and old settlers.
sentence_58: Portuguese expeditions known as [[Bandeirantes|Bandeiras]] gradually advanced the Portugal colonial [[Treaty_of_Tordesillas|original frontiers]] in South America to approximately the current Brazilian borders.
sentence_59: In this era other European powers tried to colonize parts of Brazil, in incursions that the Portuguese had to fight, notably the French [[France_Antarctique|in Rio during the 1560s]], in Maranhão during the 1610s, and the [[Dutch_Brazil|Dutch in Bahia and Pernambuco]], during the [[Dutch–Portuguese_War|Dutch–Portuguese War]], after the end of [[Iberian_Union|Iberian Union]].
sentence_60: The Portuguese colonial administration in Brazil had two objectives that would ensure colonial order and the [[Monopoly|monopoly]] of Portugal's wealthiest and largest colony: to keep under control and eradicate all forms of [[Slave_rebellion|slave rebellion]] and resistance, such as the [[Palmares_(quilombo)|Quilombo of Palmares]], and to repress all movements for [[Autonomous_administrative_division|autonomy]] or [[Independence|independence]], such as the Minas Conspiracy.
sentence_61: Main article: United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves
sentence_62: In late 1807, Spanish and Napoleonic forces threatened the security of [[Continental_Portugal|continental Portugal]], causing [[John_VI_of_Portugal|Prince Regent João]], in the name of [[Maria_I_of_Portugal|Queen Maria I]], to move the royal court from [[Lisbon|Lisbon]] to [[Transfer_of_the_Portuguese_Court_to_Brazil|Rio de Janeiro]].
sentence_63: There they established some of Brazil's first financial institutions, such as its local [[Stock_exchange|stock exchanges]], and its [[Banco_do_Brasil|National Bank]], additionally ending the Portuguese [[Monopoly|monopoly]] on Brazilian trade and opening Brazil to other nations.
sentence_64: In 1809, in retaliation for being forced into exile, the Prince Regent ordered the [[Portuguese_conquest_of_French_Guiana|Portuguese conquest of French Guiana]].
sentence_65: With the end of the [[Peninsular_War|Peninsular War]] in 1814, the courts of Europe demanded that Queen Maria I and Prince Regent João return to Portugal, deeming it unfit for the head of an ancient European monarchy to reside in a colony.
sentence_66: In 1815, to justify continuing to live in Brazil, where the royal court had thrived for six years, the Crown established the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil, and the Algarves, thus creating a [[Pluricontinental|pluricontinental]] transatlantic monarchic state.
sentence_67: However, the leadership in Portugal, resentful of the new status of its larger colony, continued to demand the return of the court to Lisbon (v. [[Liberal_Revolution_of_1820|Liberal Revolution of 1820]]).
sentence_68: In 1821, acceding to the demands of revolutionaries who had taken the city of [[Porto|Porto]], D. João VI departed for Lisbon.
sentence_69: There he swore an oath to the new constitution, leaving his son, [[Pedro_I_of_Brazil|Prince Pedro de Alcântara]], as Regent of the Kingdom of Brazil.
sentence_70: Main articles: [[Independence_of_Brazil|Independence of Brazil]] and [[Empire_of_Brazil|Empire of Brazil]]
sentence_71: Tensions between Portuguese and Brazilians increased, and the [[Portuguese_Cortes|Portuguese Cortes]], guided by the new political regime imposed by the 1820 Liberal Revolution, tried to re-establish Brazil as a colony.
sentence_72: The Brazilians refused to yield, and Prince Pedro decided to stand with them, [[Brazilian_Declaration_of_Independence|declaring the country's independence from Portugal]] on 7 September 1822.
sentence_73: A month later, Prince Pedro was declared the first [[Emperor_of_Brazil|Emperor of Brazil]], with the royal title of Dom [[Pedro_I_of_Brazil|Pedro I]], resulting in the foundation of the [[Empire_of_Brazil|Empire of Brazil]].
sentence_74: The [[Brazilian_War_of_Independence|Brazilian War of Independence]], which had already begun along this process, spread through the northern, northeastern regions and in Cisplatina province.
sentence_75: The last Portuguese soldiers surrendered on 8 March 1824; Portugal officially recognized Brazil on 29 August 1825.
sentence_76: On 7 April 1831, worn down by years of administrative turmoil and political dissent with both liberal and conservative sides of politics, including an attempt of [[Confederation_of_the_Equator|republican secession]], and unreconciled to the way that absolutists in Portugal had given in the succession of King John VI, Pedro I went to Portugal to reclaim his daughter's crown, abdicating the Brazilian throne in favor of his five-year-old son and heir (who thus became the Empire's second monarch, with the royal title of Dom [[Pedro_II_of_Brazil|Pedro II]]).
sentence_77: As the new Emperor could not exert his constitutional powers until he came of age, a [[Regency_(government)|regency]] was set up by the National Assembly.
sentence_78: In the absence of a charismatic figure who could represent a moderate face of power, during this period a series of localized rebellions took place, such as the Cabanagem in [[Grão-Pará_Province|Grão-Pará Province]], the [[Malê_Revolt|Malê Revolt]] in [[Salvador_da_Bahia|Salvador da Bahia]], the Balaiada ([[Maranhão|Maranhão]]), the Sabinada (Bahia), and the [[Ragamuffin_War|Ragamuffin War]], which began in [[Rio_Grande_do_Sul|Rio Grande do Sul]] and was supported by [[Giuseppe_Garibaldi|Giuseppe Garibaldi]].
sentence_79: These emerged from the dissatisfaction of the provinces with the central power, coupled with old and latent social tensions peculiar to a vast, slaveholding and newly independent [[Nation_state|nation state]].
sentence_80: This period of internal political and social upheaval, which included the Praieira revolt in [[Pernambuco|Pernambuco]], was overcome only at the end of the 1840s, years after the end of the regency, which occurred with the [[Dom_Pedro_II#Early_coronation|premature coronation of Pedro II]] in 1841.
sentence_81: During the last phase of the monarchy, internal political debate centered on the issue of slavery.
sentence_82: The [[Atlantic_slave_trade|Atlantic slave trade]] was abandoned in 1850, as a result of the [[United_Kingdom_of_Great_Britain_and_Ireland|British]] Aberdeen Act, but only in May 1888 after a long process of internal mobilization and debate for an ethical and legal dismantling of [[Slavery_in_Brazil|slavery in the country]], was the institution formally abolished.
sentence_83: The foreign-affairs policies of the monarchy dealt with issues with the countries of the [[Southern_Cone|Southern Cone]] with whom Brazil had borders.
sentence_84: Long after the [[Cisplatine_War|Cisplatine War]] that resulted in independence for [[Uruguay|Uruguay]], Brazil won three international wars during the 58-year reign of Pedro II.
sentence_85: These were the [[Platine_War|Platine War]], the [[Uruguayan_War|Uruguayan War]] and the devastating [[Paraguayan_War|Paraguayan War]], the largest war effort in Brazilian history.
sentence_86: Although there was no desire among the majority of Brazilians to change the country's form of government, on 15 November 1889, in disagreement with the majority of [[Imperial_Brazilian_Army|Army]] officers, as well as with rural and financial elites (for different reasons), the monarchy was overthrown by a military coup.
sentence_87: 15 November is now Republic Day, a national holiday.
sentence_88: Main articles: First Brazilian Republic, [[Vargas_Era#Estado_Novo|Vargas Era § Estado Novo]], and [[Second_Brazilian_Republic|Second Brazilian Republic]]
sentence_89: The early republican government was nothing more than a military dictatorship, with army dominating affairs both in Rio de Janeiro and in the states.
sentence_90: Freedom of the press disappeared and elections were controlled by those in power.
sentence_91: Not until 1894, following [[Encilhamento|an economic]] crisis and [[Revolta_da_Armada|a military one]], did civilians take power, remaining there until October 1930.
sentence_92: If in relation to its foreign policy, the country in this first republican period maintained a relative balance characterized by a success in resolving border disputes with neighboring countries, only broken by the Acre War (1899–1902) and [[Brazil_during_World_War_I|its involvement]] in [[World_War_I|World War I]] (1914–1918), followed by a failed attempt to exert a prominent role in the [[League_of_Nations|League of Nations]]; Internally, from the crisis of Encilhamento and the [[Revolta_da_Armada|Armada Revolts]], a prolonged cycle of financial, political and social instability began until the 1920s, keeping the country besieged by various rebellions, both civilian and military.
sentence_93: Little by little, [[Rebellions_and_revolutions_in_Brazil#1st_Republican_period_(1889-1930)|a cycle of general instability]] sparked by these crises undermined the regime to such an extent that in the wake of the murder of his running mate, the defeated opposition presidential candidate Getúlio Vargas, supported by most of the military, successfully led the October 1930 Coup.
sentence_94: Vargas and the military were supposed to assume power temporarily, but instead closed the Congress, extinguished the Constitution, ruled with emergency powers and replaced the states' governors with their own supporters.
sentence_95: In the 1930s, three failed attempts to remove Vargas and his supporters from power occurred.
sentence_96: The first was the Constitutionalist Revolution in 1932, led by the [[São_Paulo_(state)|Paulista]] [[Oligarchy|oligarchy]].
sentence_97: The second was a Communist uprising in November 1935, and the last one a putsch attempt by [[Brazilian_Integralism|local fascists]] in May 1938.
sentence_98: The 1935 uprising created a security crisis in which the Congress transferred more power to the executive.
sentence_99: The 1937 coup d'état resulted in the cancellation of the 1938 election, formalized Vargas as dictator, beginning the [[Estado_Novo_(Brazil)|Estado Novo]] era, which was noted for government brutality and censorship of the press.
sentence_100: Foreign policy during the Vargas years was marked by the antecedents and [[World_War_II|World War II]].
sentence_101: Brazil remained neutral until August 1942, when the country entered on the [[Allies_of_World_War_II|allied side]], after suffering [[Submarine_warfare#Atlantic_ocean|retaliation]] by [[Nazi_Germany|Nazi Germany]] and [[Kingdom_of_Italy#Fascist_regime_(1922–1943)|Fascist Italy]], in a strategic dispute over the South Atlantic.
sentence_102: In addition to [[Battle_of_the_Atlantic#South_Atlantic_(May_1942_–_September_1943)|its participation in the battle of the Atlantic]], Brazil also sent an [[Brazilian_Expeditionary_Force|expeditionary force]] to fight in the [[Italian_Campaign_(World_War_II)|Italian campaign]].
sentence_103: With the Allied victory in 1945 and the end of the Nazi-fascist regimes in Europe, Vargas's position became unsustainable and he was swiftly overthrown in another military coup, with democracy "reinstated" by the same army that had ended it 15 years earlier.
sentence_104: Vargas committed suicide in August 1954 amid a political crisis, after having returned to power by election in 1950.
sentence_105: Main articles: Military dictatorship in Brazil and [[History_of_Brazil_since_1985|History of Brazil since 1985]]
sentence_106: Several brief interim governments followed Vargas's suicide.
sentence_107: Juscelino Kubitschek became president in 1956 and assumed a conciliatory posture towards the [[Opposition_(politics)|political opposition]] that allowed him to govern without major crises.
sentence_108: The economy and industrial sector grew remarkably, but his greatest achievement was the construction of the new capital city of [[Brasília|Brasília]], inaugurated in 1960.
sentence_109: Kubitschek's successor, Jânio Quadros, resigned in 1961 less than a year after taking office.
sentence_110: His vice-president, João Goulart, assumed the presidency, but aroused strong political opposition and was [[1964_Brazilian_coup_d'état|deposed in April 1964]] by a coup that resulted in a military regime.
sentence_111: The new regime was intended to be transitory but gradually closed in on itself and became a full dictatorship with the promulgation of the Fifth Institutional Act in 1968.
sentence_112: Oppression was not limited to those who resorted to guerrilla tactics to fight the regime, but also reached institutional opponents, artists, journalists and other members of civil society, inside and outside the country through the infamous "[[Operation_Condor|Operation Condor]]".
sentence_113: Despite its brutality, like other [[Authoritarianism|authoritarian regimes]], due to an economic boom, known as an "economic miracle", the regime reached a peak in popularity in the early 1970s.
sentence_114: Slowly, however, the wear and tear of years of dictatorial power that had not slowed the repression, even after the defeat of the leftist guerrillas, plus the inability to deal with the economic crises of the period and popular pressure, made an opening policy inevitable, which from the regime side was led by Generals [[Ernesto_Geisel|Ernesto Geisel]] and [[Golbery_do_Couto_e_Silva|Golbery do Couto e Silva]].
sentence_115: With the enactment of the [[Amnesty_law#Brazil|Amnesty Law]] in 1979, Brazil began a slow return to democracy, which was completed during the 1980s.
sentence_116: Civilians returned to power in 1985 when José Sarney assumed the presidency.
sentence_117: He became unpopular during his tenure through failure to control the economic crisis and [[Hyperinflation|hyperinflation]] he inherited from the military regime.
sentence_118: Sarney's unsuccessful government led to the [[Brazilian_presidential_election,_1989|election in 1989]] of the almost-unknown Fernando Collor, subsequently impeached by the National Congress in 1992.
sentence_119: Collor was succeeded by his vice-president, [[Itamar_Franco|Itamar Franco]], who appointed [[Fernando_Henrique_Cardoso|Fernando Henrique Cardoso]] Minister of Finance.
sentence_120: In 1994, Cardoso produced a highly successful [[Plano_Real|Plano Real]], that, after decades of failed economic plans made by previous governments attempting to curb hyperinflation, finally stabilized the Brazilian economy.
sentence_121: Cardoso won the [[Brazilian_presidential_election,_1994|1994 election]], and [[Brazilian_presidential_election,_1998|again in 1998]].
sentence_122: The peaceful transition of power from Cardoso to his main opposition leader, [[Luiz_Inácio_Lula_da_Silva|Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva]] ([[Brazilian_presidential_election,_2002|elected in 2002]] and [[Brazilian_presidential_election,_2006|re-elected in 2006]]), was seen as proof that Brazil had achieved a long-sought political stability.
sentence_123: However, sparked by indignation and frustrations accumulated over decades from corruption (including that of then President Rouseff), police brutality, inefficiencies of the political [[The_Establishment|establishment]] and public service, [[2013_protests_in_Brazil|numerous peaceful protests]] erupted in Brazil from the middle of first term of [[Dilma_Rousseff|Dilma Rousseff]], who had succeeded Lula after winning election [[Brazilian_presidential_election,_2010|in 2010]].
sentence_124: Enhanced by political and economic crises with evidence of involvement by politicians from all the primary political parties in several [[Bribery|bribery]] and [[Tax_evasion|tax evasion]] schemes, with [[2015–16_protests_in_Brazil|large street protests for and against her]], Rousseff [[Impeachment_of_Dilma_Rousseff|was impeached]] by the [[Brazilian_Congress|Brazilian Congress]] in 2016.
sentence_125: In 2017, the Supreme Court asked for the investigation of 71 Brazilian lawmakers and nine ministers in President [[Michel_Temer|Michel Temer]]'s cabinet allegedly linked to the [[Operation_Car_Wash|Petrobras corruption scandal]].
sentence_126: President Temer is himself accused of [[Corruption_in_Brazil|corruption]].
sentence_127: In 2018, 62% of the population on a poll claimed that corruption was Brazil's biggest problem.
sentence_128: Starting in 2013, there is a total change in Brazilian politics, with the overthrow of the [[Left-wing_politics|left]] and the rise of conservatism in [[Right-wing_politics|right]].
sentence_129: With the discovery that the [[Workers'_Party_(Brazil)|PT]] governments have practically gone bankrupt in [[Petrobras|Petrobras]], [[Correios|Correios]] and many other state companies, through a great diversion of public funds and the use of their funds to bribe the [[National_Congress_of_Brazil|National Congress]], the [[Brazilian_Senate|Brazilian Senate]] and [[Judiciary|Judiciary]], in addition to the indiscriminate use of [[National_Bank_for_Economic_and_Social_Development|BNDES]] to finance socialist dictatorships in Cuba, Venezuela, Latin America, Africa and the Middle East (with Lula and Dilma openly supporting controversial figures such as [[Hugo_Chávez|Hugo Chávez]], [[Nicolás_Maduro|Nicolás Maduro]], [[Mahmoud_Ahmadinejad|Mahmoud Ahmadinejad]], [[Evo_Morales|Evo Morales]], [[Vladimir_Putin|Vladimir Putin]], [[Kim_Jong-un|Kim Jong-un]] and the [[Chinese_Communist_Party|Chinese Communist Party]], among others), also counting on the attempts of Dilma Roussef to install "Popular Councils" to replace the power of the federal deputies, [[Jair_Bolsonaro|Jair Bolsonaro]], former captain of the army and candidate of the right, is elected.
sentence_130: Through the [[Operation_Car_Wash|Operation Car Wash]], the Federal Police of Brazil has since acted on the deviations and corruption of the PT and allied parties at that time.
sentence_131: In the [[2018_Brazilian_general_election|2018 elections]], candidate [[Jair_Bolsonaro|Jair Bolsonaro]] of the [[Social_Liberal_Party_(Brazil)|Social Liberal Party]] (PSL) was elected president, who won in the second round [[Fernando_Haddad|Fernando Haddad]], of the [[Workers'_Party_(Brazil)|Workers Party]] (PT), with the support of 55.13% of the valid votes.
sentence_132: Main article: [[Geography_of_Brazil|Geography of Brazil]]
sentence_133: Brazil occupies a large area along the eastern coast of South America and includes much of the continent's interior, sharing land borders with [[Uruguay|Uruguay]] to the south; [[Argentina|Argentina]] and Paraguay to the southwest; [[Bolivia|Bolivia]] and [[Peru|Peru]] to the west; [[Colombia|Colombia]] to the northwest; and [[Venezuela|Venezuela]], [[Guyana|Guyana]], [[Suriname|Suriname]] and [[France|France]] (French overseas region of [[French_Guiana|French Guiana]]) to the north.
sentence_134: It shares a border with every South American country except [[Ecuador|Ecuador]] and [[Chile|Chile]].
sentence_135: It also encompasses a number of oceanic [[Archipelago|archipelagos]], such as [[Fernando_de_Noronha|Fernando de Noronha]], [[Rocas_Atoll|Rocas Atoll]], [[Saint_Peter_and_Saint_Paul_Archipelago|Saint Peter and Paul Rocks]], and [[Trindade_and_Martim_Vaz|Trindade and Martim Vaz]].
sentence_136: Its size, relief, climate, and natural resources make Brazil geographically diverse.
sentence_137: Including its [[Atlantic_Ocean|Atlantic]] islands, Brazil lies between latitudes [[6th_parallel_north|6°N]] and [[34th_parallel_south|34°S]], and longitudes [[28th_meridian_west|28°]] and [[74th_meridian_west|74°W]].
sentence_138: Brazil is the [[List_of_countries_and_outlying_territories_by_total_area|fifth largest]] country in the world, and third largest in the Americas, with a total area of 8,515,767.049 km (3,287,956 sq mi), including 55,455 km (21,411 sq mi) of water.
sentence_139: It spans four time zones; from UTC−5 comprising the state of [[Acre_(state)|Acre]] and the westernmost portion of [[Amazonas_(Brazilian_state)|Amazonas]], to UTC−4 in the western states, to UTC−3 in the eastern states (the [[Time_in_Brazil|national time]]) and UTC−2 in the [[List_of_islands_of_Brazil|Atlantic islands]].
sentence_140: Brazil is the longest country in the world, spanning 4,395 km (2,731 mi) from north to south.
sentence_141: Brazil is also the only country in the world that has the [[Equator|equator]] and the [[Tropic_of_Capricorn|Tropic of Capricorn]] running through it.
sentence_142: Brazilian topography is also diverse and includes hills, mountains, plains, highlands, and scrublands.
sentence_143: Much of the terrain lies between 200 metres (660 ft) and 800 metres (2,600 ft) in elevation.
sentence_144: The main upland area occupies most of the southern half of the country.
sentence_145: The northwestern parts of the plateau consist of broad, rolling terrain broken by low, rounded hills.
sentence_146: The southeastern section is more rugged, with a complex mass of ridges and mountain ranges reaching elevations of up to 1,200 metres (3,900 ft).
sentence_147: These ranges include the [[Mantiqueira_Mountains|Mantiqueira]] and [[Espinhaço_Mountains|Espinhaço]] mountains and the [[Serra_do_Mar|Serra do Mar]].
sentence_148: In the north, the Guiana Highlands form a major drainage divide, separating rivers that flow south into the [[Amazon_Basin|Amazon Basin]] from rivers that empty into the [[Orinoco|Orinoco River]] system, in Venezuela, to the north.
sentence_149: The highest point in Brazil is the [[Pico_da_Neblina|Pico da Neblina]] at 2,994 metres (9,823 ft), and the lowest is the Atlantic Ocean.
sentence_150: Brazil has a dense and complex system of rivers, one of the world's most extensive, with eight major drainage basins, all of which drain into the Atlantic.
sentence_151: Major rivers include the [[Amazon_River|Amazon]] (the world's second-longest river and the largest in terms of volume of water), the [[Paraná_River|Paraná]] and its major tributary the [[Iguazu_River|Iguaçu]] (which includes the [[Iguazu_Falls|Iguazu Falls]]), the [[Rio_Negro_(Amazon)|Negro]], São Francisco, [[Xingu_River|Xingu]], [[Madeira_River|Madeira]] and [[Tapajós|Tapajós]] rivers.
sentence_152: Main article: [[Climate_of_Brazil|Climate of Brazil]]
sentence_153: The climate of Brazil comprises a wide range of weather conditions across a large area and varied topography, but most of the country is tropical.
sentence_154: According to the [[Köppen_climate_classification|Köppen system]], Brazil hosts six major climatic subtypes: [[Desert_climate|desert]], [[Tropical_rainforest_climate|equatorial]], [[Tropical_climate|tropical]], [[Semi-arid_climate|semiarid]], [[Oceanic_climate|oceanic]] and subtropical.
sentence_155: The different climatic conditions produce environments ranging from [[Tropical_and_subtropical_moist_broadleaf_forests|equatorial rainforests]] in the north and semiarid deserts in the northeast, to [[Temperate_coniferous_forest|temperate coniferous forests]] in the south and [[Tropical_and_subtropical_grasslands,_savannas,_and_shrublands|tropical savannas]] in central Brazil.
sentence_156: Many regions have starkly different microclimates.
sentence_157: An equatorial climate characterizes much of northern Brazil.
sentence_158: There is no real [[Dry_season|dry season]], but there are some variations in the period of the year when most rain falls.
sentence_159: Temperatures average 25 °C (77 °F), with more significant temperature variation between night and day than between seasons.
sentence_160: Over central Brazil rainfall is more seasonal, characteristic of a savanna climate.
sentence_161: This region is as extensive as the Amazon basin but has a very different climate as it lies farther south at a higher altitude.
sentence_162: In the interior northeast, seasonal rainfall is even more extreme.
sentence_163: The semiarid climatic region generally receives less than 800 millimetres (31.5 in) of rain, most of which generally falls in a period of three to five months of the year and occasionally less than this, creating long periods of drought.
sentence_164: Brazil's 1877–78 [[Grande_Seca|Grande Seca]] (Great Drought), the worst in Brazil's history, caused approximately half a million deaths.
sentence_165: A similarly devastating drought occurred in 1915.
sentence_166: South of Bahia, near the coasts, and more southerly most of the state of São Paulo, the distribution of rainfall changes, with rain falling throughout the year.
sentence_167: The south enjoys subtropical conditions, with cool winters and average annual temperatures not exceeding 18 °C (64.4 °F); winter frosts and [[Snow_in_Brazil|snowfall]] are not rare in the highest areas.
sentence_168: Main articles: [[Wildlife_of_Brazil|Wildlife of Brazil]], [[Deforestation_in_Brazil|Deforestation in Brazil]], and [[Conservation_in_Brazil|Conservation in Brazil]]
sentence_169: Brazil's large territory comprises different ecosystems, such as the [[Amazon_rainforest|Amazon rainforest]], recognized as having the greatest [[Biodiversity|biological diversity]] in the world, with the [[Atlantic_Forest|Atlantic Forest]] and the [[Cerrado|Cerrado]], sustaining the greatest biodiversity.
sentence_170: In the south, the [[Araucaria|Araucaria]] pine forest grows under temperate conditions.
sentence_171: The rich wildlife of Brazil reflects the variety of natural habitats.
sentence_172: Scientists estimate that the total number of [[Wildlife_of_Brazil|plant]] and [[Wildlife_of_Brazil|animal species]] in Brazil could approach four million, mostly invertebrates.
sentence_173: Larger mammals include carnivores [[Cougar|pumas]], [[Jaguar|jaguars]], [[Ocelot|ocelots]], rare [[Bush_dog|bush dogs]], and [[Fox|foxes]], and herbivores [[Peccary|peccaries]], [[Tapir|tapirs]], anteaters, [[Sloth|sloths]], [[Opossum|opossums]], and [[Armadillo|armadillos]].
sentence_174: [[Deer|Deer]] are plentiful in the south, and many species of [[New_World_monkey|New World monkeys]] are found in the northern [[Rainforest|rain forests]].
sentence_175: Concern for the environment has grown in response to global interest in environmental issues.
sentence_176: Brazil's Amazon Basin is home to an extremely diverse array of fish species, including the [[Red-bellied_piranha|red-bellied piranha]].
sentence_177: By 2013, Brazil's "dramatic policy-driven reduction in Amazon Basin deforestation" was a "global exception in terms of forest change", according to scientific journal [[Science_(journal)|Science]].
sentence_178: From 2003 to 2011, compared to all other countries in the world, Brazil had the "largest decline in annual forest loss", as indicated in the study using high-resolution satellite maps showing global forest cover changes.
