sentence_179: The annual loss of forest cover decreased from a 2003/2004 record high of more than 40,000 square kilometres (4,000×10^ ha; 9.9×10^ acres; 15,000 sq mi) to a 2010/2011 low of under 20,000 square kilometres (2,000×10^ ha; 4.9×10^ acres; 7,700 sq mi), reversing widespread deforestation from the 1970s to 2003.
sentence_180: However, in 2019, when the [[Bolsonaro_government|Bolsonaro government]] came to power, the rate of [[Deforestation_of_the_Amazon_rainforest|deforestation of the Amazon rainforest]] increased sharply threatening to reach a tipping point after it the forest will collapse, having severe consequences for the world.
sentence_181: (see [[Tipping_points_in_the_climate_system|Tipping points in the climate system]]) This can also complicate the trade agreement with the [[European_Union|European Union]] Speaking at the [[UN_General_Assembly|UN General Assembly]], Bolsonaro criticised what he described as sensational reporting in the international media.
sentence_182: "It is a fallacy to say that the Amazon is the heritage of [[Humankind|humankind]], and a misconception, as confirmed by scientists, to say that our Amazonian forests are the lungs of world.
sentence_183: Using these fallacies, certain countries instead of helping, embarked on the media lies and behaved in a disrespectful manner and with a [[Colonialist|colonialist]] spirit."
sentence_184: he said.
sentence_185: President Jair Bolsonaro asserted Brazil's sovereignty over the [[Amazônia_Legal|Amazon]].
sentence_186: According to a 2008 GreenPeace article, the natural heritage of Brazil is severely threatened by cattle ranching and agriculture, logging, mining, resettlement, oil and gas extraction, over-fishing, wildlife trade, dams and infrastructure, water pollution, climate change, fire, and invasive species.
sentence_187: In many areas of the country, the natural environment is threatened by development.
sentence_188: The construction of highways has opened up previously remote areas for agriculture and settlement; dams have flooded valleys and inundated wildlife habitats; and mines have scarred and polluted the landscape.
sentence_189: At least 70 dams are said to be planned for the Amazon region, including the controversial [[Belo_Monte_Dam|Belo Monte]] hydroelectric dam.
sentence_190: In summer 2019, 2 states in Brazil [[Paraná_(state)|Paraná]] and [[Santa_Catarina_(state)|Santa Catarina]] banned [[Fracking|fracking]], what will have positive effects on the climate and water quality, because the [[Shale_gas|shale gas]] and [[Shale_oil|shale oil]] reserves in the state of Parana are the larger in the southern hemisphere.
sentence_191: Main articles: [[Politics_of_Brazil|Politics of Brazil]], Federal government of Brazil, and [[Elections_in_Brazil|Elections in Brazil]]
sentence_192: The form of government is a [[Democracy|democratic]] [[Federation|federative]] [[Republic|republic]], with a [[Presidential_system|presidential system]].
sentence_193: The president is both head of state and head of government of the Union and is elected for a four-year term, with the possibility of re-election for a second successive term.
sentence_194: The current president is [[Jair_Bolsonaro|Jair Bolsonaro]].
sentence_195: The previous president, [[Michel_Temer|Michel Temer]], replaced [[Dilma_Rousseff|Dilma Rousseff]] after her [[Impeachment_of_Dilma_Rousseff|impeachment]].
sentence_196: The President appoints the Ministers of State, who assist in government.
sentence_197: Legislative houses in each political entity are the main source of law in Brazil.
sentence_198: The [[National_Congress_of_Brazil|National Congress]] is the Federation's bicameral legislature, consisting of the [[Chamber_of_Deputies_of_Brazil|Chamber of Deputies]] and the [[Senate_of_Brazil|Federal Senate]].
sentence_199: Judiciary authorities exercise jurisdictional duties almost exclusively.
sentence_200: Brazil is a [[Democracy|democracy]], according to the [[Democracy_Index|Democracy Index]] 2010.
sentence_201: The political-administrative organization of the Federative Republic of Brazil comprises the Union, the states, the Federal District, and the municipalities.
sentence_202: The Union, the states, the Federal District, and the municipalities, are the "spheres of government".
sentence_203: The [[Federation|federation]] is set on five fundamental principles: sovereignty, citizenship, dignity of human beings, the social values of labor and freedom of enterprise, and political [[Pluralism_(political_theory)|pluralism]].
sentence_204: The classic tripartite branches of government (executive, legislative and judicial under a checks and balances system) are formally established by the Constitution.
sentence_205: The executive and legislative are organized [[Separation_of_powers|independently in all three spheres of government]], while the judiciary is organized only at the federal and state and Federal District spheres.
sentence_206: All members of the executive and legislative branches are directly elected.
sentence_207: Judges and other judicial officials are appointed after passing entry exams.
sentence_208: For most of its democratic history, Brazil has had a multi-party system, proportional representation.
sentence_209: Voting is compulsory for the literate between 18 and 70 years old and optional for illiterates and those between 16 and 18 or beyond 70.
sentence_210: Together with several smaller parties, four political parties stand out: [[Workers'_Party_(Brazil)|Workers' Party]] (PT), [[Brazilian_Social_Democracy_Party|Brazilian Social Democracy Party]] (PSDB), Brazilian Democratic Movement (MDB) and [[Democrats_(Brazil)|Democrats]] (DEM).
sentence_211: Fifteen political parties are represented in Congress.
sentence_212: It is common for politicians to switch parties, and thus the proportion of congressional seats held by particular parties changes regularly.
sentence_213: Almost all governmental and administrative functions are exercised by authorities and agencies affiliated to the Executive.
sentence_214: The country has more than 40 active political parties, and only one of them defines itself as a right-wing party ([[Social_Liberal_Party_(Brazil)|PSL]]), with a clear political imbalance.
sentence_215: The country has several far-left parties like PSOL, [[Workers'_Cause_Party|PCO]], PSTU, [[Brazilian_Communist_Party|PCB]], PC do B, left parties like [[Workers'_Party_(Brazil)|PT]], [[Brazilian_Socialist_Party|PSB]], [[Democratic_Labour_Party_(Brazil)|PDT]], [[Green_Party_(Brazil)|PV]], [[Sustainability_Network|Rede]] and [[Solidariedade|Solidariedade]] and center-left like [[Brazilian_Social_Democracy_Party|PSDB]], [[Democrats_(Brazil)|DEM]], PMN and Cidadania.
sentence_216: Ten parties declare themselves as the center: MDB, [[Liberal_Party_(Brazil,_2006)|PL]], [[Social_Democratic_Party_(Brazil,_2011)|PSD]], [[Christian_Labour_Party|PTC]], [[Christian_Democracy_(Brazil)|DC]], [[Republican_Party_of_the_Social_Order|PROS]], [[Avante_(political_party)|Avante]], Patriota, [[Podemos_(Brazil)|Podemos]] and [[Party_of_the_Brazilian_Woman|PMB]].
sentence_217: Five parties declare themselves as center-right: [[Brazilian_Labour_Party_(current)|PTB]], Progressistas, [[Social_Christian_Party_(Brazil)|PSC]], [[Brazilian_Labour_Renewal_Party|PRTB]] and [[Republicans_(Brazil)|Republicanos]].
sentence_218: The only party that claims to be purely liberal, without further consideration, is [[New_Party_(Brazil)|Novo]].
sentence_219: When asked about their ideological spectrum, Brazilian parties tend to give obtuse and non-conclusive answers on the subject.
sentence_220: Main articles: [[Law_of_Brazil|Law of Brazil]], [[Law_enforcement_in_Brazil|Law enforcement in Brazil]], and [[Crime_in_Brazil|Crime in Brazil]]
sentence_221: Brazilian law is based on the [[Civil_law_(legal_system)|civil law]] legal system and [[Civil_law_(legal_system)|civil law]] concepts prevail over common law practice.
sentence_222: Most of Brazilian law is codified, although non-codified statutes also represent a substantial part, playing a complementary role.
sentence_223: Court decisions set out interpretive guidelines; however, they are seldom binding on other specific cases.
sentence_224: Doctrinal works and the works of academic jurists have strong influence in law creation and in law cases.
sentence_225: The legal system is based on the [[Constitution_of_Brazil|Federal Constitution]], promulgated on 5 October 1988, and the fundamental law of Brazil.
sentence_226: All other legislation and court decisions must conform to its rules.
sentence_227: As of April 2007, there have been 53 amendments.
sentence_228: States have their own constitutions, which must not contradict the Federal Constitution.
sentence_229: Municipalities and the Federal District have "organic laws" (leis orgânicas), which act in a similar way to constitutions.
sentence_230: Legislative entities are the main source of statutes, although in certain matters judiciary and executive bodies may enact legal norms.
sentence_231: Jurisdiction is administered by the judiciary entities, although in rare situations the [[Constitution_of_Brazil|Federal Constitution]] allows the Federal Senate to pass on legal judgments.
sentence_232: There are also specialized military, labor, and electoral courts.
sentence_233: The highest court is the [[Supreme_Federal_Court|Supreme Federal Court]].
sentence_234: This system has been criticized over the last few decades for the slow pace of decision-making.
sentence_235: Lawsuits on appeal may take several years to resolve, and in some cases more than a decade elapses before definitive rulings.
sentence_236: Nevertheless, the Supreme Federal Tribunal was the first court in the world to transmit its sessions on television, and also via [[YouTube|YouTube]].
sentence_237: More recently, in December 2009, the Supreme Court adopted [[Twitter|Twitter]] to display items on the day planner of the ministers, to inform the daily actions of the Court and the most important decisions made by them.
sentence_238: Main article: [[Brazilian_Armed_Forces|Brazilian Armed Forces]]
sentence_239: The armed forces of Brazil are the [[List_of_countries_by_number_of_military_and_paramilitary_personnel|largest]] in Latin America by active personnel and the largest in terms of military equipment.
sentence_240: It consists of the [[Brazilian_Army|Brazilian Army]] (including the [[Brazilian_Army_Aviation_Command|Army Aviation Command]]), the Brazilian Navy (including the [[Brazilian_Marine_Corps|Marine Corps]] and [[Brazilian_Naval_Aviation|Naval Aviation]]), and the [[Brazilian_Air_Force|Brazilian Air Force]].
sentence_241: Brazil's conscription policy gives it one of the world's largest military forces, estimated at more than 1.6 million reservists annually.
sentence_242: Numbering close to 236,000 active personnel, the Brazilian Army has the largest number of armored vehicles in South America, including armored transports and [[Battle_tank|tanks]].
sentence_243: It is also unique in Latin America for its large, elite forces specializing in unconventional missions, the [[Brazilian_Special_Operations_Command|Brazilian Special Operations Command]], and the versatile Strategic Rapid Action Force, made up of highly mobilized and prepared Special Operations Brigade, [[Parachute_Infantry_Brigade_(Brazil)|Infantry Brigade Parachutist]], 1st Jungle Infantry Battalion (Airmobile) and 12th Brigade Light Infantry (Airmobile) able to act anywhere in the country, on short notice, to counter external aggression.
sentence_244: The states' [[Military_Police_(Brazil)|Military Police]] and the [[Military_Firefighters_Corps|Military Firefighters Corps]] are described as an ancillary forces of the Army by the constitution, but are under the control of each state's governor.
sentence_245: Brazil's navy, the second-largest in the Americas, once operated some of the most powerful warships in the world with the two [[Minas_Geraes-class_battleship|Minas Geraes-class]] [[Dreadnought|dreadnoughts]], which sparked a [[South_American_dreadnought_race|South American dreadnought race]] between Argentina, Brazil, and Chile.
sentence_246: Today, it is a [[Green-water_navy|green water]] force and has a group of specialized elite in retaking ships and naval facilities, GRUMEC, unit specially trained to protect Brazilian oil platforms along its coast.
sentence_247: It is the only navy in Latin America that operates an [[Aircraft_carrier|aircraft carrier]], [[PHM_Atlantico|PHM Atlantico]], and one of the ten navies of the world to operate one.
sentence_248: The Air Force is the largest in Latin America and has about 700 manned aircraft in service and effective about 67,000 personnel.
sentence_249: Brazil has not been invaded since 1865 during the [[Paraguayan_War|Paraguayan War]].
sentence_250: Additionally, Brazil has no contested territorial disputes with any of its neighbors and neither does it have rivalries, like Chile and Bolivia have with each other.
sentence_251: The Brazilian military has also three times intervened militarily to overthrow the Brazilian government.
sentence_252: It has built a tradition of participating in UN [[Peacekeeping|peacekeeping]] missions such as in [[Haiti|Haiti]], [[East_Timor|East Timor]] and [[Central_African_Republic|Central African Republic]].
sentence_253: Brazil signed the UN [[Treaty_on_the_Prohibition_of_Nuclear_Weapons|treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons]].
sentence_254: Main article: [[Foreign_relations_of_Brazil|Foreign relations of Brazil]]
sentence_255: Brazil's international relations are based on Article 4 of the [[Constitution_of_Brazil|Federal Constitution]], which establishes non-intervention, [[Self-determination|self-determination]], [[Internationalism_(politics)|international cooperation]] and the [[Peacebuilding|peaceful settlement of conflicts]] as the guiding principles of Brazil's relationship with other countries and multilateral organizations.
sentence_256: According to the Constitution, the [[President_of_Brazil|President]] has ultimate authority over foreign policy, while the [[National_Congress_of_Brazil|Congress]] is tasked with reviewing and considering all diplomatic nominations and [[Treaty|international treaties]], as well as legislation relating to Brazilian foreign policy.
sentence_257: Brazil's foreign policy is a by-product of the country's position as a [[Regional_power|regional power]] in [[Latin_America|Latin America]], a leader among [[Developing_countries|developing countries]], and an emerging [[World_power|world power]].
sentence_258: Brazilian foreign policy has generally been based on the principles of [[Multilateralism|multilateralism]], peaceful dispute settlement, and non-intervention in the affairs of other countries.
sentence_259: Brazil is a founding member state of the [[Community_of_Portuguese_Language_Countries|Community of Portuguese Language Countries]] (CPLP), also known as the Lusophone Commonwealth, an international organization and political association of [[Lusophone|Lusophone]] nations across four continents, where Portuguese is an official language.
sentence_260: An increasingly well-developed tool of Brazil's foreign policy is providing aid as a donor to other developing countries.
sentence_261: Brazil does not just use its growing economic strength to provide financial aid, but it also provides high levels of expertise and most importantly of all, a quiet non-confrontational diplomacy to improve governance levels.
sentence_262: Total aid is estimated to be around $1 billion per year, which includes:

list.value: technical cooperation of around $480 million ($30 million in 2010 provided directly by the Brazilian Cooperation Agency (ABC));
estimated $450 million for in-kind expertise provided by Brazilian institutions specializing in technical cooperation.

sentence_263: In addition, Brazil manages a peacekeeping mission in [[2010_Haiti_earthquake|Haiti]] ($350 million) and makes in-kind contributions to the [[World_Food_Programme|World Food Programme]] ($300 million).
sentence_264: This is in addition to humanitarian assistance and contributions to multilateral development agencies.
sentence_265: The scale of this aid places it on par with China and India.
sentence_266: The Brazilian South-South aid has been described as a "global model in waiting."
sentence_267: Main articles: [[Law_enforcement_in_Brazil|Law enforcement in Brazil]] and [[Crime_in_Brazil|Crime in Brazil]]
sentence_268: In Brazil, the [[Constitution_of_Brazil|Constitution]] establishes five different police agencies for law enforcement: Federal Police Department, [[Federal_Highway_Police_(Brazil)|Federal Highway Police]], [[Federal_Railroad_Police|Federal Railroad Police]], [[Military_Police_(Brazil)|Military Police]] and [[Civil_Police_(Brazil)|Civil Police]].
sentence_269: Of these, the first three are affiliated with federal authorities and the last two are subordinate to state governments.
sentence_270: All police forces are the responsibility of the executive branch of any of the federal or state powers.
sentence_271: The National Public Security Force also can act in public disorder situations arising anywhere in the country.
sentence_272: The country still has above-average levels of violent crime and particularly high levels of gun violence and homicide.
sentence_273: In 2012, the [[World_Health_Organization|World Health Organization]] (WHO) estimated the number of 32 deaths per 100,000 inhabitants, one of the [[List_of_countries_by_intentional_homicide_rate|highest rates of homicide of the world]].
sentence_274: The number considered tolerable by the WHO is about 10 homicides per 100,000 inhabitants.
sentence_275: In 2018, Brazil had a record 63,880 murders.
sentence_276: However, there are differences between the crime rates in the [[States_of_Brazil|Brazilian states]].
sentence_277: While in [[São_Paulo_(state)|São Paulo]] the homicide rate registered in 2013 was 10.8 deaths per 100,000 inhabitants, in [[Alagoas|Alagoas]] it was 64.7 homicides per 100,000 inhabitants.
sentence_278: Brazil also has high levels of incarceration and the third largest prison population in the world (behind only [[China|China]] and the [[United_States|United States]]), with an estimated total of approximately 700,000 prisoners around the country (June 2014), an increase of about 300% compared to the index registered in 1992.
sentence_279: The high number of prisoners eventually overloaded the Brazilian prison system, leading to a shortfall of about 200,000 accommodations.
sentence_280: Main articles: [[States_of_Brazil|States of Brazil]] and [[Municipalities_of_Brazil|Municipalities of Brazil]]
sentence_281: See also: Regions of Brazil
sentence_282: Brazil is a federation composed of 26 [[Federated_state|states]], one federal district, and the 5570 [[Municipality|municipalities]].
sentence_283: States have autonomous administrations, collect their own taxes and receive a share of taxes collected by the Federal government.
sentence_284: They have a governor and a unicameral legislative body elected directly by their voters.
sentence_285: They also have independent Courts of Law for common justice.
sentence_286: Despite this, states have much less autonomy to create their own laws than in the United States.
sentence_287: For example, criminal and civil laws can be voted by only the federal bicameral Congress and are uniform throughout the country.
sentence_288: The states and the federal district may be grouped into regions: [[Northern_Region,_Brazil|Northern]], [[Northeast_Region,_Brazil|Northeast]], [[Central-West_Region,_Brazil|Central-West]], [[Southeast_Region,_Brazil|Southeast]] and [[Southern_Region,_Brazil|Southern]].
sentence_289: The Brazilian regions are merely geographical, not political or administrative divisions, and they do not have any specific form of government.
sentence_290: Although defined by law, Brazilian regions are useful mainly for statistical purposes, and also to define the distribution of federal funds in development projects.
sentence_291: Municipalities, as the states, have autonomous administrations, collect their own taxes and receive a share of taxes collected by the Union and state government.
sentence_292: Each has a mayor and an elected legislative body, but no separate Court of Law.
sentence_293: Indeed, a Court of Law organized by the state can encompass many municipalities in a single justice administrative division called comarca (county).
sentence_294: Main article: [[Economy_of_Brazil|Economy of Brazil]]
sentence_295: See also: [[Brazilian_real|Brazilian real]], [[Agriculture_in_Brazil|Agriculture in Brazil]], [[Mining_in_Brazil|Mining in Brazil]], and [[Industry_in_Brazil|Industry in Brazil]]
sentence_296: Brazil is the largest national economy in [[Latin_America|Latin America]], the [[List_of_countries_by_GDP_(nominal)|world's ninth largest economy]] and the [[List_of_countries_by_GDP_(PPP)|eighth largest]] in [[Purchasing_power_parity|purchasing power parity]] (PPP) according to 2018 estimates.
sentence_297: Brazil has a [[Mixed_economy|mixed economy]] with abundant natural resources.
sentence_298: After rapid growth in preceding decades, the country [[2014–2016_Brazilian_economic_recession|entered an ongoing recession in 2014]] amid a political corruption scandal and nationwide protests.
sentence_299: Its [[Gross_domestic_product|Gross domestic product]] (PPP) per capita was $15,919 in 2017 putting Brazil in the 77th position according to IMF data.
sentence_300: Active in [[Agriculture|agricultural]], [[Mining|mining]], [[Manufacturing|manufacturing]] and [[Tertiary_sector_of_the_economy|service sectors]] Brazil has a labor force of over 107 million (ranking 6th worldwide) and unemployment of 6.2% (ranking 64th worldwide).
sentence_301: The country has been expanding its presence in international financial and [[Commodity_market|commodities markets]], and is one of a group of four emerging economies called the [[BRIC|BRIC countries]].
sentence_302: Brazil has been the world's largest [[Coffee_production_in_Brazil|producer of coffee]] for the last 150 years.
sentence_303: Brazil's diversified economy includes agriculture, industry, and a wide range of services.
sentence_304: [[Agriculture_in_Brazil|Agriculture]] and allied sectors like forestry, [[Logging|logging]] and [[Fishing|fishing]] accounted for 5.1% of the [[Gross_domestic_product|GDP]] in 2007.
sentence_305: Brazil is the largest producer of [[Sugar_cane|sugar cane]], [[Soybeans|soybeans]], [[Coffee|coffee]], [[Orange_(fruit)|orange]], and is the 2nd largest producer in the world of [[Papaya|papaya]], 3rd largest of [[Maize|maize]], [[Tobacco|tobacco]] and [[Pineapple|pineapple]], 4th place in [[Cotton|cotton]] and [[Cassava|cassava]], 5th place in [[Coconut|coconut]] and [[Lemon|lemon]], 6th in [[Cocoa_bean|cocoa]] and [[Avocado|avocado]], 9th in [[Rice|rice]], 10th in [[Tomato|tomato]] and 11th in [[Grape|grape]] and apple.
sentence_306: The country is also one of the 3 largest [[Banana|banana]] producers in the world, but almost all production is destined for national consumption.
sentence_307: The country also produces large quantities of [[Beans|beans]], [[Peanut|peanut]], [[Potato|potato]], [[Carrot|carrot]], [[Cashew_nuts|cashew nuts]], [[Tangerine|tangerine]], [[Persimmon|persimmon]], [[Strawberry|strawberry]], [[Guaraná|guaraná]], [[Guava|guava]], [[Açaí|açaí]], Brazil nut, [[Yerba_mate|yerba mate]], [[Wheat|wheat]], among others.
sentence_308: Part of the production is exported, and another part goes to the domestic market.
sentence_309: In the production of animal proteins, Brazil is today one of the largest countries in the world.
sentence_310: In 2019, the country was the world's largest exporter of [[Chicken_meat|chicken meat]].
sentence_311: It was also the second largest producer of [[Beef|beef]], the world's third largest producer of [[Milk|milk]], the world's fourth largest producer of [[Pork|pork]] and the seventh largest producer of [[Egg_as_food|eggs]] in the world.
sentence_312: In the mining sector, Brazil stands out in the extraction of [[Iron_ore|iron ore]] (where it is the second world exporter), [[Copper|copper]], [[Gold|gold]], [[Bauxite|bauxite]] (one of the 5 largest producers in the world), [[Manganese|manganese]] (one of the 5 largest producers in the world), [[Tin|tin]] (one of the largest producers in the world), [[Niobium|niobium]] (concentrates 98% of reserves known to the world) and [[Nickel|nickel]].
sentence_313: In terms of precious stones, Brazil is the world's largest producer of [[Amethyst|amethyst]], [[Topaz|topaz]], [[Agate|agate]] and one of the main producers of [[Tourmaline|tourmaline]], [[Emerald|emerald]], [[Aquamarine_(gemstone)|aquamarine]] and [[Garnet|garnet]].
sentence_314: [[Industry_in_Brazil|Industry in Brazil]] – from [[Automobile|automobiles]], [[Steel|steel]] and [[Petrochemical|petrochemicals]] to [[Computer|computers]], [[Aircraft|aircraft]] and [[Durable_good|consumer durables]] – accounted for 30.8% of the gross domestic product.
sentence_315: Industry is highly concentrated in metropolitan São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, [[Campinas|Campinas]], [[Porto_Alegre|Porto Alegre]], and [[Belo_Horizonte|Belo Horizonte]].
sentence_316: Brazil has become the fourth largest car market in the world.
sentence_317: Major export products include [[Fixed-wing_aircraft|aircraft]], electrical equipment, [[Automobile|automobiles]], [[Ethanol_fuel|ethanol]], [[Textile|textiles]], [[Footwear|footwear]], [[Iron_ore|iron ore]], [[Steel|steel]], [[Coffee|coffee]], [[Orange_juice|orange juice]], [[Soybean|soybeans]] and [[Corned_beef|corned beef]].
sentence_318: In total, Brazil ranks 23rd worldwide in [[List_of_countries_by_exports|value of exports]].
sentence_319: In the food industry, in 2019, Brazil was the second largest exporter of processed foods in the world.
sentence_320: In 2016, the country was the 2nd largest producer of [[Pulp_(paper)|pulp]] in the world and the 8th producer of [[Paper|paper]].
sentence_321: In the [[Footwear_industry|footwear industry]], in 2019, Brazil ranked 4th among world producers.
sentence_322: In 2019, the country was the 8th producer of [[Vehicles|vehicles]] and the 9th producer of [[Steel|steel]] in the world.
sentence_323: In 2018, the [[Chemical_industry|chemical industry]] of Brazil was the 8th in the world.
sentence_324: In [[Textile_industry|textile industry]], Brazil, although it was among the 5 largest world producers in 2013, is very little integrated in world trade.
sentence_325: Brazil pegged its currency, the [[Brazilian_real|real]], to the U.S. dollar in 1994.
sentence_326: However, after the [[1997_Asian_financial_crisis|East Asian financial crisis]], the [[1998_Russian_financial_crisis|Russian default]] in 1998 and the series of adverse financial events that followed it, the [[Central_Bank_of_Brazil|Central Bank of Brazil]] temporarily changed its [[Monetary_policy|monetary policy]] to a managed float regime scheme while undergoing a [[Currency_crisis|currency crisis]], until definitively changing the exchange regime to [[Free-float|free-float]] in January 1999.
sentence_327: Brazil received an [[International_Monetary_Fund|International Monetary Fund]] (IMF) rescue package in mid-2002 of $30.4 billion, a record sum at the time.
sentence_328: Brazil's central bank repaid the IMF loan in 2005, although it was not due to be repaid until 2006.
sentence_329: One of the issues the [[Central_Bank_of_Brazil|Central Bank of Brazil]] recently dealt with was an excess of [[Speculation|speculative]] short-term capital inflows to the country, which may have contributed to a fall in the value of the U.S. dollar against the real during that period.
sentence_330: Nonetheless, [[Foreign_direct_investment|foreign direct investment]] (FDI), related to long-term, less speculative investment in production, is estimated to be $193.8 billion for 2007.
sentence_331: [[Inflation|Inflation]] monitoring and control currently plays a major part in the Central bank's role in setting short-term [[Interest_rate|interest rates]] as a [[Monetary_policy|monetary policy]] measure.
sentence_332: Between 1993 and 2010, 7012 mergers and acquisitions with a total known value of $707 billion with the involvement of Brazilian firms were announced.
sentence_333: The year 2010 was a new record in terms of value with US$115 billion in transactions.
sentence_334: The largest transaction with involvement of Brazilian companies was the [[Vale_(mining_company)|Cia.
sentence_335: Vale do Rio Doce]] acquisition of [[Vale_Inco|Inco]] in a [[Tender_offer|tender offer]] valued at US$18.9 billion.
sentence_336: [[Corruption_in_Brazil|Corruption]] costs Brazil almost $41 billion a year alone in 2010, with 69.9% of the country's firms identifying the issue as a major constraint in successfully penetrating the global market.
sentence_337: Local government corruption is so prevalent that voters perceive it as a problem only if it surpasses certain levels, and only if a local media e.g. a radio station is present to divulge the findings of corruption charges.
sentence_338: Initiatives, like this exposure, strengthen awareness which is indicated by the Transparency International's [[Corruption_Perceptions_Index|Corruption Perceptions Index]]; ranking Brazil 69th out of 178 countries in 2012.
sentence_339: The purchasing power in Brazil is eroded by the so-called [[Brazil_cost|Brazil cost]].
sentence_340: Brazil also has a large [[Cooperative|cooperative]] sector that provides 50% of the food in the country.
sentence_341: The world's largest healthcare cooperative [[Unimed_(organization)|Unimed]] is also located in Brazil, and accounts for 32% of the healthcare insurance market in the country.
sentence_342: Main article: [[Energy_in_Brazil|Energy in Brazil]]
sentence_343: Brazil is the world's [[List_of_countries_by_total_primary_energy_consumption_and_production|tenth largest]] energy consumer with much of its energy coming from [[Renewable_energy|renewable sources]], particularly [[Hydroelectricity|hydroelectricity]] and [[Ethanol|ethanol]]; the [[Itaipu_Dam|Itaipu Dam]] is the world's largest [[Hydroelectricity|hydroelectric plant]] by energy generation, and the country has other large plants like [[Belo_Monte_Dam|Belo Monte]] and [[Tucuruí_Dam|Tucuruí]].
sentence_344: The first car with an ethanol engine was produced in 1978 and the first airplane engine running on ethanol in 2005.
sentence_345: In total electricity generation, in 2019 Brazil reached 170,000 megawatts of installed capacity, more than 75% from renewable sources (the majority, hydroelectric plants).
sentence_346: Recent oil discoveries in the [[Pre-salt_layer|Pre-salt layer]] have opened the door for a large increase in oil production.
sentence_347: The governmental agencies responsible for the energy policy are the Ministry of Mines and Energy, the National Council for Energy Policy, the [[National_Agency_of_Petroleum,_Natural_Gas_and_Biofuels_(Brazil)|National Agency of Petroleum, Natural Gas and Biofuels]], and the [[Brazilian_Electricity_Regulatory_Agency|National Agency of Electricity]].
sentence_348: In the beginning of 2020, in the production of [[Petroleum|oil]] and [[Natural_gas|natural gas]], the country exceeded 4 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, for the first time.
sentence_349: In January this year, 3.168 million barrels of oil per day and 138.753 million cubic meters of natural gas were extracted.
sentence_350: Main article: [[Tourism_in_Brazil|Tourism in Brazil]]
sentence_351: Tourism in Brazil is a growing sector and key to the economy of several regions of the country.
sentence_352: The country had 6.36 million visitors in 2015, ranking in terms of the international tourist arrivals as the main destination in South America and second in [[Latin_America|Latin America]] after [[Mexico|Mexico]].
sentence_353: Revenues from international tourists reached US$6 billion in 2010, showing a recovery from the [[Late-2000s_recession|2008–2009 economic crisis]].
sentence_354: Historical records of 5.4 million visitors and US$6.8 billion in receipts were reached in 2011.
sentence_355: Natural areas are its most popular tourism product, a combination of [[Ecotourism|ecotourism]] with [[Leisure|leisure]] and [[Recreation|recreation]], mainly sun and beach, and adventure travel, as well as cultural tourism.
sentence_356: Among the most popular destinations are the [[Amazon_Rainforest|Amazon Rainforest]], [[Beach|beaches]] and [[Dune|dunes]] in the [[Northeast_Region,_Brazil|Northeast Region]], the [[Pantanal|Pantanal]] in the [[Center-West_Region,_Brazil|Center-West Region]], beaches at [[Rio_de_Janeiro_(state)|Rio de Janeiro]] and [[Santa_Catarina_(state)|Santa Catarina]], cultural tourism in [[Minas_Gerais|Minas Gerais]] and business trips to [[São_Paulo|São Paulo]].
sentence_357: In terms of the 2015 [[Travel_and_Tourism_Competitiveness_Report|Travel and Tourism Competitiveness Index]] (TTCI), which is a measurement of the factors that make it attractive to develop business in the travel and tourism industry of individual countries, Brazil ranked in the 28st place at the world's level, third in the [[Americas|Americas]], after [[Canada|Canada]] and [[United_States|United States]].
sentence_358: Brazil's main competitive advantages are its natural resources, which ranked 1st on this criteria out of all countries considered, and ranked 23rd for its cultural resources, due to its many [[World_Heritage_site|World Heritage sites]].
sentence_359: The TTCI report notes Brazil's main weaknesses: its ground transport infrastructure remains underdeveloped (ranked 116th), with the quality of roads ranking in 105th place; and the country continues to suffer from a lack of price competitiveness (ranked 114th), due in part to high ticket taxes and airport charges, as well as high prices and high taxation.
sentence_360: Safety and security have improved significantly: 75th in 2011, up from 128th in 2008.
sentence_361: According to the [[World_Tourism_Organization|World Tourism Organization]] (WTO), international travel to Brazil accelerated in 2000, particularly during 2004 and 2005.
sentence_362: However, in 2006 a slow-down took place, and international arrivals had almost no growth in 2007–08.
sentence_363: In spite of this trend, revenues from international tourism continued to rise, from [[USD|USD]] 4 billion in 2005 to 5 billion in 2007, despite 330 000 fewer arrivals.
sentence_364: This favorable trend is the result of the strong devaluation of the US dollar against the [[Brazilian_Real|Brazilian Real]], which began in 2004, but which makes Brazil a more expensive international destination.
sentence_365: This trend changed in 2009, when both visitors and revenues fell as a result of the [[Great_Recession|Great Recession]] of 2008–09.
sentence_366: By 2010, the industry had recovered, and arrivals grew above 2006 levels to 5.2 million international visitors, and receipts from these visitors reached US$6 billion.
sentence_367: In 2011 the historical record was reached with 5.4 million visitors and US$6.8 billion in receipts.
sentence_368: Despite continuing record-breaking international tourism revenues, the number of Brazilian tourists travelling overseas has been growing steadily since 2003, resulting in a net negative [[Foreign_exchange_market|foreign exchange]] balance, as more money is spent abroad by Brazilians than comes in as receipts from international tourists visiting Brazil.
sentence_369: Tourism expenditures abroad grew from US$5.8 billion in 2006, to US$8.2 billion in 2007, a 42% increase, representing a net deficit of US$3.3 billion in 2007, as compared to US$1.5 billion in 2006, a 125% increase from the previous year.
sentence_370: This trend is caused by Brazilians taking advantage of the stronger [[Brazilian_real|Real]] to travel and making relatively cheaper expenditures abroad.
sentence_371: Brazilians traveling overseas in 2006 represented 4% of the country's population.
sentence_372: In 2005, tourism contributed with 3.2% of the country's revenues from exports of goods and services, and represented 7% of direct and indirect employment in the Brazilian economy.
sentence_373: In 2006 direct employment in the sector reached 1.9 million people.
sentence_374: Domestic tourism is a fundamental market segment for the industry, as 51 million people traveled throughout the country in 2005, and direct revenues from Brazilian tourists reached US$22 billion, 5.6 times more receipts than international tourists in 2005.
sentence_375: In 2005, [[Rio_de_Janeiro|Rio de Janeiro]], [[Foz_do_Iguaçu|Foz do Iguaçu]], [[São_Paulo|São Paulo]], Florianópolis and [[Salvador,_Bahia|Salvador]] were the most visited cities by international tourists for leisure trips.
sentence_376: The most popular destinations for business trips were [[São_Paulo|São Paulo]], [[Rio_de_Janeiro|Rio de Janeiro]] and [[Porto_Alegre|Porto Alegre]].
sentence_377: In 2006 Rio de Janeiro and [[Fortaleza|Fortaleza]] were the most popular destinations for business trips.
sentence_378: Main article: Science and technology in Brazil
sentence_379: Technological research in Brazil is largely carried out in public universities and research institutes, with the majority of funding for basic research coming from various government agencies.
sentence_380: Brazil's most esteemed technological hubs are the Oswaldo Cruz Institute, the [[Instituto_Butantan|Butantan Institute]], the Air Force's [[Brazilian_General_Command_for_Aerospace_Technology|Aerospace Technical Center]], the [[Empresa_Brasileira_de_Pesquisa_Agropecuária|Brazilian Agricultural Research Corporation]] and the INPE.
sentence_381: The [[Brazilian_Space_Agency|Brazilian Space Agency]] has the most advanced space program in Latin America, with significant resources to launch vehicles, and manufacture of [[Artificial_satellite|satellites]].
sentence_382: Owner of relative technological sophistication, the country develops [[Submarine|submarines]], aircraft, as well as being involved in space research, having a Vehicle Launch Center Light and being the only country in the [[Southern_Hemisphere|Southern Hemisphere]] the integrate team building [[International_Space_Station|International Space Station]] (ISS).
sentence_383: The country is also a pioneer in the search for oil in deep water, from where it extracts 73% of its reserves.
sentence_384: [[Uranium|Uranium]] is enriched at the [[Resende_Nuclear_Fuel_Factory|Resende Nuclear Fuel Factory]], mostly for research purposes (as Brazil obtains 88% from its electricity from [[Hydroelectricity|hydroelectricity]]) and the country's first nuclear submarine was delivered in 2015 (by France).
sentence_385: Brazil is one of the three countries in Latin America with an operational [[Synchrotron|Synchrotron]] Laboratory, a research facility on physics, chemistry, material science and life sciences, and Brazil is the only Latin American country to have a [[Semiconductor|semiconductor]] company with its own fabrication plant, the [[CEITEC|CEITEC]].
sentence_386: According to the Global Information Technology Report 2009-2010 of the World Economic Forum, Brazil is the world's 61st largest developer of information technology.
sentence_387: Brazil also has a large number of outstanding scientific personalities.
sentence_388: Among the most renowned Brazilian inventors are priests [[Bartolomeu_de_Gusmão|Bartolomeu de Gusmão]], [[Landell_de_Moura|Landell de Moura]] and Francisco João de Azevedo, besides [[Alberto_Santos-Dumont|Alberto Santos-Dumont]], Evaristo Conrado Engelberg, [[Manuel_Dias_de_Abreu|Manuel Dias de Abreu]], [[Andreas_Pavel|Andreas Pavel]] and Nélio José Nicolai.
sentence_389: Brazilian science is represented by the likes of [[César_Lattes|César Lattes]] (Brazilian [[Physicist|physicist]] Pathfinder of [[Pion|Pi Meson]]), Mário Schenberg (considered the greatest theoretical physicist of Brazil), [[José_Leite_Lopes|José Leite Lopes]] (only Brazilian physicist holder of the UNESCO Science Prize), [[Artur_Ávila|Artur Ávila]] (the first Latin American winner of the [[Fields_Medal|Fields Medal]]) and [[Fritz_Müller|Fritz Müller]] (pioneer in factual support of the theory of evolution by Charles Darwin).
sentence_390: Main article: [[Transport_in_Brazil|Transport in Brazil]]
sentence_391: Brazilian roads are the primary carriers of freight and passenger traffic.
sentence_392: The road system totaled 1.98 million km (1.23 million mi) in 2002.
sentence_393: The total of paved roads increased from 35,496 km (22,056 mi) in 1967 to 184,140 km (114,419 mi) in 2002.
sentence_394: The country has about 14,000 km (8,699 mi) of divided highways, 5,000 km (3,107 mi) only in the [[São_Paulo_(state)|State of São Paulo]].
sentence_395: Currently it's possible to travel from [[Rio_Grande,_Rio_Grande_do_Sul|Rio Grande]], in the extreme south of the country, to [[Brasília|Brasília]] (2,580 km (1,603 mi)) or [[Casimiro_de_Abreu,_Rio_de_Janeiro|Casimiro de Abreu]], in the state of [[Rio_de_Janeiro_(state)|Rio de Janeiro]] (2,045 km (1,271 mi)), only on divided highways.
sentence_396: The first investments in road infrastructure have given up in the 1920s, the government of Washington Luis, being pursued in the governments of Getúlio Vargas and Eurico Gaspar Dutra.
sentence_397: President Juscelino Kubitschek (1956–61), who designed and built the capital [[Brasília|Brasília]], was another supporter of highways.
sentence_398: Kubitschek was responsible for the installation of major car manufacturers in the country ([[Volkswagen|Volkswagen]], [[Ford_Motor_Company|Ford]] and [[General_Motors|General Motors]] arrived in Brazil during his rule) and one of the points used to attract them was support for the construction of highways.
sentence_399: With the implementation of [[Fiat|Fiat]] in 1976 ending an automobile market closed loop, from the end of the 1990s the country has received large foreign direct investments installing in its territory other major car manufacturers and utilities, such as [[Iveco|Iveco]], [[Renault|Renault]], [[Peugeot|Peugeot]], [[Citroen|Citroen]], [[Honda|Honda]], [[Mitsubishi|Mitsubishi]], [[Mercedes-Benz|Mercedes-Benz]], [[BMW|BMW]], [[Hyundai_Motor_Company|Hyundai]], [[Toyota|Toyota]] among others.
sentence_400: Brazil is the seventh most important country in the [[Auto_industry|auto industry]].
sentence_401: Brazil's [[Rail_transport|railway]] system has been declining since 1945, when emphasis shifted to [[Highway|highway]] construction.
sentence_402: The total length of railway track was 30,875 km (19,185 mi) in 2002, as compared with 31,848 km (19,789 mi) in 1970.
sentence_403: Most of the railway system belonged to the Federal Railroad Corporation RFFSA, which was privatized in 2007.
sentence_404: The [[São_Paulo_Metro|São Paulo Metro]] was the first underground transit system in Brazil.
sentence_405: The other metro systems are in [[Rio_de_Janeiro|Rio de Janeiro]], [[Porto_Alegre|Porto Alegre]], [[Recife|Recife]], [[Belo_Horizonte|Belo Horizonte]], [[Brasília|Brasília]], Teresina and [[Fortaleza|Fortaleza]].
sentence_406: The country has an extensive rail network of 28,538 kilometres (17,733 miles) in length, the tenth largest network in the world.
sentence_407: Currently, the Brazilian government, unlike the past, seeks to encourage this mode of transport; an example of this incentive is the project of the [[Rio–São_Paulo_high-speed_rail|Rio–São Paulo high-speed rail]], that will connect the two main cities of the country to carry passengers.
sentence_408: There are about 2,500 airports in Brazil, including landing fields: the second largest number in the world, after the United States.
sentence_409: São Paulo–Guarulhos International Airport, near São Paulo, is the largest and busiest airport with nearly 20 million passengers annually, while handling the vast majority of commercial traffic for the country.
sentence_410: For freight transport waterways are of importance, e.g. the [[Free_Economic_Zone_of_Manaus|industrial zones of Manaus]] can be reached only by means of the Solimões–Amazonas waterway (3,250 kilometres (2,020 miles) with 6 metres (20 feet) minimum depth).
sentence_411: The country also has 50,000 kilometres (31,000 miles) of waterways.
sentence_412: Coastal shipping links widely separated parts of the country.
sentence_413: Bolivia and Paraguay have been given free [[Port|ports]] at Santos.
sentence_414: Of the 36 deep-water ports, Santos, Itajaí, Rio Grande, Paranaguá, Rio de Janeiro, Sepetiba, Vitória, Suape, Manaus and São Francisco do Sul are the most important.
sentence_415: Bulk carriers have to wait up to 18 days before being serviced, container ships 36.3 hours on average.
sentence_416: Main article: [[Health_in_Brazil|Health in Brazil]]
sentence_417: The Brazilian [[Public_health|public health]] system, the [[Sistema_Único_de_Saúde|Unified Health System]] (SUS), is managed and provided by all levels of government, being the largest system of this type in the world.
sentence_418: On the other hand, private healthcare systems play a complementary role.
sentence_419: Public health services are universal and offered to all citizens of the country for free.
sentence_420: However, the construction and maintenance of health centers and hospitals are financed by taxes, and the country spends about 9% of its GDP on expenditures in the area.
sentence_421: In 2012, Brazil had 1.85 doctors and 2.3 hospital beds for every 1,000 inhabitants.
sentence_422: Despite all the progress made since the creation of the [[Universal_health_care|universal health care]] system in 1988, there are still several public health problems in Brazil.
sentence_423: In 2006, the main points to be solved were the high [[List_of_countries_by_infant_mortality_rate|infant]] (2.51%) and maternal mortality rates (73.1 deaths per 1000 births).
sentence_424: The number of deaths from noncommunicable diseases, such as [[Cardiovascular_diseases|cardiovascular diseases]] (151.7 deaths per 100,000 inhabitants) and [[Cancer|cancer]] (72.7 deaths per 100,000 inhabitants), also has a considerable impact on the health of the Brazilian population.
sentence_425: Finally, external but preventable factors such as car accidents, violence and suicide caused 14.9% of all deaths in the country.
sentence_426: The Brazilian health system was ranked 125th among the 191 countries evaluated by the [[World_Health_Organization|World Health Organization]] (WHO) in 2000.
sentence_427: Main article: [[Education_in_Brazil|Education in Brazil]]
sentence_428: The Federal Constitution and the Law of Guidelines and Bases of National Education determine that the Union, the [[States_of_Brazil|states]], the [[Federal_District_(Brazil)|Federal District]], and the [[Municipalities_of_Brazil|municipalities]] must manage and organize their respective education systems.
sentence_429: Each of these public educational systems is responsible for its own maintenance, which manages funds as well as the mechanisms and funding sources.
sentence_430: The constitution reserves 25% of the state budget and 18% of federal taxes and municipal taxes for education.
sentence_431: According to the [[Brazilian_Institute_of_Geography_and_Statistics|IBGE]], in 2011, the literacy rate of the population was 90.4%, meaning that 13 million (9.6% of population) people are still illiterate in the country; functional illiteracy has reached 21.6% of the population.
sentence_432: Illiteracy is highest in the Northeast, where 19.9% of the population is illiterate.
sentence_433: Higher education starts with undergraduate or sequential [[Course_(education)|courses]], which may offer different options of specialization in academic or professional careers.
sentence_434: Depending on the choice, students can improve their educational background with courses of post-graduate studies or broad sense.
sentence_435: Attending an institution of higher education is required by Law of Guidelines and Bases of Education.
sentence_436: Kindergarten, [[Elementary_school|elementary]] and medium education are required of all students, provided the student does not hold any disability, whether physical, mental, [[Visual|visual]] or [[Hearing_(sense)|hearing]].
sentence_437: The [[University_of_São_Paulo|University of São Paulo]] is the second best [[University|university]] in [[Latin_America|Latin America]], according to recent 2019 [[QS_World_University_Rankings|QS World University Rankings]].
sentence_438: Of the top 20 Latin American universities, eight are Brazilian.
sentence_439: Most of them are [[Public_university|public]].
sentence_440: Brazil's private institutions tend to be more exclusive and offer better quality education, so many high-income families send their children there.
sentence_441: The result is a segregated educational system that reflects extreme income disparities and reinforces social inequality.
sentence_442: However, efforts to change this are making impacts.
sentence_443: Main articles: [[Telecommunications_in_Brazil|Telecommunications in Brazil]] and Television in Brazil
sentence_444: See also: [[Concentration_of_media_ownership#Brazil|Concentration of media ownership § Brazil]]
sentence_445: The Brazilian press was officially born in [[Rio_de_Janeiro|Rio de Janeiro]] on 13 May 1808 with the creation of the Royal Printing National Press by the [[Prince_Regent|Prince Regent]] [[João_VI_of_Portugal|Dom João]].
sentence_446: The Gazeta do Rio de Janeiro, the first newspaper published in the country, began to circulate on 10 September 1808.
sentence_447: The [[List_of_newspapers_in_the_world_by_circulation|largest newspapers]] nowadays are [[Folha_de_S.Paulo|Folha de S.Paulo]], Super Notícia, [[O_Globo|O Globo]] and [[O_Estado_de_S._Paulo|O Estado de S. Paulo]].
sentence_448: Radio broadcasting began on 7 September 1922, with a speech by then President Pessoa, and was formalized on 20 April 1923 with the creation of "Radio Society of Rio de Janeiro."
sentence_449: Television in Brazil began officially on 18 September 1950, with the founding of TV Tupi by Assis Chateaubriand.
sentence_450: Since then television has grown in the country, creating large commercial broadcast networks such as Globo, SBT, [[RecordTV|RecordTV]], [[Rede_Bandeirantes|Bandeirantes]] and [[RedeTV!|RedeTV]].
sentence_451: Today it is the most important factor in popular culture of Brazilian society, indicated by research showing that as much as 67% of the general population follow the same daily [[Soap_opera|soap opera]] broadcast.
sentence_452: Digital Television, using the [[SBTVD|SBTVD]] standard (based on the Japanese standard [[ISDB-T|ISDB-T]]), was adopted on 29 June 2006 and launched on 2 November 2007.
sentence_453: In May 2010, the Brazilian government launched TV Brasil Internacional, an international [[Television_station|television station]], initially broadcasting to 49 countries.
sentence_454: Commercial television channels broadcast internationally include Globo Internacional, RecordTV Internacional and Band Internacional.
sentence_455: Main articles: [[Demographics_of_Brazil|Demographics of Brazil]] and [[Brazilians|Brazilians]]
sentence_456: See also: [[Immigration_to_Brazil|Immigration to Brazil]] and [[List_of_Brazilian_states_by_population_density|List of Brazilian states by population density]]
sentence_457: The population of Brazil, as recorded by the 2008 PNAD, was approximately 190 million (22.31 inhabitants per square kilometre or 57.8/sq mi), with a ratio of men to women of 0.95:1 and 83.75% of the population defined as urban.
sentence_458: The population is heavily concentrated in the Southeastern (79.8 million inhabitants) and Northeastern (53.5 million inhabitants) regions, while the two most extensive regions, the Center-West and the North, which together make up 64.12% of the Brazilian territory, have a total of only 29.1 million inhabitants.
sentence_459: The first census in Brazil was carried out in 1872 and recorded a population of 9,930,478.
sentence_460: From 1880 to 1930, 4 million Europeans arrived.
sentence_461: Brazil's population increased significantly between 1940 and 1970, because of a decline in the [[Mortality_rate|mortality rate]], even though the [[Birth_rate|birth rate]] underwent a slight decline.
sentence_462: In the 1940s the annual [[Population_growth|population growth rate]] was 2.4%, rising to 3.0% in the 1950s and remaining at 2.9% in the 1960s, as life expectancy rose from 44 to 54 years and to 72.6 years in 2007.
sentence_463: It has been steadily falling since the 1960s, from 3.04% per year between 1950 and 1960 to 1.05% in 2008 and is expected to fall to a negative value of –0.29% by 2050 thus completing the demographic transition.
sentence_464: In 2008, the illiteracy rate was 11.48% and among the [[Youth_in_Brazil|youth]] (ages 15–19) 1.74%.
sentence_465: It was highest (20.30%) in the Northeast, which had a large proportion of rural poor.
sentence_466: Illiteracy was high (24.18%) among the rural population and lower (9.05%) among the urban population.
sentence_467: Main article: Race and ethnicity in Brazil
sentence_468: According to the [[Brazilian_Institute_of_Geography_and_Statistics|National Research by Household Sample]] (PNAD) of 2008, 48.43% of the population (about 92 million) described themselves as [[White_Brazilian|White]]; 43.80% (about 83 million) as [[Pardo_Brazilians|Pardo]] ([[Brown_people|brown]]), 6.84% (about 13 million) as [[Black_Brazilian|Black]]; 0.58% (about 1.1 million) as Asian; and 0.28% (about 536 thousand) as [[Indigenous_peoples_in_Brazil|Amerindian]] (officially called indígena, Indigenous), while 0.07% (about 130 thousand) did not declare their race.
sentence_469: In 2007, the [[Fundação_Nacional_do_Índio|National Indian Foundation]] estimated that Brazil has 67 different uncontacted tribes, up from their estimate of 40 in 2005.
sentence_470: Brazil is believed to have the largest number of [[Uncontacted_peoples|uncontacted peoples]] in the world.
sentence_471: Since the arrival of the Portuguese in 1500, considerable genetic mixing between Amerindians, Europeans, and Africans has taken place in all regions of the country (with European ancestry being dominant nationwide according to the vast majority of all autosomal studies undertaken covering the entire population, accounting for between 65% to 77%).
sentence_472: Brazilian society is more [[Social_issues_in_Brazil|markedly divided by social class lines]], although a high [[Income_inequality_in_Brazil|income disparity]] is found [[Social_apartheid_in_Brazil|between race groups]], so [[Racism|racism]] and [[Class_discrimination|classism]] can be conflated.
sentence_473: Socially significant closeness to one racial group is taken in account more in the basis of appearance ([[Phenotype|phenotypes]]) rather than ancestry, to the extent that full [[Sibling|siblings]] can pertain to different "racial" groups.
sentence_474: [[Socioeconomic_status|Socioeconomic]] factors are also significant, because a minority of [[Pardo_Brazilians|pardos]] are likely to start declaring themselves White or Black if socially upward.
sentence_475: Skin color and facial features do not line quite well with ancestry (usually, Afro-Brazilians are evenly mixed and European ancestry is dominant in Whites and pardos with a significant non-European contribution, but the individual variation is great).
sentence_476: The brown population (officially called [[Pardo_Brazilians|pardo]] in Portuguese, also colloquially ) is a broad category that includes [[Caboclo|caboclos]] (assimilated Amerindians in general, and descendants of Whites and Natives), [[Mulatto|mulatos]] (descendants of primarily Whites and Afro-Brazilians) and cafuzos (descendants of Afro-Brazilians and Natives).
sentence_477: People of considerable Amerindian ancestry form the majority of the population in the Northern, Northeastern and Center-Western regions.
sentence_478: Higher percents of Blacks, mulattoes and tri-racials can be found in the eastern coast of the Northeastern region from Bahia to Paraíba and also in northern Maranhão, southern Minas Gerais and in eastern Rio de Janeiro.
sentence_479: From the 19th century, Brazil opened its borders to [[Immigration_to_Brazil|immigration]].
sentence_480: About five million people from over 60 countries migrated to Brazil between 1808 and 1972, most of them of [[Portuguese_Brazilian|Portuguese]], [[Italian_Brazilian|Italian]], [[Brazilians_of_Spanish_descent|Spanish]], [[German_Brazilian|German]], [[Ukrainian_Brazilian|Ukrainian]], [[Polish_Brazilian|Polish]], [[Jewish_Brazilian|Jewish]], Russian, [[Chinese_Brazilian|Chinese]], [[Japanese_Brazilian|Japanese]], and Arab origin.
sentence_481: Brazil has the second largest Jewish community in Latin America making up 0.06% of its population.
sentence_482: Main article: [[Religion_in_Brazil|Religion in Brazil]]
sentence_483: Further information: [[Catholic_Church_in_Brazil|Catholic Church in Brazil]] and [[Protestantism_in_Brazil|Protestantism in Brazil]]
sentence_484: [[Roman_Catholicism|Roman Catholicism]] is the country's predominant faith.
sentence_485: Brazil has the [[Catholic_Church_by_country|world's largest Catholic population]].
sentence_486: According to the 2010 Demographic Census (the PNAD survey does not inquire about religion), 64.63% of the population followed [[Roman_Catholicism_in_Brazil|Roman Catholicism]]; 22.2% [[Protestantism_in_Brazil|Protestantism]]; 2.0% Kardecist spiritism; 3.2% other religions, undeclared or undetermined; while 8.0% have no religion.
sentence_487: Religion in Brazil was formed from the meeting of the Catholic Church with the religious traditions of enslaved African peoples and indigenous peoples.
sentence_488: This confluence of faiths during the Portuguese colonization of Brazil led to the development of a diverse array of syncretistic practices within the overarching umbrella of Brazilian Catholic Church, characterized by traditional Portuguese festivities, and in some instances, [[Allan_Kardec|Allan Kardec]]'s Spiritism (a religion which incorporates elements of spiritualism and Christianity).
sentence_489: Religious pluralism increased during the 20th century, and the Protestant community has grown to include over 22% of the population.
sentence_490: The most common Protestant denominations are [[Evangelicalism|Evangelical]] [[Pentecostalism|Pentecostal]] ones.
sentence_491: Other Protestant branches with a notable presence in the country include the [[Baptists|Baptists]], [[Seventh-day_Adventist_Church|Seventh-day Adventists]], [[Lutheranism|Lutherans]] and the [[Calvinism|Reformed tradition]].
sentence_492: However, in the last ten years Protestantism, particularly in forms of Pentecostalism and Evangelicalism, has spread in Brazil, while the proportion of Catholics has dropped significantly.
sentence_493: After Protestantism, individuals professing no religion are also a significant group, exceeding 8% of the population as of the 2010 census.
sentence_494: The cities of Boa Vista, [[Salvador,_Bahia|Salvador]], and [[Porto_Velho|Porto Velho]] have the greatest proportion of [[Irreligion|Irreligious]] residents in Brazil.
sentence_495: Teresina, [[Fortaleza|Fortaleza]], and Florianópolis were the most Roman Catholic in the country.
sentence_496: [[Greater_Rio_de_Janeiro|Greater Rio de Janeiro]], not including the [[Rio_de_Janeiro|city proper]], is the most irreligious and least Roman Catholic Brazilian periphery, while [[Greater_Porto_Alegre|Greater Porto Alegre]] and Greater [[Fortaleza|Fortaleza]] are on the opposite sides of the lists, respectively.
sentence_497: In October 2009, the Brazilian Senate approved and enacted by the President of Brazil in February 2010, an agreement with the [[Holy_See|Vatican]], in which the Legal Statute of the Catholic Church in Brazil is recognized.
sentence_498: The agreement confirmed norms that were normally complied with regarding religious education in public elementary schools (which also ensures the teaching of other beliefs), marriage and spiritual assistance in prisons and hospitals.
sentence_499: The project was criticized by parliamentarians who understood the end of the secular state with the approval of the agreement.
sentence_500: Main articles: [[List_of_largest_cities_in_Brazil|List of largest cities in Brazil]] and [[Municipalities_of_Brazil|Municipalities of Brazil]]
sentence_501: According to IBGE (Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics) urban areas already concentrate 84.35% of the population, while the Southeast region remains the most populated one, with over 80 million inhabitants.
sentence_502: The largest urban agglomerations in Brazil are [[São_Paulo|São Paulo]], [[Rio_de_Janeiro|Rio de Janeiro]], and [[Belo_Horizonte|Belo Horizonte]] – all in the Southeastern Region – with 21.1, 12.3, and 5.1 million inhabitants respectively.
sentence_503: The majority of state capitals are the largest cities in their states, except for [[Vitória,_Brazil|Vitória]], the capital of Espírito Santo, and Florianópolis, the capital of Santa Catarina.
sentence_504: Main articles: [[Languages_of_Brazil|Languages of Brazil]], Portuguese language, [[Brazilian_Portuguese|Brazilian Portuguese]], and [[List_of_endangered_languages_in_Brazil|List of endangered languages in Brazil]]
sentence_505: The official language of Brazil is Portuguese (Article 13 of the [[Constitution_of_Brazil|Constitution of the Federal Republic of Brazil]]), which almost all of the population speaks and is virtually the only language used in newspapers, radio, television, and for business and administrative purposes.
sentence_506: Brazil is the only Portuguese-speaking nation in the Americas, making the language an important part of Brazilian national identity and giving it a national culture distinct from those of its Spanish-speaking neighbors.
sentence_507: [[Brazilian_Portuguese|Brazilian Portuguese]] has had its own development, mostly similar to 16th-century Central and Southern dialects of European Portuguese (despite a very substantial number of Portuguese colonial settlers, and [[Portuguese_Brazilian|more recent immigrants]], coming from [[Northern_Portugal|Northern regions]], and in minor degree Portuguese [[Macaronesia|Macaronesia]]), with a few influences from the [[Indigenous_languages_of_the_Americas|Amerindian]] and [[Languages_of_Africa|African languages]], especially [[West_Africa|West African]] and [[Bantu_languages|Bantu]] restricted to the vocabulary only.
sentence_508: As a result, the language is somewhat different, mostly in phonology, from the language of Portugal and other [[Portuguese-speaking_countries|Portuguese-speaking countries]] (the dialects of the other countries, partly because of the more recent end of [[Portuguese_Empire|Portuguese colonialism]] in these regions, have a closer connection to contemporary [[European_Portuguese|European Portuguese]]).
sentence_509: These differences are comparable to those between [[American_English|American]] and [[British_English|British English]].
sentence_510: In 1990, the [[Community_of_Portuguese_Language_Countries|Community of Portuguese Language Countries]] (CPLP), which included representatives from all countries with Portuguese as the official language, reached an agreement on the reform of the Portuguese orthography to unify the two standards then in use by Brazil on one side and the remaining lusophone countries on the other.
sentence_511: This spelling reform went into effect in Brazil on 1 January 2009.
sentence_512: In Portugal, the reform was signed into law by the President on 21 July 2008 allowing for a six-year adaptation period, during which both orthographies will co-exist.
sentence_513: The remaining CPLP countries are free to establish their own transition timetables.
sentence_514: The [[Recognition_of_sign_languages|sign language law]] legally recognized in 2002, (the law was [[Regulation|regulated]] in 2005) the use of the [[Brazilian_Sign_Language|Brazilian Sign Language]], more commonly known by its Portuguese acronym LIBRAS, in education and government services.
sentence_515: The language must be taught as a part of the [[School_of_education|education]] and [[Speech_and_language_pathology|speech and language pathology]] curricula.
sentence_516: LIBRAS teachers, instructors and translators are recognized professionals.
sentence_517: Schools and health services must provide access ("[[Inclusion_(education)|inclusion]]") to deaf people.
sentence_518: Minority languages are spoken throughout the nation.
sentence_519: One hundred and eighty [[Indigenous_languages_of_the_Americas|Amerindian languages]] are spoken in remote areas and a significant number of other languages are spoken by immigrants and their descendants.
sentence_520: In the municipality of [[São_Gabriel_da_Cachoeira|São Gabriel da Cachoeira]], [[Nheengatu_language|Nheengatu]] (a currently endangered South American [[Creole_language|creole language]] – or an 'anti-creole', according to some linguists – with mostly Indigenous Brazilian languages lexicon and Portuguese-based grammar that, together with its southern relative [[Língua_geral_paulista|língua geral paulista]], once was a major [[Lingua_franca|lingua franca]] in Brazil, being replaced by Portuguese only after governmental prohibition led by [[Suppression_of_the_Society_of_Jesus#Portugal|major political changes]]), [[Baniwa_of_Içana|Baniwa]] and Tucano languages had been granted co-official status with Portuguese.
sentence_521: There are significant communities of German (mostly the [[Riograndenser_Hunsrückisch|Brazilian Hunsrückisch]], a High German language dialect) and Italian (mostly the [[Talian_dialect|Talian]], a [[Venetian_language|Venetian]] dialect) origins in the Southern and Southeastern regions, whose ancestors' native languages were carried along to Brazil, and which, still alive there, are influenced by the Portuguese language.
sentence_522: Talian is officially a historic patrimony of [[Rio_Grande_do_Sul|Rio Grande do Sul]], and two German dialects possess co-official status in a few municipalities.
sentence_523: Italian is also recognized as ethnic language in the [[Microregions_of_Brazil|Santa Teresa]] microregion and [[Vila_Velha|Vila Velha]] (Espirito Santo state), and is taught as mandatory second language at school.
sentence_524: Learning at least one second language (generally English or Spanish) is mandatory for all the 12 grades of the mandatory [[Education_in_Brazil|education system]] (primary and [[Secondary_education|secondary education]], there called ensino fundamental and ensino médio respectively).
sentence_525: Brazil is the first country in South America to offer [[Esperanto|Esperanto]] to secondary students.
sentence_527: The core culture of Brazil is derived from [[Culture_of_Portugal|Portuguese culture]], because of its strong colonial ties with the Portuguese Empire.
sentence_528: Among other influences, the Portuguese introduced the Portuguese language, [[Catholic_Church|Roman Catholicism]] and colonial architectural styles.
sentence_529: The culture was, however, also strongly influenced by [[Ethnic_groups_of_Africa|African]], [[Indigenous_peoples_in_Brazil|indigenous]] and non-Portuguese European cultures and traditions.
sentence_530: Some aspects of Brazilian culture were influenced by the contributions of [[Italian_Brazilian|Italian]], [[German_Brazilian|German]] and other European as well as [[Japanese_Brazilian|Japanese]], [[Jewish_Brazilian|Jewish]] and Arab immigrants who arrived in large numbers in the South and Southeast of Brazil during the 19th and 20th centuries.
sentence_531: The indigenous Amerindians influenced Brazil's language and [[Brazilian_cuisine|cuisine]]; and the Africans influenced language, cuisine, [[Music_of_Brazil|music]], dance and religion.
sentence_532: [[Brazilian_art|Brazilian art]] has developed since the 16th century into different styles that range from Baroque (the dominant style in Brazil until the early 19th century) to [[Brazilian_academic_art|Romanticism]], [[Modern_art|Modernism]], [[Expressionism|Expressionism]], [[Cubism|Cubism]], [[Surrealism|Surrealism]] and [[Abstract_art|Abstractionism]].
sentence_533: [[Cinema_of_Brazil|Brazilian cinema]] dates back to the birth of the medium in the late 19th century and has gained a new level of international acclaim since the 1960s.
sentence_535: The architecture of Brazil is influenced by Europe, especially Portugal.
sentence_536: It has a history that goes back 500 years to the time when [[Pedro_Álvares_Cabral|Pedro Cabral]] discovered Brazil in 1500.
sentence_537: [[Portuguese_colonial_architecture|Portuguese colonial architecture]] was the first wave of architecture to go to Brazil.
sentence_538: It is the basis for all Brazilian architecture of later centuries.
sentence_539: In the 19th century during the time of the [[Empire_of_Brazil|Empire of Brazil]], Brazil followed European trends and adopted Neoclassical and [[Gothic_Revival_architecture|Gothic Revival architecture]].
sentence_540: Then in the 20th century especially in Brasilia, Brazil experimented with [[Modernist_architecture|Modernist architecture]].
sentence_541: The colonial architecture of Brazil dates to the early 16th century when Brazil was first explored, conquered and settled by the Portuguese.
sentence_542: The Portuguese built architecture familiar to them in Europe in their aim to colonize Brazil.
sentence_543: They built Portuguese colonial architecture which included churches, civic architecture including houses and forts in Brazilian cities and the countryside.
sentence_544: During 19th century Brazilian architecture saw the introduction of more European styles to Brazil such as Neoclassical and Gothic Revival architecture.
sentence_545: This was usually mixed with Brazilian influences from their own heritage which produced a unique form of Brazilian architecture.
sentence_546: In the 1950s the [[Modernist_architecture|modernist architecture]] was introduced when [[Brasilia|Brasilia]] was built as new federal capital in the interior of Brazil to help develop the interior.
sentence_547: The architect [[Oscar_Niemeyer|Oscar Niemeyer]] idealized and built government buildings, churches and civic buildings in the modernist style.
sentence_549: The music of Brazil was formed mainly from the fusion of European and African elements.
sentence_550: Until the nineteenth century, Portugal was the gateway to most of the influences that built Brazilian music, although many of these elements were not of Portuguese origin, but generally European.
sentence_551: The first was José Maurício Nunes Garcia, author of sacred pieces with influence of Viennese classicism.
sentence_552: The major contribution of the African element was the rhythmic diversity and some dances and instruments that had a bigger role in the development of popular music and folk, flourishing especially in the twentieth century.
sentence_553: Popular music since the late eighteenth century began to show signs of forming a characteristically Brazilian sound, with [[Samba_(music)|samba]] considered the most typical and on the UNESCO cultural heritage list.
sentence_554: [[Maracatu|Maracatu]] and [[Afoxê|Afoxê]] are two [[Afro-Brazilian|Afro-Brazilian]] music traditions that have been popularized by their appearance in the annual Brazilian Carnivals.
sentence_555: The sport of [[Capoeira|capoeira]] is usually played with its own music referred to as capoeira music, which is usually considered to be a call-and-response type of folk music.
sentence_556: Forró is a type of folk music prominent during the Festa Junina in [[Northeast_Region,_Brazil|northeastern Brazil]].
sentence_557: Jack A. Draper III, a professor of Portuguese at the [[University_of_Missouri|University of Missouri]], argues that Forró was used as a way to subdue feelings of nostalgia for a rural lifestyle.
sentence_558: [[Choro|Choro]] is a very popular music instrumental style.
sentence_559: Its origins are in 19th-century Rio de Janeiro.
sentence_560: In spite of the name, the style often has a fast and happy rhythm, characterized by virtuosity, improvisation, subtle [[Modulation_(music)|modulations]] and full of [[Syncopation|syncopation]] and [[Counterpoint|counterpoint]].
sentence_561: [[Bossa_nova|Bossa nova]] is also a well-known style of Brazilian music developed and popularized in the 1950s and 1960s.
sentence_562: The phrase "bossa nova" means literally "new trend".
sentence_563: A lyrical fusion of samba and [[Jazz|jazz]], bossa nova acquired a large following starting in the 1960s.
sentence_565: Brazilian literature dates back to the 16th century, to the writings of the first Portuguese explorers in Brazil, such as [[Pêro_Vaz_de_Caminha|Pêro Vaz de Caminha]], filled with descriptions of fauna, flora and commentary about the indigenous population that fascinated European readers.
sentence_566: Brazil produced significant works in [[Romanticism|Romanticism]] – novelists like Joaquim Manuel de Macedo and [[José_de_Alencar|José de Alencar]] wrote novels about love and pain.
sentence_567: Alencar, in his long career, also treated indigenous people as heroes in the [[Indianism_(arts)|Indigenist]] novels [[The_Guarani|O Guarani]], [[Iracema|Iracema]] and [[Ubirajara|Ubirajara]].
sentence_568: [[Machado_de_Assis|Machado de Assis]], one of his contemporaries, wrote in virtually all genres and continues to gain international prestige from critics worldwide.
sentence_569: [[Brazilian_literature#Modernism|Brazilian Modernism]], evidenced by the [[Week_of_Modern_Art|Week of Modern Art]] in 1922, was concerned with a nationalist avant-garde literature, while [[Brazilian_literature#Post-Modernism|Post-Modernism]] brought a generation of distinct poets like [[João_Cabral_de_Melo_Neto|João Cabral de Melo Neto]], Carlos Drummond de Andrade, [[Vinicius_de_Moraes|Vinicius de Moraes]], [[Cora_Coralina|Cora Coralina]], [[Graciliano_Ramos|Graciliano Ramos]], Cecília Meireles, and internationally known writers dealing with universal and regional subjects like [[Jorge_Amado|Jorge Amado]], [[João_Guimarães_Rosa|João Guimarães Rosa]], [[Clarice_Lispector|Clarice Lispector]] and Manuel Bandeira.
sentence_572: Brazilian cuisine varies greatly by region, reflecting the country's varying mix of indigenous and immigrant populations.
sentence_573: This has created a national cuisine marked by the preservation of regional differences.
sentence_574: Examples are [[Feijoada|Feijoada]], considered the country's national dish; and regional foods such as beiju, feijão tropeiro, [[Vatapá|vatapá]], [[Moqueca|moqueca]], [[Polenta|polenta]] (from Italian cuisine) and [[Acarajé|acarajé]] (from African cuisine).
sentence_575: The national beverage is [[Coffee|coffee]] and [[Cachaça|cachaça]] is Brazil's native [[Distilled_beverage|liquor]].
sentence_576: Cachaça is distilled from [[Sugarcane|sugar cane]] and is the main ingredient in the national cocktail, [[Caipirinha|Caipirinha]].
sentence_577: A typical meal consists mostly of rice and beans with [[Beef|beef]], [[Salad|salad]], [[French_fries|french fries]] and a fried egg.
sentence_578: Often, it is mixed with cassava flour ([[Farofa|farofa]]).
sentence_579: Fried potatoes, fried cassava, fried banana, fried meat and fried cheese are very often eaten in lunch and served in most typical restaurants.
sentence_580: Popular snacks are [[Pastel_(food)|pastel]] (a fried pastry); coxinha (a variation of chicken croquete); [[Pão_de_queijo|pão de queijo]] (cheese bread and cassava flour / [[Tapioca|tapioca]]); [[Pamonha|pamonha]] (corn and milk paste); [[Sfiha|esfirra]] (a variation of Lebanese pastry); [[Kibbeh|kibbeh]] (from Arabic cuisine); empanada (pastry) and empada, little salt pies filled with shrimps or heart of palm.
sentence_581: Brazil has a variety of desserts such as [[Brigadeiro|brigadeiros]] (chocolate fudge balls), [[Bolo_de_rolo|bolo de rolo]] (roll cake with [[Goiabada|goiabada]]), cocada (a coconut sweet), beijinhos (coconut truffles and clove) and romeu e julieta (cheese with goiabada).
sentence_582: Peanuts are used to make [[Paçoca|paçoca]], [[Rapadura|rapadura]] and pé-de-moleque.
sentence_583: Local common fruits like [[Açaí|açaí]], [[Cupuaçu|cupuaçu]], [[Mango|mango]], [[Papaya|papaya]], [[Cocoa_bean|cocoa]], [[Cashew|cashew]], [[Guava|guava]], [[Orange_(fruit)|orange]], [[Lime_(fruit)|lime]], [[Passionfruit|passionfruit]], [[Pineapple|pineapple]], and [[Spondias|hog plum]] are turned in [[Juice|juices]] and used to make [[Chocolate|chocolates]], [[Ice_pop|ice pops]] and [[Ice_cream|ice cream]].
sentence_585: The Brazilian film industry began in the late 19th century, during the early days of the [[Belle_Époque|Belle Époque]].
sentence_586: While there were national film productions during the early 20th century, American films such as Rio the Magnificent were made in [[Rio_de_Janeiro|Rio de Janeiro]] to promote tourism in the city.
sentence_587: The films [[Limite|Limite]] (1931) and [[Ganga_Bruta|Ganga Bruta]] (1933), the latter being produced by [[Adhemar_Gonzaga|Adhemar Gonzaga]] through the prolific studio Cinédia, were poorly received at release and failed at the box office, but are acclaimed nowadays and placed among the finest Brazilian films of all time.
sentence_588: The 1941 unfinished film [[It's_All_True_(film)|It's All True]] was divided in four segments, two of which were filmed in Brazil and directed by [[Orson_Welles|Orson Welles]]; it was originally produced as part of the United States' [[Good_Neighbor_Policy|Good Neighbor Policy]] during Getúlio Vargas' Estado Novo government.
sentence_589: During the 1960s, the [[Cinema_Novo|Cinema Novo]] movement rose to prominence with directors such as [[Glauber_Rocha|Glauber Rocha]], [[Nelson_Pereira_dos_Santos|Nelson Pereira dos Santos]], [[Paulo_Cesar_Saraceni|Paulo Cesar Saraceni]] and [[Arnaldo_Jabor|Arnaldo Jabor]].
sentence_590: Rocha's films Deus e o Diabo na Terra do Sol (1964) and [[Terra_em_Transe|Terra em Transe]] (1967) are considered to be some of the greatest and most influential in Brazilian film history.
sentence_591: During the 1990s, Brazil saw a surge of critical and commercial success with films such as [[O_Quatrilho|O Quatrilho]] ([[Fábio_Barreto|Fábio Barreto]], 1995), [[O_Que_É_Isso,_Companheiro?|O Que É Isso, Companheiro?]]
sentence_592: ([[Bruno_Barreto|Bruno Barreto]], 1997) and [[Central_Station_(film)|Central do Brasil]] ([[Walter_Salles|Walter Salles]], 1998), all of which were nominated for the [[Academy_Award_for_Best_Foreign_Language_Film|Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film]], the latter receiving a [[Academy_Award_for_Best_Actress|Best Actress]] nomination for [[Fernanda_Montenegro|Fernanda Montenegro]].
sentence_593: The 2002 crime film [[City_of_God_(2002_film)|City of God]], directed by Fernando Meirelles, was critically acclaimed, scoring 90% on [[Rotten_Tomatoes|Rotten Tomatoes]], being placed in [[Roger_Ebert|Roger Ebert]]'s Best Films of the Decade list and receiving four [[Academy_Awards|Academy Award]] nominations in 2004, including [[Academy_Award_for_Best_Director|Best Director]].
sentence_594: Notable film festivals in Brazil include the [[São_Paulo_International_Film_Festival|São Paulo]] and [[Rio_de_Janeiro_International_Film_Festival|Rio de Janeiro International Film Festivals]] and the Gramado Festival.
sentence_595: The theatre in Brazil has its origins in the period of Jesuit expansion when theater was used for the dissemination of Catholic doctrine in the 16th century.
