sentence_596: in the 17th and 18th centuries the first dramatists who appeared on the scene of European derivation was for court or private performances.
sentence_597: During the 19th century, dramatic theater gained importance and thickness, whose first representative was [[Luis_Carlos_Martins_Pena|Luis Carlos Martins Pena]] (1813–1848), capable of describing contemporary reality.
sentence_598: Always in this period the comedy of costume and comic production was imposed.
sentence_599: Significant, also in the nineteenth century, was also the playwright [[Antônio_Gonçalves_Dias|Antônio Gonçalves Dias]].
sentence_600: There were also numerous operas and orchestras.
sentence_601: The Brazilian conductor [[Antônio_Carlos_Gomes|Antônio Carlos Gomes]] became internationally known with operas like [[Il_Guarany|Il Guarany]].
sentence_602: At the end of the 19th century orchestrated dramaturgias became very popular and were accompanied with songs of famous artists like the conductress Chiquinha Gonzaga.
sentence_603: Already in the early 20th century there was the presence of theaters, entrepreneurs and actor companies, but paradoxically the quality of the products staggered, and only in 1940 the Brazilian theater received a boost of renewal thanks to the action of Paschoal Carlos Magno and his student's theater, the comedians group and the Italian actors Adolfo Celi, Ruggero Jacobbi and Aldo Calvo, founders of the Teatro Brasileiro de Comedia.
sentence_604: From the 1960s it was attended by a theater dedicated to social and religious issues and to the flourishing of schools of dramatic art.
sentence_605: The most prominent authors at this stage were [[Jorge_Andrade|Jorge Andrade]] and [[Ariano_Suassuna|Ariano Suassuna]].
sentence_607: Brazilian painting emerged in the late 16th century, influenced by [[Baroque|Baroque]], [[Rococo|Rococo]], [[Neoclassicism|Neoclassicism]], [[Romanticism|Romanticism]], [[Realism_(arts)|Realism]], [[Modernism|Modernism]], [[Expressionism|Expressionism]], [[Surrealism|Surrealism]], [[Cubism|Cubism]] and [[Abstract_art|Abstracionism]] making it a major [[Style_(visual_arts)|art style]] called [[Brazilian_academic_art|Brazilian academic art]].
sentence_608: The [[Missão_Artística_Francesa|Missão Artística Francesa]] (French Artistic Mission) arrived in Brazil in 1816 proposing the creation of an art academy modeled after the respected Académie des Beaux-Arts, with graduation courses both for artists and craftsmen for activities such as modeling, decorating, carpentry and others and bringing artists like [[Jean-Baptiste_Debret|Jean-Baptiste Debret]].
sentence_609: Upon the creation of the [[Academia_Imperial_de_Belas_Artes|Imperial Academy of Fine Arts]], new artistic movements spread across the country during the 19th century and later the event called [[Week_of_Modern_Art|Week of Modern Art]] broke definitely with academic tradition in 1922 and started a nationalist trend which was influenced by modernist arts.
sentence_610: Among the best-known Brazilian painters are Ricardo do Pilar and [[Manuel_da_Costa_Ataíde|Manuel da Costa Ataíde]] (baroque and rococo), [[Victor_Meirelles|Victor Meirelles]], [[Pedro_Américo|Pedro Américo]] and [[Almeida_Junior|Almeida Junior]] (romanticism and realism), [[Anita_Malfatti|Anita Malfatti]], [[Ismael_Nery|Ismael Nery]], [[Lasar_Segall|Lasar Segall]], [[Emiliano_di_Cavalcanti|Emiliano di Cavalcanti]], [[Vicente_do_Rego_Monteiro|Vicente do Rego Monteiro]], and [[Tarsila_do_Amaral|Tarsila do Amaral]] (expressionism, surrealism and cubism), Aldo Bonadei, [[José_Pancetti|José Pancetti]] and [[Cândido_Portinari|Cândido Portinari]] (modernism).
sentence_612: The most popular sport in Brazil is [[Association_football|football]].
sentence_613: The [[Brazil_national_football_team|Brazilian men's national team]] is ranked among the best in the world according to the [[FIFA_World_Rankings|FIFA World Rankings]], and has won the [[FIFA_World_Cup|World Cup]] tournament a record five times.
sentence_614: Volleyball, basketball, [[Auto_racing|auto racing]], and [[Martial_arts|martial arts]] also attract large audiences.
sentence_615: The [[Brazil_men's_national_volleyball_team|Brazil men's national volleyball team]], for example, currently holds the titles of the [[FIVB_Volleyball_World_League|World League]], [[FIVB_Volleyball_World_Grand_Champions_Cup|World Grand Champions Cup]], [[FIVB_Volleyball_Men's_World_Championship|World Championship]] and the [[FIVB_Volleyball_Men's_World_Cup|World Cup]].
sentence_616: In auto racing, three Brazilian drivers have won the [[Formula_One|Formula One]] world championship eight times.
sentence_617: Some sport variations have their origins in Brazil: [[Beach_soccer|beach football]], [[Futsal|futsal]] (indoor football) and [[Footvolley|footvolley]] emerged in Brazil as variations of football.
sentence_618: In martial arts, Brazilians developed [[Capoeira|Capoeira]], [[Vale_tudo|Vale tudo]], and [[Brazilian_jiu-jitsu|Brazilian jiu-jitsu]].
sentence_619: Brazil has hosted several high-profile international sporting events, like the [[1950_FIFA_World_Cup|1950 FIFA World Cup]] and recently has hosted the [[2014_FIFA_World_Cup|2014 FIFA World Cup]] and [[2019_Copa_América|2019 Copa América]].
sentence_620: The [[São_Paulo|São Paulo]] circuit, Autódromo José Carlos Pace, hosts the annual Grand Prix of Brazil.
sentence_621: São Paulo organized the [[1963_Pan_American_Games|IV Pan American Games]] in 1963, and Rio de Janeiro hosted the [[2007_Pan_American_Games|XV Pan American Games]] in 2007.
sentence_622: On 2 October 2009, Rio de Janeiro was selected to host the [[2016_Summer_Olympics|2016 Olympic Games]] and [[2016_Summer_Paralympics|2016 Paralympic Games]], making it the first South American city to host the games and second in Latin America, after [[Mexico_City|Mexico City]].
sentence_623: Furthermore, the country hosted the [[FIBA_Basketball_World_Cup|FIBA Basketball World Cups]] in [[1954_FIBA_World_Championship|1954]] and [[1963_FIBA_World_Championship|1963]].
sentence_624: At the 1963 event, the [[Brazil_national_basketball_team|Brazil national basketball team]] won one of its two world championship titles.

title: Annual plant
sentence_0: An annual plant is a plant that completes its [[Biological_life_cycle|life cycle]], from [[Germination|germination]] to the production of [[Seed|seeds]], within one [[Growing_season|growing season]], and then dies.
sentence_1: The length of growing seasons and period in which they take place vary according to geographical location, and may not correspond to the four traditional seasonal divisions of the year.
sentence_2: With respect to the traditional seasons annual plants are generally categorized into summer annuals and winter annuals.
sentence_3: Summer annuals germinate during spring or early summer and mature by autumn of the same year.
sentence_4: Winter annuals germinate during the autumn and mature during the spring or summer of the following calendar year.
sentence_5: One seed-to-seed life cycle for an annual can occur in as little as a month in some species, though most last several months.
sentence_6: [[Brassica_rapa|Oilseed rapa]] can go from seed-to-seed in about five weeks under a bank of [[Fluorescent_lamp|fluorescent lamps]].
sentence_7: This style of growing is often used in classrooms for education.
sentence_8: Many desert annuals are [[Therophyte|therophytes]], because their seed-to-seed life cycle is only weeks and they spend most of the year as seeds to survive dry conditions.
sentence_9: In cultivation, many food plants are, or are grown as, annuals, including virtually all domesticated [[Cereal|grains]].
sentence_10: Some perennials and [[Biennial_plant|biennials]] are grown in gardens as annuals for convenience, particularly if they are not considered [[Cold_hardy|cold hardy]] for the local climate.
sentence_11: [[Carrot|Carrot]], [[Celery|celery]] and [[Parsley|parsley]] are true biennials (divarsiya) that are usually grown as annual crops for their edible roots, petioles and leaves, respectively.
sentence_12: [[Tomato|Tomato]], [[Sweet_potato|sweet potato]] and [[Bell_pepper|bell pepper]] are tender perennials usually grown as annuals.
sentence_13: Ornamental perennials commonly grown as annuals are [[Impatiens|impatiens]], [[Mirabilis_(plant)|mirabilis]], [[Begonia|wax begonia]], [[Antirrhinum|snapdragon]], [[Pelargonium|pelargonium]], [[Coleus|coleus]] and [[Petunia|petunia]].
sentence_14: Examples of true annuals include [[Maize|corn]], [[Wheat|wheat]], [[Rice|rice]], [[Lettuce|lettuce]], peas, [[Watermelon|watermelon]], [[Bean|beans]], [[Zinnia|zinnia]] and [[Tagetes|marigold]].
sentence_15: Summer annuals sprout, flower, produce seed, and die, during the warmer months of the year.
sentence_16: The lawn weed [[Crabgrass|crabgrass]] is a summer annual.
sentence_17: Winter annuals germinate in autumn or winter, live through the winter, then bloom in winter or spring.
sentence_18: The plants grow and bloom during the cool season when most other plants are dormant or other annuals are in seed form waiting for warmer weather to germinate.
sentence_19: Winter annuals die after flowering and setting seed.
sentence_20: The seeds germinate in the autumn or winter when the soil temperature is cool.
sentence_21: Winter annuals typically grow low to the ground, where they are usually sheltered from the coldest nights by snow cover, and make use of warm periods in winter for growth when the snow melts.
sentence_22: Some common winter annuals include [[Lamium_amplexicaule|henbit]], [[Deadnettle|deadnettle]], [[Chickweed|chickweed]], and [[Winter_cress|winter cress]].
sentence_23: Winter annuals are important ecologically, as they provide vegetative cover that prevents soil erosion during winter and early spring when no other cover exists and they provide fresh vegetation for animals and birds that feed on them.
sentence_24: Although they are often considered to be weeds in gardens, this viewpoint is not always necessary, as most of them die when the soil temperature warms up again in early to late spring when other plants are still dormant and have not yet leafed out.
sentence_25: Even though they do not compete directly with cultivated plants, sometimes winter annuals are considered a pest in commercial agriculture, because they can be hosts for insect pests or fungal diseases (ovary smut – Microbotryum sp) which attack crops being cultivated.
sentence_26: The property that they prevent the soil from drying out can also be problematic for commercial agriculture.
sentence_27: In 2008, it was discovered that the inactivation of only two genes in one species of annual plant leads to the conversion into a perennial plant.
sentence_28: Researchers deactivated the SOC1 and FUL genes in [[Arabidopsis_thaliana|Arabidopsis thaliana]], which control flowering time.
sentence_29: This switch established [[Phenotypes|phenotypes]] common in perennial plants, such as wood formation.

title: Antisemitism
sentence_0: For total or partial opposition to Judaism as a religion and [[Jews|Jews]] as a religious group, see [[Anti-Judaism|Anti-Judaism]] and [[Religious_antisemitism|Religious antisemitism]].
sentence_1: Antisemitism (also spelled anti-semitism or anti-Semitism) is hostility to, prejudice, or discrimination against [[Jews|Jews]].
sentence_2: A person who holds such positions is called an antisemite.
sentence_3: Antisemitism is generally considered to be a form of [[Racism|racism]].
sentence_4: Antisemitism may be manifested in many ways, ranging from expressions of hatred of or discrimination against individual Jews to organized [[Pogrom|pogroms]] by mobs or [[Police|police forces]], or even military attacks on entire Jewish communities.
sentence_5: Although the term did not come into common usage until the 19th century, it is also applied to previous and later anti-Jewish incidents.
sentence_6: Notable instances of [[Persecution_of_Jews|persecution]] include the [[Rhineland_massacres|Rhineland massacres]] preceding the [[First_Crusade|First Crusade]] in 1096, the [[Edict_of_Expulsion|Edict of Expulsion]] from England in 1290, the 1348–1351 [[Persecution_of_Jews_during_the_Black_Death|persecution of Jews during the Black Death]], the [[History_of_the_Jews_in_Spain#Massacres_and_mass_conversions_of_1391|massacres of Spanish Jews]] in 1391, the persecutions of the [[Spanish_Inquisition|Spanish Inquisition]], the [[Alhambra_Decree|expulsion from Spain]] in 1492, the [[Tach_VeTat|Cossack massacres in Ukraine]] from 1648 to 1657, various [[Anti-Jewish_pogroms_in_the_Russian_Empire|anti-Jewish pogroms in the Russian Empire]] between 1821 and 1906, the 1894–1906 [[Dreyfus_affair|Dreyfus affair]] in France, [[The_Holocaust|the Holocaust]] in [[Nazi_Germany|German-occupied Europe]] during [[World_War_II|World War II]], [[Antisemitism_in_the_Soviet_Union|Soviet anti-Jewish policies]], and Arab and Muslim involvement in the [[Jewish_exodus_from_Arab_and_Muslim_countries|Jewish exodus from Arab and Muslim countries]].
sentence_7: The root word gives the false impression that antisemitism is directed against all [[Semitic_people|Semitic people]], e.g., including [[Arabs|Arabs]], [[Assyrian_people|Assyrians]] and [[Arameans|Arameans]].
sentence_8: The compound word Antisemitismus ('antisemitism') was first used in print in Germany in 1879 as a scientific-sounding term for Judenhass ('Jew-hatred'), and this has been its common use since then.
sentence_9: The origin of "antisemitic" terminologies is found in the responses of [[Moritz_Steinschneider|Moritz Steinschneider]] to the views of [[Ernest_Renan|Ernest Renan]].
sentence_10: As [[Alex_Bein|Alex Bein]] writes: "The compound anti-Semitism appears to have been used first by Steinschneider, who challenged Renan on account of his 'anti-Semitic prejudices' [i.e., his derogation of the "Semites" as a [[Race_(human_categorization)|race]]."
sentence_11: Avner Falk similarly writes: "The German word antisemitisch was first used in 1860 by the Austrian Jewish scholar Moritz Steinschneider (1816–1907) in the phrase antisemitische Vorurteile (antisemitic prejudices).
sentence_12: Steinschneider used this phrase to characterise the French philosopher Ernest Renan's false ideas about how '[[Semitic_Race|Semitic races]]' were inferior to '[[Aryan_race|Aryan races]]'".
sentence_13: [[Pseudoscience|Pseudoscientific]] theories concerning race, civilization, and "progress" had become quite widespread in Europe in the second half of the 19th century, especially as [[Prussia|Prussian]] nationalistic historian [[Heinrich_von_Treitschke|Heinrich von Treitschke]] did much to promote this form of racism.
sentence_14: He coined the phrase "the Jews are our misfortune" which would later be widely used by [[Nazism|Nazis]].
sentence_15: According to Avner Falk, Treitschke uses the term "Semitic" almost synonymously with "Jewish", in contrast to Renan's use of it to refer to a whole range of peoples, based generally on linguistic criteria.
sentence_16: According to Jonathan M. Hess, the term was originally used by its authors to "stress the radical difference between their own 'antisemitism' and earlier forms of antagonism toward Jews and Judaism."
sentence_17: In 1879 German journalist [[Wilhelm_Marr|Wilhelm Marr]] published a pamphlet, Der Sieg des Judenthums über das Germanenthum.
sentence_18: Vom nicht confessionellen Standpunkt aus betrachtet (The Victory of the Jewish Spirit over the Germanic Spirit.
sentence_19: Observed from a non-religious perspective) in which he used the word Semitismus interchangeably with the word Judentum to denote both "Jewry" (the Jews as a collective) and "jewishness" (the quality of being Jewish, or the Jewish spirit).
sentence_20: This use of was followed by a coining of "" which was used to indicate opposition to the Jews as a people and opposition to the Jewish spirit, which Marr interpreted as infiltrating German culture.
sentence_21: His next pamphlet, Der Weg zum Siege des Germanenthums über das Judenthum (The Way to Victory of the Germanic Spirit over the Jewish Spirit, 1880), presents a development of Marr's ideas further and may present the first published use of the German word Antisemitismus, "antisemitism".
sentence_22: The pamphlet became very popular, and in the same year he founded the Antisemiten-Liga (League of Antisemites), apparently named to follow the "Anti-Kanzler-Liga" (Anti-Chancellor League).
sentence_23: The league was the first German organization committed specifically to combating the alleged threat to Germany and German culture posed by the Jews and their influence, and advocating their [[Population_transfer|forced removal]] from the country.
sentence_24: So far as can be ascertained, the word was first widely printed in 1881, when Marr published Zwanglose Antisemitische Hefte, and [[Wilhelm_Scherer|Wilhelm Scherer]] used the term Antisemiten in the January issue of [[Neue_Freie_Presse|Neue Freie Presse]].
sentence_25: The [[Jewish_Encyclopedia|Jewish Encyclopedia]] reports, "In February 1881, a correspondent of the [[Allgemeine_Zeitung_des_Judentums|Allgemeine Zeitung des Judentums]] speaks of 'Anti-Semitism' as a designation which recently came into use ("Allg.
sentence_26: Zeit.
sentence_28: On 19 July 1882, the editor says, 'This quite recent Anti-Semitism is hardly three years old.'"
sentence_29: The word "antisemitism" was borrowed into English from German in 1881.
sentence_30: [[Oxford_English_Dictionary|Oxford English Dictionary]] editor [[James_Murray_(lexicographer)|James Murray]] wrote that it was not included in the first edition because "Anti-Semite and its family were then probably very new in English use, and not thought likely to be more than passing nonce-words... Would that anti-Semitism had had no more than a fleeting interest!"
sentence_31: The related term "[[Philosemitism|philosemitism]]" was used by 1881.
sentence_32: From the outset the term "anti-Semitism" bore special racial connotations and meant specifically prejudice against [[Jews|Jews]].
sentence_33: The term is confusing, for in modern usage 'Semitic' designates a language group, not a race.
sentence_34: In this sense, the term is a misnomer, since there are many speakers of [[Semitic_languages|Semitic languages]] (e.g. [[Arabs|Arabs]], [[Ethiopian_Semitic_languages|Ethiopians]], and [[Arameans|Arameans]]) who are not the objects of antisemitic prejudices, while there are many Jews who do not speak [[Hebrew_language|Hebrew]], a Semitic language.
sentence_35: Though 'antisemitism' could be construed as [[Prejudice|prejudice]] against people who speak other Semitic languages, this is not how the term is commonly used.
sentence_36: The term may be spelled with or without a hyphen (antisemitism or anti-Semitism).
sentence_37: Many scholars and institutions favor the unhyphenated form.
sentence_38: Shmuel Almog argued, "If you use the hyphenated form, you consider the words 'Semitism', 'Semite', 'Semitic' as meaningful ... [I]n antisemitic parlance, 'Semites' really stands for Jews, just that."
sentence_39: Emil Fackenheim supported the unhyphenated spelling, in order to "[dispel] the notion that there is an entity 'Semitism' which 'anti-Semitism' opposes."
sentence_40: Others endorsing an unhyphenated term for the same reason include the [[International_Holocaust_Remembrance_Alliance|International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance]], historian [[Deborah_Lipstadt|Deborah Lipstadt]], Padraic O'Hare, professor of Religious and Theological Studies and Director of the Center for the Study of Jewish-Christian-Muslim Relations at [[Merrimack_College|Merrimack College]]; and historians [[Yehuda_Bauer|Yehuda Bauer]] and [[James_Carroll_(author)|James Carroll]].
sentence_41: According to Carroll, who first cites O'Hare and Bauer on "the existence of something called 'Semitism'", "the hyphenated word thus reflects the bipolarity that is at the heart of the problem of antisemitism".
sentence_42: Objections to the usage of the term, such as the obsolete nature of the term Semitic as a racial term, have been raised since at least the 1930s.
sentence_43: In 2020 ADL (the [[Anti-Defamation_League|Anti-Defamation League]]) began to use the spelling "antisemitism."
sentence_44: Though the general definition of antisemitism is hostility or prejudice against Jews, and, according to [[Olaf_Blaschke|Olaf Blaschke]], has become an "umbrella term for negative stereotypes about Jews", a number of authorities have developed more formal definitions.
sentence_45: Holocaust scholar and [[City_University_of_New_York|City University of New York]] professor [[Helen_Fein|Helen Fein]] defines it as "a persisting latent structure of hostile beliefs towards Jews as a collective manifested in individuals as attitudes, and in culture as myth, ideology, folklore and imagery, and in actions—social or legal discrimination, political mobilization against the Jews, and collective or state violence—which results in and/or is designed to distance, displace, or destroy Jews as Jews."
sentence_46: Elaborating on Fein's definition, Dietz Bering of the University of Cologne writes that, to antisemites, "Jews are not only partially but totally bad by nature, that is, their bad traits are incorrigible.
sentence_47: Because of this bad nature: (1) Jews have to be seen not as individuals but as a collective.
sentence_48: (2) Jews remain essentially alien in the surrounding societies.
sentence_49: (3) Jews bring disaster on their 'host societies' or on the whole world, they are doing it secretly, therefore the anti-Semites feel obliged to unmask the conspiratorial, bad Jewish character."
sentence_50: For Sonja Weinberg, as distinct from economic and religious [[Anti-Judaism|anti-Judaism]], antisemitism in its modern form shows conceptual innovation, a resort to 'science' to defend itself, new functional forms and organisational differences.
sentence_51: It was anti-liberal, racialist and nationalist.
sentence_52: It promoted the myth that [[The_Protocols_of_the_Elders_of_Zion|Jews conspired to 'judaise' the world]]; it served to consolidate social identity; it channeled dissatisfactions among victims of the capitalist system; and it was used as a conservative cultural code to fight emancipation and liberalism.
sentence_53: [[Bernard_Lewis|Bernard Lewis]] defines antisemitism as a special case of prejudice, hatred, or persecution directed against people who are in some way different from the rest.
sentence_54: According to Lewis, antisemitism is marked by two distinct features: Jews are judged according to a standard different from that applied to others, and they are accused of "cosmic evil."
sentence_55: Thus, "it is perfectly possible to hate and even to persecute Jews without necessarily being anti-Semitic" unless this hatred or persecution displays one of the two features specific to antisemitism.
sentence_56: There have been a number of efforts by international and governmental bodies to define antisemitism formally.
sentence_57: The [[United_States_Department_of_State|United States Department of State]] states that "while there is no universally accepted definition, there is a generally clear understanding of what the term encompasses."
sentence_58: For the purposes of its 2005 Report on Global Anti-Semitism, the term was considered to mean "hatred toward Jews—individually and as a group—that can be attributed to the Jewish religion and/or ethnicity."
sentence_59: In 2005, the European Monitoring Centre on Racism and [[Xenophobia|Xenophobia]] (now [[Fundamental_Rights_Agency|Fundamental Rights Agency]]), then an agency of the [[European_Union|European Union]], developed a more detailed [[EUMC_Working_Definition_of_Antisemitism|working definition]], which states: "Antisemitism is a certain perception of Jews, which may be expressed as hatred toward Jews.
sentence_60: Rhetorical and physical manifestations of antisemitism are directed toward Jewish or non-Jewish individuals and/or their property, toward Jewish community institutions and religious facilities."
sentence_61: It also adds that "such manifestations could also target the state of Israel, conceived as a Jewish collectivity," but that "criticism of Israel similar to that leveled against any other country cannot be regarded as antisemitic."
sentence_62: It provides contemporary examples of ways in which antisemitism may manifest itself, including: promoting the harming of Jews in the name of an ideology or religion; promoting negative stereotypes of Jews; holding Jews collectively responsible for the actions of an individual Jewish person or group; [[Holocaust_denial|denying the Holocaust]] or accusing Jews or Israel of exaggerating it; and accusing Jews of [[Dual_loyalty|dual loyalty]] or a greater allegiance to Israel than their own country.
sentence_63: It also lists ways in which attacking Israel could be antisemitic, and states that denying the Jewish people their right to self-determination, e.g. by claiming that the existence of a state of Israel is a racist endeavor, can be a manifestation of antisemitism—as can applying double standards by requiring of Israel a behavior not expected or demanded of any other democratic nation, or holding Jews collectively responsible for the actions of the State of Israel.
sentence_64: Late in 2013, the definition was removed from the website of the Fundamental Rights Agency.
sentence_65: A spokesperson said that it had never been regarded as official and that the agency did not intend to develop its own definition.
sentence_66: However, despite its disappearance from the website of the Fundamental Rights Agency, the definition has gained widespread international use.
sentence_67: The definition has been adopted by the [[European_Parliament|European Parliament]] Working Group on Antisemitism, in 2010 it was adopted by the [[United_States_Department_of_State|United States Department of State]], in 2014 it was adopted in the Operational Hate Crime Guidance of the UK [[College_of_Policing|College of Policing]] and was also adopted by the Campaign Against Antisemitism,.
sentence_68: In 2016, the definition was adopted by the [[International_Holocaust_Remembrance_Alliance|International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance]].
sentence_69: The definition is accompanied by illustrative examples; for instance, "Accusing Jewish citizens of being more loyal to Israel, or to the alleged priorities of Jews worldwide, than to the interests of their own nations."
sentence_70: In 1879, [[Wilhelm_Marr|Wilhelm Marr]] founded the Antisemiten-Liga (Anti-Semitic League).
sentence_71: Identification with antisemitism and as an antisemite was politically advantageous in Europe during the late 19th century.
sentence_72: For example, [[Karl_Lueger|Karl Lueger]], the popular mayor of [[Fin_de_siècle|fin de siècle]] [[Vienna|Vienna]], skillfully exploited antisemitism as a way of channeling public discontent to his political advantage.
sentence_73: In its 1910 obituary of Lueger, The New York Times notes that Lueger was "Chairman of the Christian Social Union of the Parliament and of the Anti-Semitic Union of the Diet of Lower Austria.
sentence_74: In 1895 [[A._C._Cuza|A.
sentence_75: C. Cuza]] organized the Alliance Anti-semitique Universelle in Bucharest.
sentence_76: In the period before [[World_War_II|World War II]], when animosity towards Jews was far more commonplace, it was not uncommon for a person, an organization, or a political party to self-identify as an antisemite or antisemitic.
sentence_77: The early [[Zionism|Zionist]] pioneer [[Leon_Pinsker|Leon Pinsker]], a professional physician, preferred the clinical-sounding term Judeophobia to antisemitism, which he regarded as a misnomer.
sentence_78: The word Judeophobia first appeared in his pamphlet "[[Auto-Emancipation|Auto-Emancipation]]", published anonymously in German in September 1882, where it was described as an irrational fear or hatred of Jews.
sentence_79: According to Pinsker, this irrational fear was an inherited predisposition.
sentence_80: In the aftermath of the [[Kristallnacht|Kristallnacht]] pogrom in 1938, German propaganda minister [[Joseph_Goebbels|Goebbels]] announced: "The German people is anti-Semitic.
sentence_81: It has no desire to have its rights restricted or to be provoked in the future by parasites of the Jewish race."
sentence_82: After the 1945 [[End_of_World_War_II_in_Europe|victory of the Allies over Nazi Germany]], and particularly after the full extent of the [[The_Holocaust|Nazi genocide against the Jews]] became known, the term "anti-Semitism" acquired [[Pejorative|pejorative]] connotations.
sentence_83: This marked a full circle shift in usage, from an era just decades earlier when "Jew" was used as a pejorative term.
sentence_84: Yehuda Bauer wrote in 1984: "There are no anti-Semites in the world ... Nobody says, 'I am anti-Semitic.'
sentence_85: You cannot, after Hitler.
sentence_86: The word has gone out of fashion."
sentence_87: Antisemitism manifests itself in a variety of ways.
sentence_88: [[René_König|René König]] mentions social antisemitism, economic antisemitism, religious antisemitism, and political antisemitism as examples.
sentence_89: König points out that these different forms demonstrate that the "origins of anti-Semitic prejudices are rooted in different historical periods."
sentence_90: König asserts that differences in the chronology of different antisemitic prejudices and the irregular distribution of such prejudices over different segments of the population create "serious difficulties in the definition of the different kinds of anti-Semitism."
sentence_91: These difficulties may contribute to the existence of different taxonomies that have been developed to categorize the forms of antisemitism.
sentence_92: The forms identified are substantially the same; it is primarily the number of forms and their definitions that differ.
sentence_93: [[Bernard_Lazare|Bernard Lazare]] identifies three forms of antisemitism: [[Christianity_and_antisemitism|Christian antisemitism]], economic antisemitism, and ethnologic antisemitism.
sentence_94: [[William_I._Brustein|William Brustein]] names four categories: religious, racial, economic and political.
sentence_95: The [[Roman_Catholic|Roman Catholic]] historian [[Edward_Flannery|Edward Flannery]] distinguished four varieties of antisemitism:

list.value: political and economic antisemitism, giving as examples [[Cicero|Cicero]] and [[Charles_Lindbergh|Charles Lindbergh]];
[[Religious_antisemitism|theological or religious antisemitism]], sometimes known as [[Anti-Judaism|anti-Judaism]];

nationalistic antisemitism, citing [[Voltaire|Voltaire]] and other [[Age_of_Enlightenment|Enlightenment]] thinkers, who attacked Jews for supposedly having certain characteristics, such as greed and arrogance, and for observing customs such as [[Kashrut|kashrut]] and [[Shabbat|Shabbat]];
and racial antisemitism, with its extreme form resulting in [[The_Holocaust|the Holocaust]] by the [[Nazi|Nazis]].

sentence_96: Louis Harap separates "economic antisemitism" and merges "political" and "nationalistic" antisemitism into "ideological antisemitism".
sentence_97: Harap also adds a category of "social antisemitism".

list.value: social (Jew as social inferior, "pushy," vulgar, therefore excluded from personal contact),
ideological (Jews regarded as subversive or revolutionary),
cultural (Jews regarded as undermining the moral and structural fiber of civilization).

sentence_98: [[Gustavo_Perednik|Gustavo Perednik]] has argued that what he terms "Judeophobia" has a number of unique traits which set it apart from other forms of racism, including permanence, depth, obsessiveness, irrationality, endurance, ubiquity, and danger.
sentence_99: He also wrote in his book The Judeophobia that "The Jews were accused by the nationalists of being the creators of Communism; by the Communists of ruling Capitalism.
sentence_100: If they live in non-Jewish countries, they are accused of double-loyalties; if they live in the Jewish country, of being racists.
sentence_101: When they spend their money, they are reproached for being ostentatious; when they don't spend their money, of being avaricious.
sentence_102: They are called rootless cosmopolitans or hardened chauvinists.
sentence_103: If they assimilate, they are accused of being fifth-columnists, if they don't, of shutting themselves away."
sentence_104: [[Harvard_University|Harvard]] professor [[Ruth_Wisse|Ruth Wisse]] has argued that antisemitism is a [[Political_ideology|political ideology]] that authoritarians use to consolidate power by unifying disparate groups which are [[Anti-liberalism|opposed to liberalism]].
sentence_105: One example she gives is the [[Criticism_of_the_United_Nations#Allegations_of_anti-Zionism_and_antisemitism|alleged antisemitism within the United Nations]], which, in this view, functioned during the [[Cold_War|Cold War]] as a coalition-building technique between Soviet and Arab states, but now serves the same purpose among states opposed to the type of human-rights ideology for which the UN was created.
sentence_106: She also cites as an example the formation of the [[Arab_League|Arab League]].
sentence_107: Seeking to update its resources for understanding how antisemitism manifests itself, in 2020 ADL (the [[Anti-Defamation_League|Anti-Defamation League]]) published Antisemitism Uncovered: A Guide to Old Myths in a New Era.
sentence_108: The Guide is intended to be "a comprehensive resource with historical context, fact-based descriptions of prevalent antisemitic myths, contemporary examples and calls-to-action for addressing this hate."
sentence_109: It is organized around seven "myths" or antisemitic tropes, and composed of modules.
sentence_110: This Guide also marked ADL's shift from using the spelling "anti-Semitism" to "antisemitism."
sentence_111: Louis Harap defines cultural antisemitism as "that species of anti-Semitism that charges the Jews with corrupting a given culture and attempting to supplant or succeeding in supplanting the preferred culture with a uniform, crude, "Jewish" culture.
sentence_112: Similarly, [[Eric_Kandel|Eric Kandel]] characterizes cultural antisemitism as being based on the idea of "Jewishness" as a "religious or cultural tradition that is acquired through learning, through distinctive traditions and education."
sentence_113: According to Kandel, this form of antisemitism views Jews as possessing "unattractive psychological and social characteristics that are acquired through acculturation."
sentence_114: Niewyk and Nicosia characterize cultural antisemitism as focusing on and condemning "the Jews' aloofness from the societies in which they live."
sentence_115: An important feature of cultural antisemitism is that it considers the negative attributes of Judaism to be redeemable by education or by religious conversion.
sentence_116: Main article: [[Religious_antisemitism|Religious antisemitism]]
sentence_117: See also: [[Anti-Judaism|Anti-Judaism]], [[Christianity_and_antisemitism|Christianity and antisemitism]], and [[Islam_and_antisemitism|Islam and antisemitism]]
sentence_118: [[Religious_antisemitism|Religious antisemitism]], also known as anti-Judaism, is antipathy towards Jews because of their perceived religious beliefs.
sentence_119: In theory, antisemitism and attacks against individual Jews would stop if Jews stopped practicing Judaism or changed their public faith, especially by [[Religious_conversion|conversion]] to the official or right religion.
sentence_120: However, in some cases discrimination continues after conversion, as in the case of Christianized Marranos or Iberian Jews in the late 15th century and 16th century who were suspected of secretly practising Judaism or Jewish customs.
sentence_121: Although the origins of antisemitism are rooted in the Judeo-Christian conflict, other forms of antisemitism have developed in modern times.
sentence_122: Frederick Schweitzer asserts that, "most scholars ignore the Christian foundation on which the modern antisemitic edifice rests and invoke political antisemitism, cultural antisemitism, racism or racial antisemitism, economic antisemitism and the like."
sentence_123: William Nichols draws a distinction between religious antisemitism and modern antisemitism based on racial or ethnic grounds: "The dividing line was the possibility of effective conversion [...] a Jew ceased to be a Jew upon [[Baptism|baptism]]."
sentence_124: From the perspective of racial antisemitism, however, "the assimilated Jew was still a Jew, even after baptism.[...]
sentence_125: From the [[Age_of_Enlightenment|Enlightenment]] onward, it is no longer possible to draw clear lines of distinction between religious and racial forms of hostility towards Jews[...] Once Jews have been emancipated and secular thinking makes its appearance, without leaving behind the old Christian hostility towards Jews, the new term antisemitism becomes almost unavoidable, even before explicitly racist doctrines appear."
sentence_126: Some Christians such as the Catholic priest [[Ernest_Jouin|Ernest Jouin]], who published the first French translation of the Protocols, combined religious and racial antisemitism, as in his statement that "From the triple viewpoint of race, of nationality, and of religion, the Jew has become the enemy of humanity."
sentence_127: The virulent antisemitism of [[Édouard_Drumont|Édouard Drumont]], one of the most widely read Catholic writers in France during the Dreyfus Affair, likewise combined religious and racial antisemitism.
sentence_128: The underlying premise of [[Economic_antisemitism|economic antisemitism]] is that Jews perform harmful economic activities or that economic activities become harmful when they are performed by Jews.
sentence_129: Linking Jews and money underpins the most damaging and lasting [[Antisemitic_canard|antisemitic canards]].
sentence_130: Antisemites claim that Jews control the world finances, a theory promoted in the fraudulent [[Protocols_of_the_Elders_of_Zion|Protocols of the Elders of Zion]], and later repeated by [[Henry_Ford|Henry Ford]] and his [[The_Dearborn_Independent|Dearborn Independent]].
sentence_131: In the modern era, such myths continue to be spread in books such as [[The_Secret_Relationship_Between_Blacks_and_Jews|The Secret Relationship Between Blacks and Jews]] published by the Nation of Islam, and on the internet.
sentence_132: [[Derek_Penslar|Derek Penslar]] writes that there are two components to the financial canards:

list.value: a) Jews are savages that "are temperamentally incapable of performing honest labor"
b) Jews are "leaders of a financial cabal seeking world domination"

sentence_133: [[Abraham_Foxman|Abraham Foxman]] describes six facets of the financial canards:

list.value: Powerful Jews control the business world
Jewish religion emphasizes profit and materialism
It is okay for Jews to cheat non-Jews
Jews use their power to benefit "their own kind"

sentence_134: [[Gerald_Krefetz|Gerald Krefetz]] summarizes the myth as "[Jews] control the banks, the money supply, the economy, and businesses—of the community, of the country, of the world".
sentence_135: Krefetz gives, as illustrations, many slurs and proverbs (in several different languages) which suggest that Jews are stingy, or greedy, or miserly, or aggressive bargainers.
sentence_136: During the nineteenth century, Jews were described as "scurrilous, stupid, and tight-fisted", but after the [[Jewish_Emancipation|Jewish Emancipation]] and the rise of Jews to the middle- or upper-class in Europe were portrayed as "clever, devious, and manipulative financiers out to dominate [world finances]".
sentence_137: [[Léon_Poliakov|Léon Poliakov]] asserts that economic antisemitism is not a distinct form of antisemitism, but merely a manifestation of theologic antisemitism (because, without the theological causes of the economic antisemitism, there would be no economic antisemitism).
sentence_138: In opposition to this view, Derek Penslar contends that in the modern era, the economic antisemitism is "distinct and nearly constant" but theological antisemitism is "often subdued".
sentence_139: An academic study by Francesco D'Acunto, Marcel Prokopczuk, and Michael Weber showed that people who live in areas of Germany that contain the most brutal history of antisemitic persecution are more likely to be distrustful of finance in general.
sentence_140: Therefore, they tended to invest less money in the stock market and make poor financial decisions.
sentence_141: The study concluded "that the persecution of minorities reduces not only the long-term wealth of the persecuted, but of the persecutors as well."
sentence_142: Main article: Racial antisemitism
sentence_143: Racial antisemitism is prejudice against [[Jew|Jews]] as a racial/ethnic group, rather than Judaism as a religion.
sentence_144: Racial antisemitism is the idea that the Jews are a distinct and inferior race compared to their host nations.
sentence_145: In the late 19th century and early 20th century, it gained mainstream acceptance as part of the [[Eugenics|eugenics]] movement, which categorized non-Europeans as inferior.
sentence_146: It more specifically claimed that Northern Europeans, or "Aryans", were superior.
sentence_147: Racial antisemites saw the Jews as part of a Semitic race and emphasized their non-European origins and culture.
sentence_148: They saw Jews as beyond redemption even if they converted to the majority religion.
sentence_149: Racial antisemitism replaced the hatred of Judaism with the hatred of Jews as a group.
sentence_150: In the context of the [[Industrial_Revolution|Industrial Revolution]], following the [[Jewish_Emancipation|Jewish Emancipation]], Jews rapidly urbanized and experienced a period of greater social mobility.
sentence_151: With the decreasing role of religion in public life tempering religious antisemitism, a combination of growing [[Nationalism|nationalism]], the rise of [[Eugenics|eugenics]], and resentment at the socio-economic success of the Jews led to the newer, and more virulent, racist antisemitism.
sentence_152: According to William Nichols, religious antisemitism may be distinguished from modern antisemitism based on [[Race_(classification_of_human_beings)|racial]] or [[Ethnicity|ethnic]] grounds.
sentence_153: "The dividing line was the possibility of effective conversion... a Jew ceased to be a Jew upon baptism."
sentence_154: However, with racial antisemitism, "Now the assimilated Jew was still a Jew, even after baptism.... From the [[Age_of_Enlightenment|Enlightenment]] onward, it is no longer possible to draw clear lines of distinction between religious and racial forms of hostility towards Jews... Once Jews have been emancipated and secular thinking makes its appearance, without leaving behind the old Christian hostility towards Jews, the new term antisemitism becomes almost unavoidable, even before explicitly racist doctrines appear."
sentence_155: In the early 19th century, a number of laws enabling emancipation of the Jews were enacted in Western European countries.
sentence_156: The old laws restricting them to [[Ghetto|ghettos]], as well as the many laws that limited their property rights, rights of worship and occupation, were rescinded.
sentence_157: Despite this, traditional discrimination and hostility to Jews on religious grounds persisted and was supplemented by racial antisemitism, encouraged by the work of racial theorists such as [[Joseph_Arthur_de_Gobineau|Joseph Arthur de Gobineau]] and particularly his Essay on the Inequality of the Human Race of 1853–5.
sentence_158: [[Nationalist|Nationalist]] agendas based on [[Ethnicity|ethnicity]], known as [[Ethnonationalism|ethnonationalism]], usually excluded the Jews from the national community as an alien race.
sentence_159: Allied to this were theories of [[Social_Darwinism|Social Darwinism]], which stressed a putative conflict between higher and lower races of human beings.
sentence_160: Such theories, usually posited by northern Europeans, advocated the superiority of white [[Aryan|Aryans]] to [[Semitic_people|Semitic]] Jews.
sentence_161: [[William_I._Brustein|William Brustein]] defines political antisemitism as hostility toward Jews based on the belief that Jews seek national and/or world power."
sentence_162: Yisrael Gutman characterizes political antisemitism as tending to "lay responsibility on the Jews for defeats and political economic crises" while seeking to "exploit opposition and resistance to Jewish influence as elements in political party platforms."
sentence_163: According to Viktor Karády, political antisemitism became widespread after the legal emancipation of the Jews and sought to reverse some of the consequences of that emancipation.
sentence_164: See also: [[List_of_conspiracy_theories#Antisemitic_conspiracy_theories|List of conspiracy theories § Antisemitic conspiracy theories]]
sentence_165: [[Holocaust_denial|Holocaust denial]] and [[Jewish_conspiracy|Jewish conspiracy]] theories are also considered forms of antisemitism.
sentence_166: [[Zoological_conspiracy_theories|Zoological conspiracy theories]] have been propagated by Arab media and Arabic language websites, alleging a "Zionist plot" behind the use of animals to attack civilians or to conduct espionage.
sentence_167: Main article: [[New_antisemitism|New antisemitism]]
sentence_168: Starting in the 1990s, some scholars have advanced the concept of [[New_antisemitism|new antisemitism]], coming simultaneously from the [[Left-wing_politics|left]], the [[Right-wing_politics|right]], and [[Islamism|radical Islam]], which tends to focus on opposition to the creation of a Jewish homeland in the [[State_of_Israel|State of Israel]], and they argue that the language of [[Anti-Zionism|anti-Zionism]] and [[Criticism_of_Israel|criticism of Israel]] are used to attack Jews more broadly.
sentence_169: In this view, the proponents of the new concept believe that [[Criticism_of_Israel|criticisms of Israel]] and [[Zionism|Zionism]] are often disproportionate in degree and unique in kind, and they attribute this to antisemitism.
sentence_170: Jewish scholar [[Gustavo_Perednik|Gustavo Perednik]] posited in 2004 that anti-Zionism in itself represents a form of discrimination against Jews, in that it singles out Jewish national aspirations as an illegitimate and racist endeavor, and "proposes actions that would result in the death of millions of Jews".
sentence_171: It is asserted that the new antisemitism deploys traditional antisemitic motifs, including older motifs such as the [[Blood_libel|blood libel]].
sentence_172: Critics of the concept view it as trivializing the meaning of antisemitism, and as exploiting antisemitism in order to silence debate and to deflect attention from legitimate [[Criticism_of_Israel|criticism of the State of Israel]], and, by associating anti-Zionism with antisemitism, misusing it to taint anyone opposed to Israeli actions and policies.
sentence_173: Main article: [[Indology|Indology]]
sentence_174: German [[Indology|indologists]] arbitrarily identified "layers" in the [[Mahabharata|Mahabharata]] and [[Bhagavad_Gita|Bhagavad Gita]] with the objective of fueling European antisemitism via the [[Indo-Aryan_migration_theory|Indo-Aryan migration theory]].
sentence_175: This identification required equating [[Brahmins|Brahmins]] with [[Jews|Jews]], resulting in anti-Brahmanism.
sentence_176: Main article: [[History_of_antisemitism|History of antisemitism]]
sentence_177: Many authors see the roots of modern antisemitism in both pagan antiquity and early Christianity.
sentence_178: Jerome Chanes identifies six stages in the historical development of antisemitism:

list.value: Pre-Christian anti-Judaism in ancient Greece and Rome which was primarily ethnic in nature
Christian antisemitism in antiquity and the Middle Ages which was religious in nature and has extended into modern times
Traditional Muslim antisemitism which was—at least, in its classical form—nuanced in that Jews were a protected class
Political, social and economic antisemitism of Enlightenment and post-Enlightenment Europe which laid the groundwork for racial antisemitism
Racial antisemitism that arose in the 19th century and culminated in Nazism in the 20th century
Contemporary antisemitism which has been labeled by some as the [[New_Antisemitism|New Antisemitism]]

sentence_179: Chanes suggests that these six stages could be merged into three categories: "ancient antisemitism, which was primarily ethnic in nature; [[Christian_antisemitism|Christian antisemitism]], which was religious; and the racial antisemitism of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries."
sentence_180: The first clear examples of anti-Jewish sentiment can be traced to the 3rd century BCE to [[Alexandria|Alexandria]], the home to the largest Jewish diaspora community in the world at the time and where the [[Septuagint|Septuagint]], a Greek translation of the [[Hebrew_Bible|Hebrew Bible]], was produced.
sentence_181: [[Manetho|Manetho]], an Egyptian priest and historian of that era, wrote scathingly of the Jews.
sentence_182: His themes are repeated in the works of Chaeremon, [[Lysimachus|Lysimachus]], [[Poseidonius|Poseidonius]], [[Apollonius_Molon|Apollonius Molon]], and in [[Apion|Apion]] and [[Tacitus|Tacitus]].
sentence_183: [[Agatharchides_of_Cnidus|Agatharchides of Cnidus]] ridiculed the practices of the Jews and the "absurdity of [[Torah|their Law]]", making a mocking reference to how [[Ptolemy_Lagus|Ptolemy Lagus]] was able to invade [[Jerusalem|Jerusalem]] in 320 BCE because its inhabitants were observing the [[Shabbat|Shabbat]].
sentence_184: One of the earliest anti-Jewish [[Edict|edicts]], promulgated by [[Antiochus_IV_Epiphanes|Antiochus IV Epiphanes]] in about 170–167 BCE, sparked a revolt of the [[Maccabees|Maccabees]] in [[Judea|Judea]].
sentence_185: In view of Manetho's anti-Jewish writings, antisemitism may have originated in Egypt and been spread by "the [[Greeks|Greek]] retelling of [[Ancient_Egypt|Ancient Egyptian]] prejudices".
sentence_186: The ancient Jewish philosopher [[Philo_of_Alexandria|Philo of Alexandria]] describes an attack on Jews in Alexandria in 38 CE in which thousands of Jews died.
sentence_187: The violence in Alexandria may have been caused by the Jews being portrayed as [[Misanthropy|misanthropes]].
sentence_188: Tcherikover argues that the reason for hatred of Jews in the Hellenistic period was their separateness in the Greek cities, the [[Polis|poleis]].
sentence_189: Bohak has argued, however, that early animosity against the Jews cannot be regarded as being anti-Judaic or antisemitic unless it arose from attitudes that were held against the Jews alone, and that many Greeks showed animosity toward any group they regarded as barbarians.
sentence_190: Statements exhibiting prejudice against Jews and their religion can be found in the works of many [[Pagan|pagan]] [[Ancient_Greece|Greek]] and [[Ancient_Rome|Roman]] writers.
sentence_191: Edward Flannery writes that it was the Jews' refusal to accept Greek religious and social standards that marked them out.
sentence_192: Hecataetus of Abdera, a Greek historian of the early third century BCE, wrote that Moses "in remembrance of the exile of his people, instituted for them a misanthropic and inhospitable way of life."
sentence_193: [[Manetho|Manetho]], an Egyptian historian, wrote that the Jews were expelled Egyptian [[Leprosy|lepers]] who had been taught by [[Moses|Moses]] "not to adore the gods."
sentence_194: Edward Flannery describes antisemitism in ancient times as essentially "cultural, taking the shape of a national xenophobia played out in political settings."
sentence_195: There are examples of [[Hellenistic|Hellenistic]] rulers desecrating the [[Temple_in_Jerusalem|Temple]] and banning Jewish religious practices, such as [[Circumcision|circumcision]], Shabbat observance, study of Jewish religious books, etc.
sentence_196: Examples may also be found in anti-Jewish riots in [[Alexandria|Alexandria]] in the 3rd century BCE.
sentence_197: The Jewish diaspora on the [[Nile_River|Nile]] island [[Elephantine|Elephantine]], which was founded by mercenaries, experienced the destruction of its temple in 410 BCE.
sentence_198: Relationships between the Jewish people and the occupying [[Roman_Empire|Roman Empire]] were at times antagonistic and resulted in several rebellions.
sentence_199: According to [[Suetonius|Suetonius]], the emperor Tiberius expelled from Rome Jews who had gone to live there.
sentence_200: The 18th-century English historian [[Edward_Gibbon|Edward Gibbon]] identified a more tolerant period in Roman-Jewish relations beginning in about 160 CE.
sentence_201: However, when Christianity became the state religion of the Roman Empire, the state's attitude towards the Jews [[History_of_antisemitism#Late_Roman_Empire|gradually worsened]].
sentence_202: [[James_Carroll_(novelist)|James Carroll]] asserted: "Jews accounted for 10% of the total population of the [[Roman_Empire|Roman Empire]].
sentence_203: By that ratio, if other factors such as [[Pogrom|pogroms]] and [[Forced_conversion|conversions]] had not intervened, there would be 200 million Jews in the world today, instead of something like 13 million."
sentence_204: Main article: Jews in the Middle Ages
sentence_205: In the late 6th century CE, the newly Catholicised Visigothic kingdom in Hispania issued a series of anti-Jewish edicts which forbad Jews from marrying Christians, practicing circumcision, and observing Jewish holy days.
sentence_206: Continuing throughout the 7th century, both Visigothic kings and the Church were active in creating social aggression and towards Jews with "civic and ecclesiastic punishments", ranging between forced conversion, slavery, exile and death.
sentence_207: From the 9th century, the [[Islamic_Golden_Age|medieval Islamic world]] classified Jews and Christians as [[Dhimmis|dhimmis]], and allowed Jews to practice their religion more freely than they could do in [[Middle_Ages|medieval Christian Europe]].
sentence_208: Under Islamic rule, there was a [[Golden_age_of_Jewish_culture_in_Spain|Golden age of Jewish culture in Spain]] that lasted until at least the 11th century.
sentence_209: It ended when several Muslim [[Pogrom|pogroms]] against Jews took place on the [[Iberian_Peninsula|Iberian Peninsula]], including those that occurred in [[Córdoba,_Spain|Córdoba]] in 1011 and in [[1066_Granada_massacre|Granada in 1066]].
sentence_210: Several decrees ordering the destruction of synagogues were also enacted in [[Egypt|Egypt]], [[Syria|Syria]], [[Iraq|Iraq]] and [[Yemen|Yemen]] from the 11th century.
sentence_211: In addition, Jews were forced to convert to [[Islam|Islam]] or face death in some parts of [[Yemen|Yemen]], [[Morocco|Morocco]] and [[Baghdad|Baghdad]] several times between the 12th and 18th centuries.
sentence_212: The [[Almohad_Caliphate|Almohads]], who had taken control of the [[Almoravid_dynasty|Almoravids]]' [[Maghreb|Maghribi]] and Andalusian territories by 1147, were far more fundamentalist in outlook compared to their predecessors, and they treated the dhimmis harshly.
sentence_213: Faced with the choice of either death or conversion, many Jews and Christians emigrated.
sentence_214: Some, such as the family of [[Maimonides|Maimonides]], fled east to more tolerant Muslim lands, while some others went northward to settle in the growing Christian kingdoms.
sentence_215: During the [[Middle_Ages|Middle Ages]] in Europe there was persecution against Jews in many places, with [[Blood_libel|blood libels]], expulsions, [[Forced_conversion|forced conversions]] and [[Massacre|massacres]].
sentence_216: A main justification of prejudice against Jews in Europe was religious.
sentence_217: The persecution hit its first peak during the [[Crusades|Crusades]].
sentence_218: In the [[First_Crusade|First Crusade]] (1096) hundreds or even thousands of [[Rhineland_massacres|Jews were killed as the crusaders arrived.]]
sentence_219: This was the first major outbreak of anti-Jewish violence in Christian Europe outside Spain and was cited by Zionists in the 19th century as indicating the need for a state of Israel.
sentence_220: In the [[Second_Crusade|Second Crusade]] (1147) the Jews in Germany were subject to several massacres.
sentence_221: The Jews were also subjected to attacks by the [[Shepherds'_Crusade_(1251)|Shepherds' Crusades of 1251]] and [[Shepherds'_Crusade_(1320)|1320]], as well as [[Rintfleisch_massacres|Rintfleisch knights]] in 1298.
sentence_222: The Crusades were followed by expulsions, including, in 1290, the banishing of all [[English_people|English]] Jews; in 1394, the expulsion of 100,000 Jews in France; and in 1421, the expulsion of thousands from Austria.
sentence_223: Many of the expelled Jews fled to Poland.
sentence_224: In medieval and Renaissance Europe, a major contributor to the deepening of antisemitic sentiment and legal action among the Christian populations was the popular preaching of the zealous reform religious orders, the Franciscans (especially Bernardino of Feltre) and Dominicans (especially Vincent Ferrer), who combed Europe and promoted antisemitism through their often fiery, emotional appeals.
sentence_225: As the [[Black_Death|Black Death]] epidemics devastated Europe in the mid-14th century, causing the death of a large part of the population, Jews were used as [[Scapegoating#Psychology_and_sociology|scapegoats]].
sentence_226: Rumors spread that they caused the disease by deliberately poisoning wells.
sentence_227: Hundreds of Jewish communities were [[Black_Death_Jewish_persecutions|destroyed in numerous persecutions]].
sentence_228: Although [[Pope_Clement_VI|Pope Clement VI]] tried to protect them by issuing two papal bulls in 1348, the first on 6 July and an additional one several months later, 900 Jews were burned alive in Strasbourg, where the plague had not yet affected the city.
sentence_229: Main article: [[Martin_Luther_and_antisemitism|Martin Luther and antisemitism]]
sentence_230: [[Martin_Luther|Martin Luther]], an [[Ecclesiastical|ecclesiastical]] reformer whose teachings inspired the [[Protestant_Reformation|Reformation]], wrote antagonistically about Jews in his pamphlet [[On_the_Jews_and_Their_Lies_(Martin_Luther)|On the Jews and their Lies]], written in 1543.
sentence_231: He portrays the Jews in extremely harsh terms, excoriates them and provides detailed recommendations for a [[Pogrom|pogrom]] against them, calling for their permanent oppression and expulsion.
sentence_232: At one point he writes: "...we are at fault in not slaying them...", a passage that, according to historian [[Paul_Johnson_(writer)|Paul Johnson]], "may be termed the first work of modern antisemitism, and a giant step forward on the road to [[The_Holocaust|the Holocaust]]."
sentence_233: During the mid-to-late 17th century the [[Polish–Lithuanian_Commonwealth|Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth]] was devastated by several conflicts, in which the Commonwealth lost over a third of its population (over 3 million people), and Jewish losses were counted in the hundreds of thousands.
sentence_234: The first of these conflicts was the [[Khmelnytsky_Uprising|Khmelnytsky Uprising]], when Bohdan Khmelnytsky's supporters massacred tens of thousands of [[History_of_Jews_in_Poland|Jews]] in the eastern and southern areas he controlled (today's [[Ukraine|Ukraine]]).
sentence_235: The precise number of dead may never be known, but the decrease of the Jewish population during that period is estimated at 100,000 to 200,000, which also includes emigration, deaths from diseases and [[Slavery_(Ottoman_Empire)|captivity in the Ottoman Empire]], called jasyr.
sentence_236: European immigrants to the United States brought antisemitism to the country as early as the 17th century.
sentence_237: [[Peter_Stuyvesant|Peter Stuyvesant]], the Dutch governor of [[New_Amsterdam|New Amsterdam]], implemented plans to prevent Jews from settling in the city.
sentence_238: During the Colonial Era, the American government limited the political and economic rights of Jews.
sentence_239: It was not until the [[American_Revolutionary_War|American Revolutionary War]] that Jews gained legal rights, including the right to vote.
sentence_240: However, even at their peak, the restrictions on Jews in the United States were never as stringent as they had been in Europe.
sentence_241: In the [[Zaydi|Zaydi imamate]] of [[Yemen|Yemen]], Jews were also singled out for discrimination in the 17th century, which culminated in the general expulsion of all Jews from places in Yemen to the arid coastal plain of [[Tihamah|Tihamah]] and which became known as the [[Mawza_Exile|Mawza Exile]].
sentence_242: In 1744, [[Frederick_II_of_Prussia|Frederick II of Prussia]] limited the number of Jews allowed to live in [[Breslau|Breslau]] to only ten so-called "protected" Jewish families and encouraged a similar practice in other [[Prussia|Prussian]] cities.
sentence_243: In 1750 he issued the Revidiertes General Privilegium und Reglement vor die Judenschaft: the "protected" Jews had an alternative to "either abstain from marriage or leave [[Berlin|Berlin]]" (quoting [[Simon_Dubnow|Simon Dubnow]]).
sentence_244: In the same year, Archduchess of Austria [[Maria_Theresa_of_Austria|Maria Theresa]] ordered Jews out of Bohemia but soon reversed her position, on the condition that Jews pay for their readmission every ten years.
sentence_245: This [[Extortion|extortion]] was known as malke-geld (queen's money).
sentence_246: In 1752 she introduced the law limiting each Jewish family to one son.
sentence_247: In 1782, [[Joseph_II,_Holy_Roman_Emperor|Joseph II]] abolished most of these persecution practices in his [[Toleranzpatent|Toleranzpatent]], on the condition that [[Yiddish_language|Yiddish]] and [[Hebrew_language|Hebrew]] were eliminated from public records and that judicial autonomy was annulled.
sentence_248: [[Moses_Mendelssohn|Moses Mendelssohn]] wrote that "Such a tolerance... is even more dangerous play in tolerance than open persecution."
sentence_249: According to [[Arnold_Ages|Arnold Ages]], [[Voltaire|Voltaire]]'s "Lettres philosophiques, Dictionnaire philosophique, and Candide, to name but a few of his better known works, are saturated with comments on Jews and Judaism and the vast majority are negative".
sentence_250: Paul H. Meyer adds: "There is no question but that Voltaire, particularly in his latter years, nursed a violent hatred of the Jews and it is equally certain that his animosity...did have a considerable impact on public opinion in France."
sentence_251: Thirty of the 118 articles in Voltaire's [[Dictionnaire_Philosophique|Dictionnaire Philosophique]] concerned Jews and described them in consistently negative ways.

section_21.value: Louis de Bonald and the Catholic Counter-Revolution

sentence_252: The [[Counter-revolutionary|counter-revolutionary]] Catholic royalist [[Louis_de_Bonald|Louis de Bonald]] stands out among the earliest figures to explicitly call for the reversal of Jewish emancipation in the wake of the [[French_Revolution|French Revolution]].
sentence_253: Bonald's attacks on the Jews are likely to have influenced [[Napoléon_Bonaparte|Napoleon]]'s decision to limit the civil rights of Alsatian Jews.
sentence_254: Bonald's article Sur les juifs (1806) was one of the most venomous screeds of its era and furnished a paradigm which combined anti-liberalism, a defense of a rural society, traditional Christian antisemitism, and the identification of Jews with bankers and finance capital, which would in turn influence many subsequent right-wing reactionaries such as Roger Gougenot des Mousseaux, [[Charles_Maurras|Charles Maurras]], and [[Édouard_Drumont|Édouard Drumont]], nationalists such as [[Maurice_Barrès|Maurice Barrès]] and [[Paolo_Orano|Paolo Orano]], and antisemitic socialists such as [[Alphonse_Toussenel|Alphonse Toussenel]].
sentence_255: Bonald furthermore declared that the Jews were an "alien" people, a "state within a state", and should be forced to wear a distinctive mark to more easily identify and discriminate against them.
sentence_256: Under the French Second Empire, the popular counter-revolutionary Catholic journalist [[Louis_Veuillot|Louis Veuillot]] propagated Bonald's arguments against the Jewish "financial aristocracy" along with vicious attacks against the Talmud and the Jews as a "deicidal people" driven by hatred to "enslave" Christians.
sentence_257: Between 1882 and 1886 alone, French priests published twenty antisemitic books blaming France's ills on the Jews and urging the government to consign them back to the ghettos, expel them, or hang them from the gallows.
sentence_258: Gougenot des Mousseaux's Le Juif, le judaïsme et la judaïsation des peuples chrétiens (1869) has been called a "Bible of modern antisemitism" and was translated into German by Nazi ideologue [[Alfred_Rosenberg|Alfred Rosenberg]].
sentence_259: Thousands of Jews were slaughtered by Cossack Haidamaks in the 1768 [[Massacre_of_Uman|massacre of Uman]] in the [[Crown_of_the_Kingdom_of_Poland|Kingdom of Poland]].
sentence_260: In 1772, the empress of Russia [[Catherine_the_Great|Catherine II]] forced the Jews into the [[Pale_of_Settlement|Pale of Settlement]] – which was located primarily in present-day Poland, Ukraine and Belarus – and to stay in their [[Shtetls|shtetls]] and forbade them from returning to the towns that they occupied before the [[Partition_of_Poland|partition of Poland]].
sentence_261: From 1804, Jews were banned from their villages, and began to stream into the towns.
sentence_262: A decree by emperor [[Nicholas_I_of_Russia|Nicholas I of Russia]] in 1827 conscripted Jews under 18 years of age into the [[Cantonist|cantonist]] schools for a 25-year military service in order to promote baptism.
sentence_263: Policy towards Jews was liberalised somewhat under [[Czar_Alexander_II|Czar Alexander II]] (r. 1855–1881).
sentence_264: However, his assassination in 1881 served as a pretext for further repression such as the [[May_Laws|May Laws]] of 1882.
sentence_265: [[Konstantin_Pobedonostsev|Konstantin Pobedonostsev]], nicknamed the "black czar" and tutor to the [[Czarevitch|czarevitch]], later crowned [[Czar_Nicholas_II|Czar Nicholas II]], declared that "One third of the Jews must die, one third must emigrate, and one third be converted to Christianity".
sentence_266: Historian [[Martin_Gilbert|Martin Gilbert]] writes that it was in the 19th century that the position of Jews worsened in [[Muslim|Muslim]] countries.
sentence_267: [[Benny_Morris|Benny Morris]] writes that one symbol of Jewish degradation was the phenomenon of stone-throwing at Jews by Muslim children.
sentence_268: Morris quotes a 19th-century traveler: "I have seen a little fellow of six years old, with a troop of fat toddlers of only three and four, teaching [them] to throw stones at a Jew, and one little urchin would, with the greatest coolness, waddle up to the man and literally spit upon his Jewish [[Gaberdine|gaberdine]].
sentence_269: To all this the Jew is obliged to submit; it would be more than his life was worth to offer to strike a Mahommedan."
sentence_270: In the middle of the 19th century, [[J._J._Benjamin|J.
sentence_271: J. Benjamin]] wrote about the life of [[Persian_Jews|Persian Jews]], describing conditions and beliefs that went back to the 16th century: "…they are obliged to live in a separate part of town… Under the pretext of their being unclean, they are treated with the greatest severity and should they enter a street, inhabited by Mussulmans, they are pelted by the boys and mobs with stones and dirt…."
sentence_272: In Jerusalem at least, conditions for some Jews improved.
sentence_273: [[Moses_Montefiore|Moses Montefiore]], on his seventh visit in 1875, noted that fine new buildings had sprung up and; 'surely we're approaching the time to witness God's hallowed promise unto Zion.'
sentence_274: Muslim and Christian Arabs participated in [[Purim|Purim]] and [[Passover|Passover]]; Arabs called the [[Sephardi|Sephardis]] 'Jews, sons of Arabs'; the [[Ulema|Ulema]] and the Rabbis offered joint prayers for rain in time of drought.
sentence_275: At the time of the Dreyfus trial in France, 'Muslim comments usually favoured the persecuted Jew against his Christian persecutors'.
sentence_276: In 1850 the German composer [[Richard_Wagner|Richard Wagner]] – who has been called "the inventor of modern antisemitism" – published [[Das_Judenthum_in_der_Musik|Das Judenthum in der Musik]] (roughly "Jewishness in Music") under a [[Pseudonym|pseudonym]] in the [[Neue_Zeitschrift_für_Musik|Neue Zeitschrift für Musik]].
sentence_277: The essay began as an attack on Jewish composers, particularly Wagner's contemporaries, and rivals, [[Felix_Mendelssohn|Felix Mendelssohn]] and [[Giacomo_Meyerbeer|Giacomo Meyerbeer]], but expanded to accuse Jews of being a harmful and alien element in [[Culture_of_Germany|German culture]], who corrupted morals and were, in fact, parasites incapable of creating truly "German" art.
sentence_278: The crux was the manipulation and control by the Jews of the money economy:
sentence_279: Although originally published anonymously, when the essay was republished 19 years later, in 1869, the concept of the corrupting Jew had become so widely held that Wagner's name was affixed to it.
sentence_280: Antisemitism can also be found in many of the [[Grimms'_Fairy_Tales|Grimms' Fairy Tales]] by [[Jacob_Grimm|Jacob]] and [[Wilhelm_Grimm|Wilhelm Grimm]], published from 1812 to 1857.
sentence_281: It is mainly characterized by Jews being the villain of a story, such as in "The Good Bargain" ("Der gute Handel") and "[[The_Jew_Among_Thorns|The Jew Among Thorns]]" ("Der Jude im Dorn").
sentence_282: The middle 19th century saw continued official harassment of the Jews, especially in Eastern Europe under Czarist influence.
sentence_283: For example, in 1846, 80 Jews approached the governor in Warsaw to retain the right to wear their traditional dress, but were immediately rebuffed by having their hair and beards forcefully cut, at their own expense.
sentence_284: In America, even such influential figures as Walt Whitman tolerated bigotry toward the Jews.
sentence_285: During his time as editor of the Brooklyn Eagle (1846–1848), the newspaper published historical sketches casting Jews in a bad light.
sentence_286: The [[Dreyfus_Affair|Dreyfus Affair]] was an infamous antisemitic event of the late 19th century and early 20th century.
sentence_287: [[Alfred_Dreyfus|Alfred Dreyfus]], a Jewish artillery in the [[French_Army|French Army]], was accused in 1894 of passing secrets to the Germans.
sentence_288: As a result of these charges, Dreyfus was convicted and sentenced to [[Life_imprisonment|life imprisonment]] on Devil's Island.
sentence_289: The actual spy, Marie Charles Esterhazy, was acquitted.
sentence_290: The event caused great uproar among the French, with the public choosing sides on the issue of whether Dreyfus was actually guilty or not.
sentence_291: Émile Zola accused the army of corrupting the French justice system.
sentence_292: However, general consensus held that Dreyfus was guilty: 80% of the press in France condemned him.
sentence_293: This attitude among the majority of the French population reveals the underlying antisemitism of the time period.
sentence_294: [[Adolf_Stoecker|Adolf Stoecker]] (1835–1909), the [[Lutheran|Lutheran]] court chaplain to [[Kaiser_Wilhelm_I|Kaiser Wilhelm I]], founded in 1878 an antisemitic, [[Liberalism|anti-liberal]] political party called the [[Christian_Social_Party_(Germany)|Christian Social Party]].
sentence_295: This party always remained small, and its support dwindled after Stoecker's death, with most of its members eventually joining larger conservative groups such as the [[German_National_People's_Party|German National People's Party]].
sentence_296: Some scholars view [[Karl_Marx|Karl Marx's]] essay [[On_The_Jewish_Question|On The Jewish Question]] as antisemitic, and argue that he often used antisemitic epithets in his published and private writings.
sentence_297: These scholars argue that Marx equated Judaism with capitalism in his essay, helping to spread that idea.
sentence_298: Some further argue that the essay influenced [[Nazism|National Socialist]], as well as Soviet and Arab antisemites.
sentence_299: Marx himself had Jewish ancestry, and [[Albert_Lindemann|Albert Lindemann]] and [[Hyam_Maccoby|Hyam Maccoby]] have suggested that he was [[Self-hating_Jew|embarrassed by it]].
sentence_300: Others argue that Marx consistently supported Prussian Jewish communities' struggles to achieve equal political rights.
sentence_301: These scholars argue that "On the Jewish Question" is a critique of Bruno Bauer's arguments that Jews must convert to Christianity before being emancipated, and is more generally a critique of liberal rights discourses and capitalism.
sentence_302: Iain Hamphsher-Monk wrote that "This work [On The Jewish Question] has been cited as evidence for Marx's supposed anti-semitism, but only the most superficial reading of it could sustain such an interpretation."
sentence_303: David McLellan and [[Francis_Wheen|Francis Wheen]] argue that readers should interpret On the Jewish Question in the deeper context of Marx's debates with [[Bruno_Bauer|Bruno Bauer]], author of [[The_Jewish_Question|The Jewish Question]], about [[Jewish_emancipation|Jewish emancipation]] in Germany.
sentence_304: Wheen says that "Those critics, who see this as a foretaste of 'Mein Kampf', overlook one, essential point: in spite of the clumsy phraseology and crude stereotyping, the essay was actually written as a defense of the Jews.
sentence_305: It was a retort to Bruno Bauer, who had argued that Jews should not be granted full civic rights and freedoms unless they were baptised as Christians".
sentence_306: According to McLellan, Marx used the word Judentum colloquially, as meaning commerce, arguing that Germans must be emancipated from the [[Capitalist_mode_of_production_(Marxist_theory)|capitalist mode of production]] not Judaism or Jews in particular.
sentence_307: McLellan concludes that readers should interpret the essay's second half as "an extended pun at Bauer's expense".
sentence_308: See also: [[Jewish_Bolshevism|Jewish Bolshevism]] and [[Racial_policy_of_Nazi_Germany|Racial policy of Nazi Germany]]
sentence_309: Between 1900 and 1924, approximately 1.75 million Jews migrated to America, the bulk from Eastern Europe escaping [[Pogroms_in_the_Russian_Empire|the pogroms]].
sentence_310: Before 1900 American Jews had always amounted to less than 1% of America's total population, but by 1930 Jews formed about 3.5%.
sentence_311: This increase, combined with the [[Upward_social_mobility|upward social mobility]] of some Jews, contributed to a resurgence of antisemitism.
sentence_312: In the first half of the 20th century, in the US, Jews were discriminated against in employment, access to residential and resort areas, membership in clubs and organizations, and in tightened quotas on Jewish enrolment and teaching positions in colleges and universities.
sentence_313: The lynching of [[Leo_Frank|Leo Frank]] by a mob of prominent citizens in [[Marietta,_Georgia|Marietta, Georgia]] in 1915 turned the spotlight on antisemitism in the United States.
sentence_314: The case was also used to build support for the renewal of the [[Ku_Klux_Klan|Ku Klux Klan]] which had been inactive since 1870.
sentence_315: At the beginning of the 20th century, the [[Menahem_Mendel_Beilis|Beilis Trial]] in Russia represented modern incidents of [[Blood_libel|blood-libels]] in Europe.
sentence_316: During the [[Russian_Civil_War|Russian Civil War]], close to 50,000 Jews were killed in pogroms.
sentence_317: Antisemitism in America reached its peak during the [[Interwar_period|interwar period]].
sentence_318: The pioneer automobile manufacturer [[Henry_Ford|Henry Ford]] propagated antisemitic ideas in his newspaper [[The_Dearborn_Independent|The Dearborn Independent]] (published by Ford from 1919 to 1927).
sentence_319: The radio speeches of [[Father_Coughlin|Father Coughlin]] in the late 1930s attacked [[Franklin_D._Roosevelt|Franklin D. Roosevelt]]'s [[New_Deal|New Deal]] and promoted the notion of a Jewish financial conspiracy.
sentence_320: Some prominent politicians shared such views: [[Louis_T._McFadden|Louis T. McFadden]], Chairman of the [[United_States_House_Committee_on_Banking_and_Currency|United States House Committee on Banking and Currency]], blamed Jews for Roosevelt's decision to abandon the [[Gold_standard|gold standard]], and claimed that "in the United States today, the Gentiles have the slips of paper while the Jews have the lawful money".
sentence_321: In Germany, [[Nazism|Nazism]] led [[Adolf_Hitler|Adolf Hitler]] and the [[Nazi_Party|Nazi Party]], who [[Machtergreifung|came to power]] on 30 January 1933 shortly afterwards instituted repressive legislation which denied the Jews basic civil rights.
sentence_322: In September 1935, the [[Nuremberg_Laws|Nuremberg Laws]] prohibited sexual relations and marriages between "Aryans" and Jews as [[Rassenschande|Rassenschande]] ("race disgrace") and stripped all German Jews, even quarter- and [[Half-Jew|half-Jews]], of their citizenship, (their official title became "subjects of the state").
sentence_323: It instituted a pogrom on the night of 9–10 November 1938, dubbed [[Kristallnacht|Kristallnacht]], in which Jews were killed, their property destroyed and their synagogues torched.
sentence_324: Antisemitic laws, agitation and propaganda were extended to [[German-occupied_Europe|German-occupied Europe]] in the wake of conquest, often building on local antisemitic traditions.
sentence_325: In 1940 the famous aviator [[Charles_Lindbergh|Charles Lindbergh]] and many prominent Americans led the [[America_First_Committee|America First Committee]] in opposing any involvement in a European war.
sentence_326: Lindbergh alleged that Jews were pushing America to go to war against Germany.
sentence_327: Lindbergh adamantly denied being anti-Semitic, and yet he refers numerous times in his private writings – his letters and diary – to Jewish control of the media being used to pressure the U.S. to get involved in the European war.
sentence_328: In one diary entry in November 1938, he responded to Kristallnacht by writing "I do not understand these riots on the part of the Germans.
sentence_330: They have undoubtedly had a difficult Jewish problem, but why is it necessary to handle it so unreasonably?
sentence_331: ", acknowledgement on Lindbergh's part that he agreed with the Nazis that Germany had a "Jewish problem."
sentence_332: An article by Jonathan Marwil in Antisemitism, A Historical Encyclopedia of Prejudice and Persecution claims that "no one who ever knew Lindbergh thought him antisemitic" and that claims of his antisemitism were solely tied to the remarks he made in that one speech.
sentence_333: In the east the Third Reich forced Jews into ghettos [[Warsaw_Ghetto|in Warsaw]], [[Kraków_Ghetto|in Kraków]], [[Lwów_Ghetto|in Lvov]], [[Lublin_Ghetto|in Lublin]] and [[Radom_Ghetto|in Radom]].
sentence_334: After [[Operation_Barbarossa|the beginning]] of the war between Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union in 1941 a campaign of mass murder, conducted by the [[Einsatzgruppen|Einsatzgruppen]], culminated from 1942 to 1945 in systematic [[Genocide|genocide]]: [[The_Holocaust|the Holocaust]].
sentence_335: Eleven million Jews were targeted for extermination by the Nazis, and some six million were eventually killed.
