sentence_43: In 1627, the French [[Jesuit|Jesuit]] theologian [[Denis_Pétau|Denis Pétau]] (Dionysius Petavius in Latin), with his work De doctrina temporum, popularized the usage ante Christum (Latin for "Before Christ") to mark years prior to AD.
sentence_44: Further information: [[New_Year|New Year]]
sentence_45: When the reckoning from Jesus' incarnation began replacing the previous dating systems in western Europe, various people chose different Christian feast days to begin the year: Christmas, [[Annunciation|Annunciation]], or Easter.
sentence_46: Thus, depending on the time and place, the year number changed on different days in the year, which created slightly different styles in chronology:

list.value: From 25 March 753 [[Ab_urbe_condita|AUC]] (today in 1 BC), i.e., notionally from the incarnation of Jesus. That first "Annunciation style" appeared in [[Arles|Arles]] at the end of the 9th century then spread to Burgundy and northern Italy. It was not commonly used and was called calculus pisanus since it was adopted in Pisa and survived there till 1750.

From 25 December 753 AUC (today in 1 BC), i.e., notionally from the birth of Jesus. It was called "Nativity style" and had been spread by Bede together with the Anno Domini in the early Middle Ages. That reckoning of the Year of Grace from Christmas was used in France, England and most of western Europe (except Spain) until the 12th century (when it was replaced by Annunciation style) and in Germany until the second quarter of the 13th century.

From 25 March 754 AUC (today in AD 1). That second "Annunciation style" may have originated in [[Fleury_Abbey|Fleury Abbey]] in the early 11th century, but it was spread by the Cistercians. [[Florence|Florence]] adopted that style in opposition to that of Pisa, so it got the name of calculus florentinus. It soon spread in France and also in England where it became common in the late 12th century and lasted until 1752.

From Easter, starting in 754 AUC (AD 1). That mos gallicanus (French custom) bound to a [[Moveable_feast|moveable feast]] was introduced in France by king [[Philip_II_of_France|Philip Augustus]] (r. 1180–1223), maybe to establish a new style in the provinces reconquered from England. However, it never spread beyond the ruling élite.

sentence_47: With these various styles, the same day could, in some cases, be dated in 1099, 1100 or 1101.
sentence_48: See also: [[Date_of_birth_of_Jesus|Date of birth of Jesus]], [[Nativity_of_Jesus#Date_of_birth|Nativity of Jesus § Date of birth]], and [[Chronology_of_Jesus#Year_of_Jesus'_birth|Chronology of Jesus § Year of Jesus' birth]]
sentence_49: The date of birth of Jesus of Nazareth is not stated in the gospels or in any secular text, but most scholars assume a date of birth between 6 BC and 4 BC.
sentence_50: The historical evidence is too fragmentary to allow a definitive dating, but the date is estimated through two different approaches – one by analyzing references to known historical events mentioned in the Nativity accounts in the Gospels of Luke and Matthew and the second by working backwards from the estimation of the start of the [[Ministry_of_Jesus|ministry of Jesus]].
sentence_51: Further information: [[Calendar_era|Calendar era]]
sentence_52: During the first six centuries of what would come to be known as the Christian era, European countries used various systems to count years.
sentence_53: Systems in use included [[List_of_Roman_consuls|consular dating]], imperial regnal year dating, and [[Anno_Mundi|Creation dating]].
sentence_54: Although the last non-imperial consul, [[Anicius_Faustus_Albinus_Basilius|Basilius]], was appointed in 541 by Emperor [[Justinian_I|Justinian I]], later emperors through to Constans II (641–668) were appointed consuls on the first of January after their accession.
sentence_55: All of these emperors, except Justinian, used imperial post-consular years for the years of their reign, along with their regnal years.
sentence_56: Long unused, this practice was not formally abolished until Novell XCIV of the law code of [[Leo_VI_the_Wise|Leo VI]] did so in 888.
sentence_57: Another calculation had been developed by the [[Alexandria|Alexandrian]] monk [[Annianus_of_Alexandria|Annianus]] around the year AD 400, placing the Annunciation on 25 March AD 9 (Julian)—eight to ten years after the date that Dionysius was to imply.
sentence_58: Although this incarnation was popular during the early centuries of the [[Byzantine_Empire|Byzantine Empire]], years numbered from it, an Era of Incarnation, were exclusively used and are still used in [[Ethiopia|Ethiopia]].
sentence_59: This accounts for the seven- or eight-year discrepancy between the [[Gregorian_calendar|Gregorian]] and Ethiopian calendars.
sentence_60: Byzantine chroniclers like [[Maximus_the_Confessor|Maximus the Confessor]], [[George_Syncellus|George Syncellus]], and [[Theophanes_the_Confessor|Theophanes]] dated their years from Annianus' [[Genesis_creation_narrative|creation]] of the world.
sentence_61: This era, called [[Anno_Mundi|Anno Mundi]], "year of the world" (abbreviated AM), by modern scholars, began its first year on 25 March 5492 BC.
sentence_62: Later Byzantine chroniclers used Anno Mundi years from 1 September 5509 BC, the [[Byzantine_calendar|Byzantine Era]].
sentence_63: No single Anno Mundi epoch was dominant throughout the [[Christian_world|Christian world]].
sentence_64: [[Eusebius_of_Caesarea|Eusebius of Caesarea]] in his [[Chronicon_(Eusebius)|Chronicle]] used an era beginning with the birth of [[Abraham|Abraham]], dated in 2016 BC (AD 1 = 2017 Anno Abrahami).
sentence_65: Spain and Portugal continued to date by the [[Spanish_Era|Spanish Era]] (also called [[Era_of_the_Caesars|Era of the Caesars]]), which began counting from 38 BC, well into the Middle Ages.
sentence_66: In 1422, [[Portugal|Portugal]] became the last Catholic country to adopt the Anno Domini system.
sentence_67: The Era of Martyrs, which numbered years from the accession of [[Diocletian|Diocletian]] in 284, who launched the most severe [[Persecution_of_Christians|persecution of Christians]], was used by the [[Coptic_Orthodox_Church_of_Alexandria|Church of Alexandria]] and is still used, officially, by the Coptic Orthodox and [[Coptic_Catholic_Church|Coptic Catholic]] churches.
sentence_68: It was also used by the [[Ethiopian_Orthodox_Tewahedo_Church|Ethiopian]] church.
sentence_69: Another system was to date from the [[Crucifixion_of_Jesus|crucifixion of Jesus]], which as early as [[Hippolytus_(writer)|Hippolytus]] and [[Tertullian|Tertullian]] was believed to have occurred in the consulate of the Gemini (AD 29), which appears in some [[Middle_Ages|medieval]] manuscripts.
sentence_70: Main article: [[Common_Era|Common Era]]
sentence_71: Alternative names for the Anno Domini era include vulgaris aerae (found 1615 in Latin), "Vulgar Era" (in English, as early as 1635), "Christian Era" (in English, in 1652), "[[Common_Era|Common Era]]" (in English, 1708), and "Current Era".
sentence_72: Since 1856, the alternative abbreviations [[Common_Era|CE and BCE]] (sometimes written C.E. and B.C.E.) are sometimes used in place of AD and BC.
sentence_73: The "Common/Current Era" ("CE") terminology is often preferred by those who desire a term that does not explicitly make religious references.
sentence_74: For example, Cunningham and Starr (1998) write that "B.C.E./C.E.
sentence_75: […] do not presuppose faith in [[Jesus_Christ|Christ]] and hence are more appropriate for interfaith dialog than the conventional B.C./A.D."
sentence_76: Upon its foundation, the [[Republic_of_China_(1912–1949)|Republic of China]] adopted the [[Minguo_Era|Minguo Era]] but used the Western calendar for international purposes.
sentence_77: The translated term was (xī yuán; 'Western Era').
sentence_78: Later, in 1949, the [[People's_Republic_of_China|People's Republic of China]] adopted (gōngyuán; 'Common Era') for all purposes domestic and foreign.

section_6.value: No year zero: start and end of a century

sentence_79: Further information: [[Year_zero|Year zero]], [[Astronomical_year_numbering|Astronomical year numbering]], [[Millennium|Millennium]], [[Century|Century]], and [[Decade|Decade]]
sentence_80: In the AD year numbering system, whether applied to the [[Julian_calendar|Julian]] or [[Gregorian_calendar|Gregorian calendars]], AD 1 is immediately preceded by 1 BC, with nothing in between them (there was no [[Year_0|year zero]]).
sentence_81: There are debates as to whether a new decade, century, or millennium begins on a year ending in zero or one.
sentence_82: For computational reasons, [[Astronomical_year_numbering|astronomical year numbering]] and the [[ISO_8601|ISO 8601]] standard designate years so that AD 1 = year 1, 1 BC = year 0, 2 BC = year −1, etc.
sentence_83: In common usage, ancient dates are expressed in the Julian calendar, but ISO 8601 uses the Gregorian calendar and astronomers may use a variety of time scales depending on the application.
sentence_84: Thus dates using the year 0 or negative years may require further investigation before being converted to BC or AD.

title: Alexander the Great
sentence_0: This article is about the ancient king of Macedonia.
sentence_1: For other uses, see [[Alexander_the_Great_(disambiguation)|Alexander the Great (disambiguation)]].
sentence_2: Alexander III of Macedon ([[Greek_language|Greek]]: Αλέξανδρος Γʹ ὁ Μακεδών, [[Alexander|Aléxandros]] III ho Makedȏn; 20/21 July 356 BC – 10/11 June 323 BC), commonly known as Alexander the Great ([[Greek_language|Greek]]: ὁ Μέγας, ho Mégas), was a king ([[Basileus|basileus]]) of the [[Ancient_Greece|ancient Greek]] kingdom of [[Macedonia_(ancient_kingdom)|Macedon]] and a member of the [[Argead_dynasty|Argead dynasty]].
sentence_3: He was born in [[Pella|Pella]] in 356 BC and succeeded his father Philip II to the throne at the age of 20.
sentence_4: He spent most of his ruling years on an unprecedented military campaign through [[Western_Asia|western Asia]] and northeast Africa, and by the age of thirty, he had created one of the [[List_of_largest_empires|largest empires]] of the ancient world, stretching from [[Greece|Greece]] to northwestern [[Historical_India|India]].
sentence_5: He was undefeated in battle and is widely considered one of history's most successful military commanders.
sentence_6: During his youth, Alexander was tutored by [[Aristotle|Aristotle]] until age 16.
sentence_7: After Philip's assassination in 336 BC, he succeeded his father to the throne and inherited a strong kingdom and an experienced army.
sentence_8: Alexander was awarded the generalship of Greece and used this authority to launch his father's pan-Hellenic project to lead the Greeks in the conquest of [[Persia|Persia]].
sentence_9: In 334 BC, he invaded the [[Achaemenid_Empire|Achaemenid Empire]] (Persian Empire) and began a [[Wars_of_Alexander_the_Great|series of campaigns]] that lasted 10 years.
sentence_10: Following the conquest of [[Anatolia|Anatolia]], Alexander broke the power of Persia in a series of decisive battles, most notably the battles of [[Battle_of_Issus|Issus]] and [[Battle_of_Gaugamela|Gaugamela]].
sentence_11: He subsequently overthrew Persian King [[Darius_III|Darius III]] and conquered the Achaemenid Empire in its entirety.
sentence_12: At that point, his empire stretched from the [[Adriatic_Sea|Adriatic Sea]] to the [[Beas_River|Beas River]].
sentence_13: Alexander endeavoured to reach the "ends of the world and the Great Outer Sea" and [[Indian_campaign_of_Alexander_the_Great|invaded India]] in 326 BC, winning an important victory over the [[Pauravas|Pauravas]] at the Battle of the Hydaspes.
sentence_14: He eventually turned back at the demand of his homesick troops, dying in [[Babylon|Babylon]] in 323 BC, the city that he planned to establish as his capital, without executing a series of planned campaigns that would have begun with an invasion of [[Arabian_Peninsula|Arabia]].
sentence_15: In the years following [[Death_of_Alexander_the_Great|his death]], a [[Wars_of_the_Diadochi|series of civil wars]] tore his empire apart, resulting in the establishment of several states ruled by the Diadochi, Alexander's surviving generals and heirs.
sentence_16: Alexander's legacy includes the [[Cultural_diffusion|cultural diffusion]] and syncretism which his conquests engendered, such as [[Greco-Buddhism|Greco-Buddhism]].
sentence_17: He founded some [[List_of_cities_founded_by_Alexander_the_Great|twenty cities that bore his name]], most notably [[Alexandria|Alexandria]] in Egypt.
sentence_18: Alexander's settlement of Greek colonists and the resulting spread of [[Culture_of_Greece|Greek culture]] in the east resulted in a new [[Hellenistic_civilization|Hellenistic civilization]], aspects of which were still evident in the traditions of the [[Byzantine_Empire|Byzantine Empire]] in the mid-15th century AD and the presence of [[Cappadocian_Greeks|Greek speakers in central]] and [[Pontic_Greeks|far eastern Anatolia]] until the [[Greek_genocide|Greek genocide]] and the population exchange in the 1920s.
sentence_19: Alexander became legendary as a [[Hero|classical hero]] in the mould of [[Achilles|Achilles]], and he features prominently in the history and mythic traditions of both Greek and non-Greek cultures.
sentence_20: He was undefeated in battle and became the measure against which military leaders compared themselves.
sentence_21: [[Military_academy|Military academies]] throughout the world still teach his tactics.
sentence_22: He is often ranked among the most influential people in history.
sentence_23: Alexander was born in [[Pella|Pella]], the capital of the [[Macedonia_(ancient_kingdom)|Kingdom of Macedon]], on the sixth day of the ancient Greek month of [[Hekatombaion|Hekatombaion]], which probably corresponds to 20 July 356 BC, although the exact date is uncertain.
sentence_24: He was the son of the king of Macedon, Philip II, and his fourth wife, [[Olympias|Olympias]], the daughter of [[Neoptolemus_I_of_Epirus|Neoptolemus I]], king of [[Epirus_(ancient_state)|Epirus]].
sentence_25: Although Philip had seven or eight wives, Olympias was his principal wife for some time, likely because she gave birth to Alexander.
sentence_26: Several legends surround Alexander's birth and childhood.
sentence_27: According to the ancient Greek biographer [[Plutarch|Plutarch]], on the eve of the consummation of her marriage to Philip, Olympias dreamed that her womb was struck by a thunderbolt that caused a flame to spread "far and wide" before dying away.
sentence_28: Sometime after the wedding, Philip is said to have seen himself, in a dream, securing his wife's womb with a [[Seal_(emblem)|seal]] engraved with a lion's image.
sentence_29: Plutarch offered a variety of interpretations of these dreams: that Olympias was pregnant before her marriage, indicated by the sealing of her womb; or that Alexander's father was [[Zeus|Zeus]].
sentence_30: Ancient commentators were divided about whether the ambitious Olympias promulgated the story of Alexander's divine parentage, variously claiming that she had told Alexander, or that she dismissed the suggestion as impious.
sentence_31: On the day Alexander was born, Philip was preparing a [[Siege|siege]] on the city of [[Potidea|Potidea]] on the peninsula of [[Chalcidice|Chalcidice]].
sentence_32: That same day, Philip received news that his general [[Parmenion|Parmenion]] had defeated the combined [[Illyria|Illyrian]] and [[Paeonian|Paeonian]] armies and that his horses had won at the [[Ancient_Olympic_Games|Olympic Games]].
sentence_33: It was also said that on this day, the [[Temple_of_Artemis|Temple of Artemis]] in [[Ephesus|Ephesus]], one of the [[Seven_Wonders_of_the_Ancient_World|Seven Wonders of the World]], burnt down.
sentence_34: This led [[Hegesias_of_Magnesia|Hegesias of Magnesia]] to say that it had burnt down because [[Artemis|Artemis]] was away, attending the birth of Alexander.
sentence_35: Such legends may have emerged when Alexander was king, and possibly at his instigation, to show that he was superhuman and destined for greatness from conception.
sentence_36: In his early years, Alexander was raised by a nurse, [[Lanike|Lanike]], sister of Alexander's future general [[Cleitus_the_Black|Cleitus the Black]].
sentence_37: Later in his childhood, Alexander was tutored by the strict [[Leonidas_of_Epirus|Leonidas]], a relative of his mother, and by [[Lysimachus_of_Acarnania|Lysimachus of Acarnania]].
sentence_38: Alexander was raised in the manner of noble Macedonian youths, learning to read, play the [[Lyre|lyre]], ride, fight, and hunt.
sentence_39: When Alexander was ten years old, a trader from [[Thessaly|Thessaly]] brought Philip a horse, which he offered to sell for thirteen [[Attic_talent|talents]].
sentence_40: The horse refused to be mounted, and Philip ordered it away.
sentence_41: Alexander, however, detecting the horse's fear of its own shadow, asked to tame the horse, which he eventually managed.
sentence_42: Plutarch stated that Philip, overjoyed at this display of courage and ambition, kissed his son tearfully, declaring: "My boy, you must find a kingdom big enough for your ambitions.
sentence_43: Macedon is too small for you", and bought the horse for him.
sentence_44: Alexander named it [[Bucephalas|Bucephalas]], meaning "ox-head".
sentence_45: Bucephalas carried Alexander as far as [[India|India]].
sentence_46: When the animal died (because of old age, according to Plutarch, at age thirty), Alexander named a city after him, [[Alexandria_Bucephalous|Bucephala]].
sentence_47: When Alexander was 13, Philip began to search for a [[Tutor|tutor]], and considered such academics as [[Isocrates|Isocrates]] and [[Speusippus|Speusippus]], the latter offering to resign from his stewardship of the [[Platonic_Academy|Academy]] to take up the post.
sentence_48: In the end, Philip chose [[Aristotle|Aristotle]] and provided the Temple of the Nymphs at [[Mieza,_Macedonia|Mieza]] as a classroom.
sentence_49: In return for teaching Alexander, Philip agreed to rebuild Aristotle's hometown of [[Stageira|Stageira]], which Philip had razed, and to repopulate it by buying and freeing the ex-citizens who were slaves, or pardoning those who were in exile.
sentence_50: Mieza was like a boarding school for Alexander and the children of Macedonian nobles, such as [[Ptolemy_I_Soter|Ptolemy]], [[Hephaistion|Hephaistion]], and [[Cassander|Cassander]].
sentence_51: Many of these students would become his friends and future generals, and are often known as the 'Companions'.
sentence_52: Aristotle taught Alexander and his companions about medicine, philosophy, morals, religion, logic, and art.
sentence_53: Under Aristotle's tutelage, Alexander developed a passion for the works of [[Homer|Homer]], and in particular the [[Iliad|Iliad]]; Aristotle gave him an annotated copy, which Alexander later carried on his campaigns.
sentence_54: During his youth, Alexander was also acquainted with Persian exiles at the Macedonian court, who received the protection of Philip II for several years as they opposed [[Artaxerxes_III|Artaxerxes III]].
sentence_55: Among them were [[Artabazos_II|Artabazos II]] and his daughter [[Barsine|Barsine]], future mistress of Alexander, who resided at the Macedonian court from 352 to 342 BC, as well as [[Amminapes|Amminapes]], future [[Satrap|satrap]] of Alexander, or a Persian nobleman named [[Sisines|Sisines]].
sentence_56: This gave the Macedonian court a good knowledge of Persian issues, and may even have influenced some of the innovations in the management of the Macedonian state.
sentence_57: [[Suda|Suda]] writes that, also, [[Anaximenes_of_Lampsacus|Anaximenes of Lampsacus]] was one of his teachers.
sentence_58: Anaximenes, also accompanied him on his campaigns.
sentence_59: Main articles: Philip II of Macedon and [[Rise_of_Macedon|Rise of Macedon]]
sentence_60: Further information: [[History_of_Macedonia_(ancient_kingdom)|History of Macedonia (ancient kingdom)]]
sentence_61: At the age of 16, Alexander's education under Aristotle ended.
sentence_62: Philip waged war against [[Byzantium|Byzantion]], leaving Alexander in charge as regent and [[Heir_apparent|heir apparent]].
sentence_63: During Philip's absence, the [[Thracians|Thracian]] [[Maedi|Maedi]] revolted against Macedonia.
sentence_64: Alexander responded quickly, driving them from their territory.
sentence_65: He colonized it with Greeks, and founded a city named [[Alexandropolis_Maedica|Alexandropolis]].
sentence_66: Upon Philip's return, he dispatched Alexander with a small force to subdue revolts in southern [[Thrace|Thrace]].
sentence_67: Campaigning against the Greek city of [[Perinthus|Perinthus]], Alexander is reported to have saved his father's life.
sentence_68: Meanwhile, the city of [[Amphissa_(city)|Amphissa]] began to work lands that were sacred to [[Apollo|Apollo]] near [[Delphi|Delphi]], a sacrilege that gave Philip the opportunity to further intervene in Greek affairs.
sentence_69: Still occupied in Thrace, he ordered Alexander to muster an army for a campaign in southern Greece.
sentence_70: Concerned that other Greek states might intervene, Alexander made it look as though he was preparing to attack Illyria instead.
sentence_71: During this turmoil, the Illyrians invaded Macedonia, only to be repelled by Alexander.
sentence_72: Philip and his army joined his son in 338 BC, and they marched south through [[Thermopylae|Thermopylae]], taking it after stubborn resistance from its Theban garrison.
sentence_73: They went on to occupy the city of [[Elatea|Elatea]], only a few days' march from both [[Athens|Athens]] and [[Thebes,_Greece|Thebes]].
sentence_74: The Athenians, led by [[Demosthenes|Demosthenes]], voted to seek alliance with Thebes against Macedonia.
sentence_75: Both Athens and Philip sent embassies to win Thebes' favour, but Athens won the contest.
sentence_76: Philip marched on Amphissa (ostensibly acting on the request of the [[Amphictyonic_League|Amphictyonic League]]), capturing the mercenaries sent there by Demosthenes and accepting the city's surrender.
sentence_77: Philip then returned to Elatea, sending a final offer of peace to Athens and Thebes, who both rejected it.
sentence_78: As Philip marched south, his opponents blocked him near [[Chaeronea|Chaeronea]], [[Boeotia|Boeotia]].
sentence_79: During the ensuing [[Battle_of_Chaeronea_(338_BC)|Battle of Chaeronea]], Philip commanded the right wing and Alexander the left, accompanied by a group of Philip's trusted generals.
sentence_80: According to the ancient sources, the two sides fought bitterly for some time.
sentence_81: Philip deliberately commanded his troops to retreat, counting on the untested Athenian [[Hoplites|hoplites]] to follow, thus breaking their line.
sentence_82: Alexander was the first to break the Theban lines, followed by Philip's generals.
sentence_83: Having damaged the enemy's cohesion, Philip ordered his troops to press forward and quickly routed them.
sentence_84: With the Athenians lost, the Thebans were surrounded.
sentence_85: Left to fight alone, they were defeated.
sentence_86: After the victory at Chaeronea, Philip and Alexander marched unopposed into the Peloponnese, welcomed by all cities; however, when they reached [[Sparta|Sparta]], they were refused, but did not resort to war.
sentence_87: At [[Ancient_Corinth|Corinth]], Philip established a "Hellenic Alliance" (modelled on the old [[Second_Persian_invasion_of_Greece#Hellenic_alliance|anti-Persian alliance]] of the [[Greco-Persian_Wars|Greco-Persian Wars]]), which included most Greek city-states except Sparta.
sentence_88: Philip was then named [[Hegemon|Hegemon]] (often translated as "Supreme Commander") of this league (known by modern scholars as the League of Corinth), and announced his plans to attack the [[Achaemenid_Empire|Persian Empire]].
sentence_89: When Philip returned to Pella, he fell in love with and married [[Cleopatra_Eurydice_of_Macedon|Cleopatra Eurydice]] in 338 BC, the niece of his general [[Attalus_(general)|Attalus]].
sentence_90: The marriage made Alexander's position as heir less secure, since any son of Cleopatra Eurydice would be a fully Macedonian heir, while Alexander was only half-Macedonian.
sentence_91: During the [[Banquet|wedding banquet]], a drunken Attalus publicly prayed to the gods that the union would produce a legitimate heir.
sentence_92: In 337 BC, Alexander fled Macedon with his mother, dropping her off with her brother, King [[Alexander_I_of_Epirus|Alexander I of Epirus]] in [[Dodona|Dodona]], capital of the [[Molossians|Molossians]].
sentence_93: He continued to Illyria, where he sought refuge with one or more Illyrian kings, perhaps with [[Glaucias_of_Taulantii|Glaukias]], and was treated as a guest, despite having defeated them in battle a few years before.
sentence_94: However, it appears Philip never intended to disown his politically and militarily trained son.
sentence_95: Accordingly, Alexander returned to Macedon after six months due to the efforts of a family friend, [[Demaratus_(hetairos)|Demaratus]], who mediated between the two parties.
sentence_96: In the following year, the Persian [[Satrap|satrap]] (governor) of [[Caria|Caria]], [[Pixodarus_of_Caria|Pixodarus]], offered his eldest daughter to Alexander's half-brother, Philip Arrhidaeus.
sentence_97: Olympias and several of Alexander's friends suggested this showed Philip intended to make Arrhidaeus his heir.
sentence_98: Alexander reacted by sending an actor, [[Thessalus_(actor)|Thessalus]] of Corinth, to tell Pixodarus that he should not offer his daughter's hand to an illegitimate son, but instead to Alexander.
sentence_99: When Philip heard of this, he stopped the negotiations and scolded Alexander for wishing to marry the daughter of a Carian, explaining that he wanted a better bride for him.
sentence_100: Philip exiled four of Alexander's friends, [[Harpalus|Harpalus]], [[Nearchus|Nearchus]], [[Ptolemy_I_Soter|Ptolemy]] and [[Erigyius|Erigyius]], and had the Corinthians bring Thessalus to him in chains.
sentence_101: Further information: [[Government_of_Macedonia_(ancient_kingdom)|Government of Macedonia (ancient kingdom)]]
sentence_102: In summer 336 BC, while at [[Vergina|Aegae]] attending the wedding of his daughter Cleopatra to Olympias's brother, [[Alexander_I_of_Epirus|Alexander I of Epirus]], Philip was assassinated by the captain of his [[Somatophylax|bodyguards]], Pausanias.
sentence_103: As Pausanias tried to escape, he tripped over a vine and was killed by his pursuers, including two of Alexander's companions, [[Perdiccas|Perdiccas]] and [[Leonnatus|Leonnatus]].
sentence_104: Alexander was proclaimed king on the spot by the nobles and [[Ancient_Macedonian_military|army]] at the age of 20.
sentence_105: Alexander began his reign by eliminating potential rivals to the throne.
sentence_106: He had his cousin, the former [[Amyntas_IV_of_Macedon|Amyntas IV]], executed.
sentence_107: He also had two Macedonian princes from the region of [[Lyncestis|Lyncestis]] killed, but spared a third, [[Alexander_Lyncestes|Alexander Lyncestes]].
sentence_108: Olympias had Cleopatra Eurydice and Europa, her daughter by Philip, burned alive.
sentence_109: When Alexander learned about this, he was furious.
sentence_110: Alexander also ordered the murder of Attalus, who was in command of the advance guard of the army in Asia Minor and Cleopatra's uncle.
sentence_111: Attalus was at that time corresponding with Demosthenes, regarding the possibility of defecting to Athens.
sentence_112: Attalus also had severely insulted Alexander, and following Cleopatra's murder, Alexander may have considered him too dangerous to leave alive.
sentence_113: Alexander spared Arrhidaeus, who was by all accounts mentally disabled, possibly as a result of poisoning by Olympias.
sentence_114: News of Philip's death roused many states into revolt, including Thebes, Athens, Thessaly, and the Thracian tribes north of Macedon.
sentence_115: When news of the revolts reached Alexander, he responded quickly.
sentence_116: Though advised to use diplomacy, Alexander mustered 3,000 Macedonian cavalry and rode south towards Thessaly.
sentence_117: He found the Thessalian army occupying the pass between [[Mount_Olympus|Mount Olympus]] and [[Mount_Ossa_(Greece)|Mount Ossa]], and ordered his men to ride over Mount Ossa.
sentence_118: When the Thessalians awoke the next day, they found Alexander in their rear and promptly surrendered, adding their cavalry to Alexander's force.
sentence_119: He then continued south towards the Peloponnese.
sentence_120: Alexander stopped at Thermopylae, where he was recognized as the leader of the Amphictyonic League before heading south to Corinth.
sentence_121: Athens sued for peace and Alexander pardoned the rebels.
sentence_122: The famous [[Diogenes_and_Alexander|encounter between Alexander and Diogenes the Cynic]] occurred during Alexander's stay in Corinth.
sentence_123: When Alexander asked Diogenes what he could do for him, the philosopher disdainfully asked Alexander to stand a little to the side, as he was blocking the sunlight.
sentence_124: This reply apparently delighted Alexander, who is reported to have said "But verily, if I were not Alexander, I would like to be Diogenes."
sentence_125: At Corinth, Alexander took the title of Hegemon ("leader") and, like Philip, was appointed commander for the coming war against Persia.
sentence_126: He also received news of a Thracian uprising.
sentence_127: Main article: [[Alexander's_Balkan_campaign|Alexander's Balkan campaign]]
sentence_128: Before crossing to Asia, Alexander wanted to safeguard his northern borders.
sentence_129: In the spring of 335 BC, he advanced to suppress several revolts.
sentence_130: Starting from [[Amphipolis|Amphipolis]], he travelled east into the country of the "Independent Thracians"; and at Mount Haemus, the Macedonian army attacked and defeated the Thracian forces manning the heights.
sentence_131: The Macedonians marched into the country of the [[Triballi|Triballi]], and defeated their army near the Lyginus river (a [[List_of_tributaries_of_the_Danube|tributary of the Danube]]).
sentence_132: Alexander then marched for three days to the [[Danube|Danube]], encountering the [[Getae|Getae]] tribe on the opposite shore.
sentence_133: Crossing the river at night, he surprised them and forced their army to retreat after the first cavalry [[Skirmish|skirmish]].
sentence_134: News then reached Alexander that [[Cleitus_(Dardania)|Cleitus]], King of Illyria, and [[King_Glaukias|King Glaukias]] of the [[Taulantii|Taulantii]] were in open revolt against his authority.
sentence_135: Marching west into Illyria, Alexander defeated each in turn, forcing the two rulers to flee with their troops.
sentence_136: With these victories, he secured his northern frontier.
sentence_137: While Alexander campaigned north, the Thebans and Athenians rebelled once again.
sentence_138: Alexander immediately headed south.
sentence_139: While the other cities again hesitated, Thebes decided to fight.
sentence_140: The Theban resistance was ineffective, and Alexander razed the city and divided its territory between the other Boeotian cities.
sentence_141: The end of Thebes cowed Athens, leaving all of Greece temporarily at peace.
sentence_142: Alexander then set out on his Asian campaign, leaving [[Antipater|Antipater]] as regent.
sentence_143: According to ancient writers [[Demosthenes|Demosthenes]] called Alexander "Margites" ([[Greek_language|Greek]]: Μαργίτης) and a boy.
sentence_144: Greeks used the word Margites to describe fool and useless people, on account of the [[Margites|Margites]].
sentence_145: Main articles: [[Wars_of_Alexander_the_Great|Wars of Alexander the Great]] and [[Chronology_of_the_expedition_of_Alexander_the_Great_into_Asia|Chronology of the expedition of Alexander the Great into Asia]]
sentence_146: Further information: [[Battle_of_the_Granicus|Battle of the Granicus]], [[Siege_of_Halicarnassus|Siege of Halicarnassus]], and [[Siege_of_Miletus|Siege of Miletus]]
sentence_147: In 336 BC Philip II had already sent [[Parmenion|Parmenion]], with [[Amyntas_(son_of_Andromenes)|Amyntas]], Andromenes and [[Attalus_(general)|Attalus]], and an army of 10,000 men into [[Anatolia|Anatolia]] to make preparations for an invasion to free the Greeks living on the western coast and islands from Achaemenid rule.
sentence_148: At first, all went well.
sentence_149: The Greek cities on the western coast of Anatolia revolted until the news arrived that Philip had been murdered and had been succeeded by his young son Alexander.
sentence_150: The Macedonians were demoralized by Philip's death and were subsequently defeated near [[Magnesia_on_the_Meander|Magnesia]] by the Achaemenids under the command of the mercenary [[Memnon_of_Rhodes|Memnon of Rhodes]].
sentence_151: Taking over the invasion project of Philip II, Alexander's army crossed the [[Hellespont|Hellespont]] in 334 BC with approximately 48,100 soldiers, 6,100 cavalry and a fleet of 120 ships with crews numbering 38,000, drawn from Macedon and various Greek city-states, mercenaries, and feudally raised soldiers from [[Thrace|Thrace]], [[Paionia|Paionia]], and [[Illyria|Illyria]].
sentence_152: He showed his intent to conquer the entirety of the Persian Empire by throwing a spear into Asian soil and saying he accepted Asia as a gift from the gods.
sentence_153: This also showed Alexander's eagerness to fight, in contrast to his father's preference for diplomacy.
sentence_154: After an initial victory against Persian forces at the [[Battle_of_the_Granicus|Battle of the Granicus]], Alexander accepted the surrender of the Persian provincial capital and treasury of Sardis; he then proceeded along the [[Ionia|Ionian]] coast, granting autonomy and democracy to the cities.
sentence_155: Miletus, held by Achaemenid forces, required a delicate siege operation, with Persian naval forces nearby.
sentence_156: Further south, at [[Halicarnassus|Halicarnassus]], in [[Caria|Caria]], Alexander successfully waged his first large-scale [[Siege|siege]], eventually forcing his opponents, the mercenary captain [[Memnon_of_Rhodes|Memnon of Rhodes]] and the Persian [[Satrap|satrap]] of Caria, [[Orontobates|Orontobates]], to withdraw by sea.
sentence_157: Alexander left the government of Caria to a member of the Hecatomnid dynasty, [[Ada_of_Caria|Ada]], who adopted Alexander.
sentence_158: From Halicarnassus, Alexander proceeded into mountainous [[Lycia|Lycia]] and the [[Pamphylia|Pamphylian]] plain, asserting control over all coastal cities to deny the Persians naval bases.
sentence_159: From Pamphylia onwards the coast held no major ports and Alexander moved inland.
sentence_160: At [[Termessos|Termessos]], Alexander humbled but did not storm the Pisidian city.
sentence_161: At the ancient Phrygian capital of [[Gordium|Gordium]], Alexander "undid" the hitherto unsolvable [[Gordian_Knot|Gordian Knot]], a feat said to await the future "king of [[Asia_Minor|Asia]]".
sentence_162: According to the story, Alexander proclaimed that it did not matter how the knot was undone and hacked it apart with his sword.
sentence_163: Further information: [[Battle_of_Issus|Battle of Issus]] and [[Siege_of_Tyre_(332_BC)|Siege of Tyre (332 BC)]]
sentence_164: In spring 333 BC, Alexander crossed the [[Taurus_Mountains|Taurus]] into [[Cilicia|Cilicia]].
sentence_165: After a long pause due to an illness, he marched on towards Syria.
sentence_166: Though outmanoeuvered by Darius' significantly larger army, he marched back to Cilicia, where he defeated Darius at Issus.
sentence_167: Darius fled the battle, causing his army to collapse, and left behind his wife, his two daughters, his mother [[Sisygambis|Sisygambis]], and a fabulous treasure.
sentence_168: He offered a [[Peace_treaty|peace treaty]] that included the lands he had already lost, and a ransom of 10,000 [[Attic_talent|talents]] for his family.
sentence_169: Alexander replied that since he was now king of Asia, it was he alone who decided territorial divisions.
sentence_170: Alexander proceeded to take possession of [[Ancient_Syria|Syria]], and most of the coast of the [[Levant|Levant]].
sentence_171: In the following year, 332 BC, he was forced to attack [[Tyre,_Lebanon|Tyre]], which he captured after a long and difficult [[Siege_of_Tyre_(332_BC)|siege]].
sentence_172: The men of military age were massacred and the women and children sold into [[Slavery|slavery]].
sentence_173: Further information: [[Siege_of_Gaza|Siege of Gaza]]
sentence_174: When Alexander destroyed Tyre, most of the towns on the route to [[Egypt|Egypt]] quickly capitulated.
sentence_175: However, Alexander met with resistance at [[Gaza_City|Gaza]].
sentence_176: The stronghold was heavily fortified and built on a hill, requiring a siege.
sentence_177: When "his engineers pointed out to him that because of the height of the mound it would be impossible... this encouraged Alexander all the more to make the attempt".
sentence_178: After three unsuccessful assaults, the stronghold fell, but not before Alexander had received a serious shoulder wound.
sentence_179: As in Tyre, men of military age were put to the sword and the women and children were sold into slavery.
sentence_180: Alexander advanced on Egypt in later 332 BC, where he was regarded as a liberator.
sentence_181: He was pronounced son of the deity [[Amun|Amun]] at the [[Oracle|Oracle]] of [[Siwa_Oasis|Siwa Oasis]] in the [[Ancient_Libya|Libyan]] desert.
sentence_182: Henceforth, Alexander often referred to [[Zeus-Ammon|Zeus-Ammon]] as his true father, and after his death, currency depicted him adorned with the [[Horns_of_Ammon|Horns of Ammon]] as a symbol of his divinity.
sentence_183: During his stay in Egypt, he founded [[Alexandria|Alexandria-by-Egypt]], which would become the prosperous capital of the [[Ptolemaic_Kingdom|Ptolemaic Kingdom]] after his death.
sentence_184: Further information: [[Battle_of_Gaugamela|Battle of Gaugamela]]
sentence_185: Leaving Egypt in 331 BCE, Alexander marched eastward into [[Achaemenid_Assyria|Achaemenid Assyria]] in [[Upper_Mesopotamia|Upper Mesopotamia]] (now northern [[Iraq|Iraq]]) and defeated Darius again at the [[Battle_of_Gaugamela|Battle of Gaugamela]].
sentence_186: Darius once more fled the field, and Alexander chased him as far as [[Erbil|Arbela]].
sentence_187: Gaugamela would be the final and decisive encounter between the two.
sentence_188: Darius fled over the mountains to [[Ecbatana|Ecbatana]] (modern [[Hamadan|Hamadan]]) while Alexander captured [[Babylon|Babylon]].
sentence_189: Further information: [[Battle_of_the_Persian_Gate|Battle of the Persian Gate]]
sentence_190: From Babylon, Alexander went to [[Susa|Susa]], one of the [[Achaemenid_Empire|Achaemenid]] capitals, and captured its treasury.
sentence_191: He sent the bulk of his army to the Persian ceremonial capital of [[Persepolis|Persepolis]] via the Persian [[Royal_Road|Royal Road]].
sentence_192: Alexander himself took selected troops on the direct route to the city.
sentence_193: He then stormed the pass of the [[Persian_Gates|Persian Gates]] (in the modern [[Zagros_Mountains|Zagros Mountains]]) which had been blocked by a Persian army under [[Ariobarzanes_(satrap_of_Persis)|Ariobarzanes]] and then hurried to Persepolis before its garrison could loot the treasury.
sentence_194: On entering Persepolis, Alexander allowed his troops to loot the city for several days.
sentence_195: Alexander stayed in Persepolis for five months.
sentence_196: During his stay a fire broke out in the eastern palace of [[Xerxes_I|Xerxes I]] and spread to the rest of the city.
sentence_197: Possible causes include a drunken accident or deliberate revenge for the burning of the [[Acropolis_of_Athens|Acropolis of Athens]] during the [[Greco-Persian_Wars|Second Persian War]] by Xerxes; [[Plutarch|Plutarch]] and [[Diodorus|Diodorus]] allege that Alexander's companion, the [[Hetaera|hetaera]] [[Thaïs|Thaïs]], instigated and started the fire.
sentence_198: Even as he watched the city burn, Alexander immediately began to regret his decision.
sentence_199: [[Plutarch|Plutarch]] claims that he ordered his men to put out the fires, but that the flames had already spread to most of the city.
sentence_200: [[Quintus_Curtius_Rufus|Curtius]] claims that Alexander did not regret his decision until the next morning.
sentence_201: Plutarch recounts an anecdote in which Alexander pauses and talks to a fallen statue of Xerxes as if it were a live person:

section_17.value: Fall of the Empire and the East

sentence_202: Alexander then chased Darius, first into Media, and then Parthia.
sentence_203: The Persian king no longer controlled his own destiny, and was taken prisoner by [[Bessus|Bessus]], his [[Bactria|Bactrian]] satrap and kinsman.
sentence_204: As Alexander approached, Bessus had his men fatally stab the Great King and then declared himself Darius' successor as Artaxerxes V, before retreating into Central Asia to launch a [[Guerrilla_warfare|guerrilla]] campaign against Alexander.
sentence_205: Alexander buried Darius' remains next to his Achaemenid predecessors in a regal funeral.
sentence_206: He claimed that, while dying, Darius had named him as his successor to the Achaemenid throne.
sentence_207: The Achaemenid Empire is normally considered to have fallen with Darius.
sentence_208: Alexander viewed Bessus as a usurper and set out to defeat him.
sentence_209: This campaign, initially against Bessus, turned into a grand tour of central Asia.
sentence_210: Alexander founded a series of new cities, all called Alexandria, including modern [[Kandahar|Kandahar]] in Afghanistan, and [[Alexandria_Eschate|Alexandria Eschate]] ("The Furthest") in modern [[Tajikistan|Tajikistan]].
sentence_211: The campaign took Alexander through [[Media_(region)|Media]], [[Parthia|Parthia]], [[Aria_(satrapy)|Aria]] (West Afghanistan), [[Drangiana|Drangiana]], [[Arachosia|Arachosia]] (South and Central Afghanistan), [[Bactria|Bactria]] (North and Central Afghanistan), and [[Scythia|Scythia]].
sentence_212: In 329 BC, Spitamenes, who held an undefined position in the satrapy of Sogdiana, betrayed Bessus to [[Ptolemy_I_Soter|Ptolemy]], one of Alexander's trusted companions, and Bessus was executed.
sentence_213: However, when, at some point later, Alexander was on the [[Syr_Darya|Jaxartes]] dealing with an incursion by a horse nomad army, Spitamenes raised Sogdiana in revolt.
sentence_214: Alexander personally defeated the Scythians at the [[Battle_of_Jaxartes|Battle of Jaxartes]] and immediately launched a campaign against Spitamenes, defeating him in the Battle of Gabai.
sentence_215: After the defeat, Spitamenes was killed by his own men, who then sued for peace.
sentence_216: During this time, Alexander adopted some elements of Persian dress and customs at his court, notably the custom of proskynesis, either a symbolic kissing of the hand, or prostration on the ground, that Persians showed to their social superiors.
sentence_217: The Greeks regarded the gesture as the province of [[Deities|deities]] and believed that Alexander meant to deify himself by requiring it.
sentence_218: This cost him the sympathies of many of his countrymen, and he eventually abandoned it.
sentence_219: A plot against his life was revealed, and one of his officers, [[Philotas|Philotas]], was executed for failing to alert Alexander.
sentence_220: The death of the son necessitated the death of the father, and thus [[Parmenion|Parmenion]], who had been charged with guarding the treasury at [[Ecbatana|Ecbatana]], was assassinated at Alexander's command, to prevent attempts at vengeance.
sentence_221: Most infamously, Alexander personally killed the man who had saved his life at Granicus, [[Cleitus_the_Black|Cleitus the Black]], during a violent drunken altercation at [[Maracanda|Maracanda]] (modern day [[Samarkand|Samarkand]] in [[Uzbekistan|Uzbekistan]]), in which Cleitus accused Alexander of several judgmental mistakes and most especially, of having forgotten the Macedonian ways in favour of a corrupt oriental lifestyle.
sentence_222: Later, in the Central Asian campaign, a second plot against his life was revealed, this one instigated by his own royal [[Page_(servant)|pages]].
sentence_223: His official historian, [[Callisthenes|Callisthenes]] of [[Olynthus|Olynthus]], was implicated in the plot, and in the [[Anabasis_of_Alexander|Anabasis of Alexander]], [[Arrian|Arrian]] states that Callisthenes and the pages were then tortured on the [[Rack_(torture)|rack]] as punishment, and likely died soon after.
sentence_224: It remains unclear if Callisthenes was actually involved in the plot, for prior to his accusation he had fallen out of favour by leading the opposition to the attempt to introduce proskynesis.
sentence_225: When Alexander set out for Asia, he left his general [[Antipater|Antipater]], an experienced military and political leader and part of Philip II's "Old Guard", in charge of Macedon.
sentence_226: Alexander's sacking of Thebes ensured that Greece remained quiet during his absence.
sentence_227: The one exception was a call to arms by Spartan king [[Agis_III|Agis III]] in 331 BC, whom Antipater defeated and killed in the [[Battle_of_Megalopolis|battle of Megalopolis]].
sentence_228: Antipater referred the Spartans' punishment to the League of Corinth, which then deferred to Alexander, who chose to pardon them.
sentence_229: There was also considerable friction between Antipater and Olympias, and each complained to Alexander about the other.
sentence_230: In general, Greece enjoyed a period of peace and prosperity during Alexander's campaign in Asia.
sentence_231: Alexander sent back vast sums from his conquest, which stimulated the economy and increased trade across his empire.
sentence_232: However, Alexander's constant demands for troops and the migration of Macedonians throughout his empire depleted Macedon's strength, greatly weakening it in the years after Alexander, and ultimately led to its subjugation by Rome after the Third Macedonian War (171–168 BC).
sentence_233: Main article: [[Indian_campaign_of_Alexander_the_Great|Indian campaign of Alexander the Great]]
sentence_234: After the death of Spitamenes and his marriage to Roxana (Raoxshna in [[Old_Iranian|Old Iranian]]) to cement relations with his new satrapies, Alexander turned to the [[Indian_subcontinent|Indian subcontinent]].
sentence_235: He invited the chieftains of the former satrapy of [[Gandhara|Gandhara]] (a region presently straddling eastern [[Afghanistan|Afghanistan]] and northern [[Pakistan|Pakistan]]), to come to him and submit to his authority.
sentence_236: [[Omphis|Omphis]] (Indian name [[Ambhi|Ambhi]]), the ruler of [[Taxila|Taxila]], whose kingdom extended from the [[Indus|Indus]] to the Hydaspes (Jhelum), complied, but the chieftains of some hill clans, including the Aspasioi and Assakenoi sections of the Kambojas (known in Indian texts also as Ashvayanas and Ashvakayanas), refused to submit.
sentence_237: [[Ambhi|Ambhi]] hastened to relieve Alexander of his apprehension and met him with valuable presents, placing himself and all his forces at his disposal.
sentence_238: Alexander not only returned Ambhi his title and the gifts but he also presented him with a wardrobe of "Persian robes, gold and silver ornaments, 30 horses and 1,000 talents in gold".
sentence_239: Alexander was emboldened to divide his forces, and Ambhi assisted [[Hephaestion|Hephaestion]] and [[Perdiccas|Perdiccas]] in constructing a bridge over the Indus where it bends at Hund, supplied their troops with provisions, and received Alexander himself, and his whole army, in his capital city of Taxila, with every demonstration of friendship and the most liberal hospitality.
sentence_240: On the subsequent advance of the [[Macedon|Macedonian]] king, Taxiles accompanied him with a force of 5,000 men and took part in the battle of the Hydaspes River.
sentence_241: After that victory he was sent by Alexander in pursuit of [[Porus|Porus]] (Indian name Puru), to whom he was charged to offer favourable terms, but narrowly escaped losing his life at the hands of his old enemy.
sentence_242: Subsequently, however, the two rivals were reconciled by the personal mediation of Alexander; and Taxiles, after having contributed zealously to the equipment of the fleet on the Hydaspes, was entrusted by the king with the government of the whole territory between that river and the Indus.
sentence_243: A considerable accession of power was granted him after the death of [[Philip_(son_of_Machatas)|Philip]], son of Machatas; and he was allowed to retain his authority at the death of Alexander himself (323 BC), as well as in the subsequent partition of the provinces at Triparadisus, 321 BC.
sentence_244: In the winter of 327/326 BC, Alexander personally led a campaign against the Aspasioi of [[Kunar_Valley|Kunar]] valleys, the Guraeans of the [[Panjkora|Guraeus]] valley, and the Assakenoi of the [[Swat_(Pakistan)|Swat]] and [[Buner_Valley|Buner]] valleys.
sentence_245: A fierce contest ensued with the Aspasioi in which Alexander was wounded in the shoulder by a dart, but eventually the Aspasioi lost.
sentence_246: Alexander then faced the Assakenoi, who fought against him from the strongholds of Massaga, Ora and [[Aornos|Aornos]].
sentence_247: The fort of Massaga was reduced only after days of bloody fighting, in which Alexander was wounded seriously in the ankle.
sentence_248: According to [[Quintus_Curtius_Rufus|Curtius]], "Not only did Alexander slaughter the entire population of Massaga, but also did he reduce its buildings to rubble."
sentence_249: A similar slaughter followed at Ora.
sentence_250: In the aftermath of Massaga and Ora, numerous Assakenians fled to the fortress of [[Aornos|Aornos]].
sentence_251: Alexander followed close behind and captured the strategic hill-fort after four bloody days.
sentence_252: After Aornos, Alexander crossed the Indus and fought and won an epic battle against [[Porus|King Porus]], who ruled a region lying between the Hydaspes and the Acesines ([[Chenab|Chenab]]), in what is now the [[Punjab_region|Punjab]], in the Battle of the Hydaspes in 326 BC.
sentence_253: Alexander was impressed by Porus' bravery, and made him an ally.
sentence_254: He appointed Porus as satrap, and added to Porus' territory land that he did not previously own, towards the south-east, up to the Hyphasis ([[Beas|Beas]]).
sentence_255: Choosing a local helped him control these lands so distant from Greece.
sentence_256: Alexander founded two cities on opposite sides of the Hydaspes river, naming one [[Alexandria_Bucephalous|Bucephala]], in honour of his horse, who died around this time.
sentence_257: The other was [[Nicaea_(Punjab)|Nicaea]] (Victory), thought to be located at the site of modern-day [[Mong,_Punjab|Mong, Punjab]].
sentence_258: [[Philostratus_the_Elder|Philostratus the Elder]] in the [[Life_of_Apollonius_of_Tyana|Life of Apollonius of Tyana]] writes that in the army of Porus there was an elephant who fought brave against Alexander's army and Alexander dedicated it to the [[Helios|Helios]] (Sun) and named it Ajax, because he thought that a so great animal deserved a great name.
sentence_259: The elephant had gold rings around its tusks and an inscription was on them written in Greek: "Alexander the son of Zeus dedicates Ajax to the Helios" (ΑΛΕΞΑΝΔΡΟΣ Ο ΔΙΟΣ ΤΟΝ ΑΙΑΝΤΑ ΤΩΙ ΗΛΙΩΙ).
sentence_260: East of Porus' kingdom, near the [[Ganges_River|Ganges River]], was the [[Nanda_dynasty|Nanda Empire]] of Magadha, and further east, the [[Gangaridai|Gangaridai Empire]] of [[Bengal|Bengal]] region of the [[Indian_subcontinent|Indian subcontinent]].
sentence_261: Fearing the prospect of facing other large armies and exhausted by years of campaigning, Alexander's army mutinied at the [[Beas_River|Hyphasis River (Beas)]], refusing to march farther east.
sentence_262: This river thus marks the easternmost extent of Alexander's conquests.
sentence_263: Alexander tried to persuade his soldiers to march farther, but his general [[Coenus_(general)|Coenus]] pleaded with him to change his opinion and return; the men, he said, "longed to again see their parents, their wives and children, their homeland".
sentence_264: Alexander eventually agreed and turned south, marching along the [[Indus_River|Indus]].
sentence_265: Along the way his army conquered the [[Malhi|Malhi]] (in modern-day [[Multan|Multan]]) and other Indian tribes and Alexander sustained an injury during the siege.
sentence_266: Alexander sent much of his army to Carmania (modern southern [[Iran|Iran]]) with general [[Craterus|Craterus]], and commissioned a fleet to explore the [[Persian_Gulf|Persian Gulf]] shore under his admiral [[Nearchus|Nearchus]], while he led the rest back to Persia through the more difficult southern route along the [[Gedrosia|Gedrosian Desert]] and [[Makran|Makran]].
sentence_267: Alexander reached Susa in 324 BC, but not before losing many men to the harsh desert.
sentence_268: Discovering that many of his [[Satrap|satraps]] and military governors had misbehaved in his absence, Alexander executed several of them as examples on his way to [[Susa|Susa]].
sentence_269: As a gesture of thanks, he paid off the debts of his soldiers, and announced that he would send over-aged and disabled veterans back to Macedon, led by Craterus.
sentence_270: His troops misunderstood his intention and mutinied at the town of [[Opis|Opis]].
sentence_271: They refused to be sent away and criticized his adoption of Persian customs and dress and the introduction of Persian officers and soldiers into Macedonian units.
sentence_272: After three days, unable to persuade his men to back down, Alexander gave Persians command posts in the army and conferred Macedonian military titles upon Persian units.
sentence_273: The Macedonians quickly begged forgiveness, which Alexander accepted, and held a great banquet for several thousand of his men at which he and they ate together.
sentence_274: In an attempt to craft a lasting harmony between his Macedonian and Persian subjects, Alexander [[Susa_weddings|held a mass marriage]] of his senior officers to Persian and other noblewomen at Susa, but few of those marriages seem to have lasted much beyond a year.
sentence_275: Meanwhile, upon his return to Persia, Alexander learned that guards of the [[Tomb_of_Cyrus_the_Great|tomb of Cyrus the Great]] in [[Pasargadae|Pasargadae]] had desecrated it, and swiftly executed them.
sentence_276: Alexander admired [[Cyrus_the_Great|Cyrus the Great]], from an early age reading Xenophon's [[Cyropaedia|Cyropaedia]], which described Cyrus's heroism in battle and governance as a king and legislator.
sentence_277: During his visit to Pasargadae Alexander ordered his architect [[Aristobulus_of_Cassandreia|Aristobulus]] to decorate the interior of the sepulchral chamber of Cyrus' tomb.
sentence_278: Afterwards, Alexander travelled to Ecbatana to retrieve the bulk of the Persian treasure.
sentence_279: There, his closest friend and possible lover, [[Hephaestion|Hephaestion]], died of illness or poisoning.
sentence_280: Hephaestion's death devastated Alexander, and he ordered the preparation of an expensive [[Funeral_pyre|funeral pyre]] in Babylon, as well as a decree for public mourning.
sentence_281: Back in Babylon, Alexander planned a series of new campaigns, beginning with an invasion of Arabia, but he would not have a chance to realize them, as he died shortly after Hephaestion.
sentence_282: Main article: [[Death_of_Alexander_the_Great|Death of Alexander the Great]]
sentence_283: On either 10 or 11 June 323 BC, Alexander died in the palace of [[Nebuchadnezzar_II|Nebuchadnezzar II]], in [[Babylon|Babylon]], at age 32.
sentence_284: There are two different versions of Alexander's death and details of the death differ slightly in each.
sentence_285: [[Plutarch|Plutarch]]'s account is that roughly 14 days before his death, Alexander entertained admiral [[Nearchus|Nearchus]], and spent the night and next day drinking with [[Medius_of_Larissa|Medius of Larissa]].
sentence_286: He developed a fever, which worsened until he was unable to speak.
sentence_287: The common soldiers, anxious about his health, were granted the right to file past him as he silently waved at them.
sentence_288: In the second account, [[Diodorus_Siculus|Diodorus]] recounts that Alexander was struck with pain after downing a large bowl of unmixed wine in honour of [[Heracles|Heracles]], followed by 11 days of weakness; he did not develop a fever and died after some agony.
sentence_289: [[Arrian|Arrian]] also mentioned this as an alternative, but Plutarch specifically denied this claim.
sentence_290: Given the propensity of the Macedonian aristocracy to assassination, foul play featured in multiple accounts of his death.
sentence_291: Diodorus, Plutarch, Arrian and [[Justin_(historian)|Justin]] all mentioned the theory that Alexander was poisoned.
sentence_292: Justin stated that Alexander was the victim of a poisoning conspiracy, Plutarch dismissed it as a fabrication, while both Diodorus and Arrian noted that they mentioned it only for the sake of completeness.
sentence_293: The accounts were nevertheless fairly consistent in designating [[Antipater|Antipater]], recently removed as Macedonian viceroy, and at odds with Olympias, as the head of the alleged plot.
sentence_294: Perhaps taking his summons to Babylon as a death sentence, and having seen the fate of Parmenion and Philotas, Antipater purportedly arranged for Alexander to be poisoned by his son Iollas, who was Alexander's wine-pourer.
sentence_295: There was even a suggestion that Aristotle may have participated.
sentence_296: The strongest argument against the poison theory is the fact that twelve days passed between the start of his illness and his death; such long-acting poisons were probably not available.
sentence_297: However, in a 2003 BBC documentary investigating the death of Alexander, Leo Schep from the New Zealand National Poisons Centre proposed that the plant white hellebore ([[Veratrum_album|Veratrum album]]), which was known in antiquity, may have been used to poison Alexander.
sentence_298: In a 2014 manuscript in the journal [[Clinical_Toxicology|Clinical Toxicology]], Schep suggested Alexander's wine was spiked with Veratrum album, and that this would produce poisoning symptoms that match the course of events described in the [[Alexander_Romance|Alexander Romance]].
sentence_299: Veratrum album poisoning can have a prolonged course and it was suggested that if Alexander was poisoned, Veratrum album offers the most plausible cause.
sentence_300: Another poisoning explanation put forward in 2010 proposed that the circumstances of his death were compatible with poisoning by water of the river Styx (modern-day [[Mavroneri|Mavroneri]] in Arcadia, Greece) that contained [[Calicheamicin|calicheamicin]], a dangerous compound produced by bacteria.
sentence_301: Several [[Natural_causes|natural causes]] (diseases) have been suggested, including [[Malaria|malaria]] and [[Typhoid_fever|typhoid fever]].
sentence_302: A 1998 article in the New England Journal of Medicine attributed his death to typhoid fever complicated by [[Bowel_perforation|bowel perforation]] and ascending paralysis.
sentence_303: Another recent analysis suggested pyogenic (infectious) spondylitis or [[Meningitis|meningitis]].
sentence_304: Other illnesses fit the symptoms, including [[Acute_pancreatitis|acute pancreatitis]] and [[West_Nile_virus|West Nile virus]].
sentence_305: Natural-cause theories also tend to emphasize that Alexander's health may have been in general decline after years of heavy drinking and severe wounds.
sentence_306: The anguish that Alexander felt after [[Hephaestion|Hephaestion]]'s death may also have contributed to his declining health.
sentence_307: See also: [[Tomb_of_Alexander_the_Great|Tomb of Alexander the Great]]
sentence_308: Alexander's body was laid in a gold anthropoid [[Sarcophagus|sarcophagus]] that was filled with honey, which was in turn placed in a gold casket.
sentence_309: According to Aelian, a seer called Aristander foretold that the land where Alexander was laid to rest "would be happy and unvanquishable forever".
sentence_310: Perhaps more likely, the successors may have seen possession of the body as a symbol of legitimacy, since burying the prior king was a [[Royal_prerogative|royal prerogative]].
sentence_311: While Alexander's funeral cortege was on its way to Macedon, Ptolemy seized it and took it temporarily to Memphis.
sentence_312: His successor, [[Ptolemy_II_Philadelphus|Ptolemy II Philadelphus]], transferred the sarcophagus to Alexandria, where it remained until at least [[Late_Antiquity|late Antiquity]].
sentence_313: [[Ptolemy_IX_Lathyros|Ptolemy IX Lathyros]], one of Ptolemy's final successors, replaced Alexander's sarcophagus with a glass one so he could convert the original to coinage.
sentence_314: The recent discovery of an [[Kasta_Tomb|enormous tomb]] in northern Greece, at [[Amphipolis|Amphipolis]], dating from the time of Alexander the Great has given rise to speculation that its original intent was to be the burial place of Alexander.
sentence_315: This would fit with the intended destination of Alexander's funeral cortege.
sentence_316: However, the memorial was found to be dedicated to the dearest friend of Alexander the Great, [[Hephaestion|Hephaestion]].
sentence_317: [[Pompey|Pompey]], [[Julius_Caesar|Julius Caesar]] and [[Augustus|Augustus]] all visited the tomb in Alexandria, where Augustus, allegedly, accidentally knocked the nose off.
sentence_318: [[Caligula|Caligula]] was said to have taken Alexander's breastplate from the tomb for his own use.
sentence_319: Around AD 200, Emperor [[Septimius_Severus|Septimius Severus]] closed Alexander's tomb to the public.
sentence_320: His son and successor, [[Caracalla|Caracalla]], a great admirer, visited the tomb during his own reign.
sentence_321: After this, details on the fate of the tomb are hazy.
sentence_322: The so-called "[[Alexander_Sarcophagus|Alexander Sarcophagus]]", discovered near Sidon and now in the [[Istanbul_Archaeology_Museum|Istanbul Archaeology Museum]], is so named not because it was thought to have contained Alexander's remains, but because its bas-reliefs depict Alexander and his companions fighting the Persians and hunting.
sentence_323: It was originally thought to have been the sarcophagus of [[Abdalonymus|Abdalonymus]] (died 311 BC), the king of Sidon appointed by Alexander immediately following the [[Battle_of_Issus|battle of Issus]] in 331.
sentence_324: However, more recently, it has been suggested that it may date from earlier than Abdalonymus' death.
sentence_325: [[Demades|Demades]] likened the Macedonian army, after the death of Alexander, to the blinded [[Cyclops|Cyclops]], due to the many random and disorderly movements that it made.
sentence_326: In addition, Leosthenes, also, likened the anarchy between the generals, after Alexander's death, to the blinded Cyclops "who after he had lost his eye went feeling and groping about with his hands before him, not knowing where to lay them".
sentence_327: Main articles: [[Partition_of_Babylon|Partition of Babylon]] and Diadochi
sentence_328: Alexander's death was so sudden that when reports of his death reached Greece, they were not immediately believed.
sentence_329: Alexander had no obvious or legitimate heir, his son Alexander IV by Roxane being born after Alexander's death.
sentence_330: According to Diodorus, Alexander's companions asked him on his deathbed to whom he bequeathed his kingdom; his laconic reply was "tôi kratistôi"—"to the strongest".
sentence_331: Another theory is that his successors wilfully or erroneously misheard "tôi Kraterôi"—"to Craterus", the general leading his Macedonian troops home and newly entrusted with the regency of Macedonia.
sentence_332: Arrian and Plutarch claimed that Alexander was speechless by this point, implying that this was an apocryphal story.
sentence_333: Diodorus, Curtius and Justin offered the more plausible story that Alexander passed his [[Seal_(device)|signet ring]] to [[Perdiccas|Perdiccas]], a bodyguard and leader of the companion cavalry, in front of witnesses, thereby nominating him.
sentence_334: Perdiccas initially did not claim power, instead suggesting that Roxane's baby would be king, if male; with himself, [[Craterus|Craterus]], Leonnatus, and Antipater as guardians.
sentence_335: However, the infantry, under the command of [[Meleager_(general)|Meleager]], rejected this arrangement since they had been excluded from the discussion.
sentence_336: Instead, they supported Alexander's half-brother Philip Arrhidaeus.
sentence_337: Eventually, the two sides reconciled, and after the birth of Alexander IV, he and Philip III were appointed joint kings, albeit in name only.
sentence_338: Dissension and rivalry soon afflicted the Macedonians, however.
sentence_339: The satrapies handed out by Perdiccas at the [[Partition_of_Babylon|Partition of Babylon]] became power bases each general used to bid for power.
sentence_340: After the assassination of Perdiccas in 321 BC, Macedonian unity collapsed, and 40 years of war between "The Successors" (Diadochi) ensued before the Hellenistic world settled into four stable power blocs: [[Ptolemaic_Kingdom|Ptolemaic]] Egypt, [[Seleucid_Empire|Seleucid]] Mesopotamia and Central Asia, [[Attalid_dynasty|Attalid]] Anatolia, and [[Antigonid_dynasty|Antigonid]] Macedon.
sentence_341: In the process, both Alexander IV and Philip III were murdered.
sentence_342: [[Diodorus_Siculus|Diodorus]] stated that Alexander had given detailed written instructions to Craterus some time before his death.
sentence_343: Craterus started to carry out Alexander's commands, but the successors chose not to further implement them, on the grounds they were impractical and extravagant.
sentence_344: Nevertheless, Perdiccas read Alexander's will to his troops.
sentence_345: Alexander's will called for military expansion into the southern and western Mediterranean, monumental constructions, and the intermixing of Eastern and Western populations.
sentence_346: It included:

list.value: Construction of a monumental tomb for his father Philip, "to match the greatest of the [[Egyptian_pyramids|pyramids of Egypt]]"
Erection of great temples in [[Delos|Delos]], [[Delphi|Delphi]], [[Dodona|Dodona]], [[Dium|Dium]], [[Amphipolis|Amphipolis]], and a monumental temple to [[Athena|Athena]] at [[Troy|Troy]]
Conquest of Arabia and the entire Mediterranean basin

Development of cities and the "transplant of populations from Asia to Europe and in the opposite direction from Europe to Asia, in order to bring the largest continent to common unity and to friendship by means of intermarriage and family ties"

sentence_347: Alexander earned the epithet "the Great" due to his unparalleled success as a military commander.
sentence_348: He never lost a battle, despite typically being outnumbered.
sentence_349: This was due to use of terrain, phalanx and cavalry tactics, bold strategy, and the fierce loyalty of his troops.
sentence_350: The [[Macedonian_phalanx|Macedonian phalanx]], armed with the sarissa, a spear 6 metres (20 ft) long, had been developed and perfected by Philip II through rigorous training, and Alexander used its speed and manoeuvrability to great effect against larger but more disparate Persian forces.
sentence_351: Alexander also recognized the potential for disunity among his diverse army, which employed various languages and weapons.
sentence_352: He overcame this by being personally involved in battle, in the manner of a Macedonian king.
sentence_353: In his first battle in Asia, at Granicus, Alexander used only a small part of his forces, perhaps 13,000 infantry with 5,000 cavalry, against a much larger Persian force of 40,000.
sentence_354: Alexander placed the phalanx at the center and cavalry and archers on the wings, so that his line matched the length of the Persian cavalry line, about 3 km (1.86 mi).
sentence_355: By contrast, the Persian infantry was stationed behind its cavalry.
sentence_356: This ensured that Alexander would not be outflanked, while his phalanx, armed with long pikes, had a considerable advantage over the Persians' scimitars and [[Javelins|javelins]].
sentence_357: Macedonian losses were negligible compared to those of the Persians.
sentence_358: At Issus in 333 BC, his first confrontation with Darius, he used the same deployment, and again the central phalanx pushed through.
sentence_359: Alexander personally led the charge in the center, routing the opposing army.
sentence_360: At the decisive encounter with Darius at Gaugamela, Darius equipped his chariots with scythes on the wheels to break up the phalanx and equipped his cavalry with pikes.
sentence_361: Alexander arranged a double phalanx, with the center advancing at an angle, parting when the chariots bore down and then reforming.
sentence_362: The advance was successful and broke Darius' center, causing the latter to flee once again.
sentence_363: When faced with opponents who used unfamiliar fighting techniques, such as in Central Asia and India, Alexander adapted his forces to his opponents' style.
sentence_364: Thus, in [[Bactria|Bactria]] and [[Sogdiana|Sogdiana]], Alexander successfully used his javelin throwers and archers to prevent outflanking movements, while massing his cavalry at the center.
sentence_365: In India, confronted by Porus' elephant corps, the Macedonians opened their ranks to envelop the elephants and used their sarissas to strike upwards and dislodge the elephants' handlers.
sentence_366: Greek biographer [[Plutarch|Plutarch]] (c. 45 – c. 120 AD) describes Alexander's appearance as:
sentence_367: The semi-legendary [[Alexander_romance|Alexander Romance]] also suggests that Alexander exhibited [[Heterochromia_iridum|heterochromia iridum]]: that one eye was dark and the other light.
sentence_368: British historian [[Peter_Green_(historian)|Peter Green]] provided a description of Alexander's appearance, based on his review of statues and some ancient documents:
sentence_369: Historian and [[Egyptologist|Egyptologist]] [[Joann_Fletcher|Joann Fletcher]] has said that the Alexander had blond hair.
sentence_370: Ancient authors recorded that Alexander was so pleased with portraits of himself created by [[Lysippos|Lysippos]] that he forbade other sculptors from crafting his image.
sentence_371: Lysippos had often used the [[Contrapposto|contrapposto]] sculptural scheme to portray Alexander and other characters such as [[Apoxyomenos|Apoxyomenos]], [[Hermes|Hermes]] and [[Eros|Eros]].
sentence_372: Lysippos' sculpture, famous for its naturalism, as opposed to a stiffer, more static pose, is thought to be the most faithful depiction.
sentence_373: Some of Alexander's strongest personality traits formed in response to his parents.
sentence_374: His mother had huge ambitions, and encouraged him to believe it was his destiny to conquer the Persian Empire.
sentence_375: Olympias' influence instilled a sense of destiny in him, and Plutarch tells how his ambition "kept his spirit serious and lofty in advance of his years".
sentence_376: However, his father Philip was Alexander's most immediate and influential role model, as the young Alexander watched him campaign practically every year, winning victory after victory while ignoring severe wounds.
sentence_377: Alexander's relationship with his father forged the competitive side of his personality; he had a need to outdo his father, illustrated by his reckless behaviour in battle.
sentence_378: While Alexander worried that his father would leave him "no great or brilliant achievement to be displayed to the world", he also downplayed his father's achievements to his companions.
sentence_379: According to Plutarch, among Alexander's traits were a violent temper and rash, impulsive nature, which undoubtedly contributed to some of his decisions.
sentence_380: Although Alexander was stubborn and did not respond well to orders from his father, he was open to reasoned debate.
sentence_381: He had a calmer side—perceptive, logical, and calculating.
sentence_382: He had a great desire for knowledge, a love for philosophy, and was an avid reader.
sentence_383: This was no doubt in part due to Aristotle's tutelage; Alexander was intelligent and quick to learn.
sentence_384: His intelligent and rational side was amply demonstrated by his ability and success as a general.
sentence_385: He had great self-restraint in "pleasures of the body", in contrast with his lack of [[Self-control|self-control]] with alcohol.
sentence_386: Alexander was erudite and patronized both arts and sciences.
sentence_387: However, he had little interest in sports or the [[Ancient_Olympic_Games|Olympic games]] (unlike his father), seeking only the [[Homeric|Homeric]] ideals of honour (timê) and glory (kudos).
sentence_388: He had great [[Charisma|charisma]] and force of personality, characteristics which made him a great leader.
sentence_389: His unique abilities were further demonstrated by the inability of any of his generals to unite Macedonia and retain the Empire after his death—only Alexander had the ability to do so.
sentence_390: During his final years, and especially after the death of Hephaestion, Alexander began to exhibit signs of [[Megalomania|megalomania]] and [[Paranoia|paranoia]].
sentence_391: His extraordinary achievements, coupled with his own ineffable sense of destiny and the flattery of his companions, may have combined to produce this effect.
sentence_392: His [[Delusions_of_grandeur|delusions of grandeur]] are readily visible in his [[#Will|will]] and in his desire to conquer the world, in as much as he is by various sources described as having boundless ambition, an epithet, the meaning of which has descended into an historical cliché.
sentence_393: He appears to have believed himself a deity, or at least sought to deify himself.
sentence_394: Olympias always insisted to him that he was the son of Zeus, a theory apparently confirmed to him by the oracle of Amun at [[Siwa_Oasis|Siwa]].
sentence_395: He began to identify himself as the son of Zeus-Ammon.
sentence_396: Alexander adopted elements of Persian dress and customs at court, notably proskynesis, a practice of which Macedonians disapproved, and were loath to perform.
sentence_397: This behaviour cost him the sympathies of many of his countrymen.
sentence_398: However, Alexander also was a pragmatic ruler who understood the difficulties of ruling culturally disparate peoples, many of whom lived in kingdoms where the king was divine.
sentence_399: Thus, rather than megalomania, his behaviour may simply have been a practical attempt at strengthening his rule and keeping his empire together.
sentence_400: Main article: Personal relationships of Alexander the Great
sentence_401: Alexander married three times: [[Roxana|Roxana]], daughter of the [[Sogdia|Sogdian]] nobleman [[Oxyartes|Oxyartes]] of [[Bactria|Bactria]], out of love; and the Persian princesses [[Stateira_II|Stateira II]] and [[Parysatis_II|Parysatis II]], the former a daughter of [[Darius_III|Darius III]] and latter a daughter of [[Artaxerxes_III|Artaxerxes III]], for political reasons.
sentence_402: He apparently had two sons, [[Alexander_IV_of_Macedon|Alexander IV of Macedon]] by Roxana and, possibly, [[Heracles_of_Macedon|Heracles of Macedon]] from his mistress [[Barsine|Barsine]].
sentence_403: He lost another child when Roxana miscarried at Babylon.
sentence_404: Alexander also had a close relationship with his friend, general, and bodyguard [[Hephaestion|Hephaestion]], the son of a Macedonian noble.
sentence_405: Hephaestion's death devastated Alexander.
sentence_406: This event may have contributed to Alexander's failing health and detached mental state during his final months.
sentence_407: Alexander's sexuality has been the subject of speculation and controversy in modern times.
sentence_408: The Roman era writer [[Athenaeus|Athenaeus]] says, based on the scholar [[Dicaearchus|Dicaearchus]], who was Alexander's contemporary, that the king "was quite excessively keen on boys", and that Alexander sexually embraced his eunuch Bagoas in public.
sentence_409: This episode is also told by Plutarch, probably based on the same source.
sentence_410: None of Alexander's contemporaries, however, are known to have explicitly described Alexander's relationship with Hephaestion as sexual, though the pair was often compared to [[Achilles_and_Patroclus|Achilles and Patroclus]], whom classical Greek culture painted as a couple.
sentence_411: Aelian writes of Alexander's visit to [[Troy|Troy]] where "Alexander garlanded the tomb of Achilles, and Hephaestion that of [[Patroclus|Patroclus]], the latter hinting that he was a beloved of Alexander, in just the same way as Patroclus was of Achilles."
sentence_412: Some modern historians (e.g., [[Robin_Lane_Fox|Robin Lane Fox]]) believe not only that Alexander's youthful relationship with Hephaestion was sexual, but that their sexual contacts may have continued into adulthood, which went against the social norms of at least some Greek cities, such as Athens, though some modern researchers have tentatively proposed that Macedonia (or at least the Macedonian court) may have been more tolerant of homosexuality between adults.
sentence_413: Green argues that there is little evidence in ancient sources that Alexander had much carnal interest in women; he did not produce an heir until the very end of his life.
sentence_414: However, Ogden calculates that Alexander, who impregnated his partners thrice in eight years, had a higher matrimonial record than his father at the same age.
sentence_415: Two of these pregnancies — Stateira's and Barsine's — are of dubious legitimacy.
sentence_416: According to Diodorus Siculus, Alexander accumulated a harem in the style of Persian kings, but he used it rather sparingly, showing great self-control in "pleasures of the body".
sentence_417: Nevertheless, Plutarch described how Alexander was infatuated by Roxana while complimenting him on not forcing himself on her.
sentence_418: Green suggested that, in the context of the period, Alexander formed quite strong friendships with women, including [[Ada_of_Caria|Ada of Caria]], who adopted him, and even Darius' mother [[Sisygambis|Sisygambis]], who supposedly died from grief upon hearing of Alexander's death.
