sentence_156: Modern shopping areas are mostly found in [[Kızılay,_Ankara|Kızılay]], or on Tunalı Hilmi Avenue, including the modern mall of [[List_of_shopping_malls_in_Turkey#Ankara|Karum]] (named after the ancient [[Assyria|Assyrian]] merchant colonies called [[Kültepe#Kârum_Kaneš|Kârum]] that were established in [[Central_Anatolia_Region|central]] [[Anatolia|Anatolia]] at the beginning of the [[2nd_millennium_BC|2nd millennium BC]]) which is located towards the end of the Avenue; and in [[Çankaya,_Ankara|Çankaya]], the quarter with the highest elevation in the city.
sentence_157: [[Atakule|Atakule Tower]] next to [[Atakule#Atrium_shopping_mall|Atrium Mall]] in Çankaya has views over Ankara and also has a revolving restaurant at the top.
sentence_158: The symbol of the [[List_of_shopping_malls_in_Turkey#Ankara|Armada Shopping Mall]] is an [[Anchor|anchor]], and there's a large anchor monument at its entrance, as a reference to the ancient Greek name of the city, Ἄγκυρα (Ánkyra), which means anchor.
sentence_159: Likewise, the anchor monument is also related with the Spanish name of the mall, Armada, which means naval fleet.
sentence_160: As Ankara started expanding westward in the 1970s, several modern, suburbia-style developments and mini-cities began to rise along the western highway, also known as the [[Eskişehir|Eskişehir]] Road.
sentence_161: The Armada, CEPA and Kentpark malls on the highway, the Galleria, Arcadium and Gordion in Ümitköy, and a huge mall, Real in Bilkent Center, offer North American and European style shopping opportunities (these places can be reached through the Eskişehir Highway.)
sentence_162: There is also the newly expanded [[ANKAmall|ANKAmall]] at the outskirts, on the Istanbul Highway, which houses most of the well-known international brands.
sentence_163: This mall is the largest throughout the Ankara region.
sentence_164: In 2014 a few more shopping malls were open in Ankara.
sentence_165: They are Next Level and Taurus on the Boulevard of [[Mevlana|Mevlana]] (also known as [[Konya|Konya]] Road).
sentence_166: [[Turkish_State_Opera_and_Ballet|Turkish State Opera and Ballet]], the national directorate of opera and ballet companies of Turkey, has its headquarters in Ankara, and serves the city with three venues:

list.value: [[Ankara_Opera_House|Ankara Opera House]] (Opera Sahnesi, also known as Büyük Tiyatro) is the largest of the three venues for opera and ballet in Ankara.

sentence_167: Ankara is host to five classical music orchestras:

list.value: [[Bilkent_Symphony_Orchestra|Bilkent Symphony Orchestra]] (BSO) is a major symphony orchestra of Turkey.
[[Hacettepe_Symphony_Orchestra|Hacettepe Symphony Orchestra]] was founded in 2003 and is conducted by Erol Erdinç.
Başkent Oda Orkestrası (Chamber Orchestra of the Capital)

sentence_168: There are four concert halls in the city:

list.value: [[Bilkent_Concert_Hall|Bilkent Concert Hall]] is a performing arts center in Ankara. It is located in the Bilkent University campus.
[[MEB_Şura_Salonu|MEB Şura Salonu]] (also known as the Festival Hall), It is noted for its tango performances.
[[Çankaya_Çağdaş_Sanatlar_Merkezi_Concert_Hall|Çankaya Çağdaş Sanatlar Merkezi Concert Hall]] was founded in 1994.

sentence_169: The city has been host to several well-established, annual theatre, music, film festivals:

list.value: [[Ankara_International_Music_Festival|Ankara International Music Festival]], a music festival organized in the Turkish capital presenting classical music and ballet programmes.

sentence_170: Ankara also has a number of concert venues such as Eskiyeni, [[IF_Performance_Hall|IF Performance Hall]], [[Jolly_Joker_(venues_chain)|Jolly Joker]], Kite, Nefes Bar, Noxus Pub, Passage Pub and Route, which host the live performances and events of popular musicians.
sentence_171: The [[Turkish_State_Theatres|Turkish State Theatres]] also has its head office in Ankara and runs the following stages in the city:
sentence_172: In addition, the city is served by several private theatre companies, among which , who have their own stage in the city center, is a notable example.
sentence_173: There are about 50 museums in the city.
sentence_174: The [[Museum_of_Anatolian_Civilizations|Museum of Anatolian Civilizations]] (Anadolu Medeniyetleri Müzesi) is situated at the entrance of the [[Ankara_Castle|Ankara Castle]].
sentence_175: It is an old 15th century [[Bedesten|bedesten]] (covered bazaar) that has been restored and now houses a collection of [[Paleolithic|Paleolithic]], [[Neolithic|Neolithic]], [[Hittite_empire|Hatti]], [[Hittites|Hittite]], Phrygian, [[Urartu|Urartian]] and [[Roman_Empire|Roman]] works as well as a major section dedicated to Lydian treasures.
sentence_176: Anıtkabir is located on an imposing hill, which forms the Anıttepe quarter of the city, where the mausoleum of [[Mustafa_Kemal_Atatürk|Mustafa Kemal Atatürk]], founder of the Republic of Turkey, stands.
sentence_177: Completed in 1953, it is an impressive fusion of ancient and modern architectural styles.
sentence_178: An adjacent museum houses a wax statue of Atatürk, his writings, letters and personal items, as well as an exhibition of photographs recording important moments in his life and during the establishment of the Republic.
sentence_179: Anıtkabir is open every day, while the adjacent museum is open every day except Mondays.
sentence_180: [[Ethnography_Museum_of_Ankara|Ankara Ethnography Museum]] (Etnoğrafya Müzesi) is located opposite to the [[Ankara_Opera_House|Ankara Opera House]] on Talat Paşa Boulevard, in the Ulus district.
sentence_181: There is a fine collection of folkloric items, as well as artifacts from the Seljuk and Ottoman periods.
sentence_182: In front of the museum building, there is a [[Marble|marble]] and [[Bronze|bronze]] [[Equestrian_statue|equestrian statue]] of [[Mustafa_Kemal_Atatürk|Mustafa Kemal Atatürk]] (who wears a Republic era modern military uniform, with the rank [[Field_Marshal|Field Marshal]]) which was crafted in 1927 by the renowned Italian sculptor Pietro Canonica.
sentence_183: The [[State_Art_and_Sculpture_Museum|State Art and Sculpture Museum]] (Resim-Heykel Müzesi) which opened to the public in 1980 is close to the Ethnography Museum and houses a rich collection of Turkish art from the late 19th century to the present day.
sentence_184: There are also galleries which host guest exhibitions.
sentence_185: Cer Modern is the modern-arts museum of Ankara, inaugurated on 1 April 2010.
sentence_186: It is situated in the renovated building of the historic [[Turkish_State_Railways|TCDD]] Cer Atölyeleri, formerly a workshop of the [[Turkish_State_Railways|Turkish State Railways]].
sentence_187: The museum incorporates the largest exhibition hall in Turkey.
sentence_188: The museum holds periodic exhibitions of modern and contemporary art as well as hosting other contemporary arts events.
sentence_189: The War of Independence Museum (Kurtuluş Savaşı Müzesi) is located on [[Ulus_Square|Ulus Square]].
sentence_190: It was originally the first Parliament building (TBMM) of the Republic of Turkey.
sentence_191: The War of Independence was planned and directed here as recorded in various photographs and items presently on exhibition.
sentence_192: In another display, [[Wax_sculpture|wax figures]] of former presidents of the Republic of Turkey are on exhibit.
sentence_193: The [[Mehmet_Akif_Literature_Museum_Library|Mehmet Akif Literature Museum Library]] is an important literary museum and archive opened in 2011 and dedicated to [[Mehmet_Akif_Ersoy|Mehmet Akif Ersoy]] (1873–1936), the poet of the [[Turkish_National_Anthem|Turkish National Anthem]].

section_45.value: TCDD Open Air Steam Locomotive Museum

sentence_194: The [[TCDD_Open_Air_Steam_Locomotive_Museum|TCDD Open Air Steam Locomotive Museum]] is an open-air museum which traces the history of [[Steam_locomotive|steam locomotives]].
sentence_195: Ankara Aviation Museum (Hava Kuvvetleri Müzesi Komutanlığı) is located near the Istanbul Road in Etimesgut.
sentence_196: The museum opened to the public in September 1998.
sentence_197: It is home to various missiles, avionics, aviation materials and aircraft that have served in the [[Turkish_Air_Force|Turkish Air Force]] (e.g. combat aircraft such as the [[F-86_Sabre|F-86 Sabre]], [[F-100_Super_Sabre|F-100 Super Sabre]], [[F-102_Delta_Dagger|F-102 Delta Dagger]], [[F-104_Starfighter|F-104 Starfighter]], [[Northrop_F-5|F-5 Freedom Fighter]], [[F-4_Phantom_II|F-4 Phantom]]; and cargo planes such as the [[Transall_C-160|Transall C-160]].)
sentence_198: Also a Hungarian [[Mikoyan-Gurevich_MiG-21|MiG-21]], a Pakistani MiG-19, and a Bulgarian MiG-17 are on display at the museum.
sentence_199: The [[METU_Science_and_Technology_Museum|METU Science and Technology Museum]] (ODTÜ Bilim ve Teknoloji Müzesi) is located inside the [[METU|Middle East Technical University]] campus.
sentence_200: As with all other cities of Turkey, football is the most popular sport in Ankara.
sentence_201: The city has two [[Football_team|football clubs]] competing in the [[Süper_Lig|Turkish Süper Lig]]: [[MKE_Ankaragücü|Ankaragücü]], founded in 1910, is the oldest club in Ankara and is associated with Ankara's military arsenal manufacturing company MKE.
sentence_202: They were the [[Türkiye_Kupası|Turkish Cup]] winners in 1972 and 1981.
sentence_203: [[Gençlerbirliği_S.K.|Gençlerbirliği]], founded in 1923, are known as the Ankara Gale or the Poppies because of their colors: red and black.
sentence_204: They were the Turkish Cup winners in 1987 and 2001.
sentence_205: Gençlerbirliği's B team, [[Hacettepe_S.K.|Hacettepe S.K.]] (formerly known as Gençlerbirliği OFTAŞ) played in the Süper Lig but currently plays in the [[TFF_Second_League|TFF Second League]].
sentence_206: A fourth team, [[Büyükşehir_Belediye_Ankaraspor|Büyükşehir Belediye Ankaraspor]], played in the Süper Lig until 2010, when they were expelled.
sentence_207: The club was reconstituted in 2014 as [[Osmanlıspor|Osmanlıspor]] but have since returned to their old identity as [[Ankaraspor|Ankaraspor]].
sentence_208: Ankaraspor currently play in the [[TFF_First_League|TFF First League]] at the [[Osmanlı_Stadium|Osmanlı Stadium]] in the [[Sincan,_Ankara|Sincan]] district of Yenikent, outside the city center.
sentence_209: [[Keçiörengücü|Keçiörengücü]] also currently play in the [[TFF_First_League|TFF First League]].
sentence_210: Ankara has a large number of minor teams, playing at regional levels.
sentence_211: In the [[TFF_Second_League|TFF Second League]]: Mamak FK in Mamak, [[Ankara_Demirspor|Ankara Demirspor]] in Çankaya, [[Etimesgut_Belediyespor|Etimesgut Belediyespor]] in Etimesgut; in the TFF Third League: [[Çankaya_FK|Çankaya FK]] in Keçiören; Altındağspor in Altındağ; in the [[Turkish_Regional_Amateur_League|Amateur League]]: [[Turanspor|Turanspor]] in Etimesgut, Türk Telekomspor owned by the phone company in Yenimahalle, Çubukspor in Çubuk, and Bağlumspor in Keçiören.
sentence_212: In the [[Turkish_Basketball_League|Turkish Basketball League]], Ankara is represented by [[Türk_Telekom|Türk Telekom]], whose home is the [[Ankara_Arena|Ankara Arena]], and [[TED_Kolejliler|CASA TED Kolejliler]], whose home is the TOBB Sports Hall.
sentence_213: [[Halkbank_Ankara|Halkbank Ankara]] is the leading domestic powerhouse in men's volleyball, having won many championships and cups in the [[Turkish_Men's_Volleyball_League|Turkish Men's Volleyball League]] and even the [[CEV_Cup|CEV Cup]] in 2013.
sentence_214: [[Ankara_Ice_Palace|Ankara Buz Pateni Sarayı]] is where the ice skating and [[Ice_hockey|ice hockey]] competitions take place in the city.
sentence_215: There are many popular spots for [[Skateboarding|skateboarding]] which is active in the city since the 1980s.
sentence_216: Skaters in Ankara usually meet in the park near the [[Grand_National_Assembly_of_Turkey|Grand National Assembly of Turkey]].
sentence_217: The 2012-built [[THF_Sport_Hall|THF Sport Hall]] hosts the [[Turkish_Handball_Super_League|Handball Super League]] and [[Turkish_Women's_Handball_Super_League|Women's Handball Super League]] matches scheduled in Ankara.
sentence_218: Ankara has many parks and open spaces mainly established in the early years of the Republic and well maintained and expanded thereafter.
sentence_219: The most important of these parks are: [[Gençlik_Parkı|Gençlik Parkı]] (houses an [[Amusement_park|amusement park]] with a large pond for rowing), the [[Botanical_garden|Botanical garden]], Seğmenler Park, Anayasa Park, [[Kuğulu_Park|Kuğulu Park]] (famous for the swans received as a gift from the [[PRC|Chinese]] government), [[Abdi_İpekçi|Abdi İpekçi]] Park, [[Esertepe_Parkı|Esertepe Parkı]], Güven Park (see above for the monument), Kurtuluş Park (has an ice-skating rink), [[Altınpark|Altınpark]] (also a prominent exposition/fair area), Harikalar Diyarı (claimed to be Biggest Park of Europe inside city borders) and Göksu Park.
sentence_220: [[Dikmen_Vadisi|Dikmen Vadisi]] (Dikmen Valley) is a 70 hectares (170 acres) park and recreation area situated in Çankaya district.
sentence_221: Gençlik Park was depicted on the reverse of the Turkish 100 [[Turkish_lira|lira]] banknotes of 1952–1976.
sentence_222: [[Atatürk_Forest_Farm_and_Zoo|Atatürk Forest Farm and Zoo]] (Atatürk Orman Çiftliği) is an expansive recreational farming area which houses a [[Zoo|zoo]], several small agricultural farms, [[Greenhouse|greenhouses]], restaurants, a dairy farm and a brewery.
sentence_223: It is a pleasant place to spend a day with family, be it for having picnics, hiking, biking or simply enjoying good food and nature.
sentence_224: There is also an exact replica of the house where Atatürk was born in 1881, in [[Thessaloniki|Thessaloniki]], Greece.
sentence_225: Visitors to the "Çiftlik" (farm) as it is affectionately called by Ankarans, can sample such famous products of the farm such as old-fashioned beer and [[Ice_cream|ice cream]], fresh [[Dairy_product|dairy products]] and meat rolls/kebaps made on charcoal, at a traditional restaurant (Merkez Lokantası, Central Restaurant), cafés and other establishments scattered around the farm.
sentence_226: Ankara is noted, within Turkey, for the multitude of universities it is home to.
sentence_227: These include the following, several of them being among the most reputable in the country:
sentence_228: Main article: [[Turkish_Angora|Turkish Angora]]
sentence_229: Ankara is home to a world-famous domestic [[Cat_breed|cat breed]] – the [[Turkish_Angora|Turkish Angora]], called Ankara kedisi (Ankara cat) in Turkish.
sentence_230: Turkish Angoras are one of the ancient, naturally occurring cat breeds, having originated in Ankara and its surrounding region in central Anatolia.
sentence_231: They mostly have a white, silky, medium to long length coat, no undercoat and a fine bone structure.
sentence_232: There seems to be a connection between the Angora Cats and [[Persian_(cat)|Persians]], and the Turkish Angora is also a distant cousin of the [[Turkish_Van|Turkish Van]].
sentence_233: Although they are known for their shimmery white coat, there are more than twenty varieties including black, blue and reddish fur.
sentence_234: They come in [[Tabby_cat|tabby]] and tabby-white, along with smoke varieties, and are in every color other than pointed, lavender, and cinnamon (all of which would indicate breeding to an outcross.)
sentence_235: Eyes may be blue, green, or amber, or even one blue and one amber or green.
sentence_236: The [[Cat_coat_genetics#White_spotting_and_epistatic_white|W gene]] which is responsible for the white coat and blue eye is closely related to the hearing ability, and the presence of a blue eye can indicate that the cat is deaf to the side the blue eye is located.
sentence_237: However, a great many blue and [[Odd-eyed_cat|odd-eyed]] white cats have normal hearing, and even deaf cats lead a very normal life if kept indoors.
sentence_238: Ears are pointed and large, eyes are almond shaped and the head is massive with a two plane profile.
sentence_239: Another characteristic is the tail, which is often kept parallel to the back.
sentence_240: Main article: [[Angora_goat|Angora goat]]
sentence_241: The [[Angora_goat|Angora goat]] ([[Turkish_language|Turkish]]: Ankara keçisi) is a breed of [[Goat|domestic goat]] that originated in Ankara and its surrounding region in central Anatolia.
sentence_242: This breed was first mentioned in the time of [[Moses|Moses]], roughly in 1500 BC.
sentence_243: The first Angora goats were brought to Europe by [[Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor|Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor]], about 1554, but, like later imports, were not very successful.
sentence_244: Angora goats were first introduced in the United States in 1849 by Dr. James P. Davis.
sentence_245: Seven adult goats were a gift from Sultan [[Abdülmecid_I|Abdülmecid I]] in appreciation for his services and advice on the raising of cotton.
sentence_246: The [[Pile_(textile)|fleece]] taken from an Angora goat is called [[Mohair|mohair]].
sentence_247: A single goat produces between five and eight kilograms (11 and 18 [[Pound_(mass)|pounds]]) of hair per year.
sentence_248: Angoras are shorn twice a year, unlike [[Domestic_sheep|sheep]], which are shorn only once.
sentence_249: Angoras have high nutritional requirements due to their rapid hair growth.
sentence_250: A poor quality diet will curtail mohair development.
sentence_251: The United States, [[Turkey|Turkey]], and South Africa are the top producers of mohair.
sentence_252: For a long period of time, Angora goats were bred for their white coat.
sentence_253: In 1998, the Colored Angora Goat Breeders Association was set up to promote breeding of colored Angoras.
sentence_254: Today, Angora goats produce white, black (deep black to greys and silver), red (the color fades significantly as the goat gets older), and brownish fiber.
sentence_255: Angora goats were depicted on the reverse of the Turkish 50 [[Turkish_lira|lira]] banknotes of 1938–1952.
sentence_256: Main article: [[Angora_rabbit|Angora rabbit]]
sentence_257: The [[Angora_rabbit|Angora rabbit]] ([[Turkish_language|Turkish]]: Ankara tavşanı) is a variety of domestic rabbit bred for its long, soft hair.
sentence_258: The Angora is one of the oldest types of domestic rabbit, originating in Ankara and its surrounding region in central Anatolia, along with the [[Turkish_Angora|Angora cat]] and [[Angora_goat|Angora goat]].
sentence_259: The rabbits were popular pets with French royalty in the mid-18th century, and spread to other parts of Europe by the end of the century.
sentence_260: They first appeared in the United States in the early 20th century.
sentence_261: They are bred largely for their long [[Angora_wool|Angora wool]], which may be removed by [[Sheep_shearing|shearing]], combing, or [[Plucking_(hair_removal)|plucking]] (gently pulling loose wool.)
sentence_262: Angoras are bred mainly for their wool because it is silky and soft.
sentence_263: They have a humorous appearance, as they oddly resemble a fur ball.
sentence_264: Most are calm and docile but should be handled carefully.
sentence_265: Grooming is necessary to prevent the fiber from matting and felting on the rabbit.
sentence_266: A condition called "wool block" is common in Angora rabbits and should be treated quickly.
sentence_267: Sometimes they are shorn in the summer as the long fur can cause the rabbits to overheat.
sentence_268: See also: [[List_of_twin_towns_and_sister_cities_in_Turkey|List of twin towns and sister cities in Turkey]]

title: Ashoka
sentence_0: "Aśoka" and "Asoka" redirect here.
sentence_1: For other uses, see [[Ashoka_(disambiguation)|Ashoka (disambiguation)]].

sentence_2: Ashoka ([[Brahmi|Brāhmi]]: 𑀅𑀲𑁄𑀓, Asoka, [[International_Alphabet_of_Sanskrit_Transliteration|IAST]]: Aśoka, English: [[English|/əˈʃoʊkə/]]), also known as Ashoka the Great, was an Indian emperor of the [[Maurya_Empire|Maurya Dynasty]], who ruled almost all of the [[Indian_subcontinent|Indian subcontinent]] from c. 268 to 232 BCE.
sentence_3: A grandson of the dynasty's founder [[Chandragupta_Maurya|Chandragupta Maurya]], Ashoka promoted the spread of [[Buddhism|Buddhism]] across ancient [[Asia|Asia]].
sentence_4: Considered by many to be one of India's greatest emperors, Ashoka expanded Chandragupta's empire to reign over a realm stretching from present-day [[Afghanistan|Afghanistan]] in the west to [[Bangladesh|Bangladesh]] in the east.
sentence_5: It covered the entire Indian subcontinent except for parts of present-day [[Tamil_Nadu|Tamil Nadu]], [[Karnataka|Karnataka]] and [[Kerala|Kerala]].
sentence_6: The empire's capital was [[Pataliputra|Pataliputra]] (in Magadha, present-day [[Patna|Patna]]), with provincial capitals at [[Taxila|Taxila]] and [[Ujjain|Ujjain]].
sentence_7: Ashoka waged a destructive war against the state of [[Kalinga_(historical_kingdom)|Kalinga]] (modern [[Odisha|Odisha]]), which he conquered in about 260 BCE.
sentence_8: He converted to Buddhism after witnessing the mass deaths of the Kalinga War, which he had waged out of a desire for conquest and which reportedly directly resulted in more than 100,000 deaths and 150,000 deportations.
sentence_9: He is remembered for the Ashoka pillars and edicts, for sending Buddhist monks to [[Sri_Lanka|Sri Lanka]] and [[Central_Asia|Central Asia]], and for establishing monuments marking several significant sites in the life of [[Gautama_Buddha|Gautama Buddha]].
sentence_10: Beyond the [[Edicts_of_Ashoka|Edicts of Ashoka]], biographical information about him relies on legends written centuries later, such as the 2nd-century CE [[Ashokavadana|Ashokavadana]] ("Narrative of Ashoka", a part of the [[Divyavadana|Divyavadana]]), and in the Sri Lankan text [[Mahavamsa|Mahavamsa]] ("Great Chronicle").
sentence_11: The emblem of the modern [[Republic_of_India|Republic of India]] is an adaptation of the [[Lion_Capital_of_Ashoka|Lion Capital of Ashoka]].
sentence_12: His [[Sanskrit|Sanskrit]] name "Aśoka" means "painless, without sorrow" (the [[A_privativum|a privativum]] and śoka, "pain, distress").
sentence_13: In his [[Edicts_of_Ashoka|edicts]], he is referred to as Devānāmpriya (Pali Devānaṃpiya or "the Beloved of the Gods"), and Priyadarśin or Priyadarshi (Pali [[Piyadasī|Piyadasī]] or "He who regards everyone with affection").
sentence_14: His fondness for a tree is the reason for his name being connected to the "Ashoka tree" or [[Polyalthia_longifolia|Polyalthia longifolia]], and this is referenced in the [[Ashokavadana|Ashokavadana]].
sentence_15: In [[The_Outline_of_History|The Outline of History]] (1920), [[H.G._Wells|H.G.
sentence_16: Wells]] wrote, "Amidst the tens of thousands of names of monarchs that crowd the columns of history, their majesties and graciousnesses and serenities and royal highnesses and the like, the name of Ashoka shines, and shines, almost alone, a star."
sentence_17: Information about Ashoka comes from [[List_of_Edicts_of_Ashoka|his own inscriptions]]; other inscriptions that mention him or are possibly from his reign; and ancient literature, especially Buddhist texts.
sentence_18: These sources often contradict each other, although various historians have attempted to correlate their testimony.
sentence_19: Plenty is known or not known, and so, for example, while Ashoka is often attributed with building many hospitals during his time, there is no clear evidence any hospitals existed in ancient India during the 3rd century BC or that Ashoka was responsible for commissioning the construction of any.
sentence_20: Inscriptions
sentence_21: Ashoka's own inscriptions are the earliest self-representations of an imperial power in the Indian subcontinent.
sentence_22: However, these inscriptions are focused mainly on the topic of [[Ashoka's_policy_of_Dhamma|dhamma]], and provide little information regarding other aspects of the Maurya state and society.
sentence_23: Even on the topic of dhamma, the content of these inscriptions cannot be taken at face value: in words of American academic [[John_S._Strong|John S. Strong]], it is sometimes useful to think of Ashoka's messages as propaganda by a politician whose aim is to present a favourable image of himself and his administration, rather than record historical facts.
sentence_24: A small number of other inscriptions also provide some information about Ashoka.
sentence_25: For example, he finds a mention in the 2nd century [[Junagadh_rock_inscription_of_Rudradaman|Junagadh rock inscription of Rudradaman]].
sentence_26: [[Aramaic_Inscription_of_Taxila|An inscription]] discovered at [[Sirkap|Sirkap]] mentions a lost word beginning with "Priy", which is theorised to be Ashoka's title "Priyadarshi", although this is not certain.
sentence_27: Some other inscriptions, such as the [[Sohgaura_copper_plate_inscription|Sohgaura copper plate inscription]], have been tentatively dated to Ashoka's period by a section of scholars, although this is contested by others.
sentence_28: Buddhist legends
sentence_29: Much of the information about Ashoka comes from Buddhist legends, which present him as a great, ideal king.
sentence_30: These legends appear in texts that are not contemporary to Ashoka, and were composed by Buddhist authors, who used various stories to illustrate the impact of their faith on Ashoka.
sentence_31: This makes it necessary to exercise caution while relying on them for historical information.
sentence_32: Among modern scholars, opinions range from downright dismissal of these legends as mythological to acceptance of all historical portions that seem plausible.
sentence_33: The Buddhist legends about Ashoka exist in several languages, including [[Sanskrit|Sanskrit]], [[Pali|Pali]], [[Tibetic_languages|Tibetan]], [[Chinese_language|Chinese]], [[Burmese_language|Burmese]], [[Sinhala_language|Sinhala]], [[Thai_language|Thai]], [[Lao_language|Lao]], and [[Khotanese_language|Khotanese]].
sentence_34: All these legends can be traced to two primary traditions:

list.value: the North Indian tradition preserved in the Sanskrit-language texts such as [[Divyavadana|Divyavadana]] (including its constituent [[Ashokavadana|Ashokavadana]]); and Chinese sources such as A-yü wang chuan and A-yü wang ching.

the Sri Lankan tradition preserved in Pali-lanuage texts, such as [[Dipavamsa|Dipavamsa]], [[Mahavamsa|Mahavamsa]], Vamsatthapakasini (a commentary on Mahavamsa), Buddhaghosha's commentary on the Vinaya, and Samanta-pasadika.

sentence_35: There are several major differences between the two traditions.
sentence_36: For example, the Sri Lankan tradition emphasises Ashoka's role in convening the Third Buddhist council, and his dispatch of several missionaries to distant regions, including his son Mahinda to Sri Lanka.
sentence_37: However, the North Indian tradition makes no mention of these events, and describes other events not found in the Sri Lankan tradition, such as a story about another son named Kunala.
sentence_38: Even while narrating the common stories, the two traditions diverge in several ways.
sentence_39: For example, both Ashokavadana and Mahavamsa mention that Ashoka's queen Tishyarakshita had the Bodhi Tree destroyed.
sentence_40: In Ashokavadana, the queen manages to have the tree healed after she realises her mistake.
sentence_41: In the Mahavamsa, she permanently destroys the tree, but only after a branch of the tree has been transplanted in Sri Lanka.
sentence_42: In another story, both the texts describe Ashoka's unsuccessful attempts to collect a relic of Gautama Buddha from [[Ramagrama_stupa|Ramagrama]].
sentence_43: In Ashokavadana, he fails to do so because he cannot match the devotion of the Nagas who hold the relic; however, in the Mahavamsa, he fails to do so because the Buddha had destined the relic to be enshrined by king [[Dutthagamani|Dutthagamani]] of Sri Lanka.
sentence_44: Using such stories, the Mahavamsa glorifies Sri Lanka as the new preserve of Buddhism.
sentence_45: Other sources
sentence_46: Numismatic, sculptural, and archaeological evidence supplements research on Ashoka.
sentence_47: Ashoka's name appears in the lists of Mauryan kings in the various [[Puranas|Puranas]], but these texts do not provide further details about him, as their [[Brahmanism|Brahmanical]] authors were not patronised by the Mauryans.
sentence_48: Other texts, such as the [[Arthashastra|Arthashastra]] and [[Indica_(Megasthenes)|Indica of Megasthenes]], which provide general information about the Maurya period, can also be used to make inferences about Ashoka's reign.
sentence_49: However, the Arthashastra is a normative text that focuses on an ideal rather than a historical state, and its dating to the Mauryan period is a subject of debate.
sentence_50: The Indica is a lost work, and only parts of it survive in form of paraphrases in later writings.
sentence_51: The 12th-century text [[Rajatarangini|Rajatarangini]] mentions a [[Kashmiris|Kashmiri]] king [[Ashoka_(Gonandiya)|Ashoka of Gonandiya dynasty]] who built several [[Stupa|stupas]]: some scholars, such as [[Aurel_Stein|Aurel Stein]], have identified this king with the Maurya king Ashoka; others, such as Ananda W. P. Guruge dismiss this identification as inaccurate.
sentence_52: Alternative interpretation of the epigraphic evidence
sentence_53: For some scholars such as [[Christopher_I._Beckwith|Christopher I. Beckwith]], Ashoka, whose name only appears in the [[Minor_Rock_Edicts|Minor Rock Edicts]], should be differentiated from the ruler [[Priyadasi|Piyadasi]], or [[Devanampiya|Devanampiya]] Piyadasi (i.e. "Beloved of the Gods Piyadasi", "Beloved of the Gods" being a fairly widespread title for "King"), who is named as the author of the [[Major_Pillar_Edicts|Major Pillar Edicts]] and the [[Major_Rock_Edicts|Major Rock Edicts]].
sentence_54: This inscriptional evidence may suggest that these were two different rulers.
sentence_55: According to him, Piyadasi was living in the 3rd century BCE, probably the son of [[Chandragupta_Maurya|Chandragupta Maurya]] known to the Greeks as [[Amitrochates|Amitrochates]], and only advocating for piety ("[[Dharma|Dharma]]") in his [[Major_Pillar_Edicts|Major Pillar Edicts]] and [[Major_Rock_Edicts|Major Rock Edicts]], without ever mentioning [[Buddhism|Buddhism]], the [[Buddha|Buddha]] or the [[Samgha|Samgha]].
sentence_56: Also, the geographical spread of his inscription shows that Piyadasi ruled a vast Empire, contiguous with the [[Seleucid_Empire|Seleucid Empire]] in the West.
sentence_57: On the contrary, for Beckwith, Ashoka was a later king of the 1st–2nd century CE, whose name only appears explicitly in the [[Minor_Rock_Edicts|Minor Rock Edicts]] and allusively in the [[Minor_Pillar_Edicts|Minor Pillar Edicts]], and who does mention the Buddha and the [[Samgha|Samgha]], explicitly promoting Buddhism.
sentence_58: His inscriptions cover a very different and much smaller geographical area, clustering in Central India.
sentence_59: According to Beckwith, the inscriptions of this later Ashoka were typical of the later forms of "normative Buddhism", which are well attested from inscriptions and Gandhari manuscripts dated to the turn of the millennium, and around the time of the [[Kushan_Empire|Kushan Empire]].
sentence_60: The quality of the inscriptions of this Ashoka is significantly lower than the quality of the inscriptions of the earlier Piyadasi.
sentence_61: The name "A-shoka" literally means "without sorrow".
sentence_62: According to an [[Ashokavadana|Ashokavadana]] legend, his mother gave him this name because his birth removed her sorrows.
sentence_63: The name [[Priyadasi|Priyadasi]] is associated with Ashoka in the 3rd–4th century CE [[Dipavamsa|Dipavamsa]].
sentence_64: The term literally means "he who regards amiably", or "of gracious mien" ([[Sanskrit|Sanskrit]]: Priya-darshi).
sentence_65: It may have been a regnal name adopted by Ashoka.
sentence_66: Ashoka's inscriptions mention his title [[Devanampriya|Devanampiya]] (Sanskrit: Devanampriya, "Beloved of the Gods").
sentence_67: The identification of Devanampiya and Ashoka as the same person is established by the [[Maski#Minor_Rock_Edict_of_Ashoka|Maski]] and Gujarra inscriptions, which use both these terms for the king.
sentence_68: The title was adopted by other kings, including the contemporary king [[Devanampiya_Tissa_of_Anuradhapura|Devanampiya Tissa of Anuradhapura]] and Ashoka's descendant [[Dasharatha_Maurya|Dasharatha Maurya]].
sentence_69: Ashoka's own inscriptions do not describe his early life, and much of the information on this topic comes from apocryphal legends written hundreds of years after him.
sentence_70: While these legends include obviously fictitious details such as narratives of Ashoka's past lives, they include some plausible historical details about Ashoka's period.
sentence_71: The exact date of Ashoka's birth is not certain, as the extant contemporary Indian texts did not record such details.
sentence_72: It is known that he lived in the 3rd century BCE, as his inscriptions mention several contemporary rulers whose dates are known with more certainty, such as [[Antiochus_II_Theos|Antiochus II Theos]], [[Ptolemy_II_Philadelphus|Ptolemy II Philadelphus]], Antigonus II Gonatas, [[Magas_of_Cyrene|Magas of Cyrene]], and Alexander (of [[Alexander_II_of_Epirus|Epirus]] or Corinth).
sentence_73: Thus, Ashoka must have been born sometime in the late 4th century BCE or early 3rd century BCE (c. 304 BCE),
sentence_74: Ashoka's own inscriptions are fairly detailed, but make no mention of his ancestors.
sentence_75: Other sources, such as the [[Puranas|Puranas]] and the [[Mahavamsa|Mahavamsa]] state that his father was the Mauryan emperor [[Bindusara|Bindusara]], and his grandfather was [[Chandragupta_Maurya|Chandragupta]] – the founder of the Empire.
sentence_76: The Ashokavadana also names his father as Bindusara, but traces his ancestry to Buddha's contemporary king [[Bimbisara|Bimbisara]], through Ajatashatru, [[Udayin|Udayin]], Munda, Kakavarnin, Sahalin, Tulakuchi, Mahamandala, [[Prasenajit|Prasenajit]], and [[Nanda_Empire|Nanda]].
sentence_77: The 16th century Tibetan monk [[Taranatha|Taranatha]], whose account is a distorted version of the earlier traditions, describes Ashoka as the illegitimate son of king Nemita of Champarana from the daughter of a merchant.
sentence_78: Ashokavadana states that [[Mother_of_Ashoka|Ashoka's mother]] was the daughter of a Brahmin from [[Champapuri|Champa]], and was prophesized to marry a king.
sentence_79: Accordingly, her father took her to Pataliputra, where she was inducted into Bindusara's harem, and ultimately, became his chief queen.
sentence_80: The Ashokavadana does not mention her by name, although other legends provide different names for her.
sentence_81: For example, the Asokavadanamala calls her Subhadrangi.
sentence_82: The Vamsatthapakasini or Mahavamsa-tika, a commentary on Mahavamsa, calls her "Dharma" ("Dhamma" in [[Pali_language|Pali]]), and states that she belonged to the Moriya Kshatriya clan.
sentence_83: A [[Divyavadana|Divyavadana]] legend calls her Janapada-kalyani; according to scholar Ananda W. P. Guruge, this is not a name, but an epithet.
sentence_84: According to the 2nd century historian [[Appian|Appian]], Chandragupta entered into a marital alliance with the Greek ruler [[Seleucus_I_Nicator|Seleucus I Nicator]], which has led to speculation that either Chandragupta or his son Bindusara married a Greek princess.
sentence_85: However, there is no evidence that Ashoka's mother or grandmother was Greek, and the idea has been dismissed by most historians.
sentence_86: According to the Ashokavadana, Bindusara disliked Ashoka because of his rough skin.
sentence_87: One day, Bindusara asked the ascetic Pingala-vatsajiva to determine which of his sons was being worthy of his successor.
sentence_88: On the ascetic's advice, he asked all the princes to assemble at the Garden of the Golden Pavilion.
sentence_89: Ashoka was reluctant to go because his father disliked him, but his mother convinced him to do so.
sentence_90: When minister Radhagupta saw Ashoka leaving the capital for the Garden, he offered to provide the prince a royal elephant for the travel.
sentence_91: At the Garden, Pingala-vatsajiva examined the princes and realised that Ashoka would be the next king.
sentence_92: To avoid annoying Bindusara, the ascetic refused to name the successor.
sentence_93: Instead, he said that one who had the best mount, seat, drink, vessel and food would be the next king; each time, Ashoka declared that he met the criterion.
sentence_94: Later, he told Ashoka's mother that her son would be the next king, and on her advice, left the kingdom to avoid Bindusara's wrath.
sentence_95: While legends suggest that Bindusara disliked Ashoka's ugly appearance, they also state that Bindusara gave him important responsibilities, such as suppressing a revolt in Takshashila (according to north Indian tradition), and governing Ujjain (according to Sri Lankan tradition).
sentence_96: This suggests that Bindusara was impressed by the other qualities of the prince.
sentence_97: Another possibility is that he sent Ashoka to distant regions to keep him away from the imperial capital.
sentence_98: According to the Ashokavadana, Bindusara dispatched prince Ashoka to suppress a rebellion in the city of [[Taxila|Takshashila]] (present-day [[Bhir_Mound|Bhir Mound]]).
sentence_99: This episode is not mentioned in the Sri Lankan tradition, which instead states that Bindusara sent Ashoka to govern Ujjain.
sentence_100: Two other Buddhist texts – Ashoka-sutra and Kunala-sutra – state that Bindusara appointed Ashoka as a viceroy in [[Gandhara|Gandhara]] (where Takshashila was located), not Ujjain.
sentence_101: The Ashokavadana states that Bindusara provided Ashoka with a fourfold-army (comprising cavalry, elephants, chariots and infantry), but refused to provide any weapons for this army.
sentence_102: Ashoka declared that weapons would appear before him if he was worthy of being a king, and then, the deities emerged from the earth, and provided weapons to the army.
sentence_103: When Ashoka reached Takshashila, the citizens welcomed him, and told him that their rebellion was only against the evil ministers, not the king.
sentence_104: Sometime later, Ashoka was similarly welcomed in the [[Khasas|Khasa]] territory, and the gods declared that he would go on to conquer the whole earth.
sentence_105: Takshashila was a prosperous and geopolitically important city, and historical evidence proves that by Ashoka's time, it was well-connected to the Mauryan capital Pataliputra by the Uttarapatha trade route.
sentence_106: However, no extant contemporary source mentions the Takshashila rebellion, and none of Ashoka's own records state that he ever visited the city.
sentence_107: That said, the historicity of the legend about Ashoka's involvement in the Takshashila rebellion maybe corroborated by [[Aramaic_Inscription_of_Taxila|an Aramaic-language inscription]] discovered at [[Sirkap|Sirkap]] near Taxila.
sentence_108: The inscription includes a name that begins with the letters "prydr", and most scholars restore it as "Priyadarshi", which was a title of Ashoka.
sentence_109: Another evidence of Ashoka's connection to the city may be the name of the [[Dharmarajika_Stupa|Dharmarajika Stupa]] near Taxila; the name suggests that it was built by Ashoka ("Dharma-raja").
sentence_110: The story about the deities miraculously bringing weapons to Ashoka may be the text's way of deifying Ashoka; or of indicating that Bindusara – who disliked Ashoka – wanted him to fail in Takshashila.
sentence_111: According to the Mahavamsa, Bindusara appointed Ashoka as the viceroy of present-day [[Ujjain|Ujjain]] (Ujjeni), which was an important administrative and commercial centre in the Avanti province of central India.
sentence_112: This tradition is corroborated by the [[Saru_Maru|Saru Maru]] inscription discovered in central India; this inscription states that he visited the place as a prince.
sentence_113: Ashoka's own [[Major_Rock_Edicts#First_Separate_Major_Rock_Edict|rock edict]] mentions the presence of a prince viceroy at Ujjain during his reign, which further supports the tradition that he himself served as a viceroy at Ujjain.
sentence_114: Pataliputra was connected to Ujjain by multiple routes in Ashoka's time, and on the way, Ashoka entourage may have encamped at Rupnath, where his inscription has been found.
sentence_115: According to the Sri Lankan tradition, on his way to Ujjain, Ashoka visited [[Vidisha|Vidisha]], where he fell in love with a beautiful woman.
sentence_116: According to the Dipamvamsa and Mahamvamsa, the woman was [[Devi_(Ashoka's_wife)|Devi]] – the daughter of a merchant.
sentence_117: According to the Mahabodhi-vamsa, she was Vidisha-Mahadevi, and belonged to the [[Shakya|Shakya]] clan of [[Gautama_Buddha|Gautama Buddha]].
sentence_118: The Shakya connection may have been fabricated by the Buddhist chroniclers in an attempt to connect Ashoka's family to Buddha.
sentence_119: The Buddhist texts allude to her being a Buddhist in her later years, but do not describe her conversion to Buddhism.
sentence_120: Therefore, it is likely that she was already a Buddhist when she met Ashoka.
sentence_121: The Mahavamsa states that Devi gave birth to Ashoka's son [[Mahinda_(Buddhist_monk)|Mahinda]] in Ujjain, and two years later, to a daughter named [[Sanghamitta|Sanghamitta]].
sentence_122: According to the Mahavamsa, Ashoka's son Mahinda was ordained at the age of 20 years, during the sixth year of Ashoka's reign.
sentence_123: That means, Mahinda must have been 14 years old when Ashoka ascended the throne.
sentence_124: Even if Mahinda was born when Ashoka was as young as 20 years old, Ashoka must have ascended the throne at the age of 34 years, which means he must have served as a viceroy for several years.
sentence_125: Legends suggest that Ashoka was not the crown prince, and his ascension on the throne was disputed.
sentence_126: Ashokavadana states that Bindusara's eldest son Susima once slapped a bald minister on his head in jest.
sentence_127: The minister worried that after ascending the throne, Susima may jokingly hurt him with a sword.
sentence_128: Therefore, he instigated five hundred ministers to support Ashoka's claim to the throne when the time came, noting that Ashoka was predicted to become a chakravartin (universal ruler).
sentence_129: Sometime later, Takshashila rebelled again, and Bindusara dispatched Susima to curb the rebellion.
sentence_130: Shortly after, Bindusara fell ill, and expected to die soon.
sentence_131: Susima was still in Takshashila, having been unsuccessful in suppressing the rebellion.
sentence_132: Bindusara recalled him to the capital, and asked Ashoka to march to Takshashila.
sentence_133: However, the ministers told him that Ashoka was ill, and suggested that he temporarily install Ashoka on the throne until Susmia's return from Takshashila.
sentence_134: When Bindusara refused to do so, Ashoka declared that if the throne was rightfully his, the gods would crown him as the next king.
sentence_135: At that instance, the gods did so, Bindusara died, and Ashoka's authority extended to the entire world, including the Yaksha territory located above the earth, and the [[Nāga|Naga]] territory located below the earth.
sentence_136: When Susima returned to the capital, Ashoka's newly-appointed prime minister Radhagupta tricked him into a pit of charcoal.
sentence_137: Susima died a painful death, and his general Bhadrayudha became a Buddhist monk.
sentence_138: The Mahavamsa states that when Bindusara fell sick, Ashoka returned to Pataliputra from Ujjain, and gained control of the capital.
sentence_139: After his father's death, Ashoka had his eldest brother killed, and ascended the throne.
sentence_140: The text also states that Ashoka killed ninety-nine of his half-brothers, including Sumana.
sentence_141: The Dipavamsa states that he killed a hundred of his brothers, and was crowned four years later.
sentence_142: The Vamsatthapakasini adds that an Ajivika ascetic had predicted this massacre based on the interpretation of a dream of Ashoka's mother.
sentence_143: According to these accounts, only Ashoka's uterine brother Tissa was spared.
sentence_144: Other sources name the surviving brother Vitashoka, Vigatashoka, Sudatta (So-ta-to in A-yi-uang-chuan), or Sugatra (Siu-ka-tu-lu in Fen-pie-kung-te-hun).
sentence_145: The figures such as 99 and 100 are exaggerated, and seem to be a way of stating that Ashoka killed several of his brothers.
sentence_146: Taranatha states that Ashoka, who was an illegitimate son of his predecessor, killed six legitimate princes to ascend the throne.
sentence_147: It is possible that Ashoka was not the rightful heir to the throne, and killed a brother (or brothers) to acquire the throne.
sentence_148: However, the story has obviously been exaggerated by the Buddhist sources, which attempt to portray him as an evil person before his conversion to Buddhism.
sentence_149: Ashoka's Rock Edict No.
sentence_150: 5 mentions officers whose duties include supervising the welfare of "the families of his brothers, sisters, and other relatives".
sentence_151: This suggests that more than one of his brothers survived his ascension, although some scholars oppose this suggestion, arguing that the inscription talks only about the families of his brothers, not the brothers themselves.
sentence_152: According to the Sri Lankan texts Mahavamsa and the Dipavamsa, Ashoka ascended the throne 218 years after the death of Gautama Buddha, and ruled for 37 years.
sentence_153: The date of the Buddha's death is itself a matter of debate, and the North Indian tradition states that Ashoka ruled a hundred years after the Buddha's death, which has led to further debates about the date.
sentence_154: Assuming that the Sri Lankan tradition is correct, and assuming that the Buddha died in 483 BCE – a date proposed by several scholars – Ashoka must have ascended the throne in 265 BCE.
sentence_155: The Puranas state that Ashoka's father Bindusara reigned for 25 years, not 28 years as specified in the Sri Lankan tradition.
sentence_156: If this is true, Ashoka's ascension can be dated three years earlier, to 268 BCE.
sentence_157: Alternatively, if the Sri Lankan tradition is correct, but if we assume that the Buddha died in 486 BCE (a date supported by the Cantonese Dotted Record), Ashoka's ascension can be dated to 268 BCE.
sentence_158: The Mahavamsa states that Ashoka consecrated himself as the king four years after becoming a sovereign.
sentence_159: This interregnum can be explained assuming that he fought a war of succession with other sons of Bindusara during these four years.
sentence_160: The Ashokavadana contains a story about Ashoka's minister Yashas hiding the sun with his hand.
sentence_161: Professor P. H. L. Eggermont theorised that this story was a reference to a partial solar eclipse that was seen in northern India on 4 May 249 BCE.
sentence_162: According to the Ashokavadana, Ashoka went on a pilgrimage to various Buddhist sites sometime after this eclipse.
sentence_163: Ashoka's Rummindei pillar inscription states that he visited [[Lumbini|Lumbini]] during his 21st regnal year.
sentence_164: Assuming this visit was a part of the pilgrimage described in the text, and assuming that Ashoka visited Lumbini around 1–2 years after the solar eclipse, the ascension date of 268–269 BCE seems more likely.
sentence_165: However, this theory is not universally accepted.
sentence_166: For example, according to [[John_S._Strong|John S. Strong]], the event described in the Ashokavadana has nothing to do with chronology, and Eggermont's interpretation grossly ignores literary and religious context of the legend.
sentence_167: Both Sri Lankan and north Indian traditions assert that Ashoka was a violent person before his conversion to Buddhism.
sentence_168: Taranatha also states that Ashoka was initially called "Kamashoka" because he spent many years in pleasurable pursuits ([[Kama|kama]]); he was then called "Chandashoka" ("Ashoka the fierce"), because he spent some years performing extremely wicked deeds; and finally, he came to be known as Dhammashoka ("Ashoka the righteous") after his conversion to Buddhism.
sentence_169: The Ashokavadana also calls him "Chandashoka", and describes several of his cruel acts:

list.value: The ministers who had helped him ascend the throne started treating him with contempt after his ascension. To test their loyalty, Ashoka gave them the absurd order of cutting down every flower-and fruit-bearing tree. When they failed to carry out this order, Ashoka personally cut off the heads of 500 ministers.

One day, during a stroll at a park, Ashoka and his concubines came across a beautiful [[Saraca_asoca|Ashoka tree]]. The sight put him in a sensual mood, but the women did not enjoy caressing his rough skin. Sometime later, when Ashoka fell asleep, the resentful women chopped the flowers and the branches of his namesake tree. After Ashoka woke up, he burnt 500 of his concubines to death as a punishment.

Alarmed by the king's personal involvement in such massacres, the prime minister Radha-gupta proposed hiring an executioner to carry out future mass killings, so as to leave the king unsullied. Girika, a Magadha village boy who boasted that he could execute the whole of Jambudvipa, was hired for the purpose. He came to be known as Chandagirika ("Girika the fierce"), and on his request, Ashoka built a jail in Pataliputra. Called [[Ashoka's_Hell|Ashoka's Hell]], the jail looked lovely from outside, but inside it, Girika brutally tortured the prisoners.

sentence_170: The 5th century Chinese traveller [[Faxian|Faxian]] states that Ashoka personally visited the underworld to study the methods of torture there, and then invented his own methods.
sentence_171: The 7th century traveller [[Xuanzang|Xuanzang]] claims to have seen a pillar marking the site of Ashoka's "Hell".
sentence_172: The Mahavamsa also briefly alludes to Ashoka's cruelty, stating that Ashoka was earlier called Chandashoka because of his evil deeds, but came to be called Dharmashoka because of his pious acts after his conversion to Buddhism.
sentence_173: However, unlike the north Indian tradition, the Sri Lankan texts do not mention any specific evil deeds performed by Ashoka, except his killing of 99 of his brothers.
sentence_174: Such descriptions of Ashoka as an evil person before his conversion to Buddhism appear to be a fabrication of the Buddhist authors, who attempted to present the change that Buddhism brought to him as a miracle.
sentence_175: In an attempt to dramatise this change, such legends exaggerate Ashoka's past wickedness and his piousness after the conversion.

section_11.value: Kalinga war and conversion to Buddhism

sentence_176: Ashoka's own inscriptions mention that he conquered the [[Kalinga_(historical_region)|Kalinga]] region during his 8th regnal year: the destruction caused during the war made him repent violence, and in the subsequent years, he was drawn towards Buddhism.
sentence_177: Edict 13 of the [[Edicts_of_Ashoka|Edicts of Ashoka]] Rock Inscriptions expresses the great remorse the king felt after observing the destruction of Kalinga:
sentence_178: On the other hand, the Sri Lankan tradition suggests that Ashoka was already a devoted Buddhist by his 8th regnal year, having converted to Buddhism during his 4th regnal year, and having constructed 84,000 viharas during his 5th–7th regnal years.
sentence_179: The Buddhist legends make no mention of the Kalinga campaign.
sentence_180: Based on Sri Lankan tradition, some scholars – such as Eggermont – believe that Ashoka converted to Buddhism before the Kalinga war.
sentence_181: Critics of this theory argue that if Ashoka was already a Buddhist, he would not have waged the violent Kalinga War.
sentence_182: Eggermont explains this anamoly by theorising that Ashoka had his own interpretation of the "[[Middle_Way|Middle Way]]".
sentence_183: Some earlier writers believed that Ashoka dramatically converted to Buddhism after seeing the suffering caused by the war, since his Major Rock Edict 13 states that he became closer to the dhamma after the annexation of Kalinga.
sentence_184: However, even if Ashoka converted to Buddhism after the war, epigraphic evidence suggests that his conversion was a gradual process rather than a dramatic event.
sentence_185: For example, in a Minor Rock Edict issued during his 13th regnal year (five years after the Kalinga campaign), he states that he had been an [[Upasaka|upasaka]] (lay Buddhist) for more than two and a half years, but did not make much progress; in the past year, he was drawn closer to the sangha, and became a more ardent follower.
sentence_186: According to Ashoka's Major Rock Edict 13, he conquered Kalinga 8 years after his ascension to the throne.
sentence_187: The edict states that during his conquest of Kalinga, 100,000 men and animals were killed in action; many times that number "perished"; and 150,000 men and animals were carried away from Kalinga as captives.
sentence_188: Ashoka states that the repentance of these sufferings caused him to devote himself to the practice and propagation of dharma.
sentence_189: He proclaims that he now considered the slaughter, death and deportation caused during the conquest of a country painful and deplorable; and that he considered the suffering caused to the religious people and householders even more deplorable.
sentence_190: This edict has been found inscribed at several places, including Erragudi, Girnar, Kalsi, Maneshra, Shahbazgarhi and Kandahar.
sentence_191: However, is omitted in Ashoka's inscriptions found in the Kalinga region, where the Rock Edicts 13 and 14 have been replaced by two separate edicts that make no mention of Ashoka's remorse.
sentence_192: It is possible that Ashoka did not consider it politically appropriate to make such a confession to the people of Kalinga.
sentence_193: Another possibility is the Kalinga war and its consequences, as described in Ashoka's rock edicts, are "more imaginary than real": this description is meant to impress those far removed from the scene, and thus, unable to verify its accuracy.
sentence_194: Ancient sources do not mention any other military activity of Ashoka, although the 16th century writer [[Taranatha|Taranatha]] claims that Ashoka conquered the entire Jambudvipa.
sentence_195: Different sources give different accounts of Ashoka's conversion to Buddhism.
sentence_196: According to Sri Lankan tradition, Ashoka's father Bindusara was a devotee of [[Brahmanism|Brahmanism]], and his mother Dharma was a devotee of [[Ajivika|Ajivikas]].
sentence_197: The [[Samantapasadika|Samantapasadika]] states that Ashoka followed non-Buddhist sects during the first three years of his reign.
sentence_198: The Sri Lankan texts add that Ashoka was not happy with the behaviour of the Brahmins who received his alms daily.
sentence_199: His courtiers produced some Ajivika and Nigantha teachers before him, but these also failed to impress him.
sentence_200: The Dipavamsa states that Ashoka invited several non-Buddhist religious leaders to his palace, and bestowed great gifts upon them in hope that they would be able to answer a question posed by the king.
sentence_201: The text does not state what the question was, but mentions that none of the invitees were able to answer it.
sentence_202: One day, Ashoka saw a young Buddhist monk called Nigrodha (or Nyagrodha), who was looking for alms on a road in Pataliputra.
sentence_203: He was the king's nephew, although the king was not aware of this: he was a posthumous son of Ashoka's eldest brother Sumana, whom Ashoka had killed during the conflict for the throne.
sentence_204: Ashoka was impressed by Nigrodha's tranquil and fearless appearance, and asked him to teach him his faith.
sentence_205: In response, Nigrodha offered him a sermon on [[Appamada|appamada]] (earnestness).
sentence_206: Impressed by the sermon, Ashoka offered Nigrodha 400,000 silver coins and 8 daily portions of rice.
sentence_207: The king became a Buddhist [[Upasaka|upasaka]], and started visiting the [[Kukkutarama|Kukkutarama]] shrine at Pataliputra.
sentence_208: At the temple, he met the Buddhist monk [[Moggaliputta_Tissa|Moggaliputta Tissa]], and became more devoted to the Buddhist faith.
sentence_209: The veracity of this story is not certain.
sentence_210: This legend about Ashoka's search for a worthy teacher may be aimed at explaining why Ashoka did not adopt [[Jainism|Jainism]], another major contemporary faith that advocates non-violence and compassion.
sentence_211: The legend suggests that Ashoka was not attracted to Buddhism because he was looking for such a faith, rather, for a competent spiritual teacher.
sentence_212: The Sri Lankan tradition adds that during his 6th regnal year, Ashoka's son Mahinda became a Buddhist monk, and his daughter became a Buddhist nun.
sentence_213: A story in Divyavadana attributes Ashoka's conversion to the Buddhist monk Samudra, who was an ex-merchant from Shravasti.
sentence_214: According to this account, Samudra was imprisoned in Ashoka's "Hell", but saved himself using his miraculous powers.
sentence_215: When Ashoka heard about this, he visited the monk, and was further impressed by a series of miracles performed by the monk.
sentence_216: He then became a Buddhist.
sentence_217: A story in the Ashokavadana states that Samudra was a merchant's son, and was a 12-year-old boy when he met Ashoka; this account seems to be influenced by the Nigrodha story.
sentence_218: The A-yu-wang-chuan states that a 7-year-old Buddhist converted Ashoka.
sentence_219: Another story claims that the young boy ate 500 [[Brahmins|Brahmanas]] who were harassing Ashoka for being interested in Buddhism; these Brahmanas later miraculously turned into Buddhist [[Bhikku|bhikkus]] at the Kukkutarama monastery, where Ashoka paid a visit.
sentence_220: Several Buddhist establishments existed in various parts of India by the time of Ashoka's ascension.
sentence_221: It is not clear which branch of the Buddhist sangha influenced him, but the one at his capital [[Pataliputra|Pataliputra]] is a good candidate.
sentence_222: Another good candidate is the one at [[Mahabodhi_Temple|Mahabodhi]]: the Major Rock Edict 8 records his visit to the Bodhi Tree – the place of Buddha's enlightenment at Mahabodhi – after his 10th regnal year, and the minor rock edict issued during his 13th regnal year suggests that he had become a Buddhist around the same time.
sentence_223: Both Mahavamsa and Ashokavadana state that Ashoka constructed 84,000 stupas or viharas.
sentence_224: According to the Mahavamsa, this activity took place during his 5th–7th regnal years.
sentence_225: The Ashokavadana states that Ashoka collected seven out of the eight relics of Gautama Buddha, and had their portions kept in 84,000 boxes made of gold, silver, [[Cymophane|cat's eye]], and crystal.
sentence_226: He ordered the construction of 84,000 stupas throughout the earth, in towns that had a population of 100,000 or more.
sentence_227: He told Elder Yashas, a monk at the Kukkutarama monastery, that he wanted these stupas to be completed on the same day.
sentence_228: Yashas stated that he would signal the completion time by eclipsing the sun with his hand.
sentence_229: When he did so, the 84,000 stupas were completed at once.
sentence_230: The Mahavamsa states that Ashoka ordered construction of 84,000 viharas (monasteries) rather than the stupas to house the relics.
sentence_231: Like Ashokavadana, the Mahavamsa describes Ashoka's collection of the relics, but does not mention this episode in the context of the construction activities.
sentence_232: It states that Ashoka decided to construct the 84,000 viharas when Moggaliputta Tissa told him that there were 84,000 sections of the Buddha's Dhamma.
sentence_233: Ashoka himself began the construction of the Ashokarama vihara, and ordered subordinate kings to build the other viharas.
sentence_234: Ashokarama was completed by the miraculous power of Thera Indagutta, and the news about the completion of the 84,000 viharas arrived from various cities on the same day.
sentence_235: The number 84,000 is an obvious exaggeration, and it appears that in the later period, the construction of almost every old stupa was attributed to Ashoka.
sentence_236: The construction of following stupas and viharas is credited to Ashoka:

list.value: [[Nalanda|Nalanda]] Mahavihara (some portions like Sariputta Stupa), [[Bihar|Bihar]], India
[[Taxila|Taxila]] University (some portions like [[Dharmarajika|Dharmarajika]] Stupa and Kunala Stupa), [[Taxila|Taxila]], Pakistan

sentence_237: Ashoka's rock edicts suggest that during his 8th–9th regnal years, he made a pilgrimage to the Bodhi Tree, started propagating dhamma, and performed social welfare activities.
sentence_238: The welfare activities included establishment of medical treatment facilities for humans and animals; plantation of medicinal herbs; and digging of wells and plantation of trees along the roads.
sentence_239: These activities were conducted in the neighbouring kingdoms, including those of the Cholas, the Pandyas, the Satiyaputras, Tamraparni, the Greek kingdom of Antiyoka.
sentence_240: The edicts also state that during his 10th–11th regnal years, Ashoka became closer to the Buddhist sangha, and went on a tour of the empire that lasted for at least 256 days.
sentence_241: By his 12th regnal year, Ashoka had started inscribing edicts to propagate dhamma, having ordered his officers (rajjukas and pradesikas) to tour their jurisdictions every five years for inspection and for preaching dhamma.
sentence_242: By the next year, he had set up the post of the dharma-mahamatra.
sentence_243: During his 14th regnal year, he commissioned the enlargement of the stupa of Buddha Kanakamuni.
sentence_244: The Sri Lankan tradition presents a greater role for Ashoka in the Buddhist community.
sentence_245: In this tradition, Ashoka starts feeding monks on a large scale.
sentence_246: His lavish patronage to the state patronage leads to many fake monks joining the sangha.
sentence_247: The true Buddhist monks refuse to co-operate with these fake monks, and therefore, no [[Uposatha|uposatha]] ceremony is held for seven years.
sentence_248: The king attempts to eradicate the fake monks, but during this attempt, an over-zealous minister ends up killing some real monks.
sentence_249: The king then invites the elder monk [[Moggaliputta-Tissa|Moggaliputta-Tissa]], to help him expel non-Buddhists from the monastery founded by him at Pataliputra.
sentence_250: 60,000 monks ([[Bhikkhu|bhikkhus]]) convicted of being heretical are de-frocked in the ensuing process.
sentence_251: The uposatha ceremony is then held, and Tissa subsequently organises the Third Buddhist council, during the 17th regnal year of Ashoka.
sentence_252: Tissa compiles [[Kathavatthu|Kathavatthu]], a text that reaffirms Theravadin orthodoxy on several points.
sentence_253: The North Indian tradition makes no mention of these events, which has led to doubts about the historicity of the Third Buddihst council.
sentence_254: [[Richard_Gombrich|Richard Gombrich]] argues that the non-corroboration of this story by inscriptional evidence cannot be used to dismiss it as completely unhistorical, as several of Ashoka's inscriptions may have been lost.
sentence_255: Gombrich also argues that Asohka's inscriptions prove that he was interested in maintaining the "unanimity and purity" of the Sangha.
sentence_256: For example, in his Minor Rock Edict 3, Ashoka recommends the members of the Sangha to study certain texts (most of which remain unidentified).
sentence_257: Similarly, in an inscription found at Sanchi, Sarnath, and Kosam, Ashoka mandates that the dissident members of the sangha should be expelled, and expresses his desire to the Sangha remain united and flourish.
sentence_258: The 8th century Buddhist pilgrim [[Yijing_(monk)|Yijing]] records another story about Ashoka's involvement in the Buddhist sangha.
sentence_259: According to this story, the earlier king [[Bimbisara|Bimbisara]], who was a contemporary of the Gautama Buddha, once saw 18 fragments of a cloth and a stick in a dream.
sentence_260: The Buddha interpreted the dream to mean that his philosophy would be divided into 18 schools after his death, and predicted that a king called Ashoka would unite these schools over a hundred years later.
sentence_261: In the Sri Lankan tradition, [[Moggaliputta-Tissa|Moggaliputta-Tissa]] – who is patronised by Ashoka – sends out nine Buddhist missions to spread Buddhism in the "border areas" in c. 250 BCE.
sentence_262: This tradition does not credit Ashoka directly with sending these missions.
sentence_263: Each mission comprises five monks, and is headed by an elder.
sentence_264: To Sri Lanka, he sent his own son Mahinda, accompanied by four other Theras – Itthiya, Uttiya, Sambala and Bhaddasala.
sentence_265: Next, with Moggaliputta-Tissa's help, Ashoka sent Buddhist missionaries to distant regions such as Kashmir, Gandhara, Himalayas, the land of the Yonas (Greeks), Maharashtra, Suvannabhumi, and Sri Lanka.
sentence_266: The Sri Lankan tradition dates these missions to Ashoka's 18th regnal year, naming the following missionaries:

list.value: Mahadeva to Mahisa-mandala (possibly modern Mysore region)
Dhammarakkhita the Greek to Aparantaka (western India)
Soṇa and Uttara to Suvaṇṇabhūmi (possibly Lower Burma and Thailand)

sentence_267: The tradition adds that during his 19th regnal year, Ashoka's daughter Sanghamitta went to Sri Lanka to establish an order of nuns, taking a sapling of the sacred Bodhi Tree with her.
sentence_268: The North Indian tradition makes no mention of these events.
sentence_269: Ashoka's own inscriptions also appear to omit any mention of these events, recording only one of his activities during this period: in his 19th regnal year, he donated the Khalatika Cave to ascetics to provide them a shelter during the rainy season.
sentence_270: Ashoka's [[Minor_Pillar_Edicts|Pillar Edicts]] suggest that during the next year, he made pilgrimage to Lumbini – the place of Buddha's birth, and to the stupa of the Buddha Kanakamuni.
sentence_271: The Rock Edict XIII states that Ashoka's won a "dhamma victory" by sending messengers to five kings and several other kingdoms.
sentence_272: Whether these missions correspond to the Buddhist missions recorded in the Buddhist chronicles is debated.
sentence_273: Indologist [[Etienne_Lamotte|Etienne Lamotte]] argues that the "dhamma" missionaries mentioned in Ashoka's inscriptions were probably not Buddhist monks, as this "dhamma" was not same as "Buddhism".
sentence_274: Moreover, the lists of destinations of the missions and the dates of the missions mentioned in the inscriptions do not tally the ones mentioned in the Buddhist legends.
sentence_275: Other scholars, such as [[Erich_Frauwallner|Erich Frauwallner]] and [[Richard_Gombrich|Richard Gombrich]], believe that the missions mentioned in the Sri Lankan tradition are historical.
sentence_276: According to these scholars, a part of this story is corroborated by archaeological evidence: the Vinaya Nidana mentions names of five monks, who are said to have gone to the Himalayan region; three of these names have been found inscribed on relic caskets found at [[Bhilsa|Bhilsa]] (near [[Vidisha|Vidisha]]).
sentence_277: These caskets have been dated to the early 2nd century BCE, and the inscription states that the monks are of the Himalayan school.
sentence_278: The missions may have set out from Vidisha in central India, as the caskets were discovered there, and as Mahinda is said to have stayed there for a month before setting out for Sri Lanka.
sentence_279: According to Gombrich, the mission may have included representatives of other religions, and thus, Lamotte's objection about "dhamma" is not valid.
sentence_280: The Buddhist chroniclers may have decided not to mention these non-Buddhists, so as not to sideline Buddhism.
sentence_281: Frauwallner and Gombrich also believe that Ashoka was directly responsible for the missions, since only a resourceful ruler could have sponsored such activities.
sentence_282: The Sri Lankan chronicles, which belong to the Theravada school, exaggerate the role of the Theravadin monk Moggaliputta-Tissa in order to glorify their sect.
sentence_283: Some historians argue that Buddhism became a major religion because of Ashoka's royal patronage.
sentence_284: However, epigraphic evidence suggests that the spread of Buddhism in north-western India and Deccan region was less because of Ashoka's missions, and more because of merchants, traders, landowners and the artisan guilds who supported Buddhist establishments.
sentence_285: According to the Ashokavadana, Ashoka resorted to violence even after converting to Buddhism.
sentence_286: For example:

list.value: He slowly tortured Chandagirika to death in the "hell" prison.
He ordered a massacre of 18,000 heretics for a misdeed of one.
He launched a pogrom against the Jains, announcing a bounty on the head of any heretic; this results in the beheading of his own brother – Vitashoka.

sentence_287: According to the Ashokavadana, a non-Buddhist in [[Pundravardhana|Pundravardhana]] drew a picture showing the Buddha bowing at the feet of the Nirgrantha leader Jnatiputra.
sentence_288: The term nirgrantha ("free from bonds") was originally used for a pre-Jaina ascetic order, but later came to be used for Jaina monks.
sentence_289: "Jnatiputra" is identified with [[Mahavira|Mahavira]], 24th Tirthankara of [[Jainism|Jainism]].
sentence_290: The legend states that on complaint from a Buddhist devotee, Ashoka issued an order to arrest the non-Buddhist artist, and subsequently, another order to kill all the [[Ajivika|Ajivikas]] in Pundravardhana.
sentence_291: Around 18,000 followers of the Ajivika sect were executed as a result of this order.
sentence_292: Sometime later, another Nirgrantha follower in [[Pataliputra|Pataliputra]] drew a similar picture.
sentence_293: Ashoka burnt him and his entire family alive in their house.
sentence_294: He also announced an award of one dinara (silver coin) to anyone who brought him the head of a Nirgrantha heretic.
sentence_295: According to Ashokavadana, as a result of this order, his own brother was mistaken for a heretic and killed by a cowherd.
sentence_296: Ashoka realised his mistake, and withdrew the order.
sentence_297: For several reasons, scholars say, these stories of persecutions of rival sects by Ashoka appear to be clear fabrications arising out of sectarian propaganda.
sentence_298: Ashoka's last dated inscription - the [[Major_Pillar_Edicts#Major_Pillar_Edict_4|Pillar Edict 4]] is from his 26th regnal year.
sentence_299: The only source of information about Ashoka's later years are the Buddhist legends.
sentence_300: The Sri Lankan tradition states that Ashoka's queen Asandhamitta died during his 29th regnal year, and in his 32nd regnal year, his wife Tissarakkha was given the title of queen.
sentence_301: Both Mahavamsa and Ashokavadana state that Ashoka extended favours and attention to the Bodhi Tree, and a jealous Tissarakkha mistook "Bodhi" to be a mistress of Ashoka.
sentence_302: She then used black magic to make the tree wither.
sentence_303: According to the Ashokavadana, she hired a sorceress to do the job, and when Ashoka explained that "Bodhi" was the name of a tree, she had the sorceress heal the tree.
sentence_304: According to the Mahavamsa, she completely destroyed the tree, during Ashoka's 34th regnal year.
sentence_305: The Ashokavadana states that Tissarakkha (called "Tishyarakshita" here) made sexual advances towards Ashoka's son Kunala, but Kunala rejected her.
sentence_306: Subsequently, Ashoka granted Tissarakkha kingship for seven days, and during this period, she tortured and blinded Kunala.
sentence_307: Ashoka then threatened to "tear out her eyes, rip open her body with sharp rakes, impale her alive on a spit, cut off her nose with a saw, cut out her tongue with a razor."
sentence_308: Kunala regained his eyesight miraculously, and pleaded for mercy on the queen, but Ashoka had her executed anyway.
sentence_309: Kshemendra's Avadana-kalpa-lata also narrates this legend, but seeks to improve Ashoka's image by stating that he forgave the queen after Kunala regained his eyesight.
sentence_310: According to the Sri Lankan tradition, Ashoka died during his 37th regnal year, which suggests that he died around 232 BCE.
sentence_311: According to the Ashokavadana, the emperor fell severely ill during his last days.
sentence_312: He started using state funds to make donations to the Buddhist sangha, prompting his ministers to deny him access to the state treasury.
sentence_313: Ashoka then started donating his personal possessions, but was similarly restricted from doing so.
sentence_314: On his deathbed, his only possession was the half of a [[Phyllanthus_emblica|myrobalan fruit]], which he offered to the sangha as his final donation.
sentence_315: Such legends encourage generous donations to the sangha and highlight the role of the kingship in supporting the Buddhist faith.
sentence_316: Legend states that during his cremation, his body burned for seven days and nights.
sentence_317: Various sources mention five consorts of Ashoka: [[Devi_(Ashoka's_wife)|Devi]] (or Vedisa-Mahadevi-Shakyakumari), [[Karuvaki|Karuvaki]], Asandhimitra (Pali: Asandhimitta), [[Padmavati_(wife_of_Ashoka)|Padmavati]], and Tishyarakshita (Pali: Tissarakkha).
sentence_318: Kaurvaki is the only queen of Ashoka known from his own inscriptions: she is mentioned in an edict inscribed on a pillar at Allahabad.
sentence_319: The inscription names her as the mother of prince Tivara, and orders the royal officers (mahamattas) to record her religious and charitable donations.
sentence_320: According to one theory, Tishyarakshita was the regnal name of Kaurvaki.
sentence_321: According to the Mahavamsa, Ashoka's chief queen was Asandhimitta, who died four years before him.
sentence_322: It states that she was born as Ashoka's queen because in a previous life, she directed a [[Pratyekabuddha|pratyekabuddha]] to a honey merchant (who was later reborn as Ashoka).
sentence_323: Some later texts also state that she additionally gave the pratyekabuddha a piece of cloth made by her.
sentence_324: These texts include the Dasavatthuppakarana, the so-called Cambodian or Extended Mahavamsa (possibly from 9th–10th centuries), and the Trai Bhumi Katha (15th century).
sentence_325: These texts narrate another story: one day, Ashoka mocked Asandhamitta was enjoying a tasty piece of sugarcane without having earned it through her karma.
sentence_326: Asandhamitta replied that all her enjoyments resulted from merit resulting from her own karma.
sentence_327: Ashoka then challenged her to prove this by procuring 60,000 robes as an offering for monks.
sentence_328: At night, the guardian gods informed her about her past gift to the pratyekabuddha, and next day, she was able to miraculously procure the 60,000 robes.
sentence_329: An impressed Ashoka makes her his favourite queen, and even offers to make her a sovereign ruler.
sentence_330: Asandhamitta refuses the offer, but still invokes the jealousy of Ashoka's 16,000 other wives.
sentence_331: Ashoka proves her superiority by having 16,000 identical cakes baked with his royal seal hidden in only one of them.
sentence_332: Each wife is asked to choose a cake, and only Asandhamitta gets the one with the royal seal.
sentence_333: The Trai Bhumi Katha claims that it was Asandhamitta who encouraged her husband to become a Buddhist, and to construct 84,000 stupas and 84,000 viharas.
sentence_334: According to Mahavamsa, after Asandhamitta's death, Tissarakkha became the chief queen.
sentence_335: The Ashokavadana does not mention Asandhamitta at all, but does mention Tissarakkha as Tishyarakshita.
sentence_336: The Divyavadana mentions another queen called Padmavati, who was the mother of the crown-prince Kunala.
sentence_337: As mentioned above, according to the Sri Lankan tradition, Ashoka fell in love with Devi (or Vidisha-Mahadevi), as a prince in central India.
sentence_338: After Ashoka's ascention to the throne, Devi chose to remain at Vidisha than move to the royal capital Pataliputra.
sentence_339: According to the Mahavmsa, Ashoka's chief queen was Asandhamitta, not Devi: the text does not talk of any connection between the two women, so it is unlikely that Asandhamitta was another name for Devi.
sentence_340: The Sri Lankan tradition uses the word samvasa to describe the relationship between Ashoka and Devi, which modern scholars variously interpret as sexual relations outside marriage, or co-residence as a married couple.
sentence_341: Those who argue that Ashoka did not marry Devi argue that their theory is corroborated by the fact that Devi did not become Ashoka's chief queen in Pataliputra after his ascension.
sentence_342: The Dipavamsa refers to two children of Ashoka and Devi – Mahinda and [[Sanghamitta|Sanghamitta]].
sentence_343: Tivara, the son of Ashoka and Karuvaki, is the only of Ashoka's sons to be mentioned by name in the inscriptions.
sentence_344: According to North Indian tradition, Ashoka had a son named Kunala.
sentence_345: Kunala had a son named Samprati.
sentence_346: The Sri Lankan tradition mentions a son called Mahinda, who was sent to Sri Lanka as a Buddhist missionary; this son is not mentioned at all in the North Indian tradition.
sentence_347: The Chinese pilgrim [[Xuanzang|Xuanzang]] states that Mahinda was Ashoka's younger brother (Vitashoka or Vigatashoka) rather than his illgetimate son.
sentence_348: The Divyavadana mentions the crown-prince Kunala alias Dharmavivardhana, who was a son of queen Padmavati.
sentence_349: According to Faxian, Dharmavivardhana was appointed as the governor of Gandhara.
sentence_350: The Rajatarangini mentions Jalauka as a son of Ashoka.
sentence_351: According to Sri Lankan tradition, Ashoka had a daughter named Sanghamitta, who became a Buddhist nun.
sentence_352: A section of historians, such as [[Romila_Thapar|Romila Thapar]], doubt the historicity of Sanghamitta, based on the folloiwng points:

list.value: The name "Sanghamitta", which literally means the friend of the Buddhist Order (sangha), is unusual, and the story of her going to Ceylon so that the Ceylonese queen could be ordained appears to be an exaggeration.

The Mahavamsa states that she married Ashoka's nephew Agnibrahma, and the couple had a son named Sumana. The contemporary laws regarding exogamy would have forbidden such a marriage between first cousins.

According to the Mahavamsa, she was 18 years old when she was ordained as a nun. The narrative suggests that she was married two years earlier, and that her husband as well as her child were ordained. It is unlikely that she would have been allowed to become a nun with such a young child.

sentence_353: Another source mentions that Ashoka had a daughter named Charumati, who married a kshatriya named Devapala.
sentence_354: According to the Ashokavadana, Ashoka had an elder half-brother named Susima.
sentence_355: According to the Sri Lankan tradition, Ashoka killed his 99 half-brothers.
sentence_356: Various sources mention that one of Ashoka's brothers survived his ascension, and narrate stories about his role in the Buddhist community.
