list.value: According to Sri Lankan tradition, this brother was Tissa, who initially lived a luxurious life, without worrying about the world. To teach him a lesson, Ashoka put him on the throne for a few days, then accused him of being an usurper, and sentenced him to die after seven days. During these seven days, Tissa realised that the Buddhist monks gave up pleasure because they were aware of the eventual death. He then left the palace, and became an arhat.

The Theragatha commentary calls this brother Vitashoka. According to this legend, one day, Vitashoka saw a grey hair on his head, and realised that he had become old. He then retired to a monastery, and became an arhat.

Faxian calls the younger brother Mahendra, and states that Ashoka shamed him for his immoral behaviour. The brother than retired to a dark cave, where he meditated, and became an arhat. Ashoka invited him to return to the family, but he preferred to live alone on a hill. So, Ashoka had a hill built for him within Pataliputra.
The Ashoka-vadana states that Ashoka's brother was mistaken for a Nirgrantha, and killed during a massacre of the Nirgranthas ordered by Ashoka.

sentence_357: The extent of the territory controlled by Ashoka's predecessors is not certain, but it is possible that the empire of his grandfather Chandragupta extended northern India from western coast (Arabian Sea) to the eastern coast (Bay of Bengal), covering nearly two-thirds of the [[Indian_subcontinent|Indian subcontinent]].
sentence_358: Bindusara and Ashoka seem to have extended the empire southwards.
sentence_359: The distribution of Ashoka's inscriptions suggests that his empire included almost the entire [[Indian_subcontinent|Indian subcontinent]], except its southernmost parts.
sentence_360: The Rock Edicts 2 and 13 suggest that these southernmost parts were controlled by the Cholas, the Pandyas, the Keralaputras, and the Satiyaputras.
sentence_361: In the north-west, Ashoka's kingdom extended up to [[Kandahar|Kandahar]], to the east of the [[Seleucid_Empire|Seleucid Empire]] ruled by [[Antiochus_II_Theos|Antiochus II]].
sentence_362: The capital of Ashoka's empire was [[Pataliputra|Pataliputra]] in the Magadha region.
sentence_363: The Buddhist legends state that Ashoka converted to Buddhism, although this has been debated by a section of scholars.
sentence_364: The [[Minor_Rock_Edicts#Full_texts_of_the_Minor_Rock_Edicts|Minor Rock Edict 1]] leaves no doubt that Ashoka was a follower of Buddhism.
sentence_365: In this edict, he calls himself an [[Upāsaka_and_Upāsikā|upasaka]] (a lay follower of Buddhism) and a sakya (i.e. Buddhist, after Gautama Buddha's title Shakya-Muni).
sentence_366: This and several other edicts are evidence of his Buddhist affiliation:

list.value: In his Minor Rock Edict 1, Ashoka adds that he did not make much progress for a year after becoming an upasaka, but then, he "went to" the Sangha, and made more progress. It is not certain what "going to" the Sangha means – the Buddhist tradition that he lived with monks may be an exaggeration, but it clearly means that Ashoka was drawn closer to Buddhism.
In his Minor Rock Edict 3, he calls himself an upasaka, and records his faith in the Buddha and the Sangha.
In the [[Major_Rock_Edicts#Major_Rock_Edict_8|Major Rock Edict 8]], he records his visit to Sambodhi (the sacred Bodhi Tree at Bodh Gaya), ten years after his coronation.
In the [[Lumbini#Pillar_of_Ashoka|Lumbini (Rumminidei) inscription]], he records his visit to the Buddha's birthplace, and declares his reverence for the Buddha and the sangha.
In the Nigalisagar inscription, he records his doubling in size of a stupa dedicated to a former Buddha, and his visit to the site for worship.
Some of his inscriptions reflect his interest in maintaining the Buddhist sangha (see [[#Purification_of_sangha|#Purification of sangha]] below).

The [[Saru_Maru|Saru Maru]] inscription states that Ashoka dispatched the message while travelling to Upunita-vihara in Manema-desha. Although the identity of the destination is not certain, it was obviously a Buddhist monastery ([[Vihara|vihara]]).

sentence_367: A legend in the Buddhist text Vamsatthapakasini states that an Ajivika ascetic invited to interpret a dream of Ashoka's mother had predicted that he would patronise Buddhism and destroy 96 heretical sects.
sentence_368: However, such assertions are directly contradicted by Ashoka's own inscriptions.
sentence_369: Ashoka's edicts, such as the Rock Edicts 6, 7, and 12, emphasise tolerance of all sects.
sentence_370: Similarly, in his [[Major_Rock_Edicts#Major_Rock_Edict_12|Rock Edict 12]], Ashoka honours people of all faiths.
sentence_371: In his inscriptions, Ashoka dedicates caves to non-Buddhist ascetics, and repeatedly states that both Brahmins and shramanas deserved respect.
sentence_372: He also tells people "not to denigrate other sects, but to inform themselves about them".
sentence_373: In fact, there is no evidence that Buddhism was a state religion under Ashoka.
sentence_374: None of Ashoka's extant edicts record his direct donations to the Buddhists.
sentence_375: One inscription records donations by his queen [[Karuvaki|Karuvaki]], while the emperor is known to have donated the [[Barabar_Caves|Barabar Caves]] to the [[Ajivika|Ajivikas]].
sentence_376: There are some indirect references to his donations to Buddhists.
sentence_377: For example, the Nigalisagar Pillar inscription records his enlargement of the Konakamana stupa.
sentence_378: Similarly, the [[Lumbini#Pillar_of_Ashoka|Lumbini (Rumminidei) inscription]] states that he exempted the village of Buddha's birth from the land tax, and reduced the revenue tax to one-eighth.
sentence_379: Ashoka appointed the dhamma-mahamatta officers, whose duties included the welfare of various religious sects, including the Buddhist sangha, Brahmins, Ajivikas, and Nirgranthas.
sentence_380: The Rock Edicts 8 and 12, and the Pillar Edict 7, mandate donations to all religious sects.
sentence_381: Ashoka's [[Minor_Rock_Edicts#Full_texts_of_the_Minor_Rock_Edicts|Minor Rock Edict 1]] contains the phrase "amissā [[Deva_(Buddhism)|devā]]".
sentence_382: According to one interpretation, the term "amissā" derives from the word "amṛṣa" ("false"), and thus, the phrase is a reference to Ashoak's belief in "true" and "false" gods.
sentence_383: However, it is more likely that the term derives from the word "amiśra" ("not mingled"), and the phrase refers to celestial beings who did not mingle with humans.
sentence_384: The inscription claims that the righteousness generated by adoption of dhamma by the humans attracted even the celestial gods who did not mingle with humans.
sentence_385: Main article: [[Ashoka's_policy_of_Dhamma|Ashoka's policy of Dhamma]]
sentence_386: Ashoka's various inscriptions suggest that he devoted himself to the propagation of "Dharma" (Pali: Dhamma), a term that refers to the teachings of [[Gautama_Buddha|Gautama Buddha]] in the Buddhist circles.
sentence_387: However, Ashoka's own inscriptions do not mention Buddhist doctrines such as the [[Four_Noble_Truths|Four Noble Truths]] or [[Nirvana_(Buddhism)|Nirvana]].
sentence_388: The word "Dharma" has various connotations in the [[Indian_religions|Indian religions]], and can be generally translated as "law, duty, or righteousness".
sentence_389: In the Kandahar inscriptions of Ashoka, the word "Dharma" has been translated as eusebeia (Greek) and qsyt (Aramaic), which further suggests that his "Dharma" meant something more generic than Buddhism.
sentence_390: The inscriptions suggest that for Ashoka, Dharma meant "a moral polity of active social concern, religious tolerance, ecological awareness, the observance of common ethical precepts, and the renunciation of war."
sentence_391: For example:

list.value: Abolition of the death penalty (Pillar Edict IV)
Plantation of banyan trees and mango groves, and construction of resthouses and wells, every 800 metres (⁄2 mile) along the roads. (Pillar Edict 7).

Restriction on killing of animals in the royal kitchen (Rock Edict 1); the number of animals killed was limited to two peacocks and a deer daily, and in future, even these animals were not to be killed.
Provision of medical facilities for humans and animals (Rock Edict 2).
Encouragement of obedience to parents, "generosity toward priests and ascetics, and frugality in spending" (Rock Edict 3).
He "commissions officers to work for the welfare and happiness of the poor and aged" (Rock Edict 5)
Promotion of "the welfare of all beings so as to pay off his debt to living creatures and to work for their happiness in this world and the next." (Rock Edict 6)

sentence_392: Modern scholars have variously understood this dhamma as a Buddhist lay ethic, a set of politico-moral ideas, a "sort of universal religion", or as an Ashokan innovation.
sentence_393: On the other hand, it has also been interpreted as an essentially political ideology that sought to knit together a vast and diverse empire.
sentence_394: Ashoka instituted a new category of officers called the dhamma-mahamattas, who were tasked with the welfare of the aged, the infrm, the women and children, and various religious sects.
sentence_395: They were also sent on diplomatic missions to the Hellenistic kingdoms of west Asia, in order to propagate the dhamma.
sentence_396: Historically, the image of Ashoka in the global Buddhist circles was based on legends (such as those mentioned in the [[Ashokavadana|Ashokavadana]]) rather than his rock edicts.
sentence_397: This was because the Brahmi script in which these edicts were written was forgotten soon and remained undeciphered until its study by James Prinsep in the 19th century.
sentence_398: The writings of the Chinese Buddhist pilgrims such as Faxian and Xuanzang suggest that Ashoka's inscriptions mark the important sites associated with Gautama Buddha.
sentence_399: These writers attribute Buddhism-related content to Ashoka's edicts, but this content does not match with the actual text of the inscriptions as determined by modern scholars after the decipherment of the Brahmi script.
sentence_400: It is likely that the script was forgotten by the time of Faxian, who probably relied on local guides; these guides may have made up some Buddhism-related interpretations to gratify him, or may have themselves relied on faulty translations based on oral traditions.
sentence_401: Xuanzang may have encountered a similar situation, or may have taken the supposed content of the inscriptions from Faxian's writings.
sentence_402: This theory is corroborated by the fact that some Brahmin scholars are known to have similarly come up with a fanciful interpretation of Ashoka pillar inscriptions, when requested to decipher them by the 14th century Muslim king Firuz Shah Tughlaq.
sentence_403: According to Shams-i Siraj's Tarikh-i Firoz Shahi, after the king had these pillar transported from [[Topra_Kalan|Topra]] and Mirat to Delhi as war trophies, these Brahmins told him that the inscriptions prophesized that nobody would be able to remove the pillars except a king named Firuz.
sentence_404: Moreover, by this time, there were local traditions that attributed the erection of these pillars to the legendary hero [[Bhima|Bhima]].
sentence_405: According to scholars such as Richard Gombrich, Ashoka's dharma shows Buddhist influence.
sentence_406: For example, the Kalinga Separate Edict I seems to be inspired by Buddha's Advice to Sigala and his other sermons.
sentence_407: Ashoka's rock edicts declare that injuring living things is not good, and no animal should be sacrificed for slaughter.
sentence_408: However, he did not prohibit common cattle slaughter or beef eating.
sentence_409: He imposed a ban on killing of "all four-footed creatures that are neither useful nor edible", and of specific animal species including several birds, certain types of fish and bulls among others.
sentence_410: He also banned killing of female goats, sheep and pigs that were nursing their young; as well as their young up to the age of six months.
sentence_411: He also banned killing of all fish and [[Neutering|castration]] of animals during certain periods such as [[Chaturmasa|Chaturmasa]] and [[Uposatha|Uposatha]].
sentence_412: Ashoka also abolished the royal hunting of animals and restricted the slaying of animals for food in the royal residence.
sentence_413: Because he banned hunting, created many veterinary clinics and eliminated meat eating on many holidays, the Mauryan Empire under Ashoka has been described as "one of the very few instances in world history of a government treating its animals as citizens who are as deserving of its protection as the human residents".
sentence_414: It is well known that Ashoka sent dütas or emissaries to convey messages or letters, written or oral (rather both), to various people.
sentence_415: The VIth Rock Edict about "oral orders" reveals this.
sentence_416: It was later confirmed that it was not unusual to add oral messages to written ones, and the content of Ashoka's messages can be inferred likewise from the XIIIth Rock Edict: They were meant to spread his dhammavijaya, which he considered the highest victory and which he wished to propagate everywhere (including far beyond India).
sentence_417: There is obvious and undeniable trace of cultural contact through the adoption of the [[Kharosthi|Kharosthi]] script, and the idea of installing inscriptions might have travelled with this script, as [[Achaemenid|Achaemenid]] influence is seen in some of the formulations used by Ashoka in his inscriptions.
sentence_418: This indicates to us that Ashoka was indeed in contact with other cultures, and was an active part in mingling and spreading new cultural ideas beyond his own immediate walls.
sentence_419: In his rock edicts, Ashoka states that he had encouraged the transmission of Buddhism to the [[Hellenistic_period|Hellenistic kingdoms]] to the west and that the Greeks in his dominion were converts to Buddhism and recipients of his envoys:
sentence_420: It is possible, but not certain, that Ashoka received letters from Greek rulers and was acquainted with the Hellenistic royal orders in the same way as he perhaps knew of the inscriptions of the Achaemenid kings, given the presence of ambassadors of Hellenistic kings in India (as well as the dütas sent by Ashoka himself).
sentence_421: [[Dionysius_(ambassador)|Dionysius]] is reported to have been such a Greek ambassador at the court of Ashoka, sent by [[Ptolemy_II_Philadelphus|Ptolemy II Philadelphus]], who himself is mentioned in the [[Edicts_of_Ashoka|Edicts of Ashoka]] as a recipient of the Buddhist proselytism of Ashoka.
sentence_422: Some Hellenistic philosophers, such as [[Hegesias_of_Cyrene|Hegesias of Cyrene]], who probably lived under the rule of King [[Magas_of_Cyrene|Magas]], one of the supposed recipients of Buddhist emissaries from Asoka, are sometimes thought to have been influenced by Buddhist teachings.
sentence_423: The Greeks in India even seem to have played an active role in the propagation of Buddhism, as some of the emissaries of Ashoka, such as [[Dharmaraksita|Dharmaraksita]], are described in [[Pāli|Pali]] sources as leading Greek (Yona) Buddhist monks, active in spreading Buddhism (the [[Mahavamsa|Mahavamsa]], XII).
sentence_424: Some Greeks (Yavana) may have played an administrative role in the territories ruled by Ashoka.
sentence_425: The Girnar inscription of [[Rudradaman|Rudradaman]] records that during the rule of Ashoka, a Yavana Governor was in charge in the area of Girnar, [[Gujarat|Gujarat]], mentioning his role in the construction of a water reservoir.
sentence_426: It is thought that Ashoka's palace at Patna was modelled after the Achaemenid palace of [[Persepolis|Persepolis]].
sentence_427: Buddhist legends mention stories about Ashoka's past lives.
sentence_428: According to a Mahavamsa story, Ashoka, Nigrodha and Devnampiya Tissa were brothers in a previous life.
sentence_429: In that life, a [[Pratyekabuddha|pratyekabuddha]] was looking for honey to cure another, sick pratyekabuddha.
sentence_430: A woman directed him to a honey shop owned by the three brothers.
sentence_431: Ashoka generously donated honey to the pratyekabuddha, and wished to become the sovereign ruler of Jambudvipa for this act of merit.
sentence_432: The woman wished to become his queen, and was reborn as Ashoka's wife Asandhamitta.
sentence_433: Later Pali texts credit her with an additional act of merit: she gifted the pratyekabuddha a piece of cloth made by her.
sentence_434: These texts include the Dasavatthuppakarana, the so-called Cambodian or Extended Mahavamsa (possibly from 9th–10th centuries), and the Trai Bhumi Katha (15th century).
sentence_435: According to an Ashokavadana story, Ashoka was born as Jaya in a prominent family of Rajagriha.
sentence_436: When he was a little boy, he gave the Gautama Buddha dirt imagining it to be food.
sentence_437: The Buddha approved of the donation, and Jaya declared that he would become a king by this act of merit.
sentence_438: The text also state that Jaya's companion Vijaya was reborn as Ashoka's prime-minister Radhagupta.
sentence_439: In the later life, the Buddhist monk Upagupta tells Ashoka that his rough skin was caused by the impure gift of dirt in the previous life.
sentence_440: Some later texts repeat this story, without mentioning the negative implications of gifting dirt; these texts include Kumaralata's Kalpana-manditika, Aryashura's Jataka-mala, and the Maha-karma-vibhaga.
sentence_441: The Chinese writer Pao Ch'eng's Shih chia ju lai ying hua lu asserts that an insignificant act like gifting dirt could not have been meritorious enough to cause Ashoka's future greatness.
sentence_442: Instead, the text claims that in another past life, Ashoka commissioned a large number of Buddha statues as a king, and this act of merit caused him to become a great emperor in the next life.
sentence_443: The 14th century Pali-language fairy tale Dasavatthuppakarana (possibly from c. 14th century) combines the stories about the merchant's gift of honey, and the boy's gift of dirt.
sentence_444: It narrates a slightly different version of the Mahavamsa story, stating that it took place before the birth of the Gautama Buddha.
sentence_445: It then states that the merchant was reborn as the boy who gifted dirt to the Buddha; however, in this case, the Buddha his attendant to [[Ānanda|Ānanda]] to create [[Plaster|plaster]] from the dirt, which is used repair cracks in the monastery walls.
sentence_446: Besides the various stupas attributed to Ashoka, the [[Pillars_of_Ashoka|pillars erected by him]] survive at various places in the Indian subcontinent.
sentence_447: Ashoka is often credited with the beginning of stone architecture in India, possibly following the introduction of stone-building techniques by the [[Greco-Bactrian|Greeks after Alexander the Great]].
sentence_448: Before Ashoka's time, buildings were probably built in non-permanent material, such as wood, [[Bamboo|bamboo]] or thatch.
sentence_449: Ashoka may have rebuilt his palace in [[Pataliputra|Pataliputra]] by replacing wooden material by stone, and may also have used the help of foreign craftmen.
sentence_450: Ashoka also innovated by using the permanent qualities of stone for his written [[Edicts_of_Ashoka|edicts]], as well as his pillars with Buddhist symbolism.
sentence_451: Ashokan capitals were highly realistic and used a characteristic polished finish, [[Mauryan_polish|Mauryan polish]], giving a shiny appearance to the stone surface.
sentence_452: [[Lion_Capital_of_Ashoka|Lion Capital of Ashoka]], the capital of one of the pillars erected by Ashoka features a carving of a spoked wheel, known as the [[Ashoka_Chakra|Ashoka Chakra]].
sentence_453: This wheel represents the wheel of Dhamma set in motion by the Gautama Buddha, and appears on the flag of modern India.
sentence_454: This capital also features sculptures of lions, which appear on the seal of India.
sentence_455: The edicts of Ashoka are a collection of 33 inscriptions on the [[Pillars_of_Ashoka|Pillars of Ashoka]], as well as boulders and cave walls, issued during his reign.
sentence_456: These inscriptions are dispersed throughout modern-day Pakistan and India, and represent the first tangible evidence of Buddhism.
sentence_457: The edicts describe in detail the first wide expansion of Buddhism through the sponsorship of one of the most powerful kings of Indian history, offering more information about Ashoka's proselytism, moral precepts, religious precepts, and his notions of social and animal welfare.
sentence_458: Before Ashoka, the royal communications appear to have been written on perishable materials such as palm leaves, birch barks, cotton cloth, and possibly wooden boards.
sentence_459: While Ashoka's administration would have continued to use these materials, Ashoka also had his messages inscribed on rock edicts.
sentence_460: Ashoka probably got the idea of putting up these inscriptions from the neighbouring [[Achaemenid_empire|Achaemenid empire]].
sentence_461: It is likely that Ashoka's messages were also inscribed on more perishable materials, such as wood, and sent to various parts of the empire.
sentence_462: None of these records survive now.
sentence_463: Scholars are still attempting to analyse both the expressed and implied political ideas of the Edicts (particularly in regard to imperial vision), and make inferences pertaining to how that vision was grappling with problems and political realities of a "virtually subcontinental, and culturally and economically highly variegated, 3rd century BCE Indian empire.
sentence_464: Nonetheless, it remains clear that Ashoka's Inscriptions represent the earliest corpus of royal inscriptions in the Indian subcontinent, and therefore prove to be a very important innovation in royal practices."
sentence_465: Most of Ashoka's inscriptions are written in a mixture of various [[Prakrit|Prakrit]] dialects, in the [[Brahmi|Brahmi]] script.
sentence_466: Several of Ashoka's inscriptions appear to have been set up near towns, on important routes, and at places of religious significance.
sentence_467: Many of the inscriptions have been discovered in hills, rock shelters, and places of local significance.
sentence_468: Various theories have been put forward about why Ashoka or his officials chose such places, including that they were centres of megalithic cultures, were regarded as sacred spots in Ashoka's time, or that their physical grandeur may be symbolic of spiritual dominance.
sentence_469: Ashoka's inscriptions have not been found at major cities of the Maurya empire, such as Pataliputra, Vidisha, Ujjayini, and Taxila.
sentence_470: It is possible that many of these inscriptions are lost; the 7th century Chinese pilgrim [[Xuanzang|Xuanzang]] refers to some of Ashoka's pillar edicts, which have not been discovered by modern researchers.
sentence_471: It appears that Ashoka dispatched every message to his provincial governors, who in turn, relayed it to various officials in their territory.
sentence_472: For example, the [[Minor_Rock_Edicts#Full_texts_of_the_Minor_Rock_Edicts|Minor Rock Edict 1]] appears in several versions at multiple places: all the versions state that Ashoka issued the proclamation while on a tour, having spent 256 days on tour.
sentence_473: The number 256 indicates that the message was dispatched simultaneously to various places.
sentence_474: Three versions of a message, found at edicts in the neighbouring places in Karnataka (Brahmagiri, Siddapura, and Jatinga-Rameshwara), were sent from the southern province's capital Suvarnagiri to various places.
sentence_475: All three versions contain the same message, preceded by an initial greeting from the arya-putra (presumably Ashoka's son and the provincial governor) and the mahamatras (officials) in Suvarnagiri.
sentence_476: The [[Caduceus|caduceus]] appears as a symbol of the punch-marked coins of the [[Maurya_Empire|Maurya Empire]] in India, in the 3rd–2nd century BCE.
sentence_477: Numismatic research suggests that this symbol was the symbol of king Ashoka, his personal "[[Mudra|Mudra]]".
sentence_478: This symbol was not used on the pre-Mauryan punch-marked coins, but only on coins of the Maurya period, together with the [[Arched-hill_symbol|three arched-hill symbol]], the "peacock on the hill", the [[Triskelis|triskelis]] and the [[Taxila|Taxila]] mark.
sentence_479: Ashoka had almost been forgotten, but in the 19th century [[James_Prinsep|James Prinsep]] contributed in the revelation of historical sources.
sentence_480: After deciphering the [[Brahmi_script|Brahmi script]], Prinsep had originally identified the "[[Priyadasi|Priyadasi]]" of the inscriptions he found with the King of [[Ceylon|Ceylon]] [[Devanampiya_Tissa_of_Anuradhapura|Devanampiya Tissa]].
sentence_481: However, in 1837, [[George_Turnour|George Turnour]] discovered an important Sri Lankan manuscript ([[Dipavamsa|Dipavamsa]], or "Island Chronicle" ) associating Piyadasi with Ashoka:
sentence_482: Since then, the association of "Devanampriya Priyadarsin" with Ashoka was confirmed through various inscriptions, and especially confirmed in the [[Minor_Rock_Edict|Minor Rock Edict]] inscription discovered in [[Maski|Maski]], directly associating Ashoka with his regnal title Devanampriya ("Beloved-of-the-Gods"):
sentence_483: Another important historian was British [[Archaeologist|archaeologist]] [[John_Hubert_Marshall|John Hubert Marshall]], who was director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India.
sentence_484: His main interests were [[Sanchi|Sanchi]] and Sarnath, in addition to [[Harappa|Harappa]] and [[Mohenjo-daro|Mohenjodaro]].
sentence_485: Sir [[Alexander_Cunningham|Alexander Cunningham]], a British archaeologist and army engineer, and often known as the father of the Archaeological Survey of India, unveiled heritage sites like the [[Bharhut|Bharhut]] Stupa, Sarnath, Sanchi, and the Mahabodhi Temple.
sentence_486: [[Mortimer_Wheeler|Mortimer Wheeler]], a British archaeologist, also exposed Ashokan historical sources, especially the [[Taxila|Taxila]].
sentence_487: The use of Buddhist sources in reconstructing the life of Ashoka has had a strong influence on perceptions of Ashoka, as well as the interpretations of his Edicts.
sentence_488: Building on traditional accounts, early scholars regarded Ashoka as a primarily Buddhist monarch who underwent a conversion to Buddhism and was actively engaged in sponsoring and supporting the Buddhist monastic institution.
sentence_489: Some scholars have tended to question this assessment.
sentence_490: Romila Thappar writes about Ashoka that "We need to see him both as a statesman in the context of inheriting and sustaining an empire in a particular historical period, and as a person with a strong commitment to changing society through what might be called the propagation of social ethics."
sentence_491: The only source of information not attributable to Buddhist sources are the Ashokan Edicts, and these do not explicitly state that Ashoka was a Buddhist.
sentence_492: In his edicts, Ashoka expresses support for all the major religions of his time: [[Buddhism|Buddhism]], [[Vedic_Brahmanism|Brahmanism]], [[Jainism|Jainism]], and [[Ajivika|Ajivikaism]], and his edicts addressed to the population at large (there are some addressed specifically to Buddhists; this is not the case for the other religions) generally focus on moral themes members of all the religions would accept.
sentence_493: For example, Amartya Sen writes, "The Indian Emperor Ashoka in the third century BCE presented many political inscriptions in favor of tolerance and individual freedom, both as a part of state policy and in the relation of different people to each other".
sentence_494: However, the edicts alone strongly indicate that he was a Buddhist.
sentence_495: In one edict he belittles rituals, and he banned Vedic animal sacrifices; these strongly suggest that he at least did not look to the Vedic tradition for guidance.
sentence_496: Furthermore, many edicts are expressed to Buddhists alone; in one, Ashoka declares himself to be an "[[Upasaka|upasaka]]", and in another he demonstrates a close familiarity with Buddhist texts.
sentence_497: He erected rock pillars at Buddhist holy sites, but did not do so for the sites of other religions.
sentence_498: He also used the word [[Dharma_(Buddhism)|"dhamma"]] to refer to qualities of the heart that underlie moral action; this was an exclusively Buddhist use of the word.
sentence_499: However, he used the word more in the spirit than as a strict code of conduct.
sentence_500: Romila Thappar writes, "His dhamma did not derive from divine inspiration, even if its observance promised heaven.
sentence_501: It was more in keeping with the ethic conditioned by the logic of given situations.
sentence_502: His logic of Dhamma was intended to influence the conduct of categories of people, in relation to each other.
sentence_503: Especially where they involved unequal relationships."
sentence_504: Finally, he promotes ideals that correspond to the first three steps of the Buddha's graduated discourse.
sentence_505: Much of the knowledge about Ashoka comes from the [[Edicts_of_Ashoka|several inscriptions]] that he had carved on pillars and rocks throughout the empire.
sentence_506: All his inscriptions present him as compassionate and loving.
sentence_507: In the Kalinga rock edits, he addresses his people as his "children" and mentions that as a father he desires their good.
sentence_508: After Ashoka's death, the [[Maurya_Empire#Decline|Maurya empire declined]] rapidly.
sentence_509: The various Puranas provide different details about Ashoka's successors, but all agree that they had relatively short reigns.
sentence_510: The empire seems to have weakened, fragmented, and suffered an invasion from the [[Greco-Bactrian_Kingdom|Bactrian Greeks]].
sentence_511: Some historians, such as [[H._C._Raychaudhuri|H.
sentence_512: C. Raychaudhuri]], have argued that Ashoka's pacifism undermined the "military backbone" of the Maurya empire.
sentence_513: Others, such as [[Romila_Thapar|Romila Thapar]], have suggested that the extent and impact of his pacifism have been "grossly exaggerated".

list.value: Jaishankar Prasad composed Ashoka ki Chinta (Ashoka's Anxiety), a poem that portrays Ashoka's feelings during the war on Kalinga.
[[Ashok_Kumar_(film)|Ashok Kumar]] is a 1941 [[Tamil_language|Tamil]] film directed by Raja Chandrasekhar. The film stars [[Chittor_V._Nagaiah|Chittor V. Nagaiah]] as Ashoka.

Uttar-Priyadarshi (The Final Beatitude), a verse-play written by poet Agyeya depicting his redemption, was adapted to stage in 1996 by theatre director, [[Ratan_Thiyam|Ratan Thiyam]] and has since been performed in many parts of the world.
In 1973, [[Amar_Chitra_Katha|Amar Chitra Katha]] released a graphic novel based on the life of Ashoka.
In [[Piers_Anthony|Piers Anthony]]'s series of [[Space_opera|space opera]] novels, the main character mentions Ashoka as a model for administrators to strive for.
[[Aśoka_(2001_film)|Aśoka]] is a 2001 epic Indian historical drama film directed and co-written by [[Santosh_Sivan|Santosh Sivan]]. The film stars [[Shah_Rukh_Khan|Shah Rukh Khan]] as Ashoka.
In 2002, Mason Jennings released the song "Emperor Ashoka" on his [[Living_in_the_Moment_(Mason_Jennings_EP)|Living in the Moment EP]]. It is based on the life of Ashoka.
In 2013, Christopher C. Doyle released his debut novel, [[The_Mahabharata_Secret|The Mahabharata Secret]], in which he wrote about Ashoka hiding a dangerous secret for the well-being of India.
2014's [[The_Emperor's_Riddles|The Emperor's Riddles]], a fiction mystery thriller novel by Satyarth Nayak, traces the evolution of Ashoka and his esoteric legend of the Nine Unknown Men.
In 2015, [[Chakravartin_Ashoka_Samrat|Chakravartin Ashoka Samrat]], a television serial by [[Ashok_Banker|Ashok Banker]], based on the life of Ashoka, began airing on [[Colors_TV|Colors TV]].

The Legend of Kunal is an upcoming film based on the life of Kunal, the son of Ashoka. The movie will be directed by Chandraprakash Dwivedi. The role of Ashoka is to be played by [[Amitabh_Bachchan|Amitabh Bachchan]], and the role of Kunal is played by [[Arjun_Rampal|Arjun Rampal]].

[[Bharatvarsh_(TV_Series)|Bharatvarsh (TV Series)]] is an Indian television historical documentary series, hosted by actor-director [[Anupam_Kher|Anupam Kher]] on Hindi news channel [[ABP_News|ABP News]]. The series stars [[Aham_Sharma|Aham Sharma]] as Ashoka.
