sentence_1: The American Civil War (also [[Names_of_the_American_Civil_War|known by other names]]) was a civil war in the [[United_States|United States]] from 1861 to 1865, fought between [[Northern_United_States|northern states]] loyal to the [[Union_(American_Civil_War)|Union]] and [[Southern_United_States|southern states]] that had [[Secession|seceded]] to form the [[Confederate_States_of_America|Confederate States of America]].
sentence_2: The civil war began primarily as a result of the long-standing [[Origins_of_the_American_Civil_War|controversy]] over [[Slavery_in_the_United_States|the enslavement of Black people]].
sentence_3: War broke out in April 1861 when secessionist forces attacked [[Battle_of_Fort_Sumter|Fort Sumter]] in [[South_Carolina|South Carolina]], just over a month after [[Abraham_Lincoln|Abraham Lincoln]] had been [[First_inauguration_of_Abraham_Lincoln|inaugurated]] as the [[President_of_the_United_States|President of the United States]].
sentence_4: The loyalists of the Union in the North, which also included some geographically western and southern states, proclaimed support for the [[Constitution_of_the_United_States|Constitution]].
sentence_5: They faced secessionists of the Confederate States in the South, who advocated for states' rights to uphold slavery.
sentence_6: Of the 34 [[U.S._state|U.S.
sentence_7: states]] in February 1861, seven Southern [[Slave_states_and_free_states|slave states]] were declared by their state governments to have seceded from the country, and the Confederate States of America was organized in rebellion against the U.S. constitutional government.
sentence_8: The Confederacy grew to control at least a majority of territory in eleven states, and it claimed the additional states of Kentucky and Missouri by assertions from native secessionists fleeing Union authority.
sentence_9: These states were given full representation in the [[Confederate_States_Congress|Confederate Congress]] throughout the Civil War.
sentence_10: The two remaining slave states, Delaware and Maryland, were invited to join the Confederacy, but nothing substantial developed due to [[Ex_parte_Merryman|intervention]] [[Habeas_Corpus_Suspension_Act_(1863)|by federal troops]].
sentence_11: The Confederate states were never diplomatically recognized as a joint entity by the [[Federal_government_of_the_United_States|government of the United States]], nor by that of any foreign country.
sentence_12: The states that remained loyal to the [[United_States|U.S.]]
sentence_13: were known as the Union.
sentence_14: The Union and the Confederacy quickly raised volunteer and conscription armies that fought mostly in the South for four years.
sentence_15: Intense combat left between 620,000 and 750,000 soldiers dead, along with an undetermined number of [[Civilian_casualties|civilians]].
sentence_16: The Civil War remains the deadliest military conflict in American history, and accounted for more American military deaths than all other wars combined until the Vietnam War.
sentence_17: The war [[Conclusion_of_the_American_Civil_War|effectively ended]] on April 9, 1865, when Confederate General [[Robert_E._Lee|Robert E. Lee]] [[Surrender_(military)|surrendered]] to Union General [[Ulysses_S._Grant|Ulysses S. Grant]] at the [[Battle_of_Appomattox_Court_House|Battle of Appomattox Court House]].
sentence_18: Confederate generals throughout the Southern states followed suit, the last surrender on land occurring June 23.
sentence_19: Much of the South's infrastructure was destroyed, especially its railroads.
sentence_20: The Confederacy [[Conclusion_of_the_American_Civil_War#Capture_of_President_Davis_(May_10)|collapsed]], slavery was abolished, and four million enslaved Black people were freed.
sentence_21: The war-torn nation then entered the [[Reconstruction_era|Reconstruction era]] in a partially successful attempt to rebuild the country and grant [[Civil_rights|civil rights]] to freed slaves.
sentence_22: The war is one of the most studied and [[Bibliography_of_the_American_Civil_War|written about]] episodes in [[History_of_the_United_States|U.S.
sentence_23: history]], and remains the subject of cultural and [[Historiographic_issues_about_the_American_Civil_War|historiographical debate]].
sentence_24: Of particular interest are the [[Causes_of_the_Civil_War|causes of the Civil War]] and the persisting myth of the [[Lost_Cause_of_the_Confederacy|Lost Cause of the Confederacy]].
sentence_25: The American Civil War was among the earliest industrial wars.
sentence_26: Railroads, the [[Telegraph|telegraph]], steamships and [[Ironclad_warship|iron-clad]] ships, and mass-produced weapons were employed extensively.
sentence_27: The mobilization of civilian factories, mines, shipyards, banks, transportation, and food supplies all foreshadowed the impact of industrialization in [[World_War_I|World War I]], [[World_War_II|World War II]], and subsequent conflicts.
sentence_28: It remains the deadliest war in [[History_of_the_United_States|American history]].
sentence_29: By one estimate, the war claimed the lives of 10 percent of all Northern men 20–45 years old, and 30 percent of all Southern white men aged 18–40.
sentence_30: The practice of [[Slavery_in_the_United_States|slavery in the United States]] was one of the key political issues of the 19th century.
sentence_31: Slavery had been a controversial issue during the framing of the [[Constitution_of_the_United_States|Constitution]], but the issue was left unsettled.
sentence_32: In the [[1860_United_States_presidential_election|1860 presidential election]], [[Republican_Party_(United_States)|Republicans]], led by [[Abraham_Lincoln|Abraham Lincoln]], supported banning slavery in all the [[Territories_of_the_United_States|U.S.
sentence_33: territories]] (parts of the U.S. that are not states).
sentence_34: The Southern states viewed this as a violation of their constitutional rights, and as the first step in a grander Republican plan to eventually abolish slavery.
sentence_35: The three pro-Union candidates together received an overwhelming 82% majority of the votes cast nationally: Republican Lincoln's votes centered in the north, [[Democratic_Party_(United_States)|Democrat]] [[Stephen_A._Douglas|Stephen A. Douglas]]' votes were distributed nationally and [[Constitutional_Union_Party_(United_States)|Constitutional Unionist]] [[John_Bell_(Tennessee_politician)|John Bell]]'s votes centered in [[Tennessee|Tennessee]], [[Kentucky|Kentucky]], and [[Virginia|Virginia]].
sentence_36: The Republican Party, dominant in the North, secured a [[Plurality_(voting)|plurality]] of the popular votes and a majority of the electoral votes nationally; thus Lincoln was elected president.
sentence_37: He was the first Republican Party candidate to win the presidency.
sentence_38: The South was outraged, and before [[First_inauguration_of_Abraham_Lincoln|his inauguration]], seven slave states with [[Cotton|cotton]]-based economies declared secession and formed the [[Confederate_States_of_America|Confederacy]].
sentence_39: The first six to declare secession had the highest proportions of slaves in their populations, with an average of 49 percent.
sentence_40: Of those states whose legislatures resolved for secession, the first seven voted with split majorities for unionist candidates Douglas and Bell ([[Georgia_(U.S._state)|Georgia]] with 51% and [[Louisiana|Louisiana]] with 55%), or with sizable minorities for those unionists ([[Alabama|Alabama]] with 46%, [[Mississippi|Mississippi]] with 40%, [[Florida|Florida]] with 38%, [[Texas|Texas]] with 25%, and [[South_Carolina|South Carolina]], which cast [[United_States_Electoral_College|Electoral College]] votes without a popular vote for president).
sentence_41: Eight remaining slave-holding states continued to reject calls for secession.
sentence_42: Outgoing Democratic President [[James_Buchanan|James Buchanan]] and the incoming Republicans rejected secession as illegal.
sentence_43: Lincoln's [[Abraham_Lincoln's_first_inaugural_address|March 4, 1861, inaugural address]] declared that his administration would not initiate a civil war.
sentence_44: Speaking directly to the "Southern States", he attempted to calm their fears of any threats to slavery, reaffirming, "I have no purpose, directly or indirectly to interfere with the institution of slavery in the United States where it exists.
sentence_45: I believe I have no lawful right to do so, and I have no inclination to do so."
sentence_46: After Confederate forces seized numerous federal forts within territory claimed by the Confederacy, efforts at compromise failed and both sides prepared for war.
sentence_47: The Confederates assumed that [[Europe|European]] countries were so dependent on "[[King_Cotton|King Cotton]]" that they would intervene, but none did, and none recognized the new Confederate States of America.
sentence_48: Hostilities began on April 12, 1861, when Confederate forces [[Battle_of_Fort_Sumter|fired upon Fort Sumter]].
sentence_49: While in the [[Western_Theater_of_the_American_Civil_War|Western Theater]] the Union made significant permanent gains, in the [[Eastern_Theater_of_the_American_Civil_War|Eastern Theater]], the conflict was inconclusive during 1861–1862.
sentence_50: In September 1862, Lincoln issued the [[Emancipation_Proclamation|Emancipation Proclamation]], which made ending slavery a war goal.
sentence_51: To the west, the Union destroyed the Confederate river navy by summer 1862, then much of its western armies, and seized [[New_Orleans|New Orleans]].
sentence_52: The successful 1863 Union [[Siege_of_Vicksburg|siege of Vicksburg]] split the Confederacy in two at the [[Mississippi_River|Mississippi River]].
sentence_53: In 1863, [[Robert_E._Lee|Robert E. Lee]]'s Confederate incursion north ended at the [[Battle_of_Gettysburg|Battle of Gettysburg]].
sentence_54: Western successes led to [[Ulysses_S._Grant|Ulysses S. Grant]]'s command of all Union armies in 1864.
sentence_55: Inflicting an ever-tightening [[Union_blockade|naval blockade]] of Confederate ports, the Union marshaled resources and manpower to attack the Confederacy from all directions, leading to the fall of Atlanta to [[William_Tecumseh_Sherman|William Tecumseh Sherman]] and [[Sherman's_March_to_the_Sea|his march to the sea]].
sentence_56: The last significant battles raged around the [[Siege_of_Petersburg|Siege of Petersburg]].
sentence_57: Lee's escape attempt ended with his [[Battle_of_Appomattox_Court_House|surrender at Appomattox Court House]], on April 9, 1865.
sentence_58: While the military war was coming to an end, the political reintegration of the nation was to take another 12 years, known as the [[Reconstruction_era|Reconstruction era]].
sentence_59: Main articles: [[Origins_of_the_American_Civil_War|Origins of the American Civil War]] and [[Timeline_of_events_leading_to_the_American_Civil_War|Timeline of events leading to the American Civil War]]
sentence_60: The causes of secession were complex and have been controversial since the war began, but most academic scholars identify slavery as a central cause of the war.
sentence_61: James C. Bradford wrote that the issue has been further complicated by [[Historical_negationism|historical revisionists]], who have tried to offer a variety of reasons for the war.
sentence_62: Slavery was the central source of escalating political tension in the [[Timeline_of_United_States_history_(1820–1859)#1850s|1850s]].
sentence_63: The [[Republican_Party_(United_States)|Republican Party]] was determined to prevent any spread of slavery to newly formed states, and many Southern leaders had threatened secession if the Republican candidate, [[Abraham_Lincoln|Lincoln]], won the [[1860_United_States_presidential_election|1860 election]].
sentence_64: After Lincoln won, many Southern leaders felt that disunion was their only option, fearing that the loss of representation would hamper their ability to promote pro-slavery acts and policies.
sentence_65: Further information: [[Slave_Power|Slave Power]]
sentence_66: Slavery was a major cause of disunion.
sentence_67: Although there were opposing views even in the Union States, most Northern soldiers were mostly indifferent on the subject of slavery, while Confederates fought the war mainly to protect a Southern society of which slavery was an integral part.
sentence_68: From the anti-slavery perspective, the issue was primarily about whether the system of slavery was an anachronistic evil that was incompatible with [[Republicanism_in_the_United_States|republicanism]].
sentence_69: The strategy of the anti-slavery forces was containment—to stop the expansion and thus put slavery on a path to gradual extinction.
sentence_70: The slave-holding interests in the South denounced this strategy as infringing upon their Constitutional rights.
sentence_71: Southern whites believed that the emancipation of slaves would destroy the South's economy, due to the large amount of capital invested in slaves and fears of integrating the ex-slave black population.
sentence_72: In particular, Southerners feared a repeat of [[1804_Haiti_massacre|"the horrors of Santo Domingo"]], in which nearly all white people – including men, women, children, and even many sympathetic to abolition – were killed after the [[Haitian_Revolution|successful slave revolt in Haiti]].
sentence_73: Historian Thomas Fleming points to the historical phrase "a disease in the public mind" used by critics of this idea, and proposes it contributed to the segregation in the [[Jim_Crow|Jim Crow]] era following emancipation.
sentence_74: These fears were exacerbated by the [[John_Brown's_raid_on_Harpers_Ferry|1859 attempt]] of [[John_Brown_(abolitionist)|John Brown]] to instigate an armed slave rebellion in the South.
sentence_75: Slavery was illegal in much of the North, having been outlawed in the late 18th and early 19th centuries.
sentence_76: It was also fading in the border states and Southern cities, but it was expanding in the highly profitable cotton districts of the rural South and Southwest.
sentence_77: Subsequent writers on the American Civil War looked to several factors explaining the geographic divide.
sentence_78: Main article: [[Abolitionism_in_the_United_States|Abolitionism in the United States]]
sentence_79: The [[Abolitionism_in_the_United_States|abolitionists]] – those advocating the abolition of slavery – were very active in the decades leading up to the Civil War.
sentence_80: They traced their philosophical roots back to the [[Puritans|Puritans]], who strongly believed that slavery was morally wrong.
sentence_81: One of the early Puritan writings on this subject was "The Selling of Joseph," by Samuel Sewall in 1700.
sentence_82: In it, Sewall condemned slavery and the slave trade and refuted many of the era's typical justifications for slavery.
sentence_83: The [[American_Revolution|American Revolution]] and the cause of liberty added tremendous impetus to the abolitionist cause.
sentence_84: Slavery, which had been around for thousands of years, was considered "normal" and was not a significant issue of public debate prior to the Revolution.
sentence_85: The Revolution changed that and made it into an issue that had to be addressed.
sentence_86: As a result, shortly after the Revolution, the northern states quickly started outlawing slavery.
sentence_87: Even in southern states, laws were changed to limit slavery and facilitate manumission.
sentence_88: The amount of indentured servitude (temporary slavery) dropped dramatically throughout the country.
sentence_89: An [[Act_Prohibiting_Importation_of_Slaves|Act Prohibiting Importation of Slaves]] sailed through Congress with little opposition.
sentence_90: President [[Thomas_Jefferson|Thomas Jefferson]] supported it, and it went in effect on January 1, 1808.
sentence_91: [[Benjamin_Franklin|Benjamin Franklin]] and [[James_Madison|James Madison]] each helped found manumission societies.
sentence_92: Influenced by the Revolution, many individual slave owners, such as [[George_Washington|George Washington]], freed their slaves, often in their wills.
sentence_93: The number of free blacks as a proportion of the black population in the upper South increased from less than 1 percent to nearly 10 percent between 1790 and 1810 as a result of these actions.
sentence_94: The establishment of the [[Northwest_Territory|Northwest Territory]] as "free soil" – no slavery – by [[Manasseh_Cutler|Manasseh Cutler]] and [[Rufus_Putnam|Rufus Putnam]] (who both came from Puritan New England) would also prove crucial.
sentence_95: This territory (which became the states of Ohio, Michigan, Indiana, Illinois, Wisconsin and part of Minnesota) doubled the size of the United States.
sentence_96: If these had been slave states, and their electoral votes gone to Abraham Lincoln's main opponent, Lincoln would not have been elected president.
sentence_97: The Civil War would not have been fought.
sentence_98: In the decades leading up to the Civil War, the abolitionists, such as [[Theodore_Parker|Theodore Parker]], [[Ralph_Waldo_Emerson|Ralph Waldo Emerson]], [[Henry_David_Thoreau|Henry David Thoreau]] and [[Frederick_Douglass|Frederick Douglass]], repeatedly used the Puritan heritage of the country to bolster their cause.
sentence_99: The most radical anti-slavery newspaper, The Liberator, invoked the Puritans and Puritan values over a thousand times.
sentence_100: Parker, in urging New England Congressmen to support the abolition of slavery, wrote that "The son of the Puritan ... is sent to Congress to stand up for Truth and Right..."
sentence_101: By 1840 more than 15,000 people were members of abolitionist societies in the United States.
sentence_102: Abolitionism in the United States became a popular expression of [[Moralism|moralism]], and led directly to the Civil War.
sentence_103: In churches, conventions and newspapers, reformers promoted an absolute and immediate rejection of slavery.
sentence_104: Further information: [[Slave_states_and_free_states|Slave states and free states]]
sentence_105: Between 1803 and 1854, the United States achieved a vast expansion of territory through purchase, negotiation, and conquest.
sentence_106: At first, the new states carved out of these territories entering the union were apportioned equally between slave and free states.
sentence_107: Pro- and anti-slavery forces collided over the territories west of the Mississippi.
sentence_108: With the conquest of northern [[Mexico|Mexico]] west to [[Alta_California|California]] in 1848, slaveholding interests looked forward to expanding into these lands and perhaps Cuba and Central America as well.
sentence_109: Northern "free soil" interests vigorously sought to curtail any further expansion of slave territory.
sentence_110: The [[Compromise_of_1850|Compromise of 1850]] over California balanced a free-soil state with stronger fugitive slave laws for a political settlement after four years of strife in the 1840s.
sentence_111: But the states admitted following [[California|California]] were all free: [[Minnesota|Minnesota]] (1858), [[Oregon|Oregon]] (1859), and [[Kansas|Kansas]] (1861).
sentence_112: In the Southern states the question of the territorial expansion of slavery westward again became explosive.
sentence_113: Both the South and the North drew the same conclusion: "The power to decide the question of slavery for the territories was the power to determine the future of slavery itself."
sentence_114: By 1860, four doctrines had emerged to answer the question of federal control in the territories, and they all claimed they were sanctioned by the Constitution, implicitly or explicitly.
sentence_115: The first of these "conservative" theories, represented by the [[Constitutional_Union_Party_(United_States)|Constitutional Union Party]], argued that the [[Missouri_Compromise|Missouri Compromise]] apportionment of territory north for free soil and south for slavery should become a Constitutional mandate.
sentence_116: The [[Crittenden_Compromise|Crittenden Compromise]] of 1860 was an expression of this view.
sentence_117: The second doctrine of Congressional preeminence, championed by Abraham Lincoln and the Republican Party, insisted that the Constitution did not bind legislators to a policy of balance—that slavery could be excluded in a territory as it was done in the [[Northwest_Ordinance|Northwest Ordinance]] of 1787 at the discretion of Congress; thus Congress could restrict human bondage, but never establish it.
sentence_118: The [[Wilmot_Proviso|Wilmot Proviso]] announced this position in 1846.
sentence_119: Senator [[Stephen_A._Douglas|Stephen A. Douglas]] proclaimed the doctrine of territorial or "popular" sovereignty—which asserted that the settlers in a territory had the same rights as states in the Union to establish or disestablish slavery as a purely local matter.
sentence_120: The [[Kansas–Nebraska_Act|Kansas–Nebraska Act]] of 1854 legislated this doctrine.
sentence_121: In the Kansas Territory, years of [[Bleeding_Kansas|pro and anti-slavery violence]] and political conflict erupted; the congressional House of Representatives voted to admit Kansas as a free state in early 1860, but its admission did not pass the Senate until January 1861, after the departure of Southern senators.
sentence_122: The fourth theory was advocated by Mississippi Senator [[Jefferson_Davis|Jefferson Davis]], one of state sovereignty ("states' rights"), also known as the "Calhoun doctrine", named after the South Carolinian political theorist and statesman [[John_C._Calhoun|John C. Calhoun]].
sentence_123: Rejecting the arguments for federal authority or self-government, state sovereignty would empower states to promote the expansion of slavery as part of the federal union under the U.S. Constitution.
sentence_124: "States' rights" was an ideology formulated and applied as a means of advancing slave state interests through federal authority.
sentence_125: As historian Thomas L. Krannawitter points out, the "Southern demand for federal slave protection represented a demand for an unprecedented expansion of federal power."
sentence_126: These four doctrines comprised the dominant ideologies presented to the American public on the matters of slavery, the territories, and the U.S. Constitution before the 1860 presidential election.
sentence_127: The South argued that just as each state had decided to join the Union, a state had the right to secede—leave the Union—at any time.
sentence_128: Northerners (including President Buchanan) rejected that notion as opposed to the will of the [[Founding_Fathers_of_the_United_States|Founding Fathers]], who said they were setting up a perpetual union.
sentence_129: Historian James McPherson writes concerning states' rights and other non-slavery explanations:
sentence_130: [[Sectionalism|Sectionalism]] resulted from the different economies, social structure, customs, and political values of the North and South.
sentence_131: Regional tensions came to a head during the War of 1812, resulting in the [[Hartford_Convention|Hartford Convention]], which manifested Northern dissatisfaction with a foreign trade embargo that affected the industrial North disproportionately, the [[Three-Fifths_Compromise|Three-Fifths Compromise]], dilution of Northern power by new states, and a succession of Southern presidents.
sentence_132: Sectionalism increased steadily between 1800 and 1860 as the North, which phased slavery out of existence, industrialized, urbanized, and built prosperous farms, while the deep South concentrated on plantation agriculture based on slave labor, together with [[Subsistence_agriculture|subsistence agriculture]] for poor whites.
sentence_133: In the 1840s and 1850s, the issue of accepting slavery (in the guise of rejecting slave-owning bishops and missionaries) split the nation's largest religious denominations (the Methodist, Baptist, and Presbyterian churches) into separate Northern and Southern denominations.
sentence_134: Historians have debated whether economic differences between the mainly industrial North and the mainly agricultural South helped cause the war.
sentence_135: Most historians now disagree with the economic determinism of historian [[Charles_A._Beard|Charles A.
sentence_136: Beard]] in the 1920s, and emphasize that Northern and Southern economies were largely complementary.
sentence_137: While socially different, the sections economically benefited each other.
sentence_138: Owners of slaves preferred low-cost manual labor with no mechanization.
sentence_139: Northern manufacturing interests supported tariffs and protectionism while Southern planters demanded free trade.
sentence_140: The Democrats in Congress, controlled by Southerners, wrote the tariff laws in the 1830s, 1840s, and 1850s, and kept reducing rates so that the 1857 rates were the lowest since 1816.
sentence_141: The Republicans called for an increase in tariffs in the 1860 election.
sentence_142: The increases were only enacted in 1861 after Southerners resigned their seats in Congress.
sentence_143: The tariff issue was a Northern grievance.
sentence_144: However, [[Neo-Confederate|neo-Confederate]] writers have claimed it as a Southern grievance.
sentence_145: In 1860–61 none of the groups that proposed compromises to head off secession raised the tariff issue.
sentence_146: Pamphleteers North and South rarely mentioned the tariff.
sentence_147: Nationalism was a powerful force in the early 19th century, with famous spokesmen such as [[Andrew_Jackson|Andrew Jackson]] and [[Daniel_Webster|Daniel Webster]].
sentence_148: While practically all Northerners supported the Union, Southerners were split between those loyal to the entire United States (called "Unionists") and those loyal primarily to the Southern region and then the Confederacy.
sentence_149: Perceived insults to Southern collective honor included the enormous popularity of [[Uncle_Tom's_Cabin|Uncle Tom's Cabin]] (1852) and the actions of abolitionist [[John_Brown_(abolitionist)|John Brown]] in trying to incite a [[John_Brown's_raid_on_Harpers_Ferry|rebellion of slaves]] in 1859.
sentence_150: While the South moved towards a Southern nationalism, leaders in the North were also becoming more nationally minded, and they rejected any notion of splitting the Union.
sentence_151: The Republican national electoral platform of 1860 warned that Republicans regarded disunion as [[Treason|treason]] and would not tolerate it.
sentence_152: The South ignored the warnings; Southerners did not realize how ardently the North would fight to hold the Union together.
sentence_153: Main article: [[1860_United_States_presidential_election|1860 United States presidential election]]
sentence_154: The election of Abraham Lincoln in November 1860 was the final trigger for secession.
sentence_155: Efforts at compromise, including the [[Corwin_Amendment|Corwin Amendment]] and the [[Crittenden_Compromise|Crittenden Compromise]], failed.
sentence_156: Southern leaders feared that Lincoln would stop the expansion of slavery and put it on a course toward extinction.
sentence_157: The slave states, which had already become a minority in the House of Representatives, were now facing a future as a perpetual minority in the Senate and Electoral College against an increasingly powerful North.
sentence_158: Before Lincoln took office in March 1861, seven slave states had declared their secession and joined to form the Confederacy.
sentence_159: According to Lincoln, the American people had shown that they had been successful in establishing and administering a republic, but a third challenge faced the nation, maintaining a republic based on the people's vote against an attempt to overthrow it.
sentence_160: The election of Lincoln provoked the legislature of [[South_Carolina|South Carolina]] to call a state convention to consider secession.
sentence_161: Before the war, South Carolina did more than any other Southern state to advance the notion that a state had the right to [[Nullification_(U.S._Constitution)|nullify]] federal laws, and even to secede from the United States.
sentence_162: The convention summoned unanimously voted to secede on December 20, 1860, and adopted the "Declaration of the Immediate Causes Which Induce and Justify the Secession of South Carolina from the Federal Union".
sentence_163: It argued for states' rights for slave owners in the South, but contained a complaint about states' rights in the North in the form of opposition to the [[Fugitive_Slave_Law_of_1850|Fugitive Slave Act]], claiming that Northern states were not fulfilling their federal obligations under the Constitution.
sentence_164: The "cotton states" of [[Mississippi|Mississippi]], [[Florida|Florida]], [[Alabama|Alabama]], Georgia, Louisiana, and [[Texas|Texas]] followed suit, seceding in January and February 1861.
sentence_165: Among the ordinances of secession passed by the individual states, those of three—Texas, Alabama, and Virginia—specifically mentioned the plight of the "slaveholding states" at the hands of Northern abolitionists.
sentence_166: The rest make no mention of the slavery issue and are often brief announcements of the dissolution of ties by the legislatures.
sentence_167: However, at least four states—South Carolina, Mississippi, Georgia, and Texas—also passed lengthy and detailed explanations of their causes for secession, all of which laid the blame squarely on the movement to abolish slavery and that movement's influence over the politics of the Northern states.
sentence_168: The Southern states believed slaveholding was a constitutional right because of the [[Fugitive_Slave_Clause|Fugitive Slave Clause]] of the Constitution.
sentence_169: These states agreed to form a new federal government, the [[Confederate_States_of_America|Confederate States of America]], on February 4, 1861.
sentence_170: They took control of federal forts and other properties within their boundaries with little resistance from outgoing President [[James_Buchanan|James Buchanan]], whose term ended on March 4, 1861.
sentence_171: Buchanan said that the [[Dred_Scott_decision|Dred Scott decision]] was proof that the South had no reason for secession, and that the Union "was intended to be perpetual", but that "The power by force of arms to compel a State to remain in the Union" was not among the "enumerated powers granted to Congress".
sentence_172: One-quarter of the U.S. Army—the entire garrison in Texas—was surrendered in February 1861 to state forces by its commanding general, [[David_E._Twiggs|David E. Twiggs]], who then joined the Confederacy.
sentence_173: As Southerners resigned their seats in the Senate and the House, Republicans were able to pass projects that had been blocked by Southern senators before the war.
sentence_174: These included the [[Morrill_Tariff|Morrill Tariff]], land grant colleges (the [[Morrill_Land-Grant_Acts|Morrill Act]]), a [[Homestead_Acts#Homestead_Act_of_1862|Homestead Act]], a transcontinental railroad (the [[Pacific_Railroad_Acts|Pacific Railroad Acts]]), the [[National_Bank_Act|National Bank Act]], the authorization of [[United_States_Note|United States Notes]] by the [[Legal_Tender_Act_of_1862|Legal Tender Act of 1862]], and the ending of [[District_of_Columbia_Compensated_Emancipation_Act|slavery in the District of Columbia]].
sentence_175: The [[Revenue_Act_of_1861|Revenue Act of 1861]] introduced the [[Income_tax|income tax]] to help finance the war.
sentence_176: On December 18, 1860, the [[Crittenden_Compromise|Crittenden Compromise]] was proposed to re-establish the [[Missouri_Compromise|Missouri Compromise]] line by constitutionally banning slavery in territories to the north of the line while guaranteeing it to the south.
sentence_177: The adoption of this compromise likely would have prevented the secession of every Southern state apart from South Carolina, but Lincoln and the Republicans rejected it.
sentence_178: It was then proposed to hold a national referendum on the compromise.
sentence_179: The Republicans again rejected the idea, although a majority of both Northerners and Southerners would likely have voted in favor of it.
sentence_180: A pre-war February [[Peace_Conference_of_1861|Peace Conference of 1861]] met in Washington, proposing a solution similar to that of the Crittenden compromise; it was rejected by Congress.
sentence_181: The Republicans proposed an [[Corwin_Amendment|alternative compromise]] to not interfere with slavery where it existed but the South regarded it as insufficient.
sentence_182: Nonetheless, the remaining eight slave states rejected pleas to join the Confederacy following a two-to-one no-vote in Virginia's First Secessionist Convention on April 4, 1861.
sentence_183: On March 4, 1861, [[Abraham_Lincoln|Abraham Lincoln]] was sworn in as president.
sentence_184: In his [[Inauguration|inaugural address]], he argued that the Constitution was a [[Preamble_to_the_United_States_Constitution|more perfect union]] than the earlier [[Articles_of_Confederation|Articles of Confederation and Perpetual Union]], that it was a binding contract, and called any secession "legally void".
sentence_185: He had no intent to invade Southern states, nor did he intend to end slavery where it existed, but said that he would use force to maintain possession of Federal property.
sentence_186: The government would make no move to recover post offices, and if resisted, mail delivery would end at state lines.
sentence_187: Where popular conditions did not allow peaceful enforcement of Federal law, U.S. marshals and judges would be withdrawn.
sentence_188: No mention was made of bullion lost from U.S. mints in Louisiana, Georgia, and North Carolina.
sentence_189: He stated that it would be U.S. policy to only collect import duties at its ports; there could be no serious injury to the South to justify the armed revolution during his administration.
sentence_190: His speech closed with a plea for restoration of the bonds of union, famously calling on "the mystic chords of memory" binding the two regions.
sentence_191: The South sent delegations to Washington and offered to pay for the federal properties and enter into a peace treaty with the United States.
sentence_192: Lincoln rejected any negotiations with Confederate agents because he claimed the Confederacy was not a legitimate government, and that making any treaty with it would be tantamount to recognition of it as a sovereign government.
sentence_193: Secretary of State [[William_H._Seward|William Seward]], who at the time saw himself as the real governor or "prime minister" behind the throne of the inexperienced Lincoln, engaged in unauthorized and indirect negotiations that failed.
sentence_194: President Lincoln was determined to hold all remaining Union-occupied forts in the Confederacy: [[Fort_Monroe|Fort Monroe]] in Virginia, Fort Pickens, [[Fort_Jefferson_(Florida)|Fort Jefferson]] and [[Fort_Zachary_Taylor|Fort Taylor]] in Florida, and [[Fort_Sumter|Fort Sumter]] – located at the cockpit of secession in Charleston, South Carolina.
sentence_195: Main article: [[Battle_of_Fort_Sumter|Battle of Fort Sumter]]
sentence_196: Fort Sumter is located in the middle of the harbor of [[Charleston_in_the_American_Civil_War|Charleston]], South Carolina.
sentence_197: Its garrison had recently moved there to avoid incidents with local militias in the streets of the city.
sentence_198: Lincoln told its commander, [[Robert_Anderson_(Civil_War)|Maj.
sentence_199: Anderson]] to hold on until fired upon.
sentence_200: Confederate president [[Jefferson_Davis|Jefferson Davis]] ordered the surrender of the fort.
sentence_201: Anderson gave a conditional reply that the Confederate government rejected, and Davis ordered General [[P._G._T._Beauregard|P.
sentence_202: G. T. Beauregard]] to attack the fort before a relief expedition could arrive.
sentence_203: He bombarded Fort Sumter on April 12–13, forcing its capitulation.
sentence_204: The attack on Fort Sumter rallied the North to the defense of American nationalism.
sentence_205: Historian [[Allan_Nevins|Allan Nevins]] underscored the significance of the event:
sentence_206: Union leaders incorrectly assumed that only a minority of Southerners were in favor of secession and that there were large numbers of southern Unionists that could be counted on.
sentence_207: Had Northerners realized that most Southerners favored secession, they might have hesitated at attempting the enormous task of conquering a united South.
sentence_208: Lincoln called on all the states to send forces to recapture the fort and other federal properties.
sentence_209: The scale of the rebellion appeared to be small, so he called for only [[President_Lincoln's_75,000_volunteers|75,000 volunteers]] for 90 days.
sentence_210: The governor of Massachusetts had state regiments on trains headed south the next day.
sentence_211: In western Missouri, local secessionists seized [[Liberty_Arsenal|Liberty Arsenal]].
sentence_212: On May 3, 1861, Lincoln called for an additional 42,000 volunteers for a period of three years.
sentence_213: Four states in the middle and upper South had repeatedly rejected Confederate overtures, but now [[Virginia_in_the_American_Civil_War|Virginia]], [[Tennessee_in_the_American_Civil_War|Tennessee]], [[Arkansas_in_the_American_Civil_War|Arkansas]], and [[North_Carolina_in_the_American_Civil_War|North Carolina]] refused to send forces against their neighbors, declared their secession, and joined the Confederacy.
sentence_214: To reward Virginia, the Confederate capital was moved to [[Richmond,_Virginia|Richmond]].
sentence_215: Main article: [[Border_states_(American_Civil_War)|Border states (American Civil War)]]
sentence_216: [[Maryland|Maryland]], [[Delaware|Delaware]], [[Missouri|Missouri]], and [[Kentucky|Kentucky]] were slave states that were opposed to both secession and coercing the South.
sentence_217: [[West_Virginia|West Virginia]] then joined them as an additional border state after it separated from [[Virginia|Virginia]] and became a state of the [[Union_(American_Civil_War)|Union]] in 1863.
sentence_218: Maryland's territory surrounded the United States' capital of [[Washington,_D.C.,_in_the_American_Civil_War|Washington, D.C.]], and could cut it off from the North.
sentence_219: It had numerous anti-Lincoln officials who tolerated anti-army [[Baltimore_riot_of_1861|rioting in Baltimore]] and the burning of bridges, both aimed at hindering the passage of troops to the South.
sentence_220: Maryland's legislature voted overwhelmingly (53–13) to stay in the Union, but also rejected hostilities with its southern neighbors, voting to close Maryland's rail lines to prevent them from being used for war.
sentence_221: Lincoln responded by establishing [[Martial_law|martial law]] and unilaterally suspending [[Habeas_corpus|habeas corpus]] in Maryland, along with sending in militia units from the North.
sentence_222: Lincoln rapidly took control of Maryland and the District of Columbia by seizing many prominent figures, including arresting 1/3 of the members of the [[Maryland_General_Assembly|Maryland General Assembly]] on the day it reconvened.
sentence_223: All were held without trial, ignoring a ruling by the Chief Justice of the U.S. Supreme Court [[Roger_Taney|Roger Taney]], a Maryland native, that only Congress (and not the president) could suspend habeas corpus ([[Ex_parte_Merryman|Ex parte Merryman]]).
sentence_224: Federal troops imprisoned a prominent Baltimore newspaper editor, [[Frank_Key_Howard|Frank Key Howard]], Francis Scott Key's grandson, after he criticized Lincoln in an editorial for ignoring the Supreme Court Chief Justice's ruling.
sentence_225: In Missouri, an [[Missouri_Constitutional_Convention_(1861–63)|elected convention]] on secession voted decisively to remain within the Union.
sentence_226: When pro-Confederate Governor [[Claiborne_Fox_Jackson|Claiborne F. Jackson]] called out the state militia, it was attacked by federal forces under General [[Nathaniel_Lyon|Nathaniel Lyon]], who chased the governor and the rest of the State Guard to the southwestern corner of the state (see also: Missouri secession).
sentence_227: In the resulting vacuum, the convention on secession reconvened and took power as the Unionist provisional government of Missouri.
sentence_228: Kentucky did not secede; for a time, it declared itself neutral.
sentence_229: When Confederate forces entered the state in September 1861, neutrality ended and the state reaffirmed its Union status while trying to maintain slavery.
sentence_230: During a brief invasion by Confederate forces in 1861, Confederate sympathizers organized a secession convention, formed the shadow [[Confederate_Government_of_Kentucky|Confederate Government of Kentucky]], inaugurated a governor, and gained recognition from the Confederacy.
sentence_231: Its jurisdiction extended only as far as Confederate battle lines in the Commonwealth and went into exile for good after October 1862.
sentence_232: After Virginia's secession, a [[Restored_Government_of_Virginia|Unionist government]] in [[Wheeling,_West_Virginia|Wheeling]] asked 48 counties to vote on an ordinance to create a new state on October 24, 1861.
sentence_233: A voter turnout of 34 percent approved the statehood bill (96 percent approving).
sentence_234: The inclusion of 24 secessionist counties in the state and the ensuing guerrilla war engaged about 40,000 Federal troops for much of the war.
sentence_235: Congress admitted [[West_Virginia|West Virginia]] to the Union on June 20, 1863.
sentence_236: West Virginia provided about 20,000–22,000 soldiers to both the Confederacy and the Union.
sentence_237: A Unionist secession attempt occurred in [[East_Tennessee|East Tennessee]], but was suppressed by the Confederacy, which arrested over 3,000 men suspected of being loyal to the Union.
sentence_238: They were held without trial.
sentence_239: See also: [[List_of_American_Civil_War_battles|List of American Civil War battles]] and [[Military_leadership_in_the_American_Civil_War|Military leadership in the American Civil War]]
sentence_240: The Civil War was a contest marked by the ferocity and frequency of battle.
sentence_241: Over four years, 237 named battles were fought, as were many more minor actions and skirmishes, which were often characterized by their bitter intensity and high casualties.
sentence_242: In his book The American Civil War, John Keegan writes that "The American Civil War was to prove one of the most ferocious wars ever fought".
sentence_243: In many cases, without geographic objectives, the only target for each side was the enemy's soldier.
sentence_244: See also: Child soldiers in the American Civil War
sentence_245: As the first seven states began organizing a Confederacy in Montgomery, the entire U.S. army numbered 16,000.
sentence_246: However, Northern governors had begun to mobilize their militias.
sentence_247: The Confederate Congress authorized the new nation up to 100,000 troops sent by governors as early as February.
sentence_248: By May, Jefferson Davis was pushing for 100,000 men under arms for one year or the duration, and that was answered in kind by the U.S. Congress.
sentence_249: In the first year of the war, both sides had far more volunteers than they could effectively train and equip.
sentence_250: After the initial enthusiasm faded, reliance on the cohort of young men who came of age every year and wanted to join was not enough.
sentence_251: Both sides used a draft law—conscription—as a device to encourage or force volunteering; relatively few were drafted and served.
sentence_252: The Confederacy passed a draft law in April 1862 for young men aged 18 to 35; overseers of slaves, government officials, and clergymen were exempt.
sentence_253: The U.S. Congress followed in July, authorizing a militia draft within a state when it could not meet its quota with volunteers.
sentence_254: European [[History_of_Immigration_to_the_United_States#1850_to_1930|immigrants]] joined the Union Army in large numbers, including 177,000 born in Germany and 144,000 born in Ireland.
sentence_255: When the Emancipation Proclamation went into effect in January 1863, ex-slaves were energetically recruited by the states and used to meet the state quotas.
sentence_256: States and local communities offered higher and higher cash bonuses for white volunteers.
sentence_257: Congress tightened the law in March 1863.
sentence_258: Men selected in the draft could provide substitutes or, until mid-1864, pay commutation money.
sentence_259: Many eligibles pooled their money to cover the cost of anyone drafted.
sentence_260: Families used the substitute provision to select which man should go into the army and which should stay home.
sentence_261: There was much evasion and overt resistance to the draft, especially in Catholic areas.
sentence_262: The [[New_York_Draft_Riots|draft riot in New York City]] in July 1863 involved Irish immigrants who had been signed up as citizens to swell the vote of the [[Tammany_Hall|city's Democratic political machine]], not realizing it made them liable for the draft.
sentence_263: Of the 168,649 men procured for the Union through the draft, 117,986 were substitutes, leaving only 50,663 who had their services conscripted.
sentence_264: In both the North and South, the draft laws were highly unpopular.
sentence_265: In the North, some 120,000 men evaded conscription, many of them fleeing to Canada, and another 280,000 soldiers deserted during the war.
sentence_266: At least 100,000 Southerners deserted, or about 10 percent; Southern desertion was high because, according to one historian writing in 1991, the highly localized Southern identity meant that many Southern men had little investment in the outcome of the war, with individual soldiers caring more about the fate of their local area than any grand ideal.
sentence_267: In the North, "[[Bounty_jumper|bounty jumpers]]" enlisted to get the generous bonus, deserted, then went back to a second recruiting station under a different name to sign up again for a second bonus; 141 were caught and executed.
sentence_268: From a tiny frontier force in 1860, the Union and Confederate armies had grown into the "largest and most efficient armies in the world" within a few years.
sentence_269: European observers at the time dismissed them as amateur and unprofessional, but British historian [[John_Keegan|John Keegan]] concluded that each outmatched the French, Prussian and Russian armies of the time, and but for the Atlantic, would have threatened any of them with defeat.
sentence_270: The number of women who served as soldiers during the war is estimated at between 400 and 750, although an accurate count is impossible because the women had to disguise themselves as men.
sentence_271: Women also served on the Union hospital ship Red Rover and nursed Union and Confederate troops at field hospitals.
sentence_272: [[Mary_Edwards_Walker|Mary Edwards Walker]], the only woman to ever receive the [[Medal_of_Honor|Medal of Honor]], served in the Union Army and was given the medal for her efforts to treat the wounded during the war.
sentence_273: Her name was deleted from the Army Medal of Honor Roll in 1917 (along with over 900 other, male MOH recipients); however, it was restored in 1977.
sentence_274: Perman and Taylor (2010) write that historians are of two minds on why millions of men seemed so eager to fight, suffer and die over four years:
sentence_275: Main article: [[American_Civil_War_prison_camps|American Civil War prison camps]]
sentence_276: At the start of the civil war, a system of paroles operated.
sentence_277: Captives agreed not to fight until they were officially exchanged.
sentence_278: Meanwhile, they were held in camps run by their army.
sentence_279: They were paid, but they were not allowed to perform any military duties.
sentence_280: The system of exchanges collapsed in 1863 when the Confederacy refused to exchange black prisoners.
sentence_281: After that, about 56,000 of the 409,000 POWs died in prisons during the war, accounting for nearly 10 percent of the conflict's fatalities.
sentence_282: The small [[Union_Navy|U.S.
sentence_283: Navy]] of 1861 was rapidly enlarged to 6,000 officers and 45,000 men in 1865, with 671 vessels, having a tonnage of 510,396.
sentence_284: Its mission was to blockade Confederate ports, take control of the river system, defend against Confederate raiders on the high seas, and be ready for a possible war with the British [[Royal_Navy|Royal Navy]].
sentence_285: Meanwhile, the main riverine war was fought in the West, where a series of major rivers gave access to the Confederate heartland.
sentence_286: The U.S. Navy eventually gained control of the Red, Tennessee, Cumberland, Mississippi, and Ohio rivers.
sentence_287: In the East, the Navy supplied and moved army forces about and occasionally shelled Confederate installations.
sentence_288: The Civil War occurred during the early stages of the industrial revolution.
sentence_289: Many naval innovations emerged during this time, most notably the advent of the [[Ironclad_warship|ironclad warship]].
sentence_290: It began when the Confederacy, knowing they had to meet or match the Union's naval superiority, responded to the Union blockade by building or converting more than 130 vessels, including twenty-six ironclads and floating batteries.
sentence_291: Only half of these saw active service.
sentence_292: Many were equipped with ram bows, creating "ram fever" among Union squadrons wherever they threatened.
sentence_293: But in the face of overwhelming Union superiority and the Union's ironclad warships, they were unsuccessful.
sentence_294: In addition to ocean-going warships coming up the Mississippi, the Union Navy used timberclads, tinclads, and armored gunboats.
sentence_295: Shipyards at Cairo, Illinois, and St. Louis built new boats or modified steamboats for action.
sentence_296: The Confederacy experimented with the [[Submarine|submarine]] [[CSS_Hunley|CSS Hunley]], which did not work satisfactorily, and with building an ironclad ship, [[CSS_Virginia|CSS Virginia]], which was based on rebuilding a sunken Union ship, [[USS_Merrimack_(1855)|Merrimack]].
sentence_297: On its first foray on March 8, 1862, Virginia inflicted significant damage to the Union's wooden fleet, but the next day the first Union ironclad, [[USS_Monitor|USS Monitor]], arrived to challenge it in the [[Chesapeake_Bay|Chesapeake Bay]].
sentence_298: The resulting three hour [[Battle_of_Hampton_Roads|Battle of Hampton Roads]] was a draw, but it proved that ironclads were effective warships.
sentence_299: Not long after the battle, the Confederacy was forced to scuttle the Virginia to prevent its capture, while the Union built many copies of the Monitor.
sentence_300: Lacking the technology and infrastructure to build effective warships, the Confederacy attempted to obtain warships from [[United_Kingdom_of_Great_Britain_and_Ireland|Great Britain]].
sentence_301: However, this failed as Great Britain had no interest in selling warships to a nation that was at war with a far stronger enemy, and it meant it could sour relations with the [[US|US]].
sentence_302: Main article: [[Union_blockade|Union blockade]]
sentence_303: By early 1861, General [[Winfield_Scott|Winfield Scott]] had devised the [[Anaconda_Plan|Anaconda Plan]] to win the war with as little bloodshed as possible.
sentence_304: Scott argued that a Union blockade of the main ports would weaken the Confederate economy.
sentence_305: Lincoln adopted parts of the plan, but he overruled Scott's caution about 90-day volunteers.
sentence_306: Public opinion, however, demanded an immediate attack by the army to capture Richmond.
sentence_307: In April 1861, Lincoln announced the Union blockade of all Southern ports; commercial ships could not get insurance and regular traffic ended.
sentence_308: The South blundered in embargoing cotton exports in 1861 before the blockade was effective; by the time they realized the mistake, it was too late.
sentence_309: "King Cotton" was dead, as the South could export less than 10 percent of its cotton.
sentence_310: The blockade shut down the ten Confederate seaports with railheads that moved almost all the cotton, especially New Orleans, Mobile, and Charleston.
sentence_311: By June 1861, warships were stationed off the principal Southern ports, and a year later nearly 300 ships were in service.
sentence_312: Main article: [[Blockade_runners_of_the_American_Civil_War|Blockade runners of the American Civil War]]
sentence_313: British investors built small, fast, steam-driven [[Blockade_runners_of_the_American_Civil_War|blockade runners]] that traded arms and luxuries brought in from Britain through Bermuda, Cuba, and the Bahamas in return for high-priced cotton.
sentence_314: Many of the ships were designed for speed and were so small that only a small amount of cotton went out.
sentence_315: When the Union Navy seized a blockade runner, the ship and cargo were condemned as a [[Prize_of_war|prize of war]] and sold, with the proceeds given to the Navy sailors; the captured crewmen were mostly British, and they were released.
sentence_316: The Southern economy nearly collapsed during the war.
sentence_317: There were multiple reasons for this: the severe deterioration of food supplies, especially in cities, the failure of Southern railroads, the loss of control of the main rivers, foraging by Northern armies, and the seizure of animals and crops by Confederate armies.
sentence_318: Most historians agree that the blockade was a major factor in ruining the Confederate economy; however, Wise argues that the blockade runners provided just enough of a lifeline to allow Lee to continue fighting for additional months, thanks to fresh supplies of 400,000 rifles, lead, blankets, and boots that the homefront economy could no longer supply.
sentence_319: Surdam argues that the blockade was a powerful weapon that eventually ruined the Southern economy, at the cost of few lives in combat.
sentence_320: Practically, the entire Confederate cotton crop was useless (although it was sold to Union traders), costing the Confederacy its main source of income.
sentence_321: Critical imports were scarce and the coastal trade was largely ended as well.
sentence_322: The measure of the blockade's success was not the few ships that slipped through, but the thousands that never tried it.
sentence_323: Merchant ships owned in Europe could not get insurance and were too slow to evade the blockade, so they stopped calling at Confederate ports.
sentence_324: To fight an offensive war, the Confederacy purchased ships in Britain, converted them to warships, and raided American merchant ships in the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.
sentence_325: Insurance rates skyrocketed and the American flag virtually disappeared from international waters.
sentence_326: However, the same ships were reflagged with European flags and continued unmolested.
sentence_327: After the war ended, the U.S. government demanded that Britain compensate them for the damage done by the raiders outfitted in British ports.
sentence_328: Britain acquiesced to their demand, paying the U.S. $15 million in 1871.
sentence_329: Main article: [[Diplomacy_of_the_American_Civil_War|Diplomacy of the American Civil War]]
sentence_330: Although the Confederacy hoped that Britain and France would join them against the Union, this was never likely, and so they instead tried to bring Britain and France in as mediators.
sentence_331: The Union, under Lincoln and Secretary of State [[William_H._Seward|William H. Seward]] worked to block this, and threatened war if any country officially recognized the existence of the Confederate States of America.
sentence_332: In 1861, Southerners voluntarily embargoed cotton shipments, hoping to start an economic depression in Europe that would force Britain to enter the war to get cotton, but this did not work.
sentence_333: Worse, Europe developed other cotton suppliers, which they found superior, hindering the South's recovery after the war.
sentence_334: [[Cotton_diplomacy|Cotton diplomacy]] proved a failure as Europe had a surplus of cotton, while the 1860–62 crop failures in Europe made the North's grain exports of critical importance.
sentence_335: It also helped to turn European opinion further away from the Confederacy.
sentence_336: It was said that "King Corn was more powerful than King Cotton", as U.S. grain went from a quarter of the British import trade to almost half.
sentence_337: When Britain did face a cotton shortage, it was temporary, being replaced by increased cultivation in Egypt and India.
sentence_338: Meanwhile, the war created employment for arms makers, ironworkers, and ships to transport weapons.
sentence_339: Lincoln's administration failed to appeal to European public opinion.
sentence_340: Diplomats explained that the United States was not committed to the ending of slavery, and instead repeated legalistic arguments about the unconstitutionality of secession.

sentence_524: This meant that the Union now controlled the entire perimeter surrounding Richmond-Petersburg, completely cutting it off from the Confederacy.
sentence_525: Realizing that the capital was now lost, Lee decided to evacuate his army.
sentence_526: The Confederate capital fell to the [[XXV_Corps_(Union_Army)|Union XXV Corps]], composed of black troops.
sentence_527: The remaining Confederate units fled west after a defeat at [[Battle_of_Sayler's_Creek|Sayler's Creek]].
sentence_528: Main article: [[Conclusion_of_the_American_Civil_War|Conclusion of the American Civil War]]
sentence_529: Initially, Lee did not intend to surrender but planned to regroup at the [[Appomattox_Court_House_National_Historical_Park|village of Appomattox Court House]], where supplies were to be waiting and then continue the war.
sentence_530: Grant chased Lee and got in front of him so that when Lee's army reached Appomattox Court House, they were surrounded.
sentence_531: After an initial battle, Lee decided that the fight was now hopeless, and surrendered his Army of Northern Virginia on April 9, 1865, at the [[McLean_House_(Appomattox,_Virginia)|McLean House]].
sentence_532: In an untraditional gesture and as a sign of Grant's respect and anticipation of peacefully restoring Confederate states to the Union, Lee was permitted to keep his sword and his horse, [[Traveller_(horse)|Traveller]].
sentence_533: On April 14, 1865, President Lincoln was [[Abraham_Lincoln_assassination|shot]] by [[John_Wilkes_Booth|John Wilkes Booth]], a Southern sympathizer.
sentence_534: Lincoln died early the next morning.
sentence_535: Lincoln's vice president, [[Andrew_Johnson|Andrew Johnson]], was unharmed as his would-be assassin, [[George_Atzerodt|George Atzerodt]], lost his nerve, so he was immediately sworn in as president.
sentence_536: Meanwhile, Confederate forces across the South surrendered as news of Lee's surrender reached them.
sentence_537: On April 26, 1865, the same day [[Boston_Corbett|Boston Corbett]] killed Booth at a tobacco barn, General [[Joseph_E._Johnston|Joseph E. Johnston]] surrendered nearly 90,000 men of the [[Army_of_Tennessee|Army of Tennessee]] to Major General [[William_Tecumseh_Sherman|William Tecumseh Sherman]] at Bennett Place near present-day Durham, North Carolina.
sentence_538: It proved to be the largest surrender of Confederate forces.
sentence_539: On May 4, all remaining Confederate forces in Alabama and Mississippi surrendered.
sentence_540: President Johnson officially declared an end to the insurrection on May 9, 1865; Confederate president, [[Jefferson_Davis|Jefferson Davis]], was captured the following day.
sentence_541: On June 2, Kirby Smith officially surrendered his troops in the Trans-Mississippi Department.
sentence_542: On June 23, Cherokee leader [[Stand_Watie|Stand Watie]] became the last Confederate general to surrender his forces.
sentence_543: Main articles: [[Union_(American_Civil_War)|Union (American Civil War)]], [[Confederate_states_of_America|Confederate states of America]], and [[Economy_of_the_Confederate_States_of_America|Economy of the Confederate States of America]]
sentence_544: The [[Origins_of_the_American_Civil_War|causes of the war]], the reasons for its outcome, and even [[Naming_the_American_Civil_War|the name of the war itself]] are subjects of lingering contention today.
sentence_545: The North and West grew rich while the once-rich South became poor for a century.
sentence_546: The national political power of the slaveowners and rich Southerners ended.
sentence_547: Historians are less sure about the results of the postwar Reconstruction, especially regarding the second-class citizenship of the Freedmen and their poverty.
sentence_548: Historians have debated whether the Confederacy could have won the war.
sentence_549: Most scholars, including [[James_M._McPherson|James McPherson]], argue that Confederate victory was at least possible.
sentence_550: McPherson argues that the North's advantage in population and resources made Northern victory likely but not guaranteed.
sentence_551: He also argues that if the Confederacy had fought using unconventional tactics, they would have more easily been able to hold out long enough to exhaust the Union.
sentence_552: Confederates did not need to invade and hold enemy territory to win but only needed to fight a defensive war to convince the North that the cost of winning was too high.
sentence_553: The North needed to conquer and hold vast stretches of enemy territory and defeat Confederate armies to win.
sentence_554: Lincoln was not a military dictator and could continue to fight the war only as long as the American public supported a continuation of the war.
sentence_555: The Confederacy sought to win independence by out-lasting Lincoln; however, after Atlanta fell and Lincoln defeated McClellan in the election of 1864, all hope for a political victory for the South ended.
sentence_556: At that point, Lincoln had secured the support of the Republicans, War Democrats, the border states, emancipated slaves, and the neutrality of Britain and France.
sentence_557: By defeating the Democrats and McClellan, he also defeated the [[Copperheads_(politics)|Copperheads]] and their peace platform.
sentence_558: Many scholars argue that the Union held an insurmountable long-term advantage over the Confederacy in industrial strength and population.
sentence_559: Confederate actions, they argue, only delayed defeat.
sentence_560: Civil War historian [[Shelby_Foote|Shelby Foote]] expressed this view succinctly: "I think that the North fought that war with one hand behind its back ...
sentence_561: If there had been more Southern victories, and a lot more, the North simply would have brought that other hand out from behind its back.
sentence_562: I don't think the South ever had a chance to win that War."
sentence_563: A minority view among historians is that the Confederacy lost because, as [[E._Merton_Coulter|E.
sentence_564: Merton Coulter]] put it, "people did not will hard enough and long enough to win."
sentence_565: According to [[Charles_H._Wilson|Charles H. Wilson]], in The Collapse of the Confederacy, "internal conflict should figure prominently in any explanation of Confederate defeat."
sentence_566: Marxist historian Armstead Robinson agrees, pointing to class conflict in the Confederate army between the slave owners and the larger number of non-owners.
sentence_567: He argues that the non-owner soldiers grew embittered about fighting to preserve slavery and fought less enthusiastically.
sentence_568: He attributes the major Confederate defeats in 1863 at Vicksburg and Missionary Ridge to this class conflict.
sentence_569: However, most historians reject the argument.
sentence_570: [[James_M._McPherson|James M. McPherson]], after reading thousands of letters written by Confederate soldiers, found strong patriotism that continued to the end; they truly believed they were fighting for freedom and liberty.
sentence_571: Even as the Confederacy was visibly collapsing in 1864–65, he says most Confederate soldiers were fighting hard.
sentence_572: Historian Gary Gallagher cites General Sherman who in early 1864 commented, "The devils seem to have a determination that cannot but be admired."
sentence_573: Despite their loss of slaves and wealth, with starvation looming, Sherman continued, "yet I see no sign of let-up—some few deserters—plenty tired of war, but the masses determined to fight it out."
sentence_574: Also important were Lincoln's eloquence in rationalizing the national purpose and his skill in keeping the border states committed to the Union cause.
sentence_575: The Emancipation Proclamation was an effective use of the President's war powers.
sentence_576: The Confederate government failed in its attempt to get Europe involved in the war militarily, particularly Britain and France.
sentence_577: Southern leaders needed to get European powers to help break up the blockade the Union had created around the Southern ports and cities.
sentence_578: Lincoln's naval blockade was 95 percent effective at stopping trade goods; as a result, imports and exports to the South declined significantly.
sentence_579: The abundance of European cotton and Britain's hostility to the institution of slavery, along with Lincoln's Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico naval blockades, severely decreased any chance that either Britain or France would enter the war.
sentence_580: Historian Don Doyle has argued that the Union victory had a major impact on the course of world history.
sentence_581: The Union victory energized popular democratic forces.
sentence_582: A Confederate victory, on the other hand, would have meant a new birth of slavery, not freedom.
sentence_583: Historian Fergus Bordewich, following Doyle, argues that:
sentence_584: Scholars have debated what the effects of the war were on political and economic power in the South.
sentence_585: The prevailing view is that the southern planter elite retained its powerful position in the South.
sentence_586: However, a 2017 study challenges this, noting that while some Southern elites retained their economic status, the turmoil of the 1860s created greater opportunities for economic mobility in the South than in the North.
sentence_587: The war resulted in at least 1,030,000 casualties (3 percent of the population), including about 620,000 soldier deaths—two-thirds by disease, and 50,000 civilians.
sentence_588: Binghamton University historian J. David Hacker believes the number of soldier deaths was approximately 750,000, 20 percent higher than traditionally estimated, and possibly as high as 850,000.
sentence_589: The war accounted for more American deaths than in all other U.S. wars combined.
sentence_590: Based on 1860 census figures, 8 percent of all white men aged 13 to 43 died in the war, including 6 percent in the North and 18 percent in the South.
sentence_591: About 56,000 soldiers [[American_Civil_War_prison_camps|died in prison camps]] during the War.
sentence_592: An estimated 60,000 men lost limbs in the war.
sentence_593: Union army dead, amounting to 15 percent of the over two million who served, was broken down as follows:

199,790 died of disease (75 percent was due to the war, the remainder would have occurred in civilian life anyway)

sentence_594: In addition there were 4,523 deaths in the Navy (2,112 in battle) and 460 in the Marines (148 in battle).
sentence_595: Black troops made up 10 percent of the Union death toll, they amounted to 15 percent of disease deaths but less than 3 percent of those killed in battle.
sentence_596: Losses among [[African_American|African Americans]] were high, in the last year and a half and from all reported casualties, approximately 20 percent of all African Americans enrolled in the military lost their lives during the Civil War.
sentence_597: Notably, their mortality rate was significantly higher than white soldiers:
sentence_598: Confederate records compiled by historian William F. Fox list 74,524 killed and died of wounds and 59,292 died of disease.
sentence_599: Including Confederate estimates of battle losses where no records exist would bring the Confederate death toll to 94,000 killed and died of wounds.
sentence_600: Fox complained, however, that records were incomplete, especially during the last year of the war, and that battlefield reports likely under-counted deaths (many men counted as wounded in battlefield reports subsequently died of their wounds).
sentence_601: Thomas L. Livermore, using Fox's data, put the number of Confederate non-combat deaths at 166,000, using the official estimate of Union deaths from disease and accidents and a comparison of Union and Confederate enlistment records, for a total of 260,000 deaths.
sentence_602: However, this excludes the 30,000 deaths of Confederate troops in prisons, which would raise the minimum number of deaths to 290,000.
