sentence_558: The Bangladeshi diaspora contributed $15.31 billion in [[Remittance_to_Bangladesh|remittances]] in 2015.
sentence_559: Bangladesh's largest trading partners are the European Union, the United States, Japan, India, Australia, China and ASEAN.
sentence_560: Expat workers in the Middle East and Southeast Asia send back a large chunk of remittances.
sentence_561: The economy is driven by strong domestic demand.
sentence_562: During its first five years of independence Bangladesh adopted socialist policies.
sentence_563: The subsequent military regime and BNP and Jatiya Party governments restored free markets and promoted the country's private sector.
sentence_564: In 1991, finance minister [[Saifur_Rahman_(Bangladeshi_politician)|Saifur Rahman]] introduced a programme of [[Economic_liberalisation|economic liberalisation]].
sentence_565: The Bangladeshi private sector has rapidly expanded, with a number of [[List_of_conglomerates_in_Bangladesh|conglomerates]] driving the economy.
sentence_566: Major industries include textiles, [[Pharmaceuticals|pharmaceuticals]], shipbuilding, steel, electronics, energy, construction materials, chemicals, ceramics, food processing and leather goods.
sentence_567: Export-oriented industrialisation has increased with [[Fiscal_year|fiscal year]] 2018–19 exports increasing by 10.1% over the previous year to $40 billion.
sentence_568: Most export earnings are from the [[Bangladesh_textile_industry|garment-manufacturing industry]].
sentence_569: However, an insufficient power supply is a significant obstacle to Bangladesh's economic development.
sentence_570: According to the [[World_Bank|World Bank]], poor governance, corruption and weak public institutions are also major challenges.
sentence_571: In April 2010, Standard & Poor's gave Bangladesh a BB- long-term [[Credit_rating|credit rating]], below India's but above those of Pakistan and Sri Lanka.
sentence_572: Agriculture is the largest sector of the economy, making up 14.2 percent of Bangladesh's GDP in 2017 and employing about 42.7 percent of the workforce.
sentence_573: The agricultural sector impacts employment generation, poverty alleviation, [[Human_resources|human resources]] development and [[Food_security|food security]].
sentence_574: More Bangladeshis earn their living from agriculture than from any other sector.
sentence_575: The country is among the top producers of [[Rice|rice]] (fourth), [[Potatoes|potatoes]] (seventh), [[Tropical_fruits|tropical fruits]] (sixth), jute (second), and farmed fish (fifth).
sentence_576: Bangladesh is the seventh-largest [[Natural_gas_in_Bangladesh|natural gas producer]] in Asia, ahead of neighbouring Myanmar, and 56 percent of the country's electricity is generated by natural gas.
sentence_577: Major gas fields are located in the northeastern (particularly Sylhet) and southern (including Barisal and Chittagong) regions.
sentence_579: The American multinational corporation [[Chevron_Corporation|Chevron]] produces 50 percent of Bangladesh's natural gas.
sentence_580: According to geologists, the Bay of Bengal contains large, untapped gas reserves in Bangladesh's [[Exclusive_economic_zone|exclusive economic zone]].
sentence_581: Bangladesh has substantial coal reserves, with several coal mines operating in the northwest.
sentence_582: Jute exports remain significant, although the global jute trade has shrunk considerably since its World War II peak.
sentence_583: Bangladesh has one of the world's oldest tea industries, and is a major exporter of fish and seafood.
sentence_584: Bangladesh's textile and [[Bangladeshi_RMG_Sector|ready-made garment]] industries are the country's largest manufacturing sector, with 2017 exports of $34.1 billion.
sentence_585: Leather-goods manufacturing, particularly footwear, is the second-largest export sector.
sentence_586: The pharmaceutical industry meets 97 percent of domestic demand, and exports to many countries.
sentence_587: [[Shipbuilding_in_Bangladesh|Shipbuilding]] has grown rapidly, with exports to Europe.
sentence_588: [[Steel_industry_in_Bangladesh|Steel]] is concentrated in the port city of Chittagong, and the [[Ceramics_industry_in_Bangladesh|ceramics industry]] is prominent in international trade.
sentence_589: In 2005 Bangladesh was the world's 20th-largest [[List_of_countries_by_cement_production|cement]] producer, an industry dependent on [[Limestone|limestone]] imports from [[Northeast_India|northeast India]].
sentence_590: [[Food_processing|Food processing]] is a major sector, with local brands such as [[PRAN|PRAN]] increasing their international presence.
sentence_591: The [[Electronics_industry_in_Bangladesh|electronics industry]] is growing rapidly with contributions from companies like the [[Walton_Group|Walton Group]].
sentence_592: Bangladesh's defense industry includes the [[Bangladesh_Ordnance_Factories|Bangladesh Ordnance Factories]] and the [[Khulna_Shipyard|Khulna Shipyard]].
sentence_593: The service sector accounts for 51 percent of the country's GDP.
sentence_594: Bangladesh ranks with Pakistan as South Asia's second-largest banking sector.
sentence_595: The [[Dhaka_Stock_Exchange|Dhaka]] and [[Chittagong_Stock_Exchange|Chittagong Stock Exchanges]] are the country's twin financial markets.
sentence_596: Bangladesh's telecommunications industry is one of the world's fastest-growing, with 114 million cellphone subscribers in December 2013, and Grameenphone, [[Banglalink|Banglalink]], [[Robi_(company)|Robi]] and BTTB are major companies.
sentence_597: Tourism is developing, with the beach resort of [[Cox's_Bazar|Cox's Bazar]] at the center of the industry.
sentence_598: The Sylhet region, home to Bangladesh's tea gardens, also hosts a large number of visitors.
sentence_599: The country has [[List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Bangladesh|three UNESCO World Heritage Sites]] ([[Historic_Mosque_City_of_Bagerhat|the Mosque City]], the Buddhist Vihara and the [[Sundarbans|Sundarbans]]) and five [[World_Heritage_Site#Nominating_process|tentative-list]] sites.
sentence_600: Following the pioneering work of [[Akhter_Hameed_Khan|Akhter Hameed Khan]] on rural development at Bangladesh Academy for Rural Development, several [[Non-governmental_organisation|NGOs]] in Bangladesh including [[BRAC_(NGO)|BRAC]] (the world's largest NGO), and [[Grameen_Bank|Grameen Bank]], focused on rural development and poverty alleviation in the country.
sentence_601: Muhammad Yunus successfully pioneered microfinance as a sustainable tool for poverty alleviation and others followed suit.
sentence_602: As of 2015, the country had over 35 million [[Microcredit|microcredit]] borrowers.
sentence_603: In recognition of their tangible contribution to poverty alleviation, Muhammad Yunus and [[Grameen_Bank|Grameen Bank]] were jointly awarded the [[Nobel_Peace_Prize|Nobel Peace Prize]] in 2006.
sentence_605: Transport is a major sector of the economy.
sentence_606: Aviation has grown rapidly, and is dominated by the [[Flag_carrier|flag carrier]] [[Biman_Bangladesh_Airlines|Biman Bangladesh Airlines]] and other [[List_of_airlines_of_Bangladesh|privately owned airlines]].
sentence_607: Bangladesh has a [[List_of_airports_in_Bangladesh|number of airports]] including three international and several domestic STOL (short takeoff and landing) airports.
sentence_608: The busiest, [[Shahjalal_International_Airport|Shahjalal International Airport]] connects Dhaka with major destinations.
sentence_609: Bangladesh has a 2,706-kilometre (1,681-mile) long rail network operated by the state-owned [[Bangladesh_Railway|Bangladesh Railway]].
sentence_610: The total length of the country's [[List_of_roads_in_Bangladesh|road and highway network]] is nearly 21,000 kilometers (13,000 miles).
sentence_611: With 8,046 kilometres (5,000 miles) of navigable waters, Bangladesh has one of the largest inland waterway networks in the world.
sentence_612: The southeastern port of Chittagong is its busiest seaport, handling over $60 billion in annual trade (more than 80 percent of the country's export-import commerce).
sentence_615: Main articles: [[Energy_in_Bangladesh|Energy in Bangladesh]], [[Natural_gas_and_petroleum_in_Bangladesh|Natural gas and petroleum in Bangladesh]], Telecommunications in Bangladesh, and [[Water_supply_and_sanitation_in_Bangladesh|Water supply and sanitation in Bangladesh]]
sentence_616: Bangladesh had an installed electrical capacity of 20,000 megawatts in 2018, reaching 23,548 MW in 2020.
sentence_617: About 56 percent of the country's commercial energy is generated by natural gas, followed by oil, hydropower and coal.
sentence_618: Bangladesh has planned to import hydropower from [[Energy_in_Bhutan|Bhutan]] and [[Energy_in_Nepal|Nepal]].
sentence_619: A nuclear power plant is under construction with Russian support in the [[Ruppur_Nuclear_Power_Plant|Ruppur Nuclear Power Plant]] project which will add 2160 MW when fully operational.
sentence_620: The country ranks fifth worldwide in the number of [[Renewable_energy|renewable energy]] [[Green_job|green jobs]], and solar panels are increasingly used to power urban and off-grid rural areas.
sentence_621: An estimated 98 percent of the country's population had access to [[Improved_water_source|improved water sources]] by 2004 (a high percentage for a low-income country), achieved largely through the construction of [[Hand_pump|hand pumps]] with support from external donors.
sentence_622: However, in 1993 it was discovered that much of Bangladesh's groundwater (the source of drinking water for 97 percent of the rural population and a significant share of the urban population) is naturally contaminated with arsenic.
sentence_623: Another challenge is low cost recovery due to low tariffs and poor [[Economic_efficiency|economic efficiency]], especially in urban areas (where water revenue does not cover operating costs).
sentence_624: An estimated 56 percent of the population had access to adequate sanitation facilities in 2010.
sentence_625: [[Community-led_total_sanitation|Community-led total sanitation]], addressing the problem of [[Open_defecation|open defecation]] in rural areas, is credited with improving public health since its introduction in 2000.
sentence_626: Main article: [[Science_and_technology_in_Bangladesh|Science and technology in Bangladesh]]
sentence_627: See also: [[Information_technology_in_Bangladesh|Information technology in Bangladesh]] and [[Biotechnology_and_genetic_engineering_in_Bangladesh|Biotechnology and genetic engineering in Bangladesh]]
sentence_628: The [[Bangladesh_Council_of_Scientific_and_Industrial_Research|Bangladesh Council of Scientific and Industrial Research]], founded in 1973, traces its roots to the East Pakistan Regional Laboratories established in Dhaka (1955), [[Rajshahi|Rajshahi]] (1965) and Chittagong (1967).
sentence_629: Bangladesh's [[Space_agency|space agency]], [[SPARRSO|SPARRSO]], was founded in 1983 with assistance from the United States.
sentence_630: The country's first communications satellite, [[Bangabandhu-1|Bangabandhu-1]], was launched from the United States in 2018.
sentence_631: The [[Bangladesh_Atomic_Energy_Commission|Bangladesh Atomic Energy Commission]] operates a [[TRIGA|TRIGA]] research reactor at its atomic-energy facility in Savar.
sentence_632: In 2015, Bangladesh was ranked the 26th global IT outsourcing destination.
sentence_634: Bangladesh's tourist attractions include historical sites and monuments, resorts, beaches, picnic spots, forests and wildlife of various species.
sentence_635: Activities for tourists include [[Angling|angling]], water skiing, river cruising, hiking, [[Rowing_(sport)|rowing]], yachting, and [[Sea_bathing|sea bathing]].
sentence_636: The [[World_Travel_and_Tourism_Council|World Travel and Tourism Council]] (WTTC) reported in 2019 that the travel and tourism industry in Bangladesh directly generated 1,180,500 jobs in 2018 or 1.9 percent of the country's total employment.
sentence_637: According to the same report, Bangladesh experiences around 125,000 international tourist arrival per year.
sentence_638: Domestic spending generated 97.7 percent of direct travel and tourism gross domestic product (GDP) in 2012.
sentence_639: Bangladesh's world ranking in 2012 for travel and tourism's direct contribution to GDP, as a percentage of GDP, was 120 out of 140.
sentence_641: Estimates of the Bangladeshi population vary, but UN data suggests 161,376,708 (162.9 million) in 2017.
sentence_642: The 2011 census estimated 142.3 million, much less than 2007–2010 estimates of Bangladesh's population (150–170 million).
sentence_643: Bangladesh is the world's [[List_of_countries_by_population|eighth-most-populous]] nation and the most densely-populated large country in the world, ranking 7th in population density even when small countries and city-states are included.
sentence_644: The country's population-growth rate was among the highest in the world in the 1960s and 1970s, when its population grew from 65 to 110 million.
sentence_645: With the promotion of [[Birth_control|birth control]] in the 1980s, Bangladesh's growth rate began to slow.
sentence_646: Its [[Total_fertility_rate|total fertility rate]] is now 2.05, lower than India's (2.58) and Pakistan's (3.07).
sentence_647: The population is relatively young, with 34 percent aged 15 or younger and five percent 65 or older.
sentence_648: Life expectancy at birth was estimated at 72.49 years in 2016.
sentence_649: According to the World Bank, as of 2016 14.8% of the country lives below the [[International_poverty_line|international poverty line]] on less than $1.90 per day.
sentence_651: Of Bengalis, [[Bengali_Muslims|Muslims]] are the majority, followed by Hindus, [[Bengali_Christians|Christians]] and [[Bengali_Buddhists|Buddhists]].
sentence_652: The [[Adivasi|Adivasi]] population includes the Chakma, [[Marma_people|Marma]], [[Tanchangya_people|Tanchangya]], Tripuri, [[Kuki_people|Kuki]], Khiang, Khumi, [[Murang_people|Murang]], [[Mru_people_(Mrucha)|Mru]], Chak, Lushei, [[Bawm_people|Bawm]], [[Bisnupriya_Manipuri_Society|Bishnupriya Manipuri]], Khasi, Jaintia, Garo, [[Santal|Santal]], [[Munda_people|Munda]] and [[Oraon|Oraon]] tribes.
sentence_653: The Chittagong Hill Tracts region experienced unrest and an [[Chittagong_Hill_Tracts_conflict|insurgency]] from 1975 to 1997 in an autonomy movement by its indigenous people.
sentence_654: Although a peace accord was signed in 1997, the region remains militarised.
sentence_655: Bangladesh is home to a significant [[Ismaili|Ismaili]] community.
sentence_656: It hosts many [[Urdu|Urdu]]-speaking immigrants, who migrated there after the partition of India.
sentence_657: Stranded Pakistanis were given citizenship by the Supreme Court in 2008.
sentence_658: [[Rohingya_refugees_in_Bangladesh|Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh]] number at around 1 million, making Bangladesh one of the countries with the largest refugee populations in the world.
sentence_659: Further information: [[List_of_cities_and_towns_in_Bangladesh|List of cities and towns in Bangladesh]]
sentence_660: Dhaka is Bangladesh's capital and largest city and is overseen by two city corporations who manage between them the northern and southern part of the city.
sentence_661: There are 12 [[List_of_City_Corporations_of_Bangladesh|city corporations]] which hold mayoral elections: Dhaka South, Dhaka North, Chittagong, Comilla, [[Khulna|Khulna]], [[Mymensingh|Mymensingh]], [[Sylhet|Sylhet]], [[Rajshahi|Rajshahi]], Barisal, [[Rangpur,_Bangladesh|Rangpur]], Gazipur and [[Narayanganj|Narayanganj]].
sentence_662: Mayors are elected for five-year terms.
sentence_663: Altogether there are 506 urban centres in Bangladesh among which 43 cities have a population of more than 100,000.
sentence_665: The predominant language of Bangladesh is [[Bengali_language|Bengali]] (also known as Bangla).
sentence_666: Bengali is the one of the easternmost branches of the [[Indo-European_language|Indo-European language]] family.
sentence_667: It is a part of the [[Eastern_Indo-Aryan_languages|Eastern Indo-Aryan languages]] in South Asia, which developed between the 10th and 13th centuries.
sentence_668: Bengali is written using the [[Bengali_alphabet|Bengali script]].
sentence_669: In ancient Bengal, [[Sanskrit|Sanskrit]] was the language of written communication, especially by priests.
sentence_670: During the Islamic period, Sanskrit was replaced by Bengali as the [[Vernacular_language|vernacular language]].
sentence_671: The Sultans of Bengal promoted the production of Bengali literature instead of Sanskrit.
sentence_672: Bengali also received [[Persian_language|Persian]] and [[Arabic|Arabic]] loanwords during the [[Sultanate_of_Bengal|Sultanate of Bengal]].
sentence_673: Under [[Bengal_Presidency|British rule]], Bengali was significantly modernised by Europeans.
sentence_674: Modern Standard Bengali emerged as the [[Lingua_franca|lingua franca]] of the region.
sentence_675: A heavily Sanskritized version of Bengali was employed by Hindu scholars during the [[Bengali_Renaissance|Bengali Renaissance]].
sentence_676: Muslim writers such as [[Kazi_Nazrul_Islam|Kazi Nazrul Islam]] gave attention to the Persian and Arabic vocabulary of the language.
sentence_677: Today, the Bengali language standard is prescribed by the [[Bangla_Academy|Bangla Academy]] in Bangladesh.
sentence_678: More than 98 percent of people in Bangladesh speak Bengali as their native language.
sentence_679: Bengali is described as a dialect continuum where there are various [[Bengali_dialects|dialects]] spoken throughout the country.
sentence_680: Currently there is a diglossia in which much of the population are able to understand or speak Standard Colloquial Bengali and in their regional dialect, these include the most distinct dialects (some consider as separate languages) such as [[Chittagonian_language|Chittagonian]] or [[Sylheti_language|Sylheti]].
sentence_681: The [[Bangla_Bhasha_Prachalan_Ain,_1987|Bengali Language Implementation Act, 1987]] made it mandatory to use Bengali in all government affairs in Bangladesh.
sentence_682: Although laws were historically written in English, they were not translated into Bengali until the [[Bangla_Bhasha_Prachalan_Ain,_1987|Bengali Language Implementation Act of 1987]].
sentence_683: All subsequent acts, ordinances and laws have been promulgated in Bengali since 1987.
sentence_684: English is often used in the verdicts delivered by the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, and is also used in higher education.
sentence_685: The [[Chakma_language|Chakma language]] is another native Eastern Indo-Aryan language of Bangladesh.
sentence_686: It is written using the Chakma script.
sentence_687: The unique aspect of the language is that it is used by the Chakma people, who are a population with similarities to the people of East Asia, rather than the Indian subcontinent.
sentence_688: The Chakma language is endangered due to its decreasing use in schools and institutions.
sentence_689: Other tribal languages include [[Garo_language|Garo]], [[Meitei_language|Meitei]], Kokborok and [[Rakhine_language|Rakhine]].
sentence_690: Among the [[Austroasiatic_languages|Austroasiatic languages]], the [[Santali_language|Santali language]] is spoken by the Santali tribe.
sentence_691: Many of these languages are written in the Bengali script; while there is also some usage of the Latin script.
sentence_692: [[Urdu|Urdu]] has a significant heritage in Bangladesh, in particular [[Old_Dhaka|Old Dhaka]].
sentence_693: The language was introduced to Bengal in the 17th-century.
sentence_694: Traders and migrants from North India often spoke the language in Bengal, as did sections of the Bengali upper class.
sentence_695: Urdu poets lived in many parts of Bangladesh.
sentence_696: The use of Urdu became controversial during the [[Bengali_Language_Movement|Bengali Language Movement]], when the people of East Bengal resisted attempts to impose Urdu as the main official language.
sentence_697: In modern Bangladesh, the Urdu-speaking community is restricted to the country's Bihari community (formerly Stranded Pakistanis); and some sections of the [[Dhakaiyas|Old Dhakaiya]] population.
sentence_699: The constitution grants [[Freedom_of_religion|freedom of religion]] and officially makes Bangladesh a secular state, while establishing Islam as the "religion of the Republic".
sentence_700: Islam is followed by 90 percent of the population.
sentence_701: Most Bangladeshis are [[Bengali_Muslims|Bengali Muslims]], who form the largest Muslim ethnoreligious group in South Asia and the second largest in the world after the Arabs.
sentence_702: There is also a minority of non-Bengali Muslims.
sentence_703: The vast majority of Bangladeshi Muslims are [[Sunni|Sunni]], followed by minorities of [[Shia|Shia]] and [[Ahmadiya|Ahmadiya]].
sentence_705: Bangladesh has the fourth-largest Muslim population in the world, and is the third-largest Muslim-majority country (after Indonesia and Pakistan).
sentence_706: [[Sufism|Sufism]] has an extensive heritage in the region.
sentence_707: Liberal Bengali Islam sometimes clashes with orthodox movements.
sentence_708: The largest gathering of Muslims in Bangladesh is the apolitical [[Bishwa_Ijtema|Bishwa Ijtema]], held annually by the orthodox [[Tablighi_Jamaat|Tablighi Jamaat]].
sentence_709: The Ijtema is the second-largest Muslim congregation in the world, after the [[Hajj|Hajj]].
sentence_710: The [[Islamic_Foundation_Bangladesh|Islamic Foundation]] is an autonomous government agency responsible for some religious matters under state guidance, including monitoring of sighting of the moon in accordance with the lunar [[Islamic_calendar|Islamic calendar]] in order to set festival dates; as well as the charitable tradition of [[Zakat|zakat]].
sentence_711: Public holidays include the Islamic observances of Eid-ul-Fitr, Eid-al-Adha, the Prophet's Birthday, Ashura and Shab-e-Barat.
sentence_712: [[Hinduism_in_Bangladesh|Hinduism]] is followed by 8.5 percent of the population; most are Bengali Hindus, and some are members of [[Ethnic_groups_in_Bangladesh|ethnic minority groups]].
sentence_713: Bangladeshi Hindus are the country's second-largest religious group and the third-largest Hindu community in the world, after those in India and Nepal.
sentence_714: Hindus in Bangladesh are evenly distributed, with concentrations in Gopalganj, [[Dinajpur_District_(Bangladesh)|Dinajpur]], Sylhet, [[Sunamganj|Sunamganj]], Mymensingh, Khulna, Jessore, Chittagong and parts of the Chittagong Hill Tracts.
sentence_715: The festivals of Durga's Return and Krishna's Birthday are public holidays.
sentence_716: [[Buddhism_in_Bangladesh|Buddhism]] is the third-largest religion, at 0.6 percent.
sentence_717: Bangladeshi Buddhists are concentrated among ethnic groups in the Chittagong Hill Tracts (particularly the Chakma, Marma and Tanchangya peoples), while coastal Chittagong is home to a large number of [[Bengali_Buddhist|Bengali Buddhists]].
sentence_718: Although the Mahayana school of Buddhism was historically prevalent in the region, Bangladeshi Buddhists today adhere to the Theravada school.
sentence_719: Buddha's Birthday is a public holiday.
sentence_720: The chief Buddhist priests are based at a monastery in Chittagong.
sentence_721: Christianity is the fourth-largest religion, at 0.4 percent.
sentence_722: Roman Catholicism is the largest denomination among Bangladeshi Christians.
sentence_723: [[Bengali_Christians|Bengali Christians]] are spread across the country; while there are many Christians among minority ethnic groups in the Chittagong Hill Tracts (southeastern Bangladesh) and within the Garo tribe of Mymensingh (north-central Bangladesh).
sentence_724: The country also has Protestant, Baptist and Oriental Orthodox churches.
sentence_726: The Constitution of Bangladesh declares Islam the state religion, but bans religion-based politics.
sentence_727: It proclaims equal recognition of Hindus, Buddhists, Christians and people of all faiths.
sentence_728: In 1972, Bangladesh was South Asia's first constitutionally-secular country.
sentence_729: Article 12 of the constitution continues to call for secularism, the elimination of interfaith tensions and prohibits the abuse of religion for political purposes and any discrimination against, or persecution of, persons practising a particular religion.
sentence_730: Article 41 of the constitution subjects religious freedom to public order, law and morality; it gives every citizen the right to profess, practice or propagate any religion; every religious community or denomination the right to establish, maintain and manage its religious institutions; and states that no person attending any educational institution shall be required to receive religious instruction, or to take part in or to attend any religious ceremony or worship, if that instruction, ceremony or worship relates to a religion other than his own.
sentence_732: Bangladesh has a [[Literacy_rate|literacy rate]] of 72.9 percent as of 2018: 75.7% for males and 70.09% for females.
sentence_733: The country's educational system is three-tiered and heavily subsidised, with the government operating many schools at the primary, secondary and higher-secondary levels and subsidising many private schools.
sentence_734: In the tertiary-education sector, the Bangladeshi government funds over 45 state universities through the [[University_Grants_Commission_of_Bangladesh|University Grants Commission]].
sentence_735: The education system is divided into five levels: primary (first to fifth grade), junior secondary (sixth to eighth grade), secondary (ninth and tenth grade), higher secondary (11th and 12th grade) and tertiary.
sentence_736: Five years of secondary education (including junior secondary) ends with a Secondary School Certificate (SSC) examination.
sentence_737: Since 2009, the Primary Education Closing (PEC) examination has also been introduced.
sentence_738: Students who pass the PEC examination proceed to secondary or matriculation training, culminating in the SSC examination.
sentence_739: Students who pass the PEC examination proceed to three years of junior-secondary education, culminating in the [[Junior_School_Certificate|Junior School Certificate]] (JSC) examination.
sentence_740: Students who pass this examination proceed to two years of secondary education, culminating in the SSC examination.
sentence_741: Students who pass this examination proceed to two years of higher-secondary education, culminating in the Higher Secondary School Certificate (HSC) examination.
sentence_742: Education is primarily in Bengali, but English is commonly taught and used.
sentence_743: Many Muslim families send their children to part-time courses or full-time religious education in Bengali and [[Arabic_language|Arabic]] in madrasas.
sentence_744: Bangladesh conforms with [[UNESCO|UNESCO's]] [[Education_For_All|Education For All]] (EFA) objectives, the UN [[Millennium_Development_Goals|Millennium Development Goals]] (MDG) and other international declarations.
sentence_745: Article 17 of the [[Bangladesh_Constitution|Bangladesh Constitution]] provides that all children between the ages of six and ten years receive a basic education free of charge.
sentence_746: [[Universities_in_Bangladesh|Universities in Bangladesh]] are of three general types: public (government-owned and subsidized), private (privately owned universities) and international (operated and funded by international organisations).
sentence_747: They are accredited by and affiliated with the [[University_Grants_Commission_(Bangladesh)|University Grants Commission]] (UGC), created by Presidential Order 10 in 1973.
sentence_748: The country has 47 public, 105 private and two international [[List_of_universities_in_Bangladesh|universities]]; [[Bangladesh_National_University|Bangladesh National University]] has the largest enrollment, and the [[University_of_Dhaka|University of Dhaka]] (established in 1921) is the oldest.
sentence_749: University of Chittagong (established in 1966) is the largest University (Campus: Rural, 2,100 acres (8.5 km2)).
sentence_750: [[Islamic_University_of_Technology|Islamic University of Technology]], commonly known as IUT, is a subsidiary of the Organisation of the Islamic Cooperation (OIC, representing 57 countries in Asia, Africa, Europe and South America).
sentence_751: Asian University for Women in Chittagong is the preeminent South Asian liberal-arts university for women, representing 14 Asian countries; its faculty hails from notable academic institutions in North America, Europe, Asia, Australia and the Middle East.
sentence_752: As in Bangladesh, the agriculture sector is the largest contributor (more than 20%) to GDP and agricultural sciences are well developed.
sentence_753: It has 6 public research based agricultural university, and they are: Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman Agricultural University, Bangladesh Agricultural University, [[Sher-e-Bangla_Agricultural_University|Sher-e-Bangla Agricultural University]], Sylhet Agricultural University, [[Khulna_Agricultural_University|Khulna Agricultural University]], [[Chittagong_Veterinary_and_Animal_Sciences_University|Chittagong Veterinary and Animal Sciences University]].
sentence_754: BUET, CUET, KUET and RUET are Bangladesh's four public engineering universities.
sentence_755: [[BUTEX|BUTEX]] and DUET are two specialised engineering universities; BUTEX specialises in [[Textile_engineering|textile engineering]], and DUET offers higher education to diploma engineers.
sentence_756: The NITER is a specialised public-private partnership institute which provides higher education in textile engineering.
sentence_757: Science and technology universities include [[Hajee_Mohammad_Danesh_Science_&_Technology_University|Hajee Mohammad Danesh Science & Technology University]], [[Mawlana_Bhashani_Science_and_Technology_University|Mawlana Bhashani Science and Technology University]], Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman Science and Technology University, [[SUST|SUST]], JUST, PUST, NSTU and [[Patuakhali_Science_and_Technology_University|PSTU]].
sentence_758: The country's first higher education institution on [[Aerospace_engineering|aerospace engineering]], [[Bangabandhu_Sheikh_Mujibur_Rahman_Aviation_and_Aerospace_University|Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman Aviation and Aerospace University]], has been established in 2019 and is expected to launch its on-campus academic activities from the start of 2021.
sentence_759: Medical education is provided by 29 government and private [[List_of_medical_colleges_in_Bangladesh|medical colleges]].
sentence_760: All medical colleges are affiliated with the [[Ministry_of_Health_and_Family_Welfare_(Bangladesh)|Ministry of Health and Family Welfare]].
sentence_761: Bangladesh's 2015 literacy rate rose to 71 percent due to education modernisation and improved funding, with 16,087 schools and 2,363 colleges receiving Monthly Pay Order (MPO) facilities.
sentence_762: According to then education minister Nurul Islam Nahid, 27,558 madrasas and technical and vocational institutions were enlisted for the facility.
sentence_763: 6,036 educational institutions were outside MPO coverage, and the government enlisted 1,624 private schools for MPO in 2010.
sentence_765: Healthcare facilities in Bangladesh are considered less than adequate, although they have improved as poverty levels have decreased significantly.
sentence_766: Findings from a recent study in Chakaria (a rural [[Upazila|Upazila]] under Cox's Bazar District) revealed that the "village doctors", practicing allopathic medicine without formal training, were reported to have provided 65% of the healthcare sought for illness episodes occurring within 14 days prior to the survey.
sentence_767: Formally-trained providers made up only four percent of the total health workforce.
sentence_768: The Future Health Systems survey indicated significant deficiencies in the treatment practices of village doctors, with widespread harmful and inappropriate drug prescribing.
sentence_769: Receiving health care from informal providers is encouraged.
sentence_770: A 2007 study of 1,000 households in rural Bangladesh found that direct payments to formal and informal healthcare providers and indirect costs (loss of earnings because of illness) associated with illness were deterrents to accessing healthcare from qualified providers.
sentence_771: A community survey of 6,183 individuals in rural Bangladesh found a gender difference in treatment-seeking behaviour, with women less likely to seek treatment than to men.
sentence_772: The use of skilled birth attendant (SBA) services, however, rose from 2005 to 2007 among women from all socioeconomic [[Quantile|quintiles]] except the highest.
sentence_773: A health watch, a pilot community-empowerment tool, was successfully developed and implemented in south-eastern Bangladesh to improve the uptake and monitoring of public-health services.
sentence_774: Bangladesh's poor health conditions are attributed to the lack of healthcare provision by the government.
sentence_775: According to a 2010 World Bank report, 2009 healthcare spending was 3.35 percent of the country's GDP.
sentence_776: Government spending on healthcare that year was 7.9 percent of the total budget; out-of-pocket expenditures totalled 96.5 percent.
sentence_777: According to the government sources, the number of hospital beds is 8 per 10,000 population (as of 2015).
sentence_778: [[Malnutrition|Malnutrition]] has been a persistent problem in Bangladesh, with the World Bank ranking the country first in the number of malnourished children worldwide.
sentence_779: More than 54% of preschool-age children are stunted, 56% are underweight and more than 17% are wasted.
sentence_780: More than 45 percent of rural families and 76 percent of urban families were below the acceptable caloric-intake level.
sentence_781: Main articles: [[Culture_of_Bangladesh|Culture of Bangladesh]], Culture of Bengal, and [[Bengali_Renaissance|Bengali Renaissance]]
sentence_783: The recorded history of art in Bangladesh can be traced to the 3rd century BCE, when [[Terracotta|terracotta]] sculptures were made in the region.
sentence_784: In classical antiquity, a notable school of sculptural Hindu, Jain and Buddhist art developed in the Pala Empire and the Sena dynasty.
sentence_785: Islamic art evolved since the 14th century.
sentence_786: The architecture of the Bengal Sultanate saw a distinct style of domed mosques with complex niche pillars that had no minarets.
sentence_787: [[Mughal_Bengal|Mughal Bengal]]'s most celebrated artistic tradition was the weaving of [[Jamdani|Jamdani]] [[Motif_(textile_arts)|motifs]] on fine muslin, which is now classified by UNESCO as an [[Intangible_cultural_heritage|intangible cultural heritage]].
sentence_788: Jamdani motifs were similar to Iranian textile art (buta motifs) and Western textile art ([[Paisley_(design)|paisley]]).
sentence_789: The Jamdani weavers in Dhaka received imperial patronage.
sentence_790: [[Ivory|Ivory]] and [[Brass|brass]] were also widely used in Mughal art.
sentence_791: [[Pottery|Pottery]] is widely used in Bengali culture.
sentence_792: The [[Modern_art|modern art]] movement in Bangladesh took shape during the 1950s, particularly with the pioneering works of [[Zainul_Abedin|Zainul Abedin]].
sentence_793: East Bengal developed its own modernist painting and sculpture traditions, which were distinct from the art movements in West Bengal.
sentence_794: The Art Institute Dhaka has been an important center for visual art in the region.
sentence_795: Its annual [[Mangal_Shobhajatra|Bengali New Year parade]] was enlisted as an intangible cultural heritage by UNESCO in 2016.
sentence_796: Modern Bangladesh has produced many of South Asia's leading painters, including [[SM_Sultan|SM Sultan]], [[Mohammad_Kibria|Mohammad Kibria]], [[Shahabuddin_Ahmed_(artist)|Shahabuddin Ahmed]], [[Kanak_Chanpa_Chakma|Kanak Chanpa Chakma]], Kafil Ahmed, Saifuddin Ahmed, [[Qayyum_Chowdhury|Qayyum Chowdhury]], Rashid Choudhury, [[Quamrul_Hassan|Quamrul Hassan]], [[Rafiqun_Nabi|Rafiqun Nabi]] and [[Syed_Jahangir|Syed Jahangir]], among others.
sentence_797: [[Novera_Ahmed|Novera Ahmed]] and [[Nitun_Kundu|Nitun Kundu]] were the country's pioneers of modernist sculpture.
sentence_798: In recent times, photography as a medium of art has become popular.
sentence_799: Biennial Chobi Mela is considered the largest photography festival in Asia.
sentence_801: The oldest evidence of writing in Bangladesh is the Mahasthan [[Brahmi|Brahmi]] Inscription, which dates back to the 3rd century BCE.
sentence_802: In the Gupta Empire, Sanskrit literature thrived in the region.
sentence_803: Bengali developed from [[Sanskrit|Sanskrit]] and [[Magadhi_Prakrit|Magadhi Prakrit]] in the 8th to 10th century.
sentence_804: Bengali literature is a millennium-old tradition; the [[Charyapada|Charyapadas]] are the earliest examples of Bengali poetry.
sentence_805: Sufi spiritualism inspired many [[Bengali_Muslim|Bengali Muslim]] writers.
sentence_806: During the Bengal Sultanate, medieval Bengali writers were influenced by Arabic and [[Persian_literature|Persian works]].
sentence_807: The [[Chandidas|Chandidas]] are the notable lyric poets from the early Medieval Age.
sentence_808: [[Alaol|Syed Alaol]] was a noted secular poet and translator from the [[Arakan|Arakan]] region.
sentence_809: The Bengal Renaissance shaped the emergence of modern Bengali literature, including novels, short stories and science fiction.
sentence_810: Rabindranath Tagore was the first non-European laureate of the [[Nobel_Prize_in_Literature|Nobel Prize in Literature]] and is described as the Bengali Shakespeare.
sentence_811: [[Kazi_Nazrul_Islam|Kazi Nazrul Islam]] was a revolutionary poet who espoused political rebellion against colonialism and fascism.
sentence_812: [[Begum_Rokeya|Begum Rokeya]] is regarded as the pioneer feminist writer of Bangladesh.
sentence_813: Other renaissance icons included Michael Madhusudan Dutt and [[Sarat_Chandra_Chattopadhyay|Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay]].
sentence_814: The writer [[Syed_Mujtaba_Ali|Syed Mujtaba Ali]] is noted for his cosmopolitan Bengali worldview.
sentence_816: [[Shamsur_Rahman_(poet)|Shamsur Rahman]] and [[Al_Mahmud|Al Mahmud]] are considered two of the greatest Bengali poets to have emerged in the 20th century.
sentence_817: [[Farrukh_Ahmad|Farrukh Ahmad]], Sufia Kamal, [[Syed_Ali_Ahsan|Syed Ali Ahsan]], [[Ahsan_Habib|Ahsan Habib]], [[Abul_Hussain|Abul Hussain]], [[Shahid_Qadri|Shahid Qadri]], Fazal Shahbuddin, Abu Jafar Obaidullah, [[Omar_Ali_(poet)|Omar Ali]], Al Mujahidy, Syed Shamsul Huq, [[Nirmalendu_Goon|Nirmalendu Goon]], [[Abid_Azad|Abid Azad]], Sanaul Haque Khan, Hasan Hafiz, Abdul Hye Sikder, Sayeed Abubakar, Jafar Ahmad Rashed are important figures of modern Bangladeshi poetry.
sentence_818: [[Ahmed_Sofa|Ahmed Sofa]] is regarded as the most important Bangladeshi intellectual in the post-independence era.
sentence_819: [[Humayun_Ahmed|Humayun Ahmed]] was a popular writer of modern Bangladeshi [[Magical_realism|magical realism]] and science fiction.
sentence_820: Notable writers of Bangladeshi fictions include Mir Mosharraf Hossain, [[Akhteruzzaman_Elias|Akhteruzzaman Elias]], [[Alauddin_Al_Azad|Alauddin Al Azad]], [[Shahidul_Zahir|Shahidul Zahir]], [[Rashid_Karim|Rashid Karim]], [[Mahmudul_Haque|Mahmudul Haque]], [[Syed_Waliullah|Syed Waliullah]], [[Shahidullah_Kaiser|Shahidullah Kaiser]], Shawkat Osman, [[Selina_Hossain|Selina Hossain]], Shahed Ali, Abul Khayer Muslehuddin, [[Razia_Khan|Razia Khan]], [[Anisul_Hoque|Anisul Hoque]], and Abdul Mannan Syed.
sentence_821: The annual [[Ekushey_Book_Fair|Ekushey Book Fair]] and [[Hay_Festival_Dhaka|Dhaka Literature Festival]], organised by the [[Bangla_Academy|Bangla Academy]], are among the largest literary festivals in South Asia.
sentence_823: Although, as of 2015, several women occupied major political office in Bangladesh, its women continue to live under a patriarchal social regime where violence is common.
sentence_824: Whereas in India and Pakistan women participate less in the workforce as their education increases, the reverse is the case in Bangladesh.
sentence_825: Bengal has a long history of [[Feminist_activism|feminist activism]] dating back to the 19th century.
sentence_826: [[Begum_Rokeya|Begum Rokeya]] and [[Nawab_Faizunnesa|Faizunnessa Chowdhurani]] played an important role in emancipating Bengali Muslim women from [[Purdah|purdah]], prior to the country's division, as well as promoting girls' education.
sentence_827: Several women were elected to the Bengal Legislative Assembly in the British Raj.
sentence_828: The first women's magazine, [[Begum_(magazine)|Begum]], was published in 1948.
sentence_829: In 2008, Bangladeshi female workforce participation stood at 26%.
sentence_830: Women dominate [[Blue_collar|blue collar]] jobs in the Bangladeshi garment industry.
sentence_831: Agriculture, social services, healthcare and education are also major occupations for Bangladeshi women, while their employment in [[White-collar_worker|white collar]] positions has steadily increased.
sentence_833: The architectural traditions of Bangladesh have a 2,500-year-old heritage.
sentence_834: Terracotta architecture is a distinct feature of Bengal.
sentence_835: Pre-Islamic Bengali architecture reached its pinnacle in the Pala Empire, when the Pala School of Sculptural Art established grand structures such as the Somapura Mahavihara.
sentence_836: [[Islamic_architecture|Islamic architecture]] began developing under the Bengal Sultanate, when local terracotta styles influenced medieval mosque construction.
sentence_837: The [[Adina_Mosque|Adina Mosque]] of United Bengal was the largest mosque built on the [[Indian_subcontinent|Indian subcontinent]].
sentence_838: The [[Sixty_Dome_Mosque|Sixty Dome Mosque]] was the largest medieval mosque built in Bangladesh, and is a fine example of Turkic-Bengali architecture.
sentence_839: The [[Mughal_architecture|Mughal style]] replaced indigenous architecture when Bengal became a province of the Mughal Empire and influenced the development of urban housing.
sentence_840: The [[Kantajew_Temple|Kantajew Temple]] and [[Dhakeshwari_Temple|Dhakeshwari Temple]] are excellent examples of late medieval [[Hindu_temple_architecture|Hindu temple architecture]].
sentence_841: Indo-Saracenic Revival architecture, based on Indo-Islamic styles, flourished during the British period.
sentence_842: The zamindar gentry in Bangladesh built numerous Indo-Saracenic palaces and country mansions, such as the Ahsan Manzil, [[Tajhat_Palace|Tajhat Palace]], [[Uttara_Gonobhaban|Dighapatia Palace]], [[Puthia_Rajbari|Puthia Rajbari]] and [[Natore_Rajbari|Natore Rajbari]].
sentence_843: Bengali [[Vernacular_architecture|vernacular architecture]] is noted for pioneering the bungalow.
sentence_844: Bangladeshi villages consist of thatched roofed houses made of natural materials like [[Mud|mud]], straw, wood and bamboo.
sentence_845: In modern times, village bungalows are increasingly made of [[Tin|tin]].
sentence_846: [[Muzharul_Islam|Muzharul Islam]] was the pioneer of Bangladeshi modern architecture.
sentence_847: His varied works set the course of modern architectural practice in the country.
sentence_848: Islam brought leading global architects, including [[Louis_Kahn|Louis Kahn]], [[Richard_Neutra|Richard Neutra]], Stanley Tigerman, [[Paul_Rudolph_(architect)|Paul Rudolph]], Robert Boughey and Konstantinos Doxiadis, to work in erstwhile East Pakistan.
sentence_849: Louis Kahn was chosen to design the National Parliament Complex in [[Sher-e-Bangla_Nagar|Sher-e-Bangla Nagar]].
sentence_850: Kahn's monumental designs, combining regional red brick aesthetics, his own concrete and marble [[Brutalism|brutalism]] and the use of lakes to represent Bengali geography, are regarded as one of the masterpieces of the 20th century.
sentence_851: In more recent times, award-winning architects like Rafiq Azam have set the course of contemporary architecture by adopting influences from the works of Islam and Kahn.
sentence_852: [[Theatre_in_Bangladesh|Theatre in Bangladesh]] includes various forms with a history dating back to the 4th century CE.
sentence_853: It includes narrative forms, song and dance forms, supra-personae forms, performances with scroll paintings, puppet theatre and processional forms.
sentence_854: The [[Jatra_(theatre)|Jatra]] is the most popular form of Bengali folk theatre.
sentence_855: The dance traditions of Bangladesh include indigenous tribal and Bengali dance forms, as well as [[Classical_Indian_dance|classical Indian dances]], including the [[Kathak|Kathak]], [[Odissi|Odissi]] and [[Manipuri_dance|Manipuri dances]].
sentence_856: The [[Music_of_Bangladesh|music of Bangladesh]] features the [[Baul|Baul]] [[Mysticism|mystical]] tradition, listed by UNESCO as a [[Masterpiece_of_the_Oral_and_Intangible_Heritage_of_Humanity|Masterpiece of Intangible Cultural Heritage]].
sentence_857: [[Lalon|Fakir Lalon Shah]] popularized [[Baul|Baul]] music in the country in the 18th century and it has been one of the most popular music genera in the country since then.
sentence_858: Most modern [[Bauls|Bauls]] are devoted to Lalon Shah.
sentence_859: Numerous lyric-based musical traditions, varying from one region to the next, exist, including [[Gombhira|Gombhira]], [[Bhatiali|Bhatiali]] and [[Bhawaiya|Bhawaiya]].
sentence_860: Folk music is accompanied by a one-stringed instrument known as the [[Ektara|ektara]].
sentence_861: Other instruments include the [[Dotara|dotara]], dhol, flute, and [[Tabla|tabla]].
sentence_862: Bengali classical music includes [[Tagore_songs|Tagore songs]] and [[Nazrul_geeti|Nazrul Sangeet]].
sentence_863: Bangladesh has a rich tradition of [[Indian_classical_music|Indian classical music]], which uses instruments like the sitar, tabla, sarod and santoor.
sentence_864: Sabina Yasmin and [[Runa_Laila|Runa Laila]] are considered the leading playback singers in the modern time, while musician [[Ayub_Bachchu|Ayub Bachchu]] is credited with popularising Bengali rock music in Bangladesh.
sentence_865: See also: [[Textile_arts_of_Bangladesh|Textile arts of Bangladesh]] and [[Muslin_trade_in_Bengal|Muslin trade in Bengal]]
sentence_866: The [[Nakshi_Kantha|Nakshi Kantha]] is a centuries-old [[Embroidery|embroidery]] tradition for [[Quilt|quilts]], said to be indigenous to eastern Bengal (i.e. Bangladesh).
sentence_867: The sari is the national dress for Bangladeshi women.
sentence_868: Mughal Dhaka was renowned for producing the finest [[Muslin|Muslin]] saris, as well as the famed Dhakai and [[Jamdani|Jamdani]], the weaving of which is listed by UNESCO as one of the masterpieces of humanity's intangible cultural heritage.
sentence_870: The [[Shalwar_kameez|shalwar kameez]] is also widely worn by Bangladeshi women.
sentence_871: In urban areas some women can be seen in western clothing.
sentence_872: The [[Kurta|kurta]] and sherwani are the national dress of Bangladeshi men; the lungi and [[Dhoti|dhoti]] are worn by them in informal settings.
sentence_873: Aside from ethnic wear, domestically tailored [[Suit_(clothing)|suits]] and neckties are customarily worn by the country's men in offices, in schools and at social events.
sentence_874: The handloom industry supplies 60–65% of the country's clothing demand.
sentence_875: The Bengali ethnic [[Fashion_industry|fashion industry]] has flourished in the changing environment of the fashion world.
sentence_876: The retailer Aarong is one of the most successful ethnic wear brands in South Asia.
sentence_877: The development of the Bangladesh textile industry, which supplies leading international brands, has promoted the production and retail of modern Western attire locally, with the country now having a number of expanding local brands like Westecs and Yellow.
sentence_878: Bangladesh is the world's second largest garments exporter.
sentence_879: Among Bangladesh's fashion designers, [[Bibi_Russell|Bibi Russell]] has received international acclaim for her "Fashion for Development" shows.
sentence_880: Main articles: Bengali cuisine and Bangladeshi cuisine
sentence_881: [[White_rice|White rice]] is the staple of Bangladeshi cuisine, along with many vegetables and [[Lentil|lentils]].
sentence_882: Rice preparations also include Bengali [[Biryani|biryanis]], [[Pilaf|pulaos]], and [[Khichuri|khichuris]].
sentence_883: [[Mustard_(condiment)|Mustard]] sauce, ghee, [[Sunflower_oil|sunflower oil]] and fruit [[Chutney|chutneys]] are widely used in Bangladeshi cooking.
sentence_884: Fish is the main source of protein in Bengali cuisine.
sentence_885: The [[Hilsa|Hilsa]] is the national fish and immensely popular across Bangladesh.
sentence_886: Other kinds of fish eaten include [[Rohu|rohu]], [[Butterfish|butterfish]], catfish, [[Tilapia|tilapia]] and [[Barramundi|barramundi]].
sentence_887: Fish eggs are a gourmet delicacy.
sentence_888: Seafood holds an important place in Bengali cuisine, especially [[Lobster|lobsters]], [[Shrimp|shrimps]] and [[Dried_fish|dried fish]].
sentence_889: Meat consumption includes chicken, beef, [[Mutton|mutton]], [[Venison|venison]], [[Duck|duck]] and [[Squab_(food)|squab]].
sentence_890: In Chittagong, Mezban feasts are a popular tradition featuring the serving of hot beef [[Curry|curry]].
sentence_891: In Sylhet, the [[Shatkora|shatkora]] lemons are used to marinate dishes.
sentence_892: In the tribal Hill Tracts, bamboo shoot cooking is prevalent.
sentence_893: Bangladesh has a vast spread of desserts, including distinctive [[Sweets|sweets]] like [[Rasgulla|Rôshogolla]], Rôshomalai, [[Chomchom|Chomchom]], Mishti Doi and Kalojaam.
sentence_894: Pithas are traditional boiled desserts made with rice or fruits.
sentence_896: [[Naan|Naan]], [[Paratha|paratha]], [[Luchi|luchi]] and [[Bakarkhani|bakarkhani]] are the main local breads.
sentence_897: [[Milk_tea|Milk tea]] is offered to guests as a gesture of welcome and is the most common hot beverage in the country.
sentence_898: [[Kebab|Kebabs]] are widely popular across Bangladesh, particularly [[Seekh_kebab|seekh kebabs]], [[Chicken_tikka|chicken tikka]] and [[Shashlik|shashliks]].
sentence_899: Bangladesh shares its culinary heritage with the neighbouring Indian state of [[West_Bengal|West Bengal]].
sentence_900: The two regions have several differences, however.
sentence_901: In Muslim-majority Bangladesh, meat consumption is greater; whereas in Hindu-majority West Bengal, vegetarianism is more prevalent.
sentence_902: The Bangladeshi diaspora dominates the South Asian restaurant industry in many Western countries, particularly in the United Kingdom.
sentence_903: Main articles: [[Public_holidays_in_Bangladesh|Public holidays in Bangladesh]] and [[List_of_festivals_in_Bangladesh|List of festivals in Bangladesh]]
sentence_904: [[Pahela_Baishakh|Pahela Baishakh]], the Bengali new year, is the major festival of Bengali culture and sees widespread festivities.
sentence_905: Of the major holidays celebrated in Bangladesh, only Pahela Baishakh comes without any pre-existing expectations (specific religious identity, culture of gift-giving, etc.) and has become an occasion for celebrating the simpler, rural roots of the Bengal.
sentence_906: Other cultural festivals include [[Nabanna|Nabonno]], and Poush Parbon both of which are Bengali harvest festivals.
sentence_907: The Muslim festivals of Eid al-Fitr, [[Eid_al-Adha|Eid al-Adha]], [[Milad_un_Nabi|Milad un Nabi]], [[Muharram|Muharram]], [[Chand_Raat|Chand Raat]], Shab-e-Barat; the Hindu festivals of [[Durga_Puja|Durga Puja]], [[Janmashtami|Janmashtami]] and Rath Yatra; the Buddhist festival of [[Vesak|Buddha Purnima]], which marks the birth of [[Gautama_Buddha|Gautama Buddha]], and Christian festival of Christmas are [[Public_holidays_in_Bangladesh|national holidays]] in Bangladesh and see the most widespread celebrations in the country.
sentence_908: The two Eids are celebrated with long streak of public holidays and give the city-dwellers opportunity to celebrate the festivals with their families outside city.
sentence_909: Alongside are national days like the remembrance of 21 February 1952 [[Language_Movement_Day|Language Movement Day]] (declared as [[International_Mother_Language_Day|International Mother Language Day]] by [[UNESCO|UNESCO]] in 1999), [[Independence_Day_(Bangladesh)|Independence Day]] and [[Victory_day_of_Bangladesh|Victory Day]].
sentence_910: On Language Movement Day, people congregate at the [[Shaheed_Minar,_Dhaka|Shaheed Minar]] in Dhaka to remember the national heroes of the Bengali Language Movement.
sentence_911: Similar gatherings are observed at the [[National_Martyrs'_Memorial|National Martyrs' Memorial]] on Independence Day and Victory Day to remember the national heroes of the [[Bangladesh_Liberation_War|Bangladesh Liberation War]].
sentence_912: These occasions are celebrated with public ceremonies, parades, rallies by citizens, political speeches, fairs, concerts, and various other public and private events, celebrating the history and traditions of Bangladesh.
sentence_913: TV and radio stations broadcast special programs and patriotic songs, and many schools and colleges organise fairs, festivals, and concerts that draw the participation of citizens from all levels of Bangladeshi society.
sentence_915: In rural Bangladesh, several traditional indigenous sports such as Kabaddi, [[Boli_Khela|Boli Khela]], [[Lathi_Khela|Lathi Khela]] and [[Nouka_Baich|Nouka Baich]] remain fairly popular.
sentence_916: While Kabaddi is the national sport [[Cricket|cricket]] is the most popular sport in the country followed by [[Association_football|football]].
sentence_917: The [[Bangladesh_national_cricket_team|national cricket team]] participated in their first [[Cricket_World_Cup|Cricket World Cup]] in 1999 and the following year was granted [[Test_cricket|Test cricket]] status.
sentence_918: Bangladesh reached the quarter-final of the [[2015_Cricket_World_Cup|2015 Cricket World Cup]], the semi-final of the [[2017_ICC_Champions_Trophy|2017 ICC Champions Trophy]] and they reached the final of the [[Asia_Cup|Asia Cup]] 3 times – in 2012, 2016 and 2018.
sentence_919: In February 2020, the Bangladesh youth national cricket team won the men's [[2020_Under-19_Cricket_World_Cup|Under-19 Cricket World Cup]], held in South Africa.
sentence_920: This was Bangladesh's first World Cup victory.
sentence_921: Women's sports saw significant progress in the [[2010s|2010s]] decade in Bangladesh.
sentence_922: In 2018 the [[Bangladesh_women's_national_cricket_team|Bangladesh women's national cricket team]] won the [[2018_Women's_Twenty20_Asia_Cup|2018 Women's Twenty20 Asia Cup]] defeating [[India_women's_national_cricket_team|India women's national cricket team]] in the final.
sentence_923: [[Bangladesh_women's_national_football_team|Bangladesh women's national football team]] has also registered some success at regional level, especially the Under-15 and Under-18 teams.
sentence_924: [[Association_football|Football]] is the another popular sport in Bangladesh alongside cricket and is governed by the [[Bangladesh_Football_Federation|Bangladesh Football Federation]] (BFF).
sentence_925: Football tournaments are regularly organised in and outside [[Dhaka_District|Dhaka]] and football fever grips the nation during every [[FIFA_World_Cup|FIFA World Cup]].
sentence_926: On 4 November 2018, [[Bangladesh_national_under-17_football_team|Bangladesh national under-15 football team]] won the [[2018_SAFF_U-15_Championship|2018 SAFF U-15 Championship]], defeating Pakistan national under-15 football team in the final.
sentence_927: Bangladesh archers Ety Khatun and Roman Sana won several gold medals winning all the 10 [[Archery|archery]] events (both individual, and team events) in the [[2019_South_Asian_Games|2019 South Asian Games]].
sentence_928: The [[National_Sports_Council|National Sports Council]] regulates 42 sporting federations.
sentence_929: Athletics, swimming, archery, boxing, volleyball, weight-lifting and wrestling and different forms of martial arts remain popular.
sentence_931: Bangladesh has five grandmasters in chess.
sentence_932: Among them, Niaz Murshed was the first grandmaster in South Asia.
sentence_933: In 2010, mountain climber [[Musa_Ibrahim|Musa Ibrahim]] became the first Bangladeshi climber to conquer [[Mount_Everest|Mount Everest]].
sentence_934: He climbed the top of the summit of Mount Everest.
sentence_935: [[Wasfia_Nazreen|Wasfia Nazreen]] is the first Bangladeshi climber to climb the [[Seven_Summits|Seven Summits]], which are the highest mountains of each of the seven continents of the world.
sentence_936: Bangladesh hosts a number of international tournaments.
sentence_937: [[Bangabandhu_Cup|Bangabandhu Cup]] is an international football tournament hosted in the country.
sentence_938: Bangladesh hosted the South Asian Games several times.
sentence_939: In 2011, Bangladesh co-hosted the [[ICC_Cricket_World_Cup_2011|ICC Cricket World Cup 2011]] with India and Sri Lanka.
sentence_940: The [[2014_ICC_World_Twenty20|2014 ICC World Twenty20]] championship was solely hosted by Bangladesh.
sentence_941: Bangladesh hosted the [[Asia_Cup|Asia Cup]] Cricket Tournament in 2000, 2012, 2014 and 2016.
sentence_942: Main articles: [[Media_of_Bangladesh|Media of Bangladesh]] and [[Cinema_of_Bangladesh|Cinema of Bangladesh]]
sentence_943: The Bangladeshi press is diverse, outspoken and privately owned.
sentence_944: Over 200 newspapers are published in the country.
sentence_945: [[Bangladesh_Betar|Bangladesh Betar]] is the state-run radio service.
sentence_946: The [[British_Broadcasting_Corporation|British Broadcasting Corporation]] operates the popular [[BBC_Bangla|BBC Bangla]] news and current affairs service.
sentence_947: Bengali broadcasts from [[Voice_of_America|Voice of America]] are also very popular.
sentence_948: [[Bangladesh_Television|Bangladesh Television]] (BTV) is the state-owned television network.
sentence_949: There more than 20 privately owned television networks, including several news channels.
sentence_950: [[Freedom_of_the_media|Freedom of the media]] remains a major concern, due to government attempts at censorship and the harassment of journalists.
sentence_951: The [[Cinema_of_Bangladesh|cinema of Bangladesh]] dates back to 1898, when films began screening at the Crown Theatre in Dhaka.
sentence_952: The first bioscope on the subcontinent was established in Dhaka that year.
sentence_953: The [[Dhaka_Nawab_Family|Dhaka Nawab Family]] patronised the production of several [[Silent_film|silent films]] in the 1920s and 30s.
sentence_954: In 1931, the East Bengal Cinematograph Society released the first full-length feature film in Bangladesh, titled the Last Kiss.
sentence_955: The first feature film in East Pakistan, [[Mukh_O_Mukhosh|Mukh O Mukhosh]], was released in 1956.
sentence_956: During the 1960s, 25–30 films were produced annually in Dhaka.
sentence_957: By the 2000s, Bangladesh produced 80–100 films a year.
sentence_958: While the Bangladeshi film industry has achieved limited commercial success, the country has produced notable independent filmmakers.
sentence_959: [[Zahir_Raihan|Zahir Raihan]] was a prominent documentary-maker who was assassinated in 1971.
sentence_960: The late [[Tareque_Masud|Tareque Masud]] is regarded as one of Bangladesh's outstanding directors for his critically acclaimed films on social issues.
sentence_961: Masud was honoured by [[FIPRESCI|FIPRESCI]] at the 2002 [[Cannes_Film_Festival|Cannes Film Festival]] for his film [[Matir_Moina|The Clay Bird]].
sentence_962: [[Tanvir_Mokammel|Tanvir Mokammel]], [[Mostofa_Sarwar_Farooki|Mostofa Sarwar Farooki]], [[Humayun_Ahmed|Humayun Ahmed]], [[Alamgir_Kabir_(film_maker)|Alamgir Kabir]], and [[Chashi_Nazrul_Islam|Chashi Nazrul Islam]] are some of the prominent directors of Bangladeshi cinema.
sentence_963: Bangladesh have very active film society culture.
sentence_965: Now around 40 Film Society active in all over Bangladesh.
sentence_966: [[Federation_of_Film_Societies_of_Bangladesh|Federation of Film Societies of Bangladesh]] is the parent organisation of the film society movement of Bangladesh.
sentence_967: Active film societies include the Rainbow Film Society, [[Children's_Film_Society|Children's Film Society]], [[Moviyana_Film_Society|Moviyana Film Society]] and Dhaka University Film Society.
sentence_968: Main articles: [[Museums_in_Bangladesh|Museums in Bangladesh]] and [[List_of_libraries_in_Bangladesh|List of libraries in Bangladesh]]
sentence_969: The Varendra Research Museum is the oldest museum in Bangladesh.
sentence_970: It houses important collections from both the pre-Islamic and Islamic periods, including the sculptures of the Pala-Sena School of Art and the Indus Valley Civilization; as well as Sanskrit, Arabic and Persian manuscripts and inscriptions.
sentence_971: The Ahsan Manzil, the former residence of the Nawab of Dhaka, is a national museum housing collections from the British Raj.
sentence_972: It was the site of the founding conference of the All India Muslim League and hosted many British Viceroys in Dhaka.
sentence_973: The [[Tajhat_Palace|Tajhat Palace]] Museum preserves artefacts of the rich cultural heritage of North Bengal, including Hindu-Buddhist sculptures and Islamic manuscripts.
sentence_974: The [[Mymensingh_Museum|Mymensingh Museum]] houses the personal antique collections of Bengali aristocrats in central Bengal.
sentence_975: The [[Ethnological_Museum_of_Chittagong|Ethnological Museum of Chittagong]] showcases the lifestyle of various tribes in Bangladesh.
sentence_976: The [[Bangladesh_National_Museum|Bangladesh National Museum]] is located in Ramna, Dhaka and has a rich collection of antiquities.
sentence_977: The [[Liberation_War_Museum|Liberation War Museum]] documents the Bangladeshi struggle for independence and the 1971 genocide.
sentence_978: In ancient times, manuscripts were written on palm leaves, tree barks, parchment vellum and terracotta plates and preserved at monasteries known as [[Vihara|viharas]].
sentence_979: The Hussain Shahi dynasty established royal libraries during the Bengal Sultanate.
sentence_980: Libraries were established in each district of Bengal by the zamindar gentry during the Bengal Renaissance in the 19th century.
sentence_981: The trend of establishing libraries continued until the beginning of World War II.
sentence_982: In 1854, four major public libraries were opened, including the Bogra Woodburn Library, the Rangpur Public Library, the Jessore Institute Public Library and the Barisal Public Library.
sentence_983: The [[Northbrook_Hall|Northbrook Hall Public Library]] was established in Dhaka in 1882 in honour of [[Lord_Northbrook|Lord Northbrook]], the Governor-General.
sentence_984: Other libraries established in the British period included the Victoria Public Library, Natore (1901), the Sirajganj Public Library (1882), the [[Rajshahi_Public_Library|Rajshahi Public Library]] (1884), the Comilla Birchandra Library (1885), the Shah Makhdum Institute Public Library, Rajshahi (1891), the Noakhali Town Hall Public Library (1896), the Prize Memorial Library, Sylhet (1897), the Chittagong Municipality Public Library (1904) and the Varendra Research Library (1910).
sentence_985: The Great Bengal Library Association was formed in 1925.
sentence_986: The [[Central_Public_Library_(Dhaka)|Central Public Library of Dhaka]] was established in 1959.
sentence_987: The [[National_Library_of_Bangladesh|National Library of Bangladesh]] was established in 1972.
sentence_988: The [[Bishwo_Shahitto_Kendro|World Literature Center]], founded by [[Ramon_Magsaysay_Award|Ramon Magsaysay Award]] winner [[Abdullah_Abu_Sayeed|Abdullah Abu Sayeed]], is noted for operating numerous [[Mobile_library|mobile libraries]] across Bangladesh and was awarded the UNESCO Jon Amos Comenius Medal.

title: Anglican Communion
sentence_0: This article is about churches in full communion with the Archbishop of Canterbury.
sentence_1: For the Christian tradition originating in the Church of England, see [[Anglicanism|Anglicanism]].
sentence_2: "The Anglican Church" redirects here.
sentence_3: For other uses, see [[Anglican_Church_(disambiguation)|Anglican Church (disambiguation)]].
sentence_4: The Anglican Communion is the [[List_of_Christian_denominations_by_number_of_members|third largest]] Christian [[Full_communion|communion]] (after the [[Catholic_Church|Catholic Church]] and [[Eastern_Orthodox_Churches|Eastern Orthodox Church]]).
sentence_5: Founded in 1867 in London, [[England|England]], the communion currently has over 85 million members within the Church of England and other national and regional churches in [[Full_communion|full communion]].
sentence_6: The traditional origins of Anglican doctrines are summarised in the [[Thirty-nine_Articles|Thirty-nine Articles]] (1571).
sentence_7: The [[Archbishop_of_Canterbury|Archbishop of Canterbury]] (currently [[Justin_Welby|Justin Welby]]) in England acts as a focus of unity, recognised as [[Primus_inter_pares|primus inter pares]] ("first among equals"), but does not exercise authority in Anglican provinces outside of the Church of England.
sentence_8: Most, but not all member churches of the communion, are the historic national or regional [[Anglican|Anglican]] churches.
sentence_9: The Anglican Communion was founded at the Lambeth Conference in 1867 in London, England, under the leadership of [[Charles_Longley|Charles Longley]], Archbishop of Canterbury.
sentence_10: The churches of the Anglican Communion consider themselves to be part of the [[Four_Marks_of_the_Church|one, holy, catholic and apostolic church]], and to be both [[Catholic_(term)|catholic]] and [[Reformation|reformed]].
sentence_11: Although aligned with the Church of England, the communion has a multitude of beliefs, [[Liturgies|liturgies]], and practices, including [[Evangelicalism|evangelical]], [[Liberal_Christianity|liberal]] and [[Anglo-Catholic|Anglo-Catholic]].
sentence_12: Each retains their own legislative process and episcopal polity under the leadership of local [[Primate_(bishop)|primates]].
sentence_13: For some adherents, [[Anglicanism|Anglicanism]] represents a non-[[Pope|papal]] [[Catholicity|Catholicism]], for others a form of [[Protestantism|Protestantism]] though without guiding figure such as [[Martin_Luther|Luther]], [[John_Knox|Knox]], [[John_Calvin|Calvin]], [[Huldrych_Zwingli|Zwingli]] or [[John_Wesley|Wesley]], or for yet others a combination of the two.
sentence_14: Most of its 85 million members live in the [[Anglosphere|Anglosphere]] of former British territories.
sentence_15: Full participation in the sacramental life of each church is available to all communicant members.
sentence_16: Due to their historical link to England (Ecclesia Anglicana means "English Church"), some of the member churches are known as "Anglican", such as the [[Anglican_Church_of_Canada|Anglican Church of Canada]].
sentence_17: Others, for example the [[Church_of_Ireland|Church of Ireland]], the [[Scottish_Episcopal_Church|Scottish]] and [[Episcopal_Church_(United_States)|American]] Episcopal churches have official names which do not include "Anglican".
sentence_18: Additionally, there are some churches called "Anglican" which are not of the communion.
sentence_19: Main article: Anglican doctrine
sentence_20: One of the enduringly influential early resolutions of the conference was the so-called Chicago-Lambeth Quadrilateral of 1888.
sentence_21: Its intent was to provide the basis for discussions of reunion with the Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches, but it had the ancillary effect of establishing parameters of Anglican identity.
sentence_22: It establishes four principles with these words:

list.value: That, in the opinion of this Conference, the following Articles supply a basis on which approach may be by God's blessing made towards Home Reunion:
(a) The Holy Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments, as "containing all things necessary to salvation," and as being the rule and ultimate standard of faith.
(b) The [[Apostles'_Creed|Apostles' Creed]], as the Baptismal Symbol; and the [[Nicene_Creed|Nicene Creed]], as the sufficient statement of the Christian faith.

(c) The two Sacraments ordained by Christ Himself – Baptism and the [[Eucharist|Supper of the Lord]] – ministered with unfailing use of Christ's [[Words_of_Institution|Words of Institution]], and of the elements ordained by Him.
(d) The [[Historic_Episcopate|Historic Episcopate]], locally adapted in the methods of its administration to the varying needs of the nations and peoples called of God into the Unity of His Church.

sentence_23: The Anglican communion consists of forty-one autonomous [[Ecclesiastical_Province#Anglican_Communion|provinces]] each with its own [[Primate_(bishop)|primate]] and governing structure.
sentence_24: These provinces may take the form of national churches (such as in Canada, Uganda, or Japan) or a collection of nations (such as the [[West_Indies|West Indies]], [[Central_Africa|Central Africa]], or [[Southeast_Asia|Southeast Asia]]).

sentence_25: In addition to the forty-one provinces, there are five extraprovincial churches under the [[Metropolitan_bishop|metropolitical]] authority of the Archbishop of Canterbury.
