sentence_26: In addition to other member churches, the churches of the Anglican Communion are in [[Full_communion|full communion]] with the Old Catholic churches of the [[Union_of_Utrecht_(Old_Catholic)|Union of Utrecht]] and the [[Scandinavia|Scandinavian]] [[Lutheran|Lutheran]] churches of the [[Porvoo_Communion|Porvoo Communion]] in Europe, the India-based Malankara Mar Thoma Syrian and [[Malabar_Independent_Syrian_Church|Malabar Independent Syrian]] churches and the [[Philippine_Independent_Church|Philippine Independent Church]], also known as the Aglipayan Church.
sentence_27: Main article: [[History_of_the_Anglican_Communion|History of the Anglican Communion]]
sentence_28: See also: [[English_Reformation|English Reformation]]
sentence_29: Further information on the ongoing dialogue between Anglicanism and the wider Church: Anglican Communion and ecumenism
sentence_30: The churches of the Anglican Communion have traditionally held that ordination in the [[Historic_episcopate|historic episcopate]] is a core element in the validity of clerical ordinations.
sentence_31: The Roman Catholic Church, however, does not recognise Anglican orders (see [[Apostolicae_curae|Apostolicae curae]]).
sentence_32: Some [[Eastern_Orthodox|Eastern Orthodox]] churches have issued statements to the effect that Anglican orders could be accepted, yet have still reordained former Anglican clergy; other Eastern Orthodox churches have rejected Anglican orders altogether.
sentence_33: Orthodox bishop Kallistos Ware explains this apparent discrepancy as follows:
sentence_34: See also: [[Homosexuality_and_Anglicanism|Homosexuality and Anglicanism]] and [[Anglican_realignment|Anglican realignment]]
sentence_35: One effect of the Communion's dispersed authority has been the conflicts arising over divergent practices and doctrines in parts of the Communion.
sentence_36: Disputes that had been confined to the Church of England could be dealt with legislatively in that realm, but as the Communion spread out into new nations and disparate cultures, such controversies multiplied and intensified.
sentence_37: These controversies have generally been of two types: liturgical and social.
sentence_38: The first such controversy of note concerned that of the growing influence of the Catholic Revival manifested in the tractarian and so-called [[Ritualism_in_the_Church_of_England|ritualism]] controversies of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.
sentence_39: This controversy produced the [[Free_Church_of_England|Free Church of England]] and, in the United States and Canada, the [[Reformed_Episcopal_Church|Reformed Episcopal Church]].
sentence_40: Later, rapid social change and the dissipation of British [[Cultural_hegemony|cultural hegemony]] over its former colonies contributed to disputes over the role of women, the parameters of marriage and divorce, and the practices of [[Contraception|contraception]] and [[Abortion|abortion]].
sentence_41: In the late 1970s, the [[Continuing_Anglican_movement|Continuing Anglican movement]] produced a number of new church bodies in opposition to [[Ordination_of_women_in_the_Anglican_Communion|women's ordination]], prayer book changes, and the new understandings concerning marriage.
sentence_42: More recently, disagreements over homosexuality have strained the unity of the communion as well as its relationships with other Christian denominations, leading to another round of withdrawals from the Anglican Communion.
sentence_43: Some churches were founded outside the Anglican Communion in the late 20th and early 21st centuries, largely in opposition to the ordination of openly homosexual bishops and other clergy and are usually referred to as belonging to the [[Anglican_realignment|Anglican realignment]] movement, or else as "orthodox" Anglicans.
sentence_44: These disagreements were especially noted when the [[Episcopal_Church_(United_States)|Episcopal Church (US)]] consecrated an openly gay bishop in a same-sex relationship, [[Gene_Robinson|Gene Robinson]], in 2003, which led some Episcopalians to defect and found the [[Anglican_Church_in_North_America|Anglican Church in North America (ACNA)]]; then, the debate re-ignited when the Church of England agreed to allow clergy to enter into same-sex [[Civil_partnerships|civil partnerships]] in 2005.
sentence_45: The [[Church_of_Nigeria|Church of Nigeria]] opposed the Episcopal Church's decision as well as the Church of England's approval for civil partnerships.
sentence_46: "The more liberal provinces that are open to changing Church doctrine on marriage in order to allow for same-sex unions include [[Anglican_Episcopal_Church_of_Brazil|Brazil]], [[Anglican_Church_of_Canada|Canada]], [[Anglican_Church_in_Aotearoa,_New_Zealand_and_Polynesia|New Zealand]], [[Scottish_Episcopal_Church|Scotland]], [[Church_of_South_India|South India]], [[Anglican_Church_of_Southern_Africa|South Africa]], the [[Episcopal_Church_(United_States)|US]] and [[Church_in_Wales|Wales]]".
sentence_47: The Church of England does not allow same-gender marriages or blessing rites, but does permit special prayer services for same-sex couples following a civil marriage or partnership.
sentence_48: The Church of England also permits clergy to enter into same-sex civil partnerships.
sentence_49: The [[Church_of_Ireland|Church of Ireland]] has no official position on civil unions, and one senior cleric has entered into a same-sex civil partnership.
sentence_50: The Church of Ireland recognised that it will "treat civil partners the same as spouses".
sentence_51: The [[Anglican_Church_of_Australia|Anglican Church of Australia]] does not have an official position on homosexuality.
sentence_52: The conservative Anglican churches, encouraging the realignment movement, are more concentrated in the Global South.
sentence_53: For example, the [[Anglican_Church_of_Kenya|Anglican Church of Kenya]], the Church of Nigeria and the [[Church_of_Uganda|Church of Uganda]] have opposed homosexuality.
sentence_54: [[GAFCON|GAFCON]], a fellowship of conservative Anglican churches, has appointed "missionary bishops" in response to the disagreements with the perceived liberalisation in the Anglican churches in North America and Europe.
sentence_55: Debates about social theology and ethics have occurred at the same time as debates on prayer book revision and the acceptable grounds for achieving full communion with non-Anglican churches.

title: Amino acid
sentence_0: This article is about the class for chemicals.
sentence_1: For the structures and properties of the standard proteinogenic amino acids, see [[Proteinogenic_amino_acid|Proteinogenic amino acid]].
sentence_2: Amino acids are [[Organic_compound|organic compounds]] that contain [[Amine|amine]] (–NH2) and [[Carboxylic_acid|carboxyl]] (–COOH) functional groups, along with a [[Substituent|side chain]] (R group) specific to each amino acid.
sentence_3: The key [[Chemical_element|elements]] of an amino acid are [[Carbon|carbon]] (C), [[Hydrogen|hydrogen]] (H), [[Oxygen|oxygen]] (O), and [[Nitrogen|nitrogen]] (N), although other elements are found in the side chains of certain amino acids.
sentence_4: About 500 naturally occurring amino acids are known (though only 20 appear in the [[Genetic_code|genetic code]]) and can be classified in many ways.
sentence_5: They can be classified according to the core structural functional groups' locations as [[Alpha_and_beta_carbon|alpha- (α-), beta- (β-), gamma- (γ-) or delta- (δ-)]] amino acids; other categories relate to polarity, [[PH|pH]] level, and side chain group type ([[Aliphatic|aliphatic]], [[Open-chain_compound|acyclic]], [[Aromatic|aromatic]], containing [[Hydroxy_group|hydroxyl]] or [[Sulfur|sulfur]], etc.).
sentence_6: In the form of [[Protein|proteins]], amino acid [[Residue_(chemistry)|residues]] form the second-largest component ([[Water|water]] is the largest) of human [[Muscle|muscles]] and other [[Tissue_(biology)|tissues]].
sentence_7: Beyond their role as residues in proteins, amino acids participate in a number of processes such as [[Neurotransmitter|neurotransmitter]] transport and [[Biosynthesis|biosynthesis]].
sentence_8: In [[Biochemistry|biochemistry]], amino acids which have the amine group attached to the [[Alpha-carbon|(alpha-) carbon]] atom next to the carboxyl group have particular importance.
sentence_9: They are known as 2-, alpha-, or α-amino acids (generic [[Chemical_formula|formula]] H2NCHRCOOH in most cases, where R is an [[Organic_chemistry|organic]] [[Substituent|substituent]] known as a "[[Substituent|side chain]]"); often the term "amino acid" is used to refer specifically to these.
sentence_10: They include the 22 [[Proteinogenic_amino_acid|proteinogenic]] ("protein-building") amino acids, which combine into [[Peptide|peptide]] chains ("polypeptides") to form the building blocks of a vast array of [[Protein|proteins]].
sentence_11: These are all L-[[Stereoisomerism|stereoisomers]] ("[[Chirality_(chemistry)|left-handed]]" [[Isomer|isomers]]), although a few D-amino acids ("right-handed") occur in [[Bacterial_envelope|bacterial envelopes]], as a [[Neuromodulation|neuromodulator]] (D-[[Serine|serine]]), and in some [[Antibiotic|antibiotics]].
sentence_12: Twenty of the proteinogenic amino acids are encoded directly by triplet [[Codon|codons]] in the [[Genetic_code|genetic code]] and are known as "standard" amino acids.
sentence_13: The other two ("nonstandard" or "non-canonical") are [[Selenocysteine|selenocysteine]] (present in many [[Prokaryote|prokaryotes]] as well as most [[Eukaryote|eukaryotes]], but not coded directly by [[DNA|DNA]]), and [[Pyrrolysine|pyrrolysine]] (found only in some [[Archea|archaea]] and one [[Bacterium|bacterium]]).
sentence_14: Pyrrolysine and selenocysteine are encoded via variant codons; for example, selenocysteine is encoded by [[Stop_codon|stop codon]] and [[SECIS_element|SECIS element]].
sentence_15: [[N-Formylmethionine|N-formylmethionine]] (which is often the initial amino acid of proteins in bacteria, [[Mitochondrion|mitochondria]], and [[Chloroplast|chloroplasts]]) is generally considered as a form of [[Methionine|methionine]] rather than as a separate proteinogenic amino acid.
sentence_16: Codon–[[Transfer_RNA|tRNA]] combinations not found in nature can also be used to [[Expanded_genetic_code|"expand" the genetic code]] and form novel proteins known as [[Alloprotein|alloproteins]] incorporating [[Non-proteinogenic_amino_acid|non-proteinogenic amino acids]].
sentence_17: Many important proteinogenic and non-proteinogenic amino acids have biological functions.
sentence_18: For example, in the [[Human_brain|human brain]], glutamate (standard [[Glutamic_acid|glutamic acid]]) and gamma-aminobutyric acid ("GABA", nonstandard gamma-amino acid) are, respectively, the main [[Neurotransmitter#Excitatory_and_inhibitory|excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters]].
sentence_19: [[Hydroxyproline|Hydroxyproline]], a major component of the connective tissue [[Collagen|collagen]], is synthesised from [[Proline|proline]].
sentence_20: [[Glycine|Glycine]] is a biosynthetic precursor to [[Porphyrin|porphyrins]] used in [[Red_blood_cell|red blood cells]].
sentence_21: [[Carnitine|Carnitine]] is used in [[Lipid|lipid transport]].
sentence_22: Nine proteinogenic amino acids are called "[[Essential_amino_acid|essential]]" for humans because they cannot be produced from other [[Chemical_compound|compounds]] by the human body and so must be taken in as food.
sentence_23: Others may be [[Essential_amino_acid#Essentiality_vs._conditional_essentiality_in_humans|conditionally essential]] for certain ages or medical conditions.
sentence_24: Essential amino acids may also differ between [[Species|species]].
sentence_25: Because of their biological significance, amino acids are important in nutrition and are commonly used in [[Nutritional_supplement|nutritional supplements]], [[Fertilizer|fertilizers]], feed, and [[Food_technology|food technology]].
sentence_26: Industrial uses include the production of [[Pharmaceutical_drug|drugs]], [[Biodegradable_plastic|biodegradable plastics]], and [[Asymmetric_catalysis|chiral catalysts]].
sentence_27: The first few amino acids were discovered in the early 19th century.
sentence_28: In 1806, French chemists [[Louis-Nicolas_Vauquelin|Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin]] and [[Pierre_Jean_Robiquet|Pierre Jean Robiquet]] isolated a compound in [[Asparagus|asparagus]] that was subsequently named [[Asparagine|asparagine]], the first amino acid to be discovered.
sentence_29: [[Cystine|Cystine]] was discovered in 1810, although its monomer, [[Cysteine|cysteine]], remained undiscovered until 1884.
sentence_30: [[Glycine|Glycine]] and [[Leucine|leucine]] were discovered in 1820.
sentence_31: The last of the 20 common amino acids to be discovered was [[Threonine|threonine]] in 1935 by [[William_Cumming_Rose|William Cumming Rose]], who also determined the [[Essential_amino_acid|essential amino acids]] and established the minimum daily requirements of all amino acids for optimal growth.
sentence_32: The unity of the chemical category was recognized by [[Charles_Adolphe_Wurtz|Wurtz]] in 1865, but he gave no particular name to it.
sentence_33: The first use of the term "amino acid" in the English language dates from 1898, while the German term, Aminosäure, was used earlier.
sentence_34: Proteins were found to yield amino acids after enzymatic digestion or acid [[Hydrolysis|hydrolysis]].
sentence_35: In 1902, [[Hermann_Emil_Fischer|Emil Fischer]] and [[Franz_Hofmeister|Franz Hofmeister]] independently proposed that proteins are formed from many amino acids, whereby bonds are formed between the amino group of one amino acid with the carboxyl group of another, resulting in a linear structure that Fischer termed "[[Peptide|peptide]]".
sentence_36: In the structure shown at the top of the page, R represents a [[Substituent|side chain]] specific to each amino acid.
sentence_37: The [[Carbon|carbon]] atom next to the [[Carboxyl_group|carboxyl group]] is called the [[Alpha_carbon|α–carbon]].
sentence_38: Amino acids containing an [[Amino_group|amino group]] bonded directly to the alpha carbon are referred to as alpha amino acids.
sentence_39: These include amino acids such as [[Proline|proline]] which contain [[Secondary_amine|secondary amines]], which used to be often referred to as "imino acids".
sentence_40: Alpha amino acids are the most common form found in nature, but only when occurring in the L-isomer.
sentence_41: The alpha carbon is a [[Chirality_(chemistry)|chiral]] carbon atom, with the exception of [[Glycine|glycine]], which has two indistinguishable hydrogen atoms on the alpha carbon.
sentence_42: Therefore, all alpha amino acids but [[Glycine|glycine]] can exist in either of two [[Enantiomer|enantiomers]], called L or D amino acids (relative configuration), which are mirror images of each other (see also [[Chirality_(chemistry)|Chirality]]).
sentence_43: While L-amino acids represent all of the amino acids found in [[Protein|proteins]] during translation in the ribosome, D-amino acids are found in some proteins produced by enzyme after [[Translation_(biology)|translation]] and transportation to the [[Endoplasmic_reticulum|endoplasmic reticulum]], as in exotic sea-dwelling organisms such as [[Cone_snail|cone snails]].
sentence_44: They are also abundant components of the [[Peptidoglycan|peptidoglycan]] [[Cell_wall|cell walls]] of bacteria, and D-serine may act as a [[Neurotransmitter|neurotransmitter]] in the brain.
sentence_45: D-amino acids are used in [[Racemic_crystallography|racemic crystallography]] to create centrosymmetric crystals, which (depending on the protein) may allow for easier and more robust protein structure determination.
sentence_46: The L and D convention for amino acid configuration refers not to the optical activity of the amino acid itself but rather to the optical activity of the isomer of [[Glyceraldehyde|glyceraldehyde]] from which that amino acid can, in theory, be synthesized (D-glyceraldehyde is dextrorotatory; L-glyceraldehyde is levorotatory).
sentence_47: In alternative fashion, the (S) and (R) designators are used to indicate the absolute configuration.
sentence_48: Almost all of the amino acids in proteins are (S) at the α carbon, with [[Cysteine|cysteine]] being (R) and [[Glycine|glycine]] non-[[Chirality|chiral]].
sentence_49: Cysteine has its side chain in the same geometric location as the other amino acids, but the R/S terminology is reversed because [[Sulfur|sulfur]] has higher atomic number compared to the carboxyl oxygen which gives the side chain a higher priority by the Cahn–Ingold–Prelog rules, whereas the atoms in most other side chains give them lower priority compared to the carboxyl group.
sentence_50: Amino acids are designated as α- when the nitrogen atom is attached to the carbon atom adjacent to the carboxyl group: in this case the compound contains the substructure N–C–CO2.
sentence_51: Amino acids with the sub-structure N–C–C–CO2 are classified as β- amino acids.
sentence_52: γ-Amino acids contain the substructure N–C–C–C–CO2, and so on.
sentence_53: Amino acids are usually classified by the properties of their side chain into four groups.
sentence_54: The side chain can make an amino acid a [[Weak_acid|weak acid]] or a [[Weak_base|weak base]], and a [[Hydrophile|hydrophile]] if the side chain is polar or a [[Hydrophobe|hydrophobe]] if it is nonpolar.
sentence_55: The phrase "branched-chain amino acids" or BCAA refers to the amino acids having [[Aliphatic|aliphatic]] side chains that are linear; these are [[Leucine|leucine]], [[Isoleucine|isoleucine]], and [[Valine|valine]].
sentence_56: [[Proline|Proline]] is the only [[Proteinogenic|proteinogenic]] amino acid whose side-group links to the α-amino group and, thus, is also the only proteinogenic amino acid containing a secondary amine at this position.
sentence_57: In chemical terms, proline is, therefore, an [[Imino_acid|imino acid]], since it lacks a [[Amine|primary amino group]], although it is still classed as an amino acid in the current biochemical nomenclature and may also be called an "N-alkylated alpha-amino acid".
sentence_58: Main article: [[Zwitterion|Zwitterion]]
sentence_59: In aqueous solution amino acids exist in two forms (as illustrated at the right), the molecular form and the [[Zwitterion|zwitterion]] form in equilibrium with each other.
sentence_60: The two forms coexist over the pH range pK1 − 2 to pK2 + 2, which for glycine is pH 0–12.
sentence_61: The ratio of the concentrations of the two isomers is independent of pH.
sentence_62: The value of this ratio cannot be determined experimentally.
sentence_63: Because all amino acids contain amine and carboxylic acid functional groups, they are [[Amphoterism|amphiprotic]].
sentence_64: At pH = pK1 (approximately 2.2) there will be equal concentration of the species NH+ 3CH(R)CO 2H and NH+ 3CH(R)CO− 2 and at pH = pK2 (approximately 10) there will be equal concentration of the species NH+ 3CH(R)CO− 2 and NH 2CH(R)CO− 2.
sentence_65: It follows that the neutral molecule and the zwitterion are effectively the only species present at biological pH.
sentence_66: It is generally assumed that the concentration of the zwitterion is much greater than the concentration of the neutral molecule on the basis of comparisons with the known pK values of [[Amine|amines]] and [[Carboxylic_acids|carboxylic acids]].
sentence_67: At pH values between the two pKa values, the zwitterion predominates, but coexists in [[Dynamic_equilibrium|dynamic equilibrium]] with small amounts of net negative and net positive ions.
sentence_68: At the exact midpoint between the two pKa values, the trace amount of net negative and trace of net positive ions exactly balance, so that average net charge of all forms present is zero.
sentence_69: This pH is known as the [[Isoelectric_point|isoelectric point]] pI, so pI = 1/2(pKa1 + pKa2).
sentence_70: For amino acids with charged side chains, the pKa of the side chain is involved.
sentence_71: Thus for aspartate or glutamate with negative side chains, pI = 1/2(pKa1 + pKa(R)), where pKa(R) is the side chain pKa.
sentence_72: Cysteine also has potentially negative side chain with pKa(R) = 8.14, so pI should be calculated as for aspartate and glutamate, even though the side chain is not significantly charged at physiological pH.
sentence_73: For histidine, lysine, and arginine with positive side chains, pI = 1/2(pKa(R) + pKa2).
sentence_74: Amino acids have zero mobility in electrophoresis at their isoelectric point, although this behaviour is more usually exploited for peptides and proteins than single amino acids.
sentence_75: Zwitterions have minimum solubility at their isoelectric point, and some amino acids (in particular, with nonpolar side chains) can be isolated by precipitation from water by adjusting the pH to the required isoelectric point.
sentence_76: Main article: [[Proteinogenic_amino_acid|Proteinogenic amino acid]]
sentence_77: See also: [[Protein_primary_structure|Protein primary structure]] and [[Posttranslational_modification|Posttranslational modification]]
sentence_78: Amino acids are the structural units ([[Monomer|monomers]]) that make up proteins.
sentence_79: They join together to form short [[Polymer|polymer]] chains called [[Peptide|peptides]] or longer chains called either [[Polypeptides|polypeptides]] or [[Protein|proteins]].
sentence_80: These polymers are linear and unbranched, with each amino acid within the chain attached to two neighboring amino acids.
sentence_81: The process of making proteins encoded by DNA/RNA genetic material is called [[Translation_(biology)|translation]] and involves the step-by-step addition of amino acids to a growing protein chain by a [[Ribozyme|ribozyme]] that is called a [[Ribosome|ribosome]].
sentence_82: The order in which the amino acids are added is read through the [[Genetic_code|genetic code]] from an [[Messenger_RNA|mRNA]] template, which is an [[RNA|RNA]] copy of one of the organism's [[Gene|genes]].
sentence_83: Twenty-two amino acids are naturally incorporated into polypeptides and are called [[Proteinogenic|proteinogenic]] or natural amino acids.
sentence_84: Of these, 20 are encoded by the universal [[Genetic_code|genetic code]].
sentence_85: The remaining 2, [[Selenocysteine|selenocysteine]] and [[Pyrrolysine|pyrrolysine]], are incorporated into proteins by unique synthetic mechanisms.
sentence_86: [[Selenocysteine|Selenocysteine]] is incorporated when the mRNA being translated includes a [[SECIS_element|SECIS element]], which causes the UGA codon to encode selenocysteine instead of a [[Stop_codon|stop codon]].
sentence_87: [[Pyrrolysine|Pyrrolysine]] is used by some [[Methanogen|methanogenic]] [[Archaea|archaea]] in enzymes that they use to produce [[Methane|methane]].
sentence_88: It is coded for with the codon UAG, which is normally a stop codon in other organisms.
sentence_89: This UAG codon is followed by a [[PYLIS_downstream_sequence|PYLIS downstream sequence]].
sentence_90: Several independent evolutionary studies, using different types of data, have suggested that Gly, Ala, Asp, Val, Ser, Pro, Glu, Leu, Thr may belong to a group of amino acids that constituted the early genetic code, whereas Cys, Met, Tyr, Trp, His, Phe may belong to a group of amino acids that constituted later additions of the genetic code.
sentence_91: Main article: [[Non-proteinogenic_amino_acids|Non-proteinogenic amino acids]]
sentence_92: Aside from the 22 [[Proteinogenic_amino_acid|proteinogenic amino acids]], many non-proteinogenic amino acids are known.
sentence_93: Those either are not found in proteins (for example [[Carnitine|carnitine]], GABA, [[Levothyroxine|levothyroxine]]) or are not produced directly and in isolation by standard cellular machinery (for example, [[Hydroxyproline|hydroxyproline]] and [[Selenomethionine|selenomethionine]]).
sentence_94: Non-proteinogenic amino acids that are found in proteins are formed by [[Post-translational_modification|post-translational modification]], which is modification after translation during protein synthesis.
sentence_95: These modifications are often essential for the function or regulation of a protein.
sentence_96: For example, the [[Carboxylation|carboxylation]] of [[Glutamate|glutamate]] allows for better binding of [[Calcium_in_biology|calcium cations]], and [[Collagen|collagen]] contains hydroxyproline, generated by [[Hydroxylation|hydroxylation]] of [[Proline|proline]].
sentence_97: Another example is the formation of [[Hypusine|hypusine]] in the translation initiation factor [[EIF5A|EIF5A]], through modification of a lysine residue.
sentence_98: Such modifications can also determine the localization of the protein, e.g., the addition of long hydrophobic groups can cause a protein to bind to a [[Phospholipid|phospholipid]] membrane.
sentence_99: Some non-proteinogenic amino acids are not found in proteins.
sentence_100: Examples include [[2-aminoisobutyric_acid|2-aminoisobutyric acid]] and the neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid.
sentence_101: Non-proteinogenic amino acids often occur as intermediates in the [[Metabolic_pathway|metabolic pathways]] for standard amino acids – for example, [[Ornithine|ornithine]] and [[Citrulline|citrulline]] occur in the [[Urea_cycle|urea cycle]], part of amino acid [[Catabolism|catabolism]] (see below).
sentence_102: A rare exception to the dominance of α-amino acids in biology is the β-amino acid [[Beta_alanine|beta alanine]] (3-aminopropanoic acid), which is used in plants and microorganisms in the synthesis of [[Pantothenic_acid|pantothenic acid]] (vitamin B5), a component of [[Coenzyme_A|coenzyme A]].
sentence_103: Although D-isomers are uncommon in live organisms, [[Gramicidin|gramicidin]] is a polypeptide made up from mixture of D- and L-amino acids.
sentence_104: Other compounds containing D-amino acids are [[Tyrocidine|tyrocidine]] and [[Valinomycin|valinomycin]].
sentence_105: These compounds disrupt bacterial cell walls, particularly in [[Gram-positive|Gram-positive]] bacteria.
sentence_106: As of 2011, only 837 D-amino acids were found in the [[Swiss-Prot|Swiss-Prot]] database out of a total of 187 million amino acids analysed.
sentence_107: The 20 amino acids that are encoded directly by the codons of the universal [[Genetic_code|genetic code]] are called standard or canonical amino acids.
sentence_108: A modified form of methionine ([[N-Formylmethionine|N-formylmethionine]]) is often incorporated in place of methionine as the initial amino acid of proteins in bacteria, mitochondria and chloroplasts.
sentence_109: Other amino acids are called nonstandard or non-canonical.
sentence_110: Most of the nonstandard amino acids are also non-proteinogenic (i.e. they cannot be incorporated into proteins during translation), but two of them are proteinogenic, as they can be incorporated translationally into proteins by exploiting information not encoded in the universal genetic code.
sentence_111: The two nonstandard proteinogenic amino acids are [[Selenocysteine|selenocysteine]] (present in many non-eukaryotes as well as most eukaryotes, but not coded directly by DNA) and [[Pyrrolysine|pyrrolysine]] (found only in some [[Archaea|archaea]] and one [[Bacterium|bacterium]]).
sentence_112: The incorporation of these nonstandard amino acids is rare.
sentence_113: For example, 25 human proteins include selenocysteine in their primary structure, and the structurally characterized enzymes (selenoenzymes) employ selenocysteine as the catalytic [[Moiety_(chemistry)|moiety]] in their active sites.
sentence_114: Pyrrolysine and selenocysteine are encoded via variant codons.
sentence_115: For example, selenocysteine is encoded by [[Stop_codon|stop codon]] and [[SECIS_element|SECIS element]].
sentence_116: Main article: [[Essential_amino_acids|Essential amino acids]]
sentence_117: Further information: [[Protein_(nutrient)|Protein (nutrient)]] and [[Amino_acid_synthesis|Amino acid synthesis]]
sentence_118: When taken up into the human body from the diet, the 20 standard amino acids either are used to synthesize proteins, other biomolecules, or are oxidized to [[Urea|urea]] and [[Carbon_dioxide|carbon dioxide]] as a source of energy.
sentence_119: The oxidation pathway starts with the removal of the amino group by a [[Transaminase|transaminase]]; the amino group is then fed into the [[Urea_cycle|urea cycle]].
sentence_120: The other product of transamidation is a [[Keto_acid|keto acid]] that enters the [[Citric_acid_cycle|citric acid cycle]].
sentence_121: [[Glucogenic_amino_acid|Glucogenic amino acids]] can also be converted into glucose, through [[Gluconeogenesis|gluconeogenesis]].
sentence_122: Of the 20 standard amino acids, nine ([[Histidine|His]], [[Isoleucine|Ile]], [[Leucine|Leu]], [[Lysine|Lys]], [[Methionine|Met]], [[Phenylalanine|Phe]], [[Threonine|Thr]], [[Tryptophan|Trp]] and [[Valine|Val]]) are called [[Essential_amino_acid|essential amino acids]] because the [[Human_body|human body]] cannot [[Biosynthesis|synthesize]] them from other [[Chemical_compound|compounds]] at the level needed for normal growth, so they must be obtained from food.
sentence_123: In addition, [[Cysteine|cysteine]], [[Tyrosine|tyrosine]], and [[Arginine|arginine]] are considered semiessential amino acids, and taurine a semiessential aminosulfonic acid in children.
sentence_124: The metabolic pathways that synthesize these monomers are not fully developed.
sentence_125: The amounts required also depend on the age and health of the individual, so it is hard to make general statements about the dietary requirement for some amino acids.
sentence_126: Dietary exposure to the nonstandard amino acid [[Beta-Methylamino-L-alanine|BMAA]] has been linked to human neurodegenerative diseases, including [[ALS|ALS]].
sentence_127: Further information: [[Amino_acid_neurotransmitter|Amino acid neurotransmitter]]
sentence_128: In humans, non-protein amino acids also have important roles as [[Metabolic_intermediate|metabolic intermediates]], such as in the biosynthesis of the [[Neurotransmitter|neurotransmitter]] gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA).
sentence_129: Many amino acids are used to synthesize other molecules, for example:

list.value: [[Tryptophan|Tryptophan]] is a precursor of the neurotransmitter [[Serotonin|serotonin]].

[[Tyrosine|Tyrosine]] (and its precursor phenylalanine) are precursors of the [[Catecholamine|catecholamine]] [[Neurotransmitter|neurotransmitters]] [[Dopamine|dopamine]], [[Epinephrine|epinephrine]] and [[Norepinephrine|norepinephrine]] and various [[Trace_amine|trace amines]].

[[Phenylalanine|Phenylalanine]] is a precursor of [[Phenethylamine|phenethylamine]] and tyrosine in humans. In plants, it is a precursor of various [[Phenylpropanoid|phenylpropanoids]], which are important in plant metabolism.
[[Glycine|Glycine]] is a precursor of [[Porphyrin|porphyrins]] such as [[Heme|heme]].

[[Aspartate|Aspartate]], [[Glycine|glycine]], and [[Glutamine|glutamine]] are precursors of [[Nucleotide|nucleotides]]. However, not all of the functions of other abundant nonstandard amino acids are known.

sentence_130: Some nonstandard amino acids are used as [[Plant_defense_against_herbivory|defenses against herbivores]] in plants.
sentence_131: For example, [[Canavanine|canavanine]] is an analogue of [[Arginine|arginine]] that is found in many [[Legume|legumes]], and in particularly large amounts in [[Canavalia_gladiata|Canavalia gladiata]] (sword bean).
sentence_132: This amino acid protects the plants from predators such as insects and can cause illness in people if some types of legumes are eaten without processing.
sentence_133: The non-protein amino acid [[Mimosine|mimosine]] is found in other species of legume, in particular [[Leucaena_leucocephala|Leucaena leucocephala]].
sentence_134: This compound is an analogue of [[Tyrosine|tyrosine]] and can poison animals that graze on these plants.
sentence_135: Amino acids are used for a variety of applications in industry, but their main use is as additives to animal feed.
sentence_136: This is necessary, since many of the bulk components of these feeds, such as [[Soybean|soybeans]], either have low levels or lack some of the [[Essential_amino_acid|essential amino acids]]: lysine, methionine, threonine, and tryptophan are most important in the production of these feeds.
sentence_137: In this industry, amino acids are also used to chelate metal cations in order to improve the absorption of minerals from supplements, which may be required to improve the health or production of these animals.
sentence_138: The food industry is also a major consumer of amino acids, in particular, [[Glutamic_acid|glutamic acid]], which is used as a [[Flavor_enhancer|flavor enhancer]], and [[Aspartame|aspartame]] (aspartylphenylalanine 1-methyl ester) as a low-calorie [[Artificial_sweetener|artificial sweetener]].
sentence_139: Similar technology to that used for animal nutrition is employed in the human nutrition industry to alleviate symptoms of mineral deficiencies, such as anemia, by improving mineral absorption and reducing negative side effects from inorganic mineral supplementation.
sentence_140: The chelating ability of amino acids has been used in fertilizers for agriculture to facilitate the delivery of minerals to plants in order to correct mineral deficiencies, such as iron chlorosis.
sentence_141: These fertilizers are also used to prevent deficiencies from occurring and improving the overall health of the plants.
sentence_142: The remaining production of amino acids is used in the synthesis of [[Pharmaceutical_drug|drugs]] and cosmetics.
sentence_143: Similarly, some amino acids derivatives are used in pharmaceutical industry.
sentence_144: They include [[5-HTP|5-HTP]] (5-hydroxytryptophan) used for experimental treatment of depression, [[L-DOPA|L-DOPA]] (L-dihydroxyphenylalanine) for [[Parkinson's|Parkinson's]] treatment, and [[Eflornithine|eflornithine]] drug that inhibits [[Ornithine_decarboxylase|ornithine decarboxylase]] and used in the treatment of [[African_trypanosomiasis|sleeping sickness]].
sentence_145: Main article: [[Expanded_genetic_code|Expanded genetic code]]
sentence_146: Since 2001, 40 non-natural amino acids have been added into protein by creating a unique codon (recoding) and a corresponding transfer-RNA:aminoacyl – tRNA-synthetase pair to encode it with diverse physicochemical and biological properties in order to be used as a tool to exploring protein structure and function or to create novel or enhanced proteins.
sentence_147: Main article: [[Nullomers|Nullomers]]
sentence_148: Nullomers are codons that in theory code for an amino acid, however in nature there is a selective bias against using this codon in favor of another, for example bacteria prefer to use CGA instead of AGA to code for arginine.
sentence_149: This creates some sequences that do not appear in the genome.
sentence_150: This characteristic can be taken advantage of and used to create new selective cancer-fighting drugs and to prevent cross-contamination of DNA samples from crime-scene investigations.
sentence_151: Further information: [[Asymmetric_synthesis|Asymmetric synthesis]]
sentence_152: Amino acids are important as low-cost [[Feedstock|feedstocks]].
sentence_153: These compounds are used in [[Chiral_pool_synthesis|chiral pool synthesis]] as [[Enantiomer|enantiomerically pure]] building blocks.
sentence_154: Amino acids have been investigated as precursors [[Chiral_catalyst|chiral catalysts]], such as for asymmetric [[Hydrogenation|hydrogenation]] reactions, although no commercial applications exist.
sentence_155: Further information: [[Biodegradable_plastic|Biodegradable plastic]] and [[Biopolymer|Biopolymer]]
sentence_156: Amino acids have been considered as components of biodegradable polymers, which have applications as [[Environmentally_friendly|environmentally friendly]] packaging and in medicine in [[Drug_delivery|drug delivery]] and the construction of [[Prosthesis|prosthetic implants]].
sentence_157: An interesting example of such materials is [[Sodium_poly(aspartate)|polyaspartate]], a water-soluble biodegradable polymer that may have applications in disposable [[Diaper|diapers]] and agriculture.
sentence_158: Due to its solubility and ability to [[Chelation|chelate]] metal ions, polyaspartate is also being used as a biodegradeable antiscaling agent and a [[Corrosion_inhibitor|corrosion inhibitor]].
sentence_159: In addition, the aromatic amino acid [[Tyrosine|tyrosine]] has been considered as a possible replacement for [[Phenols|phenols]] such as [[Bisphenol_A|bisphenol A]] in the manufacture of [[Polycarbonate|polycarbonates]].
sentence_160: Main article: [[Amino_acid_synthesis|Amino acid synthesis]]
sentence_161: The commercial production of amino acids usually relies on mutant bacteria that overproduce individual amino acids using glucose as a carbon source.
sentence_162: Some amino acids are produced by enzymatic conversions of synthetic intermediates.
sentence_163: [[2-Aminothiazoline-4-carboxylic_acid|2-Aminothiazoline-4-carboxylic acid]] is an intermediate in one industrial synthesis of [[Cysteine|L-cysteine]] for example.
sentence_164: [[Aspartic_acid|Aspartic acid]] is produced by the addition of ammonia to [[Fumarate|fumarate]] using a lyase.
sentence_165: In plants, nitrogen is first assimilated into organic compounds in the form of [[Glutamate|glutamate]], formed from alpha-ketoglutarate and ammonia in the mitochondrion.
sentence_166: For other amino acids, plants use [[Transaminase|transaminases]] to move the amino group from glutamate to another alpha-keto acid.
sentence_167: For example, aspartate aminotransferase converts glutamate and oxaloacetate to alpha-ketoglutarate and aspartate.
sentence_168: Other organisms use transaminases for amino acid synthesis, too.
sentence_169: Nonstandard amino acids are usually formed through modifications to standard amino acids.
sentence_170: For example, [[Homocysteine|homocysteine]] is formed through the [[Transsulfuration_pathway|transsulfuration pathway]] or by the demethylation of methionine via the intermediate metabolite [[S-adenosylmethionine|S-adenosylmethionine]], while [[Hydroxyproline|hydroxyproline]] is made by a [[Post_translational_modification|post translational modification]] of [[Proline|proline]].
sentence_171: [[Microorganism|Microorganisms]] and plants synthesize many uncommon amino acids.
sentence_172: For example, some microbes make [[2-aminoisobutyric_acid|2-aminoisobutyric acid]] and [[Lanthionine|lanthionine]], which is a sulfide-bridged derivative of alanine.
sentence_173: Both of these amino acids are found in peptidic [[Lantibiotics|lantibiotics]] such as [[Alamethicin|alamethicin]].
sentence_174: However, in plants, [[1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylic_acid|1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylic acid]] is a small disubstituted cyclic amino acid that is a key intermediate in the production of the plant hormone [[Ethylene#Ethylene_as_a_plant_hormone|ethylene]].
sentence_175: Amino acids undergo the reactions expected of the constituent functional groups.
sentence_176: See also: [[Peptide_synthesis|Peptide synthesis]] and [[Peptide_bond|Peptide bond]]
sentence_177: As both the amine and carboxylic acid groups of amino acids can react to form amide bonds, one amino acid molecule can react with another and become joined through an amide linkage.
sentence_178: This [[Polymerization|polymerization]] of amino acids is what creates proteins.
sentence_179: This [[Condensation_reaction|condensation reaction]] yields the newly formed [[Peptide_bond|peptide bond]] and a molecule of water.
sentence_180: In cells, this reaction does not occur directly; instead, the amino acid is first activated by attachment to a [[Transfer_RNA|transfer RNA]] molecule through an [[Ester|ester]] bond.
sentence_181: This aminoacyl-tRNA is produced in an [[Adenosine_triphosphate|ATP]]-dependent reaction carried out by an [[Aminoacyl_tRNA_synthetase|aminoacyl tRNA synthetase]].
sentence_182: This aminoacyl-tRNA is then a substrate for the [[Ribosome|ribosome]], which catalyzes the attack of the amino group of the elongating protein chain on the ester bond.
sentence_183: As a result of this mechanism, all proteins made by ribosomes are synthesized starting at their N-terminus and moving toward their C-terminus.
sentence_184: However, not all peptide bonds are formed in this way.
sentence_185: In a few cases, peptides are synthesized by specific enzymes.
sentence_186: For example, the tripeptide [[Glutathione|glutathione]] is an essential part of the defenses of cells against oxidative stress.
sentence_187: This peptide is synthesized in two steps from free amino acids.
sentence_188: In the first step, [[Gamma-glutamylcysteine_synthetase|gamma-glutamylcysteine synthetase]] condenses [[Cysteine|cysteine]] and [[Glutamic_acid|glutamic acid]] through a peptide bond formed between the side chain carboxyl of the glutamate (the gamma carbon of this side chain) and the amino group of the cysteine.
sentence_189: This dipeptide is then condensed with [[Glycine|glycine]] by [[Glutathione_synthetase|glutathione synthetase]] to form glutathione.
sentence_190: In chemistry, peptides are synthesized by a variety of reactions.
sentence_191: One of the most-used in [[Peptide_synthesis|solid-phase peptide synthesis]] uses the aromatic oxime derivatives of amino acids as activated units.
sentence_192: These are added in sequence onto the growing peptide chain, which is attached to a solid resin support.
sentence_193: Libraries of peptides are used in drug discovery through [[High-throughput_screening|high-throughput screening]].
sentence_194: The combination of functional groups allow amino acids to be effective polydentate ligands for metal–amino acid chelates.
sentence_195: The multiple side chains of amino acids can also undergo chemical reactions.
sentence_196: Amino acids must first pass out of organelles and cells into blood circulation via [[Amino_acid_transporter|amino acid transporters]], since the amine and carboxylic acid groups are typically ionized.
sentence_197: Degradation of an amino acid, occurring in the liver and kidneys, often involves deamination by moving its amino group to alpha-ketoglutarate, forming [[Glutamate|glutamate]].
sentence_198: This process involves transaminases, often the same as those used in amination during synthesis.
sentence_199: In many vertebrates, the amino group is then removed through the [[Urea_cycle|urea cycle]] and is excreted in the form of [[Urea|urea]].
sentence_200: However, amino acid degradation can produce [[Uric_acid|uric acid]] or ammonia instead.
sentence_201: For example, [[Serine_dehydratase|serine dehydratase]] converts serine to pyruvate and ammonia.
sentence_202: After removal of one or more amino groups, the remainder of the molecule can sometimes be used to synthesize new amino acids, or it can be used for energy by entering [[Glycolysis|glycolysis]] or the [[Citric_acid_cycle|citric acid cycle]], as detailed in image at right.
sentence_203: Amino acids are bidentate ligands, forming [[Transition_metal_amino_acid_complexes|transition metal amino acid complexes]].
sentence_204: The ca. 20 canonical amino acids can be classified according to their properties.
sentence_205: Important factors are charge, [[Hydrophile|hydrophilicity]] or [[Hydrophobe|hydrophobicity]], size, and functional groups.
sentence_206: These properties influence protein structure and [[Protein–protein_interaction|protein–protein interactions]].
sentence_207: The water-soluble proteins tend to have their hydrophobic residues ([[Leucine|Leu]], [[Isoleucine|Ile]], [[Valine|Val]], [[Phenylalanine|Phe]], and [[Tryptophan|Trp]]) buried in the middle of the protein, whereas hydrophilic side chains are exposed to the aqueous solvent.
sentence_208: (Note that in [[Biochemistry|biochemistry]], a residue refers to a specific [[Monomer|monomer]] within the [[Polymer|polymeric chain]] of a [[Polysaccharide|polysaccharide]], [[Protein|protein]] or [[Nucleic_acid|nucleic acid]].)
sentence_209: The [[Integral_membrane_protein|integral membrane proteins]] tend to have outer rings of exposed [[Hydrophobic|hydrophobic]] amino acids that anchor them into the [[Lipid_bilayer|lipid bilayer]].
sentence_210: Some [[Peripheral_membrane_protein|peripheral membrane proteins]] have a patch of hydrophobic amino acids on their surface that locks onto the membrane.
sentence_211: In similar fashion, proteins that have to bind to positively charged molecules have surfaces rich with negatively charged amino acids like [[Glutamate|glutamate]] and [[Aspartate|aspartate]], while proteins binding to negatively charged molecules have surfaces rich with positively charged chains like [[Lysine|lysine]] and [[Arginine|arginine]].
sentence_212: For example, lysine and arginine are highly enriched in [[Low_complexity_regions_in_proteins|low complexity regions]] of nucleic-acid binding proteins.
sentence_213: There are various [[Hydrophobicity_scale|hydrophobicity scales]] of amino acid residues.
sentence_214: Some amino acids have special properties such as [[Cysteine|cysteine]], that can form covalent [[Disulfide_bond|disulfide bonds]] to other cysteine residues, [[Proline|proline]] that forms [[Cyclic_compound|a cycle]] to the polypeptide backbone, and [[Glycine|glycine]] that is more flexible than other amino acids.
sentence_215: Furthermore, glycine and proline are highly enriched within [[Low_complexity_regions_in_proteins|low complexity regions]] of eukaryotic and prokaryotic proteins, whereas the opposite (under-represented) has been observed for highly reactive, or complex, or hydrophobic amino acids, such as cysteine, phenylalanine, tryptophane, methionine, valine, leucine, isoleucine.
sentence_216: Many proteins undergo a range of [[Posttranslational_modification|posttranslational modifications]], whereby additional chemical groups are attached to the amino acid side chains.
sentence_217: Some modifications can produce hydrophobic [[Lipoprotein|lipoproteins]], or hydrophilic [[Glycoprotein|glycoproteins]].
sentence_218: These type of modification allow the reversible targeting of a protein to a membrane.
sentence_219: For example, the addition and removal of the fatty acid [[Palmitic_acid|palmitic acid]] to cysteine residues in some signaling proteins causes the proteins to attach and then detach from cell membranes.

sentence_222: In addition to the specific amino acid codes, placeholders are used in cases where [[Protein_sequencing|chemical]] or [[X-ray_crystallography|crystallographic]] analysis of a peptide or protein cannot conclusively determine the identity of a residue.
sentence_223: They are also used to summarise [[Conserved_sequence|conserved protein sequence]] motifs.
sentence_224: The use of single letters to indicate sets of similar residues is similar to the use of [[Nucleic_acid_notation|abbreviation codes for degenerate bases]].
