sentence_225: Unk is sometimes used instead of Xaa, but is less standard.
sentence_226: In addition, many [[Non-proteinogenic_amino_acids|nonstandard amino acids]] have a specific code.
sentence_227: For example, several peptide drugs, such as [[Bortezomib|Bortezomib]] and [[MG132|MG132]], are [[Peptide_synthesis|artificially synthesized]] and retain their [[Protecting_group|protecting groups]], which have specific codes.
sentence_228: Bortezomib is [[Pyrazinoic_acid|Pyz]]–Phe–boroLeu, and MG132 is [[Carboxybenzyl|Z]]–Leu–Leu–Leu–al.
sentence_229: To aid in the analysis of protein structure, [[Photo-reactive_amino_acid_analog|photo-reactive amino acid analogs]] are available.
sentence_230: These include photoleucine (pLeu) and photomethionine (pMet).
sentence_231: The total nitrogen content of organic matter is mainly formed by the amino groups in proteins.
sentence_232: The Total Kjeldahl Nitrogen ([[TKN|TKN]]) is a measure of nitrogen widely used in the analysis of (waste) water, soil, food, feed and organic matter in general.
sentence_233: As the name suggests, the [[Kjeldahl_method|Kjeldahl method]] is applied.
sentence_234: More sensitive methods are available.

title: Afghanistan
sentence_0: Afghanistan ([[English|/æfˈɡænɪstæn, æfˈɡɑːnɪstɑːn/]] (listen), also pronounced /ævˈɡænᵻstæn, ævˈɡɑːnᵻstɑːn/; [[Pashto|Pashto]]/[[Dari_language|Dari]]: افغانستان, Pashto: Afġānistān [[Help:IPA|[avɣɒnisˈtɒn, ab-]], Dari: Afġānestān [[Persian|[avɣɒnesˈtɒn]]), officially the Islamic Republic of Afghanistan, is a [[Landlocked_country|landlocked country]] at the crossroads of [[Central_Asia|Central]] and [[South_Asia|South Asia]].
sentence_1: Afghanistan is bordered by [[Pakistan|Pakistan]] to the east and south; [[Iran|Iran]] to the west; [[Turkmenistan|Turkmenistan]], [[Uzbekistan|Uzbekistan]], and [[Tajikistan|Tajikistan]] to the north; and [[China|China]] to the northeast.
sentence_2: Occupying 652,000 square kilometers (252,000 sq mi), it is a mountainous country with plains in the north and southwest.
sentence_3: [[Kabul|Kabul]] is the capital and largest city.
sentence_4: The population is around 32 million, composed mostly of ethnic [[Pashtuns|Pashtuns]], [[Tajiks|Tajiks]], [[Hazaras|Hazaras]], and [[Uzbeks|Uzbeks]].
sentence_5: Humans lived in what is now Afghanistan at least 50,000 years ago.
sentence_6: [[Neolithic|Settled life]] emerged in the region 9,000 years ago, evolving gradually into the [[Indus_Valley_Civilisation|Indus civilization]] ([[Shortugai|Shortugai]] site), the [[Bactria–Margiana_Archaeological_Complex|Oxus civilization]] (Dashlyji site), and the [[Helmand_culture|Helmand civilization]] ([[Mundigak|Mundigak]] site) of the 3rd millennium BCE.
sentence_7: [[Indo-Aryan_peoples|Indo-Aryans]] migrated through [[Bactria|Bactria]]-[[Margiana|Margiana]] area to [[Gandhara|Gandhara]], followed by the rise of the [[Iron_Age|Iron Age]] [[Yaz_culture|Yaz I culture]] (ca. 1500–1100 BCE), which has been closely associated with the culture depicted in the [[Avesta|Avesta]], the ancient religious texts of [[Zoroastrianism|Zoroastrianism]].
sentence_8: The region, then known as "[[Ariana|Ariana]]", fell to [[Achaemenid_Empire|Achaemenid]] Persians in the 6th century BCE, who conquered the areas to their east [[Achaemenid_conquest_of_the_Indus_Valley|as far as the Indus River]].
sentence_9: [[Alexander_the_Great|Alexander the Great]] invaded the region in the 4th century BCE, who married [[Roxana|Roxana]] in Bactria before his [[Cophen_campaign|Kabul Valley campaign]], where he faced resistance from Aspasioi and Assakan tribes.
sentence_10: The [[Greco-Bactrian_Kingdom|Greco-Bactrian Kingdom]] became the eastern end of the [[Hellenistic_period|Hellenistic world]].
sentence_11: Following the conquest by [[Maurya_Empire|Mauryan]] Indians, [[Buddhism_in_Afghanistan|Buddhism]] and [[Hinduism_in_Afghanistan|Hinduism]] flourished in the region for centuries.
sentence_12: The [[Kushan_Empire|Kushan]] emperor [[Kanishka|Kanishka]], who ruled from his twin capitals of [[Kapisi_(city)|Kapiśi]] and Puruṣapura, played an important role in the spread of [[Mahayana|Mahayana]] Buddhism to China and Central Asia.
sentence_13: Various other Buddhist and Hindu dynasties also ruled the region, including the [[Indo-Scythians|Saka]], [[Kidarites|Kidarite]], [[Hephthalites|Hephthalite]], [[Alchon_Huns|Alkhon]], [[Nezak_Huns|Nezak]], Zunbil, [[Turk_Shahi|Turk Shahi]], and [[Hindu_Shahi|Hindu Shahi]].
sentence_14: [[Muslim_conquests_of_Afghanistan|Muslims brought Islam]] to [[Sasanian_Empire|Sassanian]]-held [[Herat|Herat]] and [[Zaranj|Zaranj]] in the mid-7th century, while fuller Islamization was achieved between the 9th and 12th centuries under the [[Saffarid_dynasty|Saffarid]], [[Samanid_Empire|Samanid]], [[Ghaznavid_dynasty|Ghaznavid]], and [[Ghurid_dynasty|Ghurid]] dynasties.
sentence_15: Parts of the region were later ruled by the [[Khwarazmian_dynasty|Khwarazmian]], [[Khalji_dynasty|Khalji]], [[Timurid_Empire|Timurid]], [[Lodi_dynasty|Lodi]], [[Sur_Empire|Sur]], [[Mughal_Empire|Mughal]], and [[Safavid_dynasty|Safavid]] empires.
sentence_16: The political history of the modern state of Afghanistan began with the [[Hotak_dynasty|Hotak dynasty]], whose founder [[Mirwais_Hotak|Mirwais Hotak]] declared southern Afghanistan independent in 1709.
sentence_17: In 1747, [[Ahmad_Shah_Durrani|Ahmad Shah Durrani]] established the Durrani Empire with its capital at [[Kandahar|Kandahar]].
sentence_18: In 1776, the Durrani capital was moved to Kabul while [[Peshawar|Peshawar]] became the winter capital; the latter was lost to [[Sikh_Empire|Sikhs]] in [[Battle_of_Nowshera|1823]].
sentence_19: In the late 19th century, Afghanistan became a [[Buffer_state|buffer state]] in the "[[The_Great_Game|Great Game]]" between British India and the Russian Empire.
sentence_20: In the [[First_Anglo-Afghan_War|First Anglo-Afghan War]], the [[East_India_Company|British East India Company]] seized control of Afghanistan briefly, but following the [[Third_Anglo-Afghan_War|Third Anglo-Afghan War]] in 1919 the country was free of foreign influence, eventually becoming a monarchy under [[Amanullah_Khan|Amanullah Khan]], until almost 50 years later when [[Mohammed_Zahir_Shah|Zahir Shah]] was overthrown and a republic was established.
sentence_21: In 1978, after a second coup, Afghanistan first became a socialist state and then a Soviet protectorate, evoking the [[Soviet–Afghan_War|Soviet–Afghan War]] in the 1980s against [[Mujahideen#Afghanistan|mujahideen]] rebels.
sentence_22: By 1996, most of the country was captured by the Islamic fundamentalist [[Taliban|Taliban]], who ruled as a totalitarian regime for over five years; they were removed from power after the [[United_States_invasion_of_Afghanistan|US invasion]] in 2001 but still control a significant portion of the country.
sentence_23: The ongoing [[War_in_Afghanistan_(2001-present)|war]] between the government and the Taliban has contributed to the perpetuation of Afghanistan's problematic [[Human_rights_in_Afghanistan|human rights record]] including complications of [[Women's_rights_in_Afghanistan|women's rights]], with numerous abuses committed by both sides, such as the killing of civilians.
sentence_24: Afghanistan is a unitary presidential [[Islamic_republic|Islamic republic]].
sentence_25: The country has high levels of [[Terrorism|terrorism]], poverty, child malnutrition, and corruption.
sentence_26: It is a member of the United Nations, the [[Organisation_of_Islamic_Cooperation|Organisation of Islamic Cooperation]], the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation, the [[Group_of_77|Group of 77]], the [[Economic_Cooperation_Organization|Economic Cooperation Organization]], and the [[Non-Aligned_Movement|Non-Aligned Movement]].
sentence_27: Afghanistan's economy is the world's 96th largest, with a gross domestic product (GDP) of $72.9 billion by [[Purchasing_power_parity|purchasing power parity]]; the country fares much worse in terms of per-capita GDP (PPP), ranking 169th out of 186 countries as of 2018.
sentence_28: Main article: [[Name_of_Afghanistan|Name of Afghanistan]]
sentence_29: The [[Root_(linguistics)|root]] name "[[Afghan_(ethnonym)|Afghān]]" is, according to some scholars, derived from the name of the Aśvakan or Assakan, ancient inhabitants of the [[Hindu_Kush|Hindu Kush]] region.
sentence_30: Aśvakan literally means "horsemen", "horse breeders", or "[[Cavalry|cavalrymen]]" (from [[Aśva|aśva]] or aspa, the [[Sanskrit|Sanskrit]] and [[Avestan|Avestan]] words for "[[Horse|horse]]").
sentence_31: Historically, the ethnonym Afghān was used to refer to ethnic [[Pashtuns|Pashtuns]].
sentence_32: The Arabic and Persian form of the name, Afġān was first attested in the 10th-century geography book [[Hudud_al-'Alam|Hudud al-'Alam]].
sentence_33: The last part of the name, "[[-stan|-stan]]" is a Persian suffix for "place of."
sentence_34: Therefore, "Afghanistan" translates to "land of the Afghans," or "land of the Pashtuns" in a historical sense.
sentence_35: The modern Constitution of Afghanistan, however, states that the word "Afghan" shall apply to every [[Demographics_of_Afghanistan|citizen of Afghanistan]].
sentence_36: Main article: [[History_of_Afghanistan|History of Afghanistan]]
sentence_37: Many empires and kingdoms have also risen to power in Afghanistan, such as the [[Greco-Bactrian_Kingdom|Greco-Bactrians]], [[Indo-Scythians|Sakas]], [[Kushan_Empire|Kushans]], [[Kidarites|Kidarites]], [[Hephthalites|Hephthalites]], [[Alchon_Huns|Alkhons]], [[Nezak_Huns|Nezaks]], Zunbils, [[Turk_Shahi|Turk Shahis]], [[Hindu_Shahi|Hindu Shahis]], [[Lawik_dynasty|Lawiks]], [[Saffarid_dynasty|Saffarids]], [[Samanids|Samanids]], [[Ghaznavids|Ghaznavids]], [[Ghurid_Dynasty|Ghurids]], [[Khwarazmian_dynasty|Khwarazmians]], [[Khalji_dynasty|Khaljis]], [[Kartids|Kartids]], [[Timurid_dynasty|Timurids]], [[Lodi_dynasty|Lodis]], [[Sur_Empire|Surs]], [[Mughal_Empire|Mughals]], and [[Safavid_dynasty|Safavids]], and finally, the [[Hotak_dynasty|Hotak]] and [[Durrani_dynasty|Durrani]] dynasties, which marked the political origins of the modern state.
sentence_38: Throughout millennia several cities within the modern day Afghanistan served as capitals of various empires, namely Bactra ([[Balkh|Balkh]]), Alexandria on the Oxus ([[Ai-Khanoum|Ai-Khanoum]]), [[Kapisi_(city)|Kapisi]], [[Sigal,_Sakastan|Sigal]], [[Kabul|Kabul]], [[Kunduz|Kunduz]], [[Zaranj|Zaranj]], [[Firozkoh|Firozkoh]], [[Herat|Herat]], Ghazna ([[Ghazni|Ghazni]]), Binban ([[Bamyan|Bamyan]]), and [[Kandahar|Kandahar]].
sentence_39: The country sits at a unique nexus point where numerous civilizations have interacted and often fought.
sentence_40: It has been home to various peoples through the ages, among them the [[Ancient_Iranian_peoples|ancient Iranian peoples]] who established the dominant role of Indo-Iranian languages in the region.
sentence_41: At multiple points, the land has been incorporated within vast regional empires, among them the [[Achaemenid_Empire|Achaemenid Empire]], the [[Alexander_the_Great|Macedonian Empire]], the [[Maurya_Empire|Indian Maurya Empire]], and the [[Islamic_conquest_of_Afghanistan|Islamic Empire]].
sentence_42: For its success in resisting foreign occupation during the 19th and 20th centuries, Afghanistan has been called the "graveyard of empires," though it is unknown who coined the phrase.
sentence_43: Main article: [[Pre-Islamic_period_of_Afghanistan|Pre-Islamic period of Afghanistan]]
sentence_44: [[Excavation_(archaeology)|Excavations]] of prehistoric sites suggest that humans were living in what is now Afghanistan at least 50,000 years ago, and that farming communities in the area were among the earliest in the world.
sentence_45: An important site of early historical activities, many believe that Afghanistan compares to [[Egypt|Egypt]] in terms of the historical value of its archaeological sites.
sentence_46: [[Archaeology|Archaeological]] exploration done in the 20th century suggests that the geographical area of Afghanistan has been closely connected by culture and trade with its neighbors to the east, west, and north.
sentence_47: Artifacts typical of the [[Paleolithic|Paleolithic]], [[Mesolithic|Mesolithic]], [[Neolithic|Neolithic]], [[Bronze_Age|Bronze]], and [[Iron_Age|Iron Ages]] have been found in Afghanistan.
sentence_48: Urban civilization is believed to have begun as early as 3000 BCE, and the early city of [[Mundigak|Mundigak]] (near [[Kandahar|Kandahar]] in the south of the country) was a center of the [[Helmand_culture|Helmand culture]].
sentence_49: More recent findings established that the [[Indus_Valley_Civilisation|Indus Valley Civilisation]] stretched up towards modern-day Afghanistan, making the ancient civilization today part of Pakistan, Afghanistan, and India.
sentence_50: In more detail, it extended from what today is northwest [[Pakistan|Pakistan]] to northwest India and northeast Afghanistan.
sentence_51: An Indus Valley site has been found on the [[Oxus_River|Oxus River]] at [[Shortugai|Shortugai]] in northern Afghanistan.
sentence_52: There are several smaller IVC colonies to be found in Afghanistan as well.
sentence_53: After 2000 BCE, successive waves of semi-nomadic people from Central Asia began moving south into Afghanistan; among them were many [[Indo-European_languages|Indo-European-speaking]] [[Indo-Iranians|Indo-Iranians]].
sentence_54: These tribes later migrated further into South Asia, Western Asia, and toward Europe via the area north of the [[Caspian_Sea|Caspian Sea]].
sentence_55: The region at the time was referred to as [[Ariana|Ariana]].
sentence_56: The religion [[Zoroastrianism|Zoroastrianism]] is believed by some to have originated in what is now Afghanistan between 1800 and 800 BCE, as its founder Zoroaster is thought to have lived and died in [[Balkh|Balkh]].
sentence_57: Ancient [[Iranian_languages|Eastern Iranian languages]] may have been spoken in the region around the time of the rise of Zoroastrianism.
sentence_58: By the middle of the 6th century BCE, the Achaemenids overthrew the [[Medes|Medes]] and incorporated [[Arachosia|Arachosia]], [[Aria_(satrapy)|Aria]], and [[Bactria|Bactria]] within its eastern boundaries.
sentence_59: An inscription on the tombstone of [[Darius_I_of_Persia|Darius I of Persia]] mentions the [[Kabulistan|Kabul Valley]] in a list of the 29 countries that he had conquered.
sentence_60: [[Alexander_the_Great|Alexander the Great]] and his Macedonian forces arrived in Afghanistan in 330 BCE after defeating [[Darius_III_of_Persia|Darius III of Persia]] a year earlier in the [[Battle_of_Gaugamela|Battle of Gaugamela]].
sentence_61: Following Alexander's brief occupation, the successor state of the [[Seleucid_Empire|Seleucid Empire]] controlled the region until 305 BCE when they gave much of it to the [[Maurya_Empire|Maurya Empire]] as part of an alliance treaty.
sentence_62: The Mauryans controlled the area south of the [[Hindu_Kush|Hindu Kush]] until they were overthrown in about 185 BCE.
sentence_63: Their decline began 60 years after [[Ashoka|Ashoka]]'s rule ended, leading to the [[Hellenistic_civilization|Hellenistic]] reconquest by the [[Greco-Bactrians|Greco-Bactrians]].
sentence_64: Much of it soon broke away from them and became part of the [[Indo-Greek_Kingdom|Indo-Greek Kingdom]].
sentence_65: They were defeated and expelled by the [[Indo-Scythians|Indo-Scythians]] in the late 2nd century BCE.
sentence_66: The [[Silk_Road|Silk Road]] appeared during the first century BCE, and Afghanistan flourished with trade, with routes to China, India, Persia and north to the cities of [[Bukhara|Bukhara]], [[Samarkand|Samarkand]] and [[Khiva|Khiva]] in present-day Uzbekistan.
sentence_67: Goods and ideas were exchanged at this center point, such as Chinese silk, Persian silver and Roman gold, while the region of present Afghanistan was mining and trading [[Lapis_lazuli|lapis lazuli]] stones mainly from the [[Badakhshan|Badakhshan]] region.
sentence_68: During the first century BCE, the [[Parthian_Empire|Parthian Empire]] subjugated the region but lost it to their [[Indo-Parthian|Indo-Parthian]] vassals.
sentence_69: In the mid-to-late first century CE the vast [[Kushan_Empire|Kushan Empire]], centered in Afghanistan, became great patrons of Buddhist culture, making [[Buddhism|Buddhism]] flourish throughout the region.
sentence_70: The Kushans were overthrown by the [[Sassanid_Empire|Sassanids]] in the 3rd century CE, though the [[Indo-Sassanids|Indo-Sassanids]] continued to rule at least parts of the region.
sentence_71: They were followed by the [[Kidarite|Kidarites]] who, in turn, were replaced by the [[Hephthalites|Hephthalites]].
sentence_72: They were replaced by the [[Turk_Shahi|Turk Shahi]] in the 7th century.
sentence_73: The Buddhist Turk Shahi of Kabul was replaced by a Hindu dynasty before the Saffarids conquered the area in 870, this Hindu dynasty was called [[Hindu_Shahi|Hindu Shahi]].
sentence_74: Much of the northeastern and southern areas of the country remained dominated by [[Buddhist|Buddhist]] culture.
sentence_75: Main articles: [[Islamic_conquest_of_Afghanistan|Islamic conquest of Afghanistan]] and Mongol invasion of Central Asia
sentence_76: [[Arab|Arab]] [[Muslim|Muslims]] brought Islam to [[Herat|Herat]] and [[Zaranj|Zaranj]] in 642 CE and began spreading eastward; some of the native inhabitants they encountered accepted it while others revolted.
sentence_77: Before Islam was introduced, people of the region were mostly Buddhists and Zoroastrians, but there were also [[Surya|Surya]] and [[Nana_(Afghan_goddess)|Nana]] worshipers, [[History_of_the_Jews_in_Afghanistan|Jews]], and others.
sentence_78: The Zunbils and Kabul Shahi were first conquered in 870 CE by the [[Saffarid_Dynasty|Saffarid]] Muslims of Zaranj.
sentence_79: Later, the [[Samanids|Samanids]] extended their Islamic influence south of the [[Hindu|Hindu]] Kush.
sentence_80: It is reported that Muslims and non-Muslims still lived side by side in Kabul before the [[Ghaznavids|Ghaznavids]] rose to power in the 10th century.
sentence_81: By the 11th century, [[Mahmud_of_Ghazni|Mahmud of Ghazni]] defeated the remaining Hindu rulers and effectively [[Islamized|Islamized]] the wider region, with the exception of [[Kafiristan|Kafiristan]].
sentence_82: Mahmud made [[Ghazni|Ghazni]] into an important city and patronized intellectuals such as the historian [[Al-Biruni|Al-Biruni]] and the poet Ferdowsi.
sentence_83: The [[Ghaznavids|Ghaznavid dynasty]] was overthrown by the [[Ghurid_Dynasty|Ghurids]], whose architectural achievements included the remote [[Minaret_of_Jam|Minaret of Jam]].
sentence_84: The Ghurids controlled Afghanistan for less than a century before being conquered by the [[Khwarazmian_dynasty|Khwarazmian dynasty]] in 1215.
sentence_85: In 1219 AD, [[Genghis_Khan|Genghis Khan]] and his [[Mongol_Empire|Mongol]] army overran the region.
sentence_86: His troops are said to have annihilated the Khorasanian cities of [[Herat|Herat]] and [[Balkh|Balkh]] as well as [[Bamyan,_Afghanistan|Bamyan]].
sentence_87: The destruction caused by the Mongols forced many locals to return to an agrarian rural society.
sentence_88: Mongol rule continued with the [[Ilkhanate|Ilkhanate]] in the northwest while the [[Khalji_dynasty|Khalji dynasty]] administered the Afghan tribal areas south of the Hindu Kush until the invasion of [[Timur|Timur]] (aka Tamerlane), who established the [[Timurid_Empire|Timurid Empire]] in 1370.
sentence_89: Under the rule of [[Shah_Rukh|Shah Rukh]] the city served as the focal point of the [[Timurid_Renaissance|Timurid Renaissance]], whose glory matched [[Florence|Florence]] of the [[Italian_Renaissance|Italian Renaissance]] as the center of a cultural rebirth.
sentence_90: In the early 16th century, [[Babur|Babur]] arrived from [[Fergana|Ferghana]] and captured Kabul from the [[Arghun_dynasty|Arghun dynasty]].
sentence_91: Between the 16th and 18th century, the Uzbek Khanate of Bukhara, Iranian [[Safavid_dynasty|Safavids]], and Indian [[Mughal_Empire|Mughals]] ruled parts of the territory.
sentence_92: During the Medieval Period, the northwestern area of Afghanistan was referred to by the regional name [[Greater_Khorasan|Khorasan]].
sentence_93: Two of the four capitals of Khorasan ([[Herat|Herat]] and [[Balkh|Balkh]]) are now located in Afghanistan, while the regions of [[Kandahar_Province|Kandahar]], [[Zabul_Province|Zabulistan]], [[Ghazni|Ghazni]], [[Kabulistan|Kabulistan]], and [[Name_of_Afghanistan|Afghanistan]] formed the [[Frontier|frontier]] between Khorasan and [[Hindustan|Hindustan]].
sentence_94: However, up to the 19th century the term Khorasan was commonly used among natives to describe their country, [[George_Elphinstone,_1st_Viscount_Keith|Sir George Elphinstone]] wrote with amazement that the country known to outsiders as "Afghanistan" was referred to by its own inhabitants as "Khorasan" and that the first Afghan official whom he met at the border welcomed him to Khorasan.
sentence_95: Main articles: [[Hotak_dynasty|Hotak dynasty]] and Durrani Empire
sentence_96: In 1709, [[Mirwais_Hotak|Mirwais Hotak]], a local [[Ghilji|Ghilzai]] tribal leader, successfully rebelled against the Safavids.
sentence_97: He defeated [[George_XI_of_Kartli|Gurgin Khan]] and made Afghanistan independent.
sentence_98: Mirwais died of natural causes in 1715 and was succeeded by his brother [[Abdul_Aziz_Hotak|Abdul Aziz]], who was soon killed by Mirwais' son Mahmud for [[Treason|treason]].
sentence_99: Mahmud led the Afghan army in 1722 to the Persian capital of Isfahan, captured the city after the [[Battle_of_Gulnabad|Battle of Gulnabad]] and proclaimed himself King of Persia.
sentence_100: The Afghan dynasty was ousted from Persia by [[Nader_Shah|Nader Shah]] after the 1729 [[Battle_of_Damghan_(1729)|Battle of Damghan]].
sentence_101: In 1738, Nader Shah and his [[Afsharid_dynasty|forces]] captured Kandahar, the last Hotak stronghold, from Shah [[Hussain_Hotak|Hussain Hotak]], at which point the incarcerated 16-year-old [[Ahmad_Shah_Durrani|Ahmad Shah Durrani]] was freed and made the commander of an Afghan regiment.
sentence_102: Soon after, the Persian and Afghan forces [[Nader_Shah's_invasion_of_India|invaded India]].
sentence_103: By 1747, the [[Afghans|Afghans]] chose Durrani as their head of state.
sentence_104: Durrani and his Afghan army conquered much of present-day Afghanistan, [[Pakistan|Pakistan]], the [[Khorasan_Province|Khorasan]] and [[Quhistan|Kohistan]] provinces of Iran, and Delhi in India.
sentence_105: He defeated the Indian Maratha Empire, and one of his biggest victories was the [[Battle_of_Panipat_(1761)|1761 Battle of Panipat]].
sentence_106: In October 1772, Durrani died of natural causes and was buried at a site now adjacent to the [[Shrine_of_the_Cloak|Shrine of the Cloak]] in Kandahar.
sentence_107: He was succeeded by his son, Timur Shah, who transferred the capital of Afghanistan from Kandahar to Kabul in 1776, with [[Peshawar|Peshawar]] becoming the [[Winter_capital|winter capital]].
sentence_108: After Timur's death in 1793, the Durrani throne passed down to his son Zaman Shah, followed by Mahmud Shah, [[Shuja_Shah_Durrani|Shuja Shah]] and others.
sentence_109: Further information: [[European_influence_in_Afghanistan|European influence in Afghanistan]], [[Anglo-Afghan_Wars|Anglo-Afghan Wars]], [[Durand_Line|Durand Line]], and [[Afghan_Civil_War_(1928–1929)|Afghan Civil War (1928–1929)]]
sentence_110: By the early 19th century, the Afghan empire was under threat from the [[Qajar_dynasty|Persians]] in the west and the [[Sikh_Empire|Sikh Empire]] in the east.
sentence_111: Fateh Khan, leader of the [[Barakzai_dynasty|Barakzai tribe]], had installed 21 of his brothers in positions of power throughout the empire.
sentence_112: After his death, they rebelled and divided up the provinces of the empire between themselves.
sentence_113: During this turbulent period, Afghanistan had many temporary rulers until [[Dost_Mohammad_Khan|Dost Mohammad Khan]] declared himself emir in 1823.
sentence_114: [[Punjab|Punjab]] and [[Kashmir|Kashmir]] were lost to [[Ranjit_Singh|Ranjit Singh]], who invaded [[Khyber_Pakhtunkhwa|Khyber Pakhtunkhwa]] in March 1823 and captured the city of [[Peshawar|Peshawar]] at the [[Battle_of_Nowshera|Battle of Nowshera]].
sentence_115: In 1837, during the [[Battle_of_Jamrud|Battle of Jamrud]] near the [[Khyber_Pass|Khyber Pass]], [[Wazir_Akbar_Khan|Akbar Khan]] and the Afghan army failed to capture the [[Jamrud_Fort|Jamrud Fort]] from the [[Sikh_Khalsa_Army|Sikh Khalsa Army]], but killed Sikh Commander [[Hari_Singh_Nalwa|Hari Singh Nalwa]], thus ending the Afghan-Sikh Wars.
sentence_116: By this time the British were advancing from the east and the [[First_Anglo-Afghan_War|first major conflict]] during "[[The_Great_Game|The Great Game]]" was initiated.
sentence_117: In 1838, the British marched into Afghanistan and arrested [[Dost_Mohammad_Khan_(Emir_of_Afghanistan)|Dost Mohammad]], sent him into exile in India and replaced him with the previous ruler, [[Shah_Shujah_Durrani|Shah Shuja]].
sentence_118: Following an uprising, the [[1842_retreat_from_Kabul|1842 retreat from Kabul]] of British-Indian forces and the annihilation of [[William_George_Keith_Elphinstone|Elphinstone]]'s army, and the [[Battle_of_Kabul_(1842)|Battle of Kabul]] that led to its recapture, the British placed Dost Mohammad Khan back into power and withdrew their military forces from Afghanistan.
sentence_119: In 1878, the [[Second_Anglo-Afghan_War|Second Anglo-Afghan War]] was fought over perceived Russian influence, [[Abdur_Rahman_Khan|Abdur Rahman Khan]] replaced [[Mohammad_Ayub_Khan_(Emir_of_Afghanistan)|Ayub Khan]], and Britain gained control of Afghanistan's [[Foreign_policy|foreign relations]] as part of the [[Treaty_of_Gandamak|Treaty of Gandamak]] of 1879.
sentence_120: In 1893, [[Mortimer_Durand|Mortimer Durand]] made Amir Abdur Rahman Khan sign a controversial agreement in which the ethnic [[Pashtun_people|Pashtun]] and Baloch territories were divided by the [[Durand_Line|Durand Line]].
sentence_121: This was a standard divide and rule policy of the British and would lead to strained relations, especially with the later new state of Pakistan.
sentence_122: [[Shia_Islam_in_Afghanistan|Shia]]-dominated [[Hazarajat|Hazarajat]] and pagan [[Kafiristan|Kafiristan]] remained politically independent until being [[Muslim_conquests_of_Afghanistan|conquered]] by Abdur Rahman Khan in 1891–1896.
sentence_123: He was known as the Iron Amir for his features and his ruthless methods against tribes.
sentence_124: The Iron Amir viewed railway and telegraph lines coming from the Russian and British empires as "[[Trojan_horse|trojan horses]]" and therefore prevented railway development in Afghanistan.
sentence_125: He died in 1901, replaced by his son [[Habibullah_Khan|Habibullah Khan]].
sentence_126: During [[World_War_I|World War I]], when Afghanistan was neutral, Habibullah Khan was met by officials of the Central Powers in the [[Niedermayer–Hentig_Expedition|Niedermayer–Hentig Expedition]], to declare full independence from the United Kingdom, join them and attack British India, as part of the [[Hindu–German_Conspiracy|Hindu–German Conspiracy]].
sentence_127: Their efforts to bring Afghanistan into the Central Powers failed, but it caused discontent among the population for keeping neutrality against the British.
sentence_128: Habibullah was assassinated during a hunting trip in 1919, and [[Amanullah_Khan|Amanullah Khan]] eventually assumed power.
sentence_129: A staunch supporter of the 1915–1916 expeditions, Amanullah Khan evoked the [[Third_Anglo-Afghan_War|Third Anglo-Afghan War]], entering British India via the [[Khyber_Pass|Khyber Pass]].
sentence_130: After the end Third Anglo-Afghan War and the signing of the [[Anglo-Afghan_Treaty_of_1919|Treaty of Rawalpindi]] on 19 August 1919, King Amanullah Khan declared Afghanistan a [[Sovereign_state|sovereign]] and fully [[Independence|independent state]].
sentence_131: He moved to end his country's traditional isolation by establishing diplomatic relations with the international community, particularly with the [[Soviet_Union|Soviet Union]] and the [[Weimar_Republic|Weimar Republic]] of Germany.
sentence_132: Following a 1927–28 tour of Europe and [[Turkey|Turkey]], he introduced several reforms intended to modernize his nation.
sentence_133: A key force behind these reforms was [[Mahmud_Tarzi|Mahmud Tarzi]], an ardent supporter of the education of women.
sentence_134: He fought for Article 68 of Afghanistan's 1923 constitution, which made elementary education compulsory.
sentence_135: The institution of [[Slavery|slavery]] was abolished in 1923.
sentence_136: Khan's wife Queen [[Soraya_Tarzi|Soraya Tarzi]] was a figure during this period.
sentence_137: Some of the reforms that were put in place, such as the abolition of the traditional [[Burqa|burqa]] for women and the opening of several co-educational schools, quickly alienated many tribal and religious leaders, and this led to the [[Afghan_Civil_War_(1928–1929)|Afghan Civil War (1928–1929)]].
sentence_138: Faced with the overwhelming armed opposition, Amanullah Khan abdicated in January 1929, and soon after Kabul fell to [[Saqqawists|Saqqawist]] forces led by [[Habibullah_Kalakani|Habibullah Kalakani]].
sentence_139: Prince [[Mohammed_Nadir_Shah|Mohammed Nadir Shah]], Amanullah's cousin, in turn defeated and killed Kalakani in October 1929, and was declared King Nadir Shah.
sentence_140: He abandoned the reforms of Amanullah Khan in favor of a more gradual approach to modernization but was assassinated in 1933 by [[Abdul_Khaliq_Hazara_(assassin)|Abdul Khaliq]], a fifteen-year-old [[Hazara_people|Hazara]] student who was an [[Amanullah_loyalist|Amanullah loyalist]].
sentence_141: [[Mohammed_Zahir_Shah|Mohammed Zahir Shah]], Nadir Shah's 19-year-old son, succeeded to the throne and reigned from 1933 to 1973.
sentence_142: The [[Afghan_tribal_revolts_of_1944–1947|tribal revolts of 1944–1947]] saw Zahir Shah's reign being challenged by [[Zadran_(Pashtun_tribe)|Zadran]], [[Safi_(Pashtun_tribe)|Safi]], [[Mangal_(Pashtun_tribe)|Mangal]], and [[Wazir_(Pashtun_tribe)|Wazir]] tribesmen led by [[Mazrak_Zadran|Mazrak Zadran]], [[Salemai|Salemai]], and [[Faqir_Ipi|Mirzali Khan]], among others, many of whom were [[Amanullah_loyalism|Amanullah loyalists]].
sentence_143: Close relations with the Muslim states [[Turkey|Turkey]], the [[Kingdom_of_Iraq|Kingdom of Iraq]] and Iran/Persia were also pursued, while further international relations were sought by joining the [[League_of_Nations|League of Nations]] in 1934.
sentence_144: The 1930s saw the development of roads, infrastructure, the founding of a [[Da_Afghanistan_Bank|national bank]], and increased education.
sentence_145: Road links in the north played a large part in a growing cotton and textile industry.
sentence_146: The country built close relationships with the [[Axis_powers|Axis powers]], with Germany having the largest share in Afghan development at the time, along with Italy and [[Afghanistan-Japan_relations|Japan]].
sentence_147: Until 1946, Zahir Shah ruled with the assistance of his uncle, who held the post of [[Prime_Minister_of_Afghanistan|Prime Minister]] and continued the policies of Nadir Shah.
sentence_148: Another of Zahir Shah's uncles, [[Shah_Mahmud_Khan|Shah Mahmud Khan]], became Prime Minister in 1946 and began an experiment allowing greater political freedom, but reversed the policy when it went further than he expected.
sentence_149: He was replaced in 1953 by [[Mohammed_Daoud_Khan|Mohammed Daoud Khan]], the king's cousin and brother-in-law, and a [[Pashtuns|Pashtun]] nationalist who sought the creation of a [[Pashtunistan|Pashtunistan]], leading to highly tense relations with Pakistan.
sentence_150: During his ten years at the post until 1963, Daoud Khan pressed for social modernization reforms and sought a closer relationship with the [[Soviet_Union|Soviet Union]].
sentence_151: Afterward, the [[1964_Constitution_of_Afghanistan|1964 constitution]] was formed, and the first non-royal Prime Minister was sworn in.
sentence_152: King Zahir Shah, like his father Nadir Shah, had a policy of maintaining national independence while pursuing gradual modernization, creating nationalist feeling, and improving relations with the United Kingdom.
sentence_153: However, Afghanistan remained neutral and was neither a participant in [[World_War_II|World War II]] nor aligned with either power bloc in the [[Cold_War|Cold War]] thereafter.
sentence_154: However, it was a beneficiary of the latter rivalry as both the Soviet Union and the United States vied for influence by building Afghanistan's main highways, airports, and other vital infrastructure in the post-period.
sentence_155: On a per capita basis, Afghanistan received more Soviet [[Development_aid|development aid]] than any other country.
sentence_156: Afghanistan had, therefore, good relations with both Cold War enemies.
sentence_157: In 1973, while the King was in Italy, Daoud Khan launched a [[1973_Afghan_coup|bloodless coup]] and became the first [[President_of_Afghanistan|President of Afghanistan]], abolishing the monarchy.

sentence_158: Main articles: [[Democratic_Republic_of_Afghanistan|Democratic Republic of Afghanistan]], [[Soviet–Afghan_War|Soviet–Afghan War]], and [[Afghan_Civil_War_(1989–92)|Afghan Civil War (1989–92)]]
sentence_159: Further information: [[History_of_Afghanistan_(1978–92)|History of Afghanistan (1978–92)]]
sentence_160: In April 1978, the communist [[People's_Democratic_Party_of_Afghanistan|People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan]] (PDPA) seized power in a bloody coup d'état against then-President [[Mohammed_Daoud_Khan|Mohammed Daoud Khan]], in what is called the [[Saur_Revolution|Saur Revolution]].
sentence_161: The PDPA declared the establishment of the [[Democratic_Republic_of_Afghanistan|Democratic Republic of Afghanistan]], with its first leader named as [[People's_Democratic_Party_of_Afghanistan|People's Democratic Party]] general secretary [[Nur_Muhammad_Taraki|Nur Muhammad Taraki]].
sentence_162: This would trigger a series of events that would dramatically turn Afghanistan from a poor and secluded (albeit peaceful) country to a hotbed of international terrorism.
sentence_163: The PDPA initiated various social, symbolic and land distribution reforms that provoked strong opposition, while also brutally oppressing political dissidents.
sentence_164: This caused unrest and quickly expanded into a state of [[War_in_Afghanistan_(1978–present)|civil war]] by 1979, waged by guerrilla mujahideen (and smaller [[Maoist|Maoist]] guerillas) against regime forces countrywide.
sentence_165: It quickly turned into a [[Proxy_war|proxy war]] as the Pakistani government provided these rebels with covert training centers, the United States [[Operation_Cyclone|supported]] them through Pakistan's [[Inter-Services_Intelligence|Inter-Services Intelligence]] (ISI), and the [[Soviet_Union|Soviet Union]] sent thousands of military advisers to support the PDPA regime.
sentence_166: Meanwhile, there was increasingly hostile friction between the competing factions of the PDPA – the dominant [[Khalq|Khalq]] and the more moderate Parcham.
sentence_167: In September 1979, PDPA General Secretary Taraki was assassinated in an internal coup orchestrated by fellow Khalq member, then-Prime minister [[Hafizullah_Amin|Hafizullah Amin]], who assumed the new general secretary of the [[People's_Democratic_Party_of_Afghanistan|People's Democratic Party]].
sentence_168: The situation in the country deteriorated under Amin and thousands of people went missing.
sentence_169: Displeased with Amin's government, the [[Soviet_Army|Soviet Army]] invaded the country in December 1979, heading for Kabul and killing Amin just 3 days later.
sentence_170: A Soviet-organized regime, led by Parcham's [[Babrak_Karmal|Babrak Karmal]] but inclusive of both factions (Parcham and Khalq), filled the vacuum.
sentence_171: Soviet troops in more substantial numbers were deployed to stabilize Afghanistan under Karmal, marking the beginning of the [[Soviet–Afghan_War|Soviet–Afghan War]].
sentence_172: The United States and Pakistan, along with smaller actors like [[Saudi_Arabia|Saudi Arabia]] and [[China|China]], continued supporting the rebels, delivering billions of dollars in cash and weapons including two thousand [[FIM-92_Stinger|FIM-92 Stinger]] surface-to-air missiles.
sentence_173: Lasting nine years, the war caused the deaths of between 562,000 and 2 million Afghans, and displaced about 6 million people who subsequently fled Afghanistan, mainly to Pakistan and [[Afghans_in_Iran|Iran]].
sentence_174: Heavy air bombardment destroyed many countryside villages, millions of [[Landmine|landmines]] were planted, and some cities such as [[Herat|Herat]] and [[Kandahar|Kandahar]] were also damaged from bombardment.
sentence_175: Pakistan's [[Khyber_Pakhtunkhwa|North-West Frontier Province]] functioned as an organisational and networking base for the anti-Soviet Afghan resistance, with the province's influential [[Deobandi|Deobandi]] ulama playing a major supporting role in promoting the 'jihad'.
sentence_176: After the Soviet [[Soviet_withdrawal_from_Afghanistan|withdrawal]], the civil war [[Afghan_Civil_War_(1989-92)|ensued]] until the communist regime under People's Democratic Party leader [[Mohammad_Najibullah|Mohammad Najibullah]] collapsed in 1992.

section_13.value: Post-Cold War conflict and Taliban regime

sentence_177: See also: [[Afghan_Civil_War_(1992–96)|Afghan Civil War (1992–96)]], [[Afghan_Civil_War_(1996–2001)|Afghan Civil War (1996–2001)]], [[Taliban|Taliban]], and [[Northern_Alliance|Northern Alliance]]
sentence_178: Another civil war broke out after the [[Peshawar_Accords|creation]] of a dysfunctional coalition [[Islamic_State_of_Afghanistan|government]] between leaders of various mujahideen factions.
sentence_179: Amid a state of [[Anarchy|anarchy]] and factional infighting, various mujahideen factions committed widespread rape, murder and extortion, while Kabul was heavily bombarded and partially destroyed by the fighting.
sentence_180: Several failed reconciliations and alliances occurred between different leaders.
sentence_181: The [[Taliban|Taliban]] emerged in September 1994 as a movement and militia of students (talib) from Islamic [[Madrassas_in_Pakistan|madrassas (schools) in Pakistan]], who soon had military support from Pakistan.
sentence_182: Taking control of [[Kandahar|Kandahar]] city that year, they conquered more territories until finally driving out the government of [[Burhanuddin_Rabbani|Rabbani]] from Kabul in 1996, where they established an [[Islamic_Emirate_of_Afghanistan|emirate]] that gained international recognition from only three countries.
sentence_183: The Taliban were condemned internationally for the harsh enforcement of their interpretation of Islamic [[Sharia|sharia]] law, which resulted in the brutal treatment of many Afghans, especially [[Taliban_treatment_of_women|women]].
sentence_184: During their rule, the Taliban and their allies committed massacres against Afghan civilians, denied UN food supplies to starving civilians and conducted a policy of scorched earth, burning vast areas of fertile land and destroying tens of thousands of homes.
sentence_185: [[Battle_of_Kabul_(1992–96)|After the fall of Kabul]] to the Taliban, [[Ahmad_Shah_Massoud|Ahmad Shah Massoud]] and [[Abdul_Rashid_Dostum|Abdul Rashid Dostum]] formed the [[Northern_Alliance|Northern Alliance]], later joined by others, to resist the Taliban.
sentence_186: Dostum's forces were defeated by the Taliban during the [[Battles_of_Mazar-i-Sharif_(1997–98)|Battles of Mazar-i-Sharif (1997–98)]]; Pakistan's Chief of Army Staff, [[Pervez_Musharraf|Pervez Musharraf]], began sending thousands of Pakistanis to help the Taliban defeat the Northern Alliance.
sentence_187: By 2000 the Northern Alliance only controlled 10% of territory, cornered in the north-east.
sentence_188: On 9 September 2001, Massoud was assassinated by two Arab [[Suicide_attack|suicide attackers]] in [[Panjshir_Valley|Panjshir Valley]].
sentence_189: Around 400,000 Afghans died in internal conflicts between 1990 and 2001.
sentence_190: In October 2001, the United States [[United_States_invasion_of_Afghanistan|invaded]] Afghanistan to remove the Taliban from power after they refused to hand over [[Osama_Bin_Laden|Osama Bin Laden]], the prime suspect of the [[September_11_attacks|September 11 attacks]], who was a "guest" of the Taliban and was operating his [[Al-Qaeda|al-Qaeda]] network in Afghanistan.
sentence_191: The majority of Afghans supported the American invasion of their country.
sentence_192: During the initial invasion, US and UK forces bombed al-Qaeda training camps, and later working with the Northern Alliance, the Taliban regime came to an end.
sentence_193: Further information: [[War_in_Afghanistan_(2001–present)|War in Afghanistan (2001–present)]], [[Taliban_insurgency|Taliban insurgency]], and [[Reconstruction_in_Afghanistan|Reconstruction in Afghanistan]]
sentence_194: In December 2001, after the Taliban government was overthrown, the [[Afghan_Interim_Administration|Afghan Interim Administration]] under [[Hamid_Karzai|Hamid Karzai]] was formed.
sentence_195: The International Security Assistance Force (ISAF) was established by the [[UN_Security_Council|UN Security Council]] to help assist the [[Presidency_of_Hamid_Karzai|Karzai administration]] and provide basic security.
sentence_196: By this time, after two decades of war as well as an acute [[Famine|famine]] at the time, Afghanistan had one of the highest [[Infant_mortality|infant]] and child mortality rates in the world, the lowest life expectancy, much of the population were hungry, and infrastructure was in ruins.
sentence_197: Many foreign donors started providing aid and assistance to rebuild the war-torn country.
sentence_198: Taliban forces meanwhile began regrouping inside Pakistan, while more coalition troops entered Afghanistan to help the rebuilding process.
sentence_199: The Taliban began an [[Taliban_insurgency|insurgency]] to regain control of Afghanistan.
sentence_200: Over the next decade, ISAF and Afghan troops led many offensives against the Taliban, but failed to fully defeat them.
sentence_201: Afghanistan remains one of the poorest countries in the world because of a lack of foreign investment, [[Corruption_in_Afghanistan|government corruption]], and the Taliban insurgency.
sentence_202: Meanwhile, Karzai attempted to unite the peoples of the country, and the [[Politics_of_Afghanistan|Afghan government]] was able to build some democratic structures, adopting a constitution in 2004 with the name Islamic Republic of Afghanistan.
sentence_203: Attempts were made, often with the support of foreign donor countries, to improve the country's economy, healthcare, education, transport, and agriculture.
sentence_204: ISAF forces also began to train the [[Afghan_National_Security_Forces|Afghan National Security Forces]].
sentence_205: Following 2002, nearly five million [[Afghan_diaspora|Afghans]] were [[Repatriation|repatriated]].
sentence_206: The number of NATO troops present in Afghanistan peaked at 140,000 in 2011, dropping to about 16,000 in 2018.
sentence_207: In September 2014 [[Ashraf_Ghani|Ashraf Ghani]] became president after the [[Afghan_presidential_election,_2014|2014 presidential election]] where for the first time in Afghanistan's history power was democratically transferred.
sentence_208: On 28 December 2014, NATO formally ended ISAF combat operations in Afghanistan and transferred full security responsibility to the Afghan government.
sentence_209: The NATO-led [[Operation_Resolute_Support|Operation Resolute Support]] was formed the same day as a successor to ISAF.
sentence_210: Thousands of NATO troops remained in the country to train and advise Afghan government forces and continue their fight against the Taliban.
sentence_211: It was estimated in 2015 that "about 147,000 people have been killed in the Afghanistan war since 2001.
sentence_212: More than 38,000 of those killed have been civilians".
sentence_213: A report titled Body Count concluded that 106,000–170,000 civilians have been killed as a result of the fighting in Afghanistan at the hands of all parties to the conflict.
sentence_214: Main article: [[Geography_of_Afghanistan|Geography of Afghanistan]]
sentence_215: Afghanistan is located in South Asia and Central Asia - indeed the region particularly centered at Afghanistan is considered the "crossroads of Asia", and the country has had the nickname Heart of Asia.
sentence_216: The renowned [[Urdu|Urdu]] poet [[Muhammad_Iqbal|Muhammad Allama Iqbal]] once wrote about the country:
sentence_217: At over 652,230 km (251,830 sq mi), Afghanistan is the world's [[List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_area|41st largest country]], slightly bigger than France and smaller than Myanmar, and about the size of Texas in the United States.
sentence_218: There is no coastline, as Afghanistan is [[Landlocked|landlocked]].
sentence_219: It shares borders with Pakistan in the south and east (including Indian-claimed [[Gilgit-Baltistan|Gilgit-Baltistan]]); Iran in the west; Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan in the north; and China in the far east.
sentence_220: The geography in Afghanistan is varied, but is mostly mountainous and rugged, with some unusual mountain ridges accompanied by plateaus and river basins.
sentence_221: It is dominated by the [[Hindu_Kush|Hindu Kush]] range, the western extension of the [[Himalayas|Himalayas]] that stretches to eastern [[Tibet|Tibet]] via the [[Pamir_Mountains|Pamir Mountains]] and [[Karakoram_Mountains|Karakoram Mountains]] in Afghanistan's far north-east.
sentence_222: Most of the highest points are in the east consisting of fertile mountain valleys.
sentence_223: The Hindu Kush ends at the west-central highlands, creating plains in the north and southwest, namely the [[Turkestan|Turkestan]] Plains and the [[Sistan_Basin|Sistan Basin]]; these two regions consist of rolling grasslands and semi-deserts, and hot windy deserts, respectively.
sentence_224: Forests exist in the corridor between [[Nuristan_Province|Nuristan]] and [[Paktika_Province|Paktika]] provinces, and [[Tundra|tundra]] in the north-east.
sentence_225: The country's highest point is [[Noshaq|Noshaq]], at 7,492 m (24,580 ft) above sea level.
sentence_226: The lowest point lies in [[Jowzjan_Province|Jowzjan Province]] along the Amu River bank, at 258 m (846 ft) above sea level.
sentence_227: Despite having numerous rivers and [[List_of_dams_and_reservoirs_in_Afghanistan|reservoirs]], large parts of the country are dry.
sentence_228: The [[Endorheic_basin|endorheic]] Sistan Basin is one of the driest regions in the world.
sentence_229: The [[Amu_Darya|Amu Darya]] rises at the north of the Hindu Kush, while the nearby [[Hari_(Afghanistan)|Hari Rud]] flows west towards [[Herat|Herat]], and the [[Arghandab_River|Arghandab River]] from the central region southwards.
sentence_230: To the south and west of the Hindu Kush flow a number of streams that are tributaries of the [[Indus_River|Indus River]], such as the [[Helmand_River|Helmand River]].
sentence_231: One exception is the [[Kabul_River|Kabul River]] which flows in an easternly direction to the Indus ending at the Indian Ocean.
sentence_232: Afghanistan receives heavy snow during the winter in the [[Hindu_Kush|Hindu Kush]] and [[Pamir_Mountains|Pamir Mountains]], and the melting snow in the spring season enters the [[List_of_rivers_of_Afghanistan|rivers, lakes, and streams]].
sentence_233: However, two-thirds of the country's water flows into the neighboring countries of [[Iran|Iran]], [[Pakistan|Pakistan]], and [[Turkmenistan|Turkmenistan]].
sentence_234: As reported in 2010, the state needs more than US$2 billion to rehabilitate its irrigation systems so that the water is properly managed.
sentence_235: The northeastern Hindu Kush [[Mountain_range|mountain range]], in and around the [[Badakhshan_Province|Badakhshan Province]] of Afghanistan, is in a [[Natural_environment#Geological_activity|geologically active]] area where earthquakes may occur almost every year.
sentence_236: They can be deadly and destructive, causing [[Landslide|landslides]] in some parts or [[2009_Afghan_avalanches|avalanches]] during the winter.
sentence_237: The last strong earthquakes were in [[February_1998_Afghanistan_earthquake|1998]], which killed about 6,000 people in Badakhshan near Tajikistan.
sentence_238: This was followed by the [[2002_Hindu_Kush_earthquakes|2002 Hindu Kush earthquakes]] in which over 150 people were killed and over 1,000 injured.
sentence_239: A [[2010_Afghanistan_earthquake|2010 earthquake]] left 11 Afghans dead, over 70 injured, and more than 2,000 houses destroyed.
sentence_240: Afghanistan has a continental climate with harsh winters in the [[Hazarajat|central highlands]], the glaciated northeast (around [[Nuristan|Nuristan]]), and the [[Wakhan_Corridor|Wakhan Corridor]], where the average temperature in January is below −15 °C (5 °F) and can reach −26 °C (−15 °F), and hot summers in the low-lying areas of the [[Sistan_Basin|Sistan Basin]] of the southwest, the [[Jalalabad|Jalalabad]] basin in the east, and the [[Afghan_Turkestan|Turkestan]] plains along the [[Amu_River|Amu River]] in the north, where temperatures average over 35 °C (95 °F) in July and can go over 43 °C (109 °F).
sentence_241: The country is generally arid in the summers, with most rainfall falling between December and April.
sentence_242: The lower areas of northern and western Afghanistan are the driest, with precipitation more common in the east.
sentence_243: Although proximate to India, Afghanistan is mostly outside the [[Monsoon|monsoon]] zone, apart from [[Nuristan_Province|Nuristan Province]] which occasionally receives summer monsoon rain.
sentence_244: Main article: Wildlife of Afghanistan
sentence_245: Several types of [[Mammal|mammals]] exist throughout Afghanistan.
sentence_246: [[Snow_leopard|Snow leopards]], [[Siberian_tiger|Siberian tigers]] and [[Brown_bear|brown bears]] live in the high elevation [[Alpine_tundra|alpine tundra]] regions.
sentence_247: The [[Marco_Polo_sheep|Marco Polo sheep]] exclusively live in the [[Wakhan_Corridor|Wakhan Corridor]] region of north-east Afghanistan.
sentence_248: [[Fox|Foxes]], [[Wolves|wolves]], [[Otter|otters]], [[Deer|deer]], [[Wild_sheep|wild sheep]], [[Lynx|lynx]] and other big cats populate the mountain forest region of the east.
sentence_249: In the semi-desert northern plains, wildlife include a variety of birds, [[Hedgehog|hedgehogs]], [[Gopher|gophers]], and large carnivores such as [[Jackal|jackals]] and [[Hyena|hyenas]].
sentence_250: [[Gazelle|Gazelles]], [[Wild_boar|wild pigs]] and jackals populate the steppe plains of the south and west, while [[Mongoose|mongoose]] and [[Cheetah|cheetahs]] exist in the semi-desert south.
sentence_251: [[Marmot|Marmots]] and [[Ibex|ibex]] also live in the high mountains of Afghanistan, and pheasants exist in some parts of the country.
sentence_252: The [[Afghan_hound|Afghan hound]] is a native breed of dog known for its fast speed and its long hair; it is relatively known in the west.
sentence_253: [[Endemic|Endemic]] fauna of Afghanistan includes the [[Afghan_flying_squirrel|Afghan flying squirrel]], [[Afghan_snowfinch|Afghan snowfinch]], [[Afghanodon|Afghanodon]] (or the "[[Paghman|Paghman]] mountain salamander"), [[Stigmella_kasyi|Stigmella kasyi]], [[Vulcaniella_kabulensis|Vulcaniella kabulensis]], Afghan leopard gecko, [[Wheeleria_parviflorellus|Wheeleria parviflorellus]], amongst others.
sentence_254: Endemic flora include [[Iris_afghanica|Iris afghanica]].
sentence_255: Afghanistan has a wide variety of birds despite its relatively arid climate – an estimated 460 species of which 235 breed within.
sentence_256: The forest region of Afghanistan has vegetation such as [[Pine_tree|pine trees]], [[Spruce_tree|spruce trees]], [[Fir_tree|fir trees]] and [[Larch|larches]], whereas the steppe grassland regions consist of [[Broadleaf_tree|broadleaf trees]], short grass, perennial plants and [[Shrubland|shrublands]].
sentence_257: The colder high elevation regions are composed of hardy grasses and small flowering plants.
sentence_258: Several regions are designated [[List_of_protected_areas_of_Afghanistan|protected areas]]; there are three National Parks: [[Band-e_Amir_National_Park|Band-e Amir]], [[Wakhan|Wakhan]] and [[Nuristan|Nuristan]].
sentence_259: Main articles: [[Demographics_of_Afghanistan|Demographics of Afghanistan]] and [[Afghan_diaspora|Afghan diaspora]]
sentence_260: The population of Afghanistan was estimated at 32.9 million as of 2019 by the Afghanistan Statistics and Information Authority, whereas the UN estimates over 38.0 million.
sentence_261: About 23.9% of them are [[Urban_area|urbanite]], 71.4% live in rural areas, and the remaining 4.7% are nomadic.
sentence_262: An additional 3 million or so Afghans are temporarily housed in neighboring Pakistan and [[Afghans_in_Iran|Iran]], most of whom were born and raised in those two countries.
sentence_263: As of 2013, Afghanistan was the largest refugee-producing country in the world, a title held for 32 years.
sentence_264: The current population growth rate is 2.37%, one of the highest in the world outside of Africa.
sentence_265: This population is expected to reach 82 million by 2050 if current population trends continue.
sentence_266: The population of Afghanistan increased steadily until the 1980s, when civil war caused millions to flee to other countries such as Pakistan.
sentence_267: Millions have since returned and the war conditions has meant a high fertility rate compared to global and regional trends.
sentence_268: Afghanistan's healthcare has recovered since the turn of the century, causing falls in infant mortality and increases in life expectancy.
sentence_269: This (along with other factors such as returning refugees) caused rapid population growth in the 2000s that has only recently started to slow down.
sentence_270: Main article: [[Ethnic_groups_in_Afghanistan|Ethnic groups in Afghanistan]]
sentence_271: Afghanistan's population is divided into several [[Ethnolinguistics|ethnolinguistic]] groups.
sentence_272: The ethnicities are represented on the table on the right.
sentence_273: The percentages given are estimates only, as accurate and current statistical data on ethnicity are not available.
sentence_274: Generally the four major ethnic groups are the [[Pashtuns|Pashtuns]], [[Tajiks|Tajiks]], [[Hazaras|Hazaras]] and [[Uzbeks|Uzbeks]].
sentence_275: A further 10 other ethnic groups are recognized and each are represented in the [[Afghan_National_Anthem|Afghan National Anthem]].
sentence_276: Main article: [[Languages_of_Afghanistan|Languages of Afghanistan]]
sentence_277: [[Dari_language|Dari]] and [[Pashto|Pashto]] are the [[Official_language|official languages]] of Afghanistan; [[Bilingualism|bilingualism]] is very common.
sentence_278: Dari, which is a variety of and mutually intelligible with [[Persian_language|Persian]] (and very often called 'Farsi' by some Afghans like in [[Iran|Iran]]) functions as the [[Lingua_franca|lingua franca]] in Kabul as well as in much of the northern and northwestern parts of the country.
sentence_279: Pashto is the native tongue of the Pashtuns, although many of them are also fluent in Dari while some non-Pashtuns are fluent in Pashto.
sentence_280: Despite the Pashtuns having been dominant in Afghan politics for centuries, Dari remained the preferred language for government and bureaucracy.
sentence_281: There are a number of smaller regional languages, including [[Uzbek_language|Uzbek]], [[Turkmen_language|Turkmen]], [[Balochi_language|Balochi]], [[Pashayi_language|Pashayi]], and [[Nuristani_languages|Nuristani]].
sentence_282: When it comes to foreign languages among the populace, many are able to speak or understand [[Hindustani_language|Hindustani]] ([[Urdu|Urdu]]-[[Hindi|Hindi]]), partly due to returning Afghan refugees from Pakistan and the popularity of [[Bollywood|Bollywood]] films respectively.
sentence_283: English is also understood by some of the population, and has been gaining popularity as of the 2000s.
sentence_284: Some Afghans retain some ability of Russian, which was taught to public schools during the 1980s.
sentence_285: Main article: [[Religion_in_Afghanistan|Religion in Afghanistan]]
sentence_286: An estimated 99.7% of the Afghan population is Muslim and most are thought to adhere to the [[Sunni|Sunni]] [[Hanafi|Hanafi]] school.
sentence_287: According to [[Pew_Research_Center|Pew Research Center]], as much as 90% are of the Sunni denomination, 7% [[Shia|Shia]] and 3% [[Non-denominational_Muslim|non-denominational]].
sentence_288: The [[CIA|CIA]] Factbook variously estimates up to 89.7% Sunni or up to 15% Shia.
sentence_289: Dr [[Michael_Izady|Michael Izady]] estimated 70% of the population to be followers of Sunni Islam, 25% [[Imamiyyah|Imami Shia Islam]], 4.5% [[Isma'ilism|Ismaili Shia Islam]], and 0.5% [[Religion_in_Afghanistan#Minority_religious_groups|other religions]].
sentence_290: Thousands of Afghan Sikhs and [[Hinduism_in_Afghanistan|Hindus]] are also found in certain major cities (namely Kabul, Jalalabad, Ghazni, Kandahar) accompanied by gurdwaras and mandirs.
sentence_291: There was a small [[History_of_the_Jews_in_Afghanistan|Jewish community in Afghanistan]] who had emigrated to Israel and the United States by the end of the twentieth century; at least one Jew, [[Zablon_Simintov|Zablon Simintov]], remains, who is the caretaker of the only remaining synagogue.
sentence_292: [[Christianity_in_Afghanistan|Afghan Christians]], who number 500–8,000, practice their faith secretly due to intense societal opposition, and there are no public churches.
sentence_293: As estimated by the CIA World Factbook, 26% of the population was urbanized as of 2020.
sentence_294: This is one of the lowest figures in the world; in Asia it is only higher than [[Cambodia|Cambodia]], [[Nepal|Nepal]] and [[Sri_Lanka|Sri Lanka]].
sentence_295: Urbanization has increased rapidly, particularly in the capital [[Kabul|Kabul]], due to returning refugees from Pakistan and Iran after 2001, internally displaced people, and rural migrants.
sentence_296: Urbanization in Afghanistan has been noted to be different than traditional urbanization, in that it's centered on a few cities rather than evenly spread out nationwide.
sentence_297: The only city with over a million residents is its capital, Kabul, located in the east of the country.
sentence_298: The other large cities are located generally in the "ring" around the Central Highlands, namely [[Kandahar|Kandahar]] in the south, [[Herat|Herat]] in the west, [[Mazar-i-Sharif|Mazar-i-Sharif]] and [[Kunduz|Kunduz]] in the north, and [[Jalalabad|Jalalabad]] in the east.
sentence_299: Main articles: [[Politics_of_Afghanistan|Politics of Afghanistan]] and Constitution of Afghanistan
sentence_300: Afghanistan is an [[Islamic_republic|Islamic republic]] consisting of three branches, the executive, legislative, and judicial.
sentence_301: The nation is led by President [[Ashraf_Ghani|Ashraf Ghani]] with [[Amrullah_Saleh|Amrullah Saleh]] and Sarwar Danish as vice presidents.
sentence_302: The [[National_Assembly_of_Afghanistan|National Assembly]] is the legislature, a bicameral body having two chambers, the [[House_of_the_People_(Afghanistan)|House of the People]] and the House of Elders.
sentence_303: The [[Afghan_Supreme_Court|Supreme Court]] is led by [[Chief_Justice_of_Afghanistan|Chief Justice]] Said Yusuf Halem, the former Deputy Minister of Justice for Legal Affairs.
sentence_304: According to [[Transparency_International|Transparency International]], Afghanistan remains in the top most corrupt countries list.
sentence_305: A January 2010 report published by the [[United_Nations_Office_on_Drugs_and_Crime|United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime]] revealed that bribery consumed an amount equal to 23% of the GDP of the nation.
sentence_306: On 17 May 2020, President [[Ashraf_Ghani|Ashraf Ghani]] reached a power-sharing deal with his rival from presidential elections, [[Abdullah_Abdullah|Abdullah Abdullah]], deciding on who would manage the respected key ministries.
sentence_307: The agreement ended months-long [[Gridlock_(politics)|political deadlock]] in the country.
sentence_308: It was agreed that while Ghani will lead Afghanistan as the president, Abdullah will oversee the [[Afghan_peace_process|peace process]] with the [[Taliban|Taliban]].
sentence_309: Main articles: [[Elections_in_Afghanistan|Elections in Afghanistan]] and [[List_of_political_parties_in_Afghanistan|List of political parties in Afghanistan]]
sentence_310: One instrument of Afghan governance is the [[Loya_jirga|loya jirga]] (grand assembly), a [[Pashtuns|Pashtun]] consultative meeting that is mainly organized for choosing a new head of state, adopting a new constitution, or to settle national or regional issue such as war.
sentence_311: Loya jirgas have been held since at least 1747, with the most recent one occurring in 2013.
sentence_312: Under the 2004 constitution, both presidential and parliamentary elections are to be held every five years.
sentence_313: However, due to the disputed [[2014_Afghan_presidential_election|2014 presidential election]], the scheduled 2015 parliamentary elections were delayed until [[2018_Afghan_parliamentary_election|2018]].
sentence_314: Presidential elections use the [[Two-round_system|two-round system]]; if no candidate receives a majority of the vote in the first round, a second round will be held featuring the top two candidates.
sentence_315: Parliamentary elections have only one round and are based on the single non-transferable vote system, which allows some candidates to be elected with as little as one percent of the vote.
sentence_316: The [[Afghan_presidential_election,_2004|2004 Afghan presidential election]] was relatively peaceful, in which Hamid Karzai won in the first round with 55.4% of the votes.
sentence_317: However, the 2009 presidential election was characterized by lack of security, low voter turnout, and widespread electoral fraud, ending in Karzai's reelection.
sentence_318: The [[Afghan_presidential_election,_2014|2014 presidential election]] ended with Ashraf Ghani winning by 56.44% of the votes.
sentence_319: Political parties played a marginal role in post-2001 Afghan politics, in part due to Karzai's opposition to them.
sentence_320: In the [[Afghan_parliamentary_election,_2005|2005 parliamentary election]], the ballots did not show candidates' party affiliation, so the results were dictated by the personal prestige of the candidates.
sentence_321: Among the elected officials were a large mix of former mujahideen, [[Islamic_fundamentalists|Islamic fundamentalists]], warlords, tribal nationalists, former communists, [[Reformists|reformists]], urban professionals, royalists and several former Taliban associates.
sentence_322: In the same period, Afghanistan became the 30th highest nation in terms of female representation in the National Assembly.
sentence_323: Parties became more influential after 2009, when a new law established more stringent requirements for party registration.
sentence_324: Nearly a hundred new parties were registered after the law came into effect, and party activity increased in the 2014 elections, but party influence remained limited.
sentence_325: Main articles: [[Provinces_of_Afghanistan|Provinces of Afghanistan]] and Districts of Afghanistan
sentence_326: Afghanistan is administratively divided into 34 provinces (wilayats).
sentence_327: Each province is the size of a [[County_(United_States)|U.S. county]], having a governor and a capital.
sentence_328: The country is further divided into nearly 400 provincial districts, each of which normally covers a city or several villages.
sentence_329: Each district is represented by a district governor.
sentence_330: The [[List_of_current_governors_of_Afghanistan|provincial governors]] are appointed by the [[President_of_Afghanistan|President of Afghanistan]], and the district governors are selected by the provincial governors.
sentence_331: The provincial governors are representatives of the central government in Kabul and are responsible for all administrative and formal issues within their provinces.
sentence_332: There are also provincial councils that are elected through direct and general elections for four years.
sentence_333: The functions of provincial councils are to take part in provincial development planning and to participate in the monitoring and appraisal of other provincial governance institutions.
sentence_334: According to article 140 of the constitution and the presidential decree on electoral law, mayors of cities should be elected through free and direct elections for a four-year term.
sentence_335: In practice however, mayors are appointed by the government.
sentence_336: The following is a list of all the 34 provinces in alphabetical order:
sentence_337: Main article: [[Foreign_relations_of_Afghanistan|Foreign relations of Afghanistan]]
sentence_338: Afghanistan became a member of the United Nations in 1946.
sentence_339: It enjoys cordial relations with a number of [[NATO|NATO]] and allied nations, particularly the [[Afghanistan–United_States_relations|United States]], [[Afghanistan–Canada_relations|Canada]], [[Afghanistan–United_Kingdom_relations|United Kingdom]], [[Afghanistan–Germany_relations|Germany]], Australia, and [[Afghanistan–Turkey_relations|Turkey]].
sentence_340: In 2012, the United States and Afghanistan signed their [[U.S.–Afghanistan_Strategic_Partnership_Agreement|Strategic Partnership Agreement]] in which Afghanistan became a [[Major_non-NATO_ally|major non-NATO ally]].
sentence_341: Afghanistan has historically had strong relations with Germany, one of the first countries to recognize Afghanistan's independence in 1919; the [[Soviet_Union|Soviet Union]], which provided much aid and military training for Afghanistan's forces and includes the signing of a Treaty of Friendship in 1921 and 1978; and [[Afghanistan–India_relations|India]], with which a friendship treaty was signed in 1950.
sentence_342: Relations with [[Afghanistan–Pakistan_relations|Pakistan]] have often been tense for various reasons such as the [[Durand_Line|Durand Line]] border issue and alleged Pakistani involvement in Afghan insurgent groups.
sentence_343: Afghanistan also has diplomatic relations with neighboring [[Afghanistan–China_relations|China]], [[Afghanistan–Iran_relations|Iran]], [[Afghanistan–Tajikistan_relations|Tajikistan]], [[Foreign_relations_of_Turkmenistan#Afghanistan|Turkmenistan]], and Uzbekistan, including with regional states such as [[Afghanistan–Bangladesh_relations|Bangladesh]], [[Afghanistan–Japan_relations|Japan]], [[Foreign_relations_of_Kazakhstan|Kazakhstan]], Nepal, Russia, South Korea, and the UAE.
sentence_344: The [[Ministry_of_Foreign_Affairs_(Afghanistan)|Afghan Ministry of Foreign Affairs]] continues to develop [[Foreign_relations_of_Afghanistan|diplomatic relations]] with other countries around the world.
sentence_345: The [[United_Nations_Assistance_Mission_in_Afghanistan|United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan]] (UNAMA) was established in 2002 to help the country recover from decades of war.
sentence_346: Today, several NATO member states deploy about 17,000 troops in Afghanistan as part of the [[Resolute_Support_Mission|Resolute Support Mission]].
sentence_347: Its main purpose is to [[NATO_Training_Mission-Afghanistan|train]] the [[Afghan_National_Security_Forces|Afghan National Security Forces]].
sentence_348: Main article: [[Afghan_Armed_Forces|Afghan Armed Forces]]
sentence_349: The [[Afghan_Armed_Forces|Afghan Armed Forces]] are under the [[Ministry_of_Defense_(Afghanistan)|Ministry of Defense]], which includes the [[Afghan_Air_Force|Afghan Air Force]] (AAF) and the Afghan National Army (ANA).
sentence_350: The [[Afghan_Defense_University|Afghan Defense University]] houses various educational establishments for the Afghan Armed Forces, including the [[National_Military_Academy_of_Afghanistan|National Military Academy of Afghanistan]].
sentence_351: Main article: [[Law_enforcement_in_Afghanistan|Law enforcement in Afghanistan]]
sentence_352: Law enforcement in Afghanistan is the responsibility of the [[Afghan_National_Police|Afghan National Police]] (ANP), which is part of the [[Ministry_of_Interior_Affairs_(Afghanistan)|Ministry of Interior Affairs]].
sentence_353: The ANP consists of two primary branches, the Afghan Uniformed Police and the [[Afghan_Border_Police|Afghan Border Police]].
sentence_354: The mission of the Uniformed Police is to ensure security within Afghanistan, prevent crime, and protect property.
sentence_355: The Border Police is responsible for securing and maintaining the nation's borders with neighboring states as well as all international airports within the country.
sentence_356: Afghanistan's intelligence agency, the [[National_Directorate_of_Security|National Directorate of Security]] (NDS), assists the ANP with security matters.
sentence_357: All parts of Afghanistan are considered dangerous due to militant activities and terrorism-related incidents.
sentence_358: Kidnapping for ransom and robberies are common in major cities.
sentence_359: Every year hundreds of Afghan police are [[List_of_Afghan_security_forces_fatality_reports_in_Afghanistan|killed]] in the line of duty.
sentence_360: Afghanistan is also the world's leading [[Opium_production_in_Afghanistan|producer of opium]].
sentence_361: Afghanistan's [[Opium_poppy|opium poppy]] harvest produces more than 90% of illicit heroin globally, and more than 95% of the European supply.
sentence_362: The [[Ministry_of_Counter_Narcotics_(Afghanistan)|Afghan Ministry of Counter Narcotics]] is responsible for the monitoring and eradication of the illegal drug business.
sentence_363: See also: [[Human_rights_in_Afghanistan|Human rights in Afghanistan]], [[Women_in_Afghanistan|Women in Afghanistan]], and LGBT rights in Afghanistan
sentence_364: [[Freedom_of_expression|Freedom of expression]] and the press is permitted and promoted in the current 2004 constitution, so long as it does not threaten national or religious integrity or does not [[Defamation|defame]] individuals.
sentence_365: In 2019, [[Reporters_Without_Borders|Reporters Without Borders]] listed the media environment of Afghanistan as 121st out of 179 on its [[Press_Freedom_Index|Press Freedom Index]], with 1st being most free.
sentence_366: However many issues regarding human rights exist contrary to the law, often committed by local tribes, lawmakers and hardline clerics.
sentence_367: Journalists in Afghanistan face threat from both the security forces and insurgents.
sentence_368: The Afghan Journalists Safety Committee (AJSC) claimed in 2017 that the Afghan government accounted for 46% of the attacks on Afghans journalists, while insurgents were responsible for rest of the attacks.
sentence_369: According to Global Rights, almost 90% of women in Afghanistan have experienced physical abuse, sexual abuse, psychological abuse or forced marriage.
sentence_370: The perpetrators of these crimes are the families of the victim.
sentence_371: A 2009 proposal for a law against the violence of women could only be passed through a presidential decree.
sentence_372: In 2012, Afghanistan recorded 240 cases of [[Honor_killing|honor killing]], but the total number is believed to be much higher.
sentence_373: Of the reported honor killings, 21% were committed by the victims' husbands, 7% by their brothers, 4% by their fathers, and the rest by other relatives.
sentence_374: Homosexuality is [[Taboo|taboo]] in Afghan society; according to the Penal Code, homosexual intimacy is punished by up to a year in prison.
sentence_375: With implementing [[Sharia_law|Sharia law]] offenders can face [[Death_penalty_for_homosexuality|death]].
sentence_376: However an ancient tradition involving male homosexual acts between youngsters and older men (typically wealthy or elite people) called [[Bacha_bazi|bacha bazi]] persists.
sentence_377: This act is also illegal under the Penal Code and offenders can be imprisoned.
sentence_378: On August 14, 2020, [[UN_Human_Rights_Council|UN Human Rights Council]] experts issued a joint statement urging Afghanistan officials to prevent the killings of [[Human_rights_defenders|human rights defenders]] as there have been nine deaths of human rights defenders since January 2020.
sentence_379: Main article: [[Economy_of_Afghanistan|Economy of Afghanistan]]
sentence_380: Afghanistan's nominal GDP was $21.7 billion in 2018, or $72.9 billion by [[Purchasing_power_parity|purchasing power parity]] (PPP).
sentence_381: Its [[List_of_countries_by_GDP_(PPP)_per_capita|GDP per capita]] is $2,024 (PPP).
sentence_382: Despite having $1 trillion or more in mineral deposits, it remains one of the world's [[Least_developed_countries|least developed countries]].
sentence_383: Afghanistan's rough physical geography and its landlocked status has been cited as reasons why the country has always been among the least developed in the modern era – a factor where progress is also slowed by contemporary conflict and political instability.
sentence_384: The country imports over $7 billion worth of goods but exports only $784 million, mainly fruits and [[Nut_(fruit)|nuts]].
sentence_385: It has $2.8 billion in [[External_debt|external debt]].
sentence_386: The service sector contributed the most to the GDP (55.9%) followed by agriculture (23%) and industry (21.1%).
sentence_387: While the nation's current account deficit is largely financed with donor money, only a small portion is provided directly to the government budget.
sentence_388: The rest is provided to non-budgetary expenditure and donor-designated projects through the United Nations system and non-governmental organizations.
sentence_389: [[Da_Afghanistan_Bank|Da Afghanistan Bank]] serves as the central bank of the nation and the [[Afghan_afghani|"Afghani"]] (AFN) is the national currency, with an exchange rate of about 75 Afghanis to 1 US dollar.
sentence_390: A number of local and foreign banks operate in the country, including the [[Afghanistan_International_Bank|Afghanistan International Bank]], [[New_Kabul_Bank|New Kabul Bank]], Azizi Bank, [[Pashtany_Bank|Pashtany Bank]], [[Standard_Chartered_Bank|Standard Chartered Bank]], and the [[First_MicroFinance_Bank-Afghanistan|First Micro Finance Bank]].
sentence_391: One of the main drivers for the current economic recovery is the return of over 5 million [[Afghan_diaspora|expatriates]], who brought with them entrepreneurship and wealth-creating skills as well as much needed funds to start up businesses.
sentence_392: Many Afghans are now involved in construction, which is one of the largest industries in the country.
sentence_393: Some of the major national construction projects include the $35 billion New Kabul City next to the capital, the Aino Mena project in Kandahar, and the [[Ghazi_Amanullah_Khan_Town|Ghazi Amanullah Khan Town]] near Jalalabad.
sentence_394: Similar development projects have also begun in [[Herat|Herat]], [[Mazar-e-Sharif|Mazar-e-Sharif]], and other cities.
sentence_395: An estimated 400,000 people enter the labor market each year.
sentence_396: Several small companies and factories began operating in different parts of the country, which not only provide revenues to the government but also create new jobs.
sentence_397: Improvements to the business environment have resulted in more than $1.5 billion in [[Telecommunication|telecom]] investment and created more than 100,000 jobs since 2003.
sentence_398: [[Afghan_rug|Afghan rugs]] are becoming popular again, allowing many carpet dealers around the country to hire more workers; in 2016–17 it was the fourth most exported group of items.
sentence_399: Afghanistan is a member of [[World_Trade_Organization|WTO]], SAARC, [[Economic_Cooperation_Organization|ECO]], and [[Economy_of_the_OIC|OIC]].
sentence_400: It holds an observer status in [[Shanghai_Cooperation_Organisation|SCO]].
sentence_401: In 2018, a majority of imports come from either Iran, China, Pakistan and Kazakhstan, while 84% of exports are to Pakistan and India.
sentence_402: Agricultural production is the backbone of Afghanistan's economy and has traditionally dominated the economy, employing about 40% of the workforce as of 2018.
sentence_403: The country is known for producing [[Pomegranate_production_in_Afghanistan|pomegranates]], grapes, apricots, melons, and several other fresh and dry fruits.
sentence_404: It is also known as the world's largest producer of [[Opium_production_in_Afghanistan|opium]] – as much as 16% or more of the nation's economy is derived from the cultivation and sale of opium.
sentence_405: It is also one of the world's top producers of [[Cannabis|cannabis]].
sentence_406: [[Saffron|Saffron]], the most expensive spice, grows in Afghanistan, particularly [[Herat_Province|Herat Province]].
sentence_407: In recent years, there has been an uptick in saffron production, which authorities and farmers are trying to replace poppy cultivation.
sentence_408: Between 2012 and 2019, the saffron cultivated and produced in Afghanistan was consecutively ranked the world's best by the International Taste and Quality Institute.
sentence_409: Production hit record high in 2019 (19,469 kg of saffron), and one kilogram is sold domestically between $634 and $1147.
sentence_410: Main article: [[Mining_in_Afghanistan|Mining in Afghanistan]]
sentence_411: The country's natural resources include: coal, copper, iron ore, [[Lithium|lithium]], [[Uranium|uranium]], [[Rare_earth_element|rare earth elements]], [[Chromite|chromite]], gold, [[Zinc|zinc]], [[Talc|talc]], [[Barite|barite]], [[Sulfur|sulfur]], lead, [[Marble|marble]], precious and [[Semi-precious_stones|semi-precious stones]], natural gas, and petroleum, among other things.
sentence_412: In 2010, US and Afghan government officials estimated that untapped mineral deposits located in 2007 by the US Geological Survey are worth at least $1 trillion.
sentence_413: [[Michael_E._O'Hanlon|Michael E. O'Hanlon]] of the [[Brookings_Institution|Brookings Institution]] estimated that if Afghanistan generates about $10 billion per year from its [[Mining_in_Afghanistan|mineral deposits]], its [[Gross_national_product|gross national product]] would double and provide long-term funding for Afghan security forces and other critical needs.
sentence_414: The United States Geological Survey (USGS) estimated in 2006 that northern Afghanistan has an average 460 million m (2.9 billion bbl) of [[Crude_oil|crude oil]], 440 billion m (15.7 trillion cu ft) of natural gas, and 67 billion L (562 million US bbl) of [[Natural_gas_liquids|natural gas liquids]].
sentence_415: In 2011, Afghanistan signed an oil exploration contract with [[China_National_Petroleum_Corporation|China National Petroleum Corporation]] (CNPC) for the development of three oil fields along the Amu Darya river in the north.
sentence_416: The country has significant amounts of [[Lithium|lithium]], copper, gold, coal, iron ore, and other [[Minerals|minerals]].
sentence_417: The [[Khanashin|Khanashin]] [[Carbonatite|carbonatite]] in Helmand Province contains 1,000,000 tonnes (980,000 [[Long_ton|long tons]]; 1,100,000 [[Short_ton|short tons]]) of [[Rare_earth_element|rare earth elements]].
