sentence_2: The Bronx ([[English|/brɒŋks/]]) is a [[Boroughs_of_New_York_City|borough]] of [[New_York_City|New York City]], coextensive with Bronx County, in the [[U.S._state|U.S.
sentence_3: state]] of [[New_York_(state)|New York]], the [[County_statistics_of_the_United_States#Most_densely_populated|third-most-densely populated county in the United States]].
sentence_4: It is south of [[Westchester_County,_New_York|Westchester County]]; northeast and east of [[Manhattan|Manhattan]], across the [[Harlem_River|Harlem River]]; and north of [[Queens|Queens]], across the [[East_River|East River]].
sentence_5: The Bronx has a land area of 42 square miles (109 km) and a population of 1,418,207 in 2019.
sentence_6: Of the five boroughs, it has the fourth-largest area, fourth-highest population, and third-highest [[Population_density|population density]].
sentence_7: It is the only borough predominantly on the [[Contiguous_United_States|U.S.
sentence_8: mainland]].
sentence_9: If each borough were its own city, the Bronx would rank as the [[List_of_United_States_cities_by_population|eighth-most-populous in the U.S.]]
sentence_10: The Bronx is divided by the [[Bronx_River|Bronx River]] into a hillier section in the [[West_Bronx|west]], and a flatter eastern section.
sentence_11: East and west street names are divided by [[Jerome_Avenue|Jerome Avenue]].
sentence_12: The West Bronx was annexed to New York City in 1874, and the areas east of the Bronx River in 1895.
sentence_13: Bronx County was separated from New York County in 1914.
sentence_14: About a quarter of the Bronx's area is open space, including [[Woodlawn_Cemetery_(Bronx,_New_York)|Woodlawn Cemetery]], [[Van_Cortlandt_Park|Van Cortlandt Park]], [[Pelham_Bay_Park|Pelham Bay Park]], the [[New_York_Botanical_Garden|New York Botanical Garden]], and the [[Bronx_Zoo|Bronx Zoo]] in the borough's north and center.
sentence_15: The Thain Family Forest at The New York Botanical Garden is thousands of years old; it is New York City's largest remaining tract of the original forest that once covered the city.
sentence_16: These open spaces are situated primarily on land deliberately reserved in the late 19th century as urban development progressed north and east from Manhattan.
sentence_17: The name "Bronx" originated with Swedish-born [[Jonas_Bronck|Jonas Bronck]], who established the first settlement in the area as part of the [[New_Netherland|New Netherland]] colony in 1639.
sentence_18: The native Lenape were displaced after 1643 by European settlers.
sentence_19: In the 19th and 20th centuries, the Bronx received many immigrant and migrant groups as it was transformed into an urban community, first from various European countries (particularly [[Irish_Americans|Ireland]], [[German_Americans|Germany]], [[Italian_Americans|Italy]] and [[Eastern_Europe|Eastern Europe]]) and later from the [[Caribbean|Caribbean]] region (particularly [[Puerto_Ricans_in_the_United_States|Puerto Rico]], [[Haitian_Americans|Haiti]], [[Jamaican_Americans|Jamaica]], and the [[Dominican_Americans|Dominican Republic]]), as well as [[African_American|African American]] migrants from the [[Southern_United_States|southern United States]].
sentence_20: This cultural mix has made the Bronx a wellspring of [[Latin_music|Latin music]], [[Hip_hop_music|hip hop]] and [[Rock_music|rock]].
sentence_21: The Bronx contains the poorest [[Congressional_districts_of_the_United_States|congressional district in the United States]], the [[New_York's_15th_congressional_district|15th]].
sentence_22: There are, however, some upper-income, as well as middle-income neighborhoods such as [[Riverdale,_Bronx|Riverdale]], [[Fieldston,_Bronx|Fieldston]], [[Spuyten_Duyvil,_Bronx|Spuyten Duyvil]], [[Schuylerville,_Bronx|Schuylerville]], [[Pelham_Bay,_Bronx|Pelham Bay]], [[Pelham_Gardens,_Bronx|Pelham Gardens]], [[Morris_Park,_Bronx|Morris Park]], and [[Country_Club,_Bronx|Country Club]].
sentence_23: Parts of the Bronx saw a decline in population, livable housing and quality of life in the late 1960s, 1970s and 1980s culminating in a wave of [[Arson|arson]].
sentence_24: The [[South_Bronx|South Bronx]], in particular, experienced severe urban decay.
sentence_25: The borough experienced some redevelopment starting in the 1990s, preceding a more recent period of gentrification.
sentence_26: The Bronx was called Rananchqua by the native [[Siwanoy|Siwanoy]] band of Lenape (also known historically as the Delawares), while other [[Native_Americans_in_the_United_States|Native Americans]] knew the Bronx as Keskeskeck.
sentence_27: It was divided by the [[Aquahung|Aquahung]] River.
sentence_28: The origin of the person of [[Jonas_Bronck|Jonas Bronck]] (c. 1600–43) has been contested.
sentence_29: Documents indicate that he was a Swedish-born immigrant from [[Komstad|Komstad, Norra Ljunga parish]], in Småland, Sweden, who arrived in [[New_Netherland|New Netherland]] during the spring of 1639.
sentence_30: Bronck became the first recorded European settler in the present-day Bronx and built a farm named "Emmaus" close to what today is the corner of Willis Avenue and 132nd Street in [[Mott_Haven,_Bronx|Mott Haven]].
sentence_31: He leased land from the [[Dutch_West_India_Company|Dutch West India Company]] on the neck of the mainland immediately north of the Dutch settlement of [[History_of_Harlem#1637–1866|New Haarlem]] (on [[Manhattan_Island|Manhattan Island]]), and bought additional tracts from the local tribes.
sentence_32: He eventually accumulated 500 acres (200 ha) between the [[Harlem_River|Harlem River]] and the Aquahung, which became known as Bronck's River or the [[Bronx_River|Bronx]] [River].
sentence_33: Dutch and English settlers referred to the area as Bronck's Land.
sentence_34: The American poet [[William_Bronk|William Bronk]] was a descendant of Pieter Bronck, either Jonas Bronck's son or his younger brother, but most probably a nephew or cousin, as there was an age difference of 16 years.
sentence_35: Much work on the Swedish claim has been undertaken by Brian G. Andersson, former Commissioner of NYC's Dept.
sentence_36: of Records, who assisted in organizing a 375th Anniversary celebration in Bronck's hometown in 2014.
sentence_37: The Bronx is referred to with the [[Article_(grammar)|definite article]] as "The Bronx", both legally and colloquially.
sentence_38: The County of Bronx does not place "The" immediately before "Bronx" in formal references, unlike the coextensive Borough of the Bronx, nor does the [[United_States_Postal_Service|United States Postal Service]] in its database of Bronx addresses (the city and state mailing-address format is simply "Bronx, NY").
sentence_39: The region was apparently named after the [[Bronx_River|Bronx River]] and first appeared in the "Annexed District of The Bronx" created in 1874 out of part of [[Westchester_County,_New_York|Westchester County]].
sentence_40: It was continued in the "Borough of The Bronx", which included a larger annexation from Westchester County in 1898.
sentence_41: The use of the definite article is attributed to the style of referring to rivers.
sentence_42: A time-worn story explanation for the use of the definite article in the borough's name stems from the phrase "visiting the Broncks", referring to the settler's family.
sentence_43: The capitalization of the borough's name is sometimes disputed.
sentence_44: Generally, the definite article is lowercase in place names ("the Bronx") except in official references.
sentence_45: The definite article is capitalized ("The Bronx") at the beginning of a sentence or in any other situation when a normally lowercase word would be capitalized.
sentence_46: However, some people and groups refer to the borough with a capital letter at all times, such as Bronx Borough Historian [[Lloyd_Ultan_(historian)|Lloyd Ultan]], [[The_Bronx_County_Historical_Society|The Bronx County Historical Society]], and the Bronx-based organization Great and Glorious Grand Army of The Bronx.
sentence_47: These people say that the definite article is part of the proper name.
sentence_48: In particular, the Great and Glorious Grand Army of The Bronx is leading efforts to make the city refer to the borough with an uppercase definite article in all uses, comparing the lowercase article in the Bronx's name to "not capitalizing the 's' in 'Staten Island.'"
sentence_49: See also: [[Timeline_of_the_Bronx|Timeline of the Bronx]]
sentence_50: European colonization of the Bronx began in 1639.
sentence_51: The Bronx was originally part of [[Westchester_County,_New_York|Westchester County]], but it was ceded to [[Manhattan|New York County]] in two major parts ([[West_Bronx|West Bronx]], 1874 and East Bronx, 1895) before it became Bronx County.
sentence_52: Originally, the area was part of the Lenape's [[Lenapehoking|Lenapehoking]] territory inhabited by [[Siwanoy|Siwanoy]] of the [[Wappinger|Wappinger]] Confederacy.
sentence_53: Over time, European colonists converted the borough into farmlands.
sentence_54: See also: [[List_of_former_municipalities_in_New_York_City|List of former municipalities in New York City]]
sentence_55: The development of the Bronx is directly connected to its strategic location between [[New_England|New England]] and New York ([[Manhattan|Manhattan]]).
sentence_56: Control over the bridges across the Harlem River plagued the period of British colonial rule.
sentence_57: The King's Bridge, built in 1693 where [[Broadway_(Manhattan)|Broadway]] reached the [[Spuyten_Duyvil_Creek|Spuyten Duyvil Creek]], was a possession of [[Frederick_Philipse|Frederick Philipse]], lord of [[Philipse_Manor_Hall_State_Historic_Site|Philipse Manor]].
sentence_58: The tolls were resented by local farmers on both sides of the creek, and in 1759, Jacobus Dyckman and [[Benjamin_Palmer|Benjamin Palmer]] led them in building a free bridge across the Harlem River.
sentence_59: After the [[American_Revolutionary_War|American Revolutionary War]], the King's Bridge toll was abolished.
sentence_60: The territory now contained within Bronx County was originally part of [[Westchester_County,_New_York|Westchester County]], one of the 12 original counties of the English [[Province_of_New_York|Province of New York]].
sentence_61: The present Bronx County was contained in the town of Westchester and parts of the towns in Yonkers, [[Eastchester_(town),_New_York|Eastchester]], and [[Pelham,_New_York|Pelham]].
sentence_62: In 1846, a new town was created by division of Westchester, called West Farms.
sentence_63: The town of [[Morrisania,_Bronx|Morrisania]] was created, in turn, from West Farms in 1855.
sentence_64: In 1873, the town of [[Kingsbridge,_Bronx|Kingsbridge]] was established within the former borders of Yonkers, roughly corresponding to the modern Bronx neighborhoods of Kingsbridge, [[Riverdale,_Bronx|Riverdale]], and [[Woodlawn_Heights,_Bronx|Woodlawn Heights]].
sentence_65: Among famous settlers in the Bronx during the 19th and early 20th centuries were author [[Willa_Cather|Willa Cather]], tobacco merchant [[Pierre_Lorillard_IV|Pierre Lorillard]], and inventor [[Jordan_L._Mott|Jordan L. Mott]], who established [[Mott_Haven|Mott Haven]] to house the workers at his iron works.
sentence_66: The consolidation of the Bronx into New York City proceeded in two stages.
sentence_67: In 1873, the state legislature annexed Kingsbridge, West Farms, and Morrisania to New York, effective in 1874; the three towns were soon abolished in the process.
sentence_68: The whole territory east of the Bronx River was annexed to the city in 1895, three years before New York's consolidation with [[Brooklyn|Brooklyn]], [[Queens|Queens]], and [[Staten_Island|Staten Island]].
sentence_69: This included the Town of Westchester (which had voted against consolidation in 1894) and portions of Eastchester and Pelham.
sentence_70: The nautical community of [[City_Island,_Bronx|City Island]] voted to join the city in 1896.
sentence_71: On January 1, 1898, the consolidated [[City_of_Greater_New_York|City of New York]] was born, including the Bronx as one of the five distinct [[Borough_(New_York_City)|boroughs]] (at the same time, the Bronx's territory moved from Westchester County into [[New_York_County|New York County]], which already contained Manhattan and the rest of pre-1874 New York City).
sentence_72: On April 19, 1912, those parts of New York County which had been annexed from Westchester County in the past decades were newly constituted as Bronx County, the 62nd and last county to be created by the state, effective in 1914.
sentence_73: Bronx County's courts opened for business on January 2, 1914 (the same day that [[John_P._Mitchel|John P. Mitchel]] started work as [[Mayor_of_New_York_City|Mayor of New York City]]).
sentence_74: [[Marble_Hill,_Manhattan|Marble Hill, Manhattan]] was now connected to the Bronx, but it did not become part of that county by a historical accident due to changes in waterways.
sentence_75: The history of the Bronx during the 20th century may be divided into four periods: a boom period during 1900–29, with a population growth by a factor of six from 200,000 in 1900 to 1.3 million in 1930.
sentence_76: The [[Great_Depression|Great Depression]] and post World War II years saw a slowing of growth leading into an eventual decline.
sentence_77: The mid to late century were hard times, as the Bronx changed during 1950–85 from a predominantly moderate-income to a predominantly lower-income area with high rates of violent crime and poverty in some areas.
sentence_78: The Bronx has experienced an economic and developmental resurgence starting in the late 1980s that continues into today.
sentence_79: The Bronx was a mostly rural area for many generations, with small farms supplying the city markets.
sentence_80: In the late 19th century, however, it grew into a railroad suburb.
sentence_81: Faster transportation enabled rapid population growth in the late 19th century, involving the move from horse-drawn street cars to elevated railways and the subway system, which linked to Manhattan in 1904.
sentence_82: The South Bronx was a manufacturing center for many years and was noted as a center of [[Piano|piano]] manufacturing in the early part of the 20th century.
sentence_83: In 1919, the Bronx was the site of 63 piano factories employing more than 5,000 workers.
sentence_84: At the end of [[World_War_I|World War I]], the Bronx hosted the rather small [[Bronx_International_Exposition_of_Science,_Arts_and_Industries|1918 World's Fair]] at 177th Street and DeVoe Avenue.
sentence_85: The Bronx underwent rapid urban growth after World War I. Extensions of the [[New_York_City_Subway|New York City Subway]] contributed to the increase in population as thousands of immigrants came to the Bronx, resulting in a major boom in residential construction.
sentence_86: Among these groups, many [[Irish_Americans|Irish Americans]], [[Italian_Americans|Italian Americans]], and especially [[Jewish_Americans|Jewish Americans]] settled here.
sentence_87: In addition, [[French_American|French]], [[German_Americans|German]], [[Polish_American|Polish]], and other immigrants moved into the borough.
sentence_88: As evidence of the change in population, by 1937, 592,185 Jews lived in the Bronx (43.9% of the borough's population), while only 54,000 Jews lived in the borough in 2011.
sentence_89: Many synagogues still stand in the Bronx, but most have been converted to other uses.
sentence_90: [[Rum-running|Bootleggers]] and gangs were active in the Bronx during [[Prohibition_in_the_United_States|Prohibition]] (1920–33).
sentence_91: Irish, Italian, Jewish, and Polish gangs smuggled in most of the illegal whiskey, and the oldest sections of the borough became poverty-stricken.
sentence_92: Between 1930 and 1960, moderate and upper income Bronxites (predominantly non-Hispanic Whites) began to [[White_flight|relocate]] from the southwestern neighborhoods of the borough.
sentence_93: This migration has left a mostly poor African American and Hispanic (largely [[Puerto_Ricans_in_the_United_States|Puerto Rican]]) population in the West Bronx.
sentence_94: One significant factor that shifted the racial and economic demographics was the construction of [[Co-op_City,_Bronx|Co-op City]], built with the intent of housing middle-class residents in family-sized apartments.
sentence_95: The high-rise complex played a significant role in draining middle-class residents from older tenement buildings in the borough's southern and western fringes.
sentence_96: Most predominantly non-Hispanic White communities today [[Demographics_of_the_Bronx|are located in the eastern and northwestern sections of the borough]].
sentence_97: From the early 1960s to the early 1980s, the [[Quality_of_life|quality of life]] changed for some Bronx residents.
sentence_98: Historians and social scientists have suggested many factors, including the theory that [[Robert_Moses|Robert Moses]]' [[Cross_Bronx_Expressway|Cross Bronx Expressway]] destroyed existing residential neighborhoods and created instant slums, as put forward in [[Robert_Caro|Robert Caro]]'s biography [[The_Power_Broker|The Power Broker]].
sentence_99: Another factor in the Bronx's decline may have been the development of [[High-rise|high-rise]] [[Public_housing_in_the_United_States_and_Canada|housing projects]], particularly in the [[South_Bronx|South Bronx]].
sentence_100: Yet another factor may have been a reduction in the real estate listings and property-related financial services offered in some areas of the Bronx, such as mortgage loans or insurance policies—a process known as [[Redlining|redlining]].
sentence_101: Others have suggested a "[[Planned_shrinkage|planned shrinkage]]" of municipal services, such as fire-fighting.
sentence_102: There was also much debate as to whether rent control laws had made it less profitable (or more costly) for landlords to maintain existing buildings with their existing tenants than to abandon or destroy those buildings.
sentence_103: In the 1970s, parts of the Bronx were plagued by a wave of arson.
sentence_104: The burning of buildings was predominantly in the poorest communities, such as the South Bronx.
sentence_105: One explanation of what occurred was that landlords decided to burn their low property-value buildings and take the insurance money, as it was more lucrative to get insurance money than to refurbish or sell a building in a severely distressed area.
sentence_106: The Bronx became identified with a high rate of poverty and unemployment, which was mainly a persistent problem in the South Bronx..
sentence_107: There were also cases where tenants burnt themselves out of their apts/buildings to qualify themselves for emergency relocations by City social service agencies to better lodgings.
sentence_108: Out of 289 census tracts in the Bronx borough, 7 tracts lost more than 97% of their buildings to fire and abandonment between 1970 and 1980; another 44 tracts had more than 50% of their buildings meet the same fate.
sentence_109: By the early 1980s, the South Bronx was considered one of the most blighted urban areas in the country, with a loss of 60% of the population and 40% of housing units.
sentence_110: However, starting in the 1990s, many burned-out and run-down tenements were replaced by multi-unit housing.
sentence_111: Since the late 1980s, significant development has occurred in the Bronx, first stimulated by the city's "Ten-Year Housing Plan" and community members working to rebuild the social, economic and environmental infrastructure by creating [[Affordable_housing|affordable housing]].
sentence_112: Groups affiliated with churches in the South Bronx erected the Nehemiah Homes with about 1,000 units.
sentence_113: The grass roots organization Nos Quedamos' endeavor known as Melrose Commons began to rebuild areas in the South Bronx.
sentence_114: The [[IRT_White_Plains_Road_Line|IRT White Plains Road Line]] ([[2_(New_York_City_Subway_service)|2]] and ​[[5_(New_York_City_Subway_service)|5]] trains) began to show an increase in riders.
sentence_115: Chains such as [[Marshalls|Marshalls]], [[Staples_Inc.|Staples]], and [[Target_Corporation|Target]] opened stores in the Bronx.
sentence_116: More bank branches opened in the Bronx as a whole (rising from 106 in 1997 to 149 in 2007), although not primarily in poor or minority neighborhoods, while the Bronx still has fewer branches per person than other boroughs.
sentence_117: In 1997, the Bronx was designated an [[All_America_City|All America City]] by the National Civic League, acknowledging its comeback from the decline of the mid-century.
sentence_118: In 2006, [[The_New_York_Times|The New York Times]] reported that "construction cranes have become the borough's new visual metaphor, replacing the window decals of the 1980s in which pictures of potted plants and drawn curtains were placed in the windows of abandoned buildings."
sentence_119: The borough has experienced substantial new building construction since 2002.
sentence_120: Between 2002 and June 2007, 33,687 new units of housing were built or were under way and $4.8 billion has been invested in new housing.
sentence_121: In the first six months of 2007 alone total investment in new residential development was $965 million and 5,187 residential units were scheduled to be completed.
sentence_122: Much of the new development is springing up in formerly vacant lots across the South Bronx.
sentence_123: In addition, there is a revitalization of the existing housing market in areas such as Hunts Point, the Lower Concourse, and the neighborhoods surrounding the Third Avenue Bridge as people buy apartments and renovate them.
sentence_124: Several boutique and chain hotels have opened in recent years in the [[South_Bronx|South Bronx]].
sentence_125: New developments are underway.
sentence_126: The Bronx General Post Office on the corner of the Grand Concourse and East 149th Street is being converted into a market place, boutiques, restaurants and office space with a USPS concession.
sentence_127: The [[Kingsbridge_Armory|Kingsbridge Armory]], often cited as the largest armory in the world, is scheduled for redevelopment as the Kingsbridge National Ice Center.
sentence_128: Under consideration for future development is the construction of a platform over the [[New_York_City_Subway|New York City Subway]]'s [[Concourse_Yard|Concourse Yard]] adjacent to [[Lehman_College|Lehman College]].
sentence_129: The construction would permit approximately 2,000,000 square feet (190,000 m) of development and would cost US$350–500 million.
sentence_130: Main article: [[Geography_of_New_York_City|Geography of New York City]]
sentence_131: According to the [[U.S._Census_Bureau|U.S.
sentence_132: Census Bureau]], Bronx County has a total area of 57 square miles (150 km), of which 42 square miles (110 km) is land and 15 square miles (39 km) (27%) is water.
sentence_133: The Bronx is New York City's northernmost borough, New York State's southernmost mainland county and the only part of New York City that is almost entirely situated on the North American mainland.
sentence_134: Its [[Bedrock|bedrock]] is primarily [[Gneiss|Fordham gneiss]], a high-grade heavily banded metamorphic rock containing significant amounts of [[Feldspar|pink feldspar]].
sentence_135: Marble Hill – politically part of Manhattan but now physically attached to the Bronx – is so-called because of the formation of [[Inwood_marble|Inwood marble]] there as well as in [[Inwood,_Manhattan|Inwood, Manhattan]] and parts of the Bronx and Westchester County.
sentence_136: The [[Hudson_River|Hudson River]] separates the Bronx on the west from [[Alpine,_New_Jersey|Alpine]], [[Tenafly,_New_Jersey|Tenafly]] and [[Englewood_Cliffs|Englewood Cliffs]] in [[Bergen_County,_New_Jersey|Bergen County, New Jersey]]; the [[Harlem_River|Harlem River]] separates it from the island of [[Manhattan|Manhattan]] to the southwest; the [[East_River|East River]] separates it from [[Queens|Queens]] to the southeast; and to the east, [[Long_Island_Sound|Long Island Sound]] separates it from [[Nassau_County,_New_York|Nassau County]] in western Long Island.
sentence_137: Directly north of the Bronx are (from west to east) the adjoining [[Westchester_County,_New_York|Westchester County]] communities of Yonkers, [[Mount_Vernon,_New_York|Mount Vernon]], [[Pelham_Manor|Pelham Manor]] and [[New_Rochelle|New Rochelle]].
sentence_138: (There is also a short southern land boundary with [[Marble_Hill,_Manhattan|Marble Hill]] in the Borough of Manhattan, over the filled-in former course of the [[Spuyten_Duyvil_Creek|Spuyten Duyvil Creek]].
sentence_139: Marble Hill's postal ZIP code, telephonic [[Area_codes|area codes]] and fire service, however, are shared with the Bronx and not Manhattan.)
sentence_140: The [[Bronx_River|Bronx River]] flows south from Westchester County through the borough, emptying into the East River; it is the only entirely [[Freshwater|freshwater]] river in New York City.
sentence_141: A smaller river, the [[Hutchinson_River|Hutchinson River]] (named after the religious leader [[Anne_Hutchinson|Anne Hutchinson]], killed along its banks in 1641), passes through the East Bronx and empties into [[Eastchester_Bay|Eastchester Bay]].
sentence_142: The Bronx also includes several small islands in the [[East_River|East River]] and [[Long_Island_Sound|Long Island Sound]], such as [[City_Island,_New_York|City Island]] and [[Hart_Island_(New_York)|Hart Island]].
sentence_143: [[Rikers_Island|Rikers Island]] in the East River, home to the large jail complex for the entire city, is also part of the Bronx.
sentence_144: See also: [[List_of_smaller_islands_in_New_York_City|List of smaller islands in New York City]]
sentence_145: The Bronx's highest elevation at 280 feet (85 m) is in the northwest corner, west of [[Van_Cortlandt_Park|Van Cortlandt Park]] and in the Chapel Farm area near the [[Riverdale_Country_School|Riverdale Country School]].
sentence_146: The opposite (southeastern) side of the Bronx has four large low peninsulas or "necks" of low-lying land that jut into the waters of the East River and were once [[Salt_marsh|salt marsh]]: Hunt's Point, Clason's Point, Screvin's Neck and [[Throggs_Neck|Throggs Neck]].
sentence_147: Further up the coastline, [[Rodman's_Neck|Rodman's Neck]] lies between [[Pelham_Bay_Park|Pelham Bay Park]] in the northeast and [[City_Island,_New_York|City Island]].
sentence_148: The Bronx's irregular shoreline extends for 75 square miles (194 km).
sentence_149: See also: :Category:Parks in the Bronx
sentence_150: Although Bronx County was the third most densely populated county in the United States as of 2006 (after [[Manhattan|Manhattan]] and [[Brooklyn|Brooklyn]]), 7,000 acres (28 km) of the Bronx—about one-fifth of the Bronx's area, and one-quarter of its land area—is given over to parkland.
sentence_151: The vision of a system of major Bronx parks connected by park-like thoroughfares is usually attributed to [[John_Mullaly|John Mullaly]].
sentence_152: [[Woodlawn_Cemetery_(Bronx,_New_York)|Woodlawn Cemetery]], one of the largest cemeteries in New York City, sits on the western bank of the [[Bronx_River|Bronx River]] near Yonkers.
sentence_153: It opened in 1863, at a time when the Bronx was still considered a rural area.
sentence_154: The northern side of the borough includes the largest park in New York City—[[Pelham_Bay_Park|Pelham Bay Park]], which includes [[Orchard_Beach,_New_York|Orchard Beach]]—and the third-largest, [[Van_Cortlandt_Park|Van Cortlandt Park]], which is west of Woodlawn Cemetery and borders Yonkers.
sentence_155: Also in the northern Bronx, [[Wave_Hill_(New_York)|Wave Hill]], the former estate of [[George_Walbridge_Perkins|George W. Perkins]]—known for a historic house, gardens, changing site-specific art installations and concerts—overlooks the [[New_Jersey_Palisades|New Jersey Palisades]] from a promontory on the [[Hudson_River|Hudson]] in [[Riverdale,_Bronx|Riverdale]].
sentence_156: Nearer the borough's center, and along the [[Bronx_River|Bronx River]], is [[Bronx_Park|Bronx Park]]; its northern end houses the [[New_York_Botanical_Gardens|New York Botanical Gardens]], which preserve the last patch of the original [[Tsuga|hemlock]] forest that once covered the entire county, and its southern end the [[Bronx_Zoo|Bronx Zoo]], the largest urban zoological gardens in the United States.
sentence_157: Just south of [[Van_Cortlandt_Park|Van Cortlandt Park]] is the [[Jerome_Park_Reservoir|Jerome Park Reservoir]], surrounded by 2 miles (3 km) of stone walls and bordering several small parks in the [[Bedford_Park,_Bronx|Bedford Park]] neighborhood; the [[Reservoir|reservoir]] was built in the 1890s on the site of the former [[Jerome_Park_Racetrack|Jerome Park Racetrack]].
sentence_158: Further south is [[Crotona_Park|Crotona Park]], home to a 3.3-acre (1.3 ha) lake, 28 species of trees, and a large swimming pool.
sentence_159: The land for these parks, and many others, was bought by New York City in 1888, while land was still open and inexpensive, in anticipation of future needs and future pressures for development.
sentence_160: Some of the acquired land was set aside for the [[Grand_Concourse_(Bronx)|Grand Concourse]] and Pelham Parkway, the first of a series of boulevards and [[Parkway|parkways]] (thoroughfares lined with trees, vegetation and greenery).
sentence_161: Later projects included the Bronx River Parkway, which developed a road while restoring the riverbank and reducing pollution, [[Mosholu_Parkway|Mosholu Parkway]] and the [[Henry_Hudson_Parkway|Henry Hudson Parkway]].
sentence_162: In 2006, a five-year, $220-million program of capital improvements and natural restoration in 70 Bronx parks was begun (financed by water and sewer revenues) as part of an agreement that allowed a water filtration plant under Mosholu Golf Course in Van Cortlandt Park.
sentence_163: One major focus is on opening more of the [[Bronx_River|Bronx River]]'s banks and restoring them to a natural state.
sentence_164: See also: [[List_of_Bronx_neighborhoods|List of Bronx neighborhoods]], [[Bronx_Community_Board|Bronx Community Board]], and [[Timeline_of_town_creation_in_Downstate_New_York|Timeline of town creation in Downstate New York]]
sentence_165: The number, locations, and boundaries of the Bronx's neighborhoods (many of them sitting on the sites of 19th-century villages) have become unclear with time and successive waves of newcomers.
sentence_166: In 2006, Manny Fernandez of [[The_New_York_Times|The New York Times]] wrote,
sentence_167: Notable Bronx neighborhoods include the [[South_Bronx|South Bronx]]; Little Italy on [[Arthur_Avenue|Arthur Avenue]] in the [[Belmont,_Bronx|Belmont]] section; and [[Riverdale,_Bronx|Riverdale]].
sentence_168: Main article: East Bronx
sentence_169: ([[Bronx_Community_Board|Bronx Community Districts]] 9 [south central], 10 [east], 11 [east central] and 12 [north central] )
sentence_170: East of the [[Bronx_River|Bronx River]], the borough is relatively flat and includes four large low peninsulas, or 'necks,' of low-lying land which jut into the waters of the East River and were once saltmarsh: Hunts Point, Clason's Point, Screvin's Neck (Castle Hill Point) and [[Throgs_Neck|Throgs Neck]].
sentence_171: The East Bronx has older tenement buildings, low income public housing complexes, and multifamily homes, as well as single family homes.
sentence_172: It includes New York City's largest park: [[Pelham_Bay_Park|Pelham Bay Park]] along the [[Westchester_County,_New_York|Westchester]]-Bronx border.
sentence_173: Neighborhoods include: [[Clason's_Point,_Bronx|Clason's Point]], [[Harding_Park,_Bronx|Harding Park]], [[Soundview,_Bronx|Soundview]], [[Castle_Hill,_Bronx|Castle Hill]], [[Parkchester,_Bronx|Parkchester]] ([[Bronx_Community_Board_9|Community District 9]]); [[Throggs_Neck|Throggs Neck]], [[Country_Club,_Bronx|Country Club]], [[City_Island,_Bronx|City Island]], [[Pelham_Bay|Pelham Bay]], [[Edgewater_Park_(Bronx)|Edgewater Park]], [[Co-op_City,_Bronx|Co-op City]] ([[Bronx_Community_Board_10|Community District 10]]); [[Westchester_Square,_Bronx|Westchester Square]], [[Van_Nest|Van Nest]], [[Pelham_Parkway,_Bronx|Pelham Parkway]], [[Morris_Park,_Bronx|Morris Park]] ([[Bronx_Community_Board_11|Community District 11]]); [[Williamsbridge,_Bronx|Williamsbridge]], [[Eastchester,_Bronx|Eastchester]], [[Baychester,_Bronx|Baychester]], [[Edenwald,_Bronx|Edenwald]] and [[Wakefield,_Bronx|Wakefield]] ([[Bronx_Community_Board_12|Community District 12]]).
sentence_174: Main articles: [[City_Island,_Bronx|City Island, Bronx]] and [[Hart_Island_(Bronx)|Hart Island (Bronx)]]
sentence_175: ([[Bronx_Community_Board_10|Bronx Community District 10]])
sentence_176: City Island is located east of [[Pelham_Bay_Park|Pelham Bay Park]] in [[Long_Island_Sound|Long Island Sound]] and is known for its seafood restaurants and private waterfront homes.
sentence_177: City Island's single shopping street, City Island Avenue, is reminiscent of a small New England town.
sentence_178: It is connected to [[Rodman's_Neck|Rodman's Neck]] on the mainland by the [[City_Island_Bridge|City Island Bridge]].
sentence_179: East of City Island is [[Hart_Island_(New_York)|Hart Island]], which is uninhabited and not open to the public.
sentence_180: It once served as a prison and now houses New York City's [[Potter's_field|potter's field]] for unclaimed bodies.
sentence_181: Main article: [[West_Bronx|West Bronx]]
sentence_182: ([[Bronx_Community_Board|Bronx Community Districts]] 1 to 8, progressing roughly from south to northwest)
sentence_183: The western parts of the Bronx are hillier and are dominated by a series of parallel ridges, running south to north.
sentence_184: The West Bronx has older apartment buildings, low income public housing complexes, multifamily homes in its lower income areas as well as larger single family homes in more affluent areas such as [[Riverdale,_Bronx|Riverdale]] and [[Fieldston,_Bronx|Fieldston]].
sentence_185: It includes New York City's third-largest park: [[Van_Cortlandt_Park|Van Cortlandt Park]] along the Westchester-Bronx border.
sentence_186: The [[Grand_Concourse_(Bronx)|Grand Concourse]], a wide boulevard, runs through it, north to south.
sentence_187: ([[Bronx_Community_Board|Bronx Community Districts]] 7 [between the [[Bronx_River|Bronx]] and [[Harlem_River|Harlem Rivers]] and 8 [facing the [[Hudson_River|Hudson River]] – plus part of Board 12)
sentence_188: Neighborhoods include: Fordham-Bedford, [[Bedford_Park,_Bronx|Bedford Park]], [[Norwood,_Bronx|Norwood]], [[Kingsbridge_Heights|Kingsbridge Heights]] (Community District 7), [[Kingsbridge,_Bronx|Kingsbridge]], [[Riverdale,_Bronx|Riverdale]] ([[Bronx_Community_Board_8|Community District 8]]), and [[Woodlawn_Heights,_Bronx|Woodlawn Heights]] ([[Bronx_Community_Board_12|Community District 12]]).
sentence_189: ([[Marble_Hill,_Manhattan|Marble Hill, Manhattan]] is now connected by land to the Bronx rather than Manhattan and is served by Bronx Community District 8.)
sentence_190: Main article: [[South_Bronx|South Bronx]]
sentence_191: ([[Bronx_Community_Board|Bronx Community Districts]] 1 to 6 plus part of CD 7—progressing northwards, CDs 2, 3 and 6 border the [[Bronx_River|Bronx River]] from its mouth to [[Bronx_Park|Bronx Park]], while 1, 4, 5 and 7 face Manhattan across the [[Harlem_River|Harlem River]])
sentence_192: Like other [[Neighborhoods_in_New_York_City|neighborhoods in New York City]], the South Bronx has no official boundaries.
sentence_193: The name has been used to represent poverty in the Bronx and is applied to progressively more northern places so that by the 2000s, [[Fordham_Road|Fordham Road]] was often used as a northern limit.
sentence_194: The [[Bronx_River|Bronx River]] more consistently forms an eastern boundary.
sentence_195: The South Bronx has many high-density apartment buildings, low income public housing complexes, and multi-unit homes.
sentence_196: The South Bronx is home to the [[Bronx_County_Courthouse|Bronx County Courthouse]], Borough Hall, and other government buildings, as well as [[Yankee_Stadium|Yankee Stadium]].
sentence_197: The [[Cross_Bronx_Expressway|Cross Bronx Expressway]] bisects it, east to west.
sentence_198: The South Bronx has some of the poorest neighborhoods in the country, as well as very high crime areas.
sentence_199: Neighborhoods include: [[The_Hub,_Bronx|The Hub]] (a retail district at [[Third_Avenue|Third Avenue]] and East 149th Street), [[Port_Morris,_Bronx|Port Morris]], [[Mott_Haven,_Bronx|Mott Haven]] ([[Bronx_Community_Board_1|Community District 1]]), [[Melrose,_Bronx|Melrose]] ([[Bronx_Community_Board_1|Community District 1]] & [[Bronx_Community_Board_3|Community District 3]]), [[Morrisania|Morrisania]], [[East_Morrisania,_Bronx|East Morrisania]] [also known as Crotona Park East] ([[Bronx_Community_Board_3|Community District 3]]), [[Hunts_Point,_Bronx|Hunts Point]], [[Longwood,_Bronx|Longwood]] ([[Bronx_Community_Board_2|Community District 2]]), [[Highbridge,_Bronx|Highbridge]], [[Concourse,_Bronx|Concourse]] ([[Bronx_Community_Board_4|Community District 4]]), [[West_Farms,_Bronx|West Farms]], [[Belmont,_Bronx|Belmont]], [[East_Tremont,_Bronx|East Tremont]] ([[Bronx_Community_Board_6|Community District 6]]), [[Tremont,_Bronx|Tremont]], [[Morris_Heights,_Bronx|Morris Heights]] ([[Bronx_Community_Board_5|Community District 5]]), [[University_Heights,_Bronx|University Heights]].

sentence_202: See also: [[Transportation_in_New_York_City|Transportation in New York City]]
sentence_203: The Bronx [[Street_grid|street grid]] is irregular.
sentence_204: Like the northernmost part of [[Upper_Manhattan|upper Manhattan]], the [[West_Bronx|West Bronx]]'s hilly terrain leaves a relatively free-style street grid.
sentence_205: Much of the West Bronx's street numbering carries over from upper Manhattan, but does not match it exactly; East 132nd Street is the lowest numbered street in the Bronx.
sentence_206: This dates from the mid-19th century when the southwestern area of [[Westchester_County,_New_York|Westchester County]] west of the Bronx River, was incorporated into New York City and known as the Northside.
sentence_207: The East Bronx is considerably flatter, and the street layout tends to be more regular.
sentence_208: Only the [[Wakefield,_Bronx|Wakefield]] neighborhood picks up the street numbering, albeit at a misalignment due to Tremont Avenue's layout.
sentence_209: At the same diagonal latitude, West 262nd Street in Riverdale matches East 237th Street in Wakefield.
sentence_210: Three major north–south thoroughfares run between Manhattan and the Bronx: [[Third_Avenue|Third Avenue]], [[Park_Avenue|Park Avenue]], and [[Broadway_(Manhattan)|Broadway]].
sentence_211: Other major north–south roads include the [[Grand_Concourse_(Bronx)|Grand Concourse]], [[Jerome_Avenue|Jerome Avenue]], [[Sedgwick_Avenue|Sedgwick Avenue]], [[Webster_Avenue|Webster Avenue]], and White Plains Road.
sentence_212: Major east-west thoroughfares include [[Mosholu_Parkway|Mosholu Parkway]], [[Gun_Hill_Road_(Bronx)|Gun Hill Road]], [[Fordham_Road|Fordham Road]], Pelham Parkway, and Tremont Avenue.
sentence_213: Most east–west streets are prefixed with either East or West, to indicate on which side of Jerome Avenue they lie (continuing the similar system in Manhattan, which uses [[Fifth_Avenue|Fifth Avenue]] as the dividing line).
sentence_214: The historic [[Boston_Post_Road|Boston Post Road]], part of the long pre-revolutionary road connecting [[Boston|Boston]] with other northeastern cities, runs east–west in some places, and sometimes northeast–southwest.
sentence_215: [[Mosholu_Parkway|Mosholu]] and Pelham Parkways, with [[Bronx_Park|Bronx Park]] between them, [[Van_Cortlandt_Park|Van Cortlandt Park]] to the west and [[Pelham_Bay_Park|Pelham Bay Park]] to the east, are also linked by [[Bridle_path|bridle paths]].
sentence_216: As of the 2000 Census, approximately 61.6% of all Bronx households do not have access to a car.
sentence_217: Citywide, the percentage of autoless households is 55%.
sentence_218: Several major [[Limited_access|limited access]] highways traverse the Bronx.
sentence_219: These include:
sentence_220: Thirteen bridges and three tunnels connect the Bronx to Manhattan, and three bridges connect the Bronx to [[Queens|Queens]].
sentence_221: These are, from west to east:
sentence_222: To Manhattan: the [[Spuyten_Duyvil_Bridge|Spuyten Duyvil Bridge]], the [[Henry_Hudson_Bridge|Henry Hudson Bridge]], the [[Broadway_Bridge_(Manhattan)|Broadway Bridge]], the [[University_Heights_Bridge|University Heights Bridge]], the [[Washington_Bridge|Washington Bridge]], the Alexander Hamilton Bridge, the [[High_Bridge_(New_York_City)|High Bridge]], the Concourse Tunnel, the [[Macombs_Dam_Bridge|Macombs Dam Bridge]], the [[145th_Street_Bridge|145th Street Bridge]], the [[149th_Street_Tunnel|149th Street Tunnel]], the [[Madison_Avenue_Bridge|Madison Avenue Bridge]], the [[Park_Avenue_Bridge_(New_York_City)|Park Avenue Bridge]], the [[Lexington_Avenue_Tunnel|Lexington Avenue Tunnel]], the [[Third_Avenue_Bridge_(Manhattan)|Third Avenue Bridge]] (southbound traffic only), and the [[Willis_Avenue_Bridge|Willis Avenue Bridge]] (northbound traffic only).
sentence_223: To both Manhattan and Queens: the [[Robert_F._Kennedy_Bridge|Robert F. Kennedy Bridge]], formerly known as the Triborough Bridge.
sentence_224: To Queens: the [[Bronx–Whitestone_Bridge|Bronx–Whitestone Bridge]] and the [[Throgs_Neck_Bridge|Throgs Neck Bridge]].
sentence_225: The Bronx is served by seven [[New_York_City_Subway|New York City Subway]] services along six physical lines, with [[List_of_New_York_City_Subway_stations_in_the_Bronx|70 stations in the Bronx]]:

list.value: [[IRT_White_Plains_Road_Line|IRT White Plains Road Line]] ([[2_(New_York_City_Subway_service)|2]] and ​[[5_(New_York_City_Subway_service)|5]] trains)

sentence_226: There are also many [[MTA_Regional_Bus_Operations|MTA Regional Bus Operations]] bus routes in the Bronx.
sentence_227: This includes [[List_of_bus_routes_in_the_Bronx|local and express routes]] as well as [[Bee-Line_Bus_System|Bee-Line Bus System]] routes.
sentence_228: Two [[Metro-North_Railroad|Metro-North Railroad]] commuter rail lines (the [[Harlem_Line|Harlem Line]] and the [[Hudson_Line_(Metro-North)|Hudson Line]]) serve 11 stations in the Bronx.
sentence_229: ([[Marble_Hill_(Metro-North_station)|Marble Hill]], between the [[Spuyten_Duyvil_(Metro-North_station)|Spuyten Duyvil]] and [[University_Heights_(Metro-North_station)|University Heights]] stations, is actually in the only part of Manhattan connected to the mainland.)
sentence_230: In addition, trains serving the [[New_Haven_Line|New Haven Line]] stop at [[Fordham_(Metro-North_station)|Fordham Plaza]].
sentence_231: As part of [[Penn_Station_Access|Penn Station Access]], the 2018 MTA budget funded construction of four new stops along the New Haven Line to serve [[Hunts_Point,_Bronx|Hunts Point]], [[Parkchester,_Bronx|Parkchester]], [[Morris_Park,_Bronx|Morris Park]], and [[Co-op_City,_Bronx|Co-op City]].
sentence_232: In 2018, [[NYC_Ferry|NYC Ferry]]'s Soundview line opened, connecting the [[Soundview,_Bronx|Soundview]] landing in [[Clason_Point|Clason Point Park]] to three [[East_River|East River]] locations in Manhattan.
sentence_233: The ferry is operated by Hornblower Cruises.

sentence_235: See also: [[List_of_people_from_the_Bronx|List of people from the Bronx]]
sentence_236: The Census Bureau considers the Bronx to be the most diverse area in the country.
sentence_237: There is an 89.7 percent chance that any two residents, chosen at random, would be of different race or ethnicity.
sentence_238: The borough's most populous racial group, white, declined from 99.3% in 1920 to 44.9% in 2018.
sentence_239: The Bronx contains 532,487 housing units, with a median value of $371,800, and with an owner-occupancy rate of 19.7%, the lowest of the five boroughs.
sentence_240: There are 495,356 households, with 2.85 persons per household.
sentence_241: 59.3% of residents speak a language besides English at home, the highest rate of the five boroughs.
sentence_242: In the Bronx, the population is 7.2% under 5, 17.6% 6-18, 62.4% 19–64, and 12.8% over 65.
sentence_243: 52.9% of the population is female.
sentence_244: 35.3% of residents are foreign born.
sentence_245: The per capita income is $19,721, while the median household income is $36,593, both being the lowest of the five boroughs.
sentence_246: 27.9% of residents live below the poverty line, the highest of the five boroughs.
sentence_247: According to the 2010 Census, 53.5% of Bronx's population was of Hispanic, Latino, or Spanish origin (they may be of any race); 30.1% non-Hispanic Black or African American, 10.9% of the population was non-Hispanic White, 3.4% non-Hispanic Asian, 0.6% from some other race (non-Hispanic) and 1.2% of two or more races (non-Hispanic).
sentence_248: As of 2010, 46.29% (584,463) of Bronx residents aged five and older spoke Spanish at home, while 44.02% (555,767) spoke [[English_language|English]], 2.48% (31,361) [[Languages_of_Africa|African languages]], 0.91% (11,455) [[French_language|French]], 0.90% (11,355) [[Italian_language|Italian]], 0.87% (10,946) [[Indo-Aryan_languages|various Indic languages]], 0.70% (8,836) [[Indo-European_languages|other Indo-European languages]], and [[Chinese_language|Chinese]] was spoken at home by 0.50% (6,610) of the population over the age of five.
sentence_249: In total, 55.98% (706,783) of the Bronx's population age five and older spoke a language at home other than English.
sentence_250: A Garifuna-speaking community from [[Honduras|Honduras]] and Guatemala also makes the Bronx its home.
sentence_251: According to the 2009 American Community Survey, [[White_Americans|White Americans]] of both Hispanic and non-Hispanic origin represented over one-fifth (22.9%) of the Bronx's population.
sentence_252: However, [[Non-Hispanic_whites|non-Hispanic whites]] formed under one-eighth (12.1%) of the population, down from 34.4% in 1980.
sentence_253: Out of all five boroughs, the Bronx has the lowest number and percentage of white residents.
sentence_254: 320,640 whites called the Bronx home, of which 168,570 were non-Hispanic whites.
sentence_255: The majority of the non-Hispanic European American population is of Italian and Irish descent.
sentence_256: [[Italian_American|People of Italian descent]] numbered over 55,000 individuals and made up 3.9% of the population.
sentence_257: [[Irish_American|People of Irish descent]] numbered over 43,500 individuals and made up 3.1% of the population.
sentence_258: [[German_Americans|German Americans]] and [[Polish_Americans|Polish Americans]] made up 1.4% and 0.8% of the population respectively.
sentence_259: The Bronx is the only New York City borough with a [[Hispanic_and_Latino_Americans|Hispanic]] majority, many of whom are [[Puerto_Rican_American|Puerto Ricans]] and [[Dominican_American|Dominicans]].
sentence_260: At the 2009 American Community Survey, [[Black_Americans|Black Americans]] made the second largest group in the Bronx after Hispanics and Latinos.
sentence_261: Black people of both Hispanic and non-Hispanic origin represented over one-third (35.4%) of the Bronx's population.
sentence_262: Black people of non-Hispanic origin made up 30.8% of the population.
sentence_263: Over 495,200 Black people resided in the borough, of which 430,600 were non-Hispanic Black people.
sentence_264: Over 61,000 people identified themselves as "Sub-Saharan African" in the survey, making up 4.4% of the population.
sentence_265: Native Americans are a very small minority in the borough.
sentence_266: Only some 5,560 individuals (out of the borough's 1.4 million people) are Native American, which is equal to just 0.4% of the population.
sentence_267: In addition, roughly 2,500 people are Native Americans of non-Hispanic origin.
sentence_268: In 2009, Hispanic and Latino Americans represented 52.0% of the Bronx's population.
sentence_269: Puerto Ricans represented 23.2% of the borough's population.
sentence_270: Over 72,500 Mexicans lived in the Bronx, and they formed 5.2% of the population.
sentence_271: Cubans numbered over 9,640 members and formed 0.7% of the population.
sentence_272: In addition, over 319,000 people were of various Hispanic and Latino groups, such as Dominican, Salvadoran, and so on.
sentence_273: These groups collectively represented 22.9% of the population.
sentence_274: At the 2010 Census, 53.5% of Bronx's population was of Hispanic, Latino, or Spanish origin (they may be of any race).
sentence_275: [[Asian_Americans|Asian Americans]] are a small but sizable minority in the borough.
sentence_276: Roughly 49,600 Asians make up 3.6% of the population.
sentence_277: Roughly 13,600 Indians call the Bronx home, along with 9,800 Chinese, 6,540 Filipinos, 2,260 Vietnamese, 2,010 Koreans, and 1,100 Japanese.
sentence_278: Multiracial Americans are also a sizable minority in the Bronx.
sentence_279: People of multiracial heritage number over 41,800 individuals and represent 3.0% of the population.
sentence_280: People of mixed Caucasian and African American heritage number over 6,850 members and form 0.5% of the population.
sentence_281: People of mixed Caucasian and Native American heritage number over 2,450 members and form 0.2% of the population.
sentence_282: People of mixed Caucasian and Asian heritage number over 880 members and form 0.1% of the population.
sentence_283: People of mixed African American and Native American heritage number over 1,220 members and form 0.1% of the population.
sentence_284: The [[1930_United_States_Census|Census of 1930]] counted only 1.0% (12,930) of the Bronx's population as Negro (while making no distinct counts of Hispanic or Spanish-surname residents).
sentence_285: At the 2010 Census, there were, 1,385,108 people living in Bronx, a 3.9% increase since 2000.
sentence_286: As of the [[United_States_Census|United States Census]] of 2000, there were 1,332,650 people, 463,212 households, and 314,984 families residing in the borough.
sentence_287: The [[Population_density|population density]] was 31,709.3 inhabitants per square mile (12,242.2/km).
sentence_288: There were 490,659 housing units at an average density of 11,674.8 per square mile (4,507.4/km).
sentence_289: Recent Census estimates place total population of Bronx county at 1,392,002 as of 2012.
sentence_290: There were 463,212 households, out of which 38.1% had children under the age of 18 living with them, 31.4% were married couples living together, 30.4% had a female householder with no husband present, and 32.0% were non-families.
sentence_291: 27.4% of all households were made up of individuals, and 9.4% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older.
sentence_292: The average household size was 2.78 and the average family size was 3.37.
sentence_293: The age distribution of the population in the Bronx was as follows: 29.8% under the age of 18, 10.6% from 18 to 24, 30.7% from 25 to 44, 18.8% from 45 to 64, and 10.1% 65 years of age or older.
sentence_294: The median age was 31 years.
sentence_295: For every 100 females, there were 87.0 males.
sentence_296: The 1999 [[Median_income|median income]] for a household in the borough was $27,611, and the median income for a family was $30,682.
sentence_297: Males had a median income of $31,178 versus $29,429 for females.
sentence_298: The per capita income for the borough was $13,959.
sentence_299: About 28.0% of families and 30.7% of the population were below the [[Poverty_line|poverty line]], including 41.5% of those under age 18 and 21.3% of those age 65 or over.
sentence_300: From 2015 Census data, the [[Median_income|median income]] for a household was (in 2015 dollars) $34,299.
sentence_301: Per capita income in past 12 months (in 2015 dollars): $18,456 with persons in poverty at 30.3%.
sentence_302: Per the 2016 Census data, the [[Median_income|median income]] for a household was $35,302.
sentence_303: Per capita income was cited at $18,896.
sentence_304: Main article: [[Government_of_New_York_City|Government of New York City]]
sentence_305: Since New York City's consolidation in 1898, the Bronx has been governed by the New York City Charter that provides for a "strong" [[Mayor–council_government|mayor–council system]].
sentence_306: The centralized New York City government is responsible for public education, correctional institutions, libraries, public safety, recreational facilities, sanitation, water supply, and welfare services in the Bronx.

sentence_307: The office of [[Borough_President|Borough President]] was created in the consolidation of 1898 to balance centralization with local authority.
sentence_308: Each borough president had a powerful administrative role derived from having a vote on the [[New_York_City_Board_of_Estimate|New York City Board of Estimate]], which was responsible for creating and approving the city's budget and proposals for land use.
sentence_309: In 1989 the [[Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States|Supreme Court of the United States]] declared the Board of Estimate unconstitutional on the grounds that [[Brooklyn|Brooklyn]], the most populous borough, had no greater effective representation on the Board than [[Staten_Island|Staten Island]], the least populous borough, a violation of the [[Fourteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution|Fourteenth Amendment's]] [[Equal_Protection_Clause|Equal Protection Clause]] pursuant to the high court's 1964 "one man, one vote" decision.
sentence_310: Since 1990 the Borough President has acted as an advocate for the borough at the mayoral agencies, the [[New_York_City_Council|City Council]], the New York state government, and corporations.
sentence_311: Until March 1, 2009, the Borough President of the Bronx was [[Adolfo_Carrión_Jr.|Adolfo Carrión Jr.]], elected as a [[Democratic_Party_(United_States)|Democrat]] in 2001 and 2005 before retiring early to direct the [[White_House_Office_of_Urban_Affairs_Policy|White House Office of Urban Affairs Policy]].
sentence_312: His successor, Democratic [[New_York_State_Assembly|New York State Assembly]] member [[Ruben_Diaz,_Jr.|Rubén Díaz, Jr.]], who won a special election on April 21, 2009 by a vote of 86.3% (29,420) on the "Bronx Unity" line to 13.3% (4,646) for the Republican district leader Anthony Ribustello on the "People First" line, became Borough President on May 1.
sentence_313: All of the Bronx's currently elected public officials have first won the nomination of the [[Democratic_Party_(U.S.)|Democratic Party]] (in addition to any other endorsements).
sentence_314: Local party platforms center on affordable housing, education and economic development.
sentence_315: Controversial political issues in the Bronx include environmental issues, the cost of housing, and annexation of parkland for new [[Yankee_Stadium|Yankee Stadium]].
sentence_316: Since its separation from [[New_York_County|New York County]] on January 1, 1914, the Bronx, has had, like each of the other 61 counties of New York State, its own criminal court system and [[District_attorney|District Attorney]], the chief public prosecutor who is directly elected by popular vote.
sentence_317: [[Darcel_D._Clark|Darcel D. Clark]] has been the [[Bronx_County_District_Attorney|Bronx County District Attorney]] since 2016.
sentence_318: Her predecessor was [[Robert_T._Johnson|Robert T. Johnson]], was the District Attorney from 1989 to 2015.
sentence_319: He was the first African-American District Attorney in New York State.
sentence_320: [[Membership_of_the_New_York_City_Council|Eight members]] of the [[New_York_City_Council|New York City Council]] represent districts wholly within the Bronx (11–18), while a ninth represents a Manhattan district (8) that also includes a small area of the Bronx.
sentence_321: One of those members, [[Joel_Rivera|Joel Rivera]] (District 15), has been the Council's [[Majority_Leader|Majority Leader]] since 2002.
sentence_322: In 2008, all of them were Democrats.
sentence_323: The Bronx also has twelve [[Community_boards_of_the_Bronx|Community Boards]], appointed bodies that field complaints and advise on land use and municipal facilities and services for local residents, businesses and institutions.
sentence_324: (They are listed at [[Bronx_Community_Board|Bronx Community Boards]]).

sentence_326: [[National_Journal|National Journal]]'s neutral rating system placed all of their voting records in 2005 and 2006 somewhere between very liberal and extremely liberal.
sentence_327: 11 out of 150 members of the [[New_York_State_Assembly|New York State Assembly]] (the lower house of the state legislature) represent districts wholly within the Bronx.
sentence_328: Six [[New_York_State_Senate|State Senators]] out of 62 represent Bronx districts, half of them wholly within the County, and half straddling other counties.
sentence_329: All these legislators are Democrats who won between 65% and 100% of their districts' vote in 2006.
sentence_330: In the [[2004_United_States_presidential_election|2004 presidential election]], Senator [[John_Kerry|John Kerry]] received 81.8% of the vote in the Bronx (79.8% on the Democratic line plus 2% on the [[Working_Families_Party|Working Families Party]]'s line) while President [[George_W._Bush|George W. Bush]] received 16.3% (15.5% [[Republican_Party_(United_States)|Republican]] plus 0.85% [[Conservative_Party_of_New_York|Conservative]]).
sentence_331: In the [[2008_United_States_presidential_election|2008 presidential election]], Democrat [[Barack_Obama|Barack Obama]] improved on Kerry's showing, and took 88.7% of the vote in the Bronx to Republican [[John_McCain|John McCain]]'s 10.9%.

sentence_334: + 4.1% Working Families + 2.6% Independence) against Yonkers ex-Mayor [[John_Spencer_(mayor)|John Spencer]]'s 9.6% (8.2% Republican + 1.4% Cons.

sentence_337: In the [[2008_United_States_presidential_election|Presidential primary elections]] of February 5, 2008, Sen. Clinton won 61.2% of the Bronx's 148,636 Democratic votes against 37.8% for [[Barack_Obama|Barack Obama]] and 1.0% for the other four candidates combined ([[John_Edwards|John Edwards]], [[Dennis_Kucinich|Dennis Kucinich]], [[Bill_Richardson|Bill Richardson]] and [[Joe_Biden|Joe Biden]]).
sentence_338: On the same day, [[John_McCain|John McCain]] won 54.4% of the borough's 5,643 Republican votes, [[Mitt_Romney|Mitt Romney]] 20.8%, [[Mike_Huckabee|Mike Huckabee]] 8.2%, [[Ron_Paul|Ron Paul]] 7.4%, [[Rudy_Giuliani|Rudy Giuliani]] 5.6%, and the other candidates ([[Fred_Thompson|Fred Thompson]], [[Duncan_L._Hunter|Duncan Hunter]] and [[Alan_Keyes|Alan Keyes]]) 3.6% between them.
sentence_339: After becoming a separate county in 1914, the Bronx has supported only two Republican Presidential candidates.
sentence_340: It voted heavily for the winning Republican [[Warren_G._Harding|Warren G. Harding]] in [[United_States_presidential_election_in_New_York,_1920|1920]], but much more narrowly on a split vote for his victorious Republican successor [[Calvin_Coolidge|Calvin Coolidge]] in [[United_States_presidential_election_in_New_York,_1924|1924]] (Coolidge 79,562; [[John_W._Davis|John W. Davis]], Dem., 72,834; [[Robert_M._La_Follette,_Sr.|Robert La Follette]], 62,202 equally divided between the [[Progressive_Party_(United_States,_1924)|Progressive]] and [[Socialist_Party_of_America|Socialist]] lines).
sentence_341: Since then, the Bronx has always supported the Democratic Party's nominee for President, starting with a vote of 2–1 for the unsuccessful [[Al_Smith|Al Smith]] in 1928, followed by four 2–1 votes for the successful [[Franklin_D._Roosevelt|Franklin D. Roosevelt]].
sentence_342: (Both had been Governors of New York, but Republican former Gov.
sentence_343: [[Thomas_E._Dewey|Thomas E. Dewey]] won only 28% of the Bronx's vote in 1948 against 55% for Pres.
sentence_344: [[Harry_Truman|Harry Truman]], the winning Democrat, and 17% for Henry A. Wallace of the [[Progressive_Party_(United_States,_1948)|Progressives]].
sentence_345: It was only 32 years earlier, by contrast, that another Republican former Governor who narrowly lost the Presidency, [[Charles_Evans_Hughes|Charles Evans Hughes]], had won 42.6% of the Bronx's 1916 vote against Democratic President [[Woodrow_Wilson|Woodrow Wilson]]'s 49.8% and Socialist candidate [[Allan_Benson|Allan Benson]]'s 7.3%.)
sentence_346: The Bronx has often shown striking differences from other boroughs in [[New_York_City_mayoral_elections|elections for Mayor]].
sentence_347: The only Republican to carry the Bronx since 1914 was [[Fiorello_La_Guardia|Fiorello La Guardia]] in 1933, 1937 and 1941 (and in the latter two elections, only because his 30% to 32% vote on the [[American_Labor_Party|American Labor Party]] line was added to 22% to 23% as a Republican).
sentence_348: The Bronx was thus the only borough not carried by the successful Republican re-election campaigns of Mayors [[Rudolph_Giuliani|Rudolph Giuliani]] in 1997 and [[Michael_Bloomberg|Michael Bloomberg]] in 2005.
sentence_349: The anti-war [[Socialist_Party_of_America|Socialist]] campaign of [[Morris_Hillquit|Morris Hillquit]] in the [[New_York_City_mayoral_election,_1917|1917 mayoral election]] won over 31% of the Bronx's vote, putting him second and well ahead of the 20% won by the incumbent pro-war Fusion Mayor [[John_P._Mitchel|John P. Mitchel]], who came in second (ahead of Hillquit) everywhere else and outpolled Hillquit citywide by 23.2% to 21.7%.

sentence_350: See also: [[Economy_of_New_York_City|Economy of New York City]]
sentence_351: Shopping malls and markets in the Bronx include:
sentence_352: Prominent shopping areas in the Bronx include [[Fordham_Road|Fordham Road]], [[Bay_Plaza_Shopping_Center|Bay Plaza]] in [[Co-op_City|Co-op City]], [[The_Hub,_Bronx|The Hub]], the [[Riverdale,_Bronx|Riverdale]]/[[Kingsbridge,_Bronx|Kingsbridge]] shopping center, and [[Bruckner_Boulevard|Bruckner Boulevard]].
sentence_353: Shops are also concentrated on streets aligned underneath elevated railroad lines, including Westchester Avenue, White Plains Road, [[Jerome_Avenue|Jerome Avenue]], [[Southern_Boulevard_(Bronx)|Southern Boulevard]], and [[Broadway_(Bronx)|Broadway]].
sentence_354: The [[Bronx_Terminal_Market|Bronx Terminal Market]] contains several big-box stores, which opened in 2009 south of Yankee Stadium.
sentence_355: There are three primary shopping centers in the Bronx: The Hub, Gateway Center and Southern Boulevard.
sentence_356: The Hub–Third Avenue Business Improvement District (B.I.D.), in [[The_Hub,_Bronx|The Hub]], is the retail heart of the [[South_Bronx|South Bronx]], located where four roads converge: East 149th Street, Willis, Melrose and Third Avenues.
sentence_357: It is primarily located inside the neighborhood of [[Melrose,_Bronx|Melrose]] but also lines the northern border of Mott Haven.
sentence_358: The Hub has been called "the Broadway of the Bronx", being likened to [[Broadway_(Bronx)|the real Broadway]] in Manhattan and the northwestern Bronx.
sentence_359: It is the site of both maximum traffic and architectural density.
sentence_360: In configuration, it resembles a miniature [[Times_Square|Times Square]], a spatial "bow-tie" created by the geometry of the street.
sentence_361: The Hub is part of [[Bronx_Community_Board_1|Bronx Community Board 1]].
sentence_362: The [[Bronx_Terminal_Market|Bronx Terminal Market]], in the [[West_Bronx|West Bronx]], formerly known as Gateway Center, is a shopping center that encompasses less than one million square feet of retail space, built on a 17 acres (7 ha) site that formerly held a wholesale fruit and vegetable market also named Bronx Terminal Market as well as the former [[Bronx_House_of_Detention|Bronx House of Detention]], south of [[Yankee_Stadium|Yankee Stadium]].
sentence_363: The $500 million shopping center, which was completed in 2009, saw the construction of new buildings and two smaller buildings, one new and the other a renovation of an existing building that was part of the original market.
sentence_364: The two main buildings are linked by a six-level garage for 2,600 cars.
sentence_365: The center has earned itself a [[Leadership_in_Energy_and_Environmental_Design|LEED]] "Silver" designation in its design.
sentence_366: See also: [[Education_in_New_York_City|Education in New York City]], [[List_of_public_elementary_schools_in_New_York_City|List of public elementary schools in New York City]], and [[:Category:Charter_schools_in_New_York_(state)|:Category:Charter schools in New York (state)]]
sentence_367: Education in the Bronx is provided by a large number of public and private institutions, many of which draw students who live beyond the Bronx.
sentence_368: The [[New_York_City_Department_of_Education|New York City Department of Education]] manages public noncharter schools in the borough.
sentence_369: In 2000, public schools enrolled nearly 280,000 of the Bronx's residents over 3 years old (out of 333,100 enrolled in all pre-college schools).
sentence_370: There are also several public charter schools.
sentence_371: Private schools range from élite [[Independent_school|independent schools]] to religiously affiliated [[Parochial_schools#United_States|schools]] run by the [[Roman_Catholic_Archdiocese_of_New_York|Roman Catholic Archdiocese of New York]] and Jewish organizations.
sentence_372: A small portion of land that is between Pelham and Pelham Bay Park, with a total of 35 houses, is a part of the Bronx, but is cut off from the rest of the borough due to the way the county boundaries were established; the New York City government pays for the residents' children to go to [[Pelham_Union_Free_School_District|Pelham Union Free School District]] schools, including [[Pelham_Memorial_High_School|Pelham Memorial High School]], since that is more cost effective than sending school buses to take the students to New York City schools.
sentence_373: This arrangement has been in place since 1948.
sentence_374: In 2000, according to the [[United_States_Census|United States Census]], out of the nearly 800,000 people in the Bronx who were then at least 25 years old, 62.3% had graduated from high school and 14.6% held a bachelor's or higher college degree.
sentence_375: These percentages were lower than those for New York's other boroughs, which ranged from 68.8% (Brooklyn) to 82.6% (Staten Island) for high school graduates over 24, and from 21.8% (Brooklyn) to 49.4% (Manhattan) for college graduates.
sentence_376: (The respective state and national percentages were [NY] 79.1% & 27.4% and [US] 80.4% & 24.4%.)
sentence_377: See also: [[List_of_high_schools_in_New_York_City#Bronx|List of high schools in New York City § Bronx]]
sentence_378: In the 2000 Census, 79,240 of the nearly 95,000 Bronx residents enrolled in high school attended public schools.
sentence_379: Many public [[High_school_(North_America)|high schools]] are located in the borough including the elite [[Bronx_High_School_of_Science|Bronx High School of Science]], [[Celia_Cruz_Bronx_High_School_of_Music|Celia Cruz Bronx High School of Music]], [[DeWitt_Clinton_High_School|DeWitt Clinton High School]], [[High_School_for_Violin_and_Dance|High School for Violin and Dance]], [[Bronx_Leadership_Academy_2|Bronx Leadership Academy 2]], [[Bronx_International_High_School|Bronx International High School]], the [[School_for_Excellence|School for Excellence]], the [[Morris_Academy_for_Collaborative_Study|Morris Academy for Collaborative Study]], Wings Academy for young adults, The Bronx School for Law, Government and Justice, Validus Preparatory Academy, The Eagle Academy For Young Men, Bronx Expeditionary Learning High School, Bronx Academy of Letters, Herbert H. Lehman High School and [[High_School_of_American_Studies_at_Lehman_College|High School of American Studies]].
sentence_380: The Bronx is also home to three of New York City's most prestigious private, secular schools: [[Ethical_Culture_Fieldston_School|Fieldston]], Horace Mann, and [[Riverdale_Country_School|Riverdale Country School]].
sentence_381: High schools linked to the [[Catholic_Church|Catholic Church]] include: Saint Raymond's Academy for Girls, [[All_Hallows_High_School|All Hallows High School]], [[Fordham_Preparatory_School|Fordham Preparatory School]], [[Monsignor_Scanlan_High_School|Monsignor Scanlan High School]], [[St._Raymond_High_School_for_Boys|St.
