sentence_385: The [[SAR_Academy|SAR Academy]] and SAR High School are [[Modern_Orthodox|Modern Orthodox]] Jewish Yeshiva coeducational day schools in [[Riverdale,_Bronx|Riverdale]], with roots in Manhattan's [[Lower_East_Side|Lower East Side]].
sentence_386: In the 1990s, New York City began closing the large, public high schools in the Bronx and replacing them with small high schools.
sentence_387: Among the reasons cited for the changes were poor graduation rates and concerns about safety.
sentence_388: Schools that have been closed or reduced in size include [[John_F._Kennedy_High_School_(Bronx,_New_York)|John F. Kennedy]], [[James_Monroe_High_School_(New_York)|James Monroe]], [[William_Howard_Taft_High_School_(New_York_City)|Taft]], [[Theodore_Roosevelt_High_School_(New_York_City)|Theodore Roosevelt]], [[Adlai_E._Stevenson_High_School_(New_York_City)|Adlai Stevenson]], [[Evander_Childs_High_School|Evander Childs]], [[Christopher_Columbus_High_School_(Bronx,_New_York)|Christopher Columbus]], [[Morris_High_School_(Bronx,_New_York)|Morris]], [[Walton_High_School_(New_York_City)|Walton]], and South Bronx High Schools.
sentence_389: More recently the City has started phasing out large middle schools, also replacing them with smaller schools.
sentence_390: See also: [[List_of_colleges_and_universities_in_New_York_City|List of colleges and universities in New York City]]
sentence_391: In 2000, 49,442 (57.5%) of the 86,014 Bronx residents seeking college, graduate or professional degrees attended public institutions.
sentence_392: Several colleges and universities are located in the Bronx.
sentence_393: [[Fordham_University|Fordham University]] was founded as St. John's College in 1841 by the [[Archdiocese_of_New_York|Diocese of New York]] as the first Catholic institution of higher education in the [[Northeast_United_States|northeast]].
sentence_394: It is now officially an independent institution, but strongly embraces its [[Jesuit|Jesuit]] heritage.
sentence_395: The 85-acre (340,000 m) Bronx campus, known as Rose Hill, is the main campus of the university, and is among the largest within the city (other Fordham campuses are located in Manhattan and Westchester County).
sentence_396: Three campuses of the [[City_University_of_New_York|City University of New York]] are in the Bronx: [[Hostos_Community_College|Hostos Community College]], [[Bronx_Community_College|Bronx Community College]] (occupying the former [[University_Heights,_Bronx|University Heights]] Campus of [[New_York_University|New York University]]) and Herbert H. [[Lehman_College|Lehman College]] (formerly the uptown campus of [[Hunter_College|Hunter College]]), which offers both undergraduate and graduate degrees.
sentence_397: The [[College_of_Mount_Saint_Vincent|College of Mount Saint Vincent]] is a Catholic liberal arts college in [[Riverdale,_Bronx|Riverdale]] under the direction of the [[Sisters_of_Charity_of_New_York|Sisters of Charity of New York]].
sentence_398: Founded in 1847 as a school for girls, the academy became a degree-granting college in 1911 and began admitting men in 1974.
sentence_399: The school serves 1,600 students.
sentence_400: Its campus is also home to the [[Academy_for_Jewish_Religion_(New_York)|Academy for Jewish Religion]], a transdenominational rabbinical and cantorial school.
sentence_401: [[Manhattan_College|Manhattan College]] is a Catholic college in [[Riverdale,_Bronx|Riverdale]] which offers undergraduate programs in the arts, business, education, engineering, and science.
sentence_402: It also offers graduate programs in education and engineering.
sentence_403: [[Albert_Einstein_College_of_Medicine|Albert Einstein College of Medicine]], part of the [[Montefiore_Medical_Center|Montefiore Medical Center]], is in [[Morris_Park,_Bronx|Morris Park]].
sentence_404: The coeducational and non-sectarian [[Mercy_College_(New_York)|Mercy College]]—with its main campus in [[Dobbs_Ferry,_New_York|Dobbs Ferry]]—has a Bronx campus, located near [[Westchester_Square,_Bronx|Westchester Square]].
sentence_405: The [[State_University_of_New_York_Maritime_College|State University of New York Maritime College]] in [[Fort_Schuyler|Fort Schuyler]] ([[Throggs_Neck|Throggs Neck]])—at the far southeastern tip of the Bronx—is the national leader in maritime education and houses the [[Maritime_Industry_Museum|Maritime Industry Museum]].
sentence_406: (Directly across [[Long_Island_Sound|Long Island Sound]] is [[Kings_Point,_New_York|Kings Point]], Long Island, home of the [[United_States_Merchant_Marine_Academy|United States Merchant Marine Academy]] and the American Merchant Marine Museum.)
sentence_407: As of 2017, graduates from the university earned an average annual salary of $144,000, the highest of any university graduates in the United States.
sentence_408: In addition, the private, proprietary Monroe College, focused on preparation for business and the professions, started in the Bronx in 1933 and now has a campus in [[New_Rochelle,_New_York|New Rochelle]] (Westchester County) as well the Bronx's [[Fordham,_Bronx|Fordham]] neighborhood.
sentence_409: See also: Culture of New York City; [[Music_of_New_York_City|Music of New York City]]; [[List_of_people_from_the_Bronx|List of people from the Bronx]]; and [[List_of_Registered_Historic_Places_in_Bronx_County,_New_York|List of Registered Historic Places in Bronx County, New York]]
sentence_410: Author [[Edgar_Allan_Poe|Edgar Allan Poe]] spent the last years of his life (1846 to 1849) in the Bronx at [[Poe_Cottage|Poe Cottage]], now located at [[Kingsbridge,_Bronx|Kingsbridge]] Road and the [[Grand_Concourse_(Bronx)|Grand Concourse]].
sentence_411: A small wooden farmhouse built around 1812, the cottage once commanded unobstructed vistas over the rolling Bronx hills to the shores of [[Long_Island|Long Island]].
sentence_412: Poe moved there to get away from the Manhattan city air and crowding in hope that the then rural area would be beneficial for his wife's tuberculosis.
sentence_413: It was in the Bronx that Poe wrote one of his most famous works, [[Annabel_Lee|Annabel Lee]].
sentence_414: More than a century later, the Bronx would evolve from a hot bed of [[Latin_jazz|Latin jazz]] to an incubator of [[Hip_hop_music|hip hop]] as documented in the award-winning documentary, produced by [[City_Lore|City Lore]] and broadcast on PBS in 2006, "From Mambo to Hip Hop: A South Bronx Tale."
sentence_415: Hip Hop first emerged in the South Bronx in the early 1970s.
sentence_416: [[The_New_York_Times|The New York Times]] has identified 1520 [[Sedgwick_Avenue|Sedgwick Avenue]] "an otherwise unremarkable high-rise just north of the [[Cross_Bronx_Expressway|Cross Bronx Expressway]] and hard along the [[Major_Deegan_Expressway|Major Deegan Expressway]]" as a starting point, where [[DJ_Kool_Herc|DJ Kool Herc]] presided over parties in the community room.
sentence_417: The 2016 [[Netflix|Netflix]] series [[The_Get_Down|The Get Down]] is based on the development of hip hop in 1977 in the South Bronx.
sentence_418: Ten years earlier, the [[Bronx_Opera|Bronx Opera]] had been founded.
sentence_419: On August 11, 1973, DJ Kool Herc was a [[D.J.|D.J.]]
sentence_420: and [[M.C.|M.C.]]
sentence_421: at a party in the [[Recreation_room|recreation room]] of [[1520_Sedgwick_Avenue|1520 Sedgwick Avenue]] in the Bronx adjacent to the Cross Bronx Expressway.
sentence_422: While it was not the actual "Birthplace of Hip Hop" – the [[Genre|genre]] developed slowly in several places in the 1970s – it was verified to be the place where one of the pivotal and formative events occurred.
sentence_423: Specifically:
sentence_424: Beginning with the advent of beat match DJing, in which Bronx disc jockeys including [[Grandmaster_Flash|Grandmaster Flash]], [[Afrika_Bambaataa|Afrika Bambaataa]] and [[DJ_Kool_Herc|DJ Kool Herc]] extended the breaks of [[Funk|funk]] records, a major new musical genre emerged that sought to isolate the percussion breaks of hit funk, [[Disco|disco]] and [[Soul_music|soul]] songs.
sentence_425: As hip hop's popularity grew, performers began speaking ("[[Rapping|rapping]]") in sync with the beats, and became known as MCs or emcees.
sentence_426: The Herculoids, made up of Herc, [[Coke_La_Rock|Coke La Rock]], and Clark Kent, were the earliest to gain major fame.
sentence_427: The Bronx is referred to in hip-hop slang as "The Boogie Down Bronx", or just "The Boogie Down".
sentence_428: This was hip-hop pioneer [[KRS-One|KRS-One]]'s inspiration for his group BDP, or Boogie Down Productions, which included DJ Scott La Rock.
sentence_429: Newer hip hop artists from the Bronx include [[Big_Pun|Big Pun]], [[Lord_Tariq_and_Peter_Gunz|Lord Tariq and Peter Gunz]], Camp Lo, [[Swizz_Beatz|Swizz Beatz]], Drag-On, [[Fat_Joe|Fat Joe]], [[Terror_Squad_(group)|Terror Squad]] and [[Cory_Gunz|Cory Gunz]].
sentence_430: Hush Hip Hop Tours, a tour company founded in 2002 by local licensed sightseeing tour guide Debra Harris, has established a sightseeing tour of the Bronx showcasing the locations that helped shape hip hop culture, and features some of the pioneers of hip hop as tour guides.
sentence_431: The Bronx's recognition as an important center of [[African-American_culture|African-American culture]] has led [[Fordham_University|Fordham University]] to establish the Bronx African-American History Project (BAAHP).
sentence_432: The Bronx is the home of the [[New_York_Yankees|New York Yankees]], nicknamed "the Bronx Bombers", of [[Major_League_Baseball|Major League Baseball]].
sentence_433: The original [[Yankee_Stadium_(1923)|Yankee Stadium]] opened in 1923 on 161st Street and River Avenue, a year that saw the Yankees bring home their first of 27 [[World_Series|World Series]] Championships.
sentence_434: With the famous facade, the short right field porch and Monument Park, Yankee Stadium has been home to many of baseball's greatest players including [[Babe_Ruth|Babe Ruth]], [[Lou_Gehrig|Lou Gehrig]], [[Joe_DiMaggio|Joe DiMaggio]], [[Whitey_Ford|Whitey Ford]], [[Yogi_Berra|Yogi Berra]], [[Mickey_Mantle|Mickey Mantle]], [[Reggie_Jackson|Reggie Jackson]], [[Thurman_Munson|Thurman Munson]], [[Don_Mattingly|Don Mattingly]], [[Derek_Jeter|Derek Jeter]] and [[Mariano_Rivera|Mariano Rivera]].
sentence_435: The original stadium was the scene of [[Lou_Gehrig|Lou Gehrig]]'s Farewell Speech in 1939, Don Larsen's perfect game in the 1956 World Series, Roger Maris' record breaking 61st home run in 1961, and Reggie Jackson's 3 home runs to clinch Game 6 of the 1977 World Series.
sentence_436: The Stadium was the former home of the [[New_York_Giants|New York Giants]] of the [[National_Football_League|National Football League]] from 1956 to 1973.
sentence_437: The original Yankee Stadium closed in 2008 to make way for a new [[Yankee_Stadium|Yankee Stadium]] in which the team started play in 2009.
sentence_438: It is located north-northeast of the 1923 Yankee Stadium, on the former site of Macombs Dam Park.
sentence_439: The current Yankee Stadium is also the home of [[New_York_City_FC|New York City FC]] of [[Major_League_Soccer|Major League Soccer]], who began play in 2015.
sentence_440: Main article: [[Off-Off-Broadway|Off-Off-Broadway]]
sentence_441: The Bronx is home to several [[Off-Off-Broadway|Off-Off-Broadway]] theaters, many staging new works by immigrant playwrights from Latin America and Africa.
sentence_442: The [[Pregones_Theater|Pregones Theater]], which produces Latin American work, opened a new 130-seat theater in 2005 on Walton Avenue in the South Bronx.
sentence_443: Some artists from elsewhere in New York City have begun to converge on the area, and housing prices have nearly quadrupled in the area since 2002.
sentence_444: However rising prices directly correlate to a housing shortage across the city and the entire metro area.
sentence_445: The [[Bronx_Academy_of_Arts_and_Dance|Bronx Academy of Arts and Dance]], founded in 1998 by [[Arthur_Aviles|Arthur Aviles]] and Charles Rice-Gonzalez, provides dance, theatre and art workshops, festivals and performances focusing on contemporary and modern art in relation to race, gender, and sexuality.
sentence_446: It is home to the Arthur Aviles Typical Theatre, a contemporary dance company, and the Bronx Dance Coalition.
sentence_447: The Academy was formerly in the [[American_Bank_Note_Company_Building|American Bank Note Company Building]] before relocating to a venue on the grounds of St. Peter's Episcopal Church.
sentence_448: The [[Bronx_Museum_of_the_Arts|Bronx Museum of the Arts]], founded in 1971, exhibits 20th century and contemporary art through its central museum space and 11,000 square feet (1,000 m) of galleries.
sentence_449: Many of its exhibitions are on themes of special interest to the Bronx.
sentence_450: Its permanent collection features more than 800 works of art, primarily by artists from Africa, Asia and Latin America, including paintings, photographs, prints, drawings, and mixed media.
sentence_451: The museum was temporarily closed in 2006 while it underwent a major expansion designed by the architectural firm [[Arquitectonica|Arquitectonica]].
sentence_452: The Bronx has also become home to a peculiar poetic tribute in the form of the "[[Heinrich_Heine|Heinrich Heine]] Memorial", better known as the [[Lorelei_Fountain|Lorelei Fountain]].
sentence_453: After Heine's German birthplace of [[Düsseldorf|Düsseldorf]] had rejected, allegedly for [[Anti-Semitic|anti-Semitic]] motives, a centennial monument to the radical [[German-Jewish|German-Jewish]] poet (1797–1856), his incensed [[German-American|German-American]] admirers, including [[Carl_Schurz|Carl Schurz]], started a movement to place one instead in [[Midtown_Manhattan|Midtown Manhattan]], at [[Fifth_Avenue|Fifth Avenue]] and 59th Street.
sentence_454: However, this intention was thwarted by a combination of ethnic antagonism, aesthetic controversy and political struggles over the institutional control of public art.
sentence_455: In 1899, the memorial by [[Ernst_Gustav_Herter|Ernst Gustav Herter]] was placed in [[Joyce_Kilmer_Park|Joyce Kilmer Park]], near the [[Yankee_Stadium|Yankee Stadium]].
sentence_456: In 1999, it was moved to 161st Street and the Concourse.
sentence_457: The [[Peninsula|peninsular]] borough's maritime heritage is acknowledged in several ways.
sentence_458: occupies a former public school designed by the New York City school system's turn-of-the-last-century master architect [[C._B._J._Snyder|C.
sentence_459: B. J. Snyder]].
sentence_460: The state's [[SUNY_Maritime_College|Maritime College]] in [[Fort_Schuyler|Fort Schuyler]] (on the southeastern shore) houses the [[Maritime_Industry_Museum|Maritime Industry Museum]].
sentence_461: In addition, the Harlem River is reemerging as [[Sculling|"Scullers' Row"]] due in large part to the efforts of the Bronx River Restoration Project, a joint public-private endeavor of the city's parks department.
sentence_462: [[Canoeing|Canoeing]] and kayaking on the borough's namesake river have been promoted by the .
sentence_463: The river is also straddled by the [[New_York_Botanical_Gardens|New York Botanical Gardens]], its neighbor, the [[Bronx_Zoo|Bronx Zoo]], and a little further south, on the west shore, Bronx River Art Center.
sentence_464: "Bronx Week", traditionally held in May, originated as a one-day celebration.
sentence_465: Initiated by Bronx historian Lloyd Ultan and supported by then borough president Robert Abrams, the original one-day program was based on the "Bronx Borough Day" festival which took place in the 1920s.
sentence_466: The following year, at the height of the decade's civil unrest, the festival was extended to a one-week event.
sentence_467: In the 1980s the key event, the "Bronx Ball", was launched.
sentence_468: The week includes the Bronx Week Parade as well as inductions into the "Bronx Walk of Fame."
sentence_469: Various Bronx neighborhoods conduct their own community celebrations.
sentence_470: The Arthur Avenue "Little Italy" neighborhood conducts an annual Autumn Ferragosto Festival that celebrates Italian culture.
sentence_471: [[Hunts_Point,_Bronx|Hunts Point]] hosts an annual "Fish Parade and Summer Festival" at the start of summer.
sentence_472: [[Edgewater_Park_(Bronx)|Edgewater Park]] hosts an annual "Ragamuffin" children's walk in November.
sentence_473: There are several events to honor the borough's veterans.
sentence_474: Albanian Independence Day is also observed.
sentence_475: There are also parades to celebrate Dominican, Italian, and Irish heritage.
sentence_476: The Bronx is home to several local newspapers and radio and television studios.
sentence_477: The Bronx has several local newspapers, including The [[Bronx_News|Bronx News]], [[Parkchester|Parkchester]] News, City News, The [[Norwood_News|Norwood News]], The [[Riverdale_Press|Riverdale Press]], [[Riverdale_Review|Riverdale Review]], The Bronx Times Reporter, Inner City Press (which now has more of a focus on national issues) and [[Co-op_City|Co-op City]] Times.
sentence_478: Four non-profit news outlets, [[Norwood_News|Norwood News]], Mount Hope Monitor, [[Mott_Haven_Herald|Mott Haven Herald]] and The [[Hunts_Point,_Bronx|Hunts Point]] Express serve the borough's poorer communities.
sentence_479: The editor and co-publisher of The Riverdale Press, Bernard Stein, won the [[Pulitzer_Prize_for_Editorial_Writing|Pulitzer Prize for Editorial Writing]] for his editorials about Bronx and New York City issues in 1998.
sentence_480: (Stein graduated from the [[Bronx_High_School_of_Science|Bronx High School of Science]] in 1959.)
sentence_481: The Bronx once had its own daily newspaper, [[The_Bronx_Home_News|The Bronx Home News]], which started publishing on January 20, 1907, and merged into the [[New_York_Post|New York Post]] in 1948.
sentence_482: It became a special section of the Post, sold only in the Bronx, and eventually disappeared from view.
sentence_483: One of New York City's major non-commercial radio broadcasters is [[WFUV|WFUV]], a National Public Radio-affiliated 50,000-watt station broadcasting from [[Fordham_University|Fordham University]]'s Rose Hill campus in the Bronx.
sentence_484: The radio station's antenna is atop an apartment building owned by [[Montefiore_Medical_Center|Montefiore Medical Center]].
sentence_485: The City of New York has an official television station run by [[NYC_Media|NYC Media]] and broadcasting from [[Bronx_Community_College|Bronx Community College]], and [[Cablevision|Cablevision]] operates [[News_12_Networks|News 12 The Bronx]], both of which feature programming based in the Bronx.
sentence_486: [[Co-op_City|Co-op City]] was the first area in the Bronx, and the first in New York beyond [[Manhattan|Manhattan]], to have its own cable television provider.
sentence_487: The local [[Public-access_television|public-access television]] station [[BronxNet|BronxNet]] originates from Herbert H. Lehman College, the borough's only four year CUNY school, and provides government-access television (GATV) public affairs programming in addition to programming produced by Bronx residents.
sentence_488: The Bronx is the home of many gangs, including:

list.value: [[Dominicans_Don't_Play|Dominicans Don't Play]] – formed around 1990, it primarily targets high school students and second-generation immigrants to join their gang, and make most of their money from robberies and drug deals.
[[Trinitarios|Trinitarios]] – also formed around 1990, a spin-off of Dominicans Don't Play, mostly involved with drug, sex, and weapons trafficking

[[Latin_Kings_(gang)|Latin Kings]] – a nationwide gang whose Bronx chapter began in 1986, involved with gun and drug trafficking, extortion, credit card fraud, and auto theft as their sources of income

Ñetas – a gang that was started in 1979 in Puerto Rico. The organization began as a prison gang which gave members protection while serving their prison sentences. It eventually transformed into a drug trafficking gang.
[[Sureños|Sureños]] – made up of first- and second-generation Mexican-Americans, mainly involved in small-scale crime and gang warfare

sentence_489: See also: [[List_of_films_set_in_New_York_City|List of films set in New York City]] and [[List_of_television_shows_set_in_New_York_City|List of television shows set in New York City]]
sentence_490: Mid-20th century movies set in the Bronx portrayed densely settled, working-class, urban culture.
sentence_491: Hollywood films such as [[From_This_Day_Forward|From This Day Forward]] (1946), set in [[Highbridge,_Bronx|Highbridge]], occasionally delved into Bronx life.
sentence_492: [[Paddy_Chayefsky|Paddy Chayefsky]]'s [[Academy_Awards|Academy Award]]-winning [[Marty_(film)|Marty]] was the most notable examination of working class Bronx life was also explored by Chayefsky in his 1956 film [[The_Catered_Affair|The Catered Affair]], and in the 1993 [[Robert_De_Niro|Robert De Niro]]/[[Chazz_Palminteri|Chazz Palminteri]] film, [[A_Bronx_Tale|A Bronx Tale]], [[Spike_Lee|Spike Lee]]'s 1999 movie [[Summer_of_Sam|Summer of Sam]], centered in an [[Italian-American|Italian-American]] Bronx community, 1994's [[I_Like_It_Like_That_(film)|I Like It Like That]] that takes place in the predominantly [[Puerto_Rican_people|Puerto Rican]] neighborhood of the South Bronx, and Doughboys, the story of two Italian-American brothers in danger of losing their bakery thanks to one brother's gambling debts.
sentence_493: The Bronx's gritty urban life had worked its way into the movies even earlier, with depictions of the "[[Bronx_cheer_(gesture)|Bronx cheer]]", a loud flatulent-like sound of disapproval, allegedly first made by [[New_York_Yankees|New York Yankees]] fans.
sentence_494: The sound can be heard, for example, on the [[Spike_Jones|Spike Jones]] and His City Slickers recording of "Der Fuehrer's Face" (from the 1942 [[Disney|Disney]] [[Animated_film|animated film]] of the [[Der_Fuehrer's_Face|same name]]), repeatedly lambasting [[Adolf_Hitler|Adolf Hitler]] with: "We'll Heil!
sentence_495: (Bronx cheer) Heil!
sentence_496: (Bronx cheer) Right in Der Fuehrer's Face!"
sentence_497: Starting in the 1970s, the Bronx often symbolized violence, decay, and urban ruin.
sentence_498: The wave of arson in the South Bronx in the 1960s and 1970s inspired the observation that "The Bronx is burning": in 1974 it was the title of both a [[The_New_York_Times|The New York Times]] [[Editorial|editorial]] and a [[BBC|BBC]] [[Documentary_film|documentary film]].
sentence_499: The line entered the pop-consciousness with Game Two of the [[1977_World_Series|1977 World Series]], when a fire broke out near [[Yankee_Stadium_(1923)|Yankee Stadium]] as the team was playing the [[Los_Angeles_Dodgers|Los Angeles Dodgers]].
sentence_500: Numerous fires had previously broken out in the Bronx prior to this fire.
sentence_501: As the fire was captured on live television, announcer [[Howard_Cosell|Howard Cosell]] [[The_Bronx_Is_Burning#Summary|is wrongly remembered to have said something like]], "There it is, ladies and gentlemen: the Bronx is burning".
sentence_502: Historians of New York City frequently point to Cosell's remark as an acknowledgement of both the city and the borough's decline.
sentence_503: A new feature-length documentary film by Edwin Pagan called Bronx Burning is in production in 2006, chronicling what led up to the numerous arson-for-insurance fraud fires of the 1970s in the borough.
sentence_504: Bronx gang life was depicted in the 1974 novel The Wanderers by Bronx native [[Richard_Price_(writer)|Richard Price]] and the [[The_Wanderers_(1979_film)|1979 movie of the same name]].
sentence_505: They are set in the heart of the Bronx, showing apartment life and the then-landmark Krums ice cream parlor.
sentence_506: In the 1979 film [[The_Warriors_(film)|The Warriors]], the eponymous gang go to a meeting in [[Van_Cortlandt_Park|Van Cortlandt Park]] in the Bronx, and have to fight their way out of the borough and get back to [[Coney_Island|Coney Island]] in [[Brooklyn|Brooklyn]].
sentence_507: [[A_Bronx_Tale|A Bronx Tale]] (1993) depicts gang activities in the [[Belmont,_Bronx|Belmont]] "Little Italy" section of the Bronx.
sentence_508: The 2005 video game adaptation features levels called Pelham, Tremont, and "Gunhill" (a play off the name [[Gun_Hill_Road_(Bronx)|Gun Hill Road]]).
sentence_509: This theme lends itself to the title of [[The_Bronx_Is_Burning|The Bronx Is Burning]], an eight-part [[ESPN|ESPN]] TV mini-series (2007) about the [[New_York_Yankees|New York Yankees]]' drive to winning baseball's [[1977_World_Series|1977 World Series]].
sentence_510: The TV series emphasizes the boisterous nature of the team, led by manager [[Billy_Martin|Billy Martin]], catcher [[Thurman_Munson|Thurman Munson]] and outfielder [[Reggie_Jackson|Reggie Jackson]], as well as the malaise of the Bronx and New York City in general during that time, such as the blackout, the city's serious financial woes and near bankruptcy, the arson for insurance payments, and the election of [[Ed_Koch|Ed Koch]] as mayor.
sentence_511: The 1981 film [[Fort_Apache,_The_Bronx|Fort Apache, The Bronx]] is another film that used the Bronx's gritty image for its storyline.
sentence_512: The movie's title is from the nickname for the 41st Police Precinct in the South Bronx which was nicknamed "Fort Apache".
sentence_513: Also from 1981 is the horror film [[Wolfen_(film)|Wolfen]] making use of the rubble of the Bronx as a home for werewolf type creatures.
sentence_514: [[Knights_of_the_South_Bronx|Knights of the South Bronx]], a true story of a teacher who worked with disadvantaged children, is another film also set in the Bronx released in 2005.
sentence_515: The Bronx was the setting for the 1983 film [[Fuga_dal_Bronx|Fuga dal Bronx]], also known as Bronx Warriors 2 and Escape 2000, an Italian B-movie best known for its appearance on the television series [[Mystery_Science_Theater_3000|Mystery Science Theater 3000]].
sentence_516: The plot revolves around a sinister construction corporation's plans to depopulate, destroy and redevelop the Bronx, and a band of rebels who are out to expose the corporation's murderous ways and save their homes.
sentence_517: The film is memorable for its almost incessant use of the phrase, "Leave the Bronx!"
sentence_518: Many of the movie's scenes were filmed in [[Queens|Queens]], substituting as the Bronx.
sentence_519: [[Rumble_in_the_Bronx|Rumble in the Bronx]], filmed in Vancouver, was a 1995 [[Jackie_Chan|Jackie Chan]] [[Kung-fu|kung-fu]] film, another which popularized the Bronx to international audiences.
sentence_520: [[Last_Bronx|Last Bronx]], a 1996 Sega game played on the bad reputation of the Bronx to lend its name to an alternate version of post-Japanese bubble Tokyo, where crime and gang warfare is rampant.
sentence_521: See also: [[List_of_books_set_in_New_York_City|List of books set in New York City]]
sentence_522: The Bronx has been featured significantly in fiction literature.
sentence_523: All of the characters in [[Herman_Wouk|Herman Wouk]]'s City Boy: The Adventures of Herbie Bookbinder (1948) live in the Bronx, and about half of the action is set there.
sentence_524: [[Kate_Simon|Kate Simon]]'s Bronx Primitive: Portraits of a Childhood is directly autobiographical, a warm account of a Polish-Jewish girl in an immigrant family growing up before World War II, and living near [[Arthur_Avenue|Arthur Avenue]] and [[Tremont_Avenue|Tremont Avenue]].
sentence_525: In Jacob M. Appel's short story, "The Grand Concourse" (2007), a woman who grew up in the iconic [[Lewis_Morris|Lewis Morris]] Building returns to the [[Morrisania|Morrisania]] neighborhood with her adult daughter.
sentence_526: Similarly, in Avery Corman's book The Old Neighborhood (1980), an upper-middle class white protagonist returns to his birth neighborhood ([[Fordham_Road|Fordham Road]] and the [[Grand_Concourse_(Bronx)|Grand Concourse]]), and learns that even though the folks are poor, Hispanic and African-American, they are good people.
sentence_527: By contrast, Tom Wolfe's [[The_Bonfire_of_the_Vanities|Bonfire of the Vanities]] (1987) portrays a wealthy, white protagonist, Sherman McCoy, getting lost off the [[Bruckner_Expressway|Bruckner Expressway]] in the [[South_Bronx|South Bronx]] and having an altercation with locals.
sentence_528: A substantial piece of the last part of the book is set in the resulting riotous trial at the Bronx County Courthouse.
sentence_529: However, times change, and in 2007, [[The_New_York_Times|The New York Times]] reported that "the Bronx neighborhoods near the site of Sherman's accident are now dotted with townhouses and apartments."
sentence_530: In the same article, the Reverend [[Al_Sharpton|Al Sharpton]] (whose fictional analogue in the novel is "Reverend Bacon") asserts that "twenty years later, the cynicism of The Bonfire of the Vanities is as out of style as Tom Wolfe's wardrobe."
sentence_531: [[Don_DeLillo|Don DeLillo]]'s [[Underworld_(DeLillo_novel)|Underworld]] (1997) is also set in the Bronx and offers a perspective on the decline of the area from the 1950s onwards.
sentence_532: In poetry, the Bronx has been immortalized by one of the world's shortest couplets:
sentence_533: Nash repented 33 years after his [[Calumny|calumny]], penning in 1964 the following prose poem to the Dean of [[Bronx_Community_College|Bronx Community College]]:
sentence_534: In 2016, W. R. Rodriguez published Bronx Trilogy—consisting of the shoe shine parlor poems et al, concrete pastures of the beautiful bronx, and from the banks of brook avenue.
sentence_535: The trilogy celebrates Bronx people, places, and events.
sentence_536: [[DeWitt_Clinton_High_School|DeWitt Clinton High School]], [[St._Mary's_Park_(Bronx)|St. Mary's Park]], and Brook Avenue are a few of the schools, parks, and streets Rodriguez uses as subjects for his poems.
sentence_537: Nash's couplet "The Bronx No Thonx" and his subsequent blessing are mentioned in Bronx Accent: A Literary and Pictorial History of the Borough, edited by Llyod Ultan and Barbara Unger and published in 2000.
sentence_538: The book, which includes the work of Yiddish poets, offers a selection from [[Allen_Ginsberg|Allen Ginsberg]]'s [[Kaddish_(poem)|Kaddish]], as his Aunt Elanor and his mother, Naomi, lived near Woodlawn Cemetery.
sentence_539: Also featured is Ruth Lisa Schecther's poem, "Bronx", which is described as a celebration of the borough's landmarks.
sentence_540: There is a selection of works from poets such as Sandra María Esteves, [[Milton_Kessler|Milton Kessler]], Joan Murray, W. R. Rodriguez, Myra Shapiro, Gayl Teller, and [[Terence_Winch|Terence Wynch]].
sentence_541: "Bronx Migrations" by Michelle M. Tokarczyk is a collection that spans five decades of Tokarczyk's life in the Bronx, from her exodus in 1962 to her return in search of her childhood tenement.
sentence_542: Bronx Memoir Project: Vol. 1 is a published [[Anthology|anthology]] by the Bronx Council on the Arts and brought forth through a series of workshops meant to empower Bronx residents and shed the stigma on the Bronx's burning past.
sentence_543: The Bronx Memoir Project was created as an ongoing collaboration between the [[Bronx_Council_on_the_Arts|Bronx Council on the Arts]] and other cultural institutions, including the Bronx [[Documentary_film|Documentary]] Center, the [[Bronx_Library_Center|Bronx Library Center]], the (Edgar Allan) [[Poe_Park_Visitor_Center|Poe Park Visitor Center]], Mindbuilders, and other institutions and funded through a grant from the [[National_Endowment_for_the_Arts|National Endowment for the Arts]].
sentence_544: The goal was to develop and refine memoir fragments written by people of all walks of life that share a common bond residing within the Bronx.

sentence_546: [[Clifford_Odets|Clifford Odets]]'s play [[Awake_and_Sing!|Awake and Sing]] is set in 1933 in the Bronx.
sentence_547: The play, first produced at the [[Belasco_Theater|Belasco Theater]] in 1935, concerns a poor family living in small quarters, the struggles of the controlling parents and the aspirations of their children.
sentence_548: [[René_Marqués|René Marqués]] [[La_Carreta|The Oxcart]] (1959), concerns a rural Puerto Rican family who immigrate to the Bronx for a better life.
sentence_549: [[A_Bronx_Tale_(play)|A Bronx Tale]] is an autobiographical [[One-man_show|one-man show]] written and performed by [[Chazz_Palminteri|Chazz Palminteri]].
sentence_550: It is a coming-of-age story set in the Bronx.
sentence_551: It premiered in Los Angeles in the 1980s and then played on Off-Broadway.
sentence_552: After a film version involving Palminteri and Robert DeNiro, Palminteri performed his one-man show on Broadway and on tour in 2007.

sentence_0: The Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) is a US-based international learned society for [[Computing|computing]].
sentence_1: It was founded in 1947, and is the world's largest scientific and educational computing society.
sentence_2: The ACM is a [[Nonprofit_organization|non-profit]] professional membership group, claiming nearly 100,000 student and professional members as of 2019.
sentence_3: Its headquarters are in [[New_York_City|New York City]].
sentence_4: The ACM is an [[Umbrella_organization|umbrella organization]] for academic and scholarly interests in [[Computer_science|computer science]] ([[Informatics|informatics]]).
sentence_5: Its motto is "Advancing Computing as a Science & Profession".
sentence_6: The ACM was founded in 1947 under the name Eastern Association for Computing Machinery, which was changed the following year to the Association for Computing Machinery.
sentence_7: ACM is organized into over 171 local chapters and 37 [[Special_Interest_Group|Special Interest Groups]] (SIGs), through which it conducts most of its activities.
sentence_8: Additionally, there are over 500 college and university chapters.
sentence_9: The first student chapter was founded in 1961 at the [[University_of_Louisiana_at_Lafayette|University of Louisiana at Lafayette]]
sentence_10: Many of the SIGs, such as [[ACM_SIGGRAPH|SIGGRAPH]], SIGDA, SIGPLAN, [[SIGCSE|SIGCSE]] and SIGCOMM, sponsor regular conferences, which have become famous as the dominant venue for presenting innovations in certain fields.
sentence_11: The groups also publish a large number of specialized journals, magazines, and newsletters.
sentence_12: ACM also sponsors other computer science related events such as the worldwide [[ACM_International_Collegiate_Programming_Contest|ACM International Collegiate Programming Contest]] (ICPC), and has sponsored some other events such as the chess match between [[Garry_Kasparov|Garry Kasparov]] and the [[IBM_Deep_Blue|IBM Deep Blue]] computer.
sentence_13: Main category: Association for Computing Machinery publications
sentence_14: ACM publishes over 50 journals including the prestigious [[Journal_of_the_ACM|Journal of the ACM]], and two general magazines for computer professionals, [[Communications_of_the_ACM|Communications of the ACM]] (also known as Communications or CACM) and [[ACM_Queue|Queue]].
sentence_15: Other publications of the ACM include:

list.value: [[XRDS_(magazine)|ACM XRDS]], formerly "Crossroads", was redesigned in 2010 and is the most popular student computing magazine in the US.
[[ACM_Interactions_(magazine)|ACM Interactions]], an interdisciplinary HCI publication focused on the connections between experiences, people and technology, and the third largest ACM publication.
ACM Journal on Emerging Technologies in Computing Systems (JETC)
ACM Special Interest Group: Computers and Society (SIGCAS)
A number of journals, specific to subfields of computer science, titled ACM Transactions. Some of the more notable transactions include:
[[ACM_Transactions_on_Computational_Biology_and_Bioinformatics|IEEE/ACM Transactions on Computational Biology and Bioinformatics]] (TCBB)
[[ACM_Transactions_on_Multimedia_Computing,_Communications,_and_Applications|ACM Transactions on Multimedia Computing, Communications, and Applications]] (TOMM)
ACM Transactions on Programming Languages and Systems (TOPLAS)

sentence_16: Although Communications no longer publishes primary research, and is not considered a prestigious venue, many of the great debates and results in computing history have been published in its pages.
sentence_17: ACM has made almost all of its publications available to paid subscribers online at its [[#Digital_Library|Digital Library]] and also has a [[ACM_Guide_to_Computing_Literature|Guide to Computing Literature]].
sentence_18: Individual members additionally have access to [[Safari_Books_Online|Safari Books Online]] and Books24x7.
sentence_19: ACM also offers insurance, online courses, and other services to its members.
sentence_20: In 1997, ACM Press published Wizards and Their Wonders: Portraits in Computing ([[ISBN_(identifier)|ISBN]] 0897919602), written by Christopher Morgan, with new photographs by [[Louis_Fabian_Bachrach,_Jr.|Louis Fabian Bachrach]].
sentence_21: The book is a collection of historic and current portrait photographs of figures from the computer industry.
sentence_22: The ACM Portal is an online service of the ACM.
sentence_23: Its core are two main sections: ACM Digital Library and the [[ACM_Guide_to_Computing_Literature|ACM Guide to Computing Literature]].
sentence_24: The ACM Digital Library is the full-text collection of all articles published by the ACM in its articles, magazines and conference proceedings.
sentence_25: The Guide is a bibliography in computing with over one million entries.
sentence_26: The ACM Digital Library contains a comprehensive archive starting in the 1950s of the organization's journals, magazines, newsletters and conference proceedings.
sentence_27: Online services include a forum called Ubiquity and Tech News digest.
sentence_28: There is an extensive underlying bibliographic database containing key works of all genres from all major publishers of computing literature.
sentence_29: This secondary database is a rich discovery service known as The ACM Guide to Computing Literature.
sentence_30: ACM adopted a hybrid [[Open_access|Open Access]] (OA) publishing model in 2013.
sentence_31: Authors who do not choose to pay the OA fee must grant ACM publishing rights by either a copyright transfer agreement or a publishing license agreement.
sentence_32: ACM was a "green" publisher before the term was invented.
sentence_33: Authors may post documents on their own websites and in their institutional repositories with a link back to the ACM Digital Library's permanently maintained Version of Record.
sentence_34: All metadata in the Digital Library is open to the world, including [[Abstracts|abstracts]], linked references and citing works, citation and usage statistics, as well as all functionality and services.
sentence_35: Other than the free articles, the full-texts are accessed by subscription.
sentence_36: There is also a mounting challenge to the ACM's publication practices coming from the [[Open_access_(publishing)|open access]] movement.
sentence_37: Some authors see a centralized peer–review process as less relevant and publish on their home pages or on unreviewed sites like [[ArXiv|arXiv]].
sentence_38: Other organizations have sprung up which do their peer review entirely free and online, such as [[Journal_of_Artificial_Intelligence_Research|Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research]], [[Journal_of_Machine_Learning_Research|Journal of Machine Learning Research]] and the Journal of Research and Practice in Information Technology.
sentence_39: Main category: Members of the Association for Computing Machinery
sentence_40: In addition to student and regular members, ACM has several advanced membership grades to recognize those with multiple years of membership and "demonstrated performance that sets them apart from their peers".
sentence_41: The number of Fellows, Distinguished Members, and Senior Members cannot exceed 1%, 10%, and 25% of the total number of professional members, respectively.
sentence_42: Main article: [[ACM_Fellow|ACM Fellow]]
sentence_43: For a more comprehensive list, see [[List_of_Fellows_of_the_Association_for_Computing_Machinery|List of Fellows of the Association for Computing Machinery]].
sentence_44: The [[ACM_Fellow|ACM Fellows]] Program was established by Council of the Association for Computing Machinery in 1993 "to recognize and honor outstanding ACM members for their achievements in computer science and information technology and for their significant contributions to the mission of the ACM."
sentence_45: There are 1163 Fellows as of 2019 out of about 100,000 members.
sentence_46: In 2006, ACM began recognizing two additional membership grades, one which was called Distinguished Members.
sentence_47: Distinguished Members (Distinguished Engineers, Distinguished Scientists, and Distinguished Educators) have at least 15 years of professional experience and 5 years of continuous ACM membership and "have made a significant impact on the computing field".
sentence_48: Note that in 2006 when the Distinguished Members first came out, one of the three levels was called "Distinguished Member" and was changed about two years later to "Distinguished Educator".
sentence_49: Those who already had the Distinguished Member title had their titles changed to one of the other three titles.
sentence_50: List of Distinguished Members of the Association for Computing Machinery
sentence_51: Also in 2006, ACM began recognizing Senior Members.
sentence_52: According to the ACM, "The Senior Members Grade recognizes those ACM members with at least 10 years of professional experience and 5 years of continuous Professional Membership who have demonstrated performance through technical leadership, and technical or professional contributions".
sentence_53: Senior membership also requires 3 letters of reference
sentence_54: While not technically a membership grade, the ACM recognizes distinguished speakers on topics in computer science.
sentence_55: A distinguished speaker is appointed for a three-year period.
sentence_56: There are usually about 125 current distinguished speakers.
sentence_57: The ACM website describes these people as 'Renowned International Thought Leaders'.
sentence_58: The distinguished speaker program is overseen by a committee
sentence_59: ACM has three kinds of chapters: [[Special_Interest_Group|Special Interest Groups]], Professional Chapters, and [[ACM_Student_Chapter|Student Chapters]].
sentence_60: As of 2011, ACM has professional & SIG Chapters in 56 countries.
sentence_61: As of 2014, there exist ACM student chapters in 41 different countries.

sentence_65: Most of the SIGs also have an annual conference.
sentence_66: ACM conferences are often very popular publishing venues and are therefore very competitive.
sentence_67: For example, the 2007 [[SIGGRAPH|SIGGRAPH]] conference attracted about 30000 visitors, and CIKM only accepted 15% of the long papers that were submitted in 2005.

sentence_77: ACM is led by a Council consisting of the President, Vice-President, Treasurer, Past President, SIG Governing Board Chair, Publications Board Chair, three representatives of the SIG Governing Board, and seven Members–At–Large.
sentence_78: This institution is often referred to simply as "Council" in Communications of the ACM.

sentence_81: [[ACM-W|ACM-W]], the ACM council on [[Women_in_computing|women in computing]], supports, celebrates, and advocates internationally for the full engagement of women in computing.
sentence_82: ACM–W's main programs are regional celebrations of women in computing, ACM-W chapters, and scholarships for women CS students to attend research conferences.
sentence_83: In India and Europe these activities are overseen by ACM-W India and ACM-W Europe respectively.
sentence_84: ACM-W collaborates with organizations such as the [[Anita_Borg_Institute|Anita Borg Institute]], the National Center for Women & Information Technology (NCWIT), and [[CRA-W:_Committee_on_the_Status_of_Women_in_Computing_Research|Committee on the Status of Women in Computing Research (CRA-W)]].

sentence_88: ACM's primary partner has been the [[IEEE_Computer_Society|IEEE Computer Society]] (IEEE-CS), which is the largest subgroup of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE).

sentence_1: Acadia University is a public, predominantly undergraduate [[University|university]] located in [[Wolfville|Wolfville]], [[Nova_Scotia|Nova Scotia]], Canada with some graduate programs at the master's level and one at the doctoral level.
sentence_2: The enabling legislation consists of Acadia University Act and the Amended Acadia University Act 2000.
sentence_3: The Wolfville Campus houses Acadia University Archives and the Acadia University Art Gallery.
sentence_4: Acadia offers over 200-degree combinations in the Faculties of Arts, Pure and Applied Science, Professional Studies, and Theology.
sentence_5: The student-faculty ratio is 15:1 and the average class size is 28.
sentence_6: Open Acadia offers correspondence and distance education courses.
sentence_7: As of July 2017, Dr. Peter J. Ricketts is Acadia's current president.
sentence_8: Acadia began as an extension of Horton Academy (1828), which was founded in [[Horton,_Nova_Scotia|Horton, Nova Scotia]], by [[Baptists|Baptists]] from Nova Scotia and Queen's College (1838).
sentence_9: The college was later named Acadia College.
sentence_10: Acadia University, established at [[Wolfville,_Nova_Scotia|Wolfville, Nova Scotia]] in 1838 has a strong [[Baptist|Baptist]] religious affiliation.
sentence_11: It was designed to prepare men for the ministry and to supply education for lay members.
sentence_12: The two major Universities of the day in Nova Scotia were heavily controlled by denominational structures.
sentence_13: King's College ([[University_of_King's_College|University of King's College]]) was an [[Anglican|Anglican]] school and [[Dalhousie_University|Dalhousie University]], which was originally non-denominational, had placed itself under the control and direction of the [[Church_of_Scotland|Church of Scotland]].
sentence_14: It was the failure of Dalhousie to appoint a prominent Baptist pastor and scholar, Edmund Crawley, to the Chair of [[Classics|Classics]], as had been expected, that really thrust into the forefront of Baptist thinking the need for a college established and run by the Baptists.
sentence_15: In 1838, the Nova Scotia Baptist Education Society founded Queen's College (named for Queen Victoria).
sentence_16: The college began with 21 students in January 1839.
sentence_17: The name "Queen's College" was denied to the Baptist school, so it was renamed "Acadia College" in 1841, in reference to the history of the area as an [[Acadian|Acadian]] settlement.
sentence_18: Acadia College awarded its first degrees in 1843 and became Acadia University in 1891, established by the Acadia University Act.
sentence_19: The Granville Street Baptist Church (now First Baptist Church (Halifax)) was an instrumental and determining factor in the founding of the university.
sentence_20: It has played a supporting role throughout its history, and shares much of the credit for its survival and development.
sentence_21: Many individuals who have made significant contributions to Acadia University, including the first president John Pryor, were members of the First Baptist Church Halifax congregation.
sentence_22: Similarly, the adjacent Wolfville United Baptist Church plays a significant role in the life of the university.
sentence_23: The original charter of the college stated:
sentence_24: This was unique at the time, and a direct result of Baptists being denied entry into other schools that required religious tests of their students and staff.
sentence_25: In 1851, the power of appointing governors was transferred from the Nova Scotia Baptist Education Society to the Baptist Convention of the Maritime Provinces.
sentence_26: Charles Osborne Wickenden (architect) and J.C. Dumaresq designed the Central Building, Acadia College, 1878–79.
sentence_27: Clara Belle Marshall, from [[Mount_Hanley,_Nova_Scotia|Mount Hanley, Nova Scotia]], became the first woman to graduate from Acadia University in 1879.
sentence_28: In 1891, there were changes in the Act of Incorporation.
sentence_29: [[Andrew_R._Cobb|Andrew R. Cobb]] designed several campus buildings including: Raynor Hall Residence, 1916; , designed by Cobb in the Georgian style, and built by James Reid of [[Yarmouth,_Nova_Scotia|Yarmouth, Nova Scotia]] was opened in 1915 as Horton Academy.
sentence_30: Today, Horton Hall is the home of the Department of Psychology and Research and Graduate Studies.
sentence_31: Emmerson Hall, built in 1913, is particularly interesting for the variety of building stones used.
sentence_32: In 1967 Emmerson Hall was converted to classrooms and offices for the School of Education.
sentence_33: It is a registered Heritage Property.
sentence_34: Unveiled on 16 August 1963, a wooden and metal organ in Manning Chapel, Acadia University, is dedicated to Acadia University's war dead of the First and Second World Wars and the Korean War.
sentence_35: A book of remembrance in Manning Chapel, Acadia University was unveiled on 1 March 1998 through the efforts of the Wolfville Historical Society
sentence_36: In 1966, the Baptist denomination relinquished direct control over the University.
sentence_37: The denomination maintains nine seats on the University's Board of Governors.
sentence_38: Acadia is a laureate of Washington's Smithsonian Institution and a part of the permanent research collection of the National Museum of American History.
sentence_39: Acadia is also the only Canadian University selected for inclusion in the Education and Academia category if the Computerworld Smithsonian Award.
sentence_40: Acadia University's Board of Governors and members of the Acadia University Faculty Association (AUFA) have ratified a new covering the period 1 July 2010 to 30 June 2014.
sentence_41: The faculty of Acadia University have been on strike twice in the history of the institution.
sentence_42: The first was 24 February to 12 March 2004.
sentence_43: The second was 15 October to 5 November 2007.
sentence_44: The second strike was resolved after the province's labour minister, [[Mark_Parent|Mark Parent]], appointed a mediator, on 1 November, to facilitate an agreement.
sentence_45: In [[Maclean's|Maclean's]] 2021 Guide to Canadian Universities, Acadia was ranked second in the publication's "primarily undergraduate" Canadian university category.
sentence_46: In the same year, the publication ranked Acadia 28th, in its reputation rankings.
sentence_47: Acadia is organized into four faculties: Arts, Pure & Applied Science, Professional Studies and Theology.
sentence_48: Each faculty is further divided into departments and schools specialized in areas of teaching and research.
sentence_49: Acadia has over 15 research centres and 6 research chairs.
sentence_50: Undergraduate students have the opportunity to participate in many research opportunities in a small university setting.
sentence_51: The Division of Research & Graduate Studies is separate from the faculties and oversees graduate students as well as Acadia's research programs.
sentence_52: Acadia's research programs explore coastal environments, ethno-cultural diversity, social justice, environmental monitoring and climate change, organizational relationships, data mining, the impact of digital technologies, and lifestyle choices contributing to health and wellness.
sentence_53: Acadia's research centres include the Tidal Energy Institute, the Acadia Institute for Data Analytics, and the Beaubassin Field Station.
sentence_54: Applied research opportunities include research with local wineries and grape growers, alternative insect control techniques and technologies.
sentence_55: In 1996, Acadia University pioneered the use of mobile computing technology in a post-secondary educational environment.
sentence_56: This academic initiative, named the Acadia Advantage, integrated the use of notebook computers into the undergraduate curriculum and featured innovations in teaching.
sentence_57: By 2000, all full-time, undergraduate Acadia students were taking part in the initiative.
sentence_58: The initiative went beyond leasing notebook computers to students during the academic year, and included training, user support and the use of course-specific applications at Acadia that arguably revolutionized learning at the Wolfville, N.S. campus and beyond.
sentence_59: Because of its pioneering efforts, Acadia is a laureate of Washington's Smithsonian Institution and a part of the permanent research collection of the National Museum of American History.
sentence_60: It is the only Canadian university selected for inclusion in the Education and Academia category of the Computerworld Smithsonian Award.
sentence_61: In addition, Acadia University received the Pioneer Award for Ubiquitous Computing.
sentence_62: In 2001, it achieved high rankings in the annual [[Maclean's|Maclean's]] University Rankings, including Best Overall for Primarily Undergraduate University in their opinion survey, and it received the Canadian Information Productivity Award in 1997 as it was praised as the first university in Canada to fully utilize information technology in the undergraduate curriculum.
sentence_63: In October 2006, Dr. Dinter-Gottlieb established a commission to review the Acadia Advantage learning environment 10 years after inception.
sentence_64: The mandate of the commission was to determine how well the current Advantage program meets the needs of students, faculty, and staff and to examine how the role of technology in the postsecondary environment has changed at Acadia, and elsewhere.
sentence_65: The commission was asked to recommend changes and enhancements to the Acadia Advantage that would benefit the entire university community and ensure its sustainability.
sentence_66: Some of the recommendations coming from the Acadia Advantage Renewal Report included developing a choice of model specifications and moving from Acadia-issued, student-leased notebook computers to a student-owned computer model.
sentence_67: The compelling rationale for this was the integral role technology now plays in our lives, which was not present in 1996.
sentence_68: The University was also advised to unbundle its tuition structure so that the cost of an Acadia education is more detailed and students can understand how their investment in the future of the school is allotted.
sentence_69: In September 2008, Acadia moved to a student-owned notebook computer version of the Acadia Advantage, now named Acadia Advantage 2.0.
sentence_70: In 2017, Acadia announced the Huestis Innovation Pavilion as part of its $22.25 million Science Complex renewal project.
sentence_71: Named in honour of lead donors, Faye and David Huestis of Saint John, New Brunswick, the Pavilion is a key connection between Elliott and Huggins Halls, providing research and commercialization space.
sentence_72: The new Agri-Technology Access Centre in the Innovation Pavilion provides companies and industry organizations with better access to specialized technology, lab space, subject-matter expertise and commercialization support services, strengthening their ability to become more productive and innovative.
sentence_73: It also enables Acadia to advance its applied research strength in a key priority sector – agriculture – and expand its successful technology transfer and commercialization activities.
sentence_74: The Science Complex renewal project was supported by an investment of $15.98 million by the Federal and Provincial governments.
sentence_75: Acadia's sports teams are called the [[Acadia_Axemen|Axemen]] and [[Acadia_Axewomen|Axewomen]].
sentence_76: They participate in the Atlantic University Sports conference of [[U_Sports|U Sports]].
sentence_77: School spirit abounds with men's and women's varsity teams that have delivered more conference and national championships than any other institution in Atlantic University Sport.
sentence_78: Routinely, more than one-third of Acadia's varsity athletes also achieve Academic All-Canadian designation through Canadian Interuniversity Sport by maintaining a minimum average of 80 per cent.
sentence_79: Expansion and modernization of [[Raymond_Field|Raymond Field]] was completed in the fall of 2007 and features the installation of an eight-lane all-weather running track and a move to the same premium artificial turf used by the New England Patriots of the [[National_Football_League|National Football League]] for its main playing field.
sentence_80: The Raymond Field modernization was a gift to the university by friends, alumni, and the province.
sentence_81: War Memorial Gymnasium also saw the installation of a new playing floor to benefit its basketball and volleyball teams.
sentence_82: In September 2006, Acadia University announced its partnership with the Wolfville Tritons Swim Club and the Acadia Masters Swim Club to form the Acadia Swim Club and return competitive swimming to the university after a 14-year hiatus.
sentence_83: On 26 September 2008, the university announced its intention to return swimming to a varsity status in September 2009.

sentence_86: In 1974, Acadia was granted a coat of arms designed by the [[College_of_Arms|College of Arms]] in London, England.
sentence_87: The coat of arms is two-tone, with the school's official colours, garnet and blue, on the shield.
sentence_88: The axes represent the school's origins in a rural setting, and the determination of its founders who cleared the land and built the school on donated items and labour.
sentence_89: The open books represent the intellectual pursuits of a university, and the wolves heads are a whimsical representation of the University's location in Wolfville.
sentence_90: "In pulvere vinces" (In dust you conquer) is the motto.
sentence_91: The University seal depicts the Greek goddess of wisdom [[Athena|Athena]] in front of the first college hall.
sentence_92: The University also uses a stylized "A" as a logo for its sports teams.
sentence_93: Notable among a number of [[Fight_song|fight songs]] commonly played and sung at various events such as commencement, convocation, and athletic games are: the Acadia University [[Alma_mater|alma mater]] set to the tune of "Annie Lisle".

sentence_95: Seminary House, also known as the Ladies' Seminary, is a [[Second_Empire_architecture|Second Empire]] style-building constructed in 1878 as a home for women attending the university.
sentence_96: It was designated a [[National_Historic_Sites_of_Canada|National Historic Site of Canada]] in 1997 as Canada's oldest facility associated with the higher education of women.

sentence_98: It was designated under the provincial [[Heritage_Property_Act_(Nova_Scotia)|Heritage Property Act]] in 1989 as its construction in 1909 signified Acadia's evolution from classical college to liberal university.
sentence_99: The War Memorial House (more generally known as Barrax), which is a residence, and War Memorial Gymnasium are landmark buildings on the campus of Acadia University.

sentence_4: Alaska ([[English|/əˈlæskə/]] (listen); [[Aleut_language|Aleut]]: Alax̂sxax̂; [[Inupiaq_language|Inupiaq]]: Alaasikaq; [[Pacific_Gulf_Yupik_language|Pacific Gulf Yupik]]: Alas'kaaq; Tlingit: Anáaski; [[Russian_language|Russian]]: Аля́ска, [[Romanization_of_Russian|romanized]]: Alyáska) is a [[U.S._state|U.S.
sentence_5: state]] on the northwest extremity of the country's [[West_Coast_of_the_United_States|West Coast]], just across the [[Bering_Strait|Bering Strait]] from Asia.
sentence_6: An [[Enclave_and_exclave|exclave]] of the U.S., it borders the [[Provinces_and_territories_of_Canada|Canadian province]] of [[British_Columbia|British Columbia]] and territory of [[Yukon|Yukon]] to the east and southeast and has a [[Maritime_border|maritime border]] with Russia's [[Chukotka_Autonomous_Okrug|Chukotka Autonomous Okrug]] to the west.
sentence_7: To the north are the [[Chukchi_Sea|Chukchi]] and [[Beaufort_Sea|Beaufort]] seas of the Arctic Ocean, while the [[Pacific_Ocean|Pacific Ocean]] lies to the south and southwest.
sentence_8: Alaska is by far the [[List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_area|largest U.S. state]] by area, comprising more total area than the next three largest states [[Texas|Texas]], [[California|California]], and [[Montana|Montana]] combined, and the [[List_of_country_subdivisions_by_area|seventh-largest subnational division in the world]].
sentence_9: It is the [[List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population|third-least populous]] and the [[List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population_density|most sparsely populated]] state, but by far the continent's most populous territory located mostly north of the [[60th_parallel_north|60th parallel]], with an estimated population of 738,432 as of 2015—more than quadruple the combined populations of Northern Canada and [[Greenland|Greenland]].
sentence_10: Approximately half of Alaska's residents live within the [[Anchorage_metropolitan_area|Anchorage metropolitan area]].
sentence_11: The state capital of [[Juneau,_Alaska|Juneau]] is the second-[[List_of_United_States_cities_by_area|largest city in the United States by area]], comprising more territory than the states of [[Rhode_Island|Rhode Island]] and [[Delaware|Delaware]].
sentence_12: Alaska was occupied by various indigenous peoples for thousands of years before the arrival of Europeans.
sentence_13: The state is considered the entry point for the settlement of North America by way of the [[Bering_land_bridge|Bering land bridge]].
sentence_14: The [[Russians|Russians]] were the first Europeans to settle the area beginning in the 18th century, eventually establishing [[Russian_America|Russian America]], which spanned most of the current state.
sentence_15: The expense and difficulty of maintaining this distant possession prompted [[Alaska_Purchase|its sale to the U.S.]] in 1867 for [[US$|US$]]7.2 million, or approximately two cents per acre ($4.74/km).
sentence_16: The area went through several administrative changes before becoming organized as a [[Territories_of_the_United_States|territory]] on May 11, 1912.
sentence_17: It was admitted as the 49th state of the U.S. on January 3, 1959.
sentence_18: While it has one of the smallest state economies in the country, Alaska's [[List_of_U.S._states_by_GDP_per_capita|per capita income is among the highest]], owing to a diversified economy dominated by fishing, natural gas, and [[Petroleum|oil]], all of which it has in abundance.
sentence_19: [[United_States_armed_forces|United States armed forces]] bases and [[Tourism_in_Alaska|tourism]] are also a significant part of the [[Economy_of_Alaska|economy]]; more than half the state is federally owned public land, including a multitude of national forests, parks, and [[National_wildlife_refuge|wildlife refuges]].
sentence_20: Alaska's indigenous population is proportionally the highest of any U.S. state, at over 15 percent.
sentence_21: Close to two dozen native languages are spoken, and Alaskan Natives exercise considerable influence in local and state politics.
sentence_22: The name "Alaska" (Russian: Аля́ска, [[Romanization_of_Russian|tr.]]
sentence_23: Alyáska) was introduced in the [[Russian_America|Russian colonial period]] when it was used to refer to the [[Alaska_Peninsula|Alaska Peninsula]].
sentence_24: It was derived from an [[Aleut_language|Aleut-language]] [[Idiom|idiom]], which figuratively refers to the mainland.
sentence_25: Literally, it means object to which the action of the sea is directed.
sentence_26: Main article: [[Geography_of_Alaska|Geography of Alaska]]
sentence_27: Alaska is the northernmost and westernmost state in the United States and has the most easterly longitude in the United States because the [[Aleutian_Islands|Aleutian Islands]] extend into the [[Eastern_Hemisphere|Eastern Hemisphere]].
sentence_28: Alaska is the only non-[[Contiguous_United_States|contiguous]] U.S. state on continental North America; about 500 miles (800 km) of [[British_Columbia|British Columbia]] (Canada) separates Alaska from [[Washington_(state)|Washington]].
sentence_29: It is technically part of the [[Continental_United_States|continental U.S.]], but is sometimes not included in colloquial use; Alaska is not part of the [[Contiguous_United_States|contiguous U.S.]], often called [[Outside_(Alaska)|"the Lower 48"]].
sentence_30: The capital city, [[Juneau|Juneau]], is situated on the mainland of the North American continent but is not connected by road to the rest of the North American highway system.
sentence_31: The state is bordered by Canada's [[Yukon|Yukon]] and [[British_Columbia|British Columbia]] to the east (making it the only state to border a [[Provinces_and_territories_of_Canada|Canadian territory]]), the [[Gulf_of_Alaska|Gulf of Alaska]] and the Pacific Ocean to the south and southwest, the [[Bering_Sea|Bering Sea]], [[Bering_Strait|Bering Strait]], and [[Chukchi_Sea|Chukchi Sea]] to the west and the Arctic Ocean to the north.
sentence_32: Alaska's territorial waters touch Russia's territorial waters in the Bering Strait, as the Russian [[Big_Diomede_Island|Big Diomede Island]] and Alaskan [[Little_Diomede_Island|Little Diomede Island]] are only 3 miles (4.8 km) apart.
sentence_33: Alaska has a longer coastline than all the other U.S. states combined.
sentence_34: At 663,268 square miles (1,717,856 km) in area, Alaska is by far the largest state in the United States, and is more than twice the size of the second-largest U.S. state, [[Texas|Texas]].
sentence_35: Alaska is the seventh largest sub-national division in the world, and if it was an independent nation would be the 19th largest country in the world.
sentence_36: There are no officially defined borders demarcating the various regions of Alaska, but there are six widely accepted regions:
sentence_37: Main article: [[South_Central_Alaska|South Central Alaska]]
sentence_38: The most populous region of Alaska, containing [[Anchorage|Anchorage]], the [[Matanuska-Susitna_Valley|Matanuska-Susitna Valley]] and the [[Kenai_Peninsula|Kenai Peninsula]].
sentence_39: Rural, mostly unpopulated areas south of the [[Alaska_Range|Alaska Range]] and west of the [[Wrangell_Mountains|Wrangell Mountains]] also fall within the definition of South Central, as do the [[Prince_William_Sound|Prince William Sound]] area and the communities of [[Cordova,_Alaska|Cordova]] and [[Valdez,_Alaska|Valdez]].
sentence_40: Main article: [[Southeast_Alaska|Southeast Alaska]]
sentence_41: Also referred to as the Panhandle or Inside Passage, this is the region of Alaska closest to the rest of the United States.
sentence_42: As such, this was where most of the initial non-indigenous settlement occurred in the years following the [[Alaska_Purchase|Alaska Purchase]].
sentence_43: The region is dominated by the [[Alexander_Archipelago|Alexander Archipelago]] as well as the [[Tongass_National_Forest|Tongass National Forest]], the largest national forest in the United States.
sentence_44: It contains the state capital [[Juneau|Juneau]], the former capital [[Sitka,_Alaska|Sitka]], and [[Ketchikan|Ketchikan]], at one time Alaska's largest city.
sentence_45: The [[Alaska_Marine_Highway|Alaska Marine Highway]] provides a vital surface transportation link throughout the area, as only three communities ([[Haines,_Alaska|Haines]], [[Hyder,_Alaska|Hyder]] and Skagway) enjoy direct connections to the contiguous North American road system.
sentence_46: Main article: Alaska Interior
sentence_47: The Interior is the largest region of Alaska; much of it is uninhabited wilderness.
sentence_48: [[Fairbanks,_Alaska|Fairbanks]] is the only large city in the region.
sentence_49: [[Denali_National_Park_and_Preserve|Denali National Park and Preserve]] is located here.
sentence_50: [[Denali|Denali]], formerly Mount McKinley, is the highest mountain in North America.
sentence_51: Main article: [[Southwest_Alaska|Southwest Alaska]]
sentence_52: Southwest Alaska is a sparsely inhabited region stretching some 500 miles (800 km) inland from the Bering Sea.
sentence_53: Most of the population lives along the coast.
sentence_54: [[Kodiak_Island|Kodiak Island]] is also located in Southwest.
sentence_55: The massive [[Yukon–Kuskokwim_Delta|Yukon–Kuskokwim Delta]], one of the largest river deltas in the world, is here.
sentence_56: Portions of the [[Alaska_Peninsula|Alaska Peninsula]] are considered part of Southwest, with the remaining portions included with the Aleutian Islands (see below).
sentence_57: Main article: [[Alaska_North_Slope|Alaska North Slope]]
sentence_58: The North Slope is mostly [[Tundra|tundra]] peppered with small villages.
sentence_59: The area is known for its massive reserves of crude oil, and contains both the [[National_Petroleum_Reserve–Alaska|National Petroleum Reserve–Alaska]] and the [[Prudhoe_Bay_Oil_Field|Prudhoe Bay Oil Field]].
sentence_60: The city of [[Utqiagvik,_Alaska|Utqiagvik]], formerly known as Barrow, is the northernmost city in the United States and is located here.
sentence_61: The [[Northwest_Arctic_Borough,_Alaska|Northwest Arctic area]], anchored by [[Kotzebue,_Alaska|Kotzebue]] and also containing the [[Kobuk_River|Kobuk River]] valley, is often regarded as being part of this region.
sentence_62: However, the respective [[Inupiat_people|Inupiat]] of the North Slope and of the Northwest Arctic seldom consider themselves to be one people.
sentence_63: Main article: [[Aleutian_Islands|Aleutian Islands]]
sentence_64: More than 300 small volcanic islands make up this chain, which stretches more than 1,200 miles (1,900 km) into the Pacific Ocean.
sentence_65: Some of these islands fall in the Eastern Hemisphere, but the [[International_Date_Line|International Date Line]] was drawn west of [[180th_meridian|180°]] to keep the whole state, and thus the entire North American continent, within the same legal day.
sentence_66: Two of the islands, Attu and [[Kiska|Kiska]], were occupied by Japanese forces during World War II.
sentence_67: See also: [[Wildlife_of_Alaska|Wildlife of Alaska]]
sentence_68: With its myriad islands, Alaska has nearly 34,000 miles (55,000 km) of tidal shoreline.
sentence_69: The [[Aleutian_Islands|Aleutian Islands]] chain extends west from the southern tip of the [[Alaska_Peninsula|Alaska Peninsula]].
sentence_70: Many active [[Volcano|volcanoes]] are found in the Aleutians and in coastal regions.
sentence_71: [[Unimak_Island|Unimak Island]], for example, is home to [[Mount_Shishaldin|Mount Shishaldin]], which is an occasionally smoldering volcano that rises to 10,000 feet (3,000 m) above the North Pacific.
sentence_72: It is the most perfect volcanic cone on Earth, even more symmetrical than Japan's [[Mount_Fuji|Mount Fuji]].
sentence_73: The chain of volcanoes extends to [[Mount_Spurr|Mount Spurr]], west of Anchorage on the mainland.
sentence_74: Geologists have identified Alaska as part of [[Wrangellia|Wrangellia]], a large region consisting of multiple states and Canadian provinces in the [[Pacific_Northwest|Pacific Northwest]], which is actively undergoing [[Plate_tectonics|continent building]].
sentence_75: One of the world's largest tides occurs in [[Turnagain_Arm|Turnagain Arm]], just south of Anchorage, where tidal differences can be more than 35 feet (10.7 m).
sentence_76: Main article: [[List_of_lakes_in_Alaska|List of lakes in Alaska]]
sentence_77: Alaska has more than three million lakes.
sentence_78: [[Marshland|Marshlands]] and wetland [[Permafrost|permafrost]] cover 188,320 square miles (487,700 km) (mostly in northern, western and southwest flatlands).
sentence_79: Glacier ice covers about 28,957 square miles (75,000 km) of Alaska.
sentence_80: The [[Bering_Glacier|Bering Glacier]] is the largest glacier in North America, covering 2,008 square miles (5,200 km) alone.
sentence_81: According to an October 1998 report by the [[United_States_Bureau_of_Land_Management|United States Bureau of Land Management]], approximately 65% of Alaska is owned and managed by the [[Federal_government_of_the_United_States|U.S.
sentence_82: federal government]] as public lands, including a multitude of national forests, national parks, and [[National_wildlife_refuge|national wildlife refuges]].
sentence_83: Of these, the [[Bureau_of_Land_Management|Bureau of Land Management]] manages 87 million acres (35 million hectares), or 23.8% of the state.
sentence_84: The [[Arctic_National_Wildlife_Refuge|Arctic National Wildlife Refuge]] is managed by the [[United_States_Fish_and_Wildlife_Service|United States Fish and Wildlife Service]].
sentence_85: It is the world's largest wildlife refuge, comprising 16 million acres (6.5 million hectares).
sentence_86: Of the remaining land area, the state of Alaska owns 101 million acres (41 million hectares), its entitlement under the Alaska Statehood Act.
sentence_87: A portion of that acreage is occasionally ceded to organized boroughs, under the statutory provisions pertaining to newly formed boroughs.
sentence_88: Smaller portions are set aside for rural subdivisions and other homesteading-related opportunities.
sentence_89: These are not very popular due to the often remote and roadless locations.
sentence_90: The [[University_of_Alaska|University of Alaska]], as a [[Land_grant_university|land grant university]], also owns substantial acreage which it manages independently.
sentence_91: Another 44 million acres (18 million hectares) are owned by 12 regional, and scores of local, Native corporations created under the [[Alaska_Native_Claims_Settlement_Act|Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act]] (ANCSA) of 1971.
sentence_92: [[Alaska_Native_Regional_Corporation|Regional Native corporation]] [[Doyon,_Limited|Doyon, Limited]] often promotes itself as the largest private landowner in Alaska in advertisements and other communications.
sentence_93: Provisions of ANCSA allowing the corporations' land holdings to be sold on the open market starting in 1991 were repealed before they could take effect.
sentence_94: Effectively, the corporations hold title (including subsurface title in many cases, a privilege denied to individual Alaskans) but cannot sell the land.
sentence_95: [[Alaska_Native_Allotment_Act|Individual Native allotments]] can be and are sold on the open market, however.
sentence_96: Various private interests own the remaining land, totaling about one percent of the state.
sentence_97: Alaska is, by a large margin, the state with the smallest percentage of private land ownership when Native corporation holdings are excluded.
sentence_98: Main article: [[Climate_of_Alaska|Climate of Alaska]]
sentence_99: The climate in Southeast Alaska is a mid-latitude [[Oceanic_climate|oceanic climate]] ([[Köppen_climate_classification|Köppen climate classification]]: Cfb) in the southern sections and a subarctic oceanic climate (Köppen Cfc) in the northern parts.
sentence_100: On an annual basis, Southeast is both the wettest and warmest part of Alaska with milder temperatures in the winter and high precipitation throughout the year.
sentence_101: Juneau averages over 50 in (130 cm) of precipitation a year, and [[Ketchikan,_Alaska|Ketchikan]] averages over 150 in (380 cm).
sentence_102: This is also the only region in Alaska in which the average daytime high temperature is above freezing during the winter months.
sentence_103: The climate of [[Anchorage,_Alaska|Anchorage]] and south central Alaska is mild by Alaskan standards due to the region's proximity to the seacoast.
sentence_104: While the area gets less rain than southeast Alaska, it gets more snow, and days tend to be clearer.
sentence_105: On average, [[Anchorage,_Alaska|Anchorage]] receives 16 in (41 cm) of precipitation a year, with around 75 in (190 cm) of snow, although there are areas in the south central which receive far more snow.
sentence_106: It is a subarctic climate (Köppen: Dfc) due to its brief, cool summers.
sentence_107: The climate of [[Southwest_Alaska|Western Alaska]] is determined in large part by the [[Bering_Sea|Bering Sea]] and the [[Gulf_of_Alaska|Gulf of Alaska]].
sentence_108: It is a subarctic oceanic climate in the southwest and a continental subarctic climate farther north.
sentence_109: The temperature is somewhat moderate considering how far north the area is.
sentence_110: This region has a tremendous amount of variety in precipitation.
sentence_111: An area stretching from the northern side of the Seward Peninsula to the [[Kobuk_River|Kobuk River]] valley (i. e., the region around [[Kotzebue_Sound|Kotzebue Sound]]) is technically a [[Desert|desert]], with portions receiving less than 10 in (25 cm) of precipitation annually.
sentence_112: On the other extreme, some locations between [[Dillingham,_Alaska|Dillingham]] and [[Bethel,_Alaska|Bethel]] average around 100 in (250 cm) of precipitation.
sentence_113: The climate of the interior of Alaska is subarctic.
sentence_114: Some of the highest and lowest temperatures in Alaska occur around the area near [[Fairbanks,_Alaska|Fairbanks]].
sentence_115: The summers may have temperatures reaching into the 90s °F (the low-to-mid 30s °C), while in the winter, the temperature can fall below −60 °F (−51 °C).
sentence_116: Precipitation is sparse in the Interior, often less than 10 in (25 cm) a year, but what precipitation falls in the winter tends to stay the entire winter.
sentence_117: The highest and lowest recorded temperatures in Alaska are both in the Interior.
sentence_118: The highest is 100 °F (38 °C) in [[Fort_Yukon,_Alaska|Fort Yukon]] (which is just 8 mi or 13 km inside the arctic circle) on June 27, 1915, making Alaska tied with Hawaii as the state with the lowest high temperature in the United States.
sentence_119: The lowest official Alaska temperature is −80 °F (−62 °C) in [[Prospect_Creek,_Alaska|Prospect Creek]] on January 23, 1971, one degree above the lowest temperature recorded in continental North America (in [[Snag,_Yukon|Snag, Yukon, Canada]]).
sentence_120: The climate in the extreme north of Alaska is [[Polar_climate|Arctic]] ([[Köppen_climate_classification#GROUP_E:_Polar_climates|Köppen: ET]]) with long, very cold winters and short, cool summers.
sentence_121: Even in July, the average low temperature in [[Utqiagvik,_Alaska|Utqiagvik]] is 34 °F (1 °C).
sentence_122: Precipitation is light in this part of Alaska, with many places averaging less than 10 in (25 cm) per year, mostly as snow which stays on the ground almost the entire year.
