sentence_123: Main articles: [[Prehistory_of_Alaska|Prehistory of Alaska]] and [[History_of_Alaska|History of Alaska]]
sentence_124: Main article: Alaska Natives
sentence_125: Numerous indigenous peoples occupied Alaska for thousands of years before the arrival of European peoples to the area.
sentence_126: Linguistic and DNA studies done here have provided evidence for the settlement of North America by way of the [[Bering_land_bridge|Bering land bridge]].
sentence_127: At the [[Upward_Sun_River_site|Upward Sun River site]] in the Tanana River Valley in Alaska, remains of a six-week-old infant were found.
sentence_128: The baby's DNA showed that she belonged to a population that was genetically separate from other native groups present elsewhere in the [[New_World|New World]] at the end of the [[Pleistocene|Pleistocene]].
sentence_129: Ben Potter, the [[University_of_Alaska_Fairbanks|University of Alaska Fairbanks]] archaeologist who unearthed the remains at the Upward River Sun site in 2013, named this new group [[Ancient_Beringians|Ancient Beringians]].
sentence_130: The [[Tlingit_people|Tlingit people]] developed a society with a [[Matrilineal|matrilineal]] kinship system of property inheritance and descent in what is today Southeast Alaska, along with parts of British Columbia and the Yukon.
sentence_131: Also in Southeast were the Haida, now well known for their unique arts.
sentence_132: The [[Tsimshian|Tsimshian]] people came to Alaska from British Columbia in 1887, when President [[Grover_Cleveland|Grover Cleveland]], and later the U.S. Congress, granted them permission to settle on [[Annette_Island|Annette Island]] and found the town of [[Metlakatla,_Alaska|Metlakatla]].
sentence_133: All three of these peoples, as well as other [[Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Pacific_Northwest_Coast|indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest Coast]], experienced [[Smallpox|smallpox]] outbreaks from the late 18th through the mid-19th century, with the most devastating [[Epidemics|epidemics]] occurring in the 1830s and 1860s, resulting in high fatalities and social disruption.
sentence_134: The Aleutian Islands are still home to the [[Aleut_people|Aleut people]]'s seafaring society, although they were the first Native Alaskans to be exploited by the Russians.
sentence_135: Western and Southwestern Alaska are home to the [[Yup'ik|Yup'ik]], while their cousins the [[Alutiiq_people|Alutiiq ~ Sugpiaq]] lived in what is now Southcentral Alaska.
sentence_136: The [[Gwich'in_people|Gwich'in people]] of the northern Interior region are [[Alaskan_Athabaskans|Athabaskan]] and primarily known today for their dependence on the caribou within the much-contested [[Arctic_National_Wildlife_Refuge|Arctic National Wildlife Refuge]].
sentence_137: The North Slope and [[Little_Diomede_Island|Little Diomede Island]] are occupied by the widespread [[Inupiat_people|Inupiat people]].
sentence_138: Main articles: [[Russian_America|Russian America]], Department of Alaska, District of Alaska, [[Fairbanks_Gold_Rush|Fairbanks Gold Rush]], [[Kobuk_River_Stampede|Kobuk River Stampede]], and [[Nome_Gold_Rush|Nome Gold Rush]]
sentence_139: Some researchers believe the first Russian settlement in Alaska was established in the 17th century.
sentence_140: According to this hypothesis, in 1648 several [[Koch_(boat)|koches]] of [[Semyon_Dezhnyov|Semyon Dezhnyov]]'s expedition came ashore in Alaska by storm and founded this settlement.
sentence_141: This hypothesis is based on the testimony of Chukchi geographer Nikolai Daurkin, who had visited Alaska in 1764–1765 and who had reported on a village on the Kheuveren River, populated by "bearded men" who "pray to the [[Icons|icons]]".
sentence_142: Some modern researchers associate Kheuveren with [[Koyuk_River|Koyuk River]].
sentence_143: The first European vessel to reach Alaska is generally held to be the St. Gabriel under the authority of the surveyor [[Mikhail_Gvozdev|M.
sentence_144: S. Gvozdev]] and assistant navigator [[Ivan_Fyodorov_(navigator)|I.
sentence_145: Fyodorov]] on August 21, 1732, during an expedition of Siberian cossack A. F. Shestakov and Russian explorer [[Dmitry_Pavlutsky|Dmitry Pavlutsky]] (1729–1735).
sentence_146: Another European contact with Alaska occurred in 1741, when [[Vitus_Bering|Vitus Bering]] led an expedition for the Russian Navy aboard the St. Peter.
sentence_147: After his crew returned to Russia with [[Sea_otter|sea otter]] pelts judged to be the finest fur in the world, small associations of fur traders began to sail from the shores of Siberia toward the Aleutian Islands.
sentence_148: The first permanent European settlement was founded in 1784.
sentence_149: Between 1774 and 1800, [[Viceroyalty_of_New_Spain|Spain]] sent several [[Spanish_expeditions_to_the_Pacific_Northwest|expeditions to Alaska]] to assert its claim over the Pacific Northwest.
sentence_150: In 1789 a Spanish settlement and [[Fort_San_Miguel|fort]] were built in [[Nootka_Sound|Nootka Sound]].
sentence_151: These expeditions gave names to places such as [[Valdez,_Alaska|Valdez]], [[Bucareli_Sound|Bucareli Sound]], and [[Cordova,_Alaska|Cordova]].
sentence_152: Later, the [[Russian-American_Company|Russian-American Company]] carried out an expanded colonization program during the early-to-mid-19th century.
sentence_153: [[Sitka,_Alaska|Sitka]], renamed [[New_Archangel|New Archangel]] from 1804 to 1867, on [[Baranof_Island|Baranof Island]] in the [[Alexander_Archipelago|Alexander Archipelago]] in what is now [[Southeast_Alaska|Southeast Alaska]], became the capital of [[Russian_America|Russian America]].
sentence_154: It remained the capital after the colony was transferred to the United States.
sentence_155: The Russians never fully colonized Alaska, and the colony was never very profitable.
sentence_156: Evidence of Russian settlement in names and churches survive throughout southeast Alaska.
sentence_157: [[William_H._Seward|William H. Seward]], the [[United_States_Secretary_of_State|United States Secretary of State]], negotiated the [[Alaska_Purchase|Alaska Purchase]] (also known as Seward's Folly) with the Russians in 1867 for $7.2 million.
sentence_158: Russia's contemporary ruler [[Tsar|Tsar]] [[Alexander_II_of_Russia|Alexander II]], the [[Emperor_of_the_Russian_Empire|Emperor of the Russian Empire]], [[King_of_Poland|King of Poland]] and [[Grand_Duke_of_Finland|Grand Duke of Finland]], also planned the sale; the purchase was made on March 30, 1867.
sentence_159: Six months later the commissioners arrived in Sitka and the formal transfer was arranged; the formal flag-raising took place at Fort Sitka on October 18, 1867.
sentence_160: In the ceremony 250 uniformed U.S. soldiers marched to the governor's house at "Castle Hill", where the Russian troops lowered the Russian flag and the U.S. flag was raised.
sentence_161: This event is celebrated as [[Alaska_Day|Alaska Day]], a legal holiday on October 18.
sentence_162: Alaska was loosely governed by the military initially, and was administered as a district starting in 1884, with a governor appointed by the President of the United States.
sentence_163: A federal district court was headquartered in Sitka.
sentence_164: For most of Alaska's first decade under the United States flag, Sitka was the only community inhabited by American settlers.
sentence_165: They organized a "provisional city government", which was Alaska's first municipal government, but not in a legal sense.
sentence_166: Legislation allowing Alaskan communities to legally incorporate as cities did not come about until 1900, and [[Home_rule#Home_rule_in_the_United_States|home rule]] for cities was extremely limited or unavailable until statehood took effect in 1959.

section_15.value: Alaska as an incorporated U.S. territory

sentence_167: Main articles: [[Organic_act#List_of_organic_acts|Organic act § List of organic acts]], and Territory of Alaska
sentence_168: Starting in the 1890s and stretching in some places to the early 1910s, gold rushes in Alaska and the nearby [[Yukon|Yukon Territory]] brought thousands of miners and settlers to Alaska.
sentence_169: Alaska was officially incorporated as an organized territory in 1912.
sentence_170: Alaska's capital, which had been in [[Sitka,_Alaska|Sitka]] until 1906, was moved north to [[Juneau,_Alaska|Juneau]].
sentence_171: Construction of the [[Alaska_Governor's_Mansion|Alaska Governor's Mansion]] began that same year.
sentence_172: European immigrants from Norway and Sweden also settled in southeast Alaska, where they entered the fishing and logging industries.
sentence_173: During World War II, the [[Aleutian_Islands_Campaign|Aleutian Islands Campaign]] focused on Attu, [[Agattu|Agattu]] and [[Kiska_Island|Kiska]], all which were occupied by the [[Empire_of_Japan|Empire of Japan]].
sentence_174: During the Japanese occupation, a white American civilian and two [[United_States_Navy|United States Navy]] personnel were killed at Attu and Kiska respectively, and nearly a total of 50 Aleut civilians and eight sailors were interned in Japan.
sentence_175: About half of the Aleuts died during the period of internment.
sentence_176: [[Unalaska|Unalaska]]/[[Dutch_Harbor|Dutch Harbor]] and [[Adak,_Alaska|Adak]] became significant bases for the [[United_States_Army|United States Army]], [[United_States_Army_Air_Forces|United States Army Air Forces]] and [[United_States_Navy|United States Navy]].
sentence_177: The United States [[Lend-Lease|Lend-Lease]] program involved flying American warplanes through Canada to Fairbanks and then Nome; Soviet pilots took possession of these aircraft, ferrying them to fight the German invasion of the Soviet Union.
sentence_178: The construction of military bases contributed to the population growth of some Alaskan cities.
sentence_179: See also: Alaska Statehood Act, [[Admission_to_the_Union|Admission to the Union]], and [[List_of_U.S._states_by_date_of_admission_to_the_Union|List of U.S. states by date of admission to the Union]]
sentence_180: Statehood for Alaska was an important cause of James Wickersham early in his tenure as a congressional delegate.
sentence_181: Decades later, the statehood movement gained its first real momentum following a territorial referendum in 1946.
sentence_182: The Alaska Statehood Committee and Alaska's Constitutional Convention would soon follow.
sentence_183: Statehood supporters also found themselves fighting major battles against political foes, mostly in the U.S. Congress but also within Alaska.
sentence_184: Statehood was approved by Congress on July 7, 1958.
sentence_185: Alaska was officially proclaimed a state on January 3, 1959.
sentence_186: In 1960, the Census Bureau reported Alaska's population as 77.2% White, 3% Black, and 18.8% American Indian and Alaska Native.
sentence_187: Main article: [[1964_Alaska_earthquake|1964 Alaska earthquake]]
sentence_188: On March 27, 1964, the massive [[1964_Alaska_earthquake|Good Friday earthquake]] killed 133 people and destroyed several villages and portions of large coastal communities, mainly by the resultant [[Tsunamis|tsunamis]] and landslides.
sentence_189: It was the [[Largest_earthquakes_by_magnitude|second-most-powerful earthquake]] in recorded history, with a [[Moment_magnitude_scale|moment magnitude]] of 9.2 (more than a thousand times as powerful as the [[1989_Loma_Prieta_earthquake|1989 San Francisco earthquake]]).
sentence_190: The time of day (5:36 pm), time of year (spring) and location of the [[Epicenter|epicenter]] were all cited as factors in potentially sparing thousands of lives, particularly in Anchorage.
sentence_191: The 1968 discovery of oil at [[Prudhoe_Bay|Prudhoe Bay]] and the 1977 completion of the [[Trans-Alaska_Pipeline_System|Trans-Alaska Pipeline System]] led to an oil boom.
sentence_192: Royalty revenues from oil have funded large state budgets from 1980 onward.
sentence_193: That same year, not coincidentally, Alaska repealed its state income tax.
sentence_194: In 1989, the Exxon Valdez hit a reef in the [[Prince_William_Sound|Prince William Sound]], [[Exxon_Valdez_oil_spill|spilling]] more than 11 million U.S. gallons (42 [[Megalitre|megaliters]]) of crude oil over 1,100 miles (1,800 km) of coastline.
sentence_195: Today, the battle between philosophies of development and conservation is seen in the contentious debate over oil drilling in the [[Arctic_National_Wildlife_Refuge|Arctic National Wildlife Refuge]] and the proposed [[Pebble_Mine|Pebble Mine]].
sentence_196: The Alaska Heritage Resources Survey (AHRS) is a restricted [[Inventory|inventory]] of all reported [[Historic_site|historic]] and [[Prehistoric|prehistoric]] sites within the state of Alaska; it is maintained by the Office of History and Archaeology.
sentence_197: The survey's inventory of cultural resources includes objects, structures, buildings, sites, districts, and travel ways, with a general provision that they are more than fifty years old.
sentence_198: As of 31 January 2012, more than 35,000 sites have been reported.
sentence_199: Main article: [[Demographics_of_Alaska|Demographics of Alaska]]
sentence_200: The [[United_States_Census_Bureau|United States Census Bureau]] estimates that the population of Alaska was 731,545 on July 1, 2019, a 3.00% increase since the [[2010_United_States_Census|2010 United States Census]].
sentence_201: In 2010, Alaska ranked as the 47th state by population, ahead of [[North_Dakota|North Dakota]], [[Vermont|Vermont]], and [[Wyoming|Wyoming]] (and Washington, D.C.).
sentence_202: Estimates show North Dakota ahead as of 2018.
sentence_203: Alaska is the least densely populated state, and one of the most sparsely populated areas in the world, at 1.2 inhabitants per square mile (0.46/km), with the next state, Wyoming, at 5.8 inhabitants per square mile (2.2/km).
sentence_204: Alaska is by far the largest U.S. state by [[List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_area|area]], and the tenth wealthiest (per capita income).
sentence_205: As of November 2014, the state's unemployment rate was 6.6%.
sentence_206: As of 2018, it is one of 14 U.S. states that still have only one telephone [[Telephone_numbering_plan|area code]].
sentence_207: According to the [[2010_United_States_Census|2010 United States Census]], Alaska had a population of 710,231.
sentence_208: In terms of race and ethnicity, the state was 66.7% [[White_American|White]] (64.1% Non-Hispanic [[Non-Hispanic_Whites|White]]), 14.8% [[Native_Americans_in_the_United_States|American Indian]] and Alaska Native, 5.4% [[Asian_American|Asian]], 3.3% [[African_American|Black]] or African American, 1.0% Native Hawaiian and Other Pacific Islander, 1.6% from Some Other Race, and 7.3% from Two or More Races.
sentence_209: [[Hispanic_and_Latino_Americans|Hispanics]] or Latinos of any race made up 5.5% of the population.
sentence_210: As of 2011, 50.7% of Alaska's population younger than one year of age belonged to minority groups (i.e., did not have two parents of non-Hispanic white ancestry).
sentence_211: Further information: [[Alaska_Native_languages|Alaska Native languages]]
sentence_212: According to the 2011 [[American_Community_Survey|American Community Survey]], 83.4% of people over the age of five spoke only English at home.
sentence_213: About 3.5% spoke Spanish at home, 2.2% spoke another [[Indo-European_languages|Indo-European language]], about 4.3% spoke an Asian language (including [[Tagalog_language|Tagalog]]), and about 5.3% spoke other languages at home.
sentence_214: The [[Alaska_Native_Language_Center|Alaska Native Language Center]] at the [[University_of_Alaska_Fairbanks|University of Alaska Fairbanks]] claims that at least 20 [[Alaska_Native_languages|Alaskan native languages]] exist and there are also some languages with different dialects.
sentence_215: Most of Alaska's native languages belong to either the [[Eskimo–Aleut_languages|Eskimo–Aleut]] or [[Na-Dene_languages|Na-Dene]] language families; however, some languages are thought to be [[Language_isolate|isolates]] (e.g. [[Haida_language|Haida]]) or have not yet been classified (e.g. [[Tsimshianic_languages|Tsimshianic]]).
sentence_216: As of 2014 nearly all of Alaska's native languages were classified as either threatened, shifting, moribund, nearly extinct, or dormant languages.
sentence_217: A total of 5.2% of Alaskans speak one of the state's 20 [[Indigenous_languages_of_the_Americas|indigenous languages]], known locally as "native languages".
sentence_218: In October 2014, the governor of Alaska signed a bill declaring the state's 20 indigenous languages to have official status.
sentence_219: This bill gave them symbolic recognition as official languages, though they have not been adopted for official use within the government.
sentence_220: The 20 languages that were included in the bill are:
sentence_221: See also: [[Alaska_Native_religion|Alaska Native religion]]
sentence_222: According to statistics collected by the Association of Religion Data Archives from 2010, about 34% of Alaska residents were members of religious congregations.
sentence_223: 100,960 people identified as [[Evangelical_Protestant|Evangelical Protestants]], 50,866 as Roman Catholic, and 32,550 as mainline Protestants.
sentence_224: Roughly 4% are Mormon, 0.5% are Jewish, 1% are Muslim, 0.5% are Buddhist, 0.2% are Bahá'í, and 0.5% are Hindu.
sentence_225: The largest religious denominations in Alaska as of 2010 were the [[Catholic_Church|Catholic Church]] with 50,866 adherents, non-denominational Evangelical Protestants with 38,070 adherents, [[The_Church_of_Jesus_Christ_of_Latter-day_Saints|The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints]] with 32,170 adherents, and the [[Southern_Baptist_Convention|Southern Baptist Convention]] with 19,891 adherents.
sentence_226: Alaska has been identified, along with Pacific Northwest states Washington and Oregon, as being [[Unchurched_Belt|the least religious states of the USA]], in terms of church membership,
sentence_227: In 1795, the First [[Russian_Orthodox_Church|Russian Orthodox Church]] was established in [[Kodiak_Island_Borough,_Alaska|Kodiak]].
sentence_228: Intermarriage with Alaskan Natives helped the Russian immigrants integrate into society.
sentence_229: As a result, an increasing number of Russian Orthodox churches gradually became established within Alaska.
sentence_230: Alaska also has the largest [[Quaker|Quaker]] population (by percentage) of any state.
sentence_231: In 2009 there were 6,000 Jews in Alaska (for whom observance of [[Halakha|halakha]] [[Jewish_law_in_the_polar_regions|may pose special problems]]).
sentence_232: Alaskan Hindus often share venues and celebrations with members of other Asian religious communities, including [[Sikhism|Sikhs]] and [[Jainism|Jains]].
sentence_233: In 2010, Alaskan Hindus established the [[Sri_Ganesha_Temple_of_Alaska|Sri Ganesha Temple of Alaska]], making it the first Hindu Temple in Alaska and the northernmost Hindu Temple in the world.
sentence_234: There are an estimated 2,000–3,000 Hindus in Alaska.
sentence_235: The vast majority of Hindus live in Anchorage or Fairbanks.
sentence_236: Estimates for the number of Muslims in Alaska range from 2,000 to 5,000.
sentence_237: The [[Islamic_Community_Center_of_Anchorage,_Alaska|Islamic Community Center of Anchorage]] began efforts in the late 1990s to construct a mosque in Anchorage.
sentence_238: They broke ground on a building in south Anchorage in 2010 and were nearing completion in late 2014.
sentence_239: When completed, the mosque will be the first in the state and one of the northernmost mosques in the world.
sentence_240: There's also a [[Bahá'í_Faith|Bahá'í]] Center.
sentence_241: Main article: [[Economy_of_Alaska|Economy of Alaska]]
sentence_242: See also: [[Alaska_locations_by_per_capita_income|Alaska locations by per capita income]] and [[List_of_Alaska_companies|List of Alaska companies]]
sentence_243: The 2018 [[Gross_state_product|gross state product]] was $55 billion, 48th in the nation.
sentence_244: Its [[List_of_U.S._states_by_GDP_per_capita_(nominal)|per capita personal income]] for 2018 was $73,000, ranking 7th in the nation.
sentence_245: According to a 2013 study by Phoenix Marketing International, Alaska had the fifth-largest number of millionaires per capita in the United States, with a ratio of 6.75 percent.
sentence_246: The oil and gas industry dominates the Alaskan economy, with more than 80% of the state's revenues derived from petroleum extraction.
sentence_247: Alaska's main export product (excluding oil and natural gas) is seafood, primarily salmon, cod, Pollock and crab.
sentence_248: Agriculture represents a very small fraction of the Alaskan economy.
sentence_249: Agricultural production is primarily for consumption within the state and includes nursery stock, dairy products, vegetables, and livestock.
sentence_250: Manufacturing is limited, with most foodstuffs and general goods imported from elsewhere.
sentence_251: Employment is primarily in government and industries such as natural resource extraction, shipping, and transportation.
sentence_252: Military bases are a significant component of the economy in the Fairbanks North Star, Anchorage and Kodiak Island boroughs, as well as Kodiak.
sentence_253: Federal subsidies are also an important part of the economy, allowing the state to keep taxes low.
sentence_254: Its industrial outputs are crude petroleum, natural gas, coal, gold, precious metals, zinc and other mining, seafood processing, timber and wood products.
sentence_255: There is also a growing service and tourism sector.
sentence_256: Tourists have contributed to the economy by supporting local lodging.
sentence_257: See also: [[Natural_gas_in_Alaska|Natural gas in Alaska]] and [[Energy_law#Alaska_law|Energy law § Alaska law]]
sentence_258: Alaska has vast energy resources, although its oil reserves have been largely depleted.
sentence_259: Major oil and gas reserves were found in the [[Alaska_North_Slope|Alaska North Slope]] (ANS) and Cook Inlet basins, but according to the [[Energy_Information_Administration|Energy Information Administration]], by February 2014 Alaska had fallen to fourth place in the nation in crude oil production after Texas, North Dakota, and California.
sentence_260: Prudhoe Bay on Alaska's North Slope is still the second highest-yielding oil field in the United States, typically producing about 400,000 barrels per day (64,000 m/d), although by early 2014 North Dakota's [[Bakken_Formation|Bakken Formation]] was producing over 900,000 barrels per day (140,000 m/d).
sentence_261: Prudhoe Bay was the largest [[Conventional_oil|conventional oil]] field ever discovered in North America, but was much smaller than Canada's enormous [[Athabasca_oil_sands|Athabasca oil sands]] field, which by 2014 was producing about 1,500,000 barrels per day (240,000 m/d) of [[Unconventional_oil|unconventional oil]], and had hundreds of years of producible reserves at that rate.
sentence_262: The [[Trans-Alaska_Pipeline|Trans-Alaska Pipeline]] can transport and pump up to 2.1 million barrels (330,000 m) of crude oil per day, more than any other crude oil pipeline in the United States.
sentence_263: Additionally, substantial coal deposits are found in Alaska's bituminous, sub-bituminous, and lignite coal basins.
sentence_264: The United States Geological Survey estimates that there are 85.4 trillion cubic feet (2,420 km) of undiscovered, technically recoverable gas from natural gas hydrates on the Alaskan North Slope.
sentence_265: Alaska also offers some of the highest hydroelectric power potential in the country from its numerous rivers.
sentence_266: Large swaths of the Alaskan coastline offer wind and geothermal energy potential as well.
sentence_267: Alaska's economy depends heavily on increasingly expensive diesel fuel for heating, transportation, electric power and light.
sentence_268: Although wind and hydroelectric power are abundant and underdeveloped, proposals for statewide energy systems (e.g. with special [[Single-wire_earth_return#Use_in_interties|low-cost electric interties]]) were judged uneconomical (at the time of the report, 2001) due to low (less than 50¢/gal) fuel prices, long distances and low population.
sentence_269: The cost of a gallon of gas in urban Alaska today is usually thirty to sixty cents higher than the national average; prices in rural areas are generally significantly higher but vary widely depending on transportation costs, seasonal usage peaks, nearby petroleum development infrastructure and many other factors.
sentence_270: The [[Alaska_Permanent_Fund|Alaska Permanent Fund]] is a constitutionally authorized appropriation of oil revenues, established by voters in 1976 to manage a surplus in state petroleum revenues from oil, largely in anticipation of the then recently constructed [[Trans-Alaska_Pipeline_System|Trans-Alaska Pipeline System]].
sentence_271: The fund was originally proposed by Governor [[Keith_Harvey_Miller|Keith Miller]] on the eve of the 1969 Prudhoe Bay lease sale, out of fear that the legislature would spend the entire proceeds of the sale (which amounted to $900 million) at once.
sentence_272: It was later championed by Governor [[Jay_Hammond|Jay Hammond]] and [[Kenai,_Alaska|Kenai]] [[Alaska_House_of_Representatives|state representative]] Hugh Malone.
sentence_273: It has served as an attractive political prospect ever since, diverting revenues which would normally be deposited into the general fund.
sentence_274: The [[Alaska_Constitution|Alaska Constitution]] was written so as to discourage dedicating state funds for a particular purpose.
sentence_275: The Permanent Fund has become the rare exception to this, mostly due to the political climate of distrust existing during the time of its creation.
sentence_276: From its initial principal of $734,000, the fund has grown to $50 billion as a result of oil royalties and capital investment programs.
sentence_277: Most if not all the principal is invested conservatively outside Alaska.
sentence_278: This has led to frequent calls by Alaskan politicians for the Fund to make investments within Alaska, though such a stance has never gained momentum.
sentence_279: Starting in 1982, dividends from the fund's annual growth have been paid out each year to eligible Alaskans, ranging from an initial $1,000 in 1982 (equal to three years' payout, as the distribution of payments was held up in a lawsuit over the distribution scheme) to $3,269 in 2008 (which included a one-time $1,200 "Resource Rebate").
sentence_280: Every year, the state legislature takes out 8% from the earnings, puts 3% back into the principal for inflation proofing, and the remaining 5% is distributed to all qualifying Alaskans.
sentence_281: To qualify for the Permanent Fund Dividend, one must have lived in the state for a minimum of 12 months, maintain constant residency subject to allowable absences, and not be subject to court judgments or criminal convictions which fall under various disqualifying classifications or may subject the payment amount to civil garnishment.
sentence_282: The Permanent Fund is often considered to be one of the leading examples of a "[[Basic_income|Basic income]]" policy in the world.
sentence_283: The cost of goods in Alaska has long been higher than in the contiguous 48 states.
sentence_284: Federal government employees, particularly [[United_States_Postal_Service|United States Postal Service]] (USPS) workers and active-duty military members, receive a Cost of Living Allowance usually set at 25% of base pay because, while the cost of living has gone down, it is still one of the highest in the country.
sentence_285: Rural Alaska suffers from extremely high prices for food and consumer goods compared to the rest of the country, due to the relatively limited transportation infrastructure.
sentence_286: Due to the northern climate and short growing season, relatively little farming occurs in Alaska.
sentence_287: Most farms are in either the [[Matanuska_Valley|Matanuska Valley]], about 40 miles (64 km) northeast of [[Anchorage|Anchorage]], or on the [[Kenai_Peninsula|Kenai Peninsula]], about 60 miles (97 km) southwest of Anchorage.
sentence_288: The short 100-day growing season limits the crops that can be grown, but the long sunny summer days make for productive growing seasons.
sentence_289: The primary crops are potatoes, carrots, lettuce, and cabbage.
sentence_290: The [[Tanana_Valley|Tanana Valley]] is another notable agricultural locus, especially the [[Delta_Junction,_Alaska|Delta Junction]] area, about 100 miles (160 km) southeast of Fairbanks, with a sizable concentration of farms growing agronomic crops; these farms mostly lie north and east of [[Fort_Greely|Fort Greely]].
sentence_291: This area was largely set aside and developed under a state program spearheaded by Hammond during his second term as governor.
sentence_292: Delta-area crops consist predominantly of barley and hay.
sentence_293: West of Fairbanks lies another concentration of small farms catering to restaurants, the hotel and tourist industry, and [[Community-supported_agriculture|community-supported agriculture]].
sentence_294: Alaskan agriculture has experienced a surge in growth of market gardeners, small farms and [[Farmers'_market|farmers' markets]] in recent years, with the highest percentage increase (46%) in the nation in growth in farmers' markets in 2011, compared to 17% nationwide.
sentence_295: The [[Peony|peony]] industry has also taken off, as the growing season allows farmers to harvest during a gap in supply elsewhere in the world, thereby filling a niche in the flower market.
sentence_296: Alaska, with no counties, lacks county fairs.
sentence_297: However, a small assortment of state and local fairs (with the Alaska State Fair in [[Palmer,_Alaska|Palmer]] the largest), are held mostly in the late summer.
sentence_298: The fairs are mostly located in communities with historic or current agricultural activity, and feature local farmers exhibiting produce in addition to more high-profile commercial activities such as carnival rides, concerts and food.
sentence_299: "Alaska Grown" is used as an agricultural slogan.
sentence_300: Alaska has an abundance of seafood, with the primary fisheries in the Bering Sea and the North Pacific.
sentence_301: Seafood is one of the few food items that is often cheaper within the state than outside it.
sentence_302: Many Alaskans take advantage of salmon seasons to harvest portions of their household diet while fishing for subsistence, as well as sport.
sentence_303: This includes fish taken by hook, net or wheel.
sentence_304: Hunting for subsistence, primarily [[Caribou|caribou]], [[Moose|moose]], and [[Dall_sheep|Dall sheep]] is still common in the state, particularly in remote [[The_Bush_(Alaska)|Bush]] communities.
sentence_305: An example of a traditional native food is [[Akutaq|Akutaq]], the Eskimo ice cream, which can consist of reindeer fat, seal oil, dried fish meat and local berries.
sentence_306: Alaska's reindeer herding is concentrated on [[Seward_Peninsula|Seward Peninsula]], where wild caribou can be prevented from mingling and migrating with the domesticated reindeer.
sentence_307: Most food in Alaska is transported into the state from [[Outside_(Alaska)|"Outside"]], and shipping costs make food in the cities relatively expensive.
sentence_308: In rural areas, subsistence hunting and gathering is an essential activity because imported food is prohibitively expensive.
sentence_309: Although most small towns and villages in Alaska lie along the coastline, the cost of importing food to remote villages can be high, because of the terrain and difficult road conditions, which change dramatically, due to varying climate and precipitation changes.
sentence_310: The cost of transport can reach as high as 50¢ per pound ($1.10/kg) or more in some remote areas, during the most difficult times, if these locations can be reached at all during such inclement weather and terrain conditions.
sentence_311: The cost of delivering a 1 US gallon (3.8 L) of milk is about $3.50 in many villages where per capita income can be $20,000 or less.
sentence_312: Fuel cost per gallon is routinely twenty to thirty cents higher than the contiguous United States average, with only Hawaii having higher prices.
sentence_313: Main article: [[Transportation_in_Alaska|Transportation in Alaska]]
sentence_314: Main article: Government of Alaska
sentence_315: Like all other U.S. states, Alaska is governed as a republic, with three [[Separation_of_powers|branches of government]]: an executive branch consisting of the [[Governor_of_Alaska|governor of Alaska]] and his or her appointees which head executive departments; a [[Legislative_branch|legislative branch]] consisting of the [[Alaska_House_of_Representatives|Alaska House of Representatives]] and [[Alaska_Senate|Alaska Senate]]; and a [[Judicial_branch|judicial branch]] consisting of the Alaska Supreme Court and lower courts.
sentence_316: The state of Alaska employs approximately 16,000 people statewide.
sentence_317: The Alaska Legislature consists of a 40-member [[Alaska_House_of_Representatives|House of Representatives]] and a 20-member [[Alaska_Senate|Senate]].
sentence_318: Senators serve four-year terms and House members two.
sentence_319: The [[Governor_of_Alaska|governor of Alaska]] serves four-year terms.
sentence_320: The [[List_of_Lieutenant_Governors_of_Alaska|lieutenant governor]] runs separately from the governor in the [[Primary_election|primaries]], but during the general election, the nominee for governor and nominee for lieutenant governor run together on the same ticket.
sentence_321: Alaska's court system has four levels: the Alaska Supreme Court, the [[Alaska_Court_of_Appeals|Alaska Court of Appeals]], the superior courts and the district courts.
sentence_322: The superior and district courts are trial courts.
sentence_323: Superior courts are courts of general jurisdiction, while district courts hear only certain types of cases, including misdemeanor criminal cases and civil cases valued up to $100,000.
sentence_324: The Supreme Court and the Court of Appeals are appellate courts.
sentence_325: The Court of Appeals is required to hear appeals from certain lower-court decisions, including those regarding criminal prosecutions, juvenile delinquency, and [[Habeas_corpus|habeas corpus]].
sentence_326: The Supreme Court hears civil appeals and may in its discretion hear criminal appeals.
sentence_327: Main article: [[Politics_of_Alaska|Politics of Alaska]]
sentence_328: Further information: Political party strength in Alaska and [[Alaska_political_corruption_probe|Alaska political corruption probe]]
sentence_329: Although in its early years of statehood Alaska was a [[Democratic_Party_(United_States)|Democratic]] state, since the early 1970s it has been characterized as [[Republican_Party_(United_States)|Republican]]-leaning.
sentence_330: Local political communities have often worked on issues related to land use development, fishing, tourism, and individual rights.
sentence_331: Alaska Natives, while organized in and around their communities, have been active within the [[Alaska_Native_Regional_Corporations|Native corporations]].
sentence_332: These have been given ownership over large tracts of land, which require stewardship.
sentence_333: Alaska was formerly the only state in which possession of one ounce or less of marijuana in one's home was completely legal under state law, though the federal law remains in force.
sentence_334: The state has an independence movement favoring a vote on secession from the United States, with the Alaskan Independence Party.
sentence_335: Six [[Republican_Party_(United_States)|Republicans]] and four [[Democratic_Party_(United_States)|Democrats]] have served as governor of Alaska.
sentence_336: In addition, Republican governor Wally Hickel was elected to the office for a second term in 1990 after leaving the Republican party and briefly joining the Alaskan Independence Party ticket just long enough to be reelected.
sentence_337: He officially rejoined the Republican party in 1994.
sentence_338: Alaska's [[2014_Alaska_Measure_2|voter initiative making marijuana legal]] took effect on February 24, 2015, placing Alaska alongside Colorado and Washington as the first three U.S. states where recreational marijuana is legal.
sentence_339: The new law means people over 21 can consume small amounts of pot.
sentence_340: The first legal marijuana store opened in Valdez in October 2016.
sentence_341: To finance state government operations, Alaska depends primarily on petroleum revenues and federal subsidies.
sentence_342: This allows it to have the lowest individual tax burden in the United States.
sentence_343: It is one of five states with no [[Sales_tax|sales tax]], one of seven states with no individual [[Income_tax|income tax]], and—along with [[New_Hampshire|New Hampshire]]—one of two that has neither.
sentence_344: The Department of Revenue Tax Division reports regularly on the state's revenue sources.
sentence_345: The Department also issues an annual summary of its operations, including new state laws that directly affect the tax division.
sentence_346: In 2014 the [[Tax_Foundation|Tax Foundation]] ranked Alaska as having the fourth most "business friendly" tax policy, behind only [[Wyoming|Wyoming]], [[South_Dakota|South Dakota]], and [[Nevada|Nevada]].
sentence_347: While Alaska has no state sales tax, 89 municipalities collect a local sales tax, from 1.0 to 7.5%, typically 3–5%.
sentence_348: Other local taxes levied include raw fish taxes, hotel, motel, and bed-and-breakfast 'bed' taxes, [[Severance_tax|severance taxes]], liquor and tobacco taxes, gaming (pull tabs) taxes, tire taxes and fuel transfer taxes.
sentence_349: A part of the revenue collected from certain state taxes and license fees (such as petroleum, aviation motor fuel, telephone cooperative) is shared with municipalities in Alaska.
sentence_350: The fall in oil prices after the [[Hydraulic_fracturing_in_the_United_States|fracking boom]] in the early 2010s has decimated Alaska's state treasury, which has historically received about 85 percent of its revenue from taxes and fees imposed on oil and gas companies.
sentence_351: The state government has had to drastically reduce its budget, and has brought its budget shortfall from over $2 billion in 2016 to under $500 million by 2018.
sentence_352: In 2020, Alaska's state government budget was $4.8 billion, while projected government revenues were only $4.5 billion.
sentence_353: Main article: [[Politics_of_Alaska|Politics of Alaska]]
sentence_354: See also: [[Arctic_Policy_of_the_United_States|Arctic Policy of the United States]]
sentence_355: Alaska regularly supports [[Republican_Party_(United_States)|Republicans]] in presidential elections and has done so since statehood.
sentence_356: Republicans have won the state's [[Electoral_College_(United_States)|electoral college]] votes in all but one election that it has participated in ([[1964_United_States_presidential_election|1964]]).
sentence_357: No state has voted for a [[Democratic_Party_(United_States)|Democratic]] presidential candidate fewer times.
sentence_358: Alaska was carried by Democratic nominee [[Lyndon_B._Johnson|Lyndon B. Johnson]] during his landslide election in [[1964_United_States_presidential_election|1964]], while the [[1960_United_States_presidential_election|1960]] and [[1968_United_States_presidential_election|1968]] elections were close.
sentence_359: Since [[1972_United_States_presidential_election|1972]], however, Republicans have carried the state by large margins.
sentence_360: In [[2008_United_States_presidential_election|2008]], Republican [[John_McCain|John McCain]] defeated Democrat [[Barack_Obama|Barack Obama]] in Alaska, 59.49% to 37.83%.
sentence_361: McCain's running mate was [[Sarah_Palin|Sarah Palin]], the state's governor and the first Alaskan on a major party ticket.
sentence_362: Obama lost Alaska again in [[2012_United_States_presidential_election|2012]], but he captured 40% of the state's vote in that election, making him the first Democrat to do so since 1968.
sentence_363: The [[The_Bush_(Alaska)|Alaska Bush]], central Juneau, midtown and downtown Anchorage, and the areas surrounding the [[University_of_Alaska_Fairbanks|University of Alaska Fairbanks]] campus and Ester have been strongholds of the Democratic Party.
sentence_364: The Matanuska-Susitna Borough, the majority of Fairbanks (including North Pole and the military base), and South Anchorage typically have the strongest Republican showing.
sentence_365: As of 2004, well over half of all registered voters have chosen "non-partisan" or "undeclared" as their affiliation, despite recent attempts to close primaries to unaffiliated voters.

sentence_366: Because of its population relative to other U.S. states, Alaska has only one member in the [[United_States_House_of_Representatives|U.S.
sentence_367: House of Representatives]].
sentence_368: This seat is held by Republican [[Don_Young|Don Young]], who was re-elected to his 21st consecutive term in 2012.
sentence_369: [[Alaska's_at-large_congressional_district|Alaska's at-large congressional district]] is one of the largest parliamentary constituencies in the world by area.
sentence_370: In 2008, Governor [[Sarah_Palin|Sarah Palin]] became the first Republican woman to run on a national ticket when she became [[John_McCain|John McCain]]'s running mate.
sentence_371: She continued to be a prominent national figure even after resigning from the governor's job in July 2009.
sentence_372: [[List_of_United_States_Senators_from_Alaska|Alaska's United States senators]] belong to [[Classes_of_United_States_Senators|Class 2 and Class 3]].
sentence_373: In 2008, Democrat [[Mark_Begich|Mark Begich]], mayor of Anchorage, defeated long-time Republican senator [[Ted_Stevens|Ted Stevens]].
sentence_374: Stevens had been convicted on seven felony counts of failing to report gifts on Senate financial discloser forms one week before the election.
sentence_375: The conviction was set aside in April 2009 after evidence of prosecutorial misconduct emerged.
sentence_376: Republican [[Frank_Murkowski|Frank Murkowski]] held the state's other senatorial position.
sentence_377: After being elected governor in 2002, he resigned from the Senate and appointed his daughter, State representative [[Lisa_Murkowski|Lisa Murkowski]], as his successor.
sentence_378: She won full six-year terms in 2004, 2010 and 2016.
sentence_379: See also: [[List_of_cities_in_Alaska_by_population|List of cities in Alaska by population]], [[Alaska_locations_by_per_capita_income|Alaska locations by per capita income]], and [[List_of_boroughs_and_census_areas_in_Alaska|List of boroughs and census areas in Alaska]]
sentence_380: Alaska is not divided into [[County_(United_States)|counties]], as most of the other U.S. states, but it is divided into [[List_of_boroughs_and_census_areas_in_Alaska|boroughs]].
sentence_381: Many of the more densely populated parts of the state are part of Alaska's 16 boroughs, which function somewhat similarly to counties in other states.
sentence_382: However, unlike county-equivalents in the other 49 states, the boroughs do not cover the entire land area of the state.
sentence_383: The area not part of any borough is referred to as the Unorganized Borough.
sentence_384: The Unorganized Borough has no government of its own, but the [[U.S._Census_Bureau|U.S.
sentence_385: Census Bureau]] in cooperation with the state divided the Unorganized Borough into 11 census areas solely for the purposes of statistical analysis and presentation.
sentence_386: A recording district is a mechanism for administration of the public record in Alaska.
sentence_387: The state is divided into 34 recording districts which are centrally administered under a State Recorder.
sentence_388: All recording districts use the same acceptance criteria, fee schedule, etc., for accepting documents into the public record.
sentence_389: Whereas many U.S. states use a three-tiered system of decentralization—state/county/township—most of Alaska uses only two tiers—state/borough.
sentence_390: Owing to the low population density, most of the land is located in the Unorganized Borough.
sentence_391: As the name implies, it has no intermediate borough government but is administered directly by the state government.
sentence_392: In 2000, 57.71% of Alaska's area has this status, with 13.05% of the population.
sentence_393: Anchorage merged the city government with the Greater Anchorage Area Borough in 1975 to form the Municipality of Anchorage, containing the city proper and the communities of Eagle River, Chugiak, Peters Creek, Girdwood, Bird, and Indian.
sentence_394: Fairbanks has a separate borough (the [[Fairbanks_North_Star_Borough|Fairbanks North Star Borough]]) and municipality (the City of Fairbanks).
sentence_395: The state's most populous city is [[Anchorage,_Alaska|Anchorage]], home to 278,700 people in 2006, 225,744 of whom live in the urbanized area.
sentence_396: The richest [[Alaska_locations_by_per_capita_income|location in Alaska by per capita income]] is [[Halibut_Cove,_Alaska|Halibut Cove]] ($89,895).
sentence_397: [[Yakutat_City|Yakutat City]], Sitka, Juneau, and Anchorage are the four [[List_of_U.S._cities_by_area|largest cities in the U.S. by area]].
sentence_398: As reflected in the [[2010_United_States_Census|2010 United States Census]], Alaska has a total of 355 incorporated cities and [[Census-designated_place|census-designated places]] (CDPs).
sentence_399: The tally of cities includes four unified municipalities, essentially the equivalent of a [[Consolidated_city–county|consolidated city–county]].
sentence_400: The majority of these communities are located in the rural expanse of Alaska known as "[[The_Bush_(Alaska)|The Bush]]" and are unconnected to the contiguous North American road network.
sentence_401: The table at the bottom of this section lists the 100 largest cities and census-designated places in Alaska, in population order.
sentence_402: Of Alaska's 2010 Census population figure of 710,231, 20,429 people, or 2.88% of the population, did not live in an incorporated city or census-designated place.
sentence_403: Approximately three-quarters of that figure were people who live in urban and suburban neighborhoods on the outskirts of the city limits of Ketchikan, Kodiak, Palmer and Wasilla.
sentence_404: CDPs have not been established for these areas by the [[United_States_Census_Bureau|United States Census Bureau]], except that seven CDPs were established for the Ketchikan-area neighborhoods in the [[1980_United_States_Census|1980 Census]] (Clover Pass, Herring Cove, Ketchikan East, Mountain Point, North [[Tongass_Highway|Tongass Highway]], [[Pennock_Island|Pennock Island]] and [[Saxman,_Alaska|Saxman]] East), but have not been used since.
sentence_405: The remaining population was scattered throughout Alaska, both within organized boroughs and in the Unorganized Borough, in largely remote areas.
sentence_406: The Alaska Department of Education and Early Development administers many [[List_of_school_districts_in_Alaska|school districts]] in Alaska.
sentence_407: In addition, the state operates a boarding school, [[Mt._Edgecumbe_High_School|Mt.
sentence_408: Edgecumbe High School]] in [[Sitka,_Alaska|Sitka]], and provides partial funding for other boarding schools, including [[Nenana_Student_Living_Center|Nenana Student Living Center]] in [[Nenana,_Alaska|Nenana]] and The Galena Interior Learning Academy in [[Galena,_Alaska|Galena]].
sentence_409: There are more than a dozen [[List_of_colleges_and_universities_in_Alaska|colleges and universities in Alaska]].
sentence_410: Accredited universities in Alaska include the [[University_of_Alaska_Anchorage|University of Alaska Anchorage]], [[University_of_Alaska_Fairbanks|University of Alaska Fairbanks]], University of Alaska Southeast, and [[Alaska_Pacific_University|Alaska Pacific University]].
sentence_411: Alaska is the only state that has no institutions that are part of [[NCAA_Division_I|NCAA Division I]].
sentence_412: The Alaska Department of Labor and Workforce Development operates AVTEC, Alaska's Institute of Technology.
sentence_413: Campuses in Seward and Anchorage offer one-week to 11-month training programs in areas as diverse as Information Technology, Welding, Nursing, and Mechanics.
sentence_414: Alaska has had a problem with a "[[Brain_drain|brain drain]]".
sentence_415: Many of its young people, including most of the highest academic achievers, leave the state after high school graduation and do not return.
sentence_416: As of 2013, Alaska did not have a [[Legal_education_in_Alaska|law school]] or medical school.
sentence_417: The [[University_of_Alaska|University of Alaska]] has attempted to combat this by offering partial four-year scholarships to the top 10% of Alaska high school graduates, via the Alaska Scholars Program.
sentence_418: See also: [[Dentistry_in_rural_Alaska|Dentistry in rural Alaska]]
sentence_419: The [[Alaska_State_Troopers|Alaska State Troopers]] are Alaska's statewide police force.
sentence_420: They have a long and storied history, but were not an official organization until 1941.
sentence_421: Before the force was officially organized, law enforcement in Alaska was handled by various federal agencies.
sentence_422: Larger towns usually have their own local police and some villages rely on "Public Safety Officers" who have police training but do not carry firearms.
sentence_423: In much of the state, the troopers serve as the only police force available.
sentence_424: In addition to enforcing traffic and criminal law, wildlife Troopers enforce hunting and fishing regulations.
sentence_425: Due to the varied terrain and wide scope of the Troopers' duties, they employ a wide variety of land, air, and water patrol vehicles.
sentence_426: Many rural communities in Alaska are considered "dry", having outlawed the importation of alcoholic beverages.
sentence_427: Suicide rates for rural residents are higher than urban.
sentence_428: [[Domestic_abuse|Domestic abuse]] and other violent crimes are also at high levels in the state; this is in part linked to alcohol abuse.
sentence_429: Alaska has the highest rate of sexual assault in the nation, especially in rural areas.
sentence_430: The average age of sexually assaulted victims is 16 years old.
sentence_431: In four out of five cases, the suspects were relatives, friends or acquaintances.
sentence_432: See also: [[List_of_artists_and_writers_from_Alaska|List of artists and writers from Alaska]]
sentence_433: Some of Alaska's popular annual events are the [[Iditarod_Trail_Sled_Dog_Race|Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race]] from Anchorage to Nome, World Ice Art Championships in Fairbanks, the Blueberry Festival and Alaska Hummingbird Festival in [[Ketchikan,_Alaska|Ketchikan]], the Sitka Whale Fest, and the Stikine River Garnet Fest in [[Wrangell,_Alaska|Wrangell]].
sentence_434: The [[Stikine_River|Stikine River]] attracts the largest springtime concentration of [[American_bald_eagle|American bald eagles]] in the world.
sentence_435: The [[Alaska_Native_Heritage_Center|Alaska Native Heritage Center]] celebrates the rich heritage of Alaska's 11 cultural groups.
sentence_436: Their purpose is to encourage cross-cultural exchanges among all people and enhance self-esteem among Native people.
sentence_437: The Alaska Native Arts Foundation promotes and markets Native art from all regions and cultures in the State, using the internet.
sentence_438: Main article: Music of Alaska
sentence_439: Influences on music in Alaska include the traditional music of Alaska Natives as well as folk music brought by later immigrants from Russia and Europe.
sentence_440: Prominent musicians from Alaska include singer [[Jewel_(singer)|Jewel]], traditional Aleut flautist [[Mary_Youngblood|Mary Youngblood]], folk singer-songwriter [[Libby_Roderick|Libby Roderick]], Christian music singer-songwriter Lincoln Brewster, metal/post hardcore band [[36_Crazyfists|36 Crazyfists]] and the groups Pamyua and [[Portugal._The_Man|Portugal.
sentence_441: The Man]].
sentence_442: There are many established music festivals in Alaska, including the [[Alaska_Folk_Festival|Alaska Folk Festival]], the Fairbanks Summer Arts Festival] the Anchorage Folk Festival, the [[Athabascan_Old-Time_Fiddling_Festival|Athabascan Old-Time Fiddling Festival]], the Sitka Jazz Festival, and the [[Sitka_Summer_Music_Festival|Sitka Summer Music Festival]].
sentence_443: The most prominent orchestra in Alaska is the [[Anchorage_Symphony_Orchestra|Anchorage Symphony Orchestra]], though the Fairbanks Symphony Orchestra and [[Juneau_Symphony|Juneau Symphony]] are also notable.
sentence_444: The [[Anchorage_Opera|Anchorage Opera]] is currently the state's only professional opera company, though there are several volunteer and semi-professional organizations in the state as well.
sentence_445: The official [[List_of_U.S._state_songs|state song]] of Alaska is "[[Alaska's_Flag|Alaska's Flag]]", which was adopted in 1955; it celebrates the [[Flag_of_Alaska|flag of Alaska]].

section_41.value: Alaska in film and on television

sentence_446: See also: [[List_of_films_set_in_Alaska|List of films set in Alaska]]
sentence_447: Alaska's first independent picture entirely made in Alaska was [[The_Chechahcos|The Chechahcos]], produced by Alaskan businessman [[Austin_E._Lathrop|Austin E. Lathrop]] and filmed in and around Anchorage.
sentence_448: Released in 1924 by the Alaska Moving Picture Corporation, it was the only film the company made.
sentence_449: One of the most prominent movies filmed in Alaska is MGM's Eskimo/Mala The Magnificent, starring Alaska Native Ray Mala.
sentence_450: In 1932 an expedition set out from MGM's studios in Hollywood to Alaska to film what was then billed as "The Biggest Picture Ever Made".
sentence_451: Upon arriving in Alaska, they set up "Camp Hollywood" in Northwest Alaska, where they lived during the duration of the filming.
sentence_452: [[Louis_B._Mayer|Louis B. Mayer]] spared no expense in spite of the remote location, going so far as to hire the chef from the [[Roosevelt_Hotel_(Hollywood)|Hotel Roosevelt]] in Hollywood to prepare meals.
sentence_453: When Eskimo premiered at the [[Astor_Theatre,_New_York_City|Astor Theatre]] in New York City, the studio received the largest amount of feedback in its history.
sentence_454: Eskimo was critically acclaimed and released worldwide; as a result, Mala became an international movie star.
sentence_455: Eskimo won the first Oscar for [[Academy_Award_for_Best_Film_Editing|Best Film Editing]] at the Academy Awards, and showcased and preserved aspects of [[Inupiat_people|Inupiat]] culture on film.
sentence_456: The 1983 Disney movie [[Never_Cry_Wolf_(film)|Never Cry Wolf]] was at least partially shot in Alaska.
sentence_457: The 1991 film [[White_Fang_(1991_film)|White Fang]], based on [[Jack_London|Jack London]]'s 1906 novel and starring [[Ethan_Hawke|Ethan Hawke]], was filmed in and around [[Haines,_Alaska|Haines]].
sentence_458: [[Steven_Seagal|Steven Seagal]]'s 1994 [[On_Deadly_Ground|On Deadly Ground]], starring [[Michael_Caine|Michael Caine]], was filmed in part at the [[Worthington_Glacier|Worthington Glacier]] near [[Valdez,_Alaska|Valdez]].
sentence_459: The 1999 John Sayles film [[Limbo_(1999_film)|Limbo]], starring [[David_Strathairn|David Strathairn]], Mary Elizabeth Mastrantonio, and [[Kris_Kristofferson|Kris Kristofferson]], was filmed in Juneau.
sentence_460: The psychological thriller [[Insomnia_(2002_film)|Insomnia]], starring [[Al_Pacino|Al Pacino]] and [[Robin_Williams|Robin Williams]], was shot in Canada, but was set in Alaska.
sentence_461: The 2007 film directed by Sean Penn, [[Into_the_Wild_(film)|Into The Wild]], was partially filmed and set in Alaska.
sentence_462: The film, which is based on the novel of the same name, follows the adventures of [[Christopher_McCandless|Christopher McCandless]], who died in a remote abandoned bus along the [[Stampede_Trail|Stampede Trail]] west of [[Healy,_Alaska|Healy]] in 1992.
sentence_463: Many films and television shows set in Alaska are not filmed there; for example, [[Northern_Exposure|Northern Exposure]], set in the fictional town of Cicely, Alaska, was filmed in Roslyn, Washington.
sentence_464: The 2007 horror feature [[30_Days_of_Night_(film)|30 Days of Night]] is set in [[Utqiagvik,_Alaska|Barrow, Alaska]], but was filmed in New Zealand.
sentence_465: Many reality television shows are filmed in Alaska.
sentence_466: In 2011 the Anchorage Daily News found ten set in the state.
sentence_467: Main article: [[List_of_Alaska_state_symbols|List of Alaska state symbols]]

list.value: State motto: North to the Future
Nicknames: "The Last Frontier" or "Land of the Midnight Sun" or "Seward's Icebox"

State bird: [[Willow_ptarmigan|willow ptarmigan]], adopted by the Territorial Legislature in 1955. It is a small (15–17 in or 380–430 mm) Arctic grouse that lives among willows and on open tundra and muskeg. Plumage is brown in summer, changing to white in winter. The willow ptarmigan is common in much of Alaska.

State flower: wild/native [[Forget-me-not|forget-me-not]], adopted by the Territorial Legislature in 1917. It is a perennial found throughout Alaska, from Hyder to the Arctic Coast, and west to the Aleutians.

title: Archery
sentence_0: "Archer" and "Archers" redirect here.
sentence_1: For the animated TV show, see [[Archer_(2009_TV_series)|Archer (2009 TV series)]].
sentence_2: For other uses, see [[Archery_(disambiguation)|Archery (disambiguation)]], [[Archer_(disambiguation)|Archer (disambiguation)]], and [[Archers_(disambiguation)|Archers (disambiguation)]].
sentence_3: Archery is the art, sport, practice, or skill of using a [[Bow_(weapon)|bow]] to [[Shooting|shoot]] [[Arrow|arrows]].
sentence_4: The word comes from the [[Latin|Latin]] arcus for bow.
sentence_5: Historically, archery has been used for hunting and combat.
sentence_6: In modern times, it is mainly a competitive sport and recreational activity.
sentence_7: A person who participates in archery is typically called an archer or a bowman, and a person who is fond of or an expert at archery is sometimes called a toxophilite or a marksman.
sentence_8: Main article: [[History_of_archery|History of archery]]
sentence_9: The oldest known evidence of arrows comes from the South African site of [[Sibudu_Cave|Sibudu Cave]], where the remains of bone and stone arrowheads have been found dating approximately 60,000-70,000 years ago.
sentence_10: Based on indirect evidence, the bow also seems to have appeared or reappeared later in Eurasia, near the transition from the [[Upper_Paleolithic|Upper Paleolithic]] to the [[Mesolithic|Mesolithic]].
sentence_11: The earliest definite remains of bow and arrow from Europe are possible fragments from Germany found at Mannheim-Vogelstang dated 17,500-18,000 years ago, and at Stellmoor dated 11,000 years ago.
sentence_12: [[Azilian|Azilian]] points found in [[Grotte_du_Bichon|Grotte du Bichon]], Switzerland, alongside the remains of both a bear and a hunter, with flint fragments found in the bear's third vertebra, suggest the use of arrows at 13,500 years ago.
sentence_13: Other signs of its use in Europe come from the Stellmoor in the Ahrensburg valley north of [[Hamburg|Hamburg]], Germany and dates from the late [[Paleolithic|Paleolithic]], about 10,000–9000 BC.
sentence_14: The arrows were made of [[Pine|pine]] and consisted of a main shaft and a 15–20-centimetre-long (5 ⁄8–7 ⁄8 in) fore shaft with a [[Flint|flint]] point.
sentence_15: There are no definite earlier bows; previous pointed shafts are known, but may have been launched by [[Spear-thrower|spear-throwers]] rather than bows.
sentence_16: The [[Holmegaard_bow|oldest bows]] known so far comes from the Holmegård swamp in Denmark.
sentence_17: At the site of [[Nataruk|Nataruk]] in [[Turkana_County|Turkana County]], Kenya, [[Obsidian|obsidian]] bladelets found embedded in a skull and within the thoracic cavity of another skeleton, suggest the use of stone-tipped arrows as weapons about 10,000 years ago.
sentence_18: Bows eventually replaced the [[Spear-thrower|spear-thrower]] as the predominant means for launching shafted projectiles, on every continent except [[Australasia|Australasia]], though spear-throwers persisted alongside the bow in parts of the Americas, notably Mexico and among the [[Inuit|Inuit]].
sentence_19: Bows and arrows have been present in [[Egypt|Egyptian]] and neighboring [[Nubia|Nubian]] culture since its respective [[Predynastic_Egypt|predynastic]] and [[Pre-Kerma|Pre-Kerma]] origins.
sentence_20: In the [[Levant|Levant]], artifacts that could be arrow-shaft straighteners are known from the [[Natufian_culture|Natufian culture]], (c. 10,800–8,300 BC) onwards.
sentence_21: The [[Khiamian|Khiamian]] and [[Pre-Pottery_Neolithic_A|PPN A]] shouldered Khiam-points may well be arrowheads.
sentence_22: [[Classical_antiquity|Classical]] civilizations, notably the [[Ancient_Assyrians|Assyrians]], [[Ancient_Greece|Greeks]], [[History_of_Armenia|Armenians]], [[Achaemenid_Empire|Persians]], [[Parthia|Parthians]], [[Ancient_Rome|Romans]], [[History_of_India|Indians]], [[History_of_Korea|Koreans]], [[History_of_China|Chinese]], and [[History_of_Japan|Japanese]] fielded large numbers of archers in their armies.
sentence_23: [[Akkadian_Empire|Akkadians]] were the first to use [[Composite_bows|composite bows]] in war according to the victory stele of [[Naram-Sin_of_Akkad|Naram-Sin of Akkad]].
sentence_24: Egyptians referred to [[Nubia|Nubia]] as "Ta-Seti," or "The Land of the Bow," since the Nubians were known to be expert archers, and by the 16th Century BC Egyptians were using the composite bow in warfare.
sentence_25: The Bronze Age Aegean Cultures were able to deploy a number of state-owned specialized bow makers for warfare and hunting purposes already from the 15th century BC.
sentence_26: The [[Welsh_longbow|Welsh longbow]] proved its worth for the first time in Continental warfare at the [[Battle_of_Crécy|Battle of Crécy]].
sentence_27: In the Americas archery was widespread at European contact.
sentence_28: Archery was highly developed in [[Asia|Asia]].
sentence_29: The [[Sanskrit|Sanskrit]] term for archery, [[Dhanurveda|dhanurveda]], came to refer to martial arts in general.
sentence_30: In East Asia, [[Goguryeo|Goguryeo]], one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea was well known for its regiments of exceptionally skilled archers.
sentence_31: Main article: Mounted archery
sentence_32: Central tribesmen of Asia (after the [[Domestication_of_the_horse|domestication of the horse]]) and American Plains Indians (after gaining access to horses by Europeans) became extremely adept at archery on horseback.
sentence_33: Lightly armored, but highly mobile archers were excellently suited to warfare in the Central Asian steppes, and they formed a large part of armies that repeatedly conquered large areas of Eurasia.
sentence_34: Shorter bows are more suited to use on horseback, and the [[Composite_bow|composite bow]] enabled mounted archers to use powerful weapons.
sentence_35: Empires throughout the Eurasian landmass often strongly associated their respective "barbarian" counterparts with the usage of the bow and arrow, to the point where powerful states like the [[Han_Dynasty|Han Dynasty]] referred to their neighbors, the [[Xiong-nu|Xiong-nu]], as "Those Who Draw the Bow".
sentence_36: For example, Xiong-nu mounted bowmen made them more than a match for the Han military, and their threat was at least partially responsible for Chinese expansion into the Ordos region, to create a stronger, more powerful buffer zone against them.
sentence_37: It is possible that "barbarian" peoples were responsible for introducing archery or certain types of bows to their "civilized" counterparts—the Xiong-nu and the Han being one example.
sentence_38: Similarly, short bows seem to have been introduced to Japan by northeast Asian groups.
sentence_39: The development of [[Gunpowder_warfare|firearms]] rendered bows obsolete in warfare, although efforts were sometimes made to preserve archery practice.
sentence_40: In England and Wales, for example, the government tried to enforce practice with the longbow until the end of the 16th century.
sentence_41: This was because it was recognized that the bow had been instrumental to military success during the [[Hundred_Years'_War|Hundred Years' War]].
sentence_42: Despite the high social status, ongoing utility, and widespread pleasure of archery in Armenia, China, Egypt, England and Wales, [[Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas|America]], India, Japan, Korea, Turkey and elsewhere, almost every culture that gained access to even early firearms used them widely, to the neglect of archery.
sentence_43: Early firearms were inferior in rate-of-fire, and were very sensitive to wet weather.
sentence_44: However, they had longer effective range and were tactically superior in the common situation of soldiers shooting at each other from behind obstructions.
sentence_45: They also required significantly less training to use properly, in particular penetrating steel armor without any need to develop special musculature.
sentence_46: Armies equipped with guns could thus provide superior firepower, and highly trained archers became obsolete on the battlefield.
sentence_47: However, the bow and arrow is still an effective weapon, and archers have seen action in the 21st century.
sentence_48: Traditional archery remains in use for sport, and for hunting in many areas.
sentence_49: Early recreational archery societies included the Finsbury Archers and the Ancient Society of Kilwinning Archers.
sentence_50: The latter's annual [[Popinjay_(sport)|Papingo]] event was first recorded in 1483.
sentence_51: (In this event, archers shoot vertically from the base of an abbey tower to dislodge a wood pigeon placed approximately 30 m or 33 yards above.)
sentence_52: The Royal Company of Archers was formed in 1676 and is one of the oldest sporting bodies in the world.
sentence_53: Archery remained a small and scattered pastime, however, until the late 18th century when it experienced a fashionable revival among the [[Aristocracy|aristocracy]].
sentence_54: Sir [[Ashton_Lever|Ashton Lever]], an antiquarian and collector, formed the Toxophilite Society in London in 1781, with the patronage of [[George_III|George, the Prince of Wales]].
sentence_55: Archery societies were set up across the country, each with its own strict entry criteria and outlandish costumes.
sentence_56: Recreational archery soon became extravagant social and ceremonial events for the nobility, complete with flags, music and 21 gun salutes for the competitors.
sentence_57: The clubs were "the drawing rooms of the great country houses placed outside" and thus came to play an important role in the social networks of the local upper class.
sentence_58: As well as its emphasis on display and status, the sport was notable for its popularity with females.
sentence_59: Young women could not only compete in the contests but retain and show off their sexuality while doing so.
sentence_60: Thus, archery came to act as a forum for introductions, flirtation and romance.
sentence_61: It was often consciously styled in the manner of a [[Medieval|Medieval]] [[Tournament|tournament]] with titles and [[Laurel_wreath|laurel wreaths]] being presented as a reward to the victor.
sentence_62: General meetings were held from 1789, in which local lodges convened together to standardise the rules and ceremonies.
sentence_63: Archery was also co-opted as a distinctively British tradition, dating back to the lore of [[Robin_Hood|Robin Hood]] and it served as a patriotic form of entertainment at a time of political tension in [[Europe|Europe]].
sentence_64: The societies were also elitist, and the new [[Middle_class|middle class]] [[Bourgeoisie|bourgeoisie]] were excluded from the clubs due to their lack of social status.
sentence_65: After the [[Napoleonic_Wars|Napoleonic Wars]], the sport became increasingly popular among all classes, and it was framed as a nostalgic reimagining of the [[Industrialisation|preindustrial]] rural Britain.
sentence_66: Particularly influential was Sir [[Walter_Scott|Walter Scott]]'s 1819 novel, [[Ivanhoe|Ivanhoe]] that depicted the heroic character Lockseley winning an archery tournament.
sentence_67: The 1840s saw the second attempts at turning the recreation into a modern sport.
sentence_68: The first [[Grand_National_Archery_Society|Grand National Archery Society]] meeting was held in [[York|York]] in 1844 and over the next decade the extravagant and festive practices of the past were gradually whittled away and the rules were standardized as the 'York Round' - a series of shoots at 60 (55), 80 (73), and 100 yards (91 m).
sentence_69: [[Horace_A._Ford|Horace A. Ford]] helped to improve archery standards and pioneered new archery techniques.
sentence_70: He won the Grand National 11 times in a row and published a highly influential guide to the sport in 1856.
sentence_71: Towards the end of the 19th century, the sport experienced declining participation as alternative sports such as [[Croquet|croquet]] and [[Tennis|tennis]] became more popular among the middle class.
sentence_72: By 1889, just 50 archery clubs were left in Britain, but it was still included as a sport at the [[1900_Paris_Olympics|1900 Paris Olympics]].
sentence_73: The National Archery Association of the United States was organized in 1879 and held annual meetings, the 1910 President was Frank E Canfield.
sentence_74: Today it is known as USA Archery and is recognized by [[United_States_Olympic_&_Paralympic_Committee|United States Olympic & Paralympic Committee]].
sentence_75: In the United States, primitive archery was revived in the early 20th century.
sentence_76: The last of the [[Yahi#Yahi|Yahi Indian]] tribe, a native known as [[Ishi|Ishi]], came out of hiding in California in 1911.
sentence_77: His doctor, [[Saxton_Pope|Saxton Pope]], learned many of Ishi's traditional archery skills, and popularized them.
sentence_78: The [[Pope_and_Young_Club|Pope and Young Club]], founded in 1961 and named in honor of Pope and his friend, Arthur Young, became one of North America's leading bowhunting and conservation organizations.
sentence_79: Founded as a nonprofit scientific organization, the Club was patterned after the prestigious [[Boone_and_Crockett_Club|Boone and Crockett Club]] and advocated responsible bowhunting by promoting quality, fair chase hunting, and sound conservation practices.
sentence_80: From the 1920s, professional engineers took an interest in archery, previously the exclusive field of traditional craft experts.
sentence_81: They led the commercial development of new forms of bow including the modern [[Recurve_bow|recurve]] and compound bow.
sentence_82: These modern forms are now dominant in modern Western archery; traditional bows are in a minority.
sentence_83: In the 1980s, the skills of traditional archery were revived by American enthusiasts, and combined with the new scientific understanding.
sentence_84: Much of this expertise is available in the Traditional Bowyer's Bibles (see Further reading).
sentence_85: Modern game archery owes much of its success to [[Fred_Bear|Fred Bear]], an American bow hunter and bow manufacturer.
sentence_86: Deities and heroes in several mythologies are described as archers, including the Greek [[Artemis|Artemis]] and [[Apollo|Apollo]], the Roman [[Diana_(mythology)|Diana]] and [[Cupid|Cupid]], the Germanic [[Agilaz|Agilaz]], continuing in legends like those of [[Wilhelm_Tell|Wilhelm Tell]], [[Palnetoke|Palnetoke]], or [[Robin_Hood|Robin Hood]].
sentence_87: Armenian [[Hayk|Hayk]] and Babylonian Marduk, Indian [[Karna|Karna]] (also known as Radheya/son of Radha), [[Abhimanyu|Abhimanyu]], [[Eklavya|Eklavya]], [[Arjuna|Arjuna]], [[Bhishma|Bhishma]], [[Drona|Drona]], [[Rama|Rama]], and [[Shiva|Shiva]] were known for their shooting skills.
sentence_88: The famous archery competition of hitting the eye of a rotating fish while watching its reflection in the water bowl was one of the many archery skills depicted in the [[Mahabharata|Mahabharata]].
sentence_89: Persian [[Arash_(mythology)|Arash]] was a famous archer.
sentence_90: Earlier Greek representations of [[Heracles|Heracles]] normally depict him as an archer.
sentence_91: Archery, and the bow, play an important part in the epic poem the Odyssey, when Odysseus returns home in disguise and then bests the suitors in an archery competition after hinting at his identity by stringing and drawing his great bow that only he can draw, a similar motif is present in the Turkic heroic poem Alpamysh.
sentence_92: The Nymphai Hyperboreioi (Νύμφαι Ὑπερβόρειοι) were worshipped on the Greek island of Delos as attendants of [[Artemis|Artemis]], presiding over aspects of archery; Hekaerge (Ἑκαέργη), represented distancing, Loxo (Λοξώ), trajectory, and Oupis (Οὖπις), aim.
sentence_93: [[Houyi|Yi the archer]] and his apprentice [[Feng_Meng|Feng Meng]] appear in several early Chinese myths, and the historical character of [[Zhou_Tong_(archer)|Zhou Tong]] features in many fictional forms.
sentence_94: [[Jumong|Jumong]], the first [[Taewang|Taewang]] of the [[Goguryeo|Goguryeo]] kingdom of the [[Three_Kingdoms_of_Korea|Three Kingdoms of Korea]], is claimed by legend to have been a near-godlike archer.
sentence_95: Archery features in the story of Oguz Khagan.
sentence_96: Similarly, archery and the bow feature heavily into historical Korean identity.
sentence_97: In [[West_Africa|West African]] [[Yoruba_religion|Yoruba]] belief, [[Ochosi|Osoosi]] is one of several deities of the hunt who are identified with bow and arrow iconography and other insignia associated with archery.
sentence_98: Main article: [[Bow_and_arrow|Bow and arrow]]
sentence_99: While there is great variety in the construction details of bows (both historic and modern), all bows consist of a string attached to elastic limbs that store mechanical energy imparted by the user drawing the string.
sentence_100: Bows may be broadly split into two categories: those drawn by pulling the string directly and those that use a mechanism to pull the string.
sentence_101: Directly drawn bows may be further divided based upon differences in the method of limb construction, notable examples being [[Self_bow|self bows]], [[Laminated_bow|laminated bows]] and [[Composite_bow|composite bows]].
sentence_102: Bows can also be classified by the [[Shape|bow shape]] of the limbs when unstrung; in contrast to traditional European straight bows, a [[Recurve_bow#Recurve_bow|recurve bow]] and some types of longbow have tips that curve away from the archer when the bow is unstrung.
sentence_103: The cross-section of the limb also varies; the classic [[Longbow|longbow]] is a tall bow with narrow limbs that are D-shaped in cross section, and the [[Flatbow|flatbow]] has flat wide limbs that are approximately rectangular in cross-section.
sentence_104: [[Cable-backed_bow|Cable-backed bows]] use cords as the back of the bow; the draw weight of the bow can be adjusted by changing the tension of the cable.
sentence_105: They were widespread among [[Inuit|Inuit]] who lacked easy access to good bow wood.
sentence_106: One variety of cable-backed bow is the Penobscot bow or [[Wabenaki|Wabenaki]] bow, invented by Frank Loring (Chief Big Thunder) about 1900.
sentence_107: It consists of a small bow attached by cables on the back of a larger main bow.
sentence_108: In different cultures, the arrows are released from either the left or right side of the bow, and this affects the hand grip and position of the bow.
sentence_109: In [[Arab_archery|Arab archery]], [[Turkish_archery|Turkish archery]] and [[Kyūdō|Kyūdō]], the arrows are released from the right hand side of the bow, and this affects construction of the bow.
sentence_110: In western archery, the arrow is usually released from the left hand side of the bow for a right-handed archer.
sentence_111: Compound bows are designed to reduce the force required to hold the string at full draw, hence allowing the archer more time to aim with less muscular stress.
sentence_112: Most compound designs use cams or elliptical wheels on the ends of the limbs to achieve this.
sentence_113: A typical let-off is anywhere from 65% to 80%.
sentence_114: For example, a 60-pound (27 kg) bow with 80% let-off only requires 12 pounds-force (5.4 kgf; 53 N) to hold at full draw.
sentence_115: Up to 99% let-off is possible.
sentence_116: The compound bow was invented by [[Holless_Wilbur_Allen|Holless Wilbur Allen]] in the 1960s (a US patent was filed in 1966 and granted in 1969) and it has become the most widely used type of bow for all forms of archery in North America.
sentence_117: Mechanically drawn bows typically have a stock or other mounting, such as the [[Crossbow|crossbow]].
sentence_118: Crossbows typically have shorter draw lengths compared to compound bows.
sentence_119: Because of this, heavier draw weights are required to achieve the same energy transfer to the arrow.
sentence_120: These mechanically drawn bows also have devices to hold the tension when the bow is fully drawn.
sentence_121: They are not limited by the strength of a single archer and larger varieties have been used as [[Siege_engine|siege engines]].
sentence_122: Main article: [[Arrow|Arrow]]
sentence_123: The most common form of arrow consists of a [[Arrow_straightener|shaft]], with an [[Arrowhead|arrowhead]] at the front end, and fletchings and a [[Arrow#Nocks|nock]] at the other end.
sentence_124: Arrows across time and history have normally been carried in a container known as a quiver, which can take many different forms.
sentence_125: Shafts of arrows are typically composed of solid [[Wood|wood]], [[Bamboo|bamboo]], [[Glass-reinforced_plastic|fiberglass]], [[Aluminium_alloy|aluminium alloy]], [[Carbon_fiber|carbon fiber]], or [[Composite_material|composite materials]].
sentence_126: Wooden arrows are prone to warping.
sentence_127: Fiberglass arrows are brittle, but can be produced to uniform specifications easily.
sentence_128: Aluminium shafts were a very popular high-performance choice in the latter half of the 20th century, due to their straightness, lighter weight, and subsequently higher speed and flatter trajectories.
sentence_129: Carbon fiber arrows became popular in the 1990s because they are very light, flying even faster and flatter than aluminium arrows.
sentence_130: Today, the most popular arrows at tournaments and Olympic events are made of composite materials, in particular the X10 and A/C/E, made by [[Easton_(company)|Easton]],
sentence_131: The arrowhead is the primary functional component of the arrow.
sentence_132: Some arrows may simply use a sharpened tip of the solid shaft, but separate arrowheads are far more common, usually made from metal, stone, or other hard materials.
sentence_133: The most commonly used forms are target points, field points, and broadheads, although there are also other types, such as bodkin, judo, and blunt heads.
sentence_134: Fletching is traditionally made from bird feathers, but solid plastic vanes and thin sheet-like spin vanes are used.
sentence_135: They are attached near the nock (rear) end of the arrow with thin double sided tape, glue, or, traditionally, sinew.
sentence_136: The most common configuration in all cultures is three fletches, though as many as six have been used.
