sentence_137: Two makes the arrow unstable in flight.
sentence_138: When the arrow is three-fletched, the fletches are equally spaced around the shaft, with one placed such that it is perpendicular to the bow when nocked on the string, though variations are seen with modern equipment, especially when using the modern spin vanes.
sentence_139: This fletch is called the "index fletch" or "cock feather" (also known as "the odd vane out" or "the nocking vane"), and the others are sometimes called the "hen feathers".
sentence_140: Commonly, the cock feather is of a different color.
sentence_141: However, if archers are using fletching made of feather or similar material, they may use same color vanes, as different dyes can give varying stiffness to vanes, resulting in less precision.
sentence_142: When an arrow is four-fletched, two opposing fletches are often cock feathers, and occasionally the fletches are not evenly spaced.
sentence_143: The fletching may be either parabolic cut (short feathers in a smooth parabolic curve) or shield cut (generally shaped like half of a narrow shield), and is often attached at an angle, known as helical fletching, to introduce a stabilizing spin to the arrow while in flight.
sentence_144: Whether helical or straight fletched, when natural fletching (bird feathers) is used it is critical that all feathers come from the same side of the bird.
sentence_145: Oversized fletchings can be used to accentuate drag and thus limit the range of the arrow significantly; these arrows are called flu-flus.
sentence_146: Misplacement of fletchings can change the arrow's flight path dramatically.
sentence_147: Main article: [[Bowstring|Bowstring]]
sentence_148: [[Dacron|Dacron]] and other modern materials offer high strength for their weight and are used on most modern bows.
sentence_149: Linen and other traditional materials are still used on traditional bows.
sentence_150: Several modern methods of making a bowstring exist, such as the 'endless loop' and 'Flemish twist'.
sentence_151: Almost any fiber can be made into a bowstring.
sentence_152: The author of Arab Archery suggests the hide of a young, emaciated camel.
sentence_153: [[Njál's_saga|Njál's saga]] describes the refusal of a wife, Hallgerður, to cut her hair to make an emergency bowstring for her husband, [[Gunnar_Hámundarson|Gunnar Hámundarson]], who is then killed.
sentence_154: Main articles: [[Bracer|Bracer]], Finger tab, and Thumb ring
sentence_155: Most modern archers wear a [[Bracer_(archery)|bracer]] (also known as an arm-guard) to protect the inside of the bow arm from being hit by the string and prevent clothing from catching the bowstring.
sentence_156: The bracer does not brace the arm; the word comes from the armoury term "brassard", meaning an armoured sleeve or badge.
sentence_157: The [[Navajo_people|Navajo people]] have developed highly ornamented bracers as non-functional items of adornment.
sentence_158: Some archers (nearly all female archers) wear protection on their chests, called chestguards or plastrons.
sentence_159: The myth of the Amazons was that they had one breast removed to solve this problem.
sentence_160: Roger Ascham mentions one archer, presumably with an unusual shooting style, who wore a leather guard for his face.
sentence_161: The drawing digits are normally protected by a leather tab, glove, or thumb ring.
sentence_162: A simple tab of leather is commonly used, as is a skeleton glove.
sentence_163: Medieval Europeans probably used a complete leather glove.
sentence_164: Eurasiatic archers who used the thumb or Mongolian draw protected their thumbs, usually with leather according to the author of Arab Archery, but also with special rings of various hard materials.
sentence_165: Many surviving Turkish and Chinese examples are works of considerable art.
sentence_166: Some are so highly ornamented that the users could not have used them to loose an arrow.
sentence_167: Possibly these were items of personal adornment, and hence value, remaining extant whilst leather had virtually no intrinsic value and would also deteriorate with time.
sentence_168: In traditional [[Kyūdō|Japanese archery]] a special [[Yugake|glove]] is used that has a ridge to assist in drawing the string.
sentence_169: Main article: Release aid
sentence_170: A release aid is a mechanical device designed to give a crisp and precise loose of arrows from a compound bow.
sentence_171: In the most commonly used, the string is released by a finger-operated trigger mechanism, held in the archer's hand or attached to their wrist.
sentence_172: In another type, known as a back-tension release, the string is automatically released when drawn to a pre-determined tension.
sentence_173: Main article: [[Stabiliser_(archery)|Stabiliser (archery)]]
sentence_174: Stabilizers are mounted at various points on the bow.
sentence_175: Common with competitive archery equipment are special brackets that allow multiple stabilizers to be mounted at various angles to fine tune the bow's balance.
sentence_176: Stabilizers aid in aiming by improving the balance of the bow.
sentence_177: Sights, quivers, rests, and design of the riser (the central, non-bending part of the bow) make one side of the bow heavier.
sentence_178: One purpose of stabilizers are to offset these forces.
sentence_179: A reflex riser design will cause the top limb to lean towards the shooter.
sentence_180: In this case a heavier front stabilizer is desired to offset this action.
sentence_181: A deflex riser design has the opposite effect and a lighter front stabilizer may be used.
sentence_182: Stabilizers can reduce noise and vibration.
sentence_183: These energies are absorbed by viscoelastic polymers, gels, powders, and other materials used to build stabilizers.
sentence_184: Stabilizers improve the forgiveness and accuracy by increasing the moment of inertia of the bow to resist movement during the shooting process.
sentence_185: Lightweight carbon stabilizers with weighted ends are desirable because they improve the moment of interia while minimizing the weight added.
sentence_186: Main article: [[Bow_hunting|Bow hunting]]
sentence_187: Using archery to take game animals is known as "bow hunting".
sentence_188: Bow hunting differs markedly from hunting with firearms, as distance between hunter and prey must be much shorter to ensure a humane kill.
sentence_189: The skills and practices of bow hunting therefore emphasize very close approach to the prey, whether by still hunting, stalking, or waiting in a blind or tree stand.
sentence_190: In many countries, including much of the United States, bow hunting for large and small game is legal.
sentence_191: Bow hunters generally enjoy longer seasons than are allowed with other forms of hunting such as black powder, shotgun, or rifle.
sentence_192: Usually, compound bows are used for large game hunting due to the relatively short time it takes to master them as opposed to the longbow or recurve bow.
sentence_193: These compound bows may feature fiber optic sights, stabilizers, and other accessories designed to increase accuracy at longer distances.
sentence_194: Using a bow and arrow to take fish is known as "bow fishing".
sentence_195: Main article: Modern competitive archery
sentence_196: Competitive archery involves shooting arrows at a target for accuracy from a set distance or distances.
sentence_197: This is the most popular form of competitive archery worldwide and is called target archery.
sentence_198: A form particularly popular in Europe and [[Americas|America]] is [[Field_archery|field archery]], shot at targets generally set at various distances in a wooded setting.
sentence_199: Competitive archery in the United States is governed by USA Archery and National Field Archery Association (NFAA), which also certifies instructors.
sentence_200: Para-Archery is an adaptation of archery for athletes with a disability governed by the [[World_Archery_Federation|World Archery Federation]] (WA), and is one of the sports in the Summer [[Paralympic_Games|Paralympic Games]].
sentence_201: There are also several other lesser-known and historical forms of archery, as well as [[Archery_games|archery novelty games]] and [[Modern_competitive_archery#Flight_archery|flight archery]], where the aim is to shoot the greatest distance.

title: The Apache Software Foundation
sentence_0: The Apache Software Foundation [[English|/əˈpætʃi/]] (ASF) is an American [[Nonprofit_corporation|nonprofit corporation]] (classified as a [[501(c)(3)_organization|501(c)(3) organization]] in the United States) to support Apache software projects, including the [[Apache_HTTP_Server|Apache HTTP Server]].
sentence_1: The ASF was formed from the Apache Group and incorporated on March 25, 1999.
sentence_2: The Apache Software Foundation is a decentralized open source community of developers.
sentence_3: The software they produce is distributed under the terms of the [[Apache_License|Apache License]] and is [[Free_and_open-source_software|free and open-source software]] (FOSS).
sentence_4: The Apache projects are characterized by a collaborative, consensus-based development process and an open and pragmatic software license.
sentence_5: Each project is managed by a self-selected team of technical experts who are active contributors to the project.
sentence_6: The ASF is a [[Meritocracy|meritocracy]], implying that membership of the foundation is granted only to volunteers who have actively contributed to Apache projects.
sentence_7: The ASF is considered a second generation [[Open-source_software|open-source]] organization, in that commercial support is provided without the risk of [[Platform_lock-in|platform lock-in]].
sentence_8: Among the ASF's objectives are: to provide legal protection to volunteers working on Apache projects; to prevent the Apache brand name from being used by other organizations without permission.
sentence_9: The ASF also holds several [[ApacheCon|ApacheCon]] conferences each year, highlighting Apache projects and related technology.
sentence_10: The history of the Apache Software Foundation is linked to the Apache HTTP Server, development beginning in February 1993.
sentence_11: A group of eight developers started working on enhancing the NCSA HTTPd [[Daemon_(computing)|daemon]].
sentence_12: They came to be known as the Apache Group.
sentence_13: On March 25, 1999, the Apache Software Foundation was formed.
sentence_14: The first official meeting of the Apache Software Foundation was held on April 13, 1999, and by general consent that the initial membership list of the Apache Software Foundation, would be: [[Brian_Behlendorf|Brian Behlendorf]], [[Ken_Coar|Ken Coar]], Miguel Gonzales, Mark Cox, [[Lars_Eilebrecht|Lars Eilebrecht]], Ralf S. Engelschall, [[Roy_Fielding|Roy T. Fielding]], Dean Gaudet, Ben Hyde, [[Jim_Jagielski|Jim Jagielski]], Alexei Kosut, Martin Kraemer, [[Ben_Laurie|Ben Laurie]], Doug MacEachern, Aram Mirzadeh, [[Sameer_Parekh|Sameer Parekh]], Cliff Skolnick, Marc Slemko, William (Bill) Stoddard, Paul Sutton, [[Randy_Terbush|Randy Terbush]] and [[Dirk-Willem_van_Gulik|Dirk-Willem van Gulik]].
sentence_15: After a series of additional meetings to elect board members and resolve other legal matters regarding incorporation, the effective incorporation date of the Apache Software Foundation was set to June 1, 1999.
sentence_16: The foundation states that the [[Apache_HTTP_Server#Name|name 'Apache']] was chosen "from respect for the Native American Apache Nation, well known for their superior skills in warfare strategy and their inexhaustible endurance".
sentence_17: The Apache Software Foundation released a feature documentary, "," on June 11, 2020, detailing its history and far-reaching impact on the open-source software community.
sentence_18: See also: [[List_of_Apache_Software_Foundation_projects|List of Apache Software Foundation projects]]
sentence_19: Apache divides its [[Software_development|software development]] activities into separate semi-autonomous areas called "top-level projects" (formally known as a "Project Management Committee" in the bylaws), some of which have a number of sub-projects.
sentence_20: Unlike some other organizations that host [[Free_and_open-source_software|FOSS]] projects, before a project is hosted at Apache it has to be licensed to the ASF with a grant or contributor agreement.
sentence_21: In this way, the ASF gains the necessary intellectual property rights for the development and distribution of all its projects.
sentence_22: The Board of Directors of The Apache Software Foundation (ASF) is responsible for management and oversight of the business and affairs of the corporation in accordance with the Bylaws.
sentence_23: This includes management of the corporate assets (funds, intellectual property, trademarks, and support equipment), appointment of a President and corporate officers managing the core operations of the ASF, and allocation of corporate resources for the benefit of Apache projects.
sentence_24: Importantly, Technical decision-making authority for every Apache project is assigned to their independent project management committee; the participants in each project provide direction, not the board.
sentence_25: The board is elected annually by the ASF membership.
sentence_26: Board meetings and minutes are published on the board calendar.
sentence_27: Many other public records of our corporation are published publicly.
sentence_28: Information about Apache corporate governance and organization and how board meetings work are also available.
sentence_29: The current board of directors is:

title: Academy Awards
sentence_0: "Oscars" and "The Oscar" redirect here.
sentence_1: For other uses, see [[Oscar|Oscar]].

table.value: [[Academy_of_Motion_Picture_Arts_and_Sciences|Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences]]

sentence_2: The Academy Awards, popularly known as the Oscars, are awards for artistic and technical merit in the [[Film_industry|film industry]].
sentence_3: It is regarded as the most famous and prestigious awards in the entertainment industry.
sentence_4: Given annually by the [[Academy_of_Motion_Picture_Arts_and_Sciences|Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences]] (AMPAS), the awards are an international recognition of excellence in cinematic achievements, as assessed by the Academy's voting membership.
sentence_5: The various category winners are awarded a copy of a golden statuette as a trophy, officially called the "Academy Award of Merit", although more commonly referred to by its nickname, the "Oscar".
sentence_6: The statuette depicts a knight rendered in the [[Art_Deco|Art Deco]] style.
sentence_7: The award was originally sculpted by [[George_Stanley_(sculptor)|George Stanley]] from a design sketch by [[Cedric_Gibbons|Cedric Gibbons]].
sentence_8: AMPAS first [[1st_Academy_Awards|presented it in 1929]] at a private dinner hosted by Douglas Fairbanks in the [[Hollywood_Roosevelt_Hotel|Hollywood Roosevelt Hotel]] in what would become known as the [[1st_Academy_Awards|1st Academy Awards]].
sentence_9: The Academy Awards ceremony was first broadcast by radio in 1930 and was televised for the first time in 1953.
sentence_10: It is the oldest worldwide entertainment awards ceremony and is now televised live worldwide.
sentence_11: It is also the oldest of the [[EGOT|four major annual American entertainment awards]]; its equivalents – the [[Emmy_Award|Emmy Awards]] for television, the [[Tony_Award|Tony Awards]] for theater, and the [[Grammy_Award|Grammy Awards]] for music – are modeled after the Academy Awards.
sentence_12: They are widely cited as the most famous and prestigious competitive awards in the field of entertainment.
sentence_13: The [[92nd_Academy_Awards|92nd Academy Awards]] ceremony, honoring the [[2019_in_film|best films of 2019]], was held on February 9, 2020.
sentence_14: As with [[91st_Academy_Awards|the previous ceremony]], there was no host.
sentence_15: The ceremony was broadcast on ABC.
sentence_16: It took place at the [[Dolby_Theatre|Dolby Theatre]] in Los Angeles, California, for the 18th consecutive year.
sentence_17: This ceremony marked the first time in Oscar history that more than three films had received ten or more nominations.
sentence_18: A total of 3,140 Oscar statuettes have been awarded since its inception in 1929.
sentence_19: The [[1st_Academy_Awards|first Academy Awards]] presentation was held on May 16, 1929, at a private dinner function at the [[Hollywood_Roosevelt_Hotel|Hollywood Roosevelt Hotel]] with an audience of about 270 people.
sentence_20: The post-awards party was held at the Mayfair Hotel.
sentence_21: The cost of guest tickets for that night's ceremony was $5 ($74 in 2020 dollars).
sentence_22: Fifteen statuettes were awarded, honoring artists, directors and other participants in the film-making industry of the time, for their works during the 1927–28 period.
sentence_23: The ceremony ran for 15 minutes.
sentence_24: Winners were announced to media three months earlier.
sentence_25: That was changed for the second ceremony in 1930.
sentence_26: Since then, for the rest of the first decade, the results were given to newspapers for publication at 11:00 pm on the night of the awards.
sentence_27: This method was used until 1940, when the [[Los_Angeles_Times|Los Angeles Times]] announced the winners before the ceremony began; as a result, the Academy has, since 1941, used a sealed envelope to reveal the names of the winners.
sentence_28: The first Best Actor awarded was [[Emil_Jannings|Emil Jannings]], for his performances in [[The_Last_Command_(1928_film)|The Last Command]] and [[The_Way_of_All_Flesh_(1927_film)|The Way of All Flesh]].
sentence_29: He had to return to Europe before the ceremony, so the Academy agreed to give him the prize earlier; this made him the first Academy Award winner in history.
sentence_30: At that time, winners were recognized for the entirety of their work done in a certain category during the qualifying period; for example, Jannings received the award for two movies in which he starred during that period, and [[Janet_Gaynor|Janet Gaynor]] later won a single Oscar for performances in three films.
sentence_31: With the fourth ceremony, however, the system changed, and professionals were honored for a specific performance in a single film.
sentence_32: For the first six ceremonies, the eligibility period spanned two calendar years.
sentence_33: At the 29th ceremony, held in 1957, the Best Foreign Language Film category, now known as [[Academy_Award_for_Best_International_Feature_Film|Best International Feature Film]], was introduced.
sentence_34: Until then, foreign-language films had been honored with the Special Achievement Award.
sentence_35: Perhaps the most widely seen [[Streaking|streaker]] in history was 34-year-old Robert Opel, who streaked across the stage of The Dorothy Chandler Pavilion in Los Angeles flashing a peace sign on national US television at the 46th Academy Awards in 1974.
sentence_36: Bemused host David Niven quipped, "Isn't it fascinating to think that probably the only laugh that man will ever get in his life is by stripping off and showing his shortcomings?"
sentence_37: Later, evidence arose suggesting that Opel's appearance was facilitated as a publicity stunt by the show's producer Jack Haley Jr. Robert Metzler, the show's business manager, believed that the incident had been planned in some way; during the dress rehearsal Niven had asked Metzler's wife to borrow a pen so he could write down the famous line, which was thus not the ad-lib it appeared to be.
sentence_38: The 74th Academy Awards, held in 2002, presented the first [[Academy_Award_for_Best_Animated_Feature|Academy Award for Best Animated Feature]].
sentence_39: Since 1973, all Academy Awards ceremonies have ended with the [[Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture|Academy Award for Best Picture]].
sentence_40: Traditionally, the previous year's winner for Best Actor and Best Supporting Actor present the awards for Best Actress and Best Supporting Actress, while the previous year's winner for Best Actress and Best Supporting Actress present the awards for Best Actor and Best Supporting Actor.
sentence_41: [[Parasite_(2019_film)|Parasite]] became the first foreign-language film to win Best Picture at the [[2020_Oscars|February 9, 2020 award ceremony]].
sentence_42: [[Tom_Hanks|Tom Hanks]] announced at the [[2020_Oscars|2020 Oscar Ceremony]], the opening of the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures on December 14, 2020.
sentence_43: The museum development started in 2017 under [[Kerry_Brougher|Kerry Brougher]], but is now led by Bill Kramer.
sentence_44: The industry curated exhibits will be geared toward the history of motion picture, the art & science of film making, exhibiting trailblazing directors, actors, film makers, sound editors and more, and will house famous [[Cultural_artifact|artifacts]] from acclaimed movies like [[Ruby_slippers|Dorothy's Ruby Red Slippers]].
sentence_45: Because of [[COVID-19|COVID-19]], Academy president David Rubin and CEO Dawn Hudson announced that for the [[93rd_Academy_Awards|2021 Oscar Ceremony]], [[Streaming_service_provider|streaming movies]] not shown in theaters would be eligible, though at some point the requirement that movies be shown in theaters would return.
sentence_46: See also: [[#Awards_of_Merit_categories|§ Awards of Merit categories]]
sentence_47: The best known award is the Academy Award of Merit, more popularly known as the Oscar statuette.
sentence_48: Made of gold-plated [[Bronze|bronze]] on a black metal base, it is 13.5 in (34.3 cm) tall, weighs 8.5 lb (3.856 kg), and depicts a knight rendered in [[Art_Deco|Art Deco]] style holding a [[Crusades|crusader's]] sword standing on a reel of film with five spokes.
sentence_49: The five spokes represent the original branches of the Academy: Actors, Writers, Directors, Producers, and Technicians.
sentence_50: Sculptor [[George_Stanley_(sculptor)|George Stanley]] (who also did the Muse Fountain at the [[Hollywood_Bowl|Hollywood Bowl]]) sculpted [[Cedric_Gibbons|Cedric Gibbons]]' design.
sentence_51: The statuettes presented at the initial ceremonies were gold-plated solid bronze.
sentence_52: Within a few years, the bronze was abandoned in favor of [[Britannia_metal|Britannia metal]], a pewter-like alloy which is then plated in copper, nickel silver, and finally, 24-karat gold.
sentence_53: Due to a metal shortage during World War II, Oscars were made of painted plaster for three years.
sentence_54: Following the war, the Academy invited recipients to redeem the plaster figures for gold-plated metal ones.
sentence_55: The only addition to the Oscar since it was created is a minor streamlining of the base.
sentence_56: The original Oscar mold was cast in 1928 at the [[C.W._Shumway_&_Sons|C.W.
sentence_57: Shumway & Sons]] Foundry in [[Batavia,_Illinois|Batavia]], Illinois, which also contributed to casting the molds for the [[Vince_Lombardi_Trophy|Vince Lombardi Trophy]] and [[Emmy_Award|Emmy Award]]'s statuettes.
sentence_58: From 1983 to 2015, approximately 50 Oscars in a tin alloy with gold plating were made each year in Chicago by Illinois manufacturer [[R.S._Owens_&_Company|R.S.
sentence_59: Owens & Company]].
sentence_60: It would take between three and four weeks to manufacture 50 statuettes.
sentence_61: In 2016, the Academy returned to bronze as the core metal of the statuettes, handing manufacturing duties to [[Walden,_New_York|Walden]], New York-based Polich Tallix Fine Art Foundry.
sentence_62: While based on a digital scan of an original 1929 Oscar, the statuettes retain their modern-era dimensions and black pedestal.
sentence_63: Cast in liquid bronze from [[3D-printed|3D-printed]] ceramic molds and polished, they are then electroplated in 24-karat gold by [[Brooklyn,_New_York|Brooklyn]], New York–based Epner Technology.
sentence_64: The time required to produce 50 such statuettes is roughly three months.
sentence_65: R.S. Owens is expected to continue producing other awards for the Academy and service existing Oscars that need replating.
sentence_66: The Academy officially adopted the name "Oscar" for the trophies in 1939.
sentence_67: However, the origin of the nickname is disputed.
sentence_68: One biography of [[Bette_Davis|Bette Davis]], who was a president of the Academy in 1941, claims she named the award after her first husband, band leader Harmon Oscar Nelson.
sentence_69: A frequently mentioned originator is [[Margaret_Herrick|Margaret Herrick]], the Academy executive secretary, who, when she first saw the award in 1931, said the statuette reminded her of "Uncle Oscar", a nickname for her cousin Oscar Pierce.
sentence_70: Columnist Sidney Skolsky, who was present during Herrick's naming in 1931, wrote that "Employees have affectionately dubbed their famous statuette 'Oscar.'"
sentence_71: The Academy credits Skolsky with "the first confirmed newspaper reference" to Oscar in his column on March 16, 1934, which was written about that year's [[6th_Academy_Awards|6th Academy Awards]].
sentence_72: The 1934 awards appeared again in another early media mention of Oscar: a [[Time_(magazine)|Time magazine]] story.
sentence_73: In the ceremonies that year, [[Walt_Disney|Walt Disney]] was the first to thank the Academy for his "Oscar" during his acceptance speech.
sentence_74: To prevent information identifying the Oscar winners from leaking ahead of the ceremony, Oscar statuettes presented at the ceremony have blank baseplates.
sentence_75: Until 2010, winners returned their statuettes to the Academy and had to wait several weeks to have their names inscribed on their respective Oscars.
sentence_76: Since 2010, winners have had the option of having engraved nameplates applied to their statuettes at an inscription-processing station at the Governor's Ball, a party held immediately after the Oscar ceremony.
sentence_77: The R.S. Owens company has engraved nameplates made before the ceremony, bearing the name of every potential winner.
sentence_78: The nameplates for the non-winning nominees are later recycled.
sentence_79: Prior to 1950 Oscar statuettes were (and remain) the property of the recipient.
sentence_80: Since then the statuettes have been legally [[Encumbrance|encumbered]] by the requirement that the statuette be first offered for sale back to the Academy for US$1.
sentence_81: If a winner refuses to agree to this stipulation, then the Academy keeps the statuette.
sentence_82: Academy Awards predating this agreement have been sold in public auctions and private deals for six-figure sums.
sentence_83: In 1989 [[Mike_Todd|Michael Todd's]] grandson tried to sell Todd's [[Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture|Best Picture]] Oscar for his 1956 production of [[Around_the_World_in_80_Days_(1956_film)|Around the World in 80 Days]] to a movie prop collector.
sentence_84: The Academy earned enforcement of its statuette contract by gaining a permanent injunction against the sale.
sentence_85: In 1992, [[Harold_Russell|Harold Russell]] consigned his 1946 Oscar for Best Supporting Actor for [[The_Best_Years_of_Our_Lives|The Best Years of Our Lives]] to auction in order to raise money for his wife's medical expenses.
sentence_86: Though his decision caused controversy, the first-ever Oscar to be sold passed to a private collector on August 6, 1992 for $60,500 ($110,200 today).
sentence_87: Russell defended his action, saying, "I don't know why anybody would be critical.
sentence_88: My wife's health is much more important than sentimental reasons.
sentence_89: The movie will be here, even if Oscar isn't."
sentence_91: In December 2011, [[Orson_Welles|Orson Welles]]' 1941 Oscar for [[Citizen_Kane|Citizen Kane]] ([[Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay|Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay]]) was put up for auction, after his heirs won a 2004 court decision contending that Welles did not sign any agreement to return the statue to the Academy.
sentence_92: On December 20, 2011, it sold in an online auction for US$861,542 ($0.98 million today).
sentence_93: Some buyers have subsequently returned the statuettes to the Academy, which keeps them in its treasury.

section_7.value: Other awards presented by the Academy

sentence_94: See also: [[#Special_categories|§ Special categories]]
sentence_95: In addition to the Academy Award of Merit (Oscar award), there are nine honorary (non-competitive) awards presented by the Academy from time to time (except for the Academy Honorary Award, the Technical Achievement Award, and the Student Academy Awards, which are presented annually):

list.value: The [[Academy_Honorary_Award|Academy Honorary Award]] (annual) (which may or may not be in the form of an Oscar statuette);
The [[Irving_G._Thalberg_Memorial_Award|Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award]] (since 1938) (in the form of a bust of Thalberg);
The [[Jean_Hersholt_Humanitarian_Award|Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award]] (since 1957) (in the form of an Oscar statuette);
The Academy Scientific and Technical Awards:
Academy Award of Merit (non-competitive) (in the form of an Oscar statuette);
Scientific and Engineering Award (in the form of a bronze tablet);
[[Academy_Award_for_Technical_Achievement|Technical Achievement Award]] (annual) (in the form of a certificate);
The [[John_A._Bonner_Medal_of_Commendation|John A. Bonner Medal of Commendation]] (since 1978) (in the form of a medal);

sentence_96: The Academy also awards [[Nicholl_Fellowships_in_Screenwriting|Nicholl Fellowships in Screenwriting]].
sentence_97: Since 2004, Academy Award nomination results have been announced to the public in mid-January.
sentence_98: Prior to that, the results were announced in early February.
sentence_99: The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (AMPAS), a professional honorary organization, maintains a voting membership of over 7,000 as of 2018.
sentence_100: Academy membership is divided into different branches, with each representing a different discipline in film production.
sentence_101: Actors constitute the largest voting bloc, numbering 1,311 members (22 percent) of the Academy's composition.
sentence_102: Votes have been certified by the auditing firm [[PricewaterhouseCoopers|PricewaterhouseCoopers]] (and its predecessor [[Price_Waterhouse|Price Waterhouse]]) since the [[7th_Academy_Awards|7th Academy Awards]] in 1935.
sentence_103: The firm mails the ballots of eligible nominees to members of the Academy in December to reflect the previous eligible year with a due date sometime in January of the next year, then tabulates the votes in a process that takes thousands of hours.
sentence_104: All AMPAS members must be invited to join by the Board of Governors, on behalf of Academy Branch Executive Committees.
sentence_105: Membership eligibility may be achieved by a competitive nomination or a member may submit a name based on other significant contributions to the field of motion pictures.
sentence_106: New membership proposals are considered annually.
sentence_107: The Academy does not publicly disclose its membership, although as recently as 2007 press releases have announced the names of those who have been invited to join.
sentence_108: The 2007 release also stated that it has just under 6,000 voting members.
sentence_109: While the membership had been growing, stricter policies have kept its size steady since then.
sentence_110: In 2012, the results of a study conducted by the [[Los_Angeles_Times|Los Angeles Times]] were published describing the demographic breakdown of approximately 88% of AMPAS' voting membership.
sentence_111: Of the 5,100+ active voters confirmed, 94% were Caucasian, 77% were male, and 54% were found to be over the age of 60.
sentence_112: 33% of voting members are former nominees (14%) and winners (19%).
sentence_113: In May 2011, the Academy sent a letter advising its 6,000 or so voting members that an online system for Oscar voting would be implemented in 2013.
sentence_114: According to Rules 2 and 3 of the official Academy Awards Rules, a film must open in the previous calendar year, from midnight at the start of January 1 to midnight at the end of December 31, in [[Los_Angeles_County,_California|Los Angeles County]], California, and play for seven consecutive days, to qualify (except for the Best International Feature Film, Best Documentary Feature, and awards in short film categories).
sentence_115: Additionally, the film must be shown at least three times on each day of its qualifying run, with at least one of the daily showings starting between 6 pm and 10 pm local time.
sentence_116: The Best International Feature Film award does not require a U.S. release.
sentence_117: It requires the film to be submitted as its country's official selection.
sentence_118: The Best Documentary Feature award requires either week-long releases in both Los Angeles County and New York City during the previous calendar year, or a qualifying award at a competitive film festival from the Documentary Feature Qualifying Festival list (regardless of any public exhibition or distribution), or a submission in the International Feature Film category as its country's official selection.
sentence_119: The qualifying theatrical runs must meet the same requirements as those for non-documentary films regarding numbers and times of screenings.
sentence_120: Additionally, a film must have been reviewed by a critic from [[The_New_York_Times|The New York Times]], [[Time_Out_New_York|Time Out New York]], the [[Los_Angeles_Times|Los Angeles Times]], or [[LA_Weekly|LA Weekly]].
sentence_121: Awards in short film categories (Best Documentary Short Subject, Best Animated Short Film, and Best Live Action Short Film) have noticeably different eligibility rules from most other competitive awards.
sentence_122: First, the qualifying period for release does not coincide with a calendar year, instead covering a one-year period starting on October 1 and ending on September 30 of the calendar year before the ceremony.
sentence_123: Second, there are multiple methods of qualification.
sentence_124: The main method is a week-long theatrical release in either Los Angeles County or New York City during the eligibility period.
sentence_125: Films also can qualify by winning specified awards at one of a number of competitive film festivals designated by the Academy, also without regard to prior public distribution.
sentence_126: Finally, a film that is selected as a gold, silver, or bronze medal winner in an appropriate category of the immediately previous Student Academy Awards is also eligible (Documentary category for that award, and Animation, Narrative, Alternative, or International for the other awards).
sentence_127: The requirements for the qualifying theatrical run are also different from those for other awards.
sentence_128: Only one screening per day is required.
sentence_129: For the Documentary award, the screening must start between noon and 10 pm local time; for other awards, no specific start time is required, but the film must appear in regular theater listings with dates and screening times.
sentence_130: For example, the 2009 [[Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture|Best Picture]] winner, [[The_Hurt_Locker|The Hurt Locker]], was actually first released in 2008, but did not qualify for the [[81st_Academy_Awards|2008 awards]], as it did not play its Oscar-qualifying run in Los Angeles until mid-2009, thus qualifying for the [[82nd_Academy_Awards|2009 awards]].
sentence_131: Foreign films must include English subtitles, and each country can submit only one film for consideration in the International Feature Film category per year.
sentence_132: Rule 2 states that a film must be feature-length, defined as a minimum of 40 minutes, except for short-subject awards, and it must exist either on a [[35mm_movie_film|35 mm]] or 70 mm film print or in 24 frame/s or 48 frame/s progressive scan [[Digital_cinema|digital cinema]] format with a minimum projector resolution of 2048 by 1080 pixels.
sentence_133: Since the [[90th_Academy_Awards|90th Academy Awards]], presented in 2018, multi-part and limited series have been ineligible for the Best Documentary Feature award.
sentence_134: This followed the win of O.J.: Made in America, an eight-hour presentation that was screened in a limited release before being broadcast in five parts on ABC and [[ESPN|ESPN]], in that category in [[89th_Academy_Awards|2017]].
sentence_135: The Academy's announcement of the new rule made no direct mention of that film.
sentence_136: Producers must submit an Official Screen Credits online form before the deadline; in case it is not submitted by the defined deadline, the film will be ineligible for Academy Awards in any year.
sentence_137: The form includes the production credits for all related categories.
sentence_138: Then, each form is checked and put in a Reminder List of Eligible Releases.
sentence_139: In late December, ballots, and copies of the Reminder List of Eligible Releases are mailed to around 6,000 active members.
sentence_140: For most categories, members from each of the branches vote to determine the nominees only in their respective categories (i.e. only directors vote for directors, writers for writers, actors for actors, etc.).
sentence_141: In the special case of Best Picture, all voting members are eligible to select the nominees.
sentence_142: In all major categories, a variant of the single transferable vote is used, with each member casting a ballot with up to five nominees (ten for Best Picture) ranked preferentially.
sentence_143: In certain categories, including International Feature Film, Documentary and Animated Feature, nominees are selected by special screening committees made up of members from all branches.
sentence_144: In most categories, the winner is selected from among the nominees by [[Plurality_voting|plurality voting]] of all members.
sentence_145: Since 2009, the Best Picture winner has been chosen by instant runoff voting.
sentence_146: Since 2013, re-weighted [[Range_voting|range voting]] has been used to select the nominees for the [[Academy_Award_for_Best_Visual_Effects|Best Visual Effects]].
sentence_147: Film companies will spend as much as several million dollars on [[For_Your_Consideration_(advertising)|marketing to awards voters]] for a movie in the running for Best Picture, in attempts to improve chances of receiving Oscars and other movie awards conferred in [[Oscar_season|Oscar season]].
sentence_148: The Academy enforces rules to limit overt campaigning by its members so as to try to eliminate excesses and prevent the process from becoming undignified.
sentence_149: It has an awards czar on staff who advises members on allowed practices and levies penalties on offenders.
sentence_150: For example, a producer of the 2009 Best Picture nominee [[The_Hurt_Locker|The Hurt Locker]] was disqualified as a producer in the category when he contacted associates urging them to vote for his film and not another that was seen as the front-runner (The Hurt Locker eventually won).
sentence_151: See also: [[List_of_Academy_Awards_ceremonies|List of Academy Awards ceremonies]]
sentence_152: The major awards are presented at a live televised ceremony, commonly in late February or early March following the relevant calendar year, and six weeks after the announcement of the nominees.
sentence_153: It is the culmination of the film awards season, which usually begins during November or December of the previous year.
sentence_154: This is an elaborate extravaganza, with the invited guests walking up the red carpet in the creations of the most prominent fashion designers of the day.
sentence_155: [[Black_tie|Black tie]] dress is the most common outfit for men, although fashion may dictate not wearing a [[Bow-tie|bow-tie]], and musical performers sometimes do not adhere to this.
sentence_156: (The artists who recorded the nominees for Best Original Song quite often perform those songs live at the awards ceremony, and the fact that they are performing is often used to promote the television broadcast.)
sentence_157: The Academy Awards is the world's longest-running awards show televised live from the U.S. to all time zones in North America and worldwide, and gathers billions of viewers elsewhere throughout the world.
sentence_158: The Oscars were first televised in [[25th_Academy_Awards|1953]] by [[NBC|NBC]], which continued to broadcast the event until [[32nd_Academy_Awards|1960]], when ABC took over, televising the festivities (including the first color broadcast of the event in [[38th_Academy_Awards|1966]]) through 1970.
sentence_159: NBC regained the rights for five years (1971–75), then ABC resumed broadcast duties in [[48th_Academy_Awards|1976]] and its current contract with the Academy runs through 2028.
sentence_160: The Academy has also produced condensed versions of the ceremony for broadcast in international markets (especially those outside of the Americas) in more desirable local timeslots.
sentence_161: The ceremony was broadcast live internationally for the first time via satellite since 1970, but only two South American countries, Chile and Brazil, purchased the rights to air the broadcast.
sentence_162: By that time, the television rights to the Academy Awards had been sold in 50 countries.
sentence_163: A decade later, the rights were already being sold to 60 countries, and by [[56th_Academy_Awards|1984]], the TV rights to the Awards were licensed in 76 countries.
sentence_164: The ceremonies were moved up from late March/early April to late February, since [[76th_Academy_Awards|2004]], to help disrupt and shorten the intense [[For_Your_Consideration_(advertising)|lobbying and ad campaigns]] associated with [[Oscar_season|Oscar season]] in the film industry.
sentence_165: Another reason was because of the growing TV ratings success coinciding with the [[NCAA_Division_I_Men's_Basketball_Tournament|NCAA Basketball Tournament]], which would cut into the Academy Awards audience.
sentence_166: (In [[48th_Academy_Awards|1976]] and [[49th_Academy_Awards|1977]], ABC's regained Oscars were moved from Tuesday to Monday and went directly opposite NBC's NCAA title game.)
sentence_167: The earlier date is also to the advantage of ABC, as it now usually occurs during the highly profitable and important February [[Sweeps|sweeps]] period.
sentence_168: Some years, the ceremony is moved into the first Sunday of March to avoid a clash with the [[Winter_Olympic_Games|Winter Olympic Games]].
sentence_169: Another reason for the move to late February and early March is also to avoid the awards ceremony occurring so close to the religious holidays of [[Passover|Passover]] and Easter, which for decades had been a grievance from members and the general public.
sentence_170: Advertising is somewhat restricted, however, as traditionally no movie studios or competitors of official Academy Award sponsors may advertise during the telecast.
sentence_171: The production of the Academy Awards telecast currently holds the distinction of winning the most [[Emmy_Awards|Emmys]] in history, with 47 wins and 195 nominations overall since that award's own launch in [[21st_Academy_Awards|1949]].
sentence_172: After many years of being held on Mondays at 9:00 pm [[Eastern_Time_Zone|Eastern]]/6:00 p.m Pacific, since the [[71st_Academy_Awards|1999 ceremonies]], it was moved to Sundays at 8:30 pm ET/5:30 pm PT.
sentence_173: The reasons given for the move were that more viewers would tune in on Sundays, that Los Angeles rush-hour traffic jams could be avoided, and an earlier start time would allow viewers on the East Coast to go to bed earlier.
sentence_174: For many years the film industry opposed a Sunday broadcast because it would cut into the weekend box office.
sentence_175: In 2010, the Academy contemplated moving the ceremony even further back into January, citing TV viewers' fatigue with the film industry's long awards season.
sentence_176: However, such an accelerated schedule would dramatically decrease the voting period for its members, to the point where some voters would only have time to view the contending films streamed on their computers (as opposed to traditionally receiving the films and ballots in the mail).
sentence_177: Furthermore, a January ceremony on Sunday would clash with [[National_Football_League|National Football League]] playoff games.
sentence_178: In 2018, the Academy announced that the ceremony would be moved from late February to mid February beginning with the 92nd Academy Awards in 2020.
sentence_179: Originally scheduled for April 8, 1968, the [[40th_Academy_Awards|40th Academy Awards]] ceremony was postponed for two days, because of the [[Assassination_of_Martin_Luther_King_Jr.|assassination]] of [[Martin_Luther_King_Jr.|Dr.
sentence_180: Martin Luther King, Jr.]].
sentence_181: On March 30, 1981, the [[53rd_Academy_Awards|53rd Academy Awards]] was postponed for one day, after [[Attempted_assassination_of_Ronald_Reagan|the shooting]] of President [[Ronald_Reagan|Ronald Reagan]] and others in Washington, D.C.
sentence_182: In 1993, an In Memoriam segment was introduced, honoring those who had made a significant contribution to cinema who had died in the preceding 12 months, a selection compiled by a small committee of Academy members.
sentence_183: This segment has drawn criticism over the years for the omission of some names.
sentence_184: Criticism was also levied for many years regarding another aspect, with the segment having a "[[Popularity_contest|popularity contest]]" feel as the audience varied their applause to those who had died by the subject's cultural impact; the applause has since been muted during the telecast, and the audience is discouraged from clapping during the segment and giving silent reflection instead.
sentence_185: This segment was later followed by a commercial break.
sentence_186: In terms of broadcast length, the ceremony generally averages three and a half hours.
sentence_187: The first Oscars, in 1929, lasted 15 minutes.
sentence_188: At the other end of the spectrum, the 2002 ceremony lasted four hours and twenty-three minutes.
sentence_189: In 2010, the organizers of the Academy Awards announced winners' [[Oscar_speech|acceptance speeches]] must not run past 45 seconds.
sentence_190: This, according to organizer Bill Mechanic, was to ensure the elimination of what he termed "the single most hated thing on the show" – overly long and embarrassing displays of emotion.
sentence_191: In 2016, in a further effort to streamline speeches, winners' dedications were displayed on an on-screen ticker.
sentence_192: During the 2018 ceremony, host [[Jimmy_Kimmel|Jimmy Kimmel]] acknowledged how long the ceremony had become, by announcing that he would give a brand-new jet ski to whoever gave the shortest speech of the night (a reward won by [[Mark_Bridges_(costume_designer)|Mark Bridges]] when accepting his [[Academy_Award_for_Best_Costume_Design|Best Costume Design]] award for [[Phantom_Thread|Phantom Thread]]).
sentence_193: [[The_Wall_Street_Journal|The Wall Street Journal]] analyzed the average minutes spent across the 2014–2018 telecasts as follows: 14 on song performances; 25 on the hosts' speeches; 38 on prerecorded clips; and 78 on the awards themselves, broken into 24 on the introduction and announcement, 24 on winners walking to the stage, and 30 on their acceptance speeches.
sentence_194: Although still dominant in ratings, the viewership of the Academy Awards has steadily dropped; the [[88th_Academy_Awards|88th Academy Awards]] were the lowest-rated in the past eight years (although with increases in male and 18–49 viewership), while the show itself also faced mixed reception.
sentence_195: Following the show, [[Variety_(magazine)|Variety]] reported that ABC was, in negotiating an extension to its contract to broadcast the Oscars, seeking to have more creative control over the broadcast itself.
sentence_196: Currently and nominally, AMPAS is responsible for most aspects of the telecast, including the choice of production staff and hosting, although ABC is allowed to have some input on their decisions.
sentence_197: In August 2016, AMPAS extended its contract with ABC through 2028: the contract neither contains any notable changes nor gives ABC any further creative control over the telecast.
sentence_198: Historically, the telecast's viewership is higher when box-office hits are favored to win the Best Picture award.
sentence_199: More than 57.25 million viewers tuned to the telecast for the [[70th_Academy_Awards|70th Academy Awards]] in 1998, the year of [[Titanic_(1997_film)|Titanic]], which generated a box office haul during its initial 1997–98 run of US$600.8 million in the US, a box office record that would remain unsurpassed for years.
sentence_200: The [[76th_Academy_Awards|76th Academy Awards]] ceremony, in which The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King (pre-telecast box office earnings of US$368 million) received 11 Awards including Best Picture, drew 43.56 million viewers.
sentence_201: The most watched ceremony based on [[Nielsen_ratings|Nielsen ratings]] to date, however, was the 42nd Academy Awards (Best Picture [[Midnight_Cowboy|Midnight Cowboy]]) which drew a 43.4% household rating on April 7, 1970.
sentence_202: By contrast, ceremonies honoring films that have not performed well at the box office tend to show weaker ratings, despite how much critically acclaimed those films have been.
sentence_203: The [[78th_Academy_Awards|78th Academy Awards]] which awarded low-budget independent film [[Crash_(2004_film)|Crash]] (with a pre-Oscar gross of US$53.4 million) generated an audience of 38.64 million with a household rating of 22.91%.
sentence_204: In 2008, the [[80th_Academy_Awards|80th Academy Awards]] telecast was watched by 31.76 million viewers on average with an 18.66% household rating, the lowest-rated and least-watched ceremony at the time, in spite of celebrating 80 years of the Academy Awards.
sentence_205: The Best Picture winner of that particular ceremony was another independent film ([[No_Country_for_Old_Men_(film)|No Country for Old Men]]).
sentence_206: The 92nd Academy Awards drew an average of 23.6 million viewers—a new low.
sentence_207: The [[Academy_Film_Archive|Academy Film Archive]] holds copies of every Academy Awards ceremony since the 1949 Oscars and material on many prior ceremonies, along with ancillary material related to more recent shows.
sentence_208: Copies are held on a variety of film, video, and digital formats.
sentence_209: In 1929, the first Academy Awards were presented at a banquet dinner at the [[Hollywood_Roosevelt_Hotel|Hollywood Roosevelt Hotel]].
sentence_210: From 1930 to 1943, the ceremony alternated between two venues: the [[Ambassador_Hotel_(Los_Angeles)|Ambassador Hotel]] on Wilshire Boulevard and the Biltmore Hotel in downtown Los Angeles.
sentence_211: [[Grauman's_Chinese_Theatre|Grauman's Chinese Theatre]] in Hollywood then hosted the awards from 1944 to 1946, followed by the [[Shrine_Auditorium|Shrine Auditorium]] in Los Angeles from 1947 to 1948.
sentence_212: The [[21st_Academy_Awards|21st Academy Awards]] in 1949 were held at the Academy Award Theatre at what had been the Academy's headquarters on Melrose Avenue in Hollywood.
sentence_213: From 1950 to 1960, the awards were presented at Hollywood's [[Pantages_Theatre_(Hollywood)|Pantages Theatre]].
sentence_214: With the advent of television, the awards from 1953 to 1957 took place simultaneously in Hollywood and New York, first at the [[Majestic_Theatre_(Columbus_Circle)|NBC International Theatre]] (1953) and then at the NBC Century Theatre, after which the ceremony took place solely in Los Angeles.
sentence_215: The Oscars moved to the [[Santa_Monica_Civic_Auditorium|Santa Monica Civic Auditorium]] in [[Santa_Monica,_California|Santa Monica]], California, in 1961.
sentence_216: By 1969, the Academy decided to move the ceremonies back to Downtown Los Angeles, this time to the [[Dorothy_Chandler_Pavilion|Dorothy Chandler Pavilion]] at the [[Los_Angeles_Music_Center|Los Angeles County Music Center]].
sentence_217: In the late 1990s and early 2000s, the ceremony returned to the Shrine.
sentence_218: In 2002, Hollywood's [[Dolby_Theatre|Dolby Theatre]] (previously known as the Kodak Theatre) became the presentation's current venue.
sentence_219: In the first year of the awards, the Best Directing award was split into two categories (Drama and Comedy).
sentence_220: At times, the Best Original Score award has also been split into separate categories (Drama and Comedy/Musical).
sentence_221: From the 1930s through the 1960s, the Art Direction (now Production Design), Cinematography, and Costume Design awards were likewise split into two categories (black-and-white films and color films).
sentence_222: Prior to 2012, the Production Design award was called Art Direction, while the Makeup and Hairstyling award was called Makeup.
sentence_223: In August 2018, the Academy announced that several categories would not be televised live, but rather be recorded during commercial breaks and aired later in the ceremony.
sentence_224: Following dissent from Academy members, they announced that they would indeed air all 24 categories live.
sentence_225: This followed a number of proposals (among them, the introduction of a Popular Film category) that the Academy had announced but did not implement.
sentence_226: The Board of Governors meets each year and considers new award categories.
sentence_227: To date, the following categories have been proposed:

list.value: [[Academy_Award_for_Outstanding_Achievement_in_Popular_Film|Best Popular Film]]: proposed in 2018 for presentation at the 2019 ceremony; postponed until the 2020 ceremony at the earliest
Best Stunt Coordination: rejected every year from 1991 to 2012

sentence_228: The Special Academy Awards are voted on by special committees, rather than by the Academy membership as a whole.
sentence_229: They are not always presented on an annual basis.
sentence_230: For a list of all nine awards, see [[#Other_awards_presented_by_the_Academy|§ Other awards presented by the Academy]].

list.value: Academy Scientific and Technical Award (three different awards): since 1931
Academy Special Achievement Award: from 1972 to 1995, and again for 2017

sentence_231: Due to the positive exposure and prestige of the Academy Awards, many studios spend millions of dollars and hire publicists specifically to promote their films during what is typically called the "[[Oscar_season|Oscar season]]".
sentence_232: This has generated accusations of the Academy Awards being influenced more by marketing than by quality.
sentence_233: [[William_Friedkin|William Friedkin]], an Academy Award-winning film director and former producer of the ceremony, expressed this sentiment at a conference in New York in 2009, describing it as "the greatest promotion scheme that any industry ever devised for itself".
sentence_234: Tim Dirks, editor of [[American_Movie_Classics|AMC's]] [[Filmsite.org|filmsite.org]], has written of the Academy Awards:
sentence_235: A recent technique that has been claimed to be used during the Oscar season is the whisper campaign.
sentence_236: These campaigns are intended to spread negative perceptions of other movies nominated and are believed to be perpetrated by those that were involved in creating the movie.
sentence_237: Examples of whisper campaigns include the allegations against [[Zero_Dark_Thirty|Zero Dark Thirty]] suggesting that it justifies torture and the claim that [[Lincoln_(film)|Lincoln]] distorts history.
sentence_238: Further information: [[Oscar_bait|Oscar bait]]
sentence_239: Typical criticism of the Academy Awards for Best Picture is that among the winners and nominees there is an over-representation of romantic historical epics, biographical dramas, romantic dramedies and family melodramas, most of which are released in the U.S. the last three months of the calendar year.
sentence_240: The Oscars have been infamously known for selecting specific genres of movies to be awarded.
sentence_241: The term '[[Oscar_bait|Oscar bait]]' was coined to describe such movies.
sentence_242: This has led, at times, to more specific criticisms that the Academy is disconnected from the audience, e.g., by favoring 'Oscar bait' over audience favorites, or favoring historical melodramas over critically acclaimed movies that depict current life issues.

section_26.value: Allegations of a lack of diversity

sentence_243: The Academy Awards have long received criticism over its lack of diversity among the nominees.
sentence_244: This criticism is based on the statistics from every Academy Awards since 1929, which shows us that only 6.4% of academy award nominees have been non-white and since 1991, 11.2% of nominees have been non-white, with the rate of winners being even more polarizing.
sentence_245: More white actresses have won Oscars for [[Examples_of_yellowface|yellowface]] portrayals of Asian characters than actual Asian actresses.
sentence_246: The [[88th_Academy_Awards|88th awards ceremony]] became the target of a boycott, popularized on social media with the [[Hashtag|hashtag]] #OscarsSoWhite, based on critics' perception that its all-white acting nominee list reflected bias.
sentence_247: In response, the Academy initiated "historic" changes in membership by the year 2020.
sentence_248: Acting prizes in certain years have been criticized for not recognizing superior performances so much as being awarded for personal popularity, to make up for a "snub" for a work that proved in time to be more popular or renowned than the one actually awarded, or presented as a "career honor" to recognize a distinguished nominee's entire body of work.
sentence_249: Following the [[91st_Academy_Awards|91st Academy Awards]] in February 2019 in which the [[Netflix|Netflix]]-broadcast film [[Roma_(2018_film)|Roma]] had been nominated for ten awards including the Best Picture category, Steven Spielberg and other members of the Academy discussed changing the requirements through the Board of Governors for films as to exclude those from Netflix and other media streaming services.
sentence_250: Spielberg had been concerned that Netflix as a movie production and distribution studio could spend much more than typical Oscar-winning films and have much wider and earlier distribution than other Best Picture-nominated films, while still being able to meet the minimal theatrical-run status to qualify for an Oscar.
sentence_251: The [[United_States_Department_of_Justice|United States Department of Justice]], having heard of this potential rule change, wrote a letter to the Academy in March 2019, cautioning them that placing additional restrictions on films that originate from streaming media services without proper justification could raise anti-trust concerns against the Academy.
sentence_252: Following its April 2019 board meeting, the Academy Board of Governors agreed to retain the current rules that allow for streaming media films to be eligible for Oscars as long as they enjoy limited theatrical runs.
sentence_253: Some winners critical of the Academy Awards have boycotted the ceremonies and refused to accept their Oscars.
sentence_254: The first to do so was screenwriter [[Dudley_Nichols|Dudley Nichols]] (Best Writing in 1935 for [[The_Informer_(1935_film)|The Informer]]).
sentence_255: Nichols boycotted the [[8th_Academy_Awards|8th Academy Awards]] ceremony because of conflicts between the Academy and the Writers' Guild.
sentence_256: Nichols eventually accepted the 1935 award three years later, at the 1938 ceremony.
sentence_257: Nichols was nominated for three further Academy Awards during his career.
sentence_258: George C. Scott became the second person to refuse his award (Best Actor in 1970 for [[Patton_(film)|Patton]]) at the 43rd Academy Awards ceremony.
sentence_259: Scott described it as a "meat parade", saying, "I don't want any part of it."
sentence_260: The third person to refuse the award was [[Marlon_Brando|Marlon Brando]], who refused his award (Best Actor for 1972's [[The_Godfather|The Godfather]]), citing the film industry's discrimination and mistreatment of [[Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas|Native Americans]].
sentence_261: At the [[45th_Academy_Awards|45th Academy Awards]] ceremony, Brando sent actress and [[Civil_rights_activist|civil rights activist]] [[Sacheen_Littlefeather|Sacheen Littlefeather]] to read a 15-page speech, detailing his criticisms, which was [[Booing|booed]] by the audience.
sentence_262: At the [[89th_Academy_Awards|89th Academy Awards]] ceremony, [[Warren_Beatty|Warren Beatty]] and [[Faye_Dunaway|Faye Dunaway]] mistakenly announced [[La_La_Land_(film)|La La Land]] as the recipient of the Best Picture award, instead of [[Moonlight_(2016_film)|Moonlight]], the actual winner.
sentence_263: Beatty had been given the wrong envelope and after hesitating during the announcement, handed the envelope to Dunaway, which listed [[Emma_Stone|Emma Stone]] as Best Actress for La La Land and led to the confusion.
sentence_264: The proper winner was announced after the acceptance speeches by La La Land producers [[Fred_Berger_(producer)|Fred Berger]], [[Jordan_Horowitz|Jordan Horowitz]] and [[Marc_Platt_(producer)|Marc Platt]].
sentence_265: The [[90th_Academy_Awards|following year]], Beatty and Dunaway were invited back as presenters of the Best Picture award, which they accomplished without error.

list.value: [[Zootopia|Zootopia]]: On March 21, 2017, a copyright infringement lawsuit was filed against Disney by Esplanade Productions, a company owned by [[Gary_Goldman_(screenwriter)|Gary L. Goldman]], co-screenwriter of [[Total_Recall_(1990_film)|Total Recall]]. The lawsuit claims that Goldman (in 2000 and 2009) pitched a concept to Disney for a live-action film titled Looney, which was about a socially awkward animator who creates a self-inspired TV cartoon called Zootopia. Disney twice rejected the pitch, but Goldman accused the company of copying the name, themes, settings and character tropes. Filed with the lawsuit was a graphic of early concept artwork of characters that are claimed to appear similar to major characters from the film, including Nick Wilde, Judy Hopps, Flash and Chief Bogo. A Disney spokesperson described the lawsuit as being "ridden with patently false allegations." U.S. District Judge Michael W. Fitzgerald dismissed the infringement claims on November 8, 2017.

[[The_Shape_of_Water|The Shape of Water]]: In February 2018, the estate of [[Paul_Zindel|Paul Zindel]] initiated a lawsuit in [[United_States_District_Court_for_the_Central_District_of_California|United States District Court for the Central District of California]] against director Guillermo del Toro and associate producer Daniel Kraus, alleging that The Shape of Water "brazenly copies the story, elements, characters, and themes" of Zindel's 1969 work [[Let_Me_Hear_You_Whisper_(play)|Let Me Hear You Whisper]], which depicts a cleaning lady bonding with a dolphin and attempting to rescue it from a secret research laboratory's nefarious uses. In July 2018, Judge Percy Anderson dismissed the suit.

[[Parasite_(2019_film)|Parasite]]: On February 6, 2020, Indian film producer P. L. Thenappan threatened to take legal action against the makers of Parasite for "story theft" against his 1999 Tamil film [[Minsara_Kanna|Minsara Kanna]]. Thenappan and his lawyer had sent a letter seeking an explanation to Bong Joon-ho and the production company that made Parasite. Easwar Kuppusamy, a Madras High Court advocate who is appearing for Thenappan, said, "They can't deny that they have lifted the basic plot [of Minsara Kanna]. There are several films which have similar ideas, but an entire family going to a rich family's house and deceiving them is Minsara Kanna's plot. The only difference is that Parasite doesn't belong to the romantic genre." Some Tamil netizens agreed that the plot of the film is similar to Minsara Kanna.

sentence_266: Nine films have been disqualified before an official award ceremony because they violated the regulations:

list.value: [[The_Circus_(1928_film)|The Circus]] (1928) – The film was voluntarily removed by the Academy from competitive categories, to award [[Charlie_Chaplin|Charlie Chaplin]] a special award.
[[Hondo_(film)|Hondo]] (1953) – Removed from the Best Story ballot after letters from the producer and nominee questioned its inclusion in the category.
[[High_Society_(1955_film)|High Society]] (1955) – Withdrawn from screenwriting ballot after being mistaken for the [[High_Society_(1956_film)|1956 movie]] of the same title.

[[The_Godfather|The Godfather]] (1972) – Initially nominated for eleven awards, its nomination for Best Original Score was revoked after it was discovered that its main theme was very similar to music that [[Nino_Rota|the score's composer]] had written for an earlier film. None of its other nominations were revoked, and it received three Oscars, including Best Picture.

[[A_Place_in_the_World_(film)|A Place in the World]] (1992) – Removed from the Best Foreign Language Film ballot after it was discovered that the country who submitted the film exercised insufficient artistic control.
[[Tuba_Atlantic|Tuba Atlantic]] (2012) – Removed from the Best Live Action Short Film ballot when it was discovered that the film aired on television before its theatrical release.

[[Alone_Yet_Not_Alone|Alone Yet Not Alone]] (2014) – The film's title song, "Alone Yet Not Alone", was removed from the Best Original Song ballot after Bruce Broughton was found to have improperly contacted other members of the academy's musical branch; this was the first time that a film was removed from a ballot for ethical reasons.

sentence_267: One film was disqualified after winning the award, and had the winner return the Oscar:

list.value: [[Young_Americans_(1967_film)|Young Americans]] (1969) – Initially won the award for Best Documentary Feature, but was later revoked after it was revealed that it had opened theatrically prior to the eligibility period.

sentence_268: The following events are closely associated with the annual Academy Awards:

list.value: The 25th [[Independent_Spirit_Awards|Independent Spirit Awards]] (2010), usually held in [[Santa_Monica,_California|Santa Monica]], California the Saturday before the Oscars, marked the first time it was moved to a Friday and a change of venue to [[L.A._Live|L.A. Live]]

The annual "Night Before", traditionally held at [[The_Beverly_Hills_Hotel|the Beverly Hills Hotel]], begun in 2002 and generally known as the party of the season, benefits the Motion Picture & Television Fund, which operates a retirement home for SAG actors in the [[San_Fernando_Valley|San Fernando Valley]]
[[Elton_John_AIDS_Foundation_Academy_Award_Party|Elton John AIDS Foundation Academy Award Party]] airs the awards live at the nearby [[Pacific_Design_Center|Pacific Design Center]]
The Governors Ball is the Academy's official after-party, including dinner (until 2011), and is adjacent to the awards-presentation venue
The [[Vanity_Fair_(magazine)|Vanity Fair]] after-party, historically at the former Morton's restaurant, has been at the [[Sunset_Tower|Sunset Tower]] since 2009

sentence_269: It has become a tradition to give out gift bags to the presenters and performers at the Oscars.
sentence_270: In recent years, these gifts have also been extended to award nominees and winners.
sentence_271: The value of each of these gift bags can reach into the tens of thousands of dollars.
sentence_272: In 2014, the value was reported to be as high as US$80,000.
sentence_273: The value has risen to the point where the U.S. [[Internal_Revenue_Service|Internal Revenue Service]] issued a statement regarding the gifts and their taxable status.
sentence_274: Oscar gift bags have included vacation packages to Hawaii and Mexico and Japan, a private dinner party for the recipient and friends at a restaurant, [[Videotelephony|videophones]], a four-night stay at a hotel, watches, bracelets, spa treatments, bottles of vodka, maple salad dressing, weight-loss gummie candy and up to $25,000 worth of cosmetic treatments and rejuvenation procedures such as lip fillers and chemical peels from New York City facial plastic surgeon Konstantin Vasyukevich.
sentence_275: Some of the gifts have even had a "risque" element to them; in 2014, the adult products retailer [[Adam_&_Eve_(company)|Adam & Eve]] had a "Secret Room Gifting Suite".
sentence_276: Celebrities visiting the gifting suite included [[Judith_Hoag|Judith Hoag]], Carolyn Hennesy, [[Kate_Linder|Kate Linder]], [[Chris_Mulkey|Chris Mulkey]], [[Jim_O'Heir|Jim O'Heir]], and [[John_Salley|John Salley]].
sentence_277: From 2006 onwards, results are Live+SD; all previous years are live viewing.
sentence_278: The term "Oscar" is a registered trademark of the AMPAS; however, in the Italian language, it is used [[Generic_trademark|generically]] to refer to any award or award ceremony, regardless of which field.

title: Aarau
sentence_0: Not to be confused with [[Arau|Arau]], royal capital of [[Perlis|Perlis]], [[Malaysia|Malaysia]].
