sentence_1: Aarau (German: [[Standard_German|[ˈaːraʊ]], Swiss German: [[Alemannic_German|[ˈɑːræu̯]]) is a [[List_of_towns_in_Switzerland|town]], a [[Municipalities_of_Switzerland|municipality]], and the capital of the northern Swiss [[Cantons_of_Switzerland|canton]] of [[Aargau|Aargau]].
sentence_2: The [[List_of_towns_in_Switzerland|town]] is also the capital of the district of [[Aarau_(district)|Aarau]].
sentence_3: It is German-speaking and predominantly [[Protestant|Protestant]].
sentence_4: Aarau is situated on the Swiss plateau, in the valley of the [[Aare|Aare]], on the river's right bank, and at the southern foot of the Jura Mountains, and is west of [[Zürich|Zürich]], and 65 kilometres (40 mi) northeast of [[Bern|Bern]].
sentence_5: The municipality borders directly on the [[Canton_of_Solothurn|canton of Solothurn]] to the west.
sentence_6: It is the largest town in Aargau.
sentence_7: At the beginning of 2010 [[Rohr,_Aargau|Rohr]] became a district of Aarau.
sentence_8: The official language of Aarau is (the Swiss variety of Standard) [[Swiss_Standard_German|German]], but the main spoken language is the local variant of the Alemannic [[Swiss_German_(linguistics)|Swiss German]] dialect.
sentence_9: The old city of Aarau is situated on a rocky outcrop at a narrowing of the Aare river valley, at the southern foot of the Jura mountains.
sentence_10: Newer districts of the city lie to the south and east of the outcrop, as well as higher up the mountain, and in the valley on both sides of the Aare.
sentence_11: The neighboring municipalities are [[Küttigen|Küttigen]] to the north and [[Buchs,_Aargau|Buchs]] to the east, [[Suhr,_Aargau|Suhr]] to the south-east, [[Unterentfelden|Unterentfelden]] to the south, and [[Eppenberg-Wöschnau|Eppenberg-Wöschnau]] and [[Erlinsbach,_Aargau|Erlinsbach]] to the west.
sentence_12: Aarau and the nearby neighboring municipalities have grown together and now form an interconnected agglomeration.
sentence_13: The only exception is Unterentfelden whose settlements are divided from Aarau by the extensive forests of Gönhard and Zelgli.
sentence_14: Approximately nine-tenths of the city is south of the Aare, and one tenth is to the north.
sentence_15: It has an area, as of 2006, of 8.9 km (3.4 sq mi).
sentence_16: Of this area, 6.3% is used for agricultural purposes, while 34% is forested.
sentence_17: Of the rest of the land, 55.2% is settled (buildings or roads) and the remainder (4.5%) is non-productive (rivers or lakes).
sentence_18: The lowest elevation, 365 meters (1,198 ft), is found at the banks of the Aar, and the highest elevation, at 471 meters (1,545 ft), is the Hungerberg on the border with Küttigen.
sentence_19: A few artifacts from the [[Neolithic|Neolithic]] period were found in Aarau.
sentence_20: Near the location of the present train station, the ruins of a settlement from the [[Bronze_Age|Bronze Age]] (about 1000 BC) have been excavated.
sentence_21: The Roman road between Salodurum ([[Solothurn|Solothurn]]) and [[Vindonissa|Vindonissa]] passed through the area, along the route now covered by the Bahnhofstrasse.
sentence_22: In 1976 divers in the Aare found part of a seven-meter wide wooden bridge from the late Roman times.
sentence_23: Aarau was founded around AD 1240 by the counts of [[House_of_Kyburg|Kyburg]].
sentence_24: Aarau is first mentioned in 1248 as Arowe.
sentence_25: Around 1250 it was mentioned as Arowa.
sentence_26: However the first mention of a city sized settlement was in 1256.
sentence_27: The town was ruled from the "Rore" tower, which has been incorporated into the modern city hall.
sentence_28: In 1273 the counts of Kyburg died out.
sentence_29: Agnes of Kyburg, who had no male relations, sold the family's lands to King [[Rudolf_I|Rudolf I]] von [[Habsburg|Habsburg]].
sentence_30: He granted Aarau its city rights in 1283.
sentence_31: In the 14th century the city was expanded in two stages, and a second defensive wall was constructed.
sentence_32: A deep ditch separated the city from its "suburb;" its location is today marked by a wide street named "Graben" (meaning Ditch).
sentence_33: In 1415 Bern invaded lower Aargau with the help of Solothurn.
sentence_34: Aarau capitulated after a short resistance, and was forced to swear allegiance to the new rulers.
sentence_35: In the 16th century, the rights of the lower classes were abolished.
sentence_36: In March 1528 the citizens of Aarau allowed the introduction of Protestantism at the urging of the Bernese.
sentence_37: A growth in population during the 16th Century led to taller buildings and denser construction methods.
sentence_38: Early forms of industry developed at this time; however, unlike in other cities, no guilds were formed in Aarau.
sentence_39: On 11 August 1712, the Peace of Aarau was signed into effect.
sentence_40: This granted each [[Cantons_of_Switzerland|canton]] the right to choose their own religion thereby ending [[Catholicism|Catholicism]]'s control.
sentence_41: Starting in the early 18th century, the textile industry was established in Aarau.
sentence_42: German immigration contributed to the city's favorable conditions, in that they introduced the cotton and silk factories.
sentence_43: These highly educated immigrants were also responsible for educational reform and the [[Age_of_Enlightenment|enlightened]], revolutionary spirit that developed in Aarau.
sentence_44: On 27 December 1797, the last [[Tagsatzung|Tagsatzung]] of the Old Swiss Confederacy was held in Aarau.
sentence_45: Two weeks later a French envoy continued to foment the revolutionary opinions of the city.
sentence_46: The contrast between a high level of education and a low level of political rights was particularly great in Aarau, and the city refused to send troops to defend the Bernese border.
sentence_47: By Mid-March 1798 Aarau was occupied by French troops.
sentence_48: On 22 March 1798 Aarau was declared the capital of the [[Helvetic_Republic|Helvetic Republic]].
sentence_49: It is therefore the first capital of a unified Switzerland.
sentence_50: Parliament met in the city hall.
sentence_51: On 20 September, the capital was moved to [[Lucerne|Lucerne]].
sentence_52: In 1803, [[Napoleon_I_of_France|Napoleon]] ordered the fusion of the cantons of Aargau, Baden and Fricktal.
sentence_53: Aarau was declared the capital of the new, enlarged canton of Aargau.
sentence_54: In 1820 the city wall was torn down, with the exception of the individual towers and gates, and the defensive ditches were filled in.
sentence_55: The wooden bridge, dating from the Middle Ages, across the Aare was destroyed by floods three times in thirty years, and was replaced with a steel suspension bridge in 1851.
sentence_56: This was replaced by a concrete bridge in 1952.
sentence_57: The city was linked up to the [[Swiss_Central_Railway|Swiss Central Railway]] in 1856.
sentence_58: The textile industry in Aarau broke down in about 1850 because of the protectionist tariff policies of neighboring states.
sentence_59: Other industries had developed by that time to replace it, including the production of [[Mathematical_instrument|mathematical instruments]], shoes and cement.
sentence_60: Beginning in 1900, numerous electrical enterprises developed.
sentence_61: By the 1960s, more citizens worked in service industries or for the canton-level government than in manufacturing.
sentence_62: During the 1980s many of the industries left Aarau completely.
sentence_63: In 1802 the Canton School was established; it was the first non-parochial high school in Switzerland.
sentence_64: It developed a good reputation, and was home to Nobel Prize winners [[Albert_Einstein|Albert Einstein]], [[Paul_Karrer|Paul Karrer]], and [[Werner_Arber|Werner Arber]], as well as several Swiss politicians and authors.
sentence_65: The purchase of a manuscript collection in 1803 laid the foundation for what would become the Cantonal Library, which contains a Bible annotated by [[Huldrych_Zwingli|Huldrych Zwingli]], along with the manuscripts and incunabula.
sentence_66: More newspapers developed in the city, maintaining the revolutionary atmosphere of Aarau.
sentence_67: Beginning in 1820, Aarau has been a refuge for political refugees.
sentence_68: The urban educational and cultural opportunities of Aarau were extended through numerous new institutions.
sentence_69: A Theatre and Concert Hall was constructed in 1883, which was renovated and expanded in 1995–96.
sentence_70: The Aargau Nature Museum opened in 1922.
sentence_71: A former cloth warehouse was converted into a small theatre in 1974, and the alternative culture center KIFF (Culture in the fodder factory) was established in a former animal fodder factory.
sentence_72: The earliest use of the place name was in 1248 (in the form Arowe), and probably referred to the settlement in the area before the founding of the city.
sentence_73: It comes, along with the name of the River Aare (which was called Arula, Arola, and Araris in early times), from the German word Au, meaning [[Floodplain|floodplain]].
sentence_74: The historic old town forms an irregular square, consisting of four parts (called Stöcke).
sentence_75: To the south lies the Laurenzenvorstadt, that is, the part of the town formerly outside the city wall.
sentence_76: One characteristic of the city is its painted [[Gable|gables]], for which Aarau is sometimes called the "City of beautiful Gables".
sentence_77: The old town, Laurenzenvorstadt, government building, cantonal library, state archive and art museum are all listed as [[Swiss_inventory_of_cultural_property_of_national_and_regional_significance|heritage sites of national significance]].
sentence_78: The buildings in the old city originate, on the whole, from building projects during the 16th century, when nearly all the Middle Age period buildings were replaced or expanded.
sentence_79: The architectural development of the city ended in the 18th century, when the city began to expand beyond its (still existing) wall.
sentence_80: Most of the buildings in the "suburb" date from this time.
sentence_81: The "Schlössli" (small Castle), Rore Tower and the upper gate tower have remained nearly unchanged since the 13th century.
sentence_82: The "Schlössli" is the oldest building in the city.
sentence_83: It was already founded at the time of the establishment of the city shortly after 1200; the exact date is not known.
sentence_84: City hall was built around Rore Tower in 1515.
sentence_85: The upper gate tower stands beside the southern gate in the city wall, along the road to Lucerne and Bern.
sentence_86: The jail has been housed in it since the Middle Ages.
sentence_87: A Carillon was installed in the tower in the middle of the 20th century, the bells for which were provided by the centuries-old bell manufacturers of Aarau.
sentence_88: The town church was built between 1471 and 1478.
sentence_89: During the [[Protestant_Reformation|Reformation]], in 1528, its twelve altars and accompanying pictures were destroyed.
sentence_90: The "Justice fountain" (Gerechtskeitbrunnen) was built in 1634, and is made of French [[Limestone|limestone]]; it includes a statue of Lady Justice made of [[Sandstone|sandstone]], hence the name.
sentence_91: It was originally in the street in front of city hall, but was moved to its present location in front of the town church in 1905 due to increased traffic.
sentence_92: As of 2007, Aarau had an unemployment rate of 2.35%.
sentence_93: As of 2005, there were 48 people employed in the [[Primary_sector_of_the_economy|primary economic sector]] and about 9 businesses involved in this sector.
sentence_94: 4,181 people are employed in the secondary sector and there are 164 businesses in this sector.
sentence_95: 20,186 people are employed in the [[Tertiary_sector_of_the_economy|tertiary sector]], with 1,461 businesses in this sector.
sentence_96: This is a total of over 24,000 jobs, since Aarau's population is about 16,000 it draws workers from many surrounding communities.
sentence_97: As of 2000 there were 8,050 total workers who lived in the municipality.
sentence_98: Of these, 4,308 or about 53.5% of the residents worked outside Aarau while 17,419 people commuted into the municipality for work.
sentence_99: There were a total of 21,161 jobs (of at least 6 hours per week) in the municipality.
sentence_100: The largest employer in Aarau is the cantonal government, the offices of which are distributed across the entire city at numerous locations.
sentence_101: One of the two head offices of the Aargauer Zeitung, Switzerland's fifth largest newspaper, is located in Aarau, as are the Tele M1 television channel studios, and several radio stations.
sentence_102: Kern & Co., founded in 1819, was an internationally known geodetic instrument manufacturer based in Aarau.
sentence_103: However, it was taken over by Wild Leitz in 1988, and was closed in 1991.
sentence_104: The small scale of Aarau causes it to continually expand the borders of its growth.
sentence_105: The urban center lies in the middle of the "Golden Triangle" between [[Zürich|Zürich]], [[Bern|Bern]], and [[Basel|Basel]], and Aarau is having increasing difficulty in maintaining the independence of its economic base from the neighboring large cities.
sentence_106: The idea of merging Aarau with its neighboring suburbs has been recently discussed in the hope of arresting the slowly progressing losses.
sentence_107: Manufacture include bells, mathematical instruments, electrical goods, cotton textiles, cutlery, chemicals, shoes, and other products.
sentence_108: Aarau is famous for the quality of their instruments, cutlery and their bells.
sentence_109: Every Saturday morning there is a vegetable market in the Graben at the edge of the Old City.
sentence_110: It is supplied with regional products.
sentence_111: In the last week of September the MAG (Market of Aarauer Tradesmen) takes place there, with regional companies selling their products.
sentence_112: The "Rüeblimärt" is held in the same place on the first Wednesday in November, which is a Carrot fair.
sentence_113: The Aarau fair is held at the ice skating rink during the Spring.
sentence_114: [[Aarau_railway_station|Aarau railway station]] is a terminus of the [[S-Bahn_Zürich|S-Bahn Zürich]] on the line [[S3_(ZVV)|S3]].
sentence_115: The town is also served with public transport provided by [[Busbetrieb_Aarau_AG|Busbetrieb Aarau AG]].
sentence_116: The population of Aarau grew continuously from 1800 until about 1960, when the city reached a peak population of 17,045, more than five times its population in 1800.
sentence_117: However, since 1960 the population has fallen by 8%.
sentence_118: There are three reasons for this population loss: firstly, since the completion of Telli (a large apartment complex), the city has not had any more considerable land developments.
sentence_119: Secondly, the number of people per household has fallen; thus, the existing dwellings do not hold as many people.
sentence_120: Thirdly, population growth was absorbed by neighboring municipalities in the regional urban area, and numerous citizens of Aarau moved into the countryside.
sentence_121: This trend might have stopped since the turn of the 21st century.
sentence_122: Existing industrial developments are being used for new purposes instead of standing empty.
sentence_123: Aarau has a population (as of 31 December 2019) of 21,773.
sentence_124: As of 2008, 19.8% of the population was made up of foreign nationals.
sentence_125: Over the last 10 years the population has grown at a rate of 1%.
sentence_126: Most of the population (as of 2000) speaks German (84.5%), with Italian being second most common ( 3.3%) and Serbo-Croatian being third ( 2.9%).
sentence_127: The age distribution, as of 2008, in Aarau is; 1,296 children or 8.1% of the population are between 0 and 9 years old and 1,334 teenagers or 8.4% are between 10 and 19.
sentence_128: Of the adult population, 2,520 people or 15.8% of the population are between 20 and 29 years old.
sentence_129: 2,518 people or 15.8% are between 30 and 39, 2,320 people or 14.6% are between 40 and 49, and 1,987 people or 12.5% are between 50 and 59.
sentence_130: The senior population distribution is 1,588 people or 10.0% of the population are between 60 and 69 years old, 1,219 people or 7.7% are between 70 and 79, there are 942 people or 5.9% who are between 80 and 89,and there are 180 people or 1.1% who are 90 and older.
sentence_131: As of 2000, there were 1,365 homes with 1 or 2 persons in the household, 3,845 homes with 3 or 4 persons in the household, and 2,119 homes with 5 or more persons in the household.
sentence_132: The average number of people per household was 1.99 individuals.
sentence_133: In 2008 there were 1,594 single family homes (or 18.4% of the total) out of a total of 8,661 homes and apartments.
sentence_134: In Aarau about 74.2% of the population (between age 25–64) have completed either non-mandatory [[Education_in_Switzerland#Secondary|upper secondary education]] or additional higher education (either university or a [[Fachhochschule|Fachhochschule]]).
sentence_135: Of the school age population (in the 2008/2009 school year), there are 861 students attending [[Education_in_Switzerland#Primary|primary school]], there are 280 students attending secondary school, there are 455 students attending [[Education_in_Switzerland#Tertiary|tertiary or university level schooling]], there are 35 students who are seeking a job after school in the municipality.
sentence_136: The [[Association_football|football]] club FC Aarau play in the Stadion Brügglifeld.
sentence_137: From 1981 until 2010 they played in the top tier of the [[Swiss_football_league_system|Swiss football league system]] when they were relegated to the [[Swiss_Challenge_League|Swiss Challenge League]].
sentence_138: In the 2013/2014 they climbed back to the highest tier only to be relegated again.
sentence_139: In the 2016/17 season they will play in the Swiss Challenge League.
sentence_140: They won the [[Swiss_Cup|Swiss Cup]] in 1985 and were three times [[List_of_Swiss_football_champions|Swiss football champions]], in 1912, in 1914 and in 1993.
sentence_141: Argovia Stars play in the [[1._Liga_(ice_hockey)|MySports League]], the third highest league of Swiss ice hockey.
sentence_142: They play their home games in the 3,000-seat KeBa Aarau Arena.
sentence_143: Aarau is home to a number of sites that are listed as Swiss [[Swiss_inventory_of_cultural_property_of_national_and_regional_significance|heritage sites of national significance]].

sentence_145: There are five government buildings on the list; the Cantonal Library, which contains many pieces important to the nation's history, and Art Gallery, the old Cantonal School, the Legislature, the Cantonal Administration building, and the archives.
sentence_146: Three gardens or parks are on the list; Garten Schmidlin, Naturama Aargau and the Schlossgarten.
sentence_147: The remaining four buildings on the list are; the former Rickenbach Factory, the Crematorium, the Haus zum Erker at Rathausgasse 10 and the Restaurant Zunftstube at Pelzgasse.

sentence_149: There is also the Trade Museum which contain stained glass windows from Muri Convent and paintings.
sentence_150: Each May, Aarau plays host to the annual attracting the world's top Jazz musicians.
sentence_151: From the 2000 census, 4,473 or 28.9% are [[Roman_Catholic|Roman Catholic]], while 6,738 or 43.6% belonged to the [[Swiss_Reformed_Church|Swiss Reformed Church]].
sentence_152: Of the rest of the population, there are 51 individuals (or about 0.33% of the population) who belong to the [[Christian_Catholic_Church_of_Switzerland|Christian Catholic]] i.e. Old Catholic faith.
sentence_153: In place of a town meeting, a town assembly (Einwohnerrat) of 50 members is elected by the citizens, and follows the policy of [[Proportional_representation|proportional representation]].
sentence_154: It is responsible for approving tax levels, preparing the annual account, and the business report.
sentence_155: In addition, it can issue regulations.

sentence_158: At the district level, some elements of the government remain a direct democracy.
sentence_159: There are optional and obligatory referendums, and the population retains the right to establish an initiative.
sentence_160: The executive authority is the town council (Stadtrat).
sentence_161: The term of office is four years, and its members are elected by a [[Plurality_voting_system|plurality voting system]].
sentence_162: It leads and represents the municipality.
sentence_163: It carries out the resolutions of the assembly, and those requested by the canton and national level governments.

sentence_166: The next three most popular parties were the SVP (22.1%), the FDP (17.5%) and the Green Party (11.8%).

title: Arsenal F.C.
sentence_0: This article is about the men's football club based in England.
sentence_1: For the women's team, see [[Arsenal_W.F.C.|Arsenal W.F.C.]]
sentence_2: For other teams called Arsenal, see [[Arsenal_(disambiguation)#Association_football|Arsenal (disambiguation) § Association football]].
sentence_3: Arsenal Football Club is a professional [[Association_football|football]] club based in [[London_Borough_of_Islington|Islington]], [[London|London]], England, that plays in the [[Premier_League|Premier League]], the top flight of [[English_football_league_system|English football]].
sentence_4: The club [[List_of_football_clubs_in_England_by_competitive_honours_won|has won]] 13 [[List_of_English_football_champions#Total_titles_won|league titles]] (including one [[The_Invincibles_(football)#Arsenal|unbeaten]] title), a record 14 [[FA_Cup|FA Cups]], two [[EFL_Cup|League Cups]], 16 [[FA_Community_Shield|FA Community Shields]], the [[Football_League_Centenary_Trophy|League Centenary Trophy]], one [[UEFA_Cup_Winners'_Cup|European Cup Winners' Cup]], and one [[Inter-Cities_Fairs_Cup|Inter-Cities Fairs Cup]].
sentence_5: Arsenal was the first club from the South of England to join [[English_Football_League|The Football League]], in 1893, and they reached the [[Football_League_First_Division|First Division]] in 1904.
sentence_6: Relegated only once, in 1913, they continue the longest streak in the top division, and have won the second-most top-flight matches in English football history.
sentence_7: In the 1930s, Arsenal won five League Championships and two FA Cups, and another FA Cup and two Championships after the war.
sentence_8: In [[1970–71_Arsenal_F.C._season|1970–71]], they won their first [[Double_(association_football)#England|League and FA Cup Double]].
sentence_9: Between 1989 and 2005, they won five League titles and five FA Cups, including two more Doubles.
sentence_10: They completed the 20th century with the highest average league position.
sentence_11: [[Herbert_Chapman|Herbert Chapman]], who changed the fortunes of Arsenal forever, won the club its first silverware, and his legacy led the club to dominate the 1930s decade; Chapman, however, died prematurely of [[Pneumonia|pneumonia]] in 1934.
sentence_12: He helped introduce the [[Formation_(association_football)#WM|WM formation]], [[Floodlight#Association_football|floodlights]], and [[Squad_number_(association_football)#First_use_of_numbers|shirt numbers]]; he also added the white sleeves and brighter red to the club's jersey.
sentence_13: [[Arsène_Wenger|Arsène Wenger]] was the longest-serving manager and won the most trophies.
sentence_14: He won [[List_of_FA_Cup_winning_managers|a record]] seven FA Cups, and his title-winning team set an English record for the longest top-flight unbeaten league run at 49 games between 2003 and 2004, receiving the nickname [[The_Invincibles_(football)|The Invincibles]].
sentence_15: In 1886, [[Royal_Arsenal|Woolwich munitions]] workers founded the club as Dial Square.
sentence_16: In 1913, the club crossed the city to [[Arsenal_Stadium|Arsenal Stadium]] in Highbury, becoming close neighbours of [[Tottenham_Hotspur_F.C.|Tottenham Hotspur]], and creating the [[North_London_derby|North London derby]].
sentence_17: In 2006, they moved to the nearby [[Emirates_Stadium|Emirates Stadium]].
sentence_18: In terms of revenue, Arsenal is the [[Deloitte_Football_Money_League|ninth highest-earning]] football club in the world, earned €487.6m in [[2016–17_Arsenal_F.C._season|2016–17]] season.
sentence_19: Based on social media activity from 2014 to 2015, Arsenal's fanbase is the fifth largest in the world.
sentence_20: In 2018, [[Forbes'_list_of_the_most_valuable_football_clubs|Forbes estimated]] the club was the third most valuable in England, being worth $2.24 billion.
sentence_21: The long-standing [[Latin|Latin]] motto of the club is "Victoria Concordia Crescit" ("Victory Through Harmony").
sentence_22: Further information: [[History_of_Arsenal_F.C._(1886–1966)|History of Arsenal F.C. (1886–1966)]] and [[History_of_Arsenal_F.C._(1966–present)|History of Arsenal F.C. (1966–present)]]
sentence_23: In October 1886, Scotsman [[David_Danskin|David Danskin]] and his fellow 15 munitions workers in [[Woolwich|Woolwich]], Kent, now in South East London, formed Arsenal as Dial Square, with each member contributing sixpence and Danskin adding another three shillings to help form the club.
sentence_24: Named after the heart of the [[Royal_Arsenal|Royal Arsenal]] complex, they took the name of the whole complex a month later.
sentence_25: Royal Arsenal F.C.'s first home was [[Plumstead_Common|Plumstead Common]], though they spent most of their time in South East London playing on the other side of [[Plumstead|Plumstead]], at the [[Manor_Ground_(Plumstead)|Manor Ground]].
sentence_26: Royal Arsenal first trophies they won was the [[Kent_Senior_Cup|Kent Senior Cup]] and [[London_Charity_Cup|London Charity Cup]] in [[1889–90_in_English_football|1889–90]] and the [[London_Senior_Cup|London Senior Cup]] in [[1890–91_in_English_football|1890–91]] these were the only football association trophies Arsenal won during their time in South East London.
sentence_27: In 1891, Royal Arsenal became the first London club to turn professional.
sentence_28: Royal Arsenal renamed themselves for a second time upon becoming a limited liability company in 1893.
sentence_29: They registered their new name, Woolwich Arsenal, with [[English_Football_League|The Football League]] when the club ascended later that year.
sentence_30: Woolwich Arsenal was the first southern member of The Football League, starting out in the [[Football_League_Second_Division|Second Division]] and winning promotion to the [[Football_League_First_Division|First Division]] in 1904.
sentence_31: Falling attendances, due to financial difficulties among the munitions workers and the arrival of more accessible football clubs elsewhere in the city, led the club close to bankruptcy by 1910.
sentence_32: Businessmen [[Henry_Norris_(businessman)|Henry Norris]] and William Hall became involved in the club, and sought to move them elsewhere.
sentence_33: In 1913, soon after relegation back to the Second Division, Woolwich Arsenal moved to the new [[Arsenal_Stadium|Arsenal Stadium]] in Highbury, North London.
sentence_34: This saw their third change of name: the following year, they reduced Woolwich Arsenal to simply The Arsenal.
sentence_35: In 1919, The Football League voted to promote The Arsenal, instead of relegated local rivals [[Tottenham_Hotspur_F.C.|Tottenham Hotspur]], into the [[1919–20_Football_League|newly enlarged]] First Division, despite only listing the club sixth in the Second Division's last pre-war season of [[1914–15_Football_League#Second_Division|1914–15]].
sentence_36: Some books have speculated that the club won this election to division one by dubious means.
sentence_37: Later that year, The Arsenal started dropping "The" in official documents, gradually shifting its name for the final time towards Arsenal, as it is generally known today.
sentence_38: With a new home and First Division football, attendances were more than double those at the Manor Ground, and Arsenal's budget grew rapidly.
sentence_39: Their location and record-breaking salary offer lured star [[Huddersfield_Town_A.F.C.|Huddersfield Town]] manager [[Herbert_Chapman|Herbert Chapman]] in 1925.
sentence_40: Over the next five years, Chapman built a new Arsenal.
sentence_41: He appointed enduring new trainer [[Tom_Whittaker_(footballer)|Tom Whittaker]], implemented [[Charlie_Buchan|Charlie Buchan]]'s new twist on the nascent [[Formation_(association_football)#WM|WM formation]], captured young players like Cliff Bastin and [[Eddie_Hapgood|Eddie Hapgood]], and lavished Highbury's income on stars like [[David_Jack_(footballer)|David Jack]] and [[Alex_James_(footballer)|Alex James]].
sentence_42: With record-breaking spending and gate receipts, Arsenal quickly became known as the [[Bank_of_England_club|Bank of England club]].
sentence_43: Transformed, Chapman's Arsenal claimed their first national trophy, the [[FA_Cup|FA Cup]], in [[1930_FA_Cup_Final|1930]].
sentence_44: Two League Championships followed, in [[1930–31_Football_League|1930–31]] and [[1932–33_Football_League|1932–33]].
sentence_45: Chapman also presided over multiple off the pitch changes: white sleeves and shirt numbers were added to the kit; [[Arsenal_tube_station|a Tube station]] was named after the club; and the first of two opulent, [[Art_Deco|Art Deco]] stands was completed, with some of the first floodlights in English football.
sentence_46: Suddenly, in the middle of the [[1933–34_in_English_football|1933–34]] season, Chapman died of [[Pneumonia|pneumonia]].
sentence_47: His work was left to [[Joe_Shaw_(footballer_born_1883)|Joe Shaw]] and [[George_Allison|George Allison]], who saw out a hat-trick with the [[1933–34_Football_League|1933–34]] and [[1934–35_Football_League|1934–35]] titles, and then won the [[1935–36_FA_Cup|1936 FA Cup]] and [[1937–38_Football_League|1937–38]] title.
sentence_48: [[World_War_II|World War II]] meant The Football League was suspended for seven years, but Arsenal returned to win it in the second post-war season, [[1947–48_Football_League|1947–48]].
sentence_49: This was Tom Whittaker's first season as manager, after his promotion to succeed Allison, and the club had equalled the [[List_of_English_football_champions#List|champions of England record]].
sentence_50: They won a third FA Cup in [[1949–50_FA_Cup|1950]], and then won a record-breaking seventh championship in [[1952–53_Football_League|1952–53]].
sentence_51: However, the war had taken its toll on Arsenal.
sentence_52: The club had had more players killed than any top flight club, and debt from reconstructing the North Bank Stand bled Arsenal's resources.
sentence_53: Arsenal were not to win the League or the FA Cup for another 18 years.
sentence_54: The '53 Champions squad was old, and the club failed to attract strong enough replacements.
sentence_55: Although Arsenal were competitive during these years, their fortunes had waned; the club spent most of the 1950s and 1960s in midleague mediocrity.
sentence_56: Even former [[England_national_football_team|England]] captain [[Billy_Wright_(footballer_born_1924)|Billy Wright]] could not bring the club any success as manager, in a stint between 1962 and 1966.
sentence_57: Arsenal tentatively appointed club [[Physiotherapist|physiotherapist]] [[Bertie_Mee|Bertie Mee]] as acting manager in 1966.
sentence_58: With new assistant [[Don_Howe|Don Howe]] and new players such as [[Bob_McNab|Bob McNab]] and [[George_Graham_(footballer,_born_1944)|George Graham]], Mee led Arsenal to their first [[EFL_Cup|League Cup]] finals, in [[1967–68_Football_League_Cup|1967–68]] and [[1968–69_Football_League_Cup|1968–69]].
sentence_59: Next season saw a breakthrough: Arsenal's first competitive European trophy, the [[1969–70_Inter-Cities_Fairs_Cup|1969–70 Inter-Cities Fairs Cup]].
sentence_60: And [[1970–71_in_English_football|the season after]], an even greater triumph: Arsenal's first [[1970–71_Football_League|League]] and [[1970–71_FA_Cup|FA Cup]] [[Double_(association_football)|double]], and a new [[List_of_English_football_champions#List|champions of England record]].
sentence_61: This marked a premature high point of the decade; the Double-winning side was soon broken up and the rest of the decade was characterised by a series of near misses, starting with Arsenal finishing as FA Cup runners up in [[1971–72_FA_Cup|1972]], and First Division runners-up in [[1972–73_Football_League|1972–73]].
sentence_62: Former player [[Terry_Neill|Terry Neill]] succeeded Mee in 1976.
sentence_63: At the age of 34, he became the youngest Arsenal manager to date.
sentence_64: With new signings like [[Malcolm_Macdonald|Malcolm Macdonald]] and [[Pat_Jennings|Pat Jennings]], and a crop of talent in the side such as [[Liam_Brady|Liam Brady]] and [[Frank_Stapleton|Frank Stapleton]], the club reached a trio of FA Cup finals (1978, [[1978–79_FA_Cup|1979]] and [[1979–80_FA_Cup|1980]]), and lost the [[1980_European_Cup_Winners'_Cup_Final|1980 European Cup Winners' Cup Final]] on [[Penalty_shootout_(association_football)|penalties]].
sentence_65: The club's only trophy during this time was a last-minute 3–2 victory over [[Manchester_United_F.C.|Manchester United]] in the [[1979_FA_Cup_Final|1979 FA Cup Final]], widely regarded as a classic.
sentence_66: One of Bertie Mee's double winners, [[George_Graham_(footballer,_born_1944)|George Graham]], returned as manager in 1986, with Arsenal winning their first League Cup in [[1986–87_Football_League_Cup|1987]], Graham's first season in charge.
sentence_67: By 1988, new signings Nigel Winterburn, [[Lee_Dixon|Lee Dixon]] and [[Steve_Bould|Steve Bould]] had joined the club to complete the "famous Back Four" led by existing player [[Tony_Adams|Tony Adams]].
sentence_68: They immediately won the 1988 [[Football_League_Centenary_Trophy|Football League Centenary Trophy]], and followed it with the [[1988–89_Football_League|1988–89 Football League]] title, snatched with a last-minute goal in the [[Liverpool_0–2_Arsenal_(26_May_1989)|final game of the season]] against fellow title challengers [[Liverpool_F.C.|Liverpool]].
sentence_69: Graham's Arsenal won another title in [[1990–91_Football_League|1990–91]], losing only one match, won the [[1992–93_FA_Cup|FA Cup]] and [[1992–93_Football_League_Cup|League Cup]] double in 1993, and the [[European_Cup_Winners'_Cup|European Cup Winners' Cup]], in [[1993–94_European_Cup_Winners'_Cup|1994]].
sentence_70: Graham's reputation was tarnished when he was found to have taken kickbacks from agent [[Rune_Hauge|Rune Hauge]] for signing certain players, and he was dismissed in 1995.
sentence_71: His permanent replacement, Bruce Rioch, lasted for only one season, leaving the club after a dispute with the board of directors.
sentence_72: The club metamorphosed during the long tenure of manager [[Arsène_Wenger|Arsène Wenger]], appointed in 1996.
sentence_73: New, attacking football, an overhaul of dietary and fitness practices, and efficiency with money have defined his reign.
sentence_74: Accumulating key players from Wenger's homeland, such as [[Patrick_Vieira|Patrick Vieira]] and [[Thierry_Henry|Thierry Henry]], Arsenal won a second League and Cup double in [[1997–98_Arsenal_F.C._season|1997–98]] and a third in [[2001–02_Arsenal_F.C._season|2001–02]].
sentence_75: In addition, the club reached the final of the [[1999–2000_UEFA_Cup|1999–2000 UEFA Cup]], were victorious in the [[2002–03_FA_Cup|2003]] and [[2004–05_FA_Cup|2005]] FA Cups, and won the Premier League in 2003–04 without losing a single match, an achievement which earned the side the nickname "[[The_Invincibles_(football)|The Invincibles]]".
sentence_76: This latter feat came within a run of 49 league matches unbeaten from 7 May 2003 to 24 October 2004, a national record.
sentence_77: Arsenal finished in either first or second place in the league in eight of Wenger's first nine seasons at the club, although on no occasion were they able to retain the title.
sentence_78: The club had never progressed beyond the quarter-finals of the [[UEFA_Champions_League|Champions League]] until [[2005–06_UEFA_Champions_League|2005–06]]; in that season they became the first club from London in the competition's fifty-year history to reach [[2006_UEFA_Champions_League_Final|the final]], in which they were beaten 2–1 by [[FC_Barcelona|Barcelona]].
sentence_79: In July 2006, they moved into the [[Emirates_Stadium|Emirates Stadium]], after 93 years at Highbury.
sentence_80: Arsenal reached the final of the [[2007_Football_League_Cup_Final|2007]] and [[2011_Football_League_Cup_Final|2011]] League Cups, losing 2–1 to [[Chelsea_F.C.|Chelsea]] and [[Birmingham_City_F.C.|Birmingham City]] respectively.
sentence_81: The club had not gained a major trophy since the 2005 FA Cup until 17 May 2014 when, spearheaded by then club-record acquisition [[Mesut_Özil|Mesut Özil]], Arsenal beat [[Hull_City_A.F.C.|Hull City]] in the [[2014_FA_Cup_Final|2014 FA Cup Final]], coming back from a 2–0 deficit to win the match 3–2.
sentence_82: A year later, Arsenal appeared in the FA Cup final for the second time in a row, defeating [[Aston_Villa_F.C.|Aston Villa]] 4–0 in the [[2015_FA_Cup_Final|final]] and becoming the most successful club in the tournament's history with 12 titles, a record which Manchester United would tie the following season.
sentence_83: Arsenal later won the [[2016–17_FA_Cup|FA Cup]] for a record 13th time, defeating Chelsea 2–1 in the [[2017_FA_Cup_Final|2017 final]] and once more becoming the outright leader in terms of FA Cups won.
sentence_84: The victory also saw Wenger become the first manager in English football history to win seven FA Cups.
sentence_85: However, in that same season, Arsenal finished in the fifth position in the league, the first time they had finished outside the top four since before Wenger arrived in 1996.
sentence_86: After another unspectacular league season the following year, Wenger announced his departure from the club on 20 April 2018, after 22 years as manager.
sentence_87: His decision was met by responses of praise throughout English and world football from many pundits and former players, who also thanked him for developing them as people.
sentence_88: His final home match in charge was a 5–0 win over [[Burnley_F.C.|Burnley]] where his entrance was met to a standing ovation by supporters.
sentence_89: The final match under the Wenger era was a 1–0 away victory against Huddersfield.
sentence_90: After conducting an overhaul in the club's operating model to coincide with Wenger's departure, Basque-Spaniard [[Unai_Emery|Unai Emery]] was named as the club's new head coach on 23 May 2018.
sentence_91: He would become the club's first ever 'head coach', while also their second ever manager from outside the [[United_Kingdom|United Kingdom]].
sentence_92: In Emery's [[2018–19_Premier_League|first season]], Arsenal finished fifth in the Premier League and finished as runner-up in the [[2018–19_UEFA_Europa_League|Europa League]].
sentence_93: On 29 November 2019, Emery was sacked after a 2–1 defeat at home to [[Eintracht_Frankfurt|Eintracht Frankfurt]] in the Europa League group stages.
sentence_94: The club were on a seven-game winless run across all competitions and there was an eight-point gap to fourth place in the Premier League after 13 games.
sentence_95: Former player and assistant first team coach [[Freddie_Ljungberg|Freddie Ljungberg]] was appointed as the interim head-coach.
sentence_96: On 20 December 2019, Arsenal appointed former midfielder and club captain [[Mikel_Arteta|Mikel Arteta]] as their new head coach on a three-and-a-half-year contract.
sentence_97: He joined from Manchester City, having worked there as an assistant manager.
sentence_98: Arsenal finished the [[2019–20_Premier_League|league]] season in eighth place, their lowest finish since [[1994–95_FA_Premier_League|1994–95]], but did win their first trophy under Arteta by beating [[2020_FA_Cup_Final|Chelsea 2–1]] to earn a record-extending [[2020_FA_Cup_Final|14th FA Cup]] title.
sentence_99: Unveiled in 1888, Royal Arsenal's first [[Crest_(sports)|crest]] featured three [[Cannon|cannons]] viewed from above, pointing northwards, similar to the coat of arms of the [[Metropolitan_Borough_of_Woolwich|Metropolitan Borough of Woolwich]] (nowadays transferred to the [[Coat_of_arms_of_the_Royal_Borough_of_Greenwich|coat of arms of the Royal Borough of Greenwich]]).
sentence_100: These can sometimes be mistaken for chimneys, but the presence of a carved lion's head and a [[Cascabel_(artillery)|cascabel]] on each are clear indicators that they are cannons.
sentence_101: This was dropped after the move to Highbury in 1913, only to be reinstated in 1922, when the club adopted a crest featuring a single cannon, pointing eastwards, with the club's nickname, The Gunners, inscribed alongside it; this crest only lasted until 1925, when the cannon was reversed to point westward and its barrel slimmed down.
sentence_102: In 1949, the club unveiled a modernised crest featuring the same style of cannon below the club's name, set in [[Blackletter|blackletter]], and above the coat of arms of the [[Metropolitan_Borough_of_Islington|Metropolitan Borough of Islington]] and a scroll inscribed with the club's newly adopted Latin [[Motto|motto]], Victoria Concordia Crescit - "victory comes from harmony" – coined by the club's programme editor Harry Homer.
sentence_103: For the first time, the crest was rendered in colour, which varied slightly over the crest's lifespan, finally becoming red, gold and green.
sentence_104: Because of the numerous revisions of the crest, Arsenal were unable to [[Copyright|copyright]] it.
sentence_105: Although the club had managed to register the crest as a trademark, and had fought (and eventually won) a long legal battle with a local street trader who sold "unofficial" Arsenal merchandise, Arsenal eventually sought a more comprehensive legal protection.
sentence_106: Therefore, in 2002 they introduced a new crest featuring more modern curved lines and a simplified style, which was copyrightable.
sentence_107: The cannon once again faces east and the club's name is written in a [[Sans-serif|sans-serif]] typeface above the cannon.
sentence_108: Green was replaced by dark blue.
sentence_109: The new crest was criticised by some supporters; the Arsenal Independent Supporters' Association claimed that the club had ignored much of Arsenal's history and tradition with such a radical modern design, and that fans had not been properly consulted on the issue.
sentence_110: Until the 1960s, a badge was worn on the playing shirt only for high-profile matches such as FA Cup finals, usually in the form of a [[Monogram|monogram]] of the club's initials in red on a white background.
sentence_111: The monogram theme was developed into an [[Art_Deco|Art Deco]]-style badge on which the letters A and C framed a football rather than the letter F, the whole set within a hexagonal border.
sentence_112: This early example of a corporate logo, introduced as part of Herbert Chapman's rebranding of the club in the 1930s, was used not only on Cup Final shirts but as a design feature throughout Highbury Stadium, including above the main entrance and inlaid in the floors.
sentence_113: From 1967, a white cannon was regularly worn on the shirts, until replaced by the club crest, sometimes with the addition of the nickname "The Gunners", in the 1990s.
sentence_114: In the 2011–12 season, Arsenal celebrated their 125th anniversary.
sentence_115: The celebrations included a modified version of the current crest worn on their jerseys for the season.
sentence_116: The crest was all white, surrounded by 15 [[Oak|oak]] leaves to the right and 15 [[Laurel_wreath|laurel]] leaves to the left.
sentence_117: The oak leaves represent the 15 founding members of the club who met at the Royal Oak pub.
sentence_118: The 15 laurel leaves represent the design detail on the six pence pieces paid by the founding fathers to establish the club.
sentence_119: The laurel leaves also represent strength.
sentence_120: To complete the crest, 1886 and 2011 are shown on either sides of the motto "Forward" at the bottom of the crest.
sentence_121: For much of Arsenal's history, their home colours have been bright red shirts with white sleeves and white shorts, though this has not always been the case.
sentence_122: The choice of red is in recognition of a charitable donation from [[Nottingham_Forest_F.C.|Nottingham Forest]], soon after Arsenal's foundation in 1886.
sentence_123: Two of Dial Square's founding members, [[Fred_Beardsley|Fred Beardsley]] and [[Morris_Bates|Morris Bates]], were former Forest players who had moved to Woolwich for work.
sentence_124: As they put together the first team in the area, no kit could be found, so Beardsley and Bates wrote home for help and received a set of kit and a ball.
sentence_125: The shirt was redcurrant, a dark shade of red, and was worn with white shorts and socks with blue and white hoops.
sentence_126: In 1933, Herbert Chapman, wanting his players to be more distinctly dressed, updated the kit, adding white sleeves and changing the shade to a brighter pillar box red.
sentence_127: Two possibilities have been suggested for the origin of the white sleeves.
sentence_128: One story reports that Chapman noticed a supporter in the stands wearing a red sleeveless sweater over a white shirt; another was that he was inspired by a similar outfit worn by the cartoonist [[Tom_Webster_(cartoonist)|Tom Webster]], with whom Chapman played golf.
sentence_129: Regardless of which story is true, the red and white shirts have come to define Arsenal and the team have worn the combination ever since, aside from two seasons.
sentence_130: The first was 1966–67, when Arsenal wore all-red shirts; this proved unpopular and the white sleeves returned the following season.
sentence_131: The second was 2005–06, the last season that Arsenal played at Highbury, when the team wore commemorative redcurrant shirts similar to those worn in 1913, their first season in the stadium; the club reverted to their normal colours at the start of the next season.
sentence_132: In the 2008–09 season, Arsenal replaced the traditional all-white sleeves with red sleeves with a broad white stripe.
sentence_133: Arsenal's home colours have been the inspiration for at least three other clubs.
sentence_134: In 1909, Sparta Prague adopted a dark red kit like the one Arsenal wore at the time; in 1938, [[Hibernian_F.C.|Hibernian]] adopted the design of the Arsenal shirt sleeves in their own green and white strip.
sentence_135: In 1941, Luis Robledo, an England-schooled founder of [[Independiente_Santa_Fe|Santa Fe]] and a fan of Arsenal, selected the main colors for his newly created team.
sentence_136: In 1920, [[S.C._Braga|Sporting Clube de Braga]]'s manager returned from a game at Highbury and changed his team's green kit to a duplicate of Arsenal's red with white sleeves and shorts, giving rise to the team's nickname of Os Arsenalistas.
sentence_137: These teams still wear those designs to this day.
sentence_138: For many years Arsenal's away colours were white or navy blue.
sentence_139: However, in 1968 the FA banned navy shirts (they looked too similar to referees' black kit) so in the 1969–70 season, Arsenal introduced an away kit of yellow shirts with blue shorts.
sentence_140: This kit was worn in the 1971 FA Cup Final as Arsenal beat Liverpool to secure the double for the first time in their history.
sentence_141: The yellow and blue strip became almost as famous as their iconic red and white home kit.
sentence_142: Arsenal reached the [[1972_FA_Cup_Final|FA Cup final]] again the following year wearing the red and white home strip and were beaten by [[Leeds_United_A.F.C.|Leeds United]].
sentence_143: Arsenal then competed in three consecutive FA Cup finals between [[1978_FA_Cup_Final|1978]] and [[1980_FA_Cup_Final|1980]] wearing their "lucky" yellow and blue strip, which remained the club's away strip until the release of a green and navy away kit in 1982–83.
sentence_144: The following season, Arsenal returned to the yellow and blue scheme, albeit with a darker shade of blue than before.
sentence_145: When [[Nike,_Inc.|Nike]] took over from [[Adidas|Adidas]] as Arsenal's kit provider in 1994, Arsenal's away colours were again changed to two-tone blue shirts and shorts.
sentence_146: Since the advent of the lucrative replica kit market, the away kits have been changed regularly, with Arsenal usually releasing both away and third choice kits.
sentence_147: During this period the designs have been either all blue designs, or variations on the traditional yellow and blue, such as the metallic gold and navy strip used in the 2001–02 season, the yellow and dark grey used from 2005 to 2007, and the yellow and maroon of 2010 to 2013.
sentence_148: Until 2014, the away kit was changed every season, and the outgoing away kit became the third-choice kit if a new home kit was being introduced in the same year.
sentence_149: Since [[Puma_SE|Puma]] began manufacturing Arsenal's kits in 2014, new home, away and third kits are released every single season.
sentence_150: From the 2019–20 season Arsenal's kits will be manufactured by Adidas.
sentence_151: Before joining the Football League, Arsenal played briefly on [[Plumstead_Common|Plumstead Common]], then at the [[Manor_Ground,_Plumstead|Manor Ground]] in [[Plumstead|Plumstead]], then spent three years between 1890 and 1893 at the nearby [[Invicta_Ground|Invicta Ground]].
sentence_152: Upon joining the Football League in 1893, the club returned to the Manor Ground and installed stands and [[Terrace_(stadium)|terracing]], upgrading it from just a field.
sentence_153: Arsenal continued to play their home games there for the next twenty years (with two exceptions in the 1894–95 season), until the move to north London in 1913.
sentence_154: Widely referred to as Highbury, [[Arsenal_Stadium|Arsenal Stadium]] was the club's home from September 1913 until May 2006.
sentence_155: The original stadium was designed by the renowned football architect Archibald Leitch, and had a design common to many football grounds in the UK at the time, with a single covered stand and three open-air banks of terracing.
sentence_156: The entire stadium was given a massive overhaul in the 1930s: new [[Art_Deco|Art Deco]] West and East stands were constructed, opening in 1932 and 1936 respectively, and a roof was added to the North Bank terrace, which was bombed during the Second World War and not restored until 1954.
sentence_157: Highbury could hold more than 60,000 spectators at its peak, and had a capacity of 57,000 until the early 1990s.
sentence_158: The [[Taylor_Report|Taylor Report]] and Premier League regulations obliged Arsenal to convert Highbury to an all-seater stadium in time for the 1993–94 season, thus reducing the capacity to 38,419 seated spectators.
sentence_159: This capacity had to be reduced further during [[UEFA_Champions_League|Champions League]] matches to accommodate additional advertising boards, so much so that for two seasons, from 1998 to 2000, Arsenal played Champions League home matches at [[Wembley_Stadium_(1923)|Wembley]], which could house more than 70,000 spectators.
sentence_160: Expansion of Highbury was restricted because the East Stand had been designated as a [[Grade_II_listed|Grade II listed]] building and the other three stands were close to residential properties.
sentence_161: These limitations prevented the club from maximising matchday revenue during the 1990s and first decade of the 21st century, putting them in danger of being left behind in the football boom of that time.
sentence_162: After considering various options, in 2000 Arsenal proposed building a new 60,361-capacity stadium at Ashburton Grove, since named the [[Emirates_Stadium|Emirates Stadium]], about 500 metres south-west of Highbury.
sentence_163: The project was initially delayed by red tape and rising costs, and construction was completed in July 2006, in time for the start of the 2006–07 season.
sentence_164: The stadium was named after its sponsors, the airline company [[Emirates_(airline)|Emirates]], with whom the club signed the largest sponsorship deal in English football history, worth around £100 million.
sentence_165: Some fans referred to the ground as Ashburton Grove, or the Grove, as they did not agree with corporate sponsorship of stadium names.
sentence_166: The stadium will be officially known as Emirates Stadium until at least 2028, and the airline will be the club's shirt sponsor until at least 2024.
sentence_167: From the start of the 2010–11 season on, the stands of the stadium have been officially known as North Bank, East Stand, West Stand and Clock end.
sentence_168: Arsenal's players train at the [[Shenley_Training_Centre|Shenley Training Centre]] in Hertfordshire, a purpose-built facility which opened in 1999.
sentence_169: Before that the club used facilities on a nearby site owned by the University College of London Students' Union.
sentence_170: Until 1961 they had trained at Highbury.
sentence_171: Arsenal's [[Arsenal_F.C._Academy|Academy under-18]] teams play their home matches at Shenley, while the [[Arsenal_F.C._Reserves|reserves]] play their games at [[Meadow_Park_(Borehamwood)|Meadow Park]], which is also the home of [[Borehamwood_F.C.|Boreham Wood F.C.]] Both the [[Arsenal_F.C._Academy|Academy under-18]] & the [[Arsenal_F.C._Reserves|reserves]] occasionally play their big games at the Emirates in front of a crowd reduced to only the lower west stand.
sentence_172: Further information: Arsenal F.C. supporters and [[AFTV|AFTV]]
sentence_173: Arsenal's fanbase are referred to as "Gooners" - the name derived from the club's nickname "The Gunners".
sentence_174: Virtually all home matches sell out; in 2007–08 Arsenal had the second-highest average League attendance for an English club (60,070, which was 99.5% of available capacity), and, as of 2015, the third-highest all-time average attendance.
sentence_175: Arsenal have the seventh highest average attendance of European football clubs only behind [[Borussia_Dortmund|Borussia Dortmund]], [[FC_Barcelona|FC Barcelona]], [[Manchester_United_F.C.|Manchester United]], [[Real_Madrid_C.F.|Real Madrid]], [[FC_Bayern_Munich|Bayern Munich]], and [[FC_Schalke_04|Schalke]].
sentence_176: The club's location, adjoining wealthy areas such as [[Canonbury|Canonbury]] and [[Barnsbury|Barnsbury]], mixed areas such as [[Islington|Islington]], [[Holloway,_London|Holloway]], Highbury, and the adjacent [[London_Borough_of_Camden|London Borough of Camden]], and largely working-class areas such as [[Finsbury_Park_(district)|Finsbury Park]] and [[Stoke_Newington|Stoke Newington]], has meant that Arsenal's supporters have come from a variety of social classes.
sentence_177: Much of the Afro-Caribbean support comes from the neighbouring [[London_Borough_of_Hackney|London Borough of Hackney]] and a large portion of the South Asian Arsenal supporters commute to the stadium from [[Wembley_Park|Wembley Park]], North West of the capital.
sentence_178: There was also traditionally a large Irish community that followed Arsenal, with the nearby [[Archway,_London|Archway]] area having a particularly large community, but Irish migration to North London is much lower than in the 1960s or 1970s.
sentence_179: Like all major English football clubs, Arsenal have a number of domestic supporters' clubs, including the Arsenal Football Supporters' Club, which works closely with the club, and the Arsenal Independent Supporters' Association, which maintains a more independent line.
sentence_180: The [[Arsenal_Supporters'_Trust|Arsenal Supporters' Trust]] promotes greater participation in ownership of the club by fans.
sentence_181: The club's supporters also publish [[Fanzine|fanzines]] such as The Gooner, Gunflash and the satirical Up The Arse!.
sentence_182: In addition to the usual English [[Football_chant|football chants]], supporters sing "One-Nil to the Arsenal" (to the tune of "[[Go_West_(song)|Go West]]").
sentence_183: There have always been Arsenal supporters outside London, and since the advent of satellite television, a supporter's attachment to a football club has become less dependent on geography.
sentence_184: Consequently, Arsenal have a significant number of fans from beyond London and all over the world; in 2007, 24 UK, 37 Irish and 49 other overseas supporters clubs were affiliated with the club.
sentence_185: A 2011 report by SPORT+MARKT estimated Arsenal's global fanbase at 113 million.
sentence_186: The club's social media activity was the fifth highest in world football during the 2014–15 season.
sentence_187: Main articles: [[North_London_derby|North London derby]], [[Arsenal_F.C.–Manchester_United_F.C._rivalry|Arsenal F.C.–Manchester United F.C. rivalry]], and [[Arsenal_F.C.–Chelsea_F.C._rivalry|Arsenal F.C.–Chelsea F.C. rivalry]]
sentence_188: Arsenal's longest-running and deepest rivalry is with their nearest major neighbours, [[Tottenham_Hotspur_F.C.|Tottenham Hotspur]]; matches between the two are referred to as [[North_London_derby|North London derbies]].
sentence_189: Other rivalries within London include those with [[Chelsea_F.C.|Chelsea]], [[Fulham_F.C.|Fulham]] and [[West_Ham_United_F.C.|West Ham United]].
sentence_190: In addition, Arsenal and Manchester United developed a strong on-pitch rivalry in the late 1980s, which intensified in recent years when both clubs were competing for the Premier League title – so much so that a 2003 [[Online_poll|online poll]] by the [[Football_Fans_Census|Football Fans Census]] listed Manchester United as Arsenal's biggest rivals, followed by Tottenham and Chelsea.
sentence_191: A 2008 poll listed the Tottenham rivalry as more important.
sentence_192: The club mascot is Gunnersaurus Rex, a smiling, 7-foot-tall green dinosaur, who first appeared at a home match against Manchester City in August 1994 (or 1993).
sentence_193: He is based on a drawing by then 11-year-old Peter Lovell, whose design and another similar idea won a Junior Gunners contest; his official back story is that he hatched from an egg found during renovations at Highbury.
sentence_194: In 2019 he won a Twitter honour, the online World Cup of Football Mascots.
sentence_195: Gunnersaurus attends both men's and women's home games in addition to community activities.
sentence_196: The same person, Jerry Quy, has been inside the suit from the start; in early October 2020, as part of cost-cutting brought about by the [[COVID-19_pandemic_in_England|COVID-19 pandemic]], the club made him redundant from that and his other part-time job in supporter liaison, together with 55 full-time employees, although they later said Gunnersaurus could return after spectators were allowed back in stadiums.
sentence_197: An online fundraiser was begun for Quy, and [[Mesut_Özil|Mesut Özil]] offered to pay his salary himself as long as he remains with Arsenal.
sentence_198: Further information: [[Ownership_of_Arsenal_F.C.|Ownership of Arsenal F.C.]]
sentence_199: The largest shareholder on the Arsenal board is American sports tycoon [[Stan_Kroenke|Stan Kroenke]].
sentence_200: Kroenke first launched a bid for the club in April 2007, and faced competition for shares from Red and White Securities, which acquired its first shares off [[David_Dein|David Dein]] in August 2007.
sentence_201: Red & White Securities was co-owned by Russian billionaire Alisher Usmanov and Iranian London-based financier [[Farhad_Moshiri_(businessman)|Farhad Moshiri]], though Usmanov bought Moshiri's stake in 2016.
sentence_202: Kroenke came close to the 30% takeover threshold in November 2009, when he increased his holding to 18,594 shares (29.9%).
sentence_203: In April 2011, Kroenke achieved a full takeover by purchasing the shareholdings of Nina Bracewell-Smith and [[Danny_Fiszman|Danny Fiszman]], taking his shareholding to 62.89%.
sentence_204: As of May 2017, Kroenke owns 41,721 shares (67.05%) and Red & White Securities own 18,695 shares (30.04%).
sentence_205: In January 2018, Kroenke expanded his ownership, buying twenty-two more shares taking his total ownership to 67.09% In August 2018, Kroenke bought out Usmanov for 550 million pounds giving him more than 90% of the shares and giving him the required stake to complete the buyout of the remaining shares making him the sole owner.
sentence_206: [[Ivan_Gazidis|Ivan Gazidis]] has been the club's Chief executive since 2009.
sentence_207: Arsenal's parent company, Arsenal Holdings plc, operates as a non-quoted [[Public_limited_company|public limited company]], whose ownership is considerably different from that of other football clubs.
sentence_208: Only 62,219 shares in Arsenal have been issued, and they are not traded on a public exchange such as the [[FTSE_Group|FTSE]] or [[Alternative_Investment_Market|AIM]]; instead, they are traded relatively infrequently on the [[ICAP_(company)|ICAP]] Securities and Derivatives Exchange, a specialist market.
sentence_209: On 29 May 2017, a single share in Arsenal had a [[Mid_price|mid price]] of £18,000, which sets the club's [[Market_capitalisation|market capitalisation]] value at approximately £1,119.9m.
sentence_210: Most football clubs are not listed on an exchange, which makes direct comparisons of their values difficult.
sentence_211: Consultants Brand Finance valued the club's brand and intangible assets at $703m in 2015, and consider Arsenal an AAA global brand.
sentence_212: Business magazine [[Forbes|Forbes]] [[Forbes'_list_of_the_most_valuable_football_clubs|valued]] Arsenal as a whole at $2.238 billion (£1.69 billion) in 2018, ranked third in English football.
sentence_213: Research by the Henley Business School also ranked Arsenal second in English football, modelling the club's value at £1.118 billion in 2015.
sentence_214: Arsenal's financial results for the [[2014–15_Arsenal_F.C._season|2014–15]] season show group revenue of £344.5m, with a profit before tax of £24.7m.
sentence_215: The footballing core of the business showed a revenue of £329.3m.
sentence_216: The [[Deloitte_Football_Money_League|Deloitte Football Money League]] is a publication that homogenises and compares clubs' annual revenue.
sentence_217: They put Arsenal's footballing revenue at £331.3m (€435.5m), ranking Arsenal seventh among world football clubs.
sentence_218: Arsenal and [[Deloitte|Deloitte]] both list the match day revenue generated by the Emirates Stadium as £100.4m, more than any other football stadium in the world.
sentence_219: Arsenal have appeared in a number of media "firsts".
sentence_220: On 22 January 1927, their match at Highbury against [[Sheffield_United_F.C.|Sheffield United]] was the first English League match to be broadcast live on radio.
sentence_221: A decade later, on 16 September 1937, an exhibition match between Arsenal's first team and the reserves was the first football match in the world to be televised live.
sentence_222: Arsenal also featured in the first edition of the [[BBC|BBC]]'s [[Match_of_the_Day|Match of the Day]], which screened highlights of their match against Liverpool at [[Anfield|Anfield]] on 22 August 1964.
sentence_223: [[Sky_UK|Sky]]'s coverage of Arsenal's January 2010 match against [[Manchester_United_F.C.|Manchester United]] was the first live public broadcast of a sports event on [[3D_television|3D television]].
sentence_224: As one of the most successful teams in the country, Arsenal have often featured when football is depicted in the arts in Britain.
sentence_225: They formed the backdrop to one of the earliest football-related novels, [[The_Arsenal_Stadium_Mystery_(novel)|The Arsenal Stadium Mystery]] (1939), which was [[The_Arsenal_Stadium_Mystery|made into a film]] in the same year.
sentence_226: The story centres on a [[Friendly_match|friendly match]] between Arsenal and an amateur side, one of whose players is poisoned while playing.
sentence_227: Many Arsenal players appeared as themselves in the film and manager [[George_Allison|George Allison]] was given a speaking part.
sentence_228: The book [[Fever_Pitch|Fever Pitch]] by [[Nick_Hornby|Nick Hornby]] was an autobiographical account of Hornby's life and relationship with football and Arsenal in particular.
sentence_229: Published in 1992, it formed part of the revival and rehabilitation of football in British society during the 1990s.
sentence_230: The book was twice adapted for the cinema – the [[Fever_Pitch_(1997_film)|1997 British film]] focuses on Arsenal's 1988–89 title win, and a [[Fever_Pitch_(2005_film)|2005 American version]] features a fan of baseball's [[Boston_Red_Sox|Boston Red Sox]].
sentence_231: Arsenal have often been stereotyped as a [[Defender_(association_football)|defensive]] and "boring" side, especially during the 1970s and 1980s; many comedians, such as Eric Morecambe, made jokes about this at the team's expense.
sentence_232: The theme was repeated in the 1997 film [[The_Full_Monty|The Full Monty]], in a scene where the lead actors move in a line and raise their hands, deliberately mimicking the Arsenal defence's [[Offside_trap|offside trap]], in an attempt to co-ordinate their [[Striptease|striptease]] routine.
sentence_233: Another film reference to the club's defence comes in the film [[Plunkett_&_Macleane|Plunkett & Macleane]], in which two characters are named Dixon and Winterburn after Arsenal's long-serving full backs – the right-sided [[Lee_Dixon|Lee Dixon]] and the left-sided Nigel Winterburn.
sentence_234: In 1985, Arsenal founded a [[Corporate_social_responsibility|community scheme]], "Arsenal in the Community", which offered sporting, social inclusion, educational and charitable projects.
sentence_235: The club support a number of charitable causes directly and in 1992 established The Arsenal Charitable Trust, which by 2006 had raised more than £2 million for local causes.
sentence_236: An ex-professional and celebrity football team associated with the club also raised money by playing charity matches.
sentence_237: The club launched the Arsenal for Everyone initiative in 2008 as an annual celebration of the diversity of the Arsenal family.
sentence_238: In the 2009–10 season Arsenal announced that they had raised a record breaking £818,897 for the [[Great_Ormond_Street_Hospital_Children's_Charity|Great Ormond Street Hospital Children's Charity]].
sentence_239: The original target was £500,000.
sentence_240: [[Save_the_Children|Save the Children]] has been Arsenal global charity partner since 2011 and have worked together in numerous projects to improve safety and well-being for vulnerable children in London and abroad.
sentence_241: On 3 September 2016 The Arsenal Foundation has donated £1m to build football pitches for children in London, Indonesia, Iraq, Jordan and Somalia thanks to The Arsenal Foundation Legends Match against Milan Glorie at the Emirates Stadium.
sentence_242: On 3 June 2018, Arsenal played Real Madrid in the Corazon Classic Match 2018 at the Bernabeu, where the proceeds went to Realtoo Real Madrid Foundation projects that are aimed at the most vulnerable children.
sentence_243: In addition there will be a return meeting on 8 September 2018 at the Emirates stadium where proceeds will go towards the Arsenal foundation.
sentence_244: Further information: [[List_of_Arsenal_F.C._records_and_statistics|List of Arsenal F.C. records and statistics]]
sentence_245: Arsenal's tally of 13 League Championships is the [[List_of_English_football_champions#Total_titles_won|third highest]] in English football, after Manchester United (20) and Liverpool (19), and they were the first club [[List_of_English_football_champions#Football_League_First_Division_(1892–1992)|to reach]] a seventh and an eighth League Championship.
sentence_246: As of June 2020, they are one of seven teams, the others being Manchester United, [[Blackburn_Rovers_F.C.|Blackburn Rovers]], [[Chelsea_F.C.|Chelsea]], [[Manchester_City_F.C.|Manchester City]], [[Leicester_City_F.C.|Leicester City]] and Liverpool, to have won the Premier League since its formation in 1992.
sentence_247: They hold the highest number of FA Cup trophies, with 14.
sentence_248: The club is one of only six clubs to have won the FA Cup twice in succession, in 2002 and 2003, and 2014 and 2015.
sentence_249: Arsenal have achieved three League and FA Cup "[[Double_(association_football)#England|Doubles]]" (in 1971, 1998 and 2002), a feat only previously achieved by Manchester United (in 1994, 1996 and 1999).
sentence_250: They were the first side in English football to complete the FA Cup and League Cup double, in 1993.
sentence_251: Arsenal were also the first London club to reach the final of the UEFA Champions League, in 2006, losing the final 2–1 to [[FC_Barcelona|Barcelona]].
sentence_252: Arsenal have one of the best top-flight records in history, having finished below fourteenth only seven times.
sentence_253: They have won the second most top flight league matches in English football, and have also accumulated the second most points, whether calculated by two points per win or by the contemporary points value.
sentence_254: They have been in the top flight for the most consecutive seasons (95 as of 2020–21).
sentence_255: Arsenal also have the highest average league finishing position for the 20th century, with an average league placement of 8.5.
sentence_256: Arsenal hold the record for the longest run of unbeaten League matches (49 between May 2003 and October 2004).
sentence_257: This included all 38 matches of their title-winning [[2003–04_in_English_football|2003–04]] season, when Arsenal became only the second club to finish a top-flight campaign unbeaten, after [[Preston_North_End_F.C.|Preston North End]] (who played only 22 matches) in [[1888–89_in_English_football|1888–89]].
sentence_258: They also hold the record for the longest top flight win streak.
sentence_259: Arsenal set a Champions League record during the 2005–06 season by going ten matches without conceding a goal, beating the previous best of seven set by [[A.C._Milan|A.C.
sentence_260: Milan]].
sentence_261: They went a record total stretch of 995 minutes without letting an opponent score; the streak ended in [[2006_UEFA_Champions_League_Final|the final]], when [[Samuel_Eto'o|Samuel Eto'o]] scored a 76th-minute equaliser for Barcelona.
sentence_262: David O'Leary holds the record for Arsenal appearances, having played 722 first-team matches between 1975 and 1993.
sentence_263: Fellow [[Centre_half|centre half]] and former captain [[Tony_Adams_(footballer)|Tony Adams]] comes second, having played 669 times.
sentence_264: The record for a [[Goalkeeper_(association_football)|goalkeeper]] is held by [[David_Seaman|David Seaman]], with 564 appearances.
sentence_265: [[Thierry_Henry|Thierry Henry]] is the club's top goalscorer with 228 goals in all competitions between 1999 and 2012, having surpassed [[Ian_Wright|Ian Wright]]'s total of 185 in October 2005.
sentence_266: Wright's record had stood since September 1997, when he overtook the longstanding total of 178 goals set by winger Cliff Bastin in 1939.
sentence_267: Henry also holds the club record for goals scored in the League, with 175, a record that had been held by Bastin until February 2006.
sentence_268: Arsenal's record home attendance is 73,707, for a [[UEFA_Champions_League|UEFA Champions League]] match against [[RC_Lens|RC Lens]] on 25 November 1998 at [[Wembley_Stadium_(1923)|Wembley Stadium]], where the club formerly played home European matches because of the limits on Highbury's capacity.
sentence_269: The record attendance for an Arsenal match at Highbury is 73,295, for a 0–0 draw against [[Sunderland_A.F.C.|Sunderland]] on 9 March 1935, while that at Emirates Stadium is 60,161, for a 2–2 draw with Manchester United on 3 November 2007.

sentence_282: Main article: [[List_of_Arsenal_F.C._managers|List of Arsenal F.C. managers]]
sentence_283: The club's current manager is [[Mikel_Arteta|Mikel Arteta]].
sentence_284: The club's previous manager was [[Unai_Emery|Unai Emery]], who was appointed in May 2018.
sentence_285: There have been nineteen permanent and six caretaker managers of Arsenal since the appointment of the club's first professional manager, [[Thomas_Mitchell_(football_manager)|Thomas Mitchell]] in 1897.
sentence_286: The club's longest-serving manager, in terms of both length of tenure and number of games overseen, is [[Arsène_Wenger|Arsène Wenger]], who managed the club between 1996 and 2018.
sentence_287: Two Arsenal managers have died in the job – [[Herbert_Chapman|Herbert Chapman]] and [[Tom_Whittaker_(footballer)|Tom Whittaker]].
sentence_288: Main article: [[List_of_Arsenal_F.C._records_and_statistics#Honours_and_achievements|List of Arsenal F.C. records and statistics § Honours and achievements]]
sentence_289: See also: [[Arsenal_F.C._seasons|Arsenal F.C. seasons]] and [[Arsenal_F.C._Under-23s_and_Academy#Honours|Arsenal F.C. Under-23s and Academy § Honours]]
sentence_290: Arsenal's first ever silverware was won as the Royal Arsenal in 1890.
sentence_291: The [[Kent_County_Football_Association#County_Cup_Competitions|Kent Junior Cup]], won by Royal Arsenal's reserves, was the club's first trophy, while the first team's first trophy came three weeks later when they won the [[Kent_Senior_Cup|Kent Senior Cup]].
sentence_292: Their first national senior honour came in 1930, when they won the [[FA_Cup|FA Cup]].
sentence_293: The club enjoyed further success in the 1930s, winning another FA Cup and five [[Football_League_First_Division|Football League First Division]] titles.
sentence_294: Arsenal won their first league and cup [[Double_(association_football)#England|double]] in the [[1970–71_in_English_football|1970–71 season]] and twice repeated the feat, in [[1997–98_in_English_football|1997–98]] and [[2001–02_in_English_football|2001–02]], as well as winning a cup double of the FA Cup and [[Football_League_Cup|League Cup]] in [[1992–93_in_English_football|1992–93]].
sentence_295: Seasons in bold are seasons when the club won a [[Double_(association_football)|Double]] of the league and FA Cup, or of the FA Cup and League Cup.
sentence_296: The [[2003–04_Arsenal_F.C._season|2003–04]] season was the only 38-match league season [[The_Invincibles_(football)|unbeaten]] in English football history.
sentence_297: A special gold version of the Premier League trophy was commissioned and presented to the club the following season.
sentence_298: As of 29 August 2020.
sentence_299: Main article: [[Arsenal_F.C._in_European_football|Arsenal F.C. in European football]]

sentence_300: Main article: [[List_of_Arsenal_F.C._records_and_statistics#County_FAs|List of Arsenal F.C. records and statistics § County FAs]]
sentence_301: When the FA Cup was the only national [[Football_association|football association]] competition available to Arsenal, the other football association competitions were County Cups, and they made up many of the matches the club played during a season.
sentence_302: Arsenal's first first-team trophy was a County Cup, the inaugural [[Kent_Senior_Cup|Kent Senior Cup]].
sentence_303: Arsenal became ineligible for the [[London_Football_Association|London Cups]] when the club turned professional in 1891, and rarely participated in County Cups after this.
sentence_304: Due to the club's original location within the borders of both the London and [[Kent_County_Football_Association|Kent]] Football Associations, Arsenal competed in and won trophies organised by each.
sentence_305: Main article: [[List_of_Arsenal_F.C._records_and_statistics#Other|List of Arsenal F.C. records and statistics § Other]]
sentence_306: During Arsenal's history, the club has participated in and won a variety of pre-season and friendly honours.
sentence_307: These include Arsenal's own pre-season competition the [[Emirates_Cup|Emirates Cup]], begun in 2007.
sentence_308: During the wars, previous competitions were widely suspended and the club had to participate in wartime competitions.
sentence_309: During WWII, Arsenal won several of these.
sentence_310: Further information: [[Arsenal_W.F.C.|Arsenal W.F.C.]]
sentence_311: [[Arsenal_Women_F.C.|Arsenal Women]] is the women's football club affiliated to Arsenal.
sentence_312: Founded as Arsenal Ladies F.C. in 1987 by [[Vic_Akers|Vic Akers]], they turned semi-professional in 2002 and are currently managed by Clair Wheatley.
sentence_313: Akers currently holds the role of Honorary President of Arsenal Women.
sentence_314: As part of the festivities surrounding their 30th anniversary in 2017, the club announced that they were changing their formal name to Arsenal Women F.C., and would use "Arsenal" in all references except rare cases where there might be confusion with the men's side.
sentence_315: Arsenal Women are the most successful team in [[Women's_football_in_England|English women's football]] having won a total of 58 trophies.
sentence_316: In the 2008–09 season, they won all three major English trophies – the [[FA_Women's_Premier_League|FA Women's Premier League]], [[FA_Women's_Cup|FA Women's Cup]] and [[FA_Women's_Premier_League_Cup|FA Women's Premier League Cup]], and, as of 2017, were the only English side to have won the UEFA Women's Cup or [[UEFA_Women's_Champions_League|UEFA Women's Champions League]], having won the Cup in the 2006–07 season as part of a unique [[The_Quadruple#Women's_Football|quadruple]].
sentence_317: The men's and women's clubs are formally separate entities but have quite close ties; Arsenal Women are entitled to play once a season at the Emirates Stadium, though they usually play their home matches at [[Meadow_Park_(Borehamwood)|Meadow Park]] in Borehamwood.

title: Andhra Pradesh
sentence_0: "Andhra" redirects here.
sentence_1: For other uses, see [[Andhra_(disambiguation)|Andhra (disambiguation)]].
