sentence_106: It was to set up an autonomous Bulgarian principality spanning Moesia, [[Macedonia_(region)|Macedonia]] and [[Thrace|Thrace]], roughly on the territories of the [[Second_Bulgarian_Empire|Second Bulgarian Empire]], and this day is now [[Public_holidays_in_Bulgaria|a public holiday]] called [[Liberation_Day_(Bulgaria)|National Liberation Day]].
sentence_107: The other [[Great_Powers#History|Great Powers]] immediately rejected the treaty out of fear that such a large country in the [[Balkans|Balkans]] might threaten their interests.
sentence_108: It was superseded by the [[Treaty_of_Berlin,_1878|Treaty of Berlin]], signed on 13 July.
sentence_109: It provided for a much smaller state, the Principality of Bulgaria, only comprising Moesia and the region of [[Sofia|Sofia]], and leaving large populations of ethnic Bulgarians outside the new country.
sentence_110: This significantly contributed to Bulgaria's militaristic foreign affairs approach during the first half of the 20th century.
sentence_111: The Bulgarian principality won [[Serbo-Bulgarian_War|a war against Serbia]] and incorporated the semi-autonomous Ottoman territory of [[Eastern_Rumelia|Eastern Rumelia]] in 1885, proclaiming itself an independent state on 5 October 1908.
sentence_112: In the years following independence, Bulgaria increasingly militarized and was often referred to as "the Balkan [[Prussia|Prussia]]".
sentence_113: It became involved in three consecutive conflicts between 1912 and 1918—two [[Balkan_Wars|Balkan Wars]] and [[World_War_I|World War I]].
sentence_114: After a disastrous defeat in the [[Second_Balkan_War|Second Balkan War]], Bulgaria again found itself fighting on the losing side as a result of its alliance with the [[Central_Powers|Central Powers]] in World War I.
sentence_115: Despite fielding more than a quarter of its population in a 1,200,000-strong army and achieving several decisive victories at [[Battle_of_Doiran_(1917)|Doiran]] and [[Battle_of_Monastir_(1917)|Monastir]], the country capitulated in 1918.
sentence_116: The war resulted in significant territorial losses and a total of 87,500 soldiers killed.
sentence_117: More than 253,000 refugees from the lost territories [[Immigrated|immigrated]] to Bulgaria from 1912 to 1929, placing additional strain on the already ruined national economy.
sentence_118: The resulting political unrest led to the establishment of a royal [[Authoritarianism|authoritarian dictatorship]] by Tsar Boris III (1918–1943).
sentence_119: Bulgaria entered World War II in 1941 as a member of [[Axis_Powers|the Axis]] but declined to participate in [[Operation_Barbarossa|Operation Barbarossa]] and [[Rescue_of_the_Bulgarian_Jews|saved its Jewish population]] from deportation to [[Nazi_concentration_camps|concentration camps]].
sentence_120: The sudden death of Boris III in mid-1943 pushed the country into political turmoil as the war turned against Germany, and the communist guerrilla movement gained momentum.
sentence_121: The government of [[Bogdan_Filov|Bogdan Filov]] subsequently failed to achieve peace with the Allies.
sentence_122: Bulgaria did not comply with Soviet demands to expel German forces from its territory, resulting in a declaration of war and an invasion by the USSR in September 1944.
sentence_123: The communist-dominated [[Fatherland_Front_(Bulgaria)|Fatherland Front]] took power, ended participation in the Axis and joined the Allied side until the war ended.
sentence_124: Bulgaria suffered little war damage and the Soviet Union demanded no reparations.
sentence_125: But all wartime territorial gains, with the notable exception of [[Treaty_of_Craiova|Southern Dobrudzha]], were lost.
sentence_126: The left-wing coup d'état of 9 September 1944 led to the abolition of the monarchy and [[People's_Court_(Bulgaria)|the executions]] of some 1,000–3,000 dissidents, war criminals, and members of the former royal elite.
sentence_127: But it was not until 1946 that a one-party [[People's_republic|people's republic]] was instituted following a referendum.
sentence_128: It fell into the Soviet sphere of influence under the leadership of [[Georgi_Dimitrov|Georgi Dimitrov]] (1946–1949), who established a repressive, rapidly industrializing [[Stalinism|Stalinist]] state.
sentence_129: By the mid-1950s standards of living rose significantly and political repressions eased.
sentence_130: The Soviet-style [[Planned_economy|planned economy]] saw some experimental market-oriented policies emerging under [[Todor_Zhivkov|Todor Zhivkov]] (1954–1989).
sentence_131: Compared to wartime levels, national GDP increased five-fold and per capita GDP quadrupled by the 1980s, although severe debt spikes took place in 1960, 1977 and 1980.
sentence_132: Zhivkov's daughter, [[Lyudmila_Zhivkova|Lyudmila]], bolstered national pride by promoting Bulgarian heritage, culture and arts worldwide.
sentence_133: Facing declining birth rates among the ethnic Bulgarian majority, in 1984 Zhivkov's government forced the minority ethnic Turks to adopt Slavic names in an attempt to erase their identity and assimilate them.
sentence_134: These policies resulted in the emigration of some 300,000 ethnic Turks to Turkey.
sentence_135: The Communist Party was forced to give up its political monopoly on 10 November 1989 under the influence of the [[Revolutions_of_1989|Revolutions of 1989]].
sentence_136: Zhivkov resigned and Bulgaria embarked on a transition to a parliamentary democracy.
sentence_137: The first free elections in June 1990 were won by the Communist Party, now rebranded as the [[Bulgarian_Socialist_Party|Bulgarian Socialist Party]].
sentence_138: A [[Constitution_of_Bulgaria|new constitution]] that provided for a relatively weak elected president and for a prime minister accountable to the legislature was adopted in July 1991.
sentence_139: The new system initially failed to improve living standards or create economic growth—the average quality of life and economic performance remained lower than under communism well into the early 2000s.
sentence_140: After 2001 economic, political and geopolitical conditions improved greatly, and Bulgaria achieved high Human Development status in 2003.
sentence_141: It became a member of [[NATO|NATO]] in 2004 and participated in the [[War_in_Afghanistan_(2001–present)|War in Afghanistan]].
sentence_142: After several years of reforms it joined the [[European_Union|European Union]] and [[European_Single_Market|single market]] in 2007 despite Brussels' concerns about government corruption.
sentence_143: Bulgaria hosted the 2018 [[Presidency_of_the_Council_of_the_European_Union|Presidency of the Council of the European Union]] at the National Palace of Culture in Sofia.
sentence_144: The [[2020_Bulgarian_protests|2020 Bulgarian protests]] were triggered on 9 July 2020 when the Presidency of Bulgaria was raided by police and prosecutors as a result of a long-lasting conflict between the prime minister [[Boyko_Borisov|Boyko Borisov]] and the president [[Rumen_Radev|Rumen Radev]].
sentence_145: Main article: [[Geography_of_Bulgaria|Geography of Bulgaria]]
sentence_146: Bulgaria occupies a portion of the eastern [[Balkans|Balkan]] peninsula, bordering five countries—[[Greece|Greece]] and [[Turkey|Turkey]] to the south, [[North_Macedonia|North Macedonia]] and [[Serbia|Serbia]] to the west, and [[Romania|Romania]] to the north.
sentence_147: The land borders have a total length of 1,808 kilometres (1,123 mi), and the coastline has a length of 354 kilometres (220 mi).
sentence_148: Its total area of 110,994 square kilometres (42,855 sq mi) ranks it as the world's 105th-largest country.
sentence_149: Bulgaria's geographic coordinates are [[43rd_parallel_north|43° N]] 25° E.
sentence_150: The most notable topographical features are the [[Danubian_Plain_(Bulgaria)|Danubian Plain]], the [[Balkan_Mountains|Balkan Mountains]], the [[Thracian_Plain|Thracian Plain]], and the [[Rila|Rila]]-[[Rhodope_Mountains|Rhodope]] massif.
sentence_151: The southern edge of the Danubian Plain slopes upward into the foothills of the Balkans, while the [[Danube|Danube]] defines the border with Romania.
sentence_152: The [[Thracia|Thracian]] Plain is roughly triangular, beginning southeast of [[Sofia|Sofia]] and broadening as it reaches the [[Bulgarian_Black_Sea_Coast|Black Sea coast]].
sentence_153: The Balkan mountains run laterally through the middle of the country from west to east.
sentence_154: The mountainous southwest has two distinct [[Glacial_landform|alpine type]] ranges - [[Rila|Rila]] and [[Pirin|Pirin]], which border the lower but more extensive [[Rhodope_Mountains|Rhodope Mountains]] to the east, and various medium altitude mountains to west, northwest and south, like [[Vitosha|Vitosha]], [[Osogovo|Osogovo]] and [[Belasitsa|Belasitsa]].
sentence_155: [[Musala|Musala]], at 2,925 metres (9,596 ft), is the highest point in both Bulgaria and the Balkan peninsula.
sentence_156: The Black Sea coast is the country's lowest point.
sentence_157: Plains occupy about one third of the territory, while plateaux and hills occupy 41%.
sentence_158: Most rivers are short and with low water levels.
sentence_159: The longest river located solely in Bulgarian territory, the [[Iskar_(river)|Iskar]], has a length of 368 kilometres (229 mi).
sentence_160: The [[Struma_River|Struma]] and the [[Maritsa|Maritsa]] are two major rivers in the south.
sentence_161: Bulgaria has a varied and changeable climate, which results from being positioned at the meeting point of the [[Mediterranean_climate|Mediterranean]], [[Oceanic_climate|Oceanic]] and Continental air masses combined with the barrier effect of its mountains.
sentence_162: Northern Bulgaria averages 1 °C (1.8 °F) cooler, and registers 200 millimetres (7.9 in) more precipitation, than the regions south of the Balkan mountains.
sentence_163: Temperature amplitudes vary significantly in different areas.
sentence_164: The lowest recorded temperature is −38.3 °C (−36.9 °F), while the highest is 45.2 °C (113.4 °F).
sentence_165: [[Precipitation_(meteorology)|Precipitation]] averages about 630 millimetres (24.8 in) per year, and varies from 500 millimetres (19.7 in) in [[Dobrudja|Dobrudja]] to more than 2,500 millimetres (98.4 in) in the mountains.
sentence_166: Continental air masses bring significant amounts of snowfall during winter.
sentence_167: The interaction of climatic, hydrological, geological and topographical conditions has produced a relatively wide variety of plant and animal species.
sentence_168: Bulgaria's [[Biodiversity|biodiversity]], one of the richest in Europe, [[List_of_protected_areas_of_Bulgaria|is conserved]] in three national parks, 11 nature parks, 10 [[Biosphere_reserve|biosphere reserves]] and 565 protected areas.
sentence_169: Ninety-three of the 233 [[Mammal|mammal]] species of Europe are found in Bulgaria, along with 49% of [[Butterfly|butterfly]] and 30% of [[Vascular_plant|vascular plant]] species.
sentence_170: Overall, 41,493 plant and animal species are present.
sentence_171: Larger mammals with sizable populations include [[Deer|deer]] (106,323 individuals), [[Wild_boar|wild boars]] (88,948), [[Jackal|jackals]] (47,293) and [[Fox|foxes]] (32,326).
sentence_172: [[Partridge|Partridges]] number some 328,000 individuals, making them the most widespread [[Game_(hunting)|gamebird]].
sentence_173: A third of all nesting birds in Bulgaria can be found in [[Rila_National_Park|Rila National Park]], which also hosts Arctic and alpine species at high altitudes.
sentence_174: Flora includes more than 3,800 vascular plant species of which 170 are [[Endemism|endemic]] and 150 are considered endangered.
sentence_175: A checklist of larger [[Fungi|fungi]] in Bulgaria by the Institute of Botany identifies more than 1,500 species.
sentence_176: More than 35% of the land area is covered by forests.
sentence_177: In 1998, the Bulgarian government adopted the National Biological Diversity Conservation Strategy, a comprehensive programme seeking the preservation of local ecosystems, protection of endangered species and conservation of genetic resources.
sentence_178: Bulgaria has some of the largest [[Natura_2000|Natura 2000]] areas in Europe covering 33.8% of its territory.
sentence_179: It also achieved its [[Kyoto_Protocol|Kyoto Protocol]] objective of reducing [[Carbon_dioxide_emissions|carbon dioxide emissions]] by 30% from 1990 to 2009.
sentence_180: Bulgaria ranks 30th in the 2018 [[Environmental_Performance_Index|Environmental Performance Index]], but scores low on air quality.
sentence_181: [[Particulates|Particulate]] levels are the highest in Europe, especially in urban areas affected by automobile traffic and coal-based power stations.
sentence_182: One of these, the [[Lignite|lignite]]-fired [[Maritsa_Iztok_Complex|Maritsa Iztok-2]] station, is causing the highest damage to health and the environment in the European Union.
sentence_183: Pesticide use in agriculture and antiquated industrial sewage systems produce extensive soil and water pollution.
sentence_184: Water quality began to improve in 1998 and has maintained a trend of moderate improvement.
sentence_185: Over 75% of surface rivers meet European standards for good quality.
sentence_186: Main article: [[Politics_of_Bulgaria|Politics of Bulgaria]]
sentence_187: Bulgaria is a [[Parliamentary_democracy|parliamentary democracy]] where the [[Prime_Minister_of_Bulgaria|prime minister]] is the head of government and the most powerful executive position.
sentence_188: The political system has three branches—legislative, executive and judicial, with [[Universal_suffrage|universal suffrage]] for [[Citizen|citizens]] at least 18 years old.
sentence_189: The [[Constitution_of_Bulgaria|Constitution]] also provides possibilities of direct democracy, namely petitions and national [[Referendum|referenda]].
sentence_190: Elections are supervised by an independent Central Election Commission that includes members from all major political parties.
sentence_191: Parties must register with the commission prior to participating in a national election.
sentence_192: Normally, the prime minister-elect is the leader of the party receiving the most votes in parliamentary elections, although this is not always the case.
sentence_193: Unlike the prime minister, presidential domestic power is more limited.
sentence_194: The directly elected [[President_of_Bulgaria|president]] serves as head of state and [[Commander-in-chief|commander-in-chief]] of the armed forces, and has the authority to return a bill for further debate, although the parliament can override the presidential veto by a simple majority vote.
sentence_195: Political parties gather in the [[National_Assembly_(Bulgaria)|National Assembly]], a body of 240 deputies elected to four-year terms by direct popular vote.
sentence_196: The National Assembly has the power to enact laws, approve the budget, schedule presidential elections, select and dismiss the prime minister and other ministers, declare war, deploy troops abroad, and ratify international treaties and agreements.
sentence_197: Overall, Bulgaria displays a pattern of unstable governments.
sentence_198: [[Boyko_Borisov|Boyko Borisov]] is serving his third term as prime minister since 2009, when his centre-right, pro-EU party [[GERB|GERB]] won [[Bulgarian_parliamentary_election,_2009|the general election]] and ruled as a [[Minority_government|minority government]] with 117 seats in the National Assembly.
sentence_199: His first government resigned on 20 February 2013 after [[Protests_against_the_Borisov_cabinet|nationwide protests]] caused by high costs of utilities, low living standards, corruption and the perceived failure of the democratic system.
sentence_200: The protest wave was notable for self-immolations, spontaneous demonstrations and a strong sentiment against political parties.
sentence_201: The subsequent [[Bulgarian_parliamentary_election,_2013|snap elections in May]] resulted in a narrow win for [[GERB|GERB]], but the [[Bulgarian_Socialist_Party|Bulgarian Socialist Party]] eventually formed a government led by Plamen Oresharski after Borisov failed to secure parliamentary support.
sentence_202: The Oresharski government resigned in July 2014 amid continuing [[2013–14_Bulgarian_protests_against_the_Oresharski_cabinet|large-scale protests]].
sentence_203: A caretaker government took over and called the [[Bulgarian_parliamentary_election,_2014|October 2014 elections]] which resulted in a third GERB victory, but a total of eight parties entered parliament.
sentence_204: Borisov [[Second_Borisov_Government|formed a coalition]] with several right-wing parties, but resigned again after the candidate backed by his party failed to win the [[Bulgarian_presidential_election,_2016|2016 Presidential election]].
sentence_205: The [[Bulgarian_parliamentary_election,_2017|March 2017 snap election]] was again won by GERB, but with 95 seats in Parliament.
sentence_206: They formed a coalition with the far-right [[United_Patriots|United Patriots]], who hold 27 seats.
sentence_207: [[Freedom_House|Freedom House]] has reported a continuing deterioration of democratic governance after 2009, citing reduced media independence, stalled reforms, abuse of authority at the highest level and increased dependence of local administrations on the central government.
sentence_208: Bulgaria is still [[Freedom_in_the_World|listed as "Free"]], with a political system designated as a semi-consolidated democracy, albeit with deteriorating scores.
sentence_209: The [[Democracy_Index|Democracy Index]] defines it as a "Flawed democracy".
sentence_210: A 2018 survey by the Institute for Economics and Peace reported that less than 15% of respondents considered elections to be fair.
sentence_211: Bulgaria has a [[Civil_law_(legal_system)|civil law]] legal system.
sentence_212: The judiciary is overseen by the Ministry of Justice.
sentence_213: The Supreme Administrative Court and the Supreme Court of Cassation are the highest courts of appeal and oversee the application of laws in subordinate courts.
sentence_214: The Supreme Judicial Council manages the system and appoints judges.
sentence_215: The legal system is regarded by both domestic and international observers as one of Europe's most inefficient due to pervasive lack of transparency and corruption.
sentence_216: Law enforcement is carried out by organisations mainly subordinate to the [[Ministry_of_Interior_(Bulgaria)|Ministry of the Interior]].
sentence_217: The [[National_Police_Service_(Bulgaria)|General Directorate of National Police]] (GDNP) combats general crime and maintains public order.
sentence_218: GDNP fields 26,578 police officers in its local and national sections.
sentence_219: The bulk of criminal cases are transport-related, followed by [[Theft|theft]] and drug-related crime; [[List_of_countries_by_intentional_homicide_rate|homicide rates are low]].
sentence_220: The Ministry of the Interior also heads the Border Police Service and the [[Gendarmerie_(Bulgaria)|National Gendarmerie]]—a specialized branch for anti-terrorist activity, crisis management and riot control.
sentence_221: Counterintelligence and national security are the responsibility of the State Agency for National Security.
sentence_222: Main articles: [[Provinces_of_Bulgaria|Provinces of Bulgaria]] and [[Municipalities_of_Bulgaria|Municipalities of Bulgaria]]
sentence_223: Bulgaria is a [[Unitary_state|unitary state]].
sentence_224: Since the 1880s, the number of territorial management units has varied from seven to 26.
sentence_225: Between 1987 and 1999 the administrative structure consisted of nine provinces (oblasti, singular [[Oblast|oblast]]).
sentence_226: A new administrative structure was adopted in parallel with the decentralization of the economic system.
sentence_227: It includes 27 provinces and a metropolitan capital province (Sofia-Grad).
sentence_228: All areas take their names from their respective capital cities.
sentence_229: The provinces are subdivided into 265 [[Municipalities_of_Bulgaria|municipalities]].
sentence_230: Municipalities are run by mayors, who are elected to four-year terms, and by directly elected municipal councils.
sentence_231: Bulgaria is a highly centralized state where the [[Government_of_Bulgaria|Council of Ministers]] directly appoints regional governors and all provinces and municipalities are heavily dependent on it for funding.
sentence_232: Main articles: [[Foreign_relations_of_Bulgaria|Foreign relations of Bulgaria]] and [[Military_of_Bulgaria|Military of Bulgaria]]
sentence_233: Bulgaria became a member of the [[United_Nations|United Nations]] in 1955 and since 1966 has been a non-permanent member of the [[United_Nations_Security_Council|Security Council]] three times, most recently from 2002 to 2003.
sentence_234: It was also among the founding nations of the [[Organization_for_Security_and_Co-operation_in_Europe|Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe]] (OSCE) in 1975.
sentence_235: Euro-Atlantic integration has been a priority since the fall of communism, although the communist leadership also had aspirations of leaving the Warsaw Pact and joining the [[European_Communities|European Communities]] by 1987.
sentence_236: Bulgaria signed the European Union [[Treaty_of_Accession_2005|Treaty of Accession]] on 25 April 2005, and became a full member of the European Union on 1 January 2007.
sentence_237: In addition, it has a tripartite economic and diplomatic collaboration with Romania and Greece, good ties with China and [[Vietnam|Vietnam]] and a historical relationship with [[Russia|Russia]].
sentence_238: Bulgaria deployed significant numbers of both civilian and military advisors in Soviet-allied countries like Nicaragua and [[Great_Socialist_People's_Libyan_Arab_Jamahiriya|Libya]] during the [[Cold_War|Cold War]].
sentence_239: The first deployment of foreign troops on Bulgarian soil since World War II occurred in 2001, when the country hosted six [[KC-135_Stratotanker|KC-135 Stratotanker]] aircraft and 200 support personnel for the war effort in Afghanistan.
sentence_240: International military relations were further expanded with accession to [[NATO|NATO]] in March 2004 and the US-Bulgarian Defence Cooperation Agreement signed in April 2006.
sentence_241: [[Bezmer_Air_Base|Bezmer]] and Graf Ignatievo air bases, the [[Novo_Selo_Range|Novo Selo]] training range, and a logistics centre in [[Aytos_Logistics_Center|Aytos]] subsequently became [[List_of_joint_US-Bulgarian_military_bases|joint military training facilities]] cooperatively used by the United States and Bulgarian militaries.
sentence_242: Despite its active international defence collaborations, Bulgaria ranks as among the most peaceful countries globally, tying 6th alongside Iceland regarding domestic and international conflicts, and 26th on average in the [[Global_Peace_Index|Global Peace Index]].
sentence_243: Domestic defence is the responsibility of the all-volunteer [[Bulgarian_armed_forces|Bulgarian armed forces]], composed of [[Bulgarian_land_forces|land forces]], [[Bulgarian_Navy|navy]] and an air force.
sentence_244: The land forces consist of two mechanized brigades and eight independent regiments and battalions; the air force operates 106 aircraft and air defence systems in six air bases, and the navy operates various ships, helicopters and coastal defence weapons.
sentence_245: Active troops dwindled from 152,000 in 1988 to 31,300 in 2017, supplemented by 3,000 reservists and 16,000 paramilitary.
sentence_246: Inventory is mostly made up of Soviet equipment like [[Mikoyan_MiG-29|Mikoyan MiG-29]] and [[Sukhoi_Su-25|Sukhoi Su-25]] jets, [[S-300_missile_system|S-300PT]] air defence systems and [[SS-21_Scarab|SS-21 Scarab]] short-range ballistic missiles.
sentence_247: Main article: [[Economy_of_Bulgaria|Economy of Bulgaria]]
sentence_248: Bulgaria has an open, [[Developing_country|upper middle income]] range [[Market_economy|market economy]] where the private sector accounts for more than 70% of GDP.
sentence_249: From a largely agricultural country with a predominantly rural population in 1948, by the 1980s Bulgaria had transformed into an industrial economy with scientific and technological research at the top of its budgetary expenditure priorities.
sentence_250: The loss of [[COMECON|COMECON]] markets in 1990 and the subsequent "[[Shock_therapy_(economics)|shock therapy]]" of the planned system caused a steep decline in industrial and agricultural production, ultimately followed by an economic collapse in 1997.
sentence_251: The economy largely recovered during a period of rapid growth several years later, but the average salary of 1,036 leva ($615) per month remains the lowest in the EU.
sentence_252: More than a fifth of the labour force are employed on a [[Minimum_wage|minimum wage]] of $1.16 per hour.
sentence_253: A [[Balanced_budget|balanced budget]] was achieved in 2003 and the country began running a [[Budget_surplus|surplus]] the following year.
sentence_254: Expenditures amounted to $21.15 billion and revenues were $21.67 billion in 2017.
sentence_255: Most government spending on institutions is earmarked for security.
sentence_256: The ministries of defence, the interior and justice are allocated the largest share of the annual government budget, whereas those responsible for the environment, tourism and energy receive the least amount of funding.
sentence_257: Taxes form the bulk of government revenue at 30% of GDP.
sentence_258: Bulgaria has some of the lowest corporate income tax rates in the EU at a flat 10% rate.
sentence_259: The tax system is two-tier.
sentence_260: [[Value_added_tax|Value added tax]], [[Excise_duties|excise duties]], corporate and personal income tax are national, whereas real estate, inheritance, and vehicle taxes are levied by local authorities.
sentence_261: Strong economic performance in the early 2000s reduced [[Government_debt|government debt]] from 79.6% in 1998 to 14.1% in 2008.
sentence_262: It has since increased to 28.7% of GDP by 2016, but remains the third lowest in the EU.
sentence_263: The [[Yugozapaden|Yugozapaden]] planning area is the most developed region with a [[Per_capita|per capita]] gross domestic product ([[Purchasing_power_parity|PPP]]) of $29,816 in 2018.
sentence_264: It includes the capital city and the surrounding [[Sofia_Province|Sofia Province]], which alone generate 42% of national gross domestic product despite hosting only 22% of the population.
sentence_265: [[GDP|GDP]] per capita (in PPS) and the cost of living in 2019 stood at 53 and 52.8% of the EU average (100%), respectively.
sentence_266: National PPP GDP was estimated at $143.1 billion in 2016, with a per capita value of $20,116.
sentence_267: Economic growth statistics take into account illegal transactions from the [[Informal_economy|informal economy]], which is the largest in the EU as a percentage of economic output.
sentence_268: The [[Bulgarian_National_Bank|Bulgarian National Bank]] issues the national currency, [[Bulgarian_lev|lev]], which is pegged to the euro at a rate of 1.95583 levа per euro.
sentence_269: After several consecutive years of high growth, repercussions of the [[Financial_crisis_of_2007–2008|financial crisis of 2007–2008]] resulted in a 3.6% contraction of GDP in 2009 and increased unemployment.
sentence_270: Industrial output declined 10%, mining by 31%, and ferrous and metal production marked a 60% drop.
sentence_271: Positive growth was restored in 2010 but intercompany debt exceeded $59 billion, meaning that 60% of all Bulgarian companies were mutually indebted.
sentence_272: By 2012, it had increased to $97 billion, or 227% of GDP.
sentence_273: The government implemented strict austerity measures with IMF and EU encouragement to some positive fiscal results, but the social consequences of these measures, such as increased [[Economic_inequality|income inequality]] and accelerated outward migration, have been "catastrophic" according to the [[International_Trade_Union_Confederation|International Trade Union Confederation]].
sentence_274: Siphoning of public funds to the families and relatives of politicians from incumbent parties has resulted in fiscal and welfare losses to society.
sentence_275: Bulgaria ranks 71st in the [[Corruption_Perceptions_Index|Corruption Perceptions Index]] and experiences the worst levels of [[Corruption|corruption]] in the European Union, a phenomenon that remains a source of profound public discontent.
sentence_276: Along with organized crime, corruption has resulted in a rejection of the country's [[Schengen_Area|Schengen Area]] application and withdrawal of foreign investment.
sentence_277: Government officials reportedly engage in embezzlement, influence trading, government procurement violations and bribery with impunity.
sentence_278: Government procurement in particular is a critical area in corruption risk.
sentence_279: An estimated 10 billion leva ($5.99 billion) of state budget and [[Structural_Funds_and_Cohesion_Fund|European cohesion]] funds are spent on public tenders each year; nearly 14 billion ($8.38 billion) were spent on public contracts in 2017 alone.
sentence_280: A large share of these contracts are awarded to a few politically connected companies amid widespread irregularities, procedure violations and tailor-made award criteria.
sentence_281: Despite repeated criticism from the [[European_Commission|European Commission]], EU institutions refrain from taking measures against Bulgaria because it supports Brussels on a number of issues, unlike [[Poland|Poland]] or [[Hungary|Hungary]].
sentence_282: The labour force is 3.36 million people, of whom 6.8% are employed in agriculture, 26.6% in industry and 66.6% in the services sector.
sentence_283: Extraction of metals and minerals, production of [[Chemical_industry|chemicals]], [[Machinery_industry|machine building]], steel, biotechnology, tobacco and food processing and [[Refined_petroleum_fuel|petroleum refining]] are among the major industrial activities.
sentence_284: Mining alone employs 24,000 people and generates about 5% of the country's GDP; the number of employed in all mining-related industries is 120,000.
sentence_285: Bulgaria is Europe's fifth-largest coal producer.
sentence_286: Local deposits of coal, iron, copper and lead are vital for the manufacturing and energy sectors.
sentence_287: The main destinations of Bulgarian exports outside the EU are Turkey, China and the United States, while Russia and Turkey are by far the largest import partners.
sentence_288: Most of the exports are manufactured goods, machinery, chemicals, fuel products and food.
sentence_289: Two-thirds of food and agricultural exports go to [[OECD|OECD]] countries.
sentence_290: Although cereal and vegetable output dropped by 40% between 1990 and 2008, output in grains has since increased, and the 2016–2017 season registered the biggest grain output in a decade.
sentence_291: [[Maize|Maize]], [[Barley|barley]], [[Oats|oats]] and [[Rice|rice]] are also grown.
sentence_292: Quality [[Turkish_tobacco|Oriental tobacco]] is a significant industrial crop.
sentence_293: Bulgaria is also the largest producer globally of [[Lavender_oil|lavender]] and rose oil, both widely used in fragrances.
sentence_294: Within the services sector, [[Tourism_in_Bulgaria|tourism]] is a significant contributor to economic growth.
sentence_295: [[Sofia|Sofia]], [[Plovdiv|Plovdiv]], Veliko Tarnovo, coastal resorts Albena, [[Golden_Sands|Golden Sands]] and [[Sunny_Beach|Sunny Beach]] and winter resorts [[Bansko|Bansko]], [[Pamporovo|Pamporovo]] and Borovets are some of the locations most visited by tourists.
sentence_296: Most visitors are Romanian, Turkish, Greek and German.
sentence_297: Tourism is additionally encouraged through the [[100_Tourist_Sites_of_Bulgaria|100 Tourist Sites]] system.
sentence_298: Main article: [[Science_and_technology_in_Bulgaria|Science and technology in Bulgaria]]
sentence_299: Spending on research and development amounts to 0.78% of GDP, and the bulk of public R&D funding goes to the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences (BAS).
sentence_300: Private businesses accounted for more than 73% of R&D expenditures and employed 42% of Bulgaria's 22,000 researchers in 2015.
sentence_301: The same year, Bulgaria ranked 39th out of 50 countries in the [[Bloomberg_Innovation_Index|Bloomberg Innovation Index]], the highest score being in education (24th) and the lowest in value-added manufacturing (48th).
sentence_302: Chronic government underinvestment in research since 1990 has forced many professionals in science and engineering to leave Bulgaria.
sentence_303: Despite the lack of funding, research in chemistry, [[Materials_science|materials science]] and [[Physics|physics]] remains strong.
sentence_304: Antarctic research is actively carried out through the [[St._Kliment_Ohridski_Base|St.
sentence_305: Kliment Ohridski Base]] on [[Livingston_Island|Livingston Island]] in [[Western_Antarctica|Western Antarctica]].
sentence_306: The [[Information_and_communication_technologies|information and communication technologies]] (ICT) sector generates three per cent of economic output and employs 40,000 to 51,000 software engineers.
sentence_307: Bulgaria was known as a "Communist [[Silicon_Valley|Silicon Valley]]" during the Soviet era due to its key role in [[COMECON|COMECON]] computing technology production.
sentence_308: The country is a regional leader in [[Supercomputer|high performance computing]]: it operates Avitohol, the most powerful supercomputer in Southeast Europe, and will host one of the eight petascale [[European_High-Performance_Computing_Joint_Undertaking|EuroHPC]] supercomputers.
sentence_309: Bulgaria has made numerous contributions to [[Space_exploration|space exploration]].
sentence_310: These include two scientific satellites, more than 200 payloads and 300 experiments in Earth orbit, as well as [[Bulgarian_cosmonaut_program|two cosmonauts]] since 1971.
sentence_311: Bulgaria was the first country to grow [[Wheat|wheat]] and vegetables [[Plants_in_space|in space]] with its [[SVET_plant_growth_system|Svet]] [[Greenhouse|greenhouses]] on the [[Mir_space_station|Mir space station]].
sentence_312: It was involved in the development of the [[Granat|Granat]] [[Gamma-ray_astronomy|gamma-ray observatory]] and the Vega program, particularly in modelling trajectories and guidance [[Algorithms|algorithms]] for both Vega probes.
sentence_313: Bulgarian instruments have been used in the [[Exploration_of_Mars|exploration of Mars]], including a spectrometer that took the first high quality spectroscopic images of Martian moon [[Phobos_(moon)|Phobos]] with the [[Phobos_2|Phobos 2]] probe.
sentence_314: [[Cosmic_ray|Cosmic radiation]] en route to and around the planet has been mapped by [[Liulin_type_instruments|Liulin-ML]] dosimeters on the [[ExoMars_Trace_Gas_Orbiter|ExoMars TGO]].
sentence_315: [[RADOM-7|Variants]] of these instruments have also been fitted on the [[International_Space_Station|International Space Station]] and the [[Chandrayaan-1|Chandrayaan-1]] lunar probe.
sentence_316: Another lunar mission, [[SpaceIL|SpaceIL]]'s Beresheet, was also equipped with a Bulgarian-manufactured imaging payload.
sentence_317: Bulgaria's first geostationary communications satellite—[[BulgariaSat-1|BulgariaSat-1]]—was launched by SpaceX in 2017.
sentence_318: Main articles: [[Energy_in_Bulgaria|Energy in Bulgaria]] and [[Transport_in_Bulgaria|Transport in Bulgaria]]
sentence_319: Telephone services are widely available, and a central digital trunk line connects most regions.
sentence_320: [[Vivacom|Vivacom]] (BTC) serves more than 90% of fixed lines and is one of the three operators providing mobile services, along with [[Mtel_(Bulgaria)|A1]] and [[Telenor_(Bulgaria)|Telenor]].
sentence_321: [[Internet|Internet]] penetration stood at 66.8% of the population aged 16–74 and 75.1% of households, in 2019.
sentence_322: Bulgaria's strategic geographic location and well-developed energy sector make it a key European energy centre despite its lack of significant fossil fuel deposits.
sentence_323: Thermal power plants generate 48.9% of electricity, followed by [[Nuclear_power|nuclear power]] from the [[Kozloduy_Nuclear_Power_Plant|Kozloduy reactors]] (34.8%) and [[Renewable_energy|renewable sources]] (16.3%).
sentence_324: Equipment for a second nuclear power station at [[Belene_Nuclear_Power_Plant|Belene]] has been acquired, but the fate of the project remains uncertain.
sentence_325: Installed capacity amounts to 12,668 MW, allowing Bulgaria to exceed domestic demand and export energy.
sentence_326: The national road network has a total length of 19,512 kilometres (12,124 mi), of which 19,235 kilometres (11,952 mi) are paved.
sentence_327: Railroads are a major mode of freight transportation, although highways carry a progressively larger share of freight.
sentence_328: Bulgaria has 6,238 kilometres (3,876 mi) of railway track and currently a total of 81 kilometres (50 miles) of [[High-speed_rail|high-speed lines]] are in operation.
sentence_329: Rail links are available with Romania, Turkey, Greece, and Serbia, and express trains serve direct routes to [[Kyiv|Kyiv]], [[Minsk|Minsk]], [[Moscow|Moscow]] and [[Saint_Petersburg|Saint Petersburg]].
sentence_330: Sofia and Plovdiv are the country's air travel hubs, while Varna and Burgas are the principal maritime trade ports.
sentence_331: Main article: [[Demographics_of_Bulgaria|Demographics of Bulgaria]]
sentence_332: The population of Bulgaria is 7,364,570 people according to the 2011 national census.
sentence_333: The majority of the population, 72.5%, reside in urban areas.
sentence_334: As of 2019, Sofia is the most populated urban centre with 1,241,675 people, followed by [[Plovdiv|Plovdiv]] (346,893), [[Varna|Varna]] (336,505), [[Burgas|Burgas]] (202,434) and [[Ruse,_Bulgaria|Ruse]] (142,902).
sentence_335: [[Bulgarians|Bulgarians]] are the main ethnic group and constitute 84.8% of the population.
sentence_336: Turkish and [[Roma_in_Bulgaria|Roma]] minorities account for 8.8 and 4.9%, respectively; some 40 smaller minorities account for 0.7%, and 0.8% do not self-identify with an ethnic group.
sentence_337: Former [[National_Statistical_Institute_(Bulgaria)|Statistics]] head [[Reneta_Indzhova|Reneta Indzhova]] has disputed the 2011 census figures, suggesting the actual population is smaller than reported.
sentence_338: The Roma minority is usually underestimated in census data and may represent up to 11% of the population.
sentence_339: Population density is 65 per square kilometre, almost half the European Union average.
sentence_340: In 2018 the average [[Total_fertility_rate|total fertility rate]] (TFR) across Bulgaria was 1.56 children per woman, below the replacement rate of 2.1, it remains considerably below the high of 5.83 children per woman in 1905.
sentence_341: Bulgaria subsequently has one of the oldest populations in the world, with the average age of 43 years.
sentence_342: Bulgaria is in a state of demographic crisis.
sentence_343: It has had negative population growth since the early 1990s, when the economic collapse caused a long-lasting emigration wave.
sentence_344: Some 937,000 to 1,200,000 people—mostly young adults—left the country by 2005.
sentence_345: The majority of children are born to unmarried women.
sentence_346: Furthermore, a third of all households consist of only one person and 75.5% of families do not have children under the age of 16.
sentence_347: The resulting birth rates are among the lowest in the world while [[Death_rate|death rates]] are among the highest.
sentence_348: High death rates result from a combination of an ageing population, a high number of people at risk of poverty and a weak healthcare system.
sentence_349: More than 80% of all deaths are due to [[Cancer|cancer]] and [[Cardiovascular_conditions|cardiovascular conditions]]; nearly a fifth of those are avoidable.
sentence_350: Mortality rates can be sharply reduced to levels below the EU average through timely and adequate access to medical services, which the healthcare system does not provide fully.
sentence_351: Although [[Healthcare_in_Bulgaria|healthcare in Bulgaria]] is nominally universal, [[Out-of-pocket_expenses|out-of-pocket expenses]] account for nearly half of all healthcare spending, which significantly limits access to medical care.
sentence_352: Other problems disrupting care provision are the emigration of doctors due to low wages, understaffed and under-equipped regional hospitals, supply shortages and frequent changes to the basic service package for those insured.
sentence_353: The 2018 Bloomberg Health Care Efficiency Index ranked Bulgaria last out of 56 countries.
sentence_354: Average [[Life_expectancy|life expectancy]] is 74.8 years compared with an EU average of 80.99 and a world average of 72.38.
sentence_355: Public expenditures for education are far below the European Union average as well.
sentence_356: Educational standards were once high, but have declined significantly since the early 2000s.
sentence_357: Bulgarian students were among the highest-scoring in the world in terms of reading in 2001, performing better than their Canadian and German counterparts; by 2006, scores in reading, math and science had dropped.
sentence_358: By 2018, [[Programme_for_International_Student_Assessment|Programme for International Student Assessment]] studies found 47% of pupils in the 9th grade to be [[Functional_illiteracy|functionally illiterate]] in reading and natural sciences.
sentence_359: Average basic [[Literacy|literacy]] stands high at 98.4% with no significant difference between sexes.
sentence_360: The [[Ministry_of_Education_and_Science_(Bulgaria)|Ministry of Education and Science]] partially funds public schools, colleges and universities, sets criteria for textbooks and oversees the publishing process.
sentence_361: Education in primary and secondary public schools is free and compulsory.
sentence_362: The process spans through 12 grades, where grades one through eight are primary and nine through twelve are secondary level.
sentence_363: Higher education consists of a 4-year bachelor degree and a 1-year master's degree.
sentence_364: Bulgaria's highest-ranked higher education institution is [[Sofia_University|Sofia University]].
sentence_365: Bulgarian is the only language with official status and native for 85% of the population.
sentence_366: It belongs to the Slavic group of languages, but it has a number of grammatical peculiarities, shared with its closest relative [[Macedonian_language|Macedonian]], that set it apart from other Slavic languages: these include a complex verbal morphology (which also codes for distinctions in [[Evidentiality|evidentiality]]), the absence of noun cases and [[Infinitives|infinitives]], and the use of a suffixed definite article.
sentence_367: Other major languages are [[Turkish_language|Turkish]] and [[Romani_language|Romani]], which according to the 2011 census were spoken natively by 9.1% and 4.2% respectively.
sentence_368: The country scores high in [[Gender_equality|gender equality]], ranking 18th in the 2018 [[Global_Gender_Gap_Report|Global Gender Gap Report]].
sentence_369: Although [[Women's_suffrage|women's suffrage]] was enabled relatively late, in 1937, women today have equal political rights, high workforce participation and legally mandated [[Equal_pay_for_equal_work|equal pay]].
sentence_370: Bulgaria has the highest ratio of female ICT researchers in the EU, as well as the second-highest ratio of females in the technology sector at 44.6% of the workforce.
sentence_371: High levels of female participation are a legacy of the Socialist era.
sentence_372: Main article: [[Religion_in_Bulgaria|Religion in Bulgaria]]
sentence_373: More than three-quarters of Bulgarians subscribe to [[Eastern_Orthodoxy|Eastern Orthodoxy]].
sentence_374: [[Sunni_Muslims|Sunni Muslims]] are the second-largest religious community and constitute 10% of Bulgaria's overall religious makeup, although a majority of them are not observant and find the use of [[Islamic_veil|Islamic veils]] in schools unacceptable.
sentence_375: Less than 3% of the population are affiliated with [[Religion_in_Bulgaria|other religions]] and 11.8% are irreligious or do not self-identify with a religion.
sentence_376: The [[Bulgarian_Orthodox_Church|Bulgarian Orthodox Church]] gained [[Autocephalous|autocephalous]] status in AD 927, and has 12 dioceses and over 2,000 priests.
sentence_377: Bulgaria is a secular state with guaranteed religious freedom by constitution, but Orthodoxy is designated as a "traditional" religion.
sentence_378: Main article: [[Culture_of_Bulgaria|Culture of Bulgaria]]
sentence_379: Contemporary Bulgarian culture blends the formal culture that helped forge a national consciousness towards the end of Ottoman rule with millennia-old folk traditions.
sentence_380: An essential element of Bulgarian folklore is fire, used to banish evil spirits and illnesses.
sentence_381: Many of these are personified as witches, whereas other creatures like [[Slavic_dragon|zmey]] and [[Samodiva_(mythology)|samodiva]] (veela) are either benevolent guardians or ambivalent tricksters.
sentence_382: Some rituals against evil spirits have survived and are still practised, most notably [[Kukeri|kukeri]] and [[Survakane|survakari]].
sentence_383: [[Martenitsa|Martenitsa]] is also widely celebrated.
sentence_384: [[Nestinarstvo|Nestinarstvo]], a ritual fire-dance of Thracian origin, is included in the list of [[UNESCO_Intangible_Cultural_Heritage_Lists|UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage]].
sentence_385: [[List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Bulgaria|Nine historical and natural objects]] are [[UNESCO_World_Heritage_Site|UNESCO World Heritage Sites]]: [[Pirin_National_Park|Pirin National Park]], [[Srebarna_Nature_Reserve|Sreburna Nature Reserve]], the [[Madara_Rider|Madara Rider]], the Thracian tombs in [[Thracian_Tomb_of_Sveshtari|Sveshtari]] and [[Thracian_Tomb_of_Kazanlak|Kazanlak]], the [[Rila_Monastery|Rila Monastery]], the [[Boyana_Church|Boyana Church]], the [[Rock-hewn_Churches_of_Ivanovo|Rock-hewn Churches of Ivanovo]] and the ancient city of [[Nesebar|Nesebar]].
sentence_386: The Rila Monastery was established by Saint [[John_of_Rila|John of Rila]], Bulgaria's [[Patron_saint|patron saint]], whose life has been the subject of numerous literary accounts since Medieval times.
sentence_387: The establishment of the [[Preslav_Literary_School|Preslav]] and [[Ohrid_Literary_School|Ohrid]] literary schools in the 10th century is associated with a golden period in Bulgarian literature during the [[Middle_Ages|Middle Ages]].
sentence_388: The schools' emphasis on Christian [[Religious_text|scriptures]] made the Bulgarian Empire a centre of Slavic culture, bringing Slavs under the influence of Christianity and providing them with [[Old_Church_Slavonic|a written language]].
sentence_389: Its alphabet, [[Cyrillic|Cyrillic]] script, was developed by the Preslav Literary School.
sentence_390: The [[Tarnovo_Literary_School|Tarnovo Literary School]], on the other hand, is associated with a Silver age of literature defined by high-quality manuscripts on historical or mystical themes under the [[Asen_dynasty|Asen]] and [[House_of_Shishman|Shishman]] dynasties.
sentence_391: Many literary and artistic masterpieces were destroyed by the Ottoman conquerors, and artistic activities did not re-emerge until the National Revival in the 19th century.
sentence_392: The enormous body of work of [[Ivan_Vazov|Ivan Vazov]] (1850–1921) covered every genre and touched upon every facet of Bulgarian society, bridging pre-Liberation works with literature of the newly established state.
sentence_393: Notable later works are [[Bay_Ganyo|Bay Ganyo]] by [[Aleko_Konstantinov|Aleko Konstantinov]], the [[Friedrich_Nietzsche|Nietzschean]] poetry of [[Pencho_Slaveykov|Pencho Slaveykov]], the [[Symbolism_(arts)|Symbolist]] poetry of [[Peyo_Yavorov|Peyo Yavorov]] and Dimcho Debelyanov, the [[Marxism|Marxist]]-inspired works of [[Geo_Milev|Geo Milev]] and [[Nikola_Vaptsarov|Nikola Vaptsarov]], and the [[Socialist_Realism|Socialist realism]] novels of Dimitar Dimov and [[Dimitar_Talev|Dimitar Talev]].
sentence_394: Tzvetan Todorov is a notable contemporary author, while Bulgarian-born Elias Canetti was awarded the [[Nobel_Prize_in_Literature|Nobel Prize in Literature]] in 1981.
sentence_395: А religious visual arts heritage includes [[Fresco|frescoes]], [[Mural|murals]] and [[Icon|icons]], many produced by the medieval [[Painting_of_the_Tarnovo_Artistic_School|Tarnovo Artistic School]].
sentence_396: Like literature, it was not until the National Revival when Bulgarian visual arts began to reemerge.
sentence_397: [[Zahari_Zograf|Zahari Zograf]] was a pioneer of the visual arts in the pre-Liberation era.
sentence_398: After the Liberation, Ivan Mrkvička, Anton Mitov, [[Vladimir_Dimitrov|Vladimir Dimitrov]], [[Tsanko_Lavrenov|Tsanko Lavrenov]] and [[Zlatyu_Boyadzhiev|Zlatyu Boyadzhiev]] introduced newer styles and substance, depicting scenery from Bulgarian villages, old towns and historical subjects.
sentence_399: [[Christo|Christo]] is the most famous Bulgarian artist of the 21st century, known for his outdoor installations.
sentence_400: Folk music is by far the most extensive traditional art and has slowly developed throughout the ages as a fusion of Far Eastern, Oriental, medieval Eastern Orthodox and standard Western European tonalities and modes.
sentence_401: Bulgarian folk music has a distinctive sound and uses a wide range of traditional instruments, such as [[Gadulka|gadulka]], gaida, kaval and [[Davul|tupan]].
sentence_402: A distinguishing feature is extended rhythmical time, which has no equivalent in the rest of European music.
sentence_403: The State Television Female Vocal Choir won a [[Grammy_Award|Grammy Award]] in 1990 for its performances of Bulgarian folk music.
sentence_404: Written musical composition can be traced back to the works of [[Yoan_Kukuzel|Yoan Kukuzel]] (c. 1280–1360), but modern classical music began with Emanuil Manolov, who composed the first Bulgarian [[Opera|opera]] in 1890.
sentence_405: [[Pancho_Vladigerov|Pancho Vladigerov]] and [[Petko_Staynov|Petko Staynov]] further enriched [[Symphony|symphony]], ballet and opera, which singers [[Ghena_Dimitrova|Ghena Dimitrova]], [[Boris_Christoff|Boris Christoff]], [[Ljuba_Welitsch|Ljuba Welitsch]] and [[Nicolai_Ghiaurov|Nicolai Ghiaurov]] elevated to a world-class level.
sentence_406: Bulgarian performers have gained acclaim in other genres like [[Electropop|electropop]] ([[Mira_Aroyo|Mira Aroyo]]), [[Jazz|jazz]] (Milcho Leviev) and blends of jazz and folk ([[Ivo_Papazov|Ivo Papazov]]).
sentence_407: The [[Bulgarian_National_Radio|Bulgarian National Radio]], [[BTV_(Bulgaria)|bTV]] and daily newspapers [[Trud_(Bulgarian_newspaper)|Trud]], [[Dnevnik_(Bulgaria)|Dnevnik]] and [[24_Chasa|24 Chasa]] are some of the largest national media outlets.
sentence_408: [[Media_of_Bulgaria|Bulgarian media]] were described as generally unbiased in their reporting in the early 2000s and print media had no legal restrictions.
sentence_409: Since then, [[Freedom_of_the_press|freedom of the press]] has deteriorated to the point where Bulgaria scores 111th globally in the World Press Freedom Index, lower than all European Union members and membership candidate states.
sentence_410: The government has diverted EU funds to sympathetic media outlets and bribed others to be less critical on problematic topics, while attacks against individual journalists have increased.
sentence_411: Collusion between politicians, oligarchs and the media is widespread.
sentence_412: [[Bulgarian_cuisine|Bulgarian cuisine]] is similar to that of other Balkan countries and demonstrates strong Turkish and Greek influences.
sentence_413: [[Yogurt|Yogurt]], lukanka, banitsa, [[Shopska_salad|shopska salad]], [[Lyutenitsa|lyutenitsa]] and kozunak are among the best-known local foods.
sentence_414: Meat consumption is lower than the European average, given a cultural preference for a large variety of salads.
sentence_415: Bulgaria was the world's second-largest wine exporter until 1989, but has since lost that position.
sentence_416: The 2016 harvest yielded 128 million litres of wine, of which 62 million was exported mainly to Romania, Poland and Russia.
sentence_417: [[Mavrud|Mavrud]], Rubin, [[Siroka_Melniska|Shiroka melnishka]], [[Dimiat|Dimiat]] and [[Misket_Cherven|Cherven Misket]] are the typical grapes used in [[Bulgarian_wine|Bulgarian wine]].
sentence_418: Rakia is a traditional fruit [[Brandy|brandy]] that was consumed in Bulgaria as early as the 14th century.
sentence_419: Main article: [[Sport_in_Bulgaria|Sport in Bulgaria]]
sentence_420: Bulgaria appeared at the [[1896_Summer_Olympics|first modern Olympic games]] in 1896, when it was represented by [[Gymnastics_at_the_1896_Summer_Olympics|gymnast]] [[Charles_Champaud|Charles Champaud]].
sentence_421: Since then, Bulgarian athletes have won 52 gold, 89 silver, and 83 bronze medals, ranking 25th in the [[All-time_Olympic_Games_medal_table|all-time medal table]].
sentence_422: [[Olympic_weightlifting|Weight-lifting]] is a signature sport of Bulgaria.
sentence_423: Coach [[Ivan_Abadjiev|Ivan Abadzhiev]] developed innovative training practices that have produced many Bulgarian world and Olympic champions in weight-lifting since the 1980s.
sentence_424: Bulgarian athletes have also excelled in [[Wrestling|wrestling]], [[Boxing|boxing]], gymnastics, volleyball and [[Tennis|tennis]].
sentence_425: Stefka Kostadinova is the reigning [[List_of_world_records_in_athletics|world record]] holder in the women's [[High_jump|high jump]] at 2.09 metres (6 feet 10 inches), achieved during the [[1987_World_Championships_in_Athletics|1987 World Championships]].
sentence_426: [[Grigor_Dimitrov|Grigor Dimitrov]] is the first Bulgarian tennis player in the Top 3 [[ATP_Rankings#Current_rankings|ATP Rankings]].
sentence_427: [[Association_football|Football]] is the most popular sport in the country by a substantial margin.
sentence_428: The [[Bulgaria_national_football_team|national football team]]'s best performance was a semi-final at the [[1994_FIFA_World_Cup|1994 FIFA World Cup]], when the squad was spearheaded by forward [[Hristo_Stoichkov|Hristo Stoichkov]].
sentence_429: Stoichkov is the most successful Bulgarian player of all time; he was awarded the [[European_Golden_Shoe|Golden Boot]] and the [[Ballon_d'Or|Golden Ball]] and was considered one of the best in the world while playing for [[FC_Barcelona|FC Barcelona]] in the 1990s.
sentence_430: [[PFC_CSKA_Sofia|CSKA]] and [[PFC_Levski_Sofia|Levski]], both based in Sofia, are the most successful clubs domestically and [[Eternal_derby_of_Bulgarian_football|long-standing rivals]].
sentence_431: [[PFC_Ludogorets_Razgrad|Ludogorets]] is remarkable for having advanced from the local fourth division to the [[2014–15_UEFA_Champions_League|2014–15 UEFA Champions League]] group stage in a mere nine years.
sentence_432: Placed 39th in 2018, it is Bulgaria's highest-ranked club in [[UEFA|UEFA]].

title: Ancient Egypt
sentence_0: For the British history magazine, see [[Ancient_Egypt_(magazine)|Ancient Egypt (magazine)]].
sentence_1: "Ancient Egyptian" redirects here.
sentence_2: For the language, see [[Egyptian_language|Egyptian language]].
sentence_3: Ancient Egypt was a [[Civilization|civilization]] of ancient [[North_Africa|North Africa]], concentrated along the lower reaches of the [[Nile|Nile River]], situated in the place that is now the country [[Egypt|Egypt]].
sentence_4: Ancient Egyptian civilization followed [[Prehistoric_Egypt|prehistoric Egypt]] and coalesced around 3100 [[Anno_Domini|BC]] (according to [[Conventional_Egyptian_chronology|conventional Egyptian chronology]]) with the political unification of [[Upper_and_Lower_Egypt|Upper and Lower Egypt]] under [[Menes|Menes]] (often identified with [[Narmer|Narmer]]).
sentence_5: The [[History_of_ancient_Egypt|history of ancient Egypt]] occurred as a series of stable kingdoms, separated by periods of relative instability known as Intermediate Periods: the [[Old_Kingdom_of_Egypt|Old Kingdom]] of the [[Early_Bronze_Age|Early Bronze Age]], the [[Middle_Kingdom_of_Egypt|Middle Kingdom]] of the [[Middle_Bronze_Age|Middle Bronze Age]] and the [[New_Kingdom_of_Egypt|New Kingdom]] of the [[Late_Bronze_Age|Late Bronze Age]].
sentence_6: Egypt reached the pinnacle of its power in the New Kingdom, ruling much of [[Nubia|Nubia]] and a sizable portion of the [[Near_East|Near East]], after which it entered a period of slow decline.
sentence_7: During the course of its history Egypt was invaded or conquered by a number of foreign powers, including the [[Hyksos|Hyksos]], the [[Ancient_Libya|Libyans]], the [[Nubians|Nubians]], the [[Assyria|Assyrians]], the [[History_of_Achaemenid_Egypt|Achaemenid Persians]], and the [[Macedon|Macedonians]] under the command of [[Alexander_the_Great|Alexander the Great]].
sentence_8: The Greek [[Ptolemaic_Kingdom|Ptolemaic Kingdom]], formed in the aftermath of Alexander's death, ruled Egypt until 30 BC, when, under [[Cleopatra|Cleopatra]], it fell to the [[Roman_Empire|Roman Empire]] and became [[Egypt_(Roman_province)|a Roman province]].
sentence_9: The success of ancient Egyptian civilization came partly from its ability to adapt to the conditions of the [[Ancient_Egyptian_agriculture|Nile River valley for agriculture]].
sentence_10: The predictable [[Flooding_of_the_Nile|flooding]] and controlled [[Irrigation|irrigation]] of the fertile valley produced surplus crops, which supported a more dense population, and [[Social_change|social development]] and culture.
sentence_11: With resources to spare, the [[Administration_(government)|administration]] sponsored mineral exploitation of the valley and surrounding desert regions, the early development of an independent [[Egyptian_hieroglyphs|writing system]], the organization of collective construction and agricultural projects, trade with surrounding regions, and [[Military_of_ancient_Egypt|a military]] intended to assert Egyptian dominance.
sentence_12: Motivating and organizing these activities was a bureaucracy of elite [[Egyptian_writing|scribes]], religious leaders, and administrators under the control of a [[Pharaoh|pharaoh]], who ensured the cooperation and unity of the Egyptian people in the context of an elaborate system of [[Ancient_Egyptian_religion|religious beliefs]].
sentence_13: The many achievements of the ancient Egyptians include the quarrying, [[Surveying|surveying]] and construction techniques that supported the building of monumental [[Egyptian_pyramids|pyramids]], [[Egyptian_temple|temples]], and obelisks; a system of [[Egyptian_mathematics|mathematics]], a practical and effective system of medicine, irrigation systems and agricultural production techniques, the first known planked boats, [[Egyptian_faience|Egyptian faience]] and glass technology, new forms of [[Ancient_Egyptian_literature|literature]], and the [[Egyptian–Hittite_peace_treaty|earliest known peace treaty]], made with the Hittites.
sentence_14: Ancient Egypt has left a lasting legacy.
sentence_15: Its [[Art_of_ancient_Egypt|art]] and [[Ancient_Egyptian_architecture|architecture]] were widely copied, and its antiquities carried off to far corners of the world.
sentence_16: Its monumental ruins have inspired the imaginations of travelers and writers for centuries.
sentence_17: A newfound respect for antiquities and excavations in the early modern period by Europeans and Egyptians led to the [[Egyptology|scientific investigation]] of Egyptian civilization and a greater appreciation of its cultural legacy.
sentence_18: Main articles: [[History_of_ancient_Egypt|History of ancient Egypt]] and [[Population_history_of_Egypt|Population history of Egypt]]
sentence_19: The [[Nile|Nile]] has been the lifeline of its region for much of human history.
sentence_20: The fertile floodplain of the Nile gave humans the opportunity to develop a settled [[Ancient_Egyptian_agriculture|agricultural economy]] and a more sophisticated, centralized society that became a cornerstone in the history of human civilization.
sentence_21: [[Nomadic|Nomadic]] [[Anatomically_modern_human|modern human]] [[Hunter-gatherer|hunter-gatherers]] began living in the Nile valley through the end of the [[Pleistocene|Middle Pleistocene]] some 120,000 years ago.
sentence_22: By the late [[Paleolithic|Paleolithic]] period, the arid climate of Northern Africa became increasingly hot and dry, forcing the populations of the area to concentrate along the river region.
sentence_23: Main article: [[Predynastic_Egypt|Predynastic Egypt]]
sentence_24: In Predynastic and [[Early_Dynastic_Period_(Egypt)|Early Dynastic]] times, the [[African_humid_period|Egyptian climate was much less arid than it is today]].
sentence_25: Large regions of Egypt were covered in treed [[Savanna|savanna]] and traversed by herds of grazing [[Ungulates|ungulates]].
sentence_26: Foliage and fauna were far more prolific in all environs and the Nile region supported large populations of waterfowl.
sentence_27: Hunting would have been common for Egyptians, and this is also the period when many animals were first [[Domestication|domesticated]].
sentence_28: By about [[6th_millennium_BC|5500 BC]], small tribes living in the Nile valley had developed into a series of cultures demonstrating firm control of agriculture and [[Animal_husbandry|animal husbandry]], and identifiable by their [[Ancient_Egyptian_pottery|pottery]] and personal items, such as combs, bracelets, and beads.
sentence_29: The largest of these early cultures in upper (Southern) Egypt was the [[Badarian_culture|Badarian culture]], which probably originated in the Western Desert; it was known for its high quality ceramics, [[Stone_tool|stone tools]], and its use of copper.
sentence_30: The Badari was followed by the [[Naqada_culture|Naqada culture]]: the [[Amratian_culture|Amratian]] (Naqada I), the [[Gerzeh_culture|Gerzeh]] (Naqada II), and [[Semainean|Semainean]] (Naqada III).
sentence_31: These brought a number of technological improvements.
sentence_32: As early as the Naqada I Period, predynastic Egyptians imported [[Obsidian|obsidian]] from [[History_of_Ethiopia|Ethiopia]], used to shape blades and other objects from [[Lithic_flake|flakes]].
sentence_33: In Naqada II times, early evidence exists of contact with the [[Near_East|Near East]], particularly [[Canaan|Canaan]] and the [[Byblos|Byblos]] coast.
sentence_34: Over a period of about 1,000 years, the Naqada culture developed from a few small farming communities into a powerful civilization whose leaders were in complete control of the people and resources of the Nile valley.
sentence_35: Establishing a power center at [[Nekhen|Nekhen]] (in Greek, Hierakonpolis), and later at [[Abydos,_Egypt|Abydos]], [[Naqada_III|Naqada III]] leaders expanded their control of Egypt northwards along the [[Nile_Delta|Nile]].
sentence_36: They also traded with [[Nubia|Nubia]] to the south, the oases of the [[Libyan_Desert|western desert]] to the west, and the cultures of the [[Eastern_Mediterranean|eastern Mediterranean]] and [[Near_East|Near East]] to the east, initiating a period of [[Egypt-Mesopotamia_relations|Egypt-Mesopotamia relations]].
sentence_37: The Naqada culture manufactured a diverse selection of material goods, reflective of the increasing power and wealth of the elite, as well as societal personal-use items, which included combs, small statuary, painted pottery, high quality [[Hand_drill_(hieroglyph)|decorative stone vases]], [[Cosmetic_palette|cosmetic palettes]], and jewelry made of gold, lapis, and ivory.
sentence_38: They also developed a [[Ceramic_glaze|ceramic glaze]] known as [[Egyptian_faience|faience]], which was used well into the Roman Period to decorate cups, amulets, and figurines.
sentence_39: During the last predynastic phase, the Naqada culture began using written symbols that eventually were developed into a full system of [[Egyptian_hieroglyphs|hieroglyphs]] for writing the ancient Egyptian language.
sentence_40: Main article: [[Early_Dynastic_Period_(Egypt)|Early Dynastic Period (Egypt)]]
sentence_41: The Early Dynastic Period was approximately contemporary to the early Sumerian-[[Akkadian_Empire|Akkadian]] civilisation of Mesopotamia and of ancient [[Elam|Elam]].
sentence_42: The third-century BC Egyptian priest [[Manetho|Manetho]] grouped the long line of kings from [[Menes|Menes]] to his own time into 30 dynasties, a system still used today.
sentence_43: He began his official history with the king named "Meni" (or Menes in Greek) who was believed to have united the two kingdoms of [[Upper_Egypt|Upper]] and Lower Egypt.
sentence_44: The transition to a unified state happened more gradually than ancient Egyptian writers represented, and there is no contemporary record of Menes.
sentence_45: Some scholars now believe, however, that the mythical Menes may have been the king [[Narmer|Narmer]], who is depicted wearing royal regalia on the ceremonial Narmer Palette, in a symbolic act of unification.
sentence_46: In the Early Dynastic Period, which began about 3000 BC, the first of the Dynastic kings solidified control over lower Egypt by establishing a capital at [[Memphis,_Egypt|Memphis]], from which he could control the [[Labour_force|labour force]] and agriculture of the fertile delta region, as well as the lucrative and critical [[Trade_route|trade routes]] to the [[Levant|Levant]].
sentence_47: The increasing power and wealth of the kings during the early dynastic period was reflected in their elaborate [[Mastaba|mastaba]] tombs and mortuary cult structures at Abydos, which were used to celebrate the deified king after his death.
sentence_48: The strong institution of kingship developed by the kings served to legitimize state control over the land, labour, and resources that were essential to the survival and growth of ancient Egyptian civilization.
sentence_49: Main article: [[Old_Kingdom_of_Egypt|Old Kingdom of Egypt]]
sentence_50: Major advances in architecture, art, and technology were made during the [[Old_Kingdom|Old Kingdom]], fueled by the increased [[Agricultural_productivity|agricultural productivity]] and resulting population, made possible by a well-developed central administration.
sentence_51: Some of ancient Egypt's crowning achievements, the [[Giza_Necropolis|Giza pyramids]] and [[Great_Sphinx_of_Giza|Great Sphinx]], were constructed during the Old Kingdom.
sentence_52: Under the direction of the [[Vizier_(Ancient_Egypt)|vizier]], state officials collected taxes, coordinated irrigation projects to improve [[Crop_yield|crop yield]], drafted peasants to work on construction projects, and established a [[Criminal_law|justice system]] to maintain peace and order.
sentence_53: With the rising importance of central administration in Egypt a new class of educated scribes and officials arose who were granted estates by the king in payment for their services.
sentence_54: Kings also made land grants to their mortuary cults and local temples, to ensure that these institutions had the resources to worship the king after his death.
sentence_55: Scholars believe that five centuries of these practices slowly eroded the economic vitality of Egypt, and that the economy could no longer afford to support a large centralized administration.
sentence_56: As the power of the kings diminished, regional governors called [[Nomarch|nomarchs]] began to challenge the supremacy of the office of king.
sentence_57: This, coupled with [[4.2_kiloyear_event|severe droughts]] between 2200 and 2150 BC, is believed to have caused the country to enter the 140-year period of famine and strife known as the First Intermediate Period.
sentence_58: Main article: [[First_Intermediate_Period_of_Egypt|First Intermediate Period of Egypt]]
sentence_59: After Egypt's [[Central_government|central government]] collapsed at the end of the Old Kingdom, the administration could no longer support or stabilize the country's economy.
sentence_60: Regional governors could not rely on the king for help in times of crisis, and the ensuing food shortages and political disputes escalated into famines and small-scale civil wars.
sentence_61: Yet despite difficult problems, local leaders, owing no tribute to the king, used their new-found independence to establish a thriving culture in the provinces.
sentence_62: Once in control of their own resources, the provinces became economically richer—which was demonstrated by larger and better burials among all social classes.
sentence_63: In bursts of creativity, provincial artisans adopted and adapted cultural motifs formerly restricted to the royalty of the Old Kingdom, and scribes developed literary styles that expressed the [[Optimism|optimism]] and originality of the period.
sentence_64: Free from their loyalties to the king, local rulers began competing with each other for territorial control and [[Political_power|political power]].
sentence_65: By 2160 BC, rulers in [[Herakleopolis|Herakleopolis]] controlled Lower Egypt in the north, while a rival clan based in [[Thebes,_Egypt|Thebes]], the [[Intef_I|Intef family]], took control of Upper Egypt in the south.
sentence_66: As the Intefs grew in power and expanded their control northward, a clash between the two rival dynasties became inevitable.
sentence_67: Around 2055 BC the northern Theban forces under [[Mentuhotep_II|Nebhepetre Mentuhotep II]] finally defeated the Herakleopolitan rulers, reuniting the Two Lands.
sentence_68: They inaugurated a period of economic and cultural renaissance known as the [[Middle_Kingdom_of_Egypt|Middle Kingdom]].
sentence_69: Main article: [[Middle_Kingdom_of_Egypt|Middle Kingdom of Egypt]]
sentence_70: The kings of the Middle Kingdom restored the country's stability and prosperity, thereby stimulating a resurgence of art, literature, and monumental building projects.
sentence_71: Mentuhotep II and his [[Eleventh_Dynasty_of_Egypt|Eleventh Dynasty]] successors ruled from Thebes, but the vizier [[Amenemhat_I|Amenemhat I]], upon assuming the kingship at the beginning of the [[Twelfth_dynasty_of_Egypt|Twelfth Dynasty]] around 1985 BC, shifted the kingdom's capital to the city of [[Itjtawy|Itjtawy]], located in Faiyum.
sentence_72: From Itjtawy, the kings of the Twelfth Dynasty undertook a far-sighted [[Land_reclamation|land reclamation]] and irrigation scheme to increase agricultural output in the region.
sentence_73: Moreover, the military reconquered territory in [[Nubia|Nubia]] that was rich in quarries and gold mines, while laborers built a defensive structure in the Eastern Delta, called the "[[Walls_of_the_Ruler|Walls of the Ruler]]", to defend against foreign attack.
sentence_74: With the kings having secured the country militarily and politically and with vast agricultural and mineral wealth at their disposal, the nation's population, arts, and religion flourished.
sentence_75: In contrast to elitist Old Kingdom attitudes towards the gods, the Middle Kingdom displayed an increase in expressions of personal piety.
sentence_76: Middle Kingdom literature featured sophisticated themes and characters written in a confident, eloquent style.
sentence_77: The [[Relief|relief]] and portrait sculpture of the period captured subtle, individual details that reached new heights of technical sophistication.
sentence_78: The last great ruler of the Middle Kingdom, [[Amenemhat_III|Amenemhat III]], allowed [[Semitic_languages|Semitic]]-speaking [[Canaan|Canaanite]] settlers from the [[Near_East|Near East]] into the Delta region to provide a sufficient labour force for his especially active mining and building campaigns.
sentence_79: These ambitious building and mining activities, however, combined with severe [[Flooding_of_the_Nile|Nile floods]] later in his reign, strained the economy and precipitated the slow decline into the Second Intermediate Period during the later Thirteenth and Fourteenth dynasties.
sentence_80: During this decline, the Canaanite settlers began to assume greater control of the Delta region, eventually coming to power in Egypt as the [[Hyksos|Hyksos]].

section_6.value: Second Intermediate Period (1674–1549 BC) and the Hyksos

sentence_81: Main article: [[Second_Intermediate_Period_of_Egypt|Second Intermediate Period of Egypt]]
sentence_82: Around 1785 BC, as the power of the Middle Kingdom kings weakened, a [[Western_Asia|Western Asian]] people called the [[Hyksos|Hyksos]], who had already settled in the Delta, seized control of Egypt and established their capital at [[Avaris|Avaris]], forcing the former central government to retreat to [[Thebes,_Egypt|Thebes]].
sentence_83: The king was treated as a vassal and expected to pay tribute.
sentence_84: The Hyksos ("foreign rulers") retained Egyptian models of government and identified as kings, thereby integrating Egyptian elements into their culture.
sentence_85: They and other invaders introduced new tools of warfare into Egypt, most notably the [[Composite_bow|composite bow]] and the horse-drawn [[Chariot|chariot]].
sentence_86: After retreating south, the native Theban kings found themselves trapped between the Canaanite Hyksos ruling the north and the Hyksos' [[Nubian_people|Nubian]] allies, the [[Kingdom_of_Kush|Kushites]], to the south.
sentence_87: After years of vassalage, Thebes gathered enough strength to challenge the Hyksos in a conflict that lasted more than 30 years, until 1555 BC.
sentence_88: The kings [[Seqenenre_Tao_II|Seqenenre Tao II]] and [[Kamose|Kamose]] were ultimately able to defeat the [[Nubians|Nubians]] to the south of Egypt, but failed to defeat the Hyksos.
sentence_89: That task fell to Kamose's successor, [[Ahmose_I|Ahmose I]], who successfully waged a series of campaigns that permanently eradicated the Hyksos' presence in Egypt.
sentence_90: He established a new dynasty and, in the New Kingdom that followed, the military became a central priority for the kings, who sought to expand Egypt's borders and attempted to gain mastery of the [[Ancient_Near_East|Near East]].
sentence_91: Main article: [[New_Kingdom_of_Egypt|New Kingdom of Egypt]]
sentence_92: The New Kingdom pharaohs established a period of unprecedented prosperity by securing their borders and strengthening diplomatic ties with their neighbours, including the Mitanni Empire, [[Assyria|Assyria]], and [[Canaan|Canaan]].
sentence_93: Military campaigns waged under [[Thutmose_I|Tuthmosis I]] and his grandson [[Thutmose_III|Tuthmosis III]] extended the influence of the pharaohs to the largest empire Egypt had ever seen.
sentence_94: Beginning with [[Merneptah|Merneptah]] the rulers of Egypt adopted the title of [[Pharaoh|pharaoh]].
sentence_95: Between their reigns, [[Hatshepsut|Hatshepsut]], a queen who established herself as pharaoh, launched many building projects, including restoration of temples damaged by the Hyksos, and sent trading expeditions to [[Land_of_Punt|Punt]] and the Sinai.
sentence_96: When Tuthmosis III died in 1425 BC, Egypt had an empire extending from [[Niya_(kingdom)|Niya]] in north west [[Syria|Syria]] to the Fourth Cataract of the Nile in [[Nubia|Nubia]], cementing loyalties and opening access to critical imports such as [[Bronze|bronze]] and [[Wood|wood]].
sentence_97: The New Kingdom pharaohs began a large-scale building campaign to promote the god [[Amun|Amun]], whose growing cult was based in [[Karnak|Karnak]].
sentence_98: They also constructed monuments to glorify their own achievements, both real and imagined.
sentence_99: The Karnak temple is the largest Egyptian temple ever built.
sentence_100: Around 1350 BC, the stability of the New Kingdom was threatened when Amenhotep IV ascended the throne and instituted a series of radical and chaotic reforms.
sentence_101: Changing his name to [[Akhenaten|Akhenaten]], he touted the previously obscure [[Solar_deity|sun deity]] [[Aten|Aten]] as the [[God|supreme deity]], suppressed the worship of most other deities, and moved the capital to the new city of Akhetaten (modern-day [[Amarna|Amarna]]).
sentence_102: He was devoted to his new [[Atenism|religion]] and [[Amarna_art|artistic style]].
sentence_103: After his death, the cult of the Aten was quickly abandoned and the traditional religious order restored.
sentence_104: The subsequent pharaohs, [[Tutankhamun|Tutankhamun]], [[Ay|Ay]], and [[Horemheb|Horemheb]], worked to erase all mention of Akhenaten's heresy, now known as the Amarna Period.
sentence_105: Around 1279 BC, [[Ramesses_II|Ramesses II]], also known as Ramesses the Great, ascended the throne, and went on to build more temples, erect more statues and obelisks, and sire more children than any other pharaoh in history.
sentence_106: A bold military leader, Ramesses II led his army against the [[Hittites|Hittites]] in the [[Battle_of_Kadesh|Battle of Kadesh]] (in modern [[Syria|Syria]]) and, after fighting to a stalemate, finally agreed to the first recorded [[Egyptian–Hittite_peace_treaty|peace treaty]], around 1258 BC.
sentence_107: Egypt's wealth, however, made it a tempting target for invasion, particularly by the [[Ancient_Libya|Libyan]] Berbers to the west, and the [[Sea_Peoples|Sea Peoples]], a conjectured confederation of seafarers from the [[Aegean_Sea|Aegean Sea]].
sentence_108: Initially, the military was able to repel these invasions, but Egypt eventually lost control of its remaining territories in southern [[Canaan|Canaan]], much of it falling to the Assyrians.
sentence_109: The effects of external threats were exacerbated by internal problems such as corruption, tomb robbery, and civil unrest.
sentence_110: After regaining their power, the high priests at the [[Precinct_of_Amun-Re|temple of Amun]] in Thebes accumulated vast tracts of land and wealth, and their expanded power splintered the country during the Third Intermediate Period.
sentence_111: Main article: [[Third_Intermediate_Period_of_Egypt|Third Intermediate Period of Egypt]]
sentence_112: Following the death of [[Ramesses_XI|Ramesses XI]] in 1078 BC, [[Smendes|Smendes]] assumed authority over the northern part of Egypt, ruling from the city of [[Tanis,_Egypt|Tanis]].
sentence_113: The south was effectively controlled by the [[Theban_High_Priests_of_Amun_(21st_and_22nd_Dynasty)|High Priests of Amun at Thebes]], who recognized Smendes in name only.
sentence_114: During this time, Libyans had been settling in the western delta, and chieftains of these settlers began increasing their autonomy.
sentence_115: Libyan princes took control of the delta under [[Shoshenq_I|Shoshenq I]] in 945 BC, founding the so-called Libyan or Bubastite dynasty that would rule for some 200 years.
sentence_116: Shoshenq also gained control of southern Egypt by placing his family members in important priestly positions.
sentence_117: Libyan control began to erode as a rival dynasty in the delta arose in [[Leontopolis|Leontopolis]], and [[Cushi|Kushites]] threatened from the south.
sentence_118: Around 727 BC the Kushite king [[Piye|Piye]] invaded northward, seizing control of Thebes and eventually the Delta, which established the [[25th_Dynasty|25th Dynasty]].
sentence_119: During the 25th Dynasty, Pharaoh [[Taharqa|Taharqa]] created an empire nearly as large as the [[New_Kingdom|New Kingdom]]'s.
sentence_120: Twenty-fifth Dynasty pharaohs built, or restored, temples and monuments throughout the Nile valley, including at Memphis, Karnak, Kawa, and Jebel Barkal.
