sentence_121: During this period, the Nile valley saw the first widespread construction of [[Nubian_pyramids|pyramids (many in modern Sudan)]] since the Middle Kingdom.
sentence_122: Egypt's far-reaching prestige declined considerably toward the end of the Third Intermediate Period.
sentence_123: Its foreign allies had fallen under the [[Assyria|Assyrian]] sphere of influence, and by 700 BC war between the two states became inevitable.
sentence_124: Between 671 and 667 BC the Assyrians began the [[Assyrian_conquest_of_Egypt|Assyrian conquest of Egypt]].
sentence_125: The reigns of both [[Taharqa|Taharqa]] and his successor, [[Tantamani|Tanutamun]], were filled with constant conflict with the Assyrians, against whom Egypt enjoyed several victories.
sentence_126: Ultimately, the Assyrians pushed the Kushites back into Nubia, occupied Memphis, and [[Sack_of_Thebes|sacked the temples of Thebes]].
sentence_127: Main articles: [[Late_Period_of_ancient_Egypt|Late Period of ancient Egypt]] and [[History_of_Persian_Egypt|History of Persian Egypt]]
sentence_128: The Assyrians left control of Egypt to a series of vassals who became known as the Saite kings of the [[Twenty-sixth_dynasty_of_Egypt|Twenty-Sixth Dynasty]].
sentence_129: By 653 BC, the Saite king Psamtik I was able to oust the Assyrians with the help of Greek mercenaries, who were recruited to form Egypt's first [[Ancient_Egyptian_navy|navy]].
sentence_130: [[Colonies_in_antiquity|Greek influence]] expanded greatly as the [[Polis|city-state]] of [[Naucratis|Naukratis]] became the home of Greeks in the Nile Delta.
sentence_131: The Saite kings based in the new capital of [[Sais,_Egypt|Sais]] witnessed a brief but spirited resurgence in the economy and culture, but in 525 BC, the powerful Persians, led by [[Cambyses_II_of_Persia|Cambyses II]], began their conquest of Egypt, eventually capturing the pharaoh [[Psamtik_III|Psamtik III]] at the [[Battle_of_Pelusium_(343_BC)|Battle of Pelusium]].
sentence_132: Cambyses II then assumed the formal title of pharaoh, but ruled Egypt from Iran, leaving Egypt under the control of a satrapy.
sentence_133: A few successful revolts against the Persians marked the 5th century BC, but Egypt was never able to permanently overthrow the Persians.
sentence_134: Following its annexation by Persia, Egypt was joined with [[Cyprus|Cyprus]] and [[Phoenicia|Phoenicia]] in the sixth [[Satrap|satrapy]] of the [[Achaemenid_Empire|Achaemenid Persian Empire]].
sentence_135: This first period of Persian rule over Egypt, also known as the [[Twenty-Seventh_Dynasty|Twenty-Seventh Dynasty]], ended in 402 BC, when Egypt regained independence under a series of native dynasties.
sentence_136: The last of these dynasties, the [[Thirtieth_Dynasty_of_Egypt|Thirtieth]], proved to be the last native royal house of ancient Egypt, ending with the kingship of [[Nectanebo_II|Nectanebo II]].
sentence_137: A brief restoration of Persian rule, sometimes known as the [[Achaemenid_Empire|Thirty-First Dynasty]], began in 343 BC, but shortly after, in 332 BC, the Persian ruler Mazaces handed Egypt over to [[Alexander_the_Great|Alexander the Great]] without a fight.
sentence_138: Main article: [[Ptolemaic_Kingdom|Ptolemaic Kingdom]]
sentence_139: In 332 BC, [[Alexander_the_Great|Alexander the Great]] conquered Egypt with little resistance from the [[Persia|Persians]] and was welcomed by the Egyptians as a deliverer.
sentence_140: The administration established by Alexander's successors, the [[Ancient_Macedonians|Macedonian]] [[Ptolemaic_Kingdom|Ptolemaic Kingdom]], was based on an Egyptian model and based in the new [[Capital_(political)|capital city]] of [[Alexandria|Alexandria]].
sentence_141: The city showcased the power and prestige of Hellenistic rule, and became a [[Seat_of_Wisdom|seat of learning]] and culture, centered at the famous [[Library_of_Alexandria|Library of Alexandria]].
sentence_142: The [[Lighthouse_of_Alexandria|Lighthouse of Alexandria]] lit the way for the many ships that kept trade flowing through the city—as the Ptolemies made commerce and revenue-generating enterprises, such as papyrus manufacturing, their top priority.
sentence_143: [[Hellenistic_civilization|Hellenistic culture]] did not supplant native Egyptian culture, as the Ptolemies supported time-honored traditions in an effort to secure the loyalty of the populace.
sentence_144: They built new temples in Egyptian style, supported traditional cults, and portrayed themselves as pharaohs.
sentence_145: Some traditions merged, as Greek and [[Egyptian_mythology|Egyptian gods]] were [[Syncretic_religion|syncretized]] into composite deities, such as [[Serapis|Serapis]], and classical Greek forms of sculpture influenced traditional Egyptian motifs.
sentence_146: Despite their efforts to appease the Egyptians, the Ptolemies were challenged by native rebellion, bitter family rivalries, and the powerful mob of Alexandria that formed after the death of [[Ptolemy_IV_Philopator|Ptolemy IV]].
sentence_147: In addition, as [[Ancient_Rome|Rome]] relied more heavily on imports of grain from Egypt, the [[Ancient_Rome|Romans]] took great interest in the political situation in the country.
sentence_148: Continued Egyptian revolts, ambitious politicians, and powerful opponents from the [[Near_East|Near East]] made this situation unstable, leading Rome to send forces to secure the country as a province of its empire.
sentence_149: Main article: [[Egypt_(Roman_province)|Egypt (Roman province)]]
sentence_150: Egypt became a province of the [[Roman_Empire|Roman Empire]] in 30 BC, following the defeat of [[Mark_Antony|Marc Antony]] and [[History_of_Ptolemaic_Egypt|Ptolemaic]] Queen [[Cleopatra_VII|Cleopatra VII]] by [[Octavian|Octavian]] (later Emperor Augustus) in the [[Battle_of_Actium|Battle of Actium]].
sentence_151: The Romans relied heavily on grain shipments from Egypt, and the Roman army, under the control of a prefect appointed by the Emperor, quelled rebellions, strictly enforced the collection of heavy taxes, and prevented attacks by bandits, which had become a notorious problem during the period.
sentence_152: Alexandria became an increasingly important center on the trade route with the orient, as exotic luxuries were in high demand in Rome.
sentence_153: Although the Romans had a more hostile attitude than the Greeks towards the Egyptians, some traditions such as mummification and worship of the traditional gods continued.
sentence_154: The art of mummy portraiture flourished, and some Roman emperors had themselves depicted as pharaohs, though not to the extent that the Ptolemies had.
sentence_155: The former lived outside Egypt and did not perform the ceremonial functions of Egyptian kingship.
sentence_156: Local administration became Roman in style and closed to native Egyptians.
sentence_157: From the mid-first century AD, [[Christianity|Christianity]] took root in Egypt and it was originally seen as another cult that could be accepted.
sentence_158: However, it was an uncompromising religion that sought to win converts from [[Ancient_Egyptian_religion|Egyptian Religion]] and Greco-Roman religion and threatened popular religious traditions.
sentence_159: This led to the persecution of converts to Christianity, culminating in the great purges of [[Diocletian|Diocletian]] starting in 303, but eventually Christianity won out.
sentence_160: In 391 the Christian Emperor [[Theodosius_I|Theodosius]] introduced legislation that banned pagan rites and closed temples.
sentence_161: Alexandria became the scene of great anti-pagan riots with public and private religious imagery destroyed.
sentence_162: As a consequence, Egypt's native religious culture was continually in decline.
sentence_163: While the native population continued to speak [[Egyptian_language|their language]], the ability to read [[Egyptian_hieroglyphs|hieroglyphic writing]] slowly disappeared as the role of the Egyptian temple priests and priestesses diminished.
sentence_164: The temples themselves were sometimes converted to [[Church_(building)|churches]] or abandoned to the desert.
sentence_165: In the fourth century, as the Roman Empire divided, Egypt found itself in the Eastern Empire with its capital at Constantinople.
sentence_166: In the waning years of the Empire, Egypt fell to the [[Sasanian_Egypt|Sasanian Persian]] army in the [[Sasanian_conquest_of_Egypt|Sasanian conquest of Egypt]] (618–628).
sentence_167: It was then recaptured by the Roman Emperor [[Heraclius|Heraclius]] (629–639), and was finally captured by Muslim Rashidun army in 639–641, ending Roman rule.
sentence_168: The [[Pharaoh|pharaoh]] was the absolute monarch of the country and, at least in theory, wielded complete control of the land and its resources.
sentence_169: The king was the supreme military commander and head of the government, who relied on a bureaucracy of officials to manage his affairs.
sentence_170: In charge of the administration was his second in command, the [[Vizier_(Ancient_Egypt)|vizier]], who acted as the king's representative and coordinated land surveys, the treasury, building projects, the legal system, and the [[Archives|archives]].
sentence_171: At a regional level, the country was divided into as many as 42 administrative regions called [[Nome_(Egypt)|nomes]] each governed by a [[Nomarch|nomarch]], who was accountable to the vizier for his jurisdiction.
sentence_172: The [[Egyptian_temple|temples]] formed the backbone of the economy.
sentence_173: Not only were they [[Place_of_worship|houses of worship]], but were also responsible for collecting and storing the kingdom's wealth in a system of [[Granary|granaries]] and treasuries administered by overseers, who redistributed grain and goods.
sentence_174: Much of the economy was centrally organized and strictly controlled.
sentence_175: Although the ancient Egyptians did not use [[Currency|coinage]] until the [[Late_Period_of_ancient_Egypt|Late period]], they did use a type of money-barter system, with standard sacks of grain and the [[Deben_(unit)|deben]], a weight of roughly 91 grams (3 oz) of copper or silver, forming a common denominator.
sentence_176: Workers were paid in grain; a simple laborer might earn 5​⁄2 sacks (200 kg or 400 lb) of grain per month, while a foreman might earn 7​⁄2 sacks (250 kg or 550 lb).
sentence_177: Prices were fixed across the country and recorded in lists to facilitate trading; for example a shirt cost five copper deben, while a cow cost 140 deben.
sentence_178: Grain could be traded for other goods, according to the fixed price list.
sentence_179: During the fifth century BC coined money was introduced into Egypt from abroad.
sentence_180: At first the coins were used as standardized pieces of [[Precious_metal|precious metal]] rather than true money, but in the following centuries international traders came to rely on coinage.
sentence_181: Egyptian society was highly stratified, and social status was expressly displayed.
sentence_182: Farmers made up the bulk of the population, but agricultural produce was owned directly by the state, temple, or noble family that owned the land.
sentence_183: Farmers were also subject to a labor tax and were required to work on irrigation or construction projects in a [[Corvée|corvée]] system.
sentence_184: Artists and craftsmen were of higher status than farmers, but they were also under state control, working in the shops attached to the temples and paid directly from the state treasury.
sentence_185: Scribes and officials formed the upper class in ancient Egypt, known as the "white kilt class" in reference to the bleached linen garments that served as a mark of their rank.
sentence_186: The upper class prominently displayed their social status in art and literature.
sentence_187: Below the nobility were the priests, physicians, and engineers with specialized training in their field.
sentence_188: It is unclear whether [[Slavery|slavery]] as understood today existed in ancient Egypt, there is difference of opinions among authors.
sentence_189: The ancient Egyptians viewed men and women, including people from all social classes, as essentially equal under the law, and even the lowliest [[Peasant|peasant]] was entitled to petition the [[Vizier_(Ancient_Egypt)|vizier]] and his court for redress.
sentence_190: Although slaves were mostly used as indentured servants, they were able to buy and sell their servitude, work their way to freedom or nobility, and were usually treated by [[Physician|doctors]] in the workplace.
sentence_191: Both men and women had the right to own and sell property, make contracts, marry and divorce, receive inheritance, and pursue legal disputes in court.
sentence_192: Married couples could own property jointly and protect themselves from divorce by agreeing to marriage contracts, which stipulated the financial obligations of the husband to his wife and children should the marriage end.
sentence_193: Compared with their counterparts in ancient Greece, Rome, and even more modern places around the world, ancient Egyptian women had a greater range of personal choices, legal rights, and opportunities for achievement.
sentence_194: Women such as [[Hatshepsut|Hatshepsut]] and [[Cleopatra_VII|Cleopatra VII]] even became pharaohs, while others wielded power as [[God's_Wife_of_Amun|Divine Wives of Amun]].
sentence_195: Despite these freedoms, [[Women_in_ancient_Egypt|ancient Egyptian women]] did not often take part in official roles in the administration, aside from the royal high priestesses, apparently served only secondary roles in the temples (not much data for many dynasties), and were not so likely to be as educated as men.
sentence_196: The head of the legal system was officially the pharaoh, who was responsible for enacting laws, delivering justice, and maintaining law and order, a concept the ancient Egyptians referred to as [[Ma'at|Ma'at]].
sentence_197: Although no legal codes from ancient Egypt survive, court documents show that Egyptian law was based on a common-sense view of right and wrong that emphasized reaching agreements and resolving conflicts rather than strictly adhering to a complicated set of statutes.
sentence_198: Local councils of elders, known as Kenbet in the New Kingdom, were responsible for ruling in court cases involving small claims and minor disputes.
sentence_199: More serious cases involving murder, major land transactions, and tomb robbery were referred to the Great Kenbet, over which the vizier or pharaoh presided.
sentence_200: Plaintiffs and defendants were expected to represent themselves and were required to swear an oath that they had told the truth.
sentence_201: In some cases, the state took on both the role of prosecutor and judge, and it could torture the accused with beatings to obtain a confession and the names of any co-conspirators.
sentence_202: Whether the charges were trivial or serious, court scribes documented the complaint, testimony, and verdict of the case for future reference.
sentence_203: Punishment for minor crimes involved either imposition of fines, beatings, facial mutilation, or exile, depending on the severity of the offense.
sentence_204: Serious crimes such as murder and tomb robbery were punished by execution, carried out by decapitation, drowning, or [[Impalement|impaling]] the criminal on a stake.
sentence_205: Punishment could also be extended to the criminal's family.
sentence_206: Beginning in the New Kingdom, [[Oracle|oracles]] played a major role in the legal system, dispensing justice in both civil and criminal cases.
sentence_207: The procedure was to ask the god a "yes" or "no" question concerning the right or wrong of an issue.
sentence_208: The god, carried by a number of priests, rendered judgement by choosing one or the other, moving forward or backward, or pointing to one of the answers written on a piece of papyrus or an [[Ostracon|ostracon]].
sentence_209: Main article: [[Ancient_Egyptian_agriculture|Ancient Egyptian agriculture]]
sentence_210: See also: [[Gardens_of_ancient_Egypt|Gardens of ancient Egypt]]
sentence_211: A combination of favorable geographical features contributed to the success of ancient Egyptian culture, the most important of which was the rich [[Fertile_soil|fertile soil]] resulting from annual inundations of the Nile River.
sentence_212: The ancient Egyptians were thus able to produce an abundance of food, allowing the population to devote more time and resources to cultural, technological, and artistic pursuits.
sentence_213: [[Land_management|Land management]] was crucial in ancient Egypt because taxes were assessed based on the amount of land a person owned.
sentence_214: Farming in Egypt was dependent on the cycle of the Nile River.
sentence_215: The Egyptians recognized three seasons: [[Season_of_the_Inundation|Akhet]] (flooding), [[Season_of_the_Emergence|Peret]] (planting), and [[Season_of_the_Harvest|Shemu]] (harvesting).
sentence_216: The flooding season lasted from June to September, depositing on the river's banks a layer of mineral-rich silt ideal for growing crops.
sentence_217: After the floodwaters had receded, the [[Growing_season|growing season]] lasted from October to February.
sentence_218: Farmers plowed and planted seeds in the fields, which were irrigated with ditches and canals.
sentence_219: Egypt received little rainfall, so farmers relied on the Nile to water their crops.
sentence_220: From March to May, farmers used [[Sickle|sickles]] to harvest their crops, which were then [[Threshing|threshed]] with a [[Flail|flail]] to separate the straw from the grain.
sentence_221: [[Winnowing|Winnowing]] removed the [[Chaff|chaff]] from the grain, and the grain was then ground into flour, brewed to make beer, or stored for later use.
sentence_222: The ancient Egyptians cultivated [[Emmer|emmer]] and [[Barley|barley]], and several other cereal grains, all of which were used to make the two main food staples of bread and beer.
sentence_223: [[Flax|Flax]] plants, uprooted before they started flowering, were grown for the fibers of their stems.
sentence_224: These fibers were split along their length and spun into thread, which was used to weave sheets of [[Linen|linen]] and to make clothing.
sentence_225: [[Papyrus|Papyrus]] growing on the banks of the Nile River was used to make paper.
sentence_226: Vegetables and fruits were grown in garden plots, close to habitations and on higher ground, and had to be watered by hand.
sentence_227: Vegetables included leeks, garlic, melons, squashes, pulses, lettuce, and other crops, in addition to grapes that were made into wine.
sentence_228: The Egyptians believed that a balanced relationship between people and [[Animal|animals]] was an essential element of the cosmic order; thus humans, animals and plants were believed to be members of a single whole.
sentence_229: Animals, both [[Domestication|domesticated]] and [[Wildlife|wild]], were therefore a critical source of spirituality, companionship, and sustenance to the ancient Egyptians.
sentence_230: [[Ancient_Egyptian_cattle|Cattle]] were the most important livestock; the administration collected taxes on livestock in regular [[Cattle_count|censuses]], and the size of a herd reflected the prestige and importance of the estate or temple that owned them.
sentence_231: In addition to cattle, the ancient Egyptians kept sheep, goats, and pigs.
sentence_232: [[Poultry|Poultry]], such as ducks, geese, and pigeons, were captured in nets and bred on farms, where they were force-fed with dough to fatten them.
sentence_233: The Nile provided a plentiful source of [[Fish|fish]].
sentence_234: Bees were also domesticated from at least the Old Kingdom, and provided both honey and wax.
sentence_235: The ancient Egyptians used donkeys and oxen as [[Working_animal|beasts of burden]], and they were responsible for plowing the fields and trampling seed into the soil.
sentence_236: The slaughter of a fattened ox was also a central part of an offering ritual.
sentence_237: Horses were introduced by the [[Hyksos|Hyksos]] in the [[Second_Intermediate_Period|Second Intermediate Period]].
sentence_238: Camels, although known from the New Kingdom, were not used as beasts of burden until the Late Period.
sentence_239: There is also evidence to suggest that [[North_African_elephant|elephants]] were briefly utilized in the Late Period but largely abandoned due to lack of [[Grazing|grazing]] land.
sentence_240: [[Cats_in_ancient_Egypt|Cats]], dogs, and monkeys were common family pets, while more exotic pets imported from the heart of Africa, such as [[Sub-Saharan_Africa|Sub-Saharan African]] [[Lion|lions]], were reserved for royalty.
sentence_241: [[Herodotus|Herodotus]] observed that the Egyptians were the only people to keep their animals with them in their houses.
sentence_242: During the Late Period, the worship of the gods in their animal form was extremely popular, such as the cat goddess [[Bastet_(mythology)|Bastet]] and the ibis god [[Thoth|Thoth]], and these animals were kept in large numbers for the purpose of ritual sacrifice.
sentence_243: Further information: [[Mining_industry_of_Egypt|Mining industry of Egypt]] and Stone quarries of ancient Egypt
sentence_244: Egypt is rich in building and decorative stone, copper and lead ores, gold, and semiprecious stones.
sentence_245: These [[Natural_resource|natural resources]] allowed the ancient Egyptians to build monuments, sculpt statues, make tools, and fashion jewelry.
sentence_246: Embalmers used salts from the [[Wadi_El_Natrun|Wadi Natrun]] for [[Mummy|mummification]], which also provided the [[Gypsum|gypsum]] needed to make plaster.
sentence_247: Ore-bearing [[Rock_formation|rock formations]] were found in distant, inhospitable wadis in the [[Eastern_Desert|Eastern Desert]] and the Sinai, requiring large, state-controlled expeditions to obtain natural resources found there.
sentence_248: There were extensive [[Gold_mining|gold mines]] in [[Nubia|Nubia]], and one of the first maps known is of a gold mine in this region.
sentence_249: The [[Wadi_Hammamat|Wadi Hammamat]] was a notable source of granite, greywacke, and gold.
sentence_250: [[Flint|Flint]] was the first mineral collected and used to make tools, and flint handaxes are the earliest pieces of evidence of habitation in the Nile valley.
sentence_251: Nodules of the mineral were carefully flaked to make blades and arrowheads of moderate hardness and durability even after copper was adopted for this purpose.
sentence_252: Ancient Egyptians were among the first to use minerals such as [[Sulfur|sulfur]] as cosmetic substances.
sentence_253: The Egyptians worked deposits of the [[Lead|lead ore]] [[Galena|galena]] at Gebel Rosas to make net sinkers, plumb bobs, and small figurines.
sentence_254: Copper was the most important metal for toolmaking in ancient Egypt and was smelted in furnaces from [[Malachite|malachite]] ore mined in the Sinai.
sentence_255: Workers collected gold by washing the nuggets out of sediment in [[Alluvium|alluvial deposits]], or by the more labor-intensive process of grinding and washing gold-bearing quartzite.
sentence_256: Iron deposits found in upper Egypt were utilized in the Late Period.
sentence_257: High-quality building stones were abundant in Egypt; the ancient Egyptians quarried limestone all along the Nile valley, granite from Aswan, and basalt and sandstone from the wadis of the Eastern Desert.
sentence_258: Deposits of decorative stones such as [[Porphyry_(geology)|porphyry]], greywacke, [[Alabaster|alabaster]], and [[Carnelian|carnelian]] dotted the Eastern Desert and were collected even before the First Dynasty.
sentence_259: In the Ptolemaic and Roman Periods, miners worked deposits of [[Emerald|emeralds]] in Wadi Sikait and [[Amethyst|amethyst]] in [[Wadi_el-Hudi|Wadi el-Hudi]].
sentence_260: Main article: [[Ancient_Egyptian_trade|Ancient Egyptian trade]]
sentence_261: The ancient Egyptians engaged in trade with their [[Foreign_contacts_of_ancient_Egypt|foreign neighbors]] to obtain rare, exotic goods not found in Egypt.
sentence_262: In the [[Predynastic_Egypt|Predynastic Period]], they established trade with Nubia to obtain gold and incense.
sentence_263: They also established trade with Palestine, as evidenced by Palestinian-style oil jugs found in the burials of the First Dynasty pharaohs.
sentence_264: An Egyptian colony stationed in southern [[Canaan|Canaan]] dates to slightly before the First Dynasty.
sentence_265: [[Narmer|Narmer]] had Egyptian pottery produced in Canaan and exported back to [[Egypt|Egypt]].
sentence_266: By the Second Dynasty at latest, ancient Egyptian trade with [[Byblos|Byblos]] yielded a critical source of quality timber not found in Egypt.
sentence_267: By the Fifth Dynasty, trade with [[Land_of_Punt|Punt]] provided gold, aromatic resins, ebony, ivory, and wild animals such as monkeys and baboons.
sentence_268: Egypt relied on trade with [[Anatolia|Anatolia]] for essential quantities of tin as well as supplementary supplies of copper, both metals being necessary for the manufacture of bronze.
sentence_269: The ancient Egyptians prized the blue stone [[Lapis_lazuli|lapis lazuli]], which had to be imported from far-away [[Afghanistan|Afghanistan]].
sentence_270: Egypt's Mediterranean trade partners also included [[Ancient_Greece|Greece]] and Crete, which provided, among other goods, supplies of [[Olive_oil|olive oil]].
sentence_271: In exchange for its luxury imports and raw materials, Egypt mainly exported grain, gold, linen, and papyrus, in addition to other finished goods including glass and stone objects.
sentence_272: Main article: [[Egyptian_language|Egyptian language]]
sentence_273: The [[Egyptian_language|Egyptian language]] is a northern [[Afro-Asiatic_languages|Afro-Asiatic]] language closely related to the [[Berber_languages|Berber]] and [[Semitic_languages|Semitic languages]].
sentence_274: It has the second longest known history of any language (after [[Sumerian_language|Sumerian]]), having been written from c. 3200 BC to the Middle Ages and remaining as a spoken language for longer.
sentence_275: The phases of ancient Egyptian are [[Old_Egyptian|Old Egyptian]], [[Middle_Egyptian|Middle Egyptian]] (Classical Egyptian), [[Late_Egyptian|Late Egyptian]], [[Demotic_(Egyptian)|Demotic]] and [[Coptic_language|Coptic]].
sentence_276: Egyptian writings do not show dialect differences before Coptic, but it was probably spoken in regional dialects around Memphis and later Thebes.
sentence_277: Ancient Egyptian was a [[Synthetic_language|synthetic language]], but it became more analytic later on.
sentence_278: Late Egyptian developed prefixal definite and indefinite [[Article_(grammar)|articles]], which replaced the older inflectional [[Suffix|suffixes]].
sentence_279: There was a change from the older [[Verb–subject–object|verb–subject–object]] [[Word_order|word order]] to [[Subject–verb–object|subject–verb–object]].
sentence_280: The Egyptian [[Egyptian_hieroglyphs|hieroglyphic]], [[Hieratic|hieratic]], and demotic scripts were eventually replaced by the more phonetic Coptic alphabet.
sentence_281: Coptic is still used in the liturgy of the [[Coptic_Orthodox_Church_of_Alexandria|Egyptian Orthodox Church]], and traces of it are found in modern [[Egyptian_Arabic|Egyptian Arabic]].
sentence_282: Ancient Egyptian has 25 consonants similar to those of other Afro-Asiatic languages.
sentence_283: These include pharyngeal and emphatic consonants, voiced and voiceless stops, voiceless fricatives and voiced and voiceless [[Affricate_consonant|affricates]].
sentence_284: It has three long and three short vowels, which expanded in Late Egyptian to about nine.
sentence_285: The basic word in Egyptian, similar to Semitic and Berber, is a [[Semitic_root|triliteral]] or biliteral root of consonants and semiconsonants.
sentence_286: Suffixes are added to form words.
sentence_287: The verb conjugation corresponds to the person.
sentence_288: For example, the triconsonantal skeleton S-Ḏ-M is the semantic core of the word 'hear'; its basic conjugation is sḏm, 'he hears'.
sentence_289: If the subject is a noun, suffixes are not added to the verb: sḏm ḥmt, 'the woman hears'.
sentence_290: Adjectives are derived from nouns through a process that Egyptologists call [[Arabic_grammar|nisbation]] because of its similarity with Arabic.
sentence_291: The word order is predicate–subject in verbal and adjectival sentences, and subject–predicate in nominal and adverbial sentences.
sentence_292: The subject can be moved to the beginning of sentences if it is long and is followed by a resumptive pronoun.
sentence_293: Verbs and nouns are negated by the [[Grammatical_particle|particle]] n, but nn is used for adverbial and adjectival sentences.
sentence_294: [[Stress_(linguistics)|Stress]] falls on the ultimate or penultimate syllable, which can be open (CV) or closed (CVC).
sentence_295: [[Egyptian_hieroglyphs|Hieroglyphic writing]] dates from c. 3000 BC, and is composed of hundreds of symbols.
sentence_296: A hieroglyph can represent a word, a sound, or a silent determinative; and the same symbol can serve different purposes in different contexts.
sentence_297: Hieroglyphs were a formal script, used on stone monuments and in tombs, that could be as detailed as individual works of art.
sentence_298: In day-to-day writing, scribes used a cursive form of writing, called [[Hieratic|hieratic]], which was quicker and easier.
sentence_299: While formal hieroglyphs may be read in rows or columns in either direction (though typically written from right to left), hieratic was always written from right to left, usually in horizontal rows.
sentence_300: A new form of writing, [[Demotic_(Egyptian)|Demotic]], became the prevalent writing style, and it is this form of writing—along with formal hieroglyphs—that accompany the Greek text on the Rosetta Stone.
sentence_301: Around the first century AD, the Coptic alphabet started to be used alongside the Demotic script.
sentence_302: Coptic is a modified [[Greek_alphabet|Greek alphabet]] with the addition of some Demotic signs.
sentence_303: Although formal hieroglyphs were used in a ceremonial role until the fourth century, towards the end only a small handful of priests could still read them.
sentence_304: As the traditional religious establishments were disbanded, knowledge of hieroglyphic writing was mostly lost.
sentence_305: Attempts to decipher them date to the Byzantine and Islamic periods in Egypt, but only in the 1820s, after the discovery of the Rosetta Stone and years of research by [[Thomas_Young_(scientist)|Thomas Young]] and [[Jean-François_Champollion|Jean-François Champollion]], were hieroglyphs [[Decipherment_of_ancient_Egyptian_scripts|substantially deciphered]].
sentence_306: Main article: [[Ancient_Egyptian_literature|Ancient Egyptian literature]]
sentence_307: Writing first appeared in association with kingship on labels and tags for items found in royal tombs.
sentence_308: It was primarily an occupation of the scribes, who worked out of the Per Ankh institution or the House of Life.
sentence_309: The latter comprised offices, libraries (called House of Books), laboratories and observatories.
sentence_310: Some of the best-known pieces of ancient Egyptian literature, such as the [[Pyramid_Texts|Pyramid]] and [[Coffin_Texts|Coffin Texts]], were written in Classical Egyptian, which continued to be the language of writing until about 1300 BC.
sentence_311: Late Egyptian was spoken from the New Kingdom onward and is represented in [[Ramesside_Period|Ramesside]] administrative documents, love poetry and tales, as well as in Demotic and Coptic texts.
sentence_312: During this period, the tradition of writing had evolved into the tomb autobiography, such as those of [[Harkhuf|Harkhuf]] and [[Weni_the_Elder|Weni]].
sentence_313: The genre known as [[Sebayt|Sebayt]] ("instructions") was developed to communicate teachings and guidance from famous nobles; the [[Ipuwer_Papyrus|Ipuwer papyrus]], a poem of lamentations describing [[Natural_disaster|natural disasters]] and social upheaval, is a famous example.
sentence_314: The [[Story_of_Sinuhe|Story of Sinuhe]], written in [[Middle_Egyptian|Middle Egyptian]], might be the classic of Egyptian literature.
sentence_315: Also written at this time was the [[Westcar_Papyrus|Westcar Papyrus]], a set of stories told to [[Khufu|Khufu]] by his sons relating the marvels performed by priests.
sentence_316: The [[Instruction_of_Amenemope|Instruction of Amenemope]] is considered a masterpiece of Near Eastern literature.
sentence_317: Towards the end of the New Kingdom, the [[Late_Egyptian|vernacular language]] was more often employed to write popular pieces like the [[Story_of_Wenamun|Story of Wenamun]] and the [[Instruction_of_Any|Instruction of Any]].
sentence_318: The former tells the story of a noble who is robbed on his way to buy cedar from Lebanon and of his struggle to return to Egypt.
sentence_319: From about 700 BC, narrative stories and instructions, such as the popular Instructions of Onchsheshonqy, as well as personal and business documents were written in the [[Demotic_(Egyptian)|demotic]] script and phase of Egyptian.
sentence_320: Many stories written in demotic during the Greco-Roman period were set in previous historical eras, when Egypt was an independent nation ruled by great pharaohs such as [[Ramesses_II|Ramesses II]].
sentence_321: Further information: [[Clothing_in_ancient_Egypt|Clothing in ancient Egypt]], [[Dance_in_ancient_Egypt|Dance in ancient Egypt]], and [[Music_of_Egypt#Old_Kingdom|Music of Egypt § Old Kingdom]]
sentence_322: Most ancient Egyptians were farmers tied to the land.
sentence_323: Their dwellings were restricted to immediate family members, and were constructed of [[Mudbrick|mudbrick]] designed to remain cool in the heat of the day.
sentence_324: Each home had a kitchen with an open roof, which contained a grindstone for milling grain and a small oven for baking the bread.
sentence_325: [[Ancient_Egyptian_pottery|Ceramics]] served as household wares for the storage, preparation, transport, and consumption of food, drink, and raw materials.
sentence_326: Walls were painted white and could be covered with dyed linen wall hangings.
sentence_327: Floors were covered with reed mats, while wooden stools, beds raised from the floor and individual tables comprised the furniture.
sentence_328: The ancient Egyptians placed a great value on hygiene and appearance.
sentence_329: Most bathed in the Nile and used a pasty soap made from [[Animal_fat|animal fat]] and chalk.
sentence_330: Men shaved their entire bodies for cleanliness; perfumes and aromatic ointments covered bad odors and soothed skin.
sentence_331: Clothing was made from simple linen sheets that were bleached white, and both men and women of the upper classes wore wigs, jewelry, and [[Beauty_and_Cosmetics_in_Ancient_Egypt|cosmetics]].
sentence_332: Children went without clothing until maturity, at about age 12, and at this age males were circumcised and had their heads shaved.
sentence_333: Mothers were responsible for taking care of the children, while the father provided the family's income.
sentence_334: Music and dance were popular entertainments for those who could afford them.
sentence_335: Early instruments included flutes and harps, while instruments similar to trumpets, oboes, and pipes developed later and became popular.
sentence_336: In the New Kingdom, the Egyptians played on bells, cymbals, tambourines, drums, and imported [[Lute|lutes]] and [[Lyre|lyres]] from Asia.
sentence_337: The [[Sistrum|sistrum]] was a rattle-like [[Musical_instrument|musical instrument]] that was especially important in religious ceremonies.
sentence_338: The ancient Egyptians enjoyed a variety of leisure activities, including games and music.
sentence_339: [[Senet|Senet]], a board game where pieces moved according to random chance, was particularly popular from the earliest times; another similar game was [[Mehen_(game)|mehen]], which had a circular gaming board.
sentence_340: "[[Hounds_and_Jackals|Hounds and Jackals]]" also known as 58 holes is another example of board games played in ancient Egypt.
sentence_341: The first complete set of this game was discovered from a [[List_of_Theban_tombs|Theban tomb]] of the Egyptian pharaoh [[Amenemhat_IV|Amenemhat IV]] that dates to the [[13th_Dynasty|13th Dynasty]].
sentence_342: Juggling and [[Ball_game|ball games]] were popular with children, and wrestling is also documented in a tomb at [[Beni_Hasan|Beni Hasan]].
sentence_343: The wealthy members of ancient Egyptian society enjoyed [[Hunting,_fishing_and_animals_in_ancient_Egypt|hunting, fishing]], and boating as well.
sentence_344: The excavation of the workers' village of [[Deir_el-Medina|Deir el-Medina]] has resulted in one of the most thoroughly documented accounts of community life in the ancient world, which spans almost four hundred years.
sentence_345: There is no comparable site in which the organization, social interactions, and working and living conditions of a community have been studied in such detail.
sentence_346: Main article: [[Ancient_Egyptian_cuisine|Ancient Egyptian cuisine]]
sentence_347: Egyptian cuisine remained remarkably stable over time; indeed, the [[Egyptian_cuisine|cuisine of modern Egypt]] retains some striking similarities to the cuisine of the ancients.
sentence_348: The staple diet consisted of bread and beer, supplemented with vegetables such as onions and garlic, and fruit such as dates and figs.
sentence_349: Wine and meat were enjoyed by all on feast days while the upper classes indulged on a more regular basis.
sentence_350: Fish, meat, and fowl could be salted or dried, and could be cooked in stews or roasted on a grill.
sentence_351: Main article: [[Ancient_Egyptian_architecture|Ancient Egyptian architecture]]
sentence_352: The architecture of ancient Egypt includes some of the most famous structures in the world: the [[Giza_pyramid_complex|Great Pyramids of Giza]] and the [[Karnak|temples at Thebes]].
sentence_353: Building projects were organized and funded by the state for religious and commemorative purposes, but also to reinforce the wide-ranging power of the pharaoh.
sentence_354: The ancient Egyptians were skilled builders; using only simple but effective tools and sighting instruments, architects could build large stone structures with great accuracy and precision that is still envied today.
sentence_355: The domestic dwellings of elite and ordinary Egyptians alike were constructed from perishable materials such as mudbricks and wood, and have not survived.
sentence_356: Peasants lived in simple homes, while the palaces of the elite and the pharaoh were more elaborate structures.
sentence_357: A few surviving New Kingdom palaces, such as those in [[Malkata|Malkata]] and [[Amarna|Amarna]], show richly decorated walls and floors with scenes of people, birds, water pools, deities and geometric designs.
sentence_358: Important structures such as temples and tombs that were intended to last forever were constructed of stone instead of mudbricks.
sentence_359: The architectural elements used in the world's first large-scale stone building, [[Djoser|Djoser]]'s mortuary complex, include [[Post_and_lintel|post and lintel]] supports in the papyrus and lotus motif.
sentence_360: The earliest preserved ancient [[Egyptian_temple|Egyptian temples]], such as those at Giza, consist of single, enclosed halls with roof slabs supported by columns.
sentence_361: In the New Kingdom, architects added the [[Pylon_(architecture)|pylon]], the open [[Courtyard|courtyard]], and the enclosed [[Hypostyle|hypostyle]] hall to the front of the temple's sanctuary, a style that was standard until the Greco-Roman period.
sentence_362: The earliest and most popular tomb architecture in the Old Kingdom was the [[Mastaba|mastaba]], a flat-roofed rectangular structure of mudbrick or stone built over an underground [[Chamber_tomb|burial chamber]].
sentence_363: The [[Pyramid_of_Djoser|step pyramid of Djoser]] is a series of stone mastabas stacked on top of each other.
sentence_364: Pyramids were built during the Old and Middle Kingdoms, but most later rulers abandoned them in favor of less conspicuous rock-cut tombs.
sentence_365: The use of the pyramid form continued in private tomb chapels of the New Kingdom and in the royal [[Nubian_pyramids|pyramids of Nubia]].
sentence_366: Main articles: [[Art_of_ancient_Egypt|Art of ancient Egypt]] and [[Portraiture_in_ancient_Egypt|Portraiture in ancient Egypt]]
sentence_367: The ancient Egyptians produced art to serve functional purposes.
sentence_368: For over 3500 years, artists adhered to artistic forms and iconography that were developed during the Old Kingdom, following a strict set of principles that resisted foreign influence and internal change.
sentence_369: These artistic standards—simple lines, shapes, and flat areas of color combined with the characteristic flat projection of figures with no indication of spatial depth—created a sense of order and balance within a composition.
sentence_370: Images and text were intimately interwoven on tomb and temple walls, coffins, stelae, and even statues.
sentence_371: The [[Narmer_Palette|Narmer Palette]], for example, displays figures that can also be read as hieroglyphs.
sentence_372: Because of the rigid rules that governed its highly stylized and symbolic appearance, ancient Egyptian art served its political and religious purposes with precision and clarity.
sentence_373: Ancient Egyptian artisans used stone as a medium for carving statues and fine reliefs, but used wood as a cheap and easily carved substitute.
sentence_374: Paints were obtained from minerals such as iron ores (red and yellow ochres), copper ores (blue and green), soot or charcoal (black), and limestone (white).
sentence_375: Paints could be mixed with [[Gum_arabic|gum arabic]] as a binder and pressed into cakes, which could be moistened with water when needed.
sentence_376: Pharaohs used [[Relief|reliefs]] to record victories in battle, royal decrees, and religious scenes.
sentence_377: Common citizens had access to pieces of [[Funerary_art|funerary art]], such as [[Ushabti|shabti]] statues and books of the dead, which they believed would protect them in the afterlife.
sentence_378: During the Middle Kingdom, [[Wooden_tomb_model|wooden or clay models]] depicting scenes from everyday life became popular additions to the tomb.
sentence_379: In an attempt to duplicate the activities of the living in the [[Afterlife|afterlife]], these models show laborers, houses, boats, and even military formations that are scale representations of the ideal ancient Egyptian afterlife.
sentence_380: Despite the homogeneity of ancient Egyptian art, the styles of particular times and places sometimes reflected changing cultural or political attitudes.
sentence_381: After the invasion of the Hyksos in the Second Intermediate Period, [[Minoan_civilization|Minoan]]-style frescoes were found in [[Avaris|Avaris]].
sentence_382: The most striking example of a politically driven change in artistic forms comes from the Amarna Period, where figures were radically altered to conform to [[Akhenaten|Akhenaten]]'s revolutionary religious ideas.
sentence_383: This style, known as [[Amarna_art|Amarna art]], was quickly abandoned after Akhenaten's death and replaced by the traditional forms.
sentence_384: Main article: [[Ancient_Egyptian_religion|Ancient Egyptian religion]]
sentence_385: Beliefs in the divine and in the afterlife were ingrained in ancient Egyptian civilization from its inception; pharaonic rule was based on the [[Divine_Right_of_Kings|divine right of kings]].
sentence_386: The Egyptian pantheon was populated by [[Egyptian_pantheon|gods]] who had supernatural powers and were called on for help or protection.
sentence_387: However, the gods were not always viewed as benevolent, and Egyptians believed they had to be appeased with offerings and prayers.
sentence_388: The structure of this [[Ancient_Egyptian_deities|pantheon]] changed continually as new deities were promoted in the hierarchy, but priests made no effort to organize the diverse and sometimes conflicting [[Egyptian_mythology|myths]] and stories into a coherent system.
sentence_389: These various conceptions of divinity were not considered contradictory but rather layers in the multiple facets of reality.
sentence_390: Gods were worshiped in cult [[Egyptian_temple|temples]] administered by priests acting on the king's behalf.
sentence_391: At the center of the temple was the cult statue in a shrine.
sentence_392: Temples were not places of public worship or congregation, and only on select feast days and celebrations was a shrine carrying the statue of the god brought out for public worship.
sentence_393: Normally, the god's domain was sealed off from the outside world and was only accessible to temple officials.
sentence_394: Common citizens could worship private statues in their homes, and amulets offered protection against the forces of chaos.
sentence_395: After the New Kingdom, the pharaoh's role as a spiritual intermediary was de-emphasized as religious customs shifted to direct worship of the gods.
sentence_396: As a result, priests developed a system of [[Oracle|oracles]] to communicate the will of the gods directly to the people.
sentence_397: The Egyptians believed that every human being was composed of physical and spiritual parts or aspects.
sentence_398: In addition to the body, each person had a Å¡wt (shadow), a ba (personality or soul), a ka (life-force), and a name.
sentence_399: The heart, rather than the brain, was considered the seat of thoughts and emotions.
sentence_400: After death, the spiritual aspects were released from the body and could move at will, but they required the physical remains (or a substitute, such as a statue) as a permanent home.
sentence_401: The ultimate goal of the deceased was to rejoin his ka and ba and become one of the "blessed dead", living on as an akh, or "effective one".
sentence_402: For this to happen, the deceased had to be judged worthy in a trial, in which the heart was weighed against a "[[Maat#The_afterlife|feather of truth]]."
sentence_403: If deemed worthy, the deceased could continue their existence on earth in spiritual form.
sentence_404: If they were not deemed worthy, their heart was eaten by Ammit the Devourer and they were erased from the Universe.
sentence_405: Main article: [[Ancient_Egyptian_funerary_practices|Ancient Egyptian funerary practices]]
sentence_406: The ancient Egyptians maintained an elaborate set of burial customs that they believed were necessary to ensure immortality after death.
sentence_407: These customs involved preserving the body by [[Mummy|mummification]], performing burial ceremonies, and interring with the body goods the deceased would use in the afterlife.
sentence_408: Before the Old Kingdom, bodies buried in desert pits were naturally preserved by [[Desiccation|desiccation]].
sentence_409: The arid, desert conditions were a boon throughout the history of ancient Egypt for burials of the poor, who could not afford the elaborate burial preparations available to the elite.
sentence_410: Wealthier Egyptians began to bury their dead in stone tombs and use artificial mummification, which involved removing the [[Organ_(anatomy)|internal organs]], wrapping the body in linen, and burying it in a rectangular stone sarcophagus or wooden coffin.
sentence_411: Beginning in the Fourth Dynasty, some parts were preserved separately in [[Canopic_jar|canopic jars]].
sentence_412: By the New Kingdom, the ancient Egyptians had perfected the art of mummification; the best technique took 70 days and involved removing the internal organs, removing the brain through the nose, and desiccating the body in a mixture of salts called [[Natron|natron]].
sentence_413: The body was then wrapped in linen with protective amulets inserted between layers and placed in a decorated anthropoid coffin.
sentence_414: Mummies of the Late Period were also placed in painted [[Cartonnage|cartonnage]] mummy cases.
sentence_415: Actual preservation practices declined during the Ptolemaic and Roman eras, while greater emphasis was placed on the outer appearance of the mummy, which was decorated.
sentence_416: Wealthy Egyptians were buried with larger quantities of luxury items, but all burials, regardless of social status, included goods for the deceased.
sentence_417: [[Ancient_Egyptian_funerary_texts|Funerary texts]] were often included in the grave, and, beginning in the New Kingdom, so were [[Ushabti|shabti]] statues that were believed to perform manual labor for them in the afterlife.
sentence_418: Rituals in which the deceased was magically re-animated accompanied burials.
sentence_419: After burial, living relatives were expected to occasionally bring food to the tomb and recite prayers on behalf of the deceased.
sentence_420: Main article: [[Military_of_ancient_Egypt|Military of ancient Egypt]]
sentence_421: Further information: [[Ancient_Egyptian_navy|Ancient Egyptian navy]]
sentence_422: The ancient Egyptian military was responsible for defending Egypt against foreign invasion, and for maintaining Egypt's domination in the [[Ancient_Near_East|ancient Near East]].
sentence_423: The military protected mining expeditions to the Sinai during the Old Kingdom and fought civil wars during the First and Second Intermediate Periods.
sentence_424: The military was responsible for maintaining fortifications along important trade routes, such as those found at the city of [[Buhen|Buhen]] on the way to Nubia.
sentence_425: Forts also were constructed to serve as military bases, such as the fortress at Sile, which was a base of operations for expeditions to the [[Levant|Levant]].
sentence_426: In the New Kingdom, a series of pharaohs used the standing Egyptian army to attack and conquer [[Kingdom_of_Kush|Kush]] and parts of the Levant.
sentence_427: Typical military equipment included [[Bow_(weapon)|bows and arrows]], spears, and round-topped shields made by stretching [[Leather|animal skin]] over a wooden frame.
sentence_428: In the New Kingdom, the military began using [[Chariotry_in_ancient_Egypt|chariots]] that had earlier been introduced by the Hyksos invaders.
sentence_429: Weapons and armor continued to improve after the adoption of bronze: shields were now made from solid wood with a bronze buckle, spears were tipped with a bronze point, and the [[Khopesh|khopesh]] was adopted from Asiatic soldiers.
sentence_430: The pharaoh was usually depicted in art and literature riding at the head of the army; it has been suggested that at least a few pharaohs, such as [[Seqenenre_Tao_II|Seqenenre Tao II]] and his sons, did do so.
sentence_431: However, it has also been argued that "kings of this period did not personally act as frontline war leaders, fighting alongside their troops."
sentence_432: Soldiers were recruited from the general population, but during, and especially after, the New Kingdom, mercenaries from Nubia, Kush, and Libya were hired to fight for Egypt.
sentence_433: Main article: [[Ancient_Egyptian_technology|Ancient Egyptian technology]]
sentence_434: In technology, medicine, and mathematics, ancient Egypt achieved a relatively high standard of productivity and sophistication.
sentence_435: Traditional [[Empiricism|empiricism]], as evidenced by the [[Edwin_Smith_Papyrus|Edwin Smith]] and [[Ebers_Papyrus|Ebers papyri]] (c. 1600 BC), is first credited to Egypt.
sentence_436: The Egyptians created their own alphabet and [[Decimal|decimal system]].
sentence_437: Even before the Old Kingdom, the ancient Egyptians had developed a glassy material known as [[Egyptian_faience|faience]], which they treated as a type of artificial semi-precious stone.
sentence_438: Faience is a non-clay ceramic made of [[Silicon_dioxide|silica]], small amounts of [[Calcium_oxide|lime]] and [[Sodium_oxide|soda]], and a colorant, typically copper.
sentence_439: The material was used to make beads, tiles, figurines, and small wares.
sentence_440: Several methods can be used to create faience, but typically production involved application of the powdered materials in the form of a paste over a clay core, which was then fired.
sentence_441: By a related technique, the ancient Egyptians produced a pigment known as [[Egyptian_blue|Egyptian blue]], also called blue frit, which is produced by fusing (or [[Sintering|sintering]]) silica, copper, lime, and an alkali such as natron.
sentence_442: The product can be ground up and used as a pigment.
sentence_443: The ancient Egyptians could fabricate a wide variety of objects from glass with great skill, but it is not clear whether they developed the process independently.
sentence_444: It is also unclear whether they made their own raw glass or merely imported pre-made ingots, which they melted and finished.
sentence_445: However, they did have technical expertise in making objects, as well as adding [[Micromineral|trace elements]] to control the color of the finished glass.
sentence_446: A range of colors could be produced, including yellow, red, green, blue, purple, and white, and the glass could be made either transparent or opaque.
sentence_447: Main article: Ancient Egyptian medicine
sentence_448: The medical problems of the ancient Egyptians stemmed directly from their environment.
sentence_449: Living and working close to the Nile brought hazards from [[Malaria|malaria]] and debilitating [[Schistosomiasis|schistosomiasis]] parasites, which caused liver and intestinal damage.
sentence_450: Dangerous wildlife such as crocodiles and hippos were also a common threat.
sentence_451: The lifelong labors of farming and building put stress on the spine and joints, and traumatic injuries from construction and warfare all took a significant toll on the body.
sentence_452: The grit and sand from stone-ground flour abraded teeth, leaving them susceptible to [[Abscess|abscesses]] (though [[Dental_caries|caries]] were rare).
sentence_453: The diets of the wealthy were rich in sugars, which promoted [[Periodontitis|periodontal disease]].
sentence_454: Despite the flattering physiques portrayed on tomb walls, the overweight mummies of many of the upper class show the effects of a life of overindulgence.
sentence_455: Adult [[Life_expectancy|life expectancy]] was about 35 for men and 30 for women, but reaching adulthood was difficult as about one-third of the population died in infancy.
sentence_456: Ancient Egyptian physicians were renowned in the ancient Near East for their healing skills, and some, such as [[Imhotep|Imhotep]], remained famous long after their deaths.
sentence_457: [[Herodotus|Herodotus]] remarked that there was a high degree of specialization among Egyptian physicians, with some treating only the head or the stomach, while others were eye-doctors and dentists.
sentence_458: Training of physicians took place at the Per Ankh or "House of Life" institution, most notably those headquartered in [[Bubastis|Per-Bastet]] during the New Kingdom and at [[Abydos,_Egypt|Abydos]] and [[Sais,_Egypt|Saïs]] in the Late period.
sentence_459: [[Medical_papyri|Medical papyri]] show empirical knowledge of anatomy, injuries, and practical treatments.
sentence_460: Wounds were treated by bandaging with raw meat, white linen, sutures, nets, pads, and swabs soaked with honey to prevent infection, while [[Opium|opium]], [[Thyme|thyme]], and [[Atropa_belladonna|belladona]] were used to relieve pain.
sentence_461: The earliest records of burn treatment describe burn dressings that use the milk from mothers of male babies.
sentence_462: Prayers were made to the goddess [[Isis|Isis]].
sentence_463: Moldy bread, honey, and copper salts were also used to prevent infection from dirt in burns.
sentence_464: Garlic and onions were used regularly to promote good health and were thought to relieve [[Asthma|asthma]] symptoms.
sentence_465: Ancient Egyptian surgeons stitched wounds, set [[Broken_bones|broken bones]], and amputated diseased limbs, but they recognized that some injuries were so serious that they could only make the patient comfortable until death occurred.
sentence_466: Early [[Egyptians|Egyptians]] knew how to assemble planks of wood into a [[Hull_(ship)|ship hull]] and had mastered advanced forms of [[Shipbuilding|shipbuilding]] as early as 3000 BC.
sentence_467: The [[Archaeological_Institute_of_America|Archaeological Institute of America]] reports that the oldest [[Plank_(wood)|planked]] ships known are the [[Abydos_boats|Abydos boats]].
sentence_468: A group of 14 discovered ships in [[Abydos,_Egypt|Abydos]] were constructed of wooden planks "sewn" together.
sentence_469: Discovered by Egyptologist David O'Connor of [[New_York_University|New York University]], woven straps were found to have been used to lash the planks together, and [[Cyperus_papyrus|reeds]] or grass stuffed between the planks helped to seal the seams.
sentence_470: Because the ships are all buried together and near a mortuary belonging to [[Khasekhemwy|Pharaoh Khasekhemwy]], originally they were all thought to have belonged to him, but one of the 14 ships dates to 3000 BC, and the associated pottery jars buried with the vessels also suggest earlier dating.
sentence_471: The ship dating to 3000 BC was 75 feet (23 m) long and is now thought to perhaps have belonged to an earlier pharaoh, perhaps one as early as [[Hor-Aha|Hor-Aha]].
sentence_472: Early Egyptians also knew how to assemble planks of wood with [[Treenail|treenails]] to fasten them together, using [[Pitch_(resin)|pitch]] for caulking the seams.
sentence_473: The "[[Khufu_ship|Khufu ship]]", a 43.6-metre (143 ft) vessel sealed into a pit in the [[Giza_pyramid_complex|Giza pyramid complex]] at the foot of the [[Great_Pyramid_of_Giza|Great Pyramid of Giza]] in the [[Fourth_dynasty_of_Egypt|Fourth Dynasty]] around 2500 BC, is a full-size surviving example that may have filled the symbolic function of a [[Solar_barque|solar barque]].
sentence_474: Early Egyptians also knew how to fasten the planks of this ship together with [[Mortise_and_tenon|mortise and tenon]] joints.
sentence_475: Large seagoing ships are known to have been heavily used by the Egyptians in their trade with the city states of the eastern Mediterranean, especially [[Byblos|Byblos]] (on the coast of modern-day Lebanon), and in several expeditions down the Red Sea to the [[Land_of_Punt|Land of Punt]].
sentence_476: In fact one of the earliest Egyptian words for a seagoing ship is a "Byblos Ship", which originally defined a class of Egyptian seagoing ships used on the Byblos run; however, by the end of the Old Kingdom, the term had come to include large seagoing ships, whatever their destination.
sentence_477: In 2011, archaeologists from Italy, the United States, and Egypt excavating a dried-up lagoon known as [[Mersa_Gawasis|Mersa Gawasis]] have unearthed traces of an ancient harbor that once launched early voyages like [[Hatshepsut|Hatshepsut]]'s Punt expedition onto the open ocean.
sentence_478: Some of the site's most evocative evidence for the ancient Egyptians' seafaring prowess include large ship timbers and hundreds of feet of ropes, made from papyrus, coiled in huge bundles.
sentence_479: In 2013 a team of Franco-Egyptian archaeologists discovered what is believed to be the world's oldest port, dating back about 4500 years, from the time of King [[Cheops|Cheops]] on the Red Sea coast near Wadi el-Jarf (about 110 miles south of [[Suez|Suez]]).
sentence_480: In 1977, an ancient north–south canal dating to the [[Middle_Kingdom_of_Egypt|Middle Kingdom of Egypt]] was discovered extending from [[Lake_Timsah|Lake Timsah]] to the Ballah Lakes.
sentence_481: It was dated to the [[Middle_Kingdom_of_Egypt|Middle Kingdom of Egypt]] by extrapolating dates of ancient sites constructed along its course.
sentence_482: Main article: [[Ancient_Egyptian_mathematics|Ancient Egyptian mathematics]]
sentence_483: The earliest attested examples of mathematical calculations date to the predynastic Naqada period, and show a fully developed [[Egyptian_numerals|numeral system]].
sentence_484: The importance of mathematics to an educated Egyptian is suggested by a New Kingdom fictional letter in which the writer proposes a scholarly competition between himself and another scribe regarding everyday calculation tasks such as accounting of land, labor, and grain.
sentence_485: Texts such as the [[Rhind_Mathematical_Papyrus|Rhind Mathematical Papyrus]] and the [[Moscow_Mathematical_Papyrus|Moscow Mathematical Papyrus]] show that the ancient Egyptians could perform the four basic mathematical operations—addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division—use fractions, calculate the areas of rectangles, triangles, and circles and compute the volumes of boxes, columns and pyramids.
sentence_486: They understood basic concepts of [[Egyptian_algebra|algebra]] and [[Egyptian_geometry|geometry]], and could solve simple sets of [[Simultaneous_equations|simultaneous equations]].
sentence_487: [[Mathematical_notation|Mathematical notation]] was decimal, and based on hieroglyphic signs for each power of ten up to one million.
sentence_488: Each of these could be written as many times as necessary to add up to the desired number; so to write the number eighty or eight hundred, the symbol for ten or one hundred was written eight times respectively.
sentence_489: Because their methods of calculation could not handle most fractions with a numerator greater than one, they had to write [[Egyptian_fraction|fractions]] as the sum of several fractions.
sentence_490: For example, they resolved the fraction two-fifths into the sum of one-third + one-fifteenth.
sentence_491: Standard tables of values facilitated this.
sentence_492: Some [[Vulgar_fraction|common fractions]], however, were written with a special glyph—the equivalent of the modern two-thirds is shown on the right.
sentence_493: Ancient Egyptian mathematicians knew the [[Pythagorean_theorem|Pythagorean theorem]] as an empirical formula.
sentence_494: They were aware, for example, that a triangle had a right angle opposite the hypotenuse when its sides were in a 3–4–5 ratio.
sentence_495: They were able to estimate the area of a [[Circle|circle]] by subtracting one-ninth from its diameter and squaring the result:
sentence_496: a reasonable approximation of the formula [[Pi|π]]r.
sentence_497: The [[Golden_ratio|golden ratio]] seems to be reflected in many Egyptian constructions, including the [[Egyptian_pyramids|pyramids]], but its use may have been an unintended consequence of the ancient Egyptian practice of combining the use of knotted ropes with an intuitive sense of proportion and harmony.
sentence_498: Main article: [[Population_history_of_Egypt|Population history of Egypt]]
sentence_499: Further information: [[Ancient_Egyptian_race_controversy|Ancient Egyptian race controversy]] and [[Black_Egyptian_hypothesis|Black Egyptian hypothesis]]
sentence_500: A team led by [[Johannes_Krause|Johannes Krause]] managed the first reliable sequencing of the genomes of 90 mummified individuals in 2017 from northern Egypt (buried near modern-day Cairo), which constituted "the first reliable data set obtained from ancient Egyptians using high-throughput DNA sequencing methods."
sentence_501: Whilst not conclusive, because of the non-exhaustive time frame (New Kingdom to Roman period) and restricted location that the mummies represent, their study nevertheless showed that these ancient Egyptians "closely resembled ancient and modern Near Eastern populations, especially those in the [[Levant|Levant]], and had almost no DNA from sub-Saharan Africa.
sentence_502: What's more, the genetics of the mummies remained remarkably consistent even as different powers—including Nubians, Greeks, and Romans—conquered the empire."
sentence_503: Later, however, something did alter the genomes of Egyptians.
sentence_504: Some 15% to 20% of modern Egyptians' DNA reflects sub-Saharan ancestry, but the ancient mummies had only 6–15% sub-Saharan DNA.
sentence_505: They called for additional research to be undertaken.
sentence_506: Other genetic studies show much greater levels of sub-Saharan African ancestry in the current-day populations of southern as opposed to northern Egypt, and anticipate that mummies from southern Egypt would contain greater levels of sub-Saharan African ancestry than Lower Egyptian mummies.
sentence_507: See also: [[Egyptian_Revival_architecture|Egyptian Revival architecture]] and Tourism in Egypt
sentence_508: The culture and monuments of ancient Egypt have left a lasting legacy on the world.
sentence_509: Egyptian civilization significantly influenced the [[Kingdom_of_Kush|Kingdom of Kush]] and [[Meroë|Meroë]] with both adopting Egyptian religious and architectural norms (hundreds of [[Nubian_pyramids|pyramids]] (6–30 meters high) were built in Egypt/Sudan), as well as using Egyptian writing as the basis of the [[Meroitic_script|Meroitic script]].
sentence_510: Meroitic is the oldest written language in Africa, other than Egyptian, and was used from the 2nd century BC until the early 5th century AD.
sentence_511: The cult of the goddess [[Isis|Isis]], for example, became popular in the [[Roman_Empire|Roman Empire]], as obelisks and other relics were transported back to Rome.
sentence_512: The Romans also imported building materials from Egypt to erect Egyptian-style structures.
sentence_513: Early historians such as [[Herodotus|Herodotus]], [[Strabo|Strabo]], and [[Diodorus_Siculus|Diodorus Siculus]] studied and wrote about the land, which Romans came to view as a place of mystery.
sentence_514: During the [[Middle_Ages|Middle Ages]] and the [[Renaissance|Renaissance]], Egyptian pagan culture was in decline after the rise of Christianity and later [[Islam|Islam]], but interest in Egyptian antiquity continued in the writings of medieval scholars such as [[Dhul-Nun_al-Misri|Dhul-Nun al-Misri]] and [[Al-Maqrizi|al-Maqrizi]].
sentence_515: In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, European travelers and tourists brought back antiquities and wrote stories of their journeys, leading to a wave of Egyptomania across Europe.
sentence_516: This renewed interest sent collectors to Egypt, who took, purchased, or were given many important antiquities.
sentence_517: [[Napoleon|Napoleon]] arranged the first studies in [[Egyptology|Egyptology]] when he brought some 150 scientists and artists to study and document Egypt's [[Natural_history|natural history]], which was published in the [[Description_de_l'Égypte|Description de l'Égypte]].
sentence_518: In the 20th century, the Egyptian Government and archaeologists alike recognized the importance of cultural respect and integrity in excavations.
sentence_519: The [[Supreme_Council_of_Antiquities|Supreme Council of Antiquities]] now approves and oversees all excavations, which are aimed at finding information rather than treasure.
sentence_520: The council also supervises museums and monument reconstruction programs designed to preserve the historical legacy of Egypt.
