sentence_330: Also, Atlanta is within a few hours driving distance of many of the universities that make up the [[Southeastern_Conference|Southeastern Conference]], college football's most profitable and popular conference, and annually hosts the [[SEC_Championship_Game|SEC Championship Game]].
sentence_331: Other annual college football events include the [[Chick-fil-A_Kickoff_Game|Chick-fil-A Kickoff Game]], the [[Celebration_Bowl|Celebration Bowl]], the MEAC/SWAC Challenge, and the [[Peach_Bowl|Chick-fil-A Peach Bowl]] which is one of College Football's major New Year's Six Bowl games and a college football playoff bowl.
sentence_332: Atlanta additionally hosted the [[2018_College_Football_Playoff_National_Championship|2018 College Football Playoff National Championship]].
sentence_333: Atlanta regularly hosts a variety of sporting events.
sentence_334: Most famous was the Centennial [[1996_Summer_Olympics|1996 Summer Olympics]].
sentence_335: The city has hosted the super bowl three times: [[Super_Bowl_XXVIII|Super Bowl XXVIII]] in 1994, [[Super_Bowl_XXXIV|Super Bowl XXXIV]] in 2000, and [[Super_Bowl_LIII|Super Bowl LIII]] in 2019.
sentence_336: In professional golf, [[The_Tour_Championship|The Tour Championship]], the final [[PGA_Tour|PGA Tour]] event of the season, is played annually at [[East_Lake_Golf_Club|East Lake Golf Club]].
sentence_337: In 2001 and 2011, Atlanta hosted the [[PGA_Championship|PGA Championship]], one of the four [[Men's_major_golf_championships|major championships]] in men's professional golf, at the [[Atlanta_Athletic_Club|Atlanta Athletic Club]].
sentence_338: In 2011, Atlanta hosted professional wrestling's annual [[WrestleMania_XXVII|WrestleMania]].
sentence_339: In soccer, Atlanta has hosted numerous international friendlies and [[CONCACAF_Gold_Cup|CONCACAF Gold Cup]] matches.
sentence_340: The city has hosted the [[NCAA_Men's_Division_I_Basketball_Championship|NCAA Final Four]] Men's Basketball Championship five times, most recently in [[2020_NCAA_Men's_Division_I_Basketball_Tournament|2020]].
sentence_341: [[Running|Running]] is a popular local sport, and the city declares itself to be "Running City USA".
sentence_342: The city hosts the [[Peachtree_Road_Race|Peachtree Road Race]], the world's largest [[10K_run|10 km race]], annually on [[Independence_Day_(United_States)|Independence Day]].
sentence_343: Atlanta also hosts the nation's largest [[Thanksgiving_(United_States)|Thanksgiving]] day [[Half_marathon|half marathon]], which starts and ends at [[Georgia_State_Stadium|Georgia State Stadium]].
sentence_344: The [[Atlanta_Marathon|Atlanta Marathon]], which starts and ends at [[Centennial_Olympic_Park|Centennial Olympic Park]], routes through many of the city's historic landmarks, and its 2020 running will coincide with the U.S. Olympic marathon trials for the [[2020_Summer_Olympics|2020 Summer Olympics]].
sentence_345: Main article: [[Parks_in_Atlanta|Parks in Atlanta]]
sentence_346: Atlanta's 343 parks, nature preserves, and gardens cover 3,622 acres (14.66 km), which amounts to only 5.6% of the city's total acreage, compared to the national average of just over 10%.
sentence_347: However, 64% of Atlantans live within a 10-minute walk of a park, a percentage equal to the national average.
sentence_348: In its 2013 ParkScore ranking, [[The_Trust_for_Public_Land|The Trust for Public Land]] reported that among the park systems of the 50 most populous U.S. cities, Atlanta's park system received a ranking of 31.
sentence_349: [[Piedmont_Park|Piedmont Park]], in [[Midtown_Atlanta|Midtown]], is Atlanta's most iconic green space.
sentence_350: The park, which underwent a major renovation and expansion in recent years, attracts visitors from across the region and hosts cultural events throughout the year.
sentence_351: Other notable city parks include [[Centennial_Olympic_Park|Centennial Olympic Park]], a legacy of the [[1996_Summer_Olympics|1996 Summer Olympics]] that forms the centerpiece of the city's tourist district; [[Woodruff_Park|Woodruff Park]], which anchors the campus of [[Georgia_State_University|Georgia State University]]; [[Grant_Park_(Atlanta)|Grant Park]], home to [[Zoo_Atlanta|Zoo Atlanta]]; Chastain Park, which houses an amphitheater used for live music concerts; and the under construction [[Westside_Reservoir_Park|Westside Park at Bellwood Quarry]], the 280-acre green space and reservoir project slated to become the city's largest park when fully complete in the 2020s.
sentence_352: The Chattahoochee River National Recreation Area, in the northwestern corner of the city, preserves a 48 mi (77 km) stretch of the river for public recreation opportunities.
sentence_353: The Atlanta Botanical Garden, adjacent to Piedmont Park, contains formal gardens, including a Japanese garden and a rose garden, woodland areas, and a conservatory that includes indoor exhibits of plants from [[Tropical_rainforest|tropical rainforests]] and [[Desert|deserts]].
sentence_354: The [[BeltLine|BeltLine]], a former rail corridor that forms a 22 mi (35 km) loop around Atlanta's core, has been transformed into a series of [[City_park|parks]], connected by a multi-use trail, increasing Atlanta's park space by 40%.
sentence_355: Atlanta offers resources and opportunities for amateur and participatory sports and recreation.
sentence_356: Golf and tennis are popular in Atlanta, and the city contains six public golf courses and 182 tennis courts.
sentence_357: Facilities along the [[Chattahoochee_River|Chattahoochee River]] cater to watersports enthusiasts, providing the opportunity for kayaking, canoeing, fishing, boating, or tubing.
sentence_358: The city's only skate park, a 15,000 square feet (1,400 m) facility that offers bowls, curbs, and smooth-rolling concrete mounds, is at [[Historic_Fourth_Ward_Park|Historic Fourth Ward Park]].
sentence_359: Main articles: [[Government_of_Atlanta|Government of Atlanta]], [[List_of_mayors_of_Atlanta|List of mayors of Atlanta]], and [[Crime_in_Atlanta|Crime in Atlanta]]
sentence_360: Atlanta is governed by a mayor and the [[Atlanta_City_Council|Atlanta City Council]].
sentence_361: The city council consists of 15 representatives—one from each of the city's 12 districts and three at-large positions.
sentence_362: The mayor may veto a bill passed by the council, but the council can override the veto with a two-thirds majority.
sentence_363: The mayor of Atlanta is [[Keisha_Lance_Bottoms|Keisha Lance Bottoms]], a Democrat elected on a nonpartisan ballot whose first term in office began on January 2, 2018.
sentence_364: Every mayor elected since 1973 has been black.
sentence_365: In 2001, Shirley Franklin became the first woman to be elected mayor of Atlanta, and the first African-American woman to serve as mayor of a major Southern city.
sentence_366: Atlanta city politics suffered from a notorious reputation for corruption during the 1990s administration of Mayor [[Bill_Campbell_(mayor)|Bill Campbell]], who was convicted by a federal jury in 2006 on three counts of tax evasion in connection with gambling winnings during trips he took with city contractors.
sentence_367: As the [[List_of_capitals_in_the_United_States|state capital]], Atlanta is the site of most of Georgia's state government.
sentence_368: The [[Georgia_State_Capitol|Georgia State Capitol]] building, located downtown, houses the offices of the [[Governor_of_Georgia|governor]], lieutenant governor and secretary of state, as well as the [[Georgia_General_Assembly|General Assembly]].
sentence_369: The [[Georgia_Governor's_Mansion|Governor's Mansion]] is in a residential section of Buckhead.
sentence_370: Atlanta serves as the regional hub for many arms of the federal bureaucracy, including the [[Federal_Reserve_Bank_of_Atlanta|Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta]] and the [[Centers_for_Disease_Control_and_Prevention|Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC).
sentence_371: The City of Atlanta annexed the CDC into its territory effective January 1, 2018.
sentence_372: Atlanta also plays an important role in the federal judiciary system, containing the [[United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_Eleventh_Circuit|United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit]] and the [[United_States_District_Court_for_the_Northern_District_of_Georgia|United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia]].
sentence_373: Historically, Atlanta has been a stronghold for the [[Democratic_Party_(United_States)|Democratic Party]].
sentence_374: Although municipal elections are officially nonpartisan, nearly all of the city's elected officials are registered Democrats.
sentence_375: The city is split among 14 state house districts and four state senate districts, all held by Democrats.
sentence_376: At the federal level, Atlanta is split between two congressional districts.
sentence_377: Most of the city is in the 5th district, formerly represented by Democrat [[John_Lewis|John Lewis]] and now vacant.
sentence_378: A small portion in the north is in the 11th district, represented by [[Republican_Party_(United_States)|Republican]] [[Barry_Loudermilk|Barry Loudermilk]].

section_25.value: Law enforcement, fire, and EMS services

sentence_379: The city is served by the [[Atlanta_Police_Department|Atlanta Police Department]], which numbers 2,000 officers and oversaw a 40% decrease in the city's crime rate between 2001 and 2009.
sentence_380: Specifically, homicide decreased by 57%, rape by 72%, and violent crime overall by 55%.
sentence_381: Crime is down across the country, but Atlanta's improvement has occurred at more than twice the national rate.
sentence_382: Nevertheless, Forbes ranked Atlanta as the sixth most dangerous city in the United States in 2012.
sentence_383: Aggravated assaults, burglaries and robberies were down from 2014.
sentence_384: Mexican drug cartels thrive in Atlanta.
sentence_385: 145 gangs operate in Atlanta.
sentence_386: The [[Atlanta_Fire_Rescue_Department|Atlanta Fire Rescue Department]] provides fire protection and first responder emergency medical services to the city from its 35 fire stations.
sentence_387: In 2017, AFRD responded to over 100,000 calls for service over a coverage area of 135.7 square miles (351.5 square kilometres).
sentence_388: The department also protects Hartsfield–Jackson with 5 fire stations on the property; serving over 1 million passengers from over 100 different countries.
sentence_389: The department protects over 3000 highrise buildings, 23 miles (37 kilometres) of the rapid rail system, and 60 miles (97 kilometres) of interstate highway.
sentence_390: Emergency ambulance services are provided to city residents by hospital based [[Grady_EMS|Grady EMS]] (Fulton County), and American Medical Response (DeKalb County).
sentence_391: Atlanta in January 2017 declared the city was a "welcoming city" and "will remain open and welcoming to all".
sentence_392: Nonetheless, Atlanta does not consider itself to be a "[[Sanctuary_city|sanctuary city]]".
sentence_393: Atlanta Mayor [[Keisha_Lance_Bottoms|Keisha Lance Bottoms]] said: "Our city does not support ICE.
sentence_394: We don't have a relationship with the U.S.
sentence_395: Marshal[s] Service.
sentence_396: We closed our detention center to ICE detainees, and we would not pick up people on an immigration violation."
sentence_397: Main articles: [[List_of_colleges_and_universities_in_metropolitan_Atlanta|List of colleges and universities in metropolitan Atlanta]], [[Atlanta_Public_Schools|Atlanta Public Schools]], and List of private schools in Atlanta
sentence_398: Due to more than 15 colleges and universities in Atlanta, it is considered one of the nation's largest hubs for [[Higher_education|higher education]].
sentence_399: The [[Georgia_Institute_of_Technology|Georgia Institute of Technology]] is a prominent public research university in [[Midtown_Atlanta|Midtown]].
sentence_400: It offers highly ranked degree programs in engineering, design, industrial management, the sciences, and architecture.
sentence_401: The [[University_of_Georgia|University of Georgia]], chartered in 1785, is one of the top public research universities in the nation with [[Carnegie_Classification_of_Institutions_of_Higher_Education|"Highest Research Activity"]] and based about an hour away in [[Athens,_Georgia|Athens]]; however, the Atlanta Center of its [[Terry_College_of_Business|Terry College of Business]] is in the [[Buckhead|Buckhead]] area of Atlanta and the university has a metropolitan Atlanta Gwinnett Campus that occupies 60,000 square feet of the Intellicenter.
sentence_402: [[Georgia_State_University|Georgia State University]] is a major public research university in [[Downtown_Atlanta|Downtown Atlanta]]; it is the largest of the 29 public colleges and universities in the [[University_System_of_Georgia|University System of Georgia]] and is a significant contributor to the revitalization of the city's central business district.
sentence_403: Atlanta is home to nationally renowned private colleges and universities, most notably [[Emory_University|Emory University]], a leading liberal arts and research institution that operates Emory Healthcare, the largest health care system in [[Georgia_(U.S._state)|Georgia]].
sentence_404: The City of Atlanta annexed Emory into its territory effective January 1, 2018.
sentence_405: The [[Atlanta_University_Center|Atlanta University Center]] is also in the city; it is the largest contiguous consortium of [[Historically_black_colleges_and_universities|historically black colleges]] in the nation, comprising [[Spelman_College|Spelman College]], [[Clark_Atlanta_University|Clark Atlanta University]], [[Morehouse_College|Morehouse College]], and Morehouse School of Medicine.
sentence_406: Atlanta contains a campus of the [[Savannah_College_of_Art_and_Design|Savannah College of Art and Design]], a private art and design university that has proven to be a major factor in the recent growth of Atlanta's visual art community.
sentence_407: Atlanta and nearby Athens also boast [[American_Bar_Association|American Bar Association]] accredited law schools: [[Atlanta's_John_Marshall_Law_School|Atlanta's John Marshall Law School]], Emory University School of Law, [[Georgia_State_University_College_of_Law|Georgia State University College of Law]] and [[University_of_Georgia_School_of_Law|University of Georgia School of Law]].
sentence_408: The Atlanta Regional Council of Higher Education (ARCHE) is dedicated to strengthening synergy among 19 public and private colleges and universities in the Atlanta region.
sentence_409: Participating Atlanta region colleges and universities partner on joint-degree programs, cross-registration, library services, and cultural events.
sentence_410: Fifty-five thousand students are enrolled in 106 schools in [[Atlanta_Public_Schools|Atlanta Public Schools]] (APS), some of which are operated as charter schools.
sentence_411: Atlanta is served by many private schools including, without limitation, [[Atlanta_Jewish_Academy|Atlanta Jewish Academy]], Atlanta International School, [[The_Westminster_Schools|The Westminster Schools]], Pace Academy, The Lovett School, The Paideia School, Holy Innocents' Episcopal School and [[Catholic_Church|Roman Catholic]] parochial schools operated by the [[Archdiocese_of_Atlanta|Archdiocese of Atlanta]].
sentence_412: In 2018 the City of Atlanta annexed a portion of DeKalb County containing the [[Centers_for_Disease_Control|Centers for Disease Control]] and [[Emory_University|Emory University]]; this portion will be zoned to the DeKalb County School District until 2024, when it will transition into APS.
sentence_413: In 2017 the number of children living in the annexed territory who attended public schools was nine.
sentence_414: Main article: [[Media_in_Atlanta|Media in Atlanta]]
sentence_415: The primary network-affiliated television stations in Atlanta are WXIA-TV 11 ([[NBC|NBC]]), WGCL-TV 46 ([[CBS|CBS]]), WSB-TV 2 (ABC), and WAGA-TV 5 ([[Fox_Broadcasting_Company|Fox]]).
sentence_416: Other major commercial stations include WPXA-TV 14 ([[Ion_Television|Ion]]), [[WPCH-TV|WPCH-TV]] 17 ([[Independent_station_(North_America)|Ind.
sentence_417: ]]), WUVG-TV 34 ([[Univision|Univision]]), WUPA 69 (CW), and WATL 36 ([[MyNetworkTV|MyNetworkTV]]).
sentence_418: WPXA-TV, WUVG-TV, WAGA-TV and WUPA are network [[Owned-and-operated_station|O&O]]'s.
sentence_419: The Atlanta metropolitan area is served by two public television stations (both PBS member stations), and two public radio stations.
sentence_420: WGTV 8 is the flagship station of the statewide Georgia Public Television network, while [[WPBA_(TV)|WPBA]] is owned by [[Atlanta_Public_Schools|Atlanta Public Schools]].
sentence_421: Georgia Public Radio is listener-funded and comprises one NPR member station, [[WABE|WABE]], a classical music station operated by [[Atlanta_Public_Schools|Atlanta Public Schools]].
sentence_422: The second public radio, listerner-funded NPR member station is [[WCLK|WCLK]], a jazz music station owned and operated by [[Clark_Atlanta_University|Clark Atlanta University]].
sentence_423: Atlanta is served by [[The_Atlanta_Journal-Constitution|The Atlanta Journal-Constitution]], its only major daily newspaper with wide distribution.
sentence_424: The Atlanta Journal-Constitution is the result of a 1950 merger between The Atlanta Journal and The Atlanta Constitution, with staff consolidation occurring in 1982 and separate publication of the morning Constitution and afternoon Journal ceasing in 2001.
sentence_425: [[Alternative_weekly|Alternative weekly]] newspapers include [[Creative_Loafing_(Atlanta)|Creative Loafing]], which has a weekly print circulation of 80,000.
sentence_426: [[Atlanta_(magazine)|Atlanta]] magazine is an award-winning, monthly general-interest magazine based in and covering Atlanta.
sentence_427: Main article: [[Transportation_in_Atlanta|Transportation in Atlanta]]
sentence_428: For transportation in the Atlanta metropolitan area, see [[Atlanta_metropolitan_area#Transportation|Atlanta metropolitan area § Transportation]].
sentence_429: Atlanta's transportation infrastructure comprises a complex network that includes a [[Heavy_rail|heavy rail]] [[Rapid_transit|rapid transit]] system, a light rail [[Streetcar|streetcar]] loop, a multi-county bus system, [[Amtrak|Amtrak]] service via the [[Crescent_(train)|Crescent]], multiple freight train lines, an [[Interstate_Highway_System|Interstate Highway System]], several airports, including the world's busiest, and over 45 miles (72 km) of bike paths.
sentence_430: Atlanta has a network of freeways that radiate out from the city, and automobiles are the dominant means of transportation in the region.
sentence_431: Three major [[Interstate_highways|interstate highways]] converge in Atlanta: [[Interstate_20|I-20]] (east-west), [[Interstate_75|I-75]] (northwest-southeast), and [[Interstate_85|I-85]] (northeast-southwest).
sentence_432: The latter two combine in the middle of the city to form the [[Downtown_Connector|Downtown Connector]] (I-75/85), which carries more than 340,000 vehicles per day and is one of the most congested segments of interstate highway in the United States.
sentence_433: Atlanta is mostly encircled by [[Interstate_285_(Georgia)|Interstate 285]], a [[Beltway|beltway]] locally known as "the Perimeter" that has come to mark the boundary between "Inside the Perimeter" (ITP), the city and close-in suburbs, and "Outside the Perimeter" (OTP), the outer suburbs and exurbs.
sentence_434: The heavy reliance on automobiles for transportation in Atlanta has resulted in traffic, commute, and air pollution rates that rank among the worst in the country.
sentence_435: The City of Atlanta has a higher than average percentage of households without a car.
sentence_436: In 2015, 15.2 percent of Atlanta households lacked a car, and increased slightly to 16.4 percent in 2016.
sentence_437: The national average is 8.7 percent in 2016.
sentence_438: Atlanta averaged 1.31 cars per household in 2016, compared to a national average of 1.8.
sentence_439: The [[Metropolitan_Atlanta_Rapid_Transit_Authority|Metropolitan Atlanta Rapid Transit Authority]] (MARTA) provides public transportation in the form of buses, heavy rail, and a downtown light rail loop.
sentence_440: Notwithstanding heavy automotive usage in Atlanta, the city's [[Rapid_transit|subway]] system is the [[List_of_United_States_Rapid_Transit_systems_by_Ridership|eighth busiest in the country]].
sentence_441: MARTA rail lines connect key destinations, such as the airport, Downtown, Midtown, Buckhead, and Perimeter Center.
sentence_442: However, significant destinations, such as Emory University and [[Cumberland,_Georgia|Cumberland]], remain unserved.
sentence_443: As a result, a 2011 [[Brookings_Institution|Brookings Institution]] study placed Atlanta 91st of 100 metro areas for transit accessibility.
sentence_444: [[Emory_University|Emory University]] operates its [[The_Cliff_(Emory)|Cliff]] shuttle buses with 200,000 boardings per month, while private minibuses supply [[Buford_Highway|Buford Highway]].
sentence_445: [[Amtrak|Amtrak]], the national rail passenger system, provides service to Atlanta via the [[Crescent_(train)|Crescent train]] (New York–New Orleans), which stops at [[Peachtree_Station|Peachtree Station]].
sentence_446: In 2014, the [[Atlanta_Streetcar|Atlanta Streetcar]] opened to the public.
sentence_447: The streetcar's line, which is also known as the Downtown Loop, runs 2.7 miles (4.3 km) around the downtown tourist areas of [[Peachtree_Center|Peachtree Center]], [[Centennial_Olympic_Park|Centennial Olympic Park]], the [[Martin_Luther_King_Jr._National_Historical_Park|Martin Luther King Jr. National Historical Park]], and Sweet Auburn.
sentence_448: The Atlanta Streetcar line is also being expanded on in the coming years to include a wider range of Atlanta's neighborhoods and important places of interest, with a total of over 50 miles (80 km) of track in the plan.
sentence_449: [[Hartsfield–Jackson_Atlanta_International_Airport|Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport]] is the world's busiest airport as measured by [[World's_busiest_airports_by_passenger_traffic|passenger traffic]] and [[World's_busiest_airports_by_traffic_movements|aircraft traffic]].
sentence_450: The facility offers air service to over 150 U.S. destinations and more than 75 international destinations in 50 countries, with over 2,500 arrivals and departures daily.
sentence_451: [[Delta_Air_Lines|Delta Air Lines]] maintains its largest hub at the airport.
sentence_452: Situated 10 miles (16 km) south of downtown, the airport covers most of the land inside a wedge formed by [[Interstate_75|Interstate 75]], [[Interstate_85|Interstate 85]], and [[Interstate_285_(Georgia)|Interstate 285]].
sentence_453: [[Cycling_in_Atlanta|Cycling]] is a growing mode of transportation in Atlanta, more than doubling since 2009, when it comprised 1.1% of all commutes (up from 0.3% in 2000).
sentence_454: Although Atlanta's lack of bike lanes and hilly topography may deter many residents from cycling, the city's transportation plan calls for the construction of 226 miles (364 km) of bike lanes by 2020, with the BeltLine helping to achieve this goal.
sentence_455: In 2012, Atlanta's first "bike track" was constructed on 10th Street in Midtown.
sentence_456: The two lane bike track runs from Monroe Drive west to Charles Allen Drive, with connections to the Beltline and Piedmont Park.
sentence_457: Starting in June 2016, Atlanta received a bike sharing program, known as Relay Bike Share, with 100 bikes in Downtown and Midtown, which expanded to 500 bikes at 65 stations as of April 2017.
sentence_458: According to the 2016 [[American_Community_Survey|American Community Survey]] (five-year average), 68.6% of working city of Atlanta residents commuted by driving alone, 7% carpooled, 10% used public transportation, and 4.6% walked.
sentence_459: About 2.1% used all other forms of transportation, including taxi, bicycle, and motorcycle.
sentence_460: About 7.6% worked at home.
sentence_461: The city has also become one of a handful of "scooter capitals", where companies like [[Lime_(transportation_company)|Lime]] and [[Bird_(company)|Bird]] have gained a major foothold by placing electric scooters on street corners and byways.
sentence_462: Main article: [[Atlanta_tree_canopy|Atlanta tree canopy]]
sentence_463: Atlanta has a reputation as a "city in a forest" due to an abundance of trees that is rare among major cities.
sentence_464: The city's [[Peachtree_Street|main street]] is named after a [[Peach|tree]], and beyond the Downtown, Midtown, and Buckhead business districts, the skyline gives way to a dense canopy of woods that spreads into the suburbs.
sentence_465: The city is home to the [[Atlanta_Dogwood_Festival|Atlanta Dogwood Festival]], an annual arts and crafts festival held one weekend during early April, when the native [[Cornus_(genus)|dogwoods]] are in bloom.
sentence_466: The nickname is factually accurate, as vegetation covers 47.9% of the city as of 2017, the highest among all major American cities, and well above the national average of 27%.
sentence_467: Atlanta's tree coverage does not go unnoticed—it was the main reason cited by [[National_Geographic_(magazine)|National Geographic]] in naming Atlanta a "Place of a Lifetime".
sentence_468: The city's lush tree canopy, which filters out pollutants and cools sidewalks and buildings, has increasingly been under assault from man and nature due to heavy rains, drought, aged forests, new pests, and urban construction.
sentence_469: A 2001 study found Atlanta's heavy tree cover declined from 48% in 1974 to 38% in 1996.
sentence_470: Community organizations and the city government are addressing the problem.
sentence_471: Trees Atlanta, a non-profit organization founded in 1985, has planted and distributed over 113,000 [[Shade_tree|shade trees]] in the city, and Atlanta's government has awarded $130,000 in grants to neighborhood groups to plant trees.
sentence_472: Fees are additionally imposed on developers that remove trees on their property per a citywide ordinance, active since 1993.
sentence_473: See also: List of sister cities in the United States
sentence_474: Atlanta has 17 sister cities, as designated by [[Sister_Cities_International|Sister Cities International]], Inc. (SCI):

title: Alabama

sentence_1: For the river, see [[Alabama_River|Alabama River]].
sentence_2: For other uses, see [[Alabama_(disambiguation)|Alabama (disambiguation)]].

sentence_3: Alabama ([[English|/ˌæləˈbæmə/]]) is a state in the [[Southern_United_States|southeastern region]] of the United States.
sentence_4: It is bordered by [[Tennessee|Tennessee]] to the north, [[Georgia_(U.S._state)|Georgia]] to the east, [[Florida|Florida]] and the [[Gulf_of_Mexico|Gulf of Mexico]] to the south, and [[Mississippi|Mississippi]] to the west.
sentence_5: Alabama is the [[List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_area|30th largest by area]] and the [[List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population|24th-most populous]] of the [[List_of_U.S._states|U.S.
sentence_6: states]].
sentence_7: With a total of 1,500 miles (2,400 km) of [[Inland_waterway|inland waterways]], Alabama has among the most of any state.
sentence_8: Alabama is nicknamed the [[Northern_flicker|Yellowhammer]] State, after the [[List_of_U.S._state_birds|state bird]].
sentence_9: Alabama is also known as the "Heart of [[Dixie|Dixie]]" and the "Cotton State".
sentence_10: The [[List_of_U.S._state_trees|state tree]] is the [[Longleaf_pine|longleaf pine]], and the [[List_of_U.S._state_flowers|state flower]] is the [[Camellia|camellia]].
sentence_11: Alabama's capital is [[Montgomery,_Alabama|Montgomery]].
sentence_12: The largest city by population is [[Birmingham,_Alabama|Birmingham]], which has long been the most industrialized city; the largest city by land area is [[Huntsville,_Alabama|Huntsville]].
sentence_13: The oldest city is [[Mobile,_Alabama|Mobile]], founded by French [[Colonists|colonists]] in 1702 as the capital of [[Louisiana_(New_France)|French Louisiana]].
sentence_14: [[Birmingham_metropolitan_area,_Alabama|Greater Birmingham]] is Alabama's largest urban economy, its most populous urban area, and its economic center.
sentence_15: From the [[American_Civil_War|American Civil War]] until [[World_War_II|World War II]], Alabama, like many states in the [[Southern_U.S.|southern U.S.]], suffered economic hardship, in part because of its continued dependence on agriculture.
sentence_16: Similar to other former slave states, Alabamian legislators employed [[Jim_Crow_laws|Jim Crow laws]] to disenfranchise and otherwise discriminate against [[African_Americans|African Americans]] from the end of the [[Reconstruction_Era|Reconstruction Era]] up until at least the 1970s.
sentence_17: Despite the growth of major industries and urban centers, [[White_American|white]] rural interests dominated the state legislature from 1901 to the 1960s.
sentence_18: During this time, urban interests and African Americans were markedly under-represented.
sentence_19: Following [[World_War_II|World War II]], Alabama grew as the state's economy changed from one primarily based on [[Agriculture|agriculture]] to one with diversified interests.
sentence_20: The state's economy in the 21st century is based on management, automotive, finance, manufacturing, aerospace, mineral extraction, healthcare, education, retail, and technology.
sentence_21: The European-American naming of the [[Alabama_River|Alabama River]] and state was derived from the [[Alabama_people|Alabama people]], a [[Muskogean_languages|Muskogean-speaking tribe]] whose members lived just below the [[Confluence|confluence]] of the [[Coosa_River|Coosa]] and [[Tallapoosa_River|Tallapoosa]] rivers on the upper reaches of the river.
sentence_22: In the [[Alabama_language|Alabama language]], the word for a person of Alabama lineage is Albaamo (or variously Albaama or Albàamo in different dialects; the plural form is Albaamaha).
sentence_23: The suggestion that "Alabama" was borrowed from the [[Choctaw_language|Choctaw language]] is unlikely.
sentence_24: The word's spelling varies significantly among historical sources.
sentence_25: The first usage appears in three accounts of the [[Hernando_de_Soto|Hernando de Soto]] expedition of 1540: [[Garcilaso_de_la_Vega_(chronicler)|Garcilaso de la Vega]] used Alibamo, while the Knight of Elvas and Rodrigo Ranjel wrote Alibamu and Limamu, respectively, in transliterations of the term.
sentence_26: As early as 1702, the French called the tribe the Alibamon, with French maps identifying the river as Rivière des Alibamons.
sentence_27: Other spellings of the name have included Alibamu, Alabamo, Albama, Alebamon, Alibama, Alibamou, Alabamu, Allibamou.
sentence_28: Sources disagree on the word's meaning.
sentence_29: Some scholars suggest the word comes from the Choctaw alba (meaning "plants" or "weeds") and amo (meaning "to cut", "to trim", or "to gather").
sentence_30: The meaning may have been "clearers of the thicket" or "herb gatherers", referring to clearing land for cultivation or collecting medicinal plants.
sentence_31: The state has numerous [[List_of_place_names_in_Alabama_of_Native_American_origin|place names of Native American origin]].
sentence_32: However, there are no correspondingly similar words in the Alabama language.
sentence_33: An 1842 article in the Jacksonville Republican proposed it meant "Here We Rest".
sentence_34: This notion was popularized in the 1850s through the writings of [[Alexander_Beaufort_Meek|Alexander Beaufort Meek]].
sentence_35: Experts in the [[Muskogean_languages|Muskogean languages]] have not found any evidence to support such a translation.
sentence_36: Main article: [[History_of_Alabama|History of Alabama]]
sentence_37: Indigenous peoples of varying cultures lived in the area for thousands of years before the advent of European colonization.
sentence_38: Trade with the northeastern tribes by the [[Ohio_River|Ohio River]] began during the Burial Mound Period (1000 BCE – 700 CE) and continued until [[European_colonization_of_the_Americas|European contact]].
sentence_39: The agrarian [[Mississippian_culture|Mississippian culture]] covered most of the state from 1000 to 1600 CE, with one of its major centers built at what is now the [[Moundville_Archaeological_Site|Moundville Archaeological Site]] in [[Moundville,_Alabama|Moundville, Alabama]].
sentence_40: This is the second-largest complex of the classic Middle Mississippian era, after [[Cahokia|Cahokia]] in present-day [[Illinois|Illinois]], which was the center of the culture.
sentence_41: Analysis of [[Artifact_(archaeology)|artifacts]] from [[Archaeological|archaeological]] excavations at Moundville were the basis of scholars' formulating the characteristics of the [[Southeastern_Ceremonial_Complex|Southeastern Ceremonial Complex]] (SECC).
sentence_42: Contrary to popular belief, the SECC appears to have no direct links to [[Mesoamerica|Mesoamerican]] culture, but developed independently.
sentence_43: The Ceremonial Complex represents a major component of the religion of the Mississippian peoples; it is one of the primary means by which their religion is understood.
sentence_44: Among the historical tribes of Native American people living in present-day Alabama at the time of European contact were the [[Cherokee|Cherokee]], an [[Iroquoian_language|Iroquoian language]] people; and the [[Muskogean|Muskogean]]-speaking [[Alabama_(people)|Alabama]] (Alibamu), [[Chickasaw|Chickasaw]], [[Choctaw|Choctaw]], [[Creek_people|Creek]], and [[Koasati|Koasati]].
sentence_45: While part of the same large language family, the Muskogee tribes developed distinct cultures and languages.
sentence_46: Main articles: [[New_France|New France]], [[Louisiana_(New_France)|Louisiana (New France)]], [[French_and_Indian_War|French and Indian War]], [[Treaty_of_Paris_(1763)|Treaty of Paris (1763)]], [[New_Spain|New Spain]], [[Louisiana_(New_Spain)|Louisiana (New Spain)]], [[West_Florida|West Florida]], [[Indian_Reserve_(1763)|Indian Reserve (1763)]], [[American_Revolutionary_War|American Revolutionary War]], [[Treaty_of_Paris_(1783)|Treaty of Paris (1783)]], [[Spanish_West_Florida|Spanish West Florida]], [[Seminole_Wars|Seminole Wars]], [[Adams–Onís_Treaty|Adams–Onís Treaty]], [[Republic_of_West_Florida|Republic of West Florida]], and [[Mississippi_Territory|Mississippi Territory]]
sentence_47: With exploration in the 16th century, the Spanish were the first Europeans to reach Alabama.
sentence_48: The expedition of [[Hernando_de_Soto|Hernando de Soto]] passed through [[Mabila|Mabila]] and other parts of the state in 1540.
sentence_49: More than 160 years later, the French founded the region's first European settlement at [[Old_Mobile_Site|Old Mobile]] in 1702.
sentence_50: The city was moved to the current site of [[Mobile,_Alabama|Mobile]] in 1711.
sentence_51: This area was claimed by the French from 1702 to 1763 as part of [[La_Louisiane|La Louisiane]].
sentence_52: After the French lost to the British in the [[Seven_Years'_War|Seven Years' War]], it became part of British [[West_Florida|West Florida]] from 1763 to 1783.
sentence_53: After the United States victory in the [[American_Revolutionary_War|American Revolutionary War]], the territory was divided between the United States and Spain.
sentence_54: The latter retained control of this western territory from 1783 until the surrender of the Spanish garrison at Mobile to U.S. forces on April 13, 1813.
sentence_55: Thomas Bassett, a [[Loyalist_(American_Revolution)|loyalist]] to the British monarchy during the Revolutionary era, was one of the earliest white settlers in the state outside Mobile.
sentence_56: He settled in the [[Tombigbee_District|Tombigbee District]] during the early 1770s.
sentence_57: The district's boundaries were roughly limited to the area within a few miles of the [[Tombigbee_River|Tombigbee River]] and included portions of what is today southern [[Clarke_County,_Alabama|Clarke County]], northernmost [[Mobile_County,_Alabama|Mobile County]], and most of [[Washington_County,_Alabama|Washington County]].
sentence_58: What is now the counties of [[Baldwin_County,_Alabama|Baldwin]] and [[Mobile_County,_Alabama|Mobile]] became part of [[Spanish_West_Florida|Spanish West Florida]] in 1783, part of the independent [[Republic_of_West_Florida|Republic of West Florida]] in 1810, and was finally added to the [[Mississippi_Territory|Mississippi Territory]] in 1812.
sentence_59: Most of what is now the northern two-thirds of Alabama was known as the [[Yazoo_lands|Yazoo lands]] beginning during the British colonial period.
sentence_60: It was claimed by the [[Province_of_Georgia|Province of Georgia]] from 1767 onwards.
sentence_61: Following the Revolutionary War, it remained a part of [[Georgia_(U.S._state)|Georgia]], although heavily disputed.
sentence_62: With the exception of the area around Mobile and the Yazoo lands, what is now the lower one-third of Alabama was made part of the Mississippi Territory when it was organized in 1798.
sentence_63: The Yazoo lands were added to the territory in 1804, following the [[Yazoo_land_scandal|Yazoo land scandal]].
sentence_64: Spain kept a claim on its former Spanish West Florida territory in what would become the coastal counties until the [[Adams–Onís_Treaty|Adams–Onís Treaty]] officially ceded it to the United States in 1819.
sentence_65: Main articles: [[Organic_act#List_of_organic_acts|Organic act § List of organic acts]], [[Alabama_Territory|Alabama Territory]], [[Admission_to_the_Union|Admission to the Union]], and [[List_of_U.S._states_by_date_of_admission_to_the_Union|List of U.S. states by date of admission to the Union]]
sentence_66: Before [[Mississippi|Mississippi]]'s admission to statehood on December 10, 1817, the more sparsely settled eastern half of the territory was separated and named the [[Alabama_Territory|Alabama Territory]].
sentence_67: The [[United_States_Congress|United States Congress]] created the Alabama Territory on March 3, 1817.
sentence_68: [[St._Stephens,_Alabama|St.
sentence_69: Stephens]], now abandoned, served as the territorial capital from 1817 to 1819.
sentence_70: Alabama was admitted as the 22nd state on December 14, 1819, with Congress selecting Huntsville as the site for the first Constitutional Convention.
sentence_71: From July 5 to August 2, 1819, delegates met to prepare the new state constitution.
sentence_72: Huntsville served as temporary capital from 1819 to 1820, when the seat of government moved to [[Cahaba,_Alabama|Cahaba]] in [[Dallas_County,_Alabama|Dallas County]].
sentence_73: Cahaba, now a [[Ghost_town|ghost town]], was the first permanent state capital from 1820 to 1825.
sentence_74: The [[Alabama_Fever|Alabama Fever]] land rush was underway when the state was admitted to the Union, with settlers and land speculators pouring into the state to take advantage of fertile land suitable for cotton cultivation.
sentence_75: Part of the frontier in the 1820s and 1830s, its constitution provided for universal suffrage for white men.
sentence_76: Southeastern planters and traders from the [[Upper_South|Upper South]] brought slaves with them as the cotton [[List_of_plantations_in_Alabama|plantations in Alabama]] expanded.
sentence_77: The economy of the central [[Black_Belt_(region_of_Alabama)|Black Belt]] (named for its dark, productive soil) was built around large cotton [[Plantation_complexes_in_the_Southeastern_United_States|plantations]] whose owners' wealth grew mainly from slave labor.
sentence_78: The area also drew many poor, disfranchised people who became [[Subsistence_farmers|subsistence farmers]].
sentence_79: Alabama had an estimated population of under 10,000 people in 1810, but it increased to more than 300,000 people by 1830.
sentence_80: Most Native American tribes were [[Indian_removal|completely removed]] from the state within a few years of the passage of the [[Indian_Removal_Act|Indian Removal Act]] by Congress in 1830.
sentence_81: From 1826 to 1846, [[Tuscaloosa,_Alabama|Tuscaloosa]] served as Alabama's capital.
sentence_82: On January 30, 1846, the Alabama legislature announced it had voted to move the capital city from Tuscaloosa to [[Montgomery,_Alabama|Montgomery]].
sentence_83: The first legislative session in the new capital met in December 1847.
sentence_84: A new capitol building was erected under the direction of [[Stephen_Decatur_Button|Stephen Decatur Button]] of [[Philadelphia|Philadelphia]].
sentence_85: The first structure burned down in 1849, but was rebuilt on the same site in 1851.
sentence_86: This second capitol building in Montgomery remains to the present day.
sentence_87: It was designed by Barachias Holt of [[Exeter,_Maine|Exeter, Maine]].
sentence_88: Main articles: [[Ordinance_of_Secession|Ordinance of Secession]], [[Confederate_States_of_America|Confederate States of America]], and [[Alabama_in_the_American_Civil_War|Alabama in the American Civil War]]
sentence_89: By 1860, the population had increased to 964,201 people, of which nearly half, 435,080, were enslaved African Americans, and 2,690 were [[Free_people_of_color|free people of color]].
sentence_90: On January 11, 1861, Alabama declared its [[Secession_in_the_United_States|secession]] from the [[Union_(American_Civil_War)|Union]].
sentence_91: After remaining an independent republic for a few days, it joined the [[Confederate_States_of_America|Confederate States of America]].
sentence_92: The Confederacy's capital was initially at [[Montgomery,_Alabama|Montgomery]].
sentence_93: Alabama was heavily [[Alabama_in_the_American_Civil_War|involved in the American Civil War]].
sentence_94: Although comparatively few battles were fought in the state, Alabama contributed about 120,000 soldiers to the war effort.
sentence_95: A company of cavalry soldiers from Huntsville, Alabama, joined [[Nathan_Bedford_Forrest|Nathan Bedford Forrest]]'s battalion in [[Hopkinsville,_Kentucky|Hopkinsville, Kentucky]].
sentence_96: The company wore new uniforms with yellow trim on the sleeves, collar and coat tails.
sentence_97: This led to them being greeted with "Yellowhammer", and the name later was applied to all Alabama troops in the Confederate Army.
sentence_98: Alabama's slaves were freed by the 13th Amendment in 1865.
sentence_99: Alabama was under military rule from the end of the war in May 1865 until its official restoration to the Union in 1868.
sentence_100: From 1867 to 1874, with most white citizens barred temporarily from voting and freedmen enfranchised, many African Americans emerged as political leaders in the state.
sentence_101: Alabama was represented in Congress during this period by three African-American congressmen: [[Jeremiah_Haralson|Jeremiah Haralson]], [[Benjamin_S._Turner|Benjamin S. Turner]], and [[James_T._Rapier|James T. Rapier]].
sentence_102: Following the war, the state remained chiefly agricultural, with an economy tied to cotton.
sentence_103: During [[Reconstruction_Era|Reconstruction]], state legislators ratified a [[Constitution_of_Alabama|new state constitution]] in 1868 which created the state's first public school system and expanded women's rights.
sentence_104: Legislators funded numerous public road and railroad projects, although these were plagued with allegations of fraud and misappropriation.
sentence_105: Organized [[Insurgent|insurgent]], resistance groups tried to suppress the freedmen and Republicans.
sentence_106: Besides the short-lived original [[Ku_Klux_Klan|Ku Klux Klan]], these included the Pale Faces, [[Knights_of_the_White_Camellia|Knights of the White Camellia]], [[Red_Shirts_(Southern_United_States)|Red Shirts]], and the [[White_League|White League]].
sentence_107: Reconstruction in Alabama ended in 1874, when the Democrats regained control of the legislature and governor's office through an election dominated by fraud and violence.
sentence_108: They wrote another constitution in 1875, and the legislature passed the [[Blaine_Amendment|Blaine Amendment]], prohibiting public money from being used to finance religious-affiliated schools.
sentence_109: The same year, legislation was approved that called for [[Racial_segregation|racially segregated]] schools.
sentence_110: Railroad passenger cars were segregated in 1891.
sentence_111: After disenfranchising most African Americans and many poor whites in the 1901 constitution, the Alabama legislature passed more [[Jim_Crow_laws|Jim Crow laws]] at the beginning of the 20th century to impose segregation in everyday life.
sentence_112: The new 1901 [[Constitution_of_Alabama|Constitution of Alabama]] included provisions for [[Voter_registration|voter registration]] that effectively [[Disfranchisement_after_the_Reconstruction_Era|disenfranchised]] large portions of the population, including nearly all African Americans and Native Americans, and tens of thousands of poor whites, through making voter registration difficult, requiring a [[Poll_tax_(United_States)|poll tax]] and [[Literacy_test|literacy test]].
sentence_113: The 1901 constitution required racial segregation of public schools.
sentence_114: By 1903 only 2,980 African Americans were registered in Alabama, although at least 74,000 were [[Literate|literate]].
sentence_115: This compared to more than 181,000 African Americans eligible to vote in 1900.
sentence_116: The numbers dropped even more in later decades.
sentence_117: The state legislature passed additional racial segregation laws related to public facilities into the 1950s: jails were segregated in 1911; hospitals in 1915; toilets, hotels, and restaurants in 1928; and bus stop waiting rooms in 1945.
sentence_118: While the planter class had persuaded poor whites to vote for this legislative effort to suppress black voting, the new restrictions resulted in their disenfranchisement as well, due mostly to the imposition of a cumulative poll tax.
sentence_119: By 1941, whites constituted a slight majority of those disenfranchised by these laws: 600,000 whites vs. 520,000 African-Americans.
sentence_120: Nearly all African Americans had lost the ability to vote.
sentence_121: Despite numerous legal challenges which succeeded in overturning certain provisions, the state legislature would create new ones to maintain disenfranchisement.
sentence_122: The exclusion of blacks from the political system persisted until after passage of federal civil rights legislation in 1965 to enforce their constitutional rights as citizens.
sentence_123: The rural-dominated Alabama legislature consistently underfunded schools and services for the disenfranchised African Americans, but it did not relieve them of paying taxes.
sentence_124: Partially as a response to chronic underfunding of education for African Americans in the South, the [[Rosenwald_Fund|Rosenwald Fund]] began funding the construction of what came to be known as [[Rosenwald_School|Rosenwald Schools]].
sentence_125: In Alabama these schools were designed and the construction partially financed with Rosenwald funds, which paid one-third of the construction costs.
sentence_126: The fund required the local community and state to raise matching funds to pay the rest.
sentence_127: Black residents effectively taxed themselves twice, by raising additional monies to supply matching funds for such schools, which were built in many rural areas.
sentence_128: They often donated land and labor as well.
sentence_129: Beginning in 1913, the first 80 [[Rosenwald_Schools|Rosenwald Schools]] were built in Alabama for African-American children.
sentence_130: A total of 387 schools, seven teachers' houses, and several vocational buildings were completed by 1937 in the state.
sentence_131: Several of the [[The_Rosenwald_School_Building_Fund_and_Associated_Buildings_Multiple_Property_Submission|surviving school buildings]] in the state are now listed on the [[National_Register_of_Historic_Places|National Register of Historic Places]].
sentence_132: Continued racial discrimination and [[Lynching|lynchings]], agricultural depression, and the failure of the cotton crops due to [[Boll_weevil|boll weevil]] infestation led tens of thousands of African Americans from rural Alabama and other states to seek opportunities in northern and midwestern cities during the early decades of the 20th century as part of the [[Great_Migration_(African_American)|Great Migration]] out of the South.
sentence_133: Reflecting this emigration, the population growth rate in Alabama (see "historical populations" table below) dropped by nearly half from 1910 to 1920.
sentence_134: At the same time, many rural people migrated to the city of [[Birmingham,_Alabama|Birmingham]] to work in new industrial jobs.
sentence_135: Birmingham experienced such rapid growth it was called the "Magic City".
sentence_136: By 1920, Birmingham was the 36th-largest city in the United States.
sentence_137: Heavy industry and mining were the basis of its economy.
sentence_138: Its residents were under-represented for decades in the state legislature, which refused to redistrict after each decennial census according to population changes, as it was required by the state constitution.
sentence_139: This did not change until the late 1960s following a lawsuit and court order.
sentence_140: Industrial development related to the demands of World War II brought a level of prosperity to the state not seen since before the civil war.
sentence_141: Rural workers poured into the largest cities in the state for better jobs and a higher standard of living.
sentence_142: One example of this massive influx of workers occurred in Mobile.
sentence_143: Between 1940 and 1943, more than 89,000 people moved into the city to work for war-related industries.
sentence_144: Cotton and other [[Cash_crop|cash crops]] faded in importance as the state developed a manufacturing and service base.
sentence_145: Despite massive population changes in the state from 1901 to 1961, the rural-dominated legislature refused to reapportion House and Senate seats based on population, as required by the state constitution to follow the results of decennial censuses.
sentence_146: They held on to old representation to maintain political and economic power in agricultural areas.
sentence_147: One result was that [[Jefferson_County,_Alabama|Jefferson County]], containing Birmingham's industrial and economic powerhouse, contributed more than one-third of all tax revenue to the state, but did not receive a proportional amount in services.
sentence_148: Urban interests were consistently underrepresented in the legislature.
sentence_149: A 1960 study noted that because of rural domination, "a minority of about 25% of the total state population is in majority control of the Alabama legislature."
sentence_150: In the United States Supreme Court cases of [[Baker_v._Carr|Baker v. Carr]] (1962) and [[Reynolds_v._Sims|Reynolds v. Sims]] (1964), the court ruled that the principle of "[[One_man,_one_vote|one man, one vote]]" needed to be the basis of both houses of state legislatures, and that their districts had to be based on population rather than geographic counties.
sentence_151: In 1972, for the first time since 1901, the legislature completed the congressional redistricting based on the decennial census.
sentence_152: This benefited the urban areas that had developed, as well as all in the population who had been underrepresented for more than sixty years.
sentence_153: Other changes were made to implement representative state house and senate districts.
sentence_154: African Americans continued to press in the 1950s and 1960s to end disenfranchisement and segregation in the state through the [[Civil_rights_movement|civil rights movement]], including legal challenges.
sentence_155: In 1954, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in [[Brown_v._Board_of_Education|Brown v. Board of Education]] that public schools had to be desegregated, but Alabama was slow to comply.
sentence_156: During the 1960s, under Governor [[George_Wallace|George Wallace]], Alabama resisted compliance with federal demands for [[Desegregation|desegregation]].
sentence_157: The civil rights movement had notable events in Alabama, including the [[Montgomery_bus_boycott|Montgomery bus boycott]] (1955–56), [[Freedom_Rides|Freedom Rides]] in 1961, and 1965 [[Selma_to_Montgomery_marches|Selma to Montgomery marches]].
sentence_158: These contributed to Congressional passage and enactment of the [[Civil_Rights_Act_of_1964|Civil Rights Act of 1964]] and [[Voting_Rights_Act_of_1965|Voting Rights Act of 1965]] by the U.S. Congress.
sentence_159: Legal segregation ended in the states in 1964, but [[Jim_Crow|Jim Crow]] customs often continued until specifically challenged in court.
sentence_160: According to [[The_New_York_Times|The New York Times]], by 2017, many of Alabama's African-Americans were living in Alabama's cities such as Birmingham and Montgomery.
sentence_161: Also, the [[Black_Belt_(region_of_Alabama)|Black Belt region]] across central Alabama "is home to largely poor counties that are predominantly African-American.
sentence_162: These counties include [[Dallas_County,_Alabama|Dallas]], [[Lowndes_County,_Alabama|Lowndes]], [[Marengo_County,_Alabama|Marengo]] and [[Perry_County,_Alabama|Perry]]."
sentence_163: Alabama has made some changes since the late 20th century and has used new types of voting to increase representation.
sentence_164: In the 1980s, an omnibus redistricting case, Dillard v. Crenshaw County, challenged the [[At-large|at-large]] voting for representative seats of 180 Alabama jurisdictions, including counties and school boards.
sentence_165: At-large voting had diluted the votes of any minority in a county, as the majority tended to take all seats.
sentence_166: Despite African Americans making up a significant minority in the state, they had been unable to elect any representatives in most of the at-large jurisdictions.
sentence_167: As part of settlement of this case, five Alabama cities and counties, including [[Chilton_County,_Alabama|Chilton County]], adopted a system of [[Proportional_representation|cumulative voting]] for election of representatives in multi-seat jurisdictions.
sentence_168: This has resulted in more proportional representation for voters.
sentence_169: In another form of proportional representation, 23 jurisdictions use limited voting, as in [[Conecuh_County,_Alabama|Conecuh County]].
sentence_170: In 1982, limited voting was first tested in [[Conecuh_County,_Alabama|Conecuh County]].
sentence_171: Together use of these systems has increased the number of African Americans and women being elected to local offices, resulting in governments that are more representative of their citizens.
sentence_172: Main article: Geography of Alabama
sentence_173: See also: [[List_of_Alabama_counties|List of Alabama counties]] and [[Geology_of_Alabama|Geology of Alabama]]
sentence_174: Alabama is the thirtieth-largest state in the United States with 52,419 square miles (135,760 km) of total area: 3.2% of the area is water, making Alabama 23rd in the amount of surface water, also giving it the second-largest inland waterway system in the United States.
sentence_175: About three-fifths of the land area is a gentle plain with a general descent towards the [[Mississippi_River|Mississippi River]] and the [[Gulf_of_Mexico|Gulf of Mexico]].
sentence_176: The [[North_Alabama|North Alabama]] region is mostly mountainous, with the [[Tennessee_River|Tennessee River]] cutting a large valley and creating numerous creeks, streams, rivers, mountains, and lakes.
sentence_177: Alabama is bordered by the states of [[Tennessee|Tennessee]] to the north, [[Georgia_(U.S._state)|Georgia]] to the east, Florida to the south, and [[Mississippi|Mississippi]] to the west.
sentence_178: Alabama has coastline at the Gulf of Mexico, in the extreme southern edge of the state.
sentence_179: The state ranges in elevation from sea level at [[Mobile_Bay|Mobile Bay]] to nearly half a mile in the [[Sand_Mountain_(Alabama)|northeast]], to wit [[Mount_Cheaha|Mount Cheaha]] at 2,413 ft (735 m).
sentence_180: Alabama's land consists of 22 million acres (89,000 km) of forest or 67% of total land area.
sentence_181: Suburban [[Baldwin_County,_Alabama|Baldwin County]], along the Gulf Coast, is the largest county in the state in both land area and water area.
sentence_182: Areas in Alabama administered by the [[National_Park_Service|National Park Service]] include [[Horseshoe_Bend_National_Military_Park|Horseshoe Bend National Military Park]] near [[Alexander_City,_Alabama|Alexander City]]; [[Little_River_Canyon_National_Preserve|Little River Canyon National Preserve]] near [[Fort_Payne,_Alabama|Fort Payne]]; [[Russell_Cave_National_Monument|Russell Cave National Monument]] in [[Bridgeport,_Alabama|Bridgeport]]; [[Tuskegee_Airmen_National_Historic_Site|Tuskegee Airmen National Historic Site]] in [[Tuskegee,_Alabama|Tuskegee]]; and [[Tuskegee_Institute_National_Historic_Site|Tuskegee Institute National Historic Site]] near Tuskegee.
sentence_183: Additionally, Alabama has four National Forests: [[Conecuh_National_Forest|Conecuh]], [[Talladega_National_Forest|Talladega]], [[Tuskegee_National_Forest|Tuskegee]], and [[William_B._Bankhead_National_Forest|William B. Bankhead]].
sentence_184: Alabama also contains the [[Natchez_Trace_Parkway|Natchez Trace Parkway]], the [[Selma_To_Montgomery_National_Historic_Trail|Selma To Montgomery National Historic Trail]], and the [[Trail_of_Tears|Trail of Tears National Historic Trail]].
sentence_185: Notable natural wonders include: the [[Natural_Bridge,_Alabama|"Natural Bridge"]] rock, the longest [[Natural_bridge|natural bridge]] east of the [[Rocky_Mountains|Rockies]], located just south of [[Haleyville,_Alabama|Haleyville]]; [[Cathedral_Caverns_State_Park|Cathedral Caverns]] in [[Marshall_County,_Alabama|Marshall County]], named for its cathedral-like appearance, features one of the largest cave entrances and stalagmites in the world; Ecor Rouge in [[Fairhope,_Alabama|Fairhope]], the highest coastline point between [[Maine|Maine]] and Mexico; DeSoto Caverns in [[Childersburg,_Alabama|Childersburg]], the first officially recorded cave in the United States; [[Noccalula_Falls_Park|Noccalula Falls]] in [[Gadsden,_Alabama|Gadsden]] features a 90-foot waterfall; [[Dismals_Canyon|Dismals Canyon]] near [[Phil_Campbell,_Alabama|Phil Campbell]], home to two waterfalls, six natural bridges and allegedly served as a hideout for legendary outlaw Jesse James; Stephens Gap Cave in [[Jackson_County,_Alabama|Jackson County]] boasts a 143-foot pit, two waterfalls and is one of the most photographed wild cave scenes in America; [[Little_River_Canyon_National_Preserve|Little River Canyon]] near [[Fort_Payne,_Alabama|Fort Payne]], one of the nation's longest mountaintop rivers; [[Rickwood_Caverns_State_Park|Rickwood Caverns]] near [[Warrior,_Alabama|Warrior]] features an underground pool, blind cave fish and 260-million-year-old limestone formations; and the [[The_Walls_of_Jericho_(canyon)|Walls of Jericho]] canyon on the Alabama-[[Tennessee|Tennessee]] state line.
sentence_186: A 5-mile (8 km)-wide meteorite impact crater is located in [[Elmore_County,_Alabama|Elmore County]], just north of Montgomery.
sentence_187: This is the [[Wetumpka_crater|Wetumpka crater]], the site of "Alabama's greatest natural disaster".
sentence_188: A 1,000-foot (300 m)-wide meteorite hit the area about 80 million years ago.
sentence_189: The hills just east of downtown [[Wetumpka|Wetumpka]] showcase the eroded remains of the impact crater that was blasted into the bedrock, with the area labeled the Wetumpka crater or astrobleme ("star-wound") because of the concentric rings of fractures and zones of shattered rock that can be found beneath the surface.
sentence_190: In 2002, Christian Koeberl with the Institute of Geochemistry University of Vienna published evidence and established the site as the 157th recognized impact crater on Earth.
sentence_191: Main article: [[Climate_of_Alabama|Climate of Alabama]]
sentence_192: The state is classified as humid subtropical (Cfa) under the [[Humid_temperate_climate|Koppen Climate Classification]].
sentence_193: The average annual temperature is 64 °F (18 °C).
sentence_194: Temperatures tend to be warmer in the southern part of the state with its proximity to the Gulf of Mexico, while the northern parts of the state, especially in the [[Appalachian_Mountains|Appalachian Mountains]] in the northeast, tend to be slightly cooler.
sentence_195: Generally, Alabama has very hot summers and mild winters with copious precipitation throughout the year.
sentence_196: Alabama receives an average of 56 inches (1,400 mm) of rainfall annually and enjoys a lengthy growing season of up to 300 days in the southern part of the state.
sentence_197: Summers in Alabama are among the hottest in the U.S., with high temperatures averaging over 90 °F (32 °C) throughout the summer in some parts of the state.
sentence_198: Alabama is also prone to [[Tropical_storm|tropical storms]] and even [[Hurricane|hurricanes]].
sentence_199: Areas of the state far away from the Gulf are not immune to the effects of the storms, which often dump tremendous amounts of rain as they move inland and weaken.
sentence_200: South Alabama reports many [[Thunderstorm|thunderstorms]].
sentence_201: The Gulf Coast, around Mobile Bay, averages between 70 and 80 days per year with thunder reported.
sentence_202: This activity decreases somewhat further north in the state, but even the far north of the state reports thunder on about 60 days per year.
sentence_203: Occasionally, thunderstorms are severe with frequent [[Lightning|lightning]] and large [[Hail|hail]]; the central and northern parts of the state are most vulnerable to this type of storm.
sentence_204: Alabama ranks ninth in the number of deaths from lightning and tenth in the number of deaths from lightning strikes per capita.
sentence_205: Alabama, along with [[Oklahoma|Oklahoma]] and [[Iowa|Iowa]], has the most confirmed [[Fujita_scale|F5]] and [[Enhanced_Fujita_scale|EF5]] tornadoes of any state, according to statistics from the [[National_Climatic_Data_Center|National Climatic Data Center]] for the period January 1, 1950, to June 2013.
sentence_206: Several long-tracked F5/EF5 tornadoes have contributed to Alabama reporting more tornado fatalities since 1950 than any other state.
sentence_207: The state was affected by the [[1974_Super_Outbreak|1974 Super Outbreak]] and was devastated tremendously by the [[2011_Super_Outbreak|2011 Super Outbreak]].
sentence_208: The 2011 Super Outbreak produced a record amount of tornadoes in the state.
sentence_209: The tally reached 62.
sentence_210: The peak season for tornadoes varies from the northern to southern parts of the state.
sentence_211: Alabama is one of the few places in the world that has a secondary tornado season in November and December besides the typically severe spring.
sentence_212: The northern part—along the Tennessee River Valley—is most vulnerable.
sentence_213: The area of Alabama and Mississippi most affected by tornadoes is sometimes referred to as [[Dixie_Alley|Dixie Alley]], as distinct from the [[Tornado_Alley|Tornado Alley]] of the Southern Plains.
sentence_214: Winters are generally mild in Alabama, as they are throughout most of the Southeastern United States, with average January low temperatures around 40 °F (4 °C) in Mobile and around 32 °F (0 °C) in Birmingham.
sentence_215: Although snow is a rare event in much of Alabama, areas of the state north of Montgomery may receive a dusting of snow a few times every winter, with an occasional moderately heavy snowfall every few years.
sentence_216: Historic snowfall events include [[New_Year's_Eve_1963_snowstorm|New Year's Eve 1963 snowstorm]] and the [[1993_Storm_of_the_Century|1993 Storm of the Century]].
sentence_217: The annual average snowfall for the Birmingham area is 2 inches (51 mm) per year.
sentence_218: In the southern Gulf coast, snowfall is less frequent, sometimes going several years without any snowfall.
sentence_219: Alabama's highest temperature of 112 °F (44 °C) was recorded on September 5, 1925, in the unincorporated community of [[Centerville,_Alabama|Centerville]].
sentence_220: The record low of −27 °F (−33 °C) occurred on January 30, 1966, in [[New_Market,_Alabama|New Market]].

sentence_221: Main articles: [[List_of_amphibians_of_Alabama|List of amphibians of Alabama]], [[List_of_mammals_of_Alabama|List of mammals of Alabama]], [[List_of_reptiles_of_Alabama|List of reptiles of Alabama]], and [[Alabama_Champion_Tree_Program|Trees of Alabama]]
sentence_222: Alabama is home to a diverse array of flora and fauna in habitats that range from the Tennessee Valley, [[Appalachian_Plateau|Appalachian Plateau]], and Ridge-and-Valley Appalachians of the north to the [[Piedmont_(United_States)|Piedmont]], [[Canebrake_(region_of_Alabama)|Canebrake]], and [[Black_Belt_(region_of_Alabama)|Black Belt]] of the central region to the [[Gulf_Coastal_Plain|Gulf Coastal Plain]] and beaches along the [[Gulf_of_Mexico|Gulf of Mexico]] in the south.
sentence_223: The state is usually ranked among the top in nation for its range of overall [[Biodiversity|biodiversity]].
sentence_224: Alabama is in the subtropical coniferous forest biome and once boasted huge expanses of pine forest, which still form the largest proportion of forests in the state.
sentence_225: It currently ranks fifth in the nation for the diversity of its flora.
sentence_226: It is home to nearly 4,000 [[Pteridophyte|pteridophyte]] and [[Spermatophyte|spermatophyte]] plant species.
sentence_227: [[Indigenous_(ecology)|Indigenous]] animal species in the state include 62 [[Mammal|mammal]] [[Species|species]], 93 reptile species, 73 [[Amphibian|amphibian]] species, roughly 307 native [[Freshwater_fish|freshwater fish]] species, and 420 bird species that spend at least part of their year within the state.
sentence_228: Invertebrates include 97 [[Crayfish|crayfish]] species and 383 [[Mollusk|mollusk]] species.
sentence_229: 113 of these mollusk species have never been collected outside the state.
sentence_230: Main article: [[Demographics_of_Alabama|Demographics of Alabama]]
sentence_231: The [[United_States_Census_Bureau|United States Census Bureau]] estimates the population of Alabama was 4,903,185 on July 1, 2019, which represents an increase of 123,440 or 2.58%, since the [[2010_United_States_Census|2010 Census]].
sentence_232: This includes a natural increase since the last census of 121,054 (502,457 births minus 381,403 deaths) and an increase due to net migration of 104,991 into the state.
sentence_233: [[Immigration_to_the_United_States|Immigration]] from outside the U.S. resulted in a net increase of 31,180 people, and migration within the country produced a net gain of 73,811 people.
sentence_234: The state had 108,000 foreign-born (2.4% of the state population), of which an estimated 22.2% were undocumented (24,000).
sentence_235: The [[Center_of_population|center of population]] of Alabama is located in [[Chilton_County,_Alabama|Chilton County]], outside the town of [[Jemison,_Alabama|Jemison]].
sentence_236: According to the [[2010_United_States_Census|2010 Census]], Alabama had a population of 4,779,736.
sentence_237: The racial composition of the state was 68.5% [[White_American|White]] (67% [[Non-Hispanic_White|Non-Hispanic White]] and 1.5% [[Hispanic_White|Hispanic White]]), 26.2% [[African_American|Black or African American]], 3.9% [[Hispanic_and_Latino_Americans|Hispanic or Latino]] of any race, 1.1% Asian, 0.6% [[Native_Americans_in_the_United_States|American Indian and Alaska Native]], 0.1% [[Native_Hawaiians|Native Hawaiian]] and Other [[Pacific_Islander|Pacific Islander]], 2% from "Some Other Race", and 1.5% from "Two or More Races".
sentence_238: In 2011, 46.6% of Alabama's population younger than age 1 were minorities.
sentence_239: The largest reported ancestry groups in Alabama are: [[African_American|African]] (26.2%), [[English_American|English]] (23.6%), [[Irish_American|Irish]] (7.7%), [[German_Americans|German]] (5.7%), and [[Scots-Irish_American|Scots-Irish]] (2%).
sentence_240: Those citing "American" ancestry in Alabama are generally of English or British ancestry; many Anglo-Americans identify as having American ancestry because their roots have been in North America for so long, in some cases since the 1600s.
sentence_241: Demographers estimate that 20–23% of people in Alabama are of predominantly English ancestry and the figure is likely higher.
sentence_242: In the 1980 census, 41% of the people in Alabama identified as being of English ancestry, making them the largest ethnic group at the time.
sentence_243: Based on historic migration and settlement patterns in the southern colonies and states, demographers estimated there are more people in Alabama of Scots-Irish origins than self-reported.
sentence_244: Many people in Alabama claim Irish ancestry because of the term Scots-Irish but, based on historic immigration and settlement, their ancestors were more likely Protestant Scots-Irish coming from the northern province of [[Ulster|Ulster]], where they had been for a few generations as part of the English colonization.
sentence_245: The Scots-Irish were the largest non-English immigrant group from the British Isles before the American Revolution, and many settled in the South, later moving into the Deep South as it was developed.
sentence_246: In 1984, under the Davis–Strong Act, the state legislature established the Alabama Indian Affairs Commission.
sentence_247: Native American groups within the state had increasingly been demanding recognition as ethnic groups and seeking an end to discrimination.
sentence_248: Given the long history of slavery and associated racial segregation, the Native American peoples, who have sometimes been of mixed race, have insisted on having their cultural identification respected.
sentence_249: In the past, their self-identification was often overlooked as the state tried to impose a binary breakdown of society into white and black.
sentence_250: The state has [[State_recognized_tribes_in_the_United_States|officially recognized]] nine American Indian tribes in the state, descended mostly from the [[Five_Civilized_Tribes|Five Civilized Tribes]] of the American Southeast.
sentence_251: These are the following.

sentence_252: The state government has promoted recognition of Native American contributions to the state, including the designation in 2000 for Columbus Day to be jointly celebrated as American Indian Heritage Day.

sentence_255: Most Alabama residents (95.1% of those five and older) spoke only English at home in 2010, a minor decrease from 96.1% in 2000.
sentence_256: Alabama English is predominantly [[Southern_American_English|Southern]], and is related to South Midland speech which was taken across the border from [[Tennessee|Tennessee]].
sentence_257: In the major Southern speech region, there is the decreasing loss of the final r, for example the "boyd" pronunciation of "bird".
sentence_258: In the northern third of the state, there is a South Midland "arm" and "barb" rhyming with "form" and "orb".
sentence_259: Unique words in Alabama English include: redworm ([[Earthworm|earthworm]]), peckerwood ([[Woodpecker|woodpecker]]), snake doctor and snake feeder ([[Dragonfly|dragonfly]]), tow sack ([[Gunny_sack|burlap bag]]), plum peach ([[Clingstone_peach|clingstone]]), French harp (harmonica), and dog irons ([[Andiron|andirons]]).
