sentence_260: In the 2008 [[American_Religious_Identification_Survey|American Religious Identification Survey]], 86% of Alabama respondents reported their religion as Christian, including 6% Catholic, with 11% as having no religion.
sentence_261: The composition of other traditions is 0.5% Mormon, 0.5% Jewish, 0.5% Muslim, 0.5% Buddhist, and 0.5% Hindu.
sentence_262: Further information on Christianity in Alabama: [[History_of_Baptists_in_Alabama|History of Baptists in Alabama]], [[List_of_Baptist_churches_in_Alabama|List of Baptist churches in Alabama]], [[Episcopal_Diocese_of_Alabama|Episcopal Diocese of Alabama]], Episcopal Diocese of the Central Gulf Coast, [[Roman_Catholic_Archdiocese_of_Mobile|Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Mobile]], [[Roman_Catholic_Diocese_of_Birmingham_in_Alabama|Roman Catholic Diocese of Birmingham in Alabama]], and [[The_Church_of_Jesus_Christ_of_Latter-day_Saints_in_Alabama|The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints in Alabama]]
sentence_263: Alabama is located in the middle of the [[Bible_Belt|Bible Belt]], a region of numerous Protestant Christians.
sentence_264: Alabama has been identified as one of the most religious states in the United States, with about 58% of the population attending church regularly.
sentence_265: A majority of people in the state identify as Evangelical Protestant.
sentence_266: As of 2010, the three largest denominational groups in Alabama are the [[Southern_Baptist_Convention|Southern Baptist Convention]], [[The_United_Methodist_Church|The United Methodist Church]], and [[Nondenominational_Christianity|non-denominational]] Evangelical Protestant.
sentence_267: In Alabama, the [[Southern_Baptist_Convention|Southern Baptist Convention]] has the highest number of adherents with 1,380,121; this is followed by the [[United_Methodist_Church|United Methodist Church]] with 327,734 adherents, non-denominational Evangelical Protestant with 220,938 adherents, and the Catholic Church with 150,647 adherents.
sentence_268: Many Baptist and Methodist congregations became established in the [[Great_Awakening|Great Awakening]] of the early 19th century, when preachers proselytized across the South.
sentence_269: The [[Assemblies_of_God|Assemblies of God]] had almost 60,000 members, the [[Churches_of_Christ|Churches of Christ]] had nearly 120,000 members.
sentence_270: The [[Presbyterian_church|Presbyterian churches]], strongly associated with Scots-Irish immigrants of the 18th century and their descendants, had a combined membership around 75,000 ([[Presbyterian_Church_in_America|PCA]]—28,009 members in 108 congregations, [[PC(USA)|PC(USA)]]—26,247 members in 147 congregations, the [[Cumberland_Presbyterian_Church|Cumberland Presbyterian Church]]—6,000 members in 59 congregations, the [[Cumberland_Presbyterian_Church_in_America|Cumberland Presbyterian Church in America]]—5,000 members and fifty congregations plus the EPC and Associate Reformed Presbyterians with 230 members and nine congregations).
sentence_271: In a 2007 survey, nearly 70% of respondents could name all four of the Christian [[Canonical_Gospels|Gospels]].
sentence_272: Of those who indicated a religious preference, 59% said they possessed a "full understanding" of their faith and needed no further learning.
sentence_273: In a 2007 poll, 92% of Alabamians reported having at least some confidence in churches in the state.
sentence_274: Although in much smaller numbers, many other religious faiths are represented in the state as well, including Judaism, [[Islam|Islam]], [[Hinduism|Hinduism]], [[Buddhism|Buddhism]], [[Sikhism|Sikhism]], the [[Bahá'í_Faith|Bahá'í Faith]], and [[Unitarian_Universalism|Unitarian Universalism]].
sentence_275: Jews have been present in what is now Alabama since 1763, during the colonial era of Mobile, when [[Sephardic_Jews|Sephardic Jews]] immigrated from London.
sentence_276: The oldest Jewish congregation in the state is [[Congregation_Sha'arai_Shomayim_(Mobile,_Alabama)|Congregation Sha'arai Shomayim]] in Mobile.
sentence_277: It was formally recognized by the state legislature on January 25, 1844.
sentence_278: Later immigrants in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries tended to be Ashkenazi Jews from eastern Europe.
sentence_279: Jewish denominations in the state include two [[Orthodox_Judaism|Orthodox]], four [[Conservative_Judaism|Conservative]], ten [[Reform_Judaism|Reform]], and one Humanistic synagogue.
sentence_280: Muslims have been increasing in Alabama, with 31 mosques built by 2011, many by African-American converts.
sentence_281: Several Hindu temples and cultural centers in the state have been founded by Indian immigrants and their descendants, the best-known being the Shri Swaminarayan Mandir in [[Birmingham,_Alabama|Birmingham]], the Hindu Temple and Cultural Center of Birmingham in [[Pelham,_Alabama|Pelham]], the Hindu Cultural Center of North Alabama in [[Capshaw,_Alabama|Capshaw]], and the Hindu Mandir and Cultural Center in [[Tuscaloosa,_Alabama|Tuscaloosa]].
sentence_282: There are six [[Dharma_centre|Dharma centers]] and organizations for [[Theravada|Theravada]] [[Buddhists|Buddhists]].
sentence_283: Most monastic Buddhist temples are concentrated in southern Mobile County, near Bayou La Batre.
sentence_284: This area has attracted an [[Indochina_refugee_crisis|influx of refugees from Cambodia, Laos, and Vietnam]] during the 1970s and thereafter.
sentence_285: The four temples within a ten-mile radius of Bayou La Batre, include Chua Chanh Giac, Wat Buddharaksa, and Wat Lao Phoutthavihan.
sentence_286: The first community of adherents of the [[Bahá'í_Faith|Bahá'í Faith]] in Alabama was founded in 1896 by Paul K. Dealy, who moved from Chicago to [[Fairhope|Fairhope]].
sentence_287: Bahá'í centers in Alabama exist in [[Birmingham,_Alabama|Birmingham]], [[Huntsville,_Alabama|Huntsville]], and [[Florence,_Alabama|Florence]].
sentence_288: A [[Centers_for_Disease_Control_and_Prevention|Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] study in 2008 showed that obesity in Alabama is a problem, with most counties having more than 29% of adults obese, except for ten which had a rate between 26% and 29%.
sentence_289: Residents of the state, along with those in five other states, were least likely in the nation to be physically active during leisure time.
sentence_290: Alabama, and the southeastern U.S. in general, has one of the highest incidences of adult onset [[Diabetes_type_II|diabetes]] in the country, exceeding 10% of adults.
sentence_291: On May 14, 2019, Alabama passed the [[Human_Life_Protection_Act|Human Life Protection Act]], banning abortion at any stage of pregnancy unless there is a "serious health risk", with no exceptions for rape and [[Incest|incest]].
sentence_292: The law, if enacted, would punish doctors who perform abortions with 10 to 99 years imprisonment and be the most restrictive [[Abortion_law|abortion law]] in the country.
sentence_293: However, on October 29, 2019, U.S. District Judge [[Myron_Herbert_Thompson|Myron Thompson]] blocked the law from taking effect.
sentence_294: See also: [[Economy_of_Alabama|Economy of Alabama]] and Alabama locations by per capita income
sentence_295: The state has invested in aerospace, education, health care, banking, and various heavy industries, including automobile manufacturing, mineral extraction, steel production and [[Fabrication_(metal)|fabrication]].
sentence_296: By 2006, crop and animal production in Alabama was valued at $1.5 billion.
sentence_297: In contrast to the primarily agricultural economy of the previous century, this was only about one percent of the state's gross domestic product.
sentence_298: The number of private farms has declined at a steady rate since the 1960s, as land has been sold to developers, timber companies, and large farming conglomerates.
sentence_299: Non-agricultural employment in 2008 was 121,800 in management occupations; 71,750 in business and financial operations; 36,790 in computer-related and mathematical occupation; 44,200 in architecture and engineering; 12,410 in life, physical, and social sciences; 32,260 in community and social services; 12,770 in legal occupations; 116,250 in education, training, and library services; 27,840 in art, design and media occupations; 121,110 in healthcare; 44,750 in fire fighting, law enforcement, and security; 154,040 in food preparation and serving; 76,650 in building and grounds cleaning and maintenance; 53,230 in personal care and services; 244,510 in sales; 338,760 in office and administration support; 20,510 in farming, fishing, and forestry; 120,155 in construction and mining, gas, and oil extraction; 106,280 in installation, maintenance, and repair; 224,110 in production; and 167,160 in transportation and material moving.
sentence_300: According to the U.S. [[Bureau_of_Economic_Analysis|Bureau of Economic Analysis]], the 2008 total [[Gross_state_product|gross state product]] was $170 billion, or $29,411 per capita.
sentence_301: Alabama's 2012 GDP increased 1.2% from the previous year.
sentence_302: The single largest increase came in the area of information.
sentence_303: In 2010, per capita income for the state was $22,984.
sentence_304: The state's seasonally adjusted unemployment rate was 5.8% in April 2015.
sentence_305: This compared to a nationwide seasonally adjusted rate of 5.4%.
sentence_306: Alabama has no minimum wage and in February 2016 passed legislation preventing municipalities from setting one.
sentence_307: (A Birmingham city ordinance would have raised theirs to $10.10.)
sentence_308: As of 2018, Alabama has the sixth highest poverty rate among states in the U.S.
sentence_309: In 2017, United Nations Special Rapporteur [[Philip_Alston|Philip Alston]] toured parts of rural Alabama and observed environmental conditions he said were poorer than anywhere he had seen in the developed world.
sentence_310: The five employers that employed the most employees in Alabama in April 2011 were:
sentence_311: The next twenty largest employers, as of 2011, included:
sentence_312: Alabama's agricultural outputs include poultry and [[Egg_as_food|eggs]], cattle, fish, plant nursery items, [[Peanut|peanuts]], cotton, grains such as [[Corn_production_in_the_United_States|corn]] and [[Sorghum|sorghum]], vegetables, milk, [[Soybean|soybeans]], and peaches.
sentence_313: Although known as "[[List_of_U.S._state_nicknames|The Cotton State]]", Alabama ranks between eighth and tenth in [[Cotton_production_in_the_United_States|national cotton production]], according to various reports, with [[Texas|Texas]], [[Georgia_(U.S._state)|Georgia]] and [[Mississippi|Mississippi]] comprising the top three.
sentence_314: Alabama's industrial outputs include iron and steel products (including cast-iron and steel pipe); paper, [[Lumber|lumber]], and wood products; mining (mostly coal); plastic products; cars and trucks; and [[Apparel|apparel]].
sentence_315: In addition, Alabama produces [[Aerospace|aerospace]] and electronic products, mostly in the [[Huntsville,_Alabama|Huntsville]] area, the location of [[NASA|NASA]]'s [[George_C._Marshall_Space_Flight_Center|George C. Marshall Space Flight Center]] and the [[United_States_Army_Materiel_Command|U.S.
sentence_316: Army Materiel Command]], headquartered at [[Redstone_Arsenal|Redstone Arsenal]].
sentence_317: A great deal of Alabama's economic growth since the 1990s has been due to the state's expanding automotive manufacturing industry.
sentence_318: Located in the state are [[Honda_Manufacturing_of_Alabama|Honda Manufacturing of Alabama]], [[Hyundai_Motor_Manufacturing_Alabama|Hyundai Motor Manufacturing Alabama]], [[Mercedes-Benz_U.S._International|Mercedes-Benz U.S. International]], and [[Toyota_Motor_Manufacturing_Alabama|Toyota Motor Manufacturing Alabama]], as well as their various suppliers.
sentence_319: Since 1993, the automobile industry has generated more than 67,800 new jobs in the state.
sentence_320: Alabama currently ranks 4th in the nation for vehicle exports.
sentence_321: Automakers accounted for approximately a third of the industrial expansion in the state in 2012.
sentence_322: The eight models produced at the state's auto factories totaled combined sales of 74,335 vehicles for 2012.
sentence_323: The strongest model sales during this period were the [[Hyundai_Elantra|Hyundai Elantra]] compact car, the [[Mercedes-Benz_GL-Class|Mercedes-Benz GL-Class]] sport utility vehicle and the Honda Ridgeline sport utility truck.
sentence_324: Steel producers Outokumpu, [[Nucor|Nucor]], [[SSAB|SSAB]], ThyssenKrupp, and [[U.S._Steel|U.S.
sentence_325: Steel]] have facilities in Alabama and employ more than 10,000 people.
sentence_326: In May 2007, German steelmaker ThyssenKrupp selected [[Calvert,_Alabama|Calvert]] in [[Mobile_County,_Alabama|Mobile County]] for a 4.65 billion combined stainless and [[Carbon_steel|carbon steel]] processing facility.
sentence_327: ThyssenKrupp's stainless steel division, Inoxum, including the stainless portion of the Calvert plant, was sold to Finnish stainless steel company Outokumpu in 2012.
sentence_328: The remaining portion of the ThyssenKrupp plant had final bids submitted by [[ArcelorMittal|ArcelorMittal]] and [[Nippon_Steel|Nippon Steel]] for $1.6 billion in March 2013.
sentence_329: [[Companhia_Siderúrgica_Nacional|Companhia Siderúrgica Nacional]] submitted a combined bid for the mill at Calvert, plus a majority stake in the ThyssenKrupp mill in Brazil, for $3.8 billion.
sentence_330: In July 2013, the plant was sold to ArcelorMittal and Nippon Steel.
sentence_331: The Hunt Refining Company, a subsidiary of Hunt Consolidated, Inc., is based in Tuscaloosa and operates a refinery there.
sentence_332: The company also operates terminals in Mobile, Melvin, and [[Moundville,_Alabama|Moundville]].
sentence_333: JVC America, Inc. operates an [[Optical_disc|optical disc]] replication and packaging plant in Tuscaloosa.
sentence_334: The [[Goodyear_Tire_and_Rubber_Company|Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company]] operates a large plant in [[Gadsden,_Alabama|Gadsden]] which employs about 1,400 people.
sentence_335: It has been in operation since 1929.
sentence_336: Construction of an [[Airbus_A320_family|Airbus A320 family]] aircraft assembly plant in Mobile was formally announced by [[Airbus|Airbus]] CEO Fabrice Brégier from the Mobile Convention Center on July 2, 2012.
sentence_337: The plans include a $600 million factory at the [[Brookley_Aeroplex|Brookley Aeroplex]] for the assembly of the A319, A320 and A321 aircraft.
sentence_338: Construction began in 2013, with plans for it to become operable by 2015 and produce up to 50 aircraft per year by 2017.
sentence_339: The assembly plant is the company's first factory to be built within the United States.
sentence_340: It was announced on February 1, 2013, that Airbus had hired Alabama-based [[Hoar_Construction|Hoar Construction]] to oversee construction of the facility.
sentence_341: According to [[Business_Insider|Business Insider]], Alabama ranked 14th in most popular states to visit in 2014.
sentence_342: An estimated 26 million tourists visited the state in 2018, more than 100,000 of them from other countries including Canada, the United Kingdom, Germany and Japan.
sentence_343: In 2006, 22.3 million travellers spent $8.3 billion providing an estimated 162,000 jobs in the state.
sentence_344: The state is home to various attractions, natural features, parks and events that attract visitors from around the globe, notably the annual [[Hangout_Music_Festival|Hangout Music Festival]], held on the public beaches of [[Gulf_Shores,_Alabama|Gulf Shores]]; the [[Alabama_Shakespeare_Festival|Alabama Shakespeare Festival]], one of the ten largest [[Shakespeare_festival|Shakespeare festivals]] in the world; the [[Robert_Trent_Jones_Golf_Trail|Robert Trent Jones Golf Trail]], a collection of championship caliber golf courses distributed across the state; casinos such as Victoryland; amusement parks such as [[Alabama_Splash_Adventure|Alabama Splash Adventure]]; the [[Riverchase_Galleria|Riverchase Galleria]], one of the largest shopping centers in the southeast; [[Guntersville_Lake|Guntersville Lake]], voted the best lake in Alabama by [[Southern_Living|Southern Living]] Magazine readers; and the [[Alabama_Museum_of_Natural_History|Alabama Museum of Natural History]], the oldest museum in the state.
sentence_345: Mobile is known for having the oldest organized [[Mardi_Gras_in_Mobile,_Alabama|Mardi Gras]] celebration in the United States, beginning in 1703.
sentence_346: It was also host to the first formally organized Mardi Gras parade in the United States in 1830, a tradition that continues to this day.
sentence_347: Mardi Gras is an official state holiday in [[Mobile_County,_Alabama|Mobile]] and [[Baldwin_County,_Alabama|Baldwin]] counties.
sentence_348: In 2018, Mobile's [[Mardi_Gras_in_Mobile,_Alabama|Mardi Gras parade]] was the state's top event, producing the most tourists with an attendance of 892,811.
sentence_349: The top attraction was the [[U.S._Space_&_Rocket_Center|U.S.
sentence_350: Space & Rocket Center]] in Huntsville with an attendance of 849,981, followed by the [[Birmingham_Zoo|Birmingham Zoo]] with 543,090.
sentence_351: Of the parks and natural destinations, Alabama's Gulf Coast topped the list with 6,700,000 visitors.
sentence_352: Alabama has historically been a popular region for film shoots due to its diverse landscapes and contrast of environments.
sentence_353: Movies filmed in Alabama include: [[Close_Encounters_of_the_Third_Kind|Close Encounters of the Third Kind]], [[Get_Out|Get Out]], [[42_(film)|42]], [[Selma_(film)|Selma]], [[Big_Fish|Big Fish]], [[The_Final_Destination|The Final Destination]], [[Due_Date|Due Date]], [[Need_For_Speed_(film)|Need For Speed]] and many more.
sentence_354: [[UAB_Hospital|UAB Hospital]], [[University_of_South_Alabama|USA Health University Hospital]], Huntsville Hospital, and Children's Hospital of Alabama are the only [[Trauma_center|Level I trauma centers]] in Alabama.
sentence_355: UAB is the largest state government employer in Alabama, with a workforce of about 18,000.
sentence_356: A 2017 study found that Alabama had the least competitive health insurance market in the country, with Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Alabama having a market share of 84% followed by [[UnitedHealth_Group|UnitedHealth Group]] at 7%.
sentence_357: [[Regions_Financial_Corporation|Regions Financial Corporation]] and BBVA USA Bank are the largest banks headquartered in Alabama.
sentence_358: Birmingham-based Compass Banchshares was acquired by Spanish-based [[BBVA|BBVA]] in September 2007 with the headquarters of BBVA USA remaining in Birmingham.
sentence_359: In November 2006, Regions Financial acquired [[AmSouth_Bancorporation|AmSouth Bancorporation]], which was also headquartered in Birmingham.
sentence_360: [[SouthTrust_Corporation|SouthTrust Corporation]], another large bank headquartered in Birmingham, was acquired by [[Wachovia|Wachovia]] in 2004.
sentence_361: [[Wells_Fargo|Wells Fargo]] has a regional headquarters, an operations center campus, and a $400 million data center in Birmingham.
sentence_362: Many smaller banks are also headquartered in the Birmingham area, including ServisFirst and New South Federal Savings Bank.
sentence_363: Birmingham also serves as the headquarters for several large investment management companies, including [[Harbert_Management_Corporation|Harbert Management Corporation]].
sentence_364: Telecommunications provider AT&T, formerly [[BellSouth|BellSouth]], has a major presence in Alabama with several large offices in Birmingham.
sentence_365: Many commercial technology companies are headquartered in Huntsville, such as network access company [[ADTRAN|ADTRAN]], computer graphics company [[Intergraph|Intergraph]], and IT infrastructure company [[Avocent|Avocent]].
sentence_366: Rust International has grown to include [[Brasfield_&_Gorrie|Brasfield & Gorrie]], [[BE&K|BE&K]], [[Hoar_Construction|Hoar Construction]], and [[B.L._Harbert_International|B.L.
sentence_367: Harbert International]], which all routinely are included in the Engineering News-Record lists of top design, international construction, and engineering firms.
sentence_368: (Rust International was acquired in 2000 by [[Washington_Group_International|Washington Group International]], which was in turn acquired by San-Francisco based [[URS_Corporation|URS Corporation]] in 2007.)
sentence_369: Main article: [[Government_of_Alabama|Government of Alabama]]
sentence_370: The foundational document for Alabama's government is the [[Alabama_Constitution|Alabama Constitution]], which was ratified in 1901.
sentence_371: At almost 800 amendments and 310,000 words, it is by some accounts the world's longest constitution and is roughly forty times the length of the [[United_States_Constitution|United States Constitution]].
sentence_372: There has been a significant movement to rewrite and modernize Alabama's constitution.
sentence_373: Critics argue that Alabama's constitution maintains highly centralized power with the state legislature, leaving practically no power in local hands.
sentence_374: Most counties do not have home rule.
sentence_375: Any policy changes proposed in different areas of the state must be approved by the entire Alabama legislature and, frequently, by state referendum.
sentence_376: One criticism of the current constitution claims that its complexity and length intentionally codify segregation and racism.
sentence_377: Alabama's government is divided into three coequal branches.
sentence_378: The [[Legislative_branch|legislative branch]] is the Alabama Legislature, a bicameral assembly composed of the Alabama House of Representatives, with 105 members, and the Alabama Senate, with 35 members.
sentence_379: The Legislature is responsible for writing, debating, passing, or defeating state legislation.
sentence_380: The [[Republican_Party_(United_States)|Republican Party]] currently holds a majority in both houses of the Legislature.
sentence_381: The Legislature has the power to override a gubernatorial veto by a simple majority (most state Legislatures require a two-thirds majority to override a veto).
sentence_382: Until 1964, the state elected state senators on a geographic basis by county, with one per county.
sentence_383: It had not redistricted congressional districts since passage of its constitution in 1901; as a result, urbanized areas were grossly underrepresented.
sentence_384: It had not changed legislative districts to reflect the decennial censuses, either.
sentence_385: In [[Reynolds_v._Sims|Reynolds v. Sims]] (1964), the U.S. Supreme Court implemented the principle of "[[One_man,_one_vote|one man, one vote]]", ruling that congressional districts had to be reapportioned based on censuses (as the state already included in its constitution but had not implemented.)
sentence_386: Further, the court ruled that both houses of bicameral state legislatures had to be apportioned by population, as there was no constitutional basis for states to have geographically based systems.
sentence_387: At that time, Alabama and many other states had to change their legislative districting, as many across the country had systems that underrepresented urban areas and districts.
sentence_388: This had caused decades of underinvestment in such areas.
sentence_389: For instance, Birmingham and Jefferson County taxes had supplied one-third of the state budget, but Jefferson County received only 1/67th of state services in funding.
sentence_390: Through the legislative delegations, the Alabama legislature kept control of county governments.
sentence_391: The executive branch is responsible for the execution and oversight of laws.
sentence_392: It is headed by the [[Governor_of_Alabama|governor of Alabama]].
sentence_393: Other members of executive branch include the cabinet, the [[List_of_Lieutenant_Governors_of_Alabama|lieutenant governor of Alabama]], the [[Attorney_General_of_Alabama|Attorney General of Alabama]], the [[Alabama_Secretary_of_State|Alabama Secretary of State]], the [[Alabama_State_Treasurer|Alabama State Treasurer]], and the [[State_Auditor_of_Alabama|State Auditor of Alabama]].
sentence_394: The current governor is [[Republican_Party_(United_States)|Republican]] [[Kay_Ivey|Kay Ivey]].
sentence_395: The members of the Legislature take office immediately after the November elections.
sentence_396: Statewide officials, such as the governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general, and other constitutional officers, take office the following January.
sentence_397: The [[Judiciary|judicial branch]] is responsible for interpreting the state's [[Alabama_Constitution|Constitution]] and applying the law in state criminal and civil cases.
sentence_398: The state's highest court is the [[Supreme_Court_of_Alabama|Supreme Court of Alabama]].
sentence_399: Alabama uses partisan elections to select judges.
sentence_400: Since the 1980s judicial campaigns have become increasingly politicized.
sentence_401: The current [[Chief_justice|chief justice]] of the Alabama Supreme Court is Republican [[Tom_Parker_(judge)|Tom Parker]].
sentence_402: All sitting justices on the Alabama Supreme Court are members of the Republican Party.
sentence_403: There are two intermediate appellate courts, the Court of Civil Appeals and the Court of Criminal Appeals, and four trial courts: the circuit court (trial court of general jurisdiction), and the district, probate, and municipal courts.
sentence_404: Some critics believe the election of judges has contributed to an exceedingly high rate of executions.
sentence_405: Alabama has the highest per capita [[Capital_punishment_in_Alabama|death penalty rate]] in the country.
sentence_406: In some years, it imposes more death sentences than does [[Texas|Texas]], a state which has a population five times larger.
sentence_407: However, executions per capita are significantly higher in Texas.
sentence_408: Some of its cases have been highly controversial; the Supreme Court has overturned 24 convictions in death penalty cases.
sentence_409: It was the only state to allow judges to override jury decisions in whether or not to use a death sentence; in 10 cases judges overturned sentences of [[Life_imprisonment_without_parole|life imprisonment without parole]] (LWOP) that were voted unanimously by juries.
sentence_410: This judicial authority was removed in April 2017.
sentence_411: Taxes are collected by the [[Alabama_Department_of_Revenue|Alabama Department of Revenue]].
sentence_412: Alabama levies a 2, 4, or 5 percent [[State_income_tax|personal income tax]], depending on the amount earned and filing status.
sentence_413: Taxpayers are allowed to deduct their [[Income_tax_in_the_United_States|federal income tax]] from their Alabama state tax, even if taking the [[Standard_deduction|standard deduction]]; those who itemize can also deduct [[Federal_Insurance_Contributions_Act_tax|FICA]] (the Social Security and Medicare tax).
sentence_414: The state's general sales tax rate is 4%.
sentence_415: Sales tax rates for cities and counties are also added to purchases.
sentence_416: For example, the total sales tax rate in Mobile is 10% and there is an additional restaurant tax of 1%, which means a diner in Mobile would pay an 11% tax on a meal.
sentence_417: As of 1999, sales and excise taxes in Alabama account for 51% of all state and local revenue, compared with an average of about 36% nationwide.
sentence_418: Alabama is one of seven states that levy a tax on food at the same rate as other goods, and one of two states (the other being neighboring Mississippi) which fully taxes groceries without any offsetting relief for low-income families.
sentence_419: (Most states exempt groceries from sales tax or apply a lower tax rate.)
sentence_420: Alabama's income tax on poor working families is among the highest in the U.S. Alabama is the only state that levies income tax on a family of four with income as low as $4,600, which is barely one-quarter the federal poverty line.
sentence_421: Alabama's threshold is the lowest among the 41 states and the District of Columbia with income taxes.
sentence_422: The corporate income tax rate is currently 6.5%.
sentence_423: The overall federal, state, and local tax burden in Alabama ranks the state as the second least tax-burdened state in the country.
sentence_424: [[Property_tax|Property taxes]] are the lowest in the U.S.
sentence_425: The current state constitution requires a voter referendum to raise property taxes.
sentence_426: Since Alabama's tax structure largely depends on consumer spending, it is subject to high variable budget structure.
sentence_427: For example, in 2003, Alabama had an annual budget deficit as high as $670 million.
sentence_428: See also: [[List_of_counties_in_Alabama|List of counties in Alabama]]
sentence_429: Alabama has 67 [[County_(United_States)|counties]].
sentence_430: Each county has its own elected legislative branch, usually called the county commission.
sentence_431: It also has limited executive authority in the county.
sentence_432: Because of the constraints of the [[Alabama_Constitution|Alabama Constitution]], which centralizes power in the state legislature, only seven counties (Jefferson, Lee, Mobile, Madison, Montgomery, Shelby, and Tuscaloosa) in the state have limited [[Home_rule|home rule]].
sentence_433: Instead, most counties in the state must lobby the Local Legislation Committee of the state legislature to get simple local policies approved, ranging from waste disposal to land use zoning.
sentence_434: The state legislature has retained power over local governments by refusing to pass a constitutional amendment establishing [[Home_rule|home rule]] for counties, as recommended by the 1973 Alabama Constitutional Commission.
sentence_435: Legislative delegations retain certain powers over each county.
sentence_436: United States Supreme Court decisions in [[Baker_v._Carr|Baker v. Carr]] (1964) required that both houses have districts established on the basis of population, and redistricted after each census, to implement the principle of "one man, one vote".
sentence_437: Before that, each county was represented by one state senator, leading to under-representation in the state senate for more urbanized, populous counties.
sentence_438: The rural bias of the state legislature, which had also failed to redistrict seats in the state house, affected politics well into the 20th century, failing to recognize the rise of industrial cities and urbanized areas.
sentence_439: "The lack of home rule for counties in Alabama has resulted in the proliferation of local legislation permitting counties to do things not authorized by the state constitution.
sentence_440: Alabama's constitution has been amended more than 700 times, and almost one-third of the amendments are local in nature, applying to only one county or city.
sentence_441: A significant part of each legislative session is spent on local legislation, taking away time and attention of legislators from issues of statewide importance."
sentence_442: Alabama is an alcoholic beverage control state, meaning the state government holds a monopoly on the sale of alcohol.
sentence_443: The Alabama Alcoholic Beverage Control Board controls the sale and distribution of alcoholic beverages in the state.
sentence_444: A total of 25 of the 67 counties are "[[Dry_county|dry counties]]" which ban the sale of alcohol, and there are many dry municipalities in counties which permit alcohol sales.
sentence_445: During [[Reconstruction_Era|Reconstruction]] following the [[American_Civil_War|American Civil War]], Alabama was occupied by federal troops of the Third Military District under [[John_Pope_(military_officer)|General John Pope]].
sentence_446: In 1874, the political coalition of white Democrats known as the [[Redeemers|Redeemers]] took control of the state government from the Republicans, in part by suppressing the black vote through violence, fraud and intimidation.
sentence_447: After 1890, a coalition of White Democratic politicians passed laws to [[Racial_segregation|segregate]] and disenfranchise African American residents, a process completed in provisions of the 1901 constitution.
sentence_448: Provisions which disenfranchised blacks resulted in excluding many poor Whites.
sentence_449: By 1941 more Whites than Blacks had been disenfranchised: 600,000 to 520,000.
sentence_450: The total effects were greater on the black community, as almost all its citizens were disfranchised and relegated to separate and unequal treatment under the law.
sentence_451: From 1901 through the 1960s, the state did not redraw election districts as population grew and shifted within the state during urbanization and industrialization of certain areas.
sentence_452: As counties were the basis of election districts, the result was a rural minority that dominated state politics through nearly three-quarters of the century, until a series of federal court cases required redistricting in 1972 to meet equal representation.
sentence_453: Alabama state politics gained nationwide and international attention in the 1950s and 1960s during the [[Civil_rights_movement|civil rights movement]], when whites bureaucratically, and at times violently, resisted protests for electoral and social reform.
sentence_454: Governor [[George_Wallace|George Wallace]], the state's only four-term governor, was a controversial figure who vowed to maintain segregation.
sentence_455: Only after passage of the federal [[Civil_Rights_Act_of_1964|Civil Rights Act of 1964]] and [[Voting_Rights_Act_of_1965|Voting Rights Act of 1965]] did African Americans regain the ability to exercise suffrage, among other civil rights.
sentence_456: In many jurisdictions, they continued to be excluded from representation by [[At-large|at-large]] electoral systems, which allowed the majority of the population to dominate elections.
sentence_457: Some changes at the county level have occurred following court challenges to establish [[Single-member_districts|single-member districts]] that enable a more diverse representation among county boards.
sentence_458: In 2007, the Alabama Legislature passed, and Republican governor [[Bob_Riley|Bob Riley]] signed a resolution expressing "profound regret" over slavery and its lingering impact.
sentence_459: In a symbolic ceremony, the bill was signed in the [[Alabama_State_Capitol|Alabama State Capitol]], which housed Congress of the [[Confederate_States_of_America|Confederate States of America]].
sentence_460: In 2010, Republicans won control of both houses of the legislature for the first time in 136 years.
sentence_461: As of December 2017, there are a total of 3,326,812 registered voters, with 2,979,576 active, and the others inactive in the state.
sentence_462: Main article: [[Elections_in_Alabama|Elections in Alabama]]
sentence_463: With the [[Disfranchisement_after_Reconstruction_era|disfranchisement of Blacks]] in 1901, the state became part of the "[[Solid_South|Solid South]]", a system in which the [[Democratic_Party_(United_States)|Democratic Party]] operated as effectively the only viable political party in every Southern state.
sentence_464: For nearly a hundred years local and state elections in Alabama were decided in the Democratic Party [[Primary_election|primary]], with generally only token [[Republican_Party_(United_States)|Republican]] challengers running in the General Election.
sentence_465: Since the mid- to late 20th century, however, white conservatives started shifting to the Republican Party.
sentence_466: In Alabama, majority-white districts are now expected to regularly elect Republican candidates to federal, state and local office.
sentence_467: Members of the nine seats on the [[Supreme_Court_of_Alabama|Supreme Court of Alabama]] and all ten seats on the state appellate courts are elected to office.
sentence_468: Until 1994, no Republicans held any of the court seats.
sentence_469: In that general election, the then-incumbent chief justice, [[Ernest_C._Hornsby|Ernest C. Hornsby]], refused to leave office after losing the election by approximately 3,000 votes to Republican Perry O. Hooper, Sr..
sentence_470: Hornsby sued Alabama and defiantly remained in office for nearly a year before finally giving up the seat after losing in court.
sentence_471: This ultimately led to a collapse of support for Democrats at the ballot box in the next three or four election cycles.
sentence_472: The Democrats lost the last of the nineteen court seats in August 2011 with the resignation of the last Democrat on the bench.
sentence_473: In the early 21st century, Republicans hold all seven of the [[Political_party_strength_in_Alabama|statewide elected executive]] branch offices.
sentence_474: Republicans hold six of the eight elected seats on the Alabama State Board of Education.
sentence_475: In 2010, Republicans took large majorities of both chambers of the state legislature, giving them control of that body for the first time in 136 years.
sentence_476: The last remaining statewide Democrat, who served on the Alabama Public Service Commission was defeated in 2012.
sentence_477: Only three Republican lieutenant governors have been elected since the end of Reconstruction, when Republicans generally represented Reconstruction government, including the newly emancipated freedmen who had gained the franchise.
sentence_478: The three GOP lieutenant governors are [[Steve_Windom|Steve Windom]] (1999–2003), [[Kay_Ivey|Kay Ivey]] (2011–2017), and [[Will_Ainsworth|Will Ainsworth]] (2019–present).
sentence_479: Many local offices (county commissioners, boards of education, tax assessors, tax collectors, etc.) in the state are still held by Democrats.
sentence_480: Many rural counties have voters who are majority Democrats, resulting in local elections being decided in the Democratic primary.
sentence_481: Similarly many metropolitan and suburban counties are majority-Republican and elections are effectively decided in the Republican Primary, although there are exceptions.
sentence_482: Alabama's 67 county sheriffs are elected in partisan, [[At-large|at-large]] races, and Democrats still retain the narrow majority of those posts.
sentence_483: The current split is 35 [[Alabama_Democratic_Party|Democrats]], 31 Republicans, and one Independent Fayette.
sentence_484: However, most of the Democratic sheriffs preside over rural and less populated counties.
sentence_485: The majority of Republican sheriffs have been elected in the more urban/suburban and heavily populated counties.
sentence_486: As of 2015, the state of Alabama has one female sheriff, in [[Morgan_County,_Alabama|Morgan County, Alabama]], and ten African-American sheriffs.
sentence_487: The state's two [[United_States_Senate|U.S.
sentence_488: senators]] are Republican [[Richard_Shelby|Richard C. Shelby]] and Democrat [[Doug_Jones_(politician)|Doug Jones]].
sentence_489: Shelby was originally elected to the Senate as a Democrat in 1986 and re-elected in 1992, but switched parties immediately following the November 1994 general election.
sentence_490: In the [[United_States_House_of_Representatives|U.S.
sentence_491: House of Representatives]], the state is represented by seven members, six of whom are Republicans: ([[Bradley_Byrne|Bradley Byrne]], [[Mike_D._Rogers|Mike D. Rogers]], [[Robert_Aderholt|Robert Aderholt]], [[Morris_J._Brooks|Morris J. Brooks]], [[Martha_Roby|Martha Roby]], and [[Gary_Palmer_(politician)|Gary Palmer]]) and one Democrat: [[Terri_Sewell|Terri Sewell]] who represents the [[Black_Belt_(region_of_Alabama)|Black Belt]] as well as most of the predominantly black portions of [[Birmingham,_Alabama|Birmingham]], [[Tuscaloosa,_Alabama|Tuscaloosa]] and [[Montgomery,_Alabama|Montgomery]].
sentence_492: Main article: [[Education_in_Alabama|Education in Alabama]]
sentence_493: Public primary and secondary education in Alabama is under the purview of the Alabama State Board of Education as well as local oversight by 67 county school boards and 60 city boards of education.
sentence_494: Together, 1,496 individual schools provide education for 744,637 elementary and secondary students.
sentence_495: Public school funding is appropriated through the Alabama Legislature through the Education Trust Fund.
sentence_496: In FY 2006–2007, Alabama appropriated $3,775,163,578 for primary and secondary education.
sentence_497: That represented an increase of $444,736,387 over the previous fiscal year.
sentence_498: In 2007, more than 82 percent of schools made adequate yearly progress (AYP) toward student proficiency under the National [[No_Child_Left_Behind|No Child Left Behind]] law, using measures determined by the state of Alabama.
sentence_499: While Alabama's public education system has improved in recent decades, it lags behind in achievement compared to other states.
sentence_500: According to U.S. Census data (2000), Alabama's high school graduation rate (75%) is the fourth lowest in the U.S. (after [[Kentucky|Kentucky]], [[Louisiana|Louisiana]] and [[Mississippi|Mississippi]]).
sentence_501: The largest educational gains were among people with some college education but without degrees.
sentence_502: Generally prohibited in the West at large, [[School_corporal_punishment|school corporal punishment]] is not unusual in Alabama, with 27,260 public school students [[Paddle_(spanking)|paddled]] at least one time, according to government data for the 2011–2012 school year.
sentence_503: The rate of school corporal punishment in Alabama is surpassed by only Mississippi and Arkansas.
sentence_504: Main article: [[List_of_colleges_and_universities_in_Alabama|List of colleges and universities in Alabama]]
sentence_505: Alabama's programs of higher education include 14 four-year public universities, two-year community colleges, and 17 private, undergraduate and graduate universities.
sentence_506: In the state are four medical schools (as of fall 2015) (University of Alabama School of Medicine, [[University_of_South_Alabama|University of South Alabama]] and [[Alabama_College_of_Osteopathic_Medicine|Alabama College of Osteopathic Medicine]] and The Edward Via College of Osteopathic Medicine—Auburn Campus), two veterinary colleges ([[Auburn_University|Auburn University]] and [[Tuskegee_University|Tuskegee University]]), a dental school (University of Alabama School of Dentistry), an optometry college ([[University_of_Alabama_at_Birmingham|University of Alabama at Birmingham]]), two pharmacy schools ([[Auburn_University|Auburn University]] and [[Samford_University|Samford University]]), and five law schools ([[University_of_Alabama_School_of_Law|University of Alabama School of Law]], [[Birmingham_School_of_Law|Birmingham School of Law]], [[Cumberland_School_of_Law|Cumberland School of Law]], [[Miles_Law_School|Miles Law School]], and the [[Thomas_Goode_Jones_School_of_Law|Thomas Goode Jones School of Law]]).
sentence_507: Public, post-secondary education in Alabama is overseen by the [[Alabama_Commission_on_Higher_Education|Alabama Commission on Higher Education]] and the Alabama Department of Postsecondary Education.
sentence_508: Colleges and universities in Alabama offer degree programs from two-year associate degrees to a multitude of doctoral level programs.
sentence_509: The largest single campus is the [[University_of_Alabama|University of Alabama]], located in [[Tuscaloosa,_Alabama|Tuscaloosa]], with 37,665 enrolled for fall 2016.
sentence_510: [[Troy_University|Troy University]] was the largest institution in the state in 2010, with an enrollment of 29,689 students across four Alabama campuses ([[Troy,_Alabama|Troy]], [[Dothan,_Alabama|Dothan]], [[Montgomery,_Alabama|Montgomery]], and [[Phenix_City,_Alabama|Phenix City]]), as well as sixty learning sites in seventeen other states and eleven other countries.
sentence_511: The oldest institutions are the public [[University_of_North_Alabama|University of North Alabama]] in [[Florence,_Alabama|Florence]] and the Catholic Church-affiliated [[Spring_Hill_College|Spring Hill College]] in [[Mobile,_Alabama|Mobile]], both founded in 1830.
sentence_512: Accreditation of academic programs is through the [[Southern_Association_of_Colleges_and_Schools|Southern Association of Colleges and Schools]] (SACS) as well as other subject-focused national and international accreditation agencies such as the Association for Biblical Higher Education (ABHE), the [[Council_on_Occupational_Education|Council on Occupational Education]] (COE), and the [[Accrediting_Council_for_Independent_Colleges_and_Schools|Accrediting Council for Independent Colleges and Schools]] (ACICS).
sentence_513: According to the 2011 [[U.S._News_&_World_Report|U.S.
sentence_514: News & World Report]], Alabama had three universities ranked in the top 100 Public Schools in America (University of Alabama at 31, [[Auburn_University|Auburn University]] at 36, and [[University_of_Alabama_at_Birmingham|University of Alabama at Birmingham]] at 73).
sentence_515: According to the 2012 U.S. News & World Report, Alabama had four [[College_and_university_rankings|tier one]] universities ([[University_of_Alabama|University of Alabama]], [[Auburn_University|Auburn University]], [[University_of_Alabama_at_Birmingham|University of Alabama at Birmingham]] and [[University_of_Alabama_in_Huntsville|University of Alabama in Huntsville]]).
sentence_516: See also: :Category:Mass media in Alabama and [[List_of_newspapers_in_Alabama|List of newspapers in Alabama]]
sentence_517: Major newspapers include [[The_Birmingham_News|Birmingham News]], Mobile Press-Register, and [[Montgomery_Advertiser|Montgomery Advertiser]].
sentence_518: Major television network affiliates in Alabama include:
sentence_520: College football is extremely popular in Alabama, particularly the [[University_of_Alabama|University of Alabama]] [[Alabama_Crimson_Tide|Crimson Tide]] and [[Auburn_University|Auburn University]] [[Auburn_Tigers|Tigers]], rivals in the [[Southeastern_Conference|Southeastern Conference]].
sentence_521: In the 2013 season, Alabama averaged over 100,000 fans per game and Auburn averaged over 80,000—both numbers among the top twenty in the nation.
sentence_522: Bryant–Denny Stadium is the home of the Alabama football team, and has a [[Seating_capacity|seating capacity]] of 101,821, and is the fifth largest stadium in America.
sentence_523: Jordan-Hare Stadium is the home field of the Auburn football team and seats up to 87,451.
sentence_524: Legion Field is home for the UAB Blazers football program and the [[Birmingham_Bowl|Birmingham Bowl]].
sentence_526: [[Ladd–Peebles_Stadium|Ladd–Peebles Stadium]] in [[Mobile,_Alabama|Mobile]] is the home of the [[University_of_South_Alabama|University of South Alabama]] football team, and serves as the home of the NCAA [[Senior_Bowl|Senior Bowl]], [[Dollar_General_Bowl|Dollar General Bowl]] (formerly GoDaddy.com Bowl), and Alabama-Mississippi All Star Classic; the stadium seats 40,646.
sentence_527: In 2009, Bryant–Denny Stadium and Jordan-Hare Stadium became the homes of the Alabama High School Athletic Association state football championship games, after previously being held at Legion Field in Birmingham.
sentence_528: Main article: [[List_of_professional_sports_teams_in_Alabama|List of professional sports teams in Alabama]]
sentence_529: Alabama has several professional and semi-professional sports teams, including three minor league baseball teams.
sentence_530: The [[Talladega_Superspeedway|Talladega Superspeedway]] motorsports complex hosts a series of NASCAR events.
sentence_531: It has a [[Seating_capacity|seating capacity]] of 143,000 and is the thirteenth largest stadium in the world and sixth largest stadium in America.
sentence_532: Also, the Barber Motorsports Park has hosted [[IndyCar_Series|IndyCar Series]] and Rolex Sports Car Series races.
sentence_533: The [[ATP_Birmingham|ATP Birmingham]] was a [[World_Championship_Tennis|World Championship Tennis]] tournament held from 1973 to 1980.
sentence_534: Alabama has hosted several professional golf tournaments, such as the 1984 and 1990 [[PGA_Championship|PGA Championship]] at [[Shoal_Creek_Golf_and_Country_Club|Shoal Creek]], the [[Barbasol_Championship|Barbasol Championship]] ([[PGA_Tour|PGA Tour]]), the Mobile LPGA Tournament of Champions, [[Airbus_LPGA_Classic|Airbus LPGA Classic]], and [[Yokohama_Tire_LPGA_Classic|Yokohama Tire LPGA Classic]] ([[LPGA_Tour|LPGA Tour]]), and [[The_Tradition|The Tradition]] (Champions Tour).
sentence_537: Major airports with sustained operations in Alabama include [[Birmingham-Shuttlesworth_International_Airport|Birmingham-Shuttlesworth International Airport]] (BHM), [[Huntsville_International_Airport|Huntsville International Airport]] (HSV), [[Dothan_Regional_Airport|Dothan Regional Airport]] (DHN), [[Mobile_Regional_Airport|Mobile Regional Airport]] (MOB), [[Montgomery_Regional_Airport|Montgomery Regional Airport]] (MGM), [[Northwest_Alabama_Regional_Airport|Northwest Alabama Regional Airport]] (MSL) and [[Northeast_Alabama_Regional_Airport|Northeast Alabama Regional Airport]] (GAD).
sentence_538: For rail transport, [[Amtrak|Amtrak]] schedules the [[Crescent_(train)|Crescent]], a daily passenger train, running from New York to New Orleans with station stops at [[Anniston_station|Anniston]], [[Birmingham_station_(Alabama)|Birmingham]], and [[Tuscaloosa_station|Tuscaloosa]].
sentence_539: Alabama has six major interstate routes: [[Interstate_65_in_Alabama|Interstate 65]] (I-65) travels north–south roughly through the middle of the state; [[Interstate_20_in_Alabama|I-20]]/[[Interstate_59_in_Alabama|I-59]] travel from the central west Mississippi state line to Birmingham, where I-59 continues to the north-east corner of the state and I-20 continues east towards [[Atlanta|Atlanta]]; [[Interstate_85_in_Alabama|I-85]] originates in Montgomery and travels east-northeast to the Georgia state line, providing a main thoroughfare to Atlanta; and [[Interstate_10_in_Alabama|I-10]] traverses the southernmost portion of the state, traveling from west to east through Mobile.
sentence_540: [[Interstate_22_in_Alabama|I-22]] enters the state from [[Mississippi|Mississippi]] and connects Birmingham with [[Memphis,_Tennessee|Memphis, Tennessee]].
sentence_541: In addition, there are currently five auxiliary interstate routes in the state: [[Interstate_165_(Alabama)|I-165]] in Mobile, [[Interstate_359|I-359]] in Tuscaloosa, [[Interstate_459|I-459]] around Birmingham, [[Interstate_565|I-565]] in Decatur and Huntsville, and [[Interstate_759|I-759]] in Gadsden.
sentence_542: A sixth route, I-685, will be formed when I-85 is rerouted along a new southern bypass of Montgomery.
sentence_543: A proposed northern bypass of Birmingham will be designated as [[Interstate_422|I-422]].
sentence_544: Since a direct connection from I-22 to I-422 will not be possible, [[Interstate_222|I-222]] has been proposed, as well.
sentence_546: Highways also pass through the state, such as [[U.S._Route_11_in_Alabama|U.S.
sentence_547: Route 11]] (US-11), [[U.S._Route_29_in_Alabama|US-29]], [[U.S._Route_31_in_Alabama|US-31]], US-43, [[U.S._Route_45_in_Alabama|US-45]], [[U.S._Route_72_in_Alabama|US-72]], US-78, [[U.S._Route_80_in_Alabama|US-80]], [[U.S._Route_82_in_Alabama|US-82]], [[U.S._Route_84_in_Alabama|US-84]], [[U.S._Route_90_in_Alabama|US-90]], [[U.S._Route_98_in_Alabama|US-98]], [[U.S._Route_231_in_Alabama|US-231]], US-278, [[U.S._Route_280_in_Alabama|US-280]], US-331, [[U.S._Route_411_in_Alabama|US-411]], and [[U.S._Route_431_in_Alabama|US-431]].
sentence_548: There are four toll roads in the state: Montgomery Expressway in [[Montgomery,_Alabama|Montgomery]]; Northport/Tuscaloosa Western Bypass in [[Tuscaloosa,_Alabama|Tuscaloosa]] and [[Northport,_Alabama|Northport]]; Emerald Mountain Expressway in [[Wetumpka,_Alabama|Wetumpka]]; and Beach Express in [[Orange_Beach,_Alabama|Orange Beach]].
sentence_549: The [[Port_of_Mobile|Port of Mobile]], Alabama's only saltwater port, is a large seaport on the [[Gulf_of_Mexico|Gulf of Mexico]] with inland waterway access to the [[Midwestern_United_States|Midwest]] by way of the [[Tennessee-Tombigbee_Waterway|Tennessee-Tombigbee Waterway]].
sentence_550: The Port of Mobile was ranked 12th by tons of traffic in the United States during 2009.
sentence_551: The newly expanded container terminal at the Port of Mobile was ranked as the 25th busiest for container traffic in the nation during 2011.
sentence_552: The state's other ports are on rivers with access to the Gulf of Mexico.
