title: Amsterdam
sentence_0: For other uses, see [[Amsterdam_(disambiguation)|Amsterdam (disambiguation)]].

table.value: Population (municipality and Randstad, 2019; urban area, 2018; metro region, 2014)

sentence_1: Amsterdam ([[English|/ˈæmstərdæm/]], UK also [[English|/ˌæmstərˈdæm/]]; Dutch: [[Dutch|[ɑmstɛrˈdɑm]] (listen)) is the [[Capital_of_the_Netherlands|capital]] and most populous city of the [[Netherlands|Netherlands]] with a population of 872,680 within the city proper, 1,558,755 in the [[City_Region_of_Amsterdam|urban area]] and 2,480,394 in the [[Amsterdam_metropolitan_area|metropolitan area]].
sentence_2: Found within the [[Provinces_of_the_Netherlands|province]] of [[North_Holland|North Holland]], Amsterdam is colloquially referred to as the "[[Venice_of_the_North|Venice of the North]]", attributed by the large number of canals which form a [[World_Heritage_Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].
sentence_3: Amsterdam's name derives from Amstelredamme, indicative of the city's origin around a dam in the river [[Amstel|Amstel]].
sentence_4: Originating as a small fishing village in the late 12th century, Amsterdam became one of the most important ports in the world during the [[Dutch_Golden_Age|Dutch Golden Age]] of the 17th century, and became the leading centre for finance and [[Trade|trade]].
sentence_5: In the 19th and 20th centuries, the city expanded and many new neighbourhoods and suburbs were planned and built.
sentence_6: The 17th-century [[Canals_of_Amsterdam|canals of Amsterdam]] and the 19–20th century [[Defence_Line_of_Amsterdam|Defence Line of Amsterdam]] are on the [[UNESCO_World_Heritage_List|UNESCO World Heritage List]].
sentence_7: [[Sloten,_Amsterdam|Sloten]], annexed in 1921 by the municipality of Amsterdam, is the oldest part of the city, dating to the 9th century.
sentence_8: [[List_of_tourist_attractions_in_Amsterdam|Amsterdam's main attractions]] include its [[Canals_of_Amsterdam|historic canals]], the [[Rijksmuseum|Rijksmuseum]], the [[Van_Gogh_Museum|Van Gogh Museum]], the [[Stedelijk_Museum_Amsterdam|Stedelijk Museum]], [[Hermitage_Amsterdam|Hermitage Amsterdam]], the [[Concertgebouw|Concertgebouw]], the [[Anne_Frank_House|Anne Frank House]], the [[Nederlands_Scheepvaartmuseum|Scheepvaartmuseum]], the [[Amsterdam_Museum|Amsterdam Museum]], the [[Heineken_Experience|Heineken Experience]], the [[Royal_Palace_of_Amsterdam|Royal Palace of Amsterdam]], [[Natura_Artis_Magistra|Natura Artis Magistra]], Hortus Botanicus Amsterdam, [[NEMO_(museum)|NEMO]], the [[Red-light_district|red-light district]] and many [[Coffeeshop_(Netherlands)|cannabis coffee shops]].
sentence_9: It drew more than 5 million international visitors in 2014.
sentence_10: The city is also well known for its nightlife and festival activity; with several of its nightclubs (Melkweg, [[Paradiso_(Amsterdam)|Paradiso]]) among the world's most famous.
sentence_11: Primarily known for its artistic heritage, elaborate canal system and narrow houses with gabled [[Facade|façades]]; well-preserved legacies of the city's 17th-century Golden Age.
sentence_12: These characteristics are arguably responsible for attracting millions of Amsterdam's visitors annually.
sentence_13: [[Cycling_in_the_Netherlands|Cycling]] is key to the city's character, and there are numerous [[Cycling_infrastructure|bike paths]].
sentence_14: The [[Amsterdam_Stock_Exchange|Amsterdam Stock Exchange]] is considered the oldest "modern" securities market [[Stock_exchange|stock exchange]] in the world.
sentence_15: As the commercial capital of the Netherlands and one of the top [[Financial_centre|financial centres]] in Europe, Amsterdam is considered an [[Alpha-world_city|alpha world city]] by the [[Globalization_and_World_Cities|Globalization and World Cities]] (GaWC) study group.
sentence_16: The city is also the cultural capital of the Netherlands.
sentence_17: Many large Dutch institutions have their headquarters in the city, including: the [[Philips|Philips]] conglomerate, [[AkzoNobel|AkzoNobel]], [[Booking.com|Booking.com]], [[TomTom|TomTom]], and [[ING_Group|ING]].
sentence_18: Moreover, many of the world's largest companies are based in Amsterdam or have established their European headquarters in the city, such as leading technology companies [[Uber|Uber]], [[Netflix|Netflix]] and [[Tesla,_Inc.|Tesla]].
sentence_19: In 2012, Amsterdam was ranked the second best city to live in by the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) and 12th globally on quality of living for environment and infrastructure by Mercer.
sentence_20: The city was ranked 4th place globally as top tech hub in the Savills Tech Cities 2019 report (2nd in Europe), and 3rd in innovation by Australian innovation agency 2thinknow in their Innovation Cities Index 2009.
sentence_21: The [[Port_of_Amsterdam|Port of Amsterdam]] is the fifth largest in Europe.
sentence_22: The [[KLM|KLM]] hub and Amsterdam's main airport: [[Amsterdam_Airport_Schiphol|Schiphol]], is the Netherlands' busiest airport as well as the third busiest in [[Europe|Europe]] and 11th busiest airport in the world.
sentence_23: The Dutch capital is considered one of the most multicultural cities in the world, with at least 177 nationalities represented.
sentence_24: A few of Amsterdam's notable residents throughout [[History_of_Amsterdam|history]] include: painters [[Rembrandt|Rembrandt]] and [[Vincent_van_Gogh|Van Gogh]], the diarist [[Anne_Frank|Anne Frank]], and philosopher [[Baruch_Spinoza|Baruch Spinoza]].
sentence_25: See also [[Names_of_European_cities_in_different_languages:_A|Other names of Amsterdam]]
sentence_26: After the floods of 1170 and 1173, locals near the river Amstel built a bridge over the river and a dam across it, giving its name to the village: "Aemstelredamme".
sentence_27: The earliest recorded use of that name is in a document dated 27 October 1275, which exempted inhabitants of the village from paying bridge tolls to Count [[Floris_V,_Count_of_Holland|Floris V]].
sentence_28: This allowed the inhabitants of the village of Aemstelredamme to travel freely through the [[County_of_Holland|County of Holland]], paying no tolls at bridges, locks and dams.
sentence_29: The certificate describes the inhabitants as homines manentes apud Amestelledamme (people residing near Amestelledamme).
sentence_30: By 1327, the name had developed into Aemsterdam.
sentence_31: Main articles: [[History_of_Amsterdam|History of Amsterdam]] and [[Timeline_of_Amsterdam|Timeline of Amsterdam]]
sentence_32: Amsterdam is much younger than Dutch cities such as Nijmegen, [[Rotterdam|Rotterdam]], and [[Utrecht|Utrecht]].
sentence_33: In October 2008, historical geographer Chris de Bont suggested that the land around Amsterdam was being reclaimed as early as the late 10th century.
sentence_34: This does not necessarily mean that there was already a settlement then, since [[Reclamation_of_land|reclamation of land]] may not have been for farming—it may have been for [[Peat|peat]], for use as fuel.
sentence_35: Amsterdam was granted [[City_rights_in_the_Low_Countries|city rights]] in either 1300 or 1306.
sentence_36: From the 14th century on, Amsterdam flourished, largely from trade with the [[Hanseatic_League|Hanseatic League]].
sentence_37: In 1345, an alleged [[Blessed_Sacrament|Eucharistic miracle]] in Kalverstraat rendered the city an important place of [[Pilgrimage|pilgrimage]] until the [[Protestant_Reformation|adoption of the Protestant faith]].
sentence_38: The Miracle devotion went underground but was kept alive.
sentence_39: In the 19th century, especially after the jubilee of 1845, the devotion was revitalized and became an important national point of reference for Dutch Catholics.
sentence_40: The [[Stille_Omgang|Stille Omgang]]—a silent walk or [[Procession|procession]] in civil attire—is the expression of the pilgrimage within the Protestant Netherlands since the late 19th century.
sentence_41: In the heyday of the Silent Walk, up to 90,000 pilgrims came to Amsterdam.
sentence_42: In the 21st century, this has reduced to about 5000.
sentence_43: In the 16th century, the Dutch rebelled against [[Philip_II_of_Spain|Philip II of Spain]] and his successors.
sentence_44: The main reasons for the uprising were the imposition of new taxes, the tenth penny, and the [[Religious_persecution|religious persecution]] of Protestants by the newly introduced [[Inquisition_of_the_Netherlands|Inquisition]].
sentence_45: The revolt escalated into the [[Eighty_Years'_War|Eighty Years' War]], which ultimately led to Dutch independence.
sentence_46: Strongly pushed by [[Dutch_Revolt|Dutch Revolt]] leader [[William_the_Silent|William the Silent]], the [[Dutch_Republic|Dutch Republic]] became known for its relative religious tolerance.
sentence_47: Jews from the [[Iberian_Peninsula|Iberian Peninsula]], [[Huguenot|Huguenots]] from France, prosperous merchants and printers from [[Flanders|Flanders]], and economic and religious refugees from the Spanish-controlled parts of the [[Low_Countries|Low Countries]] found safety in Amsterdam.
sentence_48: The influx of Flemish printers and the city's intellectual tolerance made Amsterdam a centre for the European [[Freedom_of_the_press|free press]].

section_4.value: Centre of the Dutch Golden Age

sentence_49: The 17th century is considered Amsterdam's [[Dutch_Golden_Age|Golden Age]], during which it became the wealthiest city in the western world.
sentence_50: Ships sailed from Amsterdam to the Baltic Sea, North America, and Africa, as well as present-day [[Indonesia|Indonesia]], [[India|India]], [[Sri_Lanka|Sri Lanka]], and [[Brazil|Brazil]], forming the basis of a worldwide trading network.
sentence_51: Amsterdam's merchants had the largest share in both the [[Dutch_East_India_Company|Dutch East India Company]] and the [[Dutch_West_India_Company|Dutch West India Company]].
sentence_52: These companies acquired overseas possessions that later became [[Dutch_Empire|Dutch colonies]].
sentence_53: Amsterdam was Europe's most important point for the shipment of goods and was the leading [[Financial_centre|Financial centre]] of the western world.
sentence_54: In 1602, the Amsterdam office of the international trading Dutch East India Company became the world's first [[Stock_exchange|stock exchange]] by trading in its own shares.
sentence_55: The Bank of Amsterdam started operations in 1609, acting as a full-service bank for Dutch merchant bankers and as a reserve bank.
sentence_56: Amsterdam's prosperity declined during the 18th and early 19th centuries.
sentence_57: The [[Anglo-Dutch_Wars|wars]] of the [[Dutch_Republic|Dutch Republic]] with [[Kingdom_of_England|England]] and France took their toll on Amsterdam.
sentence_58: During the [[Napoleonic_Wars|Napoleonic Wars]], Amsterdam's significance reached its lowest point, with Holland being absorbed into the [[First_French_Empire|French Empire]].
sentence_59: However, the later establishment of the [[United_Kingdom_of_the_Netherlands|United Kingdom of the Netherlands]] in 1815 marked a turning point.
sentence_60: The end of the 19th century is sometimes called Amsterdam's second Golden Age.
sentence_61: New museums, a railway station, and the [[Concertgebouw|Concertgebouw]] were built; in this same time, the [[Industrial_Revolution|Industrial Revolution]] reached the city.
sentence_62: The Amsterdam–Rhine Canal was dug to give Amsterdam a direct connection to the [[Rhine|Rhine]], and the [[North_Sea_Canal|North Sea Canal]] was dug to give the port a shorter connection to the [[North_Sea|North Sea]].
sentence_63: Both projects dramatically improved commerce with the rest of Europe and the world.
sentence_64: In 1906, [[Joseph_Conrad|Joseph Conrad]] gave a brief description of Amsterdam as seen from the seaside, in The Mirror of the Sea.
sentence_65: Shortly before the First World War, the city started to expand again, and new suburbs were built.
sentence_66: Even though the Netherlands remained neutral in this war, Amsterdam suffered a food shortage, and heating fuel became scarce.
sentence_67: The shortages sparked riots in which several people were killed.
sentence_68: These riots are known as the Aardappeloproer (Potato rebellion).
sentence_69: People started looting stores and warehouses in order to get supplies, mainly food.
sentence_70: On 1 January 1921, after a flood in 1916, the depleted municipalities of Durgerdam, Holysloot, Zunderdorp and [[Schellingwoude|Schellingwoude]], all lying north of Amsterdam, were, at their own request, annexed to the city.
sentence_71: Between the wars, the city continued to expand, most notably to the west of the Jordaan district in the [[Frederik_Hendrikbuurt|Frederik Hendrikbuurt]] and surrounding neighbourhoods.
sentence_72: [[Nazi_Germany|Nazi Germany]] [[Battle_of_the_Netherlands|invaded the Netherlands]] on 10 May 1940 and took control of the country.
sentence_73: Some Amsterdam citizens sheltered Jews, thereby exposing themselves and their families to a high risk of being imprisoned or sent to concentration camps.
sentence_74: More than 100,000 Dutch Jews were deported to [[Nazi_concentration_camps|Nazi concentration camps]], of whom some 60,000 lived in Amsterdam.
sentence_75: In response, the Dutch Communist Party organised the [[February_strike|February strike]] attended by 300,000 people to protest against the raids.
sentence_76: Perhaps the most famous deportee was the young Jewish girl [[Anne_Frank|Anne Frank]], who died in the [[Bergen-Belsen_concentration_camp|Bergen-Belsen concentration camp]].
sentence_77: At the end of the Second World War, communication with the rest of the country broke down, and food and fuel became scarce.
sentence_78: Many citizens travelled to the countryside to forage.
sentence_79: Dogs, cats, [[Sugar|raw sugar]] beets, and [[Tulip|tulip]] bulbs—cooked to a pulp—were consumed to stay alive.
sentence_80: Many trees in Amsterdam were cut down for fuel, and wood was taken from the houses, apartments and other buildings of deported Jews.
sentence_81: Many new suburbs, such as [[Osdorp|Osdorp]], [[Slotervaart_(neighborhood)|Slotervaart]], [[Slotermeer|Slotermeer]] and [[Geuzenveld|Geuzenveld]], were built in the years after the Second World War.
sentence_82: These suburbs contained many public parks and wide-open spaces, and the new buildings provided improved housing conditions with larger and brighter rooms, gardens, and balconies.
sentence_83: Because of the war and other events of the 20th century, almost the entire city centre had fallen into disrepair.
sentence_84: As society was changing, politicians and other influential figures made plans to redesign large parts of it.
sentence_85: There was an increasing demand for office buildings, and also for new roads, as the automobile became available to most people.
sentence_86: A [[Amsterdam_Metro|metro]] started operating in 1977 between the new suburb of [[Bijlmermeer|Bijlmermeer]] in the city's [[Amsterdam-Zuidoost|Zuidoost]] (southeast) exclave and the centre of Amsterdam.
sentence_87: Further plans were to build a new highway above the metro to connect [[Amsterdam_Centraal_station|Amsterdam Centraal]] and the city centre with other parts of the city.
sentence_88: The required large-scale demolitions began in Amsterdam's former Jewish neighbourhood.
sentence_89: Smaller streets, such as the Jodenbreestraat and Weesperstraat, were widened and almost all houses and buildings were demolished.
sentence_90: At the peak of the demolition, the Nieuwmarktrellen ([[Nieuwmarkt_Riots|Nieuwmarkt Riots]]) broke out; the rioters expressed their fury about the demolition caused by the restructuring of the city.
sentence_91: As a result, the demolition was stopped and the highway into the city's centre was never fully built; only the metro was completed.
sentence_92: Only a few streets remained widened.
sentence_93: The new city hall was built on the almost completely demolished Waterlooplein.
sentence_94: Meanwhile, large private organisations, such as Stadsherstel Amsterdam, were founded to restore the entire city centre.
sentence_95: Although the success of this struggle is visible today, efforts for further restoration are still ongoing.
sentence_96: The entire city centre has reattained its former splendour and, as a whole, is now a [[Protected_area|protected area]].
sentence_97: Many of its buildings have become monuments, and in July 2010 the [[Grachtengordel_(Amsterdam)|Grachtengordel]] (the three concentric canals: Herengracht, Keizersgracht, and Prinsengracht) was added to the [[World_Heritage_Site|UNESCO World Heritage List]].
sentence_98: In the early years of the 21st century, the Amsterdam city centre has attracted large numbers of tourists: between 2012 and 2015, the annual number of visitors rose from 10 to 17 million.
sentence_99: Real estate prices have surged, and local shops are making way for tourist-oriented ones, making the centre unaffordable for the city's inhabitants.
sentence_100: These developments have evoked comparisons with [[Venice_(Italy)|Venice]], a city thought to be overwhelmed by the tourist influx.
sentence_101: Construction of a metro line connecting the part of the city north of the river (or lake) [[IJ_(Amsterdam)|IJ]] to the centre was started in 2003.
sentence_102: The project was controversial because its cost had exceeded its budget by a factor three by 2008, because of fears of damage to buildings in the centre, and because construction had to be halted and restarted multiple times.
sentence_103: The metro line was completed in 2018.
sentence_104: Since 2014, renewed focus has been given to urban regeneration and renewal, especially in areas directly bordering the city centre, such as [[Frederik_Hendrikbuurt|Frederik Hendrikbuurt]].
sentence_105: This urban renewal and expansion of the traditional centre of the city—with the construction on artificial islands of the new eastern [[IJburg|IJburg]] neighbourhood—is part of the Structural Vision Amsterdam 2040 initiative.
sentence_106: Amsterdam is located in the Western Netherlands, in the province of [[North_Holland|North Holland]], the capital of which is not Amsterdam, but rather [[Haarlem|Haarlem]].
sentence_107: The river [[Amstel|Amstel]] ends in the city centre and connects to a large number of canals that eventually terminate in the [[IJ_(Amsterdam)|IJ]].
sentence_108: Amsterdam is about 2 metres (6.6 feet) below sea level.
sentence_109: The surrounding land is flat as it is formed of large [[Polder|polders]].
sentence_110: A man-made forest, [[Amsterdamse_Bos|Amsterdamse Bos]], is in the southwest.
sentence_111: Amsterdam is connected to the [[North_Sea|North Sea]] through the long [[North_Sea_Canal|North Sea Canal]].
sentence_112: Amsterdam is intensely urbanised, as is the [[Amsterdam_metropolitan_area|Amsterdam metropolitan area]] surrounding the city.
sentence_113: Comprising 219.4 km (84.7 sq mi) of land, the city proper has 4,457 inhabitants per km and 2,275 houses per km.
sentence_114: Parks and [[Nature_reserve|nature reserves]] make up 12% of Amsterdam's land area.
sentence_115: Amsterdam has more than 100 km (60 mi) of [[Canals_of_Amsterdam|canals]], most of which are navigable by boat.
sentence_116: The city's three main canals are the Prinsengracht, Herengracht, and Keizersgracht.
sentence_117: In the [[Middle_Ages|Middle Ages]], Amsterdam was surrounded by a moat, called the [[Singel|Singel]], which now forms the innermost ring in the city, and gives the city centre a horseshoe shape.
sentence_118: The city is also served by a [[Port_of_Amsterdam|seaport]].
sentence_119: It has been compared with [[Venice|Venice]], due to its division into about 90 islands, which are linked by more than 1,200 bridges.
sentence_120: Amsterdam has an [[Oceanic_climate|oceanic climate]] ([[Köppen_climate_classification|Köppen]] Cfb) strongly influenced by its proximity to the [[North_Sea|North Sea]] to the west, with prevailing westerly winds.
sentence_121: While winters are cool and summers warm, temperatures vary year by year.
sentence_122: There can occasionally be cold, snowy winters and hot, humid summers.
sentence_123: Amsterdam, as well as most of the North Holland province, lies in [[United_States_Department_of_Agriculture|USDA]] [[Hardiness_zone|Hardiness zone]] 8b.
sentence_124: Frosts mainly occur during spells of easterly or northeasterly winds from the inner European continent.
sentence_125: Even then, because Amsterdam is surrounded on three sides by large bodies of water, as well as having a significant [[Urban_heat_island|heat-island effect]], nights rarely fall below −5 °C (23 °F), while it could easily be −12 °C (10 °F) in Hilversum, 25 km (16 mi) southeast.
sentence_126: Summers are moderately warm with a number of hot days every month.
sentence_127: The average daily high in August is 22.1 °C (72 °F), and 30 °C (86 °F) or higher is only measured on average on 2.5 days, placing Amsterdam in AHS Heat Zone 2.
sentence_128: The record extremes range from −19.7 °C (−3.5 °F) to 36.3 °C (97.3 °F).
sentence_129: Days with more than 1 mm (0.04 in) of [[Precipitation|precipitation]] are common, on average 133 days per year.
sentence_130: Amsterdam's average annual precipitation is 838 mm (33 in).
sentence_131: A large part of this precipitation falls as light rain or brief showers.
sentence_132: Cloudy and damp days are common during the cooler months of October through March.
sentence_133: In 1300, Amsterdam's population was around 1,000 people.
sentence_134: While many towns in Holland experienced population decline during the 15th and 16th centuries, Amsterdam's population grew, mainly due to the rise of the profitable [[Baltic_maritime_trade_(c._1400–1800)|Baltic maritime trade]] after the Burgundian victory in the Dutch–Hanseatic War.
sentence_135: Still, the population of Amsterdam was only modest compared to the towns and cities of Flanders and Brabant, which comprised the most urbanised area of the Low Countries.
sentence_136: This changed when, during the [[Dutch_Revolt|Dutch Revolt]], many people from the Southern Netherlands fled to the North, especially after [[Fall_of_Antwerp|Antwerp fell to Spanish forces]] in 1585.
sentence_137: Jewish people from Spain, Portugal and Eastern Europe similarly settled in Amsterdam, as did Germans and Scandinavians.
sentence_138: In thirty years, Amsterdam's population more than doubled between 1585 and 1610.
sentence_139: By 1600, its population was around 50,000.
sentence_140: During the 1660s, Amsterdam's population reached 200,000.
sentence_141: The city's growth levelled off and the population stabilised around 240,000 for most of the 18th century.
sentence_142: In 1750, Amsterdam was the [[List_of_largest_European_cities_in_history|fourth largest city in western Europe]], behind London (676,000), Paris (560,000) and Naples (324,000).
sentence_143: This was all the more remarkable as Amsterdam was neither the capital city nor the seat of government of the [[Dutch_Republic|Dutch Republic]], which itself was a much smaller state than England, France or the [[Ottoman_Empire|Ottoman Empire]].
sentence_144: In contrast to those other metropolises, Amsterdam was also surrounded by large towns such as [[Leiden|Leiden]] (about 67,000), [[Rotterdam|Rotterdam]] (45,000), [[Haarlem|Haarlem]] (38,000), and [[Utrecht|Utrecht]] (30,000).
sentence_145: The city's population declined in the early 19th century, dipping under 200,000 in 1820.
sentence_146: By the second half of the 19th century, industrialisation spurred renewed growth.
sentence_147: Amsterdam's population hit an all-time high of 872,000 in 1959, before declining in the following decades due to government-sponsored suburbanisation to so-called groeikernen (growth centres) such as [[Purmerend|Purmerend]] and [[Almere|Almere]].
sentence_148: Between 1970 and 1980, Amsterdam experienced its sharp population decline, peaking at a net loss of 25,000 people in 1973.
sentence_149: By 1985 the city had only 675,570 residents.
sentence_150: This was soon followed by reurbanisation and [[Gentrification|gentrification]], leading to renewed population growth in the 2010s.
sentence_151: Also in the 2010s, much of Amsterdam's population growth was due to immigration to the city.
sentence_152: Amsterdam's population is expected to top its previous high in 2019, reaching 873,000.
