sentence_72: Main articles: [[List_of_protected_areas_of_British_Columbia|List of protected areas of British Columbia]] and [[List_of_British_Columbia_Provincial_Parks|List of British Columbia Provincial Parks]]
sentence_73: There are 14 designations of parks and protected areas in the province that reflect the different administration and creation of these areas in a modern context.
sentence_74: There are 141 ecological reserves, 35 provincial marine parks, 7 provincial heritage sites, 6 [[National_Historic_Sites_of_Canada|National Historic Sites of Canada]], 4 [[National_park|national parks]] and 3 national park reserves.
sentence_75: 12.5% of the province's area (114,000 km or 44,000 sq mi) is considered protected under one of the 14 different designations that includes over 800 distinct areas.
sentence_76: British Columbia contains seven of [[National_Parks_of_Canada|Canada's national parks]] and National Park Reserves:

list.value: [[Gwaii_Haanas_National_Park_Reserve_and_Haida_Heritage_Site|Gwaii Haanas National Park Reserve and Haida Heritage Site]]

sentence_77: British Columbia contains a large number of [[Provincial_park|provincial parks]], run by BC Parks under the aegis of the Ministry of Environment.
sentence_78: British Columbia's provincial parks system is the second largest parks system in Canada, the largest being Canada's National Parks system).
sentence_79: Another tier of parks in British Columbia are [[Regional_park|regional parks]], which are maintained and run by [[List_of_regional_districts_of_British_Columbia|the province's regional districts]].
sentence_80: The Ministry of Forests operates forest recreation sites.
sentence_81: In addition to these areas, over 47,000 square kilometres (18,000 sq mi) of [[Arable_land|arable land]] are protected by the [[Agricultural_Land_Reserve|Agricultural Land Reserve]].
sentence_82: White spruce or [[Picea_engelmannii|Engelmann spruce]] and their hybrids occur in 12 of the 14 [[Biogeoclimatic_zones_of_British_Columbia|biogeoclimatic zones of British Columbia]] (Coates et al.
sentence_84: Common types of trees present in BC's forests include [[Thuja_plicata|Western Redcedar]], [[Chamaecyparis_nootkatensis|Yellow-cedar]], [[Juniperus_scopulorum|Rocky Mountain juniper]], [[Pinus_contorta|Lodgepole pine]], [[Pinus_ponderosa|Ponderosa or yellow pine]], [[Pinus_albicaulis|Whitebark pine]], [[Pinus_flexilis|Limber pine]], [[Western_white_pine|Western white pine]], [[Larix_occidentalis|Western larch]], [[Larix_laricina|Tamarack]], [[Larix_lyallii|Alpine larch]], [[Picea_glauca|White spruce]], [[Picea_engelmannii|Engelmann spruce]], [[Picea_sitchensis|Sitka spruce]], [[Picea_mariana|Black spruce]], [[Abies_grandis|Grand fir]], [[Abies_amabilis|Amabilis fir]], [[Abies_lasiocarpa|Subalpine fir]], [[Tsuga_heterophylla|Western hemlock]], [[Tsuga_mertensiana|Mountain hemlock]], [[Pseudotsuga_menziesii_var._menziesii|Douglas-fir]], [[Taxus_brevifolia|Western yew]], [[Cornus_nuttallii|Pacific dogwood]], [[Acer_macrophyllum|Bigleaf maple]], [[Acer_glabrum|Douglas maple]], [[Acer_circinatum|Vine maple]], [[Arbutus_menziesii|Arbutus]], [[Crataegus_douglasii|Black hawthorn]], [[Rhamnus_purshiana|Cascara]], [[Quercus_garryana|Garry oak]], [[Malus_fusca|Pacific crab apple]], [[Prunus_virginiana|Choke cherry]], [[Prunus_pensylvanica|Pin cherry]], [[Prunus_emarginata|Bitter cherry]], [[Alnus_rubra|Red alder]], [[Alnus_tenuifolia|Mountain alder]], [[Betula_papyrifera|Paper birch]], [[Betula_occidentalis|Water birch]], [[Populus_trichocarpa|Black cottonwood]], [[Populus_balsamifera|Balsam poplar]], [[Populus_tremuloides|Trembling aspen]].
sentence_85: Main article: Wild and medicinal plants of British Columbia
sentence_86: Plant foods traditionally contributed only a part of the total food intake of coastal [[First_Nations|First Nations]] peoples of British Columbia, though they contributed to most of the material good produced.
sentence_87: Among the plant foods used, berries, some roots (for example the Camas Lily – part of the [[Camassia|Camassia]] family), cambium noodles (inner bark of [[Tsuga|hemlock]]), and seaweeds were (and to an extent still are) important.
sentence_88: Animal products were traditionally far more important than plant foods in terms of quantity consumed, but the huge nutritional diversity provided by native plants largely contributes to the health of First Nations peoples of British Columbia.
sentence_89: (Before [[Colonization|colonization]], British Columbia had the densest aboriginal population of any region in what is now called Canada.)
sentence_90: [[Environment_Canada|Environment Canada]] subdivides British Columbia into six [[Ecozones_of_Canada|ecozones]]:
sentence_91: Main article: [[History_of_British_Columbia|History of British Columbia]]
sentence_92: Main articles: [[Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Pacific_Northwest_Coast|Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest Coast]], [[Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Northwest_Plateau|Indigenous peoples of the Northwest Plateau]], and [[The_Canadian_Crown_and_Aboriginal_peoples|The Canadian Crown and Aboriginal peoples]]
sentence_93: The area now known as British Columbia is home to First Nations groups that have a deep history with a significant number of indigenous languages.
sentence_94: There are more than 200 First Nations in BC.
sentence_95: Prior to contact (with non-Aboriginal people), human history is known from oral histories of First Nations groups, archaeological investigations, and from early records from explorers encountering societies early in the period.
sentence_96: The arrival of [[Paleoindians|Paleoindians]] from [[Beringia|Beringia]] took place between 20,000 and 12,000 years ago.
sentence_97: [[Hunter-gatherer|Hunter-gatherer]] families were the main social structure from 10,000 to 5,000 years ago.
sentence_98: The nomadic population lived in non-permanent structures foraging for nuts, berries and edible roots while hunting and trapping larger and small game for food and furs.
sentence_99: Around 5,000 years ago individual groups started to focus on resources available to them locally.
sentence_100: Thus with the passage of time there is a pattern of increasing regional generalization with a more sedentary lifestyle.
sentence_101: These indigenous populations evolved over the next 5,000 years across a large area into many groups with shared traditions and customs.
sentence_102: To the northwest of the province are the peoples of the [[Na-Dene_languages|Na-Dene languages]], which include the [[Athapaskan_languages|Athapaskan-speaking peoples]] and the [[Tlingit_people|Tlingit]], who lived on the islands of southern Alaska and northern British Columbia.
sentence_103: The Na-Dene language group is believed to be linked to the [[Yeniseian_languages|Yeniseian languages]] of Siberia.
sentence_104: The [[Dene|Dene]] of the western Arctic may represent a distinct wave of migration from Asia to North America.
sentence_105: The Interior of British Columbia was home to the [[Salishan_languages|Salishan language]] groups such as the [[Secwepemc|Shuswap (Secwepemc)]], [[Okanagan_people|Okanagan]] and Athabaskan language groups, primarily the [[Dakelh|Dakelh]] (Carrier) and the Tsilhqot'in.
sentence_106: The inlets and valleys of the British Columbia coast sheltered large, distinctive populations, such as the Haida, [[Kwakwaka'wakw|Kwakwaka'wakw]] and [[Nuu-chah-nulth_people|Nuu-chah-nulth]], sustained by the region's abundant salmon and shellfish.
sentence_107: These peoples developed complex cultures dependent on the [[Western_red_cedar|western red cedar]] that included wooden houses, seagoing whaling and war canoes and elaborately carved [[Potlatch|potlatch]] items and [[Totem_poles|totem poles]].
sentence_108: Contact with Europeans brought a series of devastating epidemics of diseases from Europe the people had no immunity to.
sentence_109: The result was a dramatic population collapse, culminating in the 1862 Smallpox outbreak in Victoria that spread throughout the coast.
sentence_110: European settlement did not bode well for the remaining native population of British Columbia.
sentence_111: Colonial officials deemed colonists could make better use of the land than the First Nations people, and thus the land territory be owned by the colonists.
sentence_112: To ensure colonists would be able to settle properly and make use of the land, First Nations were forcibly relocated onto reserves, which were often too small to support their way of life.
sentence_113: By the 1930s, British Columbia had over 1500 reserves.
sentence_114: See also: [[Oregon_boundary_dispute|Oregon boundary dispute]]
sentence_115: The British, during the colonial period, spread across the world claiming territories and building the [[British_Empire|British Empire]].
sentence_116: Lands now known as British Columbia were added to the empire during the 19th century.
sentence_117: Originally established under the auspices of the [[Hudson's_Bay_Company|Hudson's Bay Company]], colonies were established (Vancouver Island, the mainland) that were amalgamated, then entered Confederation as British Columbia in 1871 as part of the Dominion of Canada.
sentence_118: During the 1770s, [[Smallpox|smallpox]] killed at least 30% of the Pacific Northwest [[First_Nations|First Nations]].
sentence_119: This devastating epidemic was the first in a series; the Great Smallpox Epidemic of 1862 killed 50% of the native population.
sentence_120: The arrival of Europeans began around the mid-18th century, as fur traders entered the area to harvest [[Sea_otter|sea otters]].
sentence_121: While it is thought [[Francis_Drake|Sir Francis Drake]] may have explored the British Columbian coast in 1579, it was [[Juan_José_Pérez_Hernández|Juan Pérez]] who completed the first documented voyage, which took place in 1774.
sentence_122: [[Juan_Francisco_de_la_Bodega_y_Quadra|Juan Francisco de la Bodega y Quadra]] explored the coast in 1775.
sentence_123: In doing so, Pérez and Quadra reasserted the [[Spanish_Empire|Spanish]] claim for the [[Pacific_coast|Pacific coast]], first made by [[Vasco_Núñez_de_Balboa|Vasco Núñez de Balboa]] in 1513.
sentence_124: The explorations of [[James_Cook|James Cook]] in 1778 and [[George_Vancouver|George Vancouver]] in 1792–93 established British jurisdiction over the coastal area north and west of the Columbia River.
sentence_125: In 1793, [[Sir_Alexander_Mackenzie|Sir Alexander Mackenzie]] was the first European to journey across North America overland to the Pacific Ocean, inscribing a stone marking his accomplishment on the shoreline of [[Dean_Channel|Dean Channel]] near [[Bella_Coola,_British_Columbia|Bella Coola]].
sentence_126: His expedition theoretically established British sovereignty inland, and a succession of other fur company explorers charted the maze of rivers and mountain ranges between the Canadian Prairies and the Pacific.
sentence_127: Mackenzie and other explorers—notably [[John_Finlay_(fur_trader)|John Finlay]], [[Simon_Fraser_(explorer)|Simon Fraser]], [[Samuel_Black|Samuel Black]], and [[David_Thompson_(explorer)|David Thompson]]—were primarily concerned with extending the fur trade, rather than political considerations.
sentence_128: In 1794, by the third of a series of agreements known as the [[Nootka_Convention|Nootka Conventions]], [[Spanish_Empire|Spain]] conceded its claims of exclusivity in the Pacific.
sentence_129: This opened the way for formal claims and colonization by other powers, including Britain, but because of the [[Napoleonic_Wars|Napoleonic Wars]], there was little British action on its claims in the region until later.
sentence_130: The establishment of [[Trading_post|trading posts]] under the auspices of the [[North_West_Company|North West Company]] and the Hudson's Bay Company (HBC), effectively established a permanent British presence in the region.
sentence_131: The Columbia District was broadly defined as being south of 54°40 north latitude, (the southern limit of [[Russian_colonization_of_the_Americas|Russian America]]), north of Mexican-controlled California, and west of the [[Rocky_Mountains|Rocky Mountains]].
sentence_132: It was, by the [[Treaty_of_1818|Anglo-American Convention of 1818]], under the "joint occupancy and use" of citizens of the United States and subjects of Britain (which is to say, the fur companies).
sentence_133: This co-occupancy was ended with the Oregon Treaty of 1846.
sentence_134: The major supply route was the [[York_Factory_Express|York Factory Express]] between [[Hudson_Bay|Hudson Bay]] and [[Fort_Vancouver|Fort Vancouver]].
sentence_135: Some of the early outposts grew into settlements, communities, and cities.
sentence_136: Among the places in British Columbia that began as fur trading posts are Fort St. John (established 1794); [[Hudson's_Hope,_British_Columbia|Hudson's Hope]] (1805); [[Fort_Nelson,_British_Columbia|Fort Nelson]] (1805); [[Fort_St._James,_British_Columbia|Fort St. James]] (1806); [[Prince_George,_British_Columbia|Prince George]] (1807); Kamloops (1812); [[Fort_Langley,_British_Columbia|Fort Langley]] (1827); [[Fort_Victoria_(British_Columbia)|Fort Victoria]] (1843); Yale (1848); and Nanaimo (1853).
sentence_137: Fur company posts that became cities in what is now the United States include [[Vancouver,_Washington|Vancouver, Washington]] ([[Fort_Vancouver|Fort Vancouver]]), formerly the "capital" of Hudson's Bay operations in the Columbia District, [[Colville,_Washington|Colville, Washington]] and [[Walla_Walla,_Washington|Walla Walla, Washington]] (old [[Fort_Nez_Percés|Fort Nez Percés]]).
sentence_138: With the amalgamation of the two fur trading companies in 1821, modern-day British Columbia existed in three fur trading departments.
sentence_139: The bulk of the central and northern interior was organized into the [[New_Caledonia_(Canada)|New Caledonia]] district, administered from Fort St. James.
sentence_140: The interior south of the [[Thompson_River|Thompson River]] [[Drainage_basin|watershed]] and north of the Columbia was organized into the Columbia District, administered from Fort Vancouver on the lower Columbia River.
sentence_141: The northeast corner of the province east of the Rockies, known as the Peace River Block, was attached to the much larger [[District_of_Athabasca|Athabasca District]], headquartered in [[Fort_Chipewyan,_Alberta|Fort Chipewyan]], in present-day Alberta.
sentence_142: Until 1849, these districts were a wholly unorganized area of [[British_North_America|British North America]] under the [[De_facto|de facto]] jurisdiction of HBC administrators; however, unlike [[Rupert's_Land|Rupert's Land]] to the north and east, the territory was not a concession to the company.
sentence_143: Rather, it was simply granted a monopoly to trade with the First Nations inhabitants.
sentence_144: All that was changed with the westward extension of American exploration and the concomitant overlapping claims of territorial sovereignty, especially in the southern [[Columbia_River_drainage_basin|Columbia Basin]] (within present day Washington and [[Oregon|Oregon]]).
sentence_145: In 1846, the Oregon Treaty divided the territory along the [[49th_parallel_north|49th parallel]] to the [[Strait_of_Georgia|Strait of Georgia]], with the area south of this boundary (excluding Vancouver Island and the [[Gulf_Islands|Gulf Islands]]) transferred to sole American sovereignty.
sentence_146: The Colony of Vancouver Island was created in 1849, with Victoria designated as the capital.
sentence_147: New Caledonia, as the whole of the mainland rather than just its north-central Interior came to be called, continued to be an unorganized territory of British North America, "administered" by individual HBC trading post managers.
sentence_148: Main articles: [[Colony_of_British_Columbia_(1858–66)|Colony of British Columbia (1858–66)]] and [[Richard_Clement_Moody|Richard Clement Moody]]
sentence_149: With the [[Fraser_Canyon_Gold_Rush|Fraser Canyon Gold Rush]] in 1858, an influx of Americans into New Caledonia prompted the [[Secretary_of_State_for_the_Colonies|colonial office]] to designate the mainland as the Colony of British Columbia.
sentence_150: When news of the [[Fraser_Canyon_Gold_Rush|Fraser Canyon Gold Rush]] reached London, Richard Clement Moody was hand-picked by the [[Colonial_Office|Colonial Office]], under [[Sir_Edward_Bulwer-Lytton|Sir Edward Bulwer-Lytton]], to establish British order and to transform the newly established Colony of British Columbia into the British Empire's "bulwark in the farthest west" and "found a second England on the shores of the Pacific".
sentence_151: Lytton desired to send to the colony "representatives of the best of British culture, not just a police force": he sought men who possessed "courtesy, high breeding and urbane knowledge of the world" and he decided to send Moody, whom the Government considered to be the "English gentleman and British Officer" at the head of the [[Royal_Engineers,_Columbia_Detachment|Royal Engineers, Columbia Detachment]].
sentence_152: Moody and his family arrived in British Columbia in December 1858, commanding the [[Royal_Engineers,_Columbia_Detachment|Royal Engineers, Columbia Detachment]].
sentence_153: He was sworn in as the first [[Lieutenant-Governor_of_British_Columbia|Lieutenant-Governor of British Columbia]] and appointed Chief Commissioner of Lands and Works for British Columbia.
sentence_154: On the advice of Lytton, Moody hired [[Robert_Burnaby|Robert Burnaby]] as his personal secretary.
sentence_155: In British Columbia, Moody "wanted to build a city of beauty in the wilderness" and planned his city as an iconic visual metaphor for British dominance, "styled and located with the objective of reinforcing the authority of the crown and of the robe".
sentence_156: Subsequent to the enactment of the Pre-emption Act of 1860, Moody settled the [[Lower_Mainland|Lower Mainland]].
sentence_157: He selected the site and founded the new capital, [[New_Westminster|New Westminster]].
sentence_158: He selected the site due to the strategic excellence of its position and the quality of its port.
sentence_159: He was also struck by the majestic beauty of the site, writing in his letter to Blackwood,
sentence_160: Lord Lytton "forgot the practicalities of paying for clearing and developing the site and the town" and the efforts of Moody's engineers were continuously hampered by insufficient funds, which, together with the continuous opposition of [[James_Douglas_(governor)|Douglas]], "made it impossible for Moody's design to be fulfilled".
sentence_161: Moody and the Royal Engineers also built an extensive road network, including what would become [[Kingsway_(Vancouver)|Kingsway]], connecting New Westminster to False Creek, the North Road between [[Port_Moody|Port Moody]] and New Westminster, and the [[Cariboo_Road|Cariboo Road]] and [[Stanley_Park|Stanley Park]].
sentence_162: He named [[Burnaby_Lake|Burnaby Lake]] after his private secretary [[Robert_Burnaby|Robert Burnaby]] and named Port Coquitlam's 400-foot "Mary Hill" after his wife.
sentence_163: As part of the surveying effort, several tracts were designated "government reserves", which included [[Stanley_Park|Stanley Park]] as a military reserve (a strategic location in case of an American invasion).
sentence_164: The Pre-emption Act did not specify conditions for distributing the land, so large parcels were snapped up by speculators, including 3,750 acres (1,517 hectares) by Moody himself.
sentence_165: For this he was criticized by local newspapermen for [[Land_grabbing|land grabbing]].
sentence_166: Moody designed the first [[Coat_of_arms_of_British_Columbia|coat of arms of British Columbia]].
sentence_167: [[Port_Moody|Port Moody]] is named after him.
sentence_168: It was established at the end of a trail that connected New Westminster with Burrard Inlet to defend New Westminster from potential attack from the US.
sentence_169: By 1862, the Cariboo Gold Rush, attracting an additional 5000 miners, was underway, and Douglas hastened construction of the Great North Road (commonly known now as the [[Cariboo_Wagon_Road|Cariboo Wagon Road]]) up the [[Fraser_Canyon|Fraser Canyon]] to the prospecting region around Barkerville.
sentence_170: By the time of this gold rush, the character of the colony was changing, as a more stable population of British colonists settled in the region, establishing businesses, opening [[Sawmill|sawmills]], and engaging in [[Fishery|fishing]] and agriculture.
sentence_171: With this increased stability, objections to the colony's absentee governor and the lack of responsible government began to be vocalised, led by the influential editor of the [[New_Westminster|New Westminster]] British Columbian and future premier, [[John_Robson_(politician)|John Robson]].
sentence_172: A series of petitions requesting an assembly were ignored by Douglas and the colonial office until Douglas was eased out of office in 1864.
sentence_173: Finally, the colony would have both an assembly and a resident governor.
sentence_174: A series of gold rushes in various parts of the province followed, the largest being the Cariboo Gold Rush in 1862, forcing the colonial administration into deeper debt as it struggled to meet the extensive infrastructure needs of far-flung boom communities like Barkerville and [[Lillooet|Lillooet]], which sprang up overnight.
sentence_175: The Vancouver Island colony was facing financial crises of its own, and pressure to merge the two eventually [[Colony_of_British_Columbia_(1866–71)|succeeded in 1866]], when the colony of British Columbia was amalgamated with the Colony of Vancouver Island to form the [[Colony_of_British_Columbia_(1866–71)|Colony of British Columbia (1866–71)]], which was, in turn, succeeded by the present day province of British Columbia following the [[Canadian_Confederation|Canadian Confederation]] of 1871.
sentence_176: The Confederation League, including such figures as [[Amor_De_Cosmos|Amor De Cosmos]], [[John_Robson_(politician)|John Robson]], and [[Robert_Beaven|Robert Beaven]], led the chorus pressing for the colony to join Canada, which had been created out of three British North American colonies in 1867 (the [[Province_of_Canada|Province of Canada]], [[Nova_Scotia|Nova Scotia]] and [[New_Brunswick|New Brunswick]]).
sentence_177: Several factors motivated this agitation, including the fear of annexation to the United States, the overwhelming debt created by rapid population growth, the need for government-funded services to support this population, and the economic depression caused by the end of the gold rush.
sentence_178: With the agreement by the Canadian government to extend the [[Canadian_Pacific_Railway|Canadian Pacific Railway]] to British Columbia and to assume the colony's debt, British Columbia became the sixth province to join [[Canadian_Confederation|Confederation]] on July 20, 1871.
sentence_179: The borders of the province were not completely settled.
sentence_180: The Treaty of Washington sent the [[Pig_War_(1859)|Pig War]] San Juan Islands Border dispute to arbitration in 1871 and in 1903, the province's territory shrank again after the [[Alaska_boundary_dispute|Alaska boundary dispute]] settled the vague boundary of the [[Alaska_Panhandle|Alaska Panhandle]].
sentence_181: Population in British Columbia continued to expand as the province's [[Mining|mining]], forestry, [[Agriculture|agriculture]], and [[Fishery|fishing]] sectors were developed.
sentence_182: Mining activity was particularly notable throughout the Mainland, particularly in the [[Boundary_Country|Boundary Country]], in the [[Slocan_Valley|Slocan]], in the West Kootenay around Trail, the East Kootenay (the southeast corner of the province), the Fraser Canyon, the [[Cariboo_District|Cariboo]], the [[Omineca_Country|Omineca]] and the [[Cassiar_Country|Cassiar]], so much so a common epithet for the Mainland, even after provincehood, was "the Gold Colony".
sentence_183: Agriculture attracted settlers to the fertile Fraser Valley, and cattle ranchers and later fruit growers came to the drier grasslands of the Thompson River area, the Cariboo, the [[Chilcotin_District|Chilcotin]], and the Okanagan.
sentence_184: Forestry drew workers to the lush temperate rainforests of the coast, which was also the locus of a growing fishery.
sentence_185: The completion of the railway in 1885 was a huge boost to the province's economy, facilitating the transportation of the region's considerable resources to the east.
sentence_186: The milltown of Granville, known as Gastown, near the mouth of the [[Burrard_Inlet|Burrard Inlet]] was selected as the terminus of the railway, prompting the incorporation of the City as Vancouver in 1886.
sentence_187: The completion of the [[Port_of_Vancouver|Port of Vancouver]] spurred rapid growth, and in less than fifty years the city surpassed [[Winnipeg|Winnipeg]], [[Manitoba|Manitoba]], as the largest in [[Western_Canada|Western Canada]].
sentence_188: The early decades of the province were ones in which issues of land use—specifically, its settlement and development—were paramount.
sentence_189: This included expropriation from First Nations people of their land, control over its resources, as well as the ability to trade in some resources (such as the fishery).
sentence_190: Establishing a [[Labor_force|labour force]] to develop the province was problematic from the start, and British Columbia was the locus of immigration from Europe, China, Japan and India.
sentence_191: The influx of a non-[[Ethnic_groups_in_Europe|European]] population stimulated resentment from the dominant ethnic groups, resulting in agitation (much of it successful) to restrict the ability of [[Asian_people|Asian people]] to immigrate to British Columbia through the imposition of a [[Tax_per_head|head tax]].
sentence_192: This resentment culminated in mob attacks against Chinese and Japanese immigrants in Vancouver in 1887 and 1907.
sentence_193: The subsequent [[Komagata_Maru_incident|Komagata Maru incident]] in 1914, where hundreds of Indians were denied entry into Vancouver, was also a direct result of the anti-Asian resentment at the time.
sentence_194: By 1923, almost all [[Chinese_Immigration_Act,_1923|Chinese immigration had been blocked]] except for merchants, professionals, students and investors.
sentence_195: Meanwhile, the province continued to grow.
sentence_196: In 1914, the last spike of a second transcontinental rail line, the [[Grand_Trunk_Pacific_Railway|Grand Trunk Pacific]], linking north-central British Columbia from the Yellowhead Pass through Prince George to Prince Rupert was driven at [[Fort_Fraser,_British_Columbia|Fort Fraser]].
sentence_197: This opened up the North Coast and the [[Bulkley_Valley|Bulkley Valley]] region to new economic opportunities.
sentence_198: What had previously been an almost exclusively fur trade and subsistence economy soon became a locus for forestry, farming, and mining.
sentence_199: In [[World_War_I|World War I]], the province responded strongly to the call to assist the British Empire against its German foes in French and Belgian battlefields.
sentence_200: About 55,570 of the 400,000 British Columbian residents, the highest per-capita rate in Canada, responded to the military needs.
sentence_201: Horseriders from the province's Interior region and First Nations soldiers made contributions to Vimy Ridge and other battles.
sentence_202: About 6,225 men from the province died in combat.
sentence_203: When the men returned from the [[First_World_War|First World War]], they discovered the recently enfranchised women of the province had helped vote in the [[Prohibition_in_Canada|prohibition]] of liquor in an effort to end the social problems associated with the hard-core drinking Vancouver and the rest of the province was famous for until the war.
sentence_204: Because of pressure from veterans, prohibition was quickly relaxed so the "soldier and the working man" could enjoy a drink, but widespread unemployment among veterans was hardened by many of the available jobs being taken by European immigrants and disgruntled veterans organized a range of "soldier parties" to represent their interests, variously named Soldier-Farmer, Soldier-Labour, and Farmer-Labour Parties.
sentence_205: These formed the basis of the fractured labour-political spectrum that would generate a host of fringe leftist and rightist parties, including those who would eventually form the [[Co-operative_Commonwealth_Federation|Co-operative Commonwealth]] and the early Social Credit splinter groups.
sentence_206: The advent of [[Prohibition_in_the_United_States|prohibition in the United States]] created new opportunities, and many found employment or at least profit in cross-border liquor smuggling.
sentence_207: Much of Vancouver's prosperity and opulence in the 1920s results from this "pirate economy", although growth in forestry, fishing and mining continued.
sentence_208: By the end of the 1920s, the end of prohibition in the U.S., combined with the onset of the [[Great_Depression|Great Depression]], plunged the province into economic destitution during the 1930s.
sentence_209: Compounding the already dire local economic situation, tens of thousands of men from colder parts of Canada swarmed into Vancouver, creating huge [[Hobo|hobo]] jungles around False Creek and the Burrard Inlet rail yards, including the old Canadian Pacific Railway mainline [[Right-of-way_(transportation)|right-of-way]] through the heart of the city's downtown (at Hastings and Carrall).
sentence_210: Increasingly desperate times led to intense political organizing efforts, an occupation of the main Post Office at Granville and [[Hastings_Street_(Vancouver)|Hastings]] which was violently put down by the police and an effective imposition of [[Martial_law|martial law]] on the docks for almost three years.
sentence_211: A Vancouver contingent for the On-to-Ottawa Trek was organized and seized a train, which was loaded with thousands of men bound for the capital but was met by a [[Gatling_gun|Gatling gun]] straddling the tracks at Mission; the men were arrested and sent to work camps for the duration of the Depression.
sentence_212: There were some signs of economic life beginning to return to normal towards the end of the 1930s, but it was the onset of World War II which transformed the national economy and ended the hard times of the Depression.
sentence_213: Because of the war effort, women entered the workforce as never before.
sentence_214: British Columbia has long taken advantage of its location on the Pacific Ocean to have close relations with [[East_Asia|East Asia]] and [[South_Asia|South Asia]].
sentence_215: This closeness has often caused friction between cultures which has sometimes escalated into racist animosity towards those of Asian descent.
sentence_216: This was most manifest during the Second World War when many people of [[Japanese_Canadian_internment|Japanese descent were relocated]] or interned in the Interior region of the province.
sentence_217: During the [[Second_World_War|Second World War]] the mainstream BC Liberal and [[British_Columbia_Conservative_Party|BC Conservative]] Parties of British Columbia united in a formal coalition government under new Liberal leader [[John_Hart_(Canadian_politician)|John Hart]], who replaced [[Thomas_Dufferin_Pattullo|Duff Pattullo]] when the latter failed to win a majority in the [[1941_British_Columbia_general_election|1941 election]].
sentence_218: While the Liberals won the most seats, they actually received fewer votes than the socialist Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (CCF).
sentence_219: Pattullo was unwilling to form a coalition with the rival Conservatives led by [[Royal_Maitland|Royal Maitland]] and was replaced by Hart, who formed a coalition cabinet made up of five Liberal and three Conservative ministers.
sentence_220: The CCF was invited to join the coalition but refused.
sentence_221: The pretext for continuing the coalition after the end of the Second World War was to prevent the CCF, which had won a surprise victory in [[Saskatchewan|Saskatchewan]] in 1944, from ever coming to power in British Columbia.
sentence_222: The CCF's popular vote was high enough in the [[1945_British_Columbia_general_election|1945 election]] that they were likely to have won three-way contests and could have formed government; however, the coalition prevented that by uniting the anti-[[Socialism|socialist]] vote.
sentence_223: In the post-war environment the government initiated a series of infrastructure projects, notably the completion of Highway 97 north of Prince George to the Peace River Block, a section called the John Hart Highway and also public hospital insurance.
sentence_224: In 1947 the reins of the Coalition were taken over by [[Byron_Ingemar_Johnson|Byron Ingemar Johnson]].
sentence_225: The Conservatives had wanted their new leader [[Herbert_Anscomb|Herbert Anscomb]] to be premier, but the Liberals in the Coalition refused.
sentence_226: Johnson led the coalition to the highest percentage of the popular vote in British Columbia history (61%) in the [[1949_British_Columbia_general_election|1949 election]].
sentence_227: This victory was attributable to the popularity of his government's spending programmes, despite rising criticism of corruption and abuse of power.
sentence_228: During his tenure, major infrastructures continued to expand, such as the agreement with [[Rio_Tinto_Alcan|Alcan Aluminum]] to build the town of Kitimat with an aluminum smelter and the large [[Kemano_Generating_Station|Kemano Hydro Project]].
sentence_229: Johnson achieved popularity for flood relief efforts during the 1948 flooding of the Fraser Valley, which was a major blow to that region and to the province's economy.
sentence_230: On February 13, 1950, a [[1950_British_Columbia_B-36_crash|Convair B-36B crashed]] in northern British Columbia after jettisoning a Mark IV [[Atomic_bomb|atomic bomb]].
sentence_231: This was the first such [[United_States_military_nuclear_incident_terminology|nuclear weapon loss]] in history.
sentence_232: Increasing tension between the Liberal and Conservative coalition partners led the Liberal Party executive to vote to instruct Johnson to terminate the arrangement.
sentence_233: Johnson ended the coalition and dropped his Conservative cabinet ministers, including [[Deputy_Prime_Minister|Deputy Premier]] and Finance minister Herbert Anscomb, precipitating the [[1952_British_Columbia_general_election|general election of 1952]].
sentence_234: A referendum on electoral reform prior to this election had instigated an elimination ballot (similar to a [[Ranked_voting_systems|preferential ballot]]), where voters could select second and third choices.
sentence_235: The intent of the ballot, as campaigned for by Liberals and Conservatives, was that their supporters would list the rival party in lieu of the CCF, but this plan backfired when a large group of voters from all major parties, including the CCF, voted for the fringe British Columbia Social Credit Party (Socreds), who wound up with the largest number of seats in the House (19), only one seat ahead of the CCF, despite the CCF having 34.3% of the vote to Social Credit's 30.18%.
sentence_236: The Social Credit Party, led by rebel former Conservative MLA [[W._A._C._Bennett|W.
sentence_237: A. C. Bennett]], formed a [[Minority_government|minority government]] backed by the Liberals and Conservatives (with 6 and 4 seats respectively).
sentence_238: Bennett began a series of fiscal reforms, preaching a new variety of [[Populism|populism]] as well as waxing eloquent on progress and development, laying the ground for a [[1953_British_Columbia_general_election|second election in 1953]] in which the new Bennett regime secured a majority of seats, with 38% of the vote.
sentence_239: Secure with that majority, Bennett returned the province to the first-past-the-post system thereafter, which is still in use.
sentence_240: With the election of the Social Credit Party, British Columbia embarked on a phase of rapid [[Economic_development|economic development]].
sentence_241: Bennett and his party governed the province for the next twenty years, during which time the government initiated an ambitious programme of infrastructure development, fuelled by a sustained economic boom in the forestry, mining, and energy sectors.
sentence_242: During these two decades, the government [[Nationalization|nationalized]] British Columbia Electric and the British Columbia Power Company, as well as smaller electric companies, renaming the entity [[BC_Hydro|BC Hydro]].
sentence_243: [[West_Kootenay_Power_and_Light|West Kootenay Power and Light]] remained independent of BC Hydro, being owned and operated by [[Cominco|Cominco]], though tied into the regional power grid.
sentence_244: By the end of the 1960s, several major dams had been begun or completed in—among others—the [[Peace_River_(Canada)|Peace]], Columbia, and [[Nechako_River|Nechako River]] watersheds (the Nechako Diversion to [[Kemano|Kemano]], was to supply power to the [[Alcan_Inc.|Alcan Inc.]] aluminum smelter at Kitimat, and was not part of the provincial power grid but [[Independent_Power_Producers_in_British_Columbia|privately owned]]).
sentence_245: Major transmission deals were concluded, most notably the [[Columbia_River_Treaty|Columbia River Treaty]] between Canada and the United States.
sentence_246: The province's economy was also boosted by unprecedented growth in the forest sector, as well as oil and gas development in the province's northeast.
sentence_247: The 1950s and 1960s were also marked by development in the province's transportation infrastructure.
sentence_248: In 1960, the government established [[BC_Ferries|BC Ferries]] as a [[Crown_corporations_of_Canada|crown corporation]], to provide a marine extension of the provincial highway system, also supported by federal grants as being part of the [[Trans-Canada_Highway|Trans-Canada Highway]] system.
sentence_249: That system was improved and expanded through the construction of new highways and bridges, and paving of existing highways and provincial roads.
sentence_250: Vancouver and Victoria became cultural centres as poets, authors, artists, musicians, as well as dancers, actors, and haute cuisine chefs flocked to its scenery and warmer temperatures, with the cultural and entrepreneurial community bolstered by many [[Draft_dodgers|Draft dodgers]] from the United States.
sentence_251: Tourism also played a role in the economy.
sentence_252: The rise of Japan and other Pacific economies was a boost to British Columbia's economy, primarily because of exports of lumber products and unprocessed coal and trees.
sentence_253: Politically and socially, the 1960s brought a period of significant social ferment.
sentence_254: The divide between the [[Left-wing_politics|political left]] and right, which had prevailed in the province since the Depression and the rise of the [[Labour_movement|labour movement]], sharpened as so-called [[Capitalism|free enterprise]] parties coalesced into the de facto coalition represented by Social Credit—in opposition to the [[Social_democracy|social democratic]] [[New_Democratic_Party_(Canada)|New Democratic Party]], the successor to the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation.
sentence_255: As the province's economy blossomed, so did labour-management tensions.
sentence_256: Tensions emerged, also, from the counterculture movement of the late 1960s, of which Vancouver and Nanaimo were centres.
sentence_257: The conflict between [[Hippie|hippies]] and [[List_of_mayors_of_Vancouver|Vancouver mayor]] [[Tom_Campbell_(Canadian_politician)|Tom Campbell]] was particularly legendary, culminating in the [[Gastown_riots|Gastown riots]] of 1971.
sentence_258: By the end of the decade, with social tensions and dissatisfaction with the [[Status_quo|status quo]] rising, the Bennett government's achievements could not stave off its growing unpopularity.
sentence_259: On August 27, 1969, the Social Credit Party was re-elected in a general election for what would be Bennett's final term in power.
sentence_260: At the start of the 1970s, the economy was quite strong because of rising coal prices and an increase in annual allowable cuts in the forestry sector, but BC Hydro reported its first loss, which was the beginning of the end for Bennett and the Social Credit Party.
sentence_261: The Socreds were forced from power in the August 1972 election, paving the way for a provincial New Democratic Party (NDP) government under [[Dave_Barrett|Dave Barrett]].
sentence_262: Under Barrett, the large provincial surplus soon became a deficit, although changes to the accounting system makes it likely some of the deficit was carried over from the previous Social Credit regime and its "two sets of books", as WAC Bennett had once referred to his system of fiscal management.
sentence_263: The brief three-year ("Thousand Days") period of NDP governance brought several lasting changes to the province, most notably the creation of the Agricultural Land Reserve, intended to protect farmland from redevelopment, and the [[Insurance_Corporation_of_British_Columbia|Insurance Corporation of British Columbia]], a crown corporation charged with a monopoly on providing single-payer basic automobile insurance.
sentence_264: Perceptions the government had instituted reforms either too swiftly or that were too far-reaching, coupled with growing labour disruptions led to the ouster of the NDP in the [[1975_British_Columbia_general_election|1975 general election]].
sentence_265: Social Credit, under W.A.C. Bennett's son, [[Bill_Bennett|Bill Bennett]], was returned to office.
sentence_266: Under the younger Bennett's government, 85% of the province's land base was transferred from Government Reserve to management by the Ministry of Forests, reporting of deputy ministers was centralized to the Premier's Office, and NDP-instigated social programs were rolled back, with then-Human Resources Minister infamously demonstrating a golden shovel to highlight his welfare policy, although the new-era Socreds also reinforced and backed certain others instigated by the NDP—notably the creation of the [[Whistler,_British_Columbia|Resort Municipality of Whistler]], whose special status including Sunday drinking, then an anomaly in BC.
sentence_267: Also during the "MiniWac" regime (a reference to his father's acronym, WAC) certain money-losing Crown-owned assets were "privatized" in a mass giveaway of shares in the British Columbia Resources Investment Corporation, "BCRIC", with the "Brick shares" soon becoming near-worthless.
sentence_268: Towards the end of his tenure in power, Bennett oversaw the completion of several [[Megaproject|megaprojects]] meant to stimulate the economy and win votes – unlike most right-wing parties, British Columbia's Social Credit actively practised government stimulation of the economy.
sentence_269: Most notable of these was the winning of a world's fair for Vancouver, which came in the form of [[Expo_86|Expo 86]], to which was tied the construction of the [[British_Columbia_Highway_5|Coquihalla Highway]] and Vancouver's [[SkyTrain_(Vancouver)|SkyTrain]] system.
sentence_270: The Coquihalla Highway project became the subject of a scandal after revelations the premier's brother bought large tracts of land needed for the project before it was announced to the public, and also because of graft investigations of the huge cost overruns on the project.
sentence_271: Both investigations were derailed in the media by a still further scandal, the [[Doman_Scandal|Doman Scandal]], in which the premier and millionaire backer Herb Doman were investigated for insider-trading and [[Securities_fraud|securities fraud]].
sentence_272: Nonetheless, the Socreds were re-elected in 1979 under Bennett, who led the party until 1986.
sentence_273: As the province entered a sustained [[Recession|recession]], Bennett's popularity and media image were in decline.
sentence_274: On April 1, 1983, Premier Bennett overstayed his constitutional limits of power by exceeding the legal tenure of a government, and the [[Lieutenant_Governor_of_British_Columbia|Lieutenant-Governor]], [[Henry_Pybus_Bell-Irving|Henry Pybus Bell-Irving]], was forced to call Bennett to [[Government_House_(British_Columbia)|Government House]] to resolve the impasse, and an election was called for April 30, while in the meantime government cheques were covered by special emergency warrants as the Executive Council no longer had signing authority because of the constitutional crisis.
sentence_275: Campaigning on a platform of moderation, Bennett won an unexpected majority.
sentence_276: After several weeks of silence in the aftermath, a sitting of the [[Legislative_Assembly_of_British_Columbia|House]] was finally called and in the [[Speech_from_the_throne|speech from the throne]] the Socreds instituted a programme of fiscal cutbacks dubbed "restraint", which had been a buzzword for moderation during the campaign.
sentence_277: The programme included cuts to "motherhood" issues of the left, including the human rights branch, the offices of the Ombudsman and Rentalsman, women's programs, environmental and cultural programs, while still supplying mass capital infusions to corporate British Columbia.
sentence_278: This sparked a backlash, with tens of thousands of people in the streets the next day after the budget speech, and through the course of a summer repeated large demonstrations of up to 100,000 people.
sentence_279: This became known as the 1983 [[Solidarity_Crisis|Solidarity Crisis]], from the name of the Solidarity Coalition, a huge grassroots opposition movement mobilized, consisting of organized labour and community groups, with the British Columbia Federation of Labour forming a separate organization of unions, Operation Solidarity, under the direction of [[Jack_Munro|Jack Munro]], then-President of the [[International_Woodworkers_of_America|International Woodworkers of America]] (IWA), the most powerful of the province's resource unions.
sentence_280: Tens of thousands participated in protests and many felt a [[General_strike|general strike]] would be the inevitable result unless the government backed down from its policies they had claimed were only about restraint and not about recrimination against the NDP and the left.
sentence_281: Just as a strike at Pacific Press ended, which had crippled the political management of the public agenda by the publishers of the province's major papers, the movement collapsed after an apparent deal was struck by union leader and IWA president, Jack Munro and Premier Bennett.
sentence_282: A tense winter of blockades at various job sites around the province ensued, as among the new laws were those enabling non-union labour to work on large projects and other sensitive labour issues, with companies from Alberta and other provinces brought in to compete with union-scale British Columbia companies.
sentence_283: Despite the tension, Bennett's last few years in power were relatively peaceful as economic and political momentum grew on the megaprojects associated with Expo, and Bennett was to end his career by hosting [[Charles,_Prince_of_Wales|Prince Charles]] and [[Diana,_Princess_of_Wales|Lady Diana]] on their visit to open Expo 86.
sentence_284: His retirement being announced, a Social Credit convention was scheduled for the Whistler Resort, which came down to a three-way shooting match between Bud Smith, the Premier's right-hand man but an unelected official, Social Credit party grande dame [[Grace_McCarthy|Grace McCarthy]], and the charismatic but eccentric Bill Vander Zalm.
sentence_285: Bill Vander Zalm became the new Socred leader when Smith threw his support to him rather than see McCarthy win, and led the party to victory in the election later that year.
sentence_286: Vander Zalm was later involved in a conflict of interest scandal following the sale of Fantasy Gardens, a Christian and [[Culture_of_the_Netherlands|Dutch culture]] [[Amusement_park|theme park]] built by the Premier, to [[Tan_Yu|Tan Yu]], a [[Filipino_Chinese|Filipino Chinese]] gambling kingpin.
sentence_287: There were also concerns over Yu's application to the government for a bank licence, and lurid stories from flamboyant realtor [[Faye_Leung_(businesswoman)|Faye Leung]] of a party in the "Howard Hughes Suite" on the top two floors of the Bayshore Inn, where Tan Yu had been staying, with reports of a [[Bag_of_money|bag of money]] in a brown paper bag passed from Yu to Vander Zalm during the goings-on.
sentence_288: These scandals forced Vander Zalm's resignation, and Rita Johnston became premier of the province.
sentence_289: Johnston presided over the end of Social Credit power, calling an election which led to the reducing of the party's caucus to only two seats, and the revival of the long-defunct British Columbia Liberal Party as Opposition to the victorious NDP under former Vancouver mayor [[Mike_Harcourt|Mike Harcourt]].
sentence_290: In 1988, [[David_Lam_(real_estate_entrepreneur)|David Lam]] was appointed as British Columbia's twenty-fifth Lieutenant-Governor, and was the province's first Lieutenant-Governor of Chinese origin.
sentence_291: With an estimated population of 5.1 million as of 2020, British Columbia is Canada's third-most populous province, after [[Ontario|Ontario]] and [[Quebec|Quebec]].
sentence_292: See also: [[List_of_cities_in_British_Columbia|List of cities in British Columbia]], [[List_of_metropolitan_areas_in_British_Columbia|List of metropolitan areas in British Columbia]], [[List_of_municipalities_in_British_Columbia|List of municipalities in British Columbia]], and [[List_of_regional_districts_of_British_Columbia|List of regional districts of British Columbia]]
sentence_293: Half of all British Columbians live in the Metro Vancouver area, which includes Vancouver, [[Surrey,_British_Columbia|Surrey]], [[Burnaby|Burnaby]], [[Richmond,_British_Columbia|Richmond]], [[Coquitlam|Coquitlam]], [[Langley,_British_Columbia_(district_municipality)|Langley (district municipality)]], [[Delta,_British_Columbia|Delta]], [[North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)|North Vancouver (district municipality)]], Maple Ridge, [[New_Westminster|New Westminster]], [[Port_Coquitlam|Port Coquitlam]], [[North_Vancouver_(city)|North Vancouver (city)]], [[West_Vancouver|West Vancouver]], [[Port_Moody|Port Moody]], [[Langley,_British_Columbia_(city)|Langley (city)]], [[White_Rock,_British_Columbia|White Rock]], [[Pitt_Meadows|Pitt Meadows]], [[Bowen_Island|Bowen Island]], [[Anmore|Anmore]], [[Lions_Bay,_British_Columbia|Lions Bay]], and [[Belcarra|Belcarra]], with adjacent unincorporated areas (including the [[University_Endowment_Lands|University Endowment Lands]]) represented in the regional district as the [[List_of_regional_district_electoral_areas_in_British_Columbia|electoral area]] known as [[Greater_Vancouver_Electoral_Area_A,_British_Columbia|Greater Vancouver Electoral Area A]].
sentence_294: The metropolitan area has [[List_of_First_Nations_governments_in_British_Columbia|seventeen Indian reserves]], but they are outside of the regional district's jurisdiction and are not represented in its government.
sentence_295: The second largest concentration of British Columbia population is at the southern tip of Vancouver Island, which is made up of the 13 municipalities of Greater Victoria, [[Victoria,_British_Columbia|Victoria]], [[Saanich,_British_Columbia|Saanich]], Esquimalt, Oak Bay, View Royal, [[Highlands,_British_Columbia|Highlands]], [[Colwood,_British_Columbia|Colwood]], [[Langford,_British_Columbia|Langford]], [[Central_Saanich,_British_Columbia|Central Saanich]]/[[Saanichton,_British_Columbia|Saanichton]], [[North_Saanich,_British_Columbia|North Saanich]], [[Sidney,_British_Columbia|Sidney]], [[Metchosin,_British_Columbia|Metchosin]], Sooke, which are part of the [[Capital_Regional_District|Capital Regional District]].
sentence_296: The metropolitan area also includes several Indian reserves (the governments of which are not part of the regional district).
sentence_297: Almost half of the Vancouver Island population is in Greater Victoria.
sentence_298: British Columbia is the most diverse province in Canada; as of 2016, the province had the highest proportion of [[Visible_minority|visible minorities]] in the country.
sentence_299: The five largest pan-ethnic groups in the province are [[European_Canadians|Europeans]] (64%), [[East_Asian_Canadians|East Asians]] (15%), [[South_Asian_Canadians|South Asians]] (8%), [[Aboriginal_Canadian|Aboriginals]] (6%) and [[Southeast_Asia|Southeast Asians]] (4%).

table_2.caption: Top ethnic origins in BC (2016 Census)

sentence_300: Note: Statistics represent both single (for example, "German") and multiple (for example, "Chinese-English") responses to the 2016 Census, and thus do not add up to 100%.
sentence_301: All items are self-identified.
sentence_302: The largest denominations by number of adherents according to the [[Canada_2011_Census|2011 census]] were [[Christianity|Christianity]] with 1,930,415 (44.6%); [[Irreligion|irreligion]] (atheist, agnostic, and so on.)
sentence_303: with 1,908,285 (44.1%); [[Sikhism|Sikhism]] with 201,110 (4.7%); [[Buddhism|Buddhism]] with 90,620 (2.1%); [[Islam|Islam]] with 79,310 (1.8%); and [[Hinduism|Hinduism]] with 45,795 (1.1%).
sentence_304: Of the 4,648,055 population counted by the 2016 census, 4,598,415 people completed the section about language.
sentence_305: Of these, 4,494,995 gave singular responses to the question regarding their first language.
sentence_306: The languages most commonly reported were the following:
