sentence_307: BC's economy is diverse, with service-producing industries accounting for the largest portion of the province's GDP.
sentence_308: It is the terminus of two transcontinental railways, and the site of 27 major marine cargo and passenger terminals.
sentence_309: Though less than 5% of its vast 944,735 square kilometres (364,764 sq mi) land is [[Arable_land|arable]], the province is agriculturally rich (particularly in the [[Fraser_Valley|Fraser]] and Okanagan valleys), because of milder weather near the coast and in certain sheltered southern valleys.
sentence_310: Its climate encourages [[Outdoor_recreation|outdoor recreation]] and [[Tourism|tourism]], though its economic mainstay has long been [[Resource_extraction|resource extraction]], principally logging, farming, and mining.
sentence_311: Vancouver, the province's largest city, serves as the headquarters of many western-based natural resource companies.
sentence_312: It also benefits from a strong housing market and a per capita income well above the national average.
sentence_313: While the coast of British Columbia and some valleys in the south-central part of the province have mild weather, the majority of its land mass experiences a cold-winter-temperate climate similar to the rest of Canada.
sentence_314: The Northern Interior region has a [[Subarctic_climate|subarctic climate]] with very cold winters.
sentence_315: The climate of Vancouver is by far the mildest winter climate of the major Canadian cities, with nighttime January temperatures averaging above the freezing point.
sentence_316: British Columbia has a history of being a resource dominated economy, centred on the forestry industry but also with fluctuating importance in mining.
sentence_317: Employment in the resource sector has fallen steadily as a percentage of employment, and new jobs are mostly in the construction and retail/service sectors.
sentence_318: It now has the highest percentage of service industry jobs in the west, comprising 72% of industry (compared to 60% Western Canadian average).
sentence_319: The largest section of this employment is in finance, insurance, real estate and corporate management; however, many areas outside of metropolitan areas are still heavily reliant on resource extraction.
sentence_320: With its film industry known as [[Hollywood_North|Hollywood North]], the Vancouver region is the third-largest feature film production location in North America, after [[Los_Angeles|Los Angeles]] and [[New_York_City|New York City]].
sentence_321: The economic history of British Columbia is replete with tales of [[Business_cycle|dramatic upswings and downswings]], and this [[Boom_and_bust|boom and bust]] pattern has influenced the politics, culture and business climate of the province.
sentence_322: Economic activity related to mining in particular has widely fluctuated with changes in commodity prices over time, with documented costs to community health.
sentence_323: In 2017, British Columbia had the fourth-largest GDP in Canada, with a GDP of [[Canadian_dollar|CA$]]282 billion and a GDP per capita of $57,335.
sentence_324: British Columbia's [[Debt-to-GDP_ratio|debt-to-GDP ratio]] is edging up to 15.0% in [[Fiscal_year|fiscal year]] 2019–20, and it is expected to reach 16.1% by 2021–22.
sentence_325: British Columbia's economy experienced strong growth in 2017, with its annual performance outpacing the Canadian average for a fourth consecutive year.
sentence_326: In 2017, British Columbia's real GDP growth of 3.9% ranked second among Canadian provinces.
sentence_327: Main articles: Politics of British Columbia and [[Monarchy_in_British_Columbia|Monarchy in British Columbia]]
sentence_328: The Lieutenant-Governor, [[Janet_Austin|Janet Austin]], is the Queen of Canada's representative in the province.
sentence_329: During the absence of the [[Lieutenant_Governor|Lieutenant-Governor]], the [[Cabinet_of_Canada|Governor General in Council]] may appoint an administrator to execute the duties of the office.
sentence_330: In practice, this is usually the [[British_Columbia_Court_of_Appeal|Chief Justice of British Columbia]].
sentence_331: British Columbia has an 87-member elected Legislative Assembly, elected by the [[Plurality_voting_system|plurality voting system]], though from 2003 to 2009 there was significant debate about switching to a single transferable vote system called [[BC-STV|BC-STV]].
sentence_332: The government of the day appoints ministers for various portfolios, what are officially part of the Executive Council, of whom the premier is chair.
sentence_333: The province is governed by the British Columbia New Democratic Party (BC NDP) under Premier [[John_Horgan|John Horgan]].
sentence_334: The 2017 provincial election saw the Liberal Party take 43 seats, the NDP take 41, and the [[British_Columbia_Green_Party|British Columbia Green Party]] take 3.
sentence_335: No party met the minimum of 44 seats for a majority, therefore leading to the first minority government since 1953.
sentence_336: Following the election, the Greens entered into negotiations with both the Liberals and NDP, eventually announcing they would support the current NDP minority.
sentence_337: Previously, the right-of-centre British Columbia Liberal Party governed the province for 16 years between 2001 and 2017, and won the largest landslide election in British Columbia history in 2001, with 77 of 79 seats.
sentence_338: The legislature became more evenly divided between the Liberals and NDP following the 2005 (46 Liberal seats of 79) and 2009 (49 Liberal seats of 85) provincial elections.
sentence_339: The NDP and its predecessor the [[Co-operative_Commonwealth_Federation|Co-operative Commonwealth Federation]] (CCF) have been the main opposition force to right-wing parties since the 1930s and have ruled with majority governments in 1972–1975 and 1991–2001.
sentence_340: The Green Party plays a larger role in the politics of British Columbia than Green parties do in most other jurisdictions in Canada.
sentence_341: After a breakthrough election in 2001 (12.39%), the party's vote share declined (2005 – 9.17%, 2009 – 8.09%, 2013 – 8.13%) before increasing again to a record high of 16.84% at the 2017 election.
sentence_342: The British Columbia Liberal Party is not related to the federal Liberal Party and does not share the same ideology.
sentence_343: Instead, the BC Liberal party is a rather diverse coalition, made up of the remnants of the Social Credit Party, many [[Liberal_Party_of_Canada|federal Liberals]], federal Conservatives, and those who would otherwise support right-of-centre or free enterprise parties.
sentence_344: Historically, there have commonly been [[Third_party_(politics)|third parties]] present in the legislature (including the Liberals themselves from 1952 to 1975); the [[Green_Party_of_British_Columbia|BC Green Party]] are the current third party in British Columbia, with three seats in the legislature.
sentence_345: Prior to the rise of the Liberal Party, British Columbia's main political party was the British Columbia Social Credit Party which ruled British Columbia for 20 continuous years.
sentence_346: While sharing some ideology with the current Liberal government, they were more right-wing although undertook nationalization of various important monopolies, notably BC Hydro and BC Ferries.
sentence_347: British Columbia is known for having politically active labour [[Trade_union|unions]] who have traditionally supported the NDP or its predecessor, the CCF.
sentence_348: British Columbia's political history is typified by scandal and a cast of colourful characters, beginning with various colonial-era land scandals and abuses of power by early officials (such as those that led to [[McGowan's_War|McGowan's War]] in 1858–59).
sentence_349: Notable scandals in Social Credit years included the [[Robert_Bonner_(politician)|Robert Bonner]] Affair and the Fantasy Gardens scandal which forced Premier Bill Vander Zalm to resign and ended the Social Credit era.
sentence_350: NDP scandals included Bingogate, which brought down NDP Premier Mike Harcourt, and the alleged scandal named Casinogate which drove NDP Premier Glen Clark to resign.
sentence_351: A variety of scandals plagued the 2001–2017 Liberal government, including Premier Gordon Campbell's arrest for drunk driving in Maui and the resignation of various cabinet ministers because of conflict-of-interest allegations.
sentence_352: A Christmas Eve raid on the Parliament Buildings in Victoria, including the Premier's Office, resulted in charges only for ministerial aides, although key cabinet members from the time have since resigned.
sentence_353: The case, currently in preliminary hearings in the courts and relating to the sale of BC Rail to CN Rail, may not reach trial because of the mass of evidence and various procedural problems.
sentence_354: Campbell eventually resigned in late 2010 due to opposition to his government's plan to introduce a [[Harmonized_Sales_Tax|Harmonized Sales Tax]] (HST) and was replaced by [[Christy_Clark|Christy Clark]] as premier in a 2011 BC Liberal leadership election.
sentence_355: British Columbia is underrepresented in the [[Senate_of_Canada|Senate of Canada]], leading Premier Christy Clark to refuse to cooperate with the federal government's reforms for senate appointments to be made based on the recommendations of a new advisory board that would use non-partisan criteria.
sentence_356: Hours after that plan was unveiled in Ottawa on December 3, 2015, Clark issued a statement that it did "not address what's been wrong with the Senate since the beginning".
sentence_357: The imbalance in representation in that House is apparent when considering population size.
sentence_358: The six senators from BC constitute only one for every 775,000 people vs. one for every 75,000 in P.E.I. which has four senators.
sentence_359: Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have much smaller populations than BC, yet each has ten senators according to a Global News summary.
sentence_360: Correcting this imbalance would require a constitutional amendment, but that is unlikely to be supported by the Atlantic provinces.
sentence_361: The government of British Columbia has designated several [[Symbols_of_British_Columbia|official symbols]]:

list.value: Coat of arms: [[Coat_of_arms_of_British_Columbia|Coat of arms of British Columbia]]

sentence_362: The flag of British Columbia is not protected and is in the public domain, but the coat of arms is protected by law.
sentence_363: No one may "without the permission of the minister, assume, display or use the Coat of Arms of British Columbia or a design so closely resembling it as to be likely to deceive."
sentence_364: British Columbia was the second Canadian jurisdiction (after [[Ontario|Ontario]]) to legalize [[Same-sex_marriage_in_Canada|same-sex marriage]].
sentence_365: [[Affordable_housing_in_Canada|Housing affordability]] is of concern to British Columbians.
sentence_366: In April 2016 the government of British Columbia declared a public health emergency due to overdoses on the illicit opioid [[Fentanyl|Fentanyl]].
sentence_367: As of November 2016, there had been 755 cases of Fentanyl overdose.
sentence_368: June 2020 was the worst month for illicit drug overdose deaths in B.C. history, with 177 deaths.
sentence_369: There was a reported increase in the number of overdoses with extreme fentanyl concentration in April, May and June 2020 compared to previous months.
sentence_370: Transportation played a huge role in British Columbia's history.
sentence_371: The Rocky Mountains and the ranges west of them constituted a significant obstacle to overland travel until the completion of the transcontinental railway in 1885.
sentence_372: The Peace River Canyon through the Rocky Mountains was the route the earliest explorers and fur traders used.
sentence_373: Fur trade routes were only marginally used for access to British Columbia through the mountains.
sentence_374: Travel from the rest of Canada before 1885 meant the difficulty of overland travel via the United States, around [[Cape_Horn|Cape Horn]] or overseas from Asia.
sentence_375: Nearly all travel and freight to and from the region occurred via the Pacific Ocean, primarily through the ports of Victoria and New Westminster.
sentence_376: Until the 1930s, rail was the only means of overland travel to and from the rest of Canada; travellers using motor vehicles needed to journey through the United States.
sentence_377: With the construction of the Inter-Provincial Highway in 1932 (now known as the [[Crowsnest_Highway|Crowsnest Pass Highway]]), and later the [[Trans-Canada_Highway|Trans-Canada Highway]], road transportation evolved into the preferred mode of overland travel to and from the rest of the country.
sentence_378: Main article: [[List_of_British_Columbia_provincial_highways|List of British Columbia provincial highways]]
sentence_379: Because of its size and rugged, varying topography, British Columbia requires thousands of kilometres of provincial highways to connect its communities.
sentence_380: British Columbia's roads systems were notoriously poorly maintained and dangerous until a concentrated programme of improvement was initiated in the 1950s and 1960s.
sentence_381: There are now [[Controlled-access_highway|freeways]] in Greater Victoria, the Lower Mainland, and Central Interior of the province.
sentence_382: Much of the rest of the province, where traffic volumes are generally low, is accessible by well-maintained generally high-mobility two-lane [[Arterial_road|arterial highways]] with additional passing lanes in mountainous areas and usually only a few stop-controlled intersections outside the main urban areas.
sentence_383: A couple of busy intercity corridors outside Greater Vancouver feature more heavily signalized limited-mobility arterial highways that are mostly four-lane and often divided by portable median [[Traffic_barrier|traffic barriers]].
sentence_384: Highway 1 on [[Vancouver_Island|Vancouver Island]] and Highway 97 through the Okanagan Valley are medium- to high-volume roadways with variable posted speeds that range from 50 km/h (31 mph) to maximums just slightly lower than the principal grade-separated highways.
sentence_385: Numerous traffic lights operate in place of [[Interchange_(road)|interchanges]] on both arterials as long-term cost-cutting measures.
sentence_386: Signalization along both these highways is heaviest through urban areas and along inter-urban sections where traffic volumes are similar to and sometimes higher than the freeways, but where funding is not available for upgrades to interchanges or construction of high-mobility alternative routes or bypasses.
sentence_387: The building and maintenance of provincial highways is the responsibility of the [[British_Columbia_Ministry_of_Transportation|British Columbia Ministry of Transportation]] and Infrastructure.
sentence_388: There are only five major routes to the rest of Canada.
sentence_389: From south to north they are: [[British_Columbia_provincial_highway_3|BC Highway 3]] through the Crowsnest Pass, the [[Vermilion_Pass|Vermilion Pass]] (Highway 93 in both [[British_Columbia_Highway_93|British Columbia]] and [[Alberta_Highway_93|Alberta]]), the [[Kicking_Horse_Pass|Kicking Horse Pass]], the latter being used by the Trans-Canada Highway entering Alberta through [[Banff_National_Park|Banff National Park]], the [[Yellowhead_Highway|Yellowhead Highway]] (16) through [[Jasper_National_Park|Jasper National Park]], and Highway 2 through [[Dawson_Creek|Dawson Creek]].
sentence_390: There are also several highway crossings to the adjoining American states of Washington, Idaho, and Montana.
sentence_391: The longest highway is Highway 97, running 2,081 kilometres (1,293 mi) from the British Columbia-Washington border at [[Osoyoos,_British_Columbia|Osoyoos]] north to [[Watson_Lake,_Yukon|Watson Lake, Yukon]] and which includes the British Columbia portion of the [[Alaska_Highway|Alaska Highway]].
sentence_392: Prior to 1979, surface public transit was administered by BC Hydro, the provincially owned electricity utility.
sentence_393: Subsequently, the province established [[BC_Transit|BC Transit]] to oversee and operate all municipal transportation systems.
sentence_394: In 1998, the Greater Vancouver Transportation Authority, now [[TransLink_(British_Columbia)|TransLink]], a separate authority for routes within the Greater Vancouver Regional District, was established.
sentence_395: Some smaller island communities, such as [[Gabriola_Island|Gabriola Island]] and, formerly, [[Pender_Island|Pender Island]] operate routes independent of BC Transit or TransLink.
sentence_396: BC Transit has recently expanded to provide intercity routes, particularly in the Northern region of British Columbia.
sentence_397: Other intercity routes were introduced connecting southern communities in preparation of the cancellation of Greyhound Canada's pullout from Western Canada, though options for intercity bus travel are still extremely limited.
sentence_398: Public transit in British Columbia consists mainly of diesel buses, although Vancouver is also serviced by a fleet of [[Trolleybus|trolleybuses]].
sentence_399: Several experimental buses are being tested such as [[Hybrid_electric_vehicle|hybrid]] buses that have both gasoline and electric engines.
sentence_400: Additionally, there are CNG-fueled buses being tested and used in Nanaimo and Kamloops systems.
sentence_401: British Columbia also tested a fleet of Hydrogen-fueled buses for the Vancouver-Whistler Winter Olympics in 2010.
sentence_402: TransLink operates [[SkyTrain_(Vancouver)|SkyTrain]], an automated [[Rapid_transit|metro]] system serving the cities of Vancouver, Burnaby, New Westminster, Surrey, Richmond, Coquitlam, and Port Moody.
sentence_403: In 2009, the Canada Line SkyTrain was completed, linking Vancouver International Airport and the city of Richmond to downtown Vancouver bringing the total to three operating metro lines.
sentence_404: A new extension to Coquitlam and [[Port_Moody|Port Moody]] (the [[Evergreen_Extension|Evergreen Extension]] of the [[Millennium_Line|Millennium Line]]) was completed in December 2016.
sentence_405: There is planning for an extension of the Millennium Line through Vancouver City to the [[University_of_British_Columbia|University of British Columbia]].
sentence_406: Turnstiles have been added to all existing stations in the system.
sentence_407: In the past, SkyTrain used a proof of payment honour system.
sentence_408: In the capital city of Victoria BC Transit and the provincial government's infrastructure ministry are working together to create a bus rapid transit from the Westshore communities to downtown Victoria.
sentence_409: In [[Kamloops|Kamloops]], there is a bus rapid transit GPS trial underway to see how bus rapid transit affects smaller cities, rather than larger ones, like Victoria and Vancouver.
sentence_410: See also: Canadian Pacific Railway in British Columbia
sentence_411: Rail development expanded greatly in the decades after the [[Canadian_Pacific_Railway|Canadian Pacific Railway]] was completed, in 1885, and was the chief mode of long-distance surface transportation until the expansion and improvement of the provincial highways system began in the 1950s.
sentence_412: Two major routes through the Yellowhead Pass competed with the Canadian Pacific Railway – the [[Grand_Trunk_Pacific|Grand Trunk Pacific]], terminating at Prince Rupert, and the [[Canadian_Northern_Railway|Canadian Northern Railway]], terminating at Vancouver.
sentence_413: The British Columbia Electric Railway provided rail services in Victoria and Vancouver between the nineteenth century and mid twentieth century.
sentence_414: The Pacific Great Eastern line supplemented this service, providing a north–south route between interior resource communities and the coast.
sentence_415: The Pacific Great Eastern (later known as British Columbia Railway and now owned by Canadian National Railway) connects Fort St James, Fort Nelson, and [[Tumbler_Ridge,_British_Columbia|Tumbler Ridge]] with [[North_Vancouver_(city)|North Vancouver]].
sentence_416: The E&N Railway, rebranded as [[Southern_Railway_of_Vancouver_Island|Southern Railway of Vancouver Island]], formerly served the commercial and passenger train markets of Vancouver Island.
sentence_417: Service along the route is now minimal.
sentence_418: Vancouver Island was also host to the last logging railway in North America until its closure in 2017.
sentence_419: Current passenger services in British Columbia are limited.
sentence_420: [[Via_Rail_Canada|Via Rail Canada]] operates six long-distance trains on two lines.
sentence_421: Local services are limited to two regions, with [[TransLink_(British_Columbia)|TransLink]] providing rapid transit and commuter services in the [[Lower_Mainland|Lower Mainland]] and by the [[Seton_Lake_Indian_Band|Seton Lake Indian Band]] South of [[Lillooet|Lillooet]] with the [[Kaoham_Shuttle|Kaoham Shuttle]].
sentence_422: [[Amtrak|Amtrak]] runs international passenger service between Vancouver, [[Seattle|Seattle]], and intermediate points.
sentence_423: Several [[Heritage_railway|heritage railways]] operate within the province, including the White Pass & Yukon Route that runs between [[Alaska|Alaska]] and the [[Yukon|Yukon]] via British Columbia.
sentence_424: [[BC_Ferries|BC Ferries]] was established as a provincial crown corporation in 1960 to provide passenger and vehicle ferry service between Vancouver Island and the Lower Mainland as a cheaper and more reliable alternative to the service operated by the Canadian Pacific Railway and other private operators.
sentence_425: It now operates 25 routes among the [[List_of_islands_of_British_Columbia|islands of British Columbia]], as well as between the islands and the mainland.
sentence_426: Ferry service to Washington is offered by the [[Washington_State_Ferries|Washington State Ferries]] (between [[Sidney,_British_Columbia|Sidney]] and [[Anacortes,_Washington|Anacortes]]) and [[MV_Coho|Black Ball Transport]] (between Victoria and [[Port_Angeles,_Washington|Port Angeles, Washington]]).
sentence_427: Ferry service over inland lakes and rivers is provided by the [[British_Columbia_Ministry_of_Transportation_and_Infrastructure|Ministry of Transportation and Infrastructure]].
sentence_428: Various other coastal ferries are operated privately.
sentence_429: Commercial ocean transport is of vital importance.
sentence_430: Major ports are at Vancouver, [[Roberts_Bank|Roberts Bank]] (near [[Tsawwassen,_British_Columbia|Tsawwassen]]), Prince Rupert, and Victoria.
sentence_431: Of these, the [[Port_of_Vancouver|Port of Vancouver]] is the most important, being the largest in Canada and the most diversified in North America.
sentence_432: Vancouver, Victoria, and Prince Rupert are also major ports of call for [[Cruise_ship|cruise ships]].
sentence_433: In 2007, a large maritime [[Containerization|container port]] was opened in Prince Rupert with an inland sorting port in Prince George.
sentence_434: Main article: [[List_of_airports_in_British_Columbia|List of airports in British Columbia]]
sentence_435: There are over 200 airports throughout British Columbia, the major ones being the [[Vancouver_International_Airport|Vancouver International Airport]], the [[Victoria_International_Airport|Victoria International Airport]], the [[Kelowna_International_Airport|Kelowna International Airport]], and the [[Abbotsford_International_Airport|Abbotsford International Airport]], the first three of which each served over 1,000,000 passengers in 2005.
sentence_436: As of 2017, Vancouver International Airport is the [[List_of_the_busiest_airports_in_Canada|2nd busiest airport]] in the country and the second biggest International Gateway on the west coast (after Los Angeles) with an estimated 26.4 million travellers passing through in 2019.
sentence_437: Given its varied mountainous terrain and its coasts, lakes, rivers, and forests, British Columbia has long been enjoyed for pursuits like hiking and camping, rock climbing and mountaineering, [[Hunting|hunting]] and [[Fishing|fishing]].
sentence_438: Water sports, both motorized and non-motorized, are enjoyed in many places.
sentence_439: [[Sea_kayak|Sea kayaking]] opportunities abound on the British Columbia coast with its [[Fjord|fjords]].
sentence_440: [[Whitewater_rafting|Whitewater rafting]] and [[Kayak|kayaking]] are popular on many inland rivers.
sentence_441: [[Sailing|Sailing]] and sailboarding are widely enjoyed.
sentence_442: In winter, [[Cross-country_skiing|cross-country]] and telemark skiing are much enjoyed, and in recent decades high-quality [[Alpine_skiing|downhill]] [[Skiing|skiing]] has been developed in the Coast Mountain range and the Rockies, as well as in the southern areas of the Shuswap Highlands and the [[Columbia_Mountains|Columbia Mountains]].
sentence_443: [[Snowboarding|Snowboarding]] has mushroomed in popularity since the early 1990s.
sentence_444: The [[2010_Winter_Olympics|2010 Winter Olympics]] downhill events were held in [[Whistler_Blackcomb|Whistler Blackcomb]] area of the province, while the indoor events were conducted in the Vancouver area.
sentence_445: In Vancouver and Victoria (as well as some other cities), opportunities for [[Jogging|joggers]] and bicyclists have been developed.
sentence_446: Cross-country bike touring has been popular since the [[Bicycle_gearing|ten-speed]] bike became available many years ago.
sentence_447: Since the advent of the more robust mountain bike, trails in more rugged and wild places have been developed for them.
sentence_448: A 2016 poll on global biking website Pinkbike rated BC as the top destination mountain bikers would like to ride.
sentence_449: Some of the province's retired rail beds have been converted and maintained for hiking, biking, and cross-country skiing.
sentence_450: Longboarding is also a popular activity because of the hilly geography of the region.
sentence_451: [[Equestrianism|Horseback riding]] is enjoyed by many British Columbians.
sentence_452: Opportunities for [[Trail_riding|trail riding]], often into especially scenic areas, have been established for tourists in numerous areas of the province.
sentence_453: British Columbia also has strong participation levels in many other sports, including [[Golf|golf]], [[Tennis|tennis]], [[Association_football|soccer]], [[Ice_hockey|hockey]], [[Canadian_football|Canadian football]], [[Rugby_union|rugby union]], [[Lacrosse|lacrosse]], [[Baseball|baseball]], [[Softball|softball]], basketball, curling, [[Disc_golf|disc golf]], [[Ultimate_Canada|Ultimate]] and [[Figure_skating|figure skating]].
sentence_454: British Columbia has produced many outstanding athletes, especially in aquatic and [[Winter_sport|winter sports]].
sentence_455: Consistent with both increased tourism and increased participation in diverse recreations by British Columbians has been the proliferation of lodges, [[Chalet|chalets]], bed and breakfasts, motels, hotels, fishing camps, and park-camping facilities in recent decades.
sentence_456: In certain areas, there are businesses, non-profit societies, or municipal governments dedicated to promoting [[Ecotourism|ecotourism]] in their region.
sentence_457: A number of British Columbia farmers offer visitors to combine tourism with farm work, for example, through the WWOOF Canada program.
sentence_458: British Columbia is home to a comprehensive public education system.
sentence_459: Instruction is offered in both of Canada's official languages.
sentence_460: As of 2006 there were 59 anglophone school districts throughout the province.
sentence_461: As of the same year, 44 of them offered French immersion programs.
sentence_462: [[Conseil_scolaire_francophone_de_la_Colombie-Britannique|Conseil scolaire francophone de la Colombie-Britannique]], established in 1995, operates French-language public schools throughout the entire province.
sentence_463: In September 2014 there were 11,000 international students in BC public K-12 schools and about 3,000 international students in other BC K-12 schools.
sentence_464: See also: [[Higher_education_in_British_Columbia|Higher education in British Columbia]]
sentence_465: Public universities and colleges include:
sentence_466: British Columbia is also home to 11 [[List_of_private_universities_in_Canada|private colleges and universities]] located throughout the province, including:
sentence_467: Two [[United_States|American]] universities ([[Fairleigh_Dickinson_University|Fairleigh Dickinson University]] and [[Northeastern_University|Northeastern University]]) also have degree-granting campuses located in [[Vancouver|Vancouver]].

title: Adelaide
sentence_0: This article is about the Australian metropolis.
sentence_1: For the local government area, see [[City_of_Adelaide|City of Adelaide]].
sentence_2: For other uses, see [[Adelaide_(disambiguation)|Adelaide (disambiguation)]].
sentence_3: Adelaide [[English|/ˈædəleɪd/]] (listen) (AD-ə-layd) is the [[List_of_Australian_capital_cities|capital city]] of the state of [[South_Australia|South Australia]], and the [[List_of_cities_in_Australia_by_population|fifth-most populous city of Australia]].
sentence_4: The [[Demonym|demonym]] Adelaidean is used to denote the city and the residents of Adelaide.
sentence_5: Adelaide is situated on the Adelaide Plains north of the [[Fleurieu_Peninsula|Fleurieu Peninsula]], between the [[Gulf_St_Vincent|Gulf St Vincent]] in the west and the Mount Lofty Ranges in the east.
sentence_6: Its metropolitan area extends 20 km (12 mi) from the coast to the [[Adelaide_Hills|foothills]] of the Mount Lofty Ranges, and stretches 96 km (60 mi) from Gawler in the north to [[Sellicks_Beach|Sellicks Beach]] in the south.
sentence_7: Named in honour of [[Adelaide_of_Saxe-Meiningen|Queen Adelaide]], consort to [[William_IV_of_the_United_Kingdom|King William IV]], the city was founded in 1836 as the planned capital for the only freely-settled British province in Australia.
sentence_8: [[William_Light|Colonel William Light]], one of Adelaide's founding fathers, designed the city centre and chose its location close to the [[River_Torrens|River Torrens]], in the area originally inhabited by the [[Kaurna_people|Kaurna people]] and known as [[Tarndanyangga|Tarndanyangga]] ("place of the red kangaroo").
sentence_9: Light's design, now [[Australian_National_Heritage_List|listed as national heritage]], set out the city centre in a [[Grid_plan|grid layout]] known as "[[Light's_Vision|Light's Vision]]", interspaced by wide boulevards and large public squares, and entirely surrounded by [[Adelaide_Parklands|parklands]].
sentence_10: Early colonial Adelaide was shaped by the diversity and wealth of its free settlers, in contrast to the convict history of other Australian cities.
sentence_11: Until the [[Post-war|post-war]] era, it was Australia's third-largest city.
sentence_12: It has been noted for its leading examples of religious freedom and progressive political reforms, and became known as the "City of Churches" due to its diversity of faiths.
sentence_13: Today, Adelaide is noted for its many festivals and sporting events, its [[South_Australian_wine|food and wine]], its coastline and hills, and its large defence and manufacturing sectors.
sentence_14: Adelaide's [[Quality_of_life|quality of life]] has ranked consistently highly in various measures through the 21st century.
sentence_15: As South Australia's government and commercial centre, Adelaide is the site of many governmental and financial institutions.
sentence_16: Most of these are concentrated in the [[Adelaide_city_centre|city centre]] along the cultural boulevards of [[North_Terrace,_Adelaide|North Terrace]] and [[King_William_Street,_Adelaide|King William Street]].
sentence_17: Main article: [[History_of_Adelaide|History of Adelaide]]
sentence_18: Before its proclamation as a British settlement in 1836, the area around Adelaide was inhabited by the indigenous [[Kaurna|Kaurna]] people, one of many [[Australian_Aborigine|Aboriginal]] nations in South Australia.
sentence_19: The city and [[Adelaide_park_lands|parklands]] area was known as Tarntanya, or [[Tarndanyangga|Tarndanyangga]] in the [[Kaurna_language|Kaurna language]].
sentence_20: The surrounding area was an open grassy plain with patches of trees and shrub which had been managed by hundreds of generations.
sentence_21: Kaurna country encompassed the plains which stretched north and south of Tarntanya as well as the wooded foothills of the Mt Lofty Ranges.
sentence_22: The River Torrens was known as the Karrawirra Pari (red gum forest river).
sentence_23: About 300 Kaurna populated the Adelaide area, and were referred to by the settlers as the Cowandilla.
sentence_24: The Kaurna language was a complex one, reflecting their sophisticated culture and deep environmental knowledge.
sentence_25: Within a few decades of European settlement of South Australia, Kaurna culture and language were almost completely destroyed.
sentence_26: Extensive documentation by early missionaries and other researchers has enabled a modern revival of both, which has included a commitment by local and state governments to rename or include Kaurna names for many local places.
sentence_27: South Australia was officially established as a British Province in England in February 1836.
sentence_28: The first [[Governor_of_South_Australia|governor]] proclaimed the commencement of colonial government in South Australia on 28 December 1836, near [[The_Old_Gum_Tree|The Old Gum Tree]] in what is now the suburb of Glenelg North.
sentence_29: The event is commemorated in South Australia as [[Proclamation_Day_(South_Australia)|Proclamation Day]].
sentence_30: The site of the colony's capital was surveyed and laid out by Colonel [[William_Light|William Light]], the first Surveyor-General of South Australia, with his own original, unique, topographically sensitive design.
sentence_31: Claims of the design being by the architect George Strickland Kingston have been thoroughly debunked.
sentence_32: The city was named after [[Queen_Adelaide|Queen Adelaide]].
sentence_33: Adelaide was established as a planned colony of free immigrants, promising civil liberties and freedom from religious persecution, based upon the ideas of [[Edward_Gibbon_Wakefield|Edward Gibbon Wakefield]].
sentence_34: Wakefield had read accounts of Australian settlement while in prison in London for attempting to abduct an heiress, and realised that the eastern colonies suffered from a lack of available labour, due to the practice of giving land grants to all arrivals.
sentence_35: Wakefield's idea was for the Government to survey and sell the land at a rate that would maintain land values high enough to be unaffordable for labourers and journeymen.
sentence_36: Funds raised from the sale of land were to be used to bring out working-class emigrants, who would have to work hard for the monied settlers to ever afford their own land.
sentence_37: As a result of this policy, Adelaide does not share [[Convictism_in_Australia|the convict settlement history]] of other Australian cities like Sydney, [[Brisbane|Brisbane]] and [[Hobart|Hobart]].
sentence_38: As it was believed that in a colony of free settlers there would be little crime, no provision was made for a [[Prison|gaol]] in Colonel Light's 1837 plan.
sentence_39: But by mid-1837 the [[South_Australian_Register|South Australian Register]] was warning of escaped convicts from New South Wales and tenders for a temporary gaol were sought.
sentence_40: Following a burglary, a murder, and two attempted murders in Adelaide during March 1838, Governor Hindmarsh created the South Australian Police Force (now the South Australia Police) in April 1838 under 21-year-old [[Henry_Inman_(police_commander)|Henry Inman]].
sentence_41: The first sheriff, Samuel Smart, was wounded during a robbery, and on 2 May 1838 one of the offenders, Michael Magee, became the first person to be hanged in South Australia.
sentence_42: William Baker Ashton was appointed governor of the temporary gaol in 1839, and in 1840 George Strickland Kingston was commissioned to design Adelaide's new gaol.
sentence_43: Construction of [[Adelaide_Gaol|Adelaide Gaol]] commenced in 1841.
sentence_44: Adelaide's early history was marked by economic uncertainty and questionable leadership.
sentence_45: The first governor of South Australia, [[John_Hindmarsh|John Hindmarsh]], clashed frequently with others, in particular the Resident Commissioner, [[James_Hurtle_Fisher|James Hurtle Fisher]].
sentence_46: The rural area surrounding Adelaide was surveyed by Light in preparation to sell a total of over 405 km (156 sq mi) of land.
sentence_47: Adelaide's early economy started to get on its feet in 1838 with the arrival of livestock from [[Victoria_(Australia)|Victoria]], [[New_South_Wales|New South Wales]] and Tasmania.
sentence_48: Wool production provided an early basis for the South Australian economy.
sentence_49: By 1860, wheat farms had been established from [[Encounter_Bay|Encounter Bay]] in the south to [[Clare,_South_Australia|Clare]] in the north.
sentence_50: [[George_Gawler|George Gawler]] took over from Hindmarsh in late 1838 and, despite being under orders from the Select Committee on South Australia in Britain not to undertake any public works, promptly oversaw construction of a governor's house, the [[Adelaide_Gaol|Adelaide Gaol]], police barracks, a hospital, a customs house and a wharf at [[Port_Adelaide|Port Adelaide]].
sentence_51: Gawler was recalled and replaced by [[George_Edward_Grey|George Edward Grey]] in 1841.
sentence_52: Grey slashed public expenditure against heavy opposition, although its impact was negligible at this point: silver was discovered in [[Glen_Osmond,_South_Australia|Glen Osmond]] that year, agriculture was well underway, and other mines sprung up all over the state, aiding Adelaide's commercial development.
sentence_53: The city exported meat, wool, wine, fruit and wheat by the time Grey left in 1845, contrasting with a low point in 1842 when one-third of Adelaide houses were abandoned.
sentence_54: Trade links with the rest of the Australian states were established after the [[Murray_River|Murray River]] was successfully navigated in 1853 by [[Francis_Cadell_(explorer)|Francis Cadell]], an Adelaide resident.
sentence_55: South Australia became a self-governing colony in 1856 with the ratification of a new constitution by the British parliament.
sentence_56: Secret ballots were introduced, and a bicameral parliament was elected on 9 March 1857, by which time 109,917 people lived in the province.
sentence_57: In 1860 the [[Thorndon_Park|Thorndon Park]] reservoir was opened, finally providing an alternative water source to the now turbid River Torrens.
sentence_58: Gas street lighting was implemented in 1867, the [[University_of_Adelaide|University of Adelaide]] was founded in 1874, the [[South_Australian_Art_Gallery|South Australian Art Gallery]] opened in 1881 and the [[Happy_Valley_Reservoir|Happy Valley Reservoir]] opened in 1896.
sentence_59: In the 1890s Australia was affected by a severe economic depression, ending a hectic era of land booms and tumultuous expansionism.
sentence_60: Financial institutions in Melbourne and banks in Sydney closed.
sentence_61: The national fertility rate fell and immigration was reduced to a trickle.
sentence_62: The value of South Australia's exports nearly halved.
sentence_63: Drought and poor harvests from 1884 compounded the problems, with some families leaving for Western Australia.
sentence_64: Adelaide was not as badly hit as the larger gold-rush cities of Sydney and Melbourne, and silver and lead discoveries at Broken Hill provided some relief.
sentence_65: Only one year of deficit was recorded, but the price paid was retrenchments and lean public spending.
sentence_66: Wine and copper were the only industries not to suffer a downturn.
sentence_67: Adelaide was Australia's third largest city for most of the 20th century.
sentence_68: Electric street lighting was introduced in 1900 and electric trams were transporting passengers in 1909.
sentence_69: 28,000 men were sent to fight in World War I.
sentence_70: Historian F. W. Crowley examined the reports of visitors in the early 20th century, noting that "many visitors to Adelaide admired the [[Light's_Vision|foresighted planning]] of its founders", as well as pondering the riches of the young city.
sentence_71: Adelaide enjoyed a postwar boom, entering a time of relative prosperity.
sentence_72: Its population grew, and it became the third most populous metropolitan area in the country, after Sydney and Melbourne.
sentence_73: Its prosperity was short-lived, with the return of droughts and the [[Great_Depression|Great Depression]] of the 1930s.
sentence_74: It later returned to fortune under strong government leadership.
sentence_75: Secondary industries helped reduce the state's dependence on [[Primary_sector_of_industry|primary industries]].
sentence_76: World War II brought industrial stimulus and diversification to Adelaide under the [[Thomas_Playford_IV|Playford]] Government, which advocated Adelaide as a safe place for manufacturing due to its less vulnerable location.
sentence_77: Shipbuilding was expanded at the nearby port of [[Whyalla,_South_Australia|Whyalla]].
sentence_78: The South Australian Government in this period built on former wartime manufacturing industries but neglected cultural facilities which meant South Australia's economy lagged behind.
sentence_79: International manufacturers like General Motors [[Holden|Holden]] and Chrysler made use of these factories around the Adelaide area in suburbs like [[Elizabeth,_South_Australia|Elizabeth]], completing its transformation from an agricultural service centre to a 20th-century city.
sentence_80: The [[Mannum–Adelaide_pipeline|Mannum–Adelaide pipeline]] brought [[River_Murray|River Murray]] water to Adelaide in 1955 and [[Adelaide_International_Airport|an airport]] opened at [[West_Beach,_South_Australia|West Beach]] in 1955.
sentence_81: [[Flinders_University|Flinders University]] and the Flinders Medical Centre were established in the 1960s at Bedford Park, south of the city.
sentence_82: Today, Flinders Medical Centre is one of the largest teaching hospitals in South Australia.
sentence_83: In the post-war years around the early 1960s Adelaide was surpassed by Brisbane as Australia's third largest city.
sentence_84: The [[Don_Dunstan|Dunstan Governments]] of the 1970s saw something of an Adelaide 'cultural revival', establishing a wide array of social reforms.
sentence_85: The city became noted for its progressivism as South Australia became the first Australian state or territory to [[LGBT_rights_in_South_Australia|decriminalise homosexuality]] between consenting adults in 1975.
sentence_86: It also became a centre for the arts, building upon the biennial "[[Adelaide_Festival_of_Arts|Adelaide Festival of Arts]]" that commenced in 1960.
sentence_87: Adelaide hosted the [[Formula_One|Formula One]] Australian Grand Prix between 1985 and 1996 on a street circuit in the city's east parklands; it moved to Melbourne in 1996.
sentence_88: The [[State_Bank_of_South_Australia|State Bank]] collapsed in 1991 during an economic recession; the effects lasted until 2004, when Standard & Poor's reinstated South Australia's AAA credit rating.
sentence_89: From [[1999_Adelaide_500|1999]] until [[2020_Adelaide_500|2020]], the [[Adelaide_500|Adelaide 500]] [[Supercars_Championship|Supercars]] race has made use of sections of the former Formula One circuit.
sentence_90: Adelaide's tallest building, built in 1988, was originally known as the State Bank Building.
sentence_91: In 1991 it was renamed the Santos Building and in 2006 it was renamed [[Westpac_House|Westpac House]], and it is currently the 160th tallest building in Australia.
sentence_92: In the early years of the 21st century, a significant increase in the state government's spending on Adelaide's infrastructure occurred.
sentence_93: The [[Mike_Rann|Rann government]] invested A$535 million in a major upgrade of the Adelaide Oval to enable [[Australian_Football_League|Australian Football League]] to be played in the city centre and more than A$2 [[Billion|billion]] to build a new [[Royal_Adelaide_Hospital|Royal Adelaide Hospital]] on land adjacent to the Adelaide Railway Station.
sentence_94: The Glenelg tramline was extended through the city to Hindmarsh down to East Terrace and the suburban railway line extended south to Seaford.
sentence_95: Following a period of stagnation in the 1990s and 2000s, Adelaide began several major developments and redevelopments.
sentence_96: The Adelaide Convention Centre was redeveloped and expanded at a cost of A$350 million beginning in 2012.
sentence_97: Three historic buildings were adapted for modern use: the [[Torrens_Building|Torrens Building]] in Victoria Square as the Adelaide campus for Carnegie Mellon University, University College London, and Torrens University; the Stock Exchange building as the Science Exchange of the Royal Institution Australia; and the Glenside Psychiatric Hospital as the Adelaide Studios of the [[South_Australian_Film_Corporation|SA Film Corporation]].
sentence_98: The government also invested more than A$2 billion to build a [[Desalination|desalination]] plant, powered by renewable energy, as an 'insurance policy' against droughts affecting Adelaide's [[Water_supply|water supply]].
sentence_99: The [[Adelaide_Festival|Adelaide Festival]], [[Adelaide_Fringe_Festival|Fringe]], and [[Womadelaide|Womadelaide]] became annual events.
sentence_100: Adelaide is north of the Fleurieu Peninsula, on the Adelaide Plains between the Gulf St Vincent and the low-lying Mount Lofty Ranges.
sentence_101: The city stretches 20 km (12 mi) from the coast to the foothills, and 90 km (56 mi) from Gawler at its northern extent to [[Sellicks_Beach,_South_Australia|Sellicks Beach]] in the south.
sentence_102: According to the Regional Development Australia, an Australian government planning initiative, the "Adelaide Metropolitan Region" has a total land area of 870 km (340 sq mi), while a more expansive definition by the Australian Bureau of Statistics defines a "Greater Adelaide" statistical area totalling 3,259.8 km (1,258.6 sq mi).
sentence_103: The city sits at an average elevation of 50 metres (160 ft) above sea level.
sentence_104: Mount Lofty, east of the Adelaide metropolitan region in the Adelaide Hills at an elevation of 727 metres (2,385 ft), is the tallest point of the city and in the state south of [[Burra,_South_Australia|Burra]].
sentence_105: Much of Adelaide was bushland before British settlement, with some variation – sandhills, swamps and marshlands were prevalent around the coast.
sentence_106: The loss of the sandhills to urban development had a particularly destructive effect on the coastline due to erosion.
sentence_107: Where practical, the government has implemented programs to rebuild and vegetate sandhills at several of Adelaide's beachside suburbs.
sentence_108: Much of the original vegetation has been cleared with what is left to be found in reserves such as the [[Cleland_Conservation_Park|Cleland Conservation Park]] and Belair National Park.
sentence_109: A number of creeks and rivers flow through the Adelaide region.
sentence_110: The largest are the Torrens and Onkaparinga catchments.
sentence_111: Adelaide relies on its many reservoirs for water supply with the [[Happy_Valley_Reservoir|Happy Valley Reservoir]] supplying around 40% and the much larger [[Mount_Bold_Reservoir|Mount Bold Reservoir]] 10% of Adelaide's domestic requirements respectively.
sentence_112: Adelaide and its surrounding area is one of the most seismically active regions in Australia.
sentence_113: On 1 March 1954 at 3:40 am Adelaide experienced its largest recorded earthquake to date, with the epicentre 12 km from the city centre at [[Darlington,_South_Australia|Darlington]], and a reported magnitude of 5.6.
sentence_114: There have been smaller earthquakes in 2010, 2011, 2014, 2017, and 2018.
sentence_115: The uplands of the [[Adelaide_Hills|Adelaide Hills]], part of the southern Mount Lofty Ranges to the east of Adelaide, are defined on their western side by a number of arcuate faults (the Para, Eden, Clarendon and Willunga Faults), and consist of rocks such as [[Siltstone|siltstone]], [[Dolomite_(rock)|dolomite]] and [[Quartzite|quartzite]], dating from the [[Neoproterozoic|Neoproterozoic]] to the middle [[Cambrian|Cambrian]], laid down in the Adelaide Rift Complex, the oldest part of the [[Adelaide_Superbasin|Adelaide Superbasin]].
sentence_116: Most of the Adelaide metropolitan area lies in the downthrown St Vincent Basin and its embayments, including the Adelaide Plains Sub-basin, and the Golden Grove, Noarlunga and Willunga Embayments.
sentence_117: These basins contain deposits of [[Tertiary|Tertiary]] marine and non-marine sands and limestones, which form important aquifers.
sentence_118: These deposits are overlain by [[Quaternary|Quaternary]] [[Alluvial_fan|alluvial fans]] and piedmont slope deposits, derived from erosion of the uplands, consisting of sands, clays and gravels, interfingering to the west with [[Marine_transgression|transgressive]] [[Pleistocene|Pleistocene]] to [[Holocene|Holocene]] marine sands and coastal sediments of the shoreline of Gulf St Vincent.
sentence_119: Further information: [[William_Light|William Light]]
sentence_120: Adelaide is a planned city, designed by the first Surveyor-General of South Australia, Colonel [[William_Light|William Light]].
sentence_121: His plan, sometimes referred to as "Light's Vision" (also the name of a statue of him on [[Montefiore_Hill|Montefiore Hill]]), arranged Adelaide in a [[Grid_plan|grid]], with five squares in the [[Adelaide_city_centre|Adelaide city centre]] and a ring of parks, known as the [[Adelaide_Parklands|Adelaide Parklands]], surrounding it.
sentence_122: Light's selection of the location for the city was initially unpopular with the early settlers, as well as South Australia's first governor, John Hindmarsh, due to its distance from the harbour at Port Adelaide, and the lack of fresh water there.
sentence_123: Light successfully persisted with his choice of location against this initial opposition.
sentence_124: Recent evidence suggests that Light worked closely with George Kingston as well as a team of men to set out Adelaide, using various templates for city plans going back to [[Ancient_Greece|Ancient Greece]], including [[Italian_Renaissance|Italian Renaissance]] designs and the similar layouts of the American cities [[Philadelphia|Philadelphia]] and [[Savannah,_Georgia|Savannah]]–which, like Adelaide, follow the same layout of a central city square, four complementing city squares surrounding it and a parklands area that surround the city centre.
sentence_125: The benefits of Light's design are numerous: Adelaide has had wide multi-lane roads from its beginning, an easily navigable cardinal direction grid layout and an expansive green ring around the city centre.
sentence_126: There are two sets of [[Ring_road|ring roads]] in Adelaide that have resulted from the original design.
sentence_127: The [[City_Ring_Route,_Adelaide|inner ring route]] ([[A21_road_(Australia)|A21]]) borders the parklands, and the outer route ([[A3_road_(South_Australia)|A3]]/[[South_Road,_Adelaide|A13]]/[[A16_highway_(Australia)|A16]]/[[A17_highway_(Australia)|A17]]) completely bypasses the inner city via (in clockwise order) [[Grand_Junction_Road|Grand Junction Road]], Hampstead Road, Ascot Avenue, [[Portrush_Road|Portrush Road]], [[Cross_Road,_Adelaide|Cross Road]] and [[South_Road,_Adelaide|South Road]].
sentence_128: Suburban expansion has to some extent outgrown Light's original plan.
sentence_129: Numerous former outlying villages and "country towns", as well as the satellite city of [[Elizabeth,_South_Australia|Elizabeth]], have been enveloped by its [[Urban_sprawl|suburban sprawl]].
sentence_130: Expanding developments in the Adelaide Hills region led to the construction of the [[South_Eastern_Freeway|South Eastern Freeway]] to cope with growth, which has subsequently led to new developments and further improvements to that transport corridor.
sentence_131: Similarly, the booming development in Adelaide's [[City_of_Onkaparinga|South]] led to the construction of the [[Southern_Expressway_(Australia)|Southern Expressway]].
sentence_132: New roads are not the only transport infrastructure developed to cope with the urban growth.
sentence_133: The [[O-Bahn_Busway|O-Bahn Busway]] is an example of a unique solution to [[Tea_Tree_Gully,_South_Australia|Tea Tree Gully's]] transport woes in the 1980s.
sentence_134: The development of the nearby suburb of [[Golden_Grove,_South_Australia|Golden Grove]] in the late 1980s is an example of well-thought-out urban planning.
sentence_135: In the 1960s, a [[Metropolitan_Adelaide_Transport_Study|Metropolitan Adelaide Transport Study]] Plan was proposed to cater for the future growth of the city.
sentence_136: The plan involved the construction of freeways, [[Controlled-access_highway|expressways]] and the upgrade of certain aspects of the public transport system.
sentence_137: The then premier [[Steele_Hall|Steele Hall]] approved many parts of the plan and the government went as far as purchasing land for the project.
sentence_138: The later [[Australian_Labor_Party|Labor]] government elected under [[Don_Dunstan|Don Dunstan]] shelved the plan, but allowed the purchased land to remain vacant, should the future need for freeways arise.
sentence_139: In 1980, the [[Liberal_party_of_Australia|Liberal party]] won government and premier David Tonkin committed his government to selling off the land acquired for the MATS plan, ensuring that even when needs changed, the construction of most MATS-proposed freeways would be impractical.
sentence_140: Some parts of this land have been used for transport, (e.g. the O-Bahn Busway and Southern Expressway), while most has been progressively subdivided for residential use.
sentence_141: In 2008, the [[Government_of_South_Australia|SA Government]] announced plans for a network of [[Transport-oriented_development|transport-oriented developments]] across the Adelaide metropolitan area and purchased a [[Clipsal_site_development|10 hectare industrial site]] at [[Bowden,_South_Australia|Bowden]] for $52.5 million as the first of these developments.
sentence_142: The site covers 102,478 square metres, or about 10 hectares, and is bounded by Park Terrace to the south, the Adelaide to Outer Harbour railway line to the west, Drayton Street to the north and Sixth and Seventh Streets to the east.
sentence_143: Main article: Australian residential architectural styles
sentence_144: Historically, Adelaide's suburban residential areas have been characterised by single-storey detached houses built on 1,000-square-metre (⁄4-acre) blocks.
sentence_145: A relative lack of suitable, locally-available timber for construction purposes led to the early development of a brick-making industry, as well as the use of stone, for houses and other buildings.
sentence_146: By 1891 68% of houses were built of stone, 15% of timber, and 10% of brick, with brick also being widely used in stone houses for quoins, door and window surrounds, and chimneys and fireplaces.
sentence_147: There is a wide variety in the styles of these houses.
sentence_148: Until the 1960s most of the more substantial houses were built of red brick, though many front walls were of ornamental stone.
sentence_149: Then cream bricks became fashionable, and in the 1970s, deep red and brown bricks became popular.
sentence_150: Until the 1970s, roofs tended to be clad with (painted) [[Corrugated_iron|corrugated iron]] or tiles (cement or clay, usually red "terracotta").
sentence_151: Since then, Colorbond corrugated steel has dominated.
sentence_152: Most roofs are pitched; flat roofs are not common.
sentence_153: Up to the 1970s, most houses were of "double brick" construction on concrete footings, with timber floors laid on joists supported by "dwarf walls".
sentence_154: Later houses have mainly been of "[[Brick_veneer|brick veneer]]" construction – structural [[Framing_(construction)|timber]] or, more recently, [[Steel_frame#Cold-formed_steel_frames|lightweight steel]] frame on a [[Concrete_slab|concrete slab]] [[Foundation_(engineering)|foundation]], lined with [[Gyprock|Gyprock]], and with an outer skin of brickwork, to cope with Adelaide's [[Shrink–swell_capacity|reactive soils]], particularly Keswick Clay, black earth and some red-brown earth soils.
sentence_155: The use of precast concrete panels for floor and wall construction has also increased.
sentence_156: In addition to this, a significant factor in Adelaide's suburban history is the role of the South Australian Housing Trust.
sentence_157: Main article: [[Climate_of_Adelaide|Climate of Adelaide]]
sentence_158: Adelaide has a [[Mediterranean_climate|mediterranean climate]] ([[Köppen_climate_classification|Köppen climate classification]]: Csa).
sentence_159: The city has hot, dry summers and cool winters with moderate rainfall.
sentence_160: Most [[Precipitation|precipitation]] falls in the winter months, leading to the suggestion that the climate be classified as a "cold monsoon".
sentence_161: Rainfall is unreliable, light and infrequent throughout summer, although heavy falls can occur.
sentence_162: In contrast, the winter has fairly reliable rainfall with June being the wettest month of the year, averaging around 80 mm.
sentence_163: [[Frost|Frosts]] are occasional, with the most notable occurrences in July 1908 and July 1982.
sentence_164: Hail is also common in winter.
sentence_165: Adelaide is a windy city with significant [[Wind_chill|wind chill]] in winter, which makes the temperature seem colder than it actually is.
sentence_166: Snowfall in the metropolitan area is extremely uncommon, although light and sporadic falls in the nearby hills and at Mount Lofty occur during winter.
sentence_167: Dewpoints in the summer typically range from 8 to 10 °C (46 to 50 °F).
sentence_168: There are usually several days in summer where the temperature reaches 40.0 °C (104.0 °F) or above; the frequency of these temperatures has been [[Climate_of_Adelaide#Climate_data_and_extremes|increasing in recent years]].
sentence_169: The average sea temperature ranges from 13.7 °C (56.7 °F) in August to 21.2 °C (70.2 °F) in February.
sentence_170: Adelaide has been consistently listed in the world's top 10 [[Global_Liveability_Ranking|most liveable cities]] through the 2010s by The Economist Intelligence Unit, although it dropped to tenth place in 2018 after holding fifth position in the previous three years.
sentence_171: It was ranked the [[Most_liveable_city|most liveable city]] in Australia by the [[Property_Council_of_Australia|Property Council of Australia]], based on surveys of residents' views of their own city, between 2010 and 2013, dropping to second place in 2014.
sentence_172: Greener spaces for sustainable living is an initiative that has proven to create happier residents and is one of the factors that contributes to Adelaide making the top 10 of the world's most liveable cities.
sentence_173: For a relatively small city it boasts [[Adelaide_Park_Lands|29 large public parks]] as well as a [[Adelaide_Botanic_Garden|botanical garden]] in the heart of the city.
sentence_174: The reduction of Adelaide's tree canopy cover over recent years due to excessive tree removal for new construction has led to the creation of an [[Urban_heat_island|urban heat island]], an increase in the cost of housing and a decrease of overall state of well-being.
sentence_175: Main article: [[Government_of_South_Australia|Government of South Australia]]
sentence_176: Adelaide, as the capital of South Australia, is the seat of the [[Government_of_South_Australia|Government of South Australia]] as well as the bicameral [[Parliament_of_South_Australia|Parliament of South Australia]], which consists of the [[Lower_house|lower house]] known as the [[South_Australian_House_of_Assembly|House of Assembly]] and the upper house known as the [[South_Australian_Legislative_Council|Legislative Council]].
sentence_177: [[South_Australian_state_elections|General elections]] are held every four years, the last being the [[2018_South_Australian_state_election|2018 election]].
sentence_178: As Adelaide is South Australia's capital and most populous city, the [[Government_of_South_Australia|State Government]] co-operates extensively with the [[City_of_Adelaide|City of Adelaide]].
sentence_179: In 2006, the Ministry for the City of Adelaide was created to facilitate the State Government's collaboration with the [[Adelaide_City_Council|Adelaide City Council]] and the Lord Mayor to improve Adelaide's image.
sentence_180: The State Parliament's Capital City Committee is also involved in the governance of the City of Adelaide, being primarily concerned with the planning of Adelaide's urban development and growth.
sentence_181: Reflecting South Australia's status as Australia's most centralised state, Adelaide elects a substantial majority of the South Australian House of Assembly.
sentence_182: Of the 47 seats in the chamber, 34 seats (three-quarters of the legislature) are based in Adelaide, and two rural seats include Adelaide suburbs.
sentence_183: Further information: [[Local_government_areas_of_South_Australia|Local government areas of South Australia]]
sentence_184: The Adelaide metropolitan area is divided between nineteen [[Local_Government_Areas_of_South_Australia|local government areas]].
sentence_185: At its centre, the [[City_of_Adelaide|City of Adelaide]] administers the [[Adelaide_city_centre|Adelaide city centre]], North Adelaide, and the surrounding [[Adelaide_Parklands|Adelaide Parklands]].
sentence_186: It is the oldest municipal authority in Australia and was established in 1840, when Adelaide and Australia's first mayor, [[James_Hurtle_Fisher|James Hurtle Fisher]], was elected.
sentence_187: From 1919 onwards, the City has had a [[List_of_Mayors_and_Lord_Mayors_of_Adelaide|Lord Mayor]], the current being Lord Mayor The Right Honourable [[Sandy_Verschoor|Sandy Verschoor]].
sentence_188: Adelaide's inhabitants are known as Adelaideans.
sentence_189: Compared with Australia's four other major state capitals, Adelaide is growing at a much slower rate.
sentence_190: In 2017, it had a metropolitan population (including suburbs) of more than 1,345,777, making it Australia's fifth-largest city.
sentence_191: Some 77% of the population of South Australia are residents of the Adelaide metropolitan area, making South Australia one of the most centralised states.
sentence_192: Major areas of population growth in recent years have been in outer suburbs such as [[Mawson_Lakes,_South_Australia|Mawson Lakes]] and Golden Grove.
sentence_193: Adelaide's inhabitants occupy 366,912 houses, 57,695 semi-detached, row terrace or town houses and 49,413 flats, units or apartments.
sentence_194: About one sixth (17.1%) of the population had university qualifications.
sentence_195: The number of Adelaideans with vocational qualifications (such as tradespersons) fell from 62.1% of the labour force in the 1991 census to 52.4% in the 2001 census.
sentence_196: Adelaide is ageing more rapidly than other Australian capital cities.
sentence_197: More than a quarter (27.5%) of Adelaide's population is aged 55 years or older, in comparison to the national average of 25.6%.
sentence_198: Adelaide has the lowest number of children (under-15-year-olds), who comprised 17.7% of the population, compared to the national average of 19.3%.
sentence_199: At the 2016 census, the most commonly nominated ancestries were:
sentence_200: Overseas-born Adelaideans composed 31.8% of the total population at the 2016 census.
sentence_201: The five largest groups of overseas-born were from England (6.2%), India (2%), China (1.8%), Italy (1.3%) and Vietnam (1.1%).
sentence_202: Suburbs including Newton, [[Payneham,_South_Australia|Payneham]] and [[Campbelltown,_South_Australia|Campbelltown]] in the east and [[Torrensville,_South_Australia|Torrensville]], [[West_Lakes,_South_Australia|West Lakes]] and [[Fulham,_South_Australia|Fulham]] to the west, have large [[Greek_Australian|Greek]] and Italian communities.
sentence_203: The Italian consulate is located in the eastern suburb of [[Payneham,_South_Australia|Payneham]].
sentence_204: Large [[Vietnamese_Australian|Vietnamese]] populations are settled in the north-western suburbs of [[Woodville,_South_Australia|Woodville]], [[Kilkenny,_South_Australia|Kilkenny]], [[Pennington,_South_Australia|Pennington]], [[Mansfield_Park,_South_Australia|Mansfield Park]] and [[Athol_Park,_South_Australia|Athol Park]] and also [[Parafield_Gardens,_South_Australia|Parafield Gardens]] and [[Pooraka,_South_Australia|Pooraka]] in Adelaide's north.
sentence_205: Migrants from [[Indian_Australian|India]] and [[Sri_Lankan_Australian|Sri Lanka]] have settled into inner suburban areas of Adelaide including the inner northern suburbs of [[Blair_Athol,_South_Australia|Blair Athol]], Kilburn and Enfield and the inner southern suburbs of [[Plympton,_South_Australia|Plympton]], [[Park_Holme,_South_Australia|Park Holme]] and Kurralta Park.
sentence_206: Suburbs such as [[Para_Hills,_South_Australia|Para Hills]], [[Salisbury,_South_Australia|Salisbury]], [[Ingle_Farm,_South_Australia|Ingle Farm]] and [[Blair_Athol,_South_Australia|Blair Athol]] in the north and [[Findon,_South_Australia|Findon]], [[West_Croydon,_South_Australia|West Croydon]] and [[Seaton,_South_Australia|Seaton]] and other Western suburbs have sizeable [[Afghan_Australian|Afghan]] communities.
sentence_207: [[Chinese_Australian|Chinese migrants]] favour settling in the eastern and north eastern suburbs including [[Kensington_Gardens,_South_Australia|Kensington Gardens]], [[Greenacres,_South_Australia|Greenacres]], Modbury and [[Golden_Grove,_South_Australia|Golden Grove]].
sentence_208: [[Mawson_Lakes,_South_Australia|Mawson Lakes]] has a large international student population, due to its proximity to the University of South Australia campus.
sentence_209: 1.4% of the population, or 18,403 people, identified as [[Indigenous_Australians|Indigenous Australians]] ([[Aboriginal_Australians|Aboriginal Australians]] and [[Torres_Strait_Islanders|Torres Strait Islanders]]) in 2016.
sentence_210: At the 2016 census, 75.4% of the population spoke [[Australian_English|English]] at home.
sentence_211: The other languages most commonly spoken at home were Italian (2.1%), [[Standard_Mandarin|Standard Mandarin]] (2.1%), Greek (1.7%) Vietnamese (1.4%), and [[Cantonese|Cantonese]] (0.7%).
sentence_212: Adelaide was founded on a vision of religious tolerance that attracted a wide variety of religious practitioners.
sentence_213: This led to it being known as The City of Churches.
sentence_214: But approximately 28% of the population expressed no religious affiliation in the 2011 Census, compared with the national average of 22.3%, making Adelaide one of Australia's least religious cities.
sentence_215: Over half of the population of Adelaide identifies as Christian, with the largest denominations being [[Roman_Catholic_Church_in_Australia|Catholic]] (21.3%), [[Anglican_Church_of_Australia|Anglican]] (12.6%), [[Uniting_Church_in_Australia|Uniting Church]] (7.6%) and [[Eastern_Orthodox_Church|Eastern Orthodox]] (3.5%).
sentence_216: The Jewish community of the city dates back to 1840.
sentence_217: Eight years later, 58 Jews lived in the city.
sentence_218: A synagogue was built in 1871, when 435 Jews lived in the city.
sentence_219: Many took part in the city councils, such as Judah Moss Solomon (1852–66) and others after him.
sentence_220: Three Jews have been elected to the position of city mayor.
sentence_221: In 1968, the Jewish population of Adelaide numbered about 1,200; in 2001, according to the Australian census, 979 persons declared themselves to be Jewish by religion.
sentence_222: In 2011, over 1,000 Jews were living in the city, operating an [[Orthodox_Judaism|orthodox]] and a [[Reform_Judaism|reform]] school, in addition to a virtual Jewish museum.
sentence_223: The "[[Afghan_(Australia)|Afghan]]" community in Australia first became established in the 1860s when camels and their Pathan, Punjabi, Baluchi and Sindhi handlers began to be used to open up settlement in the continent's arid interior.
sentence_224: Until eventually superseded by the advent of the railways and motor vehicles, camels played an invaluable economic and social role in transporting heavy loads of goods to and from isolated settlements and mines.
sentence_225: This is acknowledged by the name of [[The_Ghan|The Ghan]], the passenger train operating between Adelaide, Alice Springs, and Darwin.
sentence_226: The [[Central_Adelaide_Mosque|Central Adelaide Mosque]] is regarded as Australia's oldest permanent mosque; an earlier [[Marree_Mosque|mosque at Marree]] in northern South Australia, dating from 1861 to 1862 and subsequently abandoned or demolished, has now been rebuilt.
sentence_227: South Australia's largest employment sectors are health care and social assistance, surpassing manufacturing in SA as the largest employer since 2006–07.
sentence_228: In 2009–10, manufacturing in SA had average annual employment of 83,700 persons compared with 103,300 for health care and social assistance.
sentence_229: Health care and social assistance represented nearly 13% of the state average annual employment.
sentence_230: The [[Adelaide_Hills_wine_region|Adelaide Hills wine region]] is an iconic and viable economic region for both the state and country in terms of wine production and sale.
sentence_231: The 2014 vintage is reported as consisting of 5,836 t (5,744 long tons; 6,433 short tons) red grapes crushed valued at A$8,196,142 and 12,037 t (11,847 long tons; 13,269 short tons) white grapes crushed valued at $14,777,631.
sentence_232: The retail trade is the second largest employer in SA (2009–10), with 91,900 jobs, and 12 per cent of the state workforce.
sentence_233: Manufacturing, defence technology, high-tech electronic systems and research, commodity export and corresponding service industries all play a role in the SA economy.
sentence_234: Almost half of all cars produced in Australia were made in Adelaide at the [[General_Motors_Holden|General Motors Holden]] plant in [[Elizabeth,_South_Australia|Elizabeth]].
sentence_235: The site ceased operating in November 2017.
sentence_236: The [[State_Bank_of_South_Australia|collapse of the State Bank in 1992]] resulted in large levels of state public debt (as much as A$4 billion).
sentence_237: The collapse meant that successive governments enacted lean budgets, cutting spending, which was a setback to the further economic development of the city and state.
sentence_238: The debt has more recently been reduced with the State Government once again receiving a AAA+ Credit Rating.
sentence_239: The global media conglomerate [[News_Corporation_(1980–2013)|News Corporation]] was founded in, and until 2004 incorporated in, Adelaide and it is still considered its 'spiritual' home by [[Rupert_Murdoch|Rupert Murdoch]].
sentence_240: Australia's largest oil company, [[Santos_Limited|Santos]], prominent South Australian brewery, [[Coopers_Brewery|Coopers]], and national retailer Harris Scarfe also call Adelaide their home.
sentence_241: The city has been chosen to be the site of the new Australian space center.
sentence_242: South Australia is already home to over 80 organisations which employ 800 people in the space sector.
sentence_243: The Prime Minister Scott Morrison stated the "agency will act as a launching pad to triple Australia's space economy to $12 billion and create up to 20,000 jobs by 2030."
sentence_244: Adelaide is home to a large proportion of Australia's defence industries, which contribute over A$1 billion to South Australia's Gross State Product.
sentence_245: The principal government military research institution, the [[Defence_Science_and_Technology_Organisation|Defence Science and Technology Organisation]], and other defence technology organisations such as [[BAE_Systems_Australia|BAE Systems Australia]] and Lockheed Martin Australia, are north of Salisbury and west of Elizabeth in an area now called "Edinburgh Parks", adjacent to [[RAAF_Base_Edinburgh|RAAF Base Edinburgh]].
sentence_246: Others, such as Saab Systems and Raytheon, are in or near [[Technology_Park,_Adelaide|Technology Park]].
sentence_247: [[ASC_Pty_Ltd|ASC Pty Ltd]], is based in the industrial suburb of Osborne and is also a part of [[Technology_Park,_Adelaide|Technology Park]].
sentence_248: South Australia was charged with constructing Australia's [[Collins_class_submarine|Collins class submarines]] and more recently the A$6 billion contract to construct the [[Royal_Australian_Navy|Royal Australian Navy]]'s new [[Hobart_class_destroyer|air-warfare destroyers]].
sentence_249: As of November 2015, Greater Adelaide had an unemployment rate of 7.4% with a youth unemployment rate of 15%.
sentence_250: The median weekly individual income for people aged 15 years and over was $447 per week in 2006, compared with $466 nationally.
sentence_251: The median family income was $1,137 per week, compared with $1,171 nationally.
sentence_252: Adelaide's housing and living costs are substantially lower than that of other Australian cities, with housing being notably cheaper.
sentence_253: The median Adelaide house price is half that of Sydney and two-thirds that of Melbourne.
sentence_254: The three-month trend unemployment rate to March 2007 was 6.2%.
sentence_255: The Northern suburbs' unemployment rate is disproportionately higher than the other regions of Adelaide at 8.3%, while the East and South are lower than the Adelaide average at 4.9% and 5.0% respectively.
sentence_256: Over the decade March 2001 – March 2010, Metropolitan Adelaide median house prices approximately tripled.
sentence_257: (approx.
sentence_258: 285% – approx.
sentence_259: 11%p.a. compounding) In the five years March 2007 – March 2012, prices increased by approx.
sentence_260: 27% – approx.
sentence_261: 5%p.a. compounding.
sentence_262: March 2012 – March 2017 saw a further increase of 19% – approx.
sentence_263: 3.5%p.a. compounding.
