sentence_265: Each quarter, The Alternative and Direct Investment Securities Association (ADISA) publishes a list of median house sale prices by suburb and Local Government Area.
sentence_266: (Previously, this was done by REISA) Due to the small sizes of many of Adelaide's suburbs, the low volumes of sales in these suburbs, and (over time) the huge variations in the numbers of sales in a suburb in a quarter, statistical analysis of "the most expensive suburb" is unreliable; the suburbs appearing in the "top 10 most expensive suburbs this quarter" list is constantly varying.
sentence_267: Quarterly Reports for the last two years can be found on the REISA website.
sentence_268: Main article: [[South_Australia#Education|Education in South Australia]]
sentence_269: Education forms an increasingly important part of the city's economy, with the [[Government_of_South_Australia|South Australian Government]] and educational institutions attempting to position Adelaide as "Australia's education hub" and marketing it as a "Learning City."
sentence_270: The number of international students studying in Adelaide has increased rapidly in recent years to 30,726 in 2015, of which 1,824 were secondary school students.
sentence_271: In addition to the city's existing institutions, foreign institutions have been attracted to set up campuses to increase its attractiveness as an education hub.
sentence_272: Adelaide is the birthplace of three Nobel laureates, [[List_of_Australian_Nobel_laureates#Australian_laureates_by_birthplace|more than any other Australian city]]: physicist [[William_Lawrence_Bragg|William Lawrence Bragg]] and pathologists [[Howard_Florey|Howard Florey]] and [[Robin_Warren|Robin Warren]], all of whom completed secondary and tertiary education at [[St_Peter's_College,_Adelaide|St Peter's College]] and the [[University_of_Adelaide|University of Adelaide]].
sentence_273: At the level of primary and secondary education, there are two systems of school education.
sentence_274: There is a public system operated by the South Australian Government and a private system of independent and Catholic schools.
sentence_275: [[List_of_schools_in_South_Australia|All schools]] provide education under the South Australian Certificate of Education (SACE) or, to a lesser extent, the [[International_Baccalaureate|International Baccalaureate]] (IB), with Adelaide having the highest number of IB schools in Australia.
sentence_276: There are three public universities local to Adelaide, as well as one private university and three constituent colleges of foreign universities.
sentence_277: [[Flinders_University_of_South_Australia|Flinders University of South Australia]], the [[University_of_Adelaide|University of Adelaide]], the University of South Australia and [[Torrens_University_Australia|Torrens University Australia]]—part of the [[Laureate_International_Universities|Laureate International Universities]] are based in Adelaide.
sentence_278: The University of Adelaide was ranked in the top 150 universities worldwide.
sentence_279: Flinders ranked in the top 250 and Uni SA in the top 300.
sentence_280: Torrens University Australia is part of an international network of over 70 higher education institutions in more than 30 countries worldwide.
sentence_281: The historic Torrens Building in [[Victoria_Square,_Adelaide|Victoria Square]] houses Carnegie Mellon University's [[Heinz_College_Australia|Heinz College Australia]], and [[University_College_London|University College London]]'s School of Energy and Resources (Australia), and constitute the city's international university precinct.
sentence_282: The [[University_of_Adelaide|University of Adelaide]], with 25,000 students, is Australia's third-oldest university and a member of the leading "[[Group_of_Eight_(Australian_universities)|Group of Eight]]".
sentence_283: It has five campuses throughout the state, including two in the city-centre, and a campus in Singapore.
sentence_284: The University of South Australia, with 37,000 students, has two North Terrace campuses, three other campuses in the metropolitan area and campuses at [[Whyalla,_South_Australia|Whyalla]] and [[Mount_Gambier,_South_Australia|Mount Gambier]].
sentence_285: [[Flinders_University|Flinders University]], with 25,184 domestic and international students, is in the southern suburb of [[Bedford_Park,_South_Australia|Bedford Park]], alongside the Flinders Medical Centre, another campus in neighbouring [[Tonsley,_South_Australia|Tonsley]], and maintains a small city campus in Victoria Square.
sentence_286: The plaza on the Bedford Park campus was revamped in 2014 and officially re-opened in 2016.
sentence_287: There are several South Australian TAFE (Technical and Further Education) campuses in the metropolitan area that provide a range of vocational education and training.
sentence_288: The Adelaide College of the Arts, as a school of TAFE SA, provides nationally recognised training in visual and performing arts.
sentence_289: In addition to the universities, Adelaide is home to a number of research institutes, including the [[Royal_Institution_of_Australia|Royal Institution of Australia]], established in 2009 as a counterpart to the two-hundred-year-old [[Royal_Institution|Royal Institution]] of Great Britain.
sentence_290: Many of the organisations involved in research tend to be geographically clustered throughout the Adelaide metropolitan area:

list.value: The east end of [[North_Terrace,_Adelaide|North Terrace]]: [[SA_Pathology|SA Pathology]]; [[Hanson_Institute|Hanson Institute]]; [[Royal_Adelaide_Hospital|RAH]]; [[National_Wine_Centre_of_Australia|National Wine Centre]].

The west end of North Terrace: [[South_Australian_Health_and_Medical_Research_Institute|South Australian Health and Medical Research Institute]] (SAHMRI), located next to the new [[Royal_Adelaide_Hospital|Royal Adelaide Hospital]].

The [[Waite_Research_Precinct|Waite Research Precinct]]: [[South_Australian_Research_and_Development_Institute|SARDI]] Head Office and Plant Research Centre; [[Australian_Wine_Research_Institute|AWRI]]; ACPFG; [[CSIRO|CSIRO]] research laboratories. SARDI also has establishments at Glenside and [[West_Beach,_South_Australia|West Beach]].
Edinburgh, South Australia: [[Defence_Science_and_Technology_Organisation|DSTO]]; [[BAE_Systems|BAE Systems]] (Australia); [[Lockheed_Martin|Lockheed Martin]] Australia Electronic Systems.

[[Technology_Park_Adelaide|Technology Park]] ([[Mawson_Lakes,_South_Australia|Mawson Lakes]]): BAE Systems; [[Optus|Optus]]; [[Raytheon|Raytheon]]; Topcon; Lockheed Martin Australia Electronic Systems.

Research Park at [[Thebarton,_South_Australia|Thebarton]]: businesses involved in materials engineering, biotechnology, environmental services, information technology, industrial design, laser/optics technology, health products, engineering services, radar systems, telecommunications and petroleum services.
Science Park (adjacent to Flinders University): Playford Capital.

The [[Basil_Hetzel|Basil Hetzel]] Institute for Translational Health Research in [[Woodville,_South_Australia|Woodville]] the research arm of the [[Queen_Elizabeth_Hospital,_Adelaide|Queen Elizabeth Hospital, Adelaide]]
The Joanna Briggs Institute, a global research collaboration for evidence-based healthcare with its headquarters in North Adelaide.

sentence_291: See also: [[South_Australia#Cultural_life|South Australia § Cultural life]], [[Department_of_the_Premier_and_Cabinet_(South_Australia)#Arts_and_culture|Department of the Premier and Cabinet (South Australia) § Arts and culture]], and [[List_of_festivals_in_Australia#South_Australia|List of festivals in Australia § South Australia]]
sentence_292: While established as a British province, and very much English in terms of its culture, Adelaide attracted immigrants from other parts of Europe early on, including German and other European non-conformists escaping religious persecution.
sentence_293: The first German Lutherans arrived in 1838 bringing with them the [[Vine_cuttings|vine cuttings]] that they used to found the acclaimed wineries of the [[Barossa_Valley|Barossa Valley]].
sentence_294: The [[Royal_Adelaide_Show|Royal Adelaide Show]] is an annual [[Agricultural_show|agricultural show]] and [[State_fair|state fair]], established in 1839 and now a huge event held in the [[Adelaide_Showground|Adelaide Showground]] annually.
sentence_295: Adelaide's arts scene flourished in the 1960s and 1970s with the support of successive premiers from both major political parties.
sentence_296: The renowned [[Adelaide_Festival_of_Arts|Adelaide Festival of Arts]] was established in 1960 under Thomas Playford, which in the same year spawned an unofficial uncurated series of performances and exhibits which grew into the [[Adelaide_Fringe|Adelaide Fringe]].
sentence_297: Construction of the [[Adelaide_Festival_Centre|Adelaide Festival Centre]] began under Steele Hall in 1970 and was completed under the subsequent government of Don Dunstan, who also established the [[South_Australian_Film_Corporation|South Australian Film Corporation]] in 1972 and the [[State_Opera_of_South_Australia|State Opera of South Australia]] in 1976.
sentence_298: Over time, the Adelaide Festival expanded to include Adelaide Writers' Week and [[WOMADelaide|WOMADelaide]], and other separate festivals were established, such as the Adelaide Cabaret Festival (2002), the Adelaide Festival of Ideas (1999), the [[Adelaide_Film_Festival|Adelaide Film Festival]] (2013), FEAST (1999, a [[LGBT_culture|queer culture]]) and Tasting Australia (1997, a food and wine affair).
sentence_299: With the Festival, the Fringe, WOMADelaide, Writers' Week and the [[Adelaide_500|Adelaide 500]] street motor racing event (along with evening music concerts) all happening in early March, the period has become known colloquially as "Mad March".
sentence_300: In 2014, [[Ghil'ad_Zuckermann|Ghil'ad Zuckermann]] founded the [[Adelaide_Language_Festival|Adelaide Language Festival]].
sentence_301: There are many international cultural fairs, most notably the German Schützenfest and Greek [[Glendi|Glendi]].
sentence_302: Adelaide is home to the [[Adelaide_Christmas_Pageant|Adelaide Christmas Pageant]], the world's largest [[Santa_Claus_parade|Christmas parade]].
sentence_303: As the state capital, Adelaide is home to a great number of cultural institutions with many along the boulevard of [[North_Terrace,_Adelaide|North Terrace]].
sentence_304: The [[Art_Gallery_of_South_Australia|Art Gallery of South Australia]], with around 35,000 works, holds Australia's second largest state-based collection.
sentence_305: Adjacent are the [[South_Australian_Museum|South Australian Museum]] and [[State_Library_of_South_Australia|State Library of South Australia]], while the [[Adelaide_Botanic_Garden|Adelaide Botanic Garden]], [[National_Wine_Centre|National Wine Centre]] and [[Tandanya_National_Aboriginal_Cultural_Institute|Tandanya National Aboriginal Cultural Institute]] are nearby in the [[East_End,_Adelaide|East End]] of the city.
sentence_306: In the back of the State Library lies the [[Migration_Museum,_Adelaide|Migration Museum]], Australia's oldest museum of its kind.
sentence_307: Further west, the [[Lion_Arts_Centre|Lion Arts Centre]] is home to [[ACE_Open|ACE Open]], which showcases contemporary art, [[Dance_Hub_SA|Dance Hub SA]] and other studio and arts industry office spaces.
sentence_308: The [[Mercury_Cinema|Mercury Cinema]] and [[JamFactory|JamFactory]] (ceramics and design gallery) are just around the corner.
sentence_309: The Adelaide Festival Centre (which includes the Dunstan Playhouse, Festival Theatre and Space Theatre), on the banks of the Torrens, is the focal point for much of the cultural activity in the city and home to the [[State_Theatre_Company_of_South_Australia|State Theatre Company of South Australia]].
sentence_310: Other live music and theatre venues include the Adelaide Entertainment Centre; [[Adelaide_Oval|Adelaide Oval]]; [[Memorial_Drive_Park|Memorial Drive Park]]; [[Thebarton_Theatre|Thebarton Theatre]]; [[Adelaide_Town_Hall|Adelaide Town Hall]]; [[Her_Majesty's_Theatre|Her Majesty's Theatre]]; [[Queen's_Theatre,_Adelaide|Queen's Theatre]]; Holden Theatres and the Hopgood Theatre.
sentence_311: The [[Lion_Arts_Factory|Lion Arts Factory]], within the Lion Arts Centre, hosts contemporary music in a wide range of genres, as does "[[The_Gov|The Gov]]" in [[Hindmarsh,_South_Australia|Hindmarsh]].
sentence_312: The city also has numerous smaller theatres, pubs and cabaret bars which host performances.
sentence_313: Further information: [[Music_of_Adelaide|Music of Adelaide]]
sentence_314: In 2015, it was said that there were now more live music venues per capita in Adelaide than any other capital city in the southern hemisphere, [[Lonely_Planet|Lonely Planet]] labelled Adelaide "Australia's live music city", and the city was recognised as a "[[City_of_Music_(UNESCO)|City of Music]]" by the [[UNESCO_Creative_Cities_Network|UNESCO Creative Cities Network]].
sentence_315: In addition to its own WOMADelaide, Adelaide attracts several touring music festivals, including Creamfields, Laneway and [[Groovin'_the_Moo|Groovin']].
sentence_316: Adelaide has produced musical groups and individuals who have achieved national and international fame.
sentence_317: These include the [[Adelaide_Symphony_Orchestra|Adelaide Symphony Orchestra]], the Adelaide Youth Orchestra, rock bands [[The_Angels_(Australian_band)|The Angels]], [[Cold_Chisel|Cold Chisel]], [[The_Superjesus|The Superjesus]], [[Wolf_&_Cub|Wolf & Cub]], roots/blues group [[The_Audreys|The Audreys]], internationally acclaimed metal acts [[I_Killed_The_Prom_Queen|I Killed The Prom Queen]] and [[Double_Dragon_(band)|Double Dragon]], popular Australian hip-hop outfit [[Hilltop_Hoods|Hilltop Hoods]], pop acts like [[Sia_Furler|Sia]], [[Orianthi|Orianthi]], [[Guy_Sebastian|Guy Sebastian]], and [[Wes_Carr|Wes Carr]], as well as internationally successful tribute act, The [[Australian_Pink_Floyd_Show|Australian Pink Floyd Show]].
sentence_318: Noted rocker [[Jimmy_Barnes|Jimmy Barnes]] (formerly lead vocalist with Cold Chisel) spent most of his youth in the northern suburb of [[Elizabeth,_South_Australia|Elizabeth]].
sentence_319: Paul Kelly grew up in Adelaide and was head prefect at [[Rostrevor_College|Rostrevor College]].
sentence_320: The first Australian Idol winner, Guy Sebastian, hails from the north-eastern suburb of [[Golden_Grove,_South_Australia|Golden Grove]].
sentence_321: Adelaide plays host to two of Australia's leading contemporary dance companies.
sentence_322: The [[Australian_Dance_Theatre|Australian Dance Theatre]] and [[Dance_Hub_SA|Dance Hub SA]] (formerly Leigh Warren & Dancers) contribute to state festivals and perform nationally and internationally.
sentence_323: [[Restless_Dance_Theatre|Restless Dance Theatre]] is also based in Adelaide and is nationally recognised for working with disabled and non-disabled dancers to use movement as a means of expression.
sentence_324: Newspapers in Adelaide are dominated by [[News_Corp_Australia|News Corporation]] publications—Adelaide being the birthplace of News Corporation itself.
sentence_325: The only South Australian daily newspaper is [[The_Advertiser_(Adelaide)|The Advertiser]], published by News Corporation six days a week.
sentence_326: The same group publishes a Sunday paper, the [[Sunday_Mail_(Adelaide)|Sunday Mail]].
sentence_327: There are eleven suburban community newspapers published weekly, known collectively as the [[Messenger_Newspapers|Messenger Newspapers]], also published by a subsidiary of News Corporation.
sentence_328: The Independent Weekly was a small independent newspaper providing an alternative view, but ceased publishing its print edition in November 2010 and now exists as a digital daily newsletter only, [[InDaily|InDaily]].
sentence_329: [[The_Adelaide_Review|The Adelaide Review]] is a free paper published monthly, and other independent magazine-style papers are published, but are not as widely available.
sentence_330: Adelaide is served by numerous digital free-to-air television channels:
sentence_331: All of the five Australian national television networks broadcast both [[High-definition_television|high-definition digital]] and standard-definition digital television services in Adelaide.
sentence_332: They share three transmission towers on the ridge near the summit of Mount Lofty.
sentence_333: There are two other transmission sites at 25 [[Grenfell_Street|Grenfell Street]], Adelaide and [[Elizabeth_Downs,_South_Australia|Elizabeth Downs]].
sentence_334: The two government-funded stations are run by the [[Australian_Broadcasting_Corporation|Australian Broadcasting Corporation]] ([[ABS_(TV_station)|ABC South Australia]]) and the [[Special_Broadcasting_Service|Special Broadcasting Service]] (SBS).
sentence_335: The [[Seven_Network|Seven Network]] and [[Network_Ten|Network Ten]] both own their Adelaide stations ([[SAS-7|SAS-7]] and ADS-10 respectively).
sentence_336: Adelaide's [[NWS-9|NWS-9]] is part of the [[Nine_Network|Nine Network]].
sentence_337: Adelaide also has a [[Community_television_in_Australia|community television]] station, [[Channel_44_(Adelaide)|Channel 44]].
sentence_338: As part of a nationwide phase-out of analogue television in Australia, Adelaide's analogue television service was shut down on 2 April 2013.
sentence_339: The Foxtel [[Pay_TV|pay TV]] service is also available via cable or satellite to the entire metropolitan area.
sentence_340: All the major broadcasting networks also operate online on-demand television services, alongside internet-only services such as [[Stan_(company)|Stan]], [[Fetch_TV|Fetch TV]], [[Netflix|Netflix]], YouTube, [[Disney+|Disney+]], and [[Kayo_Sports|Kayo Sports]].
sentence_341: See also: [[List_of_radio_stations_in_Australia#Adelaide|List of radio stations in Australia § Adelaide]]
sentence_342: There are 20 radio stations that serve the metropolitan area, as well as four stations that serve only parts of the metropolitan area; six commercial stations, six community stations, six national stations and two narrowcast stations.
sentence_343: [[DAB+|DAB+]] digital radio has been broadcasting in metropolitan Adelaide since 20 May 2009, and currently offers a choice of 41 stations all operated by the existing licensed radio broadcasters, which includes high-quality simulcast of all AM and FM stations.
sentence_344: Main article: [[Crime_in_South_Australia#Adelaide|Crime in South Australia § Adelaide]]
sentence_345: Main article: [[Sport_in_South_Australia|Sport in South Australia]]
sentence_346: The main sports played professionally in Adelaide are [[Australian_Rules_football|Australian Rules football]], association football (soccer), [[Cricket|cricket]], [[Netball|netball]], and basketball.
sentence_347: Adelaide is the home of two [[Australian_Football_League|Australian Football League]] teams: the [[Adelaide_Football_Club|Adelaide Football Club]] and [[Port_Adelaide_Football_Club|Port Adelaide Football Club]], and one [[A-League|A-League]] soccer team, [[Adelaide_United|Adelaide United]].
sentence_348: A local [[Australian_rules_football|Australian rules football]] league, the [[South_Australian_National_Football_League|SANFL]], is made up of 10 teams from around Adelaide.
sentence_349: The SANFL has been in operation since 1877 when it began as the South Australian Football Association (SAFL) before changing its name to the SANFL in 1927.
sentence_350: The SANFL is the oldest surviving football league of any code played in Australia.
sentence_351: Adelaide has developed a strong culture of attracting crowds to major sporting events.
sentence_352: Until the completion of the 2012–14 renovation and upgrade of the [[Adelaide_Oval|Adelaide Oval]], most large sporting events took place at either [[AAMI_Stadium|AAMI Stadium]] (the then home base of the [[Adelaide_Crows|Adelaide Crows]], and the then [[Port_Adelaide_Football_Club|Port Adelaide's]] home game venue), or the historic [[Adelaide_Oval|Adelaide Oval]], home of the [[Southern_Redbacks|Southern Redbacks]] and the [[Adelaide_Strikers|Adelaide Strikers]] cricket teams.
sentence_353: Since completion of the upgrade, home games for Adelaide Crows and Port Adelaide now take place at Adelaide Oval.
sentence_354: Since 1884, [[Adelaide_Oval|Adelaide Oval]] has also hosted an international cricket test every summer, along with a number of [[One_Day_International|One Day International]] cricket matches.
sentence_355: [[Memorial_Drive_Park|Memorial Drive Park]], adjacent to the Adelaide Oval, used to host Davis Cup and other major tennis events, including the Australian Open and the Adelaide International.
sentence_356: Adelaide's professional association football team, [[Adelaide_United|Adelaide United]], play in the A-League.
sentence_357: Founded in 2003, their home ground is [[Hindmarsh_Stadium|Hindmarsh Stadium]], which has a capacity of 17,000 and is one of the few [[Soccer-specific_stadium|purpose-built soccer stadia]] in Australia.
sentence_358: Prior to United's foundation, [[Adelaide_City_FC|Adelaide City]] and [[West_Adelaide_SC|West Adelaide]] represented the city in the [[National_Soccer_League|National Soccer League]].
sentence_359: The two sides, which contest the [[Adelaide_derby|Adelaide derby]] against one another, now play in the [[National_Premier_Leagues_South_Australia|National Premier Leagues South Australia]].
sentence_360: For two years, 1997 and 1998, Adelaide was represented in Australia's top level [[Rugby_league|rugby league]], after the [[New_South_Wales_Rugby_League|New South Wales Rugby League]] had played a single game per season at the Adelaide Oval for five years starting in 1991.
sentence_361: The [[Adelaide_Rams|Adelaide Rams]] were formed and played in the breakaway [[Super_League_(Australia)|Super League]] (SL) competition in [[1997_Super_League_(Australia)_season|1997]] before moving to the new [[National_Rugby_League|National Rugby League]] in [[1998_NRL_season|1998]].
sentence_362: Initially playing at the Adelaide Oval, the club moved to the more suitable Hindmarsh Stadium late in the 1998 season.
sentence_363: As part of a peace deal with the [[Australian_Rugby_League|Australian Rugby League]] to end the Super League war, the club's owners [[News_Limited|News Limited]] (who were also owners of the SL) suddenly closed the club only weeks before the start of the [[1999_NRL_season|1999 season]].
sentence_364: Adelaide has two professional basketball teams, the men's team being the [[Adelaide_36ers|Adelaide 36ers]] which plays in the [[National_Basketball_League_(Australasia)|National Basketball League]] (NBL) and the women's team, the [[Adelaide_Lightning|Adelaide Lightning]] which plays in the [[Women's_National_Basketball_League|Women's National Basketball League]] (WNBL).
sentence_365: Both teams play their home games at the [[Titanium_Security_Arena|Titanium Security Arena]].
sentence_366: Adelaide has a professional [[Netball|netball]] team, the [[Adelaide_Thunderbirds|Adelaide Thunderbirds]], which plays in the national netball competition, the [[Suncorp_Super_Netball|Suncorp Super Netball]] championship, with home games played at [[Priceline_Stadium|Priceline Stadium]].
sentence_367: The Thunderbirds occasionally play games or finals at the Titanium Security Arena, while international netball matches are usually played at the 10,500 seat Adelaide Entertainment Centre.
sentence_368: The Titanium Security Arena has a capacity of 8,000 and is the largest purpose-built basketball stadium in Australia.
sentence_369: Since 1999 Adelaide and its surrounding areas have hosted the [[Tour_Down_Under|Tour Down Under]] bicycle race, organised and directed by Adelaide-based [[Michael_Turtur|Michael Turtur]].
sentence_370: Turtur won an [[Summer_Olympics|Olympic]] gold medal for Australia in the [[Cycling_at_the_1984_Summer_Olympics|4000m Team pursuit]] at the [[1984_Summer_Olympics|1984 Los Angeles Olympics]].
sentence_371: The Tour Down Under is the largest cycling event outside Europe and was the first event outside Europe to be granted [[UCI_ProTour|UCI ProTour]] status.
sentence_372: Adelaide maintains a franchise in the [[Australian_Baseball_League|Australian Baseball League]], the [[Adelaide_Bite|Adelaide Bite]].
sentence_373: They have been playing since 2009, and their home stadium (until 2016) was [[Norwood_Oval|Norwood Oval]].
sentence_374: From 2016 the team moved to the [[Diamond_Sports_Stadium|Diamond Sports Stadium]] located near the [[Adelaide_International_Airport|Adelaide International Airport]] due to renovations at Norwood.
sentence_375: Its name stems from the local [[Great_Australian_Bight|Great Australian Bight]], and from the abundance of local [[Great_White_Shark|Great White Sharks]].
sentence_376: Adelaide also has an Ice Hockey team, [[Adelaide_Adrenaline|Adelaide Adrenaline]] in the [[Australian_Ice_Hockey_League|Australian Ice Hockey League]] (AIHL).
sentence_377: It was national champions in 2009 and plays its games at the [[Ice_Arena_(Adelaide)|IceArenA]].
sentence_378: The Australian Grand Prix for World Championship [[Formula_One|Formula One]] racing was hosted by Adelaide from 1985 to 1995 on the [[Adelaide_Street_Circuit|Adelaide Street Circuit]] which was laid out in the city's East End as well as the eastern parklands including the [[Victoria_Park,_Adelaide|Victoria Park Racecourse]].
sentence_379: The Grand Prix became a source of pride, and losing the event to Melbourne in a surprise announcement in mid-1993 left a void that has since been filled with the highly successful [[Adelaide_500|Clipsal 500]] for [[V8_Supercar|V8 Supercar]] racing, held on a modified version of the same street circuit.
sentence_380: The Classic Adelaide, a [[Rallying|rally]] of classic sporting vehicles, is also held in the city and its surrounds.
sentence_381: Adelaide formerly had three horse racing venues.
sentence_382: [[Victoria_Park,_Adelaide|Victoria Park]], [[Cheltenham_Park_Racecourse|Cheltenham Park Racecourse]], both of which have now closed, and [[Morphettville_Racecourse|Morphettville Racecourse]] that remains the home of the [[South_Australian_Jockey_Club|South Australian Jockey Club]].
sentence_383: It also has [[Globe_Derby_Park_(harness_racing)|Globe Derby Park]] for Harness racing that opened in 1969, and by 1973 had become Adelaide's premier harness racing venue taking over from the [[Adelaide_Showgrounds|Wayville Showgrounds]], as well as [[Greyhound_Park|Greyhound Park]] for [[Greyhound_racing|greyhound racing]] that opened in 1972.
sentence_384: The [[World_Solar_Challenge|World Solar Challenge]] race attracts teams from around the world, most of which are fielded by universities or corporations, although some are fielded by high schools.
sentence_385: The race has a 20-years' history spanning nine races, with the inaugural event taking place in 1987.
sentence_386: Adelaide hosted the 2012 World Bowls Championships at Lockleys Bowling Club, becoming the third city in the world to have held the championships twice, having previously hosted the event in 1996.
sentence_387: Dirt track speedway is also popular in Adelaide with three operating speedways.
sentence_388: Adelaide Motorsport Park, located adjacent to the [[Adelaide_International_Raceway|Adelaide International Raceway]] road racing circuit at [[Virginia,_South_Australia|Virginia]] (24 km (15 mi) north of the city centre) has been in continuous operation since 1979 after the closure of the popular [[Rowley_Park_Speedway|Rowley Park Speedway]].
sentence_389: [[Gillman_Speedway|Gillman Speedway]] located in the semi-industrial suburb of Gillman, has been in operation since 1998 and caters to [[Motorcycle_speedway|Motorcycle speedway]] and Sidecars, while the Sidewinders Speedway located in [[Wingfield,_South_Australia|Wingfield]] is also a motorcycle speedway dedicated to Under-16 riders and has been in operation since 1978.
sentence_390: In 2016 backed my South Australia's Peregrine Group owners of OTR (On the run service stations and 24/7-hour convenient stores) opened up a multi-purpose facility; a state-of-the-art motorsporting park and a hotel alongside its newer OTR service station outside a small township of Tailem Bend currently named [[The_Bend_Motorsport_Park|The Bend Motorsport Park]].
sentence_391: Design for thrill seekers and rev-heads the facility currently host South Australia's second V8 Supercars motoring event during a round in August and hopes to bring in other major international motoring events such as SBK Superbikes and other well established [[FIA|FIA]] motoring events.
sentence_392: Adelaide is home to the [[Great_Southern_Slam|Great Southern Slam]], the world's largest [[Roller_derby|roller derby]] tournament.
sentence_393: The tournament has been held biennially over Australia's Queen's Birthday holiday weekend since 2010.
sentence_394: In 2014 and 2016 the tournament featured 45 teams playing in two divisions.
sentence_395: In 2018 the tournament has expanded to 48 teams competing in three divisions.
sentence_396: Main article: [[Transport_in_Adelaide|Transport in Adelaide]]
sentence_397: Being centrally located on the Australian mainland, Adelaide forms a strategic transport hub for east–west and north–south routes.
sentence_398: The city itself has a metropolitan public transport system managed by and known as the [[Adelaide_Metro|Adelaide Metro]].
sentence_399: The Adelaide Metro consists of a contracted bus system including the [[O-Bahn_Busway|O-Bahn Busway]], [[Railways_in_Adelaide|6 commuter rail lines]] (diesel and electric), and a small tram network operating between inner suburb [[Hindmarsh,_South_Australia|Hindmarsh]], the city centre, and seaside [[Glenelg_tram_line|Glenelg]].
sentence_400: Tramways were largely dismantled in the 1950s, but saw a revival in the 2010s with upgrades and extensions.
sentence_401: Road transport in Adelaide has historically been easier than many of the other Australian cities, with a well-defined city layout and wide multiple-lane roads from the beginning of its development.
sentence_402: Adelaide was known as a "twenty-minute city", with commuters having been able to travel from metropolitan outskirts to the city proper in roughly twenty minutes.
sentence_403: However, such arterial roads often experience traffic congestion as the city grows.
sentence_404: The Adelaide metropolitan area has one freeway and four expressways.
sentence_405: In order of construction, they are:

list.value: The [[South_Eastern_Freeway|South Eastern Freeway]] (M1), connects the south-east corner of the Adelaide Plain to the Adelaide Hills and beyond to [[Murray_Bridge,_South_Australia|Murray Bridge]] and Tailem Bend, where it then continues as National Highway 1 south-east to Melbourne.

The [[Southern_Expressway_(Australia)|Southern Expressway]] (M2), connecting the outer southern suburbs with the inner southern suburbs and the city centre. It duplicates the route of [[South_Road|South Road]].

The [[North-South_Motorway|North-South Motorway]] (M2), is an ongoing major project that will become the major north–south corridor, replacing most of what is now [[South_Road|South Road]], connecting the [[Southern_Expressway_(Adelaide)|Southern Expressway]] and the [[Northern_Expressway|Northern Expressway]] via a motorway with no traffic lights. As of 2020 the motorway's northern half is complete (save for a small link under construction at [[Croydon_Park,_South_Australia|Croydon Park]]), connecting the Northern Expressway to Adelaide's inner north-west; the section running through Adelaide's inner west and inner south-west is awaiting funding.

The [[Port_River_Expressway|Port River Expressway]] (A9), connects Port Adelaide and [[Outer_Harbor,_South_Australia|Outer Harbor]] to Port Wakefield Road at the northern "entrance" to the metropolitan area.

The [[Northern_Expressway|Northern Expressway]] (Max Fatchen Expressway) (M2), is the northern suburbs bypass route connecting the Sturt Highway (National Highway 20) via the [[Gawler_Bypass|Gawler Bypass]] to Port Wakefield Road at a point a few kilometres north of the Port River Expressway connection.
The [[Northern_Connector|Northern Connector]], completed in 2020, links the North South Motorway to the Northern Expressway.

sentence_406: The Adelaide metropolitan area has two commercial airports, [[Adelaide_Airport|Adelaide Airport]] and [[Parafield_Airport|Parafield Airport]].
sentence_407: Adelaide Airport, in Adelaide's south-western suburbs, serves in excess of 8 million passengers annually.
sentence_408: Parafield Airport, Adelaide's second airport 18 kilometres (11 miles) north of the city centre, is used for small aircraft, pilot training and recreational aviation purposes.
sentence_409: Parafield Airport served as Adelaide's main aerodrome until the opening of the Adelaide Airport in February 1955.
sentence_410: Adelaide airport serves many international and domestic destinations including all Australian state capitals.
sentence_411: Adelaide is also home to a military airport, known as [[RAAF_Base_Edinburgh|Edinburgh Airport]], located in the northern suburbs.
sentence_412: It was built in 1955 in a joint initiative with the UK for weapon development.
sentence_413: Adelaide's two largest hospitals are the [[Royal_Adelaide_Hospital|Royal Adelaide Hospital]] (RAH) in the city centre, a teaching hospital affiliated with the University of Adelaide (800 beds), and the Flinders Medical Centre (580 beds) in Bedford Park, affiliated with Flinders University.
sentence_414: The RAH also operates additional campuses for specialist care throughout the suburbs including the Hampstead Rehabilitation Centre (150 beds) in Northfield and the [[Glenside_Hospital_(Adelaide)|Glenside Campus]] (129 beds) for acute mental health services.
sentence_415: Other major public hospitals are the Women's and Children's Hospital (305 beds), in North Adelaide; the [[Queen_Elizabeth_Hospital,_Adelaide|Queen Elizabeth Hospital]] (340 beds) in Woodville; Modbury Hospital (178 beds) in Modbury; and the [[Lyell_McEwin_Hospital|Lyell McEwin Hospital]] (198 beds) in Elizabeth.
sentence_416: Numerous private hospitals are also located throughout the city, with the largest operators being not-for-profits Adelaide Community Healthcare Alliance (3 hospitals) and [[Sisters_of_the_Little_Company_of_Mary|Calvary Care]] (4 hospitals).
sentence_417: In 2017, the RAH was relocated from the city's [[East_End,_Adelaide|East End]] to a new AU$2.3 billion facility built over former railyards in the West End.
sentence_418: The state-of-the-art hospital forms part of a new biomedical precinct called BioMed City that colocates the [[South_Australian_Health_and_Medical_Research_Institute|South Australian Health and Medical Research Institute]] (SAHMRI), the University of Adelaide Health and Medical Sciences building, the University of South Australia's Health Innovation Building, and the state's Dental Hospital.
sentence_419: SAHMRI is building a $300 million second facility due to be completed by 2022 to house the Australian Bragg Centre with Australia's first [[Proton_therapy|proton therapy]] unit.
sentence_420: There are also plans for the Women's and Children's Hospital to be relocated to the precinct adjacent the RAH by 2024.
sentence_421: The largest provider of community health care within Adelaide is the not-for-profit [[Royal_District_Nursing_Service_(South_Australia)|Royal District Nursing Service]] (RDNS), which provides out of hospital care and hospital avoidance care.
sentence_422: Adelaide's energy requirements were originally met by the [[Adelaide_Electric_Supply_Company|Adelaide Electric Supply Company]], which was nationalised by the [[Thomas_Playford_IV|Playford]] government in 1946, becoming the [[Electricity_Trust_of_South_Australia|Electricity Trust of South Australia]] (ETSA).
sentence_423: Despite significant public opposition and the Labor party's anti-privatisation stance which left the Liberal party one vote short of the numbers needed to pass the legislation, ETSA was privatised by the [[John_Olsen|Olsen]] Government in 1999 by way of a 200-year lease for the distribution network (ETSA Utilities, later renamed [[SA_Power_Networks|SA Power Networks]]) and the outright purchase of ETSA Power by the [[Cheung_Kong_Holdings|Cheung Kong Holdings]] for $3.5 billion (11 times ETSA's annual earnings) after Labor MP [[Trevor_Crothers|Trevor Crothers]] resigned from the party and voted with the government.
sentence_424: The electricity retail market was opened to competition in 2003 and although competition was expected to result in lower retail costs, prices increased by 23.7% in the market's first year.
sentence_425: In 2004 the privatisation was deemed to be a failure with consumers paying 60% more for their power and with the state government estimated to lose $3 billion in power generation net income in the first ten years of privatisation.
sentence_426: In 2012, the industry came under scrutiny for allegedly reducing supply by shutting down generators during periods of peak demand to force prices up.
sentence_427: Increased media attention also revealed that in 2009 the state government had approved a 46% increase in retail prices to cover expected increases in the costs of generation while generation costs had in fact fallen 35% by 2012.
sentence_428: South Australia has the highest retail price for electricity in the country.
sentence_429: Privatisation led to competition from a variety of companies who now separately provide for the generation, transmission, distribution and retail sales of gas and electricity.
sentence_430: Electricity generation comes from a range of technologies and operators.
sentence_431: [[ElectraNet|ElectraNet]] operates the high-voltage electricity transmission network.
sentence_432: [[SA_Power_Networks|SA Power Networks]] distributes electricity to end users.
sentence_433: The largest electricity and gas retailing companies are also the largest generating companies.
sentence_434: The largest fossil fuel power stations are the [[Torrens_Island_Power_Station|Torrens Island Power Station]] gas-fired plant operated by [[AGL_Energy|AGL Energy]] and the [[Pelican_Point_Power_Station|Pelican Point Power Station]] operated by [[Engie|Engie]].
sentence_435: South Australia also has wind and solar power and connections to the national grid.
sentence_436: [[Natural_gas|Gas]] is supplied from the [[Moomba,_South_Australia|Moomba]] Gas Processing Plant in the [[Cooper_Basin|Cooper Basin]] via the [[Moomba_Adelaide_Pipeline_System|Moomba Adelaide Pipeline System]] and the [[SEAGas_pipeline|SEAGas pipeline]] from [[Victoria,_Australia|Victoria]].
sentence_437: In 2011, South Australia generated 18% of its electricity from [[Wind_power|wind power]], and had 51% of the installed capacity of wind generators in Australia.
sentence_438: Due to almost universal blackouts within the city during September 2016, the state worked with [[Tesla,_Inc.|Tesla]] to produce the world's largest electricity battery at [[Hornsdale_Wind_Farm|Hornsdale Power Reserve]] which has increased that state's electrical security to the extent in which large blackouts are no longer an event.
sentence_439: The provision of water services is by the government-owned SA Water.
sentence_440: Adelaide's water is supplied from its seven reservoirs: [[Mount_Bold_Reservoir|Mount Bold]], [[Happy_Valley_Reservoir|Happy Valley]], [[Myponga_Reservoir|Myponga]], [[Millbrook_Reservoir|Millbrook]], [[Hope_Valley_Reservoir|Hope Valley]], [[Little_Para_Reservoir|Little Para]] and South Para.
sentence_441: The yield from these reservoir catchments can be as little as 10% of the city's requirements (90GL per annum) in drought years and about 60% in average years.
sentence_442: The remaining demand is met by the pumping of water from the [[River_Murray|River Murray]].
sentence_443: A sea-water desalination plant capable of supplying 100GL per annum was built during the 2001–2009 drought; however, it operated at about 8% of its capacity until 2019.
sentence_444: In December 2018, the State and Federal Governments agreed to fund a $2m study to determine how the plant could be used to reduce reliance on river water, in an effort to help save the Murray River basin and mouth (including the [[Coorong|Coorong]]) from further ecological damage.
sentence_445: AdelaideFree WiFi is a citywide free [[WiFi|WiFi]] network covering most of the inner city areas of Adelaide, primarily the [[Adelaide_city_centre|Adelaide CBD]] and Northern Adelaide precincts.
sentence_446: It was officially launched at the Adelaide Central Markets on Tuesday 25 June 2014.
sentence_447: It is provided by [[Internode_(ISP)|Internode]], with infrastructure provided by outdoor [[Cisco|Cisco]] WiFi N access points attached to the top of lighting poles, as well as inside cafes and businesses across the city.
