sentence_0: Dame Agatha Mary Clarissa Christie, Lady Mallowan, [[Dame_Commander_of_the_Order_of_the_British_Empire|DBE]] (née Miller; 15 September 1890 – 12 January 1976) was an English writer known for her sixty-six detective novels and fourteen short story collections, particularly those revolving around fictional detectives [[Hercule_Poirot|Hercule Poirot]] and [[Miss_Marple|Miss Marple]].
sentence_1: She also wrote the world's longest-running play, [[The_Mousetrap|The Mousetrap]], which was performed in the [[West_End_theatre|West End]] from 1952 to 2020, as well as six novels under the pseudonym Mary Westmacott.
sentence_2: In 1971, she was made a [[Dame|Dame]] (DBE) for her contributions to literature.
sentence_3: [[Guinness_World_Records|Guinness World Records]] lists Christie as the best-selling fiction writer of all time, her novels having sold more than two billion copies.
sentence_4: Christie was born into a wealthy upper-middle-class family in [[Torquay|Torquay]], Devon, and was largely home-schooled.
sentence_5: She was initially an unsuccessful writer with six consecutive rejections, but this changed in 1920 when [[The_Mysterious_Affair_at_Styles|The Mysterious Affair at Styles]], featuring detective Hercule Poirot, was published.
sentence_6: Her first husband was [[Archie_Christie|Archibald Christie]]; they married in 1914 and had one child before divorcing in 1928.
sentence_7: During both World Wars, she served in hospital dispensaries, acquiring a thorough knowledge of the poisons which featured in many of her novels, short stories, and plays.
sentence_8: Following her marriage to [[Archaeologist|archaeologist]] Max Mallowan in 1930, she spent several months each year on [[Excavation_(archaeology)|digs]] in the Middle East and used her first-hand knowledge of his profession in her fiction.
sentence_9: According to [[Index_Translationum|Index Translationum]], she remains the [[List_of_most-translated_individual_authors|most-translated individual author]].
sentence_10: [[And_Then_There_Were_None|And Then There Were None]] is one of the [[List_of_best-selling_books|highest-selling books]] of all time, with approximately 100 million sales.
sentence_11: Christie's stage play The Mousetrap holds the world record for the longest initial run.
sentence_12: It opened at the [[Ambassadors_Theatre_(London)|Ambassadors Theatre]] in the West End of London on 25 November 1952, and by September 2018 there had been more than 27,500 performances.
sentence_13: The play was closed down in March 2020 due to the [[COVID-19_pandemic|coronavirus pandemic]].
sentence_14: In 1955, Christie was the first recipient of the Mystery Writers of America's Grand Master Award.
sentence_15: Later that year, [[Witness_for_the_Prosecution_(play)|Witness for the Prosecution]] received an [[Edgar_Award|Edgar Award]] for best play.
sentence_16: In 2013, she was voted the best crime writer and [[The_Murder_of_Roger_Ackroyd|The Murder of Roger Ackroyd]] the best crime novel ever by 600 professional novelists of the [[Crime_Writers'_Association|Crime Writers' Association]].
sentence_17: In September 2015, And Then There Were None was named the "World's Favourite Christie" in a vote sponsored by the author's estate.
sentence_18: Most of Christie's books and short stories have been adapted for television, radio, video games, and graphic novels.
sentence_19: More than thirty feature films are based on her work.
sentence_20: Agatha Mary Clarissa Miller was born on 15 September 1890 into a wealthy upper-middle-class family in [[Torquay|Torquay]], Devon.
sentence_21: She was the youngest of three children born to [[Frederick_Alvah_Miller|Frederick Alvah Miller]], "a [[Gentleman|gentleman]] of substance", and his wife [[Clarissa_Miller|Clarissa Margaret ("Clara") Miller]] née Boehmer.
sentence_22: Christie's mother Clara was born in [[Dublin|Dublin]] in 1854 to [[British_Army_during_the_Victorian_Era|British Army]] officer [[Frederick_Boehmer|Frederick Boehmer]] and his wife Mary Ann Boehmer (née West).
sentence_23: Boehmer died in [[Jersey|Jersey]] in 1863, leaving his widow to raise Clara and her brothers on a meagre income.
sentence_24: Two weeks after Boehmer's death, Mary's sister Margaret West married widowed dry goods merchant [[Nathaniel_Frary_Miller|Nathaniel Frary Miller]], a US citizen.
sentence_25: To assist Mary financially, they agreed to foster nine-year-old Clara; the family settled in [[Timperley|Timperley]], Cheshire.
sentence_26: Margaret and Nathaniel had no children together, but Nathaniel had a seventeen-year-old son, Fred Miller, from his previous marriage.
sentence_27: Fred was born in [[New_York_City|New York City]] and travelled extensively after leaving his Swiss boarding school.
sentence_28: He and Clara were married in London in 1878.
sentence_29: Their first child, [[Margaret_Watts|Margaret Frary ("Madge")]], was born in Torquay in 1879.
sentence_30: The second, [[Louis_Montant_Miller|Louis Montant ("Monty")]], was born in [[Morristown,_New_Jersey|Morristown, New Jersey]], in 1880, while the family was on an extended visit to the United States.
sentence_31: When Fred's father died in 1869, he left Clara £2,000 (approximately equivalent to £190,000 in 2019); in 1881 they used this to buy the leasehold of a villa in Torquay named [[Ashfield,_Torquay|Ashfield]].
sentence_32: It was here that their third and last child, Agatha, was born in 1890.
sentence_33: She described her childhood as "very happy".
sentence_34: The Millers lived mainly in Devon but often visited her step-grandmother/great-aunt Margaret Miller in [[Ealing|Ealing]] and maternal grandmother Mary Boehmer in [[Bayswater|Bayswater]].
sentence_35: A year was spent abroad with her family, in the [[Pyrenees|French Pyrenees]], Paris, Dinard, and [[Guernsey|Guernsey]].
sentence_36: Because her siblings were so much older, and there were few children in their neighbourhood, Christie spent much of her time playing alone with her pets and imaginary companions.
sentence_37: She eventually made friends with other girls in Torquay, noting that "one of the highlights of my existence" was her appearance with them in a youth production of [[Gilbert_and_Sullivan|Gilbert and Sullivan]]'s [[The_Yeomen_of_the_Guard|The Yeomen of the Guard]], in which she played the hero, Colonel Fairfax.
sentence_38: According to Christie, Clara believed she should not learn to read until she was eight; thanks to her curiosity, she was reading by age four.
sentence_39: Her sister had been sent to a boarding school, but their mother insisted that Christie receive a home education.
sentence_40: As a result, her parents and sister supervised her studies in reading, writing, and basic arithmetic, a subject she particularly enjoyed.
sentence_41: They also taught her music, and she learned to play the piano and the mandolin.
sentence_42: Christie was a voracious reader from an early age.
sentence_43: Among her earliest memories were reading children's books by [[Mary_Louisa_Molesworth|Mrs Molesworth]] and [[Edith_Nesbit|Edith Nesbit]].
sentence_44: When a little older, she moved on to the surreal verse of [[Edward_Lear|Edward Lear]] and [[Lewis_Carroll|Lewis Carroll]].
sentence_45: As an adolescent, she enjoyed works by [[Anthony_Hope|Anthony Hope]], [[Walter_Scott|Walter Scott]], [[Charles_Dickens|Charles Dickens]], and [[Alexandre_Dumas|Alexandre Dumas]].
sentence_46: In April 1901, aged 10, she wrote her first poem, "The Cowslip".
sentence_47: By 1901, her father's health had deteriorated, because of what he believed were heart problems.
sentence_48: Fred died in November 1901 from [[Pneumonia|pneumonia]] and chronic kidney disease.
sentence_49: Christie later said that her father's death when she was eleven marked the end of her childhood.
sentence_50: The family's financial situation had by this time worsened.
sentence_51: Madge married the year after their father's death and moved to [[Cheadle_Hulme|Cheadle]], [[Cheshire|Cheshire]]; Monty was overseas, serving in a British regiment.
sentence_52: Christie now lived alone at Ashfield with her mother.
sentence_53: In 1902, she began attending Miss Guyer's Girls' School in Torquay but found it difficult to adjust to the disciplined atmosphere.
sentence_54: In 1905, her mother sent her to Paris, where she was educated in a series of pensionnats (boarding schools), focusing on voice training and piano playing.
sentence_55: Deciding she lacked the temperament and talent, she gave up her goal of performing professionally as a concert pianist or an opera singer.

section_2.value: Early literary attempts, marriage, literary success: 1907–1926

sentence_56: After completing her education, Christie returned to England to find her mother ailing.
sentence_57: They decided to spend the northern winter of 1907–1908 in the warm climate of Egypt, which was then a regular tourist destination for wealthy Britons.
sentence_58: They stayed for three months at the [[Gezirah_Palace|Gezirah Palace]] Hotel in [[Cairo|Cairo]].
sentence_59: Christie attended many dances and other social functions; she particularly enjoyed watching amateur polo matches.
sentence_60: While they visited some ancient Egyptian monuments such as the [[Great_Pyramid_of_Giza|Great Pyramid of Giza]], she did not exhibit the great interest in [[Archaeology|archaeology]] and [[Egyptology|Egyptology]] that developed in her later years.
sentence_61: Returning to Britain, she continued her social activities, writing and performing in amateur theatricals.
sentence_62: She also helped put on a play called The Blue Beard of Unhappiness with female friends.
sentence_63: At eighteen, Christie wrote her first short story, "The House of Beauty", while recovering in bed from an illness.
sentence_64: It consisted of about 6,000 words on "madness and dreams", a subject of fascination for her.
sentence_65: Her biographer, [[Janet_Morgan,_Lady_Balfour_of_Burleigh|Janet Morgan]], has commented that, despite "infelicities of style", the story was "compelling".
sentence_66: (The story became an early version of her story [[While_the_Light_Lasts_and_Other_Stories|"The House of Dreams"]].)
sentence_67: Other stories followed, most of them illustrating her interest in spiritualism and the [[Paranormal|paranormal]].
sentence_68: These included "[[The_Hound_of_Death#The_Call_of_Wings|The Call of Wings]]" and "The Little Lonely God".
sentence_69: Magazines rejected all her early submissions, made under pseudonyms (including Mac Miller, Nathaniel Miller, and Sydney West); some submissions were later revised and published under her real name, often with new titles.
sentence_70: Around the same time, Christie began work on her first novel, Snow Upon the Desert.
sentence_71: Writing under the pseudonym Monosyllaba, she set the book in Cairo and drew upon her recent experiences there.
sentence_72: She was disappointed when the six publishers she contacted declined the work.
sentence_73: Clara suggested that her daughter ask for advice from the successful novelist [[Eden_Philpotts|Eden Phillpotts]], a family friend and neighbour, who responded to her enquiry, encouraged her writing, and sent her an introduction to his own literary agent, Hughes Massie, who also rejected Snow Upon the Desert but suggested a second novel.
sentence_74: Meanwhile, Christie's social activities expanded, with country house parties, riding, hunting, dances, and roller skating.
sentence_75: She had short-lived relationships with four men and an engagement to another.
sentence_76: In October 1912, she was introduced to [[Archie_Christie|Archibald "Archie" Christie]] at a dance given by [[Baron_Clifford_of_Chudleigh|Lord and Lady Clifford]] at [[Ugbrooke|Ugbrooke]], about 12 miles (19 kilometres) from Torquay.
sentence_77: The son of a [[Barrister|barrister]] in the [[Indian_Civil_Service|Indian Civil Service]], Archie was an army officer who was seconded to the [[Royal_Flying_Corps|Royal Flying Corps]] in April 1913.
sentence_78: The couple quickly fell in love.
sentence_79: Three months after their first meeting, Archie proposed marriage, and Agatha accepted.
sentence_80: With the outbreak of World War I in August 1914, Archie was sent to France to fight.
sentence_81: They married on Christmas Eve 1914 at Emmanuel Church, [[Clifton,_Bristol|Clifton, Bristol]], close to the home of his mother and stepfather, while Archie was on home leave.
sentence_82: Rising through the ranks, he was posted back to Britain in September 1918 as a colonel in the [[Air_Ministry|Air Ministry]].
sentence_83: Christie involved herself in the war effort as a member of the [[Voluntary_Aid_Detachment|Voluntary Aid Detachment]] of the [[Red_Cross|Red Cross]].
sentence_84: From October 1914 to May 1915, then from June 1916 to September 1918, she worked 3,400 hours in the Town Hall Red Cross Hospital, Torquay, first as a nurse (unpaid) then as a dispenser at £16 (approximately equivalent to £900 in 2019) a year from 1917 after qualifying as an apothecaries' assistant.
sentence_85: Her war service ended in September 1918 when Archie was reassigned to London, and they rented a flat in [[St._John's_Wood|St.
sentence_86: John's Wood]].
sentence_87: Christie had long been a fan of detective novels, having enjoyed [[Wilkie_Collins|Wilkie Collins]]'s [[The_Woman_in_White_(novel)|The Woman in White]] and [[The_Moonstone|The Moonstone]], and [[Arthur_Conan_Doyle|Arthur Conan Doyle]]'s early [[Sherlock_Holmes|Sherlock Holmes]] stories.
sentence_88: She wrote her first detective novel, [[The_Mysterious_Affair_at_Styles|The Mysterious Affair at Styles]], in 1916.
sentence_89: It featured [[Hercule_Poirot|Hercule Poirot]], a former Belgian police officer with "magnificent moustaches" and a head "exactly the shape of an egg", who had taken refuge in Britain after Germany invaded Belgium.
sentence_90: Christie's inspiration for the character came from Belgian refugees living in Torquay, and the Belgian soldiers she helped to treat as a volunteer nurse during the First World War.
sentence_91: Her original manuscript was rejected by Hodder & Stoughton and [[Methuen_Publishing|Methuen]].
sentence_92: After keeping the submission for several months, [[John_Lane_(publisher)|John Lane]] at The Bodley Head offered to accept it, provided that Christie change how the solution was revealed.
sentence_93: She did so, and signed a contract committing her next five books to The Bodley Head, which she later felt was exploitative.
sentence_94: It was published in 1920.
sentence_95: Christie settled into married life, giving birth to her only child, [[Rosalind_Hicks|Rosalind Margaret Clarissa]] (later Hicks), in August 1919 at Ashfield.
sentence_96: Archie left the Air Force at the end of the war and began working in [[The_City_of_London|the City]] financial sector at a relatively low salary.
sentence_97: They still employed a maid.
sentence_98: Her second novel, [[The_Secret_Adversary|The Secret Adversary]] (1922), featured a new detective couple [[Tommy_and_Tuppence|Tommy and Tuppence]], again published by The Bodley Head.
sentence_99: It earned her £50 (approximately equivalent to £2,800 in 2019).
sentence_100: A third novel, [[Murder_on_the_Links|Murder on the Links]], again featured Poirot, as did the short stories commissioned by [[Bruce_Ingram|Bruce Ingram]], editor of [[The_Sketch|The Sketch]] magazine, from 1923.
sentence_101: She now had no difficulty selling her work.
sentence_102: In 1922, the Christies joined an around-the-world promotional tour for the [[British_Empire_Exhibition|British Empire Exhibition]], led by Major [[Ernest_Belcher|Ernest Belcher]].
sentence_103: Leaving their daughter with Agatha's mother and sister, in ten months they travelled to South Africa, Australia, New Zealand, Hawaii, and Canada.
sentence_104: They learned to [[Surfing|surf]] prone in South Africa; then, in Waikiki, they were among the first Britons to surf standing up.
sentence_105: When they returned to England, Archie resumed work in the city, and Christie continued to work hard at her writing.
sentence_106: After living in a series of apartments in London, they bought a house in [[Sunningdale|Sunningdale]], Berkshire, which they renamed Styles after the mansion in Christie's first detective novel.
sentence_107: Christie's mother, [[Clarissa_Miller|Clarissa Miller]], died in April 1926.
sentence_108: They had been exceptionally close, and the loss sent Christie into a deep depression.
sentence_109: In August 1926, reports appeared in the press that Christie had gone to a village near [[Biarritz|Biarritz]] to recuperate from a "breakdown" caused by "overwork".
sentence_110: In August 1926, Archie asked Christie for a divorce.
sentence_111: He had fallen in love with Nancy Neele, a friend of Major Belcher.
sentence_112: On 3 December 1926, the pair quarrelled after Archie announced his plan to spend the weekend with friends, unaccompanied by his wife.
sentence_113: Christie's mother had also passed away recently.
sentence_114: Late that evening, Christie disappeared from their home.
sentence_115: The following morning, her car, a [[Morris_Cowley|Morris Cowley]], was discovered at [[Newlands_Corner|Newlands Corner]], parked above a chalk quarry with an expired driving licence and clothes inside.
sentence_116: The disappearance quickly became a news story, as the press sought to satisfy their readers' "hunger for sensation, disaster, and scandal".
sentence_117: Home secretary [[William_Joynson-Hicks|William Joynson-Hicks]] pressured police, and a newspaper offered a £100 reward (approximately equivalent to £6,000 in 2019).
sentence_118: More than a thousand police officers, 15,000 volunteers, and several aeroplanes searched the rural landscape.
sentence_119: [[Sir_Arthur_Conan_Doyle|Sir Arthur Conan Doyle]] gave a spirit medium one of Christie's gloves to find her.
sentence_120: Christie's disappearance was featured on the front page of [[The_New_York_Times|The New York Times]].
sentence_121: Despite the extensive manhunt, she was not found for another ten days.
sentence_122: On 14 December 1926, she was located at the [[Old_Swan_Hotel|Swan Hydropathic Hotel]] in [[Harrogate|Harrogate]], Yorkshire, registered as Mrs Tressa Neele (the surname of her husband's lover) from "Capetown [[Sic|sic]] S.A." (South Africa).
sentence_123: The next day, Christie left for her sister's residence at [[Abney_Hall|Abney Hall]], Cheadle, where she was sequestered "in guarded hall, gates locked, telephone cut off, and callers turned away".
sentence_124: Christie's autobiography makes no reference to the disappearance.
sentence_125: Two doctors diagnosed her as suffering from "an unquestionable genuine loss of memory", yet opinion remains divided over the reason for her disappearance.
sentence_126: Some, including her biographer Morgan, believe she disappeared during a [[Fugue_state|fugue state]].
sentence_127: The author Jared Cade concluded that Christie planned the event to embarrass her husband but did not anticipate the resulting public melodrama.
sentence_128: Christie biographer Laura Thompson provides an alternative view that Christie disappeared during a nervous breakdown, conscious of her actions but not in emotional control of herself.
sentence_129: Public reaction at the time was largely negative, supposing a publicity stunt or an attempt to frame her husband for murder.
sentence_130: In January 1927, Christie, looking "very pale", sailed with her daughter and secretary to [[Las_Palmas|Las Palmas]], Canary Islands, to "complete her convalescence", returning three months later.
sentence_131: Christie petitioned for divorce and was granted a [[Decree_nisi|decree nisi]] against her husband in April 1928, which was made absolute in October 1928.
sentence_132: Archie married Nancy Neele a week later.
sentence_133: Christie retained custody of their daughter, Rosalind, and kept the Christie surname for her writing.
sentence_134: Reflecting on the period in her autobiography, Christie wrote, "So, after illness, came sorrow, despair and heartbreak.
sentence_135: There is no need to dwell on it."
sentence_136: In 1928 Christie left England and took the [[Orient_Express|(Simplon) Orient Express]] to [[Istanbul|Istanbul]] and then to [[Baghdad|Baghdad]].
sentence_137: In Iraq, she became friends with archaeologist [[Leonard_Woolley|Leonard Woolley]] and his wife, who invited her to return to their dig in February 1930.
sentence_138: On that second trip, she met an archaeologist, thirteen years her junior, Max Mallowan.
sentence_139: In a 1977 interview, Mallowan recounted his first meeting with Christie, when he took her and a group of tourists on a tour of his expedition site in Iraq.
sentence_140: Christie and Mallowan married in [[Edinburgh|Edinburgh]] in September 1930.
sentence_141: Their marriage lasted until Christie's death in 1976.
sentence_142: She accompanied Mallowan on his archaeological expeditions, and her travels with him contributed background to several of her novels set in the Middle East.
sentence_143: Other novels (such as [[Peril_at_End_House|Peril At End House]]) were set in and around Torquay, where she was raised.
sentence_144: Christie drew on her experience of international train travel when writing her 1934 novel [[Murder_on_the_Orient_Express|Murder on the Orient Express]].
sentence_145: The Pera Palace Hotel in Istanbul, the southern terminus of the railway, claims the book was written there and maintains Christie's room as a memorial to the author.
sentence_146: Christie and Mallowan lived in [[Chelsea,_London|Chelsea]], first in Cresswell Place and later in Sheffield Terrace.
sentence_147: Both properties are now marked by [[Blue_plaque|blue plaques]].
sentence_148: In 1934, they bought Winterbrook House in [[Winterbrook|Winterbrook]], a hamlet near Wallingford.
sentence_149: This was their main residence for the rest of their lives and the place where Christie did much of her writing.
sentence_150: This house also bears a blue plaque.
sentence_151: Christie led a quiet life despite being known in Wallingford; from 1951 to 1976 she served as president of the local [[Amateur_dramatic_society|amateur dramatic society]].
sentence_152: The couple acquired the [[Greenway_Estate|Greenway Estate]] in Devon as a summer residence in 1938, which was given to the [[National_Trust_for_Places_of_Historic_Interest_or_Natural_Beauty|National Trust]] in 2000.
sentence_153: Christie frequently stayed at Abney Hall, Cheshire, which was owned by her brother-in-law, James Watts, and based at least two stories there: a short story "[[The_Adventure_of_the_Christmas_Pudding|The Adventure of the Christmas Pudding]]" in the story collection of the same name and the novel [[After_the_Funeral|After the Funeral]].
sentence_154: One Christie compendium notes that "Abney became Agatha's greatest inspiration for country-house life, with all its servants and grandeur being woven into her plots.
sentence_155: The descriptions of the fictional Chimneys, Stonygates, and other houses in her stories are mostly Abney Hall in various forms."
sentence_156: During World War II, Christie worked in the pharmacy at [[University_College_Hospital|University College Hospital]] (UCH), London, where she updated her knowledge of poisons.
sentence_157: Her later novel [[The_Pale_Horse|The Pale Horse]] was based on a suggestion from Harold Davis, the chief pharmacist at UCH.
sentence_158: In 1977, a [[Thallium_poisoning|thallium poisoning]] case was solved by British medical personnel who had read Christie's book and recognised the symptoms she described.
sentence_159: The British intelligence agency [[MI5|MI5]] investigated Christie after a character called Major Bletchley appeared in her 1941 thriller [[N_or_M?|N or M?
sentence_160: ]], which was about a hunt for a pair of deadly [[Fifth_column|fifth columnists]] in wartime England.
sentence_161: MI5 was concerned that Christie had a spy in Britain's top-secret codebreaking centre, [[Bletchley_Park|Bletchley Park]].
sentence_162: The agency's fears were allayed when Christie told her friend, the codebreaker [[Dilly_Knox|Dilly Knox]], "I was stuck there on my way by train from Oxford to London and took revenge by giving the name to one of my least lovable characters."
sentence_163: Christie was elected a fellow of the [[Royal_Society_of_Literature|Royal Society of Literature]] in 1950.
sentence_164: In honour of her many literary works, Christie was appointed [[Commander_of_the_Order_of_the_British_Empire|Commander of the Order of the British Empire]] (CBE) in the [[1956_New_Year_Honours|1956 New Year Honours]].
sentence_165: She was co-president of the Detection Club from 1958 to her death in 1976.
sentence_166: In 1961, she was awarded an honorary Doctor of Literature [[Honorary_degree|degree]] by the [[University_of_Exeter|University of Exeter]].
sentence_167: In the [[1971_New_Year_Honours|1971 New Year Honours]], she was promoted to [[Dame_Commander_of_the_Order_of_the_British_Empire|Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire]] (DBE), three years after her husband had been knighted for his archaeological work.
sentence_168: After her husband's knighthood, Christie could also be [[Style_(manner_of_address)|styled]] Lady Mallowan.
sentence_169: From 1971 to 1974, Christie's health began to fail, but she continued to write.
sentence_170: Her last novel was [[Postern_of_Fate|Postern of Fate]] in 1973.
sentence_171: Using textual analysis, Canadian researchers suggested in 2009 that Christie may have begun to suffer from [[Alzheimer's_disease|Alzheimer's disease]] or other [[Dementia|dementia]].
sentence_172: In 1946, Christie said of herself: "My chief dislikes are crowds, loud noises, gramophones and cinemas.
sentence_173: I dislike the taste of alcohol and do not like smoking.
sentence_174: I do like sun, sea, flowers, travelling, strange foods, sports, concerts, theatres, pianos, and doing embroidery."
sentence_175: Christie's works of fiction contain some objectionable character [[Stereotypes|stereotypes]], but in real life, many of her biases were positive.
sentence_176: After four years of war-torn London, Christie hoped to return some day to Syria, which she described as a "gentle fertile country and its simple people, who know how to laugh and how to enjoy life; who are idle and gay, and who have dignity, good manners, and a great sense of humour, and to whom death is not terrible".
sentence_177: Christie was a lifelong, "quietly devout" member of the Church of England, attended church regularly, and kept her mother's copy of [[The_Imitation_of_Christ|The Imitation of Christ]] by her bedside.
sentence_178: After her divorce, she stopped taking the [[Sacrament|sacrament]] of [[Eucharist|communion]].
sentence_179: The Agatha Christie Trust For Children was established in 1969, and shortly after Christie's death a charitable memorial fund was set up to "help two causes that she favoured: old people and young children".
sentence_180: Christie's obituary in [[The_Times|The Times]] notes that "she never cared much for the cinema, or for wireless and television."
sentence_181: Further,
sentence_182: Christie died peacefully on 12 January 1976 at age 85 from natural causes at home at Winterbrook House.
sentence_183: When her death was announced, two [[West_End_theatre|West End]] theatres – the [[St_Martin's_Theatre|St.
sentence_184: Martin's]], where [[The_Mousetrap|The Mousetrap]] was playing, and [[Savoy_Theatre|the Savoy]], which was home to a revival of Murder at the Vicarage – dimmed their outside lights in her honour.
sentence_185: She was buried in the nearby churchyard of St Mary's, Cholsey, in a plot she had chosen with her husband ten years before.
sentence_186: The simple funeral service was attended by about 20 newspaper and TV reporters, some having travelled from as far away as South America.
sentence_187: Thirty wreaths adorned Christie's grave, including one from the cast of her long-running play The Mousetrap and one sent "on behalf of the multitude of grateful readers" by the Ulverscroft Large Print Book Publishers.
sentence_188: Mallowan, who remarried in 1977, died in 1978 and was buried next to Christie.

section_8.value: Estate and subsequent ownership of works

sentence_189: Christie was unhappy about becoming "an employed wage slave", and for tax reasons set up a [[Private_limited_company|private company]] in 1955, Agatha Christie Limited, to hold the rights to her works.
sentence_190: In about 1959 she transferred her 278-acre home, Greenway Estate, to her daughter, [[Rosalind_Hicks|Rosalind Hicks]].
sentence_191: In 1968, when Christie was almost 80, she sold a 51% stake in Agatha Christie Limited (and the works it owned) to Booker Books (better known as [[Booker_Group#Booker_Author's_Division|Booker Author's Division]]), which by 1977 had increased its stake to 64%.
sentence_192: Agatha Christie Limited still owns the worldwide rights for more than eighty of Christie's novels and short stories, nineteen plays, and nearly forty TV films.
sentence_193: In the late 1950s, Christie had reputedly been earning around £100,000 (approximately equivalent to £2,400,000 in 2019) per year.
sentence_194: Christie sold an estimated 300 million books during her lifetime.
sentence_195: One estimate of her total earnings from more than a half-century of writing is $20 million (approximately $89.9 million in 2019).
sentence_196: As a result of her tax planning, her will left only £106,683 (approximately equivalent to £773,000 in 2019) net, which went mostly to her husband and daughter along with some smaller bequests.
sentence_197: Her remaining 36% share of Agatha Christie Limited was inherited by Hicks, who passionately preserved her mother's works, image, and legacy until her own death 28 years later.
sentence_198: The family's share of the company allowed them to appoint 50% of the board and the chairman, and retain a veto over new treatments, updated versions, and republications of her works.
sentence_199: In 2004, Hicks' obituary in [[The_Daily_Telegraph|The Telegraph]] noted that she had been "determined to remain true to her mother's vision and to protect the integrity of her creations" and disapproved of "[[Merchandising|merchandising]]" activities.
sentence_200: Upon her death on 28 October 2004, the Greenway Estate passed to her son [[Mathew_Prichard|Mathew Prichard]].
sentence_201: After his stepfather's death in 2005, Prichard donated Greenway and its contents to the [[National_Trust_for_Places_of_Historic_Interest_or_Natural_Beauty|National Trust]].
sentence_202: Christie's family and [[Trust_(law)|family trusts]], including great-grandson James Prichard, continue to own the 36% stake in Agatha Christie Limited, and remain associated with the company.
sentence_203: In 2020, James Prichard was the company's chairman.
sentence_204: [[Mathew_Prichard|Mathew Prichard]] also holds the [[Copyright|copyright]] to some of his grandmother's later literary works including The Mousetrap.
sentence_205: Christie's work continues to be developed in a range of adaptations.
sentence_206: In 1998, Booker sold its shares in Agatha Christie Limited (at the time earning £2,100,000, approximately equivalent to £3,700,000 in 2019 annual revenue) for £10,000,000 (approximately equivalent to £17,700,000 in 2019) to [[Chorion_(company)|Chorion]], whose portfolio of authors' works included the literary estates of [[Enid_Blyton|Enid Blyton]] and Dennis Wheatley.
sentence_207: In February 2012, after a management buyout, Chorion began to sell off its literary assets.
sentence_208: This included the sale of Chorion's 64% stake in Agatha Christie Limited to Acorn Media UK.
sentence_209: In 2014, [[RLJ_Companies|RLJ Entertainment Inc.]] (RJLE) acquired Acorn Media UK, renamed it [[Acorn_DVD|Acorn Media Enterprises]], and incorporated it as the RLJE UK development arm.
sentence_210: In late February 2014, media reports stated that the [[BBC|BBC]] had acquired exclusive TV rights to Christie's works in the UK (previously associated with [[ITV_(TV_network)|ITV]]) and made plans with Acorn's co-operation to air new productions for the 125th anniversary of Christie's birth in 2015.
sentence_211: As part of that deal, the BBC broadcast [[Partners_in_Crime_(UK_TV_series)|Partners in Crime]] and [[And_Then_There_Were_None_(miniseries)|And Then There Were None]], both in 2015.
sentence_212: Subsequent productions have included [[The_Witness_for_the_Prosecution_(miniseries)|The Witness for the Prosecution]] but plans to televise [[Ordeal_by_Innocence_(TV_series)|Ordeal by Innocence]] at Christmas 2017 were delayed because of controversy surrounding one of the cast members.
sentence_213: The three-part adaptation aired in April 2018.
sentence_214: A [[The_ABC_Murders_(TV_series)|three-part adaptation]] of [[The_A.B.C._Murders|The A.B.C.
sentence_215: Murders]] starring [[John_Malkovich|John Malkovich]] and [[Rupert_Grint|Rupert Grint]] began filming in June 2018 and was first broadcast in December 2018.
sentence_216: A two-part adaptation of [[The_Pale_Horse|The Pale Horse]] was broadcast on BBC1 in February 2020.
sentence_217: [[Death_Comes_as_the_End|Death Comes as the End]] will be the next BBC adaptation.
sentence_218: Main article: [[Agatha_Christie_bibliography|Agatha Christie bibliography]]
sentence_219: Christie's first published book, [[The_Mysterious_Affair_at_Styles|The Mysterious Affair at Styles]], was released in 1920 and introduced the detective [[Hercule_Poirot|Hercule Poirot]], who appeared in thirty-three of her novels and more than fifty short stories.
sentence_220: The Poirot stories are being continued by Sophie Hannah with books including The Monogram Murders, [[Closed_Casket_(novel)|Closed Casket]], and The Mystery of Three Quarters.
sentence_221: Over the years, Christie grew tired of Poirot, much as Conan Doyle did with Sherlock Holmes.
sentence_222: By the end of the 1930s, Christie wrote in her diary that she was finding Poirot "insufferable", and by the 1960s she felt he was "an egocentric creep".
sentence_223: Thompson believes Christie's occasional antipathy to her creation is overstated, and points out that "in later life she sought to protect him against misrepresentation as powerfully as if he were her own flesh and blood."
sentence_224: Unlike Conan Doyle, she resisted the temptation to kill her detective off while he was still popular.
sentence_225: She married off Poirot's "[[Dr._Watson|Watson]]", Captain Arthur Hastings, in an attempt to trim her cast commitments.
sentence_226: [[Miss_Marple|Miss Jane Marple]] was introduced in a series of short stories that began publication in December 1927 and were subsequently collected under the title [[The_Thirteen_Problems|The Thirteen Problems]].
sentence_227: Marple was a genteel, elderly spinster who solved crimes using analogies to English village life.
sentence_228: Christie said, "Miss Marple was not in any way a picture of my grandmother; she was far more fussy and spinsterish than my grandmother ever was," but her autobiography establishes a firm connection between the fictional character and Christie's step-grandmother Margaret Miller ("Auntie-Grannie") and her "Ealing cronies".
sentence_229: Both Marple and Miller "always expected the worst of everyone and everything, and were, with almost frightening accuracy, usually proved right".
sentence_230: Marple appeared in twelve novels and twenty stories.
sentence_231: During the Second World War, Christie wrote two novels, [[Curtain_(novel)|Curtain]] and [[Sleeping_Murder|Sleeping Murder]], featuring Hercule Poirot and Miss Marple, respectively.
sentence_232: Both books were sealed in a [[Bank_vault|bank vault]], and she made over the copyrights by deed of gift to her daughter and her husband to provide each with a kind of insurance policy.
sentence_233: Christie suffered a heart attack and a serious fall in 1974, after which she was unable to write.
sentence_234: Her daughter authorised the publication of Curtain in 1975, and Sleeping Murder was published posthumously in 1976.
sentence_235: These publications followed the success of the [[Murder_on_the_Orient_Express_(1974_film)|1974 film version]] of Murder on the Orient Express.
sentence_236: Shortly before the publication of Curtain, Poirot became the first fictional character to have an obituary in The New York Times, which was printed on page one on 6 August 1975.
sentence_237: Christie never wrote a novel or short story featuring both Poirot and Miss Marple.
sentence_238: In a recording discovered and released in 2008, Christie revealed the reason for this: "Hercule Poirot, a complete egoist, would not like being taught his business or having suggestions made to him by an elderly spinster lady.
sentence_239: Hercule Poirot – a professional sleuth – would not be at home at all in Miss Marple's world."
sentence_240: In 2013, the Christie family supported the release of a new Poirot story, The Monogram Murders, written by British author Sophie Hannah.
sentence_241: Hannah later published two more Poirot mysteries, [[Closed_Casket_(novel)|Closed Casket]] in 2016 and The Mystery of Three Quarters in 2018.
sentence_242: Christie has been called the "Duchess of Death", the "Mistress of Mystery", and the "Queen of Crime".
sentence_243: Early in her career, a reporter noted that "her plots are possible, logical, and always new."
sentence_244: According to Hannah, "At the start of each novel, she shows us an apparently impossible situation and we go mad wondering 'How can this be happening?'
sentence_245: Then, slowly, she reveals how the impossible is not only possible but the only thing that could have happened."
sentence_246: She developed her storytelling techniques during what has been called the [[Golden_Age_of_Detective_Fiction|"Golden Age"]] of detective fiction.
sentence_247: Author Dilys Winn called Christie "the doyenne of Coziness", a sub-genre which "featured a small village setting, a hero with faintly aristocratic family connections, a plethora of red herrings and a tendency to commit homicide with sterling silver letter openers and poisons imported from Paraguay".
sentence_248: At the end, in a Christie hallmark, the detective usually gathers the surviving suspects into one room, explains the course of their deductive reasoning, and reveals the guilty party; there are exceptions where it is left to the guilty party to explain all (such as And Then There Were None and [[Endless_Night_(novel)|Endless Night]]).
sentence_249: Christie did not limit herself to quaint English villages – the action might take place on a small island (And Then There Were None), an aeroplane ([[Death_in_the_Clouds|Death in the Clouds]]), a train (Murder on the Orient Express), a steamship ([[Death_on_the_Nile|Death on the Nile]]), a smart London flat ([[Cards_on_the_Table|Cards on the Table]]), a resort in the West Indies ([[A_Caribbean_Mystery|A Caribbean Mystery]]), or an archaeological dig ([[Murder_in_Mesopotamia|Murder in Mesopotamia]]) – but the circle of potential suspects is usually closed and intimate: family members, friends, servants, business associates, fellow travellers.
sentence_250: Stereotyped characters abound (the femme fatale, the stolid policeman, the devoted servant, the dull colonel), but these may be subverted to stymie the reader; impersonations and secret alliances are always possible.
sentence_251: There is always a motive – most often, money: "There are very few killers in Christie who enjoy murder for its own sake."
sentence_252: Professor of Pharmacology Michael C. Gerald noted that "in over half her novels, one or more victims are poisoned, albeit not always to the full satisfaction of the perpetrator."
sentence_253: Guns, knives, garrottes, tripwires, blunt instruments, and even a hatchet were also used, but "Christie never resorted to elaborate mechanical or scientific means to explain her ingenuity," according to [[Agatha_Christie's_Secret_Notebooks|John Curran]], author and literary adviser to the Christie estate.
sentence_254: Many of her clues are mundane objects: a calendar, a coffee cup, wax flowers, a beer bottle, a fireplace used during a heat wave.
sentence_255: According to crime writer [[P._D._James|P.
sentence_256: D. James]], Christie was prone to making the unlikeliest character the guilty party.
sentence_257: Alert readers could sometimes identify the culprit by identifying the least likely suspect.
sentence_258: Christie mocked this insight in her Foreword to Cards on the Table: "Spot the person least likely to have committed the crime and in nine times out of ten your task is finished.
sentence_259: Since I do not want my faithful readers to fling away this book in disgust, I prefer to warn them beforehand that this is not that kind of book."
sentence_260: On [[Desert_Island_Discs|Desert Island Discs]] in 2007, [[Brian_Aldiss|Brian Aldiss]] said Christie had told him she wrote her books up to the last chapter, then decided who the most unlikely suspect was, after which she would go back and make the necessary changes to "frame" that person.
sentence_261: Based upon a study of her working notebooks, Curran describes how Christie would first create a cast of characters, choose a setting, and then produce a list of scenes in which specific clues would be revealed; the order of scenes would be revised as she developed her plot.
sentence_262: Of necessity, the murderer had to be known to the author before the sequence could be finalised and she began to type or dictate the first draft of her novel.
sentence_263: Much of the work, particularly dialogue, was done in her head before she put it on paper.
sentence_264: In 2013, the 600 members of the [[Crime_Writers'_Association|Crime Writers' Association]] chose [[The_Murder_of_Roger_Ackroyd|The Murder of Roger Ackroyd]] as "the best [[Whodunit|whodunit]] ... ever written".
sentence_265: Author Julian Symons observed, "In an obvious sense, the book fits within the conventions ...
sentence_266: The setting is a village deep within the English countryside, Roger Ackroyd dies in his study; there is a butler who behaves suspiciously ... Every successful detective story in this period involved a deceit practised upon the reader, and here the trick is the highly original one of making the murderer the local doctor, who tells the story and acts as Poirot's Watson."
sentence_267: Critic Sutherland Scott stated, "If Agatha Christie had made no other contribution to the literature of detective fiction she would still deserve our grateful thanks" for writing this novel.
sentence_268: In September 2015, to mark her 125th birthday, And Then There Were None was named the "World's Favourite Christie" in a vote sponsored by the author's estate.
sentence_269: The novel is emblematic of both her use of formula and her willingness to discard it.
sentence_270: "And Then There Were None carries the 'closed society' type of murder mystery to extreme lengths," according to author Charles Osborne.
sentence_271: It begins with the classic set-up of potential victim(s) and killer(s) isolated from the outside world, but then violates conventions.
sentence_272: There is no detective involved in the action, no interviews of suspects, no careful search for clues, and no suspects gathered together in the last chapter to be confronted with the solution.
sentence_273: As Christie herself said, "Ten people had to die without it becoming ridiculous or the murderer being obvious."
sentence_274: Critics agreed she had succeeded: "The arrogant Mrs. Christie this time set herself a fearsome test of her own ingenuity ... the reviews, not surprisingly, were without exception wildly adulatory."
sentence_275: For information on Christie's book originally titled Ten Little Niggers, see [[And_Then_There_Were_None|And Then There Were None]].
sentence_276: Christie included stereotyped descriptions of characters in her work, especially before 1945 (when such attitudes were more commonly expressed publicly), particularly in regard to Italians, Jews, and non-Europeans.
sentence_277: For example, she described "men of [[Hebrews|Hebraic]] extraction, sallow men with hooked noses, wearing rather flamboyant jewellery" in the short story "The Soul of the Croupier" from the collection [[The_Mysterious_Mr_Quin|The Mysterious Mr Quin]].
sentence_278: In 1947, the [[Anti-Defamation_League|Anti-Defamation League]] in the US sent an official letter of complaint to Christie's American publishers, Dodd, Mead and Company, regarding perceived [[Antisemitism|antisemitism]] in her works.
sentence_279: Christie's British literary agent later wrote to her US representative, authorising American publishers to "omit the word 'Jew' when it refers to an unpleasant character in future books."
sentence_280: In [[The_Hollow|The Hollow]], published in 1946, one of the characters is "a Whitechapel Jewess with dyed hair and a voice like a [[Corncrake|corncrake]] ... a small woman with a thick nose, henna red and a disagreeable voice".
sentence_281: To contrast with the more stereotyped descriptions, Christie portrayed some "foreign" characters as victims, or potential victims, at the hands of English malefactors, such as, respectively, Olga Seminoff ([[Hallowe'en_Party|Hallowe'en Party]]) and Katrina Reiger (in the short story "How Does Your Garden Grow?").
sentence_282: Jewish characters are often seen as un-English (such as Oliver Manders in [[Three_Act_Tragedy|Three Act Tragedy]]), but they are rarely the culprits.
sentence_283: In addition to Poirot and Marple, Christie also created amateur detectives Thomas Beresford and his wife, Prudence "Tuppence" née Cowley, who appear in four novels and one collection of short stories published between 1922 and 1974.
sentence_284: Unlike her other sleuths, the Beresfords were only in their early twenties when introduced in The Secret Adversary, and were allowed to age alongside their creator.
sentence_285: She treated their stories with a lighter touch, giving them a "dash and verve" which was not universally admired by critics.
sentence_286: Their last adventure, Postern of Fate, was Christie's last novel.
sentence_287: Harley Quin was "easily the most unorthodox" of Christie's fictional detectives.
sentence_288: Inspired by Christie's affection for the figures from the [[Harlequinade|Harlequinade]], the semi-supernatural Quin always works with an elderly, conventional man called Satterthwaite.
sentence_289: The pair appear in fourteen short stories, twelve of which were collected in 1930 as The Mysterious Mr. Quin.
sentence_290: Mallowan described these tales as "detection in a fanciful vein, touching on the fairy story, a natural product of Agatha's peculiar imagination".
sentence_291: Satterthwaite also appears in a novel, Three Act Tragedy, and a short story, "[[Murder_in_the_Mews|Dead Man's Mirror]]", both of which feature Poirot.
sentence_292: Another of her lesser-known characters is Parker Pyne, a retired civil servant who assists unhappy people in an unconventional manner.
sentence_293: The twelve short stories which introduced him, [[Parker_Pyne_Investigates|Parker Pyne Investigates]] (1934), are best remembered for "The Case of the Discontented Soldier", which features Ariadne Oliver, "an amusing and satirical self-portrait of Agatha Christie".
sentence_294: Over the ensuing decades, Oliver reappeared in seven novels.
sentence_295: In most of them she assists Poirot.
sentence_296: In 1928, [[Michael_Morton_(dramatist)|Michael Morton]] adapted The Murder of Roger Ackroyd for the stage under the title [[Alibi_(play)|Alibi]].
sentence_297: The play enjoyed a respectable run, but Christie disliked the changes made to her work and, in future, preferred to write for the theatre herself.
sentence_298: The first of her own stage works was [[Black_Coffee_(play)|Black Coffee]], which received good reviews when it opened in the [[West_End_theatre|West End]] in late 1930.
sentence_299: She followed this up with adaptations of her detective novels: [[And_Then_There_Were_None_(play)|And Then There Were None]] in 1943, [[Appointment_with_Death_(play)|Appointment with Death]] in 1945, and [[The_Hollow_(play)|The Hollow]] in 1951.
sentence_300: In the 1950s, "the theatre ... engaged much of Agatha's attention."
sentence_301: She next adapted her short radio play into [[The_Mousetrap|The Mousetrap]], which premiered in the West End in 1952, produced by [[Peter_Saunders_(impresario)|Peter Saunders]].
sentence_302: Her expectations for the play were not high; she believed it would run no more than eight months.
sentence_303: It has long since made theatrical history, staging its 27,500th performance in September 2018.
sentence_304: The play closed down in March 2020, when all UK theatres shut due to the [[COVID-19_pandemic|coronavirus pandemic]].
sentence_305: In 1953, she followed this with [[Witness_for_the_Prosecution_(play)|Witness for the Prosecution]], whose [[Broadway_theatre|Broadway]] production won the [[New_York_Drama_Critics'_Circle|New York Drama Critics' Circle]] award for best foreign play of 1954 and earned Christie an [[Edgar_Award|Edgar Award]] from the Mystery Writers of America.
sentence_306: [[Spider's_Web_(play)|Spider's Web]], an original work written for actress [[Margaret_Lockwood|Margaret Lockwood]] at her request, premiered in 1954 and was also a hit.
sentence_307: she is also the first female playwright to have three plays running simultaneously in London's West End.
sentence_308: Along with The Mousetrap the plays included were Witness for the Prosecution and Spider's Web Christie said, "Plays are much easier to write than books, because you can see them in your mind's eye, you are not hampered by all that description which clogs you so terribly in a book and stops you from getting on with what's happening."
sentence_309: In a letter to her daughter, Christie said being a playwright was "a lot of fun!
sentence_311: Christie published six mainstream novels under the name Mary Westmacott, a pseudonym which gave her the freedom to explore "her most private and precious imaginative garden".
sentence_312: These books typically received better reviews than her detective and thriller fiction.
sentence_313: Of the first, [[Giant's_Bread|Giant's Bread]] published in 1930, a reviewer for The New York Times wrote, "... her book is far above the average of current fiction, in fact, comes well under the classification of a 'good book'.
sentence_314: And it is only a satisfying novel that can claim that appellation."
sentence_315: After her authorship of the first four Westmacott novels was revealed by a journalist in 1949, she wrote two more, the last in 1956.
sentence_316: The other Westmacott titles are: [[Unfinished_Portrait_(novel)|Unfinished Portrait]] (1934), Absent in the Spring (1944), The Rose and the Yew Tree (1948), [[A_Daughter's_a_Daughter|A Daughter's a Daughter]] (1952), and The Burden (1956).
sentence_317: Christie published few non-fiction works.
sentence_318: Come, Tell Me How You Live, about working on an archaeological dig, was drawn from her life with Mallowan.
sentence_319: The Grand Tour: Around the World with the Queen of Mystery is a collection of correspondence from her 1922 Grand Tour of the British empire, including South Africa, Australia, New Zealand, and Canada.
sentence_320: Agatha Christie: An Autobiography was published posthumously in 1977 and adjudged the Best Critical / Biographical Work at the 1978 Edgar Awards.
sentence_321: Many of Christie's works from 1940 onward have titles drawn from literature, with the original context of the title typically printed as an [[Epigraph_(literature)|epigraph]].
sentence_322: The inspirations for some of Christie's titles include:

list.value: [[William_Shakespeare|William Shakespeare]]'s works: [[Sad_Cypress|Sad Cypress]], [[By_the_Pricking_of_My_Thumbs|By the Pricking of My Thumbs]], [[Taken_at_the_Flood|There is a Tide ...]], [[Absent_in_the_Spring|Absent in the Spring]], and The Mousetrap, for example. Osborne notes that "Shakespeare is the writer most quoted in the works of Agatha Christie";
The [[Bible|Bible]]: [[Evil_Under_the_Sun|Evil Under the Sun]], [[The_Burden|The Burden]], and The Pale Horse;

Other works of literature: [[The_Mirror_Crack'd_from_Side_to_Side|The Mirror Crack'd from Side to Side]] (from [[Tennyson|Tennyson]]'s "[[The_Lady_of_Shalott|The Lady of Shalott]]"), [[The_Moving_Finger|The Moving Finger]] (from [[Edward_FitzGerald_(poet)|Edward FitzGerald]]'s translation of the [[Rubáiyát_of_Omar_Khayyám|Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám]]), [[The_Rose_and_the_Yew_Tree|The Rose and the Yew Tree]] (from [[T._S._Eliot|T. S. Eliot]]'s [[Four_Quartets|Four Quartets]]), Postern of Fate (from [[James_Elroy_Flecker|James Elroy Flecker]]'s "Gates of Damascus"), Endless Night (from [[William_Blake|William Blake]]'s Auguries of Innocence), N or M? (from the [[Book_of_Common_Prayer|Book of Common Prayer]]), and [[Come,_Tell_Me_How_You_Live|Come, Tell Me How You Live]] (from Lewis Carroll's [[Through_the_Looking-Glass|Through the Looking-Glass]]).

sentence_323: Christie biographer Gillian Gill said, "Christie's writing has the sparseness, the directness, the narrative pace, and the universal appeal of the fairy story, and it is perhaps as modern fairy stories for grown-up children that Christie's novels succeed."
sentence_324: Reflecting a juxtaposition of innocence and horror, numerous Christie titles were drawn from well-known children's [[Nursery_rhyme|nursery rhymes]]: And Then There Were None (from "[[And_Then_There_Were_None#19th-century_original_verses|Ten Little Niggers]]"), [[One,_Two,_Buckle_My_Shoe_(novel)|One, Two, Buckle My Shoe]] (from "[[One,_Two,_Buckle_My_Shoe|One, Two, Buckle My Shoe]]"), Five Little Pigs (from "[[This_Little_Piggy|This Little Piggy]]"), [[Crooked_House|Crooked House]] (from "[[There_Was_a_Crooked_Man|There Was a Crooked Man]]"), [[A_Pocket_Full_of_Rye|A Pocket Full of Rye]] (from "[[Sing_a_Song_of_Sixpence|Sing a Song of Sixpence]]"), [[Hickory_Dickory_Dock_(novel)|Hickory Dickory Dock]] (from "[[Hickory_Dickory_Dock|Hickory Dickory Dock]]"), and [[Three_Blind_Mice_and_Other_Stories|Three Blind Mice]] (from "[[Three_Blind_Mice|Three Blind Mice]]").
sentence_325: Christie is regularly referred to as the "Queen of Crime" or "Queen of Mystery", and is considered a master of suspense, plotting, and characterisation.
sentence_326: In 1955, she became the first recipient of the Mystery Writers of America's Grand Master Award.
sentence_327: She was named "Best Writer of the Century" and the Hercule Poirot series of books was named "Best Series of the Century" at the 2000 [[Bouchercon|Bouchercon World Mystery Convention]].
sentence_328: In 2013, she was voted "best crime writer" in a survey of 600 members of the Crime Writers' Association of professional novelists.
sentence_329: The writer [[Raymond_Chandler|Raymond Chandler]] criticised the artificiality of her books, as did Symons.
sentence_330: The literary critic [[Edmund_Wilson|Edmund Wilson]] described her prose as banal and her characterisations as superficial.
sentence_331: In 2011 Christie was named the second most financially successful crime writer of all time in the United Kingdom, after [[Ian_Fleming|Ian Fleming]], by digital crime drama TV channel [[Alibi_(TV_channel)|Alibi]] with total earnings around [[£|£]]100 million.
sentence_332: In 2012, Christie was among the people selected by the artist [[Peter_Blake_(artist)|Peter Blake]] to appear in a new version of his most famous work, the Beatles' [[Sgt._Pepper's_Lonely_Hearts_Club_Band|Sgt.
sentence_333: Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band]] album cover, "to celebrate the British cultural figures he most admires".
sentence_334: In 2015, in honour of the 125th anniversary of her birth, twenty-five contemporary mystery writers and one publisher gave their views on Christie's works.
sentence_335: Many of the authors had read Christie's novels first, before other mystery writers, in English or in their native language, influencing their own writing, and nearly all still viewed her as the "Queen of Crime" and creator of the [[Plot_twist|plot twists]] used by mystery authors.
sentence_336: Nearly all had one or more favourites among Christie's mysteries and found her books still good to read nearly 100 years after her first novel was published.
sentence_337: Just one of the twenty-five authors held with Wilson's views.
sentence_338: In 2016, one hundred years after Christie wrote her first detective story, the [[Royal_Mail|Royal Mail]] released six stamps in her honour, featuring The Mysterious Affair at Styles, The Murder of Roger Ackroyd, Murder on the Orient Express, And Then There Were None, The Body in the Library, and A Murder is Announced.
sentence_339: [[The_Guardian|The Guardian]] reported that, "Each design incorporates [[Microprinting|microtext]], UV ink and [[Thermochromic_ink|thermochromic ink]].
sentence_340: These concealed clues can be revealed using either a magnifying glass, [[Ultraviolet|UV light]] or body heat and provide pointers to the mysteries' solutions."
sentence_341: Her characters and her face appeared on the stamps of many countries like [[Dominica|Dominica]] and the [[Somali_Republic|Somali Republic]].
sentence_342: In 2020, Christie was commemorated on a [[Pound_sterling|£]]2 coin by the [[Royal_Mint|Royal Mint]] for the first time to mark the centenary of her first novel [[The_Mysterious_Affair_at_Styles|The Mysterious Affair at Styles]].
sentence_343: In her prime Christie was rarely out of the bestseller list.
sentence_344: She was the first crime writer to have 100,000 copies of ten of her titles published by [[Penguin_Books|Penguin]] on the same day in 1948.
sentence_345: As of 2018, [[Guinness_World_Records|Guinness World Records]] listed Christie as the best-selling fiction writer of all time.
sentence_346: As of 2020, her novels had sold more than two billion copies in forty-four languages.
sentence_347: Half the sales are of English-language editions, and half are translations.
sentence_348: According to [[Index_Translationum|Index Translationum]], as of 2020, she was the most-translated individual author.
sentence_349: Christie is one of the most-borrowed authors in UK libraries.
sentence_350: She is also UK's best-selling spoken-book author.
sentence_351: In 2002, 117,696 Christie audiobooks were sold, in comparison to 97,755 for [[J._K._Rowling|J.
sentence_352: K. Rowling]], 78,770 for [[Roald_Dahl|Roald Dahl]] and 75,841 for [[J._R._R._Tolkien|J.
sentence_353: R. R. Tolkien]].
sentence_354: In 2015 the Christie estate claimed And Then There Were None was "the best-selling crime novel of all time", with approximately 100 million sales, also making it one of the [[List_of_best-selling_books|highest-selling books]] of all time.
sentence_355: Main article: [[Adaptations_of_Agatha_Christie|Adaptations of Agatha Christie]]
sentence_356: Christie's works have been adapted for cinema and television.
sentence_357: The first was the 1928 British film [[The_Passing_of_Mr._Quin|The Passing of Mr. Quin]].
sentence_358: Poirot's first film appearance was in 1931 in [[Alibi_(1931_film)|Alibi]], which starred [[Austin_Trevor|Austin Trevor]] as Christie's sleuth.
sentence_359: [[Margaret_Rutherford|Margaret Rutherford]] played Marple in a series of films released in the 1960s.
sentence_360: Christie liked her acting, but considered the first film "pretty poor" and thought no better of the rest.
sentence_361: She felt differently about the 1974 film Murder on the Orient Express, directed by [[Sidney_Lumet|Sidney Lumet]], which featured major stars and high production values; her attendance at the London premiere was one of her last public outings.
sentence_362: In 2016, a new film version was released, directed by [[Kenneth_Branagh|Kenneth Branagh]], who also starred, wearing "the most extravagant mustache moviegoers have ever seen".
sentence_363: The television adaptation [[Agatha_Christie's_Poirot|Agatha Christie's Poirot]] (1989–2013), with [[David_Suchet|David Suchet]] in the title role, ran for seventy episodes over thirteen series.
sentence_364: It received nine BAFTA award nominations and won four BAFTA awards in 1990–1992.
sentence_365: The television series [[Miss_Marple_(TV_series)|Miss Marple]] (1984–1992), with [[Joan_Hickson|Joan Hickson]] as "the BBC's peerless Miss Marple", adapted all twelve Marple novels.
sentence_366: The French television series [[Les_Petits_Meurtres_d'Agatha_Christie|Les Petits Meurtres d'Agatha Christie]] (2009–2012, 2013–2020), adapted thirty-six of Christie's stories.
sentence_367: Christie's books have also been adapted for BBC Radio, [[Agatha_Christie_(video_game_series)|a video game series]], and [[Graphic_novel|graphic novels]].
sentence_368: During the First World War, Christie took a break from nursing to train for the Apothecaries Hall Examination.
sentence_369: While she subsequently found dispensing in the hospital pharmacy monotonous, and thus less enjoyable than nursing, her new knowledge provided her with a background in potentially toxic drugs.
sentence_370: Early in the Second World War, she brought her skills up to date at Torquay Hospital.
sentence_371: As Michael C. Gerald puts it, her "activities as a hospital dispenser during both World Wars not only supported the war effort but also provided her with an appreciation of drugs as therapeutic agents and poisons ...
sentence_372: These hospital experiences were also likely responsible for the prominent role physicians, nurses, and pharmacists play in her stories."
sentence_373: There were to be many medical practitioners, pharmacists, and scientists, naïve or suspicious, in Christie's cast of characters; featuring in Murder in Mesopotamia, Cards on the Table, The Pale Horse, and Mrs. McGinty's Dead, among many others.
sentence_374: Gillian Gill notes that the murder method in Christie's first detective novel, The Mysterious Affair at Styles, "comes right out of Agatha Christie's work in the hospital dispensary".
sentence_375: In an interview with journalist Marcelle Bernstein, Christie stated, "I don't like messy deaths ...
sentence_376: I'm more interested in peaceful people who die in their own beds and no one knows why."
sentence_377: With her expert knowledge, Christie had no need of poisons unknown to science, which were forbidden under [[Ronald_Knox|Ronald Knox]]'s "Ten Rules for Detective Fiction".
sentence_378: [[Arsenic_trioxide|Arsenic]], [[Aconitine|aconite]], [[Strychnine|strychnine]], [[Digoxin_toxicity|digitalis]], thallium, and other substances were used to dispatch victims in the ensuing decades.
sentence_379: In her youth, Christie showed little interest in antiquities.
sentence_380: After her marriage to Mallowan in 1930, she accompanied him on annual expeditions, spending three to four months at a time in Syria and Iraq at excavation sites at Ur, [[Nineveh|Nineveh]], [[Tell_Arpachiyah|Tell Arpachiyah]], [[Chagar_Bazar|Chagar Bazar]], [[Tell_Brak|Tell Brak]], and [[Nimrud|Nimrud]].
sentence_381: The Mallowans also took side trips whilst travelling to and from expedition sites, visiting Italy, Greece, Egypt, Iran, and the Soviet Union, among other places.
sentence_382: Their experiences travelling and living abroad are reflected in novels such as Murder on the Orient Express, Death on the Nile, and Appointment with Death.
sentence_383: For the 1931 digging season at Nineveh, Christie bought a writing table to continue her own work; in the early 1950s, she paid to add a small writing room to the team's house at Nimrud.
sentence_384: She also devoted time and effort each season in "making herself useful by photographing, cleaning, and recording finds; and restoring ceramics, which she especially enjoyed".
sentence_385: She also provided funds for the expeditions.
sentence_386: Many of the settings for Christie's books were inspired by her archaeological fieldwork in the Middle East; this is reflected in the detail with which she describes them – for instance, the [[Abu_Simbel_temples|temple of Abu Simbel]] as depicted in Death on the Nile – while the settings for They Came to Baghdad were places she and Mallowan had recently stayed.
sentence_387: Similarly, she drew upon her knowledge of daily life on a dig throughout Murder in Mesopotamia.
sentence_388: Archaeologists and experts in Middle Eastern cultures and artefacts featured in her works include Dr Eric Leidner in Murder in Mesopotamia and Signor Richetti in Death on the Nile.
sentence_389: After the Second World War, Christie chronicled her time in Syria in Come, Tell Me How You Live, which she described as "small beer – a very little book, full of everyday doings and happenings".
sentence_390: From 8 November 2001 to March 2002, [[British_Museum|The British Museum]] presented a "colourful and episodic exhibition" called Agatha Christie and Archaeology: Mystery in Mesopotamia which illustrated how her activities as a writer and as the wife of an archaeologist intertwined.
sentence_391: [[BBC_television|BBC television]] released Agatha Christie: A Life in Pictures in 2004, in which she is portrayed by [[Olivia_Williams|Olivia Williams]], [[Anna_Massey|Anna Massey]], and [[Bonnie_Wright|Bonnie Wright]] (at different stages in her life).
sentence_392: [[ITV_(TV_channel)|ITV]]'s Perspectives: "The Mystery of Agatha Christie" (2013) is hosted by David Suchet.
sentence_393: Some of Christie's fictional portrayals have explored and offered accounts of her disappearance in 1926.
sentence_394: The film [[Agatha_(film)|Agatha]] (1979), with [[Vanessa_Redgrave|Vanessa Redgrave]], has Christie sneaking away to plan revenge against her husband; Christie's heirs sued unsuccessfully to prevent the film's distribution.
sentence_395: The [[Doctor_Who|Doctor Who]] episode "[[The_Unicorn_and_the_Wasp|The Unicorn and the Wasp]]" (17 May 2008), with Fenella Woolgar, portrays Christie in her early writing career and explains her disappearance as the result of having suffered a temporary breakdown owing to a brief psychic link being formed between her and an alien wasp called the Vespiform.
sentence_396: The film [[Agatha_and_the_Truth_of_Murder|Agatha and the Truth of Murder]] (2018) sends her under cover to solve the murder of [[Florence_Nightingale|Florence Nightingale]]'s [[Goddaughter|goddaughter]], Florence Nightingale Shore.
sentence_397: A fictionalised account of Christie's disappearance is also the central theme of a Korean musical, Agatha.
sentence_398: Other portrayals, such as the Hungarian film, Kojak Budapesten (1980) create their own scenarios involving Christie's criminal skill.
sentence_399: In the TV play, Murder by the Book (1986), Christie (Dame [[Peggy_Ashcroft|Peggy Ashcroft]]) murders one of her fictional-turned-real characters, Poirot.
sentence_400: Christie features as a character in [[Gaylord_Larsen|Gaylord Larsen]]'s Dorothy and Agatha and The London Blitz Murders by [[Max_Allan_Collins|Max Allan Collins]].
sentence_401: A young Agatha is depicted in the Spanish historical television series [[Gran_Hotel_(TV_series)|Gran Hotel]] (2011) in which she finds inspiration to write her new novel while aiding local detectives.
sentence_402: In the alternative history television film [[Agatha_and_the_Curse_of_Ishtar|Agatha and the Curse of Ishtar]] (2018), Christie becomes involved in a murder case at an archaeological dig in Iraq.
sentence_403: In 2019, [[Honeysuckle_Weeks|Honeysuckle Weeks]] portrayed Christie in an episode, "No Friends Like Old Friends", in a Canadian drama, [[Frankie_Drake_Mysteries|Frankie Drake Mysteries]].
