sentence_361: Third, there was another conflict between the British and the French in the [[Second_Hundred_Years'_War|Second Hundred Years' War]] that intervened in and influenced the revolution.
sentence_362: France played a key role in assisting the Americans with money, weapons, soldiers, and naval vessels.
sentence_363: French troops fought under US command in the states, and Spanish troops in its territory west of the Mississippi River and on the Gulf of Mexico defeated British forces.
sentence_364: From 1778 to 1780, more countries with their own colonial possessions worldwide went to war against Britain for their own reasons, including the [[Dutch_Republic|Dutch Republic]] for its right to trade with its former colony in New York, and the French and Spanish to regain lost empire and prestige in the Caribbean, India, and Gibraltar.
sentence_365: Alternatively, nations in the [[First_League_of_Armed_Neutrality|League of Armed Neutrality]] including Russia, Austria, and Prussia defended the right of their merchant convoys to trade with the rebel Americans, enforced by Russian squadrons in the Mediterranean, North Atlantic and the Caribbean Sea.
sentence_366: Congress had multiple advantages if the rebellion turned into a protracted war.
sentence_367: Their prosperous state populations depended on local production for food and supplies rather than on imports from their mother country that lay six to twelve weeks away by sail.
sentence_368: They were spread across most of the North American Atlantic seaboard, stretching 1,000 miles.
sentence_369: Most farms were remote from the seaports, and controlling four or five major ports did not give British armies control over the inland areas.
sentence_370: Each state had established internal distribution systems.
sentence_371: Each former colony had a long-established system of local militia, combat-tested in support of British regulars thirteen years before to secure an expanded British Empire.
sentence_372: Together they took away French claims in North America west to the Mississippi River in the [[French_and_Indian_War|French and Indian War]].
sentence_373: The state legislatures independently funded and controlled their local militias.
sentence_374: In the American Revolution, they trained and provided Continental Line regiments to the regular army, each with their own state officer corps.
sentence_375: Motivation was also a major asset: each colonial capital had its own newspapers and printers, and the Patriots had more popular support than the Loyalists.
sentence_376: British hoped that the Loyalists would do much of the fighting, but they fought less than expected.
sentence_377: Main article: [[Continental_Army|Continental Army]]
sentence_378: See also: [[Militia_(United_States)#American_Revolutionary_War_(1775-1783)|Militia (United States) § American Revolutionary War (1775-1783)]], and [[Minutemen|Minutemen]]
sentence_379: When the war began, Congress lacked a professional army or navy, and each colony only maintained local militias.
sentence_380: Militiamen were lightly armed, had little training, and usually did not have uniforms.
sentence_381: Their units served for only a few weeks or months at a time and lacked the training and discipline of more experienced soldiers.
sentence_382: Local county militias were reluctant to travel far from home and they were unavailable for extended operations.
sentence_383: The new Continental Army suffered significantly from the lack of an effective training program and from largely inexperienced officers and sergeants, of which the latter was somewhat offset by a few senior officers.
sentence_384: Each state legislature appointed officers for both county and state militias and their regimental Continental Line officers, and although Washington was required to accept Congressional appointments, he was otherwise permitted to choose and command his own generals.
sentence_385: When properly employed, the militias' numbers helped the Continental Army overwhelm smaller British forces, as at [[Battles_of_Lexington_and_Concord|Concord]], [[Siege_of_Boston|Boston]], [[Battle_of_Bennington|Bennington]], and [[Saratoga_campaign|Saratoga]].
sentence_386: Both sides used partisan warfare, but the state militias effectively suppressed Loyalist activity when British regulars were not in the area.
sentence_387: Congress established a regular army on June 14, 1775, and appointed Washington as commander-in-chief.
sentence_388: The development of the Continental Army was always a work in progress and Washington used both his regulars and state militia throughout the war.
sentence_389: Washington designed the overall military strategy of the war in cooperation with Congress, established the principle of civilian supremacy in military affairs, personally recruited his senior office corps, and kept the states focused on a common goal.
sentence_390: For the first three years until after [[Valley_Forge|Valley Forge]], the Continental Army was largely supplemented by local state militias.
sentence_391: Initially, Washington employed the inexperienced officers and untrained troops in Fabian strategies rather than risk frontal assaults against Britain's professional soldiers and officers.
sentence_392: Over the course of the entire war, Washington lost more battles than he won, but he maintained a fighting force in the face of British field armies and never gave up fighting for the American cause.
sentence_393: The American armies were small by European standards of the era, largely attributable to limitations such as lack of powder and other [[Logistics|logistics]].
sentence_394: At the beginning of 1776, Washington commanded 20,000 men, with two-thirds enlisted in the Continental Army and the other third in the various state militias.
sentence_395: About 250,000 men served as regulars or as militia for the Revolutionary cause over eight years during wartime, but there were never more than 90,000 men under arms at one time.
sentence_396: As a whole, American officers never equaled their opponents in tactics and maneuvers, and they lost most of the pitched battles.
sentence_397: The great successes at [[Siege_of_Boston|Boston]] (1776), [[Battles_of_Saratoga|Saratoga]] (1777), and [[Siege_of_Yorktown|Yorktown]] (1781) were won from trapping the British far from base with a greater number of troops.
sentence_398: Nevertheless, after 1778, Washington's army was transformed into a more disciplined and effective force, mostly by [[Baron_von_Steuben|Baron von Steuben]]'s training.
sentence_399: Immediately after the Army emerged from Valley Forge, it proved its ability to match the British troops in action at the [[Battle_of_Monmouth|Battle of Monmouth]], including a black Rhode Island regiment fending off a British bayonet attack then counter-charging for the first time in Washington's army.
sentence_400: Here Washington came to realize that saving entire towns was not necessary, but preserving his army and keeping the revolutionary spirit alive was more important in the long run.
sentence_401: Washington informed [[Henry_Laurens|Henry Laurens]] "that the possession of our towns, while we have an army in the field, will avail them little."
sentence_402: Although Congress was responsible for the war effort and provided supplies to the troops, Washington took it upon himself to pressure the Congress and state legislatures to provide the essentials of war; there was never nearly enough.
sentence_403: Congress evolved in its committee oversight and established the Board of War, which included members of the military.
sentence_404: Because the Board of War was also a committee ensnared with its own internal procedures, Congress also created the post of Secretary of War, and appointed Major General [[Benjamin_Lincoln|Benjamin Lincoln]] in February 1781 to the position.
sentence_405: Washington worked closely with Lincoln to coordinate civilian and military authorities and took charge of training and supplying the army.
sentence_406: Main articles: [[Continental_Navy|Continental Navy]] and Continental Marines
sentence_407: Further information: [[Naval_battles_of_the_American_Revolutionary_War|Naval battles of the American Revolutionary War]]
sentence_408: During the first summer of the war, Washington began outfitting schooners and other small seagoing vessels to prey on ships supplying the British in Boston.
sentence_409: Congress established the [[Continental_Navy|Continental Navy]] on October 13, 1775, and appointed [[Esek_Hopkins|Esek Hopkins]] as the Navy's first commander.
sentence_410: The following month, Marines were organized on November 10, 1775.
sentence_411: The Continental Navy was a handful of small frigates and sloops throughout the Revolution for the most part.
sentence_412: [[John_Paul_Jones|John Paul Jones]] became the first American naval hero by capturing [[HMS_Drake_(1777)|HMS Drake]] on April 24, 1778, the first victory for any American military vessel in British waters.
sentence_413: The last was by the frigate [[USS_Alliance_(1778)|USS Alliance]] commanded by Captain [[John_Barry_(naval_officer)|John Barry]].
sentence_414: On March 10, 1783, the Alliance outgunned HMS Sybil in a 45-minute duel while escorting Spanish gold from Havana to Congress.
sentence_415: After Yorktown, all US Navy ships were sold or given away; it was the first time in America's history that it had no fighting forces on the high seas.
sentence_416: Congress primarily commissioned privateers to reduce costs and to take advantage of the large proportion of colonial sailors found in the British Empire.
sentence_417: Overall, they included 1,700 ships that successfully captured 2,283 enemy ships to damage the British effort and to enrich themselves with the proceeds from the sale of cargo and the ship itself.
sentence_418: About 55,000 sailors served aboard American privateers during the war.
sentence_419: Main article: France in the American Revolution
sentence_420: Further information: [[History_of_the_French_Navy#Louis_XVI|History of the French Navy § Louis XVI]], and [[Military_history_of_France#Ancien_Régime|Military history of France § Ancien Régime]]
sentence_421: To begin with, the Americans had no major international allies, as most nation-states watched and waited to see developments unfold in British North America.
sentence_422: Over time, the Continental Army acquitted itself well in the face of British regulars and their German auxiliaries known to all European great powers.
sentence_423: Battles such as the [[Battle_of_Bennington|Battle of Bennington]], the [[Battles_of_Saratoga|Battles of Saratoga]], and even defeats such as the Battle of Germantown, proved decisive in gaining the attention and support of powerful European nations such as [[Pacte_de_Famille|Bourbon France and Spain]] and the [[Fourth_Anglo-Dutch_War#Background|Dutch Republic]]; the latter moved from covertly supplying the Americans with weapons and supplies to overtly supporting them.
sentence_424: The decisive American victory at [[Battles_of_Saratoga|Saratoga]] spurred France to offer the Americans the [[Treaty_of_Amity_and_Commerce_(United_States–France)|Treaty of Amity and Commerce]].
sentence_425: The two nations also agreed to a defensive [[Treaty_of_Alliance_(1778)|Treaty of Alliance]] to protect their trade and also guaranteed American independence from Britain.
sentence_426: To engage the United States as a French ally militarily, the treaty was conditioned on Britain initiating a war on France to stop it from trading with the US.
sentence_427: Spain and the Dutch Republic were invited to join by both France and the United States in the treaty, but neither made a formal reply.
sentence_428: On June 13, 1778, France declared war on Great Britain, and it invoked the French military alliance with the US, which ensured additional US privateer support for French possessions in the Caribbean.
sentence_429: Washington worked closely with the soldiers and navy that France would send to America, primarily through [[Gilbert_du_Motier,_Marquis_de_Lafayette|Lafayette]] on his staff.
sentence_430: French assistance made critical contributions required to defeat General [[Charles_Cornwallis,_1st_Marquess_Cornwallis|Charles Cornwallis]] at Yorktown in 1781.

list.value: British political landscape in its 1775 American Empire

sentence_431: The British military had considerable experience of fighting in North America, most recently during the Seven Years' War which forced France to relinquish [[New_France|New France]] in 1763.
sentence_432: However, in previous conflicts they benefited from local logistics, as well as support from the colonial militia, which was not available in the American Revolutionary War.
sentence_433: Reinforcements had to come from Europe, and maintaining large armies over such distances was extremely complex; ships could take three months to cross the Atlantic, and orders from London were often outdated by the time they arrived.
sentence_434: Prior to the conflict, the colonies were largely autonomous economic and political entities, with no centralized area of ultimate strategic importance.
sentence_435: This meant that unlike Europe where the fall of a capital city often ended wars, that in America continued even after the loss of major settlements such as Philadelphia, seat of Congress, New York and Charleston.
sentence_436: British power was reliant on the Royal Navy, whose dominance allowed them to resupply their own expeditionary forces while preventing access to enemy ports.
sentence_437: However, the majority of the American population was agrarian, rather than urban; supported by the French navy and blockade runners based in the [[Dutch_Caribbean|Dutch Caribbean]], their economy was able to survive.
sentence_438: The geographical size of the colonies and limited manpower meant the British could not simultaneously conduct military operations and occupy territory without local support.
sentence_439: Debate persists over whether their defeat was inevitable; one British statesman described it as "like trying to conquer a map".
sentence_440: While [[John_E._Ferling|Ferling]] argues Patriot victory was nothing short of a miracle, [[Joseph_Ellis|Ellis]] suggests the odds always favored the Americans, especially after Howe squandered the chance of a decisive British success in 1776, an "opportunity that would never come again".
sentence_441: The US military history speculates the additional commitment of 10,000 fresh troops in 1780 would have placed British victory "within the realm of possibility".
sentence_442: Main article: [[British_Army_during_the_American_Revolutionary_War|British Army during the American Revolutionary War]]
sentence_443: See also: [[Loyalist_(American_Revolution)#Military_service|Loyalist (American Revolution) § Military service]]
sentence_444: The expulsion of France from North America in 1763 led to a drastic reduction in British troop levels in the colonies; in 1775, there only 8,500 regular soldiers among a civilian population of 2.8 million.
sentence_445: The bulk of military resources in the Americas were focused on defending sugar islands in the Caribbean; Jamaica alone generated more revenue than all thirteen American colonies combined.
sentence_446: With the end of the Seven Years' War, the permanent army in Britain was also cut back, which resulted in administrative difficulties when the war began a decade later.
sentence_447: Over the course of the war, there were four separate British commanders-in-chief, the first of whom was Thomas Gage; appointed in 1763, his initial focus was establishing British rule in former French areas of Canada.
sentence_448: Rightly or wrongly, many in London blamed the revolt on his failure to take firm action earlier, and he was relieved after the heavy losses incurred at Bunker Hill.
sentence_449: His replacement was Sir William Howe, a member of the Whig faction in Parliament who opposed the policy of coercion advocated by Lord North; Cornwallis, who later surrendered at Yorktown, was one of many senior officers who initially refused to serve in North America.
sentence_450: The 1775 campaign showed the British overestimated the capabilities of their own troops and underestimated the colonial militia, requiring a reassessment of tactics and strategy.
sentence_451: However, it allowed the Patriots to take the initiative and British authorities rapidly lost control over every colony.
sentence_452: Howe's responsibility is still debated; despite receiving large numbers of reinforcements, Bunker Hill seems to have permanently affected his self-confidence and lack of tactical flexibility meant he often failed to follow up opportunities.
sentence_453: Many of his decisions were attributed to supply problems, such as the delay in launching the New York campaign and failure to pursue Washington's beaten army.
sentence_454: Having lost the confidence of his subordinates, he was recalled after Burgoyne surrendered at Saratoga.
sentence_455: Following the failure of the Carlisle Commission, British policy changed from treating the Patriots as subjects who needed to be reconciled to enemies who had to be defeated.
sentence_456: In 1778, Howe was replaced by Sir Henry Clinton, appointed instead of Carleton who was considered overly cautious.
sentence_457: Regarded as an expert on tactics and strategy, like his predecessors Clinton was handicapped by chronic supply issues.
sentence_458: As a result, he was largely inactive in 1779 and much of 1780; in October 1780, he warned Germain of "fatal consequences" if matters did not improve.
sentence_459: In addition, Clinton's strategy was compromised by conflict with political superiors in London and his colleagues in North America, especially Admiral [[Mariot_Arbuthnot|Mariot Arbuthnot]], replaced in early 1781 by Rodney.
sentence_460: He was neither notified nor consulted when Germain approved Cornwallis' invasion of the south in 1781, and delayed sending him reinforcements believing the bulk of Washington's army was still outside New York City.
sentence_461: After the surrender at Yorktown, Clinton was relieved by Carleton, whose major task was to oversee the evacuation of Loyalists and British troops from Savannah, Charleston, and New York City.
sentence_462: Main article: [[Hessian_(soldier)|Hessian (soldier)]]
sentence_463: During the 18th century, all states commonly hired foreign soldiers, especially Britain; during the Seven Years' War, they comprised 10% of the British army and their use caused little debate.
sentence_464: When it became clear additional troops were needed to suppress the revolt in America, it was decided to employ mercenaries.
sentence_465: There were several reasons for this, including public sympathy for the Patriot cause, an historical reluctance to expand the British army and the time needed to recruit and train new regiments.
sentence_466: An alternate source was readily available in the [[Holy_Roman_Empire|Holy Roman Empire]], where many smaller states had a long tradition of renting their armies to the highest bidder.
sentence_467: The most important was [[Landgraviate_of_Hesse-Kassel|Hesse-Cassell]], known as "the Mercenary State".
sentence_468: The first supply agreements were signed by the North administration in late 1775; over the next decade, more than 40,000 Germans fought in North America, Gibraltar, South Africa and India, of whom 30,000 served in the American War.
sentence_469: Often generically referred to as "Hessians", they included men from many other states, including Hanover and Brunswick.
sentence_470: Sir Henry Clinton recommended recruiting Russian troops whom he rated very highly, having seen them in action against the [[Russo-Turkish_War_(1768–1774)|Ottomans]]; however, negotiations with [[Catherine_the_Great|Catherine the Great]] made little progress.
sentence_471: Unlike previous wars their use led to intense political debate in Britain, France, and even Germany, where Frederick the Great refused to provide passage through his territories for troops hired for the American war.
sentence_472: In March 1776, the agreements were challenged in Parliament by Whigs who objected to "coercion" in general, and especially the use of foreign soldiers to subdue "British subjects".
sentence_473: This was reflected in North America, where the employment of 'foreign mercenaries' was one of the charges levelled against George III in the Declaration of Independence.
sentence_474: American newspapers covered the parliamentary debates in detail, reprinting key speeches; when copies of the actual treaties were smuggled into the US, it confirmed fears that these mercenaries would be used against the Patriots.
sentence_475: By apparently showing Britain was determined to go to war, it made hopes of reconciliation seem naive and hopeless; combined with the Hessian reputation in Germany for rapaciousness, it led many German-American immigrants to renounce their allegiance to Britain, while increasing enlistment into the Continental Army.
sentence_476: Both sides felt Germans might be persuaded to desert, given the presence of over 150,000 German-Americans; one reason Clinton suggested employing Russians was because he felt they were less likely to defect.
sentence_477: When the first German troops arrived on [[Staten_Island|Staten Island]] in August 1776, Congress approved the printing of "handbills" promising land and citizenship to any willing to join the Patriot cause.
sentence_478: The British launched a counter-campaign claiming deserters could well be executed for meddling in a war that was not theirs.
sentence_479: German regiments were central to the British war effort; of the estimated 30,000 sent to America, some 13,000 became casualties.
sentence_480: Their service was commemorated in [[Washington_Irving|Washington Irving]]'s short story, [[The_Legend_of_Sleepy_Hollow|The Legend of Sleepy Hollow]], which features a headless Hessian soldier.
sentence_481: Main article: [[Loyalist_(American_Revolution)|Loyalist (American Revolution)]]
sentence_482: See also: [[American_Legion|American Legion]] and [[Prince_of_Wales'_American_Regiment|Prince of Wales' American Regiment]]
sentence_483: Wealthy Loyalists convinced the British government that most of the colonists were sympathetic toward the Crown; consequently, British military planners relied on recruiting Loyalists, but had trouble recruiting sufficient numbers as the Patriots had widespread support.
sentence_484: Nevertheless, they continued to deceive themselves on their level of American support as late as 1780, a year before hostilities ended.
sentence_485: Approximately 25,000 Loyalists fought for the British throughout the war.
sentence_486: Although Loyalists constituted about twenty percent of the colonial population, they were concentrated in distinct communities.
sentence_487: Many of them lived among large plantation owners in the [[Tidewater_(region)|Tidewater region]] and [[South_Carolina_in_the_American_Revolution#Early_conflicts|South Carolina]] who produced cash crops in tobacco and indigo comparable to global markets in Caribbean sugar.
sentence_488: When the British began probing the backcountry in 1777–1778, they were faced with a major problem: any significant level of organized Loyalist activity required a continued presence of British regulars.
sentence_489: The available manpower that the British had in America was insufficient to protect Loyalist territory and counter American offensives.
sentence_490: The Loyalist militias in the South constantly defeated by neighboring Patriot militia.
sentence_491: The most critical combat between the two partisan militias was at the [[Battle_of_Kings_Mountain|Battle of Kings Mountain]]; the Patriot victory irreversibly crippled any further Loyalist militia capability in the South.
sentence_492: When the early war policy was administered by General [[William_Howe,_5th_Viscount_Howe|William Howe]], the Crown's need to maintain Loyalist support prevented it from using the traditional revolt suppression methods.
sentence_493: The British cause suffered when their troops ransacked local homes during an aborted attack on Charleston in 1779 that enraged both Patriots and Loyalists.
sentence_494: After Congress rejected the [[Carlisle_Peace_Commission|Carlisle Peace Commission]] in 1778 and Westminster turned to "hard war" during Clinton's command, neutral colonists in the Carolinas often allied with the Patriots whenever brutal combat broke out between Tories and Whigs.
sentence_495: Conversely, Loyalists gained support when Patriots intimidated suspected Tories by destroying property or [[Tarring_and_feathering|tarring and feathering]].
sentence_496: A Loyalist militia unit—the [[British_Legion_(American_Revolution)|British Legion]]—provided some of the best troops in British service that it received a commission in the British Army: it was a mixed regiment of 250 dragoons and 200 infantry supported by batteries of flying artillery.
sentence_497: It was commanded by [[Banastre_Tarleton|Banastre Tarleton]] and gained a fearsome reputation in the colonies for "brutality and needless slaughter".
sentence_498: In May 1779 the British Legion was one of five regiments that formed the [[American_establishment_(British_army)|American Establishment]].
sentence_499: Main article: [[Women_in_the_American_Revolution|Women in the American Revolution]]
sentence_500: Women played various roles during the Revolutionary War; they often accompanied their husbands when permitted to do so.
sentence_501: For example, throughout the war [[Martha_Washington|Martha Washington]] was known to visit and provide aid to her husband George at various American camps, and [[Frederika_Charlotte_Riedesel|Frederika Charlotte Riedesel]] documented the [[Saratoga_campaign|Saratoga campaign]].
sentence_502: Women often accompanied armies as [[Camp_follower|camp followers]] to sell goods and perform necessary tasks in hospitals and camps.
sentence_503: They were a necessary part of eighteenth-century armies, and numbered in the thousands during the war.
sentence_504: Women also assumed military roles: aside from auxiliary tasks like treating the wounded or setting up camp, some dressed as men to directly support combat, fight, or act as spies on both sides of the Revolutionary War.
sentence_505: Anna Maria Lane joined her husband in the Army and wore men's clothes by the time the Battle of Germantown happened.
sentence_506: The Virginia General Assembly later cited her bravery: she fought while dressed as a man and "performed extraordinary military services, and received a severe wound at the battle of Germantown ... with the courage of a soldier".
sentence_507: On April 26, 1777, [[Sybil_Ludington|Sybil Ludington]] rode to alert militia forces of Putnam County, New York, and Danbury, Connecticut, to warn them of the British's approach; she has been called the "female Paul Revere".
sentence_508: A few others [[List_of_wartime_cross-dressers|disguised themselves as men]].
sentence_509: [[Deborah_Sampson|Deborah Sampson]] fought until her gender was discovered and discharged as a result; [[Sally_St._Clair|Sally St. Clair]] was killed in action during the war.
sentence_510: Main article: [[African_Americans_in_the_Revolutionary_War|African Americans in the Revolutionary War]]
sentence_511: When war began, the population of the Thirteen Colonies included an estimated 500,000 slaves, predominantly used as labor on [[Plantation_complexes_in_the_Southern_United_States|Southern plantations]].
sentence_512: In November 1775, [[John_Murray,_4th_Earl_of_Dunmore|Lord Dunmore]], the Royal Governor of Virginia, issued a [[Dunmore's_Proclamation|proclamation]] that promised freedom to any Patriot-owned slaves willing to bear arms.
sentence_513: Although the announcement helped to fill a temporary manpower shortage, white Loyalist prejudice meant recruits were eventually redirected to non-combatant roles.
sentence_514: The Loyalists' motive was to deprive Patriot planters of labor rather than to end slavery; Loyalist-owned slaves were returned.
sentence_515: The 1779 [[Philipsburg_Proclamation|Philipsburg Proclamation]] issued by Clinton extended the offer of freedom to Patriot-owned slaves throughout the colonies.
sentence_516: It persuaded entire families to escape to British lines, many of which were employed on farms to grow food for the army by removing the requirement for military service.
sentence_517: While Clinton organized the [[Black_Pioneers|Black Pioneers]], he also ensured fugitive slaves were returned to Loyalist owners with orders that they were not to be punished for their attempted escape.
sentence_518: As the war progressed, service as regular soldiers in British units became increasingly common; black Loyalists formed two regiments of the Charleston garrison in 1783.
sentence_519: Estimates of the numbers who served the British during the war vary from 25,000 to 50,000, excluding those who escaped during wartime.
sentence_520: Thomas Jefferson estimated that Virginia may have lost 30,000 slaves in total escapes.
sentence_521: In South Carolina, nearly 25,000 slaves (about 30 percent of the enslaved population) either fled, migrated, or died, which significantly disrupted the plantation economies both during and after the war.
sentence_522: [[Black_Patriot|Black Patriots]] were barred from the Continental Army until Washington convinced Congress in January 1778 that there was no other way to replace losses from disease and desertion.
sentence_523: The [[1st_Rhode_Island_Regiment|1st Rhode Island Regiment]] formed in February included former slaves whose owners were compensated; however, only 140 of its 225 soldiers were black and recruitment stopped in June 1788.
sentence_524: Ultimately, around 5,000 African-Americans served in the Continental Army and Navy in a variety of roles, while another 4,000 were employed in Patriot militia units, aboard privateers, or as teamsters, servants, and spies.
sentence_525: After the war, a small minority received land grants or Congressional pensions in old age; many others were returned to their masters post-war despite earlier promises of freedom.
sentence_526: As a Patriot victory became increasingly likely, the treatment of Black Loyalists became a point of contention; after the surrender of Yorktown in 1781, Washington insisted all escapees be returned but Cornwallis refused.
sentence_527: In 1782 and 1783, around 8,000 to 10,000 freed blacks were evacuated by the British from Charleston, Savannah, and New York; some moved onto London, while 3,000 to 4,000 settled in [[Nova_Scotia|Nova Scotia]], where they founded settlements such as [[Birchtown,_Nova_Scotia|Birchtown]].
sentence_528: White Loyalists transported 15,000 enslaved blacks to Jamaica and the [[Bahamas|Bahamas]].
sentence_529: The free Black Loyalists who migrated to the British West Indies included regular soldiers from Dunmore's [[Ethiopian_Regiment|Ethiopian Regiment]], and those from Charleston who helped garrison the [[Leeward_Islands|Leeward Islands]].
sentence_530: Main page: :Category:Native Americans in the American Revolution
sentence_531: Most [[Native_Americans_in_the_United_States|American Indians]] east of the [[Mississippi_River|Mississippi River]] were affected by the war, and many tribes were divided over how to respond to the conflict.
sentence_532: A few tribes were friendly with the colonists, but most Indians opposed the union of the Colonies as a potential threat to their territory.
sentence_533: Approximately 13,000 Indians fought on the British side, with the largest group coming from the [[Iroquois|Iroquois]] tribes who deployed around 1,500 men.
sentence_534: Early in July 1776, [[Cherokee|Cherokee]] allies of Britain attacked the short-lived [[Washington_District,_North_Carolina|Washington District]] of [[North_Carolina_Colony|North Carolina]].
sentence_535: Their defeat splintered both Cherokee settlements and people, and was directly responsible for the rise of the [[Chickamauga_Cherokee|Chickamauga Cherokee]], who perpetuated the [[Cherokee–American_wars|Cherokee–American wars]] against American settlers for decades after hostilities with Britain ended.
sentence_536: [[Muscogee_people|Creek]] and [[Seminole|Seminole]] allies of Britain fought against Americans in Georgia and South Carolina.
sentence_537: In 1778, a force of 800 Creeks destroyed American settlements along the [[Broad_River_(Georgia)|Broad River]] in Georgia.
sentence_538: Creek warriors also joined [[Thomas_Brown_(loyalist)|Thomas Brown's]] raids into South Carolina and assisted Britain during the [[Siege_of_Savannah|Siege of Savannah]].
sentence_539: Many Indians were involved in the fight between Britain and Spain on the Gulf Coast and along the British side of the Mississippi River.
sentence_540: Thousands of Creeks, [[Chickasaw|Chickasaws]], and [[Choctaw|Choctaws]] fought in major battles such as the Battle of Fort Charlotte, the [[Battle_of_Mobile_(1781)|Battle of Mobile]], and the Siege of Pensacola.
sentence_541: The [[Iroquois_Confederacy|Iroquois Confederacy]] was shattered as a result of the American Revolutionary War, whatever side they took; the [[Seneca_nation|Seneca]], [[Onondaga_(tribe)|Onondaga]], and [[Cayuga_nation|Cayuga]] tribes sided with the British; members of the Mohawks fought on both side; and many [[Tuscarora_(tribe)|Tuscarora]] and Oneida sided with the Americans.
sentence_542: To retaliate against raids on American settlement by Loyalists and their Indian allies, the Continental Army dispatched the [[Sullivan_Expedition|Sullivan Expedition]] on a punitive expedition throughout New York to cripple the Iroquois tribes that had sided with the British.
sentence_543: Mohawk leaders [[Joseph_Louis_Cook|Joseph Louis Cook]] and [[Joseph_Brant|Joseph Brant]] sided with the Americans and the British respectively, which further exacerbated the split.
sentence_544: In the [[Western_theater_of_the_American_Revolutionary_War|western theater of the American Revolutionary War]], conflicts between settlers and Indians led to lingering distrust.
sentence_545: In the [[Treaty_of_Paris_(1783)|1783 Treaty of Paris]], Great Britain ceded control of the disputed lands between the Great Lakes and the [[Ohio_River|Ohio River]], but the Indian inhabitants were not a part of the peace negotiations.
sentence_546: Tribes in the [[Northwest_Territory|Northwest Territory]] joined together as the [[Western_Confederacy|Western Confederacy]] and allied with the British to resist American settlement, and their conflict continued after the Revolutionary War as the [[Northwest_Indian_War|Northwest Indian War]].
sentence_547: [[Frederick_North,_2nd_Earl_of_Guilford|Lord North]], Prime Minister since 1770, delegated control of the war in North America to [[Lord_George_Germain|Lord George Germain]] and the [[John_Montagu,_4th_Earl_of_Sandwich|Earl of Sandwich]], who was [[First_Lord_of_the_Admiralty|head of the Royal Navy]] from 1771 to 1782.
sentence_548: Defeat at Saratoga in 1777 made it clear the revolt would not be easily suppressed, especially after the Franco-American alliance of February 1778, and French declaration of war in June.
sentence_549: With Spain also expected to join the conflict, the Royal Navy needed to prioritize either the war in America or in Europe; Germain advocated the former, Sandwich the latter.
sentence_550: British negotiators now proposed a second peace settlement to Congress.
sentence_551: The terms presented by the [[Carlisle_Peace_Commission|Carlisle Peace Commission]] included acceptance of the principle of self-government.
sentence_552: Parliament would recognize Congress as the governing body, suspend any objectionable legislation, surrender its right to local colonial taxation, and discuss including American representatives in the House of Commons.
sentence_553: In return, all property confiscated from Loyalists would be returned, British debts honored, and locally enforced martial law accepted.
sentence_554: However, Congress demanded either immediate recognition of independence, or the withdrawal of all British troops; they knew the Commission were not authorized to accept these, bringing negotiations to a rapid end.
sentence_555: When the commissioners returned to London in November 1778, they recommended a change in policy.
sentence_556: Sir Henry Clinton, the new British Commander-in-Chief in America, was ordered to stop treating the rebels as enemies, rather than subjects whose loyalty might be regained.
sentence_557: Those standing orders would be in effect for three years until Clinton was relieved.
sentence_558: North backed the Southern strategy hoping to exploit divisions between the mercantile north and slave-owning south, but after Yorktown accepted this policy had failed.
sentence_559: It was clear the war was lost, although the Royal Navy forced the French to relocate their fleet to the Caribbean in November 1781 and resumed a close blockade of American trade.
sentence_560: The resulting economic damage and rising inflation meant the US was now eager to end the war, while France was unable to provide further loans; Congress could no longer pay its soldiers.
sentence_561: On February 27, 1782 a Whig motion to end offensive war in America was carried by 19 votes.
sentence_562: North now resigned, obliging the king to invite [[Charles_Watson-Wentworth,_2nd_Marquess_of_Rockingham|Lord Rockingham]] to form a government; a consistent supporter of the Patriot cause, he made commitment to US independence a condition of doing so.
sentence_563: George III reluctantly accepted and the [[Second_Rockingham_ministry|new government]] took office on March 27, 1782; however, Rockingham died unexpectedly on July 1, and was replaced by [[Shelburne_ministry|Lord Shelburne]] who acknowledged American independence.

list.value: See also [[Treaty_of_Paris_(1783)|Treaty of Paris (1783)]] for the Anglo-American Preliminary Treaty in November 1782, and its conclusive treaty September 1783. Additional reading in European diplomatic history at [[Peace_of_Paris_(1783)|Peace of Paris (1783)]] for preliminary British treaties signed at Paris in January 1783 with France 1783, Spain 1783 with their respective conclusive treaties signed at Versailles September 1783, and the British preliminary treaty with the Dutch Republic in September 1783 at Paris, then conclusively signed in May 1784.

sentence_564: When Lord Rockingham, the Whig leader and friend of the American cause was elevated to Prime Minister, Congress consolidated its diplomatic consuls in Europe into a peace delegation at Paris.
sentence_565: All were experienced in Congressional leadership.
sentence_566: The dean of the delegation was [[Benjamin_Franklin|Benjamin Franklin]] of Pennsylvania.
sentence_567: He had become a celebrity in the French Court, but he was also an Enlightenment scientist with influence in the courts of European great powers in Prussia, England's former ally, and Austria, a Catholic empire like Spain.
sentence_568: Since the 1760s he had been an organizer of British American inter-colony cooperation, and then a colonial lobbyist to Parliament in London.
sentence_569: [[John_Adams|John Adams]] of Massachusetts had been consul to the Dutch Republic, and was a prominent early New England Patriot.
sentence_570: [[John_Jay|John Jay]] of New York had been consul to Spain and was a past president of the Continental Congress.
sentence_571: As consul to the Dutch Republic, [[Henry_Laurens|Henry Laurens]] of South Carolina had secured a preliminary agreement for a trade agreement.
sentence_572: He had been a successor to John Jay as president of Congress and with Franklin was a member of the [[American_Philosophical_Society|American Philosophical Society]].
sentence_573: Although active in the preliminaries, he was not a signer of the conclusive treaty.
sentence_574: The Whig negotiators for Lord Rockingham and his successor, Prime Minister Lord Shelburne, included long-time friend of Benjamin Franklin from his time in London, [[David_Hartley_(the_Younger)|David Hartley]] and [[Richard_Oswald_(merchant)|Richard Oswald]], who had negotiated Laurens' release from the Tower of London.
sentence_575: The Preliminary Peace signed on November 30 met four key Congressional demands: independence, territory up to the Mississippi, navigation rights into the Gulf of Mexico, and fishing rights in Newfoundland.
sentence_576: British strategy was to strengthen the US sufficiently to prevent France regaining a foothold in North America, and they had little interest in these proposals.
sentence_577: However, divisions between their opponents allowed them to negotiate separately with each to improve their overall position, starting with the American delegation in September 1782.
sentence_578: The French and Spanish sought to improve their position by creating a US dependent on them for support against Britain, thus reversing the losses of 1763.
sentence_579: Both parties tried to negotiate a settlement with Britain excluding the Americans; France proposed setting the western boundary of the US along the Appalachians, matching the British [[Royal_Proclamation_of_1763|1763 Proclamation Line]].
sentence_580: The Spanish suggested additional concessions in the vital Mississippi River Basin, but required the cession of Georgia in violation of the Franco-American alliance.
sentence_581: An Anglo-American Preliminary Peace was formally entered into in November 1782, and Congress endorsed the settlement on April 15, 1783.
sentence_582: It announced the achievement of peace with independence; the "conclusive" treaty was signed on September 2, 1783 in Paris, effective the next day September 3, when Britain signed its treaty with France.
sentence_583: John Adams, who helped draft the treaty, claimed it represented "one of the most important political events that ever happened on the globe".
sentence_584: Ratified respectively by Congress and Parliament, the final versions were exchanged in Paris the following spring.
sentence_585: On 25 November, the last British troops remaining in the US were evacuated from New York to Halifax.
sentence_587: Washington expressed astonishment that the Americans had won a war against a leading world power, referring to the American victory as "little short of a standing miracle".
sentence_588: The conflict between British subjects with the Crown against those with the Congress had lasted over eight years from 1775 to 1783.
sentence_589: The last uniformed British troops [[Evacuation_Day_(New_York)|departed]] their last east coast port cities in Savannah, Charleston, and New York City, by November 25, 1783.
sentence_590: That marked the end of British occupation in the new United States.
sentence_591: On April 9, 1783, Washington issued orders that he had long waited to give, that "all acts of hostility" were to cease immediately.
sentence_592: That same day, by arrangement with Washington, [[Guy_Carleton,_1st_Baron_Dorchester|General Carleton]] issued a similar order to British troops.
sentence_593: British troops, however, were not to evacuate until a prisoner of war exchange occurred, an effort that involved much negotiation and would take some seven months to effect.
sentence_594: As directed by a Congressional resolution of May 26 1783, all non-commissioned officers and enlisted were furloughed "to their homes" until the "definitive treaty of peace", when they would be automatically discharged.
sentence_595: The US armies were directly disbanded in the field as of Washington's General Orders on Monday June 2, 1783.
sentence_596: Once the conclusive Treaty of Paris was signed with Britain, Washington resigned as commander-in-chief at Congress, leaving for his Army retirement at Mount Vernon.
sentence_597: The expanse of territory that was now the United States was ceded from its colonial [[Homeland#Motherland|Mother country]] alone.
sentence_598: It included millions of sparsely settled acres south of the [[Great_Lakes|Great Lakes Line]] between the Appalachian Mountains and the Mississippi River.
sentence_599: The tentative colonial migration west became a flood during the years of the Revolutionary War.
sentence_600: Virginia's Kentucky County counted 150 men in 1775.
sentence_601: By 1790 fifteen years later, it numbered over 73,000 and was seeking statehood in the United States.
sentence_602: Britain's extended post-war policy for the US continued to try to establish an Indian buffer state below the Great Lakes as late as 1814 during the War of 1812.
sentence_603: The formally acquired western American lands continued to be populated by a dozen or so American Indian tribes that had been British allies for the most part.
sentence_604: Though British forts on their lands had been ceded to either the French or the British prior to the creation of the United States, Indians were not referred to in the British cession to the US.
sentence_605: While tribes were not consulted by the British for the treaty, in practice the British refused to abandon the forts on territory they formally transferred.
sentence_606: Instead they provisioned military allies for continuing frontier raids and sponsored the [[Northwest_Indian_War|Northwest Indian War (1785–1795)]].
sentence_607: British sponsorship of local warfare on the United States continued until the Anglo-American [[Jay_Treaty|Jay Treaty]] went into effect.
sentence_608: At the same time, the Spanish also sponsored war within the US by Indian proxies in its Southwest Territory ceded by France to Britain, then Britain to the Americans.
sentence_609: Of the European powers with American colonies adjacent to the newly created United States, Spain was most threatened by American independence, and it was correspondingly the most hostile to it.
sentence_610: Its territory adjacent the US was relatively undefended, so Spanish policy developed a combination of initiatives.
sentence_611: Spanish soft power diplomatically challenged the British territorial cession west to the Mississippi and the previous northern boundaries of the Floridas.
sentence_612: It imposed a high tariff on American goods, then blocked American settler access to the port of New Orleans.
sentence_613: Spanish hard power extended war alliances and arms to Southwestern Indians to resist American settlement.
sentence_614: A former Continental Army General, [[James_Wilkinson|James Wilkinson]] settled in [[History_of_Kentucky#Kentucky_in_the_American_Revolution_(1775–1783)|Kentucky County]] Virginia in 1784, and there he fostered settler secession from Virginia during the Spanish-allied [[Cherokee–American_wars|Chickamauga Cherokee war]].
sentence_615: Beginning in 1787, he received pay as Spanish Agent 13, and subsequently expanded his efforts to persuade American settlers west of the Appalachians to secede from the United States, first in the Washington administration, and later again in the Jefferson administration.
sentence_616: The total loss of life throughout the conflict is largely unknown.
sentence_617: As was typical in wars of the era, diseases such as [[Smallpox|smallpox]] claimed more lives than battle.
sentence_618: Between 1775 and 1782, a [[1775–82_North_American_smallpox_epidemic|smallpox epidemic]] broke out throughout North America, killing an estimated 130,000 among all its populations in those revolutionary war years.
sentence_619: Historian [[Joseph_Ellis|Joseph Ellis]] suggests that Washington's decision to have his troops [[Variolation|inoculated]] against the disease was one of his most important decisions.
sentence_620: Up to 70,000 American Patriots died during active military service.
sentence_621: Of these, approximately 6,800 were killed in battle, while at least 17,000 died from disease.
sentence_622: The majority of the latter died while [[Prisoners_of_war|prisoners of war]] of the British, mostly in the [[Prisoners_in_the_American_Revolutionary_War|prison ships]] in New York Harbor.
sentence_623: The number of Patriots seriously wounded or disabled by the war has been estimated from 8,500 to 25,000.
sentence_624: The French suffered 2,112 killed in combat in the United States.
sentence_625: The Spanish lost a total of 124 killed and 247 wounded in West Florida.
sentence_626: A British report in 1781 puts their total Army deaths at 6,046 in North America (1775–1779).
sentence_627: Approximately 7,774 [[Germans_in_the_American_Revolution#Allies_of_Great_Britain|Germans]] died in British service in addition to 4,888 deserters; of the former, it is estimated 1,800 were killed in combat.
sentence_628: The American Revolution established the United States with its numerous civil liberties and set an example to overthrow both monarchy and colonial governments.
sentence_629: The United States has the world's oldest written constitution, and the constitutions of other free countries often bear a striking resemblance to the US Constitution – often word-for-word in places.
sentence_630: It inspired the French, Haitian, Latin American Revolutions, and others into the modern era.
sentence_631: Although the Revolution eliminated many forms of inequality, it did little to change the status of women, despite the role they played in winning independence.
sentence_632: Most significantly, it failed to end slavery which continued to be a serious social and political issue and caused divisions that would ultimately end in [[American_Civil_War|civil war]].
sentence_633: While many were uneasy over the contradiction of demanding liberty for some, yet denying it to others, the dependence of southern states on slave labour made abolition too great a challenge.
sentence_634: Between 1774 to 1780, many of the states banned the importation of slaves, but the institution itself continued.
sentence_635: In 1782, Virginia passed a law permitting manumission and over the next eight years more than 10,000 slaves were given their freedom.
sentence_636: With support from Benjamin Franklin, in 1790 the [[Quakers|Quakers]] petitioned Congress to abolish slavery; the number of abolitionist movements greatly increased, and by 1804 all the northern states had outlawed it.
sentence_637: However, even many like Adams who viewed slavery as a 'foul contagion' opposed the 1790 petition as a threat to the Union.
sentence_638: In 1808, Jefferson passed legislation [[Act_Prohibiting_Importation_of_Slaves|banning the importation of slaves]], but allowed the domestic slave trade to continue, arguing the federal government had no right to regulate individual states.
sentence_639: After the first U.S. postage stamp was issued in 1849 the U.S. Post Office frequently issued commemorative stamps celebrating the various people and events of the Revolutionary War.
sentence_640: The first such stamp was the 'Liberty Bell' issue of 1926.

title: Bird
sentence_0: For other uses, see [[Bird_(disambiguation)|Bird (disambiguation)]] and [[Birds_(disambiguation)|Birds (disambiguation)]].
sentence_1: "Aves" and "Avifauna" redirect here.
sentence_2: For other uses, see [[Aves_(disambiguation)|Aves (disambiguation)]] and [[Avifauna_(disambiguation)|Avifauna (disambiguation)]].
sentence_3: Birds are a group of [[Warm-blooded|warm-blooded]] [[Vertebrate|vertebrates]] constituting the [[Class_(biology)|class]] Aves [[English|/ˈeɪviːz/]], characterized by [[Feather|feathers]], toothless beaked jaws, the [[Oviparity|laying]] of [[Eggshell|hard-shelled]] eggs, a high [[Metabolism|metabolic]] rate, a four-chambered [[Heart|heart]], and a strong yet lightweight [[Bird_skeleton|skeleton]].
sentence_4: Birds live worldwide and range in size from the 5 cm (2 in) [[Bee_hummingbird|bee hummingbird]] to the 2.75 m (9 ft) [[Common_ostrich|ostrich]].
sentence_5: There are about ten thousand living species, more than half of which are [[Passerine|passerine]], or "perching" birds.
sentence_6: Birds have [[Glossary_of_bird_terms#wings|wings]] whose development varies according to species; the only known groups without wings are the extinct [[Moa|moa]] and [[Elephant_bird|elephant birds]].
sentence_7: Wings, which evolved from [[Forelimb|forelimbs]], gave birds the ability to fly, although further evolution has led to the loss of flight in some birds, including [[Ratite|ratites]], [[Penguin|penguins]], and diverse [[Endemism|endemic]] island species.
sentence_8: The digestive and respiratory systems of birds are also uniquely adapted for flight.
sentence_9: Some bird species of aquatic environments, particularly [[Seabird|seabirds]] and some [[Water_bird|waterbirds]], have further evolved for swimming.
sentence_10: Birds are a group of [[Feathered_dinosaur|feathered]] [[Theropod|theropod]] [[Dinosaur|dinosaurs]], and constitute the [[Origin_of_birds|only living dinosaurs]].
sentence_11: Likewise, birds are considered [[Reptile|reptiles]] in the modern [[Cladistics|cladistic]] sense of the term, and their closest living relatives are the [[Crocodilia|crocodilians]].
sentence_12: Birds are descendants of the primitive [[Avialae|avialans]] (whose members include [[Archaeopteryx|Archaeopteryx]]) which first appeared about 160 million years ago (mya) in China.
sentence_13: According to DNA evidence, modern birds (Neornithes) evolved in the [[Middle_Cretaceous|Middle]] to [[Late_Cretaceous|Late Cretaceous]], and diversified dramatically around the time of the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene_extinction_event|Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event]] 66 mya, which killed off the [[Pterosaur|pterosaurs]] and all non-avian dinosaurs.
sentence_14: Many [[Social_animal|social species]] pass on knowledge across generations, which is considered [[Animal_culture#Examples_of_culturally_transmitted_behaviors_in_birds|a form of culture]].
sentence_15: Birds are social, communicating with visual signals, calls, and [[Bird_vocalization|songs]], and participating in such behaviours as [[Helpers_at_the_nest|cooperative breeding]] and hunting, [[Flocking_(behavior)|flocking]], and [[Mobbing_(animal_behavior)|mobbing]] of predators.
sentence_16: The vast majority of bird species are socially (but not necessarily sexually) monogamous, usually for one breeding season at a time, sometimes for years, but rarely for life.
sentence_17: Other species have breeding systems that are [[Polygyny_in_animals|polygynous]] (one male with many females) or, rarely, [[Polyandry_in_nature|polyandrous]] (one female with many males).
sentence_18: Birds produce offspring by laying eggs which are fertilised through [[Sexual_reproduction|sexual reproduction]].
sentence_19: They are usually laid in a nest and [[Avian_incubation|incubated]] by the parents.
sentence_20: Most birds have an extended period of parental care after hatching.
sentence_21: Many species of birds are economically important as food for human consumption and raw material in manufacturing, with [[Poultry|domesticated]] and [[Game_(hunting)|undomesticated]] birds being important sources of eggs, meat, and feathers.
sentence_22: [[Songbird|Songbirds]], parrots, and other species are popular as pets.
sentence_23: [[Guano|Guano]] (bird excrement) is harvested for use as a fertiliser.
sentence_24: Birds figure throughout human culture.
sentence_25: About 120 to 130 species have become [[Bird_extinction|extinct]] due to human activity since the 17th century, and hundreds more before then.
sentence_26: Human activity threatens about 1,200 bird species with extinction, though efforts are underway to protect them.
sentence_27: Recreational [[Birdwatching|birdwatching]] is an important part of the [[Ecotourism|ecotourism]] industry.
sentence_28: Main article: [[Evolution_of_birds|Evolution of birds]]
sentence_29: The first [[Biological_classification|classification]] of birds was developed by [[Francis_Willughby|Francis Willughby]] and [[John_Ray|John Ray]] in their 1676 volume Ornithologiae.
sentence_30: [[Carl_Linnaeus|Carl Linnaeus]] modified that work in 1758 to devise the [[Taxonomic_classification|taxonomic classification]] system currently in use.
sentence_31: Birds are categorised as the [[Class_(biology)|biological class]] Aves in Linnaean taxonomy.
sentence_32: [[Phylogenetic_taxonomy|Phylogenetic taxonomy]] places Aves in the dinosaur [[Clade|clade]] [[Theropoda|Theropoda]].
sentence_33: Aves and a sister group, the order [[Crocodilia|Crocodilia]], contain the only living representatives of the reptile clade [[Archosauria|Archosauria]].
sentence_34: During the late 1990s, Aves was most commonly defined [[Phylogenetics|phylogenetically]] as all descendants of the [[Most_recent_common_ancestor|most recent common ancestor]] of modern birds and [[Archaeopteryx|Archaeopteryx lithographica]].
sentence_35: However, an earlier definition proposed by [[Jacques_Gauthier|Jacques Gauthier]] gained wide currency in the 21st century, and is used by many scientists including adherents of the [[Phylocode|Phylocode]] system.
sentence_36: Gauthier defined Aves to include only the [[Crown_group|crown group]] of the set of modern birds.
sentence_37: This was done by excluding most groups known only from [[Fossils|fossils]], and assigning them, instead, to the broader group Avialae, in part to avoid the uncertainties about the placement of Archaeopteryx in relation to animals traditionally thought of as theropod dinosaurs.
sentence_38: Gauthier and de Queiroz identified four different definitions for the same biological name "Aves", which is a problem.
sentence_39: The authors proposed to reserve the term Aves only for the crown group consisting of the last common ancestor of all living birds and all of its descendants, which corresponds to meaning number 4 below.
sentence_40: He assigned other names to the other groups.

list.value: Aves can mean all [[Archosaur|archosaurs]] closer to birds than to [[Crocodile|crocodiles]] (alternately [[Avemetatarsalia|Avemetatarsalia]])
Aves can mean those advanced archosaurs with feathers (alternately [[Avifilopluma|Avifilopluma]])
Aves can mean those feathered dinosaurs that fly (alternately [[Avialae|Avialae]])
Aves can mean the last common ancestor of all the currently living birds and all of its descendants (a "[[Crown_group|crown group]]", in this sense synonymous with Neornithes)

sentence_41: Under the fourth definition Archaeopteryx, traditionally considered one of the earliest members of Aves, is removed from this group, becoming a non-avian dinosaur instead.
sentence_42: These proposals have been adopted by many researchers in the field of palaeontology and [[Bird_evolution|bird evolution]], though the exact definitions applied have been inconsistent.
sentence_43: Avialae, initially proposed to replace the traditional fossil content of Aves, is often used synonymously with the vernacular term "bird" by these researchers.
sentence_44: Most researchers define Avialae as branch-based clade, though definitions vary.
sentence_45: Many authors have used a definition similar to "all [[Theropod|theropods]] closer to birds than to [[Deinonychus|Deinonychus]]", with [[Troodon|Troodon]] being sometimes added as a second external specifier in case it is closer to birds than to Deinonychus.
sentence_46: Avialae is also occasionally defined as an [[Phylogenetic_nomenclature#Phylogenetic_definitions|apomorphy-based clade]] (that is, one based on physical characteristics).
sentence_47: [[Jacques_Gauthier|Jacques Gauthier]], who named Avialae in 1986, re-defined it in 2001 as all dinosaurs that possessed feathered [[Wing|wings]] used in flapping [[Bird_flight|flight]], and the birds that descended from them.
sentence_48: Despite being currently one of the most widely used, the crown-group definition of Aves has been criticised by some researchers.
sentence_49: Lee and Spencer (1997) argued that, contrary to what Gauthier defended, this definition would not increase the stability of the clade and the exact content of Aves will always be uncertain because any defined clade (either crown or not) will have few synapomorphies distinguishing it from its closest relatives.
sentence_50: Their alternative definition is synonymous to Avifilopluma.

section_2.value: Dinosaurs and the origin of birds

sentence_51: Main article: [[Origin_of_birds|Origin of birds]]
sentence_52: Based on fossil and biological evidence, most scientists accept that birds are a specialised subgroup of [[Theropod|theropod]] [[Dinosaur|dinosaurs]], and more specifically, they are members of [[Maniraptora|Maniraptora]], a group of theropods which includes [[Dromaeosauridae|dromaeosaurids]] and [[Oviraptorosauria|oviraptorosaurs]], among others.
sentence_53: As scientists have discovered more theropods closely related to birds, the previously clear distinction between non-birds and birds has become blurred.
sentence_54: Recent discoveries in the [[Liaoning|Liaoning]] Province of northeast China, which demonstrate many small theropod [[Feathered_dinosaurs|feathered dinosaurs]], contribute to this ambiguity.
sentence_55: The consensus view in contemporary [[Paleontology|palaeontology]] is that the flying theropods, or [[Avialae|avialans]], are the closest relatives of the [[Deinonychosaur|deinonychosaurs]], which include dromaeosaurids and [[Troodontid|troodontids]].
sentence_56: Together, these form a group called [[Paraves|Paraves]].
sentence_57: Some [[Basal_(phylogenetics)|basal]] members of Deinonychosauria, such as [[Microraptor|Microraptor]], have features which may have enabled them to glide or fly.
sentence_58: The most basal deinonychosaurs were very small.
sentence_59: This evidence raises the possibility that the ancestor of all paravians may have been [[Arboreal|arboreal]], have been able to glide, or both.
sentence_60: Unlike Archaeopteryx and the non-avialan feathered dinosaurs, who primarily ate meat, recent studies suggest that the first avialans were [[Omnivore|omnivores]].
sentence_61: The [[Late_Jurassic|Late Jurassic]] Archaeopteryx is well known as one of the first [[Transitional_fossil|transitional fossils]] to be found, and it provided support for the [[Theory_of_evolution|theory of evolution]] in the late 19th century.
sentence_62: Archaeopteryx was the first fossil to display both clearly traditional reptilian characteristics—teeth, clawed fingers, and a long, lizard-like tail—as well as wings with flight feathers similar to those of modern birds.
sentence_63: It is not considered a direct ancestor of birds, though it is possibly closely related to the true ancestor.
sentence_64: See also: [[List_of_fossil_bird_genera|List of fossil bird genera]]
sentence_65: Over 40% of key traits found in modern birds evolved during the 60 million year transition from the earliest [[Avemetatarsalia|bird-line archosaurs]] to the first [[Maniraptoromorpha|maniraptoromorphs]], i.e. the first dinosaurs closer to living birds than to [[Tyrannosaurus|Tyrannosaurus rex]].
sentence_66: The loss of osteoderms otherwise common in archosaurs and acquisition of primitive feathers might have occurred early during this phase.
sentence_67: After the appearance of Maniraptoromorpha, the next 40 million years marked a continuous reduction of body size and the accumulation of [[Neoteny|neotenic]] (juvenile-like) characteristics.
sentence_68: [[Hypercarnivore|Hypercarnivory]] became increasingly less common while braincases enlarged and forelimbs became longer.
sentence_69: The integument evolved into complex, pennaceous feathers.
sentence_70: The oldest known paravian (and probably the earliest avialan) fossils come from the [[Tiaojishan_Formation|Tiaojishan Formation]] of China, which has been dated to the late [[Jurassic|Jurassic]] period ([[Oxfordian_(stage)|Oxfordian]] stage), about 160 million years ago.
sentence_71: The avialan species from this time period include [[Anchiornis_huxleyi|Anchiornis huxleyi]], [[Xiaotingia_zhengi|Xiaotingia zhengi]], and [[Aurornis_xui|Aurornis xui]].
sentence_72: The well-known probable early avialan, Archaeopteryx, dates from slightly later Jurassic rocks (about 155 million years old) from [[Germany|Germany]].
sentence_73: Many of these early avialans shared unusual anatomical features that may be ancestral to modern birds, but were later lost during bird evolution.
sentence_74: These features include enlarged claws on the second toe which may have been held clear of the ground in life, and long feathers or "hind wings" covering the hind limbs and feet, which may have been used in aerial maneuvering.
sentence_75: Avialans diversified into a wide variety of forms during the [[Cretaceous_Period|Cretaceous Period]].
sentence_76: Many groups retained [[Symplesiomorphy|primitive characteristics]], such as clawed wings and teeth, though the latter were lost independently in a number of avialan groups, including modern birds (Aves).
sentence_77: Increasingly stiff tails (especially the outermost half) can be seen in the evolution of maniraptoromorphs, and this process culminated in the appearance of the [[Pygostyle|pygostyle]], an ossification of fused tail vertebrae.
sentence_78: In the late Cretaceous, about 100 million years ago, the ancestors of all modern birds evolved a more open pelvis, allowing them to lay larger eggs compared to body size.
sentence_79: Around 95 million years ago, they evolved a better sense of smell.
sentence_80: A third stage of bird evolution starting with [[Ornithothoraces|Ornithothoraces]] (the "bird-chested" avialans) can be associated with the refining of aerodynamics and flight capabilities, and the loss or co-ossification of several skeletal features.
sentence_81: Particularly significant are the development of an enlarged, [[Keel_(bird_anatomy)|keeled]] sternum and the [[Alula|alula]], and the loss of grasping hands.
sentence_82: See also: [[Protobirds|Protobirds]] and [[Avialae|Avialae]]
sentence_83: The first large, diverse lineage of short-tailed avialans to evolve were the [[Enantiornithes|Enantiornithes]], or "opposite birds", so named because the construction of their shoulder bones was in reverse to that of modern birds.
sentence_84: Enantiornithes occupied a wide array of [[Ecological_niche|ecological niches]], from sand-probing shorebirds and fish-eaters to tree-dwelling forms and seed-eaters.
sentence_85: While they were the dominant group of avialans during the Cretaceous period, enantiornithes became extinct along with many other dinosaur groups at the end of the [[Mesozoic_era|Mesozoic era]].
sentence_86: Many species of the second major avialan lineage to diversify, the [[Euornithes|Euornithes]] (meaning "true birds", because they include the ancestors of modern birds), were semi-aquatic and specialised in eating fish and other small aquatic organisms.
sentence_87: Unlike the Enantiornithes, which dominated land-based and arboreal habitats, most early euornithes lacked [[Perching_bird|perching]] adaptations and seem to have included shorebird-like species, waders, and swimming and diving species.
sentence_88: The latter included the superficially [[Gull|gull]]-like [[Ichthyornis|Ichthyornis]] and the [[Hesperornithiformes|Hesperornithiformes]], which became so well adapted to hunting fish in marine environments that they lost the ability to fly and became primarily aquatic.
sentence_89: The early euornithes also saw the development of many traits associated with modern birds, like strongly keeled breastbones, toothless, beaked portions of their jaws (though most non-avian euornithes retained teeth in other parts of the jaws).
sentence_90: Euornithes also included the first avialans to develop true [[Pygostyle|pygostyle]] and a fully mobile fan of tail feathers, which may have replaced the "hind wing" as the primary mode of aerial maneuverability and braking in flight.
sentence_91: A study on [[Mosaic_evolution|mosaic evolution]] in the avian skull found that the [[Most_recent_common_ancestor|last common ancestor]] of all Neornithes might have had a beak similar to that of the modern [[Hook-billed_vanga|hook-billed vanga]] and a skull similar to that of the [[Eurasian_golden_oriole|Eurasian golden oriole]].
sentence_92: As both species are small aerial and canopy foraging [[Omnivore|omnivores]], a similar ecological niche was inferred for this hypothetical ancestor.
sentence_93: See also: [[Sibley–Ahlquist_taxonomy_of_birds|Sibley–Ahlquist taxonomy of birds]] and [[Dinosaur_classification|dinosaur classification]]
sentence_94: All modern birds lie within the [[Crown_group|crown group]] Aves (alternately Neornithes), which has two subdivisions: the [[Palaeognathae|Palaeognathae]], which includes the flightless [[Ratite|ratites]] (such as the [[Ostrich|ostriches]]) and the weak-flying [[Tinamou|tinamous]], and the extremely diverse [[Neognathae|Neognathae]], containing all other birds.
sentence_95: These two subdivisions are often given the [[Taxonomic_rank|rank]] of superorder, although Livezey and Zusi assigned them "cohort" rank.
sentence_96: Depending on the [[Alpha_taxonomy|taxonomic]] viewpoint, the number of known living bird species varies anywhere from 9,800 to 10,758.
sentence_97: The discovery of [[Vegavis|Vegavis]], a late Cretaceous member of the [[Anatidae|Anatidae]], proved that the diversification of modern birds started before the [[Cenozoic|Cenozoic era]].
sentence_98: The affinities of an earlier fossil, the possible [[Galliformes|galliform]] Austinornis lentus, dated to about 85 million years ago, are still too controversial to provide a fossil evidence of modern bird diversification.
sentence_99: Most studies agree on a Cretaceous age for the most recent common ancestor of modern birds but estimates range from the [[Middle_Cretaceous|Middle Cretaceous]] to the latest [[Late_Cretaceous|Late Cretaceous]].
sentence_100: Similarly, there is no agreement on whether most of the early diversification of modern birds occurred before or after the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene_extinction_event|Cretaceous–Palaeogene extinction event]].
sentence_101: This disagreement is in part caused by a divergence in the evidence; most molecular dating studies suggests a Cretaceous [[Evolutionary_radiation|evolutionary radiation]], while fossil evidence points to a Cenozoic radiation (the so-called 'rocks' versus 'clocks' controversy).
sentence_102: Previous attempts to reconcile molecular and fossil evidence have proved controversial, but more recent estimates, using a more comprehensive sample of fossils and a new way of calibrating [[Molecular_clocks|molecular clocks]], showed that while modern birds originated early in the Late Cretaceous in Western Gondwana, a pulse of diversification in all major groups occurred around the Cretaceous–Palaeogene extinction event.
sentence_103: Modern birds expanded from West Gondwana to the Laurasia through two routes.
sentence_104: One route was an Antarctic interchange in the Paleogene.
sentence_105: This can be confirmed with the presence of multiple avian groups in Australia and New Zealand.
sentence_106: The other route was probably through North American, via land bridges during the Paleocene.
sentence_107: This allowed the expansion and diversification of Neornithes into the Holarctic and Paleotropics.
sentence_108: See also: [[List_of_birds|List of birds]]
sentence_109: [[Cladogram|Cladogram]] of modern bird relationships based on Kuhl, H. et al.
sentence_111: The classification of birds is a contentious issue.
sentence_112: [[Charles_Sibley|Sibley]] and [[Jon_Ahlquist|Ahlquist]]'s Phylogeny and Classification of Birds (1990) is a landmark work on the classification of birds, although it is frequently debated and constantly revised.
sentence_113: Most evidence seems to suggest the assignment of orders is accurate, but scientists disagree about the relationships between the orders themselves; evidence from modern bird anatomy, fossils and DNA have all been brought to bear on the problem, but no strong consensus has emerged.
sentence_114: More recently, new fossil and molecular evidence is providing an increasingly clear picture of the evolution of modern bird orders.
sentence_115: As of 2020, the [[Genome|genome]] has been sequenced for at least one species in about 90% of extant avian families (218 out of 236 families recognised by the Howard and Moore Checklist).
sentence_116: See [[List_of_sequenced_animal_genomes|list of sequenced animal genomes]].
sentence_117: See also: [[Lists_of_birds_by_region|Lists of birds by region]] and [[List_of_birds_by_population|List of birds by population]]
sentence_118: Birds live and breed in most terrestrial habitats and on all seven continents, reaching their southern extreme in the snow petrel's breeding colonies up to 440 kilometres (270 mi) inland in [[Antarctica|Antarctica]].
sentence_119: The highest bird [[Biodiversity|diversity]] occurs in tropical regions.
sentence_120: It was earlier thought that this high diversity was the result of higher [[Speciation|speciation]] rates in the tropics; however recent studies found higher speciation rates in the high latitudes that were offset by greater [[Extinction|extinction]] rates than in the tropics.
sentence_121: Many species migrate annually over great distances and across oceans; several families of birds have adapted to life both on the world's oceans and in them, and some [[Seabird|seabird]] species come ashore only to breed, while some [[Penguin|penguins]] have been recorded diving up to 300 metres (980 ft) deep.
sentence_122: Many bird species have established breeding populations in areas to which they have been [[Introduced_species|introduced]] by humans.
sentence_123: Some of these introductions have been deliberate; the [[Ring-necked_pheasant|ring-necked pheasant]], for example, has been introduced around the world as a [[Game_bird|game bird]].
sentence_124: Others have been accidental, such as the establishment of wild [[Monk_parakeet|monk parakeets]] in several North American cities after their escape from captivity.
sentence_125: Some species, including [[Cattle_egret|cattle egret]], [[Yellow-headed_caracara|yellow-headed caracara]] and [[Galah|galah]], have [[Avian_range_expansion|spread naturally]] far beyond their original ranges as [[Agriculture|agricultural practices]] created suitable new habitat.
sentence_126: Main articles: [[Bird_anatomy|Bird anatomy]] and [[Bird_vision|Bird vision]]
sentence_127: See also: Egg tooth
sentence_128: Compared with other vertebrates, birds have a [[Body_plan|body plan]] that shows many unusual adaptations, mostly to facilitate [[Bird_flight|flight]].
sentence_129: The skeleton consists of very lightweight bones.
sentence_130: They have large air-filled cavities (called pneumatic cavities) which connect with the [[Respiratory_system|respiratory system]].
sentence_131: The skull bones in adults are fused and do not show [[Cranial_sutures|cranial sutures]].
sentence_132: The [[Orbit_(anatomy)|orbits]] are large and separated by a bony septum.
sentence_133: The [[Vertebral_column|spine]] has cervical, thoracic, lumbar and caudal regions with the number of cervical (neck) vertebrae highly variable and especially flexible, but movement is reduced in the anterior [[Thoracic_vertebrae|thoracic vertebrae]] and absent in the later vertebrae.
sentence_134: The last few are fused with the [[Pelvis|pelvis]] to form the synsacrum.
sentence_135: The ribs are flattened and the [[Sternum|sternum]] is keeled for the attachment of flight muscles except in the flightless bird orders.
sentence_136: The forelimbs are modified into wings.
sentence_137: The wings are more or less developed depending on the species; the only known groups that lost their wings are the [[Extinct|extinct]] [[Moa|moa]] and [[Elephant_bird|elephant birds]].
sentence_138: Like the [[Reptile|reptiles]], birds are primarily uricotelic, that is, their [[Kidney|kidneys]] extract nitrogenous waste from their bloodstream and excrete it as [[Uric_acid|uric acid]], instead of [[Urea|urea]] or [[Ammonia|ammonia]], through the ureters into the intestine.
sentence_139: Birds do not have a [[Urinary_bladder|urinary bladder]] or external urethral opening and (with exception of the [[Ostrich#Description|ostrich]]) uric acid is excreted along with faeces as a semisolid waste.
sentence_140: However, birds such as hummingbirds can be facultatively ammonotelic, excreting most of the nitrogenous wastes as ammonia.
sentence_141: They also excrete [[Creatine|creatine]], rather than [[Creatinine|creatinine]] like mammals.
sentence_142: This material, as well as the output of the intestines, emerges from the bird's [[Cloaca|cloaca]].
sentence_143: The cloaca is a multi-purpose opening: waste is expelled through it, most birds mate by [[Bird_anatomy#Reproduction|joining cloaca]], and females lay eggs from it.
sentence_144: In addition, many species of birds regurgitate [[Pellet_(ornithology)|pellets]].
sentence_145: It is a common but not universal feature of [[Altriciality|altricial]] [[Passerine|passerine]] nestlings (born helpless, under constant parental care) that instead of excreting directly into the nest, they produce a [[Fecal_sac|fecal sac]].
sentence_146: This is a mucus-covered pouch that allows parents to either dispose of the waste outside the nest or to recycle the waste through their own digestive system.
sentence_147: Males within [[Palaeognathae|Palaeognathae]] (with the exception of the [[Kiwi_(bird)|kiwis]]), the [[Anseriformes|Anseriformes]] (with the exception of [[Screamer|screamers]]), and in rudimentary forms in [[Galliformes|Galliformes]] (but fully developed in [[Cracidae|Cracidae]]) possess a [[Bird_penis|penis]], which is never present in [[Neoaves|Neoaves]].
sentence_148: The length is thought to be related to [[Sperm_competition|sperm competition]].
sentence_149: When not copulating, it is hidden within the [[Proctodeum|proctodeum]] compartment within the cloaca, just inside the vent.
sentence_150: Female birds have [[Female_sperm_storage|sperm storage]] tubules that allow sperm to remain viable long after copulation, a hundred days in some species.
sentence_151: Sperm from multiple males may [[Sperm_competition|compete]] through this mechanism.
sentence_152: Most female birds have a single [[Ovary|ovary]] and a single [[Oviduct|oviduct]], both on the left side, but there are exceptions: species in at least 16 different orders of birds have two ovaries.
sentence_153: Even these species, however, tend to have a single oviduct.
sentence_154: It has been speculated that this might be an adaptation to flight, but males have two testes, and it is also observed that the gonads in both sexes decrease dramatically in size outside the breeding season.
sentence_155: Also terrestrial birds generally have a single ovary, as does the [[Platypus|platypus]], an egg-laying mammal.
sentence_156: A more likely explanation is that the egg develops a shell while passing through the oviduct over a period of about a day, so that if two eggs were to develop at the same time, there would be a risk to survival.
sentence_157: Birds have two sexes: either [[Female|female]] or [[Male|male]].
sentence_158: The sex of birds is determined by the [[ZW_sex-determination_system|Z and W sex chromosomes]], rather than by the [[XY_sex-determination_system|X and Y chromosomes]] present in [[Mammal|mammals]].
sentence_159: Male birds have two Z chromosomes (ZZ), and female birds have a W chromosome and a Z chromosome (WZ).
sentence_160: In nearly all species of birds, an individual's sex is determined at fertilisation.
