sentence_161: However, one recent study claimed to demonstrate [[Temperature-dependent_sex_determination|temperature-dependent sex determination]] among the [[Australian_brushturkey|Australian brushturkey]], for which higher temperatures during incubation resulted in a higher female-to-male [[Sex_ratio|sex ratio]].
sentence_162: This, however, was later proven to not be the case.
sentence_163: These birds do not exhibit temperature-dependent sex determination, but temperature-dependent sex mortality.
sentence_164: Birds have one of the most complex [[Respiratory_system|respiratory systems]] of all animal groups.
sentence_165: Upon inhalation, 75% of the fresh air bypasses the lungs and flows directly into a posterior [[Parabronchi|air sac]] which extends from the lungs and connects with air spaces in the bones and fills them with air.
sentence_166: The other 25% of the air goes directly into the lungs.
sentence_167: When the bird exhales, the used air flows out of the lungs and the stored fresh air from the posterior air sac is simultaneously forced into the lungs.
sentence_168: Thus, a bird's lungs receive a constant supply of fresh air during both inhalation and exhalation.
sentence_169: Sound production is achieved using the [[Syrinx_(biology)|syrinx]], a muscular chamber incorporating multiple tympanic membranes which diverges from the lower end of the trachea; the trachea being elongated in some species, increasing the volume of vocalisations and the perception of the bird's size.
sentence_170: In birds, the main arteries taking blood away from the heart originate from the right [[Aortic_arches|aortic arch]] (or pharyngeal arch), unlike in the mammals where the left aortic arch forms this part of the [[Aorta|aorta]].
sentence_171: The postcava receives blood from the limbs via the renal portal system.
sentence_172: Unlike in mammals, the circulating [[Red_blood_cells|red blood cells]] in birds retain their [[Cell_nucleus|nucleus]].
sentence_173: The avian circulatory system is driven by a four-chambered, myogenic heart contained in a fibrous pericardial sac.
sentence_174: This pericardial sac is filled with a serous fluid for lubrication.
sentence_175: The heart itself is divided into a right and left half, each with an [[Atrium_(heart)|atrium]] and [[Ventricle_(heart)|ventricle]].
sentence_176: The atrium and ventricles of each side are separated by [[Atrioventricular_valves|atrioventricular valves]] which prevent back flow from one chamber to the next during contraction.
sentence_177: Being myogenic, the heart's pace is maintained by pacemaker cells found in the sinoatrial node, located on the right atrium.
sentence_178: The [[Sinoatrial_node|sinoatrial node]] uses calcium to cause a [[Depolarization|depolarising]] [[Signal_transduction_pathway|signal transduction pathway]] from the atrium through right and left atrioventricular bundle which communicates contraction to the ventricles.
sentence_179: The avian heart also consists of muscular arches that are made up of thick bundles of muscular layers.
sentence_180: Much like a mammalian heart, the avian heart is composed of [[Endocardial|endocardial]], [[Myocardial|myocardial]] and epicardial layers.
sentence_181: The atrium walls tend to be thinner than the ventricle walls, due to the intense ventricular contraction used to pump oxygenated blood throughout the body.
sentence_182: Avian hearts are generally larger than mammalian hearts when compared to body mass.
sentence_183: This adaptation allows more blood to be pumped to meet the high metabolic need associated with flight.
sentence_184: Birds have a very efficient system for diffusing oxygen into the blood; birds have a ten times greater surface area to [[Gas_exchange|gas exchange]] volume than mammals.
sentence_185: As a result, birds have more blood in their capillaries per unit of volume of lung than a mammal.
sentence_186: The arteries are composed of thick elastic muscles to withstand the pressure of the ventricular contractions, and become more rigid as they move away from the heart.
sentence_187: Blood moves through the arteries, which undergo [[Vasoconstriction|vasoconstriction]], and into arterioles which act as a transportation system to distribute primarily oxygen as well as nutrients to all tissues of the body.
sentence_188: As the arterioles move away from the heart and into individual organs and tissues they are further divided to increase surface area and slow blood flow.
sentence_189: Blood travels through the arterioles and moves into the capillaries where gas exchange can occur.
sentence_190: Capillaries are organized into capillary beds in tissues; it is here that blood exchanges oxygen for carbon dioxide waste.
sentence_191: In the capillary beds, blood flow is slowed to allow maximum [[Diffusion|diffusion]] of oxygen into the tissues.
sentence_192: Once the blood has become deoxygenated, it travels through venules then veins and back to the heart.
sentence_193: Veins, unlike arteries, are thin and rigid as they do not need to withstand extreme pressure.
sentence_194: As blood travels through the venules to the veins a funneling occurs called [[Vasodilation|vasodilation]] bringing blood back to the heart.
sentence_195: Once the blood reaches the heart, it moves first into the right atrium, then the right ventricle to be pumped through the lungs for further gas exchange of carbon dioxide waste for oxygen.
sentence_196: Oxygenated blood then flows from the lungs through the left atrium to the left ventricle where it is pumped out to the body.
sentence_197: The [[Nervous_system|nervous system]] is large relative to the bird's size.
sentence_198: The most developed part of the brain is the one that controls the flight-related functions, while the [[Cerebellum|cerebellum]] coordinates movement and the [[Cerebrum|cerebrum]] controls behaviour patterns, navigation, mating and [[Bird_nest|nest]] building.
sentence_199: Most birds have a poor [[Olfaction|sense of smell]] with notable exceptions including [[Kiwi_(bird)|kiwis]], [[New_World_vulture|New World vultures]] and [[Tubenoses|tubenoses]].
sentence_200: The avian [[Visual_system|visual system]] is usually highly developed.
sentence_201: Water birds have special flexible lenses, allowing [[Accommodation_(eye)|accommodation]] for vision in air and water.
sentence_202: Some species also have dual [[Fovea_centralis|fovea]].
sentence_203: Birds are [[Tetrachromacy|tetrachromatic]], possessing [[Ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] (UV) sensitive [[Cone_cell|cone cells]] in the eye as well as green, red and blue ones.
sentence_204: They also have [[Double_cone_(biology)|double cones]], likely to mediate [[Monochromacy|achromatic vision]].
sentence_205: Many birds show plumage patterns in [[Ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] that are invisible to the human eye; some birds whose sexes appear similar to the naked eye are distinguished by the presence of ultraviolet reflective patches on their feathers.
sentence_206: Male [[Blue_tit|blue tits]] have an ultraviolet reflective crown patch which is displayed in courtship by posturing and raising of their nape feathers.
sentence_207: Ultraviolet light is also used in foraging—[[Kestrel|kestrels]] have been shown to search for prey by detecting the UV reflective urine trail marks left on the ground by rodents.
sentence_208: With the exception of pigeons and a few other species, the eyelids of birds are not used in blinking.
sentence_209: Instead the eye is lubricated by the [[Nictitating_membrane|nictitating membrane]], a third eyelid that moves horizontally.
sentence_210: The nictitating membrane also covers the eye and acts as a [[Contact_lens|contact lens]] in many aquatic birds.
sentence_211: The bird retina has a fan shaped blood supply system called the [[Pecten_oculi|pecten]].
sentence_212: Eyes of most birds are large, not very round and capable of only limited movement in the orbits, typically 10-20°.
sentence_213: Birds with eyes on the sides of their heads have a wide [[Visual_field|visual field]], while birds with eyes on the front of their heads, such as owls, have binocular vision and can estimate the [[Depth_of_field|depth of field]].
sentence_214: The avian [[Ear|ear]] lacks external [[Pinna_(anatomy)|pinnae]] but is covered by feathers, although in some birds, such as the [[Asio|Asio]], [[Horned_owl|Bubo]] and [[Scops_owl|Otus]] [[Owl|owls]], these feathers form tufts which resemble ears.
sentence_215: The [[Inner_ear|inner ear]] has a [[Cochlea|cochlea]], but it is not spiral as in mammals.
sentence_216: A few species are able to use chemical defences against predators; some [[Procellariiformes|Procellariiformes]] can eject an unpleasant [[Stomach_oil|stomach oil]] against an aggressor, and some species of [[Pitohui|pitohuis]] from [[New_Guinea|New Guinea]] have a powerful [[Neurotoxin|neurotoxin]] in their skin and feathers.
sentence_217: A lack of field observations limit our knowledge, but intraspecific conflicts are known to sometimes result in injury or death.
sentence_218: The screamers ([[Anhimidae|Anhimidae]]), some jacanas ([[Jacana_(genus)|Jacana]], [[Hydrophasianus|Hydrophasianus]]), the spur-winged goose ([[Plectropterus|Plectropterus]]), the torrent duck ([[Merganetta|Merganetta]]) and nine species of lapwing ([[Vanellus|Vanellus]]) use a sharp spur on the wing as a weapon.
sentence_219: The steamer ducks ([[Tachyeres|Tachyeres]]), geese and swans (Anserinae), the solitaire ([[Pezophaps|Pezophaps]]), sheathbills ([[Chionis|Chionis]]), some guans ([[Crax|Crax]]) and stone curlews ([[Burhinus|Burhinus]]) use a bony knob on the [[Alula|alular]] metacarpal to punch and hammer opponents.
sentence_220: The jacanas [[Actophilornis|Actophilornis]] and [[Irediparra|Irediparra]] have an expanded, blade-like radius.
sentence_221: The extinct [[Xenicibis|Xenicibis]] was unique in having an elongate forelimb and massive hand which likely functioned in combat or defence as a jointed club or flail.
sentence_222: [[Cygnus_olor|Swans]], for instance, may strike with the bony spurs and bite when defending eggs or young.
sentence_223: Main articles: [[Feather|Feather]] and [[Flight_feather|Flight feather]]
sentence_224: Feathers are a feature characteristic of birds (though also present in [[Feathered_dinosaurs|some dinosaurs]] not currently considered to be true birds).
sentence_225: They facilitate [[Bird_flight|flight]], provide insulation that aids in [[Thermoregulation|thermoregulation]], and are used in display, camouflage, and signalling.
sentence_226: There are several types of feathers, each serving its own set of purposes.
sentence_227: Feathers are epidermal growths attached to the skin and arise only in specific tracts of skin called [[Pterylography|pterylae]].
sentence_228: The distribution pattern of these feather tracts (pterylosis) is used in taxonomy and systematics.
sentence_229: The arrangement and appearance of feathers on the body, called [[Plumage|plumage]], may vary within species by age, social status, and [[Sexual_dimorphism|sex]].
sentence_230: Plumage is regularly [[Moult|moulted]]; the standard plumage of a bird that has moulted after breeding is known as the "[[Glossary_of_bird_terms#basic_plumage|non-breeding]]" plumage, or—in the [[Humphrey–Parkes_terminology|Humphrey–Parkes terminology]]—"basic" plumage; breeding plumages or variations of the basic plumage are known under the Humphrey–Parkes system as "[[Glossary_of_bird_terms#alternate_plumage|alternate]]" plumages.
sentence_231: Moulting is annual in most species, although may have two moults a year, and large birds of prey may moult only once every few years.
sentence_232: Moulting patterns vary across species.
sentence_233: In passerines, [[Flight_feather|flight feathers]] are replaced one at a time with the innermost [[Glossary_of_bird_terms#primary|primary]] being the first.
sentence_234: When the fifth of sixth primary is replaced, the outermost [[Glossary_of_bird_terms#tertiaries|tertiaries]] begin to drop.
sentence_235: After the innermost tertiaries are moulted, the [[Glossary_of_bird_terms#secondaries|secondaries]] starting from the innermost begin to drop and this proceeds to the outer feathers (centrifugal moult).
sentence_236: The greater primary [[Glossary_of_bird_terms#coverts|coverts]] are moulted in synchrony with the primary that they overlap.
sentence_237: A small number of species, such as ducks and geese, lose all of their flight feathers at once, temporarily becoming flightless.
sentence_238: As a general rule, the tail feathers are moulted and replaced starting with the innermost pair.
sentence_239: Centripetal moults of tail feathers are however seen in the [[Phasianidae|Phasianidae]].
sentence_240: The centrifugal moult is modified in the tail feathers of [[Woodpecker|woodpeckers]] and [[Treecreeper|treecreepers]], in that it begins with the second innermost pair of feathers and finishes with the central pair of feathers so that the bird maintains a functional climbing tail.
sentence_241: The general pattern seen in [[Passerine|passerines]] is that the primaries are replaced outward, secondaries inward, and the tail from centre outward.
sentence_242: Before nesting, the females of most bird species gain a bare [[Brood_patch|brood patch]] by losing feathers close to the belly.
sentence_243: The skin there is well supplied with blood vessels and helps the bird in incubation.
sentence_244: Feathers require maintenance and birds preen or groom them daily, spending an average of around 9% of their daily time on this.
sentence_245: The bill is used to brush away foreign particles and to apply [[Wax|waxy]] secretions from the [[Uropygial_gland|uropygial gland]]; these secretions protect the feathers' flexibility and act as an [[Antimicrobial|antimicrobial agent]], inhibiting the growth of feather-degrading [[Bacteria|bacteria]].
sentence_246: This may be supplemented with the secretions of [[Formic_acid|formic acid]] from ants, which birds receive through a behaviour known as [[Anting_(bird_activity)|anting]], to remove feather parasites.
sentence_247: The [[Bird_anatomy#Scales|scales]] of birds are composed of the same keratin as beaks, claws, and spurs.
sentence_248: They are found mainly on the toes and [[Metatarsus|metatarsus]], but may be found further up on the ankle in some birds.
sentence_249: Most bird scales do not overlap significantly, except in the cases of [[Kingfisher|kingfishers]] and [[Woodpecker|woodpeckers]].
sentence_250: The scales of birds are thought to be [[Homology_(biology)|homologous]] to those of reptiles and mammals.
sentence_251: Main article: [[Bird_flight|Bird flight]]
sentence_252: Most birds can fly, which distinguishes them from almost all other vertebrate classes.
sentence_253: Flight is the primary means of locomotion for most bird species and is used for searching for food and for escaping from predators.
sentence_254: Birds have various adaptations for flight, including a lightweight skeleton, two large flight muscles, the pectoralis (which accounts for 15% of the total mass of the bird) and the supracoracoideus, as well as a modified forelimb ([[Wing|wing]]) that serves as an [[Airfoil|aerofoil]].
sentence_255: Wing shape and size generally determine a bird's flight style and performance; many birds combine powered, flapping flight with less energy-intensive soaring flight.
sentence_256: About 60 extant bird species are [[Flightless_bird|flightless]], as were many extinct birds.
sentence_257: Flightlessness often arises in birds on isolated islands, probably due to limited resources and the absence of land predators.
sentence_258: Although flightless, penguins use similar musculature and movements to "fly" through the water, as do some flight-capable birds such as [[Auk|auks]], [[Shearwater|shearwaters]] and [[Dipper|dippers]].
sentence_259: Most birds are [[Diurnal_animal|diurnal]], but some birds, such as many species of [[Owl|owls]] and [[Nightjar|nightjars]], are nocturnal or crepuscular (active during twilight hours), and many coastal [[Wader|waders]] feed when the tides are appropriate, by day or night.
sentence_260: [[Glossary_of_bird_terms#dietary_classification_terms_(-vores)|Birds' diets]] are varied and often include [[Nectar_(plant)|nectar]], fruit, plants, seeds, [[Carrion|carrion]], and various small animals, including other birds.
sentence_261: The [[Digestive_system|digestive system]] of birds is unique, with a [[Crop_(anatomy)|crop]] for storage and a [[Gizzard|gizzard]] that contains swallowed stones for grinding food to compensate for the lack of teeth.
sentence_262: Most birds are highly adapted for rapid digestion to aid with flight.
sentence_263: Some migratory birds have adapted to use protein stored in many parts of their bodies, including protein from the intestines, as additional energy during migration.
sentence_264: Birds that employ many strategies to obtain food or feed on a variety of food items are called generalists, while others that concentrate time and effort on specific food items or have a single strategy to obtain food are considered specialists.
sentence_265: [[Avian_foraging|Avian foraging]] strategies can vary widely by species.
sentence_266: Many birds [[Gleaning_(birds)|glean]] for insects, invertebrates, fruit, or seeds.
sentence_267: Some hunt insects by suddenly attacking from a branch.
sentence_268: Those species that seek [[Pest_(organism)|pest]] [[Insect|insects]] are considered beneficial 'biological control agents' and their presence encouraged in [[Biological_pest_control|biological pest control]] programmes.
sentence_269: Combined, insectivorous birds eat 400–500 million metric tons of arthropods annually.
sentence_270: Nectar feeders such as [[Hummingbird|hummingbirds]], [[Sunbird|sunbirds]], [[Lories_and_lorikeets|lories, and lorikeets]] amongst others have specially adapted brushy tongues and in many cases bills designed to fit [[Coevolution|co-adapted]] flowers.
sentence_271: [[Kiwi_(bird)|Kiwis]] and [[Shorebird|shorebirds]] with long bills probe for invertebrates; shorebirds' varied bill lengths and feeding methods result in the separation of [[Ecological_niche|ecological niches]].
sentence_272: [[Loon|Loons]], [[Diving_duck|diving ducks]], [[Penguin|penguins]] and [[Auks|auks]] pursue their prey underwater, using their wings or feet for propulsion, while aerial predators such as [[Sulidae|sulids]], [[Kingfisher|kingfishers]] and [[Tern|terns]] plunge dive after their prey.
sentence_273: [[Flamingo|Flamingos]], three species of [[Prion_(bird)|prion]], and some ducks are [[Filter_feeder|filter feeders]].
sentence_274: [[Geese|Geese]] and [[Dabbling_duck|dabbling ducks]] are primarily grazers.
sentence_275: Some species, including [[Frigatebird|frigatebirds]], [[Gull|gulls]], and [[Skua|skuas]], engage in [[Kleptoparasitism|kleptoparasitism]], stealing food items from other birds.
sentence_276: Kleptoparasitism is thought to be a supplement to food obtained by hunting, rather than a significant part of any species' diet; a study of [[Great_frigatebird|great frigatebirds]] stealing from [[Masked_booby|masked boobies]] estimated that the frigatebirds stole at most 40% of their food and on average stole only 5%.
sentence_277: Other birds are [[Scavenger|scavengers]]; some of these, like [[Vulture|vultures]], are specialised carrion eaters, while others, like gulls, [[Corvid|corvids]], or other birds of prey, are opportunists.
sentence_278: Water is needed by many birds although their mode of excretion and lack of [[Sweat_gland|sweat glands]] reduces the physiological demands.
sentence_279: Some desert birds can obtain their water needs entirely from moisture in their food.
sentence_280: They may also have other adaptations such as allowing their body temperature to rise, saving on moisture loss from evaporative cooling or panting.
sentence_281: Seabirds can drink seawater and have [[Salt_gland|salt glands]] inside the head that eliminate excess salt out of the nostrils.
sentence_282: Most birds scoop water in their beaks and raise their head to let water run down the throat.
sentence_283: Some species, especially of arid zones, belonging to the [[Columbidae|pigeon]], [[Estrildidae|finch]], [[Coliidae|mousebird]], [[Turnicidae|button-quail]] and [[Otididae|bustard]] families are capable of sucking up water without the need to tilt back their heads.
sentence_284: Some desert birds depend on water sources and [[Sandgrouse|sandgrouse]] are particularly well known for their daily congregations at waterholes.
sentence_285: Nesting sandgrouse and many plovers carry water to their young by wetting their belly feathers.
sentence_286: Some birds carry water for chicks at the nest in their crop or regurgitate it along with food.
sentence_287: The pigeon family, flamingos and penguins have adaptations to produce a nutritive fluid called [[Crop_milk|crop milk]] that they provide to their chicks.
sentence_288: Feathers, being critical to the survival of a bird, require maintenance.
sentence_289: Apart from physical wear and tear, feathers face the onslaught of fungi, [[Ectoparasitic|ectoparasitic]] feather mites and [[Bird_louse|bird lice]].
sentence_290: The physical condition of feathers are maintained by [[Glossary_of_bird_terms#preening|preening]] often with the application of secretions from the [[Glossary_of_bird_terms#preen_gland|preen gland]].
sentence_291: Birds also bathe in water or dust themselves.
sentence_292: While some birds dip into shallow water, more aerial species may make aerial dips into water and arboreal species often make use of dew or rain that collect on leaves.
sentence_293: Birds of arid regions make use of loose soil to dust-bathe.
sentence_294: A behaviour termed as [[Anting_(bird_activity)|anting]] in which the bird encourages ants to run through their plumage is also thought to help them reduce the ectoparasite load in feathers.
sentence_295: Many species will spread out their wings and expose them to direct sunlight and this too is thought to help in reducing fungal and ectoparasitic activity that may lead to feather damage.
sentence_296: Main article: [[Bird_migration|Bird migration]]
sentence_297: Many bird species migrate to take advantage of global differences of [[Season|seasonal]] temperatures, therefore optimising availability of food sources and breeding habitat.
sentence_298: These migrations vary among the different groups.
sentence_299: Many landbirds, [[Shorebird|shorebirds]], and [[Waterbird|waterbirds]] undertake annual long-distance migrations, usually triggered by the length of daylight as well as weather conditions.
sentence_300: These birds are characterised by a breeding season spent in the temperate or [[Polar_region|polar regions]] and a non-breeding season in the [[Tropical|tropical]] regions or opposite hemisphere.
sentence_301: Before migration, birds substantially increase body fats and reserves and reduce the size of some of their organs.
sentence_302: Migration is highly demanding energetically, particularly as birds need to cross deserts and oceans without refuelling.
sentence_303: Landbirds have a flight range of around 2,500 km (1,600 mi) and shorebirds can fly up to 4,000 km (2,500 mi), although the [[Bar-tailed_godwit|bar-tailed godwit]] is capable of non-stop flights of up to 10,200 km (6,300 mi).
sentence_304: [[Seabird|Seabirds]] also undertake long migrations, the longest annual migration being those of [[Sooty_shearwater|sooty shearwaters]], which nest in [[New_Zealand|New Zealand]] and [[Chile|Chile]] and spend the northern summer feeding in the North Pacific off Japan, [[Alaska|Alaska]] and [[California|California]], an annual round trip of 64,000 km (39,800 mi).
sentence_305: Other seabirds disperse after breeding, travelling widely but having no set migration route.
sentence_306: [[Albatross|Albatrosses]] nesting in the [[Southern_Ocean|Southern Ocean]] often undertake circumpolar trips between breeding seasons.
sentence_307: Some bird species undertake shorter migrations, travelling only as far as is required to avoid bad weather or obtain food.
sentence_308: species such as the boreal [[Finch|finches]] are one such group and can commonly be found at a location in one year and absent the next.
sentence_309: This type of migration is normally associated with food availability.
sentence_310: Species may also travel shorter distances over part of their range, with individuals from higher latitudes travelling into the existing range of conspecifics; others undertake partial migrations, where only a fraction of the population, usually females and subdominant males, migrates.
sentence_311: Partial migration can form a large percentage of the migration behaviour of birds in some regions; in Australia, surveys found that 44% of non-passerine birds and 32% of passerines were partially migratory.
sentence_312: [[Altitudinal_migration|Altitudinal migration]] is a form of short-distance migration in which birds spend the breeding season at higher altitudes and move to lower ones during suboptimal conditions.
sentence_313: It is most often triggered by temperature changes and usually occurs when [[Territory_(animal)|the normal territories]] also become inhospitable due to lack of food.
sentence_314: Some species may also be nomadic, holding no fixed territory and moving according to weather and food availability.
sentence_315: [[True_parrots|Parrots]] as a [[Family_(biology)|family]] are overwhelmingly neither migratory nor sedentary but considered to either be dispersive, irruptive, nomadic or undertake small and irregular migrations.
sentence_316: The ability of birds to return to precise locations across vast distances has been known for some time; in an experiment conducted in the 1950s, a [[Manx_shearwater|Manx shearwater]] released in [[Boston|Boston]] in the United States returned to its colony in [[Skomer|Skomer]], in Wales within 13 days, a distance of 5,150 km (3,200 mi).
sentence_317: Birds navigate during migration using a variety of methods.
sentence_318: For [[Diurnal_animal|diurnal]] migrants, the [[Sun|sun]] is used to navigate by day, and a stellar compass is used at night.
sentence_319: Birds that use the sun compensate for the changing position of the sun during the day by the use of an [[Chronobiology|internal clock]].
sentence_320: Orientation with the stellar compass depends on the position of the [[Constellation|constellations]] surrounding [[Polaris|Polaris]].
sentence_321: These are backed up in some species by their ability to sense the Earth's [[Geomagnetism|geomagnetism]] through specialised [[Photoreceptor_cell|photoreceptors]].
sentence_322: See also: [[Bird_vocalisation|Bird vocalisation]]
sentence_323: Birds communicate using primarily visual and auditory signals.
sentence_324: Signals can be interspecific (between species) and intraspecific (within species).
sentence_325: Birds sometimes use plumage to assess and assert social dominance, to display breeding condition in sexually selected species, or to make threatening displays, as in the [[Sunbittern|sunbittern]]'s mimicry of a large predator to ward off [[Hawk|hawks]] and protect young chicks.
sentence_326: Variation in plumage also allows for the identification of birds, particularly between species.
sentence_327: Visual communication among birds may also involve ritualised displays, which have developed from non-signalling actions such as preening, the adjustments of feather position, pecking, or other behaviour.
sentence_328: These displays may signal aggression or submission or may contribute to the formation of pair-bonds.
sentence_329: The most elaborate displays occur during courtship, where "dances" are often formed from complex combinations of many possible component movements; males' breeding success may depend on the quality of such displays.
sentence_330: [[Bird_vocalization|Bird calls and songs]], which are produced in the [[Syrinx_(biology)|syrinx]], are the major means by which birds communicate with [[Sound|sound]].
sentence_331: This communication can be very complex; some species can operate the two sides of the syrinx independently, allowing the simultaneous production of two different songs.
sentence_332: Calls are used for a variety of purposes, including mate attraction, evaluation of potential mates, bond formation, the claiming and maintenance of territories, the identification of other individuals (such as when parents look for chicks in colonies or when mates reunite at the start of breeding season), and the warning of other birds of potential predators, sometimes with specific information about the nature of the threat.
sentence_333: Some birds also use mechanical sounds for auditory communication.
sentence_334: The [[Coenocorypha|Coenocorypha]] [[Snipe|snipes]] of [[New_Zealand|New Zealand]] drive air through their feathers, [[Woodpecker|woodpeckers]] drum for long-distance communication, and [[Palm_cockatoo|palm cockatoos]] use tools to drum.
sentence_335: While some birds are essentially territorial or live in small family groups, other birds may form large [[Flock_(birds)|flocks]].
sentence_336: The principal benefits of flocking are [[Safety_in_numbers|safety in numbers]] and increased foraging efficiency.
sentence_337: Defence against predators is particularly important in closed habitats like forests, where [[Ambush_predation|ambush predation]] is common and multiple eyes can provide a valuable early warning system.
sentence_338: This has led to the development of many [[Mixed-species_feeding_flock|mixed-species feeding flocks]], which are usually composed of small numbers of many species; these flocks provide safety in numbers but increase potential competition for resources.
sentence_339: Costs of flocking include bullying of socially subordinate birds by more dominant birds and the reduction of feeding efficiency in certain cases.
sentence_340: Birds sometimes also form associations with non-avian species.
sentence_341: Plunge-diving [[Seabird|seabirds]] associate with [[Dolphin|dolphins]] and [[Tuna|tuna]], which push shoaling fish towards the surface.
sentence_342: [[Hornbill|Hornbills]] have a [[Mutualism_(biology)|mutualistic relationship]] with [[Dwarf_mongoose|dwarf mongooses]], in which they forage together and warn each other of nearby [[Birds_of_prey|birds of prey]] and other predators.
sentence_343: The high metabolic rates of birds during the active part of the day is supplemented by rest at other times.
sentence_344: Sleeping birds often use a type of sleep known as vigilant sleep, where periods of rest are interspersed with quick eye-opening "peeks", allowing them to be sensitive to disturbances and enable rapid escape from threats.
sentence_345: [[Swift|Swifts]] are believed to be able to sleep in flight and radar observations suggest that they orient themselves to face the wind in their roosting flight.
sentence_346: It has been suggested that there may be certain kinds of sleep which are possible even when in flight.
sentence_347: Some birds have also demonstrated the capacity to fall into [[Slow-wave_sleep|slow-wave sleep]] one [[Cerebral_hemisphere|hemisphere]] of the brain at a time.
sentence_348: The birds tend to exercise this ability depending upon its position relative to the outside of the flock.
sentence_349: This may allow the eye opposite the sleeping hemisphere to remain vigilant for [[Predator|predators]] by viewing the outer margins of the flock.
sentence_350: This adaptation is also known from [[Marine_mammal|marine mammals]].
sentence_351: [[Communal_roosting|Communal roosting]] is common because it lowers the [[Thermoregulation|loss of body heat]] and decreases the risks associated with predators.
sentence_352: Roosting sites are often chosen with regard to thermoregulation and safety.
sentence_353: Many sleeping birds bend their heads over their backs and tuck their [[Beak|bills]] in their back feathers, although others place their beaks among their breast feathers.
sentence_354: Many birds rest on one leg, while some may pull up their legs into their feathers, especially in cold weather.
sentence_355: [[Passerine|Perching birds]] have a tendon locking mechanism that helps them hold on to the perch when they are asleep.
sentence_356: Many ground birds, such as quails and pheasants, roost in trees.
sentence_357: A few parrots of the genus [[Loriculus|Loriculus]] roost hanging upside down.
sentence_358: Some [[Hummingbird|hummingbirds]] go into a nightly state of [[Torpor|torpor]] accompanied with a reduction of their metabolic rates.
sentence_359: This [[Adaptation|physiological adaptation]] shows in nearly a hundred other species, including [[Owlet-nightjar|owlet-nightjars]], [[Nightjar|nightjars]], and [[Woodswallow|woodswallows]].
sentence_360: One species, the [[Common_poorwill|common poorwill]], even enters a state of [[Hibernation|hibernation]].
sentence_361: Birds do not have sweat glands, but they may cool themselves by moving to shade, standing in water, panting, increasing their surface area, fluttering their throat or by using special behaviours like [[Urohidrosis|urohidrosis]] to cool themselves.
sentence_362: See also: :Category:Avian sexuality, [[Animal_sexual_behaviour#Birds|Animal sexual behaviour § Birds]], [[Seabird_breeding_behaviour|Seabird breeding behaviour]], and [[Sexual_selection_in_birds|Sexual selection in birds]]
sentence_363: Ninety-five per cent of bird species are socially monogamous.
sentence_364: These species pair for at least the length of the breeding season or—in some cases—for several years or until the death of one mate.
sentence_365: Monogamy allows for both [[Paternal_care|paternal care]] and [[Parental_investment|biparental care]], which is especially important for species in which females require males' assistance for successful brood-rearing.
sentence_366: Among many socially monogamous species, [[Extra-pair_copulation|extra-pair copulation]] (infidelity) is common.
sentence_367: Such behaviour typically occurs between dominant males and females paired with subordinate males, but may also be the result of [[Forced_copulation|forced copulation]] in ducks and other [[Anatidae|anatids]].
sentence_368: For females, possible benefits of extra-pair copulation include getting better genes for her offspring and insuring against the possibility of infertility in her mate.
sentence_369: Males of species that engage in extra-pair copulations will closely guard their mates to ensure the parentage of the offspring that they raise.
sentence_370: Other mating systems, including [[Polygyny|polygyny]], [[Polyandry|polyandry]], polygamy, [[Polygynandry|polygynandry]], and [[Promiscuity|promiscuity]], also occur.
sentence_371: Polygamous breeding systems arise when females are able to raise broods without the help of males.
sentence_372: Some species may use more than one system depending on the circumstances.
sentence_373: Breeding usually involves some form of courtship display, typically performed by the male.
sentence_374: Most displays are rather simple and involve some type of [[Bird_vocalization|song]].
sentence_375: Some displays, however, are quite elaborate.
sentence_376: Depending on the species, these may include wing or tail drumming, dancing, aerial flights, or communal [[Lek_(mating_arena)|lekking]].
sentence_377: Females are generally the ones that drive partner selection, although in the polyandrous [[Phalaropes|phalaropes]], this is reversed: plainer males choose brightly coloured females.
sentence_378: [[Courtship_feeding|Courtship feeding]], [[Billing_(birds)|billing]] and [[Glossary_of_bird_terms#allopreening|allopreening]] are commonly performed between partners, generally after the birds have paired and mated.
sentence_379: [[Homosexuality_in_animals#Birds|Homosexual behaviour has been observed]] in males or females in numerous species of birds, including copulation, pair-bonding, and joint parenting of chicks.
sentence_380: Over 130 avian species around the world engage in sexual interactions between the same sex or homosexual behaviors.
sentence_381: "Same-sex courtship activities may involve elaborate displays, synchronized dances, gift-giving ceremonies, or behaviors at specific display areas including bowers, arenas, or leks."
sentence_382: See also: [[Bird_nest|Bird nest]]
sentence_383: Many birds actively defend a territory from others of the same species during the breeding season; maintenance of territories protects the food source for their chicks.
sentence_384: Species that are unable to defend feeding territories, such as [[Seabird|seabirds]] and [[Swift|swifts]], often breed in [[Bird_colony|colonies]] instead; this is thought to offer protection from predators.
sentence_385: Colonial breeders defend small nesting sites, and competition between and within species for nesting sites can be intense.
sentence_386: All birds lay amniotic eggs with hard shells made mostly of [[Calcium_carbonate|calcium carbonate]].
sentence_387: Hole and burrow nesting species tend to lay white or pale eggs, while open nesters lay [[Camouflage|camouflaged]] eggs.
sentence_388: There are many exceptions to this pattern, however; the ground-nesting [[Nightjar|nightjars]] have pale eggs, and camouflage is instead provided by their plumage.
sentence_389: Species that are victims of [[Brood_parasites|brood parasites]] have varying egg colours to improve the chances of spotting a parasite's egg, which forces female parasites to match their eggs to those of their hosts.
sentence_390: Bird eggs are usually laid in a [[Bird_nest|nest]].
sentence_391: Most species create somewhat elaborate nests, which can be cups, domes, plates, beds scrapes, mounds, or burrows.
sentence_392: Some bird nests, however, are extremely primitive; [[Albatross|albatross]] nests are no more than a scrape on the ground.
sentence_393: Most birds build nests in sheltered, hidden areas to avoid predation, but large or colonial birds—which are more capable of defence—may build more open nests.
sentence_394: During nest construction, some species seek out plant matter from plants with parasite-reducing toxins to improve chick survival, and feathers are often used for nest insulation.
sentence_395: Some bird species have no nests; the cliff-nesting [[Common_guillemot|common guillemot]] lays its eggs on bare rock, and male [[Emperor_penguin|emperor penguins]] keep eggs between their body and feet.
sentence_396: The absence of nests is especially prevalent in ground-nesting species where the newly hatched young are precocial.
sentence_397: [[Egg_incubation|Incubation]], which optimises temperature for chick development, usually begins after the last egg has been laid.
sentence_398: In monogamous species incubation duties are often shared, whereas in polygamous species one parent is wholly responsible for incubation.
sentence_399: Warmth from parents passes to the eggs through [[Brood_patch|brood patches]], areas of bare skin on the abdomen or breast of the incubating birds.
sentence_400: Incubation can be an energetically demanding process; adult albatrosses, for instance, lose as much as 83 grams (2.9 oz) of body weight per day of incubation.
sentence_401: The warmth for the incubation of the eggs of [[Megapode|megapodes]] comes from the sun, decaying vegetation or volcanic sources.
sentence_402: Incubation periods range from 10 days (in [[Woodpecker|woodpeckers]], [[Cuckoo|cuckoos]] and [[Passerine|passerine]] birds) to over 80 days (in albatrosses and [[Kiwi_(bird)|kiwis]]).
sentence_403: The diversity of characteristics of birds is great, sometimes even in closely related species.
sentence_404: Several avian characteristics are compared in the table below.
sentence_405: Main article: [[Parental_care_in_birds|Parental care in birds]]
sentence_406: At the time of their hatching, chicks range in development from helpless to independent, depending on their species.
sentence_407: Helpless chicks are termed [[Altricial|altricial]], and tend to be born small, [[Blindness|blind]], immobile and naked; chicks that are mobile and feathered upon hatching are termed precocial.
sentence_408: Altricial chicks need help [[Thermoregulation|thermoregulating]] and must be brooded for longer than precocial chicks.
sentence_409: The young of many bird species do not precisely fit into either the precocial or altricial category, having some aspects of each and thus fall somewhere on an "altricial-precocial spectrum".
sentence_410: Chicks at neither extreme but favoring one or the other may be termed [[Glossary_of_bird_terms#semi-precocial|semi-precocial]] or [[Glossary_of_bird_terms#semi-altricial|semi-altricial]].
sentence_411: The length and nature of parental care varies widely amongst different orders and species.
sentence_412: At one extreme, parental care in [[Megapode|megapodes]] ends at hatching; the newly hatched chick digs itself out of the nest mound without parental assistance and can fend for itself immediately.
sentence_413: At the other extreme, many seabirds have extended periods of parental care, the longest being that of the [[Great_frigatebird|great frigatebird]], whose chicks take up to six months to [[Fledge|fledge]] and are fed by the parents for up to an additional 14 months.
sentence_414: The chick guard stage describes the period of breeding during which one of the adult birds is permanently present at the nest after chicks have hatched.
sentence_415: The main purpose of the guard stage is to aid offspring to thermoregulate and protect them from predation.
sentence_416: In some species, both parents care for nestlings and fledglings; in others, such care is the responsibility of only one sex.
sentence_417: In some species, [[Helpers_at_the_nest|other members]] of the same species—usually close relatives of the breeding pair, such as offspring from previous broods—will help with the raising of the young.
sentence_418: Such alloparenting is particularly common among the [[Corvida|Corvida]], which includes such birds as the true [[Corvidae|crows]], [[Australian_magpie|Australian magpie]] and [[Fairy-wren|fairy-wrens]], but has been observed in species as different as the [[Rifleman_(bird)|rifleman]] and [[Red_kite|red kite]].
sentence_419: Among most groups of animals, [[Paternal_care|male parental care]] is rare.
sentence_420: In birds, however, it is quite common—more so than in any other vertebrate class.
sentence_421: Although territory and nest site defence, incubation, and chick feeding are often shared tasks, there is sometimes a [[Division_of_labour|division of labour]] in which one mate undertakes all or most of a particular duty.
sentence_422: The point at which chicks [[Fledge|fledge]] varies dramatically.
sentence_423: The chicks of the [[Synthliboramphus|Synthliboramphus]] murrelets, like the [[Ancient_murrelet|ancient murrelet]], leave the nest the night after they hatch, following their parents out to sea, where they are raised away from terrestrial predators.
sentence_424: Some other species, such as ducks, move their chicks away from the nest at an early age.
sentence_425: In most species, chicks leave the nest just before, or soon after, they are able to fly.
sentence_426: The amount of parental care after fledging varies; albatross chicks leave the nest on their own and receive no further help, while other species continue some supplementary feeding after fledging.
sentence_427: Chicks may also follow their parents during their first [[Bird_migration|migration]].
sentence_428: Main article: [[Brood_parasite|Brood parasite]]
sentence_429: [[Brood_parasitism|Brood parasitism]], in which an egg-layer leaves her eggs with another individual's brood, is more common among birds than any other type of organism.
sentence_430: After a parasitic bird lays her eggs in another bird's nest, they are often accepted and raised by the host at the expense of the host's own brood.
sentence_431: Brood parasites may be either obligate brood parasites, which must lay their eggs in the nests of other species because they are incapable of raising their own young, or non-obligate brood parasites, which sometimes lay eggs in the nests of [[Conspecific|conspecifics]] to increase their reproductive output even though they could have raised their own young.
sentence_432: One hundred bird species, including [[Honeyguide|honeyguides]], [[Icterid|icterids]], and [[Black-headed_duck|ducks]], are obligate parasites, though the most famous are the [[Cuckoo|cuckoos]].
sentence_433: Some brood parasites are adapted to hatch before their host's young, which allows them to destroy the host's eggs by pushing them out of the nest or to kill the host's chicks; this ensures that all food brought to the nest will be fed to the parasitic chicks.
sentence_434: Main article: [[Sexual_selection_in_birds|Sexual selection in birds]]
sentence_435: Birds have [[Evolution|evolved]] a variety of mating behaviours, with the [[Peafowl|peacock]] tail being perhaps the most famous example of [[Sexual_selection|sexual selection]] and the [[Fisherian_runaway|Fisherian runaway]].
sentence_436: Commonly occurring [[Sexual_dimorphism|sexual dimorphisms]] such as size and colour differences are energetically costly attributes that signal competitive breeding situations.
sentence_437: Many types of avian [[Sexual_selection|sexual selection]] have been identified; intersexual selection, also known as female choice; and intrasexual competition, where individuals of the more abundant sex compete with each other for the privilege to mate.
sentence_438: Sexually selected traits often evolve to become more pronounced in competitive breeding situations until the trait begins to limit the individual's fitness.
sentence_439: Conflicts between an individual fitness and signalling adaptations ensure that sexually selected ornaments such as plumage coloration and [[Courtship_behavior|courtship behaviour]] are "honest" traits.
sentence_440: Signals must be costly to ensure that only good-quality individuals can present these exaggerated sexual ornaments and behaviours.
sentence_441: Main article: [[Inbreeding_depression|Inbreeding depression]]
sentence_442: Inbreeding causes early death ([[Inbreeding_depression|inbreeding depression]]) in the [[Zebra_finch|zebra finch]] Taeniopygia guttata.
sentence_443: Embryo survival (that is, hatching success of fertile eggs) was significantly lower for [[Sibling|sib-sib]] mating pairs than for unrelated pairs.
sentence_444: [[Darwin's_finches|Darwin's finch]] Geospiza scandens experiences [[Inbreeding_depression|inbreeding depression]] (reduced survival of offspring) and the magnitude of this effect is influenced by environmental conditions such as low food availability.
sentence_445: Main article: Inbreeding avoidance
sentence_446: Incestuous matings by the [[Purple-crowned_fairywren|purple-crowned fairy wren]] Malurus coronatus result in severe fitness costs due to [[Inbreeding_depression|inbreeding depression]] (greater than 30% reduction in hatchability of eggs).
sentence_447: Females paired with related males may undertake extra pair matings (see [[Promiscuity#Other_animals|Promiscuity#Other animals]] for 90% frequency in avian species) that can reduce the negative effects of inbreeding.
sentence_448: However, there are ecological and demographic constraints on extra pair matings.
sentence_449: Nevertheless, 43% of broods produced by incestuously paired females contained extra pair young.
sentence_450: Inbreeding depression occurs in the [[Great_tit|great tit]] (Parus major) when the offspring produced as a result of a mating between close relatives show reduced fitness.
sentence_451: In natural populations of Parus major, inbreeding is avoided by dispersal of individuals from their birthplace, which reduces the chance of mating with a close relative.
sentence_452: [[Southern_pied_babbler|Southern pied babblers]] Turdoides bicolor appear to avoid inbreeding in two ways.
sentence_453: The first is through dispersal, and the second is by avoiding familiar group members as mates.
sentence_454: Although both males and females disperse locally, they move outside the range where genetically related individuals are likely to be encountered.
sentence_455: Within their group, individuals only acquire breeding positions when the opposite-sex breeder is unrelated.
sentence_456: [[Cooperative_breeding|Cooperative breeding]] in birds typically occurs when offspring, usually males, delay dispersal from their natal group in order to remain with the family to help rear younger kin.
sentence_457: Female offspring rarely stay at home, dispersing over distances that allow them to breed independently, or to join unrelated groups.
sentence_458: In general, inbreeding is avoided because it leads to a reduction in progeny fitness ([[Inbreeding_depression|inbreeding depression]]) due largely to the homozygous expression of deleterious recessive alleles.
sentence_459: [[Outcrossing|Cross-fertilisation]] between unrelated individuals ordinarily leads to the masking of deleterious recessive alleles in progeny.
sentence_460: Birds occupy a wide range of ecological positions.
sentence_461: While some birds are generalists, others are highly specialised in their habitat or food requirements.
sentence_462: Even within a single habitat, such as a forest, the [[Ecological_niche|niches]] occupied by different species of birds vary, with some species feeding in the [[Forest_canopy|forest canopy]], others beneath the canopy, and still others on the forest floor.
sentence_463: Forest birds may be [[Insectivore|insectivores]], [[Frugivore|frugivores]], and [[Nectarivore|nectarivores]].
sentence_464: Aquatic birds generally feed by fishing, plant eating, and piracy or [[Kleptoparasitism|kleptoparasitism]].
sentence_465: Birds of prey specialise in hunting mammals or other birds, while vultures are specialised [[Scavenger|scavengers]].
sentence_466: [[Avivore|Avivores]] are animals that are specialised at preying on birds.
sentence_467: Some nectar-feeding birds are important pollinators, and many frugivores play a key role in seed dispersal.
sentence_468: Plants and pollinating birds often [[Coevolution|coevolve]], and in some cases a flower's primary pollinator is the only species capable of reaching its nectar.
sentence_469: Birds are often important to island ecology.
sentence_470: Birds have frequently reached islands that mammals have not; on those islands, birds may fulfil ecological roles typically played by larger animals.
sentence_471: For example, in New Zealand nine species of [[Moa|moa]] were important browsers, as are the [[Kererū|kererū]] and [[Kokako|kokako]] today.
sentence_472: Today the plants of New Zealand retain the defensive adaptations evolved to protect them from the extinct moa.
sentence_473: Nesting [[Seabird|seabirds]] may also affect the ecology of islands and surrounding seas, principally through the concentration of large quantities of [[Guano|guano]], which may enrich the local soil and the surrounding seas.
sentence_474: A wide variety of avian ecology field methods, including counts, nest monitoring, and capturing and marking, are used for researching avian ecology.
sentence_475: Main article: [[Birds_in_culture|Birds in culture]]
sentence_476: Since birds are highly visible and common animals, humans have had a relationship with them since the dawn of man.
sentence_477: Sometimes, these relationships are [[Mutualism_(biology)|mutualistic]], like the cooperative honey-gathering among [[Honeyguide|honeyguides]] and African peoples such as the [[Borana_people|Borana]].
sentence_478: Other times, they may be [[Commensalism|commensal]], as when species such as the [[House_sparrow|house sparrow]] have benefited from human activities.
sentence_479: Several bird species have become commercially significant agricultural pests, and some pose an [[Bird_strike|aviation hazard]].
sentence_480: Human activities can also be detrimental, and have threatened numerous bird species with extinction ([[Hunting|hunting]], [[Avian_lead_poisoning|avian lead poisoning]], [[Pesticide|pesticides]], [[Roadkill|roadkill]], [[Wind_turbine|wind turbine]] kills and predation by pet [[Cat|cats]] and [[Dog|dogs]] are common causes of death for birds).
sentence_481: Birds can act as vectors for spreading diseases such as [[Psittacosis|psittacosis]], [[Salmonellosis|salmonellosis]], [[Campylobacteriosis|campylobacteriosis]], mycobacteriosis (avian [[Tuberculosis|tuberculosis]]), [[Avian_influenza|avian influenza]] (bird flu), [[Giardiasis|giardiasis]], and [[Cryptosporidiosis|cryptosporidiosis]] over long distances.
sentence_482: Some of these are [[Zoonosis|zoonotic diseases]] that can also be transmitted to humans.
sentence_483: See also: [[Pet#Birds|Pet § Birds]]
sentence_484: Domesticated birds raised for meat and eggs, called [[Poultry|poultry]], are the largest source of animal protein eaten by humans; in 2003, 76 million tons of poultry and 61 million tons of eggs were produced worldwide.
sentence_485: [[Chicken|Chickens]] account for much of human poultry consumption, though domesticated [[Domesticated_turkey|turkeys]], [[Domestic_duck|ducks]], and [[Domestic_goose|geese]] are also relatively common.
sentence_486: Many species of birds are also hunted for meat.
sentence_487: Bird hunting is primarily a recreational activity except in extremely undeveloped areas.
sentence_488: The most important birds hunted in North and South America are waterfowl; other widely hunted birds include pheasants, [[Wild_turkey|wild turkeys]], quail, [[Dove|doves]], [[Partridge|partridge]], [[Grouse|grouse]], [[Snipe|snipe]], and [[Woodcock|woodcock]].
sentence_489: [[Muttonbirding|Muttonbirding]] is also popular in Australia and New Zealand.
sentence_490: Although some hunting, such as that of muttonbirds, may be sustainable, hunting has led to the extinction or endangerment of dozens of species.
sentence_491: Other commercially valuable products from birds include feathers (especially the [[Down_feather|down]] of geese and ducks), which are used as insulation in clothing and bedding, and seabird faeces ([[Guano|guano]]), which is a valuable source of phosphorus and nitrogen.
sentence_492: The [[War_of_the_Pacific|War of the Pacific]], sometimes called the Guano War, was fought in part over the control of guano deposits.
sentence_493: Birds have been domesticated by humans both as pets and for practical purposes.
sentence_494: Colourful birds, such as [[Parrot_(family)|parrots]] and mynas, are bred in captivity or kept as pets, a practice that has led to the illegal trafficking of some [[Endangered_species|endangered species]].
sentence_495: [[Falcon|Falcons]] and [[Cormorant|cormorants]] have long been used for [[Falconry|hunting]] and [[Cormorant_fishing|fishing]], respectively.
sentence_496: [[Messenger_pigeon|Messenger pigeons]], used since at least 1 AD, remained important as recently as [[World_War_II|World War II]].
sentence_497: Today, such activities are more common either as hobbies, for entertainment and tourism, or for sports such as [[Pigeon_racing|pigeon racing]].
sentence_498: Amateur bird enthusiasts (called birdwatchers, twitchers or, more commonly, [[Birding|birders]]) number in the millions.
sentence_499: Many homeowners erect [[Bird_feeder|bird feeders]] near their homes to attract various species.
sentence_500: [[Bird_feeding|Bird feeding]] has grown into a multimillion-dollar industry; for example, an estimated 75% of households in Britain provide food for birds at some point during the winter.
sentence_501: Birds play prominent and diverse roles in religion and mythology.
sentence_502: In religion, birds may serve as either messengers or priests and leaders for a [[Deity|deity]], such as in the Cult of [[Makemake_(mythology)|Makemake]], in which the Tangata manu of [[Easter_Island|Easter Island]] served as chiefs or as attendants, as in the case of [[Hugin_and_Munin|Hugin and Munin]], the two [[Common_raven|common ravens]] who whispered news into the ears of the [[Norse_god|Norse god]] [[Odin|Odin]].
sentence_503: In several civilisations of [[History_of_Italy|ancient Italy]], particularly [[Etruscan_mythology|Etruscan]] and [[Ancient_Rome|Roman]] [[Religion_in_Ancient_Rome|religion]], priests were involved in [[Augur|augury]], or interpreting the words of birds while the "auspex" (from which the word "auspicious" is derived) watched their activities to foretell events.
sentence_504: They may also serve as religious symbols, as when [[Jonah|Jonah]] ([[Hebrew_language|Hebrew]]: יוֹנָה‎, [[Dove|dove]]) embodied the fright, passivity, mourning, and beauty traditionally associated with doves.
sentence_505: Birds have themselves been deified, as in the case of the [[Common_peacock|common peacock]], which is perceived as Mother Earth by the people of southern India.
sentence_506: In the ancient world, doves were used as symbols of the [[Mesopotamian_goddess|Mesopotamian goddess]] [[Inanna|Inanna]] (later known as Ishtar), the [[Ancient_Canaanite_religion|Canaanite]] mother goddess [[Asherah|Asherah]], and the Greek goddess [[Aphrodite|Aphrodite]].
sentence_507: In [[Ancient_Greece|ancient Greece]], [[Athena|Athena]], the goddess of wisdom and patron deity of the city of [[Athens|Athens]], had a [[Little_owl|little owl]] as [[Owl_of_Athena|her symbol]].
sentence_508: In religious images preserved from the Inca and Tiwanaku empires, birds are depicted in the process of transgressing boundaries between earthly and underground spiritual realms.
sentence_509: Indigenous peoples of the central Andes maintain legends of birds passing to and from metaphysical worlds.
sentence_510: Birds have featured in culture and art since prehistoric times, when they were represented in early [[Cave_painting|cave paintings]].
sentence_511: Some birds have been perceived as monsters, including the mythological [[Roc_(mythology)|Roc]] and the [[Māori_people|Māori]]'s legendary [[Poukai|Pouākai]], a giant bird capable of snatching humans.
sentence_512: Birds were later used as symbols of power, as in the magnificent [[Peacock_Throne|Peacock Throne]] of the [[Mughal_era|Mughal]] and [[History_of_Iran|Persian]] emperors.
sentence_513: With the advent of scientific interest in birds, many paintings of birds were commissioned for books.
sentence_514: Among the most famous of these bird artists was [[John_James_Audubon|John James Audubon]], whose paintings of [[List_of_North_American_birds|North American birds]] were a great commercial success in Europe and who later lent his name to the [[National_Audubon_Society|National Audubon Society]].
sentence_515: Birds are also important figures in poetry; for example, [[Homer|Homer]] incorporated [[Nightingale|nightingales]] into his [[Odyssey|Odyssey]], and [[Catullus|Catullus]] used a [[Old_World_sparrow|sparrow]] as an erotic symbol in his [[Catullus_2|Catullus 2]].
sentence_516: The relationship between an [[Albatross|albatross]] and a sailor is the central theme of [[Samuel_Taylor_Coleridge|Samuel Taylor Coleridge]]'s [[The_Rime_of_the_Ancient_Mariner|The Rime of the Ancient Mariner]], which led to the use of the [[Albatross_(metaphor)|term as a metaphor for a 'burden']].
sentence_517: Other [[English_language|English]] metaphors derive from birds; [[Vulture_fund|vulture funds]] and vulture investors, for instance, take their name from the scavenging vulture.
sentence_518: Perceptions of bird species vary across cultures.
sentence_519: [[Owl|Owls]] are associated with bad luck, [[Witchcraft|witchcraft]], and death in parts of Africa, but are regarded as wise across much of Europe.
sentence_520: [[Hoopoe|Hoopoes]] were considered sacred in [[Ancient_Egypt|Ancient Egypt]] and symbols of virtue in [[Persia|Persia]], but were thought of as thieves across much of Europe and harbingers of war in [[Scandinavia|Scandinavia]].
sentence_521: In [[Heraldry|heraldry]], birds, especially [[Eagle_(heraldry)|eagles]], often appear in coats of arms.
sentence_523: [[Birds_in_music|In music]], birdsong has influenced composers and musicians in several ways: they can be inspired by birdsong; they can intentionally imitate bird song in a composition, as [[Antonio_Vivaldi|Vivaldi]], [[Olivier_Messiaen|Messiaen]], and [[Beethoven|Beethoven]] did, along with many later composers; they can incorporate recordings of birds into their works, as [[Ottorino_Respighi|Ottorino Respighi]] first did; or like [[Beatrice_Harrison|Beatrice Harrison]] and [[David_Rothenberg|David Rothenberg]], they can duet with birds.
sentence_525: See also: [[Late_Quaternary_prehistoric_birds|Late Quaternary prehistoric birds]], [[List_of_extinct_birds|List of extinct birds]], and [[Raptor_conservation|Raptor conservation]]
sentence_526: Although human activities have allowed the expansion of a few species, such as the [[Barn_swallow|barn swallow]] and [[European_starling|European starling]], they have caused population decreases or [[Extinction|extinction]] in many other species.
sentence_527: Over a hundred bird species have gone extinct in historical times, although the most dramatic human-caused avian extinctions, eradicating an estimated 750–1800 species, occurred during the human colonisation of [[Melanesia|Melanesian]], [[Polynesia|Polynesian]], and Micronesian islands.
sentence_528: Many bird populations are declining worldwide, with 1,227 species listed as threatened by [[BirdLife_International|BirdLife International]] and the [[IUCN|IUCN]] in 2009.
sentence_529: The most commonly cited human threat to birds is [[Habitat_destruction|habitat loss]].
sentence_530: Other threats include overhunting, accidental mortality due to collisions with buildings or [[Bird_strike|vehicles]], [[Long-line_fishing|long-line fishing]] [[Bycatch|bycatch]], pollution (including [[Oil_spill|oil spills]] and pesticide use), competition and predation from nonnative [[Invasive_species|invasive species]], and climate change.
sentence_531: Governments and [[Conservation_biology|conservation]] groups work to protect birds, either by passing laws that preserve and [[Ecological_restoration|restore]] bird habitat or by establishing [[Ex-situ_conservation|captive populations]] for reintroductions.
sentence_532: Such projects have produced some successes; one study estimated that conservation efforts saved 16 species of bird that would otherwise have gone extinct between 1994 and 2004, including the [[California_condor|California condor]] and [[Norfolk_parakeet|Norfolk parakeet]].

title: Biennial plant
sentence_0: A biennial plant is a [[Flowering_plant|flowering plant]] that takes two years to complete its biological life cycle.
sentence_1: In the first year, the plant undergoes primary growth, in which its leaves, stems, and roots (vegetative structures) develop.
sentence_2: Usually, the stem of the plant remains short and the leaves are low to the ground, forming a [[Rosette_(botany)|rosette]].
sentence_3: After the first year, the plant enters a period of [[Dormancy|dormancy]] for the colder months.
sentence_4: Many biennials require a cold treatment, or [[Vernalization|vernalization]], before they will flower.
sentence_5: During the next [[Spring_(season)|spring]] or [[Summer_(season)|summer]], the stem of the biennial plant elongates greatly, or "bolts".
sentence_6: The plant then flowers, producing [[Fruit|fruits]] and [[Seed|seeds]] before it finally dies.
sentence_7: There are far fewer biennials than either perennial plants or [[Annual_plant|annual plants]].
sentence_8: Biennials do not always follow a strict two year life cycle and the majority of plants in the wild can take 3 or more years to fully mature.
sentence_9: Rosette leaf size has been found to predict when a plant may enter its second stage of flowering and seed production.
sentence_10: Alternatively, under extreme climatic conditions, a biennial plant may complete its life cycle rapidly (e.g., in three months instead of two years).
sentence_11: This is quite common in vegetable or flower seedlings that were vernalized before they were planted in the ground.
sentence_12: This behavior leads to many normally biennial plants being treated as annuals in some areas.
sentence_13: Conversely, an annual grown under extremely favorable conditions may have highly successful seed propagation, giving it the appearance of being biennial or perennial.
sentence_14: Some short-lived perennials may appear to be biennial rather than perennial.
sentence_15: True biennials flower only once, while many perennials will flower every year once mature.
sentence_16: Biennials grown for flowers, fruits, or seeds need to be grown for two years.
sentence_17: Biennials that are grown for edible leaves or roots are grown for just one year (and not grown on a second year to run to seed).
sentence_18: Examples of biennial plants are members of the [[Onion|onion]] family including [[Leek|leek]], some members of the [[Cabbage|cabbage]] family, [[Verbascum_thapsus|common mullein]], [[Parsley|parsley]], fennel, [[Lunaria|Lunaria]], [[Silverbeet|silverbeet]], [[Rudbeckia_hirta|Black-eyed Susan]], [[Dianthus_barbatus|Sweet William]], [[Aletris|colic weed]], [[Carrot|carrot]], and some [[Hollyhock|hollyhocks]].
sentence_19: Plant breeders have produced annual cultivars of several biennials that will flower the first year from seed, for example, [[Foxglove|foxglove]] and [[Matthiola_incana|stock]].

list.value: [[Annual_plant|Annual plant]] – Plant that completes its life cycle within one growing season and then dies
Perennial plant – Plant that lives for more than two years

title: African Americans
sentence_0: See also: [[African_diaspora_in_the_Americas|African diaspora in the Americas]] and [[African_immigration_to_the_United_States|African immigration to the United States]]
sentence_1: African Americans (also referred to as Black Americans or Afro-Americans) are an [[Ethnic_group|ethnic group]] of [[Americans|Americans]] with total or partial ancestry from any of the [[Black_people|black]] racial groups of [[Africa|Africa]].
sentence_2: The term African American generally denotes descendants of [[Slavery_in_the_United_States|enslaved black people]] who are from the United States, while some recent black immigrants or their children may also come to identify as African-American or may identify differently.
sentence_3: African Americans constitute the third largest ethnic group and the second largest racial group in the US, after [[White_Americans|White Americans]] and [[Hispanic_and_Latino_Americans|Hispanic and Latino Americans]].
sentence_4: Most African Americans are descendants of enslaved peoples within the boundaries of the present United States.
sentence_5: On average, African Americans are of [[West_Africa|West]]/[[Central_Africa|Central]] African and European descent, and some also have [[Native_Americans_in_the_United_States|Native American]] ancestry.
sentence_6: According to U.S. Census Bureau data, [[African_immigration_to_the_United_States|African immigrants]] generally do not self-identify as African American.
sentence_7: The overwhelming majority of African immigrants identify instead with their own respective ethnicities (≈95%).
sentence_8: Immigrants from some [[Afro-Caribbean|Caribbean]], Central American, and South American nations and their descendants may or may not also self-identify with the term.
sentence_9: [[African-American_history|African-American history]] began in the 17th century, with Africans from [[West_Africa|West Africa]] being sold to [[Atlantic_slave_trade|European slave traders]] and [[Middle_Passage|transported across the Atlantic]] to the [[Thirteen_Colonies|Thirteen Colonies]].
sentence_10: After arriving in the Americas, they were [[Slavery_in_the_colonial_United_States|sold as slaves]] to European colonists and put to work on plantations, particularly [[Plantation_complexes_in_the_Southern_United_States|in the southern colonies]].
sentence_11: A few were able to achieve freedom through manumission or escape and founded independent communities before and during the [[American_Revolution|American Revolution]].
sentence_12: After the United States was founded in 1783, most [[Slavery_in_the_United_States|black people continued to be enslaved]], being mostly concentrated in the [[Southern_United_States|American South]], with four million enslaved only [[Thirteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution|liberated]] during and at the end of the [[American_Civil_War|Civil War]] in 1865.
sentence_13: Due to [[White_supremacy|white supremacy]], most were treated as [[Second-class_citizen|second-class citizens]].
sentence_14: The [[Naturalization_Act_of_1790|Naturalization Act of 1790]] limited U.S. citizenship to whites only, and only white men who owned property could vote.
sentence_15: These circumstances changed in [[Reconstruction_Era|Reconstruction]], further development of the [[African-American_culture|black community]], participation in the great [[Military_history_of_African_Americans|military conflicts of the United States]], substantial [[Great_Migration_(African_American)|migration out of the South]], the elimination of legal [[Racial_segregation|racial segregation]], and the [[Civil_rights_movement|civil rights movement]] which sought political and social freedom.
sentence_16: In 2008, [[Barack_Obama|Barack Obama]] became the first African American to be elected President of the United States.
sentence_17: Main article: [[African-American_history|African-American history]]
sentence_18: Main articles: [[Slavery_in_the_colonial_United_States|Slavery in the colonial United States]] and [[Atlantic_slave_trade|Atlantic slave trade]]
sentence_19: The vast majority of those who were enslaved and transported in the [[Atlantic_slave_trade|transatlantic slave trade]] were people from [[Middle_Africa|Central]] and [[West_Africa|West Africa]], who had been sold by other West Africans, or by half-European "merchant princes" to European slave traders (with a small number being captured directly by the slave traders in coastal raids), who brought them to the Americas.
sentence_20: The first African slaves arrived via [[Captaincy_General_of_Santo_Domingo|Santo Domingo]] to the [[San_Miguel_de_Gualdape|San Miguel de Gualdape]] colony (most likely located in the Winyah Bay area of present-day [[South_Carolina|South Carolina]]), founded by Spanish explorer [[Lucas_Vázquez_de_Ayllón|Lucas Vázquez de Ayllón]] in 1526.
sentence_21: The ill-fated colony was almost immediately disrupted by a fight over leadership, during which the slaves revolted and fled the colony to seek refuge among local [[Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas|Native Americans]].
sentence_22: De Ayllón and many of the colonists died shortly afterwards of an epidemic and the colony was abandoned.
sentence_23: The settlers and the slaves who had not escaped returned to [[Haiti|Haiti]], whence they had come.
sentence_24: The marriage between Luisa de Abrego, a free black domestic servant from [[Seville|Seville]] and Miguel Rodríguez, a white [[Segovia|Segovian]] conquistador in 1565 in [[St._Augustine,_Florida|St.
sentence_25: Augustine]] (Spanish Florida), is the first known and recorded Christian marriage anywhere in what is now the continental United States.
sentence_26: The first recorded Africans in [[British_America|English America]] (including most of the future United States) were [[First_Africans_in_Virginia|"20 and odd negroes"]] who came to [[Jamestown,_Virginia|Jamestown]], [[Colony_of_Virginia|Virginia]] via [[Old_Point_Comfort|Cape Comfort]] in August 1619 as indentured servants.
sentence_27: As many Virginian settlers began to die from harsh conditions, more and more Africans were brought to work as laborers.
sentence_28: An indentured servant (who could be white or black) would work for several years (usually four to seven) without wages.
sentence_29: The status of indentured servants in early Virginia and Maryland was similar to slavery.
sentence_30: Servants could be bought, sold, or leased and they could be physically beaten for disobedience or running away.
sentence_31: Unlike slaves, they were freed after their term of service expired or was bought out, their children did not inherit their status, and on their release from contract they received "a year's provision of corn, double apparel, tools necessary", and a small cash payment called "freedom dues".
sentence_32: Africans could legally raise crops and cattle to purchase their freedom.
sentence_33: They raised families, married other Africans and sometimes [[Interracial_marriage|intermarried]] with Native Americans or European [[Settler|settlers]].
sentence_34: By the 1640s and 1650s, several African families owned farms around Jamestown and some became wealthy by colonial standards and purchased indentured servants of their own.
sentence_35: In 1640, the Virginia General Court recorded the earliest documentation of lifetime slavery when they sentenced [[John_Punch_(slave)|John Punch]], a Negro, to lifetime servitude under his master Hugh Gwyn for running away.
sentence_36: In the [[Spanish_Florida|Spanish Florida]] some Spanish married or had [[Placage|unions with]] Pensacola, Creek or [[List_of_ethnic_groups_of_Africa|African]] women, both slave and free, and their descendants created a mixed-race population of [[Mestizo|mestizos]] and [[Mulatto|mulattos]].
sentence_37: The Spanish encouraged slaves from the [[Province_of_Georgia|colony of Georgia]] to come to Florida as a refuge, promising freedom in exchange for conversion to [[Catholic_Church|Catholicism]].
sentence_38: [[Charles_II_of_Spain|King Charles II]] issued a royal proclamation freeing all slaves who fled to Spanish Florida and accepted conversion and baptism.
sentence_39: Most went to the area around [[St._Augustine,_Florida|St.
sentence_40: Augustine]], but escaped slaves also reached Pensacola.
sentence_41: St. Augustine had mustered an all-black [[Militia|militia]] unit defending Spanish Florida as early as 1683.
sentence_42: One of the Dutch African arrivals, [[Anthony_Johnson_(American_Colonial)|Anthony Johnson]], would later own one of the first black "slaves", [[John_Casor|John Casor]], resulting from the court ruling of a civil case.
sentence_43: The popular conception of a race-based slave system did not fully develop until the 18th century.
sentence_44: The [[Dutch_West_India_Company|Dutch West India Company]] introduced slavery in 1625 with the importation of eleven black slaves into [[New_Amsterdam|New Amsterdam]] (present-day [[New_York_City|New York City]]).
sentence_45: All the colony's slaves, however, were freed upon its surrender to the English.
sentence_46: [[Massachusetts_Bay_Colony|Massachusetts]] was the first English colony to legally recognize slavery in 1641.
sentence_47: In 1662, Virginia passed a law that children of enslaved women took the status of the mother, rather than that of the father, as under [[Common_law|common law]].
sentence_48: This legal principle was called [[Partus_sequitur_ventrum|partus sequitur ventrum]].
sentence_49: By an act of 1699, the colony ordered all free blacks deported, virtually defining as slaves all people of African descent who remained in the colony.
sentence_50: In 1670, the colonial assembly passed a law prohibiting free and baptized blacks (and Indians) from purchasing Christians (in this act meaning White Europeans) but allowing them to buy people "of their owne nation".
sentence_51: In the [[Louisiana_(New_Spain)|Spanish Louisiana]] although there was no movement toward abolition of the African slave trade, Spanish rule introduced a new law called coartación, which allowed slaves to buy their freedom, and that of others.
sentence_52: Although some did not have the money to buy their freedom that government measures on slavery allowed a high number of free blacks.
sentence_53: That brought problems to the Spaniards with the French Creoles who also populated Spanish Louisiana, French creoles cited that measure as one of the system's worst elements.
sentence_54: In spite of that, there was a greater number of slaves as the years passed, as also the entire Spanish Louisiana population increased.
sentence_55: The earliest African-American congregations and churches were organized before 1800 in both northern and southern cities following the [[First_Great_Awakening|Great Awakening]].
sentence_56: By 1775, Africans made up 20% of the population in the [[Thirteen_Colonies|American colonies]], which made them the second largest ethnic group after [[English_Americans|English Americans]].

section_2.value: From the American Revolution to the Civil War

sentence_57: Main article: [[Slavery_in_the_United_States|Slavery in the United States]]
sentence_58: During the 1770s, Africans, both enslaved and free, helped rebellious American colonists secure their independence by defeating the British in the [[American_Revolutionary_War|American Revolutionary War]].
sentence_59: African-Americans and European Americans fought side by side and were fully integrated.
sentence_60: Blacks played a role in both sides in the American Revolution.
sentence_61: Activists in the Patriot cause included [[James_Armistead|James Armistead]], [[Prince_Whipple|Prince Whipple]] and [[Oliver_Cromwell_(American_soldier)|Oliver Cromwell]].
sentence_62: In the [[Spanish_Louisiana|Spanish Louisiana]], Governor [[Bernardo_de_Gálvez|Bernardo de Gálvez]] organized Spanish free black men into two militia companies to defend [[New_Orleans|New Orleans]] during the American Revolution.
sentence_63: They fought in the 1779 battle in which Spain captured [[Baton_Rouge|Baton Rouge]] from the British.
sentence_64: Gálvez also commanded them in campaigns against the British outposts in [[Mobile,_Alabama|Mobile]], [[Alabama|Alabama]], and [[Pensacola|Pensacola]], Florida, he recruited slaves for the militia by pledging to free anyone who was seriously wounded and promised to secure a low price for coartación (buy their freedom and that of others) for those who received lesser wounds.
sentence_65: During the 1790s, Governor [[Francisco_Luis_Héctor_de_Carondelet|Francisco Luis Héctor, baron of Carondelet]] reinforced local fortifications and recruit even more free blackmen for the militia.
sentence_66: Carondelet doubled the number of free blackmen who served, creating two more militia companies—one made up of black members and the other of [[Pardo|pardo]] (mixed race).
sentence_67: Serving in the militia brought free blackmen one step closer to equality with whites, allowing them, for example, the right to carry arms and boosting their earning power.
sentence_68: However actually these privileges distanced free blackmen from enslaved blacks and encouraged them to identify with whites.
sentence_69: Slavery had been tacitly enshrined in the [[U.S._Constitution|U.S.
sentence_70: Constitution]] through provisions such as Article I, Section 2, Clause 3, commonly known as the 3/5 compromise.
sentence_71: Slavery, which by then meant almost exclusively black people, was the most important political issue in the [[Antebellum_United_States|antebellum United States]], leading to one crisis after another.
sentence_72: Among these were the [[Missouri_Compromise|Missouri Compromise]], the [[Compromise_of_1850|Compromise of 1850]], the [[Fugitive_Slave_Act|Fugitive Slave Act]], and the [[Dred_Scott_decision|Dred Scott decision]].
sentence_73: Prior to the [[American_Civil_War|Civil War]], eight serving presidents owned slaves, a practice protected by the U.S. Constitution.
