sentence_74: By 1860, there were 3.5 to 4.4 million enslaved black people in the U.S. due to the [[Atlantic_slave_trade|Atlantic slave trade]], and another 488,000–500,000 blacks lived free (with legislated limits) across the country.
sentence_75: With legislated limits imposed upon them in addition to "unconquerable prejudice" from whites according to [[Henry_Clay|Henry Clay]], some black people who weren't enslaved left the U.S. for [[Liberia|Liberia]] in Africa.
sentence_76: Liberia began as a settlement of the [[American_Colonization_Society|American Colonization Society]] (ACS) in 1821, with the abolitionist members of the ACS believing blacks would face better chances for freedom and equality in Africa.
sentence_77: The slaves not only constituted a large investment, they produced America's most valuable product and export: [[King_Cotton|cotton]].
sentence_78: They not only helped build the [[U.S._Capitol|U.S.
sentence_79: Capitol]], they built the [[White_House|White House]] and other [[District_of_Columbia|District of Columbia]] buildings.
sentence_80: ([[Washington,_D.C.|Washington]] was a slave trading center.)
sentence_81: Similar building projects existed in slaveholding states.
sentence_82: In 1863, during the [[American_Civil_War|American Civil War]], President [[Abraham_Lincoln|Abraham Lincoln]] signed the [[Emancipation_Proclamation|Emancipation Proclamation]].
sentence_83: The proclamation declared that all slaves in Confederate-held territory were free.
sentence_84: Advancing Union troops enforced the proclamation with Texas being the last state to be emancipated, in 1865.
sentence_85: Slavery in Union-held Confederate territory continued, at least on paper, until the passage of the [[Thirteenth_Amendment_to_the_U.S._Constitution|Thirteenth Amendment]] in 1865.
sentence_86: Prior to the Civil War, only white men of property could vote, and the [[Naturalization_Act_of_1790|Naturalization Act of 1790]] limited U.S. citizenship to whites only.
sentence_87: The [[Fourteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution|14th Amendment]] (1868) gave black people citizenship, and the [[Fifteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution|15th Amendment]] (1870) gave black males the right to vote (only males could vote in the U.S. at the time).
sentence_88: Main articles: [[Reconstruction_Era|Reconstruction Era]] and [[Jim_Crow_laws|Jim Crow laws]]
sentence_89: African Americans quickly set up congregations for themselves, as well as schools and community/civic associations, to have space away from white control or oversight.
sentence_90: While the post-war Reconstruction era was initially a time of progress for African Americans, that period ended in 1876.
sentence_91: By the late 1890s, Southern states enacted Jim Crow laws to enforce [[Racial_segregation|racial segregation]] and [[Disfranchisement_after_the_American_Civil_War|disenfranchisement]].
sentence_92: Segregation, which began with slavery, continued with Jim Crow laws, with signs used to show blacks where they could legally walk, talk, drink, rest, or eat.
sentence_93: For those places that were racially mixed, non-whites had to wait until all white customers were dealt with.
sentence_94: Most African Americans obeyed the Jim Crow laws, to avoid racially motivated violence.
sentence_95: To maintain self-esteem and dignity, African Americans such as [[Anthony_Overton|Anthony Overton]] and [[Mary_McLeod_Bethune|Mary McLeod Bethune]] continued to build their own [[Historically_black_colleges_and_universities|schools]], [[Black_church|churches]], banks, social clubs, and other businesses.
sentence_96: In the last decade of the 19th century, racially discriminatory laws and racial violence aimed at African Americans began to mushroom in the United States, a period often referred to as the "[[Nadir_of_American_race_relations|nadir of American race relations]]".
sentence_97: These discriminatory acts included racial segregation—upheld by the United States Supreme Court decision in [[Plessy_v._Ferguson|Plessy v. Ferguson]] in 1896—which was legally mandated by southern states and nationwide at the local level of government, voter suppression or disenfranchisement in the southern states, denial of economic opportunity or resources nationwide, and private acts of violence and mass racial violence aimed at African Americans unhindered or encouraged by government authorities.

section_4.value: Great migration and civil rights movement

sentence_98: Main articles: [[Great_Migration_(African_American)|Great Migration]] and [[Civil_rights_movement|civil rights movement]]
sentence_99: The desperate conditions of African Americans in the South sparked the [[Great_Migration_(African_American)|Great Migration]] during the first half of the 20th century which led to a growing African-American community in [[Northern_United_States|Northern]] and Western United States.
sentence_100: The rapid influx of blacks disturbed the racial balance within Northern and Western cities, exacerbating hostility between both blacks and whites in the two regions.
sentence_101: The [[Red_Summer|Red Summer]] of 1919 was marked by hundreds of deaths and higher casualties across the U.S. as a result of race riots that occurred in more than three dozen cities, such as the [[Chicago_race_riot_of_1919|Chicago race riot of 1919]] and the [[Omaha_race_riot_of_1919|Omaha race riot of 1919]].
sentence_102: Overall, blacks in Northern and Western cities experienced [[Racism_in_the_United_States|systemic discrimination]] in a plethora of aspects of life.
sentence_103: Within employment, economic opportunities for blacks were routed to the lowest-status and restrictive in potential mobility.
sentence_104: At the 1900 [[Hampton_Negro_Conference|Hampton Negro Conference]], Reverend Matthew Anderson said, "...the lines along most of the avenues of wage earning are more rigidly drawn in the North than in the South."
sentence_105: Within the housing market, stronger discriminatory measures were used in correlation to the influx, resulting in a mix of "targeted violence, [[Covenant_(law)#Exclusionary_covenants|restrictive covenants]], [[Redlining|redlining]] and racial steering".
sentence_106: While many whites defended their space with violence, intimidation, or legal tactics toward African Americans, many other whites migrated to more racially homogeneous suburban or exurban regions, a process known as [[White_flight|white flight]].
sentence_107: Despite discrimination, drawing cards for leaving the hopelessness in the South were the growth of African American institutions and communities in Northern cities.
sentence_108: Institutions included black oriented organizations (e.g., Urban League, NAACP), churches, businesses, and newspapers, as well as successes in the development in African American intellectual culture, music, and popular culture (e.g., [[Harlem_Renaissance|Harlem Renaissance]], [[Chicago_Black_Renaissance|Chicago Black Renaissance]]).
sentence_109: The [[Cotton_Club|Cotton Club]] in Harlem was a whites-only establishment, with blacks (such as [[Duke_Ellington|Duke Ellington]]) allowed to perform, but to a white audience.
sentence_110: Black Americans also found a new ground for political power in Northern cities, without the enforced disabilities of [[Jim_Crow|Jim Crow]].
sentence_111: By the 1950s, the [[Civil_rights_movement|civil rights movement]] was gaining momentum.
sentence_112: A 1955 lynching that sparked public outrage about injustice was that of [[Emmett_Till|Emmett Till]], a 14-year-old boy from Chicago.
sentence_113: Spending the summer with relatives in [[Money,_Mississippi|Money, Mississippi]], Till was killed for allegedly having [[Wolf-whistle|wolf-whistled]] at a white woman.
sentence_114: Till had been badly beaten, one of his eyes was gouged out, and he was shot in the head.
sentence_115: The visceral response to his mother's decision to have an open-casket funeral mobilized the black community throughout the U.S. Vann R. Newkirk| wrote "the trial of his killers became a pageant illuminating the tyranny of [[White_supremacy|white supremacy]]".
sentence_116: The state of Mississippi tried two defendants, but they were speedily acquitted by an [[All-white_jury|all-white jury]].
sentence_117: One hundred days after Emmett Till's murder, [[Rosa_Parks|Rosa Parks]] refused to give up her seat on the bus in Alabama—indeed, Parks told Emmett's mother [[Mamie_Till|Mamie Till]] that "the photograph of Emmett's disfigured face in the casket was set in her mind when she refused to give up her seat on the Montgomery bus."
sentence_118: The [[March_on_Washington_for_Jobs_and_Freedom|March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom]] and the conditions which brought it into being are credited with putting pressure on presidents [[John_F._Kennedy|John F. Kennedy]] and [[Lyndon_B._Johnson|Lyndon B. Johnson]].
sentence_119: Johnson put his support behind passage of the [[Civil_Rights_Act_of_1964|Civil Rights Act of 1964]] that banned discrimination in public accommodations, employment, and [[Trade_union|labor unions]], and the [[Voting_Rights_Act|Voting Rights Act]] of 1965, which expanded federal authority over states to ensure black political participation through protection of voter registration and elections.
sentence_120: By 1966, the emergence of the [[Black_Power|Black Power]] movement, which lasted from 1966 to 1975, expanded upon the aims of the civil rights movement to include economic and political self-sufficiency, and freedom from white authority.
sentence_121: During the postwar period, many African Americans continued to be economically disadvantaged relative to other Americans.
sentence_122: Average black income stood at 54 percent of that of white workers in 1947, and 55 percent in 1962.
sentence_123: In 1959, median family income for whites was $5,600, compared with $2,900 for nonwhite families.
sentence_124: In 1965, 43 percent of all black families fell into the poverty bracket, earning under $3,000 a year.
sentence_125: The Sixties saw improvements in the social and economic conditions of many black Americans.
sentence_126: From 1965 to 1969, black family income rose from 54 to 60 percent of white family income.
sentence_127: In 1968, 23 percent of black families earned under $3,000 a year, compared with 41 percent in 1960.
sentence_128: In 1965, 19 percent of black Americans had incomes equal to the national median, a proportion that rose to 27 percent by 1967.
sentence_129: In 1960, the median level of education for blacks had been 10.8 years, and by the late Sixties the figure rose to 12.2 years, half a year behind the median for whites.
sentence_130: Main article: [[Post–civil_rights_era_in_African-American_history|Post–civil rights era in African-American history]]
sentence_131: Politically and economically, African Americans have made substantial strides during the post–civil rights era.
sentence_132: In 1968, [[Shirley_Chisholm|Shirley Chisholm]] became the first Black woman elected to the [[United_States_Congress|U.S.
sentence_133: Congress]].
sentence_134: In 1989, [[Douglas_Wilder|Douglas Wilder]] became the first African American elected governor in U.S. history.
sentence_135: [[Clarence_Thomas|Clarence Thomas]] became the second African-American Supreme Court Justice.
sentence_136: In 1992, [[Carol_Moseley-Braun|Carol Moseley-Braun]] of [[Illinois|Illinois]] became the first African-American woman elected to the [[United_States_Senate|U.S.
sentence_137: Senate]].
sentence_138: There were 8,936 black officeholders in the United States in 2000, showing a net increase of 7,467 since 1970.
sentence_139: In 2001, there were 484 black mayors.
sentence_140: In 2005, the number of Africans immigrating to the United States, in a single year, surpassed the peak number who were involuntarily brought to the United States during the [[Atlantic_Slave_Trade|Atlantic Slave Trade]].
sentence_141: On November 4, 2008, [[Democratic_Party_(United_States)|Democratic]] [[United_States_Senator|Senator]] [[Barack_Obama|Barack Obama]] [[2008_United_States_presidential_election|defeated]] [[Republican_Party_(United_States)|Republican]] Senator [[John_McCain|John McCain]] to become the first African American to be elected president.
sentence_142: At least 95 percent of African-American voters voted for Obama.
sentence_143: He also received overwhelming support from young and educated whites, a majority of [[Asian_Americans|Asians]], [[Hispanic_and_Latino_Americans|Hispanics]], and [[Native_Americans_in_the_United_States|Native Americans]] picking up a number of new states in the Democratic electoral column.
sentence_144: Obama lost the overall white vote, although he won a larger proportion of white votes than any previous nonincumbent Democratic presidential candidate since [[Jimmy_Carter|Jimmy Carter]].
sentence_145: Obama was [[2012_United_States_presidential_election|reelected]] for a second and final term, by a similar margin on November 6, 2012.
sentence_146: Further information: [[Historical_racial_and_ethnic_demographics_of_the_United_States#Black_population_as_a_percentage_of_the_total_population_by_U.S._region_and_state_(1790–2010)|Historical racial and ethnic demographics of the United States § Black population as a percentage of the total population by U.S. region and state (1790–2010)]], List of U.S. communities with African-American majority populations, [[List_of_U.S._counties_with_African-American_majority_populations|List of U.S. counties with African-American majority populations]], and [[List_of_U.S._states_by_African-American_population|List of U.S. states by African-American population]]
sentence_147: In 1790, when the first [[United_States_Census|U.S.
sentence_148: Census]] was taken, Africans (including slaves and free people) numbered about 760,000—about 19.3% of the population.
sentence_149: In 1860, at the start of the [[American_Civil_War|Civil War]], the African-American population had increased to 4.4 million, but the percentage rate dropped to 14% of the overall population of the country.
sentence_150: The vast majority were slaves, with only 488,000 counted as "freemen".
sentence_151: By 1900, the black population had doubled and reached 8.8 million.
sentence_152: In 1910, about 90% of African Americans lived in the South.
sentence_153: Large numbers began migrating north looking for better job opportunities and living conditions, and to escape [[Jim_Crow_laws|Jim Crow laws]] and racial violence.
sentence_154: The [[Great_Migration_(African_American)|Great Migration]], as it was called, spanned the 1890s to the 1970s.
sentence_155: From 1916 through the 1960s, more than 6 million [[Black_people|black people]] moved north.
sentence_156: But in the 1970s and 1980s, [[New_Great_Migration|that trend reversed]], with more African Americans moving south to the [[Sun_Belt|Sun Belt]] than leaving it.
sentence_157: The following table of the African-American population in the United States over time shows that the African-American population, as a percentage of the total population, declined until 1930 and has been rising since then.

table_1.caption: African Americans in the United States

sentence_158: By 1990, the African-American population reached about 30 million and represented 12% of the U.S. population, roughly the same proportion as in 1900.
sentence_159: At the time of the [[United_States_Census_2000|2000 Census]], 54.8% of African Americans lived in the [[Southern_United_States|South]].
sentence_160: In that year, 17.6% of African Americans lived in the [[Northeastern_United_States|Northeast]] and 18.7% in the [[Midwestern_United_States|Midwest]], while only 8.9% lived in the [[Western_United_States|western]] states.
sentence_161: The west does have a sizable black population in certain areas, however.
sentence_162: California, the nation's most populous state, has the fifth largest African-American population, only behind New York, Texas, Georgia, and Florida.
sentence_163: According to the 2000 Census, approximately 2.05% of [[Black_Hispanic_and_Latino_Americans|African Americans identified as Hispanic or Latino in origin]], many of whom may be of [[Afro-Brazilian|Brazilian]], [[Puerto_Rican_people|Puerto Rican]], [[Dominican_American|Dominican]], [[Afro-Cuban|Cuban]], [[Haitian_Americans|Haitian]], or other Latin American descent.
sentence_164: The only self-reported ancestral groups larger than African Americans are the [[Irish_American|Irish]] and [[German_Americans|Germans]].
sentence_165: According to the [[2010_United_States_Census|2010 U.S. Census]], nearly 3% of people who self-identified as black had recent ancestors who immigrated from another country.
sentence_166: Self-reported [[West_Indian_American|non-Hispanic black immigrants from the Caribbean]], mostly from Jamaica and Haiti, represented 0.9% of the U.S. population, at 2.6 million.
sentence_167: Self-reported black immigrants from Sub-Saharan Africa also represented 0.9%, at about 2.8 million.
sentence_168: Additionally, self-identified [[Black_Hispanic_and_Latino_Americans|Black Hispanics]] represented 0.4% of the United States population, at about 1.2 million people, largely found within the Puerto Rican and Dominican communities.
sentence_169: Self-reported black immigrants hailing from other countries in the Americas, such as Brazil and Canada, as well as several European countries, represented less than 0.1% of the population.
sentence_170: Mixed-Race Hispanic and non-Hispanic Americans who identified as being part black, represented 0.9% of the population.
sentence_171: Of the 12.6% of United States residents who identified as black, around 10.3% were "native black American" or ethnic African Americans, who are direct descendants of West/Central Africans brought to the U.S. as slaves.
sentence_172: These individuals make up well over 80% of all blacks in the country.
sentence_173: When including [[Multiracial_American|people of mixed-race origin]], about 13.5% of the U.S. population self-identified as black or "mixed with black".
sentence_174: However, according to the U.S. census bureau, evidence from the 2000 Census indicates that many African and Caribbean immigrant ethnic groups do not identify as "Black, African Am., or Negro".
sentence_175: Instead, they wrote in their own respective ethnic groups in the "Some Other Race" write-in entry.
sentence_176: As a result, the census bureau devised a new, separate "African American" ethnic group category in 2010 for ethnic African Americans.
sentence_177: Further information: [[List_of_U.S._cities_with_large_African-American_populations|List of U.S. cities with large African-American populations]] and [[List_of_U.S._metropolitan_areas_with_large_African-American_populations|List of U.S. metropolitan areas with large African-American populations]]
sentence_178: After 100 years of African-Americans leaving the south in large numbers seeking better opportunities and treatment in the west and north, a movement known as the [[Great_Migration_(African_American)|Great Migration]], there is now a reverse trend, called the [[New_Great_Migration|New Great Migration]].
sentence_179: As with the earlier Great Migration, the New Great Migration is primarily directed toward cities and large urban areas, such as [[Atlanta|Atlanta]], [[Charlotte,_North_Carolina|Charlotte]], [[Houston|Houston]], [[Dallas|Dallas]], [[Raleigh,_North_Carolina|Raleigh]], [[Tampa|Tampa]], [[San_Antonio|San Antonio]], [[Memphis,_Tennessee|Memphis]], [[Nashville|Nashville]], [[Jacksonville|Jacksonville]], and so forth.
sentence_180: A growing percentage of African-Americans from the west and north are migrating to the southern region of the U.S. for economic and cultural reasons.
sentence_181: [[New_York_City|New York City]], [[Chicago|Chicago]], and [[Los_Angeles|Los Angeles]] have the highest decline in African Americans, while [[Atlanta|Atlanta]], [[Dallas|Dallas]], and [[Houston|Houston]] have the highest increase respectively.
sentence_182: Among cities of 100,000 or more, [[Detroit|Detroit, Michigan]] had the highest percentage of black residents of any U.S. city in 2010, with 82%.
sentence_183: Other large cities with African-American majorities include [[Jackson,_Mississippi|Jackson, Mississippi]] (79.4%), [[Miami_Gardens,_Florida|Miami Gardens, Florida]] (76.3%), [[Baltimore|Baltimore, Maryland]] (63%), [[Birmingham,_Alabama|Birmingham, Alabama]] (62.5%), [[Memphis,_Tennessee|Memphis, Tennessee]] (61%), [[New_Orleans|New Orleans, Louisiana]] (60%), [[Montgomery,_Alabama|Montgomery, Alabama]] (56.6%), [[Flint,_Michigan|Flint, Michigan]] (56.6%), [[Savannah,_Georgia|Savannah, Georgia]] (55.0%), [[Augusta,_Georgia|Augusta, Georgia]] (54.7%), [[Atlanta|Atlanta, Georgia]] (54%, see [[African_Americans_in_Atlanta|African Americans in Atlanta]]), [[Cleveland|Cleveland]], Ohio (53.3%), [[Newark,_New_Jersey|Newark, New Jersey]] (52.35%), Washington, D.C. (50.7%), [[Richmond,_Virginia|Richmond, Virginia]] (50.6%), [[Mobile,_Alabama|Mobile, Alabama]] (50.6%), [[Baton_Rouge,_Louisiana|Baton Rouge, Louisiana]] (50.4%), and [[Shreveport,_Louisiana|Shreveport, Louisiana]] (50.4%).
sentence_184: The nation's most affluent community with an African-American majority resides in [[View_Park–Windsor_Hills,_California|View Park–Windsor Hills, California]] with an annual median household income of $159,618.
sentence_185: Other largely affluent predominantly African-American communities include [[Prince_George's_County,_Maryland|Prince George's County]] in Maryland (namely [[Mitchellville,_Maryland|Mitchellville]], [[Woodmore,_Maryland|Woodmore]], and Upper Marlboro), [[DeKalb_County,_Georgia|Dekalb County]] and [[South_Fulton,_Georgia|South Fulton]] in Georgia, [[Charles_City_County,_Virginia|Charles City County]] in Virginia, [[Baldwin_Hills,_Los_Angeles|Baldwin Hills]] in California, [[Hillcrest,_Rockland_County,_New_York|Hillcrest]] and Uniondale in New York, and [[Cedar_Hill,_Texas|Cedar Hill]], [[DeSoto,_Texas|DeSoto]], and [[Missouri_City,_Texas|Missouri City]] in Texas.
sentence_186: [[Queens|Queens County, New York]] is the only county with a population of 65,000 or more where African Americans have a higher median household income than White Americans.
sentence_187: [[Seatack,_Virginia|Seatack, Virginia]] is currently the oldest African-American community in the United States.
sentence_188: It survives today with a vibrant and active civic community.
sentence_189: By 2012, African Americans had advanced greatly in education attainment.
sentence_190: Between 1995 and 2009, freshmen college enrollment for African Americans increased by 73 percent and only 15 percent for whites.
sentence_191: Black women are enrolled in college more than any other race and gender group, leading all with 9.7% enrolled according to the 2011 U.S. Census Bureau.
sentence_192: Predominantly black schools for kindergarten through twelfth grade students were common throughout the U.S. before the 1970s.
sentence_193: By 1972, however, desegregation efforts meant that only 25% of Black students were in schools with more than 90% non-white students.
sentence_194: However, since then, a trend towards re-segregation affected communities across the country: by 2011, 2.9 million African-American students were in such overwhelmingly minority schools, including 53% of Black students in school districts that were formerly under desegregation orders.
sentence_195: [[Historically_black_colleges_and_universities|Historically black colleges and universities (HBCUs)]], which were originally set up when segregated colleges did not admit African Americans, continue to thrive and educate students of all races today.
sentence_196: The majority of HBCUs were established in the [[Southeastern_United_States|southeastern United States]], [[List_of_colleges_and_universities_in_Alabama|Alabama]] has the most HBCUs of any state.
sentence_197: As late as 1947, about one third of African Americans over 65 were considered to lack the literacy to read and write their own names.
sentence_198: By 1969, [[Illiteracy|illiteracy]] as it had been traditionally defined, had been largely eradicated among younger African Americans.
sentence_199: U.S. Census surveys showed that by 1998, 89 percent of African Americans aged 25 to 29 had completed a high-school education, less than whites or Asians, but more than Hispanics.
sentence_200: On many college entrance, standardized tests and grades, African Americans have historically lagged behind whites, but some studies suggest that the [[Achievement_gap_in_the_United_States|achievement gap]] has been closing.
sentence_201: Many policy makers have proposed that this gap can and will be eliminated through policies such as [[Affirmative_action|affirmative action]], desegregation, and multiculturalism.
sentence_202: The average high school graduation rate of blacks in the United States has steadily increased to 71% in 2013.
sentence_203: Separating this statistic into component parts shows it varies greatly depending upon the state and the school district examined.
sentence_204: 38% of black males graduated in the state of New York but in Maine 97% graduated and exceeded the white male graduation rate by 11 percentage points.
sentence_205: In much of the southeastern United States and some parts of the southwestern United States the graduation rate of white males was in fact below 70% such as in Florida where 62% of white males graduated from high school.
sentence_206: Examining specific school districts paints an even more complex picture.
sentence_207: In the Detroit school district the graduation rate of black males was 20% but 7% for white males.
sentence_208: In the New York City school district 28% of black males graduate from high school compared to 57% of white males.
sentence_209: In Newark County 76% of black males graduated compared to 67% for white males.
sentence_210: Further academic improvement has occurred in 2015.
sentence_211: Roughly 23% of all blacks have bachelor's degrees.
sentence_212: In 1988, 21% of whites had obtained a bachelor's degree versus 11% of blacks.
sentence_213: In 2015, 23% of blacks had obtained a bachelor's degree versus 36% of whites.
sentence_214: Foreign born blacks, 9% of the black population, made even greater strides.
sentence_215: They exceed native born blacks by 10 percentage points.
sentence_216: Economically, African Americans have benefited from the advances made during the [[Civil_rights_era|civil rights era]], particularly among the educated, but not without the lingering effects of historical marginalisation when considered as a whole.
sentence_217: The [[Racial_inequality_in_the_United_States|racial disparity in poverty rates]] has narrowed.
sentence_218: The black middle class has grown substantially.
sentence_219: In 2010, 45% of African Americans owned their homes, compared to 67% of all Americans.
sentence_220: The [[African-American_poverty|poverty rate among African Americans]] has decreased from 26.5% in 1998 to 24.7% in 2004, compared to 12.7% for all Americans.
sentence_221: African Americans have a combined buying power of over $892 billion currently and likely over $1.1 trillion by 2012.
sentence_222: In 2002, African American-owned businesses accounted for 1.2 million of the US's 23 million businesses.
sentence_223: As of 2011 African American-owned businesses account for approximately 2 million [[US_businesses|US businesses]].
sentence_224: Black-owned businesses experienced the largest growth in number of businesses among minorities from 2002 to 2011.
sentence_225: In 2004, African-American men had the third-highest earnings of American minority groups after Asian Americans and non-Hispanic whites.
sentence_226: Twenty-five percent of blacks had [[White-collar_worker|white-collar]] occupations (management, professional, and related fields) in 2000, compared with 33.6% of Americans overall.
sentence_227: In 2001, over half of African-American households of married couples earned $50,000 or more.
sentence_228: Although in the same year African Americans were over-represented among the nation's poor, this was directly related to the disproportionate percentage of African-American families headed by single women; such families are collectively poorer, regardless of ethnicity.
sentence_229: In 2006, the median earnings of African-American men was more than black and non-black American women overall, and in all educational levels.
sentence_230: At the same time, among American men, income disparities were significant; the median income of African-American men was approximately 76 cents for every dollar of their European American counterparts, although the gap narrowed somewhat with a rise in educational level.
sentence_231: Overall, the median earnings of African-American men were 72 cents for every dollar earned of their Asian American counterparts, and $1.17 for every dollar earned by Hispanic men.
sentence_232: On the other hand, by 2006, among American women with post-secondary education, African-American women have made significant advances; the median income of African-American women was more than those of their Asian-, European- and Hispanic American counterparts with at least some college education.
sentence_233: The U.S. [[Public_sector|public sector]] is the single most important source of employment for African Americans.
sentence_234: During 2008–2010, 21.2% of all Black workers were public employees, compared with 16.3% of non-Black workers.
sentence_235: Both before and after the onset of the [[Great_Recession|Great Recession]], African Americans were 30% more likely than other workers to be employed in the public sector.
sentence_236: The public sector is also a critical source of decent-paying jobs for Black Americans.
sentence_237: For both men and women, the median wage earned by Black employees is significantly higher in the public sector than in other industries.
sentence_238: In 1999, the median income of African-American families was $33,255 compared to $53,356 of European Americans.
sentence_239: In times of economic hardship for the nation, African Americans suffer disproportionately from job loss and underemployment, with the black underclass being hardest hit.
sentence_240: The phrase "last hired and first fired" is reflected in the [[Bureau_of_Labor_Statistics|Bureau of Labor Statistics]] unemployment figures.
sentence_241: Nationwide, the October 2008 unemployment rate for African Americans was 11.1%, while the nationwide rate was 6.5%.
sentence_242: The income gap between black and white families is also significant.
sentence_243: In 2005, employed blacks earned 65% of the wages of whites, down from 82% in 1975.
sentence_244: The New York Times reported in 2006 that in [[Queens|Queens]], New York, the median income among African-American families exceeded that of white families, which the newspaper attributed to the growth in the number of two-parent black families.
sentence_245: It noted that Queens was the only county with more than 65,000 residents where that was true.
sentence_246: In 2011, it was reported that [[African-American_family_structure|72% of black babies were born to unwed mothers]].
sentence_247: The poverty rate among single-parent black families was 39.5% in 2005, according to Williams, while it was 9.9% among married-couple black families.
sentence_248: Among white families, the respective rates were 26.4% and 6% in poverty.
sentence_249: Collectively, African Americans are more involved in the American political process than other minority groups in the United States, indicated by the highest level of voter registration and participation in elections among these groups in 2004.
sentence_250: African Americans collectively attain higher levels of education than immigrants to the United States.
sentence_251: African Americans also have the highest level of [[United_States_Congress|Congressional representation]] of any minority group in the U.S.
sentence_252: Since the mid 20th century, a large majority of African Americans support the [[Democratic_Party_(United_States)|Democratic Party]].
sentence_253: In the [[2004_United_States_presidential_election|2004 Presidential Election]], Democrat [[John_Kerry|John Kerry]] received 88% of the African-American vote compared to 11% for [[Republican_Party_(United_States)|Republican]] [[George_W._Bush|George W. Bush]].
sentence_254: Although there is an African-American lobby in foreign policy, it has not had the impact that African-American organizations have had in domestic policy.
sentence_255: Many African Americans were excluded from electoral politics in the decades following the end of Reconstruction.
sentence_256: For those that could participate, until the [[New_Deal|New Deal]], African Americans were supporters of the Republican Party because it was Republican President Abraham Lincoln who helped in granting freedom to American slaves; at the time, the Republicans and Democrats represented the [[Sectionalism|sectional]] interests of the [[Northern_United_States|North]] and [[Southern_United_States|South]], respectively, rather than any specific ideology, and both [[Conservatism_in_the_United_States|conservative]] and [[Modern_liberalism_in_the_United_States|liberal]] were represented equally in both parties.
sentence_257: The African-American trend of voting for Democrats can be traced back to the 1930s during the [[Great_Depression|Great Depression]], when [[Franklin_D._Roosevelt|Franklin D. Roosevelt]]'s [[New_Deal|New Deal]] program provided economic relief to African Americans.
sentence_258: Roosevelt's [[New_Deal_coalition|New Deal coalition]] turned the Democratic Party into an organization of the working class and their liberal allies, regardless of region.
sentence_259: The African-American vote became even more solidly Democratic when Democratic presidents [[John_F._Kennedy|John F. Kennedy]] and [[Lyndon_B._Johnson|Lyndon B. Johnson]] pushed for civil rights legislation during the 1960s.
sentence_260: In 1960, nearly a third of African Americans voted for Republican [[Richard_Nixon|Richard Nixon]].
sentence_261: See also: [[African-American_LGBT_community|African-American LGBT community]]
sentence_262: According to a [[Gallup_survey|Gallup survey]], 4.6% of black or African-Americans self-identified as [[LGBT_rights_in_the_United_States|LGBT]] in 2016, while the total portion of American adults in all ethnic groups identifying as LGBT was 4.1% in 2016.
sentence_263: Further information: [[Race_and_health_in_the_United_States#African-Americans|Race and health in the United States § African-Americans]]
sentence_264: The life expectancy for black men in 2008 was 70.8 years.
sentence_265: Life expectancy for black women was 77.5 years in 2008.
sentence_266: In 1900, when information on black life expectancy started being collated, a black man could expect to live to 32.5 years and a black woman 33.5 years.
sentence_267: In 1900, white men lived an average of 46.3 years and white women lived an average of 48.3 years.
sentence_268: African-American life expectancy at birth is persistently five to seven years lower than [[European_Americans|European Americans]].
sentence_269: Black men have shorter lifespans than any other group in the US besides Native American men.
sentence_270: Black people have higher rates of [[Obesity|obesity]], [[Diabetes|diabetes]], and [[Hypertension|hypertension]] than the U.S. average.
sentence_271: For adult black men, the rate of obesity was 31.6% in 2010.
sentence_272: For adult black women, the rate of obesity was 41.2% in 2010.
sentence_273: African Americans have higher rates of mortality than any other racial or ethnic group for 8 of the top 10 causes of death.
sentence_274: In 2013, among men, black men had the highest rate of getting cancer, followed by white, Hispanic, Asian/Pacific Islander (A/PI), and American Indian/Alaska Native (AI/AN) men.
sentence_275: Among women, white women had the highest rate of getting cancer, followed by black, Hispanic, Asian/Pacific Islander, and American Indian/Alaska Native women.
sentence_276: Violence has an impact upon African-American life expectancy.
sentence_277: A report from the [[U.S._Department_of_Justice|U.S.
sentence_278: Department of Justice]] states "In 2005, homicide victimization rates for blacks were 6 times higher than the rates for whites".
sentence_279: The report also found that "94% of black victims were killed by blacks."
sentence_280: Black boys and men age 15–44 are the only race/sex category for which homicide is a top-five cause of death.
sentence_281: According to the [[Centers_for_Disease_Control_and_Prevention|Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]], African Americans have higher rates of [[Sexually_transmitted_infections|sexually transmitted infections]] (STIs) compared to whites, with 5 times the rates of [[Syphilis|syphilis]] and [[Chlamydia_infection|chlamydia]], and 7.5 times the rate of [[Gonorrhea|gonorrhea]].
sentence_282: The disproportionately high incidence of [[AIDS_in_the_United_States|HIV/AIDS among African-Americans]] has been attributed to [[Homophobia_in_the_African_American_community|homophobic]] influences and lack of access to proper healthcare.
sentence_283: The prevalence of [[AIDS|HIV/AIDS]] among black men is seven times higher than the prevalence for white men, and black men are more than nine times as likely to die from HIV/AIDS-related illness than white men.
sentence_284: Washington, D.C. has the nation's highest rate of HIV/AIDS infection, at 3%.
sentence_285: This rate is comparable to what is seen in West Africa, and is considered a severe epidemic.
sentence_286: Ray Martins, Chief Medical Officer at the Whitman-Walker Clinic, the largest provider of HIV care in Washington D.C., estimated that the actual underlying percent with HIV/AIDS in the city is "closer to five percent".
sentence_287: African Americans have several [[Obstacles_to_receiving_mental_health_services_among_African_American_youth|barriers]] for accessing mental health services.
sentence_288: [[Mental_health_counselor|Counseling]] has been frowned upon and distant in utility and proximity to many people in the African American community.
sentence_289: In 2004, a qualitative research study explored the disconnect with African Americans and mental health.
sentence_290: The study was conducted as a semi-structured discussion which allowed the focus group to express their opinions and life experiences.
sentence_291: The results revealed a couple key variables that create barriers for many African American communities to seek mental health services such as the stigma, lack of four important necessities; trust, affordability, cultural understanding and impersonal services.
sentence_292: Historically, many African American communities did not seek counseling because religion was a part of the family values.
sentence_293: African American who have a faith background are more likely to seek prayer as a coping mechanism for mental issues rather than seeking professional mental health services.
sentence_294: In 2015 a study concluded, African Americans with high value in religion are less likely to utilize mental health services compared to those who have low value in religion.
sentence_295: Most counseling approaches are westernized and do not fit within the African American culture.
sentence_296: African American families tend to resolve concerns within the family, and it is viewed by the family as a strength.
sentence_297: On the other hand, when African Americans seek counseling, they face a social backlash and are criticized.
sentence_298: They may be labeled "crazy", viewed as weak, and their pride is diminished.
sentence_299: Because of this, many African Americans instead seek mentorship within communities they trust.
sentence_300: Terminology is another barrier in relation to African Americans and mental health.
sentence_301: There is more stigma on the term [[Psychotherapy|psychotherapy]] versus counseling.
sentence_302: In one study, psychotherapy is associated with mental illness whereas counseling approaches problem-solving, guidance and help.
sentence_303: More African Americans seek assistance when it is called counseling and not psychotherapy because it is more welcoming within the cultural and community.
sentence_304: Counselors are encouraged to be aware of such barriers for the well-being of African American clients.
sentence_305: Without [[Cultural_competence_in_healthcare|cultural competency]] training in health care, many African Americans go unheard and misunderstood.
sentence_306: Although [[Suicide|suicide]] is a top-10 cause of death for men overall in the US, it is not a top-10 cause of death for black men.
sentence_307: Recent surveys of African Americans using a genetic testing service have found varied ancestries which show different tendencies by region and sex of ancestors.
sentence_308: These studies found that on average, African Americans have 73.2–82.1% [[West_African_people|West African]], 16.7%–24% European, and 0.8–1.2% Native American genetic ancestry, with large variation between individuals.
sentence_309: Genetics websites themselves have reported similar ranges, with some finding 1 or 2 percent Native American ancestry and Ancestry.com reporting an outlying percentage of European ancestry among African Americans, 29%.
sentence_310: According to a genome-wide study by Bryc et al.
sentence_311: (2009), the mixed ancestry of African Americans in varying ratios came about as the result of sexual contact between West/Central Africans (more frequently females) and Europeans (more frequently males).
sentence_312: Consequently, the 365 African Americans in their sample have a genome-wide average of 78.1% West African ancestry and 18.5% European ancestry, with large variation among individuals (ranging from 99% to 1% West African ancestry).
sentence_313: The West African ancestral component in African Americans is most similar to that in present-day speakers from the non-[[Bantu_languages|Bantu]] branches of the [[Niger-Congo_languages|Niger-Congo]] (Niger-Kordofanian) family.
sentence_314: Correspondingly, Montinaro et al.
sentence_315: (2014) observed that around 50% of the overall ancestry of African Americans traces back to the Niger-Congo-speaking [[Yoruba_people|Yoruba]] of southwestern [[Nigeria|Nigeria]] and southern [[Benin|Benin]], reflecting the centrality of this West African region in the Atlantic Slave Trade.
sentence_316: The next most frequent ancestral component found among African Americans was derived from Great Britain, in keeping with historical records.
sentence_317: It constitutes a little over 10% of their overall ancestry, and is most similar to the Northwest European ancestral component also carried by [[Barbadians|Barbadians]].
sentence_318: Zakharaia et al.
sentence_319: (2009) found a similar proportion of Yoruba associated ancestry in their African-American samples, with a minority also drawn from [[Mandenka_people|Mandenka]] and [[Bantu_peoples|Bantu]] populations.
sentence_320: Additionally, the researchers observed an average European ancestry of 21.9%, again with significant variation between individuals.
sentence_321: Bryc et al.
sentence_322: (2009) note that populations from other parts of the continent may also constitute adequate proxies for the ancestors of some African-American individuals; namely, ancestral populations from [[Guinea_Bissau|Guinea Bissau]], [[Senegal|Senegal]] and Sierra Leone in West Africa and [[Angola|Angola]] in Southern Africa.
sentence_323: Altogether, genetic studies suggest that African Americans are a multiracial people.
sentence_324: According to DNA analysis led in 2006 by [[Pennsylvania_State_University|Penn State]] geneticist [[Mark_D._Shriver|Mark D. Shriver]], around 58 percent of African Americans have at least 12.5% European ancestry (equivalent to one European great-grandparent and his/her forebears), 19.6 percent of African Americans have at least 25% European ancestry (equivalent to one European grandparent and his/her forebears), and 1 percent of African Americans have at least 50% European ancestry (equivalent to one European parent and his/her forebears).
sentence_325: According to Shriver, around 5 percent of African Americans also have at least 12.5% Native American ancestry (equivalent to one Native American great-grandparent and his/her forebears).
sentence_326: Research suggests that Native American ancestry among people who identify as African American is a result of relationships that occurred soon after slave ships arrived in the American colonies, and European ancestry is of more recent origin, often from the decades before the Civil War.
sentence_327: Africans bearing the [[Haplogroup_E-V38|E-V38]] (E1b1a) likely traversed across the [[Sahara|Sahara]], from [[East_Africa|east]] to [[West_Africa|west]], approximately 19,000 years ago.
sentence_328: [[Haplogroup_E-M2|E-M2]] (E1b1a1) likely originated in West Africa or Central Africa.
sentence_329: According to a [[Y_chromosome|Y-DNA]] study by Sims et al.
sentence_330: (2007), the majority (≈60%) of African Americans belong to various subclades of the [[Haplogroup_E-M2|E-M2]] (E1b1a1, formerly E3a) paternal haplogroup.
sentence_331: This is the most common genetic paternal lineage found today among West/Central African males, and is also a signature of the historical [[Bantu_migration|Bantu migrations]].
sentence_332: The next most frequent Y-DNA haplogroup observed among African Americans is the [[Haplogroup_R1b_(Y-DNA)|R1b]] clade, which around 15% of African Americans carry.
sentence_333: This lineage is most common today among [[Northwestern_European_people|Northwestern European males]].
sentence_334: The remaining African Americans mainly belong to the paternal haplogroup I (≈7%), which is also frequent in Northwestern Europe.
sentence_335: According to an [[Mitochondrial_DNA|mtDNA]] study by Salas et al.
sentence_336: (2005), the maternal lineages of African Americans are most similar to haplogroups that are today especially common in West Africa (>55%), followed closely by West-Central Africa and Southwestern Africa (<41%).
sentence_337: The characteristic West African haplogroups [[Haplogroup_L1_(mtDNA)|L1b]], [[Haplogroup_L2_(mtDNA)|L2b,c,d]], and [[Haplogroup_L3_(mtDNA)|L3b,d]] and West-Central African haplogroups [[Haplogroup_L1_(mtDNA)|L1c]] and [[Haplogroup_L3_(mtDNA)|L3e]] in particular occur at high frequencies among African Americans.
sentence_338: As with the paternal DNA of African Americans, contributions from other parts of the continent to their maternal gene pool are insignificant.
sentence_339: See also: Income inequality in the United States
sentence_340: Formal political, economic and social discrimination against minorities has been present throughout American history.
sentence_341: Leland T. Saito, Associate Professor of Sociology and American Studies & Ethnicity at the [[University_of_Southern_California|University of Southern California]], writes, "Political rights have been circumscribed by race, class and gender since the founding of the United States, when the right to vote was restricted to white men of property.
sentence_342: Throughout the history of the United States race has been used by whites for legitimizing and creating difference and social, economic and political exclusion."
sentence_343: African Americans have improved their social and economic standing significantly since the civil rights movement and recent decades have witnessed the expansion of a robust, African-American middle class across the United States.
sentence_344: Unprecedented access to higher education and employment in addition to representation in the highest levels of American government has been gained by African Americans in the post–civil rights era.
sentence_345: Nonetheless, widespread racism against African Americans remain an issue that undermines the development of their social status in the United States.
sentence_346: See also: [[Poverty_in_the_United_States|Poverty in the United States]] and Income inequality in the United States
sentence_347: One of the most serious and long-standing issues within African-American communities is poverty.
sentence_348: Poverty is associated with higher rates of marital stress and dissolution, physical and [[Mental_disorder|mental health]] problems, [[Disability_and_poverty|disability]], [[Cognitive_deficit|cognitive deficits]], [[Achievement_gap_in_the_United_States|low educational attainment]], and crime.
sentence_349: In 2004, almost 25% of African-American families lived below the poverty level.
sentence_350: In 2007, the average income for African Americans was approximately $34,000, compared to $55,000 for whites.
sentence_351: African Americans experience a higher rate of unemployment than the general population.
sentence_352: African Americans have a long and diverse history of [[African-American_Businesses|business ownership]].
sentence_353: Although the first [[African-American_Businesses|African-American business]] is unknown, slaves captured from West Africa are believed to have established commercial enterprises as peddlers and skilled craftspeople as far back as the 17th century.
sentence_354: Around 1900, Booker T. Washington became the most famous proponent of African-American businesses.
sentence_355: His critic and rival W. E. B. DuBois also commended business as a vehicle for African-American advancement.
sentence_356: See also: [[Race_and_crime_in_the_United_States|Race and crime in the United States]]
sentence_357: Forty percent of prison inmates are African-American.
sentence_358: African American males are more likely to be killed by police when compared to other races killed by police.
sentence_359: This is one of the factors that led to the creation of the [[Black_Lives_Matter|Black Lives Matter]] movement in 2013.
sentence_360: White women calling the police on black people also became a widely publicized issue in 2020.
sentence_361: Although in the last decade black youth have had lower rates of [[Cannabis|cannabis]] (marijuana) consumption than whites of the same age, they have disproportionately higher arrest rates than whites: in 2010, for example, blacks were 3.73 times as likely to get arrested for using cannabis than whites, despite not significantly more frequently being users.
sentence_362: After over 50 years, marriage rates for all Americans began to decline while divorce rates and out-of-wedlock births have climbed.
sentence_363: These changes have been greatest among African Americans.
sentence_364: After more than 70 years of racial parity black marriage rates began to fall behind whites.
sentence_365: Single-parent households have become common, and according to U.S. census figures released in January 2010, only 38 percent of black children live with both their parents.
sentence_366: In 2008, Democrats overwhelmingly voted 70% against [[California_Proposition_8|California Proposition 8]], African Americans voted 58% in favor of it while 42% voted against Proposition 8.
sentence_367: On May 9, 2012, Barack Obama, the first black president, became the first U.S. president to support same-sex marriage.
sentence_368: Since Obama's endorsement there has been a rapid growth in support for same-sex marriage among African Americans.
sentence_369: As of 2012, 59% of African Americans support same-sex marriage, which is higher than support among the national average (53%) and [[White_Americans|white Americans]] (50%).
sentence_370: Polls in [[North_Carolina|North Carolina]], [[Pennsylvania|Pennsylvania]], [[Missouri|Missouri]], [[Maryland|Maryland]], [[Ohio|Ohio]], Florida, and [[Nevada|Nevada]] have also shown an increase in support for same sex marriage among African Americans.
sentence_371: On November 6, 2012, [[Maryland_Question_6|Maryland]], [[Maine_Question_1,_2012|Maine]], and [[Washington_Referendum_74|Washington]] all voted for approve of same-sex marriage, along with Minnesota rejecting a [[Minnesota_Amendment_1|constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage]].
sentence_372: Exit polls in Maryland show about 50% of African Americans voted for same-sex marriage, showing a vast evolution among African Americans on the issue and was crucial in helping pass same-sex marriage in Maryland.
sentence_373: Black Americans hold far more conservative opinions on abortion, [[Affair|extramarital sex]], and raising children out of wedlock than Democrats as a whole.
sentence_374: On financial issues, however, African Americans are in line with Democrats, generally supporting a more [[Progressive_tax|progressive tax]] structure to provide more government spending on social services.
sentence_375: [[Military_history_of_African_Americans|African Americans have fought in every war]] in the [[Military_history_of_the_United_States|history of the United States]].
sentence_376: The gains made by African Americans in the [[Civil_rights_movement|civil rights movement]] and in the [[Black_Power_movement|Black Power movement]] not only obtained certain rights for African Americans, but changed American society in far-reaching and fundamentally important ways.
sentence_377: Prior to the 1950s, Black Americans in the South were subject to de jure discrimination, or [[Jim_Crow_laws|Jim Crow laws]].
sentence_378: They were often the victims of extreme cruelty and violence, sometimes resulting in deaths: by the post World War II era, African Americans became increasingly discontented with their long-standing inequality.
sentence_379: In the words of [[Martin_Luther_King_Jr.|Martin Luther King Jr.]], African Americans and their supporters challenged the nation to "rise up and live out the true meaning of its creed that all men are created equal ..."
sentence_380: The civil rights movement marked an enormous change in American social, political, economic and civic life.
sentence_381: It brought with it [[Boycott|boycotts]], [[Sit-in|sit-ins]], [[Nonviolent|nonviolent]] demonstrations and marches, court battles, bombings and other violence; prompted worldwide media coverage and intense public debate; forged enduring civic, economic and religious alliances; and disrupted and realigned the nation's two major political parties.
sentence_382: Over time, it has changed in fundamental ways the manner in which blacks and whites interact with and relate to one another.
sentence_383: The movement resulted in the removal of codified, de jure racial segregation and discrimination from American life and law, and heavily influenced other groups and movements in struggles for civil rights and social equality within American society, including the [[Free_Speech_Movement|Free Speech Movement]], the [[Disability|disabled]], the [[Feminist_movement|women's movement]], Native Americans, and [[Migrant_workers|migrant workers]].
sentence_384: See also: [[Representation_of_African_Americans_in_media|Representation of African Americans in media]] and [[African-American_newspapers|African-American newspapers]]
sentence_385: Some activists and academics contend that American news media coverage of African-American news, concerns, or dilemmas is inadequate, or that the news media present distorted images of African Americans.
sentence_386: To combat this, [[Robert_L._Johnson|Robert L. Johnson]] founded [[Black_Entertainment_Television|Black Entertainment Television]], a network that targets young African Americans and urban audiences in the United States.
sentence_387: Over the years, the network has aired such programming as [[Hip_hop_music|rap]] and [[Contemporary_R&B|R&B]] music videos, urban-oriented movies and television series, and some public affairs programs.
sentence_388: On Sunday mornings, BET would broadcast Christian programming; the network would also broadcast non-affiliated Christian programs during the early morning hours daily.
sentence_389: BET is now a global network that reaches households in the United States, Caribbean, Canada, and the United Kingdom.
sentence_390: The network has gone on to spawn several spin-off channels, including [[BET_Her|BET Her]] (originally launched as BET on Jazz), which originally showcased [[Jazz|jazz]] music-related programming, and later expanded to include general-interest urban programs as well as some R&B, [[Soul_music|soul]], and [[World_music|world music]].
sentence_391: Another network targeting African-Americans is [[TV_One_(Radio_One)|TV One]].
sentence_392: TV One's original programming was formally focused on lifestyle and entertainment-oriented shows, movies, fashion, and music programming.
sentence_393: The network also reruns classic series from as far back as the 1970s to current series such as [[Empire_(2015_TV_series)|Empire]] and Sister Circle.
sentence_394: TV One is owned by [[Urban_One|Urban One]], founded and controlled by [[Cathy_Hughes|Catherine Hughes]].
sentence_395: Urban One is one of the nation's largest radio broadcasting companies and the largest African-American-owned radio broadcasting company in the United States.
sentence_396: African-American networks that were scheduled to launch in 2009 include the Black Television News Channel founded by former Congressman [[J._C._Watts|J.
sentence_397: C. Watts]] and Better Black Television founded by [[Master_P|Percy Miller]].
sentence_398: In June 2009, [[NBC_News|NBC News]] launched a new website named [[The_Grio|The Grio]] in partnership with the production team that created the black documentary film Meeting David Wilson.
sentence_399: It is the first African-American video [[News_site|news site]] that focuses on underrepresented stories in existing national news.
sentence_400: [[The_Grio|The Grio]] consists of a broad spectrum of original video packages, news articles, and contributor blogs on topics including breaking news, politics, health, business, entertainment and Black History.
sentence_401: Other Black-owned and oriented media outlets include:

list.value: [[The_Africa_Channel|The Africa Channel]] – Dedicated to programming representing the best in African culture.
[[ASPiRE_(TV_network)|aspireTV]] – a digital cable and satellite channel owned by businessman and former basketball player [[Magic_Johnson|Magic Johnson]].
ATTV – an independent public affairs and educational channel.
[[Bounce_TV|Bounce TV]] – a digital multicast network owned by [[E._W._Scripps_Company|E. W. Scripps Company]].
[[Cleo_TV|Cleo TV]] – a sister network to [[TV_One_(U.S._TV_network)|TV One]] targeting African-American women.
[[Fox_Television_Stations#Fox_Soul|Fox Soul]] – a digital streaming channel primarily airing original talk shows and syndicated programming

[[Oprah_Winfrey_Network|Oprah Winfrey Network]] – a cable and satellite network founded by [[Oprah_Winfrey|Oprah Winfrey]] and jointly owned by [[Discovery,_Inc.|Discovery, Inc.]] and [[Harpo_Studios|Harpo Studios]]. While not exclusively targeting African Americans, much of its original programming is geared towards a similar demographic.
[[Revolt_(TV_network)|Revolt]] – a music channel owned by [[Sean_Combs|Sean "Puff Daddy" Combs]].
[[Soul_of_the_South_Network|Soul of the South Network]] – a regional broadcast network.

[[VH1|VH1]] – A female-oriented general entertainment channel owned by [[Viacom_(2005–present)|Viacom]]. Originally focused on light genres of music, the network's programming became slanted towards African American culture in recent years.

sentence_402: Further information: [[African-American_culture|African-American culture]]
sentence_403: From their earliest presence in North America, African Americans have significantly contributed literature, art, agricultural skills, cuisine, clothing styles, music, language, and social and technological innovation to American culture.
sentence_404: The cultivation and use of many agricultural products in the United States, such as [[Sweet_potato|yams]], peanuts, rice, [[Okra|okra]], [[Sorghum|sorghum]], grits, [[Watermelon|watermelon]], [[Indigo_dye|indigo dyes]], and cotton, can be traced to West African and African-American influences.
sentence_405: Notable examples include [[George_Washington_Carver|George Washington Carver]], who created 300 products from peanuts, 118 products from sweet potatoes, and 75 products from pecans; and [[George_Crum|George Crum]], a local legend incorrectly associates him with the creation of the potato chip in 1853.
sentence_406: [[Soul_food|Soul food]] is a variety of cuisine popular among African Americans.
sentence_407: It is closely related to the [[Cuisine_of_the_Southern_United_States|cuisine of the Southern United States]].
sentence_408: The descriptive terminology may have originated in the mid-1960s, when was a common definer used to describe African-American culture (for example, [[Soul_music|soul music]]).
sentence_409: African Americans were the first peoples in the United States to make fried chicken, along with [[Scottish_people|Scottish]] immigrants to the South.
sentence_410: Although the Scottish had been frying chicken before they emigrated, they lacked the spices and flavor that African Americans had used when preparing the meal.
sentence_411: The Scottish American settlers therefore adopted the African-American method of seasoning chicken.
sentence_412: However, fried chicken was generally a rare meal in the African-American community, and was usually reserved for special events or celebrations.
sentence_413: Main article: [[African-American_English|African-American English]]
sentence_414: [[African-American_English|African-American English]] is a [[Variety_(linguistics)|variety]] ([[Dialect|dialect]], [[Ethnolect|ethnolect]], and [[Sociolect|sociolect]]) of [[American_English|American English]], commonly spoken by urban working-class and largely [[Middle_class|middle-class]] African Americans.
sentence_415: African-American English evolved during the antebellum period through interaction between speakers of 16th- and 17th-century English of Great Britain and Ireland and various West African languages.
sentence_416: As a result, the variety shares parts of its [[Grammar|grammar]] and [[Phonology|phonology]] with the [[Southern_American_English|Southern American English]] dialect.
sentence_417: Where African-American English differs from Standard American English (SAE) is in certain pronunciation characteristics, tense usage and grammatical structures that were derived from West African languages, particularly those belonging to the [[Niger-Congo_languages|Niger-Congo]] family.
sentence_418: Virtually all habitual speakers of African-American English can understand and communicate in Standard American English.
sentence_419: As with all linguistic forms, AAVE's usage is influenced by various factors, including geographical, educational and socioeconomic background, as well as formality of setting.
sentence_420: Additionally, there are many literary uses of this variety of English, particularly in [[African-American_literature|African-American literature]].
sentence_421: Main article: [[African-American_names|African-American names]]
sentence_422: [[African-American_names|African-American names]] are part of the cultural traditions of African Americans.
sentence_423: Prior to the 1950s, and 1960s, most African-American names closely resembled those used within European American culture.
sentence_424: Babies of that era were generally given a few common names, with children using nicknames to distinguish the various people with the same name.
sentence_425: With the rise of 1960s civil rights movement, there was a dramatic increase in names of various origins.
sentence_426: By the 1970s, and 1980s, it had become common among African Americans to invent new names for themselves, although many of these invented names took elements from popular existing names.
sentence_427: Prefixes such as La/Le, Da/De, Ra/Re and Ja/Je, and suffixes like -ique/iqua, -isha and -aun/-awn are common, as are inventive spellings for common names.
sentence_428: The book Baby Names Now: From Classic to Cool—The Very Last Word on First Names places the origins of "La" names in African-American culture in [[New_Orleans|New Orleans]].
sentence_429: Even with the rise of inventive names, it is still common for African Americans to use biblical, historical, or traditional European names.
sentence_430: Daniel, Christopher, Michael, David, James, Joseph, and Matthew were thus among the most frequent names for African-American boys in 2013.
sentence_431: The name LaKeisha is typically considered American in origin, but has elements that were drawn from both French and West/Central African roots.
sentence_432: Names such as LaTanisha, JaMarcus, DeAndre, and Shaniqua were created in the same way.
sentence_433: Punctuation marks are seen more often within African-American names than other American names, such as the names Mo'nique and D'Andre.
sentence_434: Main article: [[Religion_of_Black_Americans|Religion of Black Americans]]
sentence_435: Further information: [[African-American_Jews|African-American Jews]], [[African-American_Muslims|African-American Muslims]], [[Black_church|Black church]], [[Hoodoo_(folk_magic)|Hoodoo (folk magic)]], and Louisiana Voodoo
sentence_436: The majority of African Americans are [[Protestant|Protestant]], many of whom follow the historically black churches.
sentence_437: The term [[Black_church|Black church]] refers to churches which minister to predominantly African-American congregations.
sentence_438: Black congregations were first established by freed slaves at the end of the 17th century, and later when slavery was abolished more African Americans were allowed to create a unique form of Christianity that was culturally influenced by African spiritual traditions.
sentence_439: According to a 2007 survey, more than half of the African-American population are part of the historically black churches.
sentence_440: The largest Protestant denomination among African Americans are the [[Baptists|Baptists]], distributed mainly in four denominations, the largest being the [[National_Baptist_Convention,_USA,_Inc.|National Baptist Convention, USA]] and the [[National_Baptist_Convention_of_America,_Inc.|National Baptist Convention of America]].
sentence_441: The second largest are the [[Methodist|Methodists]], the largest denominations are the [[African_Methodist_Episcopal_Church|African Methodist Episcopal Church]] and the [[African_Methodist_Episcopal_Zion_Church|African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church]].
sentence_442: [[Pentecostalism|Pentecostals]] are distributed among several different religious bodies, with the [[Church_of_God_in_Christ|Church of God in Christ]] as the largest among them by far.
sentence_443: About 16% of African-American Christians are members of white Protestant communions, these denominations (which include the [[United_Church_of_Christ|United Church of Christ]]) mostly have a 2 to 3% African-American membership.
sentence_444: There are also large numbers of [[Catholic_Church|Catholics]], constituting 5% of the African-American population.
sentence_445: Of the total number of [[Jehovah's_Witnesses|Jehovah's Witnesses]], 22% are black.
sentence_446: Some African Americans follow [[Islam|Islam]].
sentence_447: Historically, between 15 and 30% of enslaved Africans brought to the Americas were [[Muslim|Muslims]], but most of these Africans were converted to Christianity during the era of American slavery.
sentence_448: During the twentieth century, some African Americans converted to Islam, mainly through the influence of [[Black_nationalism|black nationalist]] groups that preached with distinctive Islamic practices; including the [[Moorish_Science_Temple_of_America|Moorish Science Temple of America]], and the largest organization, the Nation of Islam, founded in the 1930s, which attracted at least 20,000 people by 1963, prominent members included activist [[Malcolm_X|Malcolm X]] and boxer [[Muhammad_Ali|Muhammad Ali]].
sentence_449: Malcolm X is considered the first person to start the movement among African Americans towards mainstream Islam, after he left the Nation and made the [[Hajj|pilgrimage to Mecca]].
sentence_450: In 1975, Warith Deen Mohammed, the son of [[Elijah_Muhammad|Elijah Muhammad]] took control of the Nation after his father's death and guided the majority of its members to [[Sunni_Islam|orthodox Islam]].
sentence_451: [[African-American_Muslims|African-American Muslims]] constitute 20% of the total [[Islam_in_the_United_States|U.S.
sentence_452: Muslim population]], the majority are [[Sunni_Islam|Sunni]] or orthodox Muslims, some of these identify under the community of [[W._Deen_Mohammed|W.
sentence_453: Deen Mohammed]].
sentence_454: The Nation of Islam led by Louis Farrakhan has a membership ranging from 20,000–50,000 members.
sentence_455: There are relatively few African-American Jews; estimates of their number range from 20,000 to 200,000.
sentence_456: Most of these Jews are part of mainstream groups such as the [[Reform_Judaism|Reform]], [[Conservative_Judaism|Conservative]], or [[Orthodox_Judaism|Orthodox]] branches of Judaism; although there are significant numbers of people who are part of non-mainstream Jewish groups, largely the [[Black_Hebrew_Israelites|Black Hebrew Israelites]], whose beliefs include the claim that African Americans are descended from the Biblical [[Israelites|Israelites]].
sentence_457: Confirmed [[Atheism|atheists]] are less than one half of one-percent, similar to numbers for [[Hispanic|Hispanics]].
sentence_458: [[African-American_music|African-American music]] is one of the most pervasive African-American cultural influences in the United States today and is among the most dominant in mainstream popular music.
sentence_459: [[Hip_hop_music|Hip hop]], [[Rhythm_and_blues|R&B]], [[Funk|funk]], [[Rock_and_roll|rock and roll]], [[Soul_music|soul]], [[Blues|blues]], and other contemporary American musical forms originated in black communities and evolved from other black forms of music, including [[Blues|blues]], [[Doo-wop|doo-wop]], [[Barbershop_music|barbershop]], [[Ragtime|ragtime]], bluegrass, [[Jazz|jazz]], and gospel music.
sentence_460: African-American-derived musical forms have also influenced and been incorporated into virtually every other [[Popular_music|popular music]] genre in the world, including [[Country_music|country]] and [[Techno|techno]].
sentence_461: African-American genres are the most important ethnic vernacular tradition in America, as they have developed independent of African traditions from which they arise more so than any other immigrant groups, including Europeans; make up the broadest and longest lasting range of styles in America; and have, historically, been more influential, interculturally, geographically, and economically, than other American vernacular traditions.
sentence_462: African Americans have also had an important role in American dance.
sentence_463: [[Bill_T._Jones|Bill T. Jones]], a prominent modern choreographer and dancer, has included historical African-American themes in his work, particularly in the piece "Last Supper at Uncle Tom's Cabin/The Promised Land".
sentence_464: Likewise, [[Alvin_Ailey|Alvin Ailey]]'s artistic work, including his "Revelations" based on his experience growing up as an African American in the South during the 1930s, has had a significant influence on modern dance.
sentence_465: Another form of dance, [[Stepping_(African-American)|Stepping]], is an African-American tradition whose performance and competition has been formalized through the traditionally black fraternities and sororities at universities.
sentence_466: Many African-American authors have written stories, poems, and essays influenced by their experiences as African Americans.
sentence_467: [[African-American_literature|African-American literature]] is a major genre in American literature.
sentence_468: Famous examples include [[Langston_Hughes|Langston Hughes]], [[James_Baldwin_(writer)|James Baldwin]], [[Richard_Wright_(author)|Richard Wright]], [[Zora_Neale_Hurston|Zora Neale Hurston]], [[Ralph_Ellison|Ralph Ellison]], Nobel Prize winner [[Toni_Morrison|Toni Morrison]], and [[Maya_Angelou|Maya Angelou]].
sentence_469: African-American inventors have created many widely used devices in the world and have contributed to international [[Innovation|innovation]].
sentence_470: [[Norbert_Rillieux|Norbert Rillieux]] created the technique for converting sugar cane juice into white sugar crystals.
sentence_471: Moreover, Rillieux left [[Louisiana|Louisiana]] in 1854 and went to France, where he spent ten years working with the Champollions deciphering [[Egyptian_hieroglyphs|Egyptian hieroglyphics]] from the [[Rosetta_Stone|Rosetta Stone]].
sentence_472: Most slave inventors were nameless, such as the slave owned by the [[Confederate_States_of_America|Confederate]] President Jefferson Davis who designed the ship propeller used by the Confederate navy.
sentence_473: By 1913, over 1,000 inventions were patented by black Americans.
sentence_474: Among the most notable inventors were [[Jan_Matzeliger|Jan Matzeliger]], who developed the first machine to mass-produce shoes, and [[Elijah_McCoy|Elijah McCoy]], who invented automatic lubrication devices for steam engines.
sentence_475: [[Granville_Woods|Granville Woods]] had 35 patents to improve electric railway systems, including the first system to allow moving trains to communicate.
sentence_476: [[Garrett_A._Morgan|Garrett A. Morgan]] developed the first automatic traffic signal and gas mask.
sentence_477: [[Lewis_Howard_Latimer|Lewis Howard Latimer]] invented an improvement for the incandescent light bulb.
sentence_478: More recent inventors include Frederick McKinley Jones, who invented the movable refrigeration unit for food transport in trucks and trains.
sentence_479: [[Lloyd_Quarterman|Lloyd Quarterman]] worked with six other black scientists on the creation of the atomic bomb (code named the [[Manhattan_Project|Manhattan Project]].)
sentence_480: Quarterman also helped develop the first nuclear reactor, which was used in the atomically powered [[Submarine|submarine]] called the Nautilus.
sentence_481: A few other notable examples include the first successful open heart surgery, performed by Dr. [[Daniel_Hale_Williams|Daniel Hale Williams]], and the air conditioner, patented by Frederick McKinley Jones.
sentence_482: Dr. [[Mark_Dean_(computer_scientist)|Mark Dean]] holds three of the original nine patents on the computer on which all PCs are based.
sentence_483: More current contributors include [[Otis_Boykin|Otis Boykin]], whose inventions included several novel methods for manufacturing electrical components that found use in applications such as guided missile systems and computers, and Colonel [[Frederick_D._Gregory|Frederick Gregory]], who was not only the first black [[Astronaut|astronaut]] pilot but the person who redesigned the cockpits for the last three space shuttles.
sentence_484: Gregory was also on the team that pioneered the microwave instrumentation landing system.
sentence_485: The term African American carries important political overtones.
sentence_486: Earlier terms used to describe Americans of African ancestry referred more to skin color than to ancestry, and were conferred upon the group by colonists and Americans of European ancestry; people with dark skins were considered inferior in fact and in law.
sentence_487: Other terms (such as [[Colored|colored]], [[Person_of_color|person of color]], or negro) were included in the wording of various laws and legal decisions which some thought were being used as tools of [[White_supremacy|white supremacy]] and [[Oppression|oppression]].
sentence_488: A 16-page pamphlet entitled "A Sermon on the Capture of Lord Cornwallis" is notable for the attribution of its authorship to "An African American".
sentence_489: Published in 1782, the book's use of this phrase predates any other yet identified by more than 50 years.
sentence_490: In the 1980s, the term African American was advanced on the model of, for example, [[German_Americans|German American]] or [[Irish_Americans|Irish American]], to give descendants of [[Slavery_in_the_United_States|American slaves]], and other American blacks who lived through the slavery era, a heritage and a cultural base.
sentence_491: The term was popularized in black communities around the country via [[Word_of_mouth|word of mouth]] and ultimately received mainstream use after [[Jesse_Jackson|Jesse Jackson]] publicly used the term in front of a national audience in 1988.
sentence_492: Subsequently, major media outlets adopted its use.
sentence_493: Surveys show that the majority of Black Americans have no preference for African American versus Black American, although they have a slight preference for the latter in personal settings and the former in more formal settings.
sentence_494: Many African Americans have expressed a preference for the term African American because it was formed in the same way as the terms for the many other ethnic groups currently living in the United States.
sentence_495: Some argued further that, because of the historical circumstances surrounding the capture, enslavement, and systematic attempts to de-Africanize blacks in the United States under [[Slavery#Chattel_slavery|chattel slavery]], most African Americans are unable to trace their ancestry to any specific [[List_of_sovereign_states_and_dependent_territories_in_Africa|African nation]]; hence, the [[Africa|entire continent]] serves as a geographic marker.
sentence_496: The term African American embraces [[Pan-Africanism|pan-Africanism]] as earlier enunciated by prominent African thinkers such as [[Marcus_Garvey|Marcus Garvey]], [[W._E._B._Du_Bois|W.
sentence_497: E. B.
sentence_498: Du Bois]], and [[George_Padmore|George Padmore]].
sentence_499: The term Afro-[[Usonia|Usonian]], and variations of such, are more rarely used.
sentence_500: Since 1977, in an attempt to keep up with changing social opinion, the [[Federal_government_of_the_United_States|United States government]] has officially classified black people (revised to black or African American in 1997) as "having origins in any of the black racial groups of Africa."
sentence_501: Other federal offices, such as the [[United_States_Census_Bureau|U.S.
sentence_502: Census Bureau]], adhere to the [[Office_of_Management_and_Budget|Office of Management and Budget]] standards on race in their data collection and tabulation efforts.
sentence_503: In preparation for the [[2010_United_States_Census|2010 U.S. Census]], a marketing and outreach plan called 2010 Census Integrated Communications Campaign Plan (ICC) recognized and defined African Americans as black people born in the United States.
sentence_504: From the ICC perspective, African Americans are one of three groups of black people in the United States.
sentence_505: The ICC plan was to reach the three groups by acknowledging that each group has its own sense of community that is based on geography and ethnicity.
sentence_506: The best way to market the census process toward any of the three groups is to reach them through their own unique communication channels and not treat the entire black population of the U.S. as though they are all African Americans with a single ethnic and geographical background.
sentence_507: The [[Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation|Federal Bureau of Investigation]] of the [[United_States_Department_of_Justice|U.S.
