sentence_4: Athena or Athene, often given the epithet Pallas, is an [[Ancient_Greek_religion|ancient Greek goddess]] associated with wisdom, handicraft, and warfare who was later syncretized with the [[Roman_goddess|Roman goddess]] [[Minerva|Minerva]].
sentence_5: Athena was regarded as the patron and protectress of various cities across Greece, particularly the city of [[Athens|Athens]], from which she most likely received her name.
sentence_6: She's usually shown in art wearing a helmet and holding a spear.
sentence_7: Her major symbols include [[Owl_of_Athena|owls]], [[Olive_trees|olive trees]], [[Snake|snakes]], and the [[Gorgoneion|Gorgoneion]].
sentence_8: From her origin as an Aegean [[Tutelary_deity|palace goddess]], Athena was closely associated with the city.
sentence_9: She was known as Polias and Poliouchos (both derived from [[Polis|polis]], meaning "city-state"), and her temples were usually located atop the fortified [[Acropolis|acropolis]] in the central part of the city.
sentence_10: The [[Parthenon|Parthenon]] on the [[Athenian_Acropolis|Athenian Acropolis]] is dedicated to her, along with numerous other temples and monuments.
sentence_11: As the patron of craft and weaving, Athena was known as Ergane.
sentence_12: She's also a [[Women_in_ancient_warfare|warrior goddess]], and was believed to lead soldiers into battle as [[Athena_Promachos|Athena Promachos]].
sentence_13: Her main festival in Athens was the Panathenaia, which was celebrated during the month of [[Attic_calendar|Hekatombaion]] in midsummer and was the most important festival on the Athenian calendar.
sentence_14: In [[Greek_mythology|Greek mythology]], Athena was believed to have been born from the forehead of her father [[Zeus|Zeus]].
sentence_15: In the [[Founding_myth|founding myth]] of Athens, Athena bested [[Poseidon|Poseidon]] in a competition over patronage of the city by creating the first olive tree.
sentence_16: She's known as [[Athena_Parthenos|Athena Parthenos]] "Athena the Virgin," but in one archaic [[Attica|Attic]] myth, the god [[Hephaestus|Hephaestus]] tried and failed to rape her, resulting in [[Gaia|Gaia]] giving birth to [[Erichthonius_of_Athens|Erichthonius]], an important Athenian founding hero.
sentence_17: Athena was the patron goddess of heroic endeavor; she was believed to have aided the heroes [[Perseus|Perseus]], [[Heracles|Heracles]], [[Bellerophon|Bellerophon]], and [[Jason|Jason]].
sentence_18: Along with [[Aphrodite|Aphrodite]] and [[Hera|Hera]], Athena was one of the three goddesses [[Judgement_of_Paris|whose feud]] resulted in the beginning of the [[Trojan_War|Trojan War]].
sentence_19: She plays an active role in the [[Iliad|Iliad]], in which she assists the [[Achaeans_(Homer)|Achaeans]] and, in the [[Odyssey|Odyssey]], she is the divine counselor to [[Odysseus|Odysseus]].
sentence_20: In the later writings of the Roman poet [[Ovid|Ovid]], Athena was said to have competed against the mortal Arachne in a weaving competition, afterwards transforming Arachne into the first spider; Ovid also describes how she transformed [[Medusa|Medusa]] into a [[Gorgon|Gorgon]] after witnessing her being raped by Poseidon in her temple.
sentence_21: Since the [[Renaissance|Renaissance]], Athena has become an international symbol of wisdom, the arts, and [[Classics|classical learning]].
sentence_22: Western artists and [[Allegorists|allegorists]] have often used Athena as a symbol of [[Freedom|freedom]] and [[Democracy|democracy]].
sentence_23: Athena is associated with the city of [[Athens|Athens]].
sentence_24: The name of the city in ancient Greek is Ἀθῆναι (Athȇnai), a plural [[Toponym|toponym]], designating the place where—according to myth—she presided over the Athenai, a sisterhood devoted to her worship.
sentence_25: In ancient times, scholars argued whether Athena was named after Athens or Athens after Athena.
sentence_26: Now scholars generally agree that the goddess takes her name from the city; the ending -ene is common in names of locations, but rare for personal names.
sentence_27: Testimonies from different cities in [[Ancient_Greece|ancient Greece]] attest that similar [[City_goddess|city goddesses]] were worshipped in other cities and, like Athena, took their names from the cities where they were worshipped.
sentence_28: For example, in [[Mycenae|Mycenae]] there was a goddess called Mykene, whose sisterhood was known as Mykenai, whereas at [[Thebes_(Greece)|Thebes]] an analogous deity was called Thebe, and the city was known under the plural form Thebai (or Thebes, in English, where the 's' is the plural formation).
sentence_29: The name Athenai is likely of [[Pre-Greek|Pre-Greek]] origin because it contains the presumably Pre-Greek morpheme *-ān-.
sentence_30: In his dialogue [[Cratylus_(dialogue)|Cratylus]], the ancient Greek philosopher [[Plato|Plato]] (428–347 BC) gives some rather imaginative etymologies of Athena's name, based on the theories of the ancient Athenians and his own etymological speculations:
sentence_31: Thus, Plato believed that Athena's name was derived from Greek Ἀθεονόα, Atheonóa—which the later Greeks rationalised as from the deity's (θεός, theós) mind (νοῦς, noũs).
sentence_32: The second-century AD orator [[Aelius_Aristides|Aelius Aristides]] attempted to derive natural symbols from the etymological roots of Athena's names to be aether, air, earth, and moon.
sentence_33: Athena was originally the [[Aegean_civilization|Aegean]] goddess of the palace, who presided over household crafts and protected the king.
sentence_34: A single Mycenaean Greek inscription 𐀀𐀲𐀙𐀡𐀴𐀛𐀊 a-ta-na po-ti-ni-ja /Athana potnia/ appears at [[Knossos|Knossos]] in the [[Linear_B|Linear B]] tablets from the Late Minoan II-era "Room of the Chariot Tablets"; these comprise the earliest Linear B archive anywhere.
sentence_35: Although Athana potnia is often translated as "Mistress Athena", it could also mean "the [[Potnia|Potnia]] of Athana", or the Lady of Athens.
sentence_36: However, any connection to the city of Athens in the Knossos inscription is uncertain.
sentence_37: A sign series a-ta-no-dju-wa-ja appears in the still undeciphered corpus of [[Linear_A|Linear A]] tablets, written in the unclassified Minoan language.
sentence_38: This could be connected with the Linear B Mycenaean expressions a-ta-na po-ti-ni-ja and di-u-ja or di-wi-ja (Diwia, "of Zeus" or, possibly, related to a [[List_of_Mycenaean_deities#Goddesses|homonymous goddess]]), resulting in a translation "Athena of Zeus" or "divine Athena".
sentence_39: Similarly, in the Greek mythology and epic tradition, Athena figures as a daughter of Zeus (Διός θυγάτηρ; cfr. [[Dyeus|Dyeus]]).
sentence_40: However, the inscription quoted seems to be very similar to "a-ta-nū-tī wa-ya", quoted as [[Kato_Syme|SY]] Za 1 by Jan Best.
sentence_41: Best translates the initial a-ta-nū-tī, which is recurrent in line beginnings, as "I have given".
sentence_42: A [[Mycenea|Mycenean]] fresco depicts two women extending their hands towards a central figure, who is covered by an enormous figure-eight shield; this may depict the warrior-goddess with her [[Palladium_(classical_antiquity)|palladion]], or her palladion in an aniconic representation.
sentence_43: In the "[[List_of_Aegean_frescos|Procession Fresco]]" at [[Knossos|Knossos]], which was reconstructed by the Mycenaeans, two rows of figures carrying vessels seem to meet in front of a central figure, which is probably the Minoan precursor to Athena.
sentence_44: The early twentieth-century scholar [[Martin_P._Nilsson|Martin Persson Nilsson]] argued that the [[Minoan_snake_goddess_figurines|Minoan snake goddess figurines]] are early representations of Athena.
sentence_45: Nilsson and others have claimed that, in early times, Athena was either an [[Owl|owl]] herself or a [[Bird_goddess|bird goddess]] in general.
sentence_46: In the third book of the [[Odyssey|Odyssey]], she takes the form of a [[Sea_eagle_(bird)|sea-eagle]].
sentence_47: Proponents of this view argue that she dropped her prophylactic owl-mask before she lost her wings.
sentence_48: "Athena, by the time she appears in art," [[Jane_Ellen_Harrison|Jane Ellen Harrison]] remarks, "has completely shed her animal form, has reduced the shapes she once wore of snake and bird to attributes, but occasionally in [[Black_figure_pottery|black-figure vase-paintings]] she still appears with wings."
sentence_49: It is generally agreed that the cult of Athena preserves some aspects of the [[Proto-Indo-European_religion#Societal_deities|Proto-Indo-European transfunctional goddess]].
sentence_50: The cult of Athena may have also been influenced by those of Near Eastern warrior goddesses such as the [[East_Semitic|East Semitic]] [[Ishtar|Ishtar]] and the [[Ugarit|Ugaritic]] [[Anat|Anat]], both of whom were often portrayed bearing arms.
sentence_51: Classical scholar Charles Penglase notes that Athena resembles [[Inanna|Inanna]] in her role as a "terrifying warrior goddess" and that both goddesses were closely linked with creation.
sentence_52: Athena's birth from the head of Zeus may be derived from the earlier Sumerian myth of Inanna's descent into and return from the [[Ancient_Mesopotamian_Underworld|Underworld]].
sentence_53: Plato notes that the citizens of [[Sais|Sais]] in Egypt worshipped a goddess known as Neith, whom he identifies with Athena.
sentence_54: Neith was the ancient Egyptian goddess of war and hunting, who was also associated with weaving; her worship began during the Egyptian Pre-Dynastic period.
sentence_55: In Greek mythology, Athena was reported to have visited mythological sites in North Africa, including Libya's [[Triton_(mythology)|Triton River]] and the [[Phlegra_(mythology)|Phlegraean plain]].
sentence_56: Based on these similarities, the [[Sinologist|Sinologist]] [[Martin_Bernal|Martin Bernal]] created the "[[Black_Athena|Black Athena]]" hypothesis, which claimed that Neith was brought to Greece from Egypt, along with "an enormous number of features of civilization and culture in the third and second millennia".
sentence_57: The "Black Athena" hypothesis stirred up widespread controversy near the end of the twentieth century, but it has now been widely rejected by modern scholars.
sentence_58: In her aspect of Athena Polias, Athena was venerated as the goddess of the city and the protectress of the citadel.
sentence_59: In Athens, the [[Plynteria|Plynteria]], or "Feast of the Bath", was observed every year at the end of the month of Thargelion.
sentence_60: The festival lasted for five days.
sentence_61: During this period, the priestesses of Athena, or plyntrídes, performed a cleansing ritual within the [[Erechtheion|Erechtheion]], a sanctuary devoted to Athena and Poseidon.
sentence_62: Here Athena's statue was undressed, her clothes washed, and body purified.
sentence_63: Athena was worshipped at festivals such as [[Chalceia|Chalceia]] as Athena Ergane, the patroness of various crafts, especially [[Weaving|weaving]].
sentence_64: She was also the patron of metalworkers and was believed to aid in the forging of armor and weapons.
sentence_65: During the late fifth century BC, the role of goddess of philosophy became a major aspect of Athena's [[Cult_(religious_practice)|cult]].
sentence_66: As [[Athena_Promachos|Athena Promachos]], she was believed to lead soldiers into battle.
sentence_67: Athena represented the disciplined, strategic side of war, in contrast to her brother [[Ares|Ares]], the patron of violence, bloodlust, and slaughter—"the raw force of war".
sentence_68: Athena was believed to only support those fighting for a just cause and was thought to view war primarily as a means to resolve conflict.
sentence_69: The Greeks regarded Athena with much higher esteem than Ares.
sentence_70: Athena was especially worshipped in this role during the festivals of the Panathenaea and [[Pamboeotia|Pamboeotia]], both of which prominently featured displays of athletic and military prowess.
sentence_71: As the patroness of heroes and warriors, Athena was believed to favor those who used cunning and intelligence rather than brute strength.
sentence_72: In her aspect as a warrior maiden, Athena was known as [[Athena_Parthenos|Parthenos]] ( "virgin"), because, like her fellow goddesses [[Artemis|Artemis]] and [[Hestia|Hestia]], she was believed to remain perpetually a virgin.
sentence_73: Athena's most famous temple, the [[Parthenon|Parthenon]] on the [[Athenian_Acropolis|Athenian Acropolis]], takes its name from this title.
sentence_74: According to [[Károly_Kerényi|Karl Kerényi]], a scholar of Greek mythology, the name Parthenos is not merely an observation of Athena's virginity, but also a recognition of her role as enforcer of rules of sexual modesty and ritual mystery.
sentence_75: Even beyond recognition, the Athenians allotted the goddess value based on this pureness of virginity, which they upheld as a rudiment of female behavior.
sentence_76: Kerényi's study and theory of Athena explains her virginal epithet as a result of her relationship to her father Zeus and a vital, cohesive piece of her character throughout the ages.
sentence_77: This role is expressed in a number of stories about Athena.
sentence_78: [[Marinus_of_Neapolis|Marinus of Neapolis]] reports that when Christians removed the statue of the goddess from the [[Parthenon|Parthenon]], a beautiful woman appeared in a dream to [[Proclus|Proclus]], a devotee of Athena, and announced that the "Athenian Lady" wished to dwell with him.
sentence_79: Athena was not only the patron goddess of Athens, but also other cities, including [[Argos,_Peloponnese|Argos]], [[Sparta|Sparta]], [[Gortyn|Gortyn]], [[Lindos|Lindos]], and [[Larisa|Larisa]].
sentence_80: The various cults of Athena were all branches of her panhellenic cult and often proctored various initiation rites of Grecian youth, such as the passage into citizenship by young men or the passage of young women into marriage.
sentence_81: These cults were portals of a uniform socialization, even beyond mainland Greece.
sentence_82: Athena was frequently equated with [[Aphaea|Aphaea]], a local goddess of the island of [[Aegina|Aegina]], originally from [[Crete|Crete]] and also associated with [[Artemis|Artemis]] and the nymph [[Britomartis|Britomartis]].
sentence_83: In [[Arcadia_(ancient_region)|Arcadia]], she was assimilated with the ancient goddess Alea and worshiped as [[Athena_Alea|Athena Alea]].
sentence_84: Sanctuaries dedicated to Athena Alea were located in the [[Laconia|Laconian]] towns of [[Mantineia|Mantineia]] and [[Tegea|Tegea]].
sentence_85: The temple of Athena Alea in Tegea was an important religious center of ancient Greece.
sentence_86: The geographer [[Pausanias_(geographer)|Pausanias]] was informed that the temenos had been founded by [[Aleus|Aleus]].
sentence_87: Athena had a major temple on the [[Sparta#Archaeology_of_the_classical_period|Spartan Acropolis]], where she was venerated as Poliouchos and Khalkíoikos ("of the Brazen House", often [[Latin|latinized]] as Chalcioecus).
sentence_88: This epithet may refer to the fact that cult statue held there may have been made of bronze, that the walls of the temple itself may have been made of bronze, or that Athena was the patron of metal-workers.
sentence_89: Bells made of terracotta and bronze were used in Sparta as part of Athena's cult.
sentence_90: An [[Ionic_order|Ionic-style]] temple to Athena Polias was built at [[Priene|Priene]] in the fourth century BC.
sentence_91: It was designed by [[Pythius_of_Priene|Pytheos of Priene]], the same architect who designed the [[Mausoleum_at_Halicarnassus|Mausoleum at Halicarnassus]].
sentence_92: The temple was dedicated by [[Alexander_the_Great|Alexander the Great]] and [[Priene_Inscription|an inscription from the temple]] declaring his dedication is now held in the [[British_Museum|British Museum]].
sentence_93: See also: :Category:Epithets of Athena
sentence_94: Athena was known as Atrytone (Άτρυτώνη "the Unwearying"), Parthenos (Παρθένος "Virgin"), and Promachos (Πρόμαχος "she who fights in front").
sentence_95: The epithet Polias (Πολιάς "of the city"), refers to Athena's role as protectress of the city.
sentence_96: The epithet Ergane (Εργάνη "the Industrious") pointed her out as the patron of craftsmen and artisans.
sentence_97: Burkert notes that the Athenians sometimes simply called Athena "the Goddess", hē theós (ἡ θεός), certainly an ancient title.
sentence_98: After serving as the judge at the trial of [[Orestes|Orestes]] in which he was acquitted of having murdered his mother [[Clytemnestra|Clytemnestra]], Athena won the epithet Areia (Αρεία).
sentence_99: Athena was sometimes given the epithet Hippia (Ἵππια "of the horses", "equestrian"), referring to her invention of the [[Bit_(horse)|bit]], bridle, [[Chariot|chariot]], and [[Wagon|wagon]].
sentence_100: The Greek geographer [[Pausanias_(geographer)|Pausanias]] mentions in his Guide to Greece that the temple of Athena Chalinitis ("the bridler") in Corinth was located near the tomb of [[Medea|Medea]]'s children.
sentence_101: Other epithets include [[Ageleia|Ageleia]], [[Itonia|Itonia]] and Aethyia, under which she was worshiped in [[Megara|Megara]].
sentence_102: The word aíthyia (αἴθυια) signifies a "diver", also some diving bird species (possibly the [[Shearwater|shearwater]]) and figuratively, a "ship", so the name must reference Athena teaching the art of shipbuilding or navigation.
sentence_103: In a temple at Phrixa in [[Elis|Elis]], reportedly built by [[Clymenus|Clymenus]], she was known as Cydonia (Κυδωνία).
sentence_104: The Greek biographer [[Plutarch|Plutarch]] (AD 46–120) refers to an instance during the Parthenon's construction of her being called Athena [[Hygieia|Hygieia]] (Ὑγίεια, i. e. personified "Health") after inspiring a physician to a successful course of treatment.
sentence_105: In [[Homer|Homer]]'s [[Epic_poetry|epic works]], Athena's most common [[Epithets_in_Homer|epithet]] is Glaukopis (γλαυκῶπις), which usually is translated as, "bright-eyed" or "with gleaming eyes".
sentence_106: The word is a combination of glaukós (γλαυκός, meaning "gleaming, silvery", and later, "bluish-green" or "gray") and ṓps (ὤψ, "eye, face").
sentence_107: The word glaúx (γλαύξ, "little owl") is from the same root, presumably according to some, because of the bird's own distinctive eyes.
sentence_108: Athena was clearly associated with the owl from very early on; in archaic images, she is frequently depicted with an [[Owl_of_Athena|owl]] perched on her hand.
sentence_109: Through its association with Athena, the owl evolved into the national mascot of the Athenians and eventually became a symbol of wisdom.
sentence_110: In the [[Iliad|Iliad]] (4.514), the [[Odyssey|Odyssey]] (3.378), the [[Homeric_Hymns|Homeric Hymns]], and in [[Hesiod|Hesiod]]'s [[Theogony|Theogony]], Athena is also given the curious epithet Tritogeneia (Τριτογένεια), whose significance remains unclear.
sentence_111: It could mean various things, including "Triton-born", perhaps indicating that the [[Triton_(mythology)|homonymous sea-deity]] was her parent according to some early myths.
sentence_112: One myth relates the foster father relationship of this Triton towards the half-orphan Athena, whom he raised alongside his own daughter [[Pallas_(daughter_of_Triton)|Pallas]].
sentence_113: Kerényi suggests that "Tritogeneia did not mean that she came into the world on any particular river or lake, but that she was born of the water itself; for the name Triton seems to be associated with water generally."
sentence_114: In [[Ovid|Ovid]]'s [[Metamorphoses|Metamorphoses]], Athena is occasionally referred to as "Tritonia".
sentence_115: Another possible meaning may be "triple-born" or "third-born", which may refer to a triad or to her status as the third daughter of Zeus or the fact she was born from Metis, Zeus, and herself; various legends list her as being the first child after Artemis and Apollo, though other legends identify her as Zeus' first child.
sentence_116: Several scholars have suggested a connection to the [[Rigveda|Rigvedic]] god [[Trita|Trita]], who was sometimes grouped in a body of three mythological poets.
sentence_117: Michael Janda has connected the myth of Trita to the scene in the [[Iliad|Iliad]] in which the "three brothers" Zeus, Poseidon, and Hades divide the world between them, receiving the "broad sky", the sea, and the underworld respectively.
sentence_118: Janda further connects the myth of Athena being born of the head (i. e. the uppermost part) of Zeus, understanding Trito- (which perhaps originally meant "the third") as another word for "the sky".
sentence_119: In Janda's analysis of Indo-European mythology, this heavenly sphere is also associated with the mythological body of water surrounding the inhabited world (cfr. Triton's mother, [[Amphitrite|Amphitrite]]).
sentence_120: Yet another possible meaning is mentioned in [[Diogenes_Laertius|Diogenes Laertius]]' biography of [[Democritus|Democritus]], that Athena was called "Tritogeneia" because three things, on which all mortal life depends, come from her.
sentence_121: She was the daughter of Zeus, produced without a mother, so that she emerged full-grown from his forehead.
sentence_122: There was an alternative story that Zeus swallowed Metis, the goddess of counsel, while she was pregnant with Athena, so that Athena finally emerged from Zeus.
sentence_123: Being the favourite child of Zeus, she had great power.
sentence_124: In the classical Olympian pantheon, Athena was regarded as the favorite daughter of Zeus, born fully armed from his forehead.
sentence_125: The story of her birth comes in several versions.
sentence_126: The earliest mention is in Book V of the Iliad, when Ares accuses Zeus of being biased in favor of Athena because "autos egeinao" (literally "you fathered her", but probably intended as "you gave birth to her").
sentence_127: She was essentially urban and civilized, the antithesis in many respects of Artemis, goddess of the outdoors.
sentence_128: Athena was probably a pre-Hellenic goddess and was later taken over by the Greeks.
sentence_129: In the version recounted by [[Hesiod|Hesiod]] in his [[Theogony|Theogony]], Zeus married the goddess [[Metis_(mythology)|Metis]], who is described as the "wisest among gods and mortal men", and engaged in sexual intercourse with her.
sentence_130: After learning that Metis was pregnant, however, he became afraid that the unborn offspring would try to overthrow him, because Gaia and [[Ouranos|Ouranos]] had prophesied that Metis would bear children wiser than their father.
sentence_131: In order to prevent this, Zeus tricked Metis into letting him swallow her, but it was too late because Metis had already conceived.
sentence_132: A later account of the story from the [[Bibliotheca_(Pseudo-Apollodorus)|Bibliotheca]] of Pseudo-Apollodorus, written in the second century AD, makes Metis Zeus's unwilling sexual partner, rather than his wife.
sentence_133: According to this version of the story, Metis transformed into many different shapes in effort to escape Zeus, but Zeus successfully raped her and swallowed her.
sentence_134: After swallowing Metis, Zeus took six more wives in succession until he married his seventh and present wife, [[Hera|Hera]].
sentence_135: Then Zeus experienced an enormous headache.
sentence_136: He was in such pain that he ordered someone (either [[Prometheus|Prometheus]], [[Hephaestus|Hephaestus]], [[Hermes|Hermes]], [[Ares|Ares]], or Palaemon, depending on the sources examined) to cleave his head open with the labrys, the double-headed [[Minoan_civilization|Minoan]] [[Axe|axe]].
sentence_137: Athena leaped from Zeus's head, fully grown and armed.
sentence_138: The "First Homeric Hymn to Athena" states in lines 9–16 that the gods were awestruck by Athena's appearance and even [[Helios|Helios]], the god of the sun, stopped his chariot in the sky.
sentence_139: Pindar, in his "Seventh Olympian Ode", states that she "cried aloud with a mighty shout" and that "the Sky and mother Earth shuddered before her."
sentence_140: Hesiod states that Hera was so annoyed at Zeus for having given birth to a child on his own that she conceived and bore [[Hephaestus|Hephaestus]] by [[Parthenogenesis|herself]], but in Imagines (trans.
sentence_141: Fairbanks), the third-century AD Greek rhetorician [[Philostratus_the_Elder|Philostratus the Elder]] writes that Hera "rejoices" at Athena's birth "as though Athena were her daughter also."
sentence_142: The second-century AD Christian apologist [[Justin_Martyr|Justin Martyr]] takes issue with those pagans who erect at springs images of [[Persephone|Kore]], whom he interprets as Athena: "They said that Athena was the daughter of Zeus not from intercourse, but when the god had in mind the making of a world through a word ([[Logos|logos]]) his first thought was Athena."
sentence_143: According to a version of the story in a scholium on the Iliad (found nowhere else), when Zeus swallowed [[Metis_(mythology)|Metis]], she was pregnant with Athena by the [[Cyclopes|Cyclops]] Brontes.
sentence_144: The [[Etymologicum_Magnum|Etymologicum Magnum]] instead deems Athena the daughter of the [[Dactyl_(mythology)|Daktyl]] [[Itonus|Itonos]].
sentence_145: Fragments attributed by the Christian [[Eusebius_of_Caesarea|Eusebius of Caesarea]] to the semi-legendary [[Phoenicia|Phoenician]] historian [[Sanchuniathon|Sanchuniathon]], which Eusebius thought had been written before the [[Trojan_war|Trojan war]], make Athena instead the daughter of [[Cronus|Cronus]], a king of [[Byblos|Byblos]] who visited "the inhabitable world" and bequeathed [[Attica|Attica]] to Athena.
sentence_146: Athena's epithet Pallas is derived either from πάλλω, meaning "to brandish [as a weapon]", or, more likely, from παλλακίς and related words, meaning "youth, young woman".
sentence_147: On this topic, Walter Burkert says "she is the Pallas of Athens, Pallas Athenaie, just as Hera of Argos is Here Argeie."
sentence_148: In later times, after the original meaning of the name had been forgotten, the Greeks invented myths to explain its origin, such as those reported by the Epicurean philosopher [[Philodemus|Philodemus]] and the Bibliotheca of Pseudo-Apollodorus, which claim that Pallas was originally a separate entity, whom Athena had slain in combat.
sentence_149: In one version of the myth, [[Pallas_(daughter_of_Triton)|Pallas]] was the daughter of the sea-god [[Triton_(mythology)|Triton]]; she and Athena were childhood friends, but Athena accidentally killed her during a friendly [[Sparring|sparring]] match.
sentence_150: Distraught over what she had done, Athena took the name Pallas for herself as a sign of her grief.
sentence_151: In another version of the story, [[Pallas_(Giant)|Pallas]] was a [[Giants_(Greek_mythology)|Gigante]]; Athena slew him during the [[Gigantomachy|Gigantomachy]] and flayed off his skin to make her cloak, which she wore as a victory trophy.
sentence_152: In an alternative variation of the same myth, Pallas was instead Athena's father, who attempted to assault his own daughter, causing Athena to kill him and take his skin as a trophy.
sentence_153: The [[Palladium_(classical_antiquity)|palladion]] was a statue of Athena that was said to have stood in her temple on the Trojan Acropolis.
sentence_154: Athena was said to have carved the statue herself in the likeness of her dead friend Pallas.
sentence_155: The statue had special talisman-like properties and it was thought that, as long as it was in the city, Troy could never fall.
sentence_156: When the Greeks captured Troy, [[Cassandra|Cassandra]], the daughter of [[Priam|Priam]], clung to the palladion for protection, but [[Ajax_the_Lesser|Ajax the Lesser]] violently tore her away from it and dragged her over to the other captives.
sentence_157: Athena was infuriated by this violation of her protection.
sentence_158: Although Agamemnon attempted to placate her anger with sacrifices, Athena sent a storm at Cape Kaphereos to destroy almost the entire Greek fleet and scatter all of the surviving ships across the Aegean.
sentence_159: In Homer's Iliad, Athena, as a war goddess, inspired and fought alongside the Greek heroes; her aid was synonymous with military prowess.
sentence_160: Also in the Iliad, Zeus, the chief god, specifically assigned the sphere of war to Ares, the god of war, and Athena.
sentence_161: Athena's moral and military superiority to Ares derived in part from the fact that she represented the intellectual and civilized side of war and the virtues of justice and skill, whereas Ares represented mere blood lust.
sentence_162: Her superiority also derived in part from the vastly greater variety and importance of her functions and from the patriotism of Homer's predecessors, Ares being of foreign origin.
sentence_163: In the Iliad, Athena was the divine form of the heroic, martial ideal: she personified excellence in close combat, victory, and glory.
sentence_164: The qualities that led to victory were found on the aegis, or breastplate, that Athena wore when she went to war: fear, strife, defense, and assault.
sentence_165: Athena appears in Homer's Odyssey as the tutelary deity of Odysseus, and myths from later sources portray her similarly as helper of Perseus and Heracles (Hercules).
sentence_166: As the guardian of the welfare of kings, Athena became the goddess of good counsel, of prudent restraint and practical insight, as well as of war.
sentence_167: In a [[Founding_myth|founding myth]] reported by Pseudo-Apollodorus, Athena competed with [[Poseidon|Poseidon]] for the patronage of Athens.
sentence_168: They agreed that each would give the Athenians one gift and that [[Cecrops_I|Cecrops]], the king of Athens, would determine which gift was better.
sentence_169: Poseidon struck the ground with his [[Trident|trident]] and a salt water spring sprang up; this gave the Athenians access to trade and water.
sentence_170: Athens at its height was a significant sea power, defeating the [[Achaemenid_Empire|Persian]] fleet at the [[Battle_of_Salamis|Battle of Salamis]]—but the water was salty and undrinkable.
sentence_171: In an alternative version of the myth from [[Vergil|Vergil]]'s [[Georgics|Georgics]], Poseidon instead gave the Athenians the first horse.
sentence_172: Athena offered the first domesticated [[Olive_tree|olive tree]].
sentence_173: Cecrops accepted this gift and declared Athena the patron goddess of Athens.
sentence_174: The olive tree brought wood, oil, and food, and became a symbol of Athenian economic prosperity.
sentence_175: [[Robert_Graves|Robert Graves]] was of the opinion that "Poseidon's attempts to take possession of certain cities are political myths", which reflect the conflict between matriarchal and patriarchal religions.
sentence_176: Pseudo-Apollodorus records an archaic legend, which claims that [[Hephaestus|Hephaestus]] once attempted to rape Athena, but she pushed him away, causing him to [[Ejaculate|ejaculate]] on her thigh.
sentence_177: Athena wiped the [[Semen|semen]] off using a tuft of [[Wool|wool]], which she tossed into the dust, impregnating [[Gaia_(mythology)|Gaia]] and causing her to give birth to [[Erichthonius_of_Athens|Erichthonius]].
sentence_178: Athena adopted Erichthonius as her son and raised him.
sentence_179: The Roman mythographer [[Hyginus|Hyginus]] records a similar story in which Hephaestus demanded Zeus to let him marry Athena since he was the one who had smashed open Zeus's skull, allowing Athena to be born.
sentence_180: Zeus agreed to this and Hephaestus and Athena were married, but, when Hephaestus was about to consummate the union, Athena vanished from the bridal bed, causing him to ejaculate on the floor, thus impregnating Gaia with Erichthonius.
sentence_181: The geographer [[Pausanias_(geographer)|Pausanias]] records that Athena placed the infant Erichthonius into a small chest (cista), which she entrusted to the care of the three daughters of [[Cecrops_I|Cecrops]]: [[Herse|Herse]], [[Pandrosos|Pandrosos]], and [[Aglaulus,_daughter_of_Cecrops|Aglauros]] of Athens.
sentence_182: She warned the three sisters not to open the chest, but did not explain to them why or what was in it.
sentence_183: Aglauros, and possibly one of the other sisters, opened the chest.
sentence_184: Differing reports say that they either found that the child itself was a serpent, that it was guarded by a serpent, that it was guarded by two serpents, or that it had the legs of a serpent.
sentence_185: In Pausanias's story, the two sisters were driven mad by the sight of the chest's contents and hurled themselves off the [[Acropolis|Acropolis]], dying instantly, but an Attic vase painting shows them being chased by the serpent off the edge of the cliff instead.
sentence_186: Erichthonius was one of the most important founding heroes of Athens and the legend of the daughters of Cecrops was a cult myth linked to the rituals of the [[Arrhephoria|Arrhephoria]] festival.
sentence_187: Pausanias records that, during the Arrhephoria, two young girls known as the Arrhephoroi, who lived near the temple of Athena Polias, would be given hidden objects by the [[High_Priestess_of_Athena_Polias|priestess of Athena]], which they would carry on their heads down a natural underground passage.
sentence_188: They would leave the objects they had been given at the bottom of the passage and take another set of hidden objects, which they would carry on their heads back up to the temple.
sentence_189: The ritual was performed in the dead of night and no one, not even the priestess, knew what the objects were.
sentence_190: The serpent in the story may be the same one depicted coiled at Athena's feet in Pheidias's famous statue of the Athena Parthenos in the Parthenon.
sentence_191: Many of the surviving sculptures of Athena show this serpent.
sentence_192: Herodotus records that a serpent lived in a crevice on the north side of the summit of the Athenian Acropolis and that the Athenians left a honey cake for it each month as an offering.
sentence_193: On the eve of the [[Second_Persian_invasion_of_Greece|Second Persian invasion of Greece]] in 480 BC, the serpent did not eat the honey cake and the Athenians interpreted it as a sign that Athena herself had abandoned them.
sentence_194: Another version of the myth of the Athenian maidens is told in [[Metamorphoses|Metamorphoses]] by the Roman poet [[Ovid|Ovid]] (43 BC – 17 AD); in this late variant [[Hermes|Hermes]] falls in love with Herse.
sentence_195: Herse, Aglaulus, and Pandrosus go to the temple to offer sacrifices to Athena.
sentence_196: Hermes demands help from Aglaulus to seduce Herse.
sentence_197: Aglaulus demands money in exchange.
sentence_198: Hermes gives her the money the sisters have already offered to Athena.
sentence_199: As punishment for Aglaulus's greed, Athena asks the goddess [[Invidia|Envy]] to make Aglaulus jealous of Herse.
sentence_200: When Hermes arrives to seduce Herse, Aglaulus stands in his way instead of helping him as she had agreed.
sentence_201: He turns her to stone.
sentence_202: According to Pseudo-Apollodorus's Bibliotheca, Athena advised [[Argus_(son_of_Arestor)|Argos]], the builder of the [[Argo|Argo]], the ship on which the hero [[Jason|Jason]] and his band of [[Argonauts|Argonauts]] sailed, and aided in the ship's construction.
sentence_203: Pseudo-Apollodorus also records that Athena guided the hero [[Perseus_(mythology)|Perseus]] in his quest to behead [[Medusa_(mythology)|Medusa]].
sentence_204: She and [[Hermes|Hermes]], the god of travelers, appeared to Perseus after he set off on his quest and gifted him with tools he would need to kill the Gorgon.
sentence_205: Athena gave Perseus a polished bronze shield to view Medusa's reflection rather than looking at her directly and thereby avoid being turned to stone.
sentence_206: Hermes gave him an [[Adamant|adamantine]] [[Scythe|scythe]] to cut off Medusa's head.
sentence_207: When Perseus swung his blade to behead Medusa, Athena guided it, allowing his scythe to cut it clean off.
sentence_208: According to Pindar's Thirteenth Olympian Ode, Athena helped the hero [[Bellerophon|Bellerophon]] tame the winged horse [[Pegasus|Pegasus]] by giving him a [[Bit_(horse)|bit]].
sentence_209: In [[Ancient_Greek_art|ancient Greek art]], Athena is frequently shown aiding the hero [[Heracles|Heracles]].
sentence_210: She appears in four of the twelve [[Metope|metopes]] on the [[Temple_of_Zeus_at_Olympia|Temple of Zeus at Olympia]] depicting Heracles's [[Labors_of_Heracles|Twelve Labors]], including the first, in which she passively watches him slay the [[Nemean_lion|Nemean lion]], and the tenth, in which she is shown actively helping him hold up the sky.
sentence_211: She is presented as his "stern ally", but also the "gentle... acknowledger of his achievements."
sentence_212: Artistic depictions of Heracles's apotheosis show Athena driving him to Mount Olympus in her chariot and presenting him to Zeus for his deification.
sentence_213: In [[Aeschylus|Aeschylus]]'s tragedy [[Orestes_(play)|Orestes]], Athena intervenes to save [[Orestes|Orestes]] from the wrath of the [[Erinyes|Erinyes]] and presides over his trial for the murder of his mother [[Clytemnestra|Clytemnestra]].
sentence_214: When half the [[Jury|jury]] votes to acquit and the other half votes to convict, Athena casts the deciding vote to acquit Orestes and declares that, from then on, whenever a jury is tied, the defendant shall always be acquitted.
sentence_215: In [[The_Odyssey|The Odyssey]], [[Odysseus|Odysseus]]' cunning and shrewd nature quickly wins Athena's favour.
sentence_216: For the first part of the poem, however, she largely is confined to aiding him only from afar, mainly by implanting thoughts in his head during his journey home from Troy.
sentence_217: Her guiding actions reinforce her role as the "protectress of heroes," or, as mythologian [[Walter_Friedrich_Otto|Walter Friedrich Otto]] dubbed her, the "goddess of nearness," due to her mentoring and motherly probing.
sentence_218: It is not until he washes up on the shore of the island of the [[Phaeacians|Phaeacians]], where [[Nausicaa|Nausicaa]] is washing her clothes that Athena arrives personally to provide more tangible assistance.
sentence_219: She appears in Nausicaa's dreams to ensure that the princess rescues Odysseus and plays a role in his eventual escort to Ithaca.
sentence_220: Athena appears to Odysseus upon his arrival, disguised as a herdsman; she initially lies and tells him that Penelope, his wife, has remarried and that he is believed to be dead, but Odysseus lies back to her, employing skillful prevarications to protect himself.
sentence_221: Impressed by his resolve and shrewdness, she reveals herself and tells him what he needs to know in order to win back his kingdom.
sentence_222: She disguises him as an elderly beggar so that he will not be recognized by the suitors or Penelope, and helps him to defeat the suitors.
sentence_223: Athena also appears to Odysseus's son Telemachus.
sentence_224: Her actions lead him to travel around to Odysseus's comrades and ask about his father.
sentence_225: He hears stories about some of Odysseus's journey.
sentence_226: Athena's push for Telemachos's journey helps him grow into the man role, that his father once held.
sentence_227: She also plays a role in ending the resultant feud against the suitors' relatives.
sentence_228: She instructs [[Laertes|Laertes]] to throw his spear and to kill [[Eupeithes|Eupeithes]], the father of [[Antinous_son_of_Eupeithes|Antinous]].
sentence_229: The [[Gorgoneion|Gorgoneion]] appears to have originated as an [[Apotropaic_magic|apotropaic]] symbol intended to ward off evil.
sentence_230: In a late myth invented to explain the origins of the Gorgon, [[Medusa|Medusa]] is described as having been a young priestess who served in the temple of Athena in Athens.
sentence_231: Poseidon lusted after Medusa, and raped her in the temple of Athena, refusing to allow her vow of chastity to stand in his way.
sentence_232: Upon discovering the desecration of her temple, Athena transformed Medusa into a hideous monster with serpents for hair whose gaze [[Petrifaction_in_mythology_and_fiction|would turn any mortal to stone]].
sentence_233: In his Twelfth Pythian Ode, [[Pindar|Pindar]] recounts the story of how Athena invented the [[Aulos|aulos]], a kind of flute, in imitation of the lamentations of Medusa's sisters, the Gorgons, after she was beheaded by the hero [[Perseus|Perseus]].
sentence_234: According to Pindar, Athena gave the aulos to mortals as a gift.
sentence_235: Later, the comic playwright [[Melanippides|Melanippides of Melos]] (c. 480-430 BC) embellished the story in his comedy Marsyas, claiming that Athena looked in the mirror while she was playing the aulos and saw how blowing into it puffed up her cheeks and made her look silly, so she threw the aulos away and cursed it so that whoever picked it up would meet an awful death.
sentence_236: The aulos was picked up by the satyr [[Marsyas|Marsyas]], who was later killed by Apollo for his [[Hubris|hubris]].
sentence_237: Later, this version of the story became accepted as canonical and the Athenian sculptor [[Myron|Myron]] created a group of bronze sculptures based on it, which was installed before the western front of the Parthenon in around 440 BC.
sentence_238: A myth told by the early third-century BC Hellenistic poet [[Callimachus|Callimachus]] in his Hymn 5 begins with Athena bathing in a spring on [[Mount_Helicon|Mount Helicon]] at midday with one of her favorite companions, the nymph [[Chariclo|Chariclo]].
sentence_239: Chariclo's son Tiresias happened to be hunting on the same mountain and came to the spring searching for water.
sentence_240: He inadvertently saw Athena naked, so she struck him blind to ensure he would never again see what man was not intended to see.
sentence_241: Chariclo intervened on her son's behalf and begged Athena to have mercy.
sentence_242: Athena replied that she could not restore Tiresias's eyesight, so, instead, she gave him the ability to understand the language of the birds and thus foretell the future.
sentence_243: The [[Fable|fable]] of Arachne appears in [[Ovid|Ovid]]'s [[Metamorphoses|Metamorphoses]] (8 AD) (vi.5–54 and 129–145), which is nearly the only extant source for the legend.
sentence_244: The story does not appear to have been well known prior to Ovid's rendition of it and the only earlier reference to it is a brief allusion in [[Virgil|Virgil]]'s [[Georgics|Georgics]], (29 BC) (iv, 246) that does not mention Arachne by name.
sentence_245: According to Ovid, Arachne (whose name means spider in ancient Greek) was the daughter of a famous dyer in [[Tyrian_purple|Tyrian purple]] in Hypaipa of Lydia, and a weaving student of Athena.
sentence_246: She became so conceited of her skill as a weaver that she began claiming that her skill was greater than that of Athena herself.
sentence_247: Athena gave Arachne a chance to redeem herself by assuming the form of an old woman and warning Arachne not to offend the deities.
sentence_248: Arachne scoffed and wished for a weaving contest, so she could prove her skill.
sentence_249: Athena wove the scene of her victory over [[Poseidon|Poseidon]] in the contest for the patronage of Athens.
sentence_250: Athena's tapestry also depicted the 12 Olympian gods and defeat of mythological figures who challenged their authority.
sentence_251: Arachne's tapestry featured twenty-one episodes of the deities' infidelity, including [[Zeus|Zeus]] being unfaithful with [[Leda_(mythology)|Leda]], with [[Europa_(mythical)|Europa]], and with [[Danaë|Danaë]].
sentence_252: It represented the unjust and discrediting behavior of the gods towards mortals.
sentence_253: Athena admitted that Arachne's work was flawless, but was outraged at Arachne's offensive choice of subject, which displayed the failings and transgressions of the deities.
sentence_254: Finally, losing her temper, Athena destroyed Arachne's tapestry and loom, striking it with her shuttle.
sentence_255: Athena then struck Arachne across the face with her staff four times.
sentence_256: Arachne hanged herself in despair, but Athena took pity on her and brought her back from the dead in the form of a spider.
sentence_257: Main article: [[Judgement_of_Paris|Judgement of Paris]]
sentence_258: The myth of the Judgement of Paris is mentioned briefly in the [[Iliad|Iliad]], but is described in depth in an epitome of the [[Cypria|Cypria]], a lost poem of the Epic Cycle, which records that all the gods and goddesses as well as various mortals were invited to the marriage of [[Peleus|Peleus]] and [[Thetis|Thetis]] (the eventual parents of [[Achilles|Achilles]]).
sentence_259: Only [[Eris_(mythology)|Eris]], goddess of discord, was not invited.
sentence_260: She was annoyed at this, so she arrived with a golden apple inscribed with the word καλλίστῃ (kallistēi, "for the fairest"), which she threw among the goddesses.
sentence_261: Aphrodite, Hera, and Athena all claimed to be the fairest, and thus the rightful owner of the apple.
sentence_262: The goddesses chose to place the matter before Zeus, who, not wanting to favor one of the goddesses, put the choice into the hands of Paris, a [[Troy|Trojan]] prince.
sentence_263: After bathing in the spring of [[Mount_Ida|Mount Ida]] where Troy was situated, the goddesses appeared before Paris for his decision.
sentence_264: In the extant ancient depictions of the Judgement of Paris, Aphrodite is only occasionally represented nude, and Athena and Hera are always fully clothed.
sentence_265: Since the [[Renaissance|Renaissance]], however, Western paintings have typically portrayed all three goddesses as completely naked.
sentence_266: All three goddesses were ideally beautiful and Paris could not decide between them, so they resorted to bribes.
sentence_267: Hera tried to bribe Paris with power over all [[Asia|Asia]] and [[Europe|Europe]], and Athena offered fame and glory in battle, but Aphrodite promised Paris that, if he were to choose her as the fairest, she would let him marry the most beautiful woman on earth.
sentence_268: This woman was [[Helen_of_Troy|Helen]], who was already married to King [[Menelaus|Menelaus]] of [[Sparta#Prehistory|Sparta]].
sentence_269: Paris selected Aphrodite and awarded her the apple.
sentence_270: The other two goddesses were enraged and, as a direct result, sided with the Greeks in the [[Trojan_War|Trojan War]].
sentence_271: In Books V–VI of the [[Iliad|Iliad]], Athena aids the hero [[Diomedes|Diomedes]], who, in the absence of Achilles, proves himself to be the most effective Greek warrior.
sentence_272: Several artistic representations from the early sixth century BC may show Athena and Diomedes, including an early sixth-century BC shield band depicting Athena and an unidentified warrior riding on a chariot, a vase painting of a warrior with his charioteer facing Athena, and an inscribed clay plaque showing Diomedes and Athena riding in a chariot.
sentence_273: Numerous passages in the Iliad also mention Athena having previously served as the patron of Diomedes's father [[Tydeus|Tydeus]].
sentence_274: When the Trojan women go to the temple of Athena on the Acropolis to plead her for protection from Diomedes, Athena ignores them.
sentence_275: In Book XXII of the Iliad, while Achilles is chasing [[Hector|Hector]] around the walls of Troy, Athena appears to Hector disguised as his brother [[Deiphobus|Deiphobus]] and persuades him to hold his ground so that they can fight Achilles together.
sentence_276: Then, Hector throws his spear at Achilles and misses, expecting Deiphobus to hand him another, but Athena disappears instead, leaving Hector to face Achilles alone without his spear.
sentence_277: In [[Sophocles|Sophocles]]'s tragedy [[Ajax_(play)|Ajax]], she punishes Odysseus's rival [[Ajax_the_Great|Ajax the Great]], driving him insane and causing him to massacre the Achaeans' cattle, thinking that he is slaughtering the Achaeans themselves.
sentence_278: Even after Odysseus himself expresses pity for Ajax, Athena declares, "To laugh at your enemies - what sweeter laughter can there be than that?"
sentence_279: (lines 78–9).
sentence_280: Ajax later commits [[Suicide|suicide]] as a result of his humiliation.
sentence_281: Athena appears frequently in classical Greek art, including on coins and in paintings on ceramics.
sentence_282: She is especially prominent in works produced in Athens.
sentence_283: In classical depictions, Athena is usually portrayed standing upright, wearing a full-length [[Chiton_(costume)|chiton]].
sentence_284: She is most often represented dressed in armor like a male soldier and wearing a Corinthian helmet raised high atop her forehead.
sentence_285: Her shield bears at its centre the aegis with the head of the gorgon (gorgoneion) in the center and snakes around the edge.
sentence_286: Sometimes she is shown wearing the aegis as a cloak.
sentence_287: As Athena Promachos, she is shown brandishing a spear.
sentence_288: Scenes in which Athena was represented include her birth from the head of Zeus, her battle with the [[Giants_(Greek_mythology)|Gigantes]], the birth of Erichthonius, and the Judgement of Paris.
sentence_289: The [[Mourning_Athena|Mourning Athena]] or Athena Meditating is a famous relief sculpture dating to around 470-460 BC that has been interpreted to represent Athena Polias.
sentence_290: The most famous classical depiction of Athena was the [[Athena_Parthenos|Athena Parthenos]], a now-lost 11.5 m (38 ft) [[Chryselephantine|gold and ivory]] statue of her in the [[Parthenon|Parthenon]] created by the Athenian sculptor Phidias.
sentence_291: Copies reveal that this statue depicted Athena holding her shield in her left hand with [[Nike_(mythology)|Nike]], the winged goddess of victory, standing in her right.
sentence_292: Athena Polias is also represented in a Neo-Attic relief now held in the [[Virginia_Museum_of_Fine_Arts|Virginia Museum of Fine Arts]], which depicts her holding an owl in her hand and wearing her characteristic Corinthian helmet while resting her shield against a nearby [[Herma|herma]].
sentence_293: The Roman goddess Minerva adopted most of Athena's Greek iconographical associations, but was also integrated into the [[Capitoline_Triad|Capitoline Triad]].
sentence_294: Early Christian writers, such as [[Clement_of_Alexandria|Clement of Alexandria]] and [[Julius_Firmicus_Maternus|Firmicus]], denigrated Athena as representative of all the things that were detestable about paganism; they condemned her as "immodest and immoral".
sentence_295: During the Middle Ages, however, many attributes of Athena were given to the [[Virgin_Mary|Virgin Mary]], who, in fourth century portrayals, was often depicted wearing the [[Gorgoneion|Gorgoneion]].
sentence_296: Some even viewed the Virgin Mary as a warrior maiden, much like Athena Parthenos; one anecdote tells that the Virgin Mary once appeared upon the walls of Constantinople when it was under siege by the Avars, clutching a spear and urging the people to fight.
sentence_297: During the Middle Ages, Athena became widely used as a Christian symbol and allegory, and she appeared on the family crests of certain noble houses.
sentence_298: During the Renaissance, Athena donned the mantle of patron of the arts and human endeavor; allegorical paintings involving Athena were a favorite of the Italian Renaissance painters.
sentence_299: In [[Sandro_Botticelli|Sandro Botticelli]]'s painting [[Pallas_and_the_Centaur|Pallas and the Centaur]], probably painted sometime in the 1480s, Athena is the personification of chastity, who is shown grasping the forelock of a centaur, who represents lust.
sentence_300: [[Andrea_Mantegna|Andrea Mantegna]]'s 1502 painting [[Triumph_of_the_Virtues_(Mantegna)|Minerva Expelling the Vices from the Garden of Virtue]] uses Athena as the personification of Graeco-Roman learning chasing the vices of medievalism from the garden of modern scholarship.
sentence_301: Athena is also used as the personification of wisdom in [[Bartholomeus_Spranger|Bartholomeus Spranger]]'s 1591 painting The Triumph of Wisdom or Minerva Victorious over Ignorance.
sentence_302: During the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, Athena was used as a symbol for female rulers.
sentence_303: In his book A Revelation of the True Minerva (1582), [[Thomas_Blennerhassett|Thomas Blennerhassett]] portrays [[Elizabeth_I_of_England|Queen Elizabeth I of England]] as a "new Minerva" and "the greatest goddesse nowe on earth".
sentence_304: A series of paintings by [[Peter_Paul_Rubens|Peter Paul Rubens]] depict Athena as Marie de' Medici's patron and mentor; the final painting in the series goes even further and shows Marie de' Medici with Athena's iconography, as the mortal incarnation of the goddess herself.
sentence_305: The German sculptor [[Jean-Pierre-Antoine_Tassaert|Jean-Pierre-Antoine Tassaert]] later portrayed [[Catherine_II_of_Russia|Catherine II of Russia]] as Athena in a marble bust in 1774.
sentence_306: During the [[French_Revolution|French Revolution]], statues of pagan gods were torn down all throughout France, but statues of Athena were not.
sentence_307: Instead, Athena was transformed into the personification of freedom and the republic and a statue of the goddess stood in the center of the [[Place_de_la_Revolution|Place de la Revolution]] in Paris.
sentence_308: In the years following the Revolution, artistic representations of Athena proliferated.
sentence_309: A statue of Athena stands directly in front of the [[Austrian_Parliament_Building|Austrian Parliament Building]] in [[Vienna|Vienna]], and depictions of Athena have influenced other symbols of Western freedom, including the [[Statue_of_Liberty|Statue of Liberty]] and [[Britannia|Britannia]].
sentence_310: For over a century, [[Parthenon_(Nashville)|a full-scale replica of the Parthenon]] has stood in [[Nashville,_Tennessee|Nashville, Tennessee]].
sentence_311: In 1990, the curators added a gilded forty-two-foot (12.5 m) tall [[Athena_Parthenos#Replica_at_Nashville|replica of Phidias's Athena Parthenos]], built from concrete and fiberglass.
sentence_312: The state [[Seal_of_California|seal of California]] bears the image of Athena kneeling next to a brown grizzly bear.
sentence_313: Athena has occasionally appeared on modern coins, as she did on the ancient Athenian [[Drachma|drachma]].
sentence_314: Her head appears on the $50 1915-S [[Panama–Pacific_commemorative_coins|Panama-Pacific commemorative coin]].
sentence_315: One of [[Sigmund_Freud|Sigmund Freud]]'s most treasured possessions was a small, bronze sculpture of Athena, which sat on his desk.
sentence_316: Freud once described Athena as "a woman who is unapproachable and repels all sexual desires - since she displays the terrifying genitals of the Mother."
sentence_317: [[Feminism|Feminist]] views on Athena are sharply divided; some feminists regard her as a symbol of female empowerment, while others regard her as "the ultimate [[Patriarchy|patriarchal]] sell out... who uses her powers to promote and advance men rather than others of her sex."
sentence_318: In contemporary [[Wicca|Wicca]], Athena is venerated as an aspect of the [[Wiccan_views_of_divinity|Goddess]] and some Wiccans believe that she may bestow the "Owl Gift" ("the ability to write and communicate clearly") upon her worshippers.
sentence_319: Due to her status as one of the twelve Olympians, Athena is a major deity in [[Hellenism_(religion)|Hellenismos]], a [[Modern_Paganism|Neopagan]] religion which seeks to authentically revive and recreate the religion of ancient Greece in the modern world.
sentence_320: Athena is a natural patron of universities: At [[Bryn_Mawr_College|Bryn Mawr College]] in Pennsylvania a statue of Athena (a replica of the original bronze one in the arts and archaeology library) resides in the Great Hall.
sentence_321: It is traditional at exam time for students to leave offerings to the goddess with a note asking for good luck, or to repent for accidentally breaking any of the college's numerous other traditions.
sentence_322: Pallas Athena is the tutelary goddess of the international social fraternity [[Phi_Delta_Theta|Phi Delta Theta]].
sentence_323: Her owl is also a symbol of the fraternity.

title: Asterales
sentence_0: Asterales [[English|/æstəˈreɪliːz/]] is an [[Order_(biology)|order]] of [[Dicotyledon|dicotyledonous]] [[Flowering_plant|flowering plants]] that includes the large [[Family_(biology)|family]] [[Asteraceae|Asteraceae]] (or Compositae) known for composite flowers made of [[Floret#floret|florets]], and ten families related to the Asteraceae.
sentence_1: The order is a [[Cosmopolitan_distribution|cosmopolite]] (plants found throughout most of the world including desert and frigid zones), and includes mostly [[Herbaceous_plant|herbaceous]] species, although a small number of trees (such as the [[Lobelia_deckenii|giant Lobelia]] and the [[Dendrosenecio|giant Senecio]]) and shrubs are also present.
sentence_2: Asterales are organisms that seem to have evolved from one common ancestor.
sentence_3: Asterales share characteristics on [[Morphology_(biology)|morphological]] and biochemical levels.
sentence_4: [[Synapomorphies|Synapomorphies]] (a character that is shared by two or more groups through evolutionary development) include the presence in the plants of [[Oligosaccharide|oligosaccharide]] [[Inulin|inulin]], a nutrient storage molecule used instead of [[Starch|starch]]; and unique [[Stamen|stamen]] morphology.
sentence_5: The stamens are usually found around the [[Gynoecium|style]], either aggregated densely or fused into a tube, probably an [[Adaptation|adaptation]] in association with the plunger (brush; or secondary) [[Pollination|pollination]] that is common among the families of the order, wherein pollen is collected and stored on the length of the pistil.
sentence_6: The name and order Asterales is botanically venerable, dating back to at least 1926 in the [[Hutchinson_system|Hutchinson system of plant taxonomy]] when it contained only five families, of which only two are retained in the APG III classification.
sentence_7: Under the [[Cronquist_system|Cronquist system]] of taxonomic classification of flowering plants, [[Asteraceae|Asteraceae]] was the only family in the group, but newer systems (such as [[APG_II_system|APG II]] and [[APG_III_system|APG III]]) have expanded it to 11.
sentence_8: In the classification system of [[Rolf_Dahlgren|Dahlgren]] the Asterales were in the superorder Asteriflorae (also called Asteranae).
sentence_9: The order Asterales currently includes 11 families, the largest of which are the [[Asteraceae|Asteraceae]], with about 25,000 species, and the [[Campanulaceae|Campanulaceae]] ("bellflowers"), with about 2,000 species.
sentence_10: The remaining families count together for less than 1500 species.
sentence_11: The two large families are cosmopolitan, with many of their species found in the Northern Hemisphere, and the smaller families are usually confined to Australia and the adjacent areas, or sometimes South America.
sentence_12: Only the Asteraceae have composite flower heads; the other families do not, but share other characteristics such as storage of inulin that define the 11 families as more closely related to each other than to other plant families or orders such as the [[Rosids|rosids]].
sentence_13: The phylogenetic tree according to APG III for the Campanulid clade is as below.
sentence_14: The core Asterales are Stylidiaceae (six [[Genus|genera]]), APA [[Clade|clade]] (Alseuosmiaceae, Phellinaceae and Argophyllaceae, together 7 genera), MGCA clade (Menyanthaceae, Goodeniaceae, Calyceraceae, in total twenty genera), and Asteraceae (about sixteen hundred genera).
sentence_15: Other Asterales are Rousseaceae (four genera), Campanulaceae (eighty four genera) and Pentaphragmataceae (one genus).
sentence_16: All Asterales families are represented in the Southern Hemisphere; however, Asteraceae and Campanulaceae are cosmopolitan and Menyanthaceae nearly so.
sentence_17: Although most extant species of Asteraceae are herbaceous, the examination of the basal members in the family suggests that the common ancestor of the family was an arborescent plant, a tree or shrub, perhaps adapted to dry conditions, radiating from South America.
sentence_18: Less can be said about the Asterales themselves with certainty, although since several families in Asterales contain trees, the ancestral member is most likely to have been a tree or shrub.
sentence_19: Because all clades are represented in the southern hemisphere but many not in the northern hemisphere, it is natural to conjecture that there is a common southern origin to them.
sentence_20: Asterales are [[Angiosperms|angiosperms]], flowering plants that appeared about 140 million years ago.
sentence_21: The Asterales order probably originated in the [[Cretaceous|Cretaceous]] (145 – 66 [[Mya_(unit)#Symbols_y_and_yr|Mya]]) on the supercontinent [[Gondwana|Gondwana]] which broke up from 184 – 80 Mya, forming the area that is now Australia, South America, Africa, India and Antarctica.
sentence_22: Asterales contain about 14% of [[Eudicot|eudicot]] diversity.
sentence_23: From an analysis of relationships and diversities within the Asterales and with their superorders, estimates of the age of the beginning of the Asterales have been made, which range from 116 Mya to 82Mya.
sentence_24: However few fossils have been found, of the Menyanthaceae-Asteraceae clade in the [[Oligocene|Oligocene]], about 29 Mya.
sentence_25: Fossil evidence of the Asterales is rare and belongs to rather recent epochs, so the precise estimation of the order's age is quite difficult.
sentence_26: An Oligocene (34 – 23 Mya) pollen is known for Asteraceae and Goodeniaceae, and seeds from Oligocene and [[Miocene|Miocene]] (23 – 5.3 Mya) are known for Menyanthaceae and Campanulaceae respectively.
sentence_27: The Asterales, by dint of being a super-set of the family Asteraceae, include some species grown for food, including the [[Sunflower|sunflower]] (Helianthus annuus), lettuce (Lactuca sativa) and [[Chicory|chicory]] (Cichorium).
sentence_28: Many are also used as spices and traditional medicines.
sentence_29: Asterales are common plants and have many known uses.
sentence_30: For example, [[Pyrethrum|pyrethrum]] (derived from Old World members of the genus Chrysanthemum) is a natural insecticide with minimal environmental impact.
sentence_31: [[Artemisia_(genus)|Wormwood]], derived from a genus that includes the [[Sagebrush|sagebrush]], is used as a source of flavoring for [[Absinthe|absinthe]], a bitter classical liquor of European origin.

sentence_0: The economy of Azerbaijan has completed its post-Soviet transition into a major oil based economy (with the completion of the [[Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan_pipeline|Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan Pipeline]]), from one where the state played the major role.
sentence_1: The transition to oil production led to remarkable growth figures as projects came online; reaching 26.4% in 2005 (second highest [[GDP|GDP]] growth in the world in 2005 only to [[Equatorial_Guinea|Equatorial Guinea]]) and 34.6% in 2006 (world highest) before subsiding to 10.8% and 9.3% in 2008 and 2009 respectively.
sentence_2: The real GDP growth rate for 2011 was expected at 3.7% but had dropped to 0.1%.
sentence_3: Large [[Petroleum|oil]] reserves are a major contributor to [[Azerbaijan|Azerbaijan]]'s economy.
sentence_4: The national currency, the [[Azerbaijani_manat|Azerbaijani manat]], was stable in 2000, depreciating 3.8% against the dollar.
sentence_5: The budget deficit equaled 1.3% of GDP in 2000.
sentence_6: Progress on economic reform has generally lagged behind [[Macroeconomic|macroeconomic]] stabilization.
sentence_7: The government has undertaken regulatory reforms in some areas, including substantial opening of trade policy, but inefficient public administration in which commercial and regulatory interests are co-mingled limit the impact of these reforms.
sentence_8: The government has largely completed [[Privatization|privatization]] of agricultural lands and small and medium-sized enterprises.
sentence_9: In August 2000, the government launched a second-stage privatization program, in which many large state enterprises will be privatized.
sentence_10: Since 2001, the economic activity in the country is regulated by the [[Ministry_of_Economic_Development_(Azerbaijan)|Ministry of Economic Development of Azerbaijan Republic]].
sentence_11: Throughout the Soviet period, Azerbaijan had always been less developed industrially than Armenia and Georgia, two neighboring Transcaucasia countries – but also less diversified, as a result of slow investment in the non-oil sector.
sentence_12: With a history of industrial development of more than 100 years, Azerbaijan proved to be a leading nation in Southern Caucasus throughout the turmoil of the Soviet Union collapse in early 1990s until nowadays.
sentence_13: Oil remains the most prominent product of Azerbaijan's economy with cotton, natural gas and agriculture products contributing to its economic growth over the last five years.
sentence_14: More than $60 billion was invested into Azerbaijan's oil by major international oil companies in AIOC consortium operated by [[BP|BP]].
sentence_15: Oil production under the first of these PSAs, with the Azerbaijan International Operating Company, began in November 1997 and now is about 500,000 barrels per day.
sentence_16: People visit petroleum spas (or "oil spas") to bathe in the local crude in [[Naftalan,_Azerbaijan|Naftalan]] A leading [[Caviar|caviar]] producer and exporter in the past, Azerbaijan's [[Fishing_industry|fishing industry]] today is concentrated on the dwindling stocks of [[Sturgeon|sturgeon]] and [[Beluga_(sturgeon)|beluga]] in the [[Caspian_Sea|Caspian Sea]].
sentence_17: Azerbaijan shares all the problems of the former Soviet republics in making the transition from a [[Command_economy|command]] to a [[Market_economy|market economy]], but its energy resources brighten its long-term prospects.
sentence_18: Azerbaijan has begun making progress on economic reform, and old economic ties and structures are slowly being replaced.
sentence_19: An obstacle to economic progress, including stepped up foreign investment, is the continuing conflict with Armenia over the [[Nagorno-Karabakh|Nagorno-Karabakh]] region.
sentence_20: In 1992, Azerbaijan became member of the [[Economic_Cooperation_Organization|Economic Cooperation Organization]].
sentence_21: In 2002, the Azerbaijani [[Merchant_marine|merchant marine]] had 54 ships.
sentence_22: In March 2001, Azerbaijan concluded a [[Gas|gas]] agreement with Turkey, providing a future export market for Azerbaijan.
sentence_23: Azerbaijan has concluded 21 production-sharing agreements with various oil companies.
sentence_24: An export pipeline that transports Caspian oil to the Mediterranean from [[Baku|Baku]] through [[Tbilisi|Tbilisi]], [[Georgia_(country)|Georgia]] to [[Ceyhan|Ceyhan]], [[Turkey|Turkey]] (the [[Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan_pipeline|Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan Pipeline]]) became operational in 2006.
sentence_25: The pipeline is expected to generate as much as $160 billion in revenues for the country over the next 30 years.
sentence_26: The recent high price of oil is highly beneficial to Azerbaijan's economy as the nation is in the midst of an oil boom.
sentence_27: Eastern Caspian producers in Kazakhstan also have expressed interest in accessing this pipeline to transport a portion of their production.
sentence_28: In 2010, Azerbaijan entered into the top eight biggest oil suppliers to EU countries with €9.46 billion.
sentence_29: In 2011, the amount of foreign investments in Azerbaijan was $20 billion, a 61% increase from 2010.
sentence_30: According to [[Ministry_of_Economic_Development_(Azerbaijan)|Minister of Economic Development of Azerbaijan]], [[Shahin_Mustafayev|Shahin Mustafayev]], in 2011, "$15.7 billion was invested in the non-oil sector, while the rest – in the oil sector."
sentence_31: In 2012, because of its economic performance after the Soviet breakup, Azerbaijan was predicted to become "[[Tiger_economy|Tiger of Caucasus]]".
sentence_32: In 2012, [[Globalization_and_World_Cities_Research_Network|Globalization and World Cities Research Network]] study ranked Baku as a Gamma-level [[Global_city|global city]].
sentence_33: In 2015, Turkey and Azerbaijan agreed to boost mutual trade to US$15 billion by 2023.
sentence_34: The following is a chart of trend of gross domestic product of Azerbaijan at market prices with figures in USD.
sentence_35: For purchasing power parity comparisons, the US dollar was exchanged at 1,565.88 Manats only.
sentence_36: Currently, the new Manat is in use, with an exchange rate of about 1 manat = $1.10.
sentence_37: Mean graduate pay was $5.76 per manhour in 2010.
sentence_38: The following table shows the main economic indicators in 1980–2017.
sentence_39: Source: IMF
sentence_40: For more than a century the backbone of the Azerbaijani economy has been [[Petroleum|petroleum]], which represented 50 percent of Azerbaijan's GDP in 2005, and is projected to double to almost 125 percent of GDP in 2007.
sentence_41: Now that Western oil companies are able to tap deepwater oilfields untouched by the [[Soviet_Union|Soviets]] because of poor technology, Azerbaijan is considered one of the most important areas in the world for oil exploration and development.
sentence_42: Proven [[Oil_reserves|oil reserves]] in the [[Caspian_Sea|Caspian Basin]], which Azerbaijan shares with [[Russia|Russia]], [[Kazakhstan|Kazakhstan]], [[Iran|Iran]], and [[Turkmenistan|Turkmenistan]], are comparable in size to the [[North_Sea_oil|North Sea]], although exploration is still in the early stages.
sentence_43: Main article: Agriculture in Azerbaijan
sentence_44: Azerbaijan has the largest agricultural basin in the region.
sentence_45: About 54.9 percent of Azerbaijan is agricultural lands.
sentence_46: At the beginning of 2007 there were 4.76 million hectares (11.8 million acres) of utilized agricultural area.
sentence_47: In the same year the total wood resources counted 136 million cubic metres (178 million cubic yards).
sentence_48: Azerbaijan's agricultural scientific research institutes are focused on meadows and pastures, horticulture and [[Subtropical|subtropical]] crops, [[Leaf_vegetable|leaf vegetables]], [[Viticulture|viticulture]] and [[Azerbaijani_wine|wine-making]], cotton growing and [[Medicinal_plants|medicinal plants]].
sentence_49: In some lands it is profitable to grow grain, potatoes, [[Sugar_beet|sugar beets]], cotton and tobacco.
sentence_50: Livestock, [[Dairy_product|dairy products]], and wine and [[Distilled_beverage|spirits]] are also important farm products.
sentence_51: The Caspian [[Fishing_industry|fishing industry]] is concentrated on the dwindling stocks of [[Sturgeon|sturgeon]] and [[Beluga_(sturgeon)|beluga]].
sentence_52: Some portions of most products that were previously imported from abroad have begun to be produced locally (among them are Coca-Cola by Coca-Cola Bottlers LTD, beer by Baki-Kastel, parquet by Nehir and oil pipes by EUPEC Pipe Coating Azerbaijan).
sentence_53: New program which is prepared by the Europe Union is aimed to support economic diversification of Azerbaijan.
sentence_54: Program is considered for southern region Lankaran which has the lowest economic indicator and the lowest income per capita, as well as, the lowest level of investment, but at the same time, high potential for the production of garden products in high quality.
sentence_55: The program will be focused on the development of the region at the local and international levels.
sentence_56: Azerbaijan produced in 2018:
