sentence_57: In addition to smaller productions of other agricultural products, like [[Melon|melon]] (94 thousand tons), [[Pear|pear]] (52 thousand tons) and [[Apricot|apricot]] (28 thousand tons).
sentence_58: In 2007, mining and hydrocarbon industries accounted for well over 95 per cent of the Azerbaijani economy.
sentence_59: Diversification of the economy into manufacturing industries remain a long-term issue.
sentence_60: As of late 2000s, the defense industry of Azerbaijan has emerged as an autonomous entity with a growing defense production capability.
sentence_61: The ministry is cooperating with the defense sectors of Ukraine, Belarus and Pakistan.
sentence_62: Along with other contracts, Azerbaijani defence industries and Turkish companies, Azerbaijan will produce 40 mm revolver grenade launchers, 107 mm and 122 mm MLRS systems, Cobra 4×4 vehicles and joint modernization of BTR vehicles in Baku.
sentence_63: Main article: [[Banking_in_Azerbaijan|Banking in Azerbaijan]]
sentence_64: The [[Economic_growth|GDP growth rates]] observed in Azerbaijan during last years made the country one of the fastest growing economies in the world.
sentence_65: But the banking sector of Azerbaijan has yet to tap the vast growth potential that should be achievable due to the continuation of the high economic growth.
sentence_66: For this reason the banking sector remains small in relation to the size of the Azerbaijani economy.
sentence_67: Since 2002, important stages of [[Restructuring|restructuring]] of the banking system have started to be carried out.
sentence_68: Taking into consideration entry of big oil revenues in the country, as a logical result of successful oil strategy, and in this base, as the banks were ready to an effective transfer of their financial resources to the strategic goals, development strategy was made for 2002–2005.
sentence_69: By 1 April 2010, 47 banks, 631 bank branches function in Azerbaijan.
sentence_70: One of banks was founded with participation of state capital, 23 of foreign capital.
sentence_71: To the same date, 98 non-bank credit organizations operate in the republic along with banks.
sentence_72: Growth of real money incomes of population, development of trust in bank system, improving the legal bases of protection of interests of creditors and depositors, in particular launch of 'Deposits Insurance Fund' were the criteria characterizing rapid growth of deposits of population.
sentence_73: As of 1 April 2010, [[Bank_deposit|bank deposits]] of population were equal to 2,4 billion AZN.
sentence_74: 33,3% of them were long-term deposits (higher than a year).
sentence_75: As of 1 April 2010, bank credits to customers is 8.5 bn AZN, which makes 70.5% of bank assets.
sentence_76: Special weight of private sector in structure of credit investments is higher than 82% (7 bn AZN).
sentence_77: Main article: [[Communications_in_Azerbaijan|Communications in Azerbaijan]]
sentence_78: In the 21st century, a new oil and gas boom helped to improve the situation in the Azerbaijan's science and technology sectors, and the government launched a campaign aimed at modernization and [[List_of_Azerbaijani_inventions_and_discoveries|innovation]].
sentence_79: The government estimates that profits from the information technology and communication industry will grow and become comparable with those from oil production.
sentence_80: Azerbaijan has a large and steadily growing [[Internet|Internet]] sector, mostly uninfluenced by the [[Financial_crisis_of_2007–2008|financial crisis of 2007–2008]]; rapid growth is forecast for at least five more years.
sentence_81: The country has also been making progress in developing its telecoms sector.
sentence_82: The Ministry of Communications & Information Technologies (MCIT), as well as being an operator through its role in Aztelekom, is both a policy-maker and regulator.
sentence_83: Public pay phones are available for local calls and require the purchase of a token from the telephone exchange or some shops and kiosks.
sentence_84: Tokens allow a call of indefinite duration.
sentence_85: As of 2009, there were 1,397,000 main telephone lines and 1,485,000 internet users.
sentence_86: There are five [[GSM|GSM]] providers: Azercell, Bakcell, Azerfon ([[Nar_Mobile|Nar Mobile]]), Aztrank, [[Catel|Catel]] mobile network operators and one [[CDMA|CDMA]].
sentence_87: See also: [[Tourism_in_Azerbaijan|Tourism in Azerbaijan]]
sentence_88: Tourism is an important part of the economy of Azerbaijan.
sentence_89: The country was a well-known tourist spot in the 1980s.
sentence_90: However, the fall of the Soviet Union, and the [[First_Nagorno-Karabakh_War|First Nagorno-Karabakh War]] during the 1988–1994 period, damaged the tourist industry and the image of Azerbaijan as a tourist destination.
sentence_91: It was not until the 2000s that the tourism industry began to recover, and the country has since experienced a high rate of growth in the number of tourist visits and overnight stays.
sentence_92: In the recent years, Azerbaijan has also becoming a popular destination for religious, spa, and health care tourism.
sentence_93: During winter, the [[Shahdag_Winter_Complex|Shahdag Winter Complex]] offers skiing.
sentence_94: The government of Azerbaijan has set the development of Azerbaijan as an elite tourist destination a top priority.
sentence_95: It is a national strategy to make tourism a major, if not the single largest, contributor to the Azerbaijani economy.
sentence_96: These activities are regulated by the [[Ministry_of_Culture_and_Tourism_(Azerbaijan)|Ministry of Culture and Tourism of Azerbaijan]].
sentence_97: The [[List_of_Formula_One_Grands_Prix|Formula One Grand Prix]] is held in [[Baku|Baku]], the capital city and has been held here for years.
sentence_98: See also: [[Azerbaijani_manat|Azerbaijani manat]]
sentence_99: The [[Azerbaijani_manat|Azerbaijani manat]] is the currency of Azerbaijani, denominated as the [[Azerbaijani_manat|manat]], subdivided into 100 [[Azerbaijani_manat|qapik]].
sentence_100: The manat is issued by the Central Bank of Azerbaijan, the monetary authority of Azerbaijan.
sentence_101: The [[ISO_4217|ISO 4217]] abbreviation is AZN.
sentence_102: The Latinised symbol is ().
sentence_103: The manat is held in a floating [[Exchange-rate|exchange-rate]] system managed primarily against the US dollar.
sentence_104: The [[Exchange_rate|rate of exchange]] (Azerbaijani manat per US$1) for 28 January 2016, was AZN 1.60.
sentence_105: There is a complex relationship between Azerbaijan's [[Balance_of_trade|balance of trade]], inflation, measured by the consumer price index and the value of its currency.
sentence_106: Despite allowing the value of the manat to "float", Azerbaijan's [[Central_bank|central bank]] has decisive ability to control its value with relationship to other currencies.
sentence_107: Main article: [[Energy_in_Azerbaijan|Energy in Azerbaijan]]
sentence_108: Further information: [[Petroleum_industry_in_Azerbaijan|Petroleum industry in Azerbaijan]]
sentence_109: Two thirds of Azerbaijan is rich in oil and natural gas.
sentence_110: The region of the [[Lesser_Caucasus|Lesser Caucasus]] accounts for most of the country's gold, silver, iron, copper, [[Titanium|titanium]], [[Chromium|chromium]], [[Manganese|manganese]], [[Cobalt|cobalt]], [[Molybdenum|molybdenum]], complex ore and [[Antimony|antimony]].
sentence_111: In September 1994, a 30-year contract was signed between the [[State_Oil_Company_of_Azerbaijan_Republic|State Oil Company of Azerbaijan Republic]] (SOCAR) and 13 oil companies, among them [[Amoco|Amoco]], [[BP|BP]], [[ExxonMobil|ExxonMobil]], [[Lukoil|Lukoil]] and [[Statoil|Statoil]].
sentence_112: As Western oil companies are able to tap deepwater oilfields untouched by the Soviet exploitation, Azerbaijan is considered one of the most important spots in the world for oil exploration and development.
sentence_113: Meanwhile, the State Oil Fund of Azerbaijan was established as an extra-budgetary fund to ensure the [[Macroeconomy|macroeconomic]] stability, transparency in the management of oil revenue, and the safeguarding of resources for future generations.
sentence_114: Azeriqaz, a sub-company of SOCAR, intends to ensure full gasification of the country by 2021.
sentence_115: Main article: [[Transportation_in_Azerbaijan|Transportation in Azerbaijan]]
sentence_116: The convenient location of Azerbaijan on the crossroad of major international traffic arteries, such as the [[Silk_Road|Silk Road]] and the south–north corridor, highlights the strategic importance of transportation sector for the country's economy.
sentence_117: The transport sector in the country includes roads, railways, aviation, and maritime transport.
sentence_118: Azerbaijan is also an important economic hub in the transportation of raw materials.
sentence_119: The [[Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan_pipeline|Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline]] (BTC) became operational in May 2006 and extends more than 1,774 kilometers through the territories of Azerbaijan, Georgia and Turkey.
sentence_120: The BTC is designed to transport up to 50 million tons of crude oil annually and carries oil from the Caspian Sea oilfields to global markets.
sentence_121: The [[South_Caucasus_Pipeline|South Caucasus Pipeline]], also stretching through the territory of Azerbaijan, Georgia and Turkey, became operational at the end of 2006 and offers additional gas supplies to the European market from the [[Shah_Deniz_gas_field|Shah Deniz gas field]].
sentence_122: Shah Deniz is expected to produce up to 296 billion cubic meters of natural gas per year.
sentence_123: Azerbaijan also plays a major role in the EU-sponsored Silk Road Project.
sentence_124: In 2002, the Azerbaijani government established the [[Ministry_of_Transportation_(Azerbaijan)|Ministry of Transport]] with a broad range of policy and regulatory functions.
sentence_125: In the same year, the country became a member of the [[Vienna_Convention_on_Road_Traffic|Vienna Convention on Road Traffic]].
sentence_126: The highest priority being; upgrading the transport network and transforming transportation services into one of the key comparative advantages of the country, as this would be highly conducive to the development of other sectors of the economy.
sentence_127: In 2012, the construction of [[Kars–Tbilisi–Baku_railway|Kars–Tbilisi–Baku railway]] expected to provide transportation between Asia and Europe through connecting the railways of China and [[Kazakhstan|Kazakhstan]] in the east with Turkey's [[Marmaray|Marmaray]] to the European railway system in the west.
sentence_128: [[Russian_gauge|Broad gauge]] railways in 2010 stretched for 2,918 km (1,813 mi) and [[Electrified_railway|electrified railways]] numbered 1,278 km (794 mi).
sentence_129: By 2010, there were 35 airports and one [[Heliport|heliport]].
sentence_130: Single window system shares needed information through a single gateway with all organizations serving in trade field, as well as abolishes useless processes and raises the effectiveness of cooperation among different parties.
sentence_131: 73 economies implement single window system in the world.
sentence_132: [[Azerbaijan|Azerbaijan]] started to implement this system in 2009.
sentence_133: It implemented an [[E-Government|E-Government]] portal as well.
sentence_134: A single-window system was established by a decree of the [[President_of_Azerbaijan|Azerbaijani President]] issued in 2007, 30 April, in order to simplify export-import procedures, innovate customs services, and improve the trade environment.
sentence_135: According to the decree, [[Ministry_of_Justice_(Azerbaijan)|Ministry of Justice]], [[Ministry_of_Economic_Development_(Azerbaijan)|Ministry of Economic Development]], [[Ministry_of_Taxes_(Azerbaijan)|Ministry of Taxes]], [[Ministry_of_Labour_and_Social_Protection_of_the_Population_(Azerbaijan)|Ministry of Labor and Social Protection]], [[State_Social_Protection_Fund_(Azerbaijan)|State Social Protection Fund]], and [[State_Statistics_Committee_(Azerbaijan)|State Statistics Committee]] should present a proposal on the organization of entrepreneurial activities by single registration body based on single window principle.
sentence_136: The president appointed the [[State_Customs_Committee_(Azerbaijan)|State Customs Committee]] as the leading body of controlling goods and transportation passing through the borders of the country in 2008.
sentence_137: A "single authority principle" requires customs officials to be more responsible in dealing with all types of border control operations for other authorities.
sentence_138: [[Netherlands|The Netherlands]] and [[Sweden|Sweden]] were the countries of which practice studied.
sentence_139: A "single system" works on and then shares standardized information accumulated from traders to all entities taking part in international trade.
sentence_140: The practice of [[United_States|US]] was explored in this phase.
sentence_141: An "automated system" provides a single electronic statement to responsible agencies submitted by traders to be worked on and confirmed, and after that, these authorities send electronic confirmations and announcements.
sentence_142: In this case, practice of [[Mauritius|Mauritius]] and [[Singapore|Singapore]] was studied.
sentence_143: [[State_Customs_Committee_(Azerbaijan)|The Customs Committee]] formed a commission to realize the new system.
sentence_144: [[Ministry_of_Agriculture_(Azerbaijan)|Ministry of Agriculture]], [[Ministry_of_Healthcare_(Azerbaijan)|Ministry of Healthcare]], [[Ministry_of_Internal_Affairs_(Azerbaijan)|Ministry of Internal Affairs]], [[Ministry_of_Taxes_(Azerbaijan)|Ministry of Taxes]], [[Ministry_of_Transportation_(Azerbaijan)|Ministry of Transportation]], Central Bank, State Road Police, State Committee for Standardization, Metrology and Patents, State Maritime Administration were selected as important agencies to implement single window system along with the State Customs Committee.
sentence_145: The government supported Customs Committee in preparing its staff to deal with the new system by improving recruitment of local customs offices, providing with software and hardware upgrades for the system.
sentence_146: Azerbaijani government supports financially single window system.
sentence_147: In the first phase, the government realized customs clearance system on the process of border crossing to country beginning from January 1, 2009.
sentence_148: This system was free to all users.
sentence_149: Then it was expanded to Baku and Sumgayit in 2011.
sentence_150: Customs code of the Republic of Azerbaijan was amended based on the inclusion of the article on single window system which became operative on January 1, 2012.
sentence_151: After this amendment, all of Azerbaijan's 29 customs checkpoints started to implement new single window system.
sentence_152: According to the Presidential Decree (11 November 2008), "single window" principle started to be applied from 1 January 2009 on the inspection of goods and transportation at the border checkpoints.
sentence_153: Customs Committee established a commission working on the implementation of "single window" principle in customs agencies on 18 November 2008 based on the Presidential Decree of 11 November 2008.
sentence_154: Technological scheme determining the sequence of issuance of "permit" certificates was approved by the Customs Committee on 22 December 2009.
sentence_155: Scheme provided customs officers to issue "permit" certificates at border checkpoints to vehicles, which perform customs, veterinary, photo-sanitary and sanitary quarantine control activities and international automobile transportation in accordance with legislation.

title: Alaric I
sentence_0: Alaric I ([[English|/ˈælərɪk/]]; [[Gothic_language|Gothic]]: Alareiks, 𐌰𐌻𐌰𐍂𐌴𐌹𐌺𐍃, "ruler of all"; [[Latin_language|Latin]]: Alaricus; 370 (or 375) – 410 AD) was the first king of the [[Visigoths|Visigoths]], from 395 to 410.
sentence_1: He rose to leadership of the Goths who came to occupy Moesia – territory acquired a couple of decades earlier by a combined force of Goths and [[Alans|Alans]] after the [[Battle_of_Adrianople|Battle of Adrianople]].
sentence_2: Alaric began his career under the Gothic soldier [[Gainas|Gainas]], and later joined the Roman army.
sentence_3: Once an ally of Rome under the Emperor [[Theodosius_I|Theodosius]], Alaric helped defeat the [[Franks|Franks]] and other allies of a Roman usurper.
sentence_4: Despite losing many thousands of his men, he received little recognition from Rome for his efforts and left the Roman army disappointed.
sentence_5: After the death of Theodosius and the disintegration of the Roman armies in 395, he is described as [[Reiks|king]] of the [[Visigoths|Visigoths]].
sentence_6: As the leader of the only effective field force remaining in the Balkans, he sought Roman legitimacy, never quite achieving a position acceptable to himself and to the Roman authorities.
sentence_7: He operated mainly against the successive Western Roman regimes, and marched into Italy, where he died.
sentence_8: He is responsible for the [[Sack_of_Rome_(410)|sack of Rome]] in 410, one of several notable events in the [[Fall_of_the_Western_Roman_Empire|Western Roman Empire's eventual decline]].

section_0.value: Early life, federate status in the Balkans

sentence_9: According to [[Jordanes|Jordanes]], a 6th-century Roman bureaucrat of Gothic origin—who later turned his hand to history—Alaric was born on [[Peuce_Island|Peuce Island]] at the mouth of the [[Danube_Delta|Danube Delta]] in present-day [[Romania|Romania]] and belonged to the noble [[Balti_dynasty|Balti dynasty]] of the [[Thervingi|Tervingian]] [[Goths|Goths]].
sentence_10: There is no way to verify this claim.
sentence_11: Historian Douglas Boin does not make such an unequivocal assessment about Alaric's Gothic heritage and instead claims he came from either the Tervingi or the Greuthung tribes.
sentence_12: When the Goths suffered setbacks against the [[Huns|Huns]], they made a mass migration across the [[Danube|Danube]], and fought a [[Gothic_War_(376–382)|war with Rome]].
sentence_13: Alaric was probably a child during this period who grew up along Rome's periphery.
sentence_14: Alaric's upbringing was shaped by living along the border of Roman territory in a region that the Romans viewed as a veritable "backwater"; some four centuries before, the Roman poet [[Ovid|Ovid]] regarded the area along the Danube and Black Sea where Alaric was reared as a land of "barbarians", among "the most remote in the vast world."
sentence_15: Alaric's childhood in the Balkans, where the Goths had settled by way of an agreement with Theodosius, was spent in the company of veterans who had fought at the Battle of Adrianople in 378, during which they had annihilated much of the Eastern army and killed Emperor [[Valens|Valens]].
sentence_16: Imperial campaigns against the Visigoths were conducted until a treaty was reached in 382.
sentence_17: This treaty was the first foedus on imperial Roman soil and required these semi-autonomous Germanic tribes—among whom Alaric was raised—to supply troops for the Roman army in exchange for peace, control of cultivatable land, and freedom from Roman direct administrative control.
sentence_18: Correspondingly, there was hardly a region along the Roman frontier during Alaric's day without Gothic slaves and servants of one form or another.
sentence_19: For several subsequent decades, many Goths like Alaric were "called up into regular units of the eastern field army" while others served as auxiliaries in campaigns led by Theodosius against the western usurpers [[Magnus_Maximus|Magnus Maximus]] and Eugenius.

section_1.value: Rebellion against Rome, rise to Gothic leadership

sentence_20: A new phase in the relationship between the Goths and the empire resulted from the treaty signed in 382, as more and more Goths attained aristocratic rank from their service in the imperial army.
sentence_21: Alaric began his military career under the Gothic soldier [[Gainas|Gainas]], and later joined the Roman army.
sentence_22: He first appeared as leader of a mixed band of [[Goths|Goths]] and allied peoples, who invaded [[Thrace|Thrace]] in 391 but were stopped by the half-[[Vandal|Vandal]] Roman General [[Stilicho|Stilicho]].
sentence_23: While the Roman poet [[Claudian|Claudian]] belittled Alaric as "a little-known menace" terrorizing southern Thrace during this time, Alaric's abilities and forces were formidable enough to prevent the Roman Emperor [[Theodosius_I|Theodosius]] from crossing the [[Maritsa_River|Maritsa River]].
sentence_24: By 392, Alaric had entered Roman military service, which coincided with a reduction of hostilities between Goths and Romans.
sentence_25: In 394, he led a Gothic force that helped Emperor Theodosius defeat the [[Franks|Frankish]] usurper [[Arbogast_(magister_militum)|Arbogast]]—fighting at the behest of Eugenius—at the Battle of Frigidus.
sentence_26: Despite sacrificing around 10,000 of his men, who had been victims of Theodosius' callous tactical decision to overwhelm the enemies front lines using Gothic foederati, Alaric received little recognition from the emperor.
sentence_27: Alaric was among the few who survived the protracted and bloody affair.
sentence_28: Many Romans considered it their "gain" and a victory that so many Goths had died during the Battle of Frigidus River.
sentence_29: Recent biographer, Douglas Boin, posits that seeing ten thousand of his (Alaric's) dead kinsmen likely elicited questions about what kind of ruler Theodosius actually had been and whether remaining in direct Roman service was best for men like him.
sentence_30: Refused the reward he expected, which included a promotion to the position of [[Magister_militum|Magister militum]] and command of regular Roman units, Alaric mutinied and began to march against Constantinople.
sentence_31: On 17 January 395, Theodosius died of an illness, leaving his two young and incapable sons [[Arcadius|Arcadius]] and [[Flavius_Augustus_Honorius|Honorius]] in Stilicho's guardianship.
sentence_32: Modern writers regard Alaric as king of the [[Visigoths|Visigoths]] from 395.
sentence_33: According to historian Peter Heather, it is not entirely clear in the sources if Alaric rose to prominence at the time the Goths revolted following Theodosius's death, or if he had already risen within his tribe as early as the war against Eugenius.
sentence_34: Whatever the circumstances, Jordanes recorded that the new king persuaded his people to "seek a kingdom by their own exertions rather than serve others in idleness."

section_3.value: Semi-independent action in Eastern Roman interests, Eastern Roman recognition

sentence_35: Whether or not Alaric was a member of an ancient Germanic royal clan—as claimed by Jordanes and debated by historians—is less important than his emergence as a leader, the first of his kind since [[Fritigern|Fritigern]].
sentence_36: Theodosius's death left the Roman field armies collapsing and the Empire divided again between his two sons, one taking [[Byzantine_Empire|the eastern]] and the other [[Western_Roman_Empire|the western portion]] of the Empire, [[Stilicho|Stilicho]] made himself master of the West and attempted to establish control in the East as well, and led an army into Greece.
sentence_37: Alaric rebelled again.
sentence_38: Historian Roger Collins points out that while the rivalries created by the two halves of the Empire vying for power worked to Alaric's advantage and that of his people, simply being called to authority by the Gothic people did not solve the practicalities of their needs for survival.
sentence_39: He needed Roman authority in order to be supplied by Roman cities.
sentence_40: Alaric took his Gothic army on what Stilicho's propagandist [[Claudian|Claudian]] described as a "pillaging campaign" that began first in the East.
sentence_41: Burns' interpretation is that Alaric and his men were recruited by [[Rufinus_(consul)|Rufinus]]'s Eastern regime in Constantinople, and sent to [[Thessaly|Thessaly]] to stave off Stilicho's threat.
sentence_42: No battle took place.
sentence_43: Alaric's forces made their way down to Athens and along the coast, where he sought to force a new peace upon the Romans.
sentence_44: His march in 396 included passing through [[Thermopylae|Thermopylae]].
sentence_45: Stilicho's propagandist [[Claudian|Claudian]] accuses his troops of plundering for the next year or so as far south as the mountainous Peloponnese peninsula, and reports that only Stilicho's surprise attack with his western field army (having sailed from Italy) stemmed the plundering as he pushed Alaric's forces north into Epirus.
sentence_46: Zosimus adds that Stilicho's troops destroyed and pillaged too, and let Alaric's men escape with their plunder.
sentence_47: Stilicho was forced to send some of his Eastern forces home.
sentence_48: They went to Constantinople under the command of one [[Gainas|Gainas]], a Goth with a large Gothic following.
sentence_49: On arrival, Gainas murdered Rufinus, and was appointed [[Magister_militum|magister militum]] for [[Thrace|Thrace]] by [[Eutropius_(consul_399)|Eutropius]], the new supreme minister and the only eunuch consul of Rome, who, Zosimus claims, controlled Arcadius "as if he were a sheep".
sentence_50: A poem by [[Synesius|Synesius]] advises Arcadius to display manliness and remove a "skin-clad savage" (probably referring to Alaric) from the councils of power and his barbarians from the Roman army.
sentence_51: We do not know if Arcadius ever became aware of this advice, but it had no recorded effect.
sentence_52: Stilicho obtained a few more troops from the German frontier and continued to campaign indecisively against the Eastern empire; again he was opposed by Alaric and his men.
sentence_53: During the next year, 397, Eutropius personally led his troops to victory over some [[Huns|Huns]] who were marauding in Asia Minor.
sentence_54: With his position thus strengthened he declared Stilicho a public enemy, and he established Alaric as magister militum per [[Illyricum_(Roman_province)|Illyricum]] Alaric thus acquired entitlement to gold and grain for his followers and negotiations were underway for a more permanent settlement.
sentence_55: Stilicho's supporters in Milan were outraged at this seeming betrayal; meanwhile, Eutropius was celebrated in 398 by a parade through Constantinople for having achieved victory over the "wolves of the North."
sentence_56: Alaric's people were relatively quiet for the next couple of years.
sentence_57: In 399, Eutropius fell from power.
sentence_58: The new Eastern regime now felt that they could dispense with Alaric's services and they nominally transferred Alaric's province to the West.
sentence_59: This administrative change removed Alaric's Roman rank and his entitlement to legal provisioning for his men, leaving his army—the only significant force in the ravaged Balkans—as a problem for Stilicho.

section_4.value: In search of Western Roman recognition; invading Italy

sentence_60: According to historian Michael Kulikowski, sometime in the spring of 402 Alaric decided to invade Italy, but no sources from antiquity indicate to what purpose.
sentence_61: Burns suggests that Alaric was probably desperate for provisions.
sentence_62: Using Claudian as his source, historian Guy Halsall reports that Alaric's attack actually began in late 401, but since Stilicho was in Raetia "dealing with frontier issues" the two did not first confront one another in Italy until 402.
sentence_63: Alaric's entry into Italy followed the route identified in the poetry of Claudian, as he crossed the peninsula's Alpine frontier near the city of [[Aquileia|Aquileia]].
sentence_64: For a period of six to nine months, there were reports of Gothic attacks along the northern Italian roads, where Alaric was spotted by Roman townspeople.
sentence_65: Along the route on [[Via_Postumia|Via Postumia]], Alaric first encountered Stilicho.
sentence_66: Two battles were fought.
sentence_67: The first was at [[Battle_of_Pollentia|Pollentia]] on Easter Sunday, where Stilicho (according to Claudian) achieved an impressive victory, taking Alaric's wife and children prisoner, and more significantly, seizing much of the treasure that Alaric had amassed over the previous five years' worth of plundering.
sentence_68: Pursuing the retreating forces of Alaric, Stilicho offered to return the prisoners but was refused.
sentence_69: The second battle was at Verona, where Alaric was defeated for a second time.
sentence_70: Stilicho once again offered Alaric a truce and allowed him to withdraw from Italy.
sentence_71: Kulikowski explains this confusing, if not outright conciliatory behavior by stating, "given Stilicho's cold war with Constantinople, it would have been foolish to destroy as biddable and violent a potential weapon as Alaric might well prove to be".
sentence_72: Halsall's observations are similar, as he contends that the Roman general's "decision to permit Alaric's withdrawal into Pannonia makes sense if we see Alaric's force entering Stilicho's service, and Stilicho's victory being less total than Claudian would have us believe".
sentence_73: Perhaps more revealing is a report from the Greek historian Zosimus—writing a half a century later—that indicates an agreement was concluded between Stilicho and Alaric in 405, which suggests Alaric being in "western service at that point", likely stemming from arrangements made back in 402.
sentence_74: Between 404 and 405, Alaric remained in one of the four Pannonian provinces, from where he could "play East off against West while potentially threatening both".
sentence_75: Historian A.D. Lee observes, "Alaric's return to the north-west Balkans brought only temporary respite to Italy, for in 405 another substantial body of Goths and other barbarians, this time from outside the empire, crossed the middle Danube and advanced into northern Italy, where they plundered the countryside and besieged cities and towns" under their leader [[Radagaisus|Radagaisus]].
sentence_76: Although the imperial government was struggling to muster enough troops to contain these barbarian invasions, Stilicho managed to stifle the threat posed by the tribes under Radagaisus, when the latter split his forces into three separate groups.
sentence_77: Stilicho cornered Radagaisus near Florence and starved the invaders into submission.
sentence_78: Meanwhile, Alaric—bestowed with codicils of magister militum by Stilicho and now supplied by the West—awaited for one side or the other to incite him to action as Stilicho faced further difficulties from more barbarians.

section_5.value: Second invasion of Italy, agreement with Western Roman regime

sentence_79: Sometime in 406 and into 407, more large groups of barbarians, consisting primarily of [[Vandals|Vandals]], [[Sueves|Sueves]] and [[Alans|Alans]], crossed the Rhine into Gaul while about the same time a rebellion occurred in Britain.
sentence_80: Under a common soldier named [[Constantine_III_(Western_Roman_Emperor)|Constantine]] it spread to Gaul.
sentence_81: Burdened by so many enemies, Stilicho's position was strained.
sentence_82: During this crisis in 407, Alaric again marched on Italy, taking a position in Noricum (modern Austria), where he demanded a sum of 4,000 pounds of gold to buy off another full-scale invasion.
sentence_83: The Roman Senate loathed the idea of supporting Alaric; Zosimus observed that one senator famously declaimed Non est ista pax, sed pactio servitutis ("This is not peace, but a pact of servitude").
sentence_84: Stilicho paid Alaric the 4,000 pounds of gold nevertheless.
sentence_85: This agreement, sensible in view of the military situation, fatally weakened Stilicho's standing at Honorius's court.
sentence_86: Twice Stilicho had allowed Alaric to escape his grasp, and Radagaisus had advanced all the way to the outskirts of [[Florence|Florence]].

section_6.value: Renewed hostilities after Western Roman coup

sentence_87: In the East, Arcadius died on 1 May 408 and was replaced by his son Theodosius II; Stilicho seems to have planned to march to Constantinople, and to install there a regime loyal to himself.
sentence_88: He may also have intended to give Alaric a senior official position and send him against the rebels in Gaul.
sentence_89: Before Stilicho could do so, while he was away at Ticinum at the head of a small detachment, a bloody coup against his supporters took place at Honorius's court.
sentence_90: It was led by Honorius's minister, Olympius.
sentence_91: Stilicho's small escort of Goths and Huns was commanded by a Goth, [[Sarus_(Goth)|Sarus]], whose Gothic troops massacred the Hun contingent in their sleep, and then withdrew towards the cities in which their own families were billeted.
sentence_92: Stilicho ordered that Sarus's Goths should not be admitted, but, now without an army, he was forced to flee for sanctuary.
sentence_93: Agents of Olympius promised Stilicho his life, but instead betrayed and killed him.
sentence_94: Alaric was again declared an enemy of the Emperor.
sentence_95: Olympius's men then massacred the families of the federate troops (as presumed supporters of Stilicho, although they had probably rebelled against him), and the troops defected en masse to Alaric.
sentence_96: Many thousands of barbarian auxiliaries, along with their wives and children, joined Alaric in Noricum.
sentence_97: The conspirators seem to have let their main army disintegrate, and had no policy except hunting down supporters of Stilicho.
sentence_98: Italy was left without effective indigenous defence forces thereafter.
sentence_99: As a declared 'enemy of the Emperor', Alaric was denied the legitimacy that he needed to collect taxes and hold cities without large garrisons, which he could not afford to detach.
sentence_100: He again offered to move his men, this time to Pannonia, in exchange for a modest sum of money and the modest title of [[Comes|Comes]], but he was refused because Olympius's regime regarded him as a supporter of Stilicho.

section_7.value: First siege of Rome, agreed ransom

sentence_101: When Alaric was rebuffed, he led his force of around 30,000 men—many newly enlisted and understandably motivated—on a march toward Rome to avenge their murdered families.
sentence_102: He moved across the Julian Alps into Italy, probably using the route and supplies arranged for him by Stilicho, bypassing the imperial court in Ravenna which was protected by widespread marshland and had a port, and in September 408 he menaced the city of Rome, imposing a strict blockade.
sentence_103: No blood was shed this time; Alaric relied on hunger as his most powerful weapon.
sentence_104: When the ambassadors of the [[Roman_Senate|Senate]], entreating for peace, tried to intimidate him with hints of what the despairing citizens might accomplish, he laughed and gave his celebrated answer: "The thicker the hay, the easier mowed!"
sentence_105: After much bargaining, the famine-stricken citizens agreed to pay a ransom of 5,000 pounds of gold, 30,000 pounds of silver, 4,000 silken tunics, 3,000 hides dyed scarlet, and 3,000 pounds of pepper.
sentence_106: Alaric also recruited some 40,000 freed [[Goths|Gothic]] slaves.
sentence_107: Thus ended Alaric's first siege of Rome.

section_8.value: Failed agreement with the Western Romans, Alaric sets up his own emperor

sentence_108: After having provisionally agreed to the terms offered by Alaric for lifting the blockade, Honorius recanted; historian A.D. Lee highlights that one of the points of contention for the emperor was Alaric's expectation of being named head of the Roman Army, a post Honorius was not prepared to grant to Alaric.
sentence_109: When this title was not bestowed onto Alaric, he proceeded to not only "besiege Rome again in late 409, but also to proclaim a leading senator, [[Priscus_Attalus|Priscus Attalus]], as a rival emperor, from whom Alaric then received the appointment" he desired.
sentence_110: Meanwhile, Alaric's newly appointed "emperor" Attalus, who seems not to have understood the limits of his power or his dependence on Alaric, failed to take Alaric's advice and lost the grain supply in Africa to a pro-Honorian comes Africae, Heraclian.
sentence_111: Then, sometime in 409, Attalus—accompanied by Alaric—marched on Ravenna and after receiving unprecedented terms and concessions from the legitimate emperor Honorius, refused him and instead demanded that Honorius be deposed and exiled.
sentence_112: Fearing for his safety, Honorius made preparations to flee to Ravenna when a ship carrying 4,000 troops arrived from Constantinople, restoring his resolve.
sentence_113: Now that Honorius no longer felt the need to negotiate, Alaric (regretting his choice of puppet emperor) deposed Attalus, perhaps to re-open negotiations with Ravenna.
sentence_114: Main article: [[Sack_of_Rome_(410)|Sack of Rome (410)]]
sentence_115: Negotiations with Honorius might have succeeded had it not been for another intervention by [[Sarus_(Goth)|Sarus]], of the Amal family, and therefore a hereditary enemy of Alaric and his house.
sentence_116: He attacked Alaric's men.
sentence_117: Why Sarus, who had been in imperial service for years under Stilicho, acted at this moment remains a mystery, but Alaric interpreted this attack as directed by Ravenna and as bad faith from Honorius.
sentence_118: No longer would negotiations suffice for Alaric, as his patience had reached its end, which led him to march on Rome for a third and final time.
sentence_119: On 24 August 410, Alaric and his forces began the sack of Rome, an assault that lasted three days.
sentence_120: After hearing reports that Alaric had entered the city—possibly aided by Gothic slaves inside—there were reports that Emperor Honorius (safe in Ravenna) broke into "wailing and lamentation" but quickly calmed once "it was explained to him that it was the city of Rome that had met its end and not 'Roma'," his pet fowl.
sentence_121: Writing from Bethlehem, St. Jerome (Letter 127.12, to the lady Principia) lamented: "A dreadful rumour reached us from the West.
sentence_122: We heard that Rome was besieged, that the citizens were buying their safety with gold .
sentence_125: The city which had taken the whole world was itself taken; nay, it fell by famine before it fell to the sword."
sentence_126: Nonetheless, Christian apologists also cited how Alaric ordered that anyone who took shelter in a Church was to be spared.
sentence_127: When liturgical vessels were taken from the basilica of St. Peter and Alaric heard of this, he ordered them returned and had them ceremoniously restored in the church.
sentence_128: If the account from the historian [[Paulus_Orosius|Orosius]] can be seen as accurate, there was even a celebratory recognition of Christian unity by way of a procession through the streets where Romans and barbarians alike "raised a hymn to God in public"; historian Edward James concludes that such stories are likely more political rhetoric of the "noble" barbarians than a reflection of historical reality.
sentence_129: According to historian Patrick Geary, Roman booty was not the focus of Alaric's sack of Rome; he came for needed food supplies.
sentence_130: Historian Stephen Mitchell asserts that Alaric's followers seemed incapable of feeding themselves and relied on provisions "supplied by the Roman authorities."
sentence_131: Whatever Alaric's intentions were cannot be known entirely, but Kulikowski certainly sees the issue of available treasure in a different light, writing that "For three days, Alaric's Goths sacked the city, stripping it of the wealth of centuries."
sentence_132: The barbarian invaders were not gentle in their treatment of property as substantial damage was still evident into the sixth century.
sentence_133: Certainly the Roman world was shaken by the fall of the Eternal City to barbarian invaders, but as Guy Halsall emphasizes, "Rome's fall had less striking political effects.
sentence_134: Alaric, unable to treat with Honorius, remained in the political cold."
sentence_135: Kulikowski sees the situation similarly, commenting:
sentence_136: Still, the importance of Alaric cannot be "overestimated" according to Halsall, since he had desired and obtained a Roman command even though he was a barbarian; his real misfortune was being caught between the rivalry of the Eastern and Western empires and their court intrigue.
sentence_137: According to historian Peter Brown, when one compares Alaric with other barbarians, "he was almost an Elder Statesman."
sentence_138: Nonetheless, Alaric's respect for Roman institutions as a former servant to its highest office did not stay his hand in violently sacking the city that had for centuries exemplified Roman glory, leaving behind physical destruction and social disruption, while Alaric took clerics and even the emperor's sister, [[Galla_Placidia|Galla Placidia]], with him when he left the city.
sentence_139: Many other Italian communities beyond the city of Rome itself fell victim to the forces under Alaric, as Procopius (Wars 3.2.11–13) writing in the sixth-century later relates:
sentence_140: Whether Alaric's forces wrought the level of destruction described by Procopius or not cannot be known, but evidence speaks to a significant population decrease, as the number of people on the [[Grain_supply_to_the_city_of_Rome|food dole]] dropped from 800,000 in 408 to 500,000 by 419.
sentence_141: Rome's fall to the barbarians was as much a psychological blow to the empire as anything else, since some Romans citizens saw the collapse as resulting from the conversion to Christianity, while Christian apologists like Augustine (writing City of God) responded in turn.
sentence_142: Lamenting Rome's capture, famed Christian theologian [[Jerome|Jerome]], wrote how "day and night" he could not stop thinking of everyone's safety, and moreover, how Alaric had extinguished "the bright light of all the world."
sentence_143: Some contemporary Christian observers even saw Alaric—himself a Christian—as God's wrath upon a still pagan Rome.

section_10.value: Move to southern Italy, death from disease

sentence_144: Not only had Rome's sack been a significant blow to the Roman people's morale, they had also endured two years' worth of trauma brought about by fear, hunger (consequent the blockades), and illness.
sentence_145: However, the Goths were not long in the city of Rome, as only three days after the sack, Alaric marched his men south to Campania, from where he intended to sail to Sicily—probably to obtain grain and other supplies—when a storm destroyed his fleet.
sentence_146: During the early months of 411, while on his northward return journey through Italy, Alaric took ill and died at Consentia in Bruttium.
sentence_147: His cause of death was likely fever, and his body was, according to legend, buried under the riverbed of the Busento in accordance with the pagan practices of the Visigothic people.
sentence_148: The stream was temporarily turned aside from its course while the grave was dug, wherein the Gothic chief and some of his most precious spoils were interred.
sentence_149: When the work was finished, the river was turned back into its usual channel and the captives by whose hands the labor had been accomplished were put to death that none might learn their secret.
sentence_150: Alaric was succeeded in the command of the Gothic army by his brother-in-law, [[Ataulf|Ataulf]], who married Honorius' sister [[Galla_Placidia|Galla Placidia]] three years later.
sentence_151: Following in the wake of Alaric's leadership, which Kulikowski claims, had given his people "a sense of community that survived his own death...Alaric's Goths remained together inside the empire, going on to settle in Gaul.
sentence_152: There, in the province of Aquitaine, they put down roots and created the first autonomous barbarian kingdom inside the frontiers of the Roman empire."
sentence_153: The Goths were able to settle in Aquitaine only after Honorius granted the once Roman province to them, sometime in 418 or 419.
sentence_154: Not long after Alaric's exploits in Rome and Athaulf's settlement in Aquitaine, there is a "rapid emergence of Germanic barbarian groups in the West" who begin controlling many western provinces.
sentence_155: These barbarian peoples included: Vandals in Spain and Africa, Visigoths in Spain and Aquitaine, Burgundians along the upper Rhine and southern Gaul, and Franks on the lower Rhine and in northern and central Gaul.

title: Jules Verne
sentence_0: For other uses, see [[Jules_Verne_(disambiguation)|Jules Verne (disambiguation)]].

Valentine Morel

sentence_1: Jules Gabriel Verne ([[English|/vɜːrn/]]; French: [[French|[ʒyl gabʁijɛl vɛʁn]]; 8 February 1828 – 24 March 1905) was a French novelist, poet, and playwright.
sentence_2: His collaboration with the publisher Pierre-Jules Hetzel led to the creation of the [[Voyages_extraordinaires|Voyages extraordinaires]], a series of bestselling adventure novels including [[Journey_to_the_Center_of_the_Earth|Journey to the Center of the Earth]] (1864), [[Twenty_Thousand_Leagues_Under_the_Sea|Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea]] (1870), and [[Around_the_World_in_Eighty_Days|Around the World in Eighty Days]] (1872).
sentence_3: Verne is considered to be an important author in France and most of Europe, where he has had a wide influence on the literary [[Avant-garde|avant-garde]] and on [[Surrealism|surrealism]].
sentence_4: His reputation was markedly different in [[English-speaking_world|anglophone regions]] where he had often been labeled a writer of genre fiction or [[Children's_books|children's books]], largely because of the highly abridged and altered [[Jules_Verne#English_translations|translations]] in which his novels have often been printed.
sentence_5: Since the 1980s, his literary reputation has improved.
sentence_6: Verne has been the [[List_of_most-translated_individual_authors|second most-translated author in the world]] since 1979, ranking between [[Agatha_Christie|Agatha Christie]] and [[William_Shakespeare|William Shakespeare]].
sentence_7: As of 2018, he is still the 2nd .
sentence_8: He has sometimes been called the "Father of Science Fiction", a title that has also been given to [[H._G._Wells|H.
sentence_9: G. Wells]] and [[Hugo_Gernsback|Hugo Gernsback]].
sentence_10: Verne was born on 8 February 1828, on Île Feydeau, a small artificial island on the [[Loire_River|Loire River]] within the town of [[Nantes|Nantes]], in No.
sentence_11: 4 Rue Olivier-de-Clisson, the house of his maternal grandmother Dame Sophie Marie Adélaïde Julienne Allotte de La Fuÿe (née Guillochet de La Perrière).
sentence_12: His parents were Pierre Verne, an attorney originally from [[Provins|Provins]], and Sophie Allotte de La Fuÿe, a Nantes woman from a local family of navigators and shipowners, of distant [[Scottish_people|Scottish]] descent.
sentence_13: In 1829, the Verne family moved some hundred metres away to No.
sentence_14: 2 Quai Jean-Bart, where Verne's brother Paul was born the same year.
sentence_15: Three sisters, Anne "Anna" (1836), Mathilde (1839), and Marie (1842) would follow.
sentence_16: In 1834, at the age of six, Verne was sent to boarding school at 5 Place du Bouffay in Nantes.
sentence_17: The teacher, Madame Sambin, was the widow of a naval captain who had disappeared some 30 years before.
sentence_18: Madame Sambin often told the students that her husband was a shipwrecked castaway and that he would eventually return like [[Robinson_Crusoe|Robinson Crusoe]] from his desert island paradise.
sentence_19: The theme of the robinsonade would stay with Verne throughout his life and appear in many of his novels, including [[The_Mysterious_Island|The Mysterious Island]] (1874), [[Second_Fatherland|Second Fatherland]] (1900), and [[The_School_for_Robinsons|The School for Robinsons]] (1882).
sentence_20: In 1836, Verne went on to École Saint‑Stanislas, a Catholic school suiting the pious religious tastes of his father.
sentence_21: Verne quickly distinguished himself in mémoire (recitation from memory), geography, Greek, Latin, and singing.
sentence_22: In the same year, 1836, Pierre Verne bought a vacation house at 29 Rue des Réformés in the village of Chantenay (now part of Nantes) on the Loire River.
sentence_23: In his brief memoir Souvenirs d'enfance et de jeunesse (Memories of Childhood and Youth, 1890), Verne recalled a deep fascination with the river and with the many [[Merchant_vessel|merchant vessels]] navigating it.
sentence_24: He also took vacations at [[Brains,_Loire-Atlantique|Brains]], in the house of his uncle Prudent Allotte, a retired shipowner, who had gone around the world and served as mayor of Brains from 1828 to 1837.
sentence_25: Verne took joy in playing interminable rounds of the [[Game_of_the_Goose|Game of the Goose]] with his uncle, and both the game and his uncle's name would be memorialized in two late novels (The Will of an Eccentric (1900) and [[Robur_the_Conqueror|Robur the Conqueror]] (1886), respectively).
sentence_26: Legend has it that in 1839, at the age of 11, Verne secretly procured a spot as [[Cabin_boy|cabin boy]] on the three-mast ship Coralie with the intention of traveling to the Indies and bringing back a coral necklace for his cousin Caroline.
sentence_27: The evening the ship set out for the Indies, it stopped first at [[Paimboeuf|Paimboeuf]] where Pierre Verne arrived just in time to catch his son and make him promise to travel "only in his imagination".
sentence_28: It is now known that the legend is an exaggerated tale invented by Verne's first biographer, his niece Marguerite Allotte de la Füye, though it may have been inspired by a real incident.
sentence_29: In 1840, the Vernes moved again to a large apartment at No.
sentence_30: 6 Rue Jean-Jacques-Rousseau, where the family's youngest child, Marie, was born in 1842.
sentence_31: In the same year Verne entered another religious school, the Petit Séminaire de Saint-Donatien, as a lay student.
sentence_32: His unfinished novel Un prêtre en 1839 (A Priest in 1839), written in his teens and the earliest of his prose works to survive, describes the seminary in disparaging terms.
sentence_33: From 1844 to 1846, Verne and his brother were enrolled in the Lycée Royal (now the Lycée Georges-Clemenceau) in Nantes.
sentence_34: After finishing classes in rhetoric and philosophy, he took the baccalauréat at [[Rennes|Rennes]] and received the grade "Good Enough" on 29 July 1846.
sentence_35: By 1847, when Verne was 19, he had taken seriously to writing long works in the style of [[Victor_Hugo|Victor Hugo]], beginning Un prêtre en 1839 and seeing two verse tragedies, Alexandre VI and La Conspiration des poudres (The Gunpowder Plot), to completion.
sentence_36: However, his father took it for granted that Verne, being the firstborn son of the family, would not attempt to make money in literature but would instead inherit the family law practice.
sentence_37: In 1847, Verne's father sent him to Paris, primarily to begin his studies in [[Law_school|law school]], and secondarily (according to family legend) to distance him temporarily from Nantes.
sentence_38: His cousin Caroline, with whom he was in love, was married on 27 April 1847, to Émile Dezaunay, a man of 40, with whom she would have five children.
sentence_39: After a short stay in Paris, where he passed first-year law exams, Verne returned to Nantes for his father's help in preparing for the second year.
sentence_40: (Provincial law students were in that era required to go to Paris to take exams.)
sentence_41: While in Nantes, he met Rose Herminie Arnaud Grossetière, a young woman one year his senior, and fell intensely in love with her.
sentence_42: He wrote and dedicated some thirty poems to her, including La Fille de l'air (The Daughter of Air), which describes her as "blonde and enchanting / winged and transparent".
sentence_43: His passion seems to have been reciprocated, at least for a short time, but Grossetière's parents frowned upon the idea of their daughter marrying a young student of uncertain future.
sentence_44: They married her instead to Armand Terrien de la Haye, a rich landowner ten years her senior, on 19 July 1848.
sentence_45: The sudden marriage sent Verne into deep frustration.
sentence_46: He wrote a hallucinatory letter to his mother, apparently composed in a state of half-drunkenness, in which under pretext of a dream he described his misery.
sentence_47: This requited but aborted love affair seems to have permanently marked the author and his work, and his novels include a significant number of young women married against their will (Gérande in [[Master_Zacharius|Master Zacharius]] (1854), Sava in [[Mathias_Sandorf|Mathias Sandorf]] (1885), Ellen in [[A_Floating_City|A Floating City]] (1871), etc.), to such an extent that the scholar Christian Chelebourg attributed the recurring theme to a "Herminie complex".
sentence_48: The incident also led Verne to bear a grudge against his birthplace and Nantes society, which he criticized in his poem La sixième ville de France (The Sixth City of France).
sentence_49: In July 1848, Verne left Nantes again for Paris, where his father intended him to finish law studies and take up law as a profession.
sentence_50: He obtained permission from his father to rent a furnished apartment at 24 Rue de l'Ancienne-Comédie, which he shared with Édouard Bonamy, another student of Nantes origin.
sentence_51: (On his 1847 Paris visit, Verne had stayed at 2 Rue Thérèse, the house of his aunt Charuel, on the Butte Saint-Roch.)
sentence_52: Verne arrived in Paris during a time of political upheaval: the [[French_Revolution_of_1848|French Revolution of 1848]].
sentence_53: In February, [[Louis_Philippe_I|Louis Philippe I]] had been overthrown and had fled; on 24 February, a provisional government of the [[French_Second_Republic|French Second Republic]] took power, but political demonstrations continued, and social tension remained.
sentence_54: In June, barricades went up in Paris, and the government sent Louis-Eugène Cavaignac to crush the insurrection.
sentence_55: Verne entered the city shortly before the election of [[Napoleon_III|Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte]] as the first president of the Republic, a state of affairs that would last until the French coup of 1851.
sentence_56: In a letter to his family, Verne described the bombarded state of the city after the recent [[June_Days_uprising|June Days uprising]] but assured them that the anniversary of [[Bastille_Day|Bastille Day]] had gone by without any significant conflict.
sentence_57: Verne used his family connections to make an entrance into Paris society.
sentence_58: His uncle Francisque de Chatêaubourg introduced him into [[Literary_salon|literary salons]], and Verne particularly frequented those of Mme de Barrère, a friend of his mother's.
sentence_59: While continuing his law studies, he fed his passion for the theater, writing numerous plays.
sentence_60: Verne later recalled: "I was greatly under the influence of [[Victor_Hugo|Victor Hugo]], indeed, very excited by reading and re-reading his works.
sentence_61: At that time I could have recited by heart whole pages of [[The_Hunchback_of_Notre-Dame|Notre Dame de Paris]], but it was his dramatic work that most influenced me."
sentence_62: Another source of creative stimulation came from a neighbor: living on the same floor in the Rue de l'Ancienne-Comédie apartment house was a young composer, [[Aristide_Hignard|Aristide Hignard]], with whom Verne soon became good friends, and Verne wrote several texts for Hignard to set as chansons.
sentence_63: During this period, Verne's letters to his parents primarily focused on expenses and on a suddenly appearing series of violent [[Abdominal_pain|stomach cramps]], the first of many he would suffer from during his life.
sentence_64: (Modern scholars have hypothesized that he suffered from [[Colitis|colitis]]; Verne believed the illness to have been inherited from his mother's side.)
sentence_65: Rumors of an outbreak of [[Cholera|cholera]] in March 1849 exacerbated these medical concerns.
sentence_66: Yet another health problem would strike in 1851 when Verne suffered the first of four attacks of [[Facial_nerve_paralysis|facial paralysis]].
sentence_67: These attacks, rather than being [[Psychosomatic|psychosomatic]], were due to an inflammation in the [[Middle_ear|middle ear]], though this cause remained unknown to Verne during his life.
sentence_68: In the same year, Verne was required to enlist in the French military, but the sortition process spared him, to his great relief.
sentence_69: He wrote to his father: "You should already know, dear papa, what I think of the military life, and of these domestic servants in livery.
sentence_70: … You have to abandon all dignity to perform such functions."
sentence_71: Verne's strong antiwar sentiments, to the dismay of his father, would remain steadfast throughout his life.
sentence_72: Though writing profusely and frequenting the salons, Verne diligently pursued his law studies and graduated with a licence en droit in January 1851.
sentence_73: Thanks to his visits to salons, Verne came into contact in 1849 with [[Alexandre_Dumas|Alexandre Dumas]] through the mutual acquaintance of a celebrated [[Chirologist|chirologist]] of the time, the Chevalier d'Arpentigny.
sentence_74: Verne became close friends with Dumas' son, [[Alexandre_Dumas_fils|Alexandre Dumas fils]], and showed him a manuscript for a stage comedy, Les Pailles rompues (The Broken Straws).
sentence_75: The two young men revised the play together, and Dumas, through arrangements with his father, had it produced by the [[Opéra-National|Opéra-National]] at the [[Théâtre_Historique|Théâtre Historique]] in Paris, opening on 12 June 1850.
sentence_76: In 1851, Verne met with a fellow writer from Nantes, [[Pierre-Michel-François_Chevalier|Pierre-Michel-François Chevalier]] (known as "Pitre-Chevalier"), the editor-in-chief of the magazine [[Musée_des_familles|Musée des familles]] (The Family Museum).
sentence_77: Pitre-Chevalier was looking for articles about geography, history, science, and technology, and was keen to make sure that the educational component would be made accessible to large popular audiences using a straightforward prose style or an engaging fictional story.
sentence_78: Verne, with his delight in diligent research, especially in geography, was a natural for the job.
sentence_79: Verne first offered him a short [[Historical_fiction|historical]] [[Adventure_story|adventure story]], [[A_Drama_in_Mexico|The First Ships of the Mexican Navy]], written in the style of [[James_Fenimore_Cooper|James Fenimore Cooper]], whose novels had deeply influenced him.
sentence_80: Pitre-Chevalier published it in July 1851, and in the same year published a second short story by Verne, [[A_Voyage_in_a_Balloon|A Voyage in a Balloon]] (August 1851).
sentence_81: The latter story, with its combination of adventurous narrative, travel themes, and detailed historical research, would later be described by Verne as "the first indication of the line of novel that I was destined to follow".
sentence_82: Dumas fils put Verne in contact with Jules Seveste, a stage director who had taken over the directorship of the Théâtre Historique and renamed it the [[Théâtre_Lyrique|Théâtre Lyrique]].
sentence_83: Seveste offered Verne the job of secretary of the theater, with little or no salary attached.
sentence_84: Verne accepted, using the opportunity to write and produce several comic operas written in collaboration with Hignard and the prolific [[Libretto|librettist]] [[Michel_Carré|Michel Carré]].
sentence_85: To celebrate his employment at the Théâtre Lyrique, Verne joined with ten friends to found a bachelors' dining club, the Onze-sans-femme (Eleven Bachelors).
sentence_86: For some time, Verne's father pressed him to abandon his writing and begin a business as a lawyer.
sentence_87: However, Verne argued in his letters that he could only find success in literature.
sentence_88: The pressure to plan for a secure future in law reached its climax in January 1852, when his father offered Verne his own Nantes law practice.
sentence_89: Faced with this ultimatum, Verne decided conclusively to continue his literary life and refuse the job, writing: "Am I not right to follow my own instincts?
sentence_90: It's because I know who I am that I realize what I can be one day."
sentence_91: Meanwhile, Verne was spending much time at the [[Bibliothèque_nationale_de_France|Bibliothèque nationale de France]], conducting research for his stories and feeding his passion for science and recent discoveries, especially in geography.
sentence_92: It was in this period that Verne met the illustrious geographer and explorer [[Jacques_Arago|Jacques Arago]], who continued to travel extensively despite his blindness (he had lost his sight completely in 1837).
sentence_93: The two men became good friends, and Arago's innovative and witty accounts of his travels led Verne toward a newly developing genre of literature: that of [[Travel_writing|travel writing]].
sentence_94: In 1852, two new pieces from Verne appeared in the Musée des familles: [[Martin_Paz|Martin Paz]], a [[Novella|novella]] set in [[Lima|Lima]], which Verne wrote in 1851 and published 10 July through 11 August 1852, and Les Châteaux en Californie, ou, Pierre qui roule n'amasse pas mousse (The Castles in California, or, A Rolling Stone Gathers No Moss), a one-act comedy full of racy double entendres.
sentence_95: In April and May 1854, the magazine published Verne's short story [[Master_Zacharius|Master Zacharius]], an [[E._T._A._Hoffmann|E.
sentence_96: T. A. Hoffmann]]-like fantasy featuring a sharp condemnation of scientific [[Hubris|hubris]] and ambition, followed soon afterward by [[A_Winter_Amid_the_Ice|A Winter Amid the Ice]], a polar adventure story whose themes closely anticipated many of Verne's novels.
sentence_97: The Musée also published some nonfiction [[Popular_science|popular science]] articles which, though unsigned, are generally attributed to Verne.
sentence_98: Verne's work for the magazine was cut short in 1856 when he had a serious quarrel with Pitre-Chevalier and refused to continue contributing (a refusal he would maintain until 1863, when Pitre-Chevalier died, and the magazine went to new editorship).
sentence_99: While writing stories and articles for Pitre-Chevalier, Verne began to form the idea of inventing a new kind of novel, a "Roman de la Science" ("novel of science"), which would allow him to incorporate large amounts of the factual information he so enjoyed researching in the Bibliothèque.
sentence_100: He is said to have discussed the project with the elder Alexandre Dumas, who had tried something similar with an unfinished novel, Isaac Laquedem, and who enthusiastically encouraged Verne's project.
sentence_101: At the end of 1854, another outbreak of cholera led to the death of Jules Seveste, Verne's employer at the Théâtre Lyrique and by then a good friend.
sentence_102: Though his contract only held him to a further year of service, Verne remained connected to the theater for several years after Seveste's death, seeing additional productions to fruition.
sentence_103: He also continued to write plays and musical comedies, most of which were not performed.
sentence_104: In May 1856, Verne traveled to [[Amiens|Amiens]] to be the [[Best_man|best man]] at the wedding of a Nantes friend, Auguste Lelarge, to an Amiens woman named Aimée du Fraysne de Viane.
sentence_105: Verne, invited to stay with the bride's family, took to them warmly, befriending the entire household and finding himself increasingly attracted to the bride's sister, Honorine Anne Hébée Morel (née du Fraysne de Viane), a widow aged 26 with two young children.
sentence_106: Hoping to find a secure source of income, as well as a chance to court Morel in earnest, he jumped at her brother's offer to go into business with a [[Broker|broker]].
sentence_107: Verne's father was initially dubious but gave in to his son's requests for approval in November 1856.
sentence_108: With his financial situation finally looking promising, Verne won the favor of Morel and her family, and the couple were married on 10 January 1857.
sentence_109: Verne plunged into his new business obligations, leaving his work at the Théâtre Lyrique and taking up a full-time job as an agent de change on the Paris Bourse, where he became the associate of the broker Fernand Eggly.
sentence_110: Verne woke up early each morning so that he would have time to write, before going to the Bourse for the day's work; in the rest of his spare time, he continued to consort with the Onze-Sans-Femme club (all eleven of its "bachelors" had by this time gotten married).
sentence_111: He also continued to frequent the Bibliothèque to do scientific and historical research, much of which he copied onto notecards for future use—a system he would continue for the rest of his life.
sentence_112: According to the recollections of a colleague, Verne "did better in repartee than in business".
sentence_113: In July 1858, Verne and Aristide Hignard seized an opportunity offered by Hignard's brother: a sea voyage, at no charge, from [[Bordeaux|Bordeaux]] to [[Liverpool|Liverpool]] and Scotland.
sentence_114: The journey, Verne's first trip outside France, deeply impressed him, and upon his return to Paris he fictionalized his recollections to form the backbone of a semi-autobiographical novel, [[Backwards_to_Britain|Backwards to Britain]] (written in the autumn and winter of 1859–1860 and not published until 1989).
sentence_115: A second complimentary voyage in 1861 took Hignard and Verne to [[Stockholm|Stockholm]], from where they traveled to [[Oslo|Christiania]] and through Telemark.
sentence_116: Verne left Hignard in Denmark to return in haste to Paris, but missed the birth on 3 August 1861 of his only biological son, [[Michel_Verne|Michel]].
sentence_117: Meanwhile, Verne continued work on the idea of a "Roman de la Science", which he developed in a rough draft, inspired, according to his recollections, by his "love for maps and the great explorers of the world".
sentence_118: It took shape as a story of travel across Africa and would eventually become his first published novel, Five Weeks in a Balloon.
sentence_119: In 1862, through their mutual acquaintance Alfred de Bréhat, Verne came into contact with the publisher Pierre-Jules Hetzel, and submitted to him the manuscript of his developing novel, then called Voyage en Ballon.
sentence_120: Hetzel, already the publisher of [[Honoré_de_Balzac|Honoré de Balzac]], [[George_Sand|George Sand]], [[Victor_Hugo|Victor Hugo]], and other well-known authors, had long been planning to launch a high-quality family magazine in which entertaining fiction would combine with scientific education.
sentence_121: He saw Verne, with his demonstrated inclination toward scrupulously researched adventure stories, as an ideal contributor for such a magazine, and accepted the novel, giving Verne suggestions for improvement.
sentence_122: Verne made the proposed revisions within two weeks and returned to Hetzel with the final draft, now titled Five Weeks in a Balloon.
sentence_123: It was published by Hetzel on 31 January 1863.
sentence_124: To secure his services for the planned magazine, to be called the Magasin d'Éducation et de Récréation (Magazine of Education and Recreation), Hetzel also drew up a long-term contract in which Verne would give him three volumes of text per year, each of which Hetzel would buy outright for a flat fee.
sentence_125: Verne, finding both a steady salary and a sure outlet for writing at last, accepted immediately.
sentence_126: For the rest of his lifetime, most of his novels would be serialized in Hetzel's Magasin before their appearance in book form, beginning with his second novel for Hetzel, [[The_Adventures_of_Captain_Hatteras|The Adventures of Captain Hatteras]] (1864–65).
sentence_127: When The Adventures of Captain Hatteras was published in book form in 1866, Hetzel publicly announced his literary and educational ambitions for Verne's novels by saying in a preface that Verne's works would form a novel sequence called the [[Voyages_extraordinaires|Voyages extraordinaires]] (Extraordinary Voyages or Extraordinary Journeys), and that Verne's aim was "to outline all the geographical, geological, physical, and astronomical knowledge amassed by modern science and to recount, in an entertaining and picturesque format that is his own, the history of the universe".
sentence_128: Late in life, Verne confirmed that this commission had become the running theme of his novels: "My object has been to depict the earth, and not the earth alone, but the universe… And I have tried at the same time to realize a very high ideal of beauty of style.
sentence_129: It is said that there can't be any style in a novel of adventure, but it isn't true."
sentence_130: However, he also noted that the project was extremely ambitious: "Yes!
sentence_131: But the Earth is very large, and life is very short!
sentence_132: In order to leave a completed work behind, one would need to live to be at least 100 years old!"
sentence_133: Hetzel influenced many of Verne's novels directly, especially in the first few years of their collaboration, for Verne was initially so happy to find a publisher that he agreed to almost all of the changes Hetzel suggested.
sentence_134: For example, when Hetzel disapproved of the original climax of Captain Hatteras, including the death of the title character, Verne wrote an entirely new conclusion in which Hatteras survived.
sentence_135: Hetzel also rejected Verne's next submission, Paris in the Twentieth Century, believing its pessimistic view of the future and its condemnation of technological progress were too subversive for a family magazine.
sentence_136: (The manuscript, believed lost for some time after Verne's death, was finally published in 1994.)
sentence_137: The relationship between publisher and writer changed significantly around 1869 when Verne and Hetzel were brought into conflict over the manuscript for [[Twenty_Thousand_Leagues_Under_the_Sea|Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea]].
sentence_138: Verne had initially conceived of the submariner [[Captain_Nemo|Captain Nemo]] as a Polish scientist whose acts of vengeance were directed against the Russians who had killed his family during the [[January_Uprising|January uprising]].
sentence_139: Hetzel, not wanting to alienate the lucrative Russian market for Verne's books, demanded that Nemo be made an enemy of the [[Slave_trade|slave trade]], a situation that would make him an unambiguous hero.
sentence_140: Verne, after fighting vehemently against the change, finally invented a compromise in which Nemo's past is left mysterious.
sentence_141: After this disagreement, Verne became notably cooler in his dealings with Hetzel, taking suggestions into consideration but often rejecting them outright.
sentence_142: From that point, Verne published two or more volumes a year.
sentence_143: The most successful of these are: Voyage au centre de la Terre ([[Journey_to_the_Center_of_the_Earth|Journey to the Center of the Earth]], 1864); De la Terre à la Lune ([[From_the_Earth_to_the_Moon|From the Earth to the Moon]], 1865); Vingt mille lieues sous les mers ([[Twenty_Thousand_Leagues_Under_the_Sea|Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea]], 1869); and Le tour du monde en quatre-vingts jours ([[Around_the_World_in_Eighty_Days|Around the World in Eighty Days]]), which first appeared in Le Temps in 1872.
sentence_144: Verne could now live on his writings, but most of his wealth came from the stage adaptations of Le tour du monde en quatre-vingts jours (1874) and [[Michael_Strogoff|Michel Strogoff]] (1876), which he wrote with [[Adolphe_d'Ennery|Adolphe d'Ennery]].
sentence_145: In 1867, Verne bought a small boat, the Saint-Michel, which he successively replaced with the Saint-Michel II and the Saint-Michel III as his financial situation improved.
sentence_146: On board the Saint-Michel III, he sailed around Europe.
sentence_147: After his first novel, most of his stories were first serialised in the Magazine d'Éducation et de Récréation, a Hetzel biweekly publication, before being published in book form.
sentence_148: His brother Paul contributed to 40th French climbing of the Mont-Blanc and a collection of short stories – Doctor Ox – in 1874.
sentence_149: Verne became wealthy and famous.
sentence_150: Meanwhile, Michel Verne married an actress against his father's wishes, had two children by an underage mistress and buried himself in debts.
sentence_151: The relationship between father and son improved as Michel grew older.
sentence_152: Though he was raised Catholic, Verne became a deist in his later years, from about 1870 onward.
sentence_153: Some scholars believe his deist philosophy is reflected in his novels, as they often involve the notion of God or [[Divine_providence|divine providence]] but rarely mention the concept of Christ.
sentence_154: On 9 March 1886, as Verne was coming home, his twenty-six-year-old nephew, Gaston, shot at him twice with a [[Pistol|pistol]].
sentence_155: The first bullet missed, but the second one entered Verne's left leg, giving him a permanent limp that could not be overcome.
sentence_156: This incident was hushed up in the media, but Gaston spent the rest of his life in a [[Lunatic_asylum|mental asylum]].
sentence_157: After the death of both his mother and Hetzel, Jules Verne began publishing darker works.
sentence_158: In 1888, Verne entered politics and was elected town councilor of [[Amiens|Amiens]], where he championed several improvements and served for fifteen years.
sentence_159: Verne was made a Chevalier de la [[Legion_of_Honour|Légion d'honneur]] in 1870.
sentence_160: He was promoted to an Officier de la Légion d'honneur in 1892.
sentence_161: On 24 March 1905, while ill with [[Diabetes|diabetes]], Verne died at his home in [[Amiens|Amiens]], 44 Boulevard Longueville (now Boulevard Jules-Verne).
sentence_162: His son, Michel Verne, oversaw the publication of the novels [[Invasion_of_the_Sea|Invasion of the Sea]] and [[The_Lighthouse_at_the_End_of_the_World|The Lighthouse at the End of the World]] after Jules's death.
sentence_163: The Voyages extraordinaires series continued for several years afterwards at the same rate of two volumes a year.
sentence_164: It was later discovered that Michel Verne had made extensive changes in these stories, and the original versions were eventually published at the end of the 20th century by the Jules Verne Society (Société Jules Verne).
sentence_165: In 1919, Michel Verne published [[The_Barsac_Mission|The Barsac Mission]] ([[French_language|French]]: L'Étonnante Aventure de la Mission Barsac), whose original drafts contained references to [[Esperanto|Esperanto]], a language that his father had been very interested in.
sentence_166: In 1989, Verne's great-grandson discovered his ancestor's as-yet-unpublished novel Paris in the Twentieth Century, which was subsequently published in 1994.
