sentence_5: James Earl Carter Jr. (born October 1, 1924) is an American politician and philanthropist who served as the 39th [[President_of_the_United_States|president of the United States]] from 1977 to 1981.
sentence_6: A member of the [[Democratic_Party_(United_States)|Democratic Party]], he previously served as a [[Georgia_State_Senate|Georgia State Senator]] from 1963 to 1967 and as the 76th [[List_of_governors_of_Georgia|governor of Georgia]] from 1971 to 1975.
sentence_7: Since leaving the presidency, Carter has remained engaged in political and social projects as a private citizen.
sentence_8: In 2002, he was awarded the [[Nobel_Peace_Prize|Nobel Peace Prize]] for his work in co-founding the [[Carter_Center|Carter Center]].
sentence_9: Raised in [[Plains,_Georgia|Plains, Georgia]], Carter graduated from the [[United_States_Naval_Academy|United States Naval Academy]] in 1946 with a [[Bachelor_of_Science|Bachelor of Science]] degree and joined the [[United_States_Navy|United States Navy]], where he served on [[Submarine|submarines]].
sentence_10: After the death of his father in 1953, Carter left his naval career and returned home to Georgia to take up the reins of his family's peanut-growing business.
sentence_11: Carter inherited comparatively little due to his father's forgiveness of debts and the division of the estate among the children.
sentence_12: Nevertheless, his ambition to expand and grow the Carters' peanut business was fulfilled.
sentence_13: During this period, Carter was motivated to oppose the political climate of [[Racial_segregation_in_the_United_States|racial segregation]] and support the growing [[Civil_rights_movement|civil rights movement]].
sentence_14: He became an activist within the [[Democratic_Party_(United_States)|Democratic Party]].
sentence_15: From 1963 to 1967, Carter served in the [[Georgia_State_Senate|Georgia State Senate]], and in [[1970_Georgia_gubernatorial_election|1970]], he was elected as [[Governor_of_Georgia|Governor of Georgia]], defeating former Governor [[Carl_Sanders|Carl Sanders]] in the Democratic primary on an anti-segregation platform advocating [[Affirmative_action|affirmative action]] for ethnic minorities.
sentence_16: Carter remained as governor until 1975.
sentence_17: Despite being a [[Dark_horse|dark-horse candidate]] who was little known outside of [[Georgia_(U.S._state)|Georgia]] at the start of the campaign, Carter won the [[Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries,_1976|1976 Democratic presidential nomination]].
sentence_18: In the [[1976_United_States_presidential_election|general election]], Carter ran as an outsider and narrowly defeated incumbent [[Republican_Party_(United_States)|Republican]] President [[Gerald_Ford|Gerald Ford]].
sentence_19: On his second day in office, Carter [[Federal_pardons_in_the_United_States|pardoned]] all the Vietnam War [[Draft_evasion|draft evaders]] by issuing [[Proclamation_4483|Proclamation 4483]].
sentence_20: During Carter's term as president, two new cabinet-level departments, the [[United_States_Department_of_Energy|Department of Energy]] and the [[United_States_Department_of_Education|Department of Education]], were established.
sentence_21: He established a [[Energy_policy_of_the_United_States|national energy policy]] that included conservation, price control, and new technology.
sentence_22: In foreign affairs, Carter pursued the [[Camp_David_Accords|Camp David Accords]], the [[Panama_Canal_Treaties|Panama Canal Treaties]], the second round of Strategic Arms Limitation Talks (SALT II), and the return of the [[Panama_Canal_Zone|Panama Canal Zone]] to [[Panama|Panama]].
sentence_23: On the economic front, he confronted [[Stagflation|stagflation]], a persistent combination of high inflation, high unemployment and slow growth.
sentence_24: The end of his presidential tenure was marked by the 1979–1981 [[Iran_hostage_crisis|Iran hostage crisis]], the [[1979_energy_crisis|1979 energy crisis]], the [[Three_Mile_Island_nuclear_accident|Three Mile Island nuclear accident]], and the [[Soviet_invasion_of_Afghanistan|Soviet invasion of Afghanistan]].
sentence_25: In response to the invasion, Carter escalated the [[Cold_War|Cold War]] when he ended [[Détente|détente]], imposed [[United_States_grain_embargo_against_the_Soviet_Union|a grain embargo against the Soviets]], enunciated the [[Carter_Doctrine|Carter Doctrine]], and led a [[1980_Summer_Olympics_boycott|1980 Summer Olympics boycott]] in Moscow.
sentence_26: In 1980, Carter faced a challenge from Senator [[Ted_Kennedy|Ted Kennedy]] in the primaries, but he won re-nomination at the [[1980_Democratic_National_Convention|1980 Democratic National Convention]].
sentence_27: Carter lost the [[1980_United_States_presidential_election|general election]] to [[Republican_Party_(United_States)|Republican]] nominee [[Ronald_Reagan|Ronald Reagan]] in an electoral landslide.
sentence_28: He is the only president in American history to serve a full term of office and never appoint a justice to the Supreme Court.
sentence_29: [[Historical_rankings_of_presidents_of_the_United_States|Polls of historians and political scientists]] usually rank Carter as a below-average president.
sentence_30: Carter's activities since leaving the presidency have been viewed more favorably than his presidency itself.
sentence_31: In 1982, Carter established the Carter Center to promote and expand human rights.
sentence_32: He has traveled extensively to conduct peace negotiations, monitor elections, and advance disease prevention and [[Eradication_of_infectious_diseases|eradication]] in developing nations.
sentence_33: Carter is considered a key figure in the [[Habitat_for_Humanity|Habitat for Humanity]] charity.
sentence_34: He has written [[Bibliography_of_Jimmy_Carter|over 30 books]] ranging from political memoirs to poetry while continuing to actively comment on ongoing American and global affairs, such as the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
sentence_35: The earliest-serving of the five [[Living_presidents_of_the_United_States|living U.S. presidents]], Carter is the [[List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_age|longest-lived president]], the longest-retired president, the first to live 40 years after his inauguration, and the first to live beyond the age of 95.
sentence_36: James Earl Carter Jr. was born on October 1, 1924, at the Wise Sanitarium (now the [[Lillian_G._Carter_Nursing_Center|Lillian G. Carter Nursing Center]]) in [[Plains,_Georgia|Plains, Georgia]], a hospital where his mother was employed as a registered nurse.
sentence_37: Carter was the first U.S. president to be born in a hospital.
sentence_38: He was the eldest son of [[Lillian_Gordy_Carter|Bessie Lillian]] (née Gordy) and [[James_Earl_Carter_Sr.|James Earl Carter Sr.]] Carter is a descendant of [[English_people|English]] immigrant Thomas Carter, who settled in [[Virginia|Virginia]] in 1635.
sentence_39: Numerous generations of Carters lived as cotton farmers in Georgia.
sentence_40: Carter is also a descendant of [[Thomas_Cornell_(settler)|Thomas Cornell]], an ancestor of [[Cornell_University|Cornell University]]'s founder, and is distantly related to [[Richard_Nixon|Richard Nixon]] and [[Bill_Gates|Bill Gates]].
sentence_41: Plains was a boomtown of 600 people at the time of Carter's birth.
sentence_42: Carter's father was a successful local businessman, who ran a [[General_store|general store]], and was an investor in farmland.
sentence_43: Carter's father had previously served as a reserve second lieutenant in the U.S. Army [[Quartermaster_Corps_(United_States_Army)|Quartermaster Corps]] during [[World_War_I|World War I]].
sentence_44: The family moved several times during Carter Jr.'s infancy.
sentence_45: The Carters settled on a dirt road in nearby [[Archery,_Georgia|Archery]], which was almost entirely populated by impoverished [[African_American|African American]] families.
sentence_46: They eventually had three more children: [[Gloria_Carter_Spann|Gloria]], [[Ruth_Carter_Stapleton|Ruth]], and [[Billy_Carter|Billy]].
sentence_47: Carter got along well with his parents, although his mother worked long hours and was often absent in his childhood.
sentence_48: Although Earl was staunchly pro-[[Racial_segregation_in_the_United_States|segregation]], he allowed his son to befriend the black farmhands' children.
sentence_49: Carter was an enterprising teenager who was given his own acre of Earl's farmland where he grew, packaged, and sold peanuts.
sentence_50: He also rented out a section of tenant housing that he had purchased.
sentence_51: Carter attended Plains High School from 1937 to 1941.
sentence_52: By that time, Archery and Plains had been impoverished by the [[Great_Depression_in_the_United_States|Great Depression]], but the family benefited from [[New_Deal|New Deal]] farming subsidies, and Earl took a position as a community leader.
sentence_53: Young Jimmy was a diligent student with a fondness for reading.
sentence_54: A popular anecdote holds that he was passed over for [[Valedictorian|valedictorian]] after he and his friends skipped school to venture downtown in a [[Hot_rod|hot rod]].
sentence_55: Carter's truancy was mentioned in a local newspaper, although it is not clear he would have otherwise been valedictorian.
sentence_56: Carter's teacher, Julia Coleman, was an especially strong influence.
sentence_57: As an adolescent, Carter played on the Plains High School basketball team; he also joined the [[National_FFA_Organization|Future Farmers of America]] and developed a lifelong interest in woodworking.
sentence_58: Carter had long dreamed of attending the [[United_States_Naval_Academy|U.S.
sentence_59: Naval Academy]].
sentence_60: In 1941, he started undergraduate coursework in engineering at Georgia Southwestern College in nearby Americus, Georgia.
sentence_61: The following year, he transferred to the [[Georgia_Institute_of_Technology|Georgia Institute of Technology]] in Atlanta, and he earned admission to the Naval Academy in 1943.
sentence_62: He was a good student but was seen as reserved and quiet, in contrast to the academy's culture of aggressive hazing of freshmen.
sentence_63: While at the academy, Carter fell in love with Rosalynn Smith, a friend of his sister Ruth.
sentence_64: The two married shortly after his graduation in 1946.
sentence_65: He was a [[Sprint_football|sprint football]] player for the [[Navy_Midshipmen|Navy Midshipmen]].
sentence_66: Carter graduated 60th out of 820 midshipmen in the class of 1946 with a [[Bachelor_of_Science|Bachelor of Science]] degree and was commissioned as an [[Ensign_(rank)|ensign]].
sentence_67: From 1946 to 1953, Carter and Rosalynn lived in Virginia, Hawaii, Connecticut, New York and California, during his deployments in the Atlantic and [[US_Pacific_Fleet|Pacific fleets]].
sentence_68: In 1948, he began officer training for submarine duty and served aboard [[USS_Pomfret_(SS-391)|USS Pomfret]].
sentence_69: He was promoted to [[Lieutenant_(junior_grade)|lieutenant junior grade]] in 1949.
sentence_70: In 1951 he became attached to the diesel/electric USS K-1, (a.k.a. [[USS_Barracuda_(SSK-1)|USS Barracuda]]), qualified for command, and served in several duties including Executive Officer.
sentence_71: In 1952, Carter began an association with the Navy's fledgling [[Nuclear_submarine|nuclear submarine]] program, then led by Captain [[Hyman_G._Rickover|Hyman G. Rickover]].
sentence_72: Rickover's demands on his men and machines were legendary, and Carter later said that, next to his parents, Rickover was the greatest influence on his life.
sentence_73: He was sent to the Naval Reactors Branch of the [[United_States_Atomic_Energy_Commission|Atomic Energy Commission]] in Washington, D.C. for three month temporary duty, while Rosalynn moved with their children to Schenectady, New York.
sentence_74: On December 12, 1952, an accident with the experimental NRX reactor at [[Atomic_Energy_of_Canada|Atomic Energy of Canada]]'s [[Chalk_River_Laboratories|Chalk River Laboratories]] caused a partial meltdown resulting in millions of liters of radioactive water flooding the reactor building's basement.
sentence_75: This left the reactor's core ruined.
sentence_76: Carter was ordered to Chalk River to lead a U.S. maintenance crew that joined other American and Canadian service personnel to assist in the shutdown of the reactor.
sentence_77: The painstaking process required each team member to don protective gear and be lowered individually into the reactor for a few minutes at a time, limiting their exposure to radioactivity while they disassembled the crippled reactor.
sentence_78: During and after his presidency, Carter said that his experience at Chalk River had shaped his views on atomic energy and led him to cease development of a [[Neutron_bomb|neutron bomb]].
sentence_79: In March 1953, Carter began nuclear power school, a six-month non-credit course covering nuclear power plant operation at [[Union_College|Union College]] in Schenectady.
sentence_80: His intent was to eventually work aboard [[USS_Seawolf_(SSN-575)|USS Seawolf]], which was planned to be one of the first two U.S. nuclear submarines.
sentence_81: However, he never had the opportunity to serve aboard a nuclear submarine.
sentence_82: Carter's father died two months before construction of Seawolf began, and Carter sought and obtained a release from active duty to enable him to take over the family peanut business.
sentence_83: Based on that limited training, in later years Carter would nonetheless refer to himself as a "nuclear physicist".
sentence_84: Deciding to leave Schenectady proved difficult.
sentence_85: Settling after moving so much, Rosalynn had grown comfortable with their life.
sentence_86: Returning to small-town life in Plains seemed "a monumental step backward," she said later.
sentence_87: On the other hand, Carter felt restricted by the rigidity of the military and yearned to assume a path more like his father's.
sentence_88: Carter left active duty on October 9, 1953.
sentence_89: He served in the inactive [[United_States_Navy_Reserve|Navy Reserve]] until 1961, and left the service with the rank of [[Lieutenant_(navy)|lieutenant]].
sentence_90: His awards included the [[American_Campaign_Medal|American Campaign Medal]], [[World_War_II_Victory_Medal_(United_States)|World War II Victory Medal]], [[China_Service_Medal|China Service Medal]], and [[National_Defense_Service_Medal|National Defense Service Medal]].
sentence_91: Earl Carter died a relatively wealthy man, having recently been elected to the [[Georgia_House_of_Representatives|Georgia House of Representatives]].
sentence_92: However, between his forgiveness of debts and the division of his wealth among heirs, his son Jimmy inherited comparatively little.
sentence_93: For a year, Jimmy, Rosalynn, and their three sons lived in [[Public_housing|public housing]] in Plains; Carter is the only U.S. president to have lived in subsidized housing before he took office.
sentence_94: Carter was knowledgeable in scientific and technological subjects, and he set out to expand the family's peanut-growing business.
sentence_95: The transition from Navy to agribusinessman was difficult because his first-year harvest failed due to drought; Carter was compelled to open several bank lines of credit to keep the farm afloat.
sentence_96: Meanwhile, he also took classes and read up on agriculture while Rosalynn learned accounting to manage the business's books.
sentence_97: Though they barely broke even the first year, the Carters grew the business and became quite successful.
sentence_98: Racial tension was inflamed in Plains by the 1954 [[Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States|U.S.
sentence_99: Supreme Court]] anti-segregation ruling in [[Brown_v._Board_of_Education|Brown v. Board of Education]].
sentence_100: Carter was in favor of racial tolerance and integration—at one point, the local [[Citizens'_Councils|White Citizens' Council]] boycotted his peanut warehouse when he refused to join them—but he often kept those feelings to himself to avoid making enemies.
sentence_101: By 1961 he was a prominent member of the community and the Baptist Church as well as chairman of the Sumter County school board, where he began to speak more loudly in favor of school integration.
sentence_102: A [[Georgia_Senate|state Senate]] seat was opened by the dissolution of Georgia's [[County_Unit_System|County Unit System]] in 1962; Carter announced his run for the seat 15 days before the election.
sentence_103: Rosalynn, who had an instinct for politics and organization, was instrumental to his campaign.
sentence_104: The initial results showed Carter losing, but this was the result of fraudulent voting orchestrated by Joe Hurst, the Democratic Party chairman in [[Quitman_County,_Georgia|Quitman County]], with the aid of the Quitman County sheriff.
sentence_105: Carter challenged the results; when fraud was confirmed, a new election was held, which he won.
sentence_106: The [[Civil_rights_movement|civil rights movement]] was well underway when Carter took office.
sentence_107: He and his family had become staunch [[John_F._Kennedy|John F. Kennedy]] supporters.
sentence_108: Beginning in 1962, the town of Americus was the site of mass beatings and incarcerations of black protesters, echoing similar unrest throughout the country.
sentence_109: Carter remained relatively quiet on the issue at first, even as it polarized much of the county, to avoid alienating his segregationist colleagues.
sentence_110: He did speak up on a few divisive issues, giving speeches against [[Literacy_tests|literacy tests]] and against a change to the Georgia Constitution which, he felt, implied a compulsion to practice religion.
sentence_111: At the time of [[Assassination_of_John_F._Kennedy|President Kennedy's assassination]], Carter was informed by a customer of his peanut business of the killing, prompting Carter to remove himself from work and sit alone.
sentence_112: Carter later called the assassination "the greatest blow that I had suffered since my father died."
sentence_113: Carter was a diligent legislator who took speed-reading courses to keep up with the workload.
sentence_114: Within two years, his connections landed him on the state Democratic Executive Committee, where he helped rewrite the state party's rules.
sentence_115: He became chairman of the West Central Georgia Planning and Development Commission, which oversaw the disbursement of federal and state grants for projects such as historic site restoration.
sentence_116: When [[Bo_Callaway|Bo Callaway]] was elected to the [[United_States_House_of_Representatives|U.S.
sentence_117: House of Representatives]] in November 1964, Carter immediately began planning to unseat him.
sentence_118: The two had previously clashed over which two-year college would be expanded to a four-year college program by the state; Carter wanted it to go to his alma mater, Georgia Southwestern College, but Callaway wanted the funding to go to downtown [[Columbus,_Georgia|Columbus]].
sentence_119: Carter saw Callaway, a Democrat who had recently switched to the [[Republican_Party_(United_States)|Republican Party]], as a rival who represented the inherited wealth and selfishness he despised in politics.
sentence_120: Carter was re-elected in 1964 to serve a second two-year term.
sentence_121: For a time in the State Senate, he chaired its Education Committee; he also sat on the Appropriations Committee toward the end of his second term.
sentence_122: Before his term ended he contributed to a bill expanding statewide education funding and getting Georgia Southwestern a four-year program.
sentence_123: He leveraged his regional planning work, giving speeches around the district to make himself more visible to potential voters.
sentence_124: The last day of the term, he announced his run for Congress.
sentence_125: See also: [[1966_Georgia_gubernatorial_election|1966 Georgia gubernatorial election]] and [[1970_Georgia_gubernatorial_election|1970 Georgia gubernatorial election]]
sentence_126: The race for [[Georgia's_3rd_congressional_district|Georgia's 3rd congressional district]] in 1966 was shaken up in mid-May when the incumbent, Bo Callaway, dropped out and decided to run for Governor of Georgia instead.
sentence_127: Callaway had just switched from the Democratic Party to the Republican Party in 1964, and was a very strong candidate, despite being the first Republican to run for Governor of Georgia since 1876.
sentence_128: State Democrats panicked over the prospect of losing the governorship they had held since [[Reconstruction_Era|Reconstruction]].
sentence_129: Carter decided to run for governor himself.
sentence_130: In the Democratic primary he ran against the liberal former governor [[Ellis_Arnall|Ellis Arnall]] and the conservative segregationist [[Lester_Maddox|Lester Maddox]].
sentence_131: In a press conference he described his ideology as "Conservative, moderate, liberal and middle-of-the-road.
sentence_133: I believe I am a more complicated person than that."
sentence_134: He lost the Democratic primary, but drew enough votes as a third-place candidate to force Arnall into a [[Two-round_system|runoff election]] with Maddox.
sentence_135: Maddox narrowly won the runoff ballot over Arnall for the Democratic Party gubernatorial nomination.
sentence_136: In the general election, Callaway went on to win a plurality of the vote, but short of a 50 percent majority, state rules empowered the Georgia House of Representatives, which had a Democratic Party majority, to elect Maddox as governor.
sentence_137: The result was a sharp blow to Carter, who was left deeply in debt.
sentence_138: His attempt to wrest the race from Callaway had resulted in the unlikely election of the segregationist Maddox, which he considered an even worse outcome.
sentence_139: Carter returned to his agriculture business and, during the next four years, carefully planned his next campaign for governor in 1970.
sentence_140: This period was a spiritual turning point for Carter; he grew increasingly evangelical, undertaking several religious missions in other states.
sentence_141: Inspired by his sister Ruth and [[Modern_liberalism_in_the_United_States|liberal]] theologians such as [[Reinhold_Niebuhr|Reinhold Niebuhr]], he declared himself [[Born_again|Born again]], a growing movement in 1960s America.
sentence_142: His last child [[Amy_Carter|Amy]] was born during this time, on October 19, 1967.
sentence_143: Governor Maddox was constitutionally prohibited from seeking a second consecutive term as governor, and thus the liberal former governor, [[Carl_Sanders|Carl Sanders]], became Carter's main opponent in the 1970 Democratic primary.
sentence_144: Carter ran a more modern campaign this time around, employing printed graphics and statistical analysis.
sentence_145: Responding to poll data, Carter leaned more [[Conservatism_in_the_United_States|conservative]] than before.
sentence_146: He positioned himself as a [[Populism|populist]], quickly going negative against Sanders for his wealth (labeling him "Cufflinks Carl") and associating him with the national Democratic Party.
sentence_147: He accused Sanders of corruption, but when pressed by the media, could come up with no evidence.
sentence_148: Throughout the campaign, Carter sought both the black vote and the "Wallace vote," after the prominent segregationist [[George_Wallace|George Wallace]] of Alabama.
sentence_149: While he met with black figures such as [[Martin_Luther_King_Sr.|Martin Luther King Sr.]] and [[Andrew_Young|Andrew Young]], and visited many black-owned businesses, he also praised Wallace and promised to invite him to give a speech in Georgia.
sentence_150: He implied support or dislike of private schools, depending on the audience.
sentence_151: The appeal to racism became more blatant over time; Carter's senior campaign aides handed out a photograph of his opponent Sanders celebrating with black basketball players.
sentence_152: That September, Carter came ahead of Sanders in the first ballot by 49 to 38 percent, leading to a runoff.
sentence_153: The subsequent campaign grew even more bitter; despite his early support for civil rights, Carter's campaign criticized Sanders for supporting [[Martin_Luther_King_Jr.|Martin Luther King Jr.]] Carter won the runoff election with 60 percent of the vote—winning 7 percent of the black vote—and went on to win the general election easily over the Republican [[Hal_Suit|Hal Suit]], a local news anchor.
sentence_154: Once he was elected, Carter changed his tone, and began to speak against Georgia's racist politics.
sentence_155: [[Leroy_Johnson_(Georgia_politician)|Leroy Johnson]], a black state Senator, voiced his support for Carter, saying, "I understand why he ran that kind of ultra-conservative campaign.
sentence_157: I don't believe you can win this state without being a racist."
sentence_158: Carter was sworn in as the 76th Governor of Georgia on January 12, 1971.
sentence_159: He declared in his inaugural speech that "the time of racial discrimination is over.
sentence_160: ... No poor, rural, weak, or black person should ever have to bear the additional burden of being deprived of the opportunity for an education, a job or simple justice."
sentence_161: The crowd was reportedly shocked by this message, contrasting starkly with Georgia's political culture and particularly Carter's campaign.
sentence_162: The many segregationists who had supported Carter during the race felt betrayed.
sentence_163: [[Time_(magazine)|Time]] ran a story on the [[Progressivism_in_the_United_States|progressive]] "[[New_South|New South]]" governors elected that year in a May 1971 issue, featuring a cover illustration of Carter.
sentence_164: [[Lester_Maddox|Lester Maddox]], Carter's predecessor as governor, became [[Lieutenant_Governor_of_Georgia|lieutenant governor]].
sentence_165: Carter had endorsed Maddox, although the two did not campaign as a [[Ticket_(election)|ticket]].
sentence_166: The two found little common ground during their four years of service, often publicly feuding.
sentence_167: [[Richard_Russell_Jr.|Richard Russell Jr.]], then [[President_pro_tempore_of_the_United_States_Senate|President pro tempore of the United States Senate]], died in office during Carter's second week in office; the newly inaugurated governor appointed David H. Gambrell, state Democratic Party chair, to fill Russell's unexpired term in the Senate a week after Russell's death on February 1.
sentence_168: Carter was reluctant to engage in back-slapping and political favors, and the legislature found him frustrating to work with.
sentence_169: He looked to aggressively expand the governor's authority while reducing the complexity of the state government.
sentence_170: Therefore, he negotiated a bill allowing him to propose executive restructuring and to force a vote on it.
sentence_171: He implemented zero-based budgeting within state departments and added a Judicial Selection Commission to verify the credentials of judges appointed by the governor.
sentence_172: The reorganization plan was submitted in January 1972, but had a cool reception in the legislature.
sentence_173: But after two weeks of negotiations, it was passed at midnight on the last day of the session.
sentence_174: Ultimately he merged about 300 state agencies into 22—a fact he would emphasize in his presidential run—although it is disputed that there were any overall cost savings from doing so.
sentence_175: In an April 3, 1971, televised appearance, Carter was asked if he was in favor of a requirement that candidates for Governor and Lieutenant Governor of Georgia would have to run on the same ticket.
sentence_176: He replied, "I've never really thought we needed a lieutenant governor in Georgia.
sentence_177: The lieutenant governor is part of the executive branch of government and I've always felt—ever since I was in the state Senate—that the executive branches should be separate."
sentence_178: Carter later clarified he would not introduce an amendment to put such a restriction in place.
sentence_179: On July 8, 1971, during an appearance in [[Columbus,_Georgia|Columbus, Georgia]], Carter stated his intent to establish a Georgia Human Rights Council that would work toward solving issues within the state ahead of any potential violence.
sentence_180: In a July 13, 1971, news conference, Carter announced his ordering of department heads to reduce spending for the aid of preventing a $57 million deficit by the end of the 1972 fiscal year, specifying that each state department would be impacted and estimating that 5% more than revenue being taken in by the government would be lost if state departments continued full using allocated funds.
sentence_181: On January 13, 1972, Carter requested the state legislature provide funding for an Early Childhood Development Program along with prison reform programs and 48 million in pay taxes for nearly all state employees.
sentence_182: On March 1, 1972, Carter stated a possible usage of a special session of the General Assembly could take place in the event that the Justice Department opted to turn down any reapportionment plans by either the House or Senate.
sentence_183: On April 20, Carter issued the call for a special session for consideration of advisement for the usage of a three person judge federal panel for performance on four judicial reform measures.
sentence_184: In April 1972, Carter traveled to Latin and South America for a potential trade deal with Georgia.
sentence_185: Carter stated that he had met with [[President_of_Brazil|President of Brazil]] [[Emílio_Garrastazu_Médici|Emílio Garrastazu Médici]] and had been compared by some to the late President Kennedy.
sentence_186: Civil rights were a heartfelt priority for Carter.
sentence_187: He expanded the number of black state employees, judges, and board members.
sentence_188: He hired Rita Jackson Samuels, a black woman, to advise him on potential appointments.
sentence_189: He placed portraits of Martin Luther King Jr. and two other prominent black Georgians in the capitol building, even as the [[Ku_Klux_Klan|Ku Klux Klan]] picketed the unveiling ceremony.
sentence_190: Still, Carter tried to keep his conservative allies comfortable.
sentence_191: During a televised joint appearance with [[Governor_of_Florida|Governor of Florida]] [[Reubin_Askew|Reubin Askew]] on January 31, 1973, Carter stated he favored a constitutional amendment to ban busing for the purpose of expediting integration in schools.
sentence_192: He co-sponsored an anti-busing resolution with George Wallace at the 1971 National Governors Conference, which Carter also hosted.
sentence_193: After the [[Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States|U.S.
sentence_194: Supreme Court]] threw out Georgia's [[Death_penalty_in_the_United_States|death penalty]] statute in Furman v. Georgia (1972), Carter signed a revised death-penalty statute that addressed the court's objections, thus re-introducing the practice in the state.
sentence_195: Carter later regretted endorsing the death penalty, saying, "I didn't see the injustice of it as I do now."
sentence_196: Carter pushed reforms through the legislature that provided equal state aid to schools in the wealthy and poor areas of Georgia, set up community centers for mentally handicapped children, and increased educational programs for convicts.
sentence_197: He took pride in his program for the appointment of judges and state government officials.
sentence_198: Under this program, all such appointments were based on merit, rather than political influence.
sentence_199: In one of his more controversial decisions, he vetoed a plan to build a dam on Georgia's [[Flint_River_(Georgia)|Flint River]].
sentence_200: After surveying the river and the literature himself, he argued that the [[U.S._Army_Corps_of_Engineers|U.S.
sentence_201: Army Corps of Engineers]] was underestimating both the project's cost and its impact on the region.
sentence_202: The veto won the attention of environmentalists nationwide.
sentence_203: When Lieutenant [[William_Calley|William Calley]] was convicted in a military trial and sentenced to life for his role in the [[My_Lai_Massacre|My Lai Massacre]] in [[South_Vietnam|South Vietnam]], a politically polarizing issue, Carter avoided paying direct tribute to Calley.
sentence_204: He instead instituted "American Fighting Man's Day" and asked Georgians to drive for a week with their lights on in support of the military.
sentence_205: Under Georgia's constitution, Carter was ineligible to run for re-election.
sentence_206: Looking toward a potential presidential run, Carter engaged himself in national politics and public appearances.
sentence_207: He was named to several southern planning commissions and was a delegate to the [[1972_Democratic_National_Convention|1972 Democratic National Convention]], where the liberal U.S.
sentence_208: Senator [[George_McGovern|George McGovern]] was the likely presidential nominee.

sentence_211: Carter was still fairly obscure at the time, and his attempt at triangulation failed; the [[1972_United_States_presidential_election|1972 Democratic ticket]] was McGovern and Senator [[Thomas_Eagleton|Thomas Eagleton]].
sentence_212: On August 3, Carter met with Wallace in [[Birmingham,_Alabama|Birmingham, Alabama]] to discuss preventing the Democratic Party from losing in a landslide during the November elections.
sentence_213: After McGovern's loss in November 1972, Carter began meeting regularly with his fledgling campaign staff.
sentence_214: He had quietly decided to begin putting a presidential bid for 1976 together.
sentence_215: He tried unsuccessfully to become chairman of the [[National_Governors_Association|National Governors Association]] to boost his visibility.
sentence_216: On [[David_Rockefeller|David Rockefeller]]'s endorsement he was named to the [[Trilateral_Commission|Trilateral Commission]] in April 1973.
sentence_217: The following year he was named chairman of the [[Democratic_National_Committee|Democratic National Committee]]'s congressional, as well as gubernatorial, campaigns.
sentence_218: In 1973 he appeared on the game show What's My Line, where a group of celebrity panelists would try to guess his occupation.
sentence_219: None recognized him and it took several rounds of question-and-answer before movie critic [[Gene_Shalit|Gene Shalit]] correctly guessed he was a governor.
sentence_220: In May 1973, Carter warned the Democratic Party against politicizing the [[Watergate_scandal|Watergate scandal]], the occurrence of which he attributed to President [[Richard_Nixon|Richard Nixon]] exercising isolation from Americans and secrecy in his decision making.
sentence_221: Main article: [[1976_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries|1976 Democratic Party presidential primaries]]
sentence_222: On December 12, 1974, Carter announced his candidacy for [[President_of_the_United_States|President of the United States]] at the [[National_Press_Club_(United_States)|National Press Club]] in Washington, D.C. His speech contained themes of domestic inequality, optimism, and change.
sentence_223: When Carter entered the Democratic Party presidential primaries, he was considered to have little chance against nationally better-known politicians; his [[Name_recognition|name recognition]] was two percent.
sentence_224: As late as January 26, 1976, Carter was the first choice of only four percent of Democratic voters, according to a [[Gallup_poll|Gallup poll]].
sentence_225: Yet "by mid-March 1976 Carter was not only far ahead of the active contenders for the Democratic presidential nomination, he also led President [[Gerald_Ford|Ford]] by a few percentage points," according to Shoup.
sentence_226: As the [[Watergate_scandal|Watergate scandal]] of President Nixon was still fresh in the voters' minds, Carter's position as an outsider, distant from Washington, D.C., became an asset.
sentence_227: He promoted government reorganization.
sentence_228: Carter published Why Not the Best?
sentence_229: in June 1976 to help introduce himself to the American public.
sentence_230: Carter became the front-runner early on by winning the Iowa caucuses and the [[New_Hampshire_primary|New Hampshire primary]].
sentence_231: He used a two-prong strategy: in the South, which most had tacitly conceded to Alabama's [[George_Wallace|George Wallace]], Carter ran as a moderate favorite son.
sentence_232: When Wallace proved to be a spent force, Carter swept the region.
sentence_233: In the North, Carter appealed largely to conservative Christian and rural voters; he had little chance of winning a majority in most states.
sentence_234: He won several Northern states by building the largest single bloc.
sentence_235: Carter's strategy involved reaching a region before another candidate could extend influence there.
sentence_236: He had traveled over 50,000 miles (80,000 kilometres), visited 37 states, and delivered over 200 speeches before any other candidate entered the race.
sentence_237: Initially dismissed as a regional candidate, Carter proved to be the Democrat with the most effective national strategy, and he clinched the nomination.
sentence_238: The national news media discovered and promoted Carter, as Lawrence Shoup noted in his 1980 book The Carter Presidency and Beyond:
sentence_239: During his presidential campaign in April 1976, Carter responded to an interviewer and said, "I have nothing against a community that is ... trying to maintain the ethnic purity of their neighborhoods."
sentence_240: His remark was intended as supportive of [[Housing_discrimination_in_the_United_States|open-housing]] laws, but specifying opposition to government efforts to "inject black families into a white neighborhood just to create some sort of [[Racial_integration|integration]]."
sentence_241: Carter's stated positions during his campaign include public financing of congressional campaigns, his support for the creation of a federal consumer protection agency, creating a separate department for education, signing a peace treaty with the Soviet Union against the usage of nuclear weapon, reducing the defense budget, a tax proposal implementing "a substantial increase toward those who have the higher incomes" alongside a levy reduction on taxpayers with lower and middle incomes, making multiple amendments to the [[Social_Security_Act|Social Security Act]], and having a balanced budget by the end of his tenure.
sentence_242: Main article: [[1976_United_States_presidential_election|1976 United States presidential election]]
sentence_243: On July 15, 1976, Carter chose Minnesota Senator [[Walter_Mondale|Walter F. Mondale]] as his running mate.
sentence_244: He attacked Washington in his speeches, and offered a religious salve for the nation's wounds.
sentence_245: Carter and Gerald Ford faced off in three televised debates during the 1976 election.
sentence_246: The debates were the first presidential debates since 1960.
sentence_247: Carter was interviewed by Robert Scheer of [[Playboy|Playboy]] for the November 1976 issue, which hit the newsstands a couple of weeks before the election.
sentence_248: While discussing his religion's view of pride, Carter said: "I've looked on a lot of women with lust.
sentence_249: I've committed adultery in my heart many times."
sentence_250: This and his admission in another interview that he did not mind if people uttered the word "fuck" led to a media feeding frenzy and critics lamenting the erosion of boundary between politicians and their private intimate lives.
sentence_251: Carter began the race with a sizable lead over Ford, who narrowed the gap during the campaign, but lost to Carter in a narrow defeat on November 2, 1976.
sentence_252: Carter won the popular vote by 50.1 percent to 48.0 percent for Ford, and received 297 [[United_States_Electoral_College|electoral votes]] to Ford's 240.
sentence_253: Carter carried fewer states than Ford—23 states to the defeated Ford's 27—yet Carter won with the largest percentage of the popular vote (50.1 percent) of any non-incumbent since [[Dwight_Eisenhower|Dwight Eisenhower]].
sentence_254: Main article: [[Presidency_of_Jimmy_Carter|Presidency of Jimmy Carter]]
sentence_255: Carter's tenure was a time of [[Early_1980s_recession_in_the_United_States|continuing inflation and recession]], as well as an [[1979_energy_crisis|energy crisis]].
sentence_256: Among his first acts was the fulfillment of a campaign promise by issuing an [[Executive_order_(United_States)|executive order]] declaring unconditional [[Amnesty|amnesty]] for Vietnam War-era [[Draft_evasion|draft evaders]], [[Proclamation_4483|Proclamation 4483]].
sentence_257: On January 7, 1980, Carter signed known as The Chrysler Corporation Loan Guarantee Act of 1979, bailing out [[Chrysler|Chrysler Corporation]] with $3.5 billion (equivalent to $10.86 billion in 2019) in aid.
sentence_258: Carter attempted to calm various conflicts around the world, most visibly in the Middle East with the signing of the [[Camp_David_Accords|Camp David Accords]]; [[Torrijos–Carter_Treaties|giving back the Panama Canal]] to Panama; and signing the SALT II nuclear arms reduction treaty with Soviet leader [[Leonid_Brezhnev|Leonid Brezhnev]].
sentence_259: His final year was marred by the [[Iran_hostage_crisis|Iran hostage crisis]], which contributed to his losing the [[1980_United_States_presidential_election|1980 election]] to [[Ronald_Reagan|Ronald Reagan]].
sentence_260: On November 22, 1976, Carter conducted his first visit to Washington after being elected, meeting with Director of the Office of Management [[James_Lynn|James Lynn]] and [[United_States_Secretary_of_Defense|United States Secretary of Defense]] [[Donald_Rumsfeld|Donald Rumsfeld]] at the Blair House, and holding an afternoon meeting with President Ford at the White House.
sentence_261: The following day, Carter conferred with congressional leaders, expressing that his meetings with cabinet members had been "very helpful" and saying Ford had requested he seek out his assistance if needing anything.
sentence_262: On December 3, 1976, during a news conference, Carter announced his choice of [[Cyrus_R._Vance|Cyrus R. Vance]] for [[United_States_Secretary_of_State|United States Secretary of State]] and [[Bert_Lance|Bert Lance]] as his budget director.
sentence_263: On December 9, Carter was presented plans for reform on housing, transportation, and urban development during a meeting with transition advisors at the Blair House.
sentence_264: On December 13, Carter's election was confirmed by the Electoral College.
sentence_265: On December 20, Carter announced his choice of [[Juanita_M._Kreps|Juanita M. Kreps]] for [[United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce|United States Secretary of Commerce]], [[Griffin_Bell|Griffin Bell]] for [[United_States_Attorney_General|United States Attorney General]], and [[Robert_Bergland|Robert Bergland]] for [[United_States_Secretary_of_Agriculture|United States Secretary of Agriculture]].
sentence_266: On January 4, 1977, Carter told reporters that he would free himself from potential conflicts of interest by leaving his peanut business in the hands of trustees.

O'Leary]] for Administrator of the [[Federal_Energy_Administration|Federal Energy Administration]], [[William_Nordhaus|William Nordhaus]] and [[Lyle_E._Gramley|Lyle E. Gramley]] for membership on the Council of Economic Advisors, [[Anthony_M._Solomon|Anthony M. Solomon]] for Undersecretary of the Treasury for Monetary Affairs, [[C._Fred_Bergsten|C.
sentence_271: Fred Bergsten]] for Assistant Secretary of the Treasury for Monetary Affairs, and Kenneth S. Axelson for Deputy Secretary of the Treasury.
sentence_272: On April 18, 1977, Carter delivered a televised speech declaring that the U.S. energy crisis during the 1970s was the [[President_Jimmy_Carter's_Moral_Equivalent_of_War_Speech|moral equivalent of war]].
sentence_273: He encouraged energy conservation by all U.S. citizens and installed [[White_House_solar_panels|solar water heating panels on the White House]].
sentence_274: He wore sweaters to offset turning down the heat in the White House.
sentence_275: On August 4, 1977, Carter signed the [[Department_of_Energy_Organization_Act_of_1977|Department of Energy Organization Act of 1977]], forming the Department of Energy, the first new cabinet position in eleven years.
sentence_276: During the signing ceremony, Carter cited the "impending crisis of energy shortages" with causing the necessity of the legislation.
sentence_277: At the start of a September 29, 1977 news conference, under the impression he had not come across well in addressing energy during his prior press session, Carter stated that the House of Representatives had "adopted almost all" of the energy proposal he had made five months prior and called the compromise "a turning point in establishing a comprehensive energy program."
sentence_278: The following month, on October 13, Carter stated he believed in the Senate's ability to pass the energy reform bill and identified energy as "the most important domestic issue that we will face while I am in office."
sentence_279: On January 12, 1978, during a press conference, Carter said the continued discussions about his energy reform proposal had "been long and divisive and arduous" as well as hindering to national issues that needed to be addressed with the implementation of the law.
sentence_280: In an April 11, 1978 news conference, Carter said his biggest surprise "in the nature of a disappointment" since becoming president was the difficulty Congress had in passing legislation, citing the energy reform bill in particular: "I never dreamed a year ago in April when I proposed this matter to the Congress that a year later it still would not be resolved."
sentence_281: The Carter energy legislation was approved by Congress after much deliberation and modification on October 15, 1978.
sentence_282: The measure deregulated the sale of natural gas, dropped a longstanding pricing disparity between intra- and interstate gas, and created tax credits to encourage energy conservation and the use of non fossil fuels.
sentence_283: On March 1, 1979, Carter submitted a standby gasoline rationing plan per the request of Congress.
sentence_284: On April 5, he delivered an address in which he stressed the urgency of energy conservation.
sentence_285: During an April 30 news conference, Carter said it was "imperative" that the House commerce committee approve the standby gasoline rationing plan and called on Congress to pass the several other standby energy conservation plans he had proposed.
sentence_286: On July 15, 1979, Carter delivered a nationally televised address in which he identified what he believed to be a "" among the American people, under the advisement of pollster [[Pat_Caddell|Pat Caddell]] who believed Americans faced a crisis in confidence from events of the 1960s and 1970s prior to Carter taking office.
sentence_287: The address would be cited as Carter's "[[Malaise|malaise]]" speech, memorable for mixed reactions and his use of rhetoric.
sentence_288: The speech's negative reception came from a view that Carter did not state efforts on his own part to address the energy crisis and was too reliant on Americans.
sentence_289: In 1978, Carter declared a federal emergency in the neighborhood of [[Love_Canal|Love Canal]] in the city of [[Niagara_Falls,_New_York|Niagara Falls, New York]].
sentence_290: More than 800 families were evacuated from the neighborhood, which was built on top of a [[Toxic_waste|toxic waste]] landfill.
sentence_291: The [[Superfund|Superfund]] law was created in response to the situation.
sentence_292: Federal disaster money was appropriated to demolish the approximately 500 houses, the 99th Street School, and the 93rd Street School, which were built on top of the dump; and to remediate the dump and construct a containment area for the hazardous wastes.
sentence_293: This was the first time that such a process had been undertaken.
sentence_294: Carter acknowledged that several more "Love Canals" existed across the country, and that discovering such hazardous dumpsites was "one of the grimmest discoveries of our modern era".
sentence_295: Carter refused to play by Washington's rules.
sentence_296: He missed and never returned phone calls on his part.
sentence_297: He used verbal insults and had an unwillingness to return political favors, which contributed to his lack of ability to pass legislation through Congress.
sentence_298: During a press conference on February 23, 1977, Carter stated that it was "inevitable" that he would come into conflict with Congress and added that he had found "a growing sense of cooperation" with Congress and met in the past with congressional members of both parties.
sentence_299: Carter developed a bitter feeling following an unsuccessful attempt at having Congress enact the scrapping of several water projects, which he had requested during his first 100 days in office and received opposition from members of his party.
sentence_300: As a rift ensued between the White House and Congress afterward, Carter noted the liberal wing of the Democratic Party was the most ardently against his policies, attributing this to Ted Kennedy wanting the presidency.
sentence_301: Carter, thinking he had support from 74 Congressmen, issued a "hit list" of 19 projects that he claimed were "pork barrel" spending that he claimed would result in a veto on his part if included in any legislation.
sentence_302: He found himself at odds with Congressional Democrats once more, [[Speaker_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives|Speaker of the House of Representatives]] [[Tip_O'Neill|Tip O'Neill]] finding it inappropriate for a president to pursue what had traditionally been the role of Congress.
sentence_303: Carter was also weakened by a signing of bill that contained many of the "hit list" projects.
sentence_304: In a June 23, 1977 address to a fundraising dinner for the [[Democratic_National_Committee|Democratic National Committee]], Carter said, "I think it's good to point out tonight, too, that we have evolved a good working relationship with the Congress.
sentence_305: For eight years we had government by partisanship.
sentence_306: Now we have government by partnership."
sentence_307: At a July 28 news conference, assessing the first six months of his presidency, Carter spoke of his improved understanding of Congress: "I have learned to respect the Congress more in an individual basis.
sentence_308: I've been favorably impressed at the high degree of concentrated experience and knowledge that individual Members of Congress can bring on a specific subject, where they've been the chairman of a subcommittee or committee for many years and have focused their attention on this particular aspect of government life which I will never be able to do."
sentence_309: On May 10, 1979, the House voted against giving Carter authority to produce a standby gas rationing plan.
sentence_310: The following day, Carter delivered remarks in the Oval Office describing himself as shocked and embarrassed for the American government due to the vote and concluding "the majority of the House Members are unwilling to take the responsibility, the political responsibility for dealing with a potential, serious threat to our Nation."
sentence_311: He furthered that a majority of House members were placing higher importance on "local or parochial interests" and challenged the lower chamber of Congress with composing their own rationing plan in the next 90 days.
sentence_312: Carter's remarks were met with criticism by House Republicans who accused his comments of not befitting the formality a president should have in their public remarks.
sentence_313: Others pointed to 106 Democrats voting against his proposal and the bipartisan criticism potentially coming back to haunt him.
sentence_314: At the start of a July 25, 1979 news conference, Carter called on believers in the future of the US and his proposed energy program to speak with Congress as it bore the responsibility to impose his proposals.
sentence_315: Amid the energy proposal opposition, The New York Times commented that "as the comments flying up and down Pennsylvania Avenue illustrate, there is also a crisis of confidence between Congress and the President, sense of doubt and distrust that threatens to undermine the President's legislative program and become an important issue in next year's campaign."
sentence_316: Carter's presidency had an economic history of two roughly equal periods, the first two years being a time of continuing recovery from the severe 1973–75 recession, which had left fixed investment at its lowest level since the 1970 recession and unemployment at 9%, and the last two years marked by double-digit inflation, coupled with very high interest rates, oil shortages, and slow economic growth.
sentence_317: The years of 1977 and 1978 saw the creation of millions of new jobs, in part as a result of the $30 billion economic stimulus legislation - like the Public Works Employment Act of 1977 - that he proposed and Congress passed, and real median household income growth by 5%.
sentence_318: The [[1979_energy_crisis|1979 energy crisis]] ended this period of growth, however, and as both inflation and interest rates rose, economic growth, job creation, and [[Consumer_confidence|consumer confidence]] declined sharply.
sentence_319: The relatively loose [[Monetary_policy|monetary policy]] adopted by [[Federal_Reserve_Board|Federal Reserve Board]] Chairman [[G._William_Miller|G.
sentence_320: William Miller]], had already contributed to somewhat higher [[Inflation|inflation]], rising from 5.8% in 1976 to 7.7% in 1978.
sentence_321: The sudden doubling of [[Crude_oil|crude oil]] prices by [[OPEC|OPEC]], the world's leading oil exporting cartel, forced inflation to double-digit levels, averaging 11.3% in 1979 and 13.5% in 1980.
sentence_322: The sudden shortage of [[Gasoline|gasoline]] as the 1979 summer vacation season began exacerbated the problem, and would come to symbolize the crisis among the public in general; the acute shortage, originating in the shutdown of [[Amerada_Hess|Amerada Hess]] refining facilities, led to a lawsuit against the company that year by the Federal Government.
sentence_323: In 1977, Carter appointed [[Alfred_E._Kahn|Alfred E. Kahn]] to lead the Civil Aeronautics Board (CAB).

sentence_325: This coalition swiftly gained legislative results in 1978.
sentence_326: Carter signed the [[Airline_Deregulation_Act|Airline Deregulation Act]] into law on October 24, 1978.
sentence_327: The main purpose of the act was to [[Airline_deregulation|remove government control]] over fares, routes and market entry (of new airlines) from [[Commercial_aviation|commercial aviation]].

sentence_329: The Act did not remove or diminish the FAA's regulatory powers over all aspects of airline safety.
sentence_330: In 1979, Carter deregulated the American beer industry by making it legal to sell [[Malt|malt]], [[Hops|hops]], and [[Yeast|yeast]] to American [[Homebrewing|home brewers]] for the first time since the effective 1920 beginning of [[Prohibition_in_the_United_States|Prohibition in the United States]].
sentence_331: This Carter deregulation led to an increase in home brewing over the 1980s and 1990s that by the 2000s had developed into a strong craft [[Microbrewery|microbrew]] culture in the United States, with 6,266 micro breweries, brewpubs, and regional craft breweries in the United States by the end of 2017.
sentence_332: During his presidential campaign, Carter embraced healthcare reform akin to the [[Ted_Kennedy|Ted Kennedy]]-sponsored bipartisan [[Universal_health_care|universal]] [[National_health_insurance|national health insurance]].

sentence_336: During 1978, Carter also conducted meetings with Kennedy for a compromise healthcare law that proved unsuccessful.

sentence_338: Early into his term, Carter collaborated with Congress to assist in fulfilling a campaign promise to create a cabinet level education department.
sentence_339: In a February 28, 1978 address at the White House, Carter argued, "Education is far too important a matter to be scattered piecemeal among various Government departments and agencies, which are often busy with sometimes dominant concerns."
sentence_340: On February 8, 1979, the Carter administration released an outline of its plan to establish an education department and asserted enough support for the enactment to occur by June.
sentence_341: On October 17, 1979, Carter signed the [[Department_of_Education_Organization_Act|Department of Education Organization Act]] into law, establishing the [[United_States_Department_of_Education|United States Department of Education]].
sentence_342: Carter expanded the [[Head_Start_(program)|Head Start]] program with the addition of 43,000 children and families, while the percentage of nondefense dollars spent on education was doubled.
sentence_343: Carter was complimentary of the presidency of Lyndon B. Johnson and the [[89th_United_States_Congress|89th United States Congress]] for having initiated Head Start.
sentence_344: In a November 1, 1980 speech, Carter stated his administration had extended Head Start to migrant children and was "working hard right now with Senator Bentsen and with Kika de la Garza to make as much as $45 million available in Federal money in the border districts to help with the increase in school construction for the number of Mexican school children who reside here legally".

list.value: was in an odd position—he had attempted to break with traditional US policy but ended up fulfilling the goals of that tradition, which had been to break up the Arab alliance, side-line the Palestinians, build an alliance with Egypt, weaken the Soviet Union and secure Israel.

sentence_348: In an October 4, 1977 address to African officials at the United Nations, Carter stated the U.S.'s interest to "see a strong, vigorous, free, and prosperous Africa with as much of the control of government as possible in the hands of the residents of your countries" and pointed to their unified efforts on "the problem of how to resolve the Rhodesian, Zimbabwe question."
sentence_349: At a news conference later that month, Carter outlined the US wanting "to work harmoniously with South Africa in dealing with the threats to peace in Namibia and in Zimbabwe in particular" and to do away with racial issues such as apartheid and for equal opportunities in other facets of society in the region.

sentence_354: On May 16, 1979, the Senate voted in favor of President Carter lifting economic sanctions against [[Rhodesia|Rhodesia]], the vote being seen by both Rhodesia and South Africa "as a potentially fatal blow to the joint diplomacy that the United States and Britain have pursued in the region for three years and to the effort to reach a compromise between the Salisbury leaders and the guerrillas."

sentence_356: During Carter's presidency, the United States continued to support [[Indonesia|Indonesia]] as a cold war ally in spite of human rights violations in East Timor.

sentence_365: Fifty-two American diplomats and citizens were held hostage for the next 444 days until they were finally freed immediately after [[Ronald_Reagan|Ronald Reagan]] succeeded Carter as President on January 20, 1981.
sentence_366: During the crisis, Carter remained in isolation in the [[White_House|White House]] for more than 100 days, until he left to participate in the lighting of the [[National_Menorah|National Menorah]] on [[The_Ellipse|the Ellipse]].
sentence_367: A month into the affair, Carter stated his commitment to resolving the dispute without "any military action that would cause bloodshed or arouse the unstable captors of our hostages to attack them or to punish them".
sentence_368: On April 7, 1980, Carter issued Executive Order 12205, imposing economic sanctions against Iran and announced further measures being taken by members of his cabinet and the American government that he deemed necessary to ensure a safe release.
