sentence_372: On February 8, 1977, Carter stated he had urged the Soviet Union to align with the US in forming "a comprehensive test ban to stop all nuclear testing for at least an extended period of time" and that he was in favor of the Soviet Union ceasing deployment of the [[RSD-10_Pioneer|RSD-10 Pioneer]].
sentence_373: During a June 13 conference, Carter reported that the US would "beginning this week to work closely with the Soviet Union on a comprehensive test ban treaty to prohibit all testing of nuclear devices underground or in the atmosphere" and Paul Warnke would negotiate demilitarization of the Indian Ocean with the Soviet Union beginning the following week.
sentence_374: At a news conference on December 30, Carter said throughout the period of "the last few months, the United States and the Soviet Union have made great progress in dealing with a long list of important issues, the most important of which is to control the deployment of strategic nuclear weapons" and that the two countries sought to conclude SALT II talks by the spring of the following year.
sentence_375: The talk of a comprehensive test ban treaty materialized with the signing of the Strategic Arms Limitation Treaty II by Carter and [[Leonid_Brezhnev|Leonid Brezhnev]] on June 18, 1979.
sentence_376: In the [[1980_State_of_the_Union_Address|1980 State of the Union Address]], Carter emphasized the significance of relations between the two regions: "Now, as during the last 3 1/2 decades, the relationship between our country, the United States of America, and the Soviet Union is the most critical factor in determining whether the world will live at peace or be engulfed in global conflict."
sentence_377: Communists under the leadership of [[Nur_Muhammad_Taraki|Nur Muhammad Taraki]] [[Saur_Revolution|seized power in Afghanistan]] on April 27, 1978.
sentence_378: The new regime—which was divided between Taraki's extremist [[Khalq|Khalq]] faction and the more moderate Parcham—signed a treaty of friendship with the Soviet Union in December of that year.
sentence_379: Taraki's efforts to improve secular education and redistribute land were accompanied by mass executions (including of many conservative religious leaders) and political oppression unprecedented in Afghan history, igniting a revolt by mujahideen rebels.
sentence_380: Following a general uprising in April 1979, Taraki was deposed by Khalq rival [[Hafizullah_Amin|Hafizullah Amin]] in September.
sentence_381: Amin was considered a "brutal psychopath" by foreign observers; even the Soviets were alarmed by the brutality of the Afghan communists, and suspected Amin of being an agent of the U.S. [[Central_Intelligence_Agency|Central Intelligence Agency]] (CIA), although that was not the case.
sentence_382: By December, Amin's government had lost control of much of the country, prompting the Soviet Union to [[Soviet–Afghan_War|invade Afghanistan]], execute Amin, and install Parcham leader [[Babrak_Karmal|Babrak Karmal]] as president.
sentence_383: Carter was surprised by the invasion, as the consensus of the U.S. intelligence community during 1978 and 1979—reiterated as late as September 29, 1979—was that "Moscow would not intervene in force even if it appeared likely that the Khalq government was about to collapse."
sentence_384: Indeed, Carter's diary entries from November 1979 until the Soviet invasion in late December contain only two short references to Afghanistan, and are instead preoccupied with the ongoing hostage crisis in Iran.
sentence_385: In the West, the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan was considered a threat to global security and the oil supplies of the [[Persian_Gulf|Persian Gulf]].
sentence_386: Moreover, the failure to accurately predict Soviet intentions caused American officials to reappraise the Soviet threat to both Iran and Pakistan, although it is now known that those fears were overblown.
sentence_387: For example, U.S. intelligence closely followed Soviet exercises for an invasion of Iran throughout 1980, while an earlier warning from Carter's national security adviser [[Zbigniew_Brzezinski|Zbigniew Brzezinski]] that "if the Soviets came to dominate Afghanistan, they could promote a separate [[Baluchistan|Baluchistan]] ... [thus] dismembering Pakistan and Iran" took on new urgency.
sentence_388: These concerns were a major factor in the unrequited efforts of both the Carter and Reagan administrations to improve relations with Iran, and resulted in massive aid to Pakistan's [[Muhammad_Zia-ul-Haq|Muhammad Zia-ul-Haq]].
sentence_389: Zia's ties with the U.S. had been strained during Carter's presidency due to Pakistan's nuclear program and the execution of [[Ali_Bhutto|Ali Bhutto]] in April 1979, but Carter told Brzezinski and secretary of state [[Cyrus_Vance|Cyrus Vance]] as early as January 1979 that it was vital to "repair our relationships with Pakistan" in light of the unrest in Iran.
sentence_390: One initiative Carter authorized to achieve this goal was a collaboration between the CIA and Pakistan's [[Inter-Services_Intelligence|Inter-Services Intelligence]] (ISI); through the ISI, the CIA began providing some $500,000 worth of non-lethal assistance to the mujahideen on July 3, 1979—several months prior to the Soviet invasion.
sentence_391: The modest scope of this early collaboration was likely influenced by the understanding, later recounted by CIA official [[Robert_Gates|Robert Gates]], "that a substantial U.S. covert aid program" might have "raise[d] the stakes" thereby causing "the Soviets to intervene more directly and vigorously than otherwise intended."
sentence_392: In the aftermath of the invasion, Carter was determined to respond vigorously to what he considered a dangerous provocation.
sentence_393: In a televised speech, he announced sanctions on the Soviet Union, promised renewed aid to Pakistan, initiated renewed registration for the [[Selective_Service_System|Selective Service System]], and [[Carter_Doctrine|committed the U.S. to the Persian Gulf's defense]].
sentence_394: He imposed an embargo on grain shipments to the USSR, tabled consideration of SALT II, and requested a 5% annual increase in defense spending.
sentence_395: Carter also called for a boycott of the [[1980_Summer_Olympics|1980 Summer Olympics]] in Moscow.
sentence_396: British prime minister [[Margaret_Thatcher|Margaret Thatcher]] enthusiastically backed Carter's tough stance, although British intelligence believed "the CIA was being too alarmist about the Soviet threat to Pakistan."
sentence_397: The thrust of U.S. policy for the duration of the war was determined by Carter in early 1980: Carter initiated [[Operation_Cyclone|a program to arm the mujahideen through Pakistan's ISI]] and secured a pledge from Saudi Arabia to match U.S. funding for this purpose.
sentence_398: U.S. support for the mujahideen accelerated under Carter's successor, [[Ronald_Reagan|Ronald Reagan]], at a final cost to U.S. taxpayers of some $3 billion.
sentence_399: The Soviets were unable to quell the insurgency and [[Soviet_withdrawal_from_Afghanistan|withdrew from Afghanistan]] in 1989, precipitating the dissolution of the Soviet Union itself.
sentence_400: However, the decision to route U.S. aid through Pakistan led to massive fraud, as weapons sent to [[Karachi|Karachi]] were frequently sold on the local market rather than delivered to the Afghan rebels; Karachi soon "became one of the most violent cities in the world."
sentence_401: Pakistan also controlled which rebels received assistance: Of the [[Islamic_Unity_of_Afghanistan_Mujahideen|seven mujahideen groups]] supported by Zia's government, four espoused Islamic fundamentalist beliefs—and these fundamentalists received most of the funding.
sentence_402: Despite this, Carter has expressed no regrets over his decision to support what he still considers the "freedom fighters" in Afghanistan.
sentence_403: During a March 9, 1977 news conference, Carter reaffirmed his interest in having a gradual withdrawal of American troops from [[South_Korea|South Korea]] and stated he wanted South Korea to eventually have "adequate ground forces owned by and controlled by the South Korean Government to protect themselves against any intrusion from [[North_Korea|North Korea]]."
sentence_404: On May 19, [[The_Washington_Post|The Washington Post]] quoted Chief of Staff of U.S. forces in South Korea John K. Singlaub as criticizing Carter's withdrawal of troops from the Korean peninsula.
sentence_405: Later that day, Press Secretary Rex Granum announced Singlaub had been summoned to the White House by Carter, whom he also confirmed had seen the article in The Washington Post.
sentence_406: Carter relieved Singlaub of his duties two days later on May 21 following a meeting between the two.
sentence_407: On May 26, during a news conference, Carter said he believed South Korea would be able to defend themselves despite reduced American troops in the event of conflict.
sentence_408: From June 30 to July 1, 1979, Carter held meetings with President of South Korea [[Park_Chung-hee|Park Chung-hee]] at the Blue House for a discussion on relations between the US and Korea as well as Carter's interest in preserving his policy of worldwide tension reduction.
sentence_409: On April 21, 1978, Carter announced a reduction in American troops in South Korea scheduled to be released by the end of the year by two-thirds, citing a lack of action by Congress in regards to a compensatory aid package for the Seoul Government.
sentence_410: Further information: [[List_of_international_trips_made_by_the_President_of_the_United_States#Jimmy_Carter|List of international trips made by the President of the United States § Jimmy Carter]]
sentence_411: Carter made twelve international trips to twenty-five countries during his presidency.
sentence_412: Carter was the first president to make a state visit to Sub-Saharan Africa when he went to [[Nigeria|Nigeria]] in 1978.
sentence_413: His travel also included trips to [[Europe|Europe]], [[Asia|Asia]], and [[Latin_America|Latin America]].
sentence_414: He made several trips to the Middle East to broker peace negotiations.
sentence_415: His visit to [[Iran|Iran]] from December 31, 1977, to January 1, 1978, took place less than a year before the overthrow of [[Shah_Mohammad_Reza_Pahlavi|Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi]].
sentence_416: The September 21, 1977 resignation of [[Bert_Lance|Bert Lance]], who served as Director of the Office of Management and Budget in the Carter administration, came amid allegations of improper banking activities prior to his tenure and was an embarrassment to Carter.
sentence_417: Carter became the first sitting president to testify under oath as part of an investigation into that president, as a result of [[United_States_Attorney_General|United States Attorney General]] [[Griffin_Bell|Griffin Bell]] appointing [[Paul_J._Curran|Paul J. Curran]] as a special counsel to investigate loans made to the peanut business owned by Carter by a bank controlled by Bert Lance and Curran's position as special counsel not allowing him to file charges on his own.
sentence_418: Curran announced in October 1979 that no evidence had been found to support allegations that funds loaned from the National Bank of Georgia had been diverted to Carter's 1976 presidential campaign, ending the investigation.
sentence_419: Main article: [[1980_United_States_presidential_election|1980 United States presidential election]]
sentence_420: Carter later wrote that the most intense and mounting opposition to his policies came from the liberal wing of the Democratic Party, which he attributed to [[Ted_Kennedy|Ted Kennedy]]'s ambition to replace him as president.
sentence_421: After Kennedy announced his candidacy in November 1979, questions regarding his activities during his presidential bid were a frequent subject of Carter's press conferences held during the Democratic presidential primary.
sentence_422: Kennedy surprised his supporters by running a weak campaign, and Carter won most of the primaries and secured renomination.
sentence_423: However, Kennedy had mobilized the liberal wing of the Democratic Party, which gave Carter weak support in the fall election.
sentence_424: Carter and Vice President Mondale were formally nominated at the [[1980_Democratic_National_Convention|Democratic National Convention]] in [[New_York_City|New York City]].
sentence_425: Carter delivered a speech notable for its tribute to the late [[Hubert_Humphrey|Hubert Humphrey]], whom he initially called "Hubert [[Horatio_Hornblower|Horatio Hornblower]]."
sentence_426: Carter's [[1980_United_States_presidential_election|campaign for re-election]] in 1980 was one of the most difficult and least successful in history.
sentence_427: He faced strong challenges from the right (Republican [[Ronald_Reagan|Ronald Reagan]]), the center (independent [[John_B._Anderson|John B. Anderson]]), and the left (Democrat [[Ted_Kennedy|Ted Kennedy]]).
sentence_428: He had to run against his own "[[Stagflation|stagflation]]"-ridden economy, while the hostage crisis in Iran dominated the news every week.
sentence_429: He alienated liberal college students, who were expected to be his base, by re-instating registration for the military draft.
sentence_430: His campaign manager and former appointments secretary, [[Timothy_Kraft|Timothy Kraft]], stepped down some five weeks before the general election amid what turned out to have been an uncorroborated allegation of [[Cocaine|cocaine]] use.
sentence_431: On October 28, Carter and Reagan participated in the sole presidential debate of the election cycle.
sentence_432: Though initially trailing Carter by several points, Reagan experienced a surge in polling following the debate.
sentence_433: Carter was defeated by Ronald Reagan in a landslide, and the Senate [[United_States_Senate_elections,_1980|went Republican]] for the first time since 1952.
sentence_434: In his concession speech, Carter admitted that he was hurt by the outcome of the election but pledged "a very fine transition period" with President-elect Reagan.
sentence_435: Main article: Post-presidency of Jimmy Carter
sentence_436: Shortly after losing his re-election bid, Carter told the White House press corps of his intent to emulate the retirement of [[Harry_S._Truman|Harry S. Truman]] and not use his subsequent public life to enrich himself.
sentence_437: In 1982, Carter founded the [[Carter_Center|Carter Center]], a non-governmental and non-profit organization with the purpose of [[Human_rights_activists|advancing human rights]] and alleviating human [[Suffering|suffering]], including helping improve the [[Quality_of_life|quality of life]] for people in more than 80 countries.
sentence_438: In 1994, President [[Bill_Clinton|Bill Clinton]] sought Carter's assistance in a [[North_Korea|North Korea]] peace mission, during which Carter negotiated an understanding with [[Kim_Il-sung|Kim Il-sung]], with whom he went on to outline a treaty that he announced to CNN without the consent of the Clinton administration to spur American action.
sentence_439: Carter traveled to North Korea to secure the release of [[Aijalon_Gomes|Aijalon Gomes]] in August 2010, successfully negotiating his release.
sentence_440: Throughout the latter part of 2017, as tensions between the US and North Korea persisted, Carter recommended a peace treaty between the two nations, and confirmed he had offered himself to the Trump administration as a willing candidate to serve as diplomatic envoy to North Korea.
sentence_441: In October 1984, Carter was named an honorary citizen of [[Peru|Peru]] by Mayor of Cusco [[Daniel_Estrada_(politician)|Daniel Estrada]] after traveling to [[Machu_Picchu|Machu Picchu]], Carter endorsing the country's elections in 2001, and offering support to the Peruvian government following a meeting with [[President_of_Peru|President of Peru]] [[Alan_García|Alan García]] at [[Government_Palace_(Peru)|Government Palace]] in [[Lima|Lima]] in April 2009.
sentence_442: In his February 1986 talks with [[Tomás_Borge|Tomás Borge]], Carter secured the release of journalist Luis Mora and labor leader Jose Altamirano, while touring [[Nicaragua|Nicaragua]] for three days.
sentence_443: Carter conducted a tour of [[Cuba|Cuba]] in May 2002 that included meeting with [[Fidel_Castro|Fidel Castro]] and meeting political dissidents such as the [[AIDS|AIDS]] sanitarium, a medical school, a [[Biotech|biotech]] facility, an agricultural production cooperative, and a school for disabled children.
sentence_444: Carter toured Cuba again for three days in March 2011.
sentence_445: Carter's diplomatic efforts in the Middle East included a September 1981 meeting with [[Prime_Minister_of_Israel|Prime Minister of Israel]] [[Menachem_Begin|Menachem Begin]], a March 1983 tour of [[Egypt|Egypt]] that included meeting with members of the [[Palestine_Liberation_Organization|Palestine Liberation Organization]], a December 2008 meeting with Syrian President [[Bashar_al-Assad|Bashar al-Assad]], and a June 2012 call with Jeffery Brown in which Carter stressed Egyptian military generals could be granted full power executively and legislatively in addition to being able to form a new constitution in favor of themselves in the event their announced intentions went through.
sentence_446: In 2006, Carter stated his disagreements with the domestic and foreign policies of [[Israel|Israel]] while saying he was in favor of the country, extending his criticisms to Israel's policies in [[Lebanon|Lebanon]], the [[West_Bank|West Bank]], and [[Gaza_Strip|Gaza]].
sentence_447: Carter traveled to Syria in April 2008, laying a wreath at the grave of [[Yasser_Arafat|Yasser Arafat]] in [[Ramallah|Ramallah]] and denying he had been contacted by the Bush administration in relation to meeting with [[Hamas|Hamas]] leaders.
sentence_448: In July 2007, Carter joined [[Nelson_Mandela|Nelson Mandela]] in Johannesburg, South Africa, to announce his participation in [[The_Elders_(organization)|The Elders]], a group of independent global leaders who work together on peace and human rights issues.
sentence_449: Following the announcement, Carter participated in visits to [[Darfur|Darfur]], [[Sudan|Sudan]], [[Cyprus|Cyprus]], the [[Korean_Peninsula|Korean Peninsula]], and the Middle East, among others.
sentence_450: Carter attempted traveling to [[Zimbabwe|Zimbabwe]] in November 2008, but was stopped by President [[Robert_Mugabe|Robert Mugabe]]'s government.
sentence_451: Carter held summits in Egypt and [[Tunisia|Tunisia]] in 1995–1996 to address violence in the [[African_Great_Lakes|Great Lakes region]] of [[Africa|Africa]], and played a key role in negotiation of the [[Nairobi_Agreement,_1999|Nairobi Agreement]] in 1999 between Sudan and [[Uganda|Uganda]].
sentence_452: Carter began his first year out of office with a pledge not to critique the new Reagan administration.
sentence_453: He spoke out after the [[Attempted_assassination_of_Ronald_Reagan|assassination attempt]] on Reagan, and voiced his agreement with Reagan on building neutron arms in the wake of the [[Soviet_invasion_of_Afghanistan|Soviet invasion of Afghanistan]].
sentence_454: He later disagreed with Reagan's handling of the Middle East.
sentence_455: The following year, Carter called for bipartisanship to fix American economic issues, and criticized the Reagan administration's handling of the [[Sabra_and_Shatila_massacre|Sabra and Shatila massacre]].
sentence_456: Carter responded favorably to Reagan choosing to remain within the Camp David agreement, with distaste toward what he felt was Reagan blaming his tenure for continued difficulties in policy.
sentence_457: In 1983, Carter judged the Reagan campaign with having falsified simplicity in solving issues, and criticized Reagan for a lack of attention to human rights violations.
sentence_458: In 1984, Carter stated he had been wrongly presented as weak by Reagan due to a commitment to human rights during the previous presidential election, and condemned Reagan for not making rescue efforts to retrieve four American businessmen from [[West_Beirut|West Beirut]].
sentence_459: In 1985, Carter rebuked Reagan over his handling of peace within the Middle East, his support of the [[Strategic_Defense_Initiative|Strategic Defense Initiative]], and Reagan's claim of an international conspiracy on terrorism.
sentence_460: Carter's insistence that Reagan was not preserving peace in the Middle East continued in 1987, Carter during the year also criticizing Reagan for adhering to terrorist demands, nomination of [[Robert_Bork|Robert Bork]] for the Supreme Court, and handling of the [[Persian_Gulf|Persian Gulf]].
sentence_461: During the presidency of [[George_W._Bush|George W. Bush]], Carter stated his opposition to the [[Iraq_War|Iraq War]], and what he considered an attempt on the part of Bush and [[Tony_Blair|Tony Blair]] to oust [[Saddam_Hussein|Saddam Hussein]] through the usage of "lies and misinterpretations".
sentence_462: In May 2007, Carter stated the Bush administration "has been the worst in history" in terms of its impact in foreign affairs, and later stated he was just comparing Bush's tenure to that of [[Richard_Nixon|Richard Nixon]].
sentence_463: Carter's comments received a response from the Bush administration in the form of Tony Fratto saying Carter was increasing his irrelevance with his commentary.
sentence_464: By the end of Bush's second term, Carter considered Bush's tenure disappointing, which he disclosed in comments to Forward Magazine of [[Syria|Syria]].
sentence_465: Though he praised President Obama in the early part of his tenure, Carter stated his disagreements with the use of [[Unmanned_aerial_vehicle|drone]] strikes against suspected terrorists, Obama's choice to keep [[Guantanamo_Bay_detention_camp|Guantanamo Bay detention camp]] open, and the current federal surveillance programs as disclosed by [[Edward_Snowden|Edward Snowden]] indicating that "America has no functioning democracy at this moment."
sentence_466: During the Trump presidency, Carter spoke favorably of the chance for immigration reform through Congress, and criticized Trump for his handling of the [[U.S._national_anthem_protests_(2016–present)|U.S. national anthem protests]].
sentence_467: In 2019, Carter said in response to a phone call from Trump in which Trump expressed concern that China was "getting ahead" of the United States that the reason why he agreed with Trump's assessment was due to what he said was China's lack of a record of warfare since his normalization of diplomatic relations with the country in 1979.
sentence_468: Carter was considered a potential candidate in the [[1984_United_States_presidential_election|1984]] presidential election, but did not run and instead endorsed Walter Mondale for the Democratic nomination.
sentence_469: After Mondale secured the nomination, Carter critiqued the Reagan campaign, spoke at the [[1984_Democratic_National_Convention|1984 Democratic National Convention]], and advised Mondale.
sentence_470: Following the election, in which President Reagan defeated Mondale, Carter stated the loss was predictable due to the latter's platform that included raising taxes.
sentence_471: In the [[1988_United_States_presidential_election|1988 presidential election]] cycle, Carter ruled himself out as a candidate once more and predicted Vice President [[George_H._W._Bush|George H. W. Bush]] as the Republican nominee in the general election.
sentence_472: Carter foresaw unity at the [[1988_Democratic_National_Convention|1988 Democratic National Convention]], where he delivered an address.
sentence_473: Following the election, a failed attempt by the Democrats in regaining the White House, Carter said Bush would have a more difficult presidency than Reagan due to not having the same level of popularity.
sentence_474: During the [[1992_United_States_presidential_election|1992 presidential election]], Carter met with Massachusetts Senator [[Paul_Tsongas|Paul Tsongas]] who sought out his advice.
sentence_475: Carter spoke favorably of former [[Governor_of_Arkansas|Governor of Arkansas]] [[Bill_Clinton|Bill Clinton]], and criticized [[Ross_Perot|Ross Perot]].
sentence_476: As the primary concluded, Carter spoke of the need for the [[1992_Democratic_National_Convention|1992 Democratic National Convention]] to address certain issues not focused on in the past, and campaigned for Clinton after he became the Democratic nominee in the general election, publicly stating his expectation to be consulted during the latter's presidency.
sentence_477: Carter endorsed Vice President [[Al_Gore|Al Gore]] days before the [[2000_United_States_presidential_election|2000 presidential election]], and in the years following voiced his opinion that the election was won by Gore, despite the Supreme Court handing the election to Bush in the controversial [[Bush_v._Gore|Bush v. Gore]] ruling.
sentence_478: In the [[2004_United_States_presidential_election|2004 election cycle]], Carter endorsed [[John_Kerry|John Kerry]] and spoke at the 2004 Democratic National Convention.
sentence_479: Carter also voiced concerns of another voting mishap in the state of Florida.
sentence_480: Amid the Democratic presidential primary in [[2008_United_States_presidential_election|2008]], Carter was speculated to endorse Senator [[Barack_Obama|Barack Obama]] over his main primary rival [[Hillary_Clinton|Hillary Clinton]] amid his speaking favorably of the candidate, as well as remarks from the Carter family that showed their support for Obama.
sentence_481: Carter also commented on Clinton ending her bid when superdelegates voted after the June 3 primary.
sentence_482: Leading up to the general election, Carter criticized [[John_McCain|John McCain]], who responded to Carter's comments, and warned Obama against selecting Clinton as his running mate.
sentence_483: Carter endorsed Republican [[Mitt_Romney|Mitt Romney]] for the Republican nomination during the primary season of the [[2012_United_States_presidential_election|2012 election cycle]], though he clarified his backing of Romney was due to him considering the former Massachusetts governor the candidate that could best assure a victory for President Obama.
sentence_484: Carter delivered a videotape address at the [[2012_Democratic_National_Convention|2012 Democratic National Convention]].
sentence_485: Carter was critical of Republican presidential candidate [[Donald_Trump|Donald Trump]] shortly after the latter entered the primary, and Carter predicted he would lose, noting the differing circumstances of the political climate from when he was still an active politician.
sentence_486: As the primary continued, Carter stated he would prefer Trump over his main rival [[Ted_Cruz|Ted Cruz]], though he rebuked the Trump campaign in remarks during the primary, and in his address to the [[2016_Democratic_National_Convention|2016 Democratic National Convention]].
sentence_487: In the Democratic primary, Carter voted for Senator [[Bernie_Sanders|Bernie Sanders]], and later endorsed the party's nominee, Hillary Clinton, during the Democratic National Convention.
sentence_488: In October 2017, however, Carter defended President Trump in an interview with The New York Times, criticizing the media's coverage of him.
sentence_489: "I think the media have been harder on Trump than any other president certainly that I've known about," Carter stated.
sentence_490: "I think they feel free to claim that Trump is mentally deranged and everything else without hesitation."
sentence_491: He also praised Trump for reaching out to Saudi Arabia and stated that the President has been under a stricter spotlight than his predecessors.
sentence_492: After the interview, Trump himself praised Carter's comments and thanked him over [[Twitter|Twitter]], writing "Just read the nice remarks by President Jimmy Carter about me and how badly I am treated by the press (Fake News).
sentence_493: Thank you Mr.
sentence_494: President!"
sentence_495: He has sharply criticized the [[U.S._Immigration_and_Customs_Enforcement|U.S.
sentence_496: Immigration and Customs Enforcement]] department under Trump and the administration's response to the [[Assassination_of_Jamal_Khashoggi|assassination of Jamal Khashoggi]].
sentence_497: Carter believes that Trump would not have been elected without [[Russian_interference_in_the_2016_United_States_elections|Russia's interference in the 2016 election]], and he believes "that Trump didn't actually win the election in 2016.
sentence_498: He lost the election, and he was put into office because the Russians interfered on his behalf."
sentence_499: When questioned, he agreed that Trump is an "illegitimate president".
sentence_500: Carter does not believe the Russians changed any votes during the presidential election or primaries.
sentence_501: Carter criticized the Bush administration's handling of [[Hurricane_Katrina|Hurricane Katrina]], built homes in the aftermath of [[Hurricane_Sandy|Hurricane Sandy]], and partnered with former presidents to work with [[One_America_Appeal|One America Appeal]] to help the victims of [[Hurricane_Harvey|Hurricane Harvey]] and [[Hurricane_Irma|Hurricane Irma]] in the [[Gulf_Coast_of_the_United_States|Gulf Coast]] and [[Texas|Texas]] communities, in addition to writing op-eds about the goodness seen in Americans who assist each other during natural disasters.
sentence_502: Carter attended the dedication of his presidential library and those of Presidents Ronald Reagan, George H. W. Bush, Bill Clinton, and George W. Bush.
sentence_503: He delivered eulogies at the funerals of [[Coretta_Scott_King|Coretta Scott King]] and [[Gerald_Ford|Gerald Ford]], and [[Theodore_Hesburgh|Theodore Hesburgh]].
sentence_504: As of August 2019, Carter serves as an Honorary Chair for the [[World_Justice_Project|World Justice Project]] and formerly served as one for the [[Continuity_of_Government_Commission|Continuity of Government Commission]].
sentence_505: He continues to occasionally teach [[Sunday_school|Sunday school]] at Maranatha Baptist Church.
sentence_506: Carter also teaches at [[Emory_University|Emory University]] in Atlanta, and in June 2019 was awarded tenure for 37 years of service.
sentence_507: Although Carter was "personally opposed" to [[Abortion|abortion]], he supported legalized abortion after the landmark [[US_Supreme_Court|US Supreme Court]] decision [[Roe_v._Wade|Roe v. Wade]], 410 US 113 (1973).
sentence_508: As president, he did not support increased federal funding for abortion services.
sentence_509: He was criticized by the [[American_Civil_Liberties_Union|American Civil Liberties Union]] for not doing enough to find alternatives.
sentence_510: In a March 29, 2012 interview with [[Laura_Ingraham|Laura Ingraham]], Carter expressed his current view of abortion and his wish to see the Democratic Party becoming more pro-life:
sentence_511: Carter is known for his strong opposition to the death penalty, which he expressed during his presidential campaigns.
sentence_512: In his [[Nobel_Prize|Nobel Prize]] lecture, Carter urged "prohibition of the death penalty".
sentence_513: He has continued to speak out against the death penalty in the US and abroad.
sentence_514: In a letter to the Governor of New Mexico, [[Bill_Richardson|Bill Richardson]], Carter urged the governor to sign a bill to eliminate the death penalty and institute life in prison without parole instead.
sentence_515: New Mexico abolished the [[Capital_punishment|death penalty]] in 2009.
sentence_516: Carter wrote: "As you know, the United States is one of the few countries, along with nations such as Saudi Arabia, China, and Cuba, which still carry out the death penalty despite the ongoing tragedy of wrongful conviction and gross racial and class-based disparities that make impossible the fair implementation of this ultimate punishment."
sentence_517: In 2012, Carter wrote an [[Op-ed|op-ed]] in the [[LA_Times|LA Times]] supporting passage of a state referendum which would have ended the death penalty.
sentence_518: He opened the article: "The process for administering the death penalty in the United States is broken beyond repair, and it is time to choose a more effective and moral alternative.
sentence_519: California voters will have the opportunity to do this on election day."
sentence_520: Carter has also called for commutations of death sentences for many death-row inmates, including Brian K. Baldwin (executed in 1999 in [[Alabama|Alabama]]), [[Kenneth_Foster|Kenneth Foster]] (sentence in [[Texas|Texas]] commuted in 2007) and [[Troy_Davis|Troy Davis]] (executed in Georgia in 2011).
sentence_521: In October 2000, Carter, a third-generation Southern Baptist, severed connections to the [[Southern_Baptist_Convention|Southern Baptist Convention]] over its opposition to women as pastors.
sentence_522: What led Carter to take this action was a doctrinal statement by the Convention, adopted in June 2000, advocating a [[Biblical_literalism|literal interpretation of the Bible]].
sentence_523: This statement followed a position of the Convention two years previously advocating the submission of wives to their husbands.
sentence_524: Carter described the reason for his decision as due to: "an increasing inclination on the part of Southern Baptist Convention leaders to be more rigid on what is a Southern Baptist and exclusionary of accommodating those who differ from them."
sentence_525: The New York Times called Carter's action "the highest-profile defection yet from the Southern Baptist Convention."
sentence_526: On July 15, 2009, Carter wrote an opinion piece about equality for women in which he stated that he chooses equality for women over the dictates of the leadership of what has been a lifetime religious commitment.
sentence_527: He said that the view that women are inferior is not confined to one faith, "nor, tragically does its influence stop at the walls of the church, mosque, synagogue or temple."
sentence_529: In 2014, he published A Call to Action: Women, Religion, Violence, and Power.
sentence_530: Carter has publicly expressed support both for a ban on assault weapons and for background checks of gun buyers.
sentence_531: In May 1994, Carter and former presidents [[Gerald_Ford|Gerald Ford]] and [[Ronald_Reagan|Ronald Reagan]] wrote to the [[United_States_House_of_Representatives|U.S.
sentence_532: House of Representatives]] in support of banning "semi-automatic assault guns."
sentence_533: In a February 2013 appearance on [[Piers_Morgan_Tonight|Piers Morgan Tonight]], Carter agreed that if the [[Assault_Weapons_Ban_of_2013|assault weapons ban]] did not pass it would be mainly due to lobbying by the [[National_Rifle_Association|National Rifle Association]] and its pressure on "weak-kneed" politicians.
sentence_534: Carter has stated that he supports [[Same-sex_marriage|same-sex marriage]] in civil ceremonies.
sentence_535: He has also stated that he believes [[Jesus|Jesus]] would also support it, saying "I believe Jesus would.
sentence_536: I don't have any verse in scripture.
sentence_538: I believe Jesus would approve gay marriage, but that's just my own personal belief.
sentence_539: I think Jesus would encourage any love affair if it was honest and sincere and was not damaging to anyone else, and I don't see that gay marriage damages anyone else."
sentence_540: Evangelist [[Franklin_Graham|Franklin Graham]] criticized the assertion as "absolutely wrong."
sentence_541: In October 2014, Carter argued ahead of a Supreme Court ruling that legalization of same-sex marriage should be left up to the states and not mandated by federal law.
sentence_542: Carter ignited debate in September 2009 when he stated, "I think an overwhelming portion of the intensely demonstrated animosity toward President Barack Obama is based on the fact that he is a black man, that he is African-American."

sentence_2: It is not to be confused with [[Labour_Union_(Poland)|Labour Union (Poland)]] or [[Labour_Union_(UK)|Labour Union (UK)]].
sentence_3: A trade union (or a labor union in [[American_English|American English]]), often simply called a union, is an organization of workers who have come together to achieve many common goals, such as protecting the integrity of their trade, improving safety standards, and attaining better wages, benefits (such as vacation, health care, and retirement), and working conditions through the increased bargaining power wielded by the creation of a monopoly of the workers.
sentence_4: Trade unions typically fund the formal organization, head office, and legal team functions of the trade union through regular fees or union dues.
sentence_5: The delegate staff of the trade union representation in the workforce are made up of workplace volunteers who are appointed by members in democratic elections.
sentence_6: The trade union, through an elected leadership and bargaining committee, bargains with the employer on behalf of union members ( members) and negotiates [[Labour_and_employment_law|labour contracts]] (collective bargaining) with employers.
sentence_7: The most common purpose of these associations or unions is "maintaining or improving the conditions of their [[Employment|employment]]".
sentence_8: This may include the negotiation of wages, work rules, occupational health and safety standards, complaint procedures, rules governing status of employees including promotions, just cause conditions for termination, and employment benefits.
sentence_9: Unions may organize a particular section of skilled workers ([[Craft_unionism|craft unionism]]), a cross-section of workers from various trades (general unionism), or attempt to organize all workers within a particular industry ([[Industrial_unionism|industrial unionism]]).
sentence_10: The agreements negotiated by a union are binding on the rank and file members and the employer and in some cases on other non-member workers.
sentence_11: Trade unions traditionally have a constitution which details the governance of their bargaining unit and also have governance at various levels of government depending on the industry that binds them legally to their negotiations and functioning.
sentence_12: Originating in Great Britain, trade unions became popular in many countries during the [[Industrial_Revolution|Industrial Revolution]].
sentence_13: Trade unions may be composed of individual workers, [[Professional|professionals]], [[Retiree|past workers]], students, [[Apprentice|apprentices]] or the unemployed.
sentence_14: Trade union density, or the percentage of workers belonging to a trade union, [[#Prevalence_worldwide|is highest in the Nordic countries]].
sentence_15: Since the publication of the [[History_of_Trade_Unionism|History of Trade Unionism]] (1894) by [[Sidney_Webb|Sidney]] and [[Beatrice_Webb|Beatrice Webb]], the predominant historical view is that a trade union "is a continuous association on wage earners for the purpose of maintaining or improving the conditions of their employment."
sentence_16: [[Karl_Marx|Karl Marx]] described trade unions thus: "The value of labour-power constitutes the conscious and explicit foundation of the trade unions, whose importance for the [...] working class can scarcely be overestimated.
sentence_17: The trade unions aim at nothing less than to prevent the reduction of wages below the level that is traditionally maintained in the various branches of industry.
sentence_18: That is to say, they wish to prevent the price of labour-power from falling below its value" (Capital V1, 1867, p. 1069).
