sentence_99: Back then the liberal union was known as the "Nationale Centrale der Liberale Vakbonden van België".
sentence_100: In 1930, the ACLVB-CGSLB adopted its current name.
sentence_101: Besides these "big three" there are a number of smaller unions, some more influential than others.
sentence_102: These smaller unions tend to specialize in one profession or economic sector.
sentence_103: Next to these specialized unions there is also the that rejects the pillarization of the "big three" trade unions (their affiliation with political parties).
sentence_104: There is also a small [[Flanders|Flemish]] nationalist union that exists only in the [[Flemish_language|Flemish]]-speaking part of Belgium, called the .
sentence_105: The last Belgian union worth mentioning is the very small, but highly active anarchist union called the .
sentence_106: Main article: [[List_of_trade_unions_in_Canada|List of trade unions in Canada]]
sentence_107: Canada's first trade union, the Labourers' Benevolent Association (now International Longshoremen's Association Local 273), formed in [[Saint_John,_New_Brunswick|Saint John, New Brunswick]] in 1849.
sentence_108: The union was formed when Saint John's longshoremen banded together to lobby for regular pay and a shorter workday.
sentence_109: Canadian unionism had early ties with [[United_Kingdom_of_Great_Britain_and_Ireland|Britain]] and Ireland.
sentence_110: Tradesmen who came from Britain brought traditions of the British trade union movement, and many British unions had branches in Canada.
sentence_111: Canadian unionism's ties with the United States eventually replaced those with Britain.
sentence_112: Collective bargaining was first recognized in 1945, after the strike by the [[United_Auto_Workers|United Auto Workers]] at the [[General_Motors|General Motors]]' plant in [[Oshawa,_Ontario|Oshawa, Ontario]].
sentence_113: Justice [[Ivan_Rand|Ivan Rand]] issued a landmark legal decision after the strike in [[Windsor,_Ontario|Windsor, Ontario]], involving 17,000 [[Ford|Ford]] workers.
sentence_114: He granted the union the compulsory check-off of union dues.
sentence_115: Rand ruled that all workers in a bargaining unit benefit from a union-negotiated contract.
sentence_116: Therefore, he reasoned they must pay union dues, although they do not have to join the union.
sentence_117: The post-[[World_War_II|World War II]] era also saw an increased pattern of unionization in the public service.
sentence_118: Teachers, nurses, social workers, professors and cultural workers (those employed in museums, orchestras and art galleries) all sought private-sector collective bargaining rights.
sentence_119: The Canadian Labour Congress was founded in 1956 as the national trade union center for Canada.
sentence_120: In the 1970s the federal government came under intense pressures to curtail labour cost and inflation.
sentence_121: In 1975, the [[Liberal_Party_of_Canada|Liberal]] government of [[Pierre_Trudeau|Pierre Trudeau]] introduced mandatory price and wage controls.
sentence_122: Under the new law, wages increases were monitored and those ruled to be unacceptably high were rolled back by the government.
sentence_123: Pressures on unions continued into the 1980s and '90s.
sentence_124: Private sector unions faced plant closures in many manufacturing industries and demands to reduce wages and increase productivity.
sentence_125: Public sector unions came under attack by federal and provincial governments as they attempted to reduce spending, reduce taxes and balance budgets.
sentence_126: Legislation was introduced in many jurisdictions reversing union collective bargaining rights, and many jobs were lost to contractors.
sentence_127: Prominent domestic unions in Canada include ACTRA, the Canadian Union of Postal Workers, the Canadian Union of Public Employees, the [[Public_Service_Alliance_of_Canada|Public Service Alliance of Canada]], the [[National_Union_of_Public_and_General_Employees|National Union of Public and General Employees]], and [[Unifor|Unifor]].
sentence_128: International unions active in Canada include the [[International_Alliance_of_Theatrical_Stage_Employees|International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees]], [[United_Automobile_Workers|United Automobile Workers]], United Food and Commercial Workers, and [[United_Steelworkers|United Steelworkers]].
sentence_129: Main article: [[Trade_unions_in_Colombia|Trade unions in Colombia]]
sentence_130: Until around 1990 Colombian trade unions were among the strongest in [[Latin_America|Latin America]].
sentence_131: However, the 1980s expansion of [[Paramilitarism_in_Colombia|paramilitarism in Colombia]] saw trade union leaders and members increasingly targeted for assassination, and as a result Colombia has been the most dangerous country in the world for trade unionists for several decades.
sentence_132: Between 2000 and 2010 Colombia accounted for 63.12% of trade unionists murdered globally.
sentence_133: According to the [[International_Trade_Union_Confederation|International Trade Union Confederation]] (ITUC) there were 2832 murders of trade unionists between 1 January 1986 and 30 April 2010, meaning that "on average, men and women trade unionists in Colombia have been killed at the rate of one every three days over the last 23 years."
sentence_134: Main article: [[Trade_unions_in_Costa_Rica|Trade unions in Costa Rica]]
sentence_135: In [[Costa_Rica|Costa Rica]], trade unions first appeared in the late 1800s to support workers in a variety of urban and industrial jobs, such as railroad builders and craft tradesmen.
sentence_136: After facing violent repression, such as during the 1934 United Fruit Strike, unions gained more power after the 1948 [[Costa_Rican_Civil_War|Costa Rican Civil War]].
sentence_137: Today, Costa Rican unions are strongest in the public sector, including the fields of education and medicine, but also have a strong presence in the agricultural sector.
sentence_138: In general, Costa Rican unions support government regulation of the banking, medical, and education fields, as well as improved wages and working conditions.
sentence_139: Main article: [[Trade_unions_in_Germany|Trade unions in Germany]]
sentence_140: Trade unions in Germany have a history reaching back to the [[Revolutions_of_1848_in_the_German_states|German revolution]] in 1848, and still play an important role in the [[Economy_of_Germany|German economy]] and society.
sentence_141: In 1875 the SPD, the Social Democratic Party of Germany, which is one of the biggest political parties in Germany, supported the forming of unions in Germany.
sentence_142: The most important labour organisation is the [[German_Confederation_of_Trade_Unions|German Confederation of Trade Unions]] (Deutscher Gewerkschaftsbund – DGB), which represents more than 6 million people (31 December 2011) and is the umbrella association of several single trade unions for special economic sectors.
sentence_143: The DGB is not the only Union Organization that represents the working trade.
sentence_144: There are smaller organizations, such as the CGB, which is a Christian-based confederation, that represent over 1.5 million people.
sentence_145: Main article: [[Trade_unions_in_India|Trade unions in India]]
sentence_146: In India, the Trade Union movement is generally divided on political lines.
sentence_147: According to provisional statistics from the [[Ministry_of_Labour_and_Employment_(India)|Ministry of Labour]], trade unions had a combined membership of 24,601,589 in 2002.
sentence_148: As of 2008, there are 11 Central Trade Union Organisations (CTUO) recognized by the Ministry of Labour.
sentence_149: The forming of these unions was a big deal in India.
sentence_150: It led to a big push for more regulatory laws which gave workers a lot more power.
sentence_151: [[AITUC|AITUC]] is the oldest trade union in India.
sentence_152: It is a left supported organization.
sentence_153: A trade union with nearly 2,000,000 members is the Self Employed Women's Association (SEWA) which protects the rights of Indian women working in the informal economy.
sentence_154: In addition to the protection of rights, SEWA educates, mobilizes, finances, and exalts their members' trades.
sentence_155: Multiple other organizations represent workers.
sentence_156: These organizations are formed upon different political groups.
sentence_157: These different groups allow different groups of people with different political views to join a Union.
sentence_158: Main article: [[Labor_unions_in_Japan|Labor unions in Japan]]
sentence_159: Trade unions emerged in Japan in the second half of the [[Meiji_period|Meiji period]] as the country underwent a period of rapid [[Industrialization|industrialization]].
sentence_160: Until 1945, however, the labour movement remained weak, impeded by lack of legal rights, [[Anti-union|anti-union]] legislation, management-organised factory councils, and political divisions between "cooperative" and radical unionists.
sentence_161: In the immediate aftermath of the Second World War, the [[Occupation_of_Japan|US Occupation]] authorities initially encouraged the formation of independent unions.
sentence_162: Legislation was passed that enshrined the right to organise, and membership rapidly rose to 5 million by February 1947.
sentence_163: The organisation rate, however, peaked at 55.8% in 1949 and subsequently declined to 18.2% (2006).
sentence_164: The labour movement went through a process of reorganisation from 1987 to 1991 from which emerged the present configuration of three major trade union federations, [[RENGO|Rengo]], Zenroren, and [[Zenrokyo|Zenrokyo]], along with other smaller national union organisations.
sentence_165: Before the 1990s, unions in Mexico had been historically part of a state institutional system.
sentence_166: From 1940 until the 1980s, during the worldwide spread of [[Neoliberalism|neoliberalism]] through the [[Washington_Consensus|Washington Consensus]], the Mexican unions did not operate independently, but instead as part of a state institutional system, largely controlled by the ruling party.
sentence_167: During these 40 years, the primary aim of the trade unions was not to benefit the workers, but to carry out the state's economic policy under their cosy relationship with the ruling party.
sentence_168: This economic policy, which peaked in the 1950s and 60s with the so-called "[[Mexican_Miracle|Mexican Miracle]]", saw rising incomes and improved standards of living but the primary beneficiaries were the wealthy.
sentence_169: In the 1980s, Mexico began adhering to Washington Consensus policies, selling off state industries such as railroad and telecommunications to private industries.
sentence_170: The new owners had an antagonistic attitude towards unions, which, accustomed to comfortable relationships with the state, were not prepared to fight back.
sentence_171: A movement of new unions began to emerge under a more independent model, while the former institutionalized unions had become very corrupt, violent, and led by gangsters.
sentence_172: From the 1990s onwards, this new model of independent unions prevailed, a number of them represented by the National Union of Workers / Unión Nacional de Trabajadores.
sentence_173: Current old institutions like the Oil Workers Union and the National Education Workers' Union (Sindicato Nacional de Trabajadores de la Educación, or SNTE) are examples of how the use of government benefits are not being applied to improve the quality in the investigation of the use of oil or the basic education in Mexico as long as their leaders show publicly that they are living wealthily.
sentence_174: With 1.4 million members, the teachers' union is [[Latin_America|Latin America]]'s largest; half of Mexico's government employees are teachers.
sentence_175: It controls school curriculums, and all teacher appointments.
sentence_176: Until recently, retiring teachers routinely "gave" their lifelong appointment to a relative or "sell" it for anywhere in between $4,700 and $11,800.
sentence_177: Trade unions (Danish: Fagforeninger, Norwegian: Fagforeninger/Fagforeiningar Swedish: Fackföreningar) have a long tradition in [[Scandinavia|Scandinavian]] and [[Nordic_countries|Nordic]] society.
sentence_178: Beginning in the mid-19th century, they today have a large impact on the nature of employment and workers' rights in many of the [[Nordic_countries|Nordic countries]].
sentence_179: One of the largest trade unions in [[Sweden|Sweden]] is the Swedish Confederation of Trade Unions, (LO, Landsorganisationen), incorporating unions such as the Swedish Metal Workers' Union (IF Metall = Industrifacket Metall), the Swedish Electricians' Union (Svenska Elektrikerförbundet) and the Swedish Municipality Workers' Union (Svenska Kommunalarbetareförbundet, abbreviated Kommunal).
sentence_180: One of the aims of IF Metall is to transform jobs into "good jobs", also called "developing jobs".
sentence_181: Swedish system is strongly based on the so-called Swedish model, which argues the importance of collective agreements between trade unions and employers.
sentence_182: Today, the world's highest rates of union membership are in the [[Nordic_countries|Nordic countries]].
sentence_183: As of 2018 or latest year, the percentage of workers belonging to a union (trade union density) was 90.4% in [[Iceland|Iceland]], 67.2% in [[Denmark|Denmark]], 66.1% in [[Sweden|Sweden]], 64.4 in [[Finland|Finland]] and 52.5% in [[Norway|Norway]], while it is unknown in [[Greenland|Greenland]], Faroe Islands and the [[Åland_Islands|Åland Islands]].
sentence_184: Excluding full-time students working part-time, Swedish union density was 68% in 2019.
sentence_185: In all the Nordic countries with a Ghent system—Sweden, Denmark and [[Finland|Finland]]—union density is about 70%.
sentence_186: The considerably raised membership fees of Swedish union unemployment funds implemented by the new center-right government in January 2007 caused large drops in membership in both unemployment funds and trade unions.
sentence_187: From 2006 to 2008, union density declined by six percentage points: from 77% to 71%.
sentence_188: See also: [[List_of_trade_unions_in_Spain|List of trade unions in Spain]]
sentence_189: During the [[Spanish_civil_war|Spanish civil war]] [[Anarchists|anarchists]], and [[Syndicalists|syndicalists]] took control over much of Spain.
sentence_190: Implementing worker control through a system of [[Libertarian_socialism|libertarian socialism]] with organizations like the [[Anarcho-syndicalist|anarcho-syndicalist]] [[Confederación_Nacional_del_Trabajo|CNT]] organizing throughout Spain.
sentence_191: Unions were particularly present in [[Revolutionary_Catalonia|Revolutionary Catalonia]], in which anarchists were already the basis for most of society with over 90% of industries being organized through work cooperatives.
sentence_192: The republicans, anarchists and leftists would later loose control over Spain , with [[Francisco_Franco|Francisco Franco]] becoming dictator of Spain.
sentence_193: During the fascist regime of Spain the Francoist regime saw the worker movement and union movement as a threat, Franco banned all existing trade unions and set up the government controlled [[Spanish_Syndical_Organization|Spanish Syndical Organization]] as the only legal Spanish trade union, with the organization existing to maintain Francos power.
sentence_194: Many anarchists, communists and leftist turned towards insurgent tactics as Franco implemented wide reaching authoritarian policies, with the CNT and other unions being forced underground.
sentence_195: Anarchists would operate covertly setting up local organizations and underground movements to challenge Franco.
sentence_196: On the 20 of December the [[ETA_(separatist_group)|ETA]] assassinated Luis Carrero.
sentence_197: The death of Carrero Blanco had numerous political implications.
sentence_198: By the end of 1973, the physical health of Francisco Franco had declined significantly, and it epitomized the final crisis of the Francoist regime.
sentence_199: After his death, the most conservative sector of the Francoist State, known as the búnker, wanted to influence Franco so that he would choose an ultraconservative as Prime Minister.
sentence_200: Finally, he chose Carlos Arias Navarro, who originally announced a partial relaxation of the most rigid aspects of the Francoist State, but quickly retreated under pressure from the búnker.
sentence_201: After Franco's death Arias Navarro began relaxing Spanish authoritarianism.
sentence_202: During the Spanish transition to democracy, leftist organizations became legal once again.
sentence_203: In modern Spain trade unions now contribute massively towards Spanish society, being again the main catalyst for political change in Spain, with cooperatives employing large parts of the Spanish population such as the Mondragon Corporation.
sentence_204: Trade unions today lead mass protests against the Spanish government, and are one of the main vectors of political change.
sentence_205: Main articles: [[Trade_unions_in_the_United_Kingdom|Trade unions in the United Kingdom]] and [[History_of_trade_unions_in_the_United_Kingdom|History of trade unions in the United Kingdom]]
sentence_206: Moderate [[New_Model_Union|New Model Unions]] dominated the union movement from the mid-19th century and where trade unionism was stronger than the political labour movement until the formation and growth of the [[Labour_Party_(UK)|Labour Party]] in the early years of the 20th century.
sentence_207: Trade unionism in the United Kingdom was a major factor in some of the economic crises during the 1960s and the 1970s, culminating in the "[[Winter_of_Discontent|Winter of Discontent]]" of late 1978 and early 1979, when a significant percentage of the nation's public sector workers went on strike.
sentence_208: By this stage, some 12,000,000 workers in the United Kingdom were trade union members.
sentence_209: However, the election of the [[Conservative_Party_(UK)|Conservative Party]] led by [[Margaret_Thatcher|Margaret Thatcher]] at the [[1979_United_Kingdom_general_election|general election]] in May 1979, at the expense of Labour's [[James_Callaghan|James Callaghan]], saw substantial trade union reform which saw the level of strikes fall.
sentence_210: The level of trade union membership also fell sharply in the 1980s, and continued falling for most of the 1990s.
sentence_211: The long decline of most of the industries in which manual trade unions were strong – e.g. steel, coal, printing, the docks – was one of the causes of this loss of trade union members.
sentence_212: In 2011 there were 6,135,126 members in TUC-affiliated unions, down from a peak of 12,172,508 in 1980.
sentence_213: Trade union density was 14.1% in the private sector and 56.5% in the public sector.
sentence_214: Main articles: [[Labor_unions_in_the_United_States|Labor unions in the United States]] and [[Labor_history_of_the_United_States|Labor history of the United States]]
sentence_215: Labor unions are legally recognized as representatives of workers in many industries in the United States.
sentence_216: In the United States, unions were formed based on power with the people, not over the people like the government at the time.
sentence_217: Their activity today centres on [[Collective_bargaining|collective bargaining]] over wages, benefits and working conditions for their membership, and on representing their members in disputes with management over violations of contract provisions.
sentence_218: Larger unions also typically engage in lobbying activities and supporting endorsed candidates at the state and federal level.
sentence_219: Most unions in America are aligned with one of two larger umbrella organizations: the [[AFL-CIO|AFL-CIO]] created in 1955, and the [[Change_to_Win_Federation|Change to Win Federation]] which split from the AFL-CIO in 2005.
sentence_220: Both advocate policies and legislation on behalf of workers in the United States and Canada, and take an active role in politics.
sentence_221: The AFL-CIO is especially concerned with global trade issues.
sentence_222: In 2010, the percentage of workers belonging to a union in the United States (or total labor union "density") was 11.4%, compared to 18.3% in Japan, 27.5% in Canada and 70% in Finland.
sentence_223: Union membership in the private sector has fallen under 7% – levels not seen since 1932.
sentence_224: Unions allege that employer-incited opposition has contributed to this decline in membership.
sentence_225: The most prominent unions are among [[Public_sector|public sector]] employees such as teachers, police and other non-managerial or non-executive federal, state, county and municipal employees.
sentence_226: Members of unions are disproportionately older, male and residents of the Northeast, the Midwest, and California.
sentence_227: Union workers in the private sector average 10–30% higher pay than non-union in America after controlling for individual, job, and labour market characteristics.
sentence_228: Because of their inherently governmental function, public sector workers are paid the same regardless of union affiliation or non-affiliation after controlling for individual, job, and labour market characteristics.
sentence_229: The economist [[Joseph_Stiglitz|Joseph Stiglitz]] has asserted that, "Strong unions have helped to reduce inequality, whereas weaker unions have made it easier for [[CEO|CEOs]], sometimes working with market forces that they have helped shape, to increase it."
sentence_230: The decline in unionization since the [[Second_World_War|Second World War]] in the United States has been associated with a pronounced rise in income and [[Wealth_inequality_in_the_United_States|wealth inequality]] and, since 1967, with loss of [[American_middle_class|middle class]] income.
sentence_231: The [[Association_of_Vatican_Lay_Workers|Association of Vatican Lay Workers]] represents lay employees in the Vatican.
sentence_232: Unions may organize a particular section of skilled workers ([[Craft_unionism|craft unionism]], traditionally found in Australia, Canada, Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Switzerland, the UK and the US), a cross-section of workers from various trades (general unionism, traditionally found in Australia, Belgium, Canada, Denmark, Netherlands, the UK and the US), or attempt to organize all workers within a particular industry ([[Industrial_unionism|industrial unionism]], found in Australia, Canada, Germany, Finland, Norway, South Korea, Sweden, Switzerland, the UK and the US).
sentence_233: These unions are often divided into "locals", and united in national [[List_of_federations_of_trade_unions|federations]].
sentence_234: These federations themselves will affiliate with [[International_organization|Internationals]], such as the [[International_Trade_Union_Confederation|International Trade Union Confederation]].
sentence_235: However, in Japan, union organization is slightly different due to the presence of enterprise unions, i.e. unions that are specific to a plant or company.
sentence_236: These enterprise unions, however, join industry-wide federations which in turn are members of [[RENGO|Rengo]], the Japanese national trade union confederation.
sentence_237: In [[Western_Europe|Western Europe]], professional associations often carry out the functions of a trade union.
sentence_238: In these cases, they may be negotiating for white-collar or professional workers, such as physicians, engineers or teachers.
sentence_239: Typically such trade unions refrain from politics or pursue a more liberal politics than their blue-collar counterparts.
sentence_240: A union may acquire the status of a "[[Juristic_person|juristic person]]" (an artificial legal entity), with a mandate to negotiate with employers for the workers it represents.
sentence_241: In such cases, unions have certain legal rights, most importantly the right to engage in [[Collective_bargaining|collective bargaining]] with the employer (or employers) over wages, working hours, and other [[Employment_contract|terms and conditions of employment]].
sentence_242: The inability of the parties to reach an agreement may lead to [[Industrial_action|industrial action]], culminating in either [[Strike_action|strike action]] or management [[Lockout_(industry)|lockout]], or binding arbitration.
sentence_243: In extreme cases, violent or illegal activities may develop around these events.
sentence_244: In other circumstances, unions may not have the legal right to represent workers, or the right may be in question.
sentence_245: This lack of status can range from non-recognition of a union to political or criminal prosecution of union activists and members, with many cases of violence and deaths having been recorded historically.
sentence_246: Unions may also engage in broader political or social struggle.
sentence_247: [[Social_Movement_Unionism|Social Unionism]] encompasses many unions that use their organizational strength to advocate for social policies and legislation favourable to their members or to workers in general.
sentence_248: As well, unions in some countries are closely aligned with [[Political_party|political parties]].
sentence_249: Unions are also delineated by the [[Service_model|service model]] and the [[Organizing_model|organizing model]].
sentence_250: The service model union focuses more on maintaining worker rights, providing services, and resolving disputes.
sentence_251: Alternately, the organizing model typically involves full-time [[Union_organizer|union organizers]], who work by building up confidence, strong networks, and leaders within the workforce; and confrontational campaigns involving large numbers of union members.
sentence_252: Many unions are a blend of these two philosophies, and the definitions of the models themselves are still debated.
sentence_253: In Britain, the perceived left-leaning nature of trade unions has resulted in the formation of a reactionary right-wing trade union called [[Solidarity_–_The_Union_for_British_Workers|Solidarity]] which is supported by the far-right [[British_National_Party|BNP]].
sentence_254: In Denmark, there are some newer apolitical "discount" unions who offer a very basic level of services, as opposed to the dominating Danish pattern of extensive services and organizing.
sentence_255: In contrast, in several European countries (e.g. Belgium, Denmark, the [[Netherlands|Netherlands]] and [[Switzerland|Switzerland]]), religious unions have existed for decades.
sentence_256: These unions typically distanced themselves from some of the doctrines of orthodox [[Marxism|Marxism]], such as the preference of atheism and from rhetoric suggesting that employees' interests always are in conflict with those of employers.
sentence_257: Some of these Christian unions have had some ties to centrist or conservative political movements and some do not regard strikes as acceptable political means for achieving employees' goals.
sentence_258: In [[Poland|Poland]], the biggest trade union [[Solidarity_(Polish_trade_union)|Solidarity]] emerged as an [[Anti-communism|anti-communist]] movement with [[Religious_nationalism|religious nationalist]] overtones and today it supports the right-wing Law and Justice party.
sentence_259: Although their political structure and autonomy varies widely, union leaderships are usually formed through democratic elections.
sentence_260: Some research, such as that conducted by the Australian Centre for Industrial Relations Research and Training, argues that unionized workers enjoy better conditions and wages than those who are not unionized.
sentence_261: Companies that employ workers with a union generally operate on one of several models:

list.value: A closed shop (US) or a "pre-entry closed shop" (UK) employs only people who are already union members. The compulsory hiring hall is an example of a closed shop – in this case the employer must recruit directly from the union, as well as the employee working strictly for unionized employers.
A union shop (US) or a "post-entry closed shop" (UK) employs non-union workers as well, but sets a time limit within which new employees must join a union.

An [[Agency_shop|agency shop]] requires non-union workers to pay a fee to the union for its services in negotiating their contract. This is sometimes called the [[Rand_formula|Rand formula]]. In certain situations involving state public employees in the United States, such as [[California|California]], "fair share laws" make it easy to require these sorts of payments.

An [[Open_shop|open shop]] does not require union membership in employing or keeping workers. Where a union is active, workers who do not contribute to a union may include those who approve of the union contract (free riders) and those who do not. In the United States, state level [[Right-to-work_law|right-to-work laws]] mandate the open shop in some states. In Germany only open shops are legal; that is, all discrimination based on union membership is forbidden. This affects the function and services of the union.

sentence_262: An EU case concerning Italy stated that, "The principle of trade union freedom in the Italian system implies recognition of the right of the individual not to belong to any trade union ("negative" freedom of association/trade union freedom), and the unlawfulness of discrimination liable to cause harm to non-unionized employees."
sentence_263: In Britain, previous to this EU jurisprudence, a series of laws introduced during the 1980s by Margaret Thatcher's government restricted closed and union shops.
sentence_264: All agreements requiring a worker to join a union are now illegal.
sentence_265: In the United States, the [[Taft-Hartley_Act|Taft-Hartley Act]] of 1947 outlawed the closed shop.
sentence_266: In 2006, the European Court of Human Rights found Danish closed-shop agreements to be in breach of Article 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms.
sentence_267: It was stressed that Denmark and [[Iceland|Iceland]] were among a limited number of contracting states that continue to permit the conclusion of closed-shop agreements.
sentence_268: Union law varies from country to country, as does the function of unions.
sentence_269: For example, German and Dutch unions have played a greater role in management decisions through participation in corporate boards and [[Co-determination|co-determination]] than have unions in the United States.
sentence_270: Moreover, in the United States, collective bargaining is most commonly undertaken by unions directly with employers, whereas in Austria, Denmark, Germany or Sweden, unions most often negotiate with employers associations.
sentence_271: Concerning labour market regulation in the EU, Gold (1993) and Hall (1994) have identified three distinct systems of labour market regulation, which also influence the role that unions play:

list.value: "In the Continental European System of labour market regulation, the government plays an important role as there is a strong legislative core of employee rights, which provides the basis for agreements as well as a framework for discord between unions on one side and employers or employers' associations on the other. This model was said to be found in EU core countries such as Belgium, France, Germany, the Netherlands and Italy, and it is also mirrored and emulated to some extent in the institutions of the EU, due to the relative weight that these countries had in the EU until the EU expansion by the inclusion of 10 new [[Eastern_Europe|Eastern European]] member states in 2004.

In the Anglo-Saxon System of labour market regulation, the government's legislative role is much more limited, which allows for more issues to be decided between employers and employees and any union or employers' associations which might represent these parties in the decision-making process. However, in these countries, collective agreements are not widespread; only a few businesses and a few sectors of the economy have a strong tradition of finding collective solutions in labour relations. [[Republic_of_Ireland|Ireland]] and the UK belong to this category, and in contrast to the EU core countries above, these countries first joined the EU in 1973.

In the Nordic System of labour market regulation, the government's legislative role is limited in the same way as in the Anglo-Saxon system. However, in contrast to the countries in the Anglo-Saxon system category, this is a much more widespread network of collective agreements, which covers most industries and most firms. This model was said to encompass Denmark, Finland, Norway and Sweden. Here, Denmark joined the EU in 1973, whereas Finland and Sweden joined in 1995."

sentence_272: The United States takes a more [[Laissez-faire|laissez-faire]] approach, setting some minimum standards but leaving most workers' wages and benefits to collective bargaining and market forces.
sentence_273: Thus, it comes closest to the above Anglo-Saxon model.
sentence_274: Also, the Eastern European countries that have recently entered into the EU come closest to the Anglo-Saxon model.
sentence_275: In contrast, in Germany, the relation between individual employees and employers is considered to be asymmetrical.
sentence_276: In consequence, many working conditions are not negotiable due to a strong legal protection of individuals.
sentence_277: However, the German flavor or works legislation has as its main objective to create a balance of power between employees organized in unions and employers organized in employers associations.
sentence_278: This allows much wider legal boundaries for collective bargaining, compared to the narrow boundaries for individual negotiations.
sentence_279: As a condition to obtain the legal status of a trade union, employee associations need to prove that their leverage is strong enough to serve as a counterforce in negotiations with employers.
sentence_280: If such an employees association is competing against another union, its leverage may be questioned by unions and then evaluated in a court trial.
sentence_281: In Germany, only very few professional associations obtained the right to negotiate salaries and working conditions for their members, notably the medical doctors association Marburger Bund and the pilots association Vereinigung Cockpit.
sentence_282: The engineers association [[Verein_Deutscher_Ingenieure|Verein Deutscher Ingenieure]] does not strive to act as a union, as it also represents the interests of engineering businesses.
sentence_283: Beyond the classification listed above, unions' relations with political parties vary.
sentence_284: In many countries unions are tightly bonded, or even share leadership, with a political party intended to represent the interests of the working class.
sentence_285: Typically this is a [[Left-wing|left-wing]], [[Socialist|socialist]], or [[Social_democrat|social democratic]] party, but many exceptions exist, including some of the aforementioned Christian unions.
sentence_286: In the United States, trade unions are almost always aligned with the [[Democratic_Party_(United_States)|Democratic Party]] with a few exceptions.
sentence_287: For example, the [[International_Brotherhood_of_Teamsters|International Brotherhood of Teamsters]] has supported [[Republican_Party_(United_States)|Republican Party]] candidates on a number of occasions and the [[Professional_Air_Traffic_Controllers_Organization_(1968)|Professional Air Traffic Controllers Organization]] (PATCO) endorsed [[Ronald_Reagan|Ronald Reagan]] in 1980.
sentence_288: In Britain trade union movement's relationship with the [[Labour_Party_(UK)|Labour Party]] frayed as party leadership embarked on [[Privatization|privatization]] plans at odds with what unions see as the worker's interests.
sentence_289: However, it has strengthened once more after the Labour party's election of [[Ed_Miliband|Ed Miliband]], who beat his brother [[David_Miliband|David Miliband]] to become leader of the party after Ed secured the trade union votes.
sentence_290: Additionally, in the past, there was a group known as the [[Conservative_Trade_Unionists|Conservative Trade Unionists]], or CTU, formed of people who sympathized with right wing Tory policy but were Trade Unionists.
sentence_291: Historically, the [[Republic_of_Korea|Republic of Korea]] has regulated collective bargaining by requiring employers to participate, but collective bargaining has only been legal if held in sessions before the lunar new year.
sentence_292: The largest trade union federation in the world is the [[Brussels|Brussels]]-based [[International_Trade_Union_Confederation|International Trade Union Confederation]] (ITUC), which has approximately 309 affiliated organizations in 156 countries and territories, with a combined membership of 166 million.
sentence_293: The ITUC is a federation of national trade union centres, such as the AFL-CIO in the United States and the Trades Union Congress in the United Kingdom.
sentence_294: Other global trade union organizations include the [[World_Federation_of_Trade_Unions|World Federation of Trade Unions]].
sentence_295: National and regional trade unions organizing in specific industry sectors or occupational groups also form [[Global_union_federation|global union federations]], such as [[Union_Network_International|Union Network International]], the [[International_Transport_Workers_Federation|International Transport Workers Federation]], the [[International_Federation_of_Journalists|International Federation of Journalists]], the International Arts and Entertainment Alliance or [[Public_Services_International|Public Services International]].
sentence_296: Main article: [[Opposition_to_trade_unions|Opposition to trade unions]]
sentence_297: In the United States, the outsourcing of labour to Asia, Latin America, and Africa has been partially driven by increasing costs of union partnership, which gives other countries a [[Comparative_advantage|comparative advantage]] in labour, making it more profitable to purchase disorganized, low-wage labour from these regions.
sentence_298: [[Milton_Friedman|Milton Friedman]], [[Economist|economist]] and advocate of [[Laissez-faire_capitalism|laissez-faire capitalism]], sought to show that unionization produces higher wages (for the union members) at the expense of fewer jobs, and that, if some industries are unionized while others are not, wages will tend to decline in non-unionized industries.
sentence_299: On the other hand, several studies have emphasized so-called revitalization strategies where trade unions attempt to better represent labour market outsiders, such as the unemployed and precarious workers.
sentence_300: Thus, for instance, trade unions in both Nordic and southern European countries have devised collective bargaining agreements that improved the conditions of temporary agency workers.
sentence_301: Several studies have found evidence that trade unions can reduce competitiveness due to a reduction of business profit, which can then lead to job losses as it makes the business unable to compete.
sentence_302: Unions have also been criticized by conservative economists and political groups for prolonging recessions and depressions due to discouraging investment.
sentence_303: Several sources of current news exist about the trade union movement in the world.
sentence_304: These include [[LabourStart|LabourStart]] and the official website of the international trade union movement Global Unions.
sentence_305: A source of international news about unions is RadioLabour which provides daily (Monday to Friday) news reports.
sentence_306: Labor Notes is the largest circulation cross-union publication remaining in the United States.
sentence_307: It reports news and analysis about union activity or problems facing the labour movement.
sentence_308: Another source of union news is the Workers Independent News, a news organization providing radio articles to independent and syndicated radio shows in the United States.

title: Kenesaw Mountain Landis

table.value: Judge of the [[United_States_District_Court_for_the_Northern_District_of_Illinois|United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois]]

sentence_0: Kenesaw Mountain Landis ([[English|/ˈkɛnɪsɔː ˈmaʊntɪn ˈlændɪs/]]; November 20, 1866 – November 25, 1944) was an American [[Jurist|jurist]] who served as a United States federal judge from 1905 to 1922 and the first [[Commissioner_of_Baseball|Commissioner of Baseball]] from 1920 until his death.
sentence_1: He is remembered for his handling of the [[Black_Sox_scandal|Black Sox scandal]], in which he expelled eight members of the [[1919_Chicago_White_Sox_season|Chicago White Sox]] from [[Organized_baseball|organized baseball]] for conspiring to lose the [[1919_World_Series|1919 World Series]] and repeatedly refused their reinstatement requests.
sentence_2: His firm actions and iron rule over baseball in the near quarter-century of his commissionership are generally credited with restoring public confidence in the game.
sentence_3: Born in [[Millville,_Ohio|Millville, Ohio]], Landis' given name was a spelling variation of the site of the [[Battle_of_Kennesaw_Mountain|Battle of Kennesaw Mountain]], a major battle of the [[American_Civil_War|American Civil War]] in which his father had been wounded.
sentence_4: Raised in Indiana, he became a lawyer, and then personal secretary to [[Walter_Q._Gresham|Walter Q. Gresham]], the new [[United_States_Secretary_of_State|United States Secretary of State]], in 1893.
sentence_5: He returned to private practice after Gresham died in office.
sentence_6: President [[Theodore_Roosevelt|Theodore Roosevelt]] appointed Landis as a judge of the [[United_States_District_Court_for_the_Northern_District_of_Illinois|United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois]] in 1905.
sentence_7: Landis received national attention in 1907 when he fined [[Standard_Oil_of_Indiana|Standard Oil of Indiana]] more than $29 million ($800 million in 2020) for violating federal laws forbidding rebates on railroad freight tariffs.
sentence_8: Though Landis was reversed on appeal, he was seen as a judge determined to rein in big business.
sentence_9: During and after World War I, Landis presided over several high-profile trials of draft resisters and others whom he saw as opposing the war effort.
sentence_10: He imposed heavy sentences on those who were convicted; some of the convictions were reversed on appeal, and other sentences were commuted.
sentence_11: In 1920, Landis was a leading candidate when [[American_League|American League]] and [[National_League|National League]] team owners, embarrassed by the Black Sox scandal and other instances of players throwing games, sought someone to rule over baseball.
sentence_12: Landis was given full power to act in the sport's best interest, and used that power extensively over the next quarter-century.
sentence_13: Landis was widely praised for cleaning up the game, although some of his decisions in the Black Sox matter remain controversial: supporters of [[Shoeless_Joe_Jackson|"Shoeless Joe" Jackson]] and [[Buck_Weaver|Buck Weaver]] contend that he was overly harsh with those players.
sentence_14: Others blame Landis for, in their view, delaying the [[Baseball_color_line|racial integration of baseball]].
sentence_15: Landis was elected to the [[National_Baseball_Hall_of_Fame|National Baseball Hall of Fame]] by a special vote shortly after he died in 1944.
sentence_16: Kenesaw Mountain Landis was born in [[Millville,_Ohio|Millville, Ohio]], the sixth child and fourth son of Abraham Hoch Landis, a physician, and Mary Kumler Landis, on November 20, 1866.
sentence_17: The Landises descended from Swiss Mennonites who had emigrated to Alsace before coming to the United States.
sentence_18: Abraham Landis had been wounded fighting on the Union side at the [[Battle_of_Kennesaw_Mountain|Battle of Kennesaw Mountain]] in Georgia, and when his parents proved unable to agree on a name for the new baby, Mary Landis proposed that they call him Kenesaw Mountain.
sentence_19: At the time, both spellings of "Kenesaw" were used, but in the course of time, "Kennesaw Mountain" became the accepted spelling of the battle site.
sentence_20: Abraham Landis worked in Millville as a country physician.
sentence_21: When Kenesaw was eight, the elder Landis moved his family to [[Delphi,_Indiana|Delphi, Indiana]], and subsequently to Logansport, Indiana, where the doctor purchased and ran several local farms—his war injury had caused him to scale back his medical practice.
sentence_22: Two of Kenesaw's four brothers, [[Charles_Beary_Landis|Charles Beary Landis]] and [[Frederick_Landis|Frederick Landis]], became [[Member_of_Congress|members]] of [[United_States_Congress|Congress]].
sentence_23: As "Kenny", as he was sometimes known, grew, he did an increasing share of the farm work, later stating, "I did my share—and it was a substantial share—in taking care of the 13 acres ...
sentence_24: I do not remember that I particularly liked to get up at 3:30 in the morning."
sentence_25: Kenesaw began his off-farm career at age ten as a news delivery boy.
sentence_26: He left school at 15 after an unsuccessful attempt to master [[Algebra|algebra]]; he then worked at the local general store.
sentence_27: He left that job for a position as errand boy with the [[Vandalia_Railroad_(1905–17)|Vandalia Railroad]].
sentence_28: Landis applied for a job as a brakeman, but was laughingly dismissed as too small.
sentence_29: He then worked for the Logansport Journal, and taught himself [[Shorthand|shorthand]] reporting, becoming in 1883 official court reporter for the [[Cass_County,_Indiana|Cass County]] Circuit Court.
sentence_30: Landis later wrote, "I may not have been much of a judge, nor baseball official, but I do pride myself on having been a real shorthand reporter."
sentence_31: He served in that capacity until 1886.
sentence_32: In his spare time, he became a prize-winning bicycle racer and played on and managed a baseball team.
sentence_33: Offered a professional contract as a ballplayer, he turned it down, stating that he preferred to play for the love of the game.
sentence_34: In 1886, Landis first ventured into [[Republican_Party_(United_States)|Republican Party]] politics, supporting a friend, Charles F. Griffin, for Indiana Secretary of State.
sentence_35: Griffin won, and Landis was rewarded with a civil service job in the Indiana Department of State.
sentence_36: While employed there, he applied to be an attorney.
sentence_37: At that time, in Indiana, an applicant needed only to prove that he was 21 and of good moral character, and Landis was admitted.
sentence_38: Landis opened a practice in [[Marion,_Indiana|Marion, Indiana]], but attracted few clients in his year of work there.
sentence_39: Realizing that an uneducated lawyer was unlikely to build a lucrative practice, Landis enrolled at Cincinnati's YMCA Law School (now part of [[Northern_Kentucky_University|Northern Kentucky University]]) in 1889.
sentence_40: Landis transferred to Union Law School (now part of [[Northwestern_University|Northwestern University]]) the following year, and in 1891, he took his law degree from Union and was admitted to the Illinois Bar.
sentence_41: He began a practice in Chicago, served as an assistant instructor at Union and with fellow attorney [[Clarence_Darrow|Clarence Darrow]] helped found the nonpartisan Chicago Civic Centre Club, devoted to municipal reform.
sentence_42: Landis practiced with college friend [[Frank_O._Lowden|Frank O. Lowden]]; the future commissioner and his law partner went into debt to impress potential clients, buying a law library secondhand.
sentence_43: In March 1893, President [[Grover_Cleveland|Grover Cleveland]] appointed federal judge [[Walter_Q._Gresham|Walter Q. Gresham]] as his [[United_States_Secretary_of_State|Secretary of State]], and Gresham hired Landis as his personal secretary.
sentence_44: Gresham had a long career as a political appointee in the latter part of the 19th century; though he lost his only two bids for elective office, he served in three Cabinet positions and was twice a [[Dark_horse|dark horse]] candidate for the Republican presidential nomination.
sentence_45: Although Gresham was a Republican, he had supported Cleveland (a [[Democratic_Party_(United_States)|Democrat]]) in the [[1892_United_States_presidential_election|1892 election]] because of his intense dislike for the Republican nominee, President [[Benjamin_Harrison|Benjamin Harrison]].
sentence_46: Kenesaw Landis had appeared before Judge Gresham in court.
sentence_47: According to Landis biographer J.G.
sentence_48: Taylor Spink, Gresham thought Landis "had something on the ball" and believed that Landis's shorthand skills would be of use.
sentence_49: In Washington, Landis worked hard to protect Gresham's interests in the State Department, making friends with many members of the press.
sentence_50: He was less popular among many of the Department's senior career officials, who saw him as brash.
sentence_51: When word leaked concerning President Cleveland's Hawaiian policy, the President was convinced Landis was the source of the information and demanded his dismissal.
sentence_52: Gresham defended Landis, stating that Cleveland would have to fire both of them, and the President relented, later finding out that he was mistaken in accusing Landis.
sentence_53: President Cleveland grew to like Landis, and when Gresham died in 1895, offered Landis the post of [[United_States_Ambassador_to_Venezuela|United States Ambassador to Venezuela]].
sentence_54: Landis declined the diplomatic post, preferring to return to Chicago to begin a law practice and to marry Winifred Reed, daughter of the [[Ottawa,_Illinois|Ottawa, Illinois]] postmaster.
sentence_55: The two married July 25, 1895; they had two surviving children, a boy, [[Reed_G._Landis|Reed]], and a girl, Susanne—a third child, Winifred, died almost immediately after being born.
sentence_56: Landis built a corporate law practice in Chicago; with the practice doing well, he deeply involved himself in Republican Party politics.
sentence_57: He built a close association with his friend Lowden and served as his campaign manager for [[Governor_of_Illinois|governor of Illinois]] in 1904.
sentence_58: Lowden was defeated, but would later serve two terms in the office and be a major contender for the 1920 Republican presidential nomination.
sentence_59: A seat on the [[United_States_District_Court_for_the_Northern_District_of_Illinois|United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois]] was vacant; President [[Theodore_Roosevelt|Theodore Roosevelt]] offered it to Lowden, who declined it and recommended Landis.
sentence_60: Other recommendations from Illinois politicians followed, and Roosevelt nominated Landis for the seat.
sentence_61: According to Spink, President Roosevelt wanted "a tough judge and a man sympathetic with his viewpoint in that important court"; Lowden and Landis were, like Roosevelt, on the progressive left of the Republican Party.
sentence_62: On March 18, 1905, Roosevelt transmitted the nomination to the Senate, which confirmed Landis the same afternoon, without any committee hearing; he received his commission the same day.
sentence_63: Landis's courtroom, room 627 in the [[Chicago_Federal_Building|Chicago Federal Building]], was ornate and featured two murals; one of [[John_of_England|King John]] conceding [[Magna_Carta|Magna Carta]], the other of [[Moses|Moses]] about to smash the tablets of the [[Ten_Commandments|Ten Commandments]].
sentence_64: The mahogany and marble chamber was, according to Landis biographer David Pietrusza, "just the spot for Landis's sense of the theatrical.
sentence_65: In it he would hold court for nearly the next decade and a half."
sentence_66: According to Spink, "It wasn't long before Chicago writers discovered they had a 'character' on the bench."
sentence_67: A. L. Sloan of the [[Chicago's_American|Chicago Herald-American]], a friend of Landis, recalled:
sentence_68: If Judge Landis was suspicious of an attorney's line of questioning, he would begin to wrinkle his nose, and once told a witness, "Now let's stop fooling around and tell exactly what did happen, without reciting your life's history."
sentence_69: When an elderly defendant told him that he would not be able to live to complete a five-year sentence, Landis scowled at him and asked, "Well, you can try, can't you?"
sentence_70: When a young man stood before him for sentencing after admitting to stealing jewels from a parcel, the defendant's wife stood near him, infant daughter in her arms, and Landis mused what to do about the situation.
sentence_71: After a dramatic pause, Landis ordered the young man to take his wife and daughter and go home with them, expressing his unwillingness to have the girl be the daughter of a convict.
sentence_72: According to sportswriter Ed Fitzgerald in [[SPORT_(magazine)|SPORT magazine]], "[w]omen wept unashamed and the entire courtroom burst into spontaneous, prolonged applause."
sentence_73: Landis had been a lawyer with a corporate practice; upon his elevation to the bench, corporate litigants expected him to favor them.
sentence_74: According to a 1907 magazine article about Landis, "Corporations smiled pleasantly at the thought of a corporation lawyer being on the bench.
sentence_75: They smile no more."
sentence_76: In an early case, Landis fined the [[Allis-Chalmers_Manufacturing_Company|Allis-Chalmers Manufacturing Company]] the maximum $4,000 for illegally importing workers, even though Winifred Landis's sister's husband served on the corporate board.
sentence_77: In another decision, Landis struck down a challenge to the [[Interstate_Commerce_Commission|Interstate Commerce Commission]]'s (ICC) jurisdiction over rebating, a practice banned by the Elkins Act of 1903 in which railroads and favored customers agreed that the customers would pay less than the posted tariff, which by law was to be the same for all shippers.
sentence_78: Landis's decision allowed the ICC to take action against railroads which gave rebates.
sentence_79: By the first decade of the 20th century, a number of business entities had formed themselves into [[Trust_(monopoly)|trusts]], which dominated their industries.
sentence_80: Trusts often sought to purchase or otherwise neutralize their competitors, allowing the conglomerates to raise prices to high levels.
sentence_81: In 1890, Congress had passed the [[Sherman_Anti-Trust_Act|Sherman Anti-Trust Act]], but it was not until the [[Presidency_of_Theodore_Roosevelt|Theodore Roosevelt administration]] (1901–09) that serious efforts were made to break up or control the trusts.
sentence_82: The dominant force in the oil industry was [[Standard_Oil|Standard Oil]], controlled by [[John_D._Rockefeller|John D. Rockefeller]].
sentence_83: Modern-day [[ExxonMobil|ExxonMobil]], [[Atlantic_Richfield|Atlantic Richfield]], [[Chevron_Corporation|Chevron]], Sohio, [[Amoco|Amoco]] and [[Continental_Oil|Continental Oil]] all trace their ancestry to various parts of Standard Oil.
sentence_84: In March 1906, Commissioner of Corporations James Rudolph Garfield submitted a report to President Roosevelt, alleging large-scale rebating in Standard Oil shipments.
sentence_85: Federal prosecutors in several states and territories sought indictments against components of the [[Standard_Oil_Trust|Standard Oil Trust]].
sentence_86: On June 28, 1906, [[Standard_Oil_of_Indiana|Standard Oil of Indiana]] was indicted on 6,428 counts of violation of the Elkins Act for accepting rebates on shipments on the Chicago & Alton Railroad.
sentence_87: The case was assigned to Landis.
sentence_88: Trial on the 1,903 counts that survived pretrial motions began on March 4, 1907.
sentence_89: The fact that rebates had been given was not contested; what was at issue was whether Standard Oil knew the railroad's posted rates, and if it had a duty to enquire if it did not.
sentence_90: Landis charged the jury that it "was the duty of the defendant diligently in good faith to get from the Chicago & Alton ... the lawful rate".
sentence_91: The jury found Standard Oil guilty on all 1,903 counts.
sentence_92: The maximum fine that Landis could impose was $29,240,000.
sentence_93: To aid the judge in determining the sentence, Landis issued a subpoena for Rockefeller to testify as to Standard Oil's assets.
sentence_94: The tycoon had often evaded subpoenas, not having testified in court since 1888.
sentence_95: Deputy [[United_States_marshal|United States marshals]] visited Rockefeller's several homes, as well as the estates of his friends, in the hope of finding him.
sentence_96: After several days, Rockefeller was found at his lawyer's estate, Taconic Farm in northwestern Massachusetts, and was served with the subpoena.
sentence_97: The tycoon duly came to Landis's Chicago courtroom, making his way through a mob anxious to see the proceedings.
sentence_98: Rockefeller's actual testimony, proffered after the judge made him wait through several cases and witnesses, proved to be anticlimactic, as he professed almost no knowledge of Standard Oil's corporate structure or assets.
sentence_99: On August 3, 1907, Landis pronounced sentence.
sentence_100: He fined Standard Oil the maximum penalty, $29,240,000, the largest fine imposed on a corporation to that date.
sentence_101: The corporation quickly appealed; in the meantime, Landis was lionized as a hero.
sentence_102: According to Pietrusza, "much of the nation could hardly believe a federal judge had finally cracked down on a trust—and cracked down hard ".
sentence_103: President Roosevelt, when he heard the sentence, reportedly stated, "That's bully."
sentence_104: Rockefeller was playing golf in Cleveland when he was brought a telegram containing the news.
sentence_105: Rockefeller calmly informed his golfing partners of the amount of the fine, and proceeded to shoot a personal record score, later stating, "Judge Landis will be dead a long time before this fine is paid."
sentence_106: He proved correct; the verdict and sentence were reversed by the [[United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_Seventh_Circuit|United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit]] on July 22, 1908.
sentence_107: In January 1909, the [[Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States|Supreme Court]] refused to hear the case, and in a new trial before another judge (Landis recused himself), Standard Oil was acquitted.

section_5.value: Federal League and Baby Iraene cases (1909–1917)

sentence_108: A lifelong baseball fan, Landis often slipped away from the courthouse for a [[Chicago_White_Sox|White Sox]] or [[Chicago_Cubs|Cubs]] game.
sentence_109: In 1914, the two existing [[Major_League_Baseball|major leagues]] were challenged by a new league, the [[Federal_League|Federal League]].
sentence_110: In 1915, the upstart league brought suit against the existing leagues and owners under the Sherman Act and the case was assigned to Landis.
sentence_111: Baseball owners feared that the [[Reserve_clause|reserve clause]], which forced players to sign new contracts only with their former team, and the 10-day clause, which allowed teams (but not players) to terminate player contracts on ten days notice, would be struck down by Landis.
sentence_112: Landis held hearings in late January 1915, and newspapers expected a quick decision, certainly before [[Spring_training|spring training]] began in March.
sentence_113: During the hearings, Landis admonished the parties, "Both sides must understand that any blows at the thing called baseball would be regarded by this court as a blow to a national institution".
sentence_114: When the National League's chief counsel, future Senator [[George_Wharton_Pepper|George Wharton Pepper]] referred to the activities of baseball players on [[Baseball_field|the field]] as "labor", Landis interrupted him: "As a result of 30 years of observation, I am shocked because you call playing baseball 'labor.'
sentence_115: " Landis [[Reserved_judgment|reserved judgment]], and the parties waited for his ruling.
sentence_116: Spring training passed, as did the entire regular season and [[1915_World_Series|the World Series]].
sentence_117: In December 1915, still with no word from Landis, the parties reached a settlement, and the Federal League disbanded.
sentence_118: Landis made no public statement as to the reasons for his failure to rule, though he told close friends that he had been certain the parties would reach a settlement sooner or later.
sentence_119: Most observers thought that Landis waited because he did not want to rule against the two established leagues and their contracts.
sentence_120: In 1916, Landis presided over the "Ryan Baby" or "Baby Iraene" case.
sentence_121: The recent widow of a prominent Chicago banker, Anna Dollie Ledgerwood Matters, had brought a baby girl home from a visit to Canada and claimed that the child was her late husband's posthumous heir.
sentence_122: Matters had left an estate of $250,000.
sentence_123: However, a shop girl from [[Ontario|Ontario]], Margaret Ryan, claimed the baby was hers, and brought a writ of [[Habeas_corpus|habeas corpus]] in Landis's court.
sentence_124: Ryan stated that she had given birth to the girl in an Ottawa hospital, but had been told her baby had died.
sentence_125: In the era before blood and [[DNA|DNA]] testing, Landis relied on witness testimony and awarded the child to Ryan.
sentence_126: The case brought comparisons between Landis and [[King_Solomon|King Solomon]], who had judged a similar case.
sentence_127: Landis was reversed by the Supreme Court, which held he had no jurisdiction in the matter.
sentence_128: A Canadian court later awarded the child to Ryan.
sentence_129: Although Landis was an autocrat in the courtroom, he was less so at home.
sentence_130: In a 1916 interview, he stated,
sentence_131: In early 1917, Landis considered leaving the bench and returning to private practice—though he greatly enjoyed being a judge, the salary of $7,500 was considerably lower than what he could make as an attorney.
sentence_132: The entry of the United States into World War I in April ended Landis's determination to resign; a firm supporter of the war effort, he felt he could best serve the country by remaining on the bench.
sentence_133: Despite this decision and his age, fifty, Landis wrote to [[United_States_Secretary_of_War|Secretary of War]] [[Newton_D._Baker|Newton D. Baker]], asking him to take him into the service and send him to France, where the war was raging.
sentence_134: Baker urged Landis to make speeches in support of the war instead, which he did.
sentence_135: The judge's son, [[Reed_G._Landis|Reed]], had already served briefly in the Illinois National Guard; during the war he became a pilot, and eventually an [[Flying_ace|ace]].
sentence_136: Landis's disdain for draft dodgers and other opponents of the war was evident in July 1917, when he presided over the trials of some 120 men, mostly foreign-born [[Socialist_Party_of_America|Socialists]], who had resisted the draft and rioted in [[Rockford,_Illinois|Rockford, Illinois]].
sentence_137: According to Pietrusza, Landis "was frequently brutal in his remarks" to the defendants, interrogating them on their beliefs.
sentence_138: Landis tried the case in Rockford, and found all guilty, sentencing all but three to a year and a day in jail, the maximum sentence.
sentence_139: The prisoners were ordered to register for the draft after serving their sentences—except 37, whom he ordered deported.
sentence_140: On September 5, 1917, federal officers raided the national headquarters, in Chicago, of the [[Industrial_Workers_of_the_World|Industrial Workers of the World]] (IWW, sometimes "Wobblies"), as well as 48 of the union's halls across the nation.
sentence_141: The union had opposed the war and urged members and others to refuse [[Conscription_in_the_United_States|conscription]] into the armed forces.
sentence_142: On September 28, 166 IWW leaders, including union head [[Big_Bill_Haywood|Big Bill Haywood]] were indicted in the Northern District of Illinois; their cases were assigned to Landis.
sentence_143: Some 40 of the indicted men could not be found; a few others had charges dismissed against them.
sentence_144: Ultimately, Landis presided over a trial against 113 defendants, the largest federal criminal trial to that point.
sentence_145: The trial began on April 1, 1918.
sentence_146: Landis quickly dismissed charges against a dozen defendants, including one A.C. Christ, who showed up in newly obtained army uniform.
sentence_147: Jury selection occupied a month.
sentence_148: Journalist [[John_Reed_(journalist)|John Reed]] attended the trial, and wrote of his impressions of Landis:
sentence_149: Haywood biographer Melvyn Dubofsky wrote that Landis "exercised judicial objectivity and restraint for five long months".
sentence_150: Baseball historian Harold Seymour stated that "[o]n the whole, Landis conducted the trial with restraint, despite his reputation as a foe of all radical groups."
sentence_151: Landis dismissed charges against an elderly defendant who was in obvious pain as he testified, and allowed the release of a number of prisoners on bail or on their own recognizances.
sentence_152: On August 17, 1918, following the closing argument for the prosecution (the defendants waived argument), Landis [[Jury_instructions|instructed the jury]].
sentence_153: The lead defense counsel objected to the wording of the jury charge several times, but Haywood believed it to have been fair.
sentence_154: After 65 minutes, the jury returned with guilty verdicts for all of the remaining accused, much to their shock; they had believed that Landis's charge pointed towards their acquittal.
sentence_155: When the defendants returned to court on August 29, Landis listened with patience to the defendants' [[Allocution#United_States|final pleas]].
sentence_156: For the sentencing, according to Richard Cahan in his history of Chicago's district court, "mild-mannered Landis returned a changed man".
sentence_157: Although two defendants received only ten days in jail, all others received at least a year and a day, and Haywood and fourteen others received twenty years.
sentence_158: A number of defendants, including Haywood, obtained bail during the appeal; even before Haywood's appeals were exhausted, he jumped bail and took ship for the Soviet Union.
sentence_159: The labor leader hung a portrait of Landis in his Moscow apartment, and when Haywood died in 1928, he was interred near John Reed (who had died of illness in Moscow after the [[Bolshevik_Revolution|Bolshevik Revolution]]) in the [[Kremlin_Wall_Necropolis|Kremlin Wall]]—they remain the only Americans so honored.
sentence_160: President [[Calvin_Coolidge|Calvin Coolidge]] commuted the sentences of the remaining incarcerated defendants in 1923, much to the disgust of Landis, who issued an angry statement.
sentence_161: After leaving his judgeship, Landis referred to the defendants in the Haywood case as "scum", "filth", and "slimy rats".
sentence_162: Landis hoped that the Kaiser, [[Wilhelm_II_of_Germany|Wilhelm II]] would be captured and tried in his court; he wanted to indict the Kaiser for the murder of a Chicagoan who lost his life on the [[RMS_Lusitania|RMS Lusitania]] in 1915.
sentence_163: The State Department notified Landis that [[Extradition|extradition]] treaties did not permit the rendition of the Kaiser, who fled into exile in the Netherlands as the war concluded.
sentence_164: Nevertheless, in a speech, Landis demanded that Kaiser Wilhelm, his six sons, and 5,000 German military leaders "be lined up against a wall and shot down in justice to the world and to Germany".
sentence_165: Even with the armistice in November 1918, the war-related trials continued.

sentence_178: The [[United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_Seventh_Circuit|Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals]] declined to rule on the case itself, sending it on to the Supreme Court, which on January 31, 1921, overturned the convictions and sentences by a 6–3 vote, holding that Landis should have stepped aside once he was satisfied that the affidavit was legally sufficient, leaving it for another judge to decide whether it was actually true.

section_7.value: Building trades award, controversy, and resignation (1920–1922)

sentence_208: The [[1919_World_Series|1919 World Series]] between the [[Chicago_White_Sox|Chicago White Sox]] and [[Cincinnati_Reds|Cincinnati Reds]] was much anticipated, as the nation attempted to return to normalcy in the postwar period.

sentence_225: Baseball had been governed by a three-man National Commission, consisting of American League President [[Ban_Johnson|Ban Johnson]], National League President [[John_Heydler|John Heydler]] and Cincinnati Reds owner [[Garry_Herrmann|Garry Herrmann]].

sentence_302: At the time of Landis's appointment as commissioner, it was common for professional baseball players to supplement their pay by participating in postseason "[[Barnstorm_(sports)|barnstorming]]" tours, playing on teams which would visit smaller cities and towns to play games for which admission would be charged.

section_17.value: Major-minor league relations; development of the farm system

sentence_334: At the start of Landis's commissionership, the minor league teams were for the most part autonomous of the major leagues; in fact the minor leagues independently chose to accept Landis's rule.
sentence_335: To ensure players did not become mired in the minor leagues without a chance to earn their way out, major league teams were able to draft players who played two consecutive years with the same minor league team.
sentence_336: Several minor leagues were not subject to the draft; Landis fought for the inclusion of these leagues, feeling that the non-draft leagues could prevent players from advancing as they became more skilled.
sentence_337: By 1924, he had succeeded, as the [[International_League|International League]], the final holdout, accepted the draft.
sentence_338: By the mid-1920s, major league clubs were beginning to develop "farm systems", that is, minor league teams owned or controlled by them, at which they could develop young prospects without the risk of the players being acquired by major league rivals.
sentence_339: The pioneer in this development was [[Branch_Rickey|Branch Rickey]], who then ran the St. Louis Cardinals.
sentence_340: As the 1921 National Agreement among the major and minor leagues which implemented Landis's hiring lifted a ban on major league teams owning minor league ones, Landis was limited in his avenues of attack on Rickey's schemes.
sentence_341: Developing talent at little cost thanks to Rickey, the Cardinals dominated the National League, winning nine league titles in the years from 1926 to 1946.
sentence_342: Soon after Landis's appointment, he surprised the major league owners by requiring that they disclose their minor league interests.
sentence_343: Landis fought against the practice of "covering up", using transfers between two teams controlled by the same major league team to make players ineligible for the draft.
sentence_344: His first formal act as commissioner was to declare infielder [[Phil_Todt|Phil Todt]] a free agent, dissolving his contract with the [[St._Louis_Browns|St.
sentence_345: Louis Browns]] (at the time run by Rickey, who soon thereafter moved across town to run the Cardinals); in 1928, he ruled future Hall of Famer [[Chuck_Klein|Chuck Klein]] a free agent as he held the Cardinals had tried to cover Klein up by having him play in a league where they owned two affiliates.
sentence_346: The following year, he freed [[Detroit_Tigers|Detroit Tigers]] prospect and future Hall of Famer [[Rick_Ferrell|Rick Ferrell]], who attracted a significant signing bonus from the Browns.
sentence_347: In 1936, Landis found that teenage pitching prospect [[Bob_Feller|Bob Feller]]'s signing by minor league club [[Fargo-Moorhead_Twins|Fargo-Moorhead]] had been a charade; the young pitcher was for all intents and purposes property of the Cleveland Indians.
sentence_348: However, Feller indicated that he wanted to play for Cleveland and Landis issued a ruling which required the Indians to pay damages to minor league clubs, but allowed them to retain Feller, who went on to a Hall of Fame career with the Indians.
sentence_349: Landis's attempts to crack down on "covering up" provoked the only time he was ever sued by one of his owners.
sentence_350: After the 1930 season, minor leaguer [[Fred_Bennett_(baseball)|Fred Bennett]], convinced he was being covered up by the Browns, petitioned Landis for his release.
sentence_351: Landis ruled that the Browns could either keep Bennett on their roster for the entire 1931 season, trade him, or release him.
sentence_352: Instead, Browns owner [[Phil_Ball_(baseball)|Phil Ball]] brought suit against Landis in his old court in Chicago.
sentence_353: Federal Judge [[Walter_Lindley|Walter Lindley]] ruled for Landis, noting that the agreements and rules were intended to "endow the Commissioner with all the attributes of a benevolent but absolute despot and all the disciplinary powers of the proverbial [[Pater_familias|pater familias]]".
sentence_354: Ball intended to appeal, but after a meeting between team owners and Landis in which the commissioner reminded owners of their agreement not to sue, decided to drop the case.
sentence_355: Landis had hoped that the large Cardinal farm system would become economically unfeasible; when it proved successful for the Cardinals, he had tolerated it for several years and was in a poor position to abolish it.
sentence_356: In 1938, however, finding that the Cardinals effectively controlled multiple teams in the same league (a practice disliked by Landis), he freed 70 players from their farm system.
sentence_357: As few of the players were likely prospects for the major leagues, Landis's actions generated headlines, but had little effect on the Cardinals organization, and the development of the modern farm system, whereby each major league club has several minor league teams which it uses to develop talent, proceeded apace.
sentence_358: [[Rob_Neyer|Rob Neyer]] describes Landis's effort as "a noble effort in a good cause, but it was also doomed to fail."
sentence_359: One of the most controversial aspects of Landis's commissionership is the question of race.
sentence_360: From 1884, black ballplayers were informally banned from organized baseball.
sentence_361: No black ballplayer played in organized baseball during Landis's commissionership; Rickey (then running the [[Brooklyn_Dodgers|Brooklyn Dodgers]]) broke the color line by signing [[Jackie_Robinson|Jackie Robinson]] to play for the minor league [[Montreal_Royals|Montreal Royals]] in 1946, after Landis's death.
sentence_362: Robinson became the first African-American in the major leagues since the 19th century, playing with the Dodgers beginning in 1947.
sentence_363: According to contemporary newspaper columns, at the time of his appointment as commissioner, Landis was considered a liberal on race questions; two Chicago African-American newspapers defended him against the 1921 efforts to impeach him from his judgeship.
sentence_364: However, a number of baseball authors have ascribed racism to Landis, who they say actively perpetuated baseball's color line.
sentence_365: James Bankes, in The Pittsburgh Crawfords, tracing the history of [[Pittsburgh_Crawfords|that]] [[Negro_league_baseball|Negro league]] team, states that Landis, whom the author suggests was a Southerner, made "little effort to disguise his racial prejudice during 25 years in office" and "remained a steadfast foe of integration".
sentence_366: Negro league historian John Holway termed Landis "the hard-bitten Carolinian [[Sic|sic]] Kennesaw [[Sic|sic]] Mountain Landis".
sentence_367: In a 2000 article in [[Smithsonian_(magazine)|Smithsonian magazine]], writer Bruce Watson states that Landis "upheld baseball's [[Unwritten_rules_of_baseball|unwritten ban]] on black players and did nothing to push owners toward integration".
sentence_368: A number of authors say that Landis banned major league play against black teams for fear the white teams would lose, though they ascribe various dates for this action, and the Dodgers are known to have played black teams in and around their Havana spring training base as late as 1942.
sentence_369: Landis's documented actions on race are inconsistent.
sentence_370: In 1938, Yankee [[Jake_Powell|Jake Powell]] was interviewed by a radio station, and when asked what he did in the offseason, made comments that were interpreted as meaning he worked as a police officer and beat up African Americans.
sentence_371: Landis suspended Powell for ten days.
sentence_372: In June 1942, the Negro league Kansas City Monarchs played several games against the white "[[Dizzy_Dean|Dizzy Dean]] All-Stars" at major league ballparks, attracting large crowds.
sentence_373: After three games, all won by the Monarchs, Landis ordered a fourth canceled, on the ground that the games were outdrawing major league contests.
sentence_374: On one occasion, Landis intervened in Negro league affairs, though he had no jurisdiction to do so.
sentence_375: The Crawfords lost a game to a white semi-pro team when their star catcher, [[Josh_Gibson|Josh Gibson]] dropped a pop fly, and Gibson was accused of throwing the game at the behest of gamblers.
sentence_376: Landis summoned the black catcher to his office, interviewed him, and announced that Gibson was cleared of wrongdoing.
sentence_377: In July 1942, Dodger manager [[Leo_Durocher|Leo Durocher]] charged that there was a "grapevine understanding" keeping blacks out of baseball.
sentence_378: He was summoned to Landis's Chicago office, and after emerging from a meeting with the commissioner, alleged that he had been misquoted.
sentence_379: Landis then addressed the press, and stated,
sentence_380: In his 1961 memoir, Veeck as in Wreck, longtime baseball executive and owner [[Bill_Veeck|Bill Veeck]] told of his plan, in 1942, to buy the Phillies and stock the team with Negro league stars.
sentence_381: Veeck wrote that he told Landis, who reacted with shock, and soon moved to block the purchase.
sentence_382: In his book, Veeck placed some of the blame on National League President [[Ford_Frick|Ford Frick]], but later reserved blame exclusively for Landis, whom he accused of racism, stating in a subsequent interview, "[a]fter all, a man who is named Kenesaw Mountain was not born and raised in the state of Maine."
sentence_383: However, when Veeck was asked for proof of his allegations against Landis, he stated, "I have no proof of that.
