sentence_385: According to baseball historian David Jordan, "Veeck, nothing if not a storyteller, seems to have added these embellishments, sticking in some guys in black hats, simply to juice up his tale."
sentence_386: In November 1943, Landis agreed after some persuasion that black sportswriter [[Sam_Lacy|Sam Lacy]] should make a case for integration of organized baseball before the owners' annual meeting.
sentence_387: Instead of Lacy attending the meeting, actor [[Paul_Robeson|Paul Robeson]] did.
sentence_388: Robeson, though a noted black actor and advocate of civil rights, was a controversial figure due to his affiliation with the [[Communist_Party_USA|Communist Party]].
sentence_389: The owners heard Robeson out, but at Landis's suggestion, did not ask him any questions or begin any discussion with him.
sentence_390: Neyer noted that "Landis has been blamed for delaying the integration of the major leagues, but the truth is that the owners didn't want black players in the majors any more than Landis did.
sentence_391: And it's not likely that, even if Landis hadn't died in 1944, he could have prevented Branch Rickey from bringing Jackie Robinson to the National League in 1947."
sentence_392: The [[Baseball_Writers'_Association_of_America|Baseball Writers' Association of America]] after Landis's death in 1944 renamed its [[MLB_Most_Valuable_Player_Award|Most Valuable Player Awards]] after Landis, but removed his name in 2020 with a vote of 89 percent of voting members in favor.

section_19.value: World Series and All-Star Game; other innovations

sentence_396: Landis took full jurisdiction over the World Series, as a contest between representatives of the two major leagues.
sentence_397: Landis was blamed when the umpires called a game on account of darkness with the score tied during the [[1922_World_Series|1922 World Series]], even though there was still light.
sentence_398: Landis decided that such decisions in future would be made by himself, moved forward the starting time of World Series games in future years, and announced that proceeds from the tied game would be donated to charity.
sentence_399: In the [[1932_World_Series|1932 World Series]], Landis ordered that tickets for Game One at [[Yankee_Stadium_(1923)|Yankee Stadium]] only be sold as part of strips, forcing fans to purchase tickets for all Yankee home games during that Series.
sentence_400: Bad weather and the poor economy resulted in a half-filled stadium, and Landis allowed individual game sales for Game Two.
sentence_401: During the [[1933_World_Series|1933 World Series]], he instituted a rule that only he could throw a player out of a World Series game, a rule which followed the ejection of [[Washington_Senators_(1901–60)|Washington Senator]] [[Heinie_Manush|Heinie Manush]] by umpire [[Charley_Moran|Charley Moran]].
sentence_402: [[1934_World_Series|The following year]], with the visiting Cardinals ahead of the [[Detroit_Tigers|Detroit Tigers]], 9–0 in Game Seven, he removed Cardinal [[Joe_Medwick|Joe Medwick]] from the game for his own safety when Medwick, the left fielder, was pelted with fruit by Tiger fans after Medwick had been involved in a fight with one of the Tigers.
sentence_403: Spink notes that Landis would most likely not have done so were the game within reach of the Tigers.
sentence_404: In the [[1938_World_Series|1938 World Series]], umpire Moran was hit by a wild throw and suffered facial injuries.
sentence_405: He was able to continue, but the incident caused Landis to order that World Series games and [[Major_League_Baseball_All-Star_Game|All-Star Games]] be played with six umpires.
sentence_406: The All-Star Game began in 1933; Landis had been a strong supporter of the proposal for such a contest, and after [[1933_Major_League_Baseball_All-Star_Game|the first game]] remarked, "That's a grand show, and it should be continued."
sentence_407: He never missed an All-Star Game in his lifetime; his final public appearance was at the [[1944_Major_League_Baseball_All-Star_Game|1944 All-Star Game]] in Pittsburgh.
sentence_408: In 1928, National League ball clubs proposed an innovation whereby each team's pitcher, usually the weakest hitter in the lineup, would not bat, but be replaced for the purposes of batting and base-running by a tenth player.
sentence_409: There were expectations that at the interleague meetings that year, the National League teams would vote for it, and the American League teams against it, leaving Landis to cast the deciding vote.
sentence_410: In the event, the proposal was withdrawn, and Landis did not disclose how he would have voted on this early version of the "[[Designated_hitter|designated hitter]]" rule.
sentence_411: Landis disliked the innovation of "night baseball", played in the evening with the aid of artificial light, and sought to discourage teams from it.
sentence_412: Despite this, he attended the first successful minor league night game, in [[Des_Moines,_Iowa|Des Moines, Iowa]], in 1930.
sentence_413: When major league night baseball began in the late 1930s, Landis got the owners to restrict the number of such games.
sentence_414: During World War II, many restrictions on night baseball were reduced, with the [[Washington_Senators_(1901–60)|Washington Senators]] permitted to play all their home games (except those on Sundays and holidays) at night.

section_20.value: World War II, death, and legacy

sentence_415: With the entry of the United States into World War II in late 1941, Landis wrote to President [[Franklin_D._Roosevelt|Franklin D. Roosevelt]], inquiring as to the wartime status of baseball.
sentence_416: The President responded, urging Landis to keep baseball open, foreseeing that even those fully engaged in war work would benefit from inexpensive diversions such as attending baseball games.
sentence_417: Many major leaguers enlisted or were drafted; even so Landis repeatedly stated, "We'll play as long as we can put nine men on the field."
sentence_418: Although many of the teams practiced at their normal spring training sites in 1942, beginning the following year they were required to train near their home cities or in the Northeast.
sentence_419: Landis was as virulently opposed to the [[Axis_Powers|Axis Powers]] as he had been towards the Kaiser, writing that peace would not be possible until "about fifteen thousand little Hitler, Himmlers and Hirohitos" were killed.
sentence_420: Landis retained a firm hold on baseball despite his advancing years and, in 1943, banned Phillies owner William D. Cox from baseball for betting on his own team.
sentence_421: In 1927, Landis's stance regarding gambling had been codified in the rules of baseball: "Any player, umpire, or club or league official or employee who shall bet any sum whatsoever upon any baseball game in connection with which the bettor had a duty to perform shall be declared permanently ineligible."
sentence_422: Cox was required to sell his stake in the Phillies.
sentence_423: In early October 1944, Landis checked into St. Luke's Hospital in Chicago, where his wife Winifred had been hospitalized, with a severe cold.
sentence_424: While in the hospital, he had a heart attack, causing him to miss [[1944_World_Series|the World Series]] for the first time in his commissionership.
sentence_425: He remained fully alert, and as usual signed the World Series share checks to players.
sentence_426: His contract was due to expire in January 1946; on November 17, 1944, baseball's owners voted him another seven-year term.
sentence_427: However, on November 25, he died surrounded by family, five days after his 78th birthday.
sentence_428: His longtime assistant, [[Leslie_O'Connor|Leslie O'Connor]], wept as he read the announcement for the press.
sentence_429: Landis is buried at [[Oak_Woods_Cemetery|Oak Woods Cemetery]] in Chicago.
sentence_430: Two weeks after his death, Landis was voted into the [[National_Baseball_Hall_of_Fame|National Baseball Hall of Fame]] by a special committee vote.
sentence_431: American League President [[Will_Harridge|Will Harridge]] said of Landis, "He was a wonderful man.
sentence_432: His great qualities and downright simplicity impressed themselves deeply on all who knew him."
sentence_433: Pietrusza suggests that the legend on Landis's Hall of Fame plaque is his true legacy: "His integrity and leadership established baseball in the esteem, respect, and affection of the American people."
sentence_434: Pietrusza notes that Landis was hired by the baseball owners to clean up the sport, and "no one could deny Kenesaw Mountain Landis had accomplished what he had been hired to do".

sentence_3: Count Gyula Andrássy de Csíkszentkirály et Krasznahorka (8 March 1823 – 18 February 1890) was a Hungarian statesman, who served as [[Prime_Minister_of_Hungary|Prime Minister of Hungary]] (1867–1871) and subsequently as [[List_of_foreign_ministers_of_Austria-Hungary|Foreign Minister]] of [[Austria-Hungary|Austria-Hungary]] (1871–1879).
sentence_4: Andrássy was a conservative; his foreign policies looked to expanding the Empire into Southeast Europe, preferably with British and German support, and without alienating Turkey.
sentence_5: He saw Russia as the main adversary, because of its own expansionist policies toward Slavic and Orthodox areas.
sentence_6: He distrusted Slavic nationalist movements as a threat to his multi-ethnic empire.
sentence_7: The son of Count Károly Andrássy and [[Etelka_Szapáry|Etelka Szapáry]], he was born in Oláhpatak (now in Rožňava District, [[Slovakia|Slovakia]]), [[Kingdom_of_Hungary|Kingdom of Hungary]].
sentence_8: The son of a [[Liberalism|liberal]] father who belonged to the political opposition, at a time when opposing the government was very dangerous, Andrássy at a very early age threw himself into the political struggles of the day, adopting at the outset the patriotic side.
sentence_9: [[István_Széchenyi|Count István Széchenyi]] was the first adequately to appreciate his capacity.
sentence_10: In 1845 Andrássy was appointed as president of the society for the regulation of the waters of the [[Tisza|Upper Tisza]] River.
sentence_11: In 1846, he attracted attention by publishing highly critical articles of the government in [[Lajos_Kossuth|Lajos Kossuth]]'s paper, the Pesti Hírlap.
sentence_12: He was elected as one of the Radical candidates to the [[Diet_of_Hungary|Diet]] of 1848.
sentence_13: When the Croats under Josip Jelačić attempted to have [[Međimurje|Međimurje]], which was then part of Hungary, returned to Croatia, Andrássy entered military service.
sentence_14: He was commander of the [[Gentry|gentry]] of his county, and served with distinction at the battles of Pákozd and Schwechat, as [[Artúr_Görgei|Artúr Görgei]]'s adjutant (1848).
sentence_15: Toward the end of the war, Andrássy was sent to Constantinople by the revolutionary government.
sentence_16: He was seeking to obtain the neutrality of the [[Ottoman_Empire|Ottoman Empire]], if not their support, during the struggle with Croatia.
sentence_17: After the catastrophe of [[Surrender_at_Világos|Világos]], where the Hungarians were defeated, Andrássy emigrated to London and then to Paris.
sentence_18: On 21 September 1851, he was condemned in absentia to death and was [[Hanged|hanged]] in [[Effigy|effigy]] by the Austrian government for his share in the Hungarian revolt.
sentence_19: In exile for ten years, he studied politics in what was then the centre of European diplomacy.
sentence_20: He discerned the weakness of the second French empire beneath its imposing exterior.
sentence_21: Andrássy returned to Hungary in 1858, but his position was still difficult.
sentence_22: He had never petitioned for an [[Amnesty|amnesty]], and had steadily rejected all the overtures both of the Austrian government and of the Magyar Conservatives (who would have accepted something short of full autonomy for the kingdom.)
sentence_23: He enthusiastically supported [[Ferenc_Deák|Ferenc Deák]]'s party.
sentence_24: On 21 December 1865, he was chosen vice-president of the Diet.
sentence_25: In March 1866, he was elected as president of the sub-committee appointed by the parliamentary commission to draw up the [[Austro-Hungarian_Compromise_of_1867|Austro-Hungarian Compromise of 1867]] between Austria and Hungary.
sentence_26: He originated the idea of the "Delegations" of powers.
sentence_27: It was said at that time that he was the only member of the commission who could persuade the court of the justice of the national claims.
sentence_28: After the [[Battle_of_Königgrätz|Battle of Königgrätz]], he was formally consulted by [[Emperor_Franz_Joseph|Emperor Franz Joseph]] for the first time.
sentence_29: He recommended the re-establishment of the constitution and the appointment of a responsible foreign and defence ministry.
sentence_30: On 17 February 1867 the king appointed him as the first prime minister of the Hungarian half of the newly formed Dual Monarchy of [[Austria-Hungary|Austria-Hungary]].
sentence_31: The obvious first choice had been [[Ferenc_Deák|Ferenc Deák]], one of the architects of the [[Austro-Hungarian_Compromise_of_1867|Compromise]], but he stepped down in favour of Andrássy.
sentence_32: Deák described him as "the providential statesman given to Hungary by the grace of God."
sentence_33: As premier, Andrássy by his firmness, amiability and dexterity as a debater, soon won for himself a commanding position.

sentence_37: On the outbreak of the [[Franco-Prussian_War|Franco-Prussian War]] of 1870, Andrássy resolutely defended the neutrality of the Austrian monarchy, and in his speech on 28 July 1870 warmly protested against the assumption that it was in the interests of Austria to seek to recover the position she had held in Germany before 1863.

sentence_40: Hitherto the empire of the Habsburgs had never been able to dissociate itself from its [[Holy_Roman_Empire|Holy Roman]] traditions.

sentence_47: The recovered influence of Austria was evident in the negotiations which followed the outbreak of serious disturbances in Bosnia in 1875.

sentence_50: In order to avert the risk of a general conflagration, therefore, he urged that the time had come for concerted action of the powers for the purpose of pressing the Porte to fulfil its promises.
sentence_51: A sketch of the more essential reforms followed: the recognition rather than the toleration of the [[Christianity|Christian religion]]; the abolition of the system of farming the taxes; and, in [[Bosnia_and_Herzegovina|Bosnia and Herzegovina]], where the religious was complicated by an agrarian question, the conversion of the Christian peasants into free proprietors, to rescue them from their double subjection to the Muslim Ottoman landowners.

sentence_60: In addition to the [[Austro-Hungarian_campaign_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_in_1878|occupation and administration of Bosnia-Herzegovina]], Andrássy also obtained the right to station garrisons in the [[Sanjak_of_Novi_Pazar|Sanjak of Novi Pazar]], which remained under Ottoman administration.

title: Liverpool F.C.
sentence_0: This article is about the English men's football club.
sentence_1: For the affiliated women's football club, see [[Liverpool_F.C._Women|Liverpool F.C. Women]].
sentence_2: For the Uruguayan men's football club, see [[Liverpool_F.C._(Montevideo)|Liverpool F.C. (Montevideo)]].
sentence_3: For other uses, see [[Liverpool_F.C._(disambiguation)|Liverpool F.C. (disambiguation)]].
sentence_4: Liverpool Football Club is a professional [[Association_football|football]] club in [[Liverpool|Liverpool]], England, that competes in the [[Premier_League|Premier League]], the top tier of [[English_football_league_system|English football]].
sentence_5: Domestically, the club has won nineteen [[List_of_English_football_champions#Total_titles_won|League titles]], seven [[FA_Cup|FA Cups]], a record eight [[EFL_Cup|League Cups]] and fifteen [[FA_Community_Shield|FA Community Shields]].
sentence_6: In international competitions, the club [[Liverpool_F.C._in_international_football|has won]] six [[UEFA_Champions_League|European Cups]], more than any other English club, three [[UEFA_Europa_League|UEFA Cups]], four [[UEFA_Super_Cup|UEFA Super Cups]] (also English records) and one [[FIFA_Club_World_Cup|FIFA Club World Cup]].
sentence_7: Founded in 1892, the club joined the [[English_Football_League|Football League]] the following year and has played at [[Anfield|Anfield]] since its formation.
sentence_8: Liverpool established itself as a major force in English and European football in the 1970s and 1980s, when [[Bill_Shankly|Bill Shankly]], [[Bob_Paisley|Bob Paisley]], [[Joe_Fagan|Joe Fagan]] and [[Kenny_Dalglish|Kenny Dalglish]] led the club to a combined eleven League titles and four European Cups.
sentence_9: Liverpool won two further European Cups in [[2005_UEFA_Champions_League_Final|2005]] and [[2019_UEFA_Champions_League_Final|2019]] under the management of [[Rafael_Benítez|Rafael Benítez]] and [[Jürgen_Klopp|Jürgen Klopp]], respectively, the latter of whom led Liverpool to a nineteenth League title in [[2019–20_Premier_League|2020]], the club's first during the Premier League era.
sentence_10: One of the most widely supported teams in the world, in 2019, Liverpool was the world's [[Deloitte_Football_Money_League|seventh-highest-earning]] football club, with an annual revenue of €604 million, and the world's [[Forbes'_list_of_the_most_valuable_football_clubs|eighth-most-valuable]] football club, valued at $2.183 billion.
sentence_11: Liverpool has long-standing rivalries with [[Liverpool_F.C.–Manchester_United_F.C._rivalry|Manchester United]] and Everton.
sentence_12: The team changed from red shirts and white shorts to an all-red home strip in 1964 which has been used ever since.
sentence_13: The club's anthem is "[[You'll_Never_Walk_Alone|You'll Never Walk Alone]]".
sentence_14: The club's supporters have been involved in two major tragedies: the [[Heysel_Stadium_disaster|Heysel Stadium disaster]], where escaping fans were pressed against a collapsing wall at the [[1985_European_Cup_Final|1985 European Cup Final]] in Brussels, with 39 people – mostly Italians and [[Juventus_F.C.|Juventus]] fans – dying, after which English clubs were given a five-year ban from European competition; and the [[Hillsborough_disaster|Hillsborough disaster]] in 1989, where 96 Liverpool supporters died in a [[Stampede#Human_stampedes|crush]] against perimeter fencing, which led to the elimination of fenced [[Terrace_(stadium)|standing terraces]] in favour of all-seater stadiums in the top two tiers of English football.
sentence_15: Main articles: [[History_of_Liverpool_F.C._(1892–1959)|1892–1959]], [[History_of_Liverpool_F.C._(1959–1985)|1959–85]], and [[History_of_Liverpool_F.C._(1985–present)|1985–present]]
sentence_16: Liverpool F.C. was founded following a dispute between the [[Everton_F.C.|Everton]] committee and [[John_Houlding|John Houlding]], club president and owner of the land at [[Anfield|Anfield]].
sentence_17: After eight years at the stadium, Everton relocated to [[Goodison_Park|Goodison Park]] in 1892 and Houlding founded Liverpool F.C. to play at Anfield.
sentence_18: Originally named "Everton F.C. and Athletic Grounds Ltd" (Everton Athletic for short), the club became Liverpool F.C. in March 1892 and gained official recognition three months later, after [[The_Football_Association|The Football Association]] refused to recognise the club as Everton.
sentence_19: Liverpool played their first match on 1 September 1892, a pre-season [[Exhibition_game|friendly match]] against [[Rotherham_Town_F.C._(1878)|Rotherham Town]], which they won 7–1.
sentence_20: The team Liverpool fielded against Rotherham was composed entirely of Scottish players – the players who came from Scotland to play in England in those days were known as the [[Scotch_Professors|Scotch Professors]].
sentence_21: [[List_of_Liverpool_F.C._managers|Manager]] John McKenna had recruited the players after a [[Scout_(sport)|scouting]] trip to Scotland – so they became known as the "team of Macs".
sentence_22: The team won the [[Lancashire_League_(football)|Lancashire League]] in its debut season, and joined the [[Football_League_Second_Division|Football League Second Division]] at the start of the 1893–94 season.
sentence_23: After finishing in first place the club was promoted to the [[Football_League_First_Division|First Division]], which it won in 1901 and again in 1906.
sentence_24: Liverpool reached its first [[FA_Cup_Final|FA Cup Final]] in [[1914_FA_Cup_Final|1914]], losing 1–0 to [[Burnley_F.C.|Burnley]].
sentence_25: It won consecutive League championships in 1922 and 1923, but did not win another trophy until the 1946–47 season, when the club won the First Division for a fifth time under the control of ex-[[West_Ham_Utd|West Ham Utd]] centre half [[George_Kay|George Kay]].
sentence_26: Liverpool suffered its second Cup Final defeat in 1950, playing against Arsenal.
sentence_27: The club was relegated to the Second Division in the 1953–54 season.
sentence_28: Soon after Liverpool lost 2–1 to non-league [[Worcester_City_F.C.|Worcester City]] in the 1958–59 FA Cup, [[Bill_Shankly|Bill Shankly]] was appointed manager.
sentence_29: Upon his arrival he released 24 players and converted a boot storage room at Anfield into a room where the coaches could discuss strategy; here, Shankly and other "Boot Room" members [[Joe_Fagan|Joe Fagan]], [[Reuben_Bennett|Reuben Bennett]], and [[Bob_Paisley|Bob Paisley]] began reshaping the team.
sentence_30: The club was promoted back into the First Division in 1962 and won it in 1964, for the first time in 17 years.
sentence_31: In 1965, the club won its first FA Cup.
sentence_32: In 1966, the club won the First Division but lost to [[Borussia_Dortmund|Borussia Dortmund]] in the [[1965–66_European_Cup_Winners'_Cup|European Cup Winners' Cup]] final.
sentence_33: Liverpool won both the League and the [[UEFA_Europa_League|UEFA Cup]] during the 1972–73 season, and the FA Cup again a year later.
sentence_34: Shankly retired soon afterwards and was replaced by his assistant, Bob Paisley.
sentence_35: In 1976, Paisley's second season as manager, the club won another League and UEFA Cup double.
sentence_36: The following season, the club retained the League title and won the [[UEFA_Champions_League|European Cup]] for the first time, but it lost in the 1977 FA Cup Final.
sentence_37: Liverpool retained the European Cup in 1978 and regained the First Division title in 1979.
sentence_38: During Paisley's nine seasons as manager Liverpool won 20 trophies, including three European Cups, a UEFA Cup, six League titles and three consecutive [[Football_League_Cup|League Cups]]; the only domestic trophy he did not win was the FA Cup.
sentence_39: Paisley retired in 1983 and was replaced by his assistant, Joe Fagan.
sentence_40: Liverpool won the League, League Cup and European Cup in Fagan's first season, becoming the first English side to win three trophies in a season.
sentence_41: Liverpool reached the European Cup final again in 1985, against [[Juventus_F.C.|Juventus]] at the [[King_Baudouin_Stadium|Heysel Stadium]].
sentence_42: Before kick-off, Liverpool fans breached a fence which separated the two groups of supporters, and charged the Juventus fans.
sentence_43: The resulting weight of people caused a retaining wall to collapse, killing 39 fans, mostly Italians.
sentence_44: The incident became known as the [[Heysel_Stadium_disaster|Heysel Stadium disaster]].
sentence_45: The match was played in spite of protests by both managers, and Liverpool lost 1–0 to Juventus.
sentence_46: As a result of the tragedy, English clubs were banned from participating in European competition for five years; Liverpool received a ten-year ban, which was later reduced to six years.
sentence_47: Fourteen Liverpool fans received convictions for involuntary manslaughter.
sentence_48: Fagan had announced his retirement just before the disaster and [[Kenny_Dalglish|Kenny Dalglish]] was appointed as [[Player-manager|player-manager]].
sentence_49: During his tenure, the club won another three league titles and two FA Cups, including a League and Cup "[[Double_(association_football)|Double]]" in the 1985–86 season.
sentence_50: Liverpool's success was overshadowed by the [[Hillsborough_disaster|Hillsborough disaster]]: in an FA Cup semi-final against [[Nottingham_Forest_F.C.|Nottingham Forest]] on 15 April 1989, hundreds of Liverpool fans were crushed against perimeter fencing.
sentence_51: Ninety-four fans died that day; the 95th victim died in hospital from his injuries four days later and the 96th died nearly four years later, without regaining consciousness.
sentence_52: After the Hillsborough disaster there was a government review of stadium safety.
sentence_53: The resulting [[Taylor_Report|Taylor Report]] paved the way for legislation that required top-division teams to have all-seater stadiums.
sentence_54: The report ruled that the main reason for the disaster was overcrowding due to a failure of police control.
sentence_55: Liverpool was involved in the closest finish to a league season during the 1988–89 season.
sentence_56: Liverpool finished equal with [[Arsenal_F.C.|Arsenal]] on both points and goal difference, but lost the title on total goals scored when Arsenal scored the final goal in the [[Liverpool_0–2_Arsenal_(26_May_1989)|last minute of the season]].
sentence_57: Dalglish cited the Hillsborough disaster and its repercussions as the reason for his resignation in 1991; he was replaced by former player [[Graeme_Souness|Graeme Souness]].
sentence_58: Under his leadership Liverpool won the [[1992_FA_Cup_Final|1992 FA Cup Final]], but their league performances slumped, with two consecutive sixth-place finishes, eventually resulting in his dismissal in January 1994.
sentence_59: Souness was replaced by Roy Evans, and Liverpool went on to win the 1995 Football League Cup Final.
sentence_60: While they made some title challenges under Evans, third-place finishes in 1996 and 1998 were the best they could manage, and so [[Gérard_Houllier|Gérard Houllier]] was appointed co-manager in the 1998–99 season, and became the sole manager in November 1998 after Evans resigned.
sentence_61: In 2001, Houllier's second full season in charge, Liverpool won a "[[Treble_(association_football)|Treble]]": the FA Cup, League Cup and UEFA Cup.
sentence_62: Houllier underwent major heart surgery during the 2001–02 season and Liverpool finished second in the League, behind Arsenal.
sentence_63: They won a further League Cup in 2003, but failed to mount a title challenge in the two seasons that followed.
sentence_64: Houllier was replaced by [[Rafael_Benítez|Rafael Benítez]] at the end of the 2003–04 season.
sentence_65: Despite finishing fifth in Benítez's first season, Liverpool won the [[2004–05_UEFA_Champions_League|2004–05 UEFA Champions League]], beating [[A.C._Milan|A.C.
sentence_66: Milan]] 3–2 in a [[Penalty_shoot-out_(association_football)|penalty shootout]] after the match ended with a score of 3–3.
sentence_67: The following season, Liverpool finished third in the Premier League and won the 2006 FA Cup Final, beating [[West_Ham_United_F.C.|West Ham United]] in a penalty shootout after the match finished 3–3.
sentence_68: American businessmen [[George_N._Gillett_Jr.|George Gillett]] and [[Tom_Hicks|Tom Hicks]] became the owners of the club during the 2006–07 season, in a deal which valued the club and its outstanding debts at £218.9 million.
sentence_69: The club reached the 2007 UEFA Champions League Final against Milan, as it had in 2005, but lost 2–1.
sentence_70: During the 2008–09 season Liverpool achieved 86 points, its highest Premier League points total, and finished as runners up to [[Manchester_United_F.C.|Manchester United]].
sentence_71: In the 2009–10 season, Liverpool finished seventh in the Premier League and failed to qualify for the Champions League.
sentence_72: Benítez subsequently left by mutual consent and was replaced by [[Fulham_F.C.|Fulham]] manager [[Roy_Hodgson|Roy Hodgson]].
sentence_73: At the start of the 2010–11 season Liverpool was on the verge of bankruptcy and the club's creditors asked the High Court to allow the sale of the club, overruling the wishes of Hicks and Gillett.
sentence_74: [[John_W._Henry|John W. Henry]], owner of the [[Boston_Red_Sox|Boston Red Sox]] and of [[Fenway_Sports_Group|Fenway Sports Group]], bid successfully for the club and took ownership in October 2010.
sentence_75: Poor results during the start of that season led to Hodgson leaving the club by mutual consent and former player and manager Kenny Dalglish taking over.
sentence_76: In the 2011–12 season, Liverpool secured a record 8th League Cup success and reached the FA Cup final, but finished in eighth position, the worst league finish in 18 years; this led to the sacking of Dalglish.
sentence_77: He was replaced by [[Brendan_Rodgers|Brendan Rodgers]], whose Liverpool team in the 2013–14 season mounted an unexpected title charge to finish second behind champions [[Manchester_City_F.C.|Manchester City]] and subsequently return to the Champions League, scoring 101 goals in the process, the most since the 106 scored in the [[1895–96_in_English_football|1895–96]] season.
sentence_78: Following a disappointing 2014–15 season, where Liverpool finished sixth in the league, and a poor start to the following campaign, Rodgers was sacked in October 2015.
sentence_79: Rodgers was replaced by [[Jürgen_Klopp|Jürgen Klopp]].
sentence_80: Liverpool reached the finals of the [[2015–16_Football_League_Cup|Football League Cup]] and [[2015–16_UEFA_Europa_League|UEFA Europa League]] in Klopp's first season, finishing as runner-up in both competitions.
sentence_81: The club finished second in the [[2018–19_Premier_League|2018–19 season]] with 97 points, losing only one game: a points record for a non-title winning side.
sentence_82: Klopp took Liverpool to successive Champions League finals in 2018 and 2019, with the club defeating [[Tottenham_Hotspur_F.C.|Tottenham Hotspur]] 2–0 to win the [[2019_UEFA_Champions_League_Final|2019 UEFA Champions League Final]].
sentence_83: Liverpool beat [[Clube_de_Regatas_do_Flamengo|Flamengo]] of Brazil in the [[2019_FIFA_Club_World_Cup_Final|final]] 1–0 to win the [[FIFA_Club_World_Cup|FIFA Club World Cup]] for the first time.
sentence_84: Liverpool then went on to win the [[2019–20_Premier_League|2019–20 Premier League]], winning their first top-flight league title in thirty years.
sentence_85: The club set multiple records in the season, including winning the league with seven games remaining making it the earliest any team has ever won the title, amassing a club record 99 points, and achieving a [[Football_records_and_statistics_in_England#Wins|joint-record]] 32 wins in a top-flight season.
sentence_86: For much of Liverpool's history its home colours have been all red, but when the club was founded its kit was more like the contemporary Everton kit.
sentence_87: The blue and white quartered shirts were used until 1894, when the club adopted the city's colour of red.
sentence_88: The city's symbol of the [[Liver_bird|liver bird]] was adopted as the club's badge in 1901, although it was not incorporated into the kit until 1955.
sentence_89: Liverpool continued to wear red shirts and white shorts until 1964, when manager Bill Shankly decided to change to an all red strip.
sentence_90: Liverpool played in all red for the first time against [[R.S.C._Anderlecht|Anderlecht]], as [[Ian_St._John|Ian St. John]] recalled in his autobiography:

list.value: He [Shankly] thought the colour scheme would carry psychological impact – red for danger, red for power. He came into the dressing room one day and threw a pair of red shorts to [[Ron_Yeats|Ronnie Yeats]]. "Get into those shorts and let's see how you look", he said. "Christ, Ronnie, you look awesome, terrifying. You look 7 ft tall." "Why not go the whole hog, boss?" I suggested. "Why not wear red socks? Let's go out all in red." Shankly approved and an iconic kit was born.

sentence_91: The Liverpool away strip has more often than not been all yellow or white shirts and black shorts, but there have been several exceptions.
sentence_92: An all grey kit was introduced in 1987, which was used until the 1991–92 centenary season, when it was replaced by a combination of green shirts and white shorts.
sentence_93: After various colour combinations in the 1990s, including gold and navy, bright yellow, black and grey, and [[Ecru|ecru]], the club alternated between yellow and white away kits until the 2008–09 season, when it re-introduced the grey kit.
sentence_94: A third kit is designed for European away matches, though it is also worn in domestic away matches on occasions when the current away kit clashes with a team's home kit.
sentence_95: Between 2012 and 2015, the kits were designed by [[Warrior_Sports|Warrior Sports]], who became the club's kit providers at the start of the 2012–13 season.
sentence_96: In February 2015, Warrior's parent company [[New_Balance|New Balance]] announced it would be entering the global football market, with teams sponsored by Warrior now being outfitted by New Balance.
sentence_97: The only other branded shirts worn by the club were made by [[Umbro|Umbro]] until 1985, when they were replaced by [[Adidas|Adidas]], who produced the kits until 1996 when [[Reebok|Reebok]] took over.
sentence_98: They produced the kits for 10 years before Adidas made the kits from 2006 to 2012.
sentence_99: [[Nike,_Inc.|Nike]] became the club's official kit supplier at the start of the 2020–21 season.
sentence_100: Liverpool was the first English professional club to have a sponsor's logo on its shirts, after agreeing a deal with [[Hitachi,_Ltd.|Hitachi]] in 1979.
sentence_101: Since then the club has been sponsored by [[Crown_Paints|Crown Paints]], [[Candy_(company)|Candy]], [[Carlsberg_Group|Carlsberg]] and [[Standard_Chartered|Standard Chartered]].
sentence_102: The contract with Carlsberg, which was signed in 1992, was the longest-lasting agreement in English top-flight football.
sentence_103: The association with Carlsberg ended at the start of the 2010–11 season, when Standard Chartered Bank became the club's sponsor.
sentence_104: The Liverpool badge is based on the city's liver bird, which in the past had been placed inside a shield.
sentence_105: In 1992, to commemorate the centennial of the club, a new badge was commissioned, including a representation of the [[Shankly_Gates|Shankly Gates]].
sentence_106: The next year twin flames were added at either side, symbolic of the Hillsborough memorial outside Anfield, where an [[Eternal_flame|eternal flame]] burns in memory of those who died in the Hillsborough disaster.
sentence_107: In 2012, Warrior Sports' first Liverpool kit removed the shield and gates, returning the badge to what had adorned Liverpool shirts in the 1970s; the flames were moved to the back collar of the shirt, surrounding the number 96 for the number who died at Hillsborough.
sentence_108: Main article: [[Anfield|Anfield]]
sentence_109: For information on Liverpool's abandoned proposed new stadium, see [[Stanley_Park_Stadium|Stanley Park Stadium]].
sentence_110: Anfield was built in 1884 on land adjacent to [[Stanley_Park,_Liverpool|Stanley Park]].
sentence_111: Situated 2 miles (3 km) from Liverpool city centre, it was originally used by Everton before the club moved to [[Goodison_Park|Goodison Park]] after a dispute over rent with Anfield owner John Houlding.
sentence_112: Left with an empty ground, Houlding founded Liverpool in 1892 and the club has played at Anfield ever since.
sentence_113: The capacity of the stadium at the time was 20,000, although only 100 spectators attended Liverpool's first match at Anfield.
sentence_114: The Kop was built in 1906 due to the high turnout for matches and was called the Oakfield Road Embankment initially.
sentence_115: Its first game was on 1 September 1906 when the home side beat Stoke City 1–0.
sentence_116: In 1906 the banked stand at one end of the ground was formally renamed the [[Spion_Kop_(stadiums)|Spion Kop]] after a hill in KwaZulu-Natal.
sentence_117: The hill was the site of the [[Battle_of_Spion_Kop|Battle of Spion Kop]] in the [[Second_Boer_War|Second Boer War]], where over 300 men of the Lancashire Regiment died, many of them from Liverpool.
sentence_118: At its peak, the stand could hold 28,000 spectators and was one of the largest single-tier stands in the world.
sentence_119: Many stadiums in England had stands named after Spion Kop, but Anfield's was the largest of them at the time; it could hold more supporters than some entire football grounds.
sentence_120: Anfield could accommodate more than 60,000 supporters at its peak and had a capacity of 55,000 until the 1990s, when, following recommendations from the Taylor Report, all clubs in the Premier League were obliged to convert to all-seater stadiums in time for the 1993–94 season, reducing its capacity to 45,276.
sentence_121: The findings of the report precipitated the redevelopment of the Kemlyn Road Stand, which was rebuilt in 1992, coinciding with the centenary of the club, and was known as the Centenary Stand until 2017 when it was renamed the Kenny Dalglish Stand.
sentence_122: An extra tier was added to the Anfield Road end in 1998, which further increased the capacity of the ground but gave rise to problems when it was opened.
sentence_123: A series of support poles and stanchions were inserted to give extra stability to the top tier of the stand after movement of the tier was reported at the start of the 1999–2000 season.
sentence_124: Because of restrictions on expanding the capacity at Anfield, Liverpool announced plans to move to the proposed [[Stanley_Park_Stadium|Stanley Park Stadium]] in May 2002.
sentence_125: Planning permission was granted in July 2004, and in September 2006, Liverpool City Council agreed to grant Liverpool a [[999-year_lease|999-year lease]] on the proposed site.
sentence_126: Following the takeover of the club by George Gillett and Tom Hicks in February 2007, the proposed stadium was redesigned.
sentence_127: The new design was approved by the Council in November 2007.
sentence_128: The stadium was scheduled to open in August 2011 and would hold 60,000 spectators, with [[HKS,_Inc.|HKS, Inc.]] contracted to build the stadium.
sentence_129: Construction was halted in August 2008, as Gillett and Hicks had difficulty in financing the £300 million needed for the development.
sentence_130: In October 2012, BBC Sport reported that Fenway Sports Group, the new owners of Liverpool FC, had decided to redevelop their current home at Anfield stadium, rather than building a new stadium in Stanley Park.
sentence_131: As part of the redevelopment the capacity of Anfield was to increase from 45,276 to approximately 60,000 and would cost approximately £150m.
sentence_132: When construction was completed on the new Main stand the capacity of Anfield was increased to 54,074.
sentence_133: This £100 million expansion added a third tier to the stand.
sentence_134: This was all part of a £260 million project to improve the Anfield area.
sentence_135: Jurgen Klopp the manager at the time described the stand as "impressive."
sentence_136: Liverpool is one of the best supported clubs in the world.
sentence_137: The club states that its worldwide fan base includes more than 200 officially recognised Supporters Clubs in at least 50 countries.
sentence_138: Notable groups include [[Spirit_of_Shankly|Spirit of Shankly]].
sentence_139: The club takes advantage of this support through its worldwide summer tours, which has included playing in front of 101,000 in Michigan, U.S., and 95,000 in Melbourne, Australia.
sentence_140: Liverpool fans often refer to themselves as Kopites, a reference to the fans who once stood, and now sit, on the Kop at Anfield.
sentence_141: In 2008 a group of fans decided to form a splinter club, [[A.F.C._Liverpool|A.F.C.
sentence_142: Liverpool]], to play matches for fans who had been priced out of watching Premier League football.
sentence_143: The song "[[You'll_Never_Walk_Alone|You'll Never Walk Alone]]", originally from the Rodgers and Hammerstein musical Carousel and later recorded by Liverpool musicians [[Gerry_and_the_Pacemakers|Gerry and the Pacemakers]], is the club's anthem and has been sung by the Anfield crowd since the early 1960s.
sentence_144: It has since gained popularity among fans of other clubs around the world.
sentence_145: The song's title adorns the top of the Shankly Gates, which were unveiled on 2 August 1982 in memory of former manager Bill Shankly.
sentence_146: The "You'll Never Walk Alone" portion of the Shankly Gates is also reproduced on the club's crest.
sentence_147: The club's supporters have been involved in two stadium disasters.
sentence_148: The first was the 1985 Heysel Stadium disaster, in which 39 Juventus supporters were killed.
sentence_149: They were confined to a corner by Liverpool fans who had charged in their direction; the weight of the cornered fans caused a wall to collapse.
sentence_150: [[UEFA|UEFA]] laid the blame for the incident solely on the Liverpool supporters, and banned all English clubs from European competition for five years.
sentence_151: Liverpool was banned for an additional year, preventing it from participating in the 1990–91 European Cup, even though it won the League in 1990.
sentence_152: Twenty-seven fans were arrested on suspicion of manslaughter and were extradited to Belgium in 1987 to face trial.
sentence_153: In 1989, after a five-month trial in Belgium, 14 Liverpool fans were given three-year sentences for involuntary manslaughter; half of the terms were suspended.
sentence_154: The second disaster took place during an FA Cup semi-final between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest at Hillsborough Stadium, Sheffield, on 15 April 1989.
sentence_155: Ninety-six Liverpool fans died as a consequence of overcrowding at the Leppings Lane end, in what became known as the Hillsborough disaster.
sentence_156: In the following days [[The_Sun_(United_Kingdom)|The Sun]] newspaper published an article entitled "The Truth", in which it claimed that Liverpool fans had robbed the dead and had urinated on and attacked the police.
sentence_157: Subsequent investigations proved the allegations false, leading to a boycott of the newspaper by Liverpool fans across the city and elsewhere; many still refuse to buy The Sun 30 years later.
sentence_158: Many support organisations were set up in the wake of the disaster, such as the Hillsborough Justice Campaign, which represents bereaved families, survivors and supporters in their efforts to secure justice.
sentence_159: Main articles: Merseyside derby and [[Liverpool_F.C.–Manchester_United_F.C._rivalry|Liverpool F.C.–Manchester United F.C. rivalry]]
sentence_160: Liverpool's longest-established rivalry is with fellow Liverpool team Everton, against whom they contest the Merseyside derby.
sentence_161: The rivalry stems from Liverpool's formation and the dispute with Everton officials and the then owners of Anfield.
sentence_162: The Merseyside derby is one of the few local derbies which do not enforce fan segregation, and hence has been known as the "friendly derby".
sentence_163: Since the mid-1980s, the rivalry has intensified both on and off the field and, since the inception of the Premier League in 1992, the Merseyside derby has had more players [[Ejection_(sports)|sent off]] than any other Premier League game.
sentence_164: It has been referred to as "the most ill-disciplined and explosive fixture in the Premier League".
sentence_165: In terms of support within the city, the number of Liverpool fans outweigh Everton supporters by a ratio of 2:1.
sentence_166: Liverpool's [[Liverpool_F.C.–Manchester_United_F.C._rivalry|rivalry with Manchester United]] stems from the cities' competition in the [[Industrial_Revolution|Industrial Revolution]] of the 19th century.
sentence_167: Connected by the [[Liverpool_and_Manchester_Railway|world's first inter-city railway]], by road Liverpool and Manchester are separated by approximately 30 miles (48 km) along the [[East_Lancs_Road|East Lancs Road]].
sentence_168: Ranked the two biggest clubs in England by [[France_Football|France Football]] magazine, Liverpool and Manchester United are the most successful English teams in both domestic and international competitions, and both clubs have a global fanbase.
sentence_169: Viewed as one of the biggest rivalries in world football, it is considered the most famous fixture in English football.
sentence_170: The two clubs alternated as champions between [[1963–64_Football_League_First_Division|1964]] and [[1966–67_Football_League_First_Division|1967]], and Manchester United became the first English team to win the European Cup in [[1968_European_Cup_Final|1968]], followed by Liverpool's four European Cup victories.
sentence_171: Despite the 39 league titles and nine European Cups between them the two rivals have rarely been successful at the same time – Liverpool's run of titles in the 1970s and 1980s coincided with Manchester United's 26-year title drought, and United's success in the [[Premier_League|Premier League]]-era likewise coincided with Liverpool's 30-year title drought, and the two clubs have finished first and second in the league only five times.
sentence_172: Such is the rivalry between the clubs they rarely do transfer business with each other.
sentence_173: The last player to be transferred between the two clubs was [[Phil_Chisnall|Phil Chisnall]], who moved to Liverpool from Manchester United in 1964.
sentence_174: As the owner of Anfield and founder of Liverpool, John Houlding was the club's first chairman, a position he held from its founding in 1892 until 1904.
sentence_175: John McKenna took over as chairman after Houlding's departure.
sentence_176: McKenna subsequently became President of the Football League.
sentence_177: The chairmanship changed hands many times before John Smith, whose father was a shareholder of the club, took up the role in 1973.
sentence_178: He oversaw the most successful period in Liverpool's history before stepping down in 1990.
sentence_179: His successor was [[Noel_White|Noel White]] who became chairman in 1990.
sentence_180: In August 1991 [[David_Moores|David Moores]], whose family had owned the club for more than 50 years, became chairman.
sentence_181: His uncle [[John_Moores_(merchant)|John Moores]] was also a shareholder at Liverpool and was chairman of Everton from 1961 to 1973.
sentence_182: Moores owned 51 percent of the club, and in 2004 expressed his willingness to consider a bid for his shares in Liverpool.
sentence_183: Moores eventually sold the club to American businessmen George Gillett and Tom Hicks on 6 February 2007.
sentence_184: The deal valued the club and its outstanding debts at £218.9 million.
sentence_185: The pair paid £5,000 per share, or £174.1m for the total shareholding and £44.8m to cover the club's debts.
sentence_186: Disagreements between Gillett and Hicks, and the fans' lack of support for them, resulted in the pair looking to sell the club.
sentence_187: [[Martin_Broughton|Martin Broughton]] was appointed chairman of the club on 16 April 2010 to oversee its sale.
sentence_188: In May 2010, accounts were released showing the holding company of the club to be £350m in debt (due to leveraged takeover) with losses of £55m, causing auditor [[KPMG|KPMG]] to qualify its audit opinion.
sentence_189: The group's creditors, including the [[Royal_Bank_of_Scotland|Royal Bank of Scotland]], took Gillett and Hicks to court to force them to allow the board to proceed with the sale of the club, the major asset of the holding company.
sentence_190: A High Court judge, [[Christopher_Floyd|Mr Justice Floyd]], ruled in favour of the creditors and paved the way for the sale of the club to [[Fenway_Sports_Group|Fenway Sports Group]] (formerly New England Sports Ventures), although Gillett and Hicks still had the option to appeal.
sentence_191: Liverpool was sold to Fenway Sports Group on 15 October 2010 for £300m.
sentence_192: Liverpool has been described as a global brand; a 2010 report valued the club's trademarks and associated intellectual property at £141m, an increase of £5m on the previous year.
sentence_193: Liverpool was given a brand rating of AA (Very Strong).
sentence_194: In April 2010 business magazine [[Forbes|Forbes]] ranked Liverpool as the sixth most valuable football team in the world, behind [[Manchester_United|Manchester United]], [[Real_Madrid_C.F.|Real Madrid]], Arsenal, [[FC_Barcelona|Barcelona]] and [[FC_Bayern_Munich|Bayern Munich]]; they valued the club at $822m (£532m), excluding debt.
sentence_195: Accountants [[Deloitte|Deloitte]] ranked Liverpool eighth in the [[Deloitte_Football_Money_League|Deloitte Football Money League]], which ranks the world's football clubs in terms of revenue.
sentence_196: Liverpool's income in the 2009–10 season was €225.3m.
sentence_197: According to a 2018 report by Deloitte, the club had an annual revenue of €424.2 million for the previous year, and Forbes valued the club at $1.944 billion.
sentence_198: In 2018, annual revenue increased to €513.7 million, and Forbes valued the club at $2.183 billion.

sentence_0: Harold Adrian Russell "Kim" Philby (1 January 1912 – 11 May 1988) was a British intelligence officer and a double agent for the [[Soviet_Union|Soviet Union]].
sentence_1: In 1963 he was revealed to be a member of the [[Cambridge_Five|Cambridge Five]], a spy ring which passed information to the Soviet Union during [[World_War_II|World War II]] and in the early stages of the [[Cold_War|Cold War]].
sentence_2: Of the five, Philby is believed to have been most successful in providing secret information to the Soviets.
sentence_3: Born in [[British_India|British India]], Philby was educated at [[Westminster_School|Westminster School]] and [[Trinity_College,_Cambridge|Trinity College, Cambridge]].
sentence_4: He was recruited by Soviet intelligence in 1934.
sentence_5: After leaving Cambridge, Philby worked as a journalist and covered the [[Spanish_Civil_War|Spanish Civil War]] and the [[Battle_of_France|Battle of France]].
sentence_6: In 1940 he began working for the United Kingdom's [[Secret_Intelligence_Service|Secret Intelligence Service]] (SIS or MI6).
sentence_7: By the end of the [[Second_World_War|Second World War]] he had become a high-ranking member.
sentence_8: In 1949 Philby was appointed first secretary to the [[Embassy_of_the_United_Kingdom,_Washington,_D.C.|British Embassy in Washington]] and served as chief British liaison with American intelligence agencies.
sentence_9: During his career as an intelligence officer, he passed large amounts of intelligence to the Soviet Union, including an Anglo-American plot to subvert the [[People's_Socialist_Republic_of_Albania|communist regime of Albania]].
sentence_10: He was also responsible for tipping off two other spies under suspicion of espionage, [[Donald_Maclean_(spy)|Donald Maclean]] and [[Guy_Burgess|Guy Burgess]], both of whom subsequently fled to Moscow in May 1951.
sentence_11: The defections of Maclean and Burgess cast suspicion over Philby, resulting in his resignation from MI6 in July 1951.
sentence_12: He was publicly [[Exoneration|exonerated]] in 1955, after which he resumed his career as both a journalist and a spy for SIS in [[Beirut|Beirut]].
sentence_13: In January 1963, having finally been unmasked as a Soviet agent, Philby defected to Moscow, where he lived out his life until his death in 1988.
sentence_14: Born in Ambala, [[Punjab_Province_(British_India)|Punjab]], [[British_Raj|British India]], Philby was the son of Dora Johnston and [[St_John_Philby|St John Philby]], an author, [[Arabist|Arabist]] and explorer.
sentence_15: St John was a member of the [[Indian_Civil_Service|Indian Civil Service]] (ICS) and later a civil servant in Mesopotamia and advisor to [[Ibn_Saud|King Ibn Sa'ud]] of Saudi Arabia.
sentence_16: Nicknamed "Kim" after the boy-spy in [[Rudyard_Kipling|Rudyard Kipling]]'s novel [[Kim_(novel)|Kim]], Philby attended Aldro [[Preparatory_school_(UK)|preparatory school]], an all-boys school located in [[Shackleford|Shackleford]] near Godalming in Surrey, United Kingdom.
sentence_17: In his early teens, he spent some time with the [[Bedouin|Bedouin]] in the desert of Saudi Arabia.
sentence_18: Following in the footsteps of his father, Philby continued to [[Westminster_School|Westminster School]], which he left in 1928 at the age of 16.
sentence_19: He won a scholarship to [[Trinity_College,_Cambridge|Trinity College, Cambridge]], where he studied history and economics.
sentence_20: He graduated in 1933 with a [[British_undergraduate_degree_classification#Degree_classification|2:1 degree]] in Economics.
sentence_21: At Cambridge, Philby showed his "leaning towards communism," in the words of his father.
sentence_22: Jack Philby went on to write, "The only serious question is whether Kim definitely intended to be disloyal to the government while in its service."
sentence_23: Upon Philby's graduation, [[Maurice_Dobb|Maurice Dobb]], a fellow of [[King's_College,_Cambridge|King's College, Cambridge]] and tutor in Economics, introduced him to the World Federation for the Relief of the Victims of German Fascism in Paris.
sentence_24: The World Federation for the Relief of the Victims of German Fascism was an organization that attempted to aid the people victimized by [[Fascism|fascism]] in Germany and provide education on oppositions to fascism.
sentence_25: The organization was one of several fronts operated by German Communist [[Willi_Münzenberg|Willi Münzenberg]], a member of the [[Reichstag_(Weimar_Republic)|Reichstag]] who had fled to France in 1933.
sentence_26: In [[Vienna|Vienna]], working to aid refugees from [[Nazi_Germany|Nazi Germany]], Philby met and fell in love with [[Litzi_Friedmann|Litzi Friedmann]] (born Alice Kohlmann), a young Austrian Communist of Hungarian Jewish origins.
sentence_27: Philby admired the strength of her political convictions and later recalled that at their first meeting:

sentence_29: He also delivered clothes and money to refugees from the Nazis.
sentence_30: Following the [[Austrofascism|Austrofascist]] victory in the [[Austrian_Civil_War|Austrian Civil War]], Friedmann and Philby married in February 1934, enabling her to escape to the United Kingdom with him two months later.
sentence_31: It is possible that it was a Viennese-born friend of Friedmann's in London, [[Edith_Tudor_Hart|Edith Tudor Hart]] – herself, at this time, a Soviet agent – who first approached Philby about the possibility of working for Soviet intelligence.
