sentence_158: [[John_Nicholas_Rede_Elliott|Nicholas Elliott]], an MI6 officer recently stationed in Beirut who was a friend of Philby's and had previously believed in his innocence, was tasked with attempting to secure Philby's full confession.
sentence_159: It is unclear whether Philby had been alerted, but Eleanor noted that as 1962 wore on, expressions of tension in his life "became worse and were reflected in bouts of deep depression and drinking".
sentence_160: She recalled returning home to Beirut from a sight-seeing trip in Jordan to find Philby "hopelessly drunk and incoherent with grief on the terrace of the flat," mourning the death of a little pet fox which had fallen from the balcony.
sentence_161: When Nicholas Elliott met Philby in late 1962, the first time since Golitsyn's defection, he found Philby too drunk to stand and with a bandaged head; he had fallen repeatedly and cracked his skull on a bathroom radiator, requiring stitches.
sentence_162: Philby told Elliott that he was "half expecting" to see him.
sentence_163: Elliott confronted him, saying, "I once looked up to you, Kim.
sentence_164: My God, how I despise you now.
sentence_165: I hope you've enough decency left to understand why."
sentence_166: Prompted by Elliott's accusations, Philby confirmed the charges of espionage and described his intelligence activities on behalf of the Soviets.
sentence_167: However, when Elliott asked him to sign a written statement, he hesitated and requested a delay in the interrogation.
sentence_168: Another meeting was scheduled to take place in the last week of January.
sentence_169: It has since been suggested that the whole confrontation with Elliott had been a charade to convince the KGB that Philby had to be brought back to Moscow, where he could serve as a British penetration agent of Moscow Centre.
sentence_170: On the evening of 23 January 1963, Philby vanished from Beirut, failing to meet his wife for a dinner party at the home of [[Glencairn_Balfour_Paul|Glencairn Balfour Paul]], First Secretary at the British Embassy.
sentence_171: The Dolmatova, a Soviet freighter bound for [[Odessa|Odessa]], had left Beirut that morning so abruptly that cargo was left scattered over the docks; Philby claimed that he left Beirut on board this ship.
sentence_172: However, others maintain that he escaped through Syria, overland to Soviet Armenia and thence to Russia.
sentence_173: It was not until 1 July 1963 that Philby's flight to Moscow was officially confirmed.
sentence_174: On 30 July Soviet officials announced that they had granted him political asylum in the USSR, along with Soviet citizenship.
sentence_175: When the news broke, MI6 came under criticism for failing to anticipate and block Philby's defection, though Elliott was to claim he could not have prevented Philby's flight.
sentence_176: Journalist [[Ben_Macintyre|Ben Macintyre]], author of several works on espionage, wrote in his 2014 book on Philby that MI6 might have left open the opportunity for Philby to flee to Moscow to avoid an embarrassing public trial.
sentence_177: Philby himself thought this might have been the case, according to Macintyre.
sentence_178: When [[FBI|FBI]] Director [[J._Edgar_Hoover|J.
sentence_179: Edgar Hoover]] was informed that one of MI6's top men was a spy for the Russians, he said, "Tell 'em Jesus Christ only had twelve, and one of them was a double [agent]."
sentence_180: Upon his arrival in Moscow in January 1963, Philby discovered that he was not a colonel in the KGB, as he had been led to believe.
sentence_181: He was paid 500 [[Ruble|rubles]] a month and his family was not immediately able to join him in exile.
sentence_182: It was ten years before he visited KGB headquarters.
sentence_183: Philby was under virtual house arrest, guarded, with all visitors screened by the KGB.
sentence_184: [[Mikhail_Lyubimov|Mikhail Lyubimov]], his closest KGB contact, explained that this was to guard his safety, but later admitted that the real reason was the KGB's fear that Philby would return to London.
sentence_185: Philby occupied himself by writing his memoirs, published in the UK in 1968 under the title My Silent War, not published in the Soviet Union until 1980.
sentence_186: He continued to read The Times, which was not generally available in the USSR, listened to the [[BBC_World_Service|BBC World Service]], and was an avid follower of [[Cricket|cricket]].
sentence_187: Philby's award of the [[Order_of_the_British_Empire|Order of the British Empire]] was cancelled and annulled in 1965.
sentence_188: Though Philby claimed publicly in January 1988 that he did not regret his decisions and that he missed nothing about England except some friends, [[Colman's|Colman's]] mustard, and Lea & Perrins [[Worcestershire_sauce|Worcestershire sauce]], his wife [[Rufina_Ivanovna_Pukhova|Rufina Ivanovna Pukhova]] later described Philby as "disappointed in many ways" by what he found in Moscow.
sentence_189: "He saw people suffering too much," but he consoled himself by arguing that "the ideals were right but the way they were carried out was wrong.
sentence_190: The fault lay with the people in charge."
sentence_191: Pukhova said, "he was struck by disappointment, brought to tears.
sentence_192: He said, 'Why do old people live so badly here?
sentence_193: After all, they won the war.'"
sentence_194: Philby drank heavily and suffered from loneliness and depression; according to Rufina, he had attempted suicide by slashing his wrists sometime in the 1960s.
sentence_195: Philby found work in the early 1970s in the KGB's [[Active_measures|Active Measures]] Department churning out fabricated documents.
sentence_196: Working from genuine unclassified and public CIA or US Department of State documents, Philby inserted "sinister" paragraphs regarding US plans.
sentence_197: The KGB would stamp the documents "top secret" and begin their circulation.
sentence_198: For the Soviets, Philby was an invaluable asset, ensuring the correct use of idiomatic and diplomatic English phrases in their disinformation efforts.
sentence_199: Philby died of [[Heart_failure|heart failure]] in Moscow in 1988.
sentence_200: He was given a hero's funeral, and posthumously awarded numerous medals by the Soviets: [[Order_of_Lenin|Order of Lenin]], [[Order_of_the_Red_Banner|Order of the Red Banner]], [[Order_of_Friendship_of_Peoples|Order of Friendship of Peoples]], [[Order_of_the_Great_Patriotic_War|Order of the Great Patriotic War]], [[Lenin_Medal|Lenin Medal]], [[Jubilee_Medal_"Forty_Years_of_Victory_in_the_Great_Patriotic_War_1941–1945"|Jubilee Medal "Forty Years of Victory in the Great Patriotic War 1941–1945"]].
sentence_201: In February 1934, Philby married [[Litzi_Friedmann|Litzi Friedmann]], an Austrian communist whom he had met in Vienna.
sentence_202: They subsequently moved to Britain; however, as Philby assumed the role of a fascist sympathiser, they separated.
sentence_203: Litzi lived in Paris before returning to London for the duration of the war; she ultimately settled in [[East_Germany|East Germany]].
sentence_204: While working as a correspondent in Spain, Philby began an affair with [[Frances_Doble|Frances Doble]], Lady Lindsay-Hogg, an actress and aristocratic divorcée who was an admirer of Franco and Hitler.
sentence_205: They travelled together in Spain through August 1939.
sentence_206: In 1940 he began living with Aileen Furse in London.
sentence_207: Their first three children, Josephine, John and Tommy Philby, were born between 1941 and 1944.
sentence_208: In 1946, Philby finally arranged a formal divorce from Litzi.
sentence_209: He and Aileen were married on 25 September 1946, while Aileen was pregnant with their fourth child, Miranda.
sentence_210: Their fifth child, Harry George, was born in 1950.
sentence_211: Aileen suffered from psychiatric problems, which grew more severe during the period of poverty and suspicion following the flight of Burgess and Maclean.
sentence_212: She lived separately from Philby, settling with their children in [[Crowborough|Crowborough]] while he lived first in London and later in Beirut.
sentence_213: Weakened by alcoholism and frequent sickness, she died of influenza in December 1957.
sentence_214: In 1956, Philby began an affair with Eleanor Brewer, the wife of The New York Times correspondent Sam Pope Brewer.
sentence_215: Following Eleanor's divorce, the couple married in January 1959.
sentence_216: After Philby defected to the Soviet Union in 1963, Eleanor visited him in Moscow.
sentence_217: In November 1964, after a visit to the United States, she returned, intending to settle permanently.
sentence_218: In her absence, Philby had begun an affair with Donald Maclean's wife, Melinda.
sentence_219: He and Eleanor divorced and she departed Moscow in May 1965.
sentence_220: Melinda left Maclean and briefly lived with Philby in Moscow.
sentence_221: In 1968 she returned to Maclean.
sentence_222: In 1971, Philby married [[Rufina_Pukhova|Rufina Pukhova]], a Russo-Polish woman twenty years his junior, with whom he lived until his death in 1988.

title: Latin
sentence_0: For other uses, see [[Latin_(disambiguation)|Latin (disambiguation)]].

table.value: Vulgar Latin developed into the Romance languages, 6th to 9th centuries; the formal language continued as the scholarly [[Lingua_franca|lingua franca]] of medieval Europe and [[Armenian_Kingdom_of_Cilicia|Cilicia]], as well as the [[Sacred_language|liturgical language]] of the [[Catholic_Church|Catholic Church]].

sentence_1: Latin (latīnum, [[Latin|[laˈtiːnʊ̃]] or lingua latīna, [[Latin|[ˈlɪŋɡʷa laˈtiːna]]) is a [[Classical_language|classical language]] belonging to the [[Italic_languages|Italic branch]] of the [[Indo-European_languages|Indo-European languages]].
sentence_2: Latin was originally spoken in the area around Rome, known as [[Latium|Latium]].
sentence_3: Through the power of the [[Roman_Republic|Roman Republic]], it became the dominant language in Italy, and subsequently throughout the western [[Roman_Empire|Roman Empire]].
sentence_4: Latin has contributed many words to the English language.
sentence_5: In particular, Latin (and Ancient Greek) roots are used in English descriptions of theology, [[List_of_Latin_and_Greek_words_commonly_used_in_systematic_names|the sciences]], [[List_of_medical_roots,_suffixes_and_prefixes|medicine]], and law.
sentence_6: It is the official language in the [[Holy_See|Holy See]] ([[Vatican_City|Vatican City]]).
sentence_7: By the late Roman Republic (75 BC), [[Old_Latin|Old Latin]] had been standardised into [[Classical_Latin|Classical Latin]].
sentence_8: Vulgar Latin was the colloquial form spoken during the same time and attested in inscriptions and the works of comic playwrights like [[Plautus|Plautus]] and [[Terence|Terence]] and author [[Petronius|Petronius]].
sentence_9: [[Late_Latin|Late Latin]] is the written language from the 3rd century; its colloquial form Vulgar Latin developed in the 6th to 9th centuries into the Romance languages, such as [[Italian_language|Italian]], [[Sardinian_language|Sardinian]], [[Venetian_language|Venetian]], Neapolitan, [[Sicilian_language|Sicilian]], [[Piedmontese_language|Piedmontese]], [[Lombard_language|Lombard]], [[French_language|French]], [[Franco-Provençal_language|Franco-Provençal]], [[Occitan_language|Occitan]], [[Corsican_language|Corsican]], [[Ladin_language|Ladin]], [[Friulan_language|Friulan]], [[Romansh_language|Romansh]], [[Catalan_language|Catalan]]/Valencian, [[Aragonese_language|Aragonese]], Spanish, [[Asturian_language|Asturian]], [[Galician_language|Galician]], and Portuguese.
sentence_10: Medieval Latin was used as a literary language from the 9th century to the Renaissance which used Renaissance Latin.
sentence_11: Later, Early Modern Latin and [[New_Latin|New Latin]] evolved.
sentence_12: Latin was the language of international communication, scholarship and science until well into the 18th century, when vernaculars (including the Romance languages) supplanted it.
sentence_13: [[Ecclesiastical_Latin|Ecclesiastical Latin]] remains the official language of the [[Holy_See|Holy See]] and the [[Roman_Rite|Roman Rite]] of the [[Catholic_Church|Catholic Church]].
sentence_14: Latin is a highly [[Fusional_language|inflected language]], with three distinct [[Grammatical_gender|genders]], six or seven noun cases, five declensions, four [[Grammatical_conjugation|verb conjugations]], six tenses, three persons, three moods, two [[Voice_(grammar)|voices]], two or three [[Grammatical_aspect|aspects]], and two [[Grammatical_number|numbers]].
sentence_15: The [[Latin_alphabet|Latin alphabet]] is derived from the [[Etruscan_alphabet|Etruscan]] and [[Greek_alphabet|Greek alphabets]] and ultimately from the [[Phoenician_alphabet|Phoenician alphabet]].
sentence_16: Main article: History of Latin
sentence_17: A number of historical phases of the language have been recognized, each distinguished by subtle differences in vocabulary, usage, spelling, morphology, and syntax.
sentence_18: There are no hard and fast rules of classification; different scholars emphasize different features.
sentence_19: As a result, the list has variants, as well as alternative names.
sentence_20: In addition to the historical phases, [[Ecclesiastical_Latin|Ecclesiastical Latin]] refers to the styles used by the writers of the [[Roman_Catholic_Church|Roman Catholic Church]] from [[Late_Antiquity|Late Antiquity]] onward, as well as by Protestant scholars.
sentence_21: After the Western Roman Empire fell in 476 and Germanic kingdoms took its place, the [[Germanic_people|Germanic people]] adopted Latin as a language more suitable for legal and other, more formal uses.
sentence_22: Main article: [[Old_Latin|Old Latin]]
sentence_23: The earliest known form of Latin is Old Latin, which was spoken from the Roman Kingdom to the later part of the [[Roman_Republic|Roman Republic]] period.
sentence_24: It is attested both in inscriptions and in some of the earliest extant Latin literary works, such as the comedies of [[Plautus|Plautus]] and [[Terence|Terence]].
sentence_25: The [[Latin_alphabet|Latin alphabet]] was devised from the [[Etruscan_alphabet|Etruscan alphabet]].
sentence_26: The writing later changed from what was initially either a right-to-left or a [[Boustrophedon|boustrophedon]] script to what ultimately became a strictly left-to-right script.
sentence_27: Main article: [[Classical_Latin|Classical Latin]]
sentence_28: During the late republic and into the first years of the empire, a new Classical Latin arose, a conscious creation of the orators, poets, historians and other [[Literate|literate]] men, who wrote the great works of [[Classical_literature|classical literature]], which were taught in [[Grammar|grammar]] and [[Rhetoric|rhetoric]] schools.
sentence_29: Today's instructional grammars trace their roots to such [[Roman_school|schools]], which served as a sort of informal language academy dedicated to maintaining and perpetuating educated speech.
sentence_30: Main articles: Vulgar Latin, [[Late_Latin|Late Latin]], and Romance languages
sentence_31: Philological analysis of Archaic Latin works, such as those of [[Plautus|Plautus]], which contain snippets of everyday speech, indicates that a spoken language, Vulgar Latin (termed sermo vulgi, "the speech of the masses", by [[Cicero|Cicero]]), existed concurrently with literate Classical Latin.
sentence_32: The informal language was rarely written, so philologists have been left with only individual words and phrases cited by classical authors and those found as graffiti.
sentence_33: As it was free to develop on its own, there is no reason to suppose that the speech was uniform either diachronically or geographically.
sentence_34: On the contrary, romanised European populations developed their own dialects of the language, which eventually led to the differentiation of Romance languages.
sentence_35: The [[Decline_of_the_Roman_Empire|decline of the Roman Empire]] meant a deterioration in educational standards that brought about Late Latin, a postclassical stage of the language seen in Christian writings of the time.
sentence_36: It was more in line with everyday speech, not only because of a decline in education but also because of a desire to spread the word to the masses.
sentence_37: Despite dialectal variation, which is found in any widespread language, the languages of Spain, France, Portugal, and Italy retained a remarkable unity in phonological forms and developments, bolstered by the stabilising influence of their common [[Christians|Christian]] (Roman Catholic) culture.
sentence_38: It was not until the [[Umayyad_conquest_of_Hispania|Moorish conquest of Spain]] in 711, cutting off communications between the major Romance regions, that the languages began to diverge seriously.
sentence_39: The Vulgar Latin dialect that would later become [[Romanian_language|Romanian]] diverged somewhat more from the other varieties, as it was largely separated from the unifying influences in the western part of the Empire.
sentence_40: One key marker of whether a given Romance feature was found in Vulgar Latin is to compare it with its parallel in Classical Latin.
sentence_41: If it was not preferred in Classical Latin, then it most likely came from the undocumented contemporaneous Vulgar Latin.
sentence_42: For example, the Romance for "horse" (Italian cavallo, French cheval, Spanish caballo, Portuguese cavalo and Romanian cal) came from Latin caballus.
sentence_43: However, Classical Latin used equus.
sentence_44: Therefore, caballus was most likely the spoken form.
sentence_45: Vulgar Latin began to diverge into distinct languages by the 9th century at the latest, when the earliest extant Romance writings begin to appear.
sentence_46: They were, throughout the period, confined to everyday speech, as Medieval Latin was used for writing.
sentence_47: Main article: Medieval Latin
sentence_48: Medieval Latin is the written Latin in use during that portion of the postclassical period when no corresponding Latin vernacular existed.
sentence_49: The spoken language had developed into the various incipient Romance languages; however, in the educated and official world, Latin continued without its natural spoken base.
sentence_50: Moreover, this Latin spread into lands that had never spoken Latin, such as the Germanic and Slavic nations.
sentence_51: It became useful for international communication between the member states of the [[Holy_Roman_Empire|Holy Roman Empire]] and its allies.
sentence_52: Without the institutions of the Roman empire that had supported its uniformity, medieval Latin lost its linguistic cohesion: for example, in classical Latin sum and eram are used as auxiliary verbs in the perfect and pluperfect passive, which are compound tenses.
sentence_53: Medieval Latin might use fui and fueram instead.
sentence_54: Furthermore, the meanings of many words have been changed and new vocabularies have been introduced from the vernacular.
sentence_55: Identifiable individual styles of classically incorrect Latin prevail.
sentence_56: Main article: Renaissance Latin
sentence_57: The [[Renaissance|Renaissance]] briefly reinforced the position of Latin as a spoken language by its adoption by the [[Renaissance_Humanism|Renaissance Humanists]].
sentence_58: Often led by members of the clergy, they were shocked by the accelerated dismantling of the vestiges of the classical world and the rapid loss of its literature.
sentence_59: They strove to preserve what they could and restore Latin to what it had been and introduced the practice of producing revised editions of the literary works that remained by comparing surviving manuscripts.
sentence_60: By no later than the 15th century they had replaced Medieval Latin with versions supported by the scholars of the rising universities, who attempted, by scholarship, to discover what the classical language had been.
sentence_61: Main article: [[New_Latin|New Latin]]
sentence_62: During the Early Modern Age, Latin still was the most important language of culture in Europe.
sentence_63: Therefore, until the end of the 17th century the majority of books and almost all diplomatic documents were written in Latin.
sentence_64: Afterwards, most diplomatic documents were written in [[French_language|French]] (a Romance language) and later native or other languages.
sentence_65: Main articles: [[Contemporary_Latin|Contemporary Latin]] and [[Ecclesiastical_Latin|Ecclesiastical Latin]]
sentence_66: Despite having no native speakers, Latin is still used for a variety of purposes in the contemporary world.
sentence_67: The largest organisation that retains Latin in official and quasi-official contexts is the [[Catholic_Church|Catholic Church]].
sentence_68: Latin remains the language of the [[Roman_Rite|Roman Rite]]; the [[Tridentine_Mass|Tridentine Mass]] is celebrated in Latin.
sentence_69: Although the [[Mass_of_Paul_VI|Mass of Paul VI]] is usually celebrated in the local [[Vernacular_language|vernacular language]], it can be and often is said in Latin, in part or in whole, especially at multilingual gatherings.
sentence_70: It is the official language of the [[Holy_See|Holy See]], the primary language of its [[Public_journal|public journal]], the [[Acta_Apostolicae_Sedis|Acta Apostolicae Sedis]], and the working language of the [[Roman_Rota|Roman Rota]].
sentence_71: [[Vatican_City|Vatican City]] is also home to the world's only [[Automatic_teller_machine|automatic teller machine]] that gives instructions in Latin.
sentence_72: In the [[Pontifical_university|pontifical universities]] postgraduate courses of [[Canon_law|Canon law]] are taught in Latin, and papers are written in the same language.
sentence_73: In the [[Anglican_Church|Anglican Church]], after the publication of the [[Book_of_Common_Prayer|Book of Common Prayer]] of 1559, a Latin edition was published in 1560 for use in universities such as [[Oxford_University|Oxford]] and the leading "public schools" ([[United_Kingdom|English]] private academies), where the liturgy was still permitted to be conducted in Latin.
sentence_74: There have been several Latin translations since, including a Latin edition of the 1979 USA Anglican Book of Common Prayer.
sentence_75: In the [[Western_world|Western world]], many organizations, governments and schools use Latin for their mottos due to its association with formality, tradition, and the roots of [[Western_culture|Western culture]].
sentence_76: [[Canada|Canada]]'s motto A mari usque ad mare ("from sea to sea") and most [[List_of_Canadian_provincial_and_territorial_symbols|provincial mottos]] are also in Latin.
sentence_77: The [[Victoria_Cross_(Canada)|Canadian Victoria Cross]] is modelled after the British [[Victoria_Cross|Victoria Cross]] which has the inscription "For Valour".
sentence_78: Because Canada is officially bilingual, the Canadian medal has replaced the English inscription with the Latin Pro Valore.
sentence_79: [[Spain|Spain]]'s motto PLVS VLTRA, meaning "further beyond", is also Latin in origin.
sentence_80: It is taken from the personal motto of [[Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor|Charles V]], [[Holy_Roman_Emperor|Holy Roman Emperor]] and King of Spain (as Charles I), and is a reversal of the original phrase Non terrae plus ultra ("No land further beyond").
sentence_81: This was said to have been inscribed as a warning on the [[Pillars_of_Hercules|Pillars of Hercules]] at the [[Strait_of_Gibraltar|Strait of Gibraltar]], which marked the edge of the known world.
sentence_82: Charles adopted the motto following the discovery of the New World by Columbus, and it also has metaphorical suggestions of taking risks and striving for excellence.
sentence_83: Several [[List_of_U.S._state_and_territory_mottos|states of the United States have Latin mottos]]: such as [[Connecticut|Connecticut]]'s motto Qui transtulit sustinet ("He who transplanted sustains"); [[Kansas|Kansas]]'s Ad astra per aspera ("To the stars through hardships"); [[Colorado|Colorado]]'s Nil sine numine ("Nothing without providence"); [[Michigan|Michigan]]'s Si quaeris peninsulam amoenam, circumspice ("If you seek a pleasant peninsula, look about you"); [[Missouri|Missouri]]'s [[Salus_populi_suprema_lex_esto|Salus populi suprema lex esto]] ("The health of the people should be the highest law"); [[North_Carolina|North Carolina]]'s Esse quam videri ("To be rather than to seem"); [[Virginia|Virginia]]'s [[Sic_semper_tyrannis|Sic semper tyrannis]] ("Thus always to tyrants"); and [[West_Virginia|West Virginia]]'s [[Montani_Semper_Liberi|Montani semper liberi]] ("Mountaineers are always free").
sentence_84: Many military organizations today have Latin mottos, such as Semper paratus ("always ready"), the motto of the [[United_States_Coast_Guard|United States Coast Guard]]; [[Semper_Fidelis|Semper fidelis]] ("always faithful"), the motto of the [[United_States_Marine_Corps|United States Marine Corps]]; and Per ardua ad astra ("Through adversity/struggle to the stars"), the motto of the [[Royal_Air_Force|Royal Air Force]] (RAF).
sentence_85: Some colleges and universities have adopted Latin mottos, for example [[Harvard_University|Harvard University]]'s motto is [[Veritas|Veritas]] ("truth").
sentence_86: Veritas was the goddess of truth, a daughter of Saturn, and the mother of Virtue.
sentence_87: [[Switzerland|Switzerland]] has adopted the country's Latin short name Helvetia on coins and stamps, since there is no room to use all of the nation's [[Languages_of_Switzerland|four official languages]].
sentence_88: For a similar reason, it adopted the international vehicle and internet code CH, which stands for Confœderatio Helvetica, the country's full Latin name.
sentence_89: Some films of ancient settings, such as [[Sebastiane|Sebastiane]] and [[The_Passion_of_the_Christ|The Passion of the Christ]], have been made with dialogue in Latin for the sake of realism.
sentence_90: Occasionally, Latin dialogue is used because of its association with religion or philosophy, in such film/[[Television|television]] series as [[The_Exorcist_(film)|The Exorcist]] and [[Lost_(2004_TV_series)|Lost]] ("[[Jughead_(Lost)|Jughead]]").
sentence_91: Subtitles are usually shown for the benefit of those who do not understand Latin.
sentence_92: There are also songs written with Latin lyrics.
sentence_93: The libretto for the opera-oratorio [[Oedipus_rex_(opera)|Oedipus rex]] by [[Igor_Stravinsky|Igor Stravinsky]] is in Latin.
sentence_94: The continued instruction of Latin is often seen as a highly valuable component of a liberal arts education.
sentence_95: Latin is taught at many high schools, especially in Europe and the Americas.
sentence_96: It is most common in British [[Public_school_(United_Kingdom)|public schools]] and [[Grammar_school|grammar schools]], the Italian liceo classico and [[Liceo_scientifico|liceo scientifico]], the German Humanistisches [[Gymnasium_(Germany)|Gymnasium]] and the Dutch [[Gymnasium_(school)|gymnasium]].
sentence_97: Occasionally, some media outlets, targeting enthusiasts, broadcast in Latin.
sentence_98: Notable examples include [[Radio_Bremen|Radio Bremen]] in [[Germany|Germany]], [[YLE|YLE]] radio in [[Finland|Finland]] (the [[Nuntii_Latini|Nuntii Latini]] broadcast from 1989 until it was shut down in June 2019), and Vatican Radio & Television, all of which broadcast news segments and other material in Latin.
sentence_99: There are many websites and forums maintained in Latin by enthusiasts.
sentence_100: The [[Latin_Wikipedia|Latin Wikipedia]] has more than 100,000 articles.
sentence_101: [[Italian_language|Italian]], [[French_language|French]], Portuguese, Spanish, [[Romanian_language|Romanian]], [[Catalan_language|Catalan]], [[Romansh_language|Romansh]], and other Romance languages are direct descendants of Latin.
sentence_102: There are also many Latin derivatives in English as well as a few in German, Dutch, Norwegian, Danish, and Swedish.
sentence_103: Latin is still spoken in Vatican City, a city-state situated in Rome that is the seat of the [[Catholic_Church|Catholic Church]].
sentence_104: Some inscriptions have been published in an internationally agreed, monumental, multivolume series, the [[Corpus_Inscriptionum_Latinarum|Corpus Inscriptionum Latinarum]] (CIL).
sentence_105: Authors and publishers vary, but the format is about the same: volumes detailing inscriptions with a critical apparatus stating the [[Provenance|provenance]] and relevant information.
sentence_106: The reading and interpretation of these inscriptions is the subject matter of the field of epigraphy.
sentence_107: About 270,000 inscriptions are known.
sentence_108: The works of several hundred ancient authors who wrote in Latin have survived in whole or in part, in substantial works or in fragments to be analyzed in [[Philology|philology]].
sentence_109: They are in part the subject matter of the field of [[Classics|classics]].
sentence_110: Their works were published in [[Manuscript|manuscript]] form before the invention of printing and are now published in carefully annotated printed editions, such as the Loeb Classical Library, published by Harvard University Press, or the Oxford Classical Texts, published by [[Oxford_University_Press|Oxford University Press]].
sentence_111: [[Latin_translations_of_modern_literature|Latin translations of modern literature]] such as [[The_Hobbit|The Hobbit]], Treasure Island, [[Robinson_Crusoe|Robinson Crusoe]], [[Paddington_Bear|Paddington Bear]], [[Winnie_the_Pooh|Winnie the Pooh]], [[The_Adventures_of_Tintin|The Adventures of Tintin]], [[Asterix|Asterix]], [[Harry_Potter|Harry Potter]], [[The_Little_Prince|Le Petit Prince]], [[Max_and_Moritz|Max and Moritz]], [[How_the_Grinch_Stole_Christmas!|How the Grinch Stole Christmas!
sentence_112: ]], [[The_Cat_in_the_Hat|The Cat in the Hat]], and a book of fairy tales, "fabulae mirabiles", are intended to garner popular interest in the language.
sentence_113: Additional resources include phrasebooks and resources for rendering everyday phrases and concepts into Latin, such as [[Meissner's_Latin_Phrasebook|Meissner's Latin Phrasebook]].
sentence_114: The Latin influence in English has been significant at all stages of its insular development.
sentence_115: In the [[Middle_Ages|Middle Ages]], borrowing from Latin occurred from ecclesiastical usage established by Saint [[Augustine_of_Canterbury|Augustine of Canterbury]] in the 6th century or indirectly after the [[Norman_Conquest|Norman Conquest]], through the [[Anglo-Norman_language|Anglo-Norman language]].
sentence_116: From the 16th to the 18th centuries, English writers cobbled together huge numbers of new words from Latin and Greek words, dubbed "inkhorn terms", as if they had spilled from a pot of ink.
sentence_117: Many of these words were used once by the author and then forgotten, but some useful ones survived, such as 'imbibe' and 'extrapolate'.
sentence_118: Many of the most common [[Polysyllabic|polysyllabic]] English words are of Latin origin through the medium of [[Old_French|Old French]].
sentence_119: Romance words make respectively 59%, 20% and 14% of [[English_language|English]], [[German_language|German]] and [[Dutch_language|Dutch]] vocabularies.
sentence_120: Those figures can rise dramatically when only non-compound and non-derived words are included.
sentence_121: The influence of Roman governance and [[Roman_technology|Roman technology]] on the less-developed nations under Roman dominion led to the adoption of Latin phraseology in some specialized areas, such as science, technology, medicine, and law.
sentence_122: For example, the Linnaean system of plant and animal classification was heavily influenced by [[Natural_History_(Pliny)|Historia Naturalis]], an encyclopedia of people, places, plants, animals, and things published by [[Pliny_the_Elder|Pliny the Elder]].
sentence_123: Roman medicine, recorded in the works of such physicians as [[Galen|Galen]], established that today's [[Medical_terminology|medical terminology]] would be primarily derived from Latin and Greek words, the Greek being filtered through the Latin.
sentence_124: Roman engineering had the same effect on scientific terminology as a whole.
sentence_125: Latin law principles have survived partly in a long list of Latin legal terms.
sentence_126: A few [[International_auxiliary_language|international auxiliary languages]] have been heavily influenced by Latin.
sentence_127: Interlingua is sometimes considered a simplified, modern version of the language.
sentence_128: [[Latino_sine_Flexione|Latino sine Flexione]], popular in the early 20th century, is Latin with its inflections stripped away, among other grammatical changes.
sentence_129: The Logudorese dialect of the [[Sardinian_language|Sardinian language]] is the closest contemporary language to Latin.
sentence_130: Throughout European history, an education in the classics was considered crucial for those who wished to join literate circles.
sentence_131: [[Instruction_in_Latin|Instruction in Latin]] is an essential aspect.
sentence_132: In today's world, a large number of Latin students in the US learn from Wheelock's Latin: The Classic Introductory Latin Course, Based on Ancient Authors.
sentence_133: This book, first published in 1956, was written by Frederic M. Wheelock, who received a PhD from Harvard University.
sentence_134: Wheelock's Latin has become the standard text for many American introductory Latin courses.
sentence_135: The [[Living_Latin|Living Latin]] movement attempts to teach Latin in the same way that living languages are taught, as a means of both spoken and written communication.
sentence_136: It is available at the Vatican and at some institutions in the US, such as the [[University_of_Kentucky|University of Kentucky]] and [[Iowa_State_University|Iowa State University]].
sentence_137: The British Cambridge University Press is a major supplier of Latin textbooks for all levels, such as the [[Cambridge_Latin_Course|Cambridge Latin Course]] series.
sentence_138: It has also published a subseries of children's texts in Latin by Bell & Forte, which recounts the adventures of a mouse called [[Minimus|Minimus]].
sentence_139: In the [[United_Kingdom|United Kingdom]], the [[Classical_Association|Classical Association]] encourages the study of antiquity through various means, such as publications and grants.
sentence_140: The [[University_of_Cambridge|University of Cambridge]], the [[Open_University|Open University]], a number of prestigious independent schools, for example [[Eton_College|Eton]], [[Harrow_School|Harrow]], Haberdashers' Aske's Boys' School, Merchant Taylor's School, Via Facilis and Rugby, a London-based charity, run Latin courses.
sentence_141: In the [[United_States|United States]] and in [[Canada|Canada]], the [[American_Classical_League|American Classical League]] supports every effort to further the study of classics.
sentence_142: Its subsidiaries include the [[National_Junior_Classical_League|National Junior Classical League]] (with more than 50,000 members), which encourages high school students to pursue the study of Latin, and the [[National_Senior_Classical_League|National Senior Classical League]], which encourages students to continue their study of the classics into college.
sentence_143: The league also sponsors the [[National_Latin_Exam|National Latin Exam]].
sentence_144: Classicist [[Mary_Beard_(classicist)|Mary Beard]] wrote in The Times Literary Supplement in 2006 that the reason for learning Latin is because of what was written in it.
sentence_145: Latin was or is the official language of European states:

list.value: [[Holy_See|Holy See]] – used in the diocese, with [[Italian_language|Italian]] being the official language of [[Vatican_City|Vatican City]]

[[Hungary|Hungary]] – Latin was an official language in the [[Kingdom_of_Hungary|Kingdom of Hungary]] from the 11th century to the mid 19th century, when Hungarian became the exclusive official language in 1844. The best known Latin language poet of Croatian-Hungarian origin was [[Janus_Pannonius|Janus Pannonius]].

[[Croatia|Croatia]] – Latin was the official language of [[Croatian_Parliament|Croatian Parliament]] (Sabor) from the 13th to the 19th century (1847). The oldest preserved records of the parliamentary sessions (Congregatio Regni totius Sclavonie generalis) – held in Zagreb (Zagabria), Croatia – date from 19 April 1273. An extensive Croatian Latin literature exists. Latin is still used on Croatian coins on even years.

[[Poland|Poland]], [[Kingdom_of_Poland|Kingdom of Poland]] – officially recognised and widely used between the 10th and 18th centuries, commonly used in foreign relations and popular as a second language among some of the [[Szlachta|nobility]].

sentence_146: Main article: [[Latin_phonology_and_orthography|Latin phonology and orthography]]
sentence_147: The ancient pronunciation of Latin has been reconstructed; among the data used for reconstruction are explicit statements about pronunciation by ancient authors, misspellings, puns, ancient etymologies, the spelling of Latin loanwords in other languages, and the historical development of Romance languages.
sentence_148: The consonant phonemes of Classical Latin are as follows:
sentence_149: /z/ was not native to Classical Latin.
sentence_150: It appeared in Greek loanwords starting around the first century BC, when it was probably pronounced [z] initially and doubled [zz] between vowels, in contrast to Classical Greek [dz] or [zd].
sentence_151: In Classical Latin poetry, the letter ⟨z⟩ between vowels always counts as two consonants for metrical purposes.
sentence_152: The consonant b usually sounds as [b]; however, when a t or s precedes b then it is pronounced as in [pt] or [ps].
sentence_153: Further, [[Consonant|consonants]] do not blend together.
sentence_154: So, ch, ph, and th are all sounds that would be pronounced as [ch], [ph], and [th].
sentence_155: In Latin, q is always followed by the [[Vowel|vowel]] u.
sentence_156: Together they make a [kw] sound.
sentence_157: In Old and Classical Latin, the Latin alphabet had no distinction between uppercase and lowercase, and the letters ⟨J U W⟩ did not exist.
sentence_158: In place of ⟨J U⟩, ⟨I V⟩ were used, respectively; ⟨I V⟩ represented both vowels and consonants.
sentence_159: Most of the letterforms were similar to modern uppercase, as can be seen in the inscription from the Colosseum shown at the top of the article.
sentence_160: The spelling systems used in Latin dictionaries and modern editions of Latin texts, however, normally use ⟨j u⟩ in place of Classical-era ⟨i v⟩.
sentence_161: Some systems use ⟨j v⟩ for the consonant sounds /j w/ except in the combinations ⟨gu su qu⟩ for which ⟨v⟩ is never used.
sentence_162: Some notes concerning the mapping of Latin phonemes to English graphemes are given below:

table.value: Before ⟨c⟩, ⟨x⟩, and ⟨g⟩, as ng in sing (/sɪŋ/)
When doubled ⟨ll⟩ and before ⟨i⟩, as [[Voiced_dental,_alveolar_and_postalveolar_lateral_approximants|"light L"]], [l̥] in link ([l̥ɪnk]) (l exilis)
In all other positions, as [[Voiced_dental,_alveolar_and_postalveolar_lateral_approximants|"dark L"]], [ɫ] in bowl ([boʊɫ]) (l pinguis)
Sometimes at the beginning of a syllable, or after ⟨g⟩ and ⟨s⟩, as /w/ in wine (/waɪn/)
Sometimes at the beginning of a syllable, as y (/j/) in yard (/jaɹd/)
"y" (/j/), in between vowels, becomes "i-y", being pronounced as parts of two separate syllables, as in capiō (/kapiˈjo:/)
A letter representing ⟨c⟩ + ⟨s⟩: as x in English axe (/æks/)

sentence_163: In Classical Latin, as in modern Italian, double consonant letters were pronounced as long consonant sounds distinct from short versions of the same consonants.
sentence_164: Thus the nn in Classical Latin annus "year" (and in Italian anno) is pronounced as a doubled /nn/ as in English unnamed.
sentence_165: (In English, distinctive consonant length or doubling occurs only at the boundary between two words or [[Morpheme|morphemes]], as in that example.)
sentence_166: In Classical Latin, ⟨U⟩ did not exist as a letter distinct from V; the written form ⟨V⟩ was used to represent both a vowel and a consonant.
sentence_167: ⟨Y⟩ was adopted to represent [[Upsilon|upsilon]] in loanwords from Greek, but it was pronounced like ⟨u⟩ and ⟨i⟩ by some speakers.
sentence_168: It was also used in native Latin words by confusion with Greek words of similar meaning, such as sylva and ὕλη.
sentence_169: Classical Latin distinguished between long and short vowels.
sentence_170: Then, long vowels, except for ⟨I⟩, were frequently marked using the [[Apex_(diacritic)|apex]], which was sometimes similar to an acute accent ⟨Á É Ó V́ Ý⟩.
sentence_171: Long /iː/ was written using a taller version of ⟨I⟩, called i longa "[[Long_I|long I]]": ⟨ꟾ⟩.
sentence_172: In modern texts, long vowels are often indicated by a [[Macron_(diacritic)|macron]] ⟨ā ē ī ō ū⟩, and short vowels are usually unmarked except when it is necessary to distinguish between words, when they are marked with a breve ⟨ă ĕ ĭ ŏ ŭ⟩.
sentence_173: However, they would also signify a long vowel by writing the vowel larger than other letters in a word or by repeating the vowel twice in a row.
sentence_174: The acute accent, when it is used in modern Latin texts, indicates stress, as in Spanish, rather than length.
sentence_175: Long vowels in Classical Latin are, technically, pronounced as entirely different from short vowels.
sentence_176: The difference is described in the table below:

table.value: similar to the last a in attack (/ətæk/)
does not exist in English; as ü in German Stück (/ʃtʏk/)
does not exist in English; as üh in German früh (/fʀyː/)

sentence_177: This difference in quality is posited by W. Sidney Allen in his book Vox Latina.
sentence_178: However, Andrea Calabrese has disputed that short vowels differed in quality from long vowels, based upon the observation that [ɪ] and [ʊ] do not exist even in very conservative Romance languages such as Sardinian, with the difference in vowel quality more associated with Germanic languages.
sentence_179: A vowel letter followed by ⟨m⟩ at the end of a word, or a vowel letter followed by ⟨n⟩ before ⟨s⟩ or ⟨f⟩, represented a long nasal vowel, as in monstrum [mõːstrũː].
sentence_180: Classical Latin had several diphthongs.
sentence_181: The two most common were ⟨ae au⟩.
sentence_182: ⟨oe⟩ was fairly rare, and ⟨ui eu ei⟩ were very rare, at least in native Latin words.
sentence_183: There has also been debate over whether ⟨ui⟩ is truly a diphthong in Classical Latin, due to its rarity, absence in works of Roman grammarians, and the roots of Classical Latin words (i.e. hui ce to huic, quoi to cui, etc.) not matching or being similar to the pronunciation of classical words if ⟨ui⟩ were to be considered a diphthong.
sentence_184: The sequences sometimes did not represent diphthongs.
sentence_185: ⟨ae⟩ and ⟨oe⟩ also represented a sequence of two vowels in different syllables in aēnus [aˈeː.nʊs] "of bronze" and coēpit [kɔˈeː.pɪt] "began", and ⟨au ui eu ei ou⟩ represented sequences of two vowels or of a vowel and one of the semivowels /j w/, in cavē [ˈka.weː] "beware!
sentence_186: ", cuius [ˈkʊj.jʊs] "whose", monuī [ˈmɔn.ʊ.iː] "I warned", solvī [ˈsɔɫ.wiː] "I released", dēlēvī [deːˈleː.wiː] "I destroyed", eius [ˈɛj.jʊs] "his", and novus [ˈnɔ.wʊs] "new".
sentence_187: Old Latin had more diphthongs, but most of them changed into long vowels in Classical Latin.
sentence_188: The Old Latin diphthong ⟨ai⟩ and the sequence ⟨āī⟩ became Classical ⟨ae⟩.
sentence_189: Old Latin ⟨oi⟩ and ⟨ou⟩ changed to Classical ⟨ū⟩, except in a few words whose ⟨oi⟩ became Classical ⟨oe⟩.
sentence_190: These two developments sometimes occurred in different words from the same root: for instance, Classical poena "punishment" and pūnīre "to punish".
sentence_191: Early Old Latin ⟨ei⟩ usually changed to Classical ⟨ī⟩.
sentence_192: In Vulgar Latin and the Romance languages, ⟨ae oe⟩ merged with ⟨e ē⟩.
sentence_193: During the Classical Latin period this form of speaking was deliberately avoided by well-educated speakers.
sentence_194: [[Syllable|Syllables]] in Latin are signified by the presence of diphthongs and [[Vowel|vowels]].
sentence_195: The number of syllables is the same as the number of vowel sounds.
sentence_196: Further, if a consonant separates two vowels, it will go into the syllable of the second vowel.
sentence_197: When there are two consonants between vowels, the last consonant will go with the second vowel.
sentence_198: An exception occurs when a phonetic stop and liquid come together.
sentence_199: In this situation, they are thought to be a single consonant, and as such, they will go into the syllable of the second vowel.
sentence_200: Syllables can also be seen as [[Syllable_weight|long]].
sentence_201: Within a word, a syllable may either be long by nature or long by position.
sentence_202: A syllable that is long by nature has a long vowel or diphthong.
sentence_203: On the other hand, a syllable that is long by position has a short vowel that is followed by more than one consonant.
sentence_204: There are two rules that define which syllable is [[Stress_(linguistics)|stressed]] in the Latin language.

list.value: In a word with only two syllables, the emphasis will be on the first syllable.
In a word with more than two syllables, there are two cases.
If the second-to-last syllable is long, that syllable will have stress.
If the second-to-last syllable is not long, the syllable before that one will be stressed instead.

sentence_205: Main article: [[Latin_alphabet|Latin alphabet]]
sentence_206: Latin was written in the Latin alphabet, derived from the [[Etruscan_alphabet|Etruscan alphabet]], which was in turn drawn from the [[Greek_alphabet|Greek alphabet]] and ultimately the [[Phoenician_alphabet|Phoenician alphabet]].
sentence_207: This alphabet has continued to be used over the centuries as the script for the Romance, Celtic, Germanic, Baltic, Finnic, and many Slavic languages ([[Polish_language|Polish]], Slovak, [[Slovene_language|Slovene]], [[Croatian_language|Croatian]], [[Bosnian_language|Bosnian]] and [[Czech_language|Czech]]); and it has been adopted by many languages around the world, including [[Vietnamese_language|Vietnamese]], the [[Austronesian_languages|Austronesian languages]], many [[Turkic_languages|Turkic languages]], and most languages in [[Sub-Saharan_Africa|sub-Saharan Africa]], the [[Americas|Americas]], and [[Oceania|Oceania]], making it by far the world's single most widely used writing system.
sentence_208: The number of letters in the Latin alphabet has varied.
sentence_209: When it was first derived from the Etruscan alphabet, it contained only 21 letters.
sentence_210: Later, G was added to represent /É¡/, which had previously been spelled C, and Z ceased to be included in the alphabet, as the language then had no [[Voiced_alveolar_fricative|voiced alveolar fricative]].
sentence_211: The letters Y and Z were later added to represent Greek letters, [[Upsilon|upsilon]] and [[Zeta|zeta]] respectively, in Greek loanwords.
sentence_212: W was created in the 11th century from VV.
sentence_213: It represented /w/ in Germanic languages, not Latin, which still uses V for the purpose.
sentence_214: J was distinguished from the original I only during the late Middle Ages, as was the letter U from V. Although some Latin dictionaries use J, it is rarely used for Latin text, as it was not used in classical times, but many other languages use it.
sentence_215: Classical Latin did not contain sentence [[Punctuation|punctuation]], letter case, or [[Interword_spacing|interword spacing]], but [[Apex_(diacritic)|apices]] were sometimes used to distinguish length in vowels and the [[Interpunct|interpunct]] was used at times to separate words.
sentence_216: The first line of Catullus 3, originally written as
sentence_217: or with interpunct as
sentence_218: would be rendered in a modern edition as
sentence_219: or with macrons
sentence_220: or with apices
sentence_221: The Roman cursive script is commonly found on the many [[Wax_tablet|wax tablets]] excavated at sites such as forts, an especially extensive set having been discovered at Vindolanda on [[Hadrian's_Wall|Hadrian's Wall]] in [[Great_Britain|Britain]].
sentence_222: Most notable is the fact that while most of the [[Vindolanda_tablets|Vindolanda tablets]] show spaces between words, spaces were avoided in monumental inscriptions from that era.
sentence_223: Occasionally, Latin has been written in other scripts:

list.value: The Praeneste fibula is a 7th-century BC pin with an Old Latin inscription written using the Etruscan script.

The rear panel of the early 8th-century [[Franks_Casket|Franks Casket]] has an inscription that switches from [[Old_English|Old English]] in [[Anglo-Saxon_runes|Anglo-Saxon runes]] to Latin in Latin script and to Latin in runes.

sentence_224: Main articles: [[Latin_grammar|Latin grammar]] and [[Latin_syntax|Latin syntax]]
sentence_225: Latin is a [[Synthetic_language|synthetic]], [[Fusional_language|fusional language]] in the terminology of linguistic typology.
sentence_226: In more traditional terminology, it is an inflected language, but typologists are apt to say "inflecting".
sentence_227: Words include an objective semantic element and markers specifying the grammatical use of the word.
sentence_228: The fusion of root meaning and markers produces very compact sentence elements: amō, "I love," is produced from a semantic element, ama-, "love," to which -ō, a first person singular marker, is suffixed.
sentence_229: The grammatical function can be changed by changing the markers: the word is "inflected" to express different grammatical functions, but the semantic element usually does not change.
sentence_230: (Inflection uses affixing and infixing.
sentence_231: Affixing is prefixing and suffixing.
sentence_232: Latin inflections are never prefixed.)
sentence_233: For example, amābit, "he (or she or it) will love", is formed from the same stem, amā-, to which a future tense marker, -bi-, is suffixed, and a third person singular marker, -t, is suffixed.
sentence_234: There is an inherent ambiguity: -t may denote more than one grammatical category: masculine, feminine, or neuter gender.
sentence_235: A major task in understanding Latin phrases and clauses is to clarify such ambiguities by an analysis of context.
sentence_236: All natural languages contain ambiguities of one sort or another.
sentence_237: The inflections express [[Grammatical_gender|gender]], [[Grammatical_number|number]], and case in [[Adjective|adjectives]], [[Noun|nouns]], and [[Pronoun|pronouns]], a process called declension.
sentence_238: Markers are also attached to fixed stems of verbs, to denote person, number, tense, voice, mood, and [[Grammatical_aspect|aspect]], a process called [[Grammatical_conjugation|conjugation]].
sentence_239: Some words are uninflected and undergo neither process, such as adverbs, prepositions, and interjections.
sentence_240: Main article: [[Latin_declension|Latin declension]]
sentence_241: A regular Latin noun belongs to one of five main declensions, a group of nouns with similar inflected forms.
sentence_242: The declensions are identified by the genitive singular form of the noun.
sentence_243: The first declension, with a predominant ending letter of a, is signified by the genitive singular ending of -ae.
sentence_244: The second declension, with a predominant ending letter of o, is signified by the genitive singular ending of -i.
sentence_245: The third declension, with a predominant ending letter of i, is signified by the genitive singular ending of -is.
sentence_246: The fourth declension, with a predominant ending letter of u, is signified by the genitive singular ending of -Å«s.
sentence_247: The fifth declension, with a predominant ending letter of e, is signified by the genitive singular ending of -ei.
sentence_248: There are seven Latin noun cases, which also apply to adjectives and pronouns and mark a noun's syntactic role in the sentence by means of inflections.
sentence_249: Thus, [[Word_order|word order]] is not as important in Latin as it is in English, which is less inflected.
sentence_250: The general structure and word order of a Latin sentence can therefore vary.
sentence_251: The cases are as follows:

list.value: [[Nominative_case|Nominative]] – used when the noun is the [[Subject_(grammar)|subject]] or a [[Predicate_nominative|predicate nominative]]. The thing or person acting: the girl ran: puella cucurrit, or cucurrit puella

Genitive – used when the noun is the possessor of or connected with an object: "the horse of the man", or "the man's horse"; in both instances, the word man would be in the genitive case when it is translated into Latin. It also indicates the [[Partitive|partitive]], in which the material is quantified: "a group of people"; "a number of gifts": people and gifts would be in the genitive case. Some nouns are genitive with special verbs and adjectives: The cup is full of wine. (Poculum plēnum vīnī est.) The master of the slave had beaten him. (Dominus servī eum verberāverat.)

[[Dative_case|Dative]] – used when the noun is the indirect object of the sentence, with special verbs, with certain prepositions, and if it is used as agent, reference, or even possessor: The merchant hands the stola to the woman. (Mercātor fēminae stolam trādit.)
Accusative – used when the noun is the direct object of the subject and as the object of a preposition demonstrating place to which.: The man killed the boy. (Vir puerum necāvit.)

Ablative – used when the noun demonstrates separation or movement from a source, cause, [[Agent_(grammar)|agent]] or instrument or when the noun is used as the object of certain prepositions; adverbial: You walked with the boy. (Cum puerō ambulāvistī.)

Vocative – used when the noun is used in a direct address. The vocative form of a noun is often the same as the nominative, with the exception of second-declension nouns ending in -us. The -us becomes an -e in the vocative singular. If it ends in -ius (such as fīlius), the ending is just -ī (filī), as distinct from the nominative plural (filiī) in the vocative singular: "Master!" shouted the slave. ("Domine!" clāmāvit servus.)

Locative – used to indicate a location (corresponding to the English "in" or "at"). It is far less common than the other six cases of Latin nouns and usually applies to cities and small towns and islands along with a few common nouns, such as the words domus (house), humus (ground), and rus (country). In the singular of the first and second declensions, its form coincides with the genitive (Roma becomes Romae, "in Rome"). In the plural of all declensions and the singular of the other declensions, it coincides with the ablative (Athēnae becomes Athēnīs, "at Athens"). In the fourth-declension word domus, the locative form, domī ("at home") differs from the standard form of all other cases.

sentence_252: Latin lacks both definite and indefinite [[Article_(grammar)|articles]] so puer currit can mean either "the boy is running" or "a boy is running".
sentence_253: Main article: [[Latin_declension|Latin declension]]
sentence_254: There are two types of regular Latin adjectives: first- and second- declension and third-declension.
sentence_255: They are so-called because their forms are similar or identical to first- and second-declension and third-declension nouns, respectively.
sentence_256: Latin adjectives also have comparative (more --, -er) and superlative (most --, est) forms.
sentence_257: There are also a number of Latin participles.
sentence_258: Latin numbers are sometimes declined as adjectives.
sentence_259: See Numbers below.
sentence_260: First and second-declension adjectives are declined like first-declension nouns for the feminine forms and like second-declension nouns for the masculine and neuter forms.
sentence_261: For example, for mortuus, mortua, mortuum (dead), mortua is declined like a regular first-declension noun (such as puella (girl)), mortuus is declined like a regular second-declension masculine noun (such as dominus (lord, master)), and mortuum is declined like a regular second-declension neuter noun (such as auxilium (help)).
sentence_262: Third-declension adjectives are mostly declined like normal third-declension nouns, with a few exceptions.
sentence_263: In the plural nominative neuter, for example, the ending is -ia (omnia (all, everything)), and for third-declension nouns, the plural nominative neuter ending is -a or -ia (capita (heads), animalia (animals)) They can have one, two or three forms for the masculine, feminine, and neuter nominative singular.
sentence_264: Latin participles, like English participles, are formed from a verb.
sentence_265: There are a few main types of participles: Present Active Participles, Perfect Passive Participles, Future Active Participles, and Future Passive Participles.
sentence_266: Latin sometimes uses prepositions, depending on the type of prepositional phrase being used.
sentence_267: Most prepositions are followed by a noun in either the accusative or ablative case: "apud puerum" (with the boy), with "puerum" being the accusative form of "puer", boy, and "sine puero" (without the boy, "puero" being the ablative form of "puer".
sentence_268: A few [[Adposition|adpositions]], however, govern a noun in the genitive (such as "gratia" and "tenus").
sentence_269: Main articles: [[Latin_grammar|Latin grammar]] and [[Latin_conjugation|Latin conjugation]]
sentence_270: A regular verb in Latin belongs to one of four main [[Latin_conjugation|conjugations]].
sentence_271: A conjugation is "a class of verbs with similar inflected forms."
sentence_272: The conjugations are identified by the last letter of the verb's present stem.
sentence_273: The present stem can be found by omitting the -re (-rī in deponent verbs) ending from the present infinitive form.
sentence_274: The infinitive of the first conjugation ends in -ā-re or -ā-ri (active and passive respectively): amāre, "to love," hortārī, "to exhort"; of the second conjugation by -ē-re or -ē-rī: monēre, "to warn", verērī, "to fear;" of the third conjugation by -ere, -ī: dūcere, "to lead," ūtī, "to use"; of the fourth by -ī-re, -ī-rī: audīre, "to hear," experīrī, "to attempt".
sentence_275: Irregular verbs may not follow the types or may be marked in a different way.
sentence_276: The "endings" presented above are not the suffixed infinitive markers.
sentence_277: The first letter in each case is the last of the stem so the conjugations are also called a-conjugation, e-conjugation and i-conjugation.
sentence_278: The fused infinitive ending is -re or -rī.
sentence_279: Third-conjugation stems end in a consonant: the consonant conjugation.
sentence_280: Further, there is a subset of the third conjugation, the i-stems, which behave somewhat like the fourth conjugation, as they are both i-stems, one short and the other long.
sentence_281: The stem categories descend from [[Proto-Indo-European_language|Indo-European]] and can therefore be compared to similar conjugations in other Indo-European languages.
sentence_282: There are six general "tenses" in Latin (present, imperfect, future, perfect, pluperfect and future perfect), three moods (indicative, imperative and subjunctive, in addition to the [[Infinitive|infinitive]], participle, [[Gerund|gerund]], [[Gerundive|gerundive]] and supine), three persons (first, second and third), two numbers (singular and plural), two voices (active and passive) and two [[Grammatical_aspect|aspects]] (perfective and imperfective).
sentence_283: Verbs are described by four principal parts:

list.value: The first principal part is the first-person singular, present tense, active voice, indicative mood form of the verb. If the verb is impersonal, the first principal part will be in the third-person singular.
The second principal part is the present active infinitive.

The third principal part is the first-person singular, perfect active indicative form. Like the first principal part, if the verb is impersonal, the third principal part will be in the third-person singular.

The fourth principal part is the supine form, or alternatively, the nominative singular of the perfect passive participle form of the verb. The fourth principal part can show one gender of the participle or all three genders (-us for masculine, -a for feminine and -um for neuter) in the nominative singular. The fourth principal part will be the future participle if the verb cannot be made passive. Most modern Latin dictionaries, if they show only one gender, tend to show the masculine; but many older dictionaries instead show the neuter, as it coincides with the supine. The fourth principal part is sometimes omitted for intransitive verbs, but strictly in Latin, they can be made passive if they are used impersonally, and the supine exists for such verbs.

sentence_294: After the [[History_of_Taranto|Fall of Tarentum]] (272 BC), the Romans began Hellenising, or adopting features of Greek culture, including the borrowing of Greek words, such as camera (vaulted roof), sumbolum (symbol), and balineum (bath).

sentence_304: For example, the compound adjective, omnipotens, "all-powerful," was produced from the adjectives omnis, "all", and potens, "powerful", by dropping the final s of omnis and concatenating.

sentence_0: This article is about the capital city.

sentence_4: London is the [[Capital_city|capital]] and [[Lists_of_towns_and_cities_in_England_by_population|largest city]] of [[England|England]] and the [[United_Kingdom|United Kingdom]].
sentence_5: The city stands on the [[River_Thames|River Thames]] in the south-east of England, at the head of its 50-mile (80 km) [[Estuary|estuary]] leading to the [[North_Sea|North Sea]].
sentence_6: London has been a major settlement for two millennia.
sentence_7: [[Londinium|Londinium]] was founded by the [[Roman_Empire|Romans]].
sentence_8: The [[City_of_London|City of London]], London's ancient core and financial centre − an area of just 1.12 square miles (2.9 km) and colloquially known as the Square Mile − retains boundaries that closely follow its medieval limits.
sentence_9: The adjacent [[City_of_Westminster|City of Westminster]] is an [[Inner_London|Inner London]] borough and has for centuries been the location of much of the national government.
sentence_10: Thirty one additional [[London_boroughs|boroughs]] north and south of the river also comprise modern London.
sentence_11: London is [[Greater_London_Authority|governed]] by the [[Mayor_of_London|mayor of London]] and the London Assembly.
sentence_12: London is one of the world's most important [[Global_cities|global cities]] and has been called the world's most powerful, most desirable, most influential, most visited, most expensive, sustainable, most investment-friendly, and most-popular-for-work city.
sentence_13: It exerts a considerable impact upon the arts, commerce, education, entertainment, fashion, finance, healthcare, media, professional services, research and development, tourism and transportation.
sentence_14: London ranks 26th out of 300 major cities for economic performance.
sentence_15: It is one of the largest [[Financial_centre|financial centres]] and has either the fifth- or sixth-largest [[List_of_cities_by_GDP|metropolitan area GDP]].
sentence_16: It is the most-visited city as measured by international arrivals and has the busiest city airport system as measured by passenger traffic.
sentence_17: It is the leading [[Foreign_direct_investment|investment]] destination, hosting more [[Retail#Global_top_ten_retailers|international retailers]] than any other city.
sentence_18: As of 2020, London has the [[List_of_cities_by_number_of_billionaires|second-highest number of billionaires]] of any city in Europe, after [[Moscow|Moscow]].
sentence_19: In 2019, London had the highest number of ultra high-net-worth individuals in Europe.
sentence_20: London's universities form the largest concentration of higher education institutes in Europe, and London is home to highly ranked institutions such as [[Imperial_College_London|Imperial College London]] in [[Natural_sciences|natural]] and applied sciences, and the [[London_School_of_Economics|London School of Economics]] in [[Social_sciences|social sciences]].
sentence_21: In [[2012_Summer_Olympics|2012]], London became the first city to have hosted three modern [[Summer_Olympic_Games|Summer Olympic Games]].
sentence_22: London has a diverse range of people and cultures, and more than 300 languages are spoken in the region.
sentence_23: Its estimated mid-2018 municipal population (corresponding to [[Greater_London|Greater London]]) was 8,908,081, the third-most populous of any [[List_of_European_cities_by_population_within_city_limits|city in Europe]] and accounts for 13.4% of the UK population.
sentence_24: [[Greater_London_Built-up_Area|London's urban area]] is the third [[List_of_urban_areas_in_Europe|most populous in Europe]], after Moscow and Paris, with 9,787,426 inhabitants at the 2011 census.
sentence_25: The [[London_commuter_belt|London commuter belt]] is the [[List_of_metropolitan_areas_in_Europe|second-most populous in Europe]], after the Moscow Metropolitan Area, with 14,040,163 inhabitants in 2016.
sentence_26: London contains four [[World_Heritage_Site|World Heritage Sites]]: the [[Tower_of_London|Tower of London]]; [[Kew_Gardens|Kew Gardens]]; the site comprising the [[Palace_of_Westminster|Palace of Westminster]], [[Westminster_Abbey|Westminster Abbey]], and [[St_Margaret's,_Westminster|St Margaret's Church]]; and the historic settlement in [[Greenwich|Greenwich]] where the [[Royal_Observatory,_Greenwich|Royal Observatory, Greenwich]] defines the [[Prime_Meridian|Prime Meridian]] (0° [[Longitude|longitude]]) and [[Greenwich_Mean_Time|Greenwich Mean Time]].
sentence_27: Other landmarks include [[Buckingham_Palace|Buckingham Palace]], the [[London_Eye|London Eye]], [[Piccadilly_Circus|Piccadilly Circus]], [[St_Paul's_Cathedral|St Paul's Cathedral]], [[Tower_Bridge|Tower Bridge]], [[Trafalgar_Square|Trafalgar Square]] and [[The_Shard|The Shard]].
sentence_28: London has [[List_of_museums_in_London|numerous museums]], galleries, libraries and [[Sport_in_London|sporting events]].
sentence_29: These include the [[British_Museum|British Museum]], [[National_Gallery|National Gallery]], [[Natural_History_Museum,_London|Natural History Museum]], [[Tate_Modern|Tate Modern]], [[British_Library|British Library]] and [[West_End_theatre|West End theatres]].
sentence_30: The [[London_Underground|London Underground]] is the oldest underground railway network in the world.
sentence_31: Main article: [[Etymology_of_London|Etymology of London]]
sentence_32: London is an ancient name, already attested in the first century AD, usually in the [[Latinisation_of_names|Latinised]] form [[Londinium|Londinium]]; for example, handwritten Roman tablets recovered in the city originating from AD 65/70–80 include the word Londinio ('in London').
sentence_33: Over the years, the name has attracted many mythicising explanations.
sentence_34: The earliest attested appears in [[Geoffrey_of_Monmouth|Geoffrey of Monmouth]]'s [[Historia_Regum_Britanniae|Historia Regum Britanniae]], written around 1136.
sentence_35: This had it that the name originated from a supposed [[Lud_son_of_Heli|King Lud]], who had allegedly taken over the city and named it Kaerlud.
sentence_36: Modern scientific analyses of the name must account for the origins of the different forms found in early sources: [[Latin|Latin]] (usually Londinium), [[Old_English|Old English]] (usually Lunden), and [[Welsh_language|Welsh]] (usually Llundein), with reference to the known developments over time of sounds in those different languages.
sentence_37: It is agreed that the name came into these languages from [[Common_Brittonic|Common Brythonic]]; recent work tends to reconstruct the lost Celtic form of the name as *Londonjon or something similar.
sentence_38: This was adapted into Latin as Londinium and borrowed into [[Old_English|Old English]], the ancestor-language of English.
sentence_39: The toponymy of the Common Brythonic form is much debated.
sentence_40: A prominent explanation was [[Richard_Coates|Richard Coates]]'s 1998 argument that the name derived from pre-Celtic [[Old_European_hydronymy|Old European]] *(p)lowonida, meaning "river too wide to ford".
sentence_41: Coates suggested that this was a name given to the part of the [[River_Thames|River Thames]] which flows through London; from this, the settlement gained the Celtic form of its name, *Lowonidonjon.
sentence_42: However, most work has accepted a Celtic origin for the name, and recent studies have favoured an explanation along the lines of a Celtic derivative of a [[Proto-Indo-European|Proto-Indo-European]] root *lend- ('sink, cause to sink'), combined with the Celtic suffix *-injo- or *-onjo- (used to form place-names).
sentence_43: [[Peter_Schrijver|Peter Schrijver]] has specifically suggested, on these grounds, that the name originally meant 'place that floods (periodically, tidally)'.
sentence_44: Until 1889, the name "London" applied officially to the [[City_of_London|City of London]], but since then it has also referred to the County of London and [[Greater_London|Greater London]].
sentence_45: In writing, "London" is, on occasion, [[Colloquial|colloquially]] [[Contraction_(grammar)|contracted]] to "LDN".

sentence_100: In 1637, the government of [[Charles_I_of_England|Charles I]] attempted to reform administration in the area of London.

sentence_105: After an initial advance by the [[Cavaliers|Royalists]] in 1642, culminating in the battles of [[Battle_of_Brentford_(1642)|Brentford]] and [[Battle_of_Turnham_Green|Turnham Green]], London was surrounded by a defensive perimeter wall known as the [[Lines_of_Communication_(London)|Lines of Communication]].

sentence_128: Rising [[Traffic_congestion|traffic congestion]] led to the creation of the world's first local urban rail network.
sentence_129: The [[Metropolitan_Board_of_Works|Metropolitan Board of Works]] oversaw infrastructure expansion in the capital and some of the surrounding counties; it was abolished in 1889 when the [[London_County_Council|London County Council]] was created out of those areas of the counties surrounding the capital.
sentence_130: London was [[German_strategic_bombing_during_World_War_I|bombed by the Germans]] during the [[First_World_War|First World War]], and during the [[World_War_II|Second World War]], [[The_Blitz|the Blitz]] and other bombings by the German [[Luftwaffe|Luftwaffe]] killed over 30,000 Londoners, destroying large tracts of housing and other buildings across the city.
sentence_131: Immediately after the War, the [[1948_Summer_Olympics|1948 Summer Olympics]] were held at the original [[Wembley_Stadium_(1923)|Wembley Stadium]], at a time when London was still recovering from the war.
sentence_132: From the 1940s onwards, London became home to many immigrants, primarily from [[Commonwealth_of_Nations|Commonwealth]] countries such as Jamaica, India, Bangladesh and Pakistan, making London one of the most diverse cities worldwide.
sentence_133: In 1951, the [[Festival_of_Britain|Festival of Britain]] was held on the [[South_Bank|South Bank]].
sentence_134: The [[Great_Smog|Great Smog]] of 1952 led to the [[Clean_Air_Act_1956|Clean Air Act 1956]], which ended the "[[Pea_soup_fog|pea soup fogs]]" for which London had been notorious.
sentence_135: Primarily starting in the mid-1960s, London became a centre for the worldwide [[Youth_culture|youth culture]], exemplified by the [[Swinging_London|Swinging London]] subculture associated with the [[King's_Road|King's Road]], [[Chelsea,_London|Chelsea]] and [[Carnaby_Street|Carnaby Street]].
sentence_136: The role of trendsetter was revived during the [[Punk_rock|punk]] era.
sentence_137: In 1965 London's political boundaries were expanded to take into account the growth of the urban area and a new [[Greater_London_Council|Greater London Council]] was created.
sentence_138: During [[The_Troubles|The Troubles]] in Northern Ireland, London was subjected to bombing attacks by the [[Provisional_Irish_Republican_Army|Provisional Irish Republican Army]] for two decades, starting with the [[Old_Bailey_bombing|Old Bailey bombing]] in 1973.
sentence_139: Racial inequality was highlighted by the 1981 Brixton riot.
sentence_140: Greater London's population declined steadily in the decades after the Second World War, from an estimated peak of 8.6 million in 1939 to around 6.8 million in the 1980s.
sentence_141: The principal ports for London moved downstream to [[Port_of_Felixstowe|Felixstowe]] and [[Port_of_Tilbury|Tilbury]], with the [[London_Docklands|London Docklands]] area becoming a focus for regeneration, including the [[Canary_Wharf|Canary Wharf]] development.
sentence_142: This was borne out of London's ever-increasing role as a major international financial centre during the 1980s.
sentence_143: The [[Thames_Barrier|Thames Barrier]] was completed in the 1980s to protect London against tidal surges from the [[North_Sea|North Sea]].
sentence_144: The Greater London Council was abolished in 1986, which left London without a central administration until 2000 when London-wide government was restored, with the creation of the [[Greater_London_Authority|Greater London Authority]].
sentence_145: To celebrate the start of the 21st century, the [[Millennium_Dome|Millennium Dome]], [[London_Eye|London Eye]] and [[Millennium_Bridge_(London)|Millennium Bridge]] were constructed.
sentence_146: On 6 July 2005 London was awarded the [[2012_Summer_Olympics|2012 Summer Olympics]], making London the first city to stage the [[Olympic_Games|Olympic Games]] three times.
sentence_147: On 7 July 2005, three [[London_Underground|London Underground]] trains and a [[Double-decker_bus|double-decker bus]] were bombed in a [[7_July_2005_London_bombings|series of terrorist attacks]].
sentence_148: In 2008, [[Time_(magazine)|Time]] named London alongside [[New_York_City|New York City]] and [[Hong_Kong|Hong Kong]] as [[Nylonkong|Nylonkong]], hailing it as the world's three most influential [[Global_cities|global cities]].
sentence_149: In January 2015, Greater London's population was estimated to be 8.63 million, the highest level since 1939.
sentence_150: During the [[2016_United_Kingdom_European_Union_membership_referendum|Brexit referendum]] in 2016, the UK as a whole decided to leave the European Union, but a majority of London constituencies voted to remain in the EU.
sentence_151: Main articles: [[Local_government_in_London|Local government in London]], [[History_of_local_government_in_London|History of local government in London]], and [[List_of_heads_of_London_government|List of heads of London government]]
sentence_152: The administration of London is formed of two tiers: a citywide, strategic tier and a local tier.
sentence_153: Citywide administration is coordinated by the [[Greater_London_Authority|Greater London Authority]] (GLA), while local administration is carried out by 33 smaller authorities.
sentence_154: The GLA consists of two elected components: the [[Mayor_of_London|mayor of London]], who has executive powers, and the London Assembly, which scrutinises the mayor's decisions and can accept or reject the mayor's budget proposals each year.
sentence_155: The headquarters of the GLA is [[City_Hall_(London)|City Hall]], Southwark.
sentence_156: The mayor since 2016 has been [[Sadiq_Khan|Sadiq Khan]], the first [[Muslim|Muslim]] mayor of a major Western capital.
sentence_157: The mayor's [[Statutory_planning|statutory planning]] strategy is published as the [[London_Plan|London Plan]], which was most recently revised in 2011.
sentence_158: The local authorities are the councils of the 32 [[London_borough|London boroughs]] and the [[City_of_London_Corporation|City of London Corporation]].
sentence_159: They are responsible for most local services, such as local planning, schools, [[Social_work|social services]], local roads and refuse collection.
sentence_160: Certain functions, such as [[Waste_disposal_authorities_in_London|waste management]], are provided through joint arrangements.
sentence_161: In 2009–2010 the combined revenue expenditure by London councils and the GLA amounted to just over £22 billion (£14.7 billion for the boroughs and £7.4 billion for the GLA).
sentence_162: The [[London_Fire_Brigade|London Fire Brigade]] is the [[Statute|statutory]] [[Fire_service_in_the_UK|fire and rescue service]] for Greater London.
sentence_163: It is run by the [[London_Fire_and_Emergency_Planning_Authority|London Fire and Emergency Planning Authority]] and is the third largest fire service in the world.
sentence_164: [[National_Health_Service|National Health Service]] [[Emergency_medical_services|ambulance services]] are provided by the [[London_Ambulance_Service|London Ambulance Service (LAS) NHS Trust]], the largest free-at-the-point-of-use emergency ambulance service in the world.
sentence_165: The [[London_Air_Ambulance|London Air Ambulance]] charity operates in conjunction with the LAS where required.
sentence_166: Her Majesty's Coastguard and the [[Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution|Royal National Lifeboat Institution]] operate on the [[River_Thames|River Thames]], which is under the jurisdiction of the [[Port_of_London_Authority|Port of London Authority]] from [[Teddington_Lock|Teddington Lock]] to the sea.
sentence_167: London is the seat of the [[Government_of_the_United_Kingdom|Government of the United Kingdom]].
sentence_168: Many government departments, as well as the [[Prime_Minister_of_the_United_Kingdom|prime minister's]] residence at [[10_Downing_Street|10 Downing Street]], are based close to the [[Palace_of_Westminster|Palace of Westminster]], particularly along [[Whitehall|Whitehall]].
sentence_169: There are 73 members of Parliament (MPs) from London, elected from local parliamentary [[List_of_Parliamentary_constituencies_in_Greater_London|constituencies]] in the national [[British_House_of_Commons|Parliament]].
sentence_170: As of December 2019, 49 are from the [[Labour_Party_(UK)|Labour Party]], 21 are [[Conservative_Party_(UK)|Conservatives]], and three are [[Liberal_Democrats_(UK)|Liberal Democrat]].
sentence_171: The ministerial post of [[Minister_for_London|minister for London]] was created in 1994.
sentence_172: The current Minister for London is [[Paul_Scully|Paul Scully]] MP.
sentence_173: Main article: Crime in London
sentence_174: Policing in Greater London, with the exception of the [[City_of_London|City of London]], is provided by the [[Metropolitan_Police|Metropolitan Police]], overseen by the mayor through the [[Mayor's_Office_for_Policing_and_Crime|Mayor's Office for Policing and Crime]] (MOPAC).
sentence_175: The City of London has its own police force – the [[City_of_London_Police|City of London Police]].
sentence_176: The [[British_Transport_Police|British Transport Police]] are responsible for police services on [[National_Rail|National Rail]], [[London_Underground|London Underground]], [[Docklands_Light_Railway|Docklands Light Railway]] and [[Tramlink|Tramlink]] services.
sentence_177: A fourth police force in London, the [[Ministry_of_Defence_Police|Ministry of Defence Police]], do not generally become involved with policing the general public.
sentence_178: Crime rates vary widely by area, ranging from parts with serious issues to parts considered very safe.
