sentence_179: Today crime figures are made available nationally at [[Local_authority#England|Local Authority]] and [[Ward_(England)|Ward]] level.
sentence_180: In 2015, there were 118 homicides, a 25.5% increase over 2014.
sentence_181: The Metropolitan Police have made detailed crime figures, broken down by category at borough and ward level, available on their website since 2000.
sentence_182: Recorded crime has been rising in London, notably violent crime and murder by stabbing and other means have risen.
sentence_183: There were 50 murders from the start of 2018 to mid April 2018.
sentence_184: Funding cuts to police in London are likely to have contributed to this, though other factors are also involved.
sentence_185: Main article: [[Geography_of_London|Geography of London]]
sentence_186: [[Greater_London|London]], also referred to as Greater London, is one of nine [[Regions_of_England|regions of England]] and the top-level subdivision covering most of the city's metropolis.
sentence_187: The small ancient [[City_of_London|City of London]] at its core once comprised the whole settlement, but as its urban area grew, the [[City_of_London_Corporation|Corporation of London]] resisted attempts to amalgamate the city with its suburbs, causing "London" to be defined in a number of ways for different purposes.
sentence_188: Forty per cent of Greater London is covered by the [[London_postal_district|London post town]], within which 'LONDON' forms part of postal addresses.
sentence_189: The London telephone [[Area_code|area code]] (020) covers a larger area, similar in size to Greater London, although some outer districts are excluded and some places just outside are included.
sentence_190: The Greater London boundary has been [[List_of_Greater_London_boundary_changes|aligned to the M25 motorway]] in places.
sentence_191: Outward urban expansion is now prevented by the [[Metropolitan_Green_Belt|Metropolitan Green Belt]], although the built-up area extends beyond the boundary in places, resulting in a separately defined [[Greater_London_Urban_Area|Greater London Urban Area]].
sentence_192: Beyond this is the vast [[London_commuter_belt|London commuter belt]].
sentence_193: Greater London is split for some purposes into [[Inner_London|Inner London]] and [[Outer_London|Outer London]].
sentence_194: The city is split by the River Thames into [[North_London|North]] and [[South_London|South]], with an informal [[Central_London|central London]] area in its interior.
sentence_195: The coordinates of the nominal centre of London, traditionally considered to be the original [[Eleanor_Cross|Eleanor Cross]] at [[Charing_Cross|Charing Cross]] near the junction of [[Trafalgar_Square|Trafalgar Square]] and [[Whitehall|Whitehall]], are about .
sentence_196: However the geographical centre of London, on one definition, is in the [[London_Borough_of_Lambeth|London Borough of Lambeth]], just 0.1 miles to the northeast of [[Lambeth_North_tube_station|Lambeth North tube station]].
sentence_197: Within London, both the [[City_of_London|City of London]] and the [[City_of_Westminster|City of Westminster]] have [[City_status_in_the_United_Kingdom|city status]] and both the City of London and the remainder of Greater London are [[Ceremonial_counties_of_England|counties for the purposes of lieutenancies]].
sentence_198: The area of [[Metropolitan_and_non-metropolitan_counties_of_England#Greater_London|Greater London]] includes areas that are part of the [[Historic_counties_of_England|historic counties]] of [[Middlesex|Middlesex]], Kent, [[Surrey|Surrey]], Essex and [[Hertfordshire|Hertfordshire]].
sentence_199: London's status as the capital of England, and later the United Kingdom, has never been granted or confirmed officially—by statute or in written form.
sentence_200: Its position was formed through [[Constitutional_convention_(political_custom)|constitutional convention]], making its status as de facto capital a part of the [[Constitution_of_the_United_Kingdom|UK's uncodified constitution]].
sentence_201: The capital of England was moved to London from [[Winchester|Winchester]] as the [[Palace_of_Westminster|Palace of Westminster]] developed in the 12th and 13th centuries to become the permanent location of the [[Noble_court|royal court]], and thus the political capital of the nation.
sentence_202: More recently, Greater London has been defined as a [[Regions_of_England|region of England]] and in this context is known as London.
sentence_203: Greater London encompasses a total area of 1,583 square kilometres (611 sq mi), an area which had a population of 7,172,036 in 2001 and a population density of 4,542 inhabitants per square kilometre (11,760/sq mi).
sentence_204: The extended area known as the London Metropolitan Region or the London Metropolitan Agglomeration, comprises a total area of 8,382 square kilometres (3,236 sq mi) has a population of 13,709,000 and a population density of 1,510 inhabitants per square kilometre (3,900/sq mi).
sentence_205: Modern London stands on the [[River_Thames|Thames]], its primary geographical feature, a [[Navigability|navigable]] river which crosses the city from the south-west to the east.
sentence_206: The [[Thames_Valley|Thames Valley]] is a [[Floodplain|floodplain]] surrounded by gently rolling hills including [[Parliament_Hill,_London|Parliament Hill]], [[Addington_Hills|Addington Hills]], and [[Primrose_Hill|Primrose Hill]].
sentence_207: Historically London grew up at the [[Lowest_bridging_point|lowest bridging point]] on the Thames.
sentence_208: The Thames was once a much broader, shallower river with extensive [[Marsh|marshlands]]; at high tide, its shores reached five times their present width.
sentence_209: Since the [[Victorian_era|Victorian era]] the Thames has been extensively embanked, and many of its London [[Tributaries_of_the_River_Thames|tributaries]] now flow [[Subterranean_rivers_of_London|underground]].
sentence_210: The Thames is a tidal river, and London is vulnerable to flooding.
sentence_211: The threat has increased over time because of a slow but continuous rise in [[Tide|high water]] level by the slow 'tilting' of the British Isles (up in Scotland and Northern Ireland and down in southern parts of [[England|England]], [[Wales|Wales]] and Ireland) caused by [[Post-glacial_rebound|post-glacial rebound]].
sentence_212: In 1974 a decade of work began on the construction of the [[Thames_Barrier|Thames Barrier]] across the Thames at [[Woolwich|Woolwich]] to deal with this threat.
sentence_213: While the barrier is expected to function as designed until roughly 2070, concepts for its future enlargement or redesign are already being discussed.
sentence_214: Main article: [[Climate_of_London|Climate of London]]
sentence_215: London has a temperate [[Oceanic_climate|oceanic climate]] ([[Köppen_climate_classification|Köppen]]: Cfb ).
sentence_216: Rainfall records have been kept in the city since at least 1697, when records began at Kew.
sentence_217: At Kew, the most rainfall in one month is 7.4 inches (189 mm) in November 1755 and the least is 0 inches (0 mm) in both December 1788 and July 1800.
sentence_218: Mile End also had 0 inches (0 mm) in April 1893.
sentence_219: The wettest year on record is 1903, with a total fall of 38.1 inches (969 mm) and the driest is 1921, with a total fall of 12.1 inches (308 mm).
sentence_220: The average annual precipitation amounts to about 600 mm, a value inferior to cities such as [[Rome|Rome]], [[Lisbon|Lisbon]], [[New_York_City|New York City]] and [[Sydney|Sydney]].
sentence_221: Nevertheless, despite its relatively low annual precipitation, London still receives a good amount of rainy days annually – 109.6 days on the 1.0 mm threshold – Higher than, or at least akin to, the aforementioned cities.
sentence_222: Temperature extremes in London range from 38.1 °C (100.6 °F) at Kew during August 2003 down to −21.1 °C (−6.0 °F).
sentence_223: However, an unofficial reading of −24 °C (−11 °F) was reported on 3 January 1740.
sentence_224: Conversely, the highest unofficial temperature ever known to be recorded in the United Kingdom occurred in London in the 1808 heat wave.
sentence_225: The temperature was recorded at 105 °F (40.6 °C) on 13 July.
sentence_226: It is thought that this temperature, if accurate, is one of the highest temperatures of the millennium in the United Kingdom.
sentence_227: It is thought that only days in 1513 and 1707 could have beaten this.
sentence_228: Since records began in London (first at Greenwich in 1841), the warmest month on record is July 1868, with a mean temperature of 22.5 °C (72.5 °F) at [[Greenwich|Greenwich]] whereas the coldest month is December 2010, with a mean temperature of −6.7 °C (19.9 °F) at Northolt.
sentence_229: Records for [[Atmospheric_pressure|atmospheric pressure]] have been kept at London since 1692.
sentence_230: The highest pressure ever reported is 1,050 millibars (31 inHg) on 20 January 2020, and the lowest is 945.8 millibars (27.93 inHg) on 25 December 1821.
sentence_231: Summers are generally warm, sometimes hot.
sentence_232: London's average July high is 24 °C (74 °F).
sentence_233: On average each year, London experiences 31 days above 25 °C (77.0 °F) and 4.2 days above 30.0 °C (86.0 °F) every year.
sentence_234: During the [[2003_European_heat_wave|2003 European heat wave]] there were 14 consecutive days above 30 °C (86.0 °F) and 2 consecutive days when temperatures reached 38 °C (100 °F), leading to hundreds of heat-related deaths.
sentence_235: There was also a previous spell of 15 consecutive days above 32.2 °C (90.0 °F) in 1976 which also caused many heat related deaths.
sentence_236: The previous record high was 38 °C (100 °F) in August 1911 at the Greenwich station.
sentence_237: Droughts can also, occasionally, be a problem, especially in summer.
sentence_238: Most recently in Summer 2018 and with much drier than average conditions prevailing from May to December.
sentence_239: However, the most consecutive days without rain was 73 days in the spring of 1893.
sentence_240: Winters are generally cool with little temperature variation.
sentence_241: Heavy snow is rare but snow usually happens at least once each winter.
sentence_242: Spring and autumn can be pleasant.
sentence_243: As a large city, London has a considerable [[Urban_heat_island|urban heat island]] effect, making the centre of London at times 5 °C (9 °F) warmer than the suburbs and outskirts.
sentence_244: This can be seen below when comparing London Heathrow, 15 miles (24 km) west of London, with the London Weather Centre.
sentence_245: Main articles: [[List_of_districts_of_London|List of districts of London]] and [[London_boroughs|London boroughs]]
sentence_246: London's vast urban area is often described using a set of district names, such as [[Mayfair|Mayfair]], Southwark, [[Wembley|Wembley]] and [[Whitechapel|Whitechapel]].
sentence_247: These are either informal designations, reflect the names of villages that have been absorbed by sprawl, or are superseded administrative units such as parishes or [[Metropolitan_boroughs_of_the_County_of_London|former boroughs]].
sentence_248: Such names have remained in use through tradition, each referring to a local area with its own distinctive character, but without official boundaries.
sentence_249: Since 1965 Greater London has been divided into 32 [[London_borough|London boroughs]] in addition to the ancient City of London.
sentence_250: The City of London is the main financial district, and [[Canary_Wharf|Canary Wharf]] has recently developed into a new financial and commercial hub in the [[London_Docklands|Docklands]] to the east.
sentence_251: The West End is London's main entertainment and shopping district, attracting tourists.
sentence_252: [[West_(London_sub_region)|West London]] includes expensive residential areas where properties can sell for tens of millions of pounds.
sentence_253: The average price for properties in [[Royal_Borough_of_Kensington_and_Chelsea|Kensington and Chelsea]] is over £2 million with a similarly high outlay in most of central London.
sentence_254: The [[East_End_of_London|East End]] is the area closest to the original [[Port_of_London|Port of London]], known for its high immigrant population, as well as for being one of the poorest areas in London.
sentence_255: The surrounding [[North_East_(London_sub_region)|East London]] area saw much of London's early industrial development; now, [[Brownfield_land|brownfield]] sites throughout the area are being redeveloped as part of the [[Thames_Gateway|Thames Gateway]] including the [[London_Riverside|London Riverside]] and [[Lower_Lea_Valley|Lower Lea Valley]], which was developed into the [[Olympic_Park,_London|Olympic Park]] for the [[London_2012_Olympic_bid|2012 Olympics and Paralympics]].
sentence_256: Main articles: [[Architecture_of_London|Architecture of London]], [[List_of_tallest_buildings_and_structures_in_London|List of tallest buildings and structures in London]], and [[List_of_demolished_buildings_and_structures_in_London|List of demolished buildings and structures in London]]
sentence_257: London's buildings are too diverse to be characterised by any particular architectural style, partly because of their varying ages.
sentence_258: Many grand houses and public buildings, such as the [[National_Gallery|National Gallery]], are constructed from [[Portland_stone|Portland stone]].
sentence_259: Some areas of the city, particularly those just west of the centre, are characterised by white stucco or whitewashed buildings.
sentence_260: Few structures in central London pre-date the [[Great_Fire_of_London|Great Fire]] of 1666, these being a few trace [[Ancient_Rome|Roman]] remains, the [[Tower_of_London|Tower of London]] and a few scattered [[Tudor_architecture|Tudor]] survivors in the city.
sentence_261: Further out is, for example, the [[Tudor_period|Tudor-period]] [[Hampton_Court_Palace|Hampton Court Palace]], England's oldest surviving Tudor palace, built by Cardinal [[Thomas_Wolsey|Thomas Wolsey]] c.1515.
sentence_262: Part of the varied architectural heritage are the 17th-century churches by [[Christopher_Wren|Wren]], neoclassical financial institutions such as the [[Royal_Exchange,_London|Royal Exchange]] and the [[Bank_of_England|Bank of England]], to the early 20th century [[Old_Bailey|Old Bailey]] and the 1960s [[Barbican_Estate|Barbican Estate]].
sentence_263: The disused – but soon to be rejuvenated – 1939 [[Battersea_Power_Station|Battersea Power Station]] by the river in the south-west is a local landmark, while some railway termini are excellent examples of [[Victorian_architecture|Victorian architecture]], most notably [[St_Pancras_railway_station|St.
sentence_264: Pancras]] and [[Paddington_railway_station|Paddington]].
sentence_265: The density of London varies, with high employment density in the [[Central_London|central area]] and [[Canary_Wharf|Canary Wharf]], high residential densities in [[Inner_London|inner London]], and lower densities in [[Outer_London|Outer London]].
sentence_266: [[The_Monument|The Monument]] in the City of London provides views of the surrounding area while commemorating the [[Great_Fire_of_London|Great Fire of London]], which originated nearby.
sentence_267: [[Marble_Arch|Marble Arch]] and [[Wellington_Arch|Wellington Arch]], at the north and south ends of [[Park_Lane_(road)|Park Lane]], respectively, have royal connections, as do the [[Albert_Memorial|Albert Memorial]] and [[Royal_Albert_Hall|Royal Albert Hall]] in [[Kensington|Kensington]].
sentence_268: [[Nelson's_Column|Nelson's Column]] is a nationally recognised monument in [[Trafalgar_Square|Trafalgar Square]], one of the focal points of central London.
sentence_269: Older buildings are mainly brick built, most commonly the yellow [[London_stock_brick|London stock brick]] or a warm orange-red variety, often decorated with carvings and white plaster [[Moulding_(decorative)|mouldings]].
sentence_270: In the dense areas, most of the concentration is via medium- and high-rise buildings.
sentence_271: London's skyscrapers, such as [[30_St_Mary_Axe|30 St Mary Axe]], [[Tower_42|Tower 42]], the [[Broadgate_Tower|Broadgate Tower]] and [[One_Canada_Square|One Canada Square]], are mostly in the two financial districts, the [[City_of_London|City of London]] and [[Canary_Wharf|Canary Wharf]].
sentence_272: High-rise development is restricted at certain sites if it would obstruct protected views of [[St_Paul's_Cathedral|St Paul's Cathedral]] and other historic buildings.
sentence_273: Nevertheless, there are a number of tall skyscrapers in central London (see [[Tall_buildings_in_London|Tall buildings in London]]), including the 95-storey [[Shard_London_Bridge|Shard London Bridge]], the [[List_of_tallest_buildings_in_the_United_Kingdom|tallest building in the United Kingdom]].
sentence_274: Other notable modern buildings include [[City_Hall_(London)|City Hall]] in Southwark with its distinctive oval shape, the [[Art_Deco|Art Deco]] [[BBC_Broadcasting_House|BBC Broadcasting House]] plus the Postmodernist [[British_Library|British Library]] in Somers Town/[[Kings_Cross,_London|Kings Cross]] and No 1 Poultry by [[James_Stirling_(architect)|James Stirling]].
sentence_275: What was formerly the [[Millennium_Dome|Millennium Dome]], by the Thames to the east of Canary Wharf, is now an entertainment venue called the [[The_O2_(London)|O2 Arena]].
sentence_276: The London Natural History Society suggest that London is "one of the World's Greenest Cities" with more than 40 per cent green space or open water.
sentence_277: They indicate that 2000 species of flowering plant have been found growing there and that the [[Tideway|tidal Thames]] supports 120 species of fish.
sentence_278: They also state that over 60 species of bird nest in [[Central_London|central London]] and that their members have recorded 47 species of butterfly, 1173 moths and more than 270 kinds of spider around London.
sentence_279: London's [[Wetland|wetland]] areas support nationally important populations of many water birds.
sentence_280: London has 38 [[List_of_Sites_of_Special_Scientific_Interest_in_Greater_London|Sites of Special Scientific Interest]] (SSSIs), two [[National_nature_reserve_(United_Kingdom)|national nature reserves]] and 76 [[List_of_local_nature_reserves_in_Greater_London|local nature reserves]].
sentence_281: [[Amphibians|Amphibians]] are common in the capital, including [[Smooth_newt|smooth newts]] living by the [[Tate_Modern|Tate Modern]], and [[Common_frog|common frogs]], [[Common_toad|common toads]], palmate newts and [[Great_crested_newt|great crested newts]].
sentence_282: On the other hand, native reptiles such as [[Slowworm|slowworms]], [[Common_lizard|common lizards]], [[Barred_grass_snake|barred grass snakes]] and [[Vipera_berus|adders]], are mostly only seen in [[Outer_London|Outer London]].
sentence_283: Among other inhabitants of London are 10,000 [[Red_fox|red foxes]], so that there are now 16 foxes for every square mile (2.6 square kilometres) of London.
sentence_284: These urban foxes are noticeably bolder than their country cousins, sharing the pavement with pedestrians and raising cubs in people's backyards.
sentence_285: Foxes have even sneaked into the [[Houses_of_Parliament|Houses of Parliament]], where one was found asleep on a filing cabinet.
sentence_286: Another broke into the grounds of [[Buckingham_Palace|Buckingham Palace]], reportedly killing some of Queen Elizabeth II's prized [[Pink_flamingo|pink flamingos]].
sentence_287: Generally, however, foxes and city folk appear to get along.
sentence_288: A survey in 2001 by the London-based [[Mammal_Society|Mammal Society]] found that 80 per cent of 3,779 respondents who volunteered to keep a diary of garden mammal visits liked having them around.
sentence_289: This sample cannot be taken to represent Londoners as a whole.
sentence_290: Other mammals found in [[Greater_London|Greater London]] are [[European_hedgehog|hedgehog]], [[Brown_rat|brown rat]], [[Mice|mice]], [[European_rabbit|rabbit]], [[Shrew|shrew]], vole, and [[Grey_squirrel|grey squirrel]].
sentence_291: In wilder areas of Outer London, such as [[Epping_Forest|Epping Forest]], a wide variety of mammals are found, including [[European_hare|European hare]], [[European_badger|badger]], [[Field_vole|field]], [[Bank_vole|bank]] and [[European_water_vole|water vole]], [[Wood_mouse|wood mouse]], [[Yellow-necked_mouse|yellow-necked mouse]], [[European_mole|mole]], shrew, and [[Least_weasel|weasel]], in addition to red fox, grey squirrel and hedgehog.
sentence_292: A dead [[Eurasian_otter|otter]] was found at The Highway, in [[Wapping|Wapping]], about a mile from the [[Tower_Bridge|Tower Bridge]], which would suggest that they have begun to move back after being absent a hundred years from the city.
sentence_293: Ten of England's eighteen species of [[Bat|bats]] have been recorded in Epping Forest: [[Soprano_pipistrelle|soprano]], [[Nathusius'_pipistrelle|Nathusius']] and [[Common_pipistrelle|common pipistrelles]], [[Common_noctule|common noctule]], [[Serotine|serotine]], [[Barbastelle|barbastelle]], [[Daubenton's_bat|Daubenton's]], [[Brown_long-eared_bat|brown long-eared]], [[Natterer's_bat|Natterer's]] and [[Leisler's_bat|Leisler's]].
sentence_294: Among the strange sights seen in London have been a whale in the Thames, while the BBC Two programme "Natural World: Unnatural History of London" shows [[Feral_pigeon|feral pigeons]] using the [[London_Underground|London Underground]] to get around the city, a [[Pinniped|seal]] that takes fish from [[Fishmonger|fishmongers]] outside [[Billingsgate_Fish_Market|Billingsgate Fish Market]], and foxes that will "sit" if given sausages.
sentence_295: Herds of [[Red_deer|red]] and [[Fallow_deer|fallow deer]] also roam freely within much of [[Richmond_Park|Richmond]] and [[Bushy_Park|Bushy Park]].
sentence_296: A cull takes place each November and February to ensure numbers can be sustained.
sentence_297: Epping Forest is also known for its [[Fallow_deer|fallow deer]], which can frequently be seen in herds to the north of the Forest.
sentence_298: A rare population of [[Melanistic|melanistic]], black fallow deer is also maintained at the Deer Sanctuary near [[Theydon_Bois|Theydon Bois]].
sentence_299: Muntjac deer, which escaped from deer parks at the turn of the twentieth century, are also found in the forest.
sentence_300: While Londoners are accustomed to wildlife such as birds and foxes sharing the city, more recently urban deer have started becoming a regular feature, and whole herds of fallow deer come into residential areas at night to take advantage of London's green spaces.
sentence_301: Main article: [[Demography_of_London|Demography of London]]
sentence_302: The 2011 census recorded that 2,998,264 people or 36.7% of London's population are [[Foreign-born_population_of_the_United_Kingdom|foreign-born]] making London the city with the [[Foreign_born#Cities_With_Largest_Foreign_Born_Populations|second largest immigrant population]], behind New York City, in terms of absolute numbers.
sentence_303: About 69% of children born in London in 2015 had at least one parent who was born abroad.
sentence_304: The table to the right shows the most common countries of birth of London residents.
sentence_305: Note that some of the German-born population, in 18th position, are British citizens from birth born to parents serving in the [[British_Armed_Forces|British Armed Forces]] in [[Germany|Germany]].
sentence_306: With increasing industrialisation, London's population grew rapidly throughout the 19th and early 20th centuries, and it was for some time in the late 19th and early 20th centuries the most populous city in the world.
sentence_307: Its population peaked at 8,615,245 in 1939 immediately before the outbreak of the Second World War, but had declined to 7,192,091 at the 2001 Census.
sentence_308: However, the population then grew by just over a million between the 2001 and 2011 Censuses, to reach 8,173,941 in the latter enumeration.
sentence_309: However, London's continuous urban area extends beyond the borders of Greater London and was home to 9,787,426 people in 2011, while its wider [[London_metropolitan_area|metropolitan area]] has a population of between 12 and 14 million depending on the definition used.
sentence_310: According to Eurostat, London is the [[List_of_cities_in_the_European_Union_by_population_within_city_limits|most populous city and metropolitan area of the European Union]] and the second [[List_of_metropolitan_areas_in_Europe|most populous in Europe]].
sentence_311: During the period 1991–2001 a net 726,000 immigrants arrived in London.
sentence_312: The region covers an area of 1,579 square kilometres (610 sq mi).
sentence_313: The population density is 5,177 inhabitants per square kilometre (13,410/sq mi), more than ten times that of any other [[NUTS:UK|British region]].
sentence_314: In terms of population, London is the 19th [[World's_largest_cities|largest city]] and the 18th [[List_of_metropolitan_areas_by_population|largest metropolitan]] region.
sentence_315: Children (aged younger than 14 years) constitute 21 percent of the population in Outer London, and 28 percent in Inner London; the age group aged between 15 and 24 years is 12 percent in both Outer and Inner London; those aged between 25 and 44 years are 31 percent in Outer London and 40 percent in Inner London; those aged between 45 and 64 years form 26 percent and 21 percent in Outer and Inner London respectively; while in Outer London those aged 65 and older are 13 percent, though in Inner London just 9 percent.
sentence_316: The [[Median_age|median age]] of London in 2017 is 36.5 years old.
sentence_317: Main article: [[Ethnic_groups_in_London|Ethnic groups in London]]
sentence_318: According to the [[Office_for_National_Statistics|Office for National Statistics]], based on the [[United_Kingdom_Census_2011|2011 Census]] estimates, 59.8 per cent of the 8,173,941 inhabitants of London were [[White_people|White]], with 44.9 per cent [[White_British|White British]], 2.2 per cent [[Irish_migration_to_Great_Britain|White Irish]], 0.1 per cent [[Gypsy_(term)|gypsy]]/[[Irish_traveller|Irish traveller]] and 12.1 per cent classified as [[Other_White|Other White]].
sentence_319: 20.9 per cent of Londoners are of [[British_Asian|Asian]] and mixed-Asian descent.
sentence_320: 19.7 per cent are of full Asian descent, with those of mixed-Asian heritage comprising 1.2 of the population.
sentence_321: [[British_Indian|Indians]] account for 6.6 per cent of the population, followed by [[British_Pakistanis|Pakistanis]] and [[British_Bangladeshi|Bangladeshis]] at 2.7 per cent each.
sentence_322: [[British_Chinese|Chinese]] peoples account for 1.5 per cent of the population, with [[British_Arabs|Arabs]] comprising 1.3 per cent.
sentence_323: A further 4.9 per cent are classified as "Other Asian".
sentence_324: 15.6 per cent of London's population are of [[Black_British|Black]] and mixed-Black descent.
sentence_325: 13.3 per cent are of full Black descent, with those of mixed-Black heritage comprising 2.3 per cent.
sentence_326: [[Black_British|Black Africans]] account for 7.0 per cent of London's population, with 4.2 per cent as [[British_African-Caribbean_community|Black Caribbean]] and 2.1 per cent as "Other Black".
sentence_327: 5.0 per cent are of [[Mixed_(United_Kingdom_ethnicity_category)|mixed race]].
sentence_328: As of 2007, [[Black_British|Black]] and [[British_Asian|Asian]] children outnumbered [[White_British|White British]] children by about six to four in state schools across London.
sentence_329: Altogether at the 2011 census, of London's 1,624,768 population aged 0 to 15, 46.4 per cent were White, 19.8 per cent were Asian, 19 per cent were Black, 10.8 per cent were Mixed and 4 per cent represented another ethnic group.
sentence_330: In January 2005, a survey of London's ethnic and religious diversity claimed that there were more than 300 languages spoken in London and more than 50 non-indigenous communities with a population of more than 10,000.
sentence_331: Figures from the [[Office_for_National_Statistics|Office for National Statistics]] show that, in 2010, London's foreign-born population was 2,650,000 (33 per cent), up from 1,630,000 in 1997.
sentence_332: The 2011 census showed that 36.7 per cent of [[Greater_London|Greater London]]'s population were born outside the UK.
sentence_333: A portion of the German-born population are likely to be British nationals born to parents serving in the [[British_Armed_Forces|British Armed Forces]] in Germany.
sentence_334: Estimates produced by the [[Office_for_National_Statistics|Office for National Statistics]] indicate that the five largest foreign-born groups living in London in the period July 2009 to June 2010 were those born in India, Poland, the Republic of Ireland, Bangladesh and Nigeria.
sentence_335: Main article: [[Religion_in_London|Religion in London]]
sentence_336: According to the [[2011_UK_Census|2011 Census]], the largest religious groupings are Christians (48.4 per cent), followed by those of [[Irreligion|no religion]] (20.7 per cent), [[Muslims|Muslims]] (12.4 per cent), no response (8.5 per cent), [[Hinduism|Hindus]] (5.0 per cent), [[Jews|Jews]] (1.8 per cent), [[Sikhism|Sikhs]] (1.5 per cent), [[Buddhism|Buddhists]] (1.0 per cent) and other (0.6 per cent).
sentence_337: London has traditionally been Christian, and has a [[List_of_churches_in_London|large number of churches]], particularly in the City of London.
sentence_338: The well-known [[St_Paul's_Cathedral|St Paul's Cathedral]] in the City and [[Southwark_Cathedral|Southwark Cathedral]] south of the river are [[Anglicanism|Anglican]] administrative centres, while the [[Archbishop_of_Canterbury|Archbishop of Canterbury]], principal bishop of the Church of England and worldwide [[Anglican_Communion|Anglican Communion]], has his main residence at [[Lambeth_Palace|Lambeth Palace]] in the [[London_Borough_of_Lambeth|London Borough of Lambeth]].
sentence_339: Important national and royal ceremonies are shared between [[St_Paul's_Cathedral|St Paul's]] and [[Westminster_Abbey|Westminster Abbey]].
sentence_340: The Abbey is not to be confused with nearby [[Westminster_Cathedral|Westminster Cathedral]], which is the largest [[Roman_Catholic|Roman Catholic]] cathedral in [[England_and_Wales|England and Wales]].
sentence_341: Despite the prevalence of Anglican churches, observance is very low within the Anglican denomination.
sentence_342: Church attendance continues on a long, slow, steady decline, according to Church of England statistics.
sentence_343: London is also home to sizeable [[Muslim|Muslim]], [[Hindu|Hindu]], [[Sikh|Sikh]], and [[Jewish|Jewish]] communities.
sentence_344: Notable mosques include the [[East_London_Mosque|East London Mosque]] in Tower Hamlets, which is allowed to give the Islamic call to prayer through loudspeakers, the London Central Mosque on the edge of [[Regent's_Park|Regent's Park]] and the [[Baitul_Futuh|Baitul Futuh]] of the [[Ahmadiyya_Muslim_Community|Ahmadiyya Muslim Community]].
sentence_345: Following the oil boom, increasing numbers of wealthy Middle-Eastern Arab Muslims have based themselves around [[Mayfair|Mayfair]], Kensington, and [[Knightsbridge|Knightsbridge]] in West London.
sentence_346: There are large [[Bengali_Muslim|Bengali Muslim]] communities in the eastern boroughs of [[London_Borough_of_Tower_Hamlets|Tower Hamlets]] and [[London_Borough_of_Newham|Newham]].
sentence_347: Large Hindu communities are in the north-western boroughs of [[London_Borough_of_Harrow|Harrow]] and [[London_Borough_of_Brent|Brent]], the latter of which hosts what was, until 2006, Europe's largest [[Hindu_temple|Hindu temple]], [[Neasden_Temple|Neasden Temple]].
sentence_348: London is also home to 44 Hindu temples, including the [[BAPS_Shri_Swaminarayan_Mandir_London|BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir London]].
sentence_349: There are Sikh communities in East and West London, particularly in Southall, home to one of the largest Sikh populations and the largest Sikh temple outside India.
sentence_350: The majority of [[British_Jews|British Jews]] live in London, with significant Jewish communities in [[Stamford_Hill|Stamford Hill]], [[Stanmore|Stanmore]], [[Golders_Green|Golders Green]], [[Finchley|Finchley]], [[Hampstead|Hampstead]], Hendon and [[Edgware|Edgware]] in [[North_London|North London]].
sentence_351: [[Bevis_Marks_Synagogue|Bevis Marks Synagogue]] in the [[City_of_London|City of London]] is affiliated to London's historic [[Sephardic|Sephardic]] Jewish community.
sentence_352: It is the only synagogue in Europe which has held regular services continuously for over 300 years.
sentence_353: [[Stanmore_and_Canons_Park_Synagogue|Stanmore and Canons Park Synagogue]] has the largest membership of any single Orthodox synagogue in the whole of Europe, overtaking [[Ilford|Ilford]] synagogue (also in London) in 1998.
sentence_354: The community set up the [[London_Jewish_Forum|London Jewish Forum]] in 2006 in response to the growing significance of devolved London Government.
sentence_355: The accent of a 21st-century Londoner varies widely; what is becoming more and more common amongst the under-30s however is some fusion of [[Cockney|Cockney]] with a whole array of ethnic accents, in particular [[Caribbean|Caribbean]], which help to form an accent labelled [[Multicultural_London_English|Multicultural London English]] (MLE).
sentence_356: The other widely heard and spoken accent is RP ([[Received_Pronunciation|Received Pronunciation]]) in various forms, which can often be heard in the media and many of other traditional professions and beyond, although this accent is not limited to London and South East England, and can also be heard selectively throughout the whole UK amongst certain social groupings.
sentence_357: Since the turn of the century the Cockney dialect is less common in the East End and has 'migrated' east to [[London_Borough_of_Havering|Havering]] and the county of [[Essex|Essex]].
sentence_358: Main article: [[Economy_of_London|Economy of London]]
sentence_359: London's [[Gross_regional_product|gross regional product]] in 2018 was almost £500 billion, around a quarter of [[Economy_of_the_United_Kingdom|UK GDP]].
sentence_360: London has five major business districts: the city, Westminster, Canary Wharf, Camden & Islington and Lambeth & Southwark.
sentence_361: One way to get an idea of their relative importance is to look at relative amounts of office space: Greater London had 27 million m of office space in 2001, and the City contains the most space, with 8 million m of office space.
sentence_362: London has some of the highest real estate prices in the world.
sentence_363: London is the world's most expensive office market for the last three years according to world property journal (2015) report.
sentence_364: As of 2015 the residential property in London is worth $2.2 trillion – same value as that of Brazil's annual GDP.
sentence_365: The city has the highest property prices of any European city according to the Office for National Statistics and the European Office of Statistics.
sentence_366: On average the price per square metre in central London is €24,252 (April 2014).
sentence_367: This is higher than the property prices in other G8 European capital cities; Berlin €3,306, Rome €6,188 and Paris €11,229.
sentence_368: London's finance industry is based in the [[City_of_London|City of London]] and [[Canary_Wharf|Canary Wharf]], the two major business districts in London.
sentence_369: London is one of the pre-eminent financial centres of the world as the most important location for international finance.
sentence_370: London took over as a major financial centre shortly after 1795 when the Dutch Republic collapsed before the Napoleonic armies.
sentence_371: For many bankers established in Amsterdam (e.g. Hope, Baring), this was only time to move to London.
sentence_372: The London financial elite was strengthened by a strong Jewish community from all over Europe capable of mastering the most sophisticated financial tools of the time.
sentence_373: This unique concentration of talents accelerated the transition from the Commercial Revolution to the Industrial Revolution.
sentence_374: By the end of the 19th century, Britain was the wealthiest of all nations, and London a leading [[Financial_centre|financial centre]].
sentence_375: Still, as of 2016 London tops the world rankings on the Global Financial Centres Index (GFCI), and it ranked second in A.T. Kearney's 2018 Global Cities Index.
sentence_376: London's largest industry is finance, and its [[Financial_export|financial exports]] make it a large contributor to the UK's [[Balance_of_payments|balance of payments]].
sentence_377: Around 325,000 people were employed in financial services in London until mid-2007.
sentence_378: London has over 480 overseas banks, more than any other city in the world.
sentence_379: It is also the world's biggest currency trading centre, accounting for some 37 per cent of the $5.1 trillion average daily volume, according to the BIS.
sentence_380: Over 85 per cent (3.2 million) of the employed population of greater London works in the services industries.
sentence_381: Because of its prominent global role, London's economy had been affected by the [[Financial_crisis_of_2007–2008|financial crisis of 2007–2008]].
sentence_382: However, by 2010 the city has recovered; put in place new regulatory powers, proceeded to regain lost ground and re-established London's economic dominance.
sentence_383: Along with professional services headquarters, the [[City_of_London|City of London]] is home to the [[Bank_of_England|Bank of England]], [[London_Stock_Exchange|London Stock Exchange]], and [[Lloyd's_of_London|Lloyd's of London]] insurance market.
sentence_384: Over half of the UK's top 100 listed companies (the [[FTSE_100|FTSE 100]]) and over 100 of Europe's 500 largest companies have their headquarters in central London.
sentence_385: Over 70 per cent of the FTSE 100 are within London's metropolitan area, and 75 per cent of [[Fortune_500|Fortune 500]] companies have offices in London.
sentence_386: Media companies are concentrated in London and the media distribution industry is London's second most competitive sector.
sentence_387: The [[BBC|BBC]] is a significant employer, while other broadcasters also have headquarters around the city.
sentence_388: Many [[List_of_newspapers_in_the_United_Kingdom|national newspapers]] are edited in London.
sentence_389: London is a major retail centre and in 2010 had the highest non-food retail sales of any city in the world, with a total spend of around £64.2 billion.
sentence_390: The [[Port_of_London|Port of London]] is the second-largest in the United Kingdom, handling 45 million [[Tonne|tonnes]] of cargo each year.
sentence_391: A growing number of technology companies are based in London notably in [[East_London_Tech_City|East London Tech City]], also known as Silicon Roundabout.
sentence_392: In April 2014, the city was among the first to receive a [[GeoTLD|geoTLD]].
sentence_393: In February 2014 London was ranked as the European City of the Future in the 2014/15 list by [[FDi_Magazine|FDi Magazine]].
sentence_394: The gas and electricity distribution networks that manage and operate the towers, cables and pressure systems that deliver energy to consumers across the city are managed by [[National_Grid_plc|National Grid plc]], [[SGN_(company)|SGN]] and [[UK_Power_Networks|UK Power Networks]].
sentence_395: Main article: [[Tourism_in_London|Tourism in London]]
sentence_396: London is one of the leading tourist destinations in the world and in 2015 was ranked as the most visited city in the world with over 65 million visits.
sentence_397: It is also the top city in the world by visitor cross-border spending, estimated at US$20.23 billion in 2015.
sentence_398: Tourism is one of London's prime industries, employing the equivalent of 350,000 full-time workers in 2003, and the city accounts for 54% of all inbound visitor spending in the UK.
sentence_399: As of 2016 London was the world top city destination as ranked by [[TripAdvisor|TripAdvisor]] users.
sentence_400: In 2015 the top most-visited attractions in the UK were all in London.
sentence_401: The top 10 most visited attractions were: (with visits per venue)
sentence_402: The number of hotel rooms in London in 2015 stood at 138,769, and is expected to grow over the years.
sentence_403: Main articles: [[Transport_in_London|Transport in London]] and [[Infrastructure_in_London|Infrastructure in London]]
sentence_404: Transport is one of the four main areas of policy administered by the Mayor of London, however the mayor's financial control does not extend to the longer distance rail network that enters London.
sentence_405: In 2007 he assumed responsibility for some local lines, which now form the [[London_Overground|London Overground]] network, adding to the existing responsibility for the London Underground, trams and buses.
sentence_406: The public transport network is administered by [[Transport_for_London|Transport for London]] (TfL).
sentence_407: The lines that formed the London Underground, as well as trams and buses, became part of an integrated transport system in 1933 when the [[London_Passenger_Transport_Board|London Passenger Transport Board]] or [[London_Transport_(brand)|London Transport]] was created.
sentence_408: Transport for London is now the statutory corporation responsible for most aspects of the transport system in Greater London, and is run by a board and a commissioner appointed by the [[Mayor_of_London|Mayor of London]].
sentence_409: Main article: [[Airports_of_London|Airports of London]]
sentence_410: London is a major international air transport hub with the busiest city airspace in the world.
sentence_411: Eight airports use the word London in their name, but most traffic passes through six of these.
sentence_412: Additionally, [[Airports_of_London|various other airports]] also serve London, catering primarily to [[General_aviation|general aviation]] flights.

list.value: [[London_Heathrow_Airport|London Heathrow Airport]], in [[London_Borough_of_Hillingdon|Hillingdon]], West London, was for many years the [[World's_busiest_airport|busiest airport in the world]] for international traffic, and is the major hub of the nation's flag carrier, [[British_Airways|British Airways]]. In March 2008 its fifth terminal was opened. In 2014, [[Dubai_International_Airport|Dubai]] gained from Heathrow the leading position in terms of international passenger traffic.

[[London_Gatwick_Airport|London Gatwick Airport]], south of London in [[West_Sussex|West Sussex]], handles flights to more destinations than any other UK airport and is the main base of [[EasyJet|easyJet]], the UK's largest airline by number of passengers.

[[London_Stansted_Airport|London Stansted Airport]], north-east of London in [[Essex|Essex]], has flights that serve the greatest number of European destinations of any UK airport and is the main base of [[Ryanair|Ryanair]], the world's largest international airline by number of international passengers.
[[London_Luton_Airport|London Luton Airport]], to the north of London in [[Bedfordshire|Bedfordshire]], is used by several budget airlines for short-haul flights.

[[London_City_Airport|London City Airport]], the most central airport and the one with the shortest runway, in [[London_Borough_of_Newham|Newham]], East London, is focused on business travellers, with a mixture of full-service short-haul scheduled flights and considerable [[Business_jet|business jet]] traffic.

[[London_Southend_Airport|London Southend Airport]], east of London in [[Essex|Essex]], is a smaller, regional airport that caters for short-haul flights on a limited, though growing, number of airlines. In 2017, international passengers made up over 95% of the total at Southend, the highest proportion of any London airport.

sentence_413: The [[London_Underground|London Underground]], commonly referred to as the Tube, is the oldest and third longest [[Rapid_transit|metro]] system in the world.
sentence_414: The system serves 270 [[Metro_station|stations]] and was formed from several private companies, including the world's first underground electric line, the [[City_and_South_London_Railway|City and South London Railway]].
sentence_415: It dates from 1863.
sentence_416: Over four million journeys are made every day on the Underground network, over 1 billion each year.
sentence_417: An investment programme is attempting to reduce congestion and improve reliability, including £6.5 billion (€7.7 billion) spent before the [[2012_Summer_Olympics|2012 Summer Olympics]].
sentence_418: The [[Docklands_Light_Railway|Docklands Light Railway (DLR)]], which opened in 1987, is a second, more [[Medium-capacity_rail_transport_system|local metro system]] using smaller and lighter tram-type vehicles that serve the [[London_Docklands|Docklands]], [[Greenwich|Greenwich]] and [[Lewisham|Lewisham]].
sentence_419: There are more than 360 [[Railway_stations|railway stations]] in the [[London_fare_zones|London Travelcard Zones]] on an extensive above-ground suburban railway network.
sentence_420: South London, particularly, has a high concentration of railways as it has fewer Underground lines.
sentence_421: Most rail lines terminate around the centre of London, running into [[London_station_group|eighteen terminal stations]], with the exception of the [[Thameslink_(route)|Thameslink]] trains connecting [[Bedford|Bedford]] in the north and [[Brighton|Brighton]] in the south via [[London_Luton_Airport|Luton]] and [[Gatwick_Airport|Gatwick]] airports.
sentence_422: London has Britain's busiest station by number of passengers – [[London_Waterloo_station|Waterloo]], with over 184 million people using the interchange station complex (which includes [[London_Waterloo_East_railway_station|Waterloo East]] station) each year.
sentence_423: [[Clapham_Junction_railway_station|Clapham Junction]] is the busiest station in Europe by the number of trains passing.
sentence_424: With the need for more rail capacity in London, [[Crossrail|Crossrail]] is expected to open in 2021.
sentence_425: It will be a new railway line running east to west through London and into the [[Home_Counties|Home Counties]] with a branch to [[Heathrow_Airport|Heathrow Airport]].
sentence_426: It is Europe's biggest construction project, with a £15 billion projected cost.
sentence_427: London is the centre of the [[National_Rail|National Rail]] network, with 70 per cent of rail journeys starting or ending in London.
sentence_428: Like suburban rail services, regional and inter-city trains depart from several termini around the city centre, linking London with the rest of Britain including [[Birmingham|Birmingham]], [[Brighton|Brighton]], [[Bristol|Bristol]], [[Cambridge|Cambridge]], [[Cardiff|Cardiff]], [[Chester|Chester]], [[Derby|Derby]], Holyhead (for [[Dublin|Dublin]]), [[Edinburgh|Edinburgh]], [[Exeter|Exeter]], [[Glasgow|Glasgow]], [[Leeds|Leeds]], [[Liverpool|Liverpool]], [[Nottingham|Nottingham]], [[Manchester|Manchester]], [[Newcastle_upon_Tyne|Newcastle upon Tyne]], [[Norwich|Norwich]], [[Reading,_Berkshire|Reading]], [[Sheffield|Sheffield]], [[York|York]].
sentence_429: Some international railway services to Continental Europe were operated during the 20th century as [[Boat_train|boat trains]], such as the [[Admiraal_de_Ruijter_(train)|Admiraal de Ruijter]] to [[Amsterdam|Amsterdam]] and the [[Night_Ferry|Night Ferry]] to Paris and Brussels.
sentence_430: The opening of the [[Channel_Tunnel|Channel Tunnel]] in 1994 connected London directly to the continental rail network, allowing [[Eurostar|Eurostar]] services to begin.
sentence_431: Since 2007, high-speed trains link [[St_Pancras_railway_station|St.
sentence_432: Pancras International]] with [[Lille|Lille]], [[Calais|Calais]], [[Paris|Paris]], [[Disneyland_Paris|Disneyland Paris]], [[Brussels|Brussels]], [[Amsterdam|Amsterdam]] and other European tourist destinations via the [[High_Speed_1|High Speed 1]] rail link and the [[Channel_Tunnel|Channel Tunnel]].
sentence_433: The first [[Southeastern_(train_operating_company)|high-speed domestic]] trains started in June 2009 linking [[Kent|Kent]] to London.
sentence_434: There are plans for a [[High_Speed_2|second high speed line]] linking London to the Midlands, North West England, and Yorkshire.
sentence_435: Although [[Rail_freight|rail freight]] levels are far down compared to their height, significant quantities of cargo are also carried into and out of London by rail; chiefly building materials and [[Landfill|landfill]] waste.
sentence_436: As a major hub of the British railway network, London's tracks also carry large amounts of freight for the other regions, such as [[Containerisation|container freight]] from the Channel Tunnel and [[English_Channel|English Channel]] ports, and [[Nuclear_waste|nuclear waste]] for reprocessing at [[Sellafield|Sellafield]].
sentence_437: London's bus network runs 24 hours a day, with about 8,500 buses, more than 700 bus routes and around 19,500 bus stops.
sentence_438: In 2013, the network had more than 2 billion commuter trips per year, more than the Underground.
sentence_439: Around £850 million is taken in revenue each year.
sentence_440: London has the largest wheelchair-accessible network in the world and, from the third quarter of 2007, became more accessible to hearing and visually impaired passengers as audio-visual announcements were introduced.
sentence_441: London's coach hub is [[Victoria_Coach_Station|Victoria Coach Station]], an [[Art_Deco|Art Deco]] building opened in 1932.
sentence_442: The coach station was initially run by a group of coach companies under the name of London Coastal Coaches; however, in 1970 the service and station were included in the nationalisation of the country's coach services, becoming part of the National Bus Company.
sentence_443: In 1988, the coach station was purchased by London Transport which then became [[Transport_for_London|Transport for London]].
sentence_444: Victoria Coach Station has weekly passenger numbers of over 200,000 and provides services across the UK and Europe.
sentence_445: London has a modern tram network, known as [[Tramlink|Tramlink]], centred on [[Croydon|Croydon]] in [[South_London|South London]].
sentence_446: The network has 39 stops and four routes, and carried 28 million people in 2013.
sentence_447: Since June 2008, [[Transport_for_London|Transport for London]] has completely owned Tramlink.
sentence_448: London's first and to date only cable car is the [[Emirates_Air_Line_(cable_car)|Emirates Air Line]], which opened in June 2012.
sentence_449: The cable car crosses the [[River_Thames|River Thames]], and links [[Greenwich_Peninsula|Greenwich Peninsula]] and the [[Royal_Docks|Royal Docks]] in the east of the city.
sentence_450: It is integrated with London's Oyster Card ticketing system, although special fares are charged.
sentence_451: It cost £60 million to build and carries more than 3,500 passengers every day.
sentence_452: Similar to the [[Santander_Cycles|Santander Cycles]] bike hire scheme, the cable car is sponsored in a 10-year deal by the airline [[Emirates_(airline)|Emirates]].
sentence_453: Main article: [[Cycling_in_London|Cycling in London]]
sentence_454: In the Greater London Area, around 650,000 people use a bike everyday.
sentence_455: But out of a total population of around 8.8 million, this means that just around 7% of Greater London's population use a bike on an average day.
sentence_456: This relatively low percentage of bicycle users may be due to the poor investments for cycling in London of about £110 million per year, equating to around £12 per person, which can be compared to £22 in the Netherlands.
sentence_457: [[Cycling_in_London|Cycling]] has become an increasingly popular way to get around London.
sentence_458: The launch of [[Santander_Cycles|a cycle hire scheme]] in July 2010 was successful and generally well received.
sentence_459: The [[Port_of_London|Port of London]], once the largest in the world, is now only the second-largest in the United Kingdom, handling 45 million tonnes of cargo each year as of 2009.
sentence_460: Most of this cargo passes through the [[Port_of_Tilbury|Port of Tilbury]], outside the boundary of Greater London.
sentence_461: London has river boat services on the Thames known as [[Thames_Clippers|Thames Clippers]], which offers both commuter and tourist boat services.
sentence_462: These run every 20 minutes between [[Embankment_Pier|Embankment Pier]] and [[North_Greenwich_Pier|North Greenwich Pier]].
sentence_463: The [[Woolwich_Ferry|Woolwich Ferry]], with 2.5 million passengers every year, is a frequent service linking the [[North_Circular_Road|North]] and [[South_Circular_Road,_London|South Circular]] Roads.
sentence_464: Although the majority of journeys in central London are made by public transport, car travel is common in the suburbs.
sentence_465: The [[London_Inner_Ring_Road|inner ring road]] (around the city centre), the [[A406_road|North]] and [[A205_road|South Circular]] roads (just within the suburbs), and the outer orbital motorway (the [[M25_motorway|M25]], just outside the built-up area in most places) encircle the city and are intersected by a number of busy radial routes—but very few motorways penetrate into [[Inner_London|inner London]].
sentence_466: A plan for a comprehensive network of motorways throughout the city (the [[London_Ringways|Ringways Plan]]) was prepared in the 1960s but was mostly cancelled in the early 1970s.
sentence_467: The M25 is the second-longest ring-road motorway in Europe at 117 mi (188 km) long.
sentence_468: The [[A1_road_(Great_Britain)|A1]] and [[M1_motorway|M1]] connect London to [[Leeds|Leeds]], and [[Newcastle_upon_Tyne|Newcastle]] and [[Edinburgh|Edinburgh]].
sentence_469: London is notorious for its traffic congestion; in 2009, the average speed of a car in the rush hour was recorded at 10.6 mph (17.1 km/h).
sentence_470: In 2003, a [[London_congestion_charge|congestion charge]] was introduced to reduce traffic volumes in the city centre.
sentence_471: With a few exceptions, motorists are required to pay to drive within a defined zone encompassing much of central London.
sentence_472: Motorists who are residents of the defined zone can buy a greatly reduced season pass.
sentence_473: The London government initially expected the Congestion Charge Zone to increase daily peak period Underground and bus users, reduce road traffic, increase traffic speeds, and reduce queues; however, the increase in private for hire vehicles has affected these expectations.
sentence_474: Over the course of several years, the average number of cars entering the centre of London on a weekday was reduced from 195,000 to 125,000 cars – a 35-per-cent reduction of vehicles driven per day.
sentence_475: Main article: Education in London
sentence_476: See Also: [[List_of_universities_and_higher_education_colleges_in_London|List of universities and higher education colleges in London]]
sentence_477: London is a major global centre of higher education teaching and research and has the largest concentration of higher education institutes in Europe.
sentence_478: According to the QS World University Rankings 2015/16, London has the greatest concentration of top class universities in the world and its international student population of around 110,000 is larger than any other city in the world.
sentence_479: A 2014 [[PricewaterhouseCoopers|PricewaterhouseCoopers]] report termed London the global capital of higher education.
sentence_480: A number of world-leading education institutions are based in London.
sentence_481: In the 2014/15 [[QS_World_University_Rankings|QS World University Rankings]], [[Imperial_College_London|Imperial College London]] is ranked joint-second in the world, [[University_College_London|University College London]] (UCL) is ranked fifth, and [[King's_College_London|King's College London]] (KCL) is ranked 16th.
sentence_482: The [[London_School_of_Economics|London School of Economics]] has been described as the world's leading social science institution for both teaching and research.
sentence_483: The [[London_Business_School|London Business School]] is considered one of the world's leading business schools and in 2015 its MBA programme was ranked second-best in the world by the [[Financial_Times|Financial Times]].
sentence_484: The city is also home to three of the world's top ten performing arts schools (as ranked by the 2020 QS World University Rankings): the [[Royal_College_of_Music|Royal College of Music]] (ranking 2nd in the world), the [[Royal_Academy_of_Music|Royal Academy of Music]] (ranking 4th) and the [[Guildhall_School_of_Music_and_Drama|Guildhall School of Music and Drama]] (ranking 6th).
sentence_485: With 178,735 students in London and around 48,000 in [[University_of_London_Worldwide|University of London Worldwide]], the federal [[University_of_London|University of London]] is the largest contact teaching university in the UK.
sentence_486: It includes five multi-faculty universities – [[City,_University_of_London|City]], [[King's_College_London|King's College London]], [[Queen_Mary,_University_of_London|Queen Mary]], [[Royal_Holloway|Royal Holloway]] and [[University_College_London|UCL]] – and a number of smaller and more specialised institutions including [[Birkbeck_College|Birkbeck]], the [[Courtauld_Institute_of_Art|Courtauld Institute of Art]], [[Goldsmiths,_University_of_London|Goldsmiths]], the [[London_Business_School|London Business School]], the London School of Economics, the [[London_School_of_Hygiene_&_Tropical_Medicine|London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine]], the [[Royal_Academy_of_Music|Royal Academy of Music]], the [[Central_School_of_Speech_and_Drama|Central School of Speech and Drama]], the Royal Veterinary College and the [[School_of_Oriental_and_African_Studies|School of Oriental and African Studies]].
sentence_487: Members of the University of London have their own [[University_and_college_admission|admissions]] procedures, and most award their own degrees.
sentence_488: A number of universities in London are outside the University of London system, including [[Brunel_University|Brunel University]], [[Imperial_College_London|Imperial College London]], [[Kingston_University|Kingston University]], [[London_Metropolitan_University|London Metropolitan University]], [[University_of_East_London|University of East London]], [[University_of_West_London|University of West London]], [[University_of_Westminster|University of Westminster]], [[London_South_Bank_University|London South Bank University]], [[Middlesex_University|Middlesex University]], and University of the Arts London (the largest university of art, design, fashion, communication and the performing arts in Europe).
sentence_489: In addition there are three international universities in London – [[Regent's_College|Regent's University London]], Richmond, The American International University in London and [[Schiller_International_University|Schiller International University]].
sentence_490: London is home to five major medical schools – [[Barts_and_The_London_School_of_Medicine_and_Dentistry|Barts and The London School of Medicine and Dentistry]] (part of [[Queen_Mary,_University_of_London|Queen Mary]]), [[King's_College_London_School_of_Medicine|King's College London School of Medicine]] (the largest medical school in Europe), [[Imperial_College_School_of_Medicine|Imperial College School of Medicine]], [[UCL_Medical_School|UCL Medical School]] and [[St_George's,_University_of_London|St George's, University of London]] – and has many affiliated teaching hospitals.
sentence_491: It is also a major centre for biomedical research, and three of the UK's eight [[Academic_health_science_centre|academic health science centres]] are based in the city – [[Imperial_College_Healthcare_NHS_Trust|Imperial College Healthcare]], [[King's_Health_Partners|King's Health Partners]] and [[UCL_Partners|UCL Partners]] (the largest such centre in Europe).
sentence_492: Additionally, many biomedical and biotechnology spin out companies from these research institutions are based around the city, most prominently in [[White_City,_London|White City]].
sentence_493: There are a number of business schools in London, including the [[London_School_of_Business_and_Finance|London School of Business and Finance]], [[Cass_Business_School|Cass Business School]] (part of [[City_University_London|City University London]]), [[Hult_International_Business_School|Hult International Business School]], [[ESCP_Europe|ESCP Europe]], [[European_Business_School_London|European Business School London]], [[Imperial_College_Business_School|Imperial College Business School]], the [[London_Business_School|London Business School]] and the [[UCL_School_of_Management|UCL School of Management]].
sentence_494: London is also home to many specialist arts education institutions, including the Academy of Live and Recorded Arts, Central School of Ballet, [[London_Academy_of_Music_and_Dramatic_Art|LAMDA]], [[London_College_of_Contemporary_Arts_(LCCA)|London College of Contemporary Arts (LCCA)]], [[London_Contemporary_Dance_School|London Contemporary Dance School]], [[The_Circus_Space|National Centre for Circus Arts]], [[Royal_Academy_of_Dramatic_Art|RADA]], [[Rambert_Dance_Company|Rambert School of Ballet and Contemporary Dance]], the [[Royal_College_of_Art|Royal College of Art]] and [[Trinity_Laban|Trinity Laban]].
sentence_495: The majority of primary and secondary schools and further-education colleges in London are controlled by the [[London_boroughs|London boroughs]] or otherwise state-funded; leading examples include [[Ashbourne_College|Ashbourne College]], [[Bethnal_Green_Academy|Bethnal Green Academy]], [[Brampton_Manor_Academy|Brampton Manor Academy]], [[City_and_Islington_College|City and Islington College]], [[City_of_Westminster_College|City of Westminster College]], [[David_Game_College|David Game College]], Ealing, Hammersmith and West London College, [[Leyton_Sixth_Form_College|Leyton Sixth Form College]], [[London_Academy_of_Excellence|London Academy of Excellence]], Tower Hamlets College, and [[Newham_Collegiate_Sixth_Form_Centre|Newham Collegiate Sixth Form Centre]].
sentence_496: There are also a number of private schools and colleges in London, some old and famous, such as [[City_of_London_School|City of London School]], [[Harrow_School|Harrow]], [[St_Paul's_School_(London)|St Paul's School]], Haberdashers' Aske's Boys' School, University College School, The John Lyon School, [[Highgate_School|Highgate School]] and [[Westminster_School|Westminster School]].
sentence_497: Main article: Culture of London
sentence_498: See also: [[List_of_annual_events_in_London|List of annual events in London]] and [[West_End_theatre|West End theatre]]
sentence_499: Leisure is a major part of the London economy, with a 2003 report attributing a quarter of the entire UK leisure economy to London at 25.6 events per 1000 people.
sentence_500: Globally the city is amongst the big four [[Fashion_capital|fashion capitals]] of the world, and according to official statistics, London is the world's third-busiest film production centre, presents more live comedy than any other city, and has the biggest theatre audience of any city in the world.
sentence_501: Within the [[City_of_Westminster|City of Westminster]] in London, the entertainment district of the West End has its focus around [[Leicester_Square|Leicester Square]], where London and world film [[Premiere|premieres]] are held, and [[Piccadilly_Circus|Piccadilly Circus]], with its giant electronic advertisements.
sentence_502: London's [[West_End_theatre|theatre district]] is here, as are many cinemas, bars, clubs, and restaurants, including the city's [[Chinatown,_London|Chinatown]] district (in [[Soho|Soho]]), and just to the east is [[Royal_Opera_House|Covent Garden]], an area housing speciality shops.
sentence_503: The city is the home of [[Andrew_Lloyd_Webber|Andrew Lloyd Webber]], whose musicals have dominated the West End theatre since the late 20th century.
sentence_504: The United Kingdom's [[Royal_Ballet|Royal Ballet]], [[English_National_Ballet|English National Ballet]], [[Royal_Opera,_London|Royal Opera]], and [[English_National_Opera|English National Opera]] are based in London and perform at the [[Royal_Opera_House|Royal Opera House]], the [[London_Coliseum|London Coliseum]], Sadler's Wells Theatre, and the [[Royal_Albert_Hall|Royal Albert Hall]], as well as touring the country.
sentence_505: [[Islington|Islington]]'s 1 mile (1.6 km) long Upper Street, extending northwards from [[Angel,_London|Angel]], has more bars and restaurants than any other street in the United Kingdom.
sentence_506: Europe's busiest shopping area is [[Oxford_Street|Oxford Street]], a shopping street nearly 1 mile (1.6 km) long, making it the longest shopping street in the UK.
sentence_507: Oxford Street is home to vast numbers of retailers and [[Department_stores|department stores]], including the world-famous [[Selfridges|Selfridges]] [[Flagship_store#Retailing|flagship store]].
sentence_508: [[Knightsbridge|Knightsbridge]], home to the equally renowned [[Harrods|Harrods]] [[Department_store|department store]], lies to the south-west.
sentence_509: London is home to designers [[Vivienne_Westwood|Vivienne Westwood]], [[John_Galliano|Galliano]], [[Stella_McCartney|Stella McCartney]], [[Manolo_Blahnik|Manolo Blahnik]], and Jimmy Choo, among others; its renowned art and fashion schools make it an international centre of fashion alongside Paris, [[Milan|Milan]], and New York City.
sentence_510: London offers a great variety of cuisine as a result of its ethnically diverse population.
sentence_511: Gastronomic centres include the Bangladeshi restaurants of [[Brick_Lane|Brick Lane]] and the [[Chinese_food|Chinese]] restaurants of [[Chinatown,_London|Chinatown]].
sentence_512: There is a variety of [[List_of_annual_events_in_London|annual events]], beginning with the relatively new [[New_Year's_Day_Parade|New Year's Day Parade]], a fireworks display at the [[London_Eye|London Eye]]; the world's second largest [[Street_party|street party]], the [[Notting_Hill_Carnival|Notting Hill Carnival]], is held on the late [[August_Bank_Holiday|August Bank Holiday]] each year.
sentence_513: Traditional parades include November's [[Lord_Mayor's_Show|Lord Mayor's Show]], a centuries-old event celebrating the annual appointment of a new [[Lord_Mayor_of_the_City_of_London|Lord Mayor of the City of London]] with a procession along the streets of the city, and June's Trooping the Colour, a formal military pageant performed by regiments of the [[Commonwealth_of_Nations|Commonwealth]] and [[British_Army|British]] armies to celebrate the [[Queen's_Official_Birthday|Queen's Official Birthday]].
sentence_514: The [[Boishakhi_Mela|Boishakhi Mela]] is a [[Bengali_New_Year|Bengali New Year]] festival celebrated by the [[British_Bangladeshi|British Bangladeshi]] community.
sentence_515: It is the largest open-air Asian festival in Europe.
sentence_516: After the [[Notting_Hill_Carnival|Notting Hill Carnival]], it is the second-largest street festival in the [[United_Kingdom|United Kingdom]] attracting over 80,000 visitors from across the country.
sentence_517: Main articles: London in fiction, London in film, [[List_of_television_shows_set_in_London|List of television shows set in London]], and [[London_Television_Archive|London Television Archive]]
sentence_518: London has been the setting for many works of literature.
sentence_519: The pilgrims in [[Geoffrey_Chaucer|Geoffrey Chaucer]]'s late 14th-century [[The_Canterbury_Tales|Canterbury Tales]] set out for [[Canterbury|Canterbury]] from London – specifically, from the [[The_Tabard|Tabard]] inn, Southwark.
sentence_520: [[William_Shakespeare|William Shakespeare]] spent a large part of his life living and working in London; his contemporary [[Ben_Jonson|Ben Jonson]] was also based there, and some of his work, most notably his play [[The_Alchemist_(play)|The Alchemist]], was set in the city.
sentence_521: [[A_Journal_of_the_Plague_Year|A Journal of the Plague Year]] (1722) by [[Daniel_Defoe|Daniel Defoe]] is a fictionalisation of the events of the 1665 [[Great_Plague_of_London|Great Plague]].
sentence_522: The literary centres of London have traditionally been hilly [[Hampstead|Hampstead]] and (since the early 20th century) [[Bloomsbury|Bloomsbury]].
sentence_523: Writers closely associated with the city are the diarist [[Samuel_Pepys|Samuel Pepys]], noted for his eyewitness account of the [[Great_Fire_of_London|Great Fire]]; [[Charles_Dickens|Charles Dickens]], whose representation of a foggy, snowy, grimy London of street sweepers and pickpockets has been a major influence on people's vision of early [[Victorian_era|Victorian]] London; and [[Virginia_Woolf|Virginia Woolf]], regarded as one of the foremost [[Modernist_literature|modernist]] literary figures of the 20th century.
sentence_524: Later important depictions of London from the 19th and early 20th centuries are Dickens' novels, and [[Arthur_Conan_Doyle|Arthur Conan Doyle]]'s [[Sherlock_Holmes|Sherlock Holmes]] stories.
sentence_525: Also of significance is [[Letitia_Elizabeth_Landon|Letitia Elizabeth Landon]]'s Calendar of the London Seasons (1834).
sentence_526: Modern writers pervasively influenced by the city include [[Peter_Ackroyd|Peter Ackroyd]], author of a "biography" of London, and [[Iain_Sinclair|Iain Sinclair]], who writes in the genre of [[Psychogeography|psychogeography]].
sentence_527: London has played a significant role in the film industry.
sentence_528: Major studios within or bordering London include [[Twickenham_Film_Studios|Twickenham]], [[Ealing_Studios|Ealing]], [[Shepperton_Studios|Shepperton]], [[Pinewood_Studios|Pinewood]], [[Elstree_studios|Elstree and Borehamwood]], and a [[Special_effect|special effects]] and post-production community centred in [[Soho|Soho]].
sentence_529: [[Working_Title_Films|Working Title Films]] has its headquarters in London.
sentence_530: London has been the setting for films including [[Oliver_Twist_(1948_film)|Oliver Twist]] (1948), [[Scrooge_(1951_film)|Scrooge]] (1951), [[Peter_Pan_(1953_film)|Peter Pan]] (1953), [[101_Dalmatians_(1996_film)|The 101 Dalmatians]] (1961), [[My_Fair_Lady_(film)|My Fair Lady]] (1964), [[Mary_Poppins_(film)|Mary Poppins]] (1964), [[Blowup|Blowup]] (1966), [[The_Long_Good_Friday|The Long Good Friday]] (1980), [[The_Great_Mouse_Detective|The Great Mouse Detective]] (1986), [[Notting_Hill_(film)|Notting Hill]] (1999), [[Love_Actually|Love Actually]] (2003), [[V_For_Vendetta_(film)|V For Vendetta]] (2005), Sweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Street (2008) and [[The_King's_Speech|The King's Speech]] (2010).
sentence_531: Notable actors and filmmakers from London include; [[Charlie_Chaplin|Charlie Chaplin]], [[Alfred_Hitchcock|Alfred Hitchcock]], [[Michael_Caine|Michael Caine]], [[Helen_Mirren|Helen Mirren]], [[Gary_Oldman|Gary Oldman]], [[Christopher_Nolan|Christopher Nolan]], [[Jude_Law|Jude Law]], [[Benedict_Cumberbatch|Benedict Cumberbatch]], [[Tom_Hardy|Tom Hardy]], [[Keira_Knightley|Keira Knightley]] and [[Daniel_Day-Lewis|Daniel Day-Lewis]].
sentence_532: As of 2008, the [[British_Academy_Film_Awards|British Academy Film Awards]] have taken place at the [[Royal_Opera_House|Royal Opera House]].
sentence_533: London is a major centre for television production, with studios including [[BBC_Television_Centre|BBC Television Centre]], The Fountain Studios and [[The_London_Studios|The London Studios]].
sentence_534: Many television programmes have been set in London, including the popular television soap opera [[EastEnders|EastEnders]], broadcast by the BBC since 1985.
sentence_535: London is [[List_of_museums_in_London|home to many museums]], galleries, and other institutions, many of which are free of admission charges and are major [[Tourist_attraction|tourist attractions]] as well as playing a research role.
sentence_536: The first of these to be established was the [[British_Museum|British Museum]] in [[Bloomsbury|Bloomsbury]], in 1753.
sentence_537: Originally containing antiquities, natural history specimens, and the national library, the museum now has 7 million artefacts from around the globe.
sentence_538: In 1824, the [[National_Gallery|National Gallery]] was founded to house the British national collection of Western paintings; this now occupies a prominent position in [[Trafalgar_Square|Trafalgar Square]].
sentence_539: The [[British_Library|British Library]] is the [[List_of_largest_libraries|largest library in the world]], and the national library of the United Kingdom.
sentence_540: There are many other research libraries, including the [[Wellcome_Library|Wellcome Library]] and [[Dana_Library_and_Research_Centre|Dana Centre]], as well as [[Academic_library|university libraries]], including the [[British_Library_of_Political_and_Economic_Science|British Library of Political and Economic Science]] at [[London_School_of_Economics|LSE]], the [[Imperial_College_Central_Library|Central Library]] at [[Imperial_College_London|Imperial]], the [[Maughan_Library|Maughan Library]] at [[King's_College_London|King's]], and the [[Senate_House_Libraries|Senate House Libraries]] at the [[University_of_London|University of London]].
sentence_541: In the latter half of the 19th century the locale of [[South_Kensington|South Kensington]] was developed as "[[Albertopolis|Albertopolis]]", a cultural and scientific quarter.
sentence_542: Three major national museums are there: the [[Victoria_and_Albert_Museum|Victoria and Albert Museum]] (for the [[Applied_arts|applied arts]]), the [[Natural_History_Museum,_London|Natural History Museum]], and the [[London_Science_Museum|Science Museum]].
sentence_543: The [[National_Portrait_Gallery,_London|National Portrait Gallery]] was founded in 1856 to house depictions of figures from British history; its holdings now comprise the world's most extensive collection of portraits.
sentence_544: The national gallery of British art is at [[Tate_Britain|Tate Britain]], originally established as an annexe of the National Gallery in 1897.
sentence_545: The Tate Gallery, as it was formerly known, also became a major centre for modern art; in 2000, this collection moved to [[Tate_Modern|Tate Modern]], a new gallery housed in the former [[Bankside_Power_Station|Bankside Power Station]], which was built by the [[Basel|Basel]]-based architecture firm of [[Herzog_&_de_Meuron|Herzog & de Meuron]].
sentence_546: London is one of the major classical and [[Popular_music|popular music]] capitals of the world and hosts major music corporations, such as [[Universal_Music_Group|Universal Music Group International]] and [[Warner_Music_Group|Warner Music Group]], as well as countless bands, musicians and industry professionals.
sentence_547: The city is also home to many orchestras and concert halls, such as the [[Barbican_Arts_Centre|Barbican Arts Centre]] (principal base of the [[London_Symphony_Orchestra|London Symphony Orchestra]] and the [[London_Symphony_Chorus|London Symphony Chorus]]), the [[Southbank_Centre|Southbank Centre]] ([[London_Philharmonic_Orchestra|London Philharmonic Orchestra]] and the [[Philharmonia_Orchestra|Philharmonia Orchestra]]), [[Cadogan_Hall|Cadogan Hall]] ([[Royal_Philharmonic_Orchestra|Royal Philharmonic Orchestra]]) and the [[Royal_Albert_Hall|Royal Albert Hall]] ([[The_Proms|The Proms]]).
sentence_548: London's two main opera houses are the [[Royal_Opera_House|Royal Opera House]] and the [[London_Coliseum|London Coliseum]] (home to the [[English_National_Opera|English National Opera]]).
sentence_549: The UK's largest [[Pipe_organ|pipe organ]] is at the Royal Albert Hall.
sentence_550: Other significant instruments are at the cathedrals and major churches.
sentence_551: Several [[Conservatoire|conservatoires]] are within the city: [[Royal_Academy_of_Music|Royal Academy of Music]], [[Royal_College_of_Music|Royal College of Music]], [[Guildhall_School_of_Music_and_Drama|Guildhall School of Music and Drama]] and [[Trinity_College_of_Music|Trinity Laban]].
sentence_552: London has numerous venues for rock and pop concerts, including the world's busiest indoor venue, [[The_O2_Arena|The O2 Arena]] and Wembley Arena, as well as many mid-sized venues, such as [[Brixton_Academy|Brixton Academy]], the [[Hammersmith_Apollo|Hammersmith Apollo]] and the [[Shepherd's_Bush_Empire|Shepherd's Bush Empire]].
sentence_553: Several music festivals, including the [[Wireless_Festival|Wireless Festival]], South West Four, [[Lovebox_Festival|Lovebox]], and [[Hyde_Park,_London|Hyde Park]]'s [[British_Summer_Time_(concerts)|British Summer Time]] are all held in London.
sentence_554: The city is home to the original [[Hard_Rock_Cafe|Hard Rock Cafe]] and the Abbey Road Studios, where [[The_Beatles|The Beatles]] recorded many of their hits.
sentence_555: In the 1960s, 1970s and 1980s, musicians and groups like [[Elton_John|Elton John]], [[Pink_Floyd|Pink Floyd]], [[Cliff_Richard|Cliff Richard]], [[David_Bowie|David Bowie]], [[Queen_(band)|Queen]], [[The_Kinks|The Kinks]], [[The_Rolling_Stones|The Rolling Stones]], [[The_Who|The Who]], [[Eric_Clapton|Eric Clapton]], [[Led_Zeppelin|Led Zeppelin]], [[The_Small_Faces|The Small Faces]], [[Iron_Maiden|Iron Maiden]], [[Fleetwood_Mac|Fleetwood Mac]], Elvis Costello, [[Cat_Stevens|Cat Stevens]], [[The_Police|The Police]], [[The_Cure|The Cure]], [[Madness_(band)|Madness]], [[The_Jam|The Jam]], [[Ultravox|Ultravox]], [[Spandau_Ballet|Spandau Ballet]], [[Culture_Club|Culture Club]], [[Dusty_Springfield|Dusty Springfield]], [[Phil_Collins|Phil Collins]], [[Rod_Stewart|Rod Stewart]], [[Adam_Ant|Adam Ant]], [[Status_Quo_(band)|Status Quo]] and [[Sade_(band)|Sade]], derived their sound from the streets and rhythms of London.
sentence_556: London was instrumental in the development of [[Punk_music|punk music]], with figures such as the [[Sex_Pistols|Sex Pistols]], [[The_Clash|The Clash]], and [[Vivienne_Westwood|Vivienne Westwood]] all based in the city.
sentence_557: More recent artists to emerge from the London music scene include [[George_Michael|George Michael]]'s [[Wham!|Wham!
sentence_558: ]], [[Kate_Bush|Kate Bush]], [[Seal_(musician)|Seal]], the [[Pet_Shop_Boys|Pet Shop Boys]], [[Bananarama|Bananarama]], [[Siouxsie_and_the_Banshees|Siouxsie and the Banshees]], [[Bush_(band)|Bush]], the [[Spice_Girls|Spice Girls]], [[Jamiroquai|Jamiroquai]], [[Blur_(band)|Blur]], [[McFly|McFly]], [[The_Prodigy|The Prodigy]], [[Gorillaz|Gorillaz]], [[Bloc_Party|Bloc Party]], [[Mumford_&_Sons|Mumford & Sons]], [[Coldplay|Coldplay]], [[Amy_Winehouse|Amy Winehouse]], [[Adele|Adele]], [[Sam_Smith_(singer)|Sam Smith]], [[Ed_Sheeran|Ed Sheeran]], [[Paloma_Faith|Paloma Faith]], [[Ellie_Goulding|Ellie Goulding]], [[One_Direction|One Direction]] and [[Florence_and_the_Machine|Florence and the Machine]].
sentence_559: London is also a centre for urban music.
sentence_560: In particular the genres [[UK_garage|UK garage]], [[Drum_and_bass|drum and bass]], [[Dubstep|dubstep]] and [[Grime_(music)|grime]] evolved in the city from the foreign genres of [[Hip_hop|hip hop]] and [[Reggae|reggae]], alongside local [[Drum_and_bass|drum and bass]].
