sentence_561: Music station BBC Radio 1Xtra was set up to support the rise of local [[Urban_contemporary|urban contemporary]] music both in London and in the rest of the United Kingdom.
sentence_562: Main articles: [[Parks_and_open_spaces_in_London|Parks and open spaces in London]] and [[Royal_Parks_of_London|Royal Parks of London]]
sentence_563: See also: [[List_of_Sites_of_Special_Scientific_Interest_in_Greater_London|List of Sites of Special Scientific Interest in Greater London]] and [[List_of_local_nature_reserves_in_Greater_London|List of local nature reserves in Greater London]]
sentence_564: A 2013 report by the [[City_of_London_Corporation|City of London Corporation]] said that London is the "greenest city" in Europe with 35,000 acres of public parks, woodlands and gardens.
sentence_565: The largest parks in the [[Central_London|central area of London]] are three of the eight [[Royal_Parks_of_London|Royal Parks]], namely [[Hyde_Park,_London|Hyde Park]] and its neighbour [[Kensington_Gardens|Kensington Gardens]] in the west, and [[Regent's_Park|Regent's Park]] to the north.
sentence_566: Hyde Park in particular is popular for [[#Sports|sports]] and sometimes hosts open-air concerts.
sentence_567: Regent's Park contains [[London_Zoo|London Zoo]], the world's oldest scientific zoo, and is near [[Madame_Tussauds|Madame Tussauds]] Wax Museum.
sentence_568: [[Primrose_Hill|Primrose Hill]], immediately to the north of Regent's Park, at 256 feet (78 m) is a popular spot from which to view the city skyline.
sentence_569: Close to Hyde Park are smaller Royal Parks, [[Green_Park|Green Park]] and [[St._James's_Park|St.
sentence_571: A number of large parks lie outside the city centre, including [[Hampstead_Heath|Hampstead Heath]] and the remaining Royal Parks of [[Greenwich_Park|Greenwich Park]] to the southeast and [[Bushy_Park|Bushy Park]] and [[Richmond_Park|Richmond Park]] (the largest) to the southwest, [[Hampton_Court_Park|Hampton Court Park]] is also a royal park, but, because it contains a palace, it is administered by the [[Historic_Royal_Palaces|Historic Royal Palaces]], unlike the eight [[Royal_Parks_of_London|Royal Parks]].
sentence_572: Close to Richmond Park is [[Kew_Gardens|Kew Gardens]] which has the world's largest collection of living plants.
sentence_573: In 2003, the gardens were put on the [[United_Nations_Educational,_Scientific_and_Cultural_Organization|UNESCO]] list of [[List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_of_the_United_Kingdom|World Heritage Sites]].
sentence_574: There are also parks administered by London's borough Councils, including [[Victoria_Park,_London|Victoria Park]] in the [[East_End|East End]] and Battersea Park in the centre.
sentence_575: Some more informal, semi-natural open spaces also exist, including the 320-hectare (790-acre) [[Hampstead_Heath|Hampstead Heath]] of [[North_London|North London]], and [[Epping_Forest|Epping Forest]], which covers 2,476 hectares (6,118 acres) in the east.
sentence_576: Both are controlled by the [[City_of_London_Corporation|City of London Corporation]].
sentence_577: Hampstead Heath incorporates [[Kenwood_House|Kenwood House]], a former [[Stately_home|stately home]] and a popular location in the summer months when classical musical concerts are held by the lake, attracting thousands of people every weekend to enjoy the music, scenery and fireworks.
sentence_578: Epping Forest is a popular venue for various outdoor activities, including mountain biking, walking, horse riding, golf, angling, and orienteering.
sentence_579: [[Walking_in_London|Walking is a popular recreational activity in London]].
sentence_580: Areas that provide for walks include [[Wimbledon_Common|Wimbledon Common]], [[Epping_Forest|Epping Forest]], [[Hampton_Court_Park|Hampton Court Park]], [[Hampstead_Heath|Hampstead Heath]], the eight [[Royal_Parks|Royal Parks]], canals and disused railway tracks.
sentence_581: Access to canals and rivers has improved recently, including the creation of the [[Thames_Path|Thames Path]], some 28 miles (45 km) of which is within [[Greater_London|Greater London]], and The Wandle Trail; this runs 12 miles (19 km) through [[South_London|South London]] along the [[River_Wandle|River Wandle]], a [[Tributaries_of_the_River_Thames|tributary of the River Thames]].
sentence_582: Other long distance paths, linking green spaces, have also been created, including the [[Capital_Ring|Capital Ring]], the [[Green_Chain_Walk|Green Chain Walk]], [[London_Outer_Orbital_Path|London Outer Orbital Path]] ("Loop"), [[Jubilee_Walkway|Jubilee Walkway]], [[Lea_Valley_Walk|Lea Valley Walk]], and the [[Diana,_Princess_of_Wales_Memorial_Walk|Diana, Princess of Wales Memorial Walk]].
sentence_584: London has hosted the [[Summer_Olympic_Games|Summer Olympics]] three times: in [[1908_Summer_Olympics|1908]], [[1948_Summer_Olympics|1948]], and [[2012_Summer_Olympics|2012]], making it the first city to host the modern Games three times.
sentence_585: The city was also the host of the [[Commonwealth_Games|British Empire Games]] in [[1934_British_Empire_Games|1934]].
sentence_586: In 2017, London hosted the [[2017_World_Championships_in_Athletics|World Championships in Athletics]] for the first time.
sentence_587: London's [[Sport_in_the_United_Kingdom#Popularity|most popular sport]] is [[Association_football|football]] and it has six clubs in the English [[Premier_League|Premier League]] as of the [[2020–21_Premier_League|2020–21 season]]: [[Arsenal_F.C.|Arsenal]], [[Chelsea_F.C.|Chelsea]], [[Crystal_Palace_F.C.|Crystal Palace]], [[Fulham_F.C.|Fulham]], [[Tottenham_Hotspur_F.C.|Tottenham Hotspur]], and [[West_Ham_United_F.C.|West Ham United]].
sentence_588: Other professional teams in London are [[Queens_Park_Rangers_F.C.|Queens Park Rangers]], [[Brentford_F.C.|Brentford]], [[Millwall_F.C.|Millwall]], [[Charlton_Athletic_F.C.|Charlton Athletic]], [[AFC_Wimbledon|AFC Wimbledon]], [[Leyton_Orient_F.C.|Leyton Orient]], [[Barnet_F.C.|Barnet]], [[Sutton_United_F.C.|Sutton United]], [[Bromley_F.C.|Bromley]] and [[Dagenham_&_Redbridge_F.C.|Dagenham & Redbridge]].
sentence_589: From 1924, the original [[Wembley_Stadium_(1923)|Wembley Stadium]] was the home of the [[England_national_football_team|English national football team]].
sentence_590: It hosted the [[1966_FIFA_World_Cup_Final|1966 FIFA World Cup Final]], with England defeating West Germany, and served as the venue for the [[FA_Cup_Final|FA Cup Final]] as well as [[Rugby_league|rugby league]]'s [[Challenge_Cup|Challenge Cup]] final.
sentence_591: The new [[Wembley_Stadium|Wembley Stadium]] serves exactly the same purposes and has a capacity of 90,000.
sentence_592: Two [[English_Premiership_(rugby_union)|Aviva Premiership]] rugby union teams are based in London, [[Saracens_F.C.|Saracens]] and [[Harlequin_F.C.|Harlequins]].
sentence_593: [[London_Scottish_F.C.|London Scottish]], [[London_Welsh|London Welsh]] and [[London_Irish|London Irish]] play in the [[RFU_Championship|RFU Championship]] club and other rugby union clubs in the city include Richmond F.C., Rosslyn Park F.C., Westcombe Park R.F.C.
sentence_595: [[Twickenham_Stadium|Twickenham Stadium]] in south-west London hosts home matches for the [[England_national_rugby_union_team|England national rugby union team]] and has a capacity of 82,000 now that the new south stand has been completed.
sentence_596: While [[Rugby_league|rugby league]] is more popular in the north of England, there are two professional rugby league clubs in London – the London Broncos in the second-tier [[RFL_Championship|RFL Championship]], who play at the [[Trailfinders_Sports_Ground|Trailfinders Sports Ground]] in [[West_Ealing|West Ealing]], and the third-tier [[League_1_(rugby_league)|League 1]] team, the [[London_Skolars|London Skolars]] from [[Wood_Green|Wood Green]], [[London_Borough_of_Haringey|Haringey]].
sentence_597: One of London's best-known annual sports competitions is the [[Wimbledon_Championships|Wimbledon Tennis Championships]], held at the [[All_England_Lawn_Tennis_and_Croquet_Club|All England Club]] in the south-western suburb of [[Wimbledon,_London|Wimbledon]].
sentence_598: Played in late June to early July, it is the oldest tennis tournament in the world, and widely considered the most prestigious.
sentence_599: London has two [[Test_cricket|Test cricket]] grounds, [[Lord's|Lord's]] (home of Middlesex C.C.C.)
sentence_600: in [[St_John's_Wood|St John's Wood]] and [[The_Oval|the Oval]] (home of [[Surrey_County_Cricket_Club|Surrey C.C.C.]])
sentence_602: Lord's has hosted four finals of the [[Cricket_World_Cup|Cricket World Cup]], and is known as the Home of Cricket.
sentence_603: Other key events are the annual mass-participation [[London_Marathon|London Marathon]], in which some 35,000 runners attempt a 26.2 miles (42.2 km) course around the city, and the [[University_Boat_Race|University Boat Race]] on the [[River_Thames|River Thames]] from [[Putney|Putney]] to [[Mortlake|Mortlake]].
sentence_604: Main article: [[List_of_people_from_London|List of people from London]]

title: Lacrosse
sentence_0: This article is about the team sport.
sentence_1: For other uses, see [[Lacrosse_(disambiguation)|Lacrosse (disambiguation)]].

sentence_2: Lacrosse is a [[Team_sport|team sport]] played with a [[Lacrosse_stick|lacrosse stick]] and a [[Lacrosse_ball|lacrosse ball]].
sentence_3: It is the oldest organized sport in [[North_America|North America]], with its origins in a tribal game played by the [[Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Eastern_Woodlands|indigenous peoples of the Eastern Woodlands]] and by various other [[Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas#North_America|indigenous peoples of North America]].
sentence_4: The game was extensively modified reducing the violence by European colonizers to create its current collegiate and professional form.
sentence_5: Players use the head of the lacrosse stick to carry, pass, catch, and shoot the ball into the goal.
sentence_6: The sport has four versions that have different sticks, fields, rules and equipment: [[Field_lacrosse|field lacrosse]], [[Women's_lacrosse|women's lacrosse]], [[Box_lacrosse|box lacrosse]] and [[Intercrosse|intercrosse]].
sentence_7: The men's games, field lacrosse (outdoor) and box lacrosse (indoor), are contact sports and all players wear protective gear: [[Lacrosse_helmet|helmet]], [[Lacrosse_glove|gloves]], shoulder pads, and elbow pads.
sentence_8: The women's game is played outdoors and does not allow body contact but does allow stick to stick contact.
sentence_9: The only protective gear required for women players is eyegear, while goalies wear helmets and protective pads.
sentence_10: Intercrosse is a mixed-gender non-contact sport played indoors that uses an all-plastic stick and a softer ball.
sentence_11: The modern sport is governed by [[World_Lacrosse|World Lacrosse]] and is the only international sport organization to recognize [[First_Nations|First Nations]] bands and [[Native_Americans_in_the_United_States|Native American]] tribes as sovereign nations.
sentence_12: The organization hosts the [[World_Lacrosse_Championship|World Lacrosse Championship]] for men, the Women's Lacrosse World Cup, the [[World_Indoor_Lacrosse_Championship|World Indoor Lacrosse Championship]] for box lacrosse, and the [[Under-19_World_Lacrosse_Championships|Under-19 World Lacrosse Championships]] for both men and women.
sentence_13: Each is held every four years.
sentence_14: [[Lacrosse_at_the_Summer_Olympics|Lacrosse at the Summer Olympics]] has been contested at two editions of the [[Summer_Olympic_Games|Summer Olympic Games]], [[Lacrosse_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics|1904]] and [[Lacrosse_at_the_1908_Summer_Olympics|1908]].
sentence_15: It was also held as a demonstration event at the [[Lacrosse_at_the_1928_Summer_Olympics|1928]], [[Lacrosse_at_the_1932_Summer_Olympics|1932]], and [[Lacrosse_at_the_1948_Summer_Olympics|1948]] Summer Olympics.
sentence_16: Main article: [[History_of_lacrosse|History of lacrosse]]
sentence_17: Further information: [[Lacrosse_in_Canada|Lacrosse in Canada]] and [[Lacrosse_in_the_United_States|Lacrosse in the United States]]
sentence_18: Lacrosse is based on games played by various [[Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas|Native American]] communities as early as 1100 AD.
sentence_19: By the 17th century, a version of lacrosse was well-established and was documented by [[Jesuit|Jesuit]] [[Missionary|missionary]] priests in the territory of present-day Canada.
sentence_20: In the traditional [[Aboriginal_peoples_in_Canada|aboriginal Canadian]] version, each team consisted of about 100 to 1,000 men on a field several miles (several kilometers) long.
sentence_21: These games lasted from sunup to sundown for two to three days straight and were played as part of ceremonial ritual, a kind of symbolic warfare, or to give thanks to the Creator or Master.
sentence_22: Lacrosse played a significant role in the community and religious life of tribes across the continent for many years.
sentence_23: Early lacrosse was characterized by deep spiritual involvement, befitting the spirit of combat in which it was undertaken.
sentence_24: Those who took part did so in the role of [[Warriors|warriors]], with the goal of bringing glory and honor to themselves and their tribes.
sentence_25: The game was said to be played "for the Creator" or was referred to as "The Creator's Game."
sentence_26: The French [[Jesuit_missions_in_North_America|Jesuit]] missionary [[Jean_de_Brébeuf|Jean de Brébeuf]] saw [[Wyandot_people|Huron]] tribesmen play the game during 1637 in present-day [[Ontario|Ontario]].
sentence_27: He called it la crosse, "the stick" in French.
sentence_28: The name seems to be originated from the French term for [[Field_hockey|field hockey]], le jeu de la crosse.
sentence_29: [[James_Smith_(frontiersman)|James Smith]] described in some detail a game being played in 1757 by Mohawk people "wherein now they used a wooden ball, about 3 inches (7.6 cm) in diameter, and the instrument they moved it with was a strong staff about 5 feet (1.5 m) long, with a hoop net on the end of it, large enough to contain the ball."
sentence_30: Anglophones from Montreal noticed the game being played by Mohawk people and started playing themselves in the 1830s.
sentence_31: In 1856, [[William_George_Beers|William George Beers]], a Canadian dentist, founded the [[Montreal_Lacrosse_Club|Montreal Lacrosse Club]].
sentence_32: In 1860, Beers codified the game, shortening the length of each game and reducing the number of players to 12 per team.
sentence_33: The first game played under Beers's rules was at [[Upper_Canada_College|Upper Canada College]] in 1867; they lost to the Toronto Cricket Club by a score of 3–1.
sentence_34: The new sport proved to be very popular and spread across the English-speaking world; [[List_of_the_oldest_lacrosse_teams|by 1900 there were dozens of men's clubs]] in Canada, the United States, England, Australia, and New Zealand.
sentence_35: The [[Women's_lacrosse#History|women's game was introduced]] by [[Louisa_Lumsden|Louisa Lumsden]] in Scotland in 1890.
sentence_36: The first women's club in the United States was started by [[Rosabelle_Sinclair|Rosabelle Sinclair]] at [[Bryn_Mawr_School|Bryn Mawr School]] in 1926.
sentence_37: In the United States, lacrosse during the late 1800s and first half of the 1900s was primarily a regional sport centered around the [[Mid-Atlantic_states|Mid-Atlantic states]], especially [[New_York_(state)|New York]] and [[Maryland|Maryland]].
sentence_38: However, in the last half of the 20th century, the sport spread outside this region, and can be currently found in most of the United States.
sentence_39: According to a survey conducted by [[US_Lacrosse|US Lacrosse]] in 2016, there are over 825,000 lacrosse participants nationwide and lacrosse is the fastest-growing team sport among NFHS member schools.
sentence_40: Main article: [[Field_lacrosse|Field lacrosse]]
sentence_41: Field lacrosse is the men's outdoor version of the sport.
sentence_42: There are ten players on each team: three attackmen, three midfielders, three defensemen, and one [[Goaltender_(field_lacrosse)|goalie]].
sentence_43: Each player carries a [[Lacrosse_stick|lacrosse stick]].
sentence_44: A short stick measures between 40 and 42 inches (100 and 110 cm) long and is used by attackmen and midfielders.
sentence_45: A maximum of four players on the field per team may carry a long stick which is between 52 and 72 inches (130 and 180 cm) long and is used by the three defensemen and sometimes one defensive midfielder.
sentence_46: The goalie uses a stick with a head as wide as 12 inches (30 cm) that can be between 40 and 72 inches (100 and 180 cm) long.
sentence_47: The field of play is 110 by 60 yards (101 by 55 m).
sentence_48: The goals are 6 by 6 ft (1.8 by 1.8 m) and are 80 yd (73 m) apart.
sentence_49: Each goal sits inside a circular "crease", measuring 18 ft (5.5 m) in diameter.
sentence_50: The goalie has special privileges within the crease to avoid opponents' stick checks.
sentence_51: Offensive players or their sticks may not enter into the crease at any time.
sentence_52: The mid-field line separates the field into an offensive and defensive zone for each team.
sentence_53: Each team must keep four players in its defensive zone and three players in its offensive zone at all times.
sentence_54: It does not matter which positional players satisfy the requirement, although usually the three attackmen stay in the offensive zone, the three defensemen and the goalie stay in the defensive zone, and the three middies play in both zones.
sentence_55: A team that violates this rule is offsides and either loses possession of the ball if they have it or incurs a technical foul if they do not.
sentence_56: The regulation playing time of a game is 60 minutes, divided into four periods of 15 minutes each.
sentence_57: Play is started at the beginning of each quarter and after each goal with a [[Face-off#Field_lacrosse|face-off]].
sentence_58: During a face-off, two players lay their sticks on the ground parallel to the mid-line, the two heads of their sticks on opposite sides of the ball.
sentence_59: At the whistle, the face-off-men scrap for the ball, often by "clamping" it under their stick and flicking it out to their teammates.
sentence_60: When one of the teams has possession of the ball, they bring it into their offensive zone and try to score a goal.
sentence_61: Due to the offsides rule, settled play involves six offensive players versus six defensive players and a goalie.
sentence_62: If the ball goes out of bounds, possession is awarded against the team that touched it last.
sentence_63: The exception is when the ball is shot towards the goal.
sentence_64: Missed shots that go out of bounds are awarded to the team that has the player who is the closest to the ball when and where the ball goes out.
sentence_65: During play, teams may substitute players in and out if they leave and enter the field through the substitution area, sometimes referred to as "on the fly".
sentence_66: After penalties and goals, players may freely substitute and do not have to go through the substitution area.
sentence_67: Penalties are awarded for rule violations and result in the offending team losing possession (loss of possession) or temporarily losing a player (time serving).
sentence_68: During time serving penalties, the penalized team plays with one fewer player for the duration of the penalty.
sentence_69: Time serving penalties are either releasable or non-releasable.
sentence_70: When serving a releasable penalty, the offending player may re-enter play if a goal is scored by the opposing team during the duration of the penalty.
sentence_71: Non-releasable penalties do not allow this and the player must serve the entire duration.
sentence_72: In conjunction with the offsides rule, the opponent may play with six attackers versus the penalized team's five defenders and goalie.
sentence_73: The team that has taken the penalty is said to be playing man down, while the other team is [[Power_play_(sporting_term)#Lacrosse|man up]].
sentence_74: Teams will use various lacrosse strategies to attack and defend while a player is being penalized.
sentence_75: There are two classes of rule violations that result in penalties: technical fouls and personal fouls.
sentence_76: Technical fouls, such as offsides, pushing, and holding, result in either a loss of possession or a 30-second penalty, depending on which team has the ball.
sentence_77: Personal fouls, such as cross-checking, illegal body checking, or slashing, concern actions that endanger player safety.
sentence_78: Cross-checking is when a player strikes another player with the shaft of the stick between his hands.
sentence_79: A slash is when a player strikes another player with the end of the stick anywhere besides the gloves.
sentence_80: These fouls draw 1-minute or longer penalties; the offending player must leave the field.
sentence_81: Main article: [[Box_lacrosse|Box lacrosse]]
sentence_82: Box lacrosse is played by teams of five runners plus a goalie on a [[Ice_hockey_rink|hockey rink]] where the ice has been removed or covered by artificial turf, or in an indoor soccer field.
sentence_83: The enclosed playing area is called a box, in contrast to the open playing field of the traditional game.
sentence_84: This version of the game was introduced in Canada in the 1930s to promote business for hockey arenas outside of the ice hockey season.
sentence_85: Within several years it had nearly supplanted field lacrosse in Canada.
sentence_86: The goals in box lacrosse are smaller than field lacrosse, traditionally 4 ft (1.2 m) wide and tall.
sentence_87: Also, the [[Goaltender_(box_lacrosse)|goaltender]] wears much more protective padding, including a massive chest protector and armguard combination known as "uppers", large shin guards known as leg pads (both of which must follow strict measurement guidelines), and ice hockey-style goalie masks.
sentence_88: The style of the game is quick, accelerated by the close confines of the floor and a [[Shot_clock|shot clock]].
sentence_89: The shot clock requires the attacking team to take a shot on goal within 30 seconds of gaining possession of the ball.
sentence_90: Box lacrosse is also a much more physical game.
sentence_91: Since cross checking is legal in box lacrosse, players wear rib pads and the shoulder and elbow pads are bigger and stronger than what field lacrosse players wear.
sentence_92: Box lacrosse players wear a hockey helmet with a box lacrosse cage.
sentence_93: There is no offsides in box lacrosse, the players substitute freely from their bench areas as in hockey.
sentence_94: However, most players specialize in offense or defense, so usually all five runners substitute for teammates as their team transitions between offense and defense.
sentence_95: For penalties, the offending player is sent to the [[Penalty_box|penalty box]] and his team has to play without him, or man-down, for the length of the penalty.
sentence_96: Most fouls are minor penalties and last for two minutes, major penalties for serious offenses last five minutes.
sentence_97: What separates box lacrosse (and ice hockey) from other sports is that at the top levels of professional and junior lacrosse, participating in a fight does not automatically cause an ejection, but a five-minute major penalty is given.
sentence_98: Box lacrosse is played at the highest level in the National Lacrosse League and by the Senior A divisions of the [[Canadian_Lacrosse_Association|Canadian Lacrosse Association]].
sentence_99: The National Lacrosse League (NLL) employs some minor rule changes from the Canadian Lacrosse Association (CLA) rules.
sentence_100: Notably, the goals are 4 feet 9 inches (1.45 m) wide instead of 4 feet (1.2 m) and the games are played during the winter.
sentence_101: The NLL games consist of four fifteen-minute quarters compared with three periods of twenty minutes each in CLA games.
sentence_102: NLL players may only use sticks with hollow shafts, while CLA permits solid wooden sticks.
sentence_103: Main article: [[Women's_lacrosse|Women's lacrosse]]
sentence_104: The rules of women's lacrosse differ significantly from men's lacrosse, most notably by equipment and the degree of allowable physical contact.
sentence_105: Women's lacrosse rules also differ significantly between the US and all other countries, who play by the Federation of International Lacrosse (FIL) rules.
sentence_106: Women's lacrosse does not allow physical contact, the only protective equipment worn is a mouth guard and eye-guard.
sentence_107: In the early part of the 21st century, there have been discussions of requiring headgear to prevent concussions.
sentence_108: In 2008, Florida was the first state to mandate headgear in women's lacrosse.
sentence_109: Stick checking is permitted in the women's game, but only in certain levels of play and within strict rules.
sentence_110: Women's lacrosse also does not allow players to have a pocket, or loose net, on the lacrosse stick.
sentence_111: Women start the game with a "draw" instead of a face-off.
sentence_112: The two players stand up and the ball is placed between their stick heads while their sticks are horizontal at waist-height.
sentence_113: At the whistle, the players lift their sticks into the air, trying to control where the ball goes.
sentence_114: The first modern women's lacrosse game was held at [[St_Leonards_School|St Leonards School]] in Scotland in 1890.
sentence_115: It was introduced by the school's headmistress [[Louisa_Lumsden|Louisa Lumsden]] after a visit to [[Quebec|Quebec]], where she saw it played.
sentence_116: The first women's lacrosse team in the United States was established at [[Bryn_Mawr_School|Bryn Mawr School]] in [[Baltimore,_Maryland|Baltimore, Maryland]] in 1926.
sentence_117: Both the number of players and the lines on the field differ from men's lacrosse.
sentence_118: There are 12 players in women's lacrosse and players must abide by certain boundaries that do not exist in men's play.
sentence_119: The three specific boundaries are the 8-meter (26 ft 3 in) "fan" in front of the goal (11 m [36 ft 1 in] internationally), the 12-meter (39 ft 4 in) (8 m [26 ft 3 in] internationally) half circle that surrounds the 8-meter fan, and the draw circle in the center of the field, which is used for draws to start quarters and after goals.
sentence_120: The goal circle is also positioned slightly closer to the end line in women's lacrosse compared to men's.
sentence_121: In women's lacrosse on either the offensive or defensive end, the players besides the goaltender are not able to step inside the goal circle; this becomes a "goal-circle violation".
sentence_122: However, at the women's collegiate level, a new rule has been established that allows defenders to pass through the goal circle.
sentence_123: The 8-meter fan that is in front of the goal circle has a few restrictions in it.
sentence_124: Defenders cannot stand inside the 8-meter fan longer than 3 seconds without being a stick-length away from the offensive player they are guarding.
sentence_125: This is very similar to the [[Three-second_rule|three-second rule]] in basketball.
sentence_126: A three seconds violation results in a player from the other team taking a free shot against the goalie.
sentence_127: If you are an attacker trying to shoot the ball into the goal, you are not supposed to take a shot while a defender is in "shooting space."
sentence_128: To make sure that you, the defender, are being safe, you want to lead with your [[Lacrosse_stick|lacrosse stick]] and once you are a sticks-length away, you can be in front of her.
sentence_129: Main article: [[Intercrosse|Intercrosse]]
sentence_130: Intercrosse, or soft stick lacrosse, is a non-contact form of lacrosse with a standardized set of rules using modified lacrosse equipment.
sentence_131: An intercrosse stick is different from a normal lacrosse stick, the head is made completely of plastic instead of leather or nylon pockets in traditional lacrosse sticks.
sentence_132: The ball is larger, softer and hollow, unlike a lacrosse ball, which is solid rubber.
sentence_133: Intercrosse is a competitive adult sport is popular in Quebec, Canada, as well as in many European countries, particularly in the Czech Republic.
sentence_134: Generally, teams consist of five players per side, and the field size is 20 m (66 ft) wide and 40 m (130 ft) long.
sentence_135: Goals for adults are the same size as [[Box_lacrosse|box lacrosse]], 4 ft or 1.2 m in height and width.
sentence_136: The international governing body, the Fédération Internationale d'Inter-Crosse, hosts a [[FIIC_Intercrosse_World_Championship|World Championship]] bi-annually.
sentence_137: Soft stick lacrosse is a popular way to introduce youth to the sport.
sentence_138: It can be played outdoors or indoors and has a developed curriculum for [[Physical_education|physical education]] classes.
sentence_139: Further information: [[List_of_national_lacrosse_organizations|List of national lacrosse organizations]]
sentence_140: Lacrosse has historically been played for the most part in [[Lacrosse_in_Canada|Canada]] and the [[Lacrosse_in_the_United_States|United States]], with small but dedicated lacrosse communities in the [[Lacrosse_in_England|United]] [[Lacrosse_in_Scotland|Kingdom]] and [[Lacrosse_in_Australia|Australia]].
sentence_141: Recently, however, lacrosse has begun to flourish at the international level, with teams being established around the world, particularly in Europe and East Asia.
sentence_142: Main article: [[World_Lacrosse|World Lacrosse]]
sentence_143: In August 2008, the men's international governing body, the International Lacrosse Federation, merged with the women's, the International Federation of Women's Lacrosse Associations, to form the Federation of International Lacrosse (FIL).
sentence_144: The FIL changed its name to World Lacrosse in May 2019.
sentence_145: There are currently 62 member nations of World Lacrosse.
sentence_146: World Lacrosse sponsors five world championship tournaments: the [[World_Lacrosse_Championship|World Lacrosse Championship]] for men's field, the Women's Lacrosse World Cup for women's, the [[World_Indoor_Lacrosse_Championship|World Indoor Lacrosse Championship]] for box lacrosse, and the [[Under-19_World_Lacrosse_Championships|Under-19 World Lacrosse Championships]] for men and women.
sentence_147: Each is held every four years.
sentence_148: The World Lacrosse Championship (WLC) began in 1968 as a four-team invitational tournament sponsored by the International Lacrosse Federation.
sentence_149: Until 1990, only the United States, Canada, England, and Australia had entered.
sentence_150: With the expansion of the game internationally, the [[2014_World_Lacrosse_Championship|2014 World Lacrosse Championship]] was contested by 38 countries.
sentence_151: The WLC has been dominated by the United States.
sentence_152: [[United_States_men's_national_lacrosse_team|Team USA]] has won 9 of the 12 titles, with [[Canada_men's_national_lacrosse_team|Canada]] winning the other three.
sentence_153: The Women's Lacrosse World Cup (WLWC) began in 1982.
sentence_154: The [[United_States_women's_national_lacrosse_team|United States]] has won 8 of the 10 titles, with [[Australia_women's_national_lacrosse_team|Australia]] winning the other two.
sentence_155: Canada and [[England_women's_national_lacrosse_team|England]] have always finished in the top five.
sentence_156: The 2017 tournament was held in England and featured 25 countries.
sentence_157: The first World Indoor Lacrosse Championship (WILC) was held in 2003 and contested by six nations at four sites in [[Ontario|Ontario]].
sentence_158: [[Canada_national_indoor_lacrosse_team|Canada]] won the championship by beating the [[Iroquois_men's_national_lacrosse_team|Iroquois Nationals]] 21–4 in the final.
sentence_159: The [[2015_World_Indoor_Lacrosse_Championship|2007 championship]] hosted by the [[Onondaga_Nation|Onondaga Nation]] included 13 teams.
sentence_160: Canada has dominated the competition, winning all four gold medals and never losing a game.
sentence_161: The [[Iroquois_men's_national_lacrosse_team|Iroquois Nationals]] are the men's national team representing the Six Nations of the [[Iroquois_Confederacy|Iroquois Confederacy]] in international field lacrosse competition.
sentence_162: The team was admitted to the FIL in 1987.
sentence_163: It is the only [[Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas|First Nations]] team sanctioned for international competition in any sport.
sentence_164: The Nationals placed fourth in the 1998, 2002 and 2006 World Lacrosse Championships and third in 2014.
sentence_165: The [[Iroquois_national_indoor_lacrosse_team|indoor team]] won the silver medal in all four World Indoor Lacrosse Championships.
sentence_166: In 2008, the Iroquois women's team was admitted to the FIL as the [[Haudenosaunee_women's_national_lacrosse_team|Haudenosaunee Nationals]].
sentence_167: They placed 7th at the [[2013_Women's_Lacrosse_World_Cup|2013 Women's Lacrosse World Cup]].
sentence_168: Main article: [[Lacrosse_at_the_Summer_Olympics|Lacrosse at the Summer Olympics]]
sentence_169: Field lacrosse was a medal [[Olympic_Sport|sport]] in the [[Lacrosse_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics|1904]] and the [[Lacrosse_at_the_1908_Summer_Olympics|1908]] Summer Olympics.
sentence_170: In 1904, three teams competed in the games held in [[St._Louis|St.
sentence_171: Louis]].
sentence_172: Two Canadian teams, the Winnipeg Shamrocks and a team of Mohawk people from the [[Iroquois_Confederacy|Iroquois Confederacy]], plus the local St. Louis Amateur Athletic Association team representing the United States participated.
sentence_173: The Winnipeg Shamrocks captured the gold medal.
sentence_174: The 1908 games held in [[London|London]], England, featured only two teams, representing Canada and Great Britain.
sentence_175: The Canadians again won the gold medal in a single championship match by a score of 14–10.
sentence_176: In the [[Lacrosse_at_the_1928_Summer_Olympics|1928]], [[Lacrosse_at_the_1932_Summer_Olympics|1932]], and the [[Lacrosse_at_the_1948_Summer_Olympics|1948]] Summer Olympics, lacrosse was a [[Demonstration_sport|demonstration sport]].
sentence_177: The 1928 Olympics in Amsterdam featured three teams: the United States, Canada, and Great Britain.
sentence_178: The 1932 games in Los Angeles featured a three-game exhibition between a Canadian all-star team and the United States.
sentence_179: The United States was represented by [[Johns_Hopkins_Blue_Jays_men's_lacrosse|Johns Hopkins]] in both the 1928 and 1932 Olympics.
sentence_180: The 1948 games featured an exhibition by an "All-England" team organized by the English Lacrosse Union and the collegiate lacrosse team from [[Rensselaer_Polytechnic_Institute|Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute]] representing the United States.
sentence_181: This exhibition match ended in a 5–5 tie.
sentence_182: Efforts were made to include lacrosse as an exhibition sport at the [[1996_Summer_Olympics|1996 Summer Olympics]] in [[Atlanta|Atlanta, Georgia]] and the [[2000_Summer_Olympics|2000 Summer Olympics]] in [[Sydney|Sydney, Australia]], but they were not successful.
sentence_183: An obstacle for lacrosse to return to the Olympics is insufficient international participation.
sentence_184: To be considered for the Olympics, a sport must be played on four continents and by at least 75 countries.
sentence_185: Lacrosse is played on all six continents, but as of August 2019 when Ghana joined, there are only 63 countries playing the sport.
sentence_186: The [[European_Lacrosse_Federation|European Lacrosse Federation]] (ELF) was established in 1995 and held the first [[European_Lacrosse_Championships|European Lacrosse Championships]] that year.
sentence_187: Originally an annual event, it is now held every four years, in between FIL's men's and women's championships.
sentence_188: In 2004, 12 men's and 6 women's teams played in the tournament, making it the largest international lacrosse event of the year.
sentence_189: The last men's tournament was in [[2016_European_Lacrosse_Championship|2016]], when 24 countries participated.
sentence_190: England won its ninth gold medal out of the ten tournaments played.
sentence_191: [[2015_Women's_Lacrosse_European_Championship|2015]] was the last women's tournament, when 17 teams participated in the Czech Republic.
sentence_192: England won its sixth gold medal, with Wales earning silver and Scotland bronze.
sentence_193: These three countries from Great Britain have dominated the women's championships, earning all but three medals since the tournament began in 1996.
sentence_194: There are currently 29 members of the ELF, they make up the majority of nations in the FIL.
sentence_195: The Asia Pacific Lacrosse Union was founded in 2004 by Australia, Hong Kong, South Korea and Japan.
sentence_196: It currently has 12 members and holds the Asia Pacific Championship for both men's and women's teams every two years.
sentence_197: Lacrosse was played in the [[World_Games|World Games]] for the first time at the [[2017_World_Games|2017 World Games]] held in Poland.
sentence_198: Only women's teams took part in the competition.
sentence_199: The United States won the gold medal defeating Canada in the finals.
sentence_200: Australia won the bronze medal match.
sentence_201: The [[Haudenosaunee_Nationals_women's_lacrosse_team|Haudenosaunee Nationals women's lacrosse team]] could not participate.
sentence_202: Main article: [[Lacrosse_in_the_United_States|Lacrosse in the United States]]
sentence_203: Main article: [[College_lacrosse|College lacrosse]]
sentence_204: Collegiate lacrosse in the United States is played at the [[National_Collegiate_Athletic_Association|NCAA]], [[National_Association_of_Intercollegiate_Athletics|NAIA]] and club levels.
sentence_205: There are currently 71 [[NCAA_Division_I|NCAA Division I]] men's lacrosse teams, 93 [[NCAA_Division_II|Division II]] teams, and 236 [[NCAA_Division_III|Division III]] teams.
sentence_206: Thirty-two schools participate at the NAIA level.
sentence_207: 184 men's club teams compete in the Men's Collegiate Lacrosse Association, including most universities and colleges outside the northeastern United States.
sentence_208: The [[National_College_Lacrosse_League|National College Lacrosse League]] and [[Great_Lakes_Lacrosse_League|Great Lakes Lacrosse League]] are two other lower-division club leagues.
sentence_209: In Canada, 14 teams from Ontario and Quebec play field lacrosse in the fall in the [[Canadian_University_Field_Lacrosse_Association|Canadian University Field Lacrosse Association]].
sentence_210: The first U. S. intercollegiate men's lacrosse game was played on November 22, 1877 between [[New_York_University|New York University]] and [[Manhattan_College|Manhattan College]].
sentence_211: An organizing body for the sport, the U. S. National Lacrosse Association, was founded in 1879 and the first intercollegiate lacrosse tournament was held in 1881, with [[Harvard|Harvard]] beating [[Princeton_University|Princeton]] 3–0 in the championship game.
sentence_212: Annual post-season championships were awarded by a variety of early lacrosse associations through the 1930s.
sentence_213: From 1936 to 1972, the [[United_States_Intercollegiate_Lacrosse_Association|United States Intercollegiate Lacrosse Association]] awarded the [[Wingate_Memorial_Trophy|Wingate Memorial Trophy]] to the best college lacrosse team each year.
sentence_214: The NCAA began sponsoring a men's lacrosse championship in 1971, when [[Cornell_Big_Red_men's_lacrosse|Cornell]] took the first title over [[Maryland_Terrapins_men's_lacrosse|Maryland]], 12–6.
sentence_215: [[Syracuse_Orange_men's_lacrosse|Syracuse]] has 10 Division I titles, [[Johns_Hopkins_Blue_Jays_men's_lacrosse|Johns Hopkins]] 9, and [[Princeton_Tigers_men's_lacrosse|Princeton]] 6.
sentence_216: The NCAA national championship weekend tournament draws over 80,000 fans.
sentence_217: There are currently 112 Division I women's lacrosse teams, 109 Division II teams, and 282 Division III teams.
sentence_218: There are 36 NAIA women's lacrosse teams.
sentence_219: The NCAA started sponsoring a women's lacrosse championship in 1982.
sentence_220: [[Maryland_Terrapins_women's_lacrosse|Maryland]] has traditionally dominated women's [[College_athletics|intercollegiate play]], producing many head coaches and U.S. national team players.
sentence_221: The Terrapins won seven consecutive [[NCAA_Women's_Lacrosse_Championship|NCAA championships]] from 1995 through 2001.
sentence_222: [[Princeton_Tigers_women's_lacrosse|Princeton's]] women's teams have made it to the final game seven times since 1993 and have won three NCAA titles, in 1993, 2002, and 2003.
sentence_223: In recent years, Northwestern has become a force, winning the national championship from 2005 through 2009.
sentence_224: Maryland ended Northwestern's streak by defeating the Wildcats in the 2010 final, however, Northwestern won the next two titles in 2011 and 2012.
sentence_225: Maryland again claimed the national championship in 2014, 2015, and 2017.
sentence_226: The [[Women's_Collegiate_Lacrosse_Associates|Women's Collegiate Lacrosse Associates]] (WCLA) is a collection of over 260 college club teams that are organized by [[US_Lacrosse|US Lacrosse]].
sentence_227: Teams are organized into two divisions and various leagues.
sentence_228: Main article: [[Major_League_Lacrosse|Major League Lacrosse]]
sentence_229: Major League Lacrosse (MLL) is a semi-professional field lacrosse league started in 2001 with six teams in the [[Northeastern_United_States|Northeastern United States]].
sentence_230: The league currently has nine teams in the Eastern United States and [[Denver_Outlaws|Denver]] playing a 14-game season from April to August.
sentence_231: MLL rules are based on NCAA men's rules with several exceptions, such as a 16-yard 2-point line and a 60-second shot clock.
sentence_232: MLL venues range from small stadiums with under 10,000 capacity to an [[Sports_Authority_Field_at_Mile_High|NFL stadium in Denver]] that seats 76,000.
sentence_233: Overall league average attendance is around 4,000 per game, but Denver has averaged around 10,000 per game since its founding in 2006.
sentence_234: The rookie salary is $7,000 per season and most players make between $10,000 and $20,000 per season.
sentence_235: Therefore, players have other jobs, often non-lacrosse related, and travel to games on the weekends.
sentence_236: The [[Chesapeake_Bayhawks|Chesapeake Bayhawks]], who have played in the Annapolis–Baltimore–Washington, DC area since 2001, are the most successful franchise with five championships.
sentence_237: Main article: National Lacrosse League
sentence_238: The National Lacrosse League (NLL) is a men's semi-professional [[Box_lacrosse|box lacrosse]] league in North America.
sentence_239: The NLL currently has nine teams, five in the United States and four in Canada.
sentence_240: The 18-game regular season runs from December to April; games are always on the weekends.
sentence_241: The champion is awarded the [[National_Lacrosse_League_Cup|National Lacrosse League Cup]] in early June.
sentence_242: Games are played in ice rinks with artificial turf covering the ice.
sentence_243: Venues range from NHL arenas seating 19,000 to smaller arenas with under 10,000 capacity.
sentence_244: In 2017, average attendance ranged from 3,200 per game in [[Vancouver_Stealth|Vancouver]] to over 15,000 in [[Buffalo_Bandits|Buffalo]].
sentence_245: Overall, the league averaged 9,500 people per game.
sentence_246: With an average salary around $20,000 per season, players have regular jobs, mostly non-lacrosse related, and live in different cities, flying into town for games.
sentence_247: Canadians and Native Americans make up over 90% of the players.
sentence_248: The NLL started in 1987 as the Eagle Pro Box Lacrosse League.
sentence_249: Teams in Philadelphia, New Jersey, Baltimore and Washington, DC, played a 6-game season.
sentence_250: The league operated as the Major Indoor Lacrosse League from 1989 to 1997, when there were six teams playing a 10-game schedule.
sentence_251: The current NLL name began in the [[1998_NLL_season|1998 season]], which included the first Canadian team.
sentence_252: The most successful franchises have been the [[Toronto_Rock|Toronto Rock]] and the now-defunct [[Philadelphia_Wings_(1987–2014)|Philadelphia Wings]], each has won six championships.
sentence_253: Main article: [[Premier_Lacrosse_League|Premier Lacrosse League]]
sentence_254: In October 2018, former MLL player [[Paul_Rabil|Paul Rabil]] branched away from the MLL and created the Premier Lacrosse League.
sentence_255: The PLL focuses on being a traveling lacrosse league that will bring the best players in the world to different cities in the United States.
sentence_256: Main article: [[United_Women's_Lacrosse_League|United Women's Lacrosse League]]
sentence_257: The United Women's Lacrosse League (UWLX), a four-team women's lacrosse league, was launched in 2016.
sentence_258: The teams are the [[Baltimore_Ride|Baltimore Ride]], [[Boston_Storm_(UWLX)|Boston Storm]], [[Long_Island_Sound_(UWLX)|Long Island Sound]] and [[Philadelphia_Force_(UWLX)|Philadelphia Force]].
sentence_259: Long Island won the first two championships.
sentence_260: The [[Women's_Professional_Lacrosse_League|Women's Professional Lacrosse League]] is a professional women's lacrosse league with 5 teams that started in 2018.
sentence_261: Main article: [[Lacrosse_stick|Lacrosse stick]]
sentence_262: The lacrosse stick has two parts, the head and the shaft.
sentence_263: There are three parts to the head: the scoop, sidewall, and pocket.
sentence_264: The scoop is the top of the stick that affects picking up ground ball as well as passing and shooting.
sentence_265: The sidewall is the side of the head that affects the depth of the head and the stiffness.
sentence_266: The pocket is the leather or nylon mesh attached to the sidewall and scoop.
sentence_267: A wider pocket allows an easier time catching balls, but will also cause less ball control.
sentence_268: A narrower pocket makes catching harder, but allows more ball retention and accuracy.
sentence_269: Shafts are usually made of hollow metal.
sentence_270: They are octagonal, instead of round, in order to provide a better grip.
sentence_271: Most are made of [[Aluminum|aluminum]], [[Titanium|titanium]], [[Scandium|scandium]], or alloys, but some shafts are made from other materials, including wood, plastic, carbon fiber, or [[Fiberglass|fiberglass]].
sentence_272: Stick length, both shaft and head together, is governed by NCAA regulations, which require that men's sticks be from 40 to 42 inches (100 to 110 cm) long for offensive players, 52 to 72 inches (130 to 180 cm) long for defensemen, and 40 to 72 inches (100 to 180 cm) long for goalies.
sentence_273: Women's sticks must be an overall length of 35.5–43.25 inches (90.2–109.9 cm).
sentence_274: The head must be seven to nine inches wide and the top of the ball must remain above the side walls when dropped in the pocket.
sentence_275: The goalkeeper's stick must be 35.5–48 inches (90–122 cm) long.
sentence_276: The head of the goalie's stick can up to 12 inches (30 cm) wide and the pocket may be mesh.
sentence_277: Main article: [[Lacrosse_ball|Lacrosse ball]]
sentence_278: The ball is made of solid rubber.
sentence_279: It is typically white for men's lacrosse, or yellow for women's Lacrosse; but is also produced in a wide variety of colors, such as yellow, orange or lime green according to the Men's Lacrosse Rules and Interpretations.
sentence_280: In the college level the Lacrosse ball is orange.
sentence_281: Men's field lacrosse protective equipment contains a pair of [[Lacrosse_glove|gloves]], elbow pads, shoulder pads, [[Lacrosse_helmet|helmet]], mouthguard, and [[Cleat_(shoe)|cleats]].
sentence_282: Pads differ in size and protection from player to player based on position, ability, comfort and preference.
sentence_283: For example, many attack players wear larger and more protective elbow pads to protect themselves from checks thrown at them while defenders typically wear smaller and less protective pads due to their smaller possibility of being checked and goalies usually wear no elbow pads due to the very limited opportunities of being checked.
sentence_284: A goalkeeper must also wear a large protective chest pad to cover their stomach and chest and a plastic neck guard that connects to the chin of their helmet to protect them from shots hitting their windpipe.
sentence_285: In addition, male goalkeepers are required to wear a protective cup.
sentence_286: Men's box players wear more protective gear than field players due to the increased physical contact and more permissive checking rules.
sentence_287: Cross-checking in the back is allowed by the rules.
sentence_288: Runners wear larger and heavier elbow pads and stronger shoulder pads that extend down the back of the player.
sentence_289: Most players wear rib pads as well.
sentence_290: Box goalies wear equipment very similar to ice hockey goalies, the leg blockers are somewhat smaller, although the shoulder pads are bigger than ice hockey pads.
sentence_291: Women's field players are not required to wear protective equipment besides eyegear and a mouthguard.
sentence_292: Eyegear is a metal cage covering the eyes attached with a strap around the back of the head.
sentence_293: In recent years, there has been discussion about allowing or requiring padded headgear to protect against concussions.
sentence_294: Women goalies wear a helmet, gloves, and chest protector.

title: Lamiales
sentence_0: The Lamiales are an [[Order_(biology)|order]] in the [[Asteridae|asterid]] group of [[Dicotyledon|dicotyledonous]] [[Flowering_plants|flowering plants]].
sentence_1: It includes about 23,810 [[Species|species]], 1,059 genera, and is divided into about 24 [[Family_(biology)|families]].
sentence_2: Well-known or economically important members of this order include [[Lavender|lavender]], [[Lilac|lilac]], [[Olive|olive]], [[Jasmine|jasmine]], the [[Ash_tree|ash tree]], [[Teak|teak]], [[Antirrhinum|snapdragon]], [[Sesame|sesame]], [[Psyllium|psyllium]], [[Salvia_officinalis|garden sage]], and a number of table herbs such as [[Mentha|mint]], [[Basil|basil]], and [[Rosemary|rosemary]].
sentence_3: Although exceptions often occur, [[Species|species]] in this order typically have the following characteristics:
sentence_4: The Lamiales previously had a restricted circumscription (e.g., by [[Arthur_Cronquist|Arthur Cronquist]]) that included the major families [[Lamiaceae|Lamiaceae]] (Labiatae), [[Verbenaceae|Verbenaceae]], and [[Boraginaceae|Boraginaceae]], plus a few smaller families.
sentence_5: In the classification system of [[Rolf_Dahlgren|Dahlgren]] the Lamiales were in the superorder Lamiiflorae (also called Lamianae).
sentence_6: Recent phylogenetic work has shown the Lamiales are [[Polyphyletic|polyphyletic]] with respect to order [[Scrophulariales|Scrophulariales]] and the two groups are now usually combined in a single order that also includes the former orders Hippuridales and [[Plantaginales|Plantaginales]].
sentence_7: Lamiales has become the preferred name for this much larger combined group.
sentence_8: The placement of the [[Boraginaceae|Boraginaceae]] is unclear, but phylogenetic work shows this family does not belong in Lamiales.
sentence_9: Also, the circumscription of family [[Scrophulariaceae|Scrophulariaceae]], formerly a [[Paraphyletic|paraphyletic]] group defined primarily by [[Plesiomorphic|plesiomorphic]] characters and from within which numerous other families of the Lamiales were derived, has been radically altered to create a number of smaller, better-defined, and putatively [[Monophyletic|monophyletic]] families.
sentence_10: Much research has been conducted in recent years regarding the dating the Lamiales [[Lineage_(evolution)|lineage]], although there still remains some ambiguity.
sentence_11: A 2004 study, on the molecular [[Phylogenetics|phylogenetic]] dating of [[Asterids|asterid]] flowering plants, estimated 106 million years (MY) for the stem lineage of Lamiales.
sentence_12: A 2009 study on [[Flowering_plant|angiosperm]] diversification through time, concluded an inferred age of lower [[Eocene|Eocene]], ca. 50 MY, for Lamiales.

sentence_1: The King's Royal Rifle Corps was an infantry [[Rifle_regiment|rifle regiment]] of the [[British_Army|British Army]] that was originally raised in [[British_North_America|British North America]] as the Royal American Regiment during the phase of the [[Seven_Years'_War|Seven Years' War]] in North America known as 'The French and Indian War.'
sentence_2: Subsequently numbered the 60th Regiment of Foot, the regiment served for more than 200 years throughout the [[British_Empire|British Empire]].
sentence_3: In 1958, the regiment joined the [[Oxfordshire_and_Buckinghamshire_Light_Infantry|Oxfordshire and Buckinghamshire Light Infantry]] and the [[Rifle_Brigade_(Prince_Consort's_Own)|Rifle Brigade]] in the [[Green_Jackets_Brigade|Green Jackets Brigade]] and in 1966 the three regiments were formally amalgamated to become the [[Royal_Green_Jackets|Royal Green Jackets]].
sentence_4: The KRRC became the 2nd Battalion, [[Royal_Green_Jackets|Royal Green Jackets]].
sentence_5: On the disbandment of the 1st Battalion, Royal Green Jackets in 1992, the RGJ's KRRC battalion was redesignated as the 1st Battalion, Royal Green Jackets, eventually becoming 2nd Battalion, [[The_Rifles|The Rifles]] in 2007.
sentence_6: The King's Royal Rifle Corps was raised in the American colonies in 1756 as the 62nd (Royal American) Regiment to defend the thirteen colonies against attack by the French and their Native American allies.
sentence_7: After [[Braddock_Expedition|Braddock's defeat]] in 1755, royal approval for a new regiment, as well as funds, were granted by parliament just before Christmas 1755 – hence the regiment's traditional birthday of Christmas Day.
sentence_8: However, parliamentary delays meant that it was 4 March 1756 before a special act of parliament created four battalions of 1,000 men each to include foreigners for service in the Americas.
sentence_9: A regimental history compiled in 1879 states that, in November 1755, Parliament voted the sum of £81,000 for the purpose of raising a regiment of four battalions, each one thousand strong, for service in [[British_North_America|British North America]].
sentence_10: To provide experienced personnel, Parliament passed the Commissions to Foreign Protestants Act 1756 (29 Geo.
sentence_11: 2 c. 5) [[John_Campbell,_4th_Earl_of_Loudoun|The Earl of Loudoun]], who as [[Commander-in-chief|commander-in-chief]] of the Forces in North America, was appointed [[Colonel-in-chief|colonel-in-chief]] of the regiment.
sentence_12: About fifty officers' commissions were given to Germans and Swiss, and none were allowed to rise above the rank of lieutenant-colonel.
sentence_13: According to a modern history of the regiment, the idea for creating this unique force was proposed by Jacques Prevost, a Swiss soldier and adventurer who was a friend of the [[Prince_William,_Duke_of_Cumberland|Duke of Cumberland]] (the Duke was the King's second son and also [[Commander-in-Chief_of_the_Forces|Commander-in-Chief of the Forces]]).
sentence_14: Prevost recognised the need for soldiers who understood forest warfare, unlike the regulars who were brought to America in 1755 by General [[Edward_Braddock|Edward Braddock]].
sentence_15: The regiment was intended to combine the characteristics of a [[Colonial_troops|colonial corps]] with those of a [[Foreign_volunteers|foreign legion]].
sentence_16: Swiss and German forest fighting experts, American colonists and British volunteers from other British regiments were recruited.
sentence_17: These men were Protestants, an important consideration for fighting against the predominantly Catholic French.
sentence_18: The officers were also recruited from Europe – not from the American colonies – and consisted of English, Scots, Irish, Dutch, Swiss and Germans.
sentence_19: It was the first time foreign officers were commissioned as British Army officers.
sentence_20: In total, the regiment consisted of 101 officers, 240 non-commissioned officers and 4,160 enlisted men.
sentence_21: The battalions were raised on [[Governors_Island|Governors Island]], New York.
sentence_22: The regiment was renumbered the 60th (Royal American) Regiment in February 1757 when the [[Shirley's_Regiment|50th (Shirley's)]] and [[Pepperrell's_Regiment|51st (Pepperrell's)]] foot regiments were removed from the British Army roll after their surrender at [[Fort_Oswego|Fort Oswego]].
sentence_23: Among the distinguished foreign officers given commissions in the 60th (Royal Americans) was [[Henry_Bouquet|Henry Bouquet]], a Swiss citizen, whose forward-looking ideas on tactics, training and man-management (including the unofficial introduction of the rifle and more practical clothing suited to bush-fighting) would come to be accepted as standard in the British Army many years in the future.
sentence_24: Bouquet was commanding officer of the 1st battalion, and with his fellow battalion commanders, worked to form units that were better suited to warfare in the forests and lakes of northeast America.
sentence_25: Elements of the new regiment fought at [[Siege_of_Louisbourg_(1758)|Louisbourg]] in June 1758, the [[Cape_Sable_Campaign|Cape Sable Campaign]] in September 1758 and [[Battle_of_the_Plains_of_Abraham|Quebec]] in September 1759, and finally the [[Montreal_Campaign|Montreal Campaign]] from July to September 1760 which finally wrested Canada from France.
sentence_26: At Quebec General [[James_Wolfe|James Wolfe]] is said to have granted the 60th the motto Celer et Audax (Swift and Bold).
sentence_27: To reward and maintain their service and loyalty, Parliament passed the American Protestant Soldier Naturalization Act 1762 (2 Geo.
sentence_28: 3 c. 25), which offered British naturalization to those officers, engineers and soldiers who had or would serve for two years, with certain conditions and on the model of the [[Plantation_Act_1740|Plantation Act 1740]].
sentence_29: These earlier engagements were conventional battles on the European model, but fighting during [[Pontiac's_War|Pontiac's War]] in 1763 was of a very different character.
sentence_30: The frontier war threatened the British control of North America.
sentence_31: The new regiment at first lost several outlying garrisons such as [[Fort_Michilimackinac|Fort Michilimackinac]], later a detachment fought under Bouquet's leadership at the victory of [[Battle_of_Bushy_Run|Bushy Run]] in August 1763.
sentence_32: The 60th was uniformed and equipped in a similar manner to other British regiments with red coats and cocked hats or grenadier caps, but on campaign, swords were replaced with hatchets, and coats and hats cut down for ease of movement in the woods.
sentence_33: Two additional battalions of the regiment (the 3rd and 4th battalions) were raised in England in 1775, principally of men recruited from England and Hanover in 1775 for service in the [[American_Revolutionary_War|American Revolutionary War]].
sentence_34: After assembly in the [[Isle_of_Wight|Isle of Wight]], both battalions were sent in 1776 to Florida where they were joined by detachments from 1st and 2nd Battalions.
sentence_35: These battalions were deployed to [[Georgia_(U.S._state)|Georgia]] and were involved in skirmishes at Sudbury in January 1779, the [[Battle_of_Briar_Creek|Battle of Briar Creek]] in March 1779, the [[Siege_of_Savannah|Siege of Savannah]] in October 1779 where elements from the 4th Battalion captured the Colour of the [[2nd_South_Carolina_Regiment|2nd South Carolina Regiment]], and at [[Augusta,_Georgia|Augusta]] in September 1780.
sentence_36: The 3rd and 4th battalions were disbanded in June 1783.
sentence_37: During the [[Napoleonic_Wars|Napoleonic Wars]], the regiment saw action in the [[Peninsular_War|Peninsular War]].
sentence_38: The first four battalions had been raised as regular line battalions, but in 1797 a 5th battalion had been raised on Barbados, with additional companies formed on the Isle of Wight, and equipped entirely with rifles.
sentence_39: The troops of the 5th battalion were so effective that [[Arthur_Wellesley,_1st_Duke_of_Wellington|Sir Arthur Wellesley]] recommended their use to the divisional commanders describing them as the "most useful, active and brave troops in the field".
sentence_40: A 7th battalion was raised specifically for service in the American War of 1812.

section_4.value: Anglo-Egyptian War and Second Boer War

sentence_41: After the Napoleonic Wars, the regiment received a new title: first, in 1815, its name was changed to The Duke of York's Own Rifle Corps and then, in 1830, to the King's Royal Rifle Corps (KRRC).
sentence_42: In 1858, the [[Peninsula_Barracks|Rifle Depot]] at [[Winchester|Winchester]] was made their headquarters.
sentence_43: The regiment served in the [[Anglo-Egyptian_War|Anglo-Egyptian War]] in 1882.
sentence_44: During the rest of the 1800s, the unit also was active in China, Canada ([[Wolseley_expedition|Wolseley expedition]]), Afghanistan, India, [[Myanmar|Burma]] and South Africa.
sentence_45: The regiment was deployed during the [[Second_Boer_War|Second Boer War]] from the outset playing a key role in the first battle at [[Battle_of_Talana_Hill|Talana Hill]].
sentence_46: Two officers from the regiment were awarded the [[Victoria_Cross|Victoria Cross]]; Lieutenant [[Frederick_Hugh_Sherston_Roberts|Frederick Hugh Sherston Roberts]] and Lieutenant [[Llewelyn_Alberic_Emilius_Price-Davies|Llewelyn Alberic Emilius Price-Davies]].
sentence_47: Private [[Frederick_Corbett|Frederick Corbett]] also received the Victoria Cross for his action at [[Battle_of_Kafr-el-Dawwar|Kafr Dowar]], [[Egypt|Egypt]], on 5 August 1882; his VC was later rescinded when he was convicted of embezzlement, theft, and being absent without leave.
sentence_48: Following the end of the war in South Africa, the 1st battalion was transferred to [[Malta|Malta]], where it arrived in October 1902.
sentence_49: In 1908, the Volunteers and Militia were reorganised nationally, with the former becoming the [[Territorial_Force|Territorial Force]] and the latter the [[Special_Reserve_(militia)|Special Reserve]]; the regiment now had two Reserve but no Territorial battalions.
sentence_50: The 1st Battalion landed at [[Rouen|Rouen]] as part of the [[6th_Infantry_Brigade_(United_Kingdom)|6th Brigade]] in the [[2nd_Infantry_Division_(United_Kingdom)|2nd Division]] in August 1914 for service on the [[Western_Front_(World_War_I)|Western Front]].
sentence_51: It saw action at the [[Battle_of_Mons|Battle of Mons]] in August 1914, the [[First_Battle_of_the_Marne|First Battle of the Marne]] and the [[First_Battle_of_the_Aisne|First Battle of the Aisne]] in September 1914 and [[First_Battle_of_Ypres|First Battle of Ypres]] in October 1914.
sentence_52: It fought at the [[Battle_of_Festubert|Battle of Festubert]] in May 1915, the [[Battle_of_Loos|Battle of Loos]] in September 1915 and the [[Battle_of_the_Somme|Battle of the Somme]] in Autumn 1916 before taking part in the advance to the [[Hindenburg_Line|Hindenburg Line]], the [[Battle_of_Cambrai_(1917)|Battle of Arras]] in November 1917, the [[Battle_of_Cambrai_(1917)|Battle of Cambrai]] in November 1917, the [[Second_Battle_of_the_Somme_(1918)|Second Battle of the Somme]] in Autumn 1918 and the [[Battle_of_the_Selle|Battle of the Selle]] in October 1918.
sentence_53: The 2nd Battalion landed at [[Le_Havre|Le Havre]] as part of the [[2nd_Infantry_Brigade_(United_Kingdom)|2nd Brigade]] in the [[1st_Infantry_Division_(United_Kingdom)|1st Division]] in August 1914 for service on the Western Front and saw action at the [[Battle_of_Aubers_Ridge|Battle of Aubers Ridge]] in May 1915.
sentence_54: The 3rd Battalion landed at Le Havre as part of the [[80th_Brigade_(United_Kingdom)|80th Brigade]] in the [[27th_Division_(United_Kingdom)|27th Division]] in December 1914 for service on the Western Front and saw action at the [[Second_Battle_of_Ypres|Second Battle of Ypres]] in April 1915.
sentence_55: The 4th Battalion landed at Le Havre as part of the 80th Brigade in the 27th Division in December 1914 for service on the Western Front and saw action at the Second Battle of Ypres in April 1915 but moved to [[Thessaloniki|Salonika]] in November 1915 before returning to France in June 1918.
sentence_56: The regiment did not have any territorial force battalions.
sentence_57: The 7th (Service) Battalion landed at [[Boulogne-sur-Mer|Boulogne-sur-Mer]] as part of the [[41st_Brigade_(United_Kingdom)|41st Brigade]] in the [[14th_(Light)_Division|14th (Light) Division]] in August 1914 for service on the Western Front and saw action the [[Second_Battle_of_Ypres|Second Battle of Ypres]] in May 1915, the [[Battle_of_Delville_Wood|Battle of Delville Wood]] in July 1916 and the [[Battle_of_Flers–Courcelette|Battle of Flers–Courcelette]] in September 1916 as well as the advance to the [[Hindenburg_Line|Hindenburg Line]], the [[Battle_of_Arras_(1917)|Battle of Arras]] in April 1917, the [[Battle_of_Langemarck_(1917)|Battle of Langemark]] in August 1917, the [[First_Battle_of_Passchendaele|First Battle of Passchendaele]] in October 1917 and the [[Second_Battle_of_Passchendaele|Second Battle of Passchendaele]] in November 1917 before taking part in the [[Operation_Michael|Battle of St Quentin]] in March 1918 and the [[Battle_of_the_Avre|Battle of the Avre]] in April 1918.
sentence_58: The 8th (Service) Battalion landed at Boulogne-sur-Mer as part of the 41st Brigade in the 14th (Light) Division in May 1915 for service on the Western Front and saw action most of the same battles as the 7th Battalion.
sentence_59: The 9th (Service) Battalion landed at Boulogne-sur-Mer as part of the [[42nd_Infantry_Brigade_and_Headquarters_North_West|42nd Brigade]] in the 14th (Light) Division in May 1915 for service on the Western Front and saw action most of the same battles as the 7th and 8th battalions.
sentence_60: The 10th (Service) Battalion and 11th (Service) Battalion landed at Boulogne-sur-Mer as part of the [[59th_Brigade_(United_Kingdom)|59th Brigade]] in the [[20th_(Light)_Division|20th (Light) Division]] in July 1915 for service on the Western Front and saw action at the [[Battle_of_Mont_Sorrel|Battle of Mont Sorrel]] in June 1916, the [[Battle_of_Delville_Wood|Battle of Delville Wood]] in July 1916 and the [[Battle_of_Guillemont|Battle of Guillemont]] in September 1916 as well as the [[Battle_of_Flers–Courcelette|Battle of Flers–Courcelette]] in September 1916, the [[Battle_of_Morval|Battle of Morval]] in September 1916 and the [[Battle_of_Le_Transloy|Battle of Le Transloy]] in October 1916 before taking part in the advance to the [[Hindenburg_Line|Hindenburg Line]], the [[Battle_of_Langemarck_(1917)|Battle of Langemarck]] in August 1917, the [[Battle_of_the_Menin_Road_Ridge|Battle of the Menin Road Ridge]] in September 1917, the [[Battle_of_Polygon_Wood|Battle of Polygon Wood]] in September 1917 and the [[Battle_of_Cambrai_(1917)|Battle of Cambrai]] in November 1917.
sentence_61: The 12th (Service) Battalion landed at Boulogne-sur-Mer as part of the [[60th_Brigade_(United_Kingdom)|60th Brigade]] in the 20th (Light) Division in July 1915 for service on the Western Front and saw action most of the same battles as the 10th and 11th Battalions.
sentence_62: The 13th (Service) Battalion landed at Boulogne-sur-Mer as part of the [[111th_Brigade_(United_Kingdom)|111th Brigade]] in the [[37th_Division_(United_Kingdom)|37th Division]] in July 1915 for service on the Western Front and saw action at the [[Battle_of_Morval|Battle of Morval]] in September 1916, the advance to the [[Hindenburg_Line|Hindenburg Line]] and the [[Battle_of_Arras_(1917)|Battle of Arras]] in April 1917 as well as the [[Battle_of_Passchendaele|Battle of Passchendaele]] in Autumn 1917, the [[Battle_of_Cambrai_(1917)|Battle of Cambrai]] in November 1917 and the [[Hundred_Days_Offensive|Hundred Days Offensive]] in Autumn 1918 before taking part in the Battles of the Hindenburg Line and the Final Advance in Picardy.
sentence_63: The 16th (Service) Battalion (Church Lads Brigade) landed at Le Havre as part of the [[100th_Brigade_(United_Kingdom)|100th Brigade]] in the [[33rd_Division_(United_Kingdom)|33rd Division]] in November 1915 for service on the Western Front.
sentence_64: The 17th (Service) Battalion (British Empire League) landed at Le Havre as part of the [[117th_Brigade_(United_Kingdom)|117th Brigade]] in the [[39th_Division_(United_Kingdom)|39th Division]] in March 1916 for service on the Western Front.
sentence_65: The 18th (Service) Battalion (Arts & Crafts) landed at Le Havre as part of the [[122nd_Brigade|122nd Brigade]] in the [[41st_Division_(United_Kingdom)|41st Division]] on 3 May 1916 for service on the Western Front.
sentence_66: The 20th (Service) Battalion (British Empire League Pioneers) landed at Le Havre as pioneer battalion for the [[3rd_Division_(United_Kingdom)|3rd Division]] in March 1916 for service on the Western Front.
sentence_67: The 21st (Service) Battalion (Yeoman Rifles) landed in France as part of the [[124th_Brigade|124th Brigade]] in the [[41st_Division_(United_Kingdom)|41st Division]] in May 1916 for service on the Western Front but moved to Italy in November 1917 before returning to France in March 1918.
sentence_68: Seven members of the regiment received the Victoria Cross.
sentence_69: After 1918, the unit returned to garrison duties in India, [[Mandatory_Palestine|Palestine]] and Ireland.
sentence_70: In 1922, the regiment was reduced from four to two battalions with the third and fourth being disbanded.
sentence_71: In 1926, the Regiment was reorganised as one of the first mechanised infantry regiments.
sentence_72: The 1st Battalion, KRRC, commanded initially by [[Lieutenant_colonel_(United_Kingdom)|Lieutenant Colonel]] [[William_Gott|William Gott]], was deployed to North Africa upon war's outbreak and saw action as part of the pivot group within the [[7th_Armoured_Division_(United_Kingdom)|7th Armoured Division]] at the [[Battle_of_Sidi_Rezegh|Battle of Sidi Rezegh]] in November 1941, the [[First_Battle_of_El_Alamein|First Battle of El Alamein]] in July 1942 and the [[Second_Battle_of_El_Alamein|Second Battle of El Alamein]] in October 1942 during the [[Western_Desert_Campaign|Western Desert Campaign]].
sentence_73: Rifleman [[John_Beeley|John Beeley]] was awarded a posthumous [[Victoria_Cross|Victoria Cross]] for his actions during [[Operation_Crusader|Operation Crusader]] in North Africa in late 1941.
sentence_74: The battalion, now part of the [[2nd_Armoured_Brigade_(United_Kingdom)|2nd Armoured Brigade]] of the [[1st_(United_Kingdom)_Division|1st Armoured Division]], was then engaged in action throughout the final stages of the [[Tunisian_Campaign|Tunisian Campaign]].
sentence_75: The battalion, now commanded by Lieutenant Colonel [[Edward_Alexander_Wilmot_Williams|Edward Williams]], served in the [[Italian_Campaign_(World_War_II)|Italian Campaign]] then with the independent [[9th_Armoured_Brigade_(United_Kingdom)|9th Armoured Brigade]] and finally the [[6th_Armoured_Division_(United_Kingdom)|6th Armoured Division]]'s [[61st_Infantry_Brigade_(United_Kingdom)|61st Infantry Brigade]].
sentence_76: The 2nd Battalion, KRRC, commanded by Lieutenant Colonel [[Thomas_Needham_Furnival_Wilson|Thomas Wilson]], was part of the [[British_Expeditionary_Force_(World_War_II)|British Expeditionary Force]] (BEF) that landed in France in May 1940.
sentence_77: The battalion, which was part of the [[30th_Infantry_Brigade_(United_Kingdom)|30th Infantry Brigade]], [[1st_(United_Kingdom)_Division|1st Armoured Division]], and now commanded by Lieutenant Colonel [[Euan_Miller|Euan Miller]], was lost in the [[Siege_of_Calais_(1940)|defence of Calais]], where the brigade slowed the German advance and enabled the [[Dunkirk_evacuation|Dunkirk evacuation]] to proceed.
sentence_78: The battalion was reformed in the summer of 1940 under the command of Lieutenant Colonel [[George_Erskine|George Erskine]] and transferred to the [[22nd_Armoured_Brigade_(United_Kingdom)|22nd Armoured Brigade]] of the 1st Armoured Division.
sentence_79: The reformed battalion took part in the [[Battle_of_Gazala|Battle of Gazala]] in May 1942 and the [[Second_Battle_of_El_Alamein|Second Battle of El Alamein]] in October 1942 during the [[North_African_Campaign|North African Campaign]], forming part of the Division's [[18th_Infantry_Brigade_(United_Kingdom)#Second_World_War|7th Motor Brigade]] during the latter engagement and transferring to [[4th_Infantry_Brigade_and_Headquarters_North_East#Second_World_War|4th Armoured Brigade]] in January 1943.
sentence_80: Now under Lieutenant Colonel W. Heathcote-Amory, the battalion continued serving with 4th Armoured Brigade in the [[Normandy_landings|Normandy landings]] in June 1944 and the subsequent [[Western_Front_(World_War_II)|campaign in North-West Europe]], finally leaving 1st Division six days after [[VE_Day|VE Day]].
sentence_81: Two officers of note served with the battalion in its final campaign of the war, [[Roland_Gibbs|Roland Gibbs]] and [[Edwin_Bramall|Edwin Bramall]].
sentence_82: The 1st Battalion of the [[Queen_Victoria's_Rifles|Queen Victoria's Rifles]] (QFR) was a [[Army_Reserve_(United_Kingdom)|Territorial Army]] (TA) unit which had been closely associated with the KRRC.
sentence_83: The battalion, commanded by Lieutenant Colonel J. A. M. Elison-Mccartney, was initially part of the TA [[56th_(London)_Infantry_Division|1st London Division]], serving as the division's motorcycle battalion.
sentence_84: However, like the 2nd Battalion, it was also lost in the defence of Calais in May 1940.
sentence_85: The battalion was later reformed in the United Kingdom and, in December 1940, transferred to the [[27th_Armoured_Brigade|27th Armoured Brigade]], part of the newly formed [[9th_Armoured_Division_(United_Kingdom)|9th Armoured Division]].
sentence_86: The 9th Battalion ([[The_Rangers_(British_regiment)|The Rangers]]) was deployed to the [[Mediterranean_and_Middle_East_theatre_of_World_War_II|Mediterranean theatre]] as part of the [[1st_Armoured_Brigade_(United_Kingdom)|1st Armoured Brigade]] in the 7th Armoured Division.
sentence_87: It saw action in the [[Battle_of_Greece|Greek campaign]] in April 1941 before being disbanded in August 1942.
sentence_88: In 1958 for administrative purposes, the KRRC was brigaded with the [[Oxfordshire_and_Buckinghamshire_Light_Infantry|Oxfordshire and Buckinghamshire Light Infantry]] and the [[Rifle_Brigade_(Prince_Consort's_Own)|Rifle Brigade]] to form the [[Green_Jackets_Brigade|Green Jackets Brigade]].
sentence_89: In 1958, the Regiment was re-titled the 2nd Green Jackets, the King's Royal Rifle Corps, while the two other regiments of the Green Jackets Brigade were re-titled the [[1st_Green_Jackets_(43rd_and_52nd)|1st Green Jackets (43rd and 52nd)]] and 3rd Green Jackets, the Rifle Brigade (Prince Consort's Own) respectively.
sentence_90: In 1966, the three regiments were amalgamated to form the three battalions of the [[Royal_Green_Jackets|Royal Green Jackets]].
sentence_91: The regimental collection is held by the [[Royal_Green_Jackets_(Rifles)_Museum|Royal Green Jackets (Rifles) Museum]] which is based at [[Peninsula_Barracks|Peninsula Barracks]] in [[Winchester|Winchester]].

sentence_94: There were two cadet battalions: 1st Cadet Battalion, The King's Royal Rifle Corps and Queen Victoria's Rifles Cadet Corps (re-titled the 2nd Cadet Battalion, The King's Royal Rifle Corps in 1945).
sentence_95: Over the years, the formation of the cadet battalions was changed regularly, due to the changes to do with rules and the commanding officer.
sentence_96: The 1st Cadet Battalion owes its foundation to the Reverend Freeman Wills, who was commissioned into the Volunteer Army in the rank of captain on 26 July 1890.

sentence_98: On receiving his commission he decided to form a cadet company within the 1st Cadet Battalion, the [[Queen's_Royal_Regiment_(West_Surrey)|Royal West Surrey Regiment]].
sentence_99: The Company quickly expanded to become the 2nd Cadet Battalion, the Royal West Surrey Regiment, at which point he moved the Battalion Headquarters to No.

sentence_101: In 1894 he applied to [[Prince_George,_Duke_of_Cambridge|Prince George, Duke of Cambridge]], Colonel-in-Chief, to affiliate to the Regiment, with the title of 1st Cadet Battalion, the King's Royal Rifle Corps.
sentence_102: Consent was granted on 8 November 1894 and the Battalion has remained a part of the Regiment ever since.
sentence_103: In the days of their foundation, Cadet battalions were privately organized and funded.
sentence_104: On becoming a part of the King's Royal Rifle Corps, subscriptions began to flow in and, after the commanding officer had spent nearly £1,000, the Battalion was placed on a financial basis that many Volunteer Corps would have envied.
sentence_105: There were to be many ups and down in later years, especially when recognition of the Cadet Force was withdrawn between the two World Wars, but fortunately the enthusiasm and commitment of those involved consistently triumphed over the parsimony of Governments.
sentence_106: In 1900, when volunteers were urgently needed for the Second Boer War, the Commanding Officer, Colonel Freeman Croft-Wills persuaded the War Office to accept a Company of the older Cadets, principally N.C.O.s (Non-Commissioned Officers), the company being enrolled in the City Imperial Volunteers.
sentence_107: Around 100 cadets thus served in South Africa with this unit, whilst other Cadets and ex-Cadets served in the Royal Army Medical Corps, and other units.
sentence_108: Four were killed in action, one serving with the 1st Battalion King's Royal Rifle Corps at the Battle of Dundee, and the others with units of the C.I.V.s.
sentence_109: Their comrades erected brass plaques in their memory in the Drill Hall at Sun Street.
sentence_110: These are now displayed in the Cadet Company Office here at Davies Street.
sentence_111: In recognition of this service, [[Edward_VII|King Edward VII]] granted the Battalion the honour of wearing on its accoutrements the Battle Honour "South Africa 1900–1902" (Army Order 151 of 1905).
sentence_112: The announcement of this privilege was made to the Battalion by His Majesty, [[George_V|King George V]], then Prince of Wales, when, accompanied by Her Majesty [[Mary_of_Teck|Queen Mary]], he distributed the prizes at the [[Guildhall,_London|Guildhall]] in the City of London.
sentence_113: The 1st Cadet Battalion King's Royal Rifle Corps are the only Cadet Unit in the United Kingdom to have been granted such an honour and are permitted to wear the miniature 60th Cap Badge with the single Battle Honour, and call their Cadets "Riflemen".
sentence_114: The 2nd Cadet Battalion, the King's Royal Rifle Corps was formed in 1942 when a [[Home_Guard_(United_Kingdom)|Home Guard]] instruction was issued ordering each Home Guard battalion to raise a cadet unit.
