title: Lincoln, England
sentence_0: Lincoln ([[English|/ˈlɪŋkən/]]) is a [[Cathedral_city|cathedral city]] and [[County_town|county town]] of [[Lincolnshire|Lincolnshire]] in the [[East_Midlands|East Midlands]] of England.
sentence_1: The [[Non-metropolitan_district|non-metropolitan district]] of Lincoln had a 2012 population of 94,600.
sentence_2: The 2011 census gave the urban area of Lincoln, which includes [[North_Hykeham|North Hykeham]] and [[Waddington,_Lincolnshire|Waddington]], a population of 130,200.
sentence_3: [[Roman_Britain|Roman]] [[Lindum_Colonia|Lindum Colonia]] developed from an [[Iron_Age|Iron Age]] settlement on the [[River_Witham|River Witham]].
sentence_4: The city's landmarks include [[Lincoln_Cathedral|Lincoln Cathedral]], an example of [[English_Gothic_architecture|English Gothic architecture]] and the tallest building in the world for over 200 years, and the 11th-century [[Norman_architecture|Norman]] [[Lincoln_Castle|Lincoln Castle]].
sentence_5: The city is home to the University of Lincoln and [[Bishop_Grosseteste_University|Bishop Grosseteste University]], and to both [[Lincoln_City_F.C.|Lincoln City FC]] and [[Lincoln_United_F.C.|Lincoln United FC]].
sentence_6: See also: [[Timeline_of_Lincoln|Timeline of Lincoln]]
sentence_7: The earliest origins of Lincoln can be traced to the remains of an [[Iron_Age|Iron Age]] settlement of round wooden dwellings (which were discovered by archaeologists in 1972) that have been dated to the 1st century BC.
sentence_8: This settlement was built by a deep pool (the modern [[Brayford_Pool|Brayford Pool]]) in the [[River_Witham|River Witham]] at the foot of a large hill (on which the [[Normans|Normans]] later built Lincoln Cathedral and [[Lincoln_Castle|Lincoln Castle]]).
sentence_9: The origins of the name Lincoln may come from this period, when the settlement is thought to have been named in the [[Brythonic_languages|Brittonic language]] of Iron Age Britain's [[Celts|Celtic]] inhabitants as Lindon "The Pool", presumably referring to Brayford Pool (compare the etymology of the name [[Dublin|Dublin]], from the Gaelic dubh linn "black pool").
sentence_10: The extent of this original settlement is unknown as its remains are now buried deep beneath the later Roman and medieval ruins and modern Lincoln.
sentence_11: Main article: [[Lindum_Colonia|Lindum Colonia]]
sentence_12: The Romans conquered this part of Britain in AD 48 and shortly afterwards built a legionary fortress high on a hill overlooking the natural lake formed by the widening of the [[River_Witham|River Witham]] (the modern day [[Brayford_Pool|Brayford Pool]]) and at the northern end of the [[Fosse_Way|Fosse Way]] Roman road (A46).
sentence_13: The Celtic name Lindon was subsequently [[Latin_language|Latinised]] to Lindum and given the title Colonia when it was converted into a settlement for army veterans.
sentence_14: The conversion to a colonia was made when the legion moved on to [[York|York]] (Eboracum) in AD 71.
sentence_15: Lindum colonia or more fully, Colonia Domitiana Lindensium, after the Emperor [[Domitian|Domitian]] who ruled at the time, was established within the walls of the hilltop fortress with the addition of an extension of about equal area, down the hillside to the waterside below.
sentence_16: It became a major flourishing settlement, accessible from the sea both through the [[River_Trent|River Trent]] and through the [[River_Witham|River Witham]].
sentence_17: On the basis of the patently corrupt list of British bishops who attended the [[Council_of_Arles_(314)|314 Council of Arles]], the city is now often considered to have been the capital of the province of [[Flavia_Caesariensis|Flavia Caesariensis]] which was formed during the late-3rd century [[Diocletian_Reforms|Diocletian Reforms]].
sentence_18: Subsequently, the town and its waterways fell into decline.
sentence_19: By the close of the 5th century it was largely deserted, although some occupation continued under a Praefectus Civitatis – [[Paulinus_of_York|Saint Paulinus]] visited a man holding this office in Lincoln in AD 629.
sentence_20: Main article: [[Lincoln_Castle|Lincoln Castle]]
sentence_21: Germanic tribes from the North Sea area settled Lincolnshire during the fifth and sixth centuries.
sentence_22: The Latin Lindum Colonia was shortened in their language, [[Old_English|Old English]], first to Lindocolina, then to Lincylene.
sentence_23: After the first [[Viking|Viking]] raids, the city again rose to some importance, with overseas trading connections.
sentence_24: In Viking times Lincoln was a trading centre with its own mint, by far the most important in Lincolnshire and by the end of the 10th century, comparable in output to that of [[York|York]].
sentence_25: After the establishment of the [[Danelaw|Danelaw]] in 886, Lincoln became one of the [[Five_Burghs|Five Boroughs]] in the [[East_Midlands|East Midlands]].
sentence_26: Excavations at Flaxengate reveal that the area, deserted since Roman times, received timber-framed buildings fronting a new street system in about 900.
sentence_27: Lincoln underwent an economic explosion with the settlement of the [[Danes_(Germanic_tribe)|Danes]].
sentence_28: Like York, the Upper City seems to have had purely administrative functions up to 850 or so, while the Lower City, down the hill towards the River Witham, may have been largely deserted.
sentence_29: By 950, however, the Witham banks were developed, with the Lower City resettled and the suburb of Wigford emerging as a trading centre.
sentence_30: In 1068, two years after the [[Norman_conquest_of_England|Norman conquest of England]], [[William_I_of_England|William I]] ordered [[Lincoln_Castle|Lincoln Castle]] to be built on the site of the old Roman settlement, for the same strategic reasons and controlling the same road.
sentence_31: Main articles: [[Lincoln_Cathedral|Lincoln Cathedral]] and [[Bishop_of_Lincoln|Bishop of Lincoln]]
sentence_32: Construction of the first Lincoln Cathedral, within its close or walled precinct facing the castle, began when the see was removed from the quiet backwater of [[Dorchester-on-Thames,_Oxfordshire|Dorchester-on-Thames]], Oxfordshire, and was completed in 1092; it was rebuilt after a fire but destroyed by an earthquake in 1185.
sentence_33: The rebuilt Lincoln Minster, enlarged to the east at each rebuilding, was on a magnificent scale, its [[Crossing_tower|crossing tower]] crowned by a spire reputed to have been the highest in Europe at 525 ft (160 m).
sentence_34: When completed, the central of the three spires is widely accepted to have succeeded the [[Egyptian_pyramids|Great Pyramids of Egypt]] as the tallest man-made structure in the world.
sentence_35: The Lincoln bishops were among the magnates of medieval England.
sentence_36: The [[Diocese_of_Lincoln|Diocese of Lincoln]], the largest in England, had more monasteries than the rest of England put together, and the diocese was supported by large estates.
sentence_37: When [[Magna_Carta|Magna Carta]] was drawn up in 1215, one of the witnesses was [[Hugh_of_Wells|Hugh of Wells]], [[Bishop_of_Lincoln|Bishop of Lincoln]].
sentence_38: One of only four surviving originals of the document is preserved in [[Lincoln_Castle|Lincoln Castle]].
sentence_39: Among the most famous bishops of Lincoln were [[Robert_Bloet|Robert Bloet]], the magnificent [[Justiciar|justiciar]] to [[Henry_I_of_England|Henry I]], [[Hugh_of_Avalon|Hugh of Avalon]], the cathedral builder canonised as [[St_Hugh_of_Lincoln|St Hugh of Lincoln]], [[Robert_Grosseteste|Robert Grosseteste]], the 13th century intellectual, [[Henry_Beaufort|Henry Beaufort]], chancellor of [[Henry_V_of_England|Henry V]] and [[Henry_VI_of_England|Henry VI]], [[Thomas_Rotherham|Thomas Rotherham]], a politician deeply involved in the Wars of the Roses, [[Philip_Repyngdon|Philip Repyngdon]], chaplain to [[Henry_IV_of_England|Henry IV]] and defender of [[John_Wycliffe|Wycliffe]], and [[Thomas_Wolsey|Thomas Wolsey]], the lord chancellor of [[Henry_VIII_of_England|Henry VIII]].
sentence_40: Theologian [[William_de_Montibus|William de Montibus]] was the head of the cathedral school and chancellor until his death in 1213.
sentence_41: The administrative centre was the [[Lincoln_Medieval_Bishop's_Palace|Bishop's Palace]], the third element in the central complex.
sentence_42: When it was built in the late 12th century, the Bishop's Palace was one of the most important buildings in England.
sentence_43: Built by Hugh of Lincoln, its East Hall over a vaulted undercroft is the earliest surviving example of a roofed domestic hall.
sentence_44: The chapel range and entrance tower were built by Bishop William of Alnwick, who modernised the palace in the 1430s.
sentence_45: Both Henry VIII and [[James_VI_and_I|James I]] were guests there; the palace was sacked by royalist troops during the [[English_Civil_War|civil war]] in 1648.
sentence_46: During [[The_Anarchy|the Anarchy]], in 1141 Lincoln was the site of a [[Battle_of_Lincoln_(1141)|battle]] between [[Stephen_of_England|King Stephen]] and the forces of [[Empress_Matilda|Empress Matilda]], led by her illegitimate half-brother [[Robert,_1st_Earl_of_Gloucester|Robert, 1st Earl of Gloucester]].
sentence_47: After fierce fighting in the city's streets, Stephen's forces were defeated.
sentence_48: Stephen himself was captured and taken to [[Bristol|Bristol]].
sentence_49: By 1150, Lincoln was among the wealthiest towns in England.
sentence_50: The basis of the economy was cloth and [[Wool|wool]], exported to [[Flanders|Flanders]]; Lincoln [[Weaving|weavers]] had set up a [[Guild|guild]] in 1130 to produce Lincoln Cloth, especially the fine dyed "scarlet" and "green", whose reputation was later enhanced by the legendary [[Robin_Hood|Robin Hood]] wearing woollens of [[Lincoln_green|Lincoln green]].
sentence_51: In the Guildhall that surmounts the city gate called the [[Guildhall_and_Stonebow,_Lincoln|Stonebow]], the ancient Council Chamber contains Lincoln's civic insignia, a fine collection of civic regalia.
sentence_52: Outside the precincts of cathedral and castle, the old quarter clustered around the Bailgate, and down Steep Hill to the [[High_Bridge,_Lincoln|High Bridge]], whose half-timbered housing juts out over the river.
sentence_53: There are three ancient churches: [[St_Mary_le_Wigford|St Mary le Wigford]] and [[St_Peter_at_Gowts|St Peter at Gowts]] are both 11th century in origin and [[St_Mary_Magdalene,_Bailgate,_Lincoln|St Mary Magdalene]], built in the late 13th century.
sentence_54: The last is an unusual English dedication to the saint whose cult was coming into vogue on the European continent at that time.
sentence_55: Lincoln was home to one of the five main Jewish communities in England, well established before it was officially noted in 1154.
sentence_56: In 1190, [[Antisemitism|anti-Semitic]] riots that started in [[King's_Lynn|King's Lynn]], Norfolk, spread to Lincoln; the Jewish community took refuge with royal officials, but their habitations were plundered.
sentence_57: The so-called [[Norman_House|House of Aaron]] has a two-storey street frontage that is essentially 12th century and a nearby [[Jew's_House|Jew's House]] likewise bears witness to the Jewish population.
sentence_58: In 1255, the affair called "[[Blood_libel|The Libel of Lincoln]]" in which prominent Jews of Lincoln, accused of the ritual murder of a Christian boy (the [[Little_Saint_Hugh_of_Lincoln|Little Saint Hugh of Lincoln]] in medieval folklore) were sent to the [[Tower_of_London|Tower of London]] and 18 were executed.
sentence_59: The Jews were expelled in total in 1290.
sentence_60: Thirteenth-century Lincoln was England's third largest city and a favourite of more than one king.
sentence_61: During the [[First_Barons'_War|First Barons' War]], it became caught up in the strife between the king and rebel barons who had allied with the French.
sentence_62: It was [[Battle_of_Lincoln_(1217)|here]] and at [[Dover|Dover]] that the French and Rebel army was defeated.
sentence_63: In the aftermath, the town was pillaged for having sided with [[Louis_VIII_of_France|Prince Louis]].
sentence_64: In the [[Second_Barons'_War|Second Barons' War]], of 1266, the disinherited rebels attacked the Jews of Lincoln, ransacked the synagogue, and burned the records which registered debts.
sentence_65: According to some historians, the city's fortunes began to decline in the 14th century, although others have argued that the city remained buoyant in both trade and communications well into the 15th century.
sentence_66: Thus in 1409, the city was made a county in its own right known as the County of the City of Lincoln.
sentence_67: Thereafter, additional rights being conferred on the town by successive monarchs, including those of an assay town (controlling metal manufacturing, for example).
sentence_68: The oldest surviving [[Secularity|secular]] [[Drama|drama]] in English, [[The_Interlude_of_the_Student_and_the_Girl|The Interlude of the Student and the Girl]] (c. 1300), may have originated from Lincoln.
sentence_69: Lincoln's coat of arms, not officially endorsed by the [[College_of_Arms|College of Arms]], is believed to date from the 14th century.
sentence_70: It is [[Argent_(heraldry)|Argent]] on a [[Cross_(heraldry)|cross]] [[Gules_(heraldry)|gules]] a fleur-de-lis [[Or_(heraldry)|or]].
sentence_71: The cross is believed to derive from the Diocese of Lincoln.
sentence_72: The fleur-de-lis is the symbol of the Virgin Mary, to whom the cathedral is dedicated.
sentence_73: The [[Motto|motto]] is CIVITAS LINCOLNIA (Latin for City of Lincoln).
sentence_74: The Dissolution of the Monasteries cut off Lincoln's main source of diocesan income and dried up the network of patronage controlled by the bishop.
sentence_75: No fewer than seven monasteries closed within the city alone.
sentence_76: A number of nearby abbeys were also closed, which further diminished the region's political power.
sentence_77: A symbol of Lincoln's economic and political decline came in 1549, when the cathedral's great spire rotted and collapsed and was not replaced.
sentence_78: However, the comparative poverty of post-medieval Lincoln preserved pre-medieval structures that would probably have been lost under more prosperous conditions.
sentence_79: Between 1642 and 1651, during the [[English_Civil_War|English Civil War]], Lincoln was on the frontier between the [[Cavalier|Royalist]] and [[Roundhead|Parliamentary]] forces and changed hands several times.
sentence_80: Many buildings were badly damaged.
sentence_81: Lincoln now had no major industry and no easy access to the sea.
sentence_82: While the rest of the country was beginning to prosper in the early 18th century, Lincoln suffered, travellers often commenting on what had essentially become a one-street town.
sentence_83: By the [[Georgian_era|Georgian era]], Lincoln's fortunes began to pick up, thanks in part to the [[British_Agricultural_Revolution|Agricultural Revolution]].
sentence_84: The re-opening of the [[Foss_Dyke|Foss Dyke]] canal allowed coal and other raw materials vital to industry to be brought into the city more easily.
sentence_85: Along with the economic growth of Lincoln in this period, the city boundaries were expanded to include the West Common.
sentence_86: To this day, an annual Beat the Boundaries walk takes place along the perimeter of the common.
sentence_87: Coupled with the arrival of railway links, Lincoln boomed again during the [[Industrial_Revolution|Industrial Revolution]], and several world-famous companies arose, such as [[Ruston_(engine_builder)|Ruston's]], [[Clayton_&_Shuttleworth|Clayton]]'s, [[Proctor|Proctor]]'s and William Foster's.
sentence_88: Lincoln began to excel in heavy engineering, building locomotives, steam shovels and all manner of heavy machinery.
sentence_89: A permanent military presence came with the completion of the [[The_Old_Barracks,_Lincoln|"Old Barracks"]] (now occupied by the [[Museum_of_Lincolnshire_Life|Museum of Lincolnshire Life]]) in 1857.
sentence_90: These were replaced by the "New Barracks" (now [[Sobraon_Barracks|Sobraon Barracks]]) in 1890, when [[Lincoln_Drill_Hall|Lincoln Drill Hall]] in Broadgate also opened.
sentence_91: Lincoln was hit by a [[Typhoid|typhoid]] epidemic between November 1904 and August 1905 caused by polluted drinking water from Hartsholme Lake and the [[River_Witham|River Witham]].
sentence_92: Over 1,000 people contracted the disease and fatalities totalled 113, including the man responsible for the city's water supply, Liam Kirk of Baker Crescent.
sentence_93: Near the beginning of the epidemic, Dr Alexander Cruickshank Houston installed a chlorine [[Disinfection|disinfection]] system just ahead of the poorly operating slow sand filter to kill the fatal bacteria.
sentence_94: [[Water_chlorination|Chlorination]] of the water supply continued until 1911 when a new supply was implemented.
sentence_95: The Lincoln chlorination episode was one of the first uses of the chemical to disinfect a water supply.
sentence_96: Westgate Water Tower was constructed to provide new water supplies to the city.
sentence_97: In the two [[World_war|world wars]], Lincoln switched to war production.
sentence_98: The first ever [[Tank|tanks]] were invented, designed and built in Lincoln by [[William_Foster_&_Co.|William Foster & Co.]] in the [[First_World_War|First World War]] and population growth provided more workers for even greater expansion.
sentence_99: The tanks were tested on land now covered by Tritton Road in the south-west suburbs.
sentence_100: During the [[Second_World_War|Second World War]], Lincoln produced a vast array of war goods: tanks, aircraft, munitions and military vehicles.
sentence_101: Ruston & Hornsby produced [[Diesel_engine|diesel engines]] for ships and locomotives, then by teaming up with former colleagues of [[Frank_Whittle|Frank Whittle]] and [[Power_Jets|Power Jets]] Ltd, in the early 1950s, R & H (which became RGT) opened the first production line to build [[Gas_turbine|gas turbine]] engines for land-based and sea-based energy production.
sentence_102: Its success made it the largest single employer in the city, providing over 5,000 jobs in its factory and research facilities, making it a rich takeover target for industrial conglomerates.
sentence_103: It was subsumed by [[English_Electric|English Electric]] in November 1966, which was then bought by [[General_Electric_Company|GEC]] in 1968, with diesel engine production being transferred to the Ruston Diesels Division in [[Newton-le-Willows|Newton-le-Willows]], Lancashire, at the former [[Vulcan_Foundry|Vulcan Foundry]], which was eventually bought by the German MAN Diesel (now [[MAN_Energy_Solutions|MAN Energy Solutions]]) in June 2000.
sentence_104: Pelham Works merged with [[Alstom|Alstom]] of France in the late 1980s, then was bought in 2003 by Siemens of Germany as [[Siemens_Power_Generation|Siemens Industrial Turbomachinery]].
sentence_105: This includes what is left of Napier Turbochargers.
sentence_106: Plans came early in 2008 for a new plant outside the city at Teal Park, [[North_Hykeham|North Hykeham]].
sentence_107: However, Siemens made large-scale redundancies and moved jobs to both [[Sweden|Sweden]] and the [[Netherlands|Netherlands]].
sentence_108: The factory now employs 1300 people.
sentence_109: R & H's former Beevor Foundry is now owned by Hoval Group, which makes industrial boilers ([[Woodchips|wood chip]]).
sentence_110: The Aerospace Manufacturing Facility (AMF) in Firth Road passed from Alstom Aerospace Ltd to [[Industria_de_Turbo_Propulsores|ITP Engines]] UK in January 2009.
sentence_111: Lincoln's second largest private employer is James Dawson and Son, a belting and hose manufacturer founded there in the late 19th century.
sentence_112: Its two sites are both in Tritton Road.
sentence_113: The main one, next to the University of Lincoln, used Lincoln's last coal-fired boiler, until it was replaced by a gas-powered one in July 2018.
sentence_114: Dawson's became part of the Hull-based [[Fenner_plc|Fenner]] group in the late 1970s.
sentence_115: New suburbs were built in the years after 1945, but heavy industry declined towards the end of the 20th century.
sentence_116: Nevertheless, more people in Lincoln are still employed today in building gas turbines than in any other field.
sentence_117: Much development, particularly around the Brayford area, has followed the construction of the University of Lincoln's Brayford Campus, which opened in 1996.
sentence_118: In 2012, Bishop Grosseteste teaching college was also awarded university status.
sentence_119: Lincoln's economy is based mainly on public administration, commerce, arable farming and tourism, with industrial relics like [[Ruston_(engine_builder)|Ruston]] (now Siemens) still in existence.
sentence_120: However, many of Lincoln's industrial giants have long ceased production there, leaving large empty industrial warehouse-like buildings.
sentence_121: More recently, these have become multi-occupant units, with the likes of [[Lincs_FM|Lincs FM]] radio station (in the Titanic Works) and [[LA_Fitness|LA Fitness]] gym taking up space.
sentence_122: The main employment sectors in Lincoln are public administration, education and health, which account for 34 per cent of the workforce.
sentence_123: Distribution, restaurants and hotels account for 25 per cent.
sentence_124: Like many other cities, Lincoln has developed a growing [[Information_technology|IT]] economy, with many e-commerce mail order companies set up, along with a plethora of other, more conventional small industrial businesses.
sentence_125: One reason behind the University of Lincoln was to increase inward investment and act as a springboard for small companies.
sentence_126: Its presence has also drawn many more licensed premises to the town centre around the Brayford Pool.
sentence_127: A small business unit next door to a university accommodation building, the Think Tank, opened in June 2009.
sentence_128: The [[Extra_(service_areas)|Extra]] motorway services company is based on Castle Hill, with most new UK service areas being built by Swayfields, which is the parent company.
sentence_129: There are two main electronics companies in the town: [[Chelmsford|Chelmsford]]-based [[English_Electric_Valve_Company|e2V]] (formerly [[Associated_Electrical_Industries|Associated Electrical Industries]] before 1961) is situated between Carholme Road (A57) and the [[Foss_Dyke|Foss Dyke]] next-door to Carholme Golf Club; and [[Dynex_Semiconductor|Dynex Semiconductor]] (formerly Marconi Electronic Devices) is in Doddington Road (B1190) near the A46 bypass and near [[North_Hykeham|North Hykeham]].
sentence_130: Bifrangi, an Italian company making [[Crankshaft|crankshafts]] for off-road vehicles (tractors) using a [[Screw_press|screw press]] is based at the former Tower Works owned by Smith-Clayton Forge Ltd.
sentence_131: Lincoln is the hub of a wider area encompassing satellite settlements such as Welton, Saxilby, Skellingthorpe and Washingborough, which look to Lincoln for most service and employment needs.
sentence_132: Adding them to the city's population raises it to 165,000.
sentence_133: Lincoln is the main centre for jobs and facilities in Central Lincolnshire, and performs a regional role over much of Lincolnshire and parts of Nottinghamshire.
sentence_134: According to a document entitled "Central Lincolnshire Local Plan Core Strategy", Lincoln is within a "travel-to-work" area with a population of about 300,000.
sentence_135: Since 1994 Lincoln has gained two universities, in association with its growth in the services sector.
sentence_136: New blocks of flats, restaurants and entertainment venues have appeared.
sentence_137: Entertainment venues linked to the universities include [[The_Engine_Shed|The Engine Shed]] and The Venue Cinema.
sentence_138: Around the [[B1003_road|Tritton Road (B1003)]] trading estate, new businesses have begun trading from large units with car parking.
sentence_139: Lincoln has a choice of seven large national supermarkets (Tesco, Asda, Sainsbury, Waitrose, Morrisons, Aldi and Lidl).
sentence_140: The St Mark's Square complex has [[Debenhams|Debenhams]] as its flagship store and an accompanying trading estate of well-known chain stores.
sentence_141: The city is a tourist centre for those visiting historic buildings that include the cathedral, the castle and the medieval Bishop's Palace.
sentence_142: [[The_Collection_(Lincolnshire)|The Collection]], of which the Usher Gallery is now part, is an important attraction, partly in a purpose-built venue, it currently contains over 2,000,000 objects, and was one of the four finalists for the 2006 [[Gulbenkian_Prize|Gulbenkian Prize]].
sentence_143: Any material from official archaeological excavations in Lincolnshire is eventually deposited in The Collection, so that it continues to grow.
sentence_144: Other attractions include the [[Museum_of_Lincolnshire_Life|Museum of Lincolnshire Life]] and the International Bomber Command Centre.
sentence_145: Tranquil destinations close by are [[Whisby_Nature_Park|Whisby Nature Reserve]] and [[Hartsholme_Country_Park|Hartsholme Country Park]] (including the Swanholme Lakes [[SSSI|SSSI]]), while noisier entertainment can be found at [[RAF_Waddington|Waddington airfield]], [[RAF_Scampton|Scampton airfield]] (base of the [[Royal_Air_Force|RAF's]] [[Red_Arrows|Red Arrows]] jet [[Aerobatic|aerobatic]] team), the County Showground or the Cadwell Park [[Auto_racing|motor racing]] circuit near [[Louth,_Lincolnshire|Louth]].
sentence_146: Early in December the Bailgate area holds an annual [[Lincoln_Christmas_Market|Christmas Market]] in and around the Castle grounds, shaped by the traditional German-style Christmas markets as found in cities, including Lincoln's twin town [[Neustadt_an_der_Weinstrasse|Neustadt an der Weinstrasse]].
sentence_147: In 2010, for the first time in its history, the event was cancelled due to "atrocious" snowfalls across most of the United Kingdom.
sentence_148: Lincoln has many churches and chapels in the city region.
sentence_149: Most notable is the Anglican Cathedral of St Mary, but also prominent is the Catholic Church of [[St_Hugh's_Church,_Lincoln|St Hugh's]] Among many others, there are two Baptist churches.
sentence_150: There are currently two Jewish communities.
sentence_151: A purpose-built mosque and cultural centre opened in Lincoln in 2015, becoming the first in the city.
sentence_152: Lincoln lies 157 mi (253 km) north of London, at a height of 67 ft (20.4 m) above sea level by the River Witham up to 246 ft (75.0 m) on Castle Hill.
sentence_153: It fills a gap in the [[Lincoln_Cliff|Lincoln Cliff]] escarpment running north and south through central [[Lincolnshire|Lincolnshire]] and with altitudes up to 200 feet (61 metres).
sentence_154: The city is 76 miles (123 km) north-east of [[Birmingham|Birmingham]], 32 miles (51 km) north-east of [[Nottingham|Nottingham]], 47 miles (76 km) north of [[Peterborough|Peterborough]] and 40 miles (64 km) east south-east of [[Sheffield|Sheffield]].
sentence_155: The city lies on the [[River_Witham|River Witham]], which flows through this gap.
sentence_156: Lincoln is thus divided informally into two zones, known unofficially as uphill and downhill.
sentence_157: The uphill area comprises the northern part of the city, on top of the Lincoln Cliff (to the north of the gap).
sentence_158: This area includes the historical quarter, including [[Lincoln_Cathedral|Lincoln Cathedral]], [[Lincoln_Castle|Lincoln Castle]] and the Medieval Bishop's Palace, known locally as The Bail (although described in tourist promotional literature as the Cathedral Quarter).
sentence_159: It includes residential suburbs to the north and north-east.
sentence_160: The downhill area comprises the city centre and suburbs to the south and south-west.
sentence_161: [[Steep_Hill|Steep Hill]] is a narrow, pedestrian street connecting the two (too steep for vehicular traffic).
sentence_162: It passes through an archway known as the Stonebow.
sentence_163: This divide, peculiar to Lincoln, was once an important class distinction, with uphill more affluent and downhill less so.
sentence_164: The distinction dates from the time of the [[Norman_conquest|Norman conquest]], when the religious and military elite occupied the hilltop.
sentence_165: The expansion of suburbs in both parts of the city since the mid-19th century has diluted the distinction, but uphill housing continues to fetch a premium.
sentence_166: The [[Mute_swan|mute swan]] is an iconic species for Lincoln.
sentence_167: Many pairs nest each year beside the Brayford, and they feature on the university's heraldic emblem.
sentence_168: Other bird life within the city includes [[Peregrine_falcon|peregrine falcon]], [[Tawny_owl|tawny owl]] and [[Common_kingfisher|common kingfisher]].
sentence_169: Mammals on the city edges include [[Red_fox|red fox]], [[Roe_deer|roe deer]] and [[Least_weasel|least weasel]].
sentence_170: [[European_perch|European perch]], [[Northern_pike|northern pike]] and [[Bream|bream]] are among fish seen in the Witham and Brayford.
sentence_171: Nature reserves around the city include Greetwell Hollow SSSI, Swanholme SSSI, [[Whisby_Moor|Whisby Nature Park]], [[Boultham|Boultham Mere]] and [[Hartsholme_Country_Park|Hartsholme Country Park]].
sentence_172: Since about 2016, [[Little_egret|Little egrets]] have nested in the Birchwood area and [[Eurasian_otter|otters]] have been seen in the River Witham.
sentence_173: Both species are native to Britain and repopulating the area after extermination.
sentence_174: Several invasive species of plants and animals have reached Lincoln.
sentence_175: [[Japanese_knotweed|Japanese knotweed]] and [[Himalayan_balsam|Himalayan balsam]] are Asian plant species around the River Witham.
sentence_176: [[Galinsoga|Galinsoga]] and [[Amsinckia|Amsinckia]] are American species found among city weeds.
sentence_177: [[American_mink|American mink]] are occasionally seen on the Witham.
sentence_178: Lincoln has a typical East Midland [[Maritime_climate|maritime climate]] with cool summers and mild winters.
sentence_179: The nearest [[Meteorological_Office|Met Office]] weather station is at [[RAF_Waddington|RAF Waddington]], about 4 miles (6 kilometres) to the south.
sentence_180: Temperature extremes since 1948 have ranged between 35.1 °C (95.2 °F) on 25 July 2019, and −15.6 °C (3.9 °F) in February 1956.
sentence_181: A former weather station holds the record for the lowest daytime maximum temperature recorded in England in the month of December: −9.0 °C (15.8 °F) on 17 December 1981.
sentence_182: The coldest recent temperature was −10.4 °C (13.3 °F) in December 2010, although another weather station, at [[Scampton|Scampton]], a similar distance north of the city centre, fell to −15.6 °C (3.9 °F), so equalling Waddington's record low set in 1956.
sentence_183: Closure of [[Lincoln_St_Marks_railway_station|Lincoln St Marks]] in 1985 left the city with [[Lincoln_railway_station|Lincoln Central]], soon renamed plain Lincoln, as its own station.
sentence_184: Destinations for [[East_Midlands_Railway|East Midlands Railway]] and [[Northern_Trains|Northern Trains]] services from its five platforms include [[Newark_North_Gate_railway_station|Newark]], [[Sheffield_railway_station|Sheffield]], [[Leeds_railway_station|Leeds]], [[Nottingham_railway_station|Nottingham]], [[Grimsby_railway_station|Grimsby]] and Peterborough.
sentence_185: [[London_North_Eastern_Railway|London North Eastern Railway]] runs services to [[London_King's_Cross_railway_station|London King's Cross]], calling at [[Newark_North_Gate_railway_station|Newark]], Peterborough and [[Stevenage_railway_station|Stevenage]].
sentence_186: The £19-million [[A46_road|A46]] north-west bypass opened in December 1985, with an eastern A15 bypass scheduled to commence construction in 2017, but the collapse of the contractor, [[Carillion|Carillion]], means it is now scheduled to open in May 2020.
sentence_187: The final, southern part of the Lincoln ring road is now under construction (2020).
sentence_188: B1190 is an east–west road through Lincoln, between the Nottinghamshire-Lincolnshire boundary on the (Roman) [[Foss_Dyke|Foss Dyke]] and A57 and in the east at [[Thimbleby,_Lincolnshire|Thimbleby]] on the [[A158_road|A158]] near Horncastle.
sentence_189: Until the 1980s, the only two main roads through Lincoln were the A46 and A15, both feeding traffic along the High Street.
sentence_190: At the intersection of Guildhall Street and the High Street, these met at the termination of the A57.
sentence_191: North of the city centre, the former A15, [[Riseholme,_Lincolnshire|Riseholme]] Road, is the B1226, and the old A46, [[Nettleham|Nettleham]] Road, the B1182.
sentence_192: The early northern inner ring-road, formed of Yarborough Road and Yarborough Crescent, is today numbered B1273.
sentence_193: [[East_Midlands_Airport|East Midlands Airport]], 43 miles from Lincoln, is the main international airport serving the county.
sentence_194: It mainly handles European flights with low-cost airlines.
sentence_195: [[Humberside_Airport|Humberside Airport]], 29 miles north of Lincoln, is the only airport located in the county.
sentence_196: It has a small number of flights mainly to hub airports such as [[Amsterdam|Amsterdam]].
sentence_197: [[Doncaster_Sheffield_Airport|Doncaster Sheffield Airport]] also serves Lincoln.
sentence_198: It mainly caters to low-cost airlines and lies just outside the East Midlands Region in South Yorkshire.
sentence_199: The older of Lincoln's two higher education institutions, [[Bishop_Grosseteste_University|Bishop Grosseteste University]], was started as a teacher training college linked to the [[Anglican_Church|Anglican Church]] in 1862.
sentence_200: During the 1990s, it branched out into other subject areas with a focus on the arts and drama.
sentence_201: It became a university college in 2006 with degree powers taken over from the University of Leicester.
sentence_202: The college became a university in 2012.
sentence_203: An annual graduation celebration takes place in Lincoln Cathedral.
sentence_204: Bishop Grosseteste University has not linked with the University of Lincoln.
sentence_205: The larger University of Lincoln started as the University of Lincolnshire and Humberside in 1996, when the University of Humberside opened a Lincoln campus next to [[Brayford_Pool|Brayford Pool]].
sentence_206: Lincoln School of Art and Design (which was Lincolnshire's main outlet for higher education) and Riseholme Agricultural College, previously been part of [[De_Montfort_University|De Montfort University]] in [[Leicester|Leicester]], were absorbed into the University of Lincoln in 2001, and subsequently the Lincoln campus took priority over the [[Kingston_upon_Hull|Hull]] campus.
sentence_207: Most buildings were built after 2001.
sentence_208: The name changed to the University of Lincoln in September 2002.
sentence_209: In the 2005–2006 academic year, 8,292 full-time undergraduates were studying there.
sentence_210: This rose to 11,900.
sentence_211: Further education courses in Lincoln are provided by [[Lincoln_College,_Lincolnshire|Lincoln College]], which is the largest education institution in [[Lincolnshire|Lincolnshire]], with 18,500 students, of whom 2,300 are full-time.
sentence_212: There is a specialist creative college, Access Creative, offering courses in music, media and games design to some 180 students, all full-time.
sentence_213: The school system in Lincoln is anomalous within Lincolnshire despite being part of the same [[Local_education_authority|local education authority]] (LEA), as most of the county retained the [[Grammar_schools_in_the_United_Kingdom|grammar-school]] system.
sentence_214: In 1952, [[William_Farr_School|William Farr School]] was founded in Welton, a nearby village.
sentence_215: Lincoln itself had four single-sex grammar schools until September 1974.
sentence_216: [[The_Priory_Academy_LSST|The Priory Academy LSST]] converted to academy status in 2008, in turn establishing [[The_Priory_Federation_of_Academies|The Priory Federation of Academies]].
sentence_217: [[The_Priory_Witham_Academy|The Priory Witham Academy]] was formed when the federation absorbed Moorlands Infant School, Usher Junior School and Ancaster High School.
sentence_218: The [[Priory_City_of_Lincoln_Academy|Priory City of Lincoln Academy]] was formed when the City of Lincoln Community College merged into the federation.
sentence_219: Both schools were rebuilt after substantial investment by the federation.
sentence_220: Cherry Willingham School joined the federation in 2017, becoming The Priory Pembroke Academy.
sentence_221: The Lincolnshire LEA was ranked 32nd in the country based on its proportion of pupils attaining at least 5 A–C grades at GCSE including maths and English (62.2% compared with a national average of 58.2%).
sentence_222: There are four special-needs schools in Lincoln: Fortuna Primary School (5–11 years old), Sincil Sports College (11–16), St Christopher's School (3–16) and St Francis Community Special School (2–18).
sentence_223: The local newspaper, the Lincolnshire Echo, was founded in 1894.
sentence_224: Local radio stations are [[BBC_Lincolnshire|BBC Lincolnshire]] on 94.9 FM, its commercial rival [[Lincs_FM|Lincs FM]] on 102.2FM and Lincoln City Radio on 103.6 FM a community radio station catering mainly for listeners over 50 .
sentence_225: The Lincolnite is an online mobile publication covering the greater-Lincoln area.
sentence_226: Local listeners can also receive [[Siren_FM|Siren FM]], on 107.3 FM from the University of Lincoln.
sentence_227: The student publication The Linc is available online and in print and targets the University of Lincoln's student population.
sentence_228: [[BBC_Look_North_(East_Yorkshire_and_Lincolnshire)|BBC Look North]] has a bureau in Lincoln as part of its coverage of Lincolnshire and East Yorkshire.
sentence_229: The three TV reporters based in Lincoln serve both BBC Look North and East Midlands Today.
sentence_230: ITV News also hold a newsroom in Lincoln.
sentence_231: Lincoln has a professional [[Association_football|football]] team, [[Lincoln_City_FC|Lincoln City FC]], nicknamed "The Imps", which plays at the [[Sincil_Bank|Sincil Bank]] stadium on the southern edge of the city.
sentence_232: The collapse of [[ITV_Digital|ITV Digital]], which owed Lincoln City FC more than £100,000, in 2002 saw the team faced with bankruptcy, but it was saved by a fund-raising venture among the fans, which returned ownership of the club to them, where it has remained since.
sentence_233: The club was famously the first team to be relegated from the English [[Football_League|Football League]], when automatic relegation to the [[Football_Conference|Football Conference]] was introduced from the 1986–87 season.
sentence_234: Lincoln City regained its league place at the first attempt and held onto it until the 2010–11 season, when it was again relegated to the Football Conference.
sentence_235: Its most successful era was in the early 1980s, winning promotion from the Fourth Division in 1981 and narrowly missing promotion to the Second Division in the two years that followed.
sentence_236: More recently, the club reached the quarter-finals of the FA Cup in 2017, beating several teams in the top two tiers of English football before being defeated by [[Arsenal_F.C.|Arsenal]].
sentence_237: Lincoln City was the first club managed by [[Graham_Taylor_(footballer)|Graham Taylor]], who went on to manage the [[English_national_football_team|English national football team]] from 1990 to 1993.
sentence_238: He was at Lincoln City from 1972 to 1977, during which time the club won promotion from the Fourth Division as champions in 1976.
sentence_239: The club also won the Football League Division Three North title on three separate occasions, a joint record.
sentence_240: Lincoln is also home to [[Lincoln_United_FC|Lincoln United FC]], [[Lincoln_Moorlands_Railway_FC|Lincoln Moorlands Railway FC]] and Lincoln Griffins Ladies FC.
sentence_241: Lincoln hosts upcoming sports teams and facilities such [[American_Football|American football]]'s Lincolnshire Bombers, which plays in the [[BAFA_National_Leagues|BAFA National Leagues]], the [[Lincolnshire_Bombers_Roller_Girls|Lincolnshire Bombers Roller Girls]], the Imposters Rollergirls, and hosts Lincoln Rowing centre on the River Witham.
sentence_242: [[Lindum_Hockey_Club|Lindum Hockey Club]] plays in the north of the city.
sentence_243: Since 1956 the city has played host to the Lincoln Grand Prix one-day cycle race, which for around 30 years or so has used a city-centre finishing circuit incorporating the challenging 1-in-6 cobbled ascent of Michaelgate.
sentence_244: Since 2013 the city has also boasted its own professional wrestling promotion and training academy, Lincoln Fight Factory Wrestling.
sentence_245: The [[Lincoln_Lions_(rugby_union)|Lincoln Lions]] rugby union team has been playing since 1902.
sentence_246: Two short-lived [[Greyhound_racing_in_the_United_Kingdom|greyhound racing]] tracks were opened by the Lincolnshire Greyhound Racing Association.
sentence_247: The first was the Highfield track in Hykeham Road, which opened on 13 September 1931, and the second at the Lincoln Speedway on the Rope Walk, which opened on 4 June 1932.
sentence_248: Racing at both tracks was independent as they were "flapping" tracks not affiliated to the sport's governing body the [[National_Greyhound_Racing_Club|National Greyhound Racing Club]].
sentence_249: Their dates of closure have not been found.

title: Jack Brabham
sentence_0: For the Triffids album, see [[Jack_Brabham_(album)|Jack Brabham (album)]].
sentence_1: Sir John Arthur Brabham, [[Officer_of_the_Order_of_Australia|AO]], [[Officer_of_the_Order_of_the_British_Empire|OBE]] (2 April 1926 – 19 May 2014) was an [[Formula_One_drivers_from_Australia|Australian racing driver]] who was [[Formula_One|Formula One]] World Champion in [[1959_Formula_One_season|1959]], [[1960_Formula_One_season|1960]], and 1966.
sentence_2: He was a founder of the [[Brabham|Brabham]] racing team and race car constructor that bore his name.
sentence_3: Brabham was a [[Royal_Australian_Air_Force|Royal Australian Air Force]] flight mechanic and ran a small engineering workshop before he started [[Midget_car_racing|racing midget cars]] in 1948.
sentence_4: His successes with midgets in Australian and New Zealand road racing events led to his going to Britain to further his racing career.
sentence_5: There he became part of the [[Cooper_Car_Company|Cooper Car Company]]'s racing team, building as well as racing cars.
sentence_6: He contributed to the design of the mid-engined cars that Cooper introduced to Formula One and the [[Indianapolis_500|Indianapolis 500]], and won the Formula One world championship in [[1959_Formula_One_season|1959]] and [[1960_Formula_One_season|1960]].
sentence_7: In 1962 he established his own Brabham marque with fellow Australian [[Ron_Tauranac|Ron Tauranac]], which in the 1960s became the largest manufacturer of customer racing cars in the world.
sentence_8: In the 1966 Formula One season Brabham became the first – and still, the only – man to win the Formula One world championship driving one of his own cars.
sentence_9: He was the last surviving World Champion of the 1950s.
sentence_10: Brabham retired to Australia after the 1970 Formula One season, where he bought a farm and maintained business interests, which included the [[Judd_(engine)|Engine Developments]] racing engine manufacturer and several garages.
sentence_11: John Arthur 'Jack' Brabham was born on 2 April 1926 in [[Hurstville,_New_South_Wales|Hurstville, New South Wales]], then a commuter town outside Sydney.
sentence_12: Brabham was involved with cars and mechanics from an early age.
sentence_13: At the age of 12, he learned to drive the family car and the trucks of his father's grocery business.
sentence_14: Brabham attended technical college, studying metalwork, carpentry, and technical drawing.
sentence_15: Brabham's early career continued the engineering theme.
sentence_16: At the age of 15 he left school to work, combining a job at a local garage with an evening course in mechanical engineering.
sentence_17: Brabham soon branched out into his own business selling motorbikes, which he bought and repaired for sale, using his parents' back veranda as his workshop.
sentence_18: One month after his 18th birthday on 19 May 1944 Brabham enlisted into the [[Royal_Australian_Air_Force|Royal Australian Air Force]] (RAAF).
sentence_19: Although he was keen on becoming a pilot, there was already a surplus of trained aircrew and the Air Force instead put his mechanical skills to use as a flight mechanic, of which there was a wartime shortage.
sentence_20: He was based at [[RAAF_Base_Williamtown|RAAF Station Williamtown]], where he maintained [[Bristol_Beaufighter|Bristol Beaufighters]] at [[No._5_Operational_Training_Unit_RAAF|No.
sentence_21: 5 Operational Training Unit]].
sentence_22: On his 20th birthday, 2 April 1946, Brabham was discharged from the RAAF with the rank of leading aircraftman.
sentence_23: He then started a small service, repair, and machining business in a workshop built by his uncle on a plot of land behind his grandfather's house.
sentence_24: Brabham started racing after an American friend, Johnny Schonberg, persuaded him to watch a [[Midget_car_racing|midget car]] race.
sentence_25: Midget racing was a category for small open-wheel cars racing on dirt ovals.
sentence_26: It was popular in Australia, attracting crowds of up to 40,000.
sentence_27: Brabham records that he was not taken with the idea of driving, being convinced that the drivers "were all lunatics" but he agreed to build a car with Schonberg.
sentence_28: At first Schonberg drove the homemade device, powered by a modified [[JA_Prestwich_Industries_Ltd|JAP]] motorcycle engine built by Brabham in his workshop.
sentence_29: In 1948, Schonberg's wife persuaded him to stop racing and on his suggestion Brabham took over.
sentence_30: He almost immediately found that he had a knack for the sport, winning on his third night's racing.
sentence_31: From there he was a regular competitor and winner in Midgets (known as Speedcars in Australia) at tracks such Sydney's [[Parramatta_Stadium|Cumberland Speedway]], the Sydney Showground, and the [[Sydney_Sports_Ground|Sydney Sports Ground]], as well as interstate tracks such as [[Adelaide|Adelaide]]'s Kilburn and [[Rowley_Park_Speedway|Rowley Park]] speedways and the [[Brisbane_Exhibition_Ground|Ekka]] in [[Brisbane|Brisbane]].
sentence_32: Brabham has since said that it was "terrific driver training.
sentence_33: You had to have quick reflexes: in effect you lived—or possibly died—on them."
sentence_34: Due to the time required to prepare the car, the sport also became his living.
sentence_35: Brabham won the [[Australian_Speedcar_Championship|1948 Australian Speedcar Championship]], the 1949 Australian and [[South_Australian_Speedcar_Championship|South Australian]] Speedcar championships, and the 1950–1951 Australian championship with the car.
sentence_36: After successfully running the midget at some hillclimbing events in 1951, Brabham became interested in [[Road_racing|road racing]].
sentence_37: He bought and modified a series of racing cars from the [[Cooper_Car_Company|Cooper Car Company]], a British constructor, and from 1953 concentrated on this form of racing, in which drivers compete on closed tarmac circuits.
sentence_38: He was supported by his father and by the Redex fuel additive company, although his commercially aware approach—including the title RedeX Special painted on the side of his Cooper-Bristol—did not go down well with the [[Confederation_of_Australian_Motor_Sport|Confederation of Australian Motor Sport]] (CAMS), which banned the advertisement.
sentence_39: Brabham competed in Australia and New Zealand until early 1955, taking "a long succession of victories", including the 1953 Queensland Road Racing championship.
sentence_40: During this time, he picked up the nickname "Black Jack", which has been variously attributed to his dark hair and stubble, to his "ruthless" approach on the track, and to his "propensity for maintaining a shadowy silence".
sentence_41: After the 1954 [[New_Zealand_Grand_Prix|New Zealand Grand Prix]], Brabham was persuaded by Dean Delamont, competitions manager of the [[Royal_Automobile_Club|Royal Automobile Club]] in the United Kingdom, to try a season of racing in Europe, then the international centre of road racing.
sentence_42: Upon arriving in Europe on his own in early 1955, Brabham based himself in the UK, where he bought another Cooper to race in national events.
sentence_43: His crowd-pleasing driving style initially betrayed his dirt track origins: as he put it, he took corners "by using full [steering] lock and lots of throttle".
sentence_44: Visits to the Cooper factory for parts led to a friendship with Charlie and [[John_Cooper_(car_maker)|John Cooper]], who told the story that after many requests for a drive with the factory team, Brabham was given the keys to the transporter taking the cars to a race.
sentence_45: Brabham soon "seemed to merge into Cooper Cars": he was not an employee, but he started working at Cooper daily from the midpoint of the 1955 season building a Bobtail mid-engined [[Sports_car|sports car]], intended for [[Formula_One|Formula One]], the top category of single seater racing.
sentence_46: He made his Grand Prix debut at the age of 29 driving the car at the [[1955_British_Grand_Prix|1955 British Grand Prix]].
sentence_47: It had a 2-litre engine, half a litre less than permitted, and ran slowly with a broken clutch before retiring.
sentence_48: Later in the year Brabham, again driving the Bobtail, tussled with [[Stirling_Moss|Stirling Moss]] for third place in a non-championship Formula One race at Snetterton.
sentence_49: Although Moss finished ahead, Brabham saw the race as a turning point, proving that he could compete at this level.
sentence_50: He shipped the Bobtail back to Australia, where he used it to win the 1955 Australian Grand Prix before selling it to help fund a permanent move to the UK the following year with his wife Betty and their son [[Geoff_Brabham|Geoff]].
sentence_51: Brabham briefly and unsuccessfully campaigned his own second hand Formula One [[Maserati_250F|Maserati 250F]] during 1956, but his season was saved by drives for Cooper in [[Sports_car_racing|sports cars]] and [[Formula_Two|Formula Two]], the junior category to Formula One.
sentence_52: At that time, almost all racing cars had their engines mounted at the front but Coopers were different, having the engine placed behind the driver, which improved their handling.
sentence_53: In 1957, Brabham drove another mid-engined Cooper, again only fitted with a 2-litre engine, at the [[1957_Monaco_Grand_Prix|Monaco Grand Prix]].
sentence_54: He avoided a large crash at the first corner and was running third towards the end of the race when the fuel pump mount failed.
sentence_55: After more than three hours of racing, the exhausted Brabham, who "hated to be beaten", pushed the car to the line to finish sixth.
sentence_56: The following year, he was Autocar Formula Two champion in a Cooper, while continuing to score minor points-scoring positions with the small-engined Coopers in the World Drivers' Championship and driving for [[Aston_Martin|Aston Martin]] in Sportscars.
sentence_57: His schedule necessitated a considerable amount of travel on the roads of Europe.
sentence_58: Brabham's driving on public roads was described as "safe as houses", unlike many of his contemporaries—on the way back from the [[1957_Pescara_Grand_Prix|1957 Pescara Grand Prix]], passenger [[Tony_Brooks_(racing_driver)|Tony Brooks]] took over driving after Brabham refused to overtake a long line of lorries.
sentence_59: In late 1958, Brabham rekindled his interest in flying and began taking lessons.
sentence_60: He bought his own plane and on gaining his [[Pilot_licensing_in_the_United_Kingdom|licence]] began to make heavy use of it piloting himself, his family, and members of his team around Europe to races.
sentence_61: In [[1959_Formula_One_season|1959]], Cooper obtained 2.5-litre engines for the first time and Brabham put the extra power to good use by winning his first world championship race at the season-opening [[1959_Monaco_Grand_Prix|Monaco Grand Prix]] after [[Jean_Behra|Jean Behra]]'s Ferrari and [[Stirling_Moss|Stirling Moss]]'s Cooper failed.
sentence_62: More podium places were followed by a win in the [[1959_British_Grand_Prix|British Grand Prix]] at Aintree after Brabham preserved his tyres to the end of the race, enabling him to finish ahead of Moss who had to pit to replace worn tyres.
sentence_63: This gave him a 13-point championship lead with four races to go.
sentence_64: At the Portuguese Grand Prix at Monsanto Park, Brabham was chasing race leader Moss when a backmarker moved over on him and launched the Cooper into the air.
sentence_65: The airborne car hit a telegraph pole, throwing Brabham onto the track, where he narrowly avoided being hit by one of his teammates but escaped with no serious injury.
sentence_66: With two wins each, Brabham, Moss, and Ferrari's Tony Brooks were all capable of winning the championship at the final event of the season, the United States Grand Prix at Sebring.
sentence_67: Brabham was among those up until 1 am the morning before the race working on the Cooper team cars.
sentence_68: The next day, after pacing himself behind Moss, who soon retired with a broken gearbox, he led almost to the end of the race before running out of fuel on the last lap.
sentence_69: He again pushed the car to the finish line to place fourth, although in the event this was unnecessary as his other title rival, Brooks, finished only third.
sentence_70: His championship-winning margin over Brooks was four points.
sentence_71: According to Gerald Donaldson, "some thought [his title] owed more to stealth than skill, an opinion at least partly based on Brabham's low-key presence."
sentence_72: Despite his success with Cooper, Brabham was sure he could do better.
sentence_73: He considered buying Cooper in partnership with Roy Salvadori and then in late 1959 he asked his friend [[Ron_Tauranac|Ron Tauranac]] to come to the UK and work with him, producing upgrade kits for Sunbeam Rapier and [[Triumph_Herald|Triumph Herald]] road cars at his car dealership, Jack Brabham Motors, but with the long-term aim of designing racing cars.
sentence_74: Brabham continued to drive for Cooper, but on the long flight back from the [[1960_Formula_One_season|1960 season]]-opening [[1960_Argentine_Grand_Prix|Argentine Grand Prix]], he had a heart-to-heart with John Cooper.
sentence_75: John's father Charlie and the designer [[Owen_Maddock|Owen Maddock]] had been reluctant to update their car, but although a Cooper had won in Argentina, other cars had been faster before they broke down.
sentence_76: Brabham helped design the more advanced [[Cooper_T53|Cooper T53]], including advice from Tauranac.
sentence_77: Brabham spun the new car out of the next championship race, the [[1960_Monaco_Grand_Prix|Monaco Grand Prix]], but then embarked on a series of five straight victories.
sentence_78: He won from the front at the [[1960_Dutch_Grand_Prix|Dutch]], [[1960_French_Grand_Prix|French]], and [[1960_Belgian_Grand_Prix|Belgian Grands Prix]], where title rival Moss was badly injured in a practice accident that put him out for two months.
sentence_79: Two other drivers were killed during the race.
sentence_80: At the [[1960_British_Grand_Prix|British Grand Prix]], Brabham was closing on Graham Hill's BRM before Hill spun off, leaving Brabham the victory.
sentence_81: He then came back from eighth place to second at the [[1960_Portuguese_Grand_Prix|Portuguese Grand Prix]] after sliding off on [[Tramway_track|tramlines]] and won after race leader John Surtees crashed.
sentence_82: Brabham's points total was put out of reach when the British teams withdrew from the Italian GP on safety grounds.
sentence_83: Mike Lawrence writes that Brabham's expertise in setting up the cars was a significant factor in Cooper's 1960 drivers' and constructors' titles.
sentence_84: Coventry Climax were late in producing the smaller 1.5-litre engine required for the [[1961_Formula_One_season|1961 season]] and the Cooper-Climaxes were outclassed by new mid-engined cars from Porsche, Lotus, and championship-winners Ferrari.
sentence_85: Brabham scored only three points and finished 11th in the championship.
sentence_86: He had a little more success in the non-championship Formula One races, where he ran his own private Coopers and took three victories at [[1961_Lombank_Trophy|Snetterton]] (26 March), [[1961_Brussels_Grand_Prix|Brussels]] (9 April), and [[1961_Aintree_200|Aintree]] (22 April).
sentence_87: [[1961_Indianapolis_500|The same year]], Brabham entered the famous [[Indianapolis_500|Indianapolis 500]] oval race for the first time in a modified version of the Formula One Cooper.
sentence_88: It had a 2.7-litre Climax engine producing 268 bhp (200 kW; 272 PS) compared to the 4.4-litre, 430 bhp (321 kW; 436 PS) Offenhauser engines used by the front-engined [[Roadster_(automobile)|roadsters]] driven by all the other entrants.
sentence_89: Jack qualified a respectable 17th at 145.144 mp/h (pole winner Eddie Sachs qualified at 147.481 mp/h), and while the front-engined roadsters were much faster on the long front and back straights, the rear-engined Cooper's superior handling through the turns and the shorter north and south sections kept the reigning World Champion competitive.
sentence_90: Brabham ran as high as third before finishing ninth, completing all 200 laps.
sentence_91: Although most of the doubters in the American Indycar scene claimed that rear-engine cars were for drivers who like to be pushed around, as Brabham put it, it "triggered the rear-engined revolution at Indy" and within five years most of the cars that raced at [[Indianapolis_Motor_Speedway|Indianapolis]] would be rear-engined.
sentence_92: Brabham and Tauranac set up a company called Motor Racing Developments (MRD), which produced customer racing cars, while Brabham himself continued to race for Cooper.
sentence_93: MRD produced cars for [[Formula_Junior|Formula Junior]], with the first one appearing in mid-1961.
sentence_94: Brabham left Cooper in 1962 to drive for his own team: the Brabham Racing Organisation, using cars built by Motor Racing Developments.
sentence_95: A newly introduced engine limit in Formula One of 1500 cc did not suit Brabham and he did not win a single race with a 1500 cc car.
sentence_96: His team suffered poor reliability during this period and motorsport authors Mike Lawrence and David Hodges have said that Brabham's reluctance to spend money may have cost the team results, a view echoed by Tauranac.
sentence_97: During the [[1965_Formula_One_season|1965 season]], Brabham started to consider retirement to manage his team.
sentence_98: [[Dan_Gurney|Dan Gurney]] took the lead driver role, and the team's first world championship win, while Brabham gave up his car to several other drivers towards the end of the season.
sentence_99: At the end of the season, Gurney announced his intention to leave and set up his own team and Brabham decided to carry on.
sentence_100: In 1966, a new 3-litre formula was created for Formula One.
sentence_101: The new engines under development by other suppliers all had at least 12 [[Cylinder_(engine)|cylinders]] and proved difficult to develop, being heavy and unreliable.
sentence_102: Brabham took a different approach to the problem of obtaining a suitable engine: he persuaded Australian engineering company [[Repco|Repco]] to develop a new 3-litre eight-cylinder engine for him.
sentence_103: Repco had no experience in designing complete engines.
sentence_104: Brabham had identified a supply of suitable engine blocks obtained from [[Oldsmobile|Oldsmobile]]'s aluminium alloy [[Buick_V8_engine#215|215]] engine and persuaded the company that an engine could be designed around the block, largely using existing components.
sentence_105: Brabham and Repco were aware that the engine would not compete in terms of outright power, but felt that a lightweight, reliable engine could achieve good championship results while other teams were still making their new designs reliable.
sentence_106: The combination of the Repco engine and the [[Brabham_BT19|Brabham BT19]] chassis designed by Tauranac worked.
sentence_107: At the [[1966_French_Grand_Prix|French Grand Prix]] at [[Reims-Gueux|Reims-Gueux]], Jack Brabham took his first Formula One world championship win since 1960 and became the first man to win such a race in a car of his own construction.
sentence_108: Only his two former teammates, [[Bruce_McLaren|Bruce McLaren]] and [[Dan_Gurney|Dan Gurney]], have since matched this achievement.
sentence_109: It was the first in a run of four straight wins for the Australian veteran.
sentence_110: The 40-year-old Brabham was annoyed by press stories about his age and, in a highly uncharacteristic stunt, at the [[1966_Dutch_Grand_Prix|Dutch Grand Prix]] he hobbled to his car on the starting grid before the race wearing a long false beard and leaning on a cane before going on to win the race.
sentence_111: Brabham confirmed his third championship at the [[1966_Italian_Grand_Prix|Italian Grand Prix]] and became the only driver to win the Formula One World Championship in a car that carried his own name.
sentence_112: The season also saw the fruition of Brabham's relationship with Japanese engine manufacturer [[Honda|Honda]] in Formula Two.
sentence_113: After a generally unsuccessful season in 1965, Honda revised their 1-litre engine completely.
sentence_114: Brabham won ten of the year's 16 European Formula Two races in his Brabham-Honda.
sentence_115: There was no European Formula Two championship that year, but Brabham won the Trophées de France, a championship consisting of six of the French Formula Two races.
sentence_116: In 1967, the Formula One title went to Brabham's teammate [[Denny_Hulme|Denny Hulme]].
sentence_117: Hulme had better reliability through the year, possibly due to Brabham's desire to try new parts first.
sentence_118: Despite taking pole position in the first two rounds, mechanical problems halted his chances of victory.
sentence_119: He spun numerous times in [[1967_South_African_Grand_Prix|South Africa]], and at [[1967_Monaco_Grand_Prix|Monaco]], his engine blew up at the start, and the win went to his teammate [[Denny_Hulme|Denny Hulme]].
sentence_120: At the [[1967_Dutch_Grand_Prix|Dutch Grand Prix]], he scored his first podium of the season, with second place, behind Scotsman [[Jim_Clark|Jim Clark]].
sentence_121: He retired in the [[1967_Belgian_Grand_Prix|Belgian Grand Prix]] with another blown engine.
sentence_122: He fixed this by winning the [[1967_French_Grand_Prix|French Grand Prix]] at the Bugatti Circuit in [[Le_Mans|Le Mans]].
sentence_123: He came fourth at the [[1967_British_Grand_Prix|British Grand Prix]], behind [[Chris_Amon|Chris Amon]], his teammate Hulme, and Clark.
sentence_124: At the [[1967_German_Grand_Prix|German Grand Prix]], he had a huge battle with Amon, and Brabham eventually finished ahead of the New Zealander, by only half a second.
sentence_125: Hulme was the winner.
sentence_126: At the first ever Canadian Grand Prix at [[Mosport_International_Raceway|Mosport Park]], he took a huge win, ahead of Hulme, in cold and rainy conditions.
sentence_127: At the [[1967_Italian_Grand_Prix|Italian Grand Prix]] at [[Autodromo_Nazionale_Monza|Monza]], Brabham had to finish second, only a few car lengths behind [[John_Surtees|John Surtees]], who took his last GP win.
sentence_128: Hulme retired from the race, cutting the gap to 3 points between the two, as the circus headed for the United States, at Watkins Glen for the [[1967_United_States_Grand_Prix|United States Grand Prix]].
sentence_129: Brabham outqualified his teammate, and finished fifth in the race, and with Hulme on the podium, this meant the championship chances were looking slim for Black Jack, as the circus went to [[1967_Mexican_Grand_Prix|Mexico]] for the championship deciding and final race of the season.
sentence_130: Once again, he outqualified his teammate, and needed to win, with Hulme fifth or lower.
sentence_131: But [[Jim_Clark|Jim Clark]] was simply too fast during the whole weekend, and dominated the race from pole to win, with Brabham finishing over 1 minute and 25 seconds behind.
sentence_132: Hulme finished third, and so the New Zealander won the championship, while Brabham settled for second place.
sentence_133: The team secured the Constructors' Championship, with 67 total points scored, and 23 points ahead of Lotus which scored a total of 44 points.
sentence_134: Brabham raced alongside his teammate [[Jochen_Rindt|Jochen Rindt]] during the [[1968_Formula_One_season|1968 season]].
sentence_135: It wasn't a good season for him.
sentence_136: He retired from the first seven races, before scoring two points for fifth place at the [[1968_German_Grand_Prix|German Grand Prix]].
sentence_137: He retired from the remaining four races.
sentence_138: At the end of the year, he fulfilled a desire to fly from Britain to Australia in a small twin-engined Beechcraft Queen Air.
sentence_139: Partway through the [[1969_Formula_One_season|1969 season]], Brabham suffered serious injuries to his foot in a testing accident.
sentence_140: He returned to racing before the end of the year, but promised his wife that he would retire after the season finished and sold his share of the team to Tauranac.
sentence_141: Finding no top drivers available despite coming close to bringing Rindt back to the team, Brabham decided to race for one more year.
sentence_142: He began auspiciously, winning the first race of the season, the South African Grand Prix, and then led the third race, the Monaco Grand Prix until the very last turn of the last lap.
sentence_143: Brabham was about to hold off the onrushing Rindt (the eventual 1970 F1 champion) when his front wheels locked in a skid on the sharp right turn only yards from the finish and he ended up second.
sentence_144: While leading at the British Grand Prix at Brands Hatch, he ran out of fuel at Clearways and Rindt passed him to take the win while Brabham coasted to the finish in second place.
sentence_145: After the 13th and final race of the season, the Mexican Grand Prix, Brabham did retire.
sentence_146: He had tied [[Jackie_Stewart|Jackie Stewart]] for fifth in the points standings in the season he drove at the age of 44.
sentence_147: Brabham also drove for the works Matra team during the [[1970_World_Sportscar_Championship|1970 World Sportscar Championship]] season and won the final race of the season and his final top level race at the Paris 1000 km in October that year.
sentence_148: He then made a complete break from racing and returned to Australia, to the relief of his wife who had been "scared stiff" each time he drove.
sentence_149: Following his retirement, Brabham and his family moved to a farm between Sydney and Melbourne.
sentence_150: Brabham says that he "never really wanted" the move, but his wife hoped their sons could grow up away from motorsport.
sentence_151: As well as running the new venture, he continued his interest in businesses in the UK and Australia, including a small aviation company and garages and car dealerships.
sentence_152: He also set up [[Engine_Developments_Ltd.|Engine Developments Ltd.]] in 1971 with John Judd, who had worked for Brabham on the Repco engine project in the mid 1960s.
sentence_153: The company builds engines for racing applications.
sentence_154: Brabham was also a shareholder in Jack Brabham Engines Pty Ltd., an Australian company marketing Jack Brabham memorabilia.
sentence_155: The Brabham team continued in Formula One, winning two further Drivers' Championships in the early 1980s under [[Bernie_Ecclestone|Bernie Ecclestone]]'s ownership.
sentence_156: Although the original organisation went into administration in 1992, the name was attached to a German company selling cars and accessories in 2008, and an unsuccessful attempt to set up a new Formula One team the following year.
sentence_157: On both occasions the Brabham family, which was unconnected to the ventures, announced its intention to take legal advice.
sentence_158: In September 2014, Brabham's youngest son David announced [[Project_Brabham|Project Brabham]], a new team planning to use a [[Crowdsourcing|crowdsourcing]] business model to enter the 2015 [[FIA_World_Endurance_Championship|FIA World Endurance Championship]] in the LMP2 category.
sentence_159: Despite his three titles, and although John Cooper considered him "the greatest", Formula One journalist Adam Cooper wrote in 1999 that Brabham is never listed among the Top 10 of all time, noting that "Stirling Moss and Jim Clark dominated the headlines when Jack was racing, and they still do".
sentence_160: Brabham was the first post-war racing driver to be [[Knight|knighted]] when he received the honour in 1978 for services to motorsport.
sentence_161: He has received several other honours and in 2011, the suburb of [[Brabham,_Western_Australia|Brabham]] in [[Perth|Perth]], Western Australia, was named after him.
sentence_162: A race circuit and an automotive training school were also named after him in the early 2010s.
sentence_163: In retirement, Brabham continued to be involved in motorsport events, appearing at contemporary and historic motorsport events around the world where he often drove his former Cooper and Brabham cars until the early 2000s.
sentence_164: In 1999, after competing at the [[Goodwood_Revival|Goodwood Revival]] at the age of 73 he commented that driving stopped him getting old.
sentence_165: Despite a large accident at the 2000 Revival, the first racing accident to put him in hospital overnight, he continued to drive until at least 2004.
sentence_166: By the late 2000s, ill-health was preventing him from driving in competition.
sentence_167: In addition to the deafness caused by years of motor racing without adequate ear protection, his eyesight was reduced due to [[Macular_degeneration|macular degeneration]] and he had kidney disease for which by 2009 he was receiving [[Dialysis|dialysis]] three times a week.
sentence_168: Nonetheless, that year he attended a celebration of the 50th anniversary of his first world championship at the Phillip Island Classic festival of motorsport, and in 2010 flew to Bahrain with most of the other Formula One world Drivers' Champions for a celebration of 60 years of the Formula One world championship.
sentence_169: Brabham was the oldest surviving F1 champion.
sentence_170: Brabham and Betty had three sons together: [[Geoff_Brabham|Geoff]], [[Gary_Brabham|Gary]], and David.
sentence_171: All three became involved in motorsport, with support from Brabham in their early years.
sentence_172: Between them, they have won sportscar and single-seater races and championships.
sentence_173: Geoff was an Indycar and sportscar racer who won five North American sportscar championships as well as the [[24_Hours_of_Le_Mans|24 Hours of Le Mans]], while David competed in Formula One for the Brabham team and has also won the Le Mans race as well as three Japanese and North American sportscar titles.
sentence_174: Gary also drove briefly in Formula One, although his F1 career consisted of two DNPQ's for the Life team.
sentence_175: Brabham and Betty divorced in 1994 after 43 years.
sentence_176: Brabham married his second wife, Margaret in 1995 and they lived on the [[Gold_Coast,_Queensland|Gold Coast, Queensland]].
sentence_177: Brabham's grandson [[Matthew_Brabham|Matthew]] (son of Geoff) graduated from karts in 2010 and won two ladders of the [[Mazda_Road_to_Indy|Mazda Road to Indy]], eventually racing in the [[2016_Indianapolis_500|2016 Indianapolis 500]] and winning two [[Stadium_Super_Trucks|Stadium Super Trucks]] championships.
sentence_178: Another grandson, [[Sam_Brabham|Sam]], the son of David and [[Mike_Thackwell|Lisa, whose brother Mike also was an F1 driver]], stepped up to car racing from karts in 2013 when he made his debut in the [[British_Formula_Ford_Championship|British Formula Ford Championship]].
sentence_179: The Brabham family have been involved in world-class motorsport for over 60 years.
sentence_180: Brabham made his last public appearance on 18 May 2014, appearing with one of the cars he built.
sentence_181: He died at his home on the [[Gold_Coast,_Queensland|Gold Coast]] on 19 May 2014, aged 88, following a lengthy battle with liver disease.
sentence_182: He was eating breakfast with his wife, Margaret, when he died.
sentence_183: In a statement on the family's website, Brabham's son David confirmed his father's death.
sentence_184: "It's a very sad day for all of us", David Brabham stated.
sentence_185: "My father passed away peacefully at home at the age of 88 this morning.
sentence_186: He lived an incredible life, achieving more than anyone would ever dream of and he will continue to live on through the astounding legacy he leaves behind."
sentence_187: At the time of his death, Brabham was the last surviving world champion from the 1950s era.
sentence_188: At his request, his ashes were scattered at the Tamborine Mountain Skywalk in Queensland Australia by his wife, Lady Margaret Brabham on 4 September 2014.
sentence_189: Brabham was a frequent visitor to the Skywalk.
