sentence_224: The peacetime strength of the Luftwaffe in the spring of 1939 was 370,000 men.
sentence_225: After the mobilization in 1939 almost 900,000 men served, and just before [[Operation_Barbarossa|Operation Barbarossa]] in 1941 the personnel strength had reached 1.5 million men.
sentence_226: The Luftwaffe reached its largest personnel strength during the period November 1943 to June 1944, with almost three million men and women in uniform; 1.7 million of these were male soldiers, 1 million male [[Ranks_and_insignia_of_the_German_Army_(1935–1945)#Armed_Forces_officials_(Wehrmachtbeamte)|Wehrmachtsbeamte]] and civilian employees, and almost 300,000 female and male auxiliaries (Luftwaffenhelfer).
sentence_227: In October 1944, the anti-aircraft units had 600,000 soldiers and 530,000 auxiliaries, including 60,000 male members of the Reichsarbeitsdienst, 50,000 Luftwaffenhelfer (males age 15–17), 80,000 Flakwehrmänner (males above military age) and Flak-V-soldaten (males unfit for military service), and 160,000 female Flakwaffenhelferinnen and RAD-Maiden, as well as 160,000 foreign personnel ([[Hiwi_(volunteer)|Hiwis]]).
sentence_228: Main article: [[Operational_history_of_the_Luftwaffe_(1939–45)|Operational history of the Luftwaffe (1939–45)]]
sentence_229: The Luftwaffe's [[Condor_Legion|Condor Legion]] experimented with new doctrine and aircraft during the [[Spanish_Civil_War|Spanish Civil War]].
sentence_230: It helped the [[Falange|Falange]] under [[Francisco_Franco|Francisco Franco]] to defeat the Republican forces.
sentence_231: Over 20,000 German airmen gained combat experience that would give the Luftwaffe an important advantage going into the Second World War.
sentence_232: One infamous operation was the bombing of Guernica in the [[Basque_Country_(autonomous_community)|Basque country]].
sentence_233: It is commonly assumed this attack was the result of a "terror doctrine" in Luftwaffe doctrine.
sentence_234: The raids on Guernica and [[Madrid|Madrid]] caused many civilian casualties and a wave of protests in the democracies.
sentence_235: It has been suggested that the bombing of Guernica was carried out for military tactical reasons, in support of ground operations, but the town was not directly involved in any fighting at that point in time.
sentence_236: It was not until 1942 that the Germans started to develop bombing policy in which civilians were the primary target, although [[The_Blitz|The Blitz]] on London and many other British cities involved indiscriminate bombing of civilian areas, 'nuisance raids' which could even involve the machine-gunning of civilians and livestock.
sentence_237: When World War II began, the Luftwaffe was one of the most technologically advanced air forces in the world.
sentence_238: During the [[Polish_Campaign|Polish Campaign]] that triggered the war, it quickly established air superiority, and then air supremacy.
sentence_239: It supported the German Army operations which ended the campaign in five weeks.
sentence_240: The Luftwaffe's performance was as OKL had hoped.
sentence_241: The Luftwaffe rendered invaluable support to the army, mopping up pockets of resistance.
sentence_242: Göring was delighted with the performance.
sentence_243: Command and control problems were experienced, but owing to the flexibility and improvisation of both the army and Luftwaffe, these problems were solved.
sentence_244: The Luftwaffe was to have in place a ground-to-air communication system, which played a vital role in the success of [[Fall_Gelb|Fall Gelb]].
sentence_245: In the spring of 1940, the Luftwaffe assisted the Kriegsmarine and Heer in the invasion of Norway.
sentence_246: Flying in reinforcements and winning air superiority, the Luftwaffe contributed decisively to the German conquest.
sentence_247: In the spring of 1940, the Luftwaffe contributed to the unexpected success in the [[Battle_of_France|Battle of France]].
sentence_248: It destroyed three Allied Air Forces and helped secure the defeat of France in just over six weeks.
sentence_249: However, it could not [[Battle_of_Dunkirk|destroy the British Expeditionary Force at Dunkirk]] despite intense bombing.
sentence_250: The BEF escaped to continue the war.
sentence_251: During the [[Battle_of_Britain|Battle of Britain]] in summer 1940, the Luftwaffe inflicted severe damage to the [[Royal_Air_Force|Royal Air Force]], but did not achieve the air superiority that Hitler demanded for [[Operation_Sea_Lion|the proposed invasion of Britain]], which was postponed and then cancelled in December 1940.
sentence_252: The Luftwaffe ravaged British cities during [[The_Blitz|The Blitz]], but failed to break British morale.
sentence_253: Hitler had already ordered preparations to be made for [[Operation_Barbarossa|Operation Barbarossa]], the invasion of the [[Soviet_Union|Soviet Union]].
sentence_254: In spring 1941, the Luftwaffe helped its [[Axis_powers|Axis]] partner, Italy, secure victory in the [[Balkans_Campaign_(World_War_II)|Balkans Campaign]] and continued to support Italy in the [[Mediterranean,_Middle_East_and_African_theatres_of_World_War_II|Mediterranean, Middle East and African theatres]] until May 1945.
sentence_255: In June 1941, Germany invaded the Soviet Union.
sentence_256: The Luftwaffe destroyed thousands of Soviet aircraft, yet it failed to destroy the [[Red_Air_Force|Red Air Force]] altogether.
sentence_257: Lacking strategic bombers (the very "Ural bombers" that General Wever had asked for six years before) the Luftwaffe could not strike at Soviet production centers regularly or with the needed force.
sentence_258: The [[Axis_and_Soviet_air_operations_during_Operation_Barbarossa|Axis and Soviet air operations during Operation Barbarossa]] consumed vast numbers of men and planes.
sentence_259: As the war dragged on, the Luftwaffe was eroded in strength.
sentence_260: The defeats at the [[Battle_of_Stalingrad|Battle of Stalingrad]] and [[Battle_of_Kursk|Battle of Kursk]] ensured the gradual decline of the Wehrmacht on the [[Eastern_Front_(World_War_II)|Eastern Front]].
sentence_261: British historian [[Frederick_Taylor_(historian)|Frederick Taylor]] asserts that "all sides bombed each other's cities during the war.
sentence_262: Half a million [[Soviet_Union|Soviet]] citizens, for example, died from German [[Strategic_bombing_during_World_War_II|bombing]] during the invasion and occupation of Russia.
sentence_263: That's roughly equivalent to the number of German citizens who died from Allied raids."
sentence_264: Meanwhile, the Luftwaffe continued to defend [[German-occupied_Europe|German-occupied Europe]] against the growing offensive power of [[RAF_Bomber_Command|RAF Bomber Command]] and, starting in the summer of 1942, the steadily building strength of the [[United_States_Army_Air_Forces|United States Army Air Forces]].
sentence_265: The mounting demands of the [[Defence_of_the_Reich|Defence of the Reich]] campaign gradually destroyed the Luftwaffe's fighter arm.
sentence_266: Despite its belated use of advanced turbojet and rocket propelled aircraft for bomber destroyer duties, it was overwhelmed by Allied numbers and a lack of trained pilots and fuel.
sentence_267: A last-ditch attempt, known as [[Operation_Bodenplatte|Operation Bodenplatte]], to win air superiority on 1 January 1945 failed.
sentence_268: After the Bodenplatte effort, the Luftwaffe ceased to be an effective fighting force.
sentence_269: German day and night fighter pilots claimed more than 70,000 aerial victories during World War II.
sentence_270: Of these, about 745 victories are estimated to be achieved by [[Messerschmitt_Me_262|jet fighters]].
sentence_271: [[Anti-aircraft_warfare|Flak]] shot down 25,000–30,000 Allied planes.
sentence_272: Broken down on the different Allies, about 25,000 were American planes, about 20,000 British, 46,100 Soviet, 1,274 French, 375 Polish, and 81 Dutch as well as aircraft from other Allied nationalities.
sentence_273: The highest scoring day fighter pilot was [[Erich_Hartmann|Erich Hartmann]] with 352 confirmed kills, all of them at the Eastern front against the Soviets.
sentence_274: The leading aces in the west were [[Hans-Joachim_Marseille|Hans-Joachim Marseille]] with 158 kills against planes from the British Empire ([[Royal_Air_Force|RAF]], [[Royal_Australian_Air_Force|RAAF]], and [[South_African_Air_Force|SAAF]]) and [[Georg-Peter_Eder|Georg-Peter Eder]] with 56 kills of aircraft from the [[United_States_Army_Air_Force|USAAF]] (of a total of 78).
sentence_275: The most successful night fighter pilot was [[Heinz-Wolfgang_Schnaufer|Heinz-Wolfgang Schnaufer]], who is credited with 121 kills.
sentence_276: 103 German fighter pilots shot down more than 100 enemy aircraft for a total of roughly 15,400 aerial victories.
sentence_277: Roughly a further 360 pilots claimed between 40 and 100 aerial victories for round about 21,000 victories.
sentence_278: Another 500 fighter pilots claimed between 20 and 40 victories for a total of 15,000 victories.
sentence_279: Part of the reason why German pilots scored such high victory totals was because they were in combat for the duration of the war-unlike the Allies, who rotated their flyers out of combat after a certain amount of time, German pilots flew until they were killed, captured or too badly wounded to keep flying.
sentence_280: It is relatively certain that 2,500 German fighter pilots attained ace status, having achieved at least five aerial victories.
sentence_281: These achievements were honored with 453 German single and twin-engine ([[Messerschmitt_Bf_110|Messerschmitt Bf 110]]) day fighter pilots having received the [[Knight's_Cross_of_the_Iron_Cross|Knight's Cross of the Iron Cross]].
sentence_282: 85 night fighter pilots, including 14 crew members, were awarded the Knight's Cross of the Iron Cross.
sentence_283: Some Bomber pilots were also highly successful.
sentence_284: The [[Junkers_Ju87|Stuka]] and Schlachtflieger pilot [[Hans-Ulrich_Rudel|Hans-Ulrich Rudel]] flew 2,530 ground-attack missions and claimed the destruction of more than 519 tanks and a battleship, among others.
sentence_285: He was the most highly decorated German serviceman of the Second World War.
sentence_286: The Bomber pilot [[Hansgeorg_Bätcher|Hansgeorg Bätcher]] flew more than 658 combat missions destroying numerous ships and other targets.
sentence_287: Losses on the other hand were high as well.
sentence_288: The estimated total number of destroyed and damaged for the war totaled 76,875 aircraft.
sentence_289: Of these, about 43,000 were lost in combat, the rest in operational accidents and during training.
sentence_290: By type, losses totaled 21,452 fighters, 12,037 bombers, 15,428 trainers, 10,221 twin-engine fighters, 5,548 ground attack, 6,733 reconnaissance, and 6,141 transports.
sentence_291: According to the General Staff of the Wehrmacht the losses of the flight personnel until February 1945 amounted to:
sentence_292: total: 15,082 officers and 98,568 enlisted men
sentence_293: According to official statistics, total Luftwaffe casualties, including ground personnel, amounted to 138,596 killed and 156,132 missing through 31 January 1945.
sentence_294: The failure of the Luftwaffe in the [[Defence_of_the_Reich|Defence of the Reich]] campaign was a result of a number of factors.
sentence_295: The Luftwaffe lacked an effective air defence system early in the war.
sentence_296: [[Adolf_Hitler|Adolf Hitler]]'s foreign policy had pushed Germany into war before these defences could be fully developed.
sentence_297: The Luftwaffe was forced to improvise and construct its defences during the war.
sentence_298: The daylight actions over German controlled territory were sparse in 1939–1940.
sentence_299: The responsibility of the defence of German air space fell to the Luftgaukommandos (air district commands).
sentence_300: The defence systems relied mostly on the "flak" arm.
sentence_301: The defences were not coordinated and communication was poor.
sentence_302: This lack of understanding between the flak and flying branches of the defence would plague the Luftwaffe throughout the war.
sentence_303: Hitler in particular wanted the defence to rest on anti-aircraft artillery as it gave the civilian population a "psychological crutch" no matter how ineffective the weapons.
sentence_304: Most of the battles fought by the Luftwaffe on the Western Front were against [[Circus_offensive|the RAF's "Circus" raids]] and the occasional daylight raid into German air space.
sentence_305: This was a fortunate position since the Luftwaffe's strategy of focusing its striking power on one front started to unravel with the failure of the invasion of the Soviet Union.
sentence_306: The "peripheral" strategy of the Luftwaffe between 1939 and 1940 had been to deploy its fighter defences at the edges of Axis occupied territory, with little protecting the inner depths.
sentence_307: Moreover, the front line units in the West were complaining about the poor numbers and performance of aircraft.
sentence_308: Units complained of lack of Zerstörer aircraft with all-weather capabilities and the "lack of climbing power of the Bf 109".
sentence_309: The Luftwaffe's technical edge was slipping as the only formidable new aircraft in the German arsenal was the [[Focke-Wulf_Fw_190|Focke-Wulf Fw 190]].
sentence_310: [[Generalfeldmarschall|Generalfeldmarschall]] Erhard Milch was to assist Ernst Udet with aircraft production increases and introduction of more modern types of fighter aircraft.
sentence_311: However, they explained at a meeting of the Reich Industrial Council on 18 September 1941 that the new next generation aircraft had failed to materialize, and production of obsolete types had to continue to meet the growing need for replacements.
sentence_312: The buildup of the [[Jagdwaffe|Jagdwaffe]] ("Fighter Force") was too rapid and its quality suffered.
sentence_313: It was not put under a unified command until 1943, which also affected performance of the nine Jagdgeschwader fighter wings in existence in 1939.
sentence_314: No further units were formed until 1942, and the years of 1940–1941 were wasted.
sentence_315: OKL failed to construct a strategy; instead its command style was reactionary, and its measures not as effective without thorough planning.
sentence_316: This was particularly apparent with the [[Sturmböck|Sturmböck]] squadrons, formed to replace the increasingly ineffective twin-engined Zerstörer twin-engined heavy fighter wings as the primary defense against USAAF daylight raids.
sentence_317: The Sturmböcke flew Fw 190A fighters armed with heavy 20 mm and 30 mm cannon to destroy heavy bombers, but this increased the weight and affected the performance of the Fw 190 at a time when the aircraft were meeting large numbers of equal if not superior Allied types.
sentence_318: Daytime aerial defense against the USAAF's strongly defended heavy bomber forces, particularly the [[Eighth_Air_Force|Eighth Air Force]] and the [[Fifteenth_Air_Force|Fifteenth Air Force]], had its successes through the calendar year of 1943.
sentence_319: But at the start of 1944, [[Jimmy_Doolittle#Doolittle's_breakthrough_in_fighter_tactics|Eighth AF commander Jimmy Doolittle made a major change in offensive fighter tactics]], which defeated the Luftwaffe's day fighter force from that time onwards.
sentence_320: Steadily increasing numbers of the superlative [[North_American_P-51_Mustang|North American P-51 Mustang]] single-engine fighter, leading the USAAF's bombers into German airspace defeated first the [[Heavy_fighter#Germany|Bf 110 Zerstörer]] wings, then the [[Focke-Wulf_Fw_190_operational_history#The_Sturmböcke|Fw 190A Sturmböcke]].
sentence_321: In terms of technological development, the failure to develop a long-range bomber and capable long-range fighters during this period left the Luftwaffe unable to conduct a meaningful strategic bombing campaign throughout the war.
sentence_322: However, Germany at that time suffered from limitations in raw materials such as oil and aluminium, which meant that there were insufficient resources for much beyond a tactical air force: given these circumstances, the Luftwaffe's reliance on tactical mid-range, twin engined medium bombers and short range dive-bombers was a pragmatic choice of strategy.
sentence_323: It might also be argued that the Luftwaffe's Kampfgeschwader medium and heavy bomber wings were perfectly capable of attacking strategic targets, but the lack of capable long range escort fighters left the bombers unable to carry out their missions effectively against determined and well organised fighter opposition.
sentence_324: The greatest failure for the Kampfgeschwader, however, was being saddled with an aircraft intended as a capable four-engined heavy bomber: the perpetually troubled [[Heinkel_He_177|Heinkel He 177]], whose engines were [[Heinkel_He_177#Engine_difficulties|prone to catch fire]] in flight.
sentence_325: Of the [[Heinkel_He_277#Trio_of_separate_efforts|three parallel proposals]] from the Heinkel engineering departments for a four engined version of the A-series He 177 [[Heinkel_He_277#Trio_of_separate_efforts|by February 1943]], one of these being [[Heinkel_He_277|the Heinkel firm's Amerikabomber candidate]], only one, the [[Heinkel_He_177#Further_development:_the_Heinkel_He_177B|He 177B]], emerged in the concluding months of 1943.
sentence_326: Only three airworthy prototypes of the B-series He 177 design were produced by early 1944, some three years after the first prototype flights of the [[Avro_Lancaster|Avro Lancaster]], the most successful RAF heavy bomber.
sentence_327: Another failure of procurement and equipment was the lack of a dedicated [[Naval_aviation|naval air arm]].
sentence_328: General Felmy had already expressed a desire to build a naval air arm to support Kriegsmarine operations in the Atlantic and British waters.
sentence_329: Britain was dependent on food and raw materials from its Empire and North America.
sentence_330: Felmy pressed this case firmly throughout 1938 and 1939, and, on 31 October 1939, [[Großadmiral|Großadmiral]] Erich Raeder sent a strongly worded letter to Göring in support of such proposals.
sentence_331: The early-war twin-engined [[Heinkel_He_115|Heinkel He 115]] floatplane and [[Dornier_Do_18|Dornier Do 18]] flying boat were too slow and short-ranged.
sentence_332: The then-contemporary [[Blohm_&_Voss_BV_138|Blohm & Voss BV 138]] Seedrache (seadragon) trimotor flying boat became the Luftwaffe's primary seaborne maritime patrol platform, with nearly 300 examples built; its trio of [[Junkers_Jumo_205|Junkers Jumo 205]] diesel engines gave it a 4,300 km (2,670 mi) maximum range.
sentence_333: Another Blohm und Voss design of 1940, the enormous, 46-meter wingspan six-engined Blohm und Voss BV 222 Wiking maritime patrol flying boat, would see it capable of a 6,800 km (4,200-mile) range at maximum endurance when using higher-output versions of the same [[Jumo_205|Jumo 205]] powerplants as used by the BV 138, in later years.
sentence_334: The [[Dornier_Do_217|Dornier Do 217]] would have been ideal as a land-based choice, but suffered production problems.
sentence_335: Raeder also complained about the poor standard of aerial torpedoes, although their design was the responsibility of the Wehrmacht combined military's naval arm (the Kriegsmarine), even considering production of the Japanese [[Type_91_torpedo#Provision_of_the_aerial_torpedo_technology_to_Germany|Type 91 torpedo]] used at [[Attack_on_Pearl_Harbor|Pearl Harbor]] as the Lufttorpedo LT 850 by August 1942.
sentence_336: (See both:[[Yanagi_missions|Yanagi missions]] and [[Heinkel_He_111_operational_history#Torpedo_bomber_operations|Heinkel He 111 torpedo bomber operations]])
sentence_337: Without specialised naval or land-based, purpose-designed maritime patrol aircraft, the Luftwaffe was forced to improvise.
sentence_338: The [[Focke-Wulf_Fw_200|Focke-Wulf Fw 200]] Condor airliner's airframe – engineered for civilian airliner use – lacked the structural strength for combat maneuvering at lower altitudes, making it unsuitable for use as a bomber in maritime patrol duties.
sentence_339: The Condor lacked speed, armour and bomb load capacity.
sentence_340: Sometimes the fuselage literally "broke its back" or a wing panel dropped loose from the [[Wing_root|wing root]] after a hard landing.
sentence_341: Nevertheless, this civilian transport was adapted for the long-range reconnaissance and anti-shipping roles and, between August 1940 and February 1941, Fw 200s sank 85 vessels for a claimed total of 363,000 Grt.
sentence_342: Had the Luftwaffe focused on naval aviation – particularly maritime patrol aircraft with long range, like the aforementioned diesel-powered multi-engine Blohm & Voss flying boats – Germany might well have been in a position to win the Battle of the Atlantic.
sentence_343: However, Raeder and the Kriegsmarine failed to press for naval air power until the war began, mitigating the Luftwaffe's responsibility.
sentence_344: In addition, Göring regarded any other branch of the German military developing its own aviation as an encroachment on his authority and continually frustrated the Navy's attempts to build its own airpower.
sentence_345: The absence of a strategic bomber force for the Luftwaffe, following General Wever's accidental death in the early summer of 1936 and the end of the Ural bomber program he fostered before the invasion of Poland, would not be addressed again until the authorization of the "Bomber B" design competition in July 1939, which sought to replace the medium bomber force with which the Luftwaffe was to begin the war, and the partly achieved Schnellbomber high-speed medium bomber concept with more advanced, twin-engined high speed bomber aircraft fitted with pairs of relatively [[Bomber_B#High-output_engines|"high-power" engines]] of 1,500 kW (2,000 hp) output levels and upwards each as a follow-on to the earlier Schnellbomber project, that would also be able to function as shorter range heavy bombers.
sentence_346: The spring 1942 [[Amerika_Bomber|Amerika Bomber]] program also sought to produce useful strategic bomber designs for the Luftwaffe, with their prime design priority being an advanced trans-oceanic range capability as the main aim of the project to directly attack the United States from Europe or the Azores.
sentence_347: Inevitably, both the Bomber B and Amerika Bomber programs were victims of the continued emphasis of the Wehrmacht combined military's insistence for its Luftwaffe air arm to support the Heer as its primary mission, and the damage to the German aviation industry from Allied bomber attacks.

section_16.value: Challenges in directly addressing combat pilots' issues

sentence_348: The RLM's apparent lack of a dedicated "technical-tactical" department, that would have directly been in contact with combat pilots to assess their needs for weaponry upgrades and tactical advice, had never been seriously envisioned as a critically ongoing necessity in the planning of the original German air arm.
sentence_349: The RLM did have its own Technisches Amt (T-Amt) department to handle aviation technology issues, but this was tasked with handling all aviation technology issues in the Third Reich, both military and civilian in nature, and also not known to have ever had any clear and actively administrative and consultative links with the front-line forces established for such purposes.
sentence_350: On the front-line combat side of the issue, and for direct contact with the German aviation firms making the Luftwaffe's warplanes, the Luftwaffe did have its own reasonably effective system of four military aviation test facilities, or Erprobungstellen located at three coastal sites – [[Peenemünde_Airfield|Peenemünde-West]] (also incorporating a separate facility in nearby [[Karlshagen|Karlshagen]]), [[Tarnewitz_test_site|Tarnewitz]] and [[Priwall_Peninsula|Travemünde]] – and the central inland site of [[Rechlin-Lärz_Airfield|Rechlin]], itself first established as a military airfield in late August 1918 by the German Empire, with the four-facility system commanded later in World War II by Oberst (Colonel) [[Edgar_Petersen|Edgar Petersen]].
sentence_351: However, due to lack of co-ordination between the RLM and OKL, all fighter and bomber development was oriented toward short range aircraft, as they could be produced in greater numbers, rather than quality long range aircraft, something that put the Luftwaffe at a disadvantage [[Aircraft_of_the_Battle_of_Britain#German_fighter_fuel_capacity|as early as the Battle of Britain]].
sentence_352: The "ramp-up" to production levels required to fulfill the Luftwaffe's front-line needs was also slow, not reaching maximum output until 1944.
sentence_353: Production of fighters was not [[Jägernotprogramm|given priority until 1944]]; [[Adolf_Galland|Adolf Galland]] commented that this should have occurred at least a year earlier.
sentence_354: Galland also pointed to the mistakes and challenges made in the development of the [[Messerschmitt_Me_262|Messerschmitt Me 262]] jet – which included the protracted development time required for its [[Junkers_Jumo_004|Junkers Jumo 004]] jet engines to achieve reliability.
sentence_355: German combat aircraft types that were first designed and flown in the mid-1930s had become obsolete, yet were kept in production, in particular the Ju 87 Stuka, and the Bf 109, because there were no well-developed replacement designs.
sentence_356: The failure of German production was evident from the start of the Battle of Britain.
sentence_357: By the end of 1940 the Luftwaffe had suffered heavy losses and needed to regroup.
sentence_358: Deliveries of new aircraft were insufficient to meet the drain on resources; the Luftwaffe, unlike the RAF, was failing to expand its pilot and aircraft numbers.
sentence_359: This was partly owing to production planning failures before the war and the demands of the army.
sentence_360: Nevertheless, the German aircraft industry was being outproduced in 1940.
sentence_361: In terms of fighter aircraft production, the British exceeded their production plans by 43%, while the Germans remained 40% "behind" target by the summer 1940.
sentence_362: In fact German production in fighters fell from 227 to 177 per month between July and September 1940.
sentence_363: One of the many reasons for the failure of the Luftwaffe in 1940 was that it did not have the operational and material means to destroy the British aircraft industry, something that the much-anticipated Bomber B design competition was intended to address.
sentence_364: The so-called "Göring program", had largely been predicated on the defeat of the Soviet Union in 1941.
sentence_365: After the Wehrmacht's failure in front of Moscow, industrial priorities for a possibility in increasing aircraft production were largely abandoned in favor to support the army's increased attrition rates and heavy equipment losses.
sentence_366: Erhard Milch's reforms expanded production rates.
sentence_367: In 1941 an average of 981 aircraft (including 311 fighters) were produced each month.
sentence_368: In 1942 this rose to 1,296 aircraft of which 434 were fighters.
sentence_369: Milch's planned production increases were initially opposed.
sentence_370: But in June, he was granted materials for 900 fighters per month as the average output.
sentence_371: By the Summer of 1942, Luftwaffe's operational fighter force had recovered from a low of 39% (44% for fighters and 31% for bombers) in Winter of 1941–1942, to 69% by late June (75% for fighters and 66% for bombers) in 1942.
sentence_372: However, after increased commitments in the east, overall operational ready rates fluctuated between 59% and 65% for the remaining year.
sentence_373: Throughout 1942 the Luftwaffe was out produced in fighter aircraft by 250% and in twin-engine aircraft by 196%.
sentence_374: The appointment of [[Albert_Speer|Albert Speer]] as Minister of Armaments increased production of existing designs, and the few new designs that had originated from earlier in the war.
sentence_375: However the intensification of Allied bombing caused the dispersion of production and prevented an efficient acceleration of expansion.
sentence_376: German aviation production reached about 36,000 combat aircraft for 1944.
sentence_377: However, by the time this was achieved the Luftwaffe lacked the fuel and trained pilots to make this achievement worth while.
sentence_378: The failure to maximize production immediately after the failures in the Soviet Union and North Africa ensured the Luftwaffe's effective defeat in the period of September 1943 – February 1944.
sentence_379: Despite the tactical victories won, they failed to achieve a decisive victory.
sentence_380: By the time production reached acceptable levels, as so many other factors had for the Luftwaffe – and for the entire Wehrmacht's weapons and ordnance technology as a whole – late in the war, it was "too little, too late".
sentence_381: By the late 1930s, [[Airframe|airframe]] construction methods had progressed to the point where airframes could be built to any required size, founded on the all-metal airframe design technologies pioneered by Hugo Junkers in 1915 and constantly improved upon for over two decades to follow – especially in Germany with aircraft like the Dornier Do X flying boat and the [[Junkers_G_38|Junkers G 38]] airliner.
sentence_382: However, powering such designs was a major challenge.
sentence_383: Mid-1930s aero engines were limited to about 600 hp and the first 1000 hp engines were just entering the prototype stage – for the then-new Third Reich's Luftwaffe air arm, this meant liquid-cooled inverted V12 designs like the [[Daimler-Benz_DB_601|Daimler-Benz DB 601]].
sentence_384: The [[United_States|United States]] had already gotten its start towards this goal by 1937 with two large displacement, twin-row 18-cylinder air-cooled radial engine designs of at least 46 litres (2,800 in) displacement each: the [[Pratt_&_Whitney_Double_Wasp#Design_and_development|Pratt & Whitney Double Wasp]] and the Wright Duplex-Cyclone.
sentence_385: Nazi Germany's initial need for substantially more powerful aviation engines originated with the private venture Heinkel He 119 high-speed reconnaissance design, and the ostensibly twin-"engined" [[Messerschmitt_Me_261|Messerschmitt Me 261]] for maritime reconnaissance duties – to power each of these designs, Daimler-Benz literally "doubled-up" their new, fuel-injected DB 601 engines.
sentence_386: This "doubling-up" involved placing two DB 601s side by side on either side of a common vertical-plane space frame with their crankcases' outer sides each having a mount similar to what would be used in a single-engine installation, creating a "mirror-image" centrifugal supercharger for the starboard-side component DB 601, inclining the top ends of their crankcases inwards by roughly 30º to mate with the space-frame central mount, and placing a common propeller gear reduction housing across the front ends of the two engines.
sentence_387: Such a twin-crankcased "power system" aviation engine crafted from a pair of DB 601s resulted in the 2,700 PS (1,986 kW) maximum output DB 606 "coupled" engine design for these two aircraft in February 1937, but with each of the DB 606 "coupled" engines weighing in at around 1.5 tonnes apiece.
sentence_388: The early development of the DB 606 "coupled" engines, was paralleled during the late 1930s with Daimler-Benz's simultaneous development of a 1,500 kW class engine design using a single crankcase.
sentence_389: The result was the twenty-four cylinder [[Daimler-Benz_DB_604|Daimler-Benz DB 604]] [[X_engine|X-configuration]] engine, with four banks of six cylinders each.
sentence_390: Possessing essentially the same displacement of 46.5 litres (2830 in) as the initial version of the liquid-cooled [[Junkers_Jumo_222|Junkers Jumo 222]] multibank engine, itself a "converse" choice in configuration to the DB 604 in possessing six banks of four inline cylinders apiece instead; coincidentally, both the original Jumo 222 design and the DB 604 each weighed about a third less (at some 1,080 kg/2,379 lb of dry weight) than the DB 606, but the DB 604's protracted development was diverting valuable German aviation powerplant research resources, and with more development of the "twinned-[[Daimler-Benz_DB_605|DB 605]]" based DB 610 coupled engine (itself initiated in June 1940 with top output level of 2950 PS (2,909 hp), and brought together in the same way – with the same all-up weight of 1.5 tonnes – as the DB 606 had been) giving improved results at the time, the Reich Air Ministry stopped all work on the DB 604 in September 1942.
sentence_391: Such "coupled powerplants" were the exclusive choice of power for the [[Heinkel_He_177|Heinkel He 177]]A Greif heavy bomber, mistasked from its beginnings in being intended to do moderate-angle "dive bombing" for a 30-meter wingspan class, heavy bomber design – the twin nacelles for a pair of DB 606s or 610s did reduce drag for such a combat "requirement", but the poor design of the He 177A's engine accommodations for these twin-crankcase "power systems" caused [[Heinkel_He_177#Engine_difficulties|repeated outbreaks of engine fires]], causing the "dive bombing" requirement for the He 177A to be cancelled by mid-September 1942.
sentence_392: BMW worked on what was essentially an enlarged version of its highly successful BMW 801 design from the [[Focke-Wulf_Fw_190|Focke-Wulf Fw 190]]A.
sentence_393: This led to the 53.7-litre displacement [[BMW_802|BMW 802]] in 1943, an eighteen-cylinder air-cooled radial, which nearly matched the American Duplex-Cyclone's 54.9-litre figure, but with a weight of some 1,530 kg (3,370 lb) matching that of the 24-cylinder liquid-cooled inline DB 606; and the even larger, 83.5-litre displacement [[BMW_803|BMW 803]] 28-cylinder liquid-cooled radial, which from post-war statements from BMW development personnel were each considered to be "secondary priority" development programs at best.
sentence_394: This situation with the 802 and 803 designs led to the company's engineering personnel being redirected to place all efforts on improving the 801 to develop it to its full potential.
sentence_395: The BMW 801F radial development, through its use of features coming from the 801E subtype, was able to substantially exceed the over-1,500 kW output level.
sentence_396: The two closest Allied equivalents to the 801 in configuration and displacement – the American [[Wright_R-2600#Variants|Wright Twin Cyclone]], and the Soviet [[Shvetsov_ASh-82#Variants|Shvetsov ASh-82]] radials – never had any need to be developed beyond a 1,500 kW output level, as larger-displacement, 18-cylinder radial aviation engines in both nations (the aforementioned American Double Wasp and Duplex-Cyclone) and the eventual 1945 premiere of the Soviet [[Shvetsov_ASh-73|Shvetsov ASh-73]] design, all three of which started their development before 1940, handled needs for even greater power from large radial aviation engines.
sentence_397: The twinned-up [[Daimler-Benz_DB_601|Daimler-Benz DB 601]]-based, 1,750 kW output DB 606, and its more powerful descendant, the 2,130 kW output DB 605-based DB 610, weighing some 1.5 tonnes apiece, were the only 1,500 kW-plus output level aircraft powerplants to ever be produced by Germany for Luftwaffe combat aircraft, mostly for the aforementioned Heinkel He 177A heavy bomber.
sentence_398: Even the largest-displacement inverted V12 aircraft powerplant built in Germany, the 44.52-litre (2,717 cu.
sentence_399: in.)
sentence_400: [[Daimler-Benz_DB_603|Daimler-Benz DB 603]], which saw widespread use in twin-engined designs, could not exceed the 1,500 kW output level without more development.
sentence_401: By March 1940, even the DB 603 was being "twinned-up" as the 601/606 and 605/610 had been, to become their replacement "power system": this was the strictly experimental, approximately 1.8-tonne weight apiece, twin-crankcase DB 613; capable of over 2,570 kW (3,495 PS) output, but which never left its test phase.
sentence_402: The proposed over-1,500 kW output subtypes of German aviation industry's existing piston aviation engine designs—which adhered to using just a single crankcase that were able to substantially exceed the aforementioned over-1,500 kW output level—were the DB 603 LM (1,800 kW at take-off, in production), the DB 603 N (2,205 kW at take-off, planned for 1946) and the BMW 801F (1,765 kW (2,400 PS) engines.
sentence_403: The pioneering nature of jet engine technology in the 1940s resulted in numerous development problems for both of Germany's major jet engine designs to see mass production, the [[Jumo_004|Jumo 004]] and BMW 003 (both of pioneering axial flow design), with the more powerful [[Heinkel_HeS_011|Heinkel HeS 011]] never leaving the test phase, as only 19 examples of the HeS 011 would ever be built for development.
sentence_404: Even with such dismal degrees of success for such advanced aviation powerplant designs, more and more design proposals for new German combat aircraft in the 1943–45 period centered either around the failed Jumo 222 or HeS 011 aviation powerplants for their propulsion.
sentence_405: The bomber arm was given preference and received the "better" pilots.
sentence_406: Later, fighter pilot leaders were few in numbers as a result of this.
sentence_407: As with the late shift to fighter production, the Luftwaffe pilot schools did not give the fighter pilot schools preference soon enough.
sentence_408: The Luftwaffe, OKW argued, was still an offensive weapon, and its primary focus was on producing bomber pilots.
sentence_409: This attitude prevailed until the second half of 1943.
sentence_410: During the [[Defence_of_the_Reich|Defence of the Reich]] campaign in 1943 and 1944, there were not enough commissioned fighter pilots and leaders to meet attrition rates; as the need arose to replace aircrew (as attrition rates increased), the quality of [[Defence_of_the_Reich#Pilot_selection_and_training|pilot training deteriorated]] rapidly.
sentence_411: Later this was made worse by [[Oil_Campaign_of_World_War_II|fuel shortages for pilot training]].
sentence_412: Overall this meant reduced training on operational types, formation flying, gunnery training, and combat training, and a total lack of instrument training.
sentence_413: At the beginning of the war commanders were replaced with younger commanders too quickly.
sentence_414: These younger commanders had to learn "in the field" rather than entering a front-line post fully qualified.
sentence_415: Training of formation leaders was not systematic until 1943, which was far too late, with the Luftwaffe already stretched.
sentence_416: The Luftwaffe thus lacked a cadre of staff officers to set up new combat units with carefully selected and skilled combat personnel, and pass on experience.
sentence_417: Moreover, Luftwaffe leadership from the start poached the training command, which undermined its ability to replace losses, while also planning for "short sharp campaigns", which did not pertain.
sentence_418: Moreover, no plans were laid for [[Night_fighter|night fighters]].
sentence_419: In fact, when protests were raised, [[Hans_Jeschonnek|Hans Jeschonnek]], Chief of the General Staff of the Luftwaffe, said, "First we've got to beat Russia, then we can start training!"
sentence_420: The Luftwaffe was unusual among contemporary independent air forces in possessing an organic [[Paratrooper|paratrooper]] force called [[Fallschirmjäger_(World_War_II)|Fallschirmjäger]].
sentence_421: Established in 1938, they were deployed in parachute operations in 1940 and 1941 and participated in the [[Battle_of_Fort_Eben-Emael|Battle of Fort Eben-Emael]] and the [[Battle_for_The_Hague|Battle for The Hague]] in May 1940, and during the [[Battle_of_Crete|Battle of Crete]] in May 1941.
sentence_422: However, more than 4,000 Fallschirmjäger were killed during the Crete operation.
sentence_423: Afterwards, although continuing to be trained in parachute delivery, paratroopers were only used in a parachute role for smaller-scale operations, such as [[Gran_Sasso_raid|the rescue of Benito Mussolini in 1943]].
sentence_424: Fallschirmjäger formations were mainly used as [[Light_infantry|light infantry]] in all theatres of the war.
sentence_425: Their losses were 22,041 KIA, 57,594 WIA and 44,785 MIA (until February 1945).
sentence_426: During 1942 surplus Luftwaffe personnel was used to form the [[Luftwaffe_Field_Division|Luftwaffe Field Divisions]], standard infantry divisions that were used chiefly as [[Bandit_fighting|rear echelon units]] to free up front line troops.
sentence_427: From 1943, the Luftwaffe also had an armoured division called Fallschirm-Panzer Division 1 Hermann Göring, which was expanded to a [[Panzerkorps|Panzerkorps]] in 1944.
sentence_428: Ground support and combat units from the Reichsarbeitsdienst (RAD) and the [[National_Socialist_Motor_Corps|National Socialist Motor Corps]] (NSKK) were also put at the Luftwaffe's disposal during the war.
sentence_429: In 1942 56 RAD companies served with the Luftwaffe in the West as airfield construction troops.
sentence_430: In 1943 420 RAD companies were trained as [[Anti-aircraft_artillery|anti-aircraft artillery]] (AAA) and posted to existing Luftwaffe AAA battalions in the homeland.
sentence_431: At the end of the war, these units were also fighting allied tanks.
sentence_432: Beginning in 1939 with a transport regiment, the NSKK had in 1942 a complete division sized transportation unit serving the Luftwaffe, the NSKK Transportgruppe Luftwaffe serving in France and at the Eastern front.
sentence_433: The overwhelming number of its 12,000 members were Belgian, Dutch and French collaborators.

section_21.value: War crimes and bombing of non-military targets

sentence_434: See also: [[Jägerstab|Jägerstab]], [[Luftwaffe_guards_at_concentration_camps|Luftwaffe guards at concentration camps]], and Companies involved in the Holocaust
sentence_435: In 1943 and 1944, aircraft production was moved to concentration camps in order to alleviate labor shortages and to protect production from Allied air raids.
sentence_436: The two largest aircraft factories in Germany were located at [[Mauthausen-Gusen|Mauthausen-Gusen]] and [[Mittelbau-Dora|Mittelbau-Dora]] concentration camps.
sentence_437: Aircraft parts were also manufactured at [[Flossenbürg_concentration_camp|Flossenbürg]], [[Buchenwald|Buchenwald]], [[Dachau_concentration_camp|Dachau]], [[Ravensbrück|Ravensbrück]], [[Gross-Rosen|Gross-Rosen]], [[Natzweiler|Natzweiler]], [[Herzogenbusch|Herzogenbusch]], and [[Neuengamme_concentration_camp|Neuengamme]].
sentence_438: In 1944 and 1945, as many as 90,000 concentration prisoners worked in the aviation industry, and were about one tenth of the concentration camp population over the winter of 1944–45.
sentence_439: Partly in response to the Luftwaffe's demand for more forced laborers to increase fighter production, the concentration camp more than doubled between mid-1943 (224,000) and mid-1944 (524,000).
sentence_440: Part of this increase was due to the deportation of the Hungarian Jews; the [[Jägerstab|Jägerstab]] program was used to justify the deportations to the Hungarian government.
sentence_441: Of the 437,000 Hungarian Jews deported between May and July 1944, about 320,000 were gassed on arrival at [[Auschwitz|Auschwitz]] and the remainder forced to work.
sentence_442: Only 50,000 survived.
sentence_443: Almost 1,000 fuselages of the jet fighter [[Messerschmitt_Me_262|Messerschmitt Me 262]] were produced at Gusen, a subcamp of Mauthausen and brutal Nazi labor camp, where the average life expectancy was six months.
sentence_444: By 1944, one-third of production at the crucial [[Regensburg|Regensburg]] plant that produced the Bf 109, the backbone of the Luftwaffe fighter arm, originated in Gusen and Flossenbürg alone.
sentence_445: [[Synthetic_oil|Synthetic oil]] was produced from [[Shale_oil|shale oil]] deposits by prisoners of Mittlebau-Dora as part of [[Operation_Desert_(German_fuel_project)|Operation Desert]] directed by [[Edmund_Geilenberg|Edmund Geilenberg]] in order to make up for the [[Oil_campaign_of_World_War_II|decrease in oil production due to Allied bombing]].
sentence_446: For oil production, three subcamps were constructed and 15,000 prisoners forced to work in the plant.
sentence_447: More than 3,500 people died.
sentence_448: Vaivara concentration camp in [[Estonia|Estonia]] was also established for shale oil extraction; about 20,000 prisoners worked there and more than 1,500 died at Vaivara.
sentence_449: Luftwaffe airfields were frequently maintained using forced labor.
sentence_450: Thousands of inmates from five subcamps of [[Stutthof_concentration_camp|Stutthof]] worked on the airfields.
sentence_451: Airfields and bases near several other concentration camps and [[Nazi_ghettos|ghettos]] were constructed or maintained by prisoners.
sentence_452: On the orders of the Luftwaffe, prisoners from Buchenwald and Herzogenbusch were forced to defuse bombs that had fallen around Düsseldorf and Leeuwarden respectively.
sentence_453: Thousands of Luftwaffe personnel [[Luftwaffe_guards_at_concentration_camps|worked as concentration camp guards]].
sentence_454: [[Auschwitz|Auschwitz]] included a munitions factory guarded by Luftwaffe soldiers; 2,700 Luftwaffe personnel worked as guards at Buchenwald.
sentence_455: Dozens of camps and subcamps were staffed primarily by Luftwaffe soldiers.
sentence_456: According to the [[Encyclopedia_of_Camps_and_Ghettos|Encyclopedia of Camps and Ghettos]], it was typical for camps devoted to armaments production to be run by the branch of the Wehrmacht that used the products.
sentence_457: In 1944, many Luftwaffe soldiers were transferred to concentration camps to alleviate personnel shortages.
sentence_458: Further information: [[Bandenbekämpfung|Bandenbekämpfung]] and [[List_of_Wehrmacht_and_Waffen-SS_divisions_that_committed_war_crimes_in_Italy|List of Wehrmacht and Waffen-SS divisions that committed war crimes in Italy]]
sentence_459: [[Luftwaffe_paratroopers|Luftwaffe paratroopers]] committed many war crimes in [[Crete|Crete]] following the [[Battle_of_Crete|Battle of Crete]], including the [[Alikianos_executions|Alikianos executions]], [[Massacre_of_Kondomari|Massacre of Kondomari]], and the [[Razing_of_Kandanos|Razing of Kandanos]].
sentence_460: Several Luftwaffe divisions, including the [[1st_Parachute_Division_(Germany)|1st Parachute Division]], [[2nd_Parachute_Division_(Germany)|2nd Parachute Division]], [[4th_Parachute_Division_(Germany)|4th Parachute Division]], 19th Luftwaffe Field Division, 20th Luftwaffe Field Division and the 1st Fallschirm-Panzer Division, committed war crimes in Italy, murdering hundreds of civilians.
sentence_461: Luftwaffe troops participated in the murder of Jews imprisoned in ghettos in Eastern Europe, for example assisting in the murder of 2,680 Jews at the Nemirov ghetto, participating in a series of massacres at the Opoczno ghetto, and helping to liquidate the [[Dęblin–Irena_Ghetto|Dęblin–Irena Ghetto]] by deporting thousands of Jews to the [[Treblinka_extermination_camp|Treblinka extermination camp]].
sentence_462: Between 1942 and 1944, two Luftwaffe security battalions were stationed in the [[Białowieża_Forest|Białowieża Forest]] for [[Bandenbekämpfung|Bandenbekämpfung]] operations.
sentence_463: Encouraged by Göring, they murdered thousands of Jews and other civilians.
sentence_464: Luftwaffe soldiers frequently [[Summary_execution|executed]] Polish civilians at random with baseless accuastions of being "[[Bolshevik|Bolshevik]] agents", in order to keep the population in line, or as reprisal for partisan activities.
sentence_465: The performance of the troops was measured by the [[Body_count|body count]] of people murdered.
sentence_466: Ten thousand Luftwaffe troops were stationed on the Eastern Front for such "anti-partisan" operations.
sentence_467: See also: [[Nazi_human_experimentation|Nazi human experimentation]]
sentence_468: Throughout the war, concentration camp prisoners were forced to serve as [[Human_subject_research|human guinea pigs]] in testing Luftwaffe equipment.
sentence_469: Some were carried out by Luftwaffe personnel and others were performed by the SS on the orders of the OKL.
sentence_470: In 1941, experiments with the intent of discovering means to prevent and treat [[Hypothermia|hypothermia]] were carried out for the Luftwaffe, which had lost aircrew to immersion hypothermia after ditchings.
sentence_471: The experiments were conducted at Dachau and Auschwitz.
sentence_472: [[Sigmund_Rascher|Sigmund Rascher]], a Luftwaffe doctor based at Dachau, published the results at the 1942 medical conference entitled "Medical Problems Arising from Sea and Winter".
sentence_473: Of about 400 prisoners forced to participate in cold-water experiments, 80 to 90 were killed.
sentence_474: In early 1942, prisoners at Dachau were used by Rascher in experiments to perfect ejection seats at high altitudes.
sentence_475: A [[Pressure_vessel|low-pressure chamber]] containing these prisoners was used to simulate conditions at altitudes of up to 20,000 metres (66,000 ft).
sentence_476: It was rumoured that Rascher performed [[Vivisection|vivisections]] on the brains of victims who survived the initial experiment.
sentence_477: Of the 200 subjects, 80 died from the experimentation, and the others were executed.
sentence_478: Eugen Hagen, head doctor of the Luftwaffe, infected inmates of Natzweiler concentration camp with [[Typhus|typhus]] in order to test the efficacy of proposed vaccines.
sentence_479: See also: [[Bombing_of_Wieluń|Bombing of Wieluń]] and [[Operation_Retribution_(1941)|Operation Retribution (1941)]]
sentence_480: No [[Positive_international_law|positive]] or specific [[Customary_international_law|customary]] [[International_humanitarian_law|international humanitarian law]] with respect to [[Aerial_warfare|aerial warfare]] existed prior to or during World War II.
sentence_481: This is also why no Luftwaffe officers were prosecuted at the post-World War II Allied war crime trials for the aerial raids.
sentence_482: The [[Bombing_of_Wieluń|bombing of Wieluń]] was an air raid on the [[Poland|Polish]] town of [[Wieluń|Wieluń]] by the Luftwaffe on 1 September 1939.
sentence_483: The Luftwaffe started bombing Wieluń at 04:40, five minutes before the shelling of Westerplatte, which has traditionally been considered the beginning of [[World_War_II|World War II]] in Europe.
sentence_484: The air raid on the town was one of the [[Strategic_bombing_during_World_War_II|first aerial bombings of the war]].
sentence_485: About 1,300 civilians were killed, hundreds injured, and 90 percent of the town centre was destroyed.
sentence_486: The casualty rate was more than twice as high as [[Bombing_of_Guernica|Guernica]].
sentence_487: A 1989 Sender Freies Berlin documentary stated that there were no military or industrial targets in the area, except for a small sugar factory in the outskirts of the town.
sentence_488: Furthermore, Trenkner stated that German bombers first destroyed the town's hospital.
sentence_489: Two attempts, in 1978 and 1983, to prosecute individuals for the bombing of the Wieluń hospital were dismissed by West German judges when prosecutors stated that the pilots had been unable to make out the nature of the structure due to fog.
sentence_490: [[Operation_Retribution_(1941)|Operation Retribution]] was the April 1941 [[Nazi_Germany|German]] [[Strategic_bombing|bombing]] of [[Belgrade|Belgrade]], the capital of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia.
sentence_491: The bombing deliberately targeted the killing of civilians as punishment, and resulted in 17,000 civilian deaths.
sentence_492: It occurred in the first days of the [[World_War_II|World War II]] German-led [[Axis_powers|Axis]] [[Invasion_of_Yugoslavia|invasion of Yugoslavia]].
sentence_493: The operation commenced on 6 April and concluded on 7 or 8 April, resulting in the paralysis of Yugoslav civilian and military command and control, widespread destruction in the centre of the city and many civilian casualties.
sentence_494: Following the Yugoslav capitulation, Luftwaffe engineers conducted a bomb damage assessment in Belgrade.
sentence_495: The report stated that 218.5 metric tons (215.0 long tons; 240.9 short tons) of bombs were dropped, with 10 to 14 percent being incendiaries.
sentence_496: It listed all the targets of the bombing, which included: the royal palace, the war ministry, military headquarters, the central post office, the telegraph office, passenger and goods railway stations, power stations and barracks.
sentence_497: It also mentioned that seven aerial mines were dropped, and that areas in the centre and northwest of the city had been destroyed, comprising 20 to 25 percent of its total area.
sentence_498: Some aspects of the bombing remain unexplained, particularly the use of the aerial mines.
sentence_499: In contrast, Pavlowitch states that almost 50 percent of housing in Belgrade was destroyed.
sentence_500: After the invasion, the Germans forced between 3,500 and 4,000 [[Jews|Jews]] to collect rubble that was caused by the bombing.
sentence_501: Main article: [[List_of_Luftwaffe_personnel_convicted_of_war_crimes|List of Luftwaffe personnel convicted of war crimes]]
sentence_502: Several prominent Luftwaffe commanders were convicted of war crimes, including General Alexander Löhr and Field Marshal [[Albert_Kesselring|Albert Kesselring]].

title: Liverpool
sentence_0: This article is about the English city.
sentence_1: For the football club, see [[Liverpool_F.C.|Liverpool F.C.]] For other uses, see [[Liverpool_(disambiguation)|Liverpool (disambiguation)]].

sentence_2: Liverpool is a [[City_status_in_the_United_Kingdom|city]] and [[Metropolitan_borough|metropolitan borough]] in [[Merseyside|Merseyside]], [[England|England]].
sentence_3: Its population in 2019 was approximately 498,042, making it the [[List_of_English_districts_by_population|tenth-largest English district by population]].
sentence_4: Liverpool's [[ESPON_metropolitan_areas_in_the_United_Kingdom|metropolitan area]] is the fifth-largest in the UK with a population of 2.24 million.
sentence_5: Liverpool is on the eastern side of the [[Mersey_Estuary|Mersey Estuary]] and historically lay within the ancient [[Hundred_(county_division)|hundred]] of [[West_Derby_(hundred)|West Derby]] in North West England's [[Historic_counties_of_England|county]] of [[Lancashire|Lancashire]].
sentence_6: It became a [[Borough_status_in_the_United_Kingdom|borough in 1207]], a [[City_status_in_the_United_Kingdom|city in 1880]], and a [[County_borough|county borough]] independent of Lancashire in 1889.
sentence_7: Its growth as a [[Port_of_Liverpool|major port]] was paralleled by the expansion of the city throughout the [[Industrial_Revolution|Industrial Revolution]].
sentence_8: Along with general cargo, freight, and raw materials such as coal and cotton, merchants were involved in the [[Atlantic_slave_trade|slave trade]].
sentence_9: In the 19th century, Liverpool was a major port of departure for English and Irish emigrants to [[North_America|North America]].
sentence_10: It was also home to both the [[Cunard_Line|Cunard]] and White Star Lines, and was the port of registry of the ocean liners [[RMS_Titanic|RMS Titanic]], [[RMS_Lusitania|RMS Lusitania]], [[RMS_Queen_Mary|RMS Queen Mary]], and [[RMS_Olympic|RMS Olympic]].
sentence_11: In 2019, Liverpool was ranked fifth on the list of the most visited UK cities.
sentence_12: It is noted for its [[Culture_of_Liverpool|culture]], [[Architecture_of_Liverpool|architecture]], and [[Transport_in_Liverpool|transport links]].
sentence_13: The city is closely associated with the arts, especially music; the popularity of [[The_Beatles|the Beatles]], who are widely regarded as [[Cultural_impact_of_the_Beatles|the most influential musical group in history]], cemented the city's status as a tourist destination.
sentence_14: Since then, Liverpool has continued to produce many notable musicians and record labels—musicians from the city have produced 56 [[List_of_best-selling_singles|No.
sentence_15: 1 hit singles]], more than any other city in the world.
sentence_16: It also has a long-standing reputation as the origin of various actors and actresses, artists, athletes, comedians, journalists, novelists, and poets.
sentence_17: The city has the second-highest number of art galleries, national museums, [[Listed_buildings_in_Liverpool|listed buildings]], and [[Parks_and_open_spaces_in_Liverpool|listed parks]] in the UK; only the capital, [[London|London]], has more.
sentence_18: The [[Liverpool_Maritime_Mercantile_City|Liverpool Maritime Mercantile City]] includes the [[Pier_Head|Pier Head]], [[Royal_Albert_Dock,_Liverpool|Albert Dock]], and [[William_Brown_Street|William Brown Street]].
sentence_19: In sports, the city is best known for being the home of [[Premier_League|Premier League]] football teams [[Liverpool_F.C.|Liverpool FC]] and [[Everton_F.C.|Everton FC]], with matches between the two being known as the Merseyside derby.
sentence_20: The annual [[Grand_National|Grand National]] horse race takes place at Aintree Racecourse.
sentence_21: Several areas of [[Liverpool_city_centre|Liverpool city centre]] were granted [[World_Heritage_Site|World Heritage Site]] status by [[UNESCO|UNESCO]] in 2004, and the city's vast collection of parks and open spaces has been described as the "most important in the country" by England's [[Register_of_Historic_Parks_and_Gardens_of_Special_Historic_Interest_in_England|Register of Historic Parks and Gardens of Special Historic Interest]].
sentence_22: Its status as a port city historically attracted a diverse population from a wide range of cultures, primarily [[Republic_of_Ireland|Ireland]], [[Norway|Norway]], and [[Wales|Wales]].
sentence_23: It is also home to the [[Black_people_in_Liverpool|oldest black community in the UK]] and the [[Chinatown,_Liverpool|oldest Chinese community in Europe]].
sentence_24: Natives of Liverpool (and occasionally longtime residents) are formally referred to as "Liverpudlians" but are more often called "Scousers", a reference to [[Scouse_(food)|the form of stew]] made popular by sailors in the city, which also became the most common name for the [[Scouse|local accent and dialect]].
sentence_25: The city celebrated its 800th anniversary in 2007 and was named the 2008 [[European_Capital_of_Culture|European Capital of Culture]], which it shared with the Norwegian city of [[Stavanger|Stavanger]].
sentence_26: Its designation as European Capital of Culture resulted in a sharp uptick in the city's fortunes, as the money gained from the EU was spent on regenerating large parts of the city that had become run down.
sentence_27: The name comes from the Old English lifer, meaning thick or muddy water, and pōl, meaning a pool or creek, and is first recorded around 1190 as Liuerpul.
sentence_28: According to the Cambridge Dictionary of English Place-Names, "The original reference was to a pool or tidal creek now filled up into which two streams drained".
sentence_29: The place appearing as Leyrpole, in a legal record of 1418, may also refer to Liverpool.
sentence_30: Other origins of the name have been suggested, including "elverpool", a reference to the large number of [[Eel|eels]] in the [[River_Mersey|Mersey]].
sentence_31: The adjective "Liverpudlian" was first recorded in 1833.
sentence_32: Although the Old English origin of the name Liverpool is beyond dispute, claims are sometimes made that the name Liverpool is of Welsh origin, but these are without foundation.
sentence_33: The Welsh name for Liverpool is Lerpwl, from a former English local form Leerpool.
sentence_34: This is a reduction of the form "Leverpool" with the loss of the intervocalic [v] (seen in other English names and words e.g. Daventry (Northamptonshire) > Danetry, never-do-well > ne'er-do-well).
sentence_35: In the nineteenth century, some Welsh publications used the name "Lle'r Pwll" ("(the) place (of) the pool"), a reinterpretation of Lerpwl, probably in the belief that "Lle'r Pwll" was the original form.
sentence_36: Another name, which is widely known even today, is Llynlleifiad, again a nineteenth-century coining.
sentence_37: "Llyn" is pool, but "lleifiad" has no obvious meaning.
sentence_38: Professor G. Melville Richards (1910‐1973), a pioneer of scientific toponymy in Wales, in "Place Names of North Wales", does not attempt to explain it beyond noting that "lleifiad" is used as a Welsh equivalent of "Liver".
sentence_39: A derivative form of a learned borrowing into Welsh (*llaf) of Latin lāma (slough, bog, fen) to give "lleifiad" is possible, but unproven.
sentence_40: Main articles: [[History_of_Liverpool|History of Liverpool]] and [[Timeline_of_Liverpool|Timeline of Liverpool]]
sentence_41: [[John_of_England|King John]]'s [[Letters_patent|letters patent]] of 1207 announced the foundation of the borough of Liverpool.
sentence_42: By the middle of the 16th century, the population was still around 500.
sentence_43: The original street plan of Liverpool is said to have been designed by King John near the same time it was granted a [[Royal_charter|royal charter]], making it a borough.
sentence_44: The original seven streets were laid out in an H shape: Bank Street (now Water Street), Castle Street, Chapel Street, Dale Street, Juggler Street (now High Street), Moor Street (now Tithebarn Street) and Whiteacre Street (now Old Hall Street).
sentence_45: In the 17th century there was slow progress in trade and population growth.
sentence_46: Battles for control of the town were waged during the [[English_Civil_War|English Civil War]], including an eighteen-day siege in 1644.
sentence_47: In 1699, the same year as its first recorded [[Slave_ship|slave ship]], Liverpool Merchant, set sail for Africa, Liverpool was made a parish by Act of Parliament, although arguably the legislation of 1695 that reformed the Liverpool council was of more significance to its subsequent development.
sentence_48: Since Roman times, the nearby city of [[Chester|Chester]] on the [[River_Dee,_Wales|River Dee]] had been the region's principal port on the [[Irish_Sea|Irish Sea]].
sentence_49: However, as the Dee began to silt up, maritime trade from Chester became increasingly difficult and shifted towards Liverpool on the neighbouring [[River_Mersey|River Mersey]].
sentence_50: As trade from the [[West_Indies|West Indies]], including sugar, surpassed that of Ireland and Europe, and as the [[River_Dee,_Wales|River Dee]] continued to silt up, Liverpool began to grow with increasing rapidity.
sentence_51: The first commercial [[Wet_dock|wet dock]] was built in Liverpool in 1715.
sentence_52: Substantial profits from the [[Atlantic_slave_trade|slave trade]] and tobacco helped the town to prosper and rapidly grow, although several prominent local men, including William Rathbone, [[William_Roscoe|William Roscoe]] and [[Edward_Rushton|Edward Rushton]], were at the forefront of the [[Abolitionism_in_the_United_Kingdom|local abolitionist movement]].
sentence_53: By the start of the 19th century, a large volume of trade was passing through Liverpool, and the construction of major buildings reflected this wealth.
sentence_54: In 1830, Liverpool and [[Manchester|Manchester]] became the first cities to have an intercity rail link, through the [[Liverpool_and_Manchester_Railway|Liverpool and Manchester Railway]].
sentence_55: The population continued to rise rapidly, especially during the 1840s when [[Irish_diaspora|Irish]] migrants began arriving by the hundreds of thousands as a result of the [[Irish_Potato_Famine_(1845–1849)|Great Famine]].
sentence_56: In her poem "Liverpool" (1832), which celebrates the city's worldwide commerce, [[Letitia_Elizabeth_Landon|Letitia Elizabeth Landon]] refers specifically to the Macgregor Laird expedition to the Niger River, at that time in progress.
sentence_57: Britain was a major market for cotton imported from the [[Deep_South|Deep South]] of the United States, which fed the textile industry in the country.
sentence_58: Given the crucial place cotton held in the city's economy, during the [[American_Civil_War|American Civil War]] Liverpool was, in the words of historian [[Sven_Beckert|Sven Beckert]], "the most pro-Confederate place in the world outside the [[Confederate_States_of_America|Confederacy]] itself."
sentence_59: For periods during the 19th century, the wealth of Liverpool exceeded that of London, and Liverpool's [[Custom_House,_Liverpool|Custom House]] was the single largest contributor to the British Exchequer.
sentence_60: Liverpool was the only British city ever to have its own [[Whitehall|Whitehall]] office.
sentence_61: In the early 19th century, Liverpool played a major role in the [[Antarctic|Antarctic]] [[Seal_hunting|sealing]] industry, in recognition of which [[Liverpool_Beach|Liverpool Beach]] in the [[South_Shetland_Islands|South Shetland Islands]] is named after the city.
sentence_62: As early as 1851 the city was described as "the New York of Europe".
sentence_63: During the late 19th and early 20th centuries, Liverpool was attracting [[Immigrants|immigrants]] from across Europe.
sentence_64: This resulted in the construction of a diverse array of religious buildings in the city for the new ethnic and religious groups, many of which are still in use today.
sentence_65: The [[German_Church,_Liverpool|Deutsche Kirche Liverpool]], [[Greek_Orthodox_Church_of_St_Nicholas|Greek Orthodox Church of St Nicholas]], [[Gustav_Adolf_Church,_Liverpool|Gustav Adolf Church]] and [[Princes_Road_Synagogue|Princes Road Synagogue]] were all established in the 1800s to serve Liverpool's growing German, Greek, Nordic and Jewish communities, respectively.
sentence_66: One of Liverpool's oldest surviving churches, [[St._Peter's_Roman_Catholic_Church,_Liverpool|St.
sentence_67: Peter's Roman Catholic Church]], served the Polish community in its final years as a place of worship.
sentence_68: The postwar period after the Great War was marked by social unrest, as society grappled with the massive war losses of young men, as well as trying to integrate veterans into the economy.
sentence_69: Union organising and strikes took place in numerous locations, including police strikes in London among the Metropolitan Police.
sentence_70: Numerous colonial soldiers and sailors from Africa and India, who had served with the UK, settled in Liverpool and other port cities.
sentence_71: In June 1919 they were subject to attack by whites in racial riots; residents in the port included Swedish immigrants, and both groups had to compete with native people from Liverpool for jobs and housing.
sentence_72: In this period, race riots also took place in [[Cardiff|Cardiff]], [[Newport,_Wales|Newport]] and [[Barry,_Vale_of_Glamorgan|Barry]], and there had been incidents in [[Glasgow|Glasgow]], [[South_Shields|South Shields]], [[London|London]], [[Kingston_upon_Hull|Hull]] and [[City_of_Salford|Salford]].
sentence_73: Similarly, racial riots of whites against blacks took place across the United States in numerous industrial cities, so that a black leader termed the period of time [[Red_Summer|Red Summer]].
sentence_74: In that first postwar year, there were also riots in Caribbean and South African cities.
sentence_75: The Housing Act 1919 resulted in mass council housing being built across Liverpool during the 1920s and 1930s.
sentence_76: Thousands of families were relocated from the inner-city to new suburban housing estates, based on the belief that this would improve their standard of living, though this is largely subjective.
sentence_77: Numerous private homes were also built during this era.
sentence_78: During the [[Great_Depression|Great Depression]] of the early 1930s, unemployment peaked at around 30% in the city.
sentence_79: Liverpool was the site of Britain's first provincial airport, operating from 1930.
sentence_80: During the Second World War, the critical strategic importance of Liverpool was recognised by both [[Hitler|Hitler]] and [[Winston_Churchill|Churchill]].
sentence_81: The city was heavily bombed by the Germans, suffering a [[Liverpool_Blitz|blitz]] second only to London's.
sentence_82: The pivotal Battle of the Atlantic was planned, fought and won from Liverpool.
sentence_83: The [[Luftwaffe|Luftwaffe]] made 80 [[Liverpool_Blitz|air raids on Merseyside]], killing 2,500 people and causing damage to almost half the homes in the metropolitan area.
sentence_84: Significant rebuilding followed the war, including massive housing estates and the [[Seaforth_Dock|Seaforth Dock]], the largest dock project in Britain.
sentence_85: Much of the immediate reconstruction of the city centre has been deeply unpopular.
sentence_86: It was as flawed as much subsequent town planning renewal in the 1950s and 1960s.
sentence_87: The historic portions of the city that had survived German bombing suffered extensive destruction during urban renewal.
sentence_88: Since 1952 Liverpool has been twinned with [[Cologne|Cologne]], Germany, a city which also suffered severe aerial bombing during the war.
sentence_89: A significant [[West_Indies|West Indian]] black community has existed in the city since the first two decades of the 20th century.
sentence_90: Like most British cities and industrialised towns, Liverpool became home to a significant number of [[Commonwealth_of_Nations|Commonwealth]] immigrants, beginning after World War I with colonial soldiers and sailors who had served in the area.
sentence_91: More immigrants arrived after World War II, mostly settling in older inner-city areas such as [[Toxteth|Toxteth]], where housing was less expensive.
sentence_92: The construction of suburban public housing expanded after the Second World War.
sentence_93: Some of the older inner-city areas were redeveloped for new homes.
sentence_94: In the 1960s Liverpool was the centre of the "[[Beat_music|Merseybeat]]" sound, which became synonymous with [[The_Beatles|the Beatles]] and fellow Liverpudlian rock bands.
sentence_95: Influenced by American rhythm and blues and rock music, they also in turn strongly affected American music for years and were internationally popular.
sentence_96: The [[Beatles|Beatles]] became internationally known in the early 1960s and performed for years together; they were the most commercially successful and musically influential band in popular history.
sentence_97: Their co-founder, singer, and composer [[John_Lennon|John Lennon]] was killed in New York City in 1980 after the Beatles stopped performing together.
sentence_98: Liverpool airport was renamed after him in 2002, the first British airport to be named in honour of an individual.
sentence_99: Previously part of [[Lancashire|Lancashire]], and a county borough from 1889, Liverpool in 1974 became a [[Metropolitan_borough|metropolitan borough]] within the newly created [[Metropolitan_county|metropolitan county]] of [[Merseyside|Merseyside]].
sentence_100: From the mid-1970s onwards, Liverpool's docks and traditional [[Manufacturing_industries|manufacturing industries]] declined due to restructuring of shipping and heavy industry, causing massive losses of jobs.
sentence_101: The advent of [[Containerisation|containerisation]] meant that the city's docks became largely obsolete, and dock workers were thrown out of jobs.
sentence_102: By the early 1980s unemployment rates in Liverpool were among the highest in the UK, standing at 17% by January 1982.
sentence_103: This was about half the level of unemployment that had affected the city during the Great Depression 50 years previously.
sentence_104: In the later 20th century, Liverpool's economy began to recover.
sentence_105: Since the mid-1990s the city has enjoyed growth rates higher than the national average.
sentence_106: At the end of the 20th century, Liverpool was concentrating on regeneration, a process that continues today.
sentence_107: To celebrate the [[Golden_Jubilee_of_Elizabeth_II|Golden Jubilee of Elizabeth II]] in 2002, the conservation charity [[Plantlife|Plantlife]] organised a competition to choose [[County_flower|county flowers]]; the [[Eryngium_maritimum|sea-holly]] was Liverpool's final choice.
sentence_108: Capitalising on the popularity of 1960s rock groups, such as [[The_Beatles|the Beatles]], as well as the city's world-class art galleries, museums and landmarks, tourism has also become a significant factor in Liverpool's economy.
sentence_109: In 2004, property developer [[Grosvenor_Group|Grosvenor]] started the Paradise Project, a £920 m development based on Paradise Street.
sentence_110: This produced the most significant changes to Liverpool's city centre since the post-war reconstruction.
sentence_111: Renamed 'Liverpool ONE,' the centre opened in May 2008.
sentence_112: In 2007, the city celebrated the 800th anniversary of the founding of the borough of Liverpool, for which a number of events were planned.
sentence_113: Liverpool was designated as a joint [[European_Capital_of_Culture|European Capital of Culture]] for 2008.
sentence_114: The main celebrations, in September 2008, included the erection of [[La_Princesse|La Princesse]], a large mechanical spider 20 metres high and weighing 37 tonnes, and represents the "eight legs" of Liverpool: honour, history, music, the Mersey, the ports, governance, sunshine and culture.
sentence_115: [[La_Princesse|La Princesse]] roamed the streets of the city during the festivities, and concluded by entering the [[Queensway_Tunnel|Queensway Tunnel]].
sentence_116: Spearheaded by the multi-billion-[[Pound_sterling|pound]] Liverpool ONE development, regeneration has continued through to the start of the early 2010s.
sentence_117: Some of the most significant redevelopment projects include new buildings in the [[Liverpool_City_Centre#Commercial_District|Commercial District]], the King's Dock, [[Mann_Island|Mann Island]], the [[Lime_Street,_Liverpool|Lime Street Gateway]], the [[Baltic_Triangle|Baltic Triangle]], the [[RopeWalks,_Liverpool|RopeWalks]], and the [[Edge_Lane|Edge Lane Gateway]].
sentence_118: All projects could be eclipsed by the [[Liverpool_Waters|Liverpool Waters]] scheme, which if built will cost in the region of £5.5billion and be one of the largest [[Megaproject|megaprojects]] in the UK's history.
sentence_119: Liverpool Waters is a mixed-use development planned to contain one of Europe's largest skyscraper clusters.
sentence_120: The project received outline planning permission in 2012, despite fierce opposition from such groups as [[UNESCO|UNESCO]], which claimed that it would adversely affect Liverpool's World Heritage status.
sentence_121: In June 2014, Prime Minister [[David_Cameron|David Cameron]] launched the International Festival for Business in Liverpool, the world's largest business event in 2014, and the largest in the UK since the [[Festival_of_Britain|Festival of Britain]] in 1951.
sentence_122: Liverpool has been a centre of invention and innovation.
sentence_123: Railways, transatlantic steamships, municipal trams, and electric trains were all pioneered in Liverpool as modes of mass transit.
sentence_124: In 1829 and 1836, the first railway tunnels in the world were constructed under Liverpool ([[Wapping_Tunnel|Wapping Tunnel]]).
sentence_125: From 1950 to 1951, the world's first scheduled passenger helicopter service ran between Liverpool and [[Cardiff|Cardiff]].
sentence_126: The first [[Royal_School_for_the_Blind_(Liverpool)|School for the Blind]], [[Mechanics'_Institutes|Mechanics' Institute]], High School for Girls, council house, and Juvenile Court were all founded in Liverpool.
sentence_127: Charities such as the [[RSPCA|RSPCA]], NSPCC, [[Age_Concern|Age Concern]], [[Relate|Relate]], and [[Citizen's_Advice_Bureau|Citizen's Advice Bureau]] all evolved from work in the city.
sentence_128: The first [[Lifeboat_(rescue)|lifeboat]] station, public bath and wash-house, sanitary act, medical officer for health ([[William_Henry_Duncan|William Henry Duncan]]), district nurse, [[Slum_clearance|slum clearance]], purpose-built ambulance, X-ray medical diagnosis, school of tropical medicine ([[Liverpool_School_of_Tropical_Medicine|Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine]]), motorised municipal fire-engine, free school meal, cancer research centre, and [[Zoonosis|zoonosis]] research centre all originated in Liverpool.
sentence_129: The first British Nobel Prize was awarded in 1902 to [[Ronald_Ross|Ronald Ross]], professor at the School of Tropical Medicine, the first school of its kind in the world.
sentence_130: [[Orthopaedic_surgery|Orthopaedic surgery]] was pioneered in Liverpool by [[Hugh_Owen_Thomas|Hugh Owen Thomas]], and modern medical anaesthetics by [[Thomas_Cecil_Gray|Thomas Cecil Gray]].
sentence_131: The world's first integrated sewer system was constructed in Liverpool by [[James_Newlands|James Newlands]], appointed in 1847 as the UK's first borough engineer.
sentence_132: Liverpool also founded the UK's first Underwriters' Association and the first [[Institute_of_Chartered_Accountants_in_England_and_Wales|Institute of Accountants]].
sentence_133: The Western world's first financial derivatives (cotton futures) were traded on the Liverpool Cotton Exchange in the late 1700s.
sentence_134: In the arts, Liverpool was home to the first lending library ([[The_Lyceum,_Liverpool|The Lyceum]]), athenaeum society ([[Liverpool_Athenaeum|Liverpool Athenaeum]]), arts centre ([[Bluecoat_Chambers|Bluecoat Chambers]]), and public art conservation centre ([[National_Conservation_Centre|National Conservation Centre]]).
sentence_135: It is also home to the UK's oldest surviving classical orchestra ([[Royal_Liverpool_Philharmonic_Orchestra|Royal Liverpool Philharmonic Orchestra]]) and repertory theatre ([[Liverpool_Playhouse|Liverpool Playhouse]]).
sentence_136: In 1864, [[Peter_Ellis_(architect)|Peter Ellis]] built the world's first iron-framed, curtain-walled office building, [[Oriel_Chambers|Oriel Chambers]], which was a prototype of the [[Skyscraper|skyscraper]].
sentence_137: The UK's first purpose-built department store was Compton House, completed in 1867 for the retailer J.R. Jeffrey.
sentence_138: It was the largest store in the world at the time.
sentence_139: Between 1862 and 1867, Liverpool held an annual Grand Olympic Festival.
sentence_140: Devised by [[John_Hulley|John Hulley]] and Charles Melly, these games were the first to be wholly amateur in nature and international in outlook.
sentence_141: The programme of the first modern Olympiad in [[Athens|Athens]] in 1896 was almost identical to that of the Liverpool Olympics.
sentence_142: In 1865, Hulley co-founded the National Olympian Association in Liverpool, a forerunner of the [[British_Olympic_Association|British Olympic Association]].
sentence_143: Its articles of foundation provided the framework for the International Olympic Charter.
sentence_144: Sir [[Alfred_Lewis_Jones|Alfred Lewis Jones]], a shipowner, introduced bananas to the UK via Liverpool's docks in 1884.
sentence_145: The [[Mersey_Railway|Mersey Railway]], opened in 1886, incorporated the world's first tunnel under a tidal estuary and the world's first deep-level underground stations ([[Liverpool_James_Street_railway_station|Liverpool James Street railway station]]).
sentence_146: In 1889, borough engineer [[John_Alexander_Brodie|John Alexander Brodie]] invented the football goal net.
