sentence_147: He also was a pioneer in the use of pre-fabricated housing and oversaw the construction of the UK's first ring road ([[A5058_road|A5058]]) and intercity highway ([[East_Lancashire_Road|East Lancashire Road]]), as well as the [[Queensway_Tunnel|Queensway Tunnel]] linking Liverpool and [[Birkenhead|Birkenhead]].
sentence_148: Described as "the eighth wonder of the world" at the time of its construction, it was the longest underwater tunnel in the world for 24 years.
sentence_149: In 1897, the [[Auguste_and_Louis_Lumière|Lumière brothers]] filmed Liverpool, including what is believed to be the world's first tracking shot, taken from the [[Liverpool_Overhead_Railway|Liverpool Overhead Railway]], the world's first elevated electrified railway.
sentence_150: The Overhead Railway was the first railway in the world to use electric multiple units, employ automatic signalling, and install an escalator.
sentence_151: Liverpool inventor [[Frank_Hornby|Frank Hornby]] was a visionary in toy development and manufacture, producing three of the most popular lines of toys in the 20th century: [[Meccano|Meccano]], [[Hornby_Model_Railways|Hornby Model Railways]], and [[Dinky_Toys|Dinky Toys]].
sentence_152: The [[British_Interplanetary_Society|British Interplanetary Society]], founded in Liverpool in 1933 by Phillip Ellaby Cleator, is the world's oldest existing organisation devoted to the promotion of spaceflight.
sentence_153: Its journal, the [[Journal_of_the_British_Interplanetary_Society|Journal of the British Interplanetary Society]], is the longest-running astronautical publication in the world.
sentence_154: In 1999, Liverpool was the first city outside of London to be awarded [[Blue_plaques|blue plaques]] by English Heritage in recognition of the "significant contribution made by its sons and daughters in all walks of life".
sentence_155: Liverpool is governed by a Unitary Authority, as when [[Merseyside_County_Council|Merseyside County Council]] was disbanded civic functions were returned to a district borough level.
sentence_156: However several services such as the [[Merseyside_Police|police]] and fire and rescue service, continue to be run at a county-wide level.
sentence_157: The city also elects four [[Member_of_Parliament_(United_Kingdom)|members of Parliament]] (MPs) to the [[Westminster_Parliament|Westminster Parliament]].
sentence_158: See also: [[Liverpool_City_Council|Liverpool City Council]]
sentence_159: The City of Liverpool is governed by the [[Directly_elected_mayor_of_Liverpool|Directly elected mayor of Liverpool]] and [[Liverpool_City_Council|Liverpool City Council]], and is one of six metropolitan boroughs that combine to make up the [[Liverpool_City_Region|Liverpool City Region]].
sentence_160: The mayor is elected by the citizens of Liverpool every four years and is responsible for the day-to-day running of the council.
sentence_161: The council's 90 elected councillors who represent local communities throughout the city, are responsible for scrutinising the mayor's decisions, setting the budget, and policy framework of the city.
sentence_162: The mayor's responsibility is to be a powerful voice for the city both nationally and internationally, to lead, build investor confidence, and to direct resources to economic priorities.
sentence_163: The mayor also exchanges direct dialogue with government ministers and the prime minister through his seat at the Cabinet of Mayors.
sentence_164: Discussions include pressing decision-makers in the government on local issues as well as building relationships with the other [[Directly_elected_mayors_in_England_and_Wales|directly elected mayors in England and Wales]].
sentence_165: The mayor is [[Joe_Anderson_(politician)|Joe Anderson]].
sentence_166: The City of Liverpool effectively has two mayors.
sentence_167: As well as the directly elected mayor, there is the ceremonial lord mayor (or civic mayor) who is elected by the full city council at its annual general meeting in May and stands for one year in office.
sentence_168: The lord mayor acts as the "first citizen" of Liverpool and is responsible for promoting the city, supporting local charities and community groups as well as representing the city at civic events.
sentence_169: The [[Lord_Mayor|Lord Mayor]] is Councillor Christine Banks.
sentence_170: For local elections the city is split into 30 local council wards, which in alphabetical order are:
sentence_171: During the local elections [[2011_Liverpool_Council_election|held in May 2011]], the [[Labour_Party_(UK)|Labour Party]] consolidated its control of Liverpool City Council, following on from regaining power for the first time in 12 years, during the [[2010_Liverpool_Council_election|previous elections in May 2010]].
sentence_172: The Labour Party gained 11 seats during the election, taking their total to 62 seats, compared with the 22 held by the [[Liberal_Democrats_(UK)|Liberal Democrats]].
sentence_173: Of the remaining seats, the [[Liberal_Party_(UK)|Liberal Party]] won three and [[Green_Party_of_England_and_Wales|the Green Party]] claimed two.
sentence_174: The [[Conservative_Party_(UK)|Conservative Party]], one of the three major political parties in the UK had no representation on Liverpool City Council.
sentence_175: In February 2008, Liverpool City Council was reported to be the worst-performing council in the country, receiving just a one-star rating (classified as inadequate).
sentence_176: The main cause of the poor rating was attributed to the council's poor handling of tax-payer money, including the accumulation of a £20m shortfall on Capital of Culture funding.
sentence_177: While Liverpool through most of the 19th and early 20th centuries was a municipal stronghold of Toryism, support for the Conservative Party recently has been among the lowest in any part of Britain, particularly since the [[Monetarism|monetarist]] economic policies of prime minister [[Margaret_Thatcher|Margaret Thatcher]] after her [[1979_United_Kingdom_general_election|1979 general election]] victory contributed to high unemployment in the city which did not begin to fall for many years.
sentence_178: Liverpool is one of the Labour Party's key strongholds; however the city has seen hard times under Labour governments as well, particularly in the [[Winter_of_Discontent|Winter of Discontent]] (late 1978 and early 1979) when Liverpool suffered public sector strikes along with the rest of the United Kingdom but also suffered the particularly humiliating misfortune of having grave-diggers going on strike, leaving the dead unburied.
sentence_179: The City of Liverpool is one of the six constituent local government districts of the [[Liverpool_City_Region|Liverpool City Region]].
sentence_180: Since 1 April 2014, some of the city's responsibilities have been pooled with neighbouring authorities within the metropolitan area and subsumed into the [[Liverpool_City_Region_Combined_Authority|Liverpool City Region Combined Authority]].
sentence_181: The [[Combined_authority|combined authority]] has effectively become the top-tier administrative body for the local governance of the city region and The Mayor of Liverpool, along with the five other leaders from neighbouring local government districts, take strategic decisions over economic development, transport, employment and skills, tourism, culture, housing and physical infrastructure.
sentence_182: As of July 2015, negotiations are currently taking place between the UK national government and the combined authority over a possible devolution deal to confer greater powers on the region.
sentence_183: Discussions include whether to introduce an elected 'Metro Mayor' to oversee the entire metropolitan area.
sentence_184: See also: [[List_of_Parliamentary_constituencies_on_Merseyside|List of Parliamentary constituencies on Merseyside]]
sentence_185: Liverpool has four [[United_Kingdom_constituencies|parliamentary constituencies]] entirely within the city, through which MPs are elected to represent the city in [[Parliament_of_the_United_Kingdom|Westminster]]: [[Liverpool_Riverside_(UK_Parliament_constituency)|Liverpool Riverside]], [[Liverpool_Walton_(UK_Parliament_constituency)|Liverpool Walton]], [[Liverpool_Wavertree_(UK_Parliament_constituency)|Liverpool Wavertree]] and [[Liverpool_West_Derby_(UK_Parliament_constituency)|Liverpool West Derby]].
sentence_186: At the [[2019_United_Kingdom_general_election|last general election]], all were won by Labour with representation being from [[Kim_Johnson_(politician)|Kim Johnson]], [[Dan_Carden|Dan Carden]], Paula Barker and [[Ian_Byrne_(politician)|Ian Byrne]] respectively.
sentence_187: Due to [[Constituencies_in_the_United_Kingdom_general_election,_2010|boundary changes]] prior to the 2010 election, the [[Liverpool_Garston_(UK_Parliament_constituency)|Liverpool Garston]] constituency was merged with most of [[Knowsley_South_(UK_Parliament_constituency)|Knowsley South]] to form the [[Garston_and_Halewood_(UK_Parliament_constituency)|Garston and Halewood]] cross-boundary seat.
sentence_188: At the most 2019 election this seat was won by [[Maria_Eagle|Maria Eagle]] of the Labour Party.
sentence_189: Liverpool has been described as having "the most splendid setting of any English city."
sentence_190: At (53.4, −2.98), 176 miles (283 km) northwest of London, located on the [[Liverpool_Bay|Liverpool Bay]] of the [[Irish_Sea|Irish Sea]] the city of Liverpool is built across a ridge of [[Sandstone|sandstone]] hills rising up to a height of around 230 feet (70 m) above sea-level at Everton Hill, which represents the southern boundary of the West Lancashire Coastal Plain.
sentence_191: The [[Mersey_Estuary|Mersey Estuary]] separates Liverpool from the [[Wirral_Peninsula|Wirral Peninsula]].
sentence_192: The boundaries of Liverpool are adjacent to Bootle, Crosby and [[Maghull|Maghull]] in south [[Metropolitan_Borough_of_Sefton|Sefton]] to the north, and [[Kirkby|Kirkby]], [[Huyton|Huyton]], [[Prescot|Prescot]] and Halewood in [[Metropolitan_Borough_of_Knowsley|Knowsley]] to the east.
sentence_193: Main article: [[Climate_of_Liverpool|Climate of Liverpool]]
sentence_194: Liverpool experiences a temperate [[Oceanic_climate|maritime climate]] ([[Köppen_climate_classification|Köppen]]: Cfb), like much of the British Isles, with relatively mild summers, cool winters and rainfall spread fairly evenly throughout the year.
sentence_195: Rainfall and Temperature records have been kept at Bidston since 1867, but records for atmospheric pressure go back as far as 1845.
sentence_196: Bidston closed down in 2002 but the [[Met_Office|Met Office]] also has a weather station at Crosby.
sentence_197: Since records began in 1867, temperatures have ranged from −17.6 °C (0.3 °F) on 21 December 2010 to 34.5 °C (94.1 °F) on 2 August 1990.
sentence_198: Although, Liverpool Airport recorded a temperature of 35.0 °C (95.0 °F) on 19 July 2006.
sentence_199: The lowest amount of sunshine on record was 16.5hrs in December 1927 whereas the most was 314.5hrs in July 2013.
sentence_200: Tornado activity or funnel cloud formation is very rare in and around the Liverpool area and tornadoes that do form are usually weak.
sentence_201: Recent tornadoes or funnel clouds have been seen in 1998, 2014 and 2018.
sentence_202: During the period 1981–2010, Crosby recorded an average of 32.8 days of air frost per year, which is low for the United Kingdom.
sentence_203: Snow is fairly common during the winter although heavy snow is rare.
sentence_204: Snow generally falls between November and March but can occasionally fall earlier and later.
sentence_205: In recent times, the earliest snowfall was on 1 October 2008 while the latest occurred on 15 May 2012.
sentence_206: Although historically, the earliest snowfall occurred on 4 September 1974 and the latest on 2 June 1975.
sentence_207: Rainfall, although light, is quite a common occurrence in Liverpool, with the wettest month on record being October 1787, which recorded 9.16 in (232.7 mm) of rain and the driest being February 1932, with 0.035 in (0.9 mm).
sentence_208: However, droughts can occasionally become a problem, especially, but not exclusively, in the summer, this happened most recently in 2018.
sentence_209: However, the longest run of days without any rainfall was 41 days between 16 July and 25 August 1995.
sentence_210: The driest year on record was 1991, with 18.92 in (480.5 mm) of rainfall and the wettest was 1792, with 54.25 in (1,378.0 mm).
sentence_211: Since Bidston closed down in 2002, new records are:

table.value: December record low (and all-time record low)
Coldest December (and coldest month of any kind)

sentence_212: See also: :Category:Areas of Liverpool
sentence_213: Suburbs and districts of Liverpool include:
sentence_214: In 2010 Liverpool City Council and the Primary Care Trust Commissioned The Mersey Forest to complete "A Green Infrastructure Strategy" for the city.
sentence_215: Further information: [[North_West_Green_Belt|North West Green Belt]]
sentence_216: Liverpool is a core urban element of a [[Green_belt_(United_Kingdom)|green belt]] region that extends into the wider surrounding counties, which is in place to reduce [[Urban_sprawl|urban sprawl]], prevent the towns in the conurbation from further convergence, protect the identity of outlying communities, encourage [[Brownfield|brownfield]] reuse, and preserve nearby countryside.
sentence_217: This is achieved by restricting inappropriate development within the designated areas and imposing stricter conditions on permitted building.
sentence_218: Due to being already highly built up, the city contains limited portions of protected green belt area within [[Greenfield_land|greenfield]] throughout the borough, at Fazakerley, Croxteth Hall and country park and Craven Wood, Woodfields Park and nearby golf courses in Netherley, small greenfield tracts east of the Speke area by the St Ambrose primary school, and the small hamlet of Oglet and the surrounding area south of Liverpool Airport.
sentence_219: The green belt was first drawn up in 1983 under Merseyside County Council and the size in the city amounts to 530 hectares (5.3 km; 2.0 sq mi).
sentence_220: Main article: [[Demography_of_Liverpool|Demography of Liverpool]]
sentence_221: At the [[United_Kingdom_Census_2011|2011 UK Census]] the recorded population of Liverpool was 466,415, a 6.1% increase on the figure of 439,473 recorded in the 2001 census.
sentence_222: The population of the central Liverpool local authority peaked in the 1930s with 846,101 recorded in the 1931 census, before suburbanisation and the establishment of new towns in the region.
sentence_223: As with many British cities including [[London|London]] and [[Manchester|Manchester]], the city centre covered by the Liverpool council area had experienced negative population growth since the 1931 census.
sentence_224: Much of the population loss was as a result of large-scale resettlement programmes to nearby areas introduced in the aftermath of the Second World War, with satellite towns such as [[Kirkby,_Merseyside|Kirkby]], [[Skelmersdale|Skelmersdale]] and [[Runcorn|Runcorn]] seeing a corresponding rise in their populations (Kirkby being the fastest growing town in Britain during the 1960s).
sentence_225: Liverpool's population is younger than that of England as a whole, with 42.5 per cent of its population under the age of 30, compared to an English average of 37.7 per cent.
sentence_226: As of July 2014, 66 per cent of the population was of working age.
sentence_227: Liverpool is the largest local authority by population, GDP and area in Merseyside.
sentence_228: Liverpool is typically grouped with the wider Merseyside area for the purpose of defining its metropolitan footprint, and there are several methodologies.
sentence_229: Liverpool is defined as a standalone [[NUTS_statistical_regions_of_the_United_Kingdom|NUTS3 area by the ONS for statistical purpose]], and makes up part of the NUTS2 area "Merseyside" along with East Merseyside (Knowsley, St Helens and Halton), Sefton and the Wirral.
sentence_230: The population of this area was 1,513,306 based on 2014 estimates.
sentence_231: The "[[Liverpool_Urban_Area|Liverpool Urban Area]]" is a term used by the [[Office_for_National_Statistics|Office for National Statistics]] (ONS) to denote the [[Urban_area|urban area]] around the city to the east of the [[River_Mersey|River Mersey]].
sentence_232: The contiguous built-up area extends beyond the area administered by [[Liverpool_City_Council|Liverpool City Council]] into adjoining local authority areas, particularly parts of [[Metropolitan_Borough_of_Sefton|Sefton]] and [[Metropolitan_Borough_of_Knowsley|Knowsley]].
sentence_233: As defined by ONS, the area extends as far east as [[Haydock|Haydock]] and [[St_Helens,_Merseyside|St.
sentence_234: Helens]].
sentence_235: Unlike the Metropolitan area, the Urban Area does not include The Wirral or its contiguous areas.
sentence_236: The population of this area as of 2011 was 864,211.
sentence_237: The "[[Liverpool_City_Region|Liverpool City Region]]" is an economic partnership between local authorities in Merseyside under the umbrella of the [[Liverpool_City_Region_Combined_Authority|Liverpool City Region Combined Authority]] as defined by the Mersey Partnership.
sentence_238: The area covers Merseyside and the [[Borough_of_Halton|Borough of Halton]] and has an estimated population between 1,500,000 and 2,000,000 and.
sentence_239: In 2006 ESPON (now ([[European_Observation_Network_for_Territorial_Development_and_Cohesion|European Observation Network for Territorial Development and Cohesion]]) released a study defining a "Liverpool/Birkenhead Metropolitan area" as a functional urban area consisting of contiguous urban areas, labour pool, and commuter "Travel To Work Areas".
sentence_240: The analysis grouped the [[Merseyside|Merseyside]] metropolitan county with the borough of [[Halton_(borough)|Halton]], [[Wigan|Wigan]] in Greater Manchester, the city of [[Chester|Chester]] as well as number of towns in Lancashire and Cheshire including [[Ormskirk|Ormskirk]] and [[Warrington|Warrington]], estimating the polynuclear metropolitan area to have a population of 2,241,000 people.
sentence_241: Liverpool and Manchester are sometimes considered as one large polynuclear metropolitan area, or [[Megalopolis_(city_type)|megalopolis]].
sentence_242: According to data from the 2011 census, 84.8 per cent of Liverpool's population was [[White_British|White British]], 1.4 per cent [[White_Irish|White Irish]], 2.6 per cent White Other, 4.1 per cent [[Asian_British|Asian or Asian British]] (including 1.1 per cent British Indian and 1.7 per cent British Chinese), 2.6 per cent [[Black_British|Black or Black British]] (including 1.8 per cent Black African) and 2.5 per cent [[British_Mixed-Race|mixed-race]].
sentence_243: 1.8 per cent of respondents were from other ethnic groups.
sentence_244: According to a 2014 survey, the ten most popular surnames of Liverpool (With surname origin), followed with their population are;
sentence_245: Liverpool is home to Britain's oldest [[Black_people|Black]] community, dating to at least the 1730s.
sentence_246: Some Black Liverpudlians can trace their ancestors in the city back ten generations.
sentence_247: Early Black settlers in the city included seamen, the children of traders sent to be educated, and freed slaves, since slaves entering the country after 1722 were deemed free men.
sentence_248: Since the 20th century, Liverpool is also noted for its large [[British_African-Caribbean_people|African-Caribbean]], [[Ghanaians_in_the_United_Kingdom|Ghanaian]], and [[Somalis_in_the_United_Kingdom|Somali]] communities, formed of more recent African-descended immigrants and their subsequent generations.
sentence_249: The city is also home to the oldest Chinese community in Europe; the first residents of the city's [[Chinatown,_Liverpool|Chinatown]] arrived as seamen in the 19th century.
sentence_250: The traditional Chinese gateway erected in Liverpool's Chinatown is the largest gateway outside China.
sentence_251: Liverpool also has a long-standing Filipino community.
sentence_252: [[Lita_Roza|Lita Roza]], a singer from Liverpool who was the first woman to achieve a UK number one hit, had Filipino ancestry.
sentence_253: The city is also known for its large Irish population and its historically large [[Welsh_people|Welsh]] population.
sentence_254: In 1813, 10 per cent of Liverpool's population was Welsh, leading to the city becoming known as "the capital of North Wales."
sentence_255: Following the start of the [[Great_Famine_(Ireland)|Great Irish Famine]] in the mid-19th century, up to two million Irish people travelled to Liverpool within one decade, with many subsequently departing for the United States.
sentence_256: By 1851, more than 20 per cent of the population of Liverpool was Irish.
sentence_257: At the 2001 Census, 1.17 per cent of the population were Welsh-born and 0.75 per cent were born in the [[Republic_of_Ireland|Republic of Ireland]], while 0.54 per cent were born in [[Northern_Ireland|Northern Ireland]], but many more Liverpudlians are of Welsh or Irish ancestry.
sentence_258: Other contemporary ethnicities include [[British_Indian|Indian]], [[Latin_American_migration_to_the_United_Kingdom|Latin American]], [[Malaysians_in_the_United_Kingdom|Malaysian]], and [[Yemenis_in_the_United_Kingdom|Yemeni]] communities, which number several thousand each.
sentence_259: The thousands of migrants and sailors passing through Liverpool resulted in a religious diversity that is still apparent today.
sentence_260: This is reflected in the equally diverse collection of religious buildings, including two Christian cathedrals.
sentence_261: Liverpool is known to be England's 'most Catholic city', with a Catholic population much larger than in other parts of England.
sentence_262: The parish church of Liverpool is the Anglican [[Church_of_Our_Lady_and_Saint_Nicholas,_Liverpool|Our Lady and St Nicholas]], colloquially known as "the sailors church", which has existed near the waterfront since 1257.
sentence_263: It regularly plays host to Catholic masses.
sentence_264: Other notable churches include the [[Greek_Orthodox_Church_of_St_Nicholas|Greek Orthodox Church of St Nicholas]] (built in the [[Neo-Byzantine_architecture|Neo-Byzantine architecture]] style), and the [[Gustav_Adolf_Church,_Liverpool|Gustav Adolf Church]] (the Swedish Seamen's Church, reminiscent of Nordic styles).
sentence_265: Liverpool's wealth as a port city enabled the construction of two enormous cathedrals in the 20th century.
sentence_266: The [[Liverpool_Cathedral|Anglican Cathedral]], which was designed by Sir Giles Gilbert Scott and plays host to the annual [[Liverpool_Shakespeare_Festival|Liverpool Shakespeare Festival]], has one of the longest [[Nave|naves]], largest organs and heaviest and highest peals of bells in the world.
sentence_267: The Roman Catholic [[Liverpool_Metropolitan_Cathedral|Metropolitan Cathedral]], on Mount Pleasant next to [[Liverpool_Science_Park|Liverpool Science Park]], was initially planned to be even larger.
sentence_268: Of [[Sir_Edwin_Lutyens|Sir Edwin Lutyens]]'s original design, only the crypt was completed.
sentence_269: The cathedral was eventually built to a simpler design by [[Sir_Frederick_Gibberd|Sir Frederick Gibberd]].
sentence_270: While this is on a smaller scale than Lutyens' original design it still incorporates the largest panel of [[Stained_glass|stained glass]] in the world.
sentence_271: The road running between the two cathedrals is called [[Hope_Street,_Liverpool|Hope Street]], a coincidence which pleases believers.
sentence_272: The cathedral is colloquially referred to as "Paddy's Wigwam" due to its shape.
sentence_273: Liverpool contains several synagogues, of which the Grade I listed Moorish Revival [[Princes_Road_Synagogue|Princes Road Synagogue]] is architecturally the most notable.
sentence_274: Princes Road is widely considered to be the most magnificent of Britain's Moorish Revival synagogues and one of the finest buildings in Liverpool.
sentence_275: Liverpool has a thriving Jewish community with a further two orthodox Synagogues, one in the Allerton district of the city and a second in the Childwall district of the city where a significant [[Jewish|Jewish]] community reside.
sentence_276: A third orthodox Synagogue in the Greenbank Park area of L17 has recently closed and is a listed 1930s structure.
sentence_277: There is also a [[Lubavitch|Lubavitch]] [[Chabad_House|Chabad House]] and a reform Synagogue.
sentence_278: Liverpool has had a Jewish community since the mid-18th century.
sentence_279: The Jewish population of Liverpool is around 5,000.
sentence_280: The [[Liverpool_Talmudical_College|Liverpool Talmudical College]] existed from 1914 until 1990, when its classes moved to the Childwall Synagogue.
sentence_281: Liverpool also has a [[Hindu|Hindu]] community, with a [[Mandir|Mandir]] on [[Edge_Lane|Edge Lane]], [[Edge_Hill,_Merseyside|Edge Hill]].
sentence_282: The Shri Radha Krishna Temple from the Hindu Cultural Organisation in Liverpool is located there.
sentence_283: Liverpool also has the [[Guru_Nanak|Guru Nanak]] [[Sikh|Sikh]] [[Gurdwara|Gurdwara]] in [[Wavertree|Wavertree]] and a [[Bahá'í_Faith|Bahá'í]] Centre in the same area.
sentence_284: The city had the earliest mosque in England, and possibly the UK, founded in 1887 by [[William_Abdullah_Quilliam|William Abdullah Quilliam]], a lawyer who had converted to [[Islam|Islam]], and set up the [[Liverpool_Muslim_Institute|Liverpool Muslim Institute]] in a [[Terraced_house|terraced house]] on West Derby Road.
sentence_285: The building was used as a house of worship until 1908, when it was sold to the City Council and converted into offices.
sentence_286: Plans have been accepted to re-convert the building where the mosque once stood into a museum.
sentence_287: There are three mosques in Liverpool: the largest and main one, [[Al-Rahma_mosque|Al-Rahma mosque]], in the [[Toxteth|Toxteth]] area of the city and a mosque recently opened in the [[Mossley_Hill|Mossley Hill]] district of the city.
sentence_288: The third mosque was also recently opened in Toxteth and is on [[Granby_Four_Streets|Granby Street]].
sentence_289: Natives of the city of Liverpool are referred to as Liverpudlians, and colloquially as "Scousers", a reference to "[[Scouse_(food)|scouse]]", a form of stew.
sentence_290: The word "Scouse" has also become synonymous with the [[Scouse|Liverpool accent and dialect]].
sentence_291: Many people "self-identify" as Liverpudlians or Scousers without actually being born or living within the city boundaries of Liverpool.
sentence_292: Main article: Economy of Liverpool
sentence_293: The Economy of Liverpool is one of the largest within the United Kingdom, sitting at the centre of one of the [[North_West_of_England#Economy|two core economies]] within the North West of England.
sentence_294: In 2006, the city's [[Gross_value_added|GVA]] was £7,626 million, providing a per capita figure of £17,489, which was above the North West average.
sentence_295: Liverpool's economy has seen strong growth since the mid-1990s, with its GVA increasing 71.8% between 1995 and 2006 and employment increasing 12% between 1998 and 2006.
sentence_296: GDP per capita was estimated to stand at $32,121 in 2014, and total GDP at $65.8 billion.
sentence_297: In common with much of the rest of the UK today, Liverpool's economy is dominated by [[Tertiary_sector_of_the_economy|service sector industries]], both public and private.
sentence_298: In 2007, over 60% of all employment in the city was in the public administration, education, health, banking, finance and insurance sectors.
sentence_299: Over recent years there has also been significant growth in the [[Knowledge_economy|knowledge economy]] of Liverpool with the establishment of the [[Liverpool_Knowledge_Quarter|Liverpool Knowledge Quarter]] in sectors such as media and life sciences.
sentence_300: Liverpool's rich architectural base has also helped the city become the second most filmed city in the UK outside London, including doubling for Chicago, London, Moscow, New York, Paris and Rome.
sentence_301: Another important component of Liverpool's economy are the tourism and [[Leisure_industry|leisure sectors]].
sentence_302: Liverpool is the sixth most visited UK city and one of the 100 most visited cities in the world by international tourists.
sentence_303: In 2008, during the city's [[European_Capital_of_Culture|European Capital of Culture]] celebrations, overnight visitors brought £188m into the local economy, while tourism as a whole is worth approximately £1.3bn a year to Liverpool.
sentence_304: The city's new [[Liverpool_Cruise_Terminal|cruise liner terminal]], which is situated close to the [[Pier_Head|Pier Head]], also makes Liverpool one of the few places in the world where cruise ships are able to berth right in the centre of the city.
sentence_305: Other recent developments in Liverpool such as the [[Echo_Arena|Echo Arena]] and Liverpool One have made Liverpool an important leisure centre with the latter helping to lift Liverpool into the top five retail destinations in the UK.
sentence_306: Historically, the economy of Liverpool was centred on the [[Port_of_Liverpool|city's port]] and manufacturing base, although a smaller proportion of total employment is today derived from the port.
sentence_307: Nonetheless the city remains one of the most important ports in the United Kingdom, handling over 32.2m tonnes of cargo in 2008.
sentence_308: A new multimillion-pound expansion to the Port of Liverpool, [[Liverpool2|Liverpool2]], is scheduled to be operational from the end of 2015, and is projected to greatly increase the volume of cargo which Liverpool is able to handle.
sentence_309: Liverpool is also home to the UK headquarters of many shipping lines including Japanese firm [[Nippon_Yusen|NYK]] and Danish firm [[Maersk_Line|Maersk Line]], whilst shipping firm [[Atlantic_Container_Line|Atlantic Container Line]] has recently invested significant amounts in expanding its Liverpool operations, with a new headquarters currently under construction.
sentence_310: Future plans to redevelop the city's northern dock system, in a project known as [[Liverpool_Waters|Liverpool Waters]], could see £5.5bn invested in the city over the next 50 years, creating 17,000 new jobs.
sentence_311: Car manufacturing also takes place in the city at the [[Jaguar_Land_Rover|Jaguar Land Rover]] Halewood plant where the Range Rover Evoque model is assembled.
sentence_312: Main articles: [[Architecture_of_Liverpool|Architecture of Liverpool]] and [[Liverpool_Maritime_Mercantile_City|Liverpool Maritime Mercantile City]]
sentence_313: See also: [[List_of_tallest_buildings_and_structures_in_Liverpool|List of tallest buildings and structures in Liverpool]] and [[List_of_public_art_in_Liverpool|List of public art in Liverpool]]
sentence_314: Liverpool's history means that there are a considerable variety of [[Architectural_style|architectural styles]] found within the city, ranging from 16th century [[Tudor_architecture|Tudor buildings]] to modern-day [[Contemporary_architecture|contemporary architecture]].
sentence_315: The majority of buildings in the city date from the late-18th century onwards, the period during which the city grew into one of the foremost powers in the [[British_Empire|British Empire]].
sentence_316: There are over [[Listed_buildings_in_Liverpool|2,500 listed buildings]] in Liverpool, of which 27 are Grade I listed and 85 are Grade II* listed.
sentence_317: The city also has a greater number of public sculptures than any other location in the United Kingdom aside from [[City_of_Westminster|Westminster]] and more Georgian houses than the city of [[Bath,_Somerset|Bath]].
sentence_318: This richness of architecture has subsequently seen Liverpool described by [[English_Heritage|English Heritage]], as England's finest Victorian city.
sentence_319: The value of Liverpool's architecture and design was recognised in 2004, when several areas throughout the city were declared a [[UNESCO|UNESCO]] [[World_Heritage_Site|World Heritage Site]].
sentence_320: Known as the [[Liverpool_Maritime_Mercantile_City|Liverpool Maritime Mercantile City]], the sites were added in recognition of the city's role in the development of international trade and [[Dock_(maritime)|docking]] technology.
sentence_321: As a major British port, the docks in Liverpool have historically been central to the city's development.
sentence_322: Several major docking firsts have occurred in the city including the construction of the world's first enclosed [[Wet_dock|wet dock]] (the [[Old_Dock|Old Dock]]) in 1715 and the first ever [[Hydraulic|hydraulic]] lifting [[Crane_(machine)|cranes]].
sentence_323: The best-known dock in Liverpool is the [[Royal_Albert_Dock,_Liverpool|Albert Dock]], which was constructed in 1846 and today comprises the largest single collection of Grade I listed buildings anywhere in Britain.
sentence_324: Built under the guidance of [[Jesse_Hartley|Jesse Hartley]], it was considered to be one of the most advanced docks anywhere in the world upon completion and is often attributed with helping the city to become one of the most important ports in the world.
sentence_325: The Albert Dock houses restaurants, bars, shops, two hotels as well as the [[Merseyside_Maritime_Museum|Merseyside Maritime Museum]], [[International_Slavery_Museum|International Slavery Museum]], [[Tate_Liverpool|Tate Liverpool]] and [[The_Beatles_Story|The Beatles Story]].
sentence_326: North of the city centre is [[Stanley_Dock|Stanley Dock]], home to the [[Stanley_Dock_Tobacco_Warehouse|Stanley Dock Tobacco Warehouse]], which was at the time of its construction in 1901, the world's largest building in terms of area and today stands as the world's largest brick-work building.
sentence_327: One of the most famous locations in Liverpool is the [[Pier_Head|Pier Head]], renowned for the trio of buildings – the [[Royal_Liver_Building|Royal Liver Building]], the [[Cunard_Building|Cunard Building]] and the [[Port_of_Liverpool_Building|Port of Liverpool Building]] – which sit upon it.
sentence_328: Collectively referred to as the Three Graces, these buildings stand as a testament to the great wealth in the city during the late 19th and early 20th century.
sentence_329: Built-in a variety of architectural styles, they are recognised as being the symbol of Maritime Liverpool and are regarded by many as contributing to one of the most impressive waterfronts in the world.
sentence_330: In recent years, several areas along Liverpool's waterfront have undergone significant redevelopment.
sentence_331: Amongst the notable recent developments are the [[Museum_of_Liverpool|Museum of Liverpool]], the construction of the [[Liverpool_Arena|Liverpool Arena]] and BT Convention Centre on [[King's_Dock,_Port_of_Liverpool|Kings Dock]], [[Alexandra_Tower,_Liverpool|Alexandra Tower]] and [[1_Princes_Dock|1 Princes Dock]] on [[Prince's_Dock,_Liverpool|Prince's Dock]] and [[Liverpool_Marina|Liverpool Marina]] around [[Coburg_Dock|Coburg]] and [[Brunswick_Dock|Brunswick Docks]].
sentence_332: [[The_Wheel_of_Liverpool|The Wheel of Liverpool]] opened on 25 March 2010.
sentence_333: However, plans to redevelop parts of the Liverpool have been marred by [[Controversy|controversy]].
sentence_334: In December 2016, a newly formed company called [[North_Point_Global_Ltd.|North Point Global Ltd.]] was given the rights to develop part of the docks under the "New Chinatown" banner.
sentence_335: Though heavily advertised in Liverpool, Hong Kong and Chinese cities with glossy advertisements and videos, the "New Chinatown" development failed to materialise.
sentence_336: In January 2018, the Liverpool Echo and Asia Times revealed that the site remained sans any construction, North Point Global as well as its subcontractor "Bilt" had both declared [[Bankruptcy|bankruptcy]], and the small investors (mostly middle class couples) who had already paid money for the apartments had lost most of their savings in them.
sentence_337: Five similar development projects, mostly targeting individual Chinese and Hong Kong based citizens, were suspended due to financial misappropriations.
sentence_338: Liverpool's historic position as one of the most important trading ports in the world has meant that over time many grand buildings have been constructed in the city as headquarters for shipping firms, insurance companies, banks and other large firms.
sentence_339: The great wealth this brought, then allowed for the development of grand civic buildings, which were designed to allow the local administrators to 'run the city with pride'.
sentence_340: The commercial district is centred on the Castle Street, Dale Street and Old Hall Street areas of the city, with many of the area's roads still following their [[England_in_the_Middle_Ages|medieval]] layout.
sentence_341: Having developed over a period of three centuries the area is regarded as one of the most important architectural locations in the city, as recognised by its inclusion in Liverpool's World Heritage site.
sentence_342: The oldest building in the area is the [[Grade_I|Grade I]] [[Listed_building|listed]] [[Liverpool_Town_Hall|Liverpool Town Hall]], which is located at the top of Castle Street and dates from 1754.
sentence_343: Often regarded as the city's finest piece of [[Georgian_architecture|Georgian architecture]], the building is known as one of the most extravagantly decorated civic buildings anywhere in Britain.
sentence_344: Also on Castle Street is the Grade I listed [[Bank_of_England,_Liverpool|Bank of England Building]], constructed between 1845 and 1848, as one of only three provincial branches of the national bank.
sentence_345: Amongst the other buildings in the area are the [[Tower_Buildings,_Liverpool|Tower Buildings]], [[Albion_House,_Liverpool|Albion House]] (the former White Star Line headquarters), the [[Municipal_Buildings,_Liverpool|Municipal Buildings]] and [[Oriel_Chambers|Oriel Chambers]], which is considered to be one of the earliest [[Modernist|Modernist]] style buildings ever built.
sentence_346: The area around [[William_Brown_Street|William Brown Street]] is referred to as the city's 'Cultural Quarter', owing to the presence of numerous civic buildings, including the [[William_Brown_Library|William Brown Library]], [[Walker_Art_Gallery|Walker Art Gallery]], Picton Reading Rooms and World Museum Liverpool.
sentence_347: The area is dominated by neo-classical architecture, of which the most prominent, [[St._George's_Hall,_Liverpool|St George's Hall]], is widely regarded as the best example of a neo-classical building anywhere in Europe.
sentence_348: A Grade I listed building, it was constructed between 1840 and 1855 to serve a variety of civic functions in the city and its doors are inscribed with "S.P.Q.L."
sentence_349: (Latin senatus populusque Liverpudliensis), meaning "the senate and people of Liverpool".
sentence_350: William Brown Street is also home to numerous public monuments and sculptures, including [[Wellington's_Column|Wellington's Column]] and the [[Steble_Fountain|Steble Fountain]].
sentence_351: Many others are located around the area, particularly in [[St_John's_Gardens,_Liverpool|St John's Gardens]], which was specifically developed for this purpose.
sentence_352: The William Brown Street area has been likened to a modern recreation of the Roman Forum.
sentence_353: While the majority of Liverpool's architecture dates from the mid-18th century onwards, there are several buildings that pre-date this time.
sentence_354: One of the oldest surviving buildings is [[Speke_Hall|Speke Hall]], a [[Tudor_style_architecture|Tudor]] manor house located in the south of the city, which was completed in 1598.
sentence_355: The building is one of the few remaining timber framed Tudor houses left in the [[North_of_England|north of England]] and is particularly noted for its Victorian interiors, which was added in the mid-19th century.
sentence_356: In addition to Speke Hall, many of the city's other oldest surviving buildings are also former manor houses including [[Croxteth_Hall|Croxteth Hall]] and [[Woolton_Hall|Woolton Hall]], which were completed in 1702 and 1704 respectively.
sentence_357: The oldest building within the city centre is the [[Grade_I|Grade I]] [[Listed_building|listed]] [[Bluecoat_Chambers|Bluecoat Chambers]], which was built between 1717 and 1718.
sentence_358: Constructed in British Queen Anne style, the building was influenced in part by the work of [[Christopher_Wren|Christopher Wren]] and was originally the home of the Bluecoat School (who later moved to a larger site in [[Wavertree|Wavertree]] in the south of the city).
sentence_359: Since 1908 it has acted as a centre for arts in Liverpool.
sentence_360: Liverpool is noted for having two Cathedrals, each of which imposes over the landscape around it.
sentence_361: The [[Liverpool_Cathedral|Anglican Cathedral]], which was constructed between 1904 and 1978, is the largest Cathedral in Britain and the fifth largest in the world.
sentence_362: Designed and built in [[Gothic_style|Gothic style]], it is regarded as one of the greatest buildings to have been constructed during the 20th century and was described by former British Poet Laureate, [[John_Betjeman|John Betjeman]], as 'one of the great buildings of the world'.
sentence_363: The Roman Catholic [[Liverpool_Metropolitan_Cathedral|Metropolitan Cathedral]] was constructed between 1962 and 1967 and is known as one of the first Cathedrals to break the traditional longitudinal design.
sentence_364: In recent years, many parts of Liverpool's city centre have undergone significant redevelopment and regeneration after years of decline.
sentence_365: The largest of these developments has been Liverpool One, which has seen almost £1 billion invested in the redevelopment of 42 acres (170,000 m) of land, providing new retail, commercial, residential and leisure space.
sentence_366: Around the north of the city centre several new skyscrapers have also been constructed including the [[RIBA|RIBA]] award-winning [[Unity_Buildings|Unity Buildings]] and [[West_Tower|West Tower]], which at 140m is [[List_of_tallest_buildings_and_structures_in_Liverpool|Liverpool's tallest building]].
sentence_367: Many redevelopment schemes are also in progress including [[Central_Village,_Liverpool|Central Village]] / Circus, the [[Lime_Street,_Liverpool|Lime Street]] gateway, and the highly ambitious [[Liverpool_Waters|Liverpool Waters]].
sentence_368: There are many other notable buildings in Liverpool, including the [[Art_deco|art deco]] [[Crowne_Plaza_Liverpool_John_Lennon_Airport_Hotel|former terminal building]] of [[Liverpool_John_Lennon_Airport|Speke Airport]], the [[University_of_Liverpool|University of Liverpool]]'s [[Victoria_Building,_University_of_Liverpool|Victoria Building]], (which provided the inspiration for the term [[Red_Brick_universities|Red Brick University]]), and the [[Britannia_Adelphi_Hotel|Adelphi Hotel]], which was in that past considered to be one of the finest hotels anywhere in the world.
sentence_369: The English Heritage National Register of Historic Parks describes Merseyside's Victorian Parks as collectively the "most important in the country".
sentence_370: The city of Liverpool has ten listed parks and cemeteries, including two Grade I and five Grade II*, more than any other English city apart from London.
sentence_371: Main article: [[Transport_in_Liverpool|Transport in Liverpool]]
sentence_372: Further information: [[Liverpool_city_centre#Transport|Liverpool city centre § Transport]]
sentence_373: Transport in Liverpool is primarily centred on the city's road and rail networks, both of which are extensive and provide links across the United Kingdom.
sentence_374: Liverpool has an extensive local public transport network, which is managed by [[Merseytravel|Merseytravel]], and includes buses, trains and ferries.
sentence_375: Additionally, the city also has an international airport and a major port, both of which provides links to locations outside the country.
sentence_376: As a major city, Liverpool has direct road links with many other areas within England.
sentence_377: To the east, the [[M62_motorway|M62 motorway]] connects Liverpool with [[Kingston-upon-Hull|Hull]] and along the route provides links to several large cities, including [[Manchester|Manchester]], [[Leeds|Leeds]] and [[Bradford|Bradford]].
sentence_378: The M62 also provides a connection to both the [[M6_motorway|M6]] and [[M1_motorway|M1 motorways]], providing indirect links to more distant areas including [[Birmingham|Birmingham]], London, [[Nottingham|Nottingham]], [[Preston,_Lancashire|Preston]] and [[Sheffield|Sheffield]].
sentence_379: To the west of the city, the [[Kingsway_Tunnel|Kingsway]] and [[Queensway_Tunnel|Queensway Tunnels]] connect Liverpool with the [[Wirral_Peninsula|Wirral Peninsula]], including [[Birkenhead|Birkenhead]], and [[Wallasey|Wallasey]].
sentence_380: The A41 road and [[M53_motorway|M53 motorway]], which both begin in Birkenhead, link to [[Cheshire|Cheshire]] and [[Shropshire|Shropshire]] and via the [[A55_road|A55]], to North Wales.
sentence_381: To the south, Liverpool is connected to [[Widnes|Widnes]] and [[Warrington|Warrington]] via the [[A562_road|A562]] and across the [[River_Mersey|River Mersey]] to [[Runcorn|Runcorn]], via the [[Silver_Jubilee_Bridge|Silver Jubilee]] and [[Mersey_Gateway|Mersey Gateway]] bridges.
sentence_382: Liverpool is served by two separate rail networks.
sentence_383: The local rail network is managed and run by [[Merseyrail|Merseyrail]] and provides links throughout Merseyside and beyond (see [[Liverpool#Local_travel|Local travel]] below), while the national network, which is managed by [[Network_Rail|Network Rail]], provides Liverpool with connections to major towns and cities across England.
sentence_384: The city's primary mainline station is Lime Street station, which is the terminus for several lines into the city, with numerous destinations, including London (in 2 hours 8 minutes with [[British_Rail_Class_390|Pendolino]] trains), [[Birmingham|Birmingham]], [[Newcastle_upon_Tyne|Newcastle upon Tyne]], Manchester, [[Preston,_Lancashire|Preston]], [[Leeds|Leeds]], [[Scarborough,_North_Yorkshire|Scarborough]], [[Sheffield|Sheffield]], [[Nottingham|Nottingham]] and [[Norwich|Norwich]].
sentence_385: In the south of the city, [[Liverpool_South_Parkway|Liverpool South Parkway]] provides a connection to the city's airport.
sentence_386: The [[Port_of_Liverpool|Port of Liverpool]] is one of Britain's largest ports, providing passenger ferry services across the [[Irish_Sea|Irish Sea]] to [[Belfast|Belfast]], Dublin and the [[Isle_of_Man|Isle of Man]].
sentence_387: Services are provided by several companies, including the [[Isle_of_Man_Steam_Packet_Company|Isle of Man Steam Packet Company]], [[P&O_Ferries|P&O Ferries]] and [[Stena_Line|Stena Line]].
sentence_388: In 2007, a new [[Liverpool_Cruise_Terminal|cruise terminal]] was opened in Liverpool, located alongside the [[Pier_Head|Pier Head]] in the city centre.
sentence_389: November 2016 saw the official opening of [[Liverpool2|Liverpool2]], an extension to the port that allows [[Post-Panamax#Post-Panamax_ships|post-Panamax]] vessels to dock in Liverpool.
sentence_390: [[Leeds_and_Liverpool_Canal|Leeds and Liverpool Canal]] runs into Liverpool city centre via [[Liverpool_Canal_Link|Liverpool Canal Link]] at Pier Head since 2009.
sentence_391: [[Liverpool_Cruise_Terminal|Liverpool Cruise Terminal]] in the city centre provides long-distance passenger cruises, [[Fred._Olsen_Cruise_Lines|Fred.
sentence_392: Olsen Cruise Lines]] [[MS_Black_Watch_(1971)|MS Black Watch]] and [[Cruise_&_Maritime_Voyages|Cruise & Maritime Voyages]] [[MS_Magellan|MS Magellan]] using the terminal to depart to [[Iceland|Iceland]], [[France|France]], [[Spain|Spain]] and [[Norway|Norway]].
sentence_393: [[Liverpool_John_Lennon_Airport|Liverpool John Lennon Airport]], which is located in the south of the city, provides Liverpool with direct air connections across the United Kingdom and Europe.
sentence_394: In 2008, the airport handled over 5.3 million passengers and today offers services to 68 destinations, including Berlin, Rome, Milan, Paris, Barcelona and Zürich.
sentence_395: The airport is primarily served by low-cost airlines, notably [[Ryanair|Ryanair]] and [[Easyjet|Easyjet]], although it does provide additional charter services in the summer.
sentence_396: Liverpool's [[Commuter_rail_in_the_United_Kingdom|local rail]] network is one of the busiest and most extensive in the country.
sentence_397: The network consists of three lines: the [[Northern_Line_(Merseyrail)|Northern Line]], which runs to [[Southport|Southport]], [[Ormskirk|Ormskirk]], [[Kirkby|Kirkby]] and [[Hunts_Cross|Hunts Cross]]; the [[Wirral_Line|Wirral Line]], which runs through the Mersey Railway Tunnel and has branches to [[New_Brighton,_Merseyside|New Brighton]], [[West_Kirby|West Kirby]], [[Chester|Chester]] and [[Ellesmere_Port|Ellesmere Port]]; and the [[City_Line_(Merseyrail)|City Line]], which begins at Lime Street, providing links to [[St_Helens,_Merseyside|St Helens]], [[Wigan|Wigan]], [[Preston,_Lancashire|Preston]], [[Warrington|Warrington]] and [[Manchester|Manchester]].
sentence_398: The network is predominantly electric.
sentence_399: Electrification of the City Line was completed in 2015.
sentence_400: The two lines operated by Merseyrail are the busiest British urban commuter networks outside London, covering 75 miles (121 km) of track, with an average of 110,000 passenger journeys per weekday.
sentence_401: Services are operated by the [[Merseyrail|Merseyrail]] franchise and managed by [[Merseytravel|Merseytravel]].
sentence_402: Local services on the City Line are operated by [[Northern_(train_operating_company)|Northern]] rather than Merseyrail, although the line itself remains part of the Merseyrail network.
sentence_403: Within the city centre the majority of the network is underground, with four city centre stations and over 6.5 miles (10.5 km) of tunnels.
sentence_404: Local bus services within and around Liverpool are managed by [[Merseytravel|Merseytravel]] and are run by several different companies, including [[Arriva_North_West|Arriva]] and [[Stagecoach_Merseyside|Stagecoach]].
sentence_405: The two principal termini for local buses are Queen Square Bus Station (located near Lime Street railway station) for services north and east of the city, and Liverpool One Bus Station formerly known as Paradise Street Bus Interchange (located near the [[Royal_Albert_Dock,_Liverpool|Albert Dock]]) for services to the south and east.
sentence_406: Cross-river services to the [[Metropolitan_Borough_of_Wirral|Wirral]] use roadside terminus points in Castle Street and Sir Thomas Street.
sentence_407: A night bus service also operates on Saturdays providing services from the city centre across Liverpool and Merseyside.
sentence_408: City Sights and City explorer by Maghull coaches offer a tour bus service.
sentence_409: [[National_Express|National Express]] also operates.
sentence_410: The cross river ferry service in Liverpool, known as the [[Mersey_Ferry|Mersey Ferry]], is managed and operated by [[Merseytravel|Merseytravel]], with services operating between the [[Pier_Head|Pier Head]] in Liverpool and both [[Woodside,_Merseyside|Woodside]] in [[Birkenhead|Birkenhead]] and Seacombe in [[Wallasey|Wallasey]].
sentence_411: Services operate at intervals ranging from 20 minutes at peak times, to every hour during the middle of the day and during weekends.
sentence_412: Despite remaining an important transport link between the city and the Wirral Peninsula, the Mersey Ferry has become an increasingly popular tourist attraction within the city, with daytime River Explorer Cruises providing passengers with an historical overview of the [[River_Mersey|River Mersey]] and surrounding areas.
sentence_413: In May 2014, the CityBike hire scheme was launched in the city.
sentence_414: The scheme provides access to over 1,000 bikes stationed at over 140 docking stations across the city.
sentence_415: [[National_Cycle_Route_56|National Cycle Route 56]], [[National_Cycle_Route_62|National Cycle Route 62]] and National Cycle Route 810 run through Liverpool.
sentence_416: As with other large cities, Liverpool is an important cultural centre within the United Kingdom, incorporating music, performing arts, museums and art galleries, literature and nightlife amongst others.
sentence_417: In 2008, the cultural heritage of the city was celebrated with the city holding the title of [[European_Capital_of_Culture|European Capital of Culture]], during which time a wide range of cultural celebrations took place in the city, including [[Go_Superlambananas!|Go Superlambananas!]]
sentence_418: and [[La_Princesse|La Princesse]].
sentence_419: Liverpool has also held Europe's largest music and poetry event, the [[National_Eisteddfod_of_Wales|Welsh national Eisteddfod]], three times, despite being in England, in 1884, 1900, and 1929.
sentence_420: Main articles: Music of Liverpool, [[Beat_music|Beat music]], and [[Culture_of_Liverpool|Culture of Liverpool]]
sentence_421: Liverpool is internationally known for music and is recognised by Guinness World Records as the World Capital City of Pop.
sentence_422: Musicians from the city have produced 56 No.
sentence_423: 1 singles, more than any other city in the world.
sentence_424: Both the most successful [[The_Beatles|male band]] and [[Spice_Girls|girl group]] in global music history have contained Liverpudlian members.
sentence_425: Liverpool is most famous as the birthplace of [[The_Beatles|the Beatles]] and during the 1960s was at the forefront of the [[Beat_Music|Beat Music]] movement, which would eventually lead to the [[British_Invasion|British Invasion]].
sentence_426: Many notable musicians of the time originated in the city including [[Billy_J._Kramer|Billy J. Kramer]], [[Cilla_Black|Cilla Black]], [[Gerry_and_the_Pacemakers|Gerry and the Pacemakers]] and [[The_Searchers_(band)|The Searchers]].
sentence_427: The influence of musicians from Liverpool, coupled with other cultural exploits of the time, such as the [[Liverpool_poets|Liverpool poets]], prompted American poet [[Allen_Ginsberg|Allen Ginsberg]] to proclaim that the city was "the centre of consciousness of the human universe".
sentence_428: Other musicians from Liverpool include [[Billy_Fury|Billy Fury]], [[A_Flock_of_Seagulls|A Flock of Seagulls]], [[Echo_&_the_Bunnymen|Echo & the Bunnymen]], Frankie Goes to Hollywood, [[Frankie_Vaughan|Frankie Vaughan]], [[Anathema_(band)|Anathema]], [[Ladytron|Ladytron]], [[The_Zutons|The Zutons]], [[Cast_(band)|Cast]], [[Atomic_Kitten|Atomic Kitten]] and [[Rebecca_Ferguson_(singer)|Rebecca Ferguson]].
sentence_429: [[The_La's|The La's]] 1990 hit single "[[There_She_Goes_(The_La's_song)|There She Goes]]" was described by [[Rolling_Stone|Rolling Stone]] as a "founding piece of [[Britpop|Britpop]]'s foundation."
sentence_430: The city is also home to the oldest surviving professional symphony orchestra in the UK, the [[Royal_Liverpool_Philharmonic_Orchestra|Royal Liverpool Philharmonic Orchestra]], which is based in the [[Philharmonic_Hall,_Liverpool|Philharmonic Hall]].
sentence_431: The chief conductor of the orchestra is [[Vasily_Petrenko|Vasily Petrenko]].
sentence_432: Sir [[Edward_Elgar|Edward Elgar]] dedicated his [[Pomp_and_Circumstance#March_No._1_in_D|Pomp and Circumstance March No.
sentence_433: 1]] to the Liverpool Orchestral Society, and the piece had its first performance in the city in 1901.
sentence_434: Among Liverpool's curiosities, the Austrian émigré [[Fritz_Spiegl|Fritz Spiegl]] is notable.
sentence_435: He not only became a world expert on the etymology of [[Scouse|Scouse]], but composed the music to Z-cars and the Radio 4 UK Theme.
sentence_436: The [[Liverpool_Mathew_Street_Music_Festival|Mathew Street Festival]] is an annual street festival that is one of the most important musical events in Liverpool's calendar.
sentence_437: It is Europe's largest free music event and takes place every August.
sentence_438: Other well established festivals in the city include [[Africa_Oyé|Africa Oyé]] and [[Brazilica_Festival|Brazilica]] which are the UK's largest free African and Brazilian music festivals respectively.
sentence_439: The dance music festival [[Creamfields|Creamfields]] was established by the Liverpool-based [[Cream_(nightclub)|Cream]] clubbing brand which started life as a weekly event at Nation nightclub.
sentence_440: There are numerous music venues located across the city, however the [[Echo_Arena_Liverpool|Echo Arena]] is by far the largest.
sentence_441: Opened in 2008 the 11,000-seat arena hosted the [[MTV_Europe_Music_Awards_2008|MTV Europe Music Awards]] the same year and since then has held host to world-renowned acts such as [[Andrea_Bocelli|Andrea Bocelli]], [[Beyoncé|Beyoncé]], [[Elton_John|Elton John]], [[Kanye_West|Kanye West]], [[Kasabian|Kasabian]], [[The_Killers|The Killers]], [[Lady_Gaga|Lady Gaga]], [[Oasis_(band)|Oasis]], [[Pink_(singer)|Pink]], [[Rihanna|Rihanna]], [[UB40|UB40]].
sentence_442: Liverpool has more galleries and national museums than any other city in the United Kingdom apart from London.
sentence_443: [[National_Museums_Liverpool|National Museums Liverpool]] is the only English national collection based wholly outside London.
sentence_444: The [[Tate_Liverpool|Tate Liverpool]] gallery houses the modern art collection of the Tate in the North of England and was, until the opening of [[Tate_Modern|Tate Modern]], the largest exhibition space dedicated to modern art in the United Kingdom.
sentence_445: The [[FACT_centre|FACT centre]] hosts touring multimedia exhibitions, while the [[Walker_Art_Gallery|Walker Art Gallery]] houses one of the most impressive permanent collections of [[Pre-Raphaelite|Pre-Raphaelite]] art in the world.
sentence_446: [[Sudley_House|Sudley House]] contains another major collection of pre-20th-century art.
sentence_447: Liverpool University's Victoria Building was re-opened as a public art gallery and museum to display the University's artwork and historical collections which include the largest display of art by [[John_James_Audubon|Audubon]] outside the US.
sentence_448: A number of artists have also come from the city, including painter [[George_Stubbs|George Stubbs]] who was born in Liverpool in 1724.
sentence_449: The Liverpool Biennial festival of arts runs from mid-September to late November and comprises three main sections; the International, The Independents and New Contemporaries although fringe events are timed to coincide.
sentence_450: It was during the 2004 festival that [[Yoko_Ono|Yoko Ono]]'s work "My mother is beautiful" caused widespread public protest when photographs of a naked woman's pubic area were exhibited on the main shopping street.
sentence_451: [[Felicia_Hemans|Felicia Hemans]] (née Browne) was born in Dale Street, Liverpool, in 1793, although she later moved to Flintshire, in Wales.
sentence_452: Felicia was born in Liverpool, a granddaughter of the [[Republic_of_Venice|Venetian]] consul in that city.
sentence_453: Her father's business soon brought the family to [[Denbighshire_(historic)|Denbighshire]] in North Wales, where she spent her youth.
sentence_454: They made their home near Abergele and [[St._Asaph|St.
sentence_455: Asaph]] ([[Flintshire_(historic)|Flintshire]]), and it is clear that she came to regard herself as Welsh by adoption, later referring to Wales as "Land of my childhood, my home and my dead".
sentence_456: Her first poems, dedicated to the [[George_IV_of_the_United_Kingdom|Prince of Wales]], were published in Liverpool in 1808, when she was only fourteen, arousing the interest of [[Percy_Bysshe_Shelley|Percy Bysshe Shelley]], who briefly corresponded with her.
sentence_457: A number of notable authors have visited Liverpool, including [[Daniel_Defoe|Daniel Defoe]], [[Washington_Irving|Washington Irving]], [[Thomas_De_Quincey|Thomas De Quincey]], [[Herman_Melville|Herman Melville]], [[Nathaniel_Hawthorne|Nathaniel Hawthorne]], [[Charles_Dickens|Charles Dickens]], [[Gerard_Manley_Hopkins|Gerard Manley Hopkins]] and [[Hugh_Walpole|Hugh Walpole]].
sentence_458: [[Daniel_Defoe|Daniel Defoe]], after visiting the city, described it, as "one of the wonders of Britain in his 'Tour through England and Wales'".
sentence_459: [[Herman_Melville|Herman Melville]]'s novel [[Redburn|Redburn]] deals with the first seagoing voyage of 19 years old Wellingborough Redburn between New York and Liverpool in 1839.
sentence_460: Largely autobiographical, the middle sections of the book are set in Liverpool and describe the young merchantman's wanderings, and his reflections.
sentence_461: Hawthorne was stationed in Liverpool as United States consul between 1853 and 1856.
sentence_462: Charles Dickens visited the city on numerous occasions to give public readings.
sentence_463: Hopkins served as priest at St Francis Xavier Church, Langdale St., Liverpool, between 1879 and 81.
sentence_464: Although he is not known to have ever visited Liverpool, [[Jung|Jung]] famously had a vivid dream of the city which he analysed in one of his works.
sentence_465: Of all the poets who are connected with Liverpool, perhaps the greatest is [[Constantine_P._Cavafy|Constantine P. Cavafy]], a twentieth-century Greek cultural icon, although he was born in Alexandria.
sentence_466: From a wealthy family, his father had business interests in Egypt, London and Liverpool.
sentence_467: After his father's death, Cavafy's mother brought him in 1872 at the age of nine to Liverpool where he spent part of his childhood being educated.
sentence_468: He lived first in Balmoral Road, then when the family firm crashed, he lived in poorer circumstances in Huskisson Street.
sentence_469: After his father died in 1870, Cavafy and his family settled for a while in Liverpool.
sentence_470: In 1876, his family faced financial problems due to the Long Depression of 1873, so, by 1877, they had to move back to Alexandria.
sentence_471: [[Her_Benny|Her Benny]], a novel telling the tragic story of Liverpool street urchins in the 1870s, written by Methodist preacher [[Silas_K._Hocking|Silas K. Hocking]], was a best-seller and the first book to sell a million copies in the author's lifetime.
sentence_472: The prolific writer of adventure novels, [[Harold_Edward_Bindloss|Harold Edward Bindloss]] (1866–1945), was born in Liverpool.
sentence_473: The writer, docker and political activist [[George_Garrett_(activist)|George Garrett]] was born in [[Secombe|Secombe]], on the [[Wirral_Peninsula|Wirral Peninsula]] in 1896 and was brought up in Liverpool's South end, around Park Road, the son of a fierce Liverpool–Irish Catholic mother and a staunch 'Orange' stevedore father.
sentence_474: In the 1920s and 1930s, his organisation within the Seamen's Vigilance Committees, unemployed demonstrations, and hunger marches from Liverpool became part of a wider cultural force.
sentence_475: He spoke at reconciliation meetings in sectarian Liverpool, and helped found the Unity Theatre in the 1930s as part of the Popular Front against the rise of fascism, particularly its echoes in the [[Spanish_Civil_War|Spanish Civil War]].
sentence_476: Garrett died in 1966.
sentence_477: The novelist and playwright [[James_Hanley_(novelist)|James Hanley]] (1897–1985) was born in [[Kirkdale,_Merseyside|Kirkdale]], Liverpool, in 1897 (not [[Dublin|Dublin]], nor 1901 as he generally implied) to a working-class family.
sentence_478: Hanley grew up close to the docks and much of his early writing is about seamen.
sentence_479: [[The_Furys_Chronicle|The Furys]] (1935) is first in a sequence of five loosely autobiographical novels about working-class life in Liverpool.
sentence_480: James Hanley's brother, novelist [[Gerald_Hanley|Gerald Hanley]] (1916–92) was also born in Liverpool (not [[County_Cork|County Cork]], Ireland, as he claimed).
sentence_481: While he published a number of novels he also wrote [[Radio_drama|radio plays]] for the BBC as well as some film scripts, most notably [[The_Blue_Max|The Blue Max]] (1966).
sentence_482: He was also one of several scriptwriters for a life of [[Gandhi|Gandhi]] (1964).
sentence_483: Novelist [[Beryl_Bainbridge|Beryl Bainbridge]] (1932–2010) was born in Liverpool and raised in nearby [[Formby|Formby]].
sentence_484: She was primarily known for her works of psychological fiction, often set among the English working classes.
sentence_485: Bainbridge won the [[Costa_Book_Awards|Whitbread Awards]] prize for best novel in [[1977_Whitbread_Awards|1977]] and [[1996_Whitbread_Awards|1996]] and was nominated five times for the [[Booker_Prize|Booker Prize]].
sentence_486: [[The_Times|The Times]] newspaper named Bainbridge among their list of "The 50 greatest [[British_literature|British writers]] since 1945".
sentence_487: [[J._G._Farrell|J.
sentence_488: G. Farrell]] was born in Liverpool in 1935 but left at the outbreak of war in 1939.
sentence_489: A novelist of Irish descent, Farrell gained prominence for his historical fiction, most notably his Empire Trilogy ([[Troubles_(novel)|Troubles]], [[The_Siege_of_Krishnapur|The Siege of Krishnapur]] and [[The_Singapore_Grip|The Singapore Grip]]), dealing with the political and human consequences of British colonial rule.
sentence_490: However, his career ended when he drowned in Ireland in 1979 at the age of 44.
sentence_491: [[Helen_Forrester|Helen Forrester]] was the pen name of June Bhatia (née Huband) (1919–2011), who was known for her books about her early childhood in Liverpool during the [[Great_Depression|Great Depression]], including Twopence to Cross the Mersey (1974), as well as several works of fiction.
sentence_492: During the late 1960s the city became well known for the [[Liverpool_poets|Liverpool poets]], who include [[Roger_McGough|Roger McGough]] and the late Adrian Henri.
sentence_493: An anthology of poems, [[The_Mersey_Sound_(book)|The Mersey Sound]], written by Henri, McGough and [[Brian_Patten|Brian Patten]], has sold well since it was first being published in 1967.
sentence_494: Liverpool has produced several noted writers of horror fiction, often set on Merseyside – [[Ramsey_Campbell|Ramsey Campbell]], [[Clive_Barker|Clive Barker]] and Peter Atkins among them.
sentence_495: A collection of Liverpudlian horror fiction, Spook City was edited by a Liverpool expatriate, Angus Mackenzie, and introduced by Doug Bradley, also from Liverpool.
sentence_496: Bradley is famed for portraying Barker's creation Pinhead in the Hellraiser series of films.
sentence_497: Liverpool also has a long history of performing arts, reflected in several annual theatre festivals such as the [[Liverpool_Shakespeare_Festival|Liverpool Shakespeare Festival]], which takes place inside [[Liverpool_Cathedral|Liverpool Cathedral]] and in the adjacent historic St James' Gardens every summer; the Everyword Festival of new theatre writing, the only one of its kind in the country; Physical Fest, an international festival of physical theatre; the annual festivals organised by [[Liverpool_John_Moores_University|Liverpool John Moores University]]'s drama department and the Liverpool Institute for Performing Arts; and other festivals by the large number of theatres in the city, such as the [[Liverpool_Empire_Theatre|Empire]], Epstein, [[Everyman_Theatre,_Liverpool|Everyman]], [[Liverpool_Playhouse|Playhouse]], [[Royal_Court_Theatre,_Liverpool|Royal Court]], and Unity theatres.
sentence_498: Notable actors and actresses from Liverpool include [[Arthur_Askey|Arthur Askey]], [[Tom_Baker|Tom Baker]], [[Kim_Cattrall|Kim Cattrall]], [[Jodie_Comer|Jodie Comer]], [[Stephen_Graham|Stephen Graham]], [[Rex_Harrison|Rex Harrison]], [[Jason_Isaacs|Jason Isaacs]], [[Tina_Malone|Tina Malone]], the McGann brothers (Joe, Mark, Paul, and [[Stephen_McGann|Stephen]]), [[David_Morrissey|David Morrissey]], [[Elizabeth_Morton|Elizabeth Morton]], [[Peter_Serafinowicz|Peter Serafinowicz]], [[Elisabeth_Sladen|Elisabeth Sladen]], [[Alison_Steadman|Alison Steadman]], and [[Rita_Tushingham|Rita Tushingham]].
sentence_499: Actors and actresses from elsewhere in the world have strong ties to the city, such as Canadian actor [[Mike_Myers|Mike Myers]] (whose parents were both from Liverpool) and American actress [[Halle_Berry|Halle Berry]] (whose mother was from Liverpool).
sentence_500: Liverpool has a thriving and varied nightlife, with the majority of the city's late-night bars, pubs, nightclubs, live music venues and comedy clubs being located in a number of distinct districts.
sentence_501: A 2011 [[TripAdvisor|TripAdvisor]] poll voted Liverpool as having the best nightlife of any UK city, ahead of [[Manchester|Manchester]], [[Leeds|Leeds]] and even London.
sentence_502: [[Concert_Square,_Liverpool|Concert Square]], St. Peter's Square and the adjoining Seel, Duke and [[Hardman_Street|Hardman Streets]] are home to some of Liverpool's largest and most famed nightclubs including [[St._Peter's_Roman_Catholic_Church,_Liverpool|Alma de Cuba]], [[Blue_Angel_(nightclub)|Blue Angel]], Bumper, Chibuku, Heebie Jeebies, [[Korova_(Liverpool)|Korova]], The Krazyhouse (Now Electrik Warehouse), The Magnet, [[Cream_(nightclub)|Nation]] (home of the [[Cream_(nightclub)|Cream brand]], and Medication, the UK's largest and longest-running weekly student event), Popworld as well as countless other smaller establishments and chain bars.
sentence_503: Another popular nightlife destination in the city centre is [[Mathew_Street|Mathew Street]] and the [[Liverpool_gay_quarter|Gay Quarter]], located close to the city's commercial district, this area is famed for [[The_Cavern_Club|The Cavern Club]] alongside numerous gay bars including Garlands and G-Bar.
sentence_504: The [[Royal_Albert_Dock,_Liverpool|Albert Dock]] and [[Lark_Lane,_Liverpool|Lark Lane]] in Aigburth also contain an abundance of bars and late-night venues.
sentence_505: See also: [[List_of_schools_in_Liverpool|List of schools in Liverpool]]
sentence_506: In Liverpool primary and secondary education is available in various forms supported by the state including secular, Church of England, [[Jewish|Jewish]], and Roman Catholic.
sentence_507: [[Islamic|Islamic]] education is available at primary level, but there is no secondary provision.
sentence_508: One of Liverpool's important early schools was The Liverpool Blue Coat School; founded in 1708 as a charitable school.
sentence_509: The Liverpool Blue Coat School is the top-performing school in the city with 100% 5 or more A*-C grades at GCSE resulting in the 30th best GCSE results in the country and an average point score per student of 1087.4 in A/AS levels.
sentence_510: Other notable schools include Liverpool College founded in 1840 [[Merchant_Taylors'_School,_Crosby|Merchant Taylors' School]] founded in 1620.
sentence_511: Another of Liverpool's notable senior schools is [[St._Edward's_College|St.
sentence_512: Edward's College]] situated in the West Derby area of the city.
sentence_513: Historic grammar schools, such as the [[Liverpool_Institute|Liverpool Institute High School]] and Liverpool Collegiate School—both closed in the 1980s—are still remembered as centres of academic excellence.
sentence_514: Bellerive Catholic College is the city's top-performing non-selective school, based upon GCSE results in 2007.
sentence_515: Liverpool has three universities: the [[University_of_Liverpool|University of Liverpool]], [[Liverpool_John_Moores_University|Liverpool John Moores University]] and [[Liverpool_Hope_University|Liverpool Hope University]].
sentence_516: Edge Hill University, founded as a [[Teacher-training_college|teacher-training college]] in the [[Edge_Hill,_Merseyside|Edge Hill]] district of Liverpool, is now located in [[Ormskirk|Ormskirk]] in South-West Lancashire.
sentence_517: Liverpool is also home to the Liverpool Institute for Performing Arts (LIPA).
sentence_518: The [[University_of_Liverpool|University of Liverpool]] was established in 1881 as University College Liverpool.
sentence_519: In 1884, it became part of the federal [[Victoria_University_(UK)|Victoria University]].
sentence_520: Following a Royal Charter and Act of Parliament in 1903, it became an independent university, the University of Liverpool, with the right to confer its own degrees.
sentence_521: It was the first university to offer degrees in biochemistry, architecture, civic design, veterinary science, oceanography and social science.
sentence_522: [[Liverpool_Hope_University|Liverpool Hope University]], which was formed through the merger of three colleges, the earliest of which was founded in 1844, gained university status in 2005.
sentence_523: It is the only ecumenical university in Europe.
sentence_524: It is situated on both sides of Taggart Avenue in Childwall and has a second campus in the city centre (the Cornerstone).
sentence_525: The [[Liverpool_School_of_Tropical_Medicine|Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine]], founded to address some of the problems created by trade, continues today as a post-graduate school affiliated with the [[University_of_Liverpool|University of Liverpool]] and houses an anti-venom repository.
sentence_526: [[Liverpool_John_Moores_University|Liverpool John Moores University]] was previously a [[Institute_of_technology|polytechnic]], and gained status in 1992.
sentence_527: It is named in honour of [[John_Moores_(merchant)|Sir John Moores]], one of the founders of the Littlewoods football pools and retail group, who was a major benefactor.
sentence_528: The institution was previously owned and run by Liverpool City Council.
sentence_529: It traces it lineage to the Liverpool [[Mechanics_Institute|Mechanics Institute]], opened in 1823, making it by this measure England's third-oldest university.
sentence_530: The city has one [[Further_education|further education]] college, Liverpool Community College in the city centre.
sentence_531: Liverpool City Council operates [[Burton_Manor|Burton Manor]], a residential adult education college in nearby [[Burton,_Ledsham_and_Willaston|Burton]], on the [[Wirral_Peninsula|Wirral Peninsula]].
sentence_532: There are two Jewish schools in Liverpool, both belonging to the King David Foundation.
sentence_533: [[King_David_School,_Liverpool|King David School, Liverpool]] is the High School and the King David Primary School.
sentence_534: There is also a King David Kindergarten, featured in the community centre of Harold House.
sentence_535: These schools are all run by the King David Foundation located in Harold House in Childwall; conveniently next door to the [[Childwall|Childwall]] Synagogue.
sentence_536: The City of Liverpool is the most successful footballing city in England.
sentence_537: Football is the most popular sport in the city, home to [[Everton_F.C.|Everton F.C.]] and [[Liverpool_F.C.|Liverpool F.C.]].
sentence_538: Between them, the clubs have won 28 English First Division titles, 12 [[FA_Cup|FA Cup]] titles, 10 [[EFL_Cup|League Cup]] titles, 6 [[UEFA_Champions_League|European Cup]] titles, 1 [[European_Cup_Winners'_Cup|European Cup Winners' Cup]] title, 3 [[UEFA_Europa_League|UEFA Cup]] titles, and 24 [[FA_Charity_Shield|FA Charity Shields]].
sentence_539: The clubs both compete in the [[Premier_League|Premier League]], of which they are founding members, and contest the Merseyside derby, dubbed the 'friendly derby' despite there having been more sending-offs in this fixture than any other.
sentence_540: However, unlike many other derbies, it is not rare for families in the city to contain supporters of both clubs.
sentence_541: Liverpool F.C. is the English and British club with the most European Cup titles with six, the latest in [[2019_UEFA_Champions_League_Final|2019]].
sentence_542: [[Everton_F.C.|Everton F.C.]] was founded in 1878 and play at [[Goodison_Park|Goodison Park]] and [[Liverpool_F.C.|Liverpool F.C.]] were founded in 1892 and play at [[Anfield|Anfield]].
sentence_543: Many high-profile players have played for the clubs, including [[Dixie_Dean|Dixie Dean]], [[Alan_Ball,_Jr.|Alan Ball]], [[Gary_Lineker|Gary Lineker]], [[Neville_Southall|Neville Southall]] and [[Wayne_Rooney|Wayne Rooney]] for [[Everton_F.C.|Everton F.C.]] and [[Kenny_Dalglish|Kenny Dalglish]], [[Alan_Hansen|Alan Hansen]], Kevin Keegan, Ian Rush and [[Steven_Gerrard|Steven Gerrard]] for [[Liverpool_F.C.|Liverpool F.C.]].
sentence_544: Notable managers of the clubs include Harry Catterick and [[Howard_Kendall|Howard Kendall]] of Everton, and [[Bill_Shankly|Bill Shankly]] and [[Bob_Paisley|Bob Paisley]] of Liverpool.
sentence_545: Famous professional footballers from Liverpool include [[Peter_Reid|Peter Reid]], [[Gary_Ablett_(English_footballer)|Gary Ablett]], [[Wayne_Rooney|Wayne Rooney]], [[Steven_Gerrard|Steven Gerrard]], [[Jamie_Carragher|Jamie Carragher]] and [[Tony_Hibbert|Tony Hibbert]].
sentence_546: The City of Liverpool is the only one in England to have staged top division football every single season since the formation of the [[Football_League|Football League]] in 1888, and both of the city's clubs play in high-capacity stadiums.
sentence_547: Boxing is massively popular in Liverpool.
sentence_548: The city has a proud heritage and history in the sport and is home to around 22 amateur boxing clubs, which are responsible for producing many successful boxers, such as Ike Bradley, [[Alan_Rudkin|Alan Rudkin]], [[John_Conteh|John Conteh]], Andy Holligan, [[Paul_Smith_(boxer)|Paul Smith]], [[Shea_Neary|Shea Neary]], [[Tony_Bellew|Tony Bellew]] and [[David_Price_(boxer)|David Price]].
sentence_549: The city also boasts a consistently strong amateur contingent which is highlighted by Liverpool being the most represented city on the GB Boxing team, as well as at the [[2012_London_Olympics|2012 London Olympics]], the most notable Liverpool amateur fighters include; [[George_Turpin|George Turpin]], [[Tony_Willis|Tony Willis]], [[Robin_Reid_(boxer)|Robin Reid]] and [[David_Price_(boxer)|David Price]] who have all medalled at the [[Olympic_Games|Olympic Games]].
sentence_550: Boxing events are usually hosted at the [[Echo_Arena|Echo Arena]] and [[Liverpool_Olympia|Liverpool Olympia]] within the city, although the former home of Liverpool boxing was the renowned [[Liverpool_Stadium|Liverpool Stadium]].
sentence_551: [[Aintree|Aintree]] is home to the world's most famous steeple-chase, the [[John_Smith's_Grand_National|John Smith's Grand National]] which takes place annually in early April.
sentence_552: The race meeting attracts horse owners/ jockeys from around the world to compete in the demanding 4 miles (6.4 km) and 30 fence course.
sentence_553: There have been many memorable moments of the Grand National, for instance, the 100/1 outsider Foinavon in 1967, the dominant [[Red_Rum|Red Rum]] and [[Ginger_McCain|Ginger McCain]] of the 1970s and [[Mon_Mome|Mon Mome]] (100/1) who won the 2009 meeting.
sentence_554: In 2010, the National became the first horse race to be televised in [[High-definition_television|high-definition]] in the UK.
sentence_555: The [[Royal_Liverpool_Golf_Club,_Hoylake|Royal Liverpool Golf Club]], situated in the nearby town of [[Hoylake|Hoylake]] on the Wirral Peninsula, has hosted [[The_Open_Championship|The Open Championship]] on a number of occasions, most recently in [[2014_Open_Championship|2014]].
