sentence_0: Korean ([[South_Korea|South Korean]]: /韓國語 hangugeo; [[North_Korea|North Korean]]: /朝鮮말 chosŏnmal) is an East Asian language spoken by about 77 million people.
sentence_1: It is the [[Official_language|official]] and [[National_language|national]] language of both [[Korea|Koreas]]: [[North_Korea|North Korea]] and [[South_Korea|South Korea]], with different standardized official forms used in each country.
sentence_2: It is a recognised minority language in the [[Yanbian_Korean_Autonomous_Prefecture|Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture]] and [[Changbai_Korean_Autonomous_County|Changbai Korean Autonomous County]] of Jilin province, [[China|China]].
sentence_3: It is also spoken in parts of [[Sakhalin|Sakhalin]], [[Russia|Russia]], and [[Central_Asia|Central Asia]].
sentence_4: Historical and modern linguists classify Korean as a [[Language_isolate|language isolate]]; however, it does have a few [[Extinct_language|extinct relatives]], which together with Korean itself and the [[Jeju_language|Jeju language]] (spoken in the [[Jeju_Province|Jeju Province]] and considered somewhat distinct) form the [[Koreanic_languages|Koreanic language family]].
sentence_5: The linguistic homeland of Korean is suggested to be somewhere in [[Manchuria|Manchuria]].
sentence_6: Main article: [[History_of_the_Korean_language|History of the Korean language]]
sentence_7: Modern Korean descends from [[Middle_Korean|Middle Korean]], which in turn descends from [[Old_Korean|Old Korean]], which descends from the [[Proto-Koreanic_language|Proto-Koreanic language]] which is generally suggested to have its linguistic homeland somewhere in [[Manchuria|Manchuria]].
sentence_8: Whitman (2012) suggests that the proto-Koreans, already present in northern Korea, expanded into the southern part of the [[Korean_Peninsula|Korean Peninsula]] at around 300 BC and coexisted with the descendants of the Japonic Mumun cultivators (or assimilated them).
sentence_9: Both had influence on each other and a later founder effect diminished the internal variety of both language families.
sentence_10: [[Chinese_characters|Chinese characters]] arrived in Korea (see [[Sino-Xenic_pronunciations|Sino-Xenic pronunciations]] for further information) together with [[Buddhism|Buddhism]] during the [[Proto–Three_Kingdoms_of_Korea|Proto-Three Kingdoms era]] in the 1st century BC.
sentence_11: They were adapted for Korean and became known as Hanja, and remained as the main script for writing Korean for over a millennium alongside various phonetic scripts that were later invented such as [[Idu_script|Idu]], [[Gugyeol|Gugyeol]] and [[Hyangchal|Hyangchal]].
sentence_12: Mainly privileged elites were educated to read and write in Hanja.
sentence_13: However, most of the population was illiterate.
sentence_14: In the 15th century, King Sejong the Great personally developed an [[Alphabet|alphabetic]] featural writing system known today as Hangul.
sentence_15: He felt that Hanja was inadequate to write Korean and that this was the cause of its very restricted use; Hangul was designed to either aid in reading Hanja or replace Hanja entirely.
sentence_16: Introduced in the document [[Hunminjeongeum|Hunminjeongeum]], it was called eonmun (colloquial script) and quickly spread nationwide to increase literacy in Korea.
sentence_17: Hangul was widely used by all the Korean classes but often treated as amkeul (script for women) and disregarded by privileged elites, whereas Hanja was regarded as jinseo (true text).
sentence_18: Consequently, official documents were always written in Hanja during the [[Joseon|Joseon]] era.
sentence_19: Since most people couldn't understand Hanja, Korean kings sometimes released public notices entirely written in Hangul as early as the 16th century for all Korean classes, including uneducated peasants and slaves.
sentence_20: By the 17th century, the elite class of Yangban exchanged Hangul letters with their slaves, suggesting a high literacy rate of Hangul during the Joseon era.
sentence_21: Today, Hanja is largely unused in everyday life due to its inconvenience, but it is still important for historical and linguistic studies.
sentence_22: Neither South Korea or North Korea opposes the learning of Hanja, though they are not officially used in North Korea anymore, and their usage in South Korea is mainly reserved for specific circumstances, such as newspapers, scholarly papers, and disambiguation.
sentence_23: Since the [[Korean_War|Korean War]], through 70 years of separation, North–South differences have developed in standard Korean, including variations in pronunciation and vocabulary chosen, but these minor differences can be found in any of the Korean dialects, which are still largely mutually intelligible.
sentence_24: The Korean names for the language are based on the names for Korea used in both South Korea and North Korea.
sentence_25: The English word "Korean" is derived from [[Goryeo|Goryeo]], which is thought to be the first Korean dynasty known to Western nations.
sentence_26: Korean people in the [[Post-Soviet_states|former USSR]] refer to themselves as [[Koryo-saram|Koryo-saram]] and/or Koryo-in (literally, "[[Names_of_Korea#Goryeo|Koryo/Goryeo]] person(s)"), and call the language [[Koryo-mal|Koryo-mal]].
sentence_27: In South Korea, the Korean language is referred to by many names including hanguk-eo ("Korean language"), hanguk-mal ("Korean speech") and uri-mal ("our language").
sentence_28: In "hanguk-eo" and "hanguk-mal", the first part of the word, "hanguk" was taken from the name of the [[Korean_Empire|Korean Empire]] (대한제국; 大韓帝國; Daehan Jeguk).
sentence_29: The "Han" (韓) in Hanguk and Daehan Jeguk is derived from [[Samhan|Samhan]], in reference to the [[Three_Kingdoms_of_Korea|Three Kingdoms of Korea]] (not the ancient confederacies in the southern Korean Peninsula), while "-eo" and "-mal" mean "language" and "speech", respectively.
sentence_30: Korean is also simply referred to as guk-eo, literally "national language".
sentence_31: This name is based on the same Han characters, meaning "nation" + "language" ("國語"), that are also used in Taiwan and Japan to refer to their respective national languages.
sentence_32: In North Korea and [[China|China]], the language is most often called Joseon-mal, or more formally, Joseon-o.
sentence_33: This is taken from the North Korean name for Korea (Joseon), a name retained from the [[Joseon_dynasty|Joseon dynasty]] until the proclamation of the [[Korean_Empire|Korean Empire]], which in turn was annexed by the [[Empire_of_Japan|Empire of Japan]].
sentence_34: In [[Mainland_China|mainland China]], following the establishment of diplomatic relations with South Korea in 1992, the term Cháoxiǎnyǔ or the short form Cháoyǔ has normally been used to refer to the standard language of North Korea and [[Yanbian_Korean_Autonomous_Prefecture|Yanbian]], whereas Hánguóyǔ or the short form Hányǔ is used to refer to the standard language of South Korea.
sentence_35: Some older English sources also use the spelling "Corea" to refer to the nation, and its inflected form for the language, culture and people, "Korea" becoming more popular in the late 1800s according to Google's NGram English corpus of 2015.
sentence_36: Korean is considered by most linguists to be a [[Language_isolate|language isolate]], though it is commonly included by proponents of the now generally rejected [[Altaic_languages|Altaic]] family.
sentence_37: The hypothesis that Korean could be related to Japanese has had some supporters due to some overlap in vocabulary and similar grammatical features that have been elaborated upon by such researchers as [[Samuel_Martin_(linguist)|Samuel E. Martin]] and [[Roy_Andrew_Miller|Roy Andrew Miller]].
sentence_38: [[Sergei_Anatolyevich_Starostin|Sergei Anatolyevich Starostin]] (1991) found about 25% of potential [[Cognate|cognates]] in the Japanese–Korean 100-word [[Swadesh_list|Swadesh list]].
sentence_39: Some linguists concerned with the issue, including Vovin, have argued that the indicated similarities between Japanese and Korean are not due to any genetic relationship, but rather to a [[Sprachbund|sprachbund]] effect and heavy borrowing, especially from ancient Korean into Western [[Old_Japanese|Old Japanese]].
sentence_40: A good example might be Middle Korean sàm and Japanese asá, meaning "hemp".
sentence_41: This word seems to be a cognate, but although it is well attested in Western Old Japanese and [[Northern_Ryukyuan_languages|Northern Ryukyuan languages]], in Eastern Old Japanese it only occurs in compounds, and it is only present in three dialects of the [[Southern_Ryukyuan_languages|Southern Ryukyuan language group]].
sentence_42: Also, the doublet wo meaning "hemp" is attested in Western Old Japanese and Southern Ryukyuan languages.
sentence_43: It is thus plausible to assume a borrowed term.
sentence_44: (see [[Classification_of_the_Japonic_languages|Classification of the Japonic languages]] or [[Comparison_of_Japanese_and_Korean|Comparison of Japanese and Korean]] for further details on a possible relationship.)
sentence_45: Another lesser-known theory is the [[Dravido-Korean_languages|Dravido-Korean languages]] theory which suggests a relation with Dravidian in India.
sentence_46: Some of the common features in the Korean and [[Dravidian_languages|Dravidian languages]] are that they share some similar vocabulary, are agglutinative, and follow the SOV order; in both languages, nominals and adjectives follow the same syntax, particles are post-positional, and modifiers always precede modified words.
sentence_47: However, typological similarities such as these could have arisen by chance.
sentence_48: The [[Khitan_language|Khitan language]] has many vocabulary items similar to Korean that are not found in Mongolian or Tungusic languages.
sentence_49: This suggests a strong Korean presence or influence on Khitan.
sentence_50: See also: [[Korean_diaspora|Korean diaspora]]
sentence_51: Korean is spoken by the [[Koreans|Korean people]] in both South Korea and North Korea, and by the [[Korean_diaspora|Korean diaspora]] in many countries including the [[China|People's Republic of China]], the [[United_States|United States]], [[Japan|Japan]], and [[Russia|Russia]].
sentence_52: Currently, Korean is the fourth most popular [[Foreign_language|foreign language]] in China, following English, Japanese, and Russian.
sentence_53: Korean-speaking minorities exist in these states, but because of [[Cultural_assimilation|cultural assimilation]] into host countries, not all ethnic Koreans may speak it with native fluency.
sentence_54: Korean is the official language of South Korea and North Korea.
sentence_55: It is also one of the two official languages of the [[Yanbian_Korean_Autonomous_Prefecture|Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture]].
sentence_56: In North Korea, the regulatory body is the Language Institute of the Academy of Social Sciences (사회과학원 어학연구소; 社會科學院語學硏究所, Sahoe Gwahagweon Eohag Yeonguso).
sentence_57: In South Korea, the regulatory body for Korean is the [[Seoul|Seoul]]-based National Institute of the Korean Language, which was created by presidential decree on January 23, 1991.
sentence_58: Established pursuant to Article 9, Section 2, of the Framework Act on the National Language, the [[King_Sejong_Institute|King Sejong Institute]] is a public institution set up to coordinate the government's project of propagating Korean language and culture; it also supports the King Sejong Institute, which is the institution's overseas branch.
sentence_59: The King Sejong Institute was established in response to:

list.value: An increase in the demand for Korean language education;

a rapid increase in Korean language education thanks to the spread of [[Hallyu|hallyu]], an increase in international marriage, the expansion of Korean enterprises into overseas markets, and enforcement of employment licensing system;
the need for a government-sanctioned Korean language educational institution;
the need for general support for overseas Korean language education based on a successful domestic language education program.

sentence_60: The TOPIK Korea Institute is a lifelong educational center affiliated with a variety of Korean universities in Seoul, South Korea, whose aim is to promote Korean language and culture, support local Korean teaching internationally, and facilitate cultural exchanges.
sentence_61: The institute is sometimes compared to language and culture promotion organizations such as the King Sejong Institute.
sentence_62: Unlike that organization, however, TOPIK Korea Institute operates within established universities and colleges around the world, providing educational materials.
sentence_63: In countries around the world, Korean embassies and cultural centers (한국문화원) administer TOPIK examinations.
sentence_64: Main articles: [[Korean_dialects|Korean dialects]] and [[Koreanic_languages|Koreanic languages]]
sentence_65: Korean has numerous small local [[Dialect|dialects]] (called mal (말) [literally "speech"], saturi (사투리), or bang'eon (방언 in Korean).
sentence_66: The [[Standard_language|standard language]] (pyojun-eo or pyojun-mal) of both South Korea and North Korea is based on the dialect of the area around Seoul (which, as Hanyang, was the capital of [[Joseon_Dynasty|Joseon]]-era Korea for 500 years), though the northern standard after the [[Korean_War|Korean War]] has been influenced by the dialect of [[Pyongyang|P'yŏngyang]].
sentence_67: All dialects of Korean are similar to each other and largely [[Mutually_intelligible|mutually intelligible]] (with the exception of dialect-specific phrases or non-Standard vocabulary unique to dialects), though the [[Jeju_dialect|dialect of Jeju Island]] is divergent enough to be sometimes classified as a separate language.
sentence_68: One of the more salient differences between dialects is the use of tone: speakers of the Seoul dialect make use of vowel length, whereas speakers of the [[Gyeongsang_dialect|Gyeongsang dialect]] maintain the [[Pitch-accent_language|pitch accent]] of Middle Korean.
sentence_69: Some dialects are conservative, maintaining Middle Korean sounds (such as z, β, ə) which have been lost from the standard language, whereas others are highly innovative.
sentence_70: There is substantial evidence for a history of extensive [[Dialect_levelling|dialect levelling]], or even [[Convergent_evolution|convergent evolution]] or intermixture of two or more originally distinct linguistic stocks, within the Korean language and its dialects.
sentence_71: Many Korean dialects have basic vocabulary that is etymologically distinct from vocabulary of identical meaning in Standard Korean or other dialects, for example "[[Garlic_chives|garlic chives]]" translated into Gyeongsang dialect /t͡ɕʌŋ.ɡu.d͡ʑi/ (정구지; Jeongguji) but in Standard Korean, it is /puːt͡ɕʰu/ (부추; Buchu).
sentence_72: This suggests that the Korean Peninsula may have at one time been much more linguistically diverse than it is at present.

sentence_74: Nonetheless, the separation of the two Korean states has resulted in increasing differences among the dialects that have emerged over time.
sentence_75: Since the allies of the newly-founded nations split the Korean peninsula in half after 1945, the newly formed Korean nations have since borrowed vocabulary extensively from their respective allies.
sentence_76: As the Soviet Union helped industrialize North Korea and establish it as a communist state, the North Koreans therefore borrowed a number of Russian terms.
sentence_77: Likewise, since the United States helped South Korea extensively to develop militarily, economically, and politically, South Koreans therefore borrowed extensively from English.
sentence_78: The differences among northern and southern dialects have become so significant that many North Korean defectors reportedly have had great difficulty communicating with South Koreans after having initially settled into South Korea.
sentence_79: In response to the diverging vocabularies, an app called Univoca was designed to help North Korean defectors learn South Korean terms by translating them into North Korean ones.
sentence_80: More information can be found on the page North-South differences in the Korean language.
sentence_81: Aside from the standard language, there are few clear boundaries between Korean dialects, and they are typically partially grouped according to the regions of Korea.
sentence_82: Recently, both North and South Korea's usage rate of the regional dialect have been decreasing due to social factors.

sentence_102: Note that a written syllable-final 'ㄹ', when followed by a vowel or a glide (i.e., when the next character starts with 'ㅇ'), migrates to the next syllable and thus becomes [ɾ].

sentence_115: Grammatical morphemes may change shape depending on the preceding sounds.

sentence_121: Main article: Korean grammar
sentence_122: Korean is an [[Agglutinative_language|agglutinative language]].
sentence_123: The Korean language is traditionally considered to have nine parts of speech.
sentence_124: For details, see Korean parts of speech.
sentence_125: Modifiers generally precede the modified words, and in the case of verb modifiers, can be serially appended.
sentence_126: The basic form of a Korean sentence is [[Subject–object–verb|subject–object–verb]], but the verb is the only required and immovable element and [[Word_order|word order]] is highly flexible, as in many other agglutinative languages.

sentence_127: Main articles: Korean speech levels and [[Korean_honorifics|Korean honorifics]]
sentence_128: The relationship between a speaker or writer and his or her subject and audience is paramount in Korean grammar.
sentence_129: The relationship between speaker/writer and subject referent is reflected in honorifics, whereas that between speaker/writer and audience is reflected in speech level.
sentence_130: When talking about someone superior in status, a speaker or writer usually uses special nouns or verb endings to indicate the subject's superiority.
sentence_131: Generally, someone is superior in status if they are an older relative, a stranger of roughly equal or greater age, or an employer, teacher, customer, or the like.
sentence_132: Someone is equal or inferior in status if they are a younger stranger, student, employee, or the like.
sentence_133: Nowadays, there are special endings which can be used on declarative, interrogative, and imperative sentences; and both honorific or normal sentences.
sentence_134: Honorifics in traditional Korea were strictly hierarchical.
sentence_135: The caste and estate systems possessed patterns and usages much more complex and stratified than those used today.
sentence_136: The intricate structure of the Korean honorific system flourished in traditional culture and society.
sentence_137: Honorifics in contemporary Korea are now used for people who are psychologically distant.
sentence_138: Honorifics are also used for people who are superior in status.
sentence_139: For example, older people, teachers, and employers.
sentence_140: There are seven verb [[Paradigm|paradigms]] or speech levels in Korean, and each level has its own unique set of verb endings which are used to indicate the level of formality of a situation.
sentence_141: Unlike honorifics—which are used to show respect towards the referent (the person spoken of) —speech levels are used to show respect towards a speaker's or writer's audience (the person spoken to).
sentence_142: The names of the seven levels are derived from the non-honorific imperative form of the verb (hada, "do") in each level, plus the suffix 체 ("che", Hanja: 體), which means "style".
sentence_143: The three levels with high politeness (very formally polite, formally polite, casually polite) are generally grouped together as jondaenmal (존댓말), whereas the two levels with low politeness (formally impolite, casually impolite) are banmal (반말) in Korean.
sentence_144: The remaining two levels (neutral formality with neutral politeness, high formality with neutral politeness) are neither polite nor impolite.
sentence_145: Nowadays, younger-generation speakers no longer feel obligated to lower their usual regard toward the referent.
sentence_146: It is common to see younger people talk to their older relatives with banmal (반말).
sentence_147: This is not out of disrespect, but instead it shows the intimacy and the closeness of the relationship between the two speakers.
sentence_148: Transformations in social structures and attitudes in today's rapidly changing society have brought about change in the way people speak.
sentence_149: In general, Korean lacks grammatical gender.
sentence_150: As one of the few exceptions, the third-person singular pronoun has two different forms: 그 geu (male) and 그녀 geunyeo (female).
sentence_151: Before 그녀 were invented in need of translating 'she' into Korean, 그 was the only one third-person singular pronoun, and had no grammatical gender.
sentence_152: In order to have a more complete understanding of intricacies of gender within the Korean language, we can look at the three models of language and gender that have been proposed: the deficit model, the dominance model, and the cultural difference model.
sentence_153: In the deficit model, male speech is seen as the default, and any form of speech that diverges from this norm (female speech) is seen as lesser than.
sentence_154: The dominance model sees women as lacking in power due to living within a patriarchal society.
sentence_155: The cultural difference model proposes that the difference in upbringing between men and women can explain the differences in their speech patterns.
sentence_156: It is important to look at these models so that one can better understand the misogynistic conditions that shaped the way men and women use the Korean language.
sentence_157: Korean is unique from the Romance languages and some Germanic languages in that there is no grammatical gender.
sentence_158: Rather, gendered differences in Korean can be observed through formality, intonation, word choice, etc.
sentence_159: However, one can still find stronger contrasts between the sexes within Korean speech.
sentence_160: Some examples of this can be seen in: (1) softer tone used by women in speech; (2) a married woman introducing herself as someone's mother or wife, not with her own name; (3) the presence of gender differences in titles and occupational terms (for example, a sajang is a company president and yŏsajang is a female company president.
sentence_161: ); (4) females sometimes using more tag questions and rising tones in statements, also seen in speech from children.
sentence_162: Between two people of asymmetrical status in a Korean society, people tend to emphasize differences in status for the sake of solidarity.
sentence_163: Koreans prefer to use kinship terms, rather than any other terms of reference.
sentence_164: In traditional Korean society, women have long been in disadvantaged positions.
sentence_165: Korean social structure traditionally was a patriarchically dominated family system that emphasized the maintenance of family lines.
sentence_166: This structure has tended to separate the roles of women from those of men.
sentence_167: Cho and Whitman (2019) explain that the different categories like male and female in social conditions influence the Korean language features.
sentence_168: Parallel variable solidarity and affection move the convention of speech style, especially terms of address that Jaki (자기 'you') has emerged as a gender-specific second-person pronoun used by women.

sentence_170: In contrast, the present Janey (자네 'you') is used by only men, among men, in terms of power and solidarity rules of speech style.

sentence_177: If we observe how Korean society used the question endings -ni (니) and -nya (냐), we can observe that -ni (니) was used between females and -nya (냐) was used between males.
sentence_178: In terms of the dominance model, it shows that women place themselves in a position of powerlessness in their socialization process, and this becomes manifested in their speech style.
sentence_179: While males tend to use the deferential ending (hamnida style) females frequently use the polite ending (haeyo '해요).
sentence_180: The fact that females often use the ending -yo (요) shows that this is a result of women having fewer opportunities to speak in formal settings.
sentence_181: Another female speech ending, -toraguyo (더라고요) 'I recall that …' and -kot kat ayo (것 겉아요) 'it seems that…' suggests that the speaker does not have an opinion of her own.
sentence_182: Examples of this include women speaking more passively or the use of upspeak when talking to men.
sentence_183: The use of the word 'like' was common among younger demographics, but now it is prevalent across generations.
sentence_184: Korea is a patriarchal society that had a negative attitude toward women, so a female prefix was added to the default lexicon, including terms for titles and occupations.
sentence_185: For instance, Sino Korean terms 'female' in SK morpheme ye (여) 'women,' used in ye-siin (여시인 'female poet') and ye-pise (여비서 'female secretary').
sentence_186: The male prefix adds the negligence lexicon, including discriminatory terms for women.
sentence_187: For example, for female for ye-sengmi (여성미 ' female beauty') and ye thay (여태 'female attitude ') are social terms referring to human physical characteristics.
sentence_188: Lately, sengkoy (성괴 ' cosmetic surgery monster') is used as a female gender-biased neglecting metaphor.
sentence_189: Another crucial difference between genders of men and women is the tone and pitch of their voices and how that affects the perception of politeness.
sentence_190: Upspeak Men learn to use an authoritative falling tone, and in korean culture a deeper voice is associated with being more polite.
sentence_191: In addition to the deferential speech endings being used, men are seen as more polite as well as impartial and professional.
sentence_192: When compared to women who use a rising tone in conjunction with the -yo (요) ending, they are not perceived to be as polite as men.
sentence_193: The -yo (요) ending also indicates uncertainty due to how this ending has many prefixes which indicate uncertainty and questioning.
sentence_194: While the deferential ending does not have any prefixes which can indicate uncertainty.
sentence_195: The -habnida (합니다) ending is the most polite and formal form of Korea, while the -yo (요) ending is less polite and formal which is where the perception of women being less professional originates from.
sentence_196: Hedges soften an assertion and its function as a euphemism in women's speech in terms of discourse difference.

sentence_201: Despite efforts at reform, male and female differentiation stereotypically works in Korean at lexicon, and the number of phonology, syntax, and discourse conduct gender as any other identities.
sentence_202: Korean women often use more indirect speech, obscure expressions, and cooperative communication.
sentence_203: Korean men use a more direct speech style and women use indirect speech due to their status via traditional social values.

sentence_205: Also, kilssey (글세 'well') and kunyang (그냥 'well') are typical characters for women's obscure expressions.

sentence_207: The core of the Korean vocabulary is made up of native Korean words.
sentence_208: A significant proportion of the vocabulary, especially words that denote abstract ideas, are [[Sino-Korean_vocabulary|Sino-Korean words]], either

sentence_209: The exact proportion of Sino-Korean vocabulary is a matter of debate.
sentence_210: Sohn (2001) stated 50–60%.
sentence_211: Later, the same author (2006, p. 5) gives an even higher estimate of 65%.
sentence_212: Jeong Jae-do, one of the compilers of the dictionary Urimal Keun Sajeon, asserts that the proportion is not so high.
sentence_213: He points out that Korean dictionaries compiled during the [[Korea_under_Japanese_rule|colonial period]] include many unused Sino-Korean words.
sentence_214: In his estimation, the proportion of Sino-Korean vocabulary in the Korean language might be as low as 30%.
sentence_215: Most of the vocabulary consists of two sets of words; native Korean and Sino-Korean respectively.
sentence_216: It is similar to that of English — native English words and Latinate equivalents such as water-aqua, fire-flame, sea-marine, two-dual, sun-solar, star-stellar.
sentence_217: Therefore, just like other Korean words, Korean has two sets of numeral systems.
sentence_218: However, unlike English and Latin which belong to the same Indo-European languages family and bear a certain resemblance, Korean and Chinese are [[Genetic_relationship_(linguistics)|genetically unrelated]] and the two sets of Korean words differ completely from each other.
sentence_219: All Sino-Korean [[Morpheme|morphemes]] are [[Monosyllabic_language|monosyllabic]] as in Chinese, whereas native Korean morphemes can be polysyllabic.
sentence_220: The Sino-Korean words were deliberately imported alongside corresponding Chinese characters for a written language and everything was supposed to be written in Hanja, so the coexistence of Sino-Korean would be more thorough and systematic than that of Latinate words in English.
sentence_221: To a much lesser extent, some words have also been borrowed from [[Mongolian_language|Mongolian]] and other languages.
sentence_222: The vast majority of loanwords other than Sino-Korean come from modern times, approximately 90% of which are from [[English_language|English]].
sentence_223: Many words have also been borrowed from Western languages such as [[German_language|German]] via Japanese (아르바이트 () "part-time job", 알레르기 (allereugi) "allergy", 기브스 (gibseu or gibuseu) "plaster cast used for broken bones").
sentence_224: Some Western words were borrowed indirectly via Japanese during the [[Korea_under_Japanese_rule|Japanese occupation of Korea]], taking a Japanese sound pattern, for example "dozen" > ダース dāsu > 다스 daseu.
sentence_225: Most indirect Western borrowings are now written according to current "Hangulization" rules for the respective Western language, as if borrowed directly.
sentence_226: There are a few more complicated borrowings such as "German(y)" (see [[Names_of_Germany#Korean|names of Germany]]), the first part of whose [[Exonym_and_endonym|endonym]] Deutschland [ˈdɔʏ̯t͡ʃ.lant] the Japanese approximated using the [[Kanji|kanji]] 獨逸 doitsu that were then accepted into the Korean language by their Sino-Korean pronunciation: dok + il = .
sentence_227: In South Korean official use, a number of other Sino-Korean country names have been replaced with phonetically oriented "Hangeulizations" of the countries' endonyms or English names.
sentence_228: Because of such a prevalence of English in modern South Korean culture and society, [[Lexical_borrowing|lexical borrowing]] is inevitable.
sentence_229: English-derived Korean, or '[[Konglish|Konglish]]' (콩글리쉬), is increasingly used.
sentence_230: The vocabulary of the South Korean dialect of the Korean language is roughly 5% loanwords (excluding Sino-Korean vocabulary).
sentence_231: However, due to North Korea's isolation, such influence is lacking in North Korean speech.
sentence_232: Korean uses words adapted from English in ways that may seem strange to native English speakers.
sentence_233: For example, fighting (화이팅 / 파이팅) is a term of encouragement like 'come on'/'go (on)' in English.
sentence_234: Something that is 'service' (서비스) is free or 'on the house'.
sentence_235: A building referred to as an 'aparteu' (아파트) is an 'apartment' (but in fact refers to a residence more akin to a condominium) and a type of pencil that is called a 'sharp' (샤프) is a mechanical pencil.
sentence_236: Like other borrowings, many of these idiosyncrasies, including all the examples listed above, appear to be imported into Korean via Japanese, or influenced by Japanese.
sentence_237: Many English words introduced via Japanese pronunciation have been reformed as in 멜론 (melon) which was once called 메론 (meron) as in Japanese.
sentence_238: North Korean vocabulary shows a tendency to prefer native Korean over Sino-Korean or foreign borrowings, especially with recent political objectives aimed at eliminating foreign influences on the Korean language in the North.
sentence_239: In the early years, the North Korean government tried to eliminate Sino-Korean words.
sentence_240: Consequently, South Korean may have several Sino-Korean or foreign borrowings which are not in North Korean.
sentence_241: Main articles: Hangul, [[Korean_Braille|Korean Braille]], and Hanja
sentence_242: See also: Hangul consonant and vowel tables
sentence_243: Before the creation of the modern Korean alphabet, known as Chosŏn'gŭl in North Korea and as Hangul in South Korea, people in Korea (known as [[Joseon|Joseon]] at the time) primarily wrote using [[Classical_Chinese|Classical Chinese]] alongside native phonetic writing systems that predate Hangul by hundreds of years, including [[Idu_script|idu]], [[Hyangchal|hyangchal]], [[Gugyeol|gugyeol]], and gakpil.
sentence_244: However, due to the fundamental differences between the Korean and Chinese languages and the large number of characters to be learned, the lower classes, who often didn't have the privilege of education, had much difficulty in learning how to write using Chinese characters.
sentence_245: To assuage this problem, King Sejong (r. 1418–1450) created the unique alphabet known as Hangul to promote literacy among the common people.
sentence_246: The Korean alphabet was denounced and looked down upon by the yangban aristocracy, who deemed it too easy to learn, but it gained widespread use among the common class, and was widely used to print popular novels which were enjoyed by the common class.
sentence_247: With growing Korean nationalism in the 19th century, the [[Gabo_Reform|Gabo Reformists']] push, and the promotion of Hangul in schools, in 1894, Hangul displaced Hanja as Korea's national script.
sentence_248: Hanja are still used to a certain extent in South Korea, where they are sometimes combined with Hangul, but this method is slowly declining in use, even though students learn Hanja in school.
sentence_249: Below is a chart of the Korean alphabet's symbols and their canonical [[International_Phonetic_Alphabet|IPA]] values:
sentence_250: The letters of the Korean alphabet are not written linearly like most alphabets, but instead arranged into blocks that represent syllables.
sentence_251: So, while the word bibimbap is written as eight characters in a row in English, in Korean it is written 비빔밥, as three syllable blocks in a row.
sentence_252: The syllable blocks are then written left to right, top to bottom.
sentence_253: Modern Korean is written with spaces between words, a feature not found in Chinese or Japanese (except when Japanese is written exclusively in hiragana, as in children's books).
sentence_254: Korean punctuation marks are almost identical to Western ones.
sentence_255: Traditionally, Korean was written in columns, from top to bottom, right to left, but it is now usually written in rows, from left to right, top to bottom.

sentence_256: Main article: North–South differences in the Korean language
sentence_257: The Korean language used in the North and the South exhibits differences in pronunciation, spelling, grammar and vocabulary.
sentence_258: In North Korea, [[Palatalization_(sound_change)|palatalization]] of /si/ is optional, and /t͡ɕ/ can be pronounced [z] between vowels.
sentence_259: Words that are written the same way may be pronounced differently, such as the examples below.
sentence_260: The pronunciations below are given in [[Revised_Romanization_of_Korean|Revised Romanization]], [[McCune–Reischauer|McCune–Reischauer]] and Hangul, the last of which represents what the Korean characters would be if one were to write the word as pronounced.
sentence_261: * Similar pronunciation is used in the North whenever the hanja "的" is attached to a Sino-Korean word ending in ㄴ, ㅁ or ㅇ.
sentence_262: (In the South, this rule only applies when it is attached to any single-character Sino-Korean word.)
sentence_263: See also: [[Korean_spelling_alphabet|Korean spelling alphabet]]
sentence_264: Some words are spelled differently by the North and the South, but the pronunciations are the same.

table.value: The "sai siot" ('ㅅ' used for indicating sound change) is almost never written out in the North.
When a ㄴㄴ combination is pronounced as ll, the original Hangul spelling is kept in the North, whereas the Hangul is changed in the South.

In words where the original hanja is spelt "렬" or "률" and follows a vowel, the initial ㄹ is not pronounced in the North, making the pronunciation identical with that in the South where the ㄹ is dropped in the spelling.

sentence_265: Some words have different spellings and pronunciations in the North and the South.
sentence_266: Most of the official languages of North Korea are from the northwest (Pyeongan dialect), and the standard language of South Korea is the standard language (Seoul language close to Gyeonggi- dialect).
sentence_267: some of which were given in the "Phonology" section above:

table.value: Initial r's are dropped if followed by i or y in the South Korean version of Korean.
Initial r's are demoted to an n if not followed by i or y in the South Korean version of Korean.

"Mortal enemy" and "[[Wonsu|field marshal]]" are homophones in the South. Possibly to avoid referring to [[Kim_Il-sung|Kim Il-sung]], [[Kim_Jong-il|Kim Jong-il]] or [[Kim_Jong-un|Kim Jong-un]] as the enemy, the second syllable of "enemy" is written and pronounced 쑤 in the North.

When transcribing foreign words from languages that do not have contrasts between aspirated and unaspirated stops, North Koreans generally use tensed stops for the unaspirated ones while South Koreans use aspirated stops in both cases.
In the case where ye comes after a consonant, such as in hye and pye, it is pronounced without the palatal approximate. North Korean orthography reflects this pronunciation nuance.

sentence_268: In general, when transcribing place names, North Korea tends to use the pronunciation in the original language more than South Korea, which often uses the pronunciation in English.

sentence_270: Some grammatical constructions are also different:

table.value: All similar grammar forms of verbs or adjectives that end in ㅣ in the stem (i.e. ㅣ, ㅐ, ㅔ, ㅚ, ㅟ and ㅢ) in the North use 여 instead of the South's 어.
ㅂ-irregular verbs in the North use 와 (wa) for all those with a positive ending vowel; this only happens in the South if the verb stem has only one syllable.
Although the Hangul differ, the pronunciations are the same (i.e. with the tensed ㄲ sound).

sentence_271: Some vocabulary is different between the North and the South:

table.value: 아빠트 (appateu/appat'ŭ) is also used in the North.

The Japanese pronunciation of 조선말 was used throughout Korea and Manchuria during Japanese Imperial Rule, but after liberation, the government chose the name 대한민국 (Daehanminguk) which was derived from the name immediately prior to Japanese Imperial Rule. The syllable 한 (Han) was drawn from the same source as that name (in reference to the Han people). [[Names_of_Korea#20th_century|Read more]].

동무 was originally a non-ideological word for "friend" used all over the Korean peninsula, but North Koreans later adopted it as the equivalent of the Communist term of address "comrade". As a result, to South Koreans today the word has a heavy political tinge, and so they have shifted to using other words for friend like chingu (친구) or beot (벗). South Koreans use chingu (친구) more often than beot (벗).
Such changes were made after the Korean War and the ideological battle between the anti-Communist government in the South and North Korea's communism.

sentence_272: In the North, [[Guillemet|guillemets]] 《 and 》 are the symbols used for quotes; in the South, quotation marks equivalent to the English ones, " and ", are standard, although 『 』 and 「 」 are also used.
sentence_273: For native English speakers, Korean is generally considered to be one of the most difficult languages to master despite the relative ease of learning Hangul.
sentence_274: For instance, the [[United_States|United States]]' Defense Language Institute places Korean in Category IV, which also includes Japanese, [[Chinese_language|Chinese]] (e.g. [[Standard_Mandarin|Mandarin]], [[Cantonese_language|Cantonese]] & [[Shanghainese_language|Shanghainese]]) and [[Arabic|Arabic]].
sentence_275: This means that 63 weeks of instruction (as compared to just 25 weeks for [[Italian_language|Italian]], [[French_language|French]], Portuguese and Spanish) are required to bring an English-speaking student to a limited working level of proficiency in which they have "sufficient capability to meet routine social demands and limited job requirements" and "can deal with concrete topics in past, present, and future tense."
sentence_276: Similarly, the Foreign Service Institute's School of Language Studies places Korean in Category IV, the highest level of difficulty.
sentence_277: The study of the Korean language in the United States is dominated by [[Korean_American|Korean American]] [[Heritage_language_learning|heritage language students]]; in 2007 they were estimated to form over 80% of all students of the language at non-military universities.
sentence_278: However, Sejong Institutes in the United States have noted a sharp rise in the number of people of other ethnic backgrounds studying Korean between 2009 and 2011; they attribute this to [[Korean_Wave|rising popularity]] of [[K-Pop|South Korean music]] and [[Korean_drama|television shows]].
sentence_279: In 2018 it was reported that the rise in K-Pop was responsible for the increase in people learning the language in US universities.
sentence_280: There are two widely used tests of Korean as a foreign language: the [[Korean_Language_Proficiency_Test|Korean Language Proficiency Test]] (KLPT) and the [[Test_of_Proficiency_in_Korean|Test of Proficiency in Korean]] (TOPIK).
sentence_281: The Korean Language Proficiency Test, an examination aimed at assessing non-native speakers' competence in Korean, was instituted in 1997; 17,000 people applied for the 2005 sitting of the examination.
sentence_282: The TOPIK was first administered in 1997 and was taken by 2,274 people.
sentence_283: Since then the total number of people who have taken the TOPIK has surpassed 1 million, with more than 150,000 candidates taking the test in 2012.
sentence_284: TOPIK is administered in 45 regions within South Korea and 72 nations outside of South Korea, with a significant portion being administered in Japan and North America, which would suggest the targeted audience for TOPIK is still primarily foreigners of Korean heritage.
sentence_285: This is also evident in TOPIK's website, where the examination is introduced as intended for Korean heritage students.

title: London Underground
sentence_0: This article is about the rapid transit system in London.
sentence_1: For the suburban London rail network, see [[London_Overground|London Overground]].
sentence_2: For the album by Herbie Mann, see [[London_Underground_(album)|London Underground (album)]].
sentence_3: The London Underground (also known simply as the Underground, or by its nickname the Tube) is a [[Rapid_transit|rapid transit]] system serving [[Greater_London|Greater London]] and some parts of the adjacent [[Ceremonial_counties_of_England|counties]] of Buckinghamshire, [[Essex|Essex]] and [[Hertfordshire|Hertfordshire]] in the United Kingdom.
sentence_4: The Underground has its origins in the [[Metropolitan_Railway|Metropolitan Railway]], the world's first underground passenger railway.
sentence_5: Opened in January 1863, it is now part of the [[Circle_line_(London_Underground)|Circle]], [[Hammersmith_&_City_line|Hammersmith & City]] and [[Metropolitan_line|Metropolitan lines]]; the first line to operate underground [[Electric_locomotive|electric traction trains]], the [[City_&_South_London_Railway|City & South London Railway]] in 1890, is now part of the [[Northern_line|Northern line]].
sentence_6: The network has expanded to 11 lines, and in 2017/18 was used for 1.357 billion passenger journeys, making it the world's [[List_of_metro_systems|12th busiest metro system]].
sentence_7: The 11 lines collectively handle up to 5 million passenger journeys a day.
sentence_8: The system's first tunnels were built just below the ground, using the [[Cut-and-cover|cut-and-cover]] method; later, smaller, roughly circular tunnels—which gave rise to its nickname, the Tube—were dug through at a deeper level.
sentence_9: The system has [[List_of_London_Underground_stations|270 stations]] and 250 miles (400 km) of track.
sentence_10: Despite its name, only 45% of the system is underground in tunnels, with much of the network in the outer environs of London being on the surface.
sentence_11: In addition, the Underground does not cover most southern parts of [[Greater_London|Greater London]], and there are only 29 stations south of the [[River_Thames|River Thames]].
sentence_12: The early tube lines, originally owned by several private companies, were brought together under the "UndergrounD" brand in the early 20th century and eventually merged along with the sub-surface lines and bus services in 1933 to form London Transport under the control of the [[London_Passenger_Transport_Board|London Passenger Transport Board]] (LPTB).
sentence_13: The current operator, London Underground Limited (LUL), is a wholly owned subsidiary of [[Transport_for_London|Transport for London]] (TfL), the statutory corporation responsible for the transport network in London.
sentence_14: As of 2015, 92% of operational expenditure is covered by passenger fares.
sentence_15: The [[Travelcard|Travelcard]] ticket was introduced in 1983 and [[Oyster_card|Oyster]], a contactless ticketing system, in 2003.
sentence_16: Contactless bank card payments were introduced in 2014, the first public transport system in the world to do so.
sentence_17: The LPTB commissioned many new station buildings, posters and public artworks in a [[Modernism|modernist]] style.
sentence_18: The schematic [[Tube_map|Tube map]], designed by Harry Beck in 1931, was voted a national design icon in 2006 and now includes other TfL transport systems such as the [[Docklands_Light_Railway|Docklands Light Railway]], [[London_Overground|London Overground]], [[TfL_Rail|TfL Rail]], and [[Tramlink|Tramlink]].
sentence_19: Other famous London Underground branding includes the [[#Roundel|roundel]] and [[Johnston_(typeface)|Johnston typeface]], created by Edward Johnston in 1916.
sentence_20: Main article: [[History_of_the_London_Underground|History of the London Underground]]
sentence_21: The idea of an underground railway linking the [[City_of_London|City of London]] with the urban centre was proposed in the 1830s, and the [[Metropolitan_Railway|Metropolitan Railway]] was granted permission to build such a line in 1854.
sentence_22: To prepare construction, a short test tunnel was built in 1855 in Kibblesworth, a small town with geological properties similar to London.
sentence_23: This test tunnel was used for two years in the development of the first underground train, and was later, in 1861, filled up.
sentence_24: The world's first underground railway, it opened in January 1863 between [[Paddington|Paddington]] and [[Farringdon,_London|Farringdon]] using gas-lit wooden carriages hauled by steam locomotives.
sentence_25: It was hailed as a success, carrying 38,000 passengers on the opening day, and borrowing trains from other railways to supplement the service.
sentence_26: The Metropolitan District Railway (commonly known as the [[District_Railway|District Railway]]) opened in December 1868 from South Kensington to Westminster as part of a plan for an underground "inner circle" connecting London's main-line stations.
sentence_27: The Metropolitan and District railways completed the [[Circle_line_(London_Underground)|Circle line]] in 1884, built using the [[Cut_and_cover|cut and cover]] method.
sentence_28: Both railways expanded, the District building five branches to the west reaching [[Ealing|Ealing]], [[Hounslow|Hounslow]], [[Uxbridge|Uxbridge]], [[Richmond,_London|Richmond]] and [[Wimbledon,_London|Wimbledon]] and the Metropolitan eventually extended as far as [[Verney_Junction_railway_station|Verney Junction]] in Buckinghamshire, more than 50 miles (80 km) from [[Baker_Street_tube_station|Baker Street]] and the centre of London.
sentence_29: For the first deep-level tube line, the [[City_and_South_London_Railway|City and South London Railway]], two 10 feet 2 inches (3.10 m) diameter circular tunnels were dug between [[King_William_Street,_London|King William Street]] (close to today's [[Bank–Monument_station|Monument station]]) and [[Stockwell|Stockwell]], under the roads to avoid the need for agreement with owners of property on the surface.
sentence_30: This opened in 1890 with electric locomotives that hauled carriages with small opaque windows, nicknamed padded cells.
sentence_31: The Waterloo and City Railway opened in 1898, followed by the [[Central_London_Railway|Central London Railway]] in 1900, known as the "twopenny tube".
sentence_32: These two ran electric trains in circular tunnels having diameters between 11 feet 8 inches (3.56 m) and 12 feet 2.5 inches (3.72 m), whereas the [[Great_Northern_and_City_Railway|Great Northern and City Railway]], which opened in 1904, was built to take main line trains from [[Finsbury_Park_station|Finsbury Park]] to a [[Moorgate_station|Moorgate terminus]] in the City and had 16-foot (4.9 m) diameter tunnels.
sentence_33: While steam locomotives were in use on the Underground there were contrasting health reports.
sentence_34: There were many instances of passengers collapsing whilst travelling, due to heat and pollution, leading for calls to clean the air through the installation of garden plants.
sentence_35: The Metropolitan even encouraged beards for staff to act as an air filter.
sentence_36: There were other reports claiming beneficial outcomes of using the Underground, including the designation of Great Portland Street as a "sanatorium for [sufferers of ...] [[Asthma|asthma]] and bronchial complaints", [[Tonsillitis|tonsillitis]] could be cured with acid gas and the Twopenny Tube cured [[Anorexia_(symptom)|anorexia]].
sentence_37: With the advent of electric Tube services (the Waterloo and City Railway and the Great Northern and City Railway), the [[Volk's_Electric_Railway|Volks Electric Railway]], in [[Brighton|Brighton]], and competition from electric trams, the pioneering Underground companies needed modernising.
sentence_38: In the early 20th century, the District and Metropolitan railways needed to electrify and a joint committee recommended an [[Alternating_current|AC]] system, the two companies co-operating because of the shared ownership of the inner circle.
sentence_39: The District, needing to raise the finance necessary, found an investor in the American [[Charles_Yerkes|Charles Yerkes]] who favoured a DC system similar to that in use on the City & South London and Central London railways.
sentence_40: The Metropolitan Railway protested about the change of plan, but after arbitration by the [[Board_of_Trade|Board of Trade]], the DC system was adopted.
sentence_41: Yerkes soon had control of the District Railway and established the [[Underground_Electric_Railways_Company_of_London|Underground Electric Railways Company of London]] (UERL) in 1902 to finance and operate three tube lines, the [[Baker_Street_and_Waterloo_Railway|Baker Street and Waterloo Railway]] (Bakerloo), the [[Charing_Cross,_Euston_and_Hampstead_Railway|Charing Cross, Euston and Hampstead Railway]] (Hampstead) and the [[Great_Northern,_Piccadilly_and_Brompton_Railway|Great Northern, Piccadilly and Brompton Railway]], (Piccadilly), which all opened between 1906 and 1907.
sentence_42: When the "Bakerloo" was so named in July 1906, [[The_Railway_Magazine|The Railway Magazine]] called it an undignified "gutter title".
sentence_43: By 1907 the District and Metropolitan Railways had electrified the underground sections of their lines.
sentence_44: In January 1913, the UERL acquired the [[Central_London_Railway|Central London Railway]] and the [[City_&_South_London_Railway|City & South London Railway]], as well as many of London's bus and tram operators.
sentence_45: Only the [[Metropolitan_Railway|Metropolitan Railway]], along with its subsidiaries the [[Great_Northern_&_City_Railway|Great Northern & City Railway]] and the [[East_London_Railway|East London Railway]], and the Waterloo & City Railway, by then owned by the main line [[London_and_South_Western_Railway|London and South Western Railway]], remained outside the Underground Group's control.
sentence_46: A joint marketing agreement between most of the companies in the early years of the 20th century included maps, joint publicity, through ticketing and UNDERGROUND signs, incorporating the first bullseye symbol, outside stations in Central London.
sentence_47: At the time, the term Underground was selected from three other proposed names; 'Tube' and 'Electric' were both officially rejected.
sentence_48: Ironically, the term Tube was later adopted alongside the Underground.
sentence_49: The Bakerloo line was extended north to Queen's Park to join a new electric line from Euston to [[Watford|Watford]], but [[World_War_I|World War I]] delayed construction and trains reached [[Watford_Junction_railway_station|Watford Junction]] in 1917.
sentence_50: During air raids in 1915 people used the tube stations as shelters.
sentence_51: An extension of the Central line west to [[Ealing|Ealing]] was also delayed by the war and was completed in 1920.
sentence_52: After the war government-backed financial guarantees were used to expand the network and the tunnels of the City and South London and Hampstead railways were linked at Euston and Kennington; the combined service was not named the [[Northern_line|Northern line]] until later.
sentence_53: The Metropolitan promoted housing estates near the railway with the "[[Metro-land|Metro-land]]" brand and nine housing estates were built near stations on the line.
sentence_54: Electrification was extended north from Harrow to [[Rickmansworth|Rickmansworth]], and branches opened from Rickmansworth to Watford in 1925 and from Wembley Park to Stanmore in 1932.
sentence_55: The [[Piccadilly_line|Piccadilly line]] was extended north to Cockfosters and took over District line branches to Harrow (later Uxbridge) and Hounslow.
sentence_56: In 1933, most of London's underground railways, tramway and bus services were merged to form the [[London_Passenger_Transport_Board|London Passenger Transport Board]], which used the [[London_Transport_(brand)|London Transport brand]].
sentence_57: The Waterloo & City Railway, which was by then in the ownership of the main line [[Southern_Railway_(UK)|Southern Railway]], remained with its existing owners.
sentence_58: In the same year that the London Passenger Transport Board was formed, Harry Beck's diagrammatic [[Tube_map|tube map]] first appeared.
sentence_59: In the following years, the outlying lines of the former Metropolitan Railway closed, the [[Brill_Tramway|Brill Tramway]] in 1935, and the line from [[Quainton_Road_railway_station|Quainton Road]] to [[Verney_Junction_railway_station|Verney Junction]] in 1936.
sentence_60: The 1935–40 [[New_Works_Programme|New Works Programme]] included the extension of the Central and Northern lines and the Bakerloo line to take over the Metropolitan's Stanmore branch.
sentence_61: [[World_War_II|World War II]] suspended these plans after the Bakerloo line had reached Stanmore and the Northern line [[High_Barnet_tube_station|High Barnet]] and [[Mill_Hill_East_tube_station|Mill Hill East]] in 1941.
sentence_62: Following bombing in 1940, passenger services over the [[West_London_line|West London line]] were suspended, leaving [[Olympia_(London)|Olympia exhibition centre]] without a railway service until a District line shuttle from Earl's Court began after the war.
sentence_63: After work restarted on the Central line extensions in east and west London, these were completed in 1949.
sentence_64: During the war many tube stations were used as air-raid shelters.
sentence_65: On 3 March 1943, a test of the air-raid warning sirens, together with the firing of a new type of anti-aircraft rocket, resulted in a crush of people attempting to take shelter in [[Bethnal_Green_tube_station|Bethnal Green Underground station]].
sentence_66: A total of 173 people, including 62 children, died, making this both the worst civilian disaster of World War II, and the largest loss of life in a single incident on the London Underground network.

section_7.value: London Transport Executive and Board era

sentence_67: On 1 January 1948, under the provisions of the [[Transport_Act_1947|Transport Act 1947]], the [[London_Passenger_Transport_Board|London Passenger Transport Board]] was nationalised and renamed the London Transport Executive, becoming a subsidiary transport organisation of the British Transport Commission, which was formed on the same day.
sentence_68: Under the same act, the country's main line railways were also nationalised, and their reconstruction was given priority over the maintenance of the Underground and most of the unfinished plans of the pre-war New Works Programme were shelved or postponed.
sentence_69: The District line needed new trains and an unpainted aluminium train entered service in 1953, this becoming the standard for new trains.
sentence_70: In the early 1960s, the Metropolitan line was electrified as far as [[Amersham|Amersham]], [[British_Railways|British Railways]] providing services for the former Metropolitan line stations between Amersham and Aylesbury.
sentence_71: In 1962, the British Transport Commission was abolished, and the London Transport Executive was renamed the London Transport Board, reporting directly to the Minister of Transport.
sentence_72: Also during the 1960s, the [[Victoria_line|Victoria line]] was dug under central London and, unlike the earlier tunnels, did not follow the roads above.
sentence_73: The line opened in 1968–71 with the trains being driven automatically and magnetically encoded tickets collected by automatic gates gave access to the platforms.
sentence_74: On 1 January 1970 responsibility for public transport within Greater London passed from central government to local government, in the form of the [[Greater_London_Council|Greater London Council]] (GLC), and the London Transport Board was abolished.
sentence_75: The London Transport brand continued to be used by the GLC.
sentence_76: On 28 February 1975, a southbound train on the [[Northern_City_Line|Northern City Line]] failed to stop at its [[Moorgate_station|Moorgate terminus]] and crashed into the wall at the end of the tunnel, in the [[Moorgate_tube_crash|Moorgate tube crash]].
sentence_77: There were 43 deaths and 74 injuries, the greatest loss of life during peacetime on the London Underground.
sentence_78: In 1976 the Northern City Line was taken over by British Rail and linked up with the main line railway at [[Finsbury_Park_station|Finsbury Park]], a transfer that had already been planned prior to the accident.
sentence_79: In 1979 another new tube, the [[Jubilee_line|Jubilee line]], named in honour of [[Silver_Jubilee_of_Elizabeth_II|Queen Elizabeth's Silver Jubilee]], took over the Stanmore branch from the Bakerloo line, linking it to a newly constructed tube between [[Baker_Street_tube_station|Baker Street]] and [[Charing_Cross_tube_station|Charing Cross]] stations.
sentence_80: Under the control of the GLC, London Transport introduced a system of [[London_fare_zones|fare zones]] for buses and underground trains that cut the average fare in 1981.
sentence_81: Fares increased following a legal challenge but the fare zones were retained, and in the mid-1980s the [[Travelcard|Travelcard]] and the Capitalcard were introduced.
sentence_82: In 1984 control of London Buses and the London Underground passed back to central government with the creation of [[London_Regional_Transport|London Regional Transport]] (LRT), which reported directly to the Secretary of State for Transport, still retaining the London Transport brand.
sentence_83: One person operation had been planned in 1968, but conflict with the trade unions delayed introduction until the 1980s.
sentence_84: On 18 November 1987, fire broke out in an escalator at [[King's_Cross_St._Pancras_tube_station|King's Cross St. Pancras tube station]].
sentence_85: The [[King's_Cross_fire|resulting fire]] cost the lives of 31 people and injured a further 100.
sentence_86: London Underground were strongly criticised in the aftermath for their attitude to fires underground, and publication of the report into the fire led to the resignation of senior management of both London Underground and London Regional Transport.
sentence_87: To comply with new safety regulations issued as a result of the fire, and to combat graffiti, a train refurbishment project was launched in July 1991.
sentence_88: In April 1994, the Waterloo & City Railway, by then owned by [[British_Rail|British Rail]] and known as the Waterloo & City line, was transferred to the London Underground.
sentence_89: In 1999, the [[Jubilee_line|Jubilee line]] was extended from [[Green_Park_tube_station|Green Park station]] through [[London_Docklands|Docklands]] to [[Stratford_station|Stratford station]], resulting in the closure of the short section of tunnel between Green Park and [[Charing_Cross_tube_station|Charing Cross]] stations, and including the first stations on the London Underground to have platform edge doors.
sentence_90: [[Transport_for_London|Transport for London]] (TfL) was created in 2000 as the integrated body responsible for London's transport system.
sentence_91: TfL is part of the [[Greater_London_Authority|Greater London Authority]] and is constituted as a statutory corporation regulated under local government finance rules.
sentence_92: The TfL Board is appointed by the [[Mayor_of_London|Mayor of London]], who also sets the structure and level of public transport fares in London.
sentence_93: The day-to-day running of the corporation is left to the Commissioner of Transport for London.
sentence_94: TfL eventually replaced [[London_Regional_Transport|London Regional Transport]], and discontinued the use of the London Transport brand in favour of its own brand.
sentence_95: The transfer of responsibility was staged, with transfer of control of London Underground delayed until July 2003, when London Underground Limited became an indirect subsidiary of TfL.
sentence_96: Between 2000 and 2003, London Underground was reorganised in a [[Public-Private_Partnership|Public-Private Partnership]] where private infrastructure companies (infracos) upgraded and maintained the railway.
sentence_97: This was undertaken before control passed to TfL, who were opposed to the arrangement.
sentence_98: One infraco - [[Metronet|Metronet]] - went into administration in 2007 and TfL took over the responsibilities, TfL taking over the other - [[Tube_Lines|Tube Lines]] - in 2010.
sentence_99: [[Electronic_ticket|Electronic ticketing]] in the form of the contactless [[Oyster_card|Oyster card]] was introduced in 2003.
sentence_100: London Underground services on the [[East_London_line|East London line]] ceased in 2007 so that it could be extended and converted to [[London_Overground|London Overground]] operation, and in December 2009 the Circle line changed from serving a closed loop around the centre of London to a spiral also serving Hammersmith.
sentence_101: Since September 2014, passengers have been able to use [[Contactless_payment|contactless bank cards]] on the Tube.
sentence_102: Their use has grown very quickly and now over a million contactless transactions are made on the Underground every day.
sentence_103: Main article: [[London_Underground_infrastructure|London Underground infrastructure]]
sentence_104: As of 2017, the Underground serves 270 [[Underground_station|stations]].
sentence_105: Sixteen Underground stations are outside [[Greater_London|London region]], eight on the Metropolitan line and eight on the Central line.
sentence_106: Of these, five ([[Amersham_station|Amersham]], [[Chalfont_&_Latimer_station|Chalfont & Latimer]], [[Chesham_tube_station|Chesham]], and [[Chorleywood_station|Chorleywood]] on the Metropolitan line, and [[Epping_tube_station|Epping]] on the Central line), are beyond the [[M25_motorway|M25 London Orbital motorway]].
sentence_107: Of the 32 [[London_borough|London boroughs]], six ([[London_Borough_of_Bexley|Bexley]], [[London_Borough_of_Bromley|Bromley]], [[London_Borough_of_Croydon|Croydon]], [[Royal_Borough_of_Kingston_upon_Thames|Kingston]], [[London_Borough_of_Lewisham|Lewisham]] and [[London_Borough_of_Sutton|Sutton]]) are not served by the Underground network, while [[London_Borough_of_Hackney|Hackney]] has [[Old_Street_tube_station|Old Street]] (on the Northern line Bank branch) and [[Manor_House_tube_station|Manor House]] (on the Piccadilly line) only just inside its boundaries.
sentence_108: Lewisham used to be served by the [[East_London_line|East London line]] (stations at New Cross and [[New_Cross_Gate_railway_station|New Cross Gate]]).
sentence_109: The line and the stations were transferred to the London Overground network in 2010.
sentence_110: London Underground's eleven lines total 402 kilometres (250 mi) in length, making it the fifth [[List_of_metro_systems|longest metro system in the world]].
sentence_111: These are made up of the sub-surface network and the deep-tube lines.
sentence_112: The [[Circle_line_(London_Underground)|Circle]], [[District_line|District]], [[Hammersmith_&_City_line|Hammersmith & City]], and [[Metropolitan_line|Metropolitan lines]] form the sub-surface network, with railway tunnels just below the surface and of a similar size to those on British main lines, converging on a circular bi-directional loop around zone 1.
sentence_113: The Hammersmith & City and Circle lines share stations and most of their track with each other, as well as with the Metropolitan and District lines.
sentence_114: The [[Bakerloo_line|Bakerloo]], [[Central_line_(London_Underground)|Central]], [[Jubilee_line|Jubilee]], [[Northern_line|Northern]], [[Piccadilly_line|Piccadilly]], [[Victoria_line|Victoria]] and [[Waterloo_&_City_line|Waterloo & City lines]] are deep-level tubes, with smaller trains that run in two circular tunnels (tubes) with a diameter about 11 feet 8 inches (3.56 m).
sentence_115: These lines have the exclusive use of a pair of tracks, except for the Uxbridge branch of the Piccadilly line, which shares track with the District line between Acton Town and Hanger Lane Junction and with the Metropolitan line between Rayners Lane and Uxbridge; and the Bakerloo line, which shares track with [[London_Overground|London Overground]]'s Watford DC Line for its aboveground section north of Queen's Park.
sentence_116: Fifty-five per cent of the system runs on the surface.
sentence_117: There are 20 miles (32 km) of [[Cut-and-cover|cut-and-cover]] tunnel and 93 miles (150 km) of tube tunnel.
sentence_118: Many of the central London underground stations on deep-level tube routes are higher than the running lines to assist deceleration when arriving and acceleration when departing.
sentence_119: Trains generally run on the left-hand track.
sentence_120: In some places, the tunnels are above each other (for example, the Central line east of St Paul's station), or the running tunnels are on the right (for example on the Victoria line between Warren Street and King's Cross St. Pancras, to allow cross-platform interchange with the Northern line at [[Euston_tube_station|Euston]]).
sentence_121: The lines are electrified with a four-rail DC system: a conductor rail between the rails is energised at −210 V and a rail outside the running rails at +420 V, giving a potential difference of 630 V. On the sections of line shared with mainline trains, such as the District line from East Putney to Wimbledon and Gunnersbury to Richmond, and the Bakerloo line north of Queen's Park, the centre rail is bonded to the running rails.
sentence_122: The average speed on the Underground is 20.5 mph (33.0 km/h).
sentence_123: Outside the tunnels of central London, many lines' trains tend to travel at over 40 mph (64 km/h) in the suburban and countryside areas.
sentence_124: The Metropolitan line can reach speeds of 62 mph (100 km/h).
sentence_125: The London Underground was used by 1.357 billion passengers in 2017/2018.

section_14.value: Services using former and current main lines

sentence_126: The Underground uses several railways and alignments that were built by main-line railway companies.

list.value: Bakerloo line: Between [[Queen's_Park_(London)_station|Queen's Park]] and [[Harrow_&_Wealdstone_station|Harrow & Wealdstone]] this runs over the Watford DC Line also used by [[London_Overground|London Overground]], alongside the [[London_&_North_Western_Railway|London & North Western Railway]] (LNWR) main line that opened in 1837. The route was laid out by the LNWR in 1912–15 and is part of the [[Network_Rail|Network Rail]] system.

Central line: The railway from just south of [[Leyton_tube_station|Leyton]] to just south of [[Loughton_tube_station|Loughton]] was built by [[Eastern_Counties_Railway|Eastern Counties Railway]] in 1856 on the same alignment in use today. The Underground also uses the line built in 1865 by the [[Great_Eastern_Railway|Great Eastern Railway]] (GER) between Loughton to [[Ongar_tube_station|Ongar]] via [[Epping_tube_station|Epping]]. The connection to the main line south of Leyton was closed in 1970 and removed in 1972. The line from Epping to Ongar was closed in 1994; most of the line is in use today by the heritage [[Epping_Ongar_Railway|Epping Ongar Railway]]. The line between [[Newbury_Park_tube_station|Newbury Park]] and Woodford junction (west of [[Roding_Valley_tube_station|Roding Valley]]) via Hainault was built by the GER in 1903, the connections to the main line south of Newbury Park closing in 1947 (in the Ilford direction) and 1956 (in the Seven Kings direction).

Central line: The line from just north of White City to [[Ealing_Broadway_tube_station|Ealing Broadway]] was built in 1917 by the [[Great_Western_Railway|Great Western Railway]] (GWR) and passenger service introduced by the Underground in 1920. [[North_Acton_tube_station|North Acton]] to [[West_Ruislip_tube_station|West Ruislip]] was built by GWR on behalf of the Underground in 1947–8 alongside the pre-existing tracks from Old Oak Common junction towards [[High_Wycombe_railway_station|High Wycombe]] and beyond, which date from 1904. As of May 2013, the original Old Oak Common junction to [[South_Ruislip_railway_station|South Ruislip]] route has one main-line train a day to and from Paddington.

District line: South of [[Kensington_Olympia_station|Kensington Olympia]] short sections of the 1862 [[West_London_Railway|West London Railway]] (WLR) and its 1863 West London Extension Railway (WLER) were used when District extended from Earl's Court in 1872. The District had its own bay platform at Olympia built in 1958 along with track on the bed of the 1862–3 WLR/WLER northbound. The southbound WLR/WLER became the new northbound main line at that time, and a new southbound main-line track was built through the site of former goods yard. The 1872 junction closed in 1958, and a further connection to the WLR just south of Olympia closed in 1992. The branch is now segregated.

District line: The line between Campbell Road junction (now closed), near [[Bromley-by-Bow_tube_station|Bromley-by-Bow]], and [[Barking_station|Barking]] was built by the [[London,_Tilbury_&_Southend_Railway|London, Tilbury & Southend Railway]] (LTSR) in 1858. The slow tracks were built 1903–05, when District services were extended from [[Bow_Road|Bow Road]] (though there were no District services east of [[East_Ham_tube_station|East Ham]] from 1905 to 1932). The slow tracks were shared with LTSR stopping and goods trains until segregated by 1962, when main-line trains stopped serving intermediate stations.

District line: The railway from Barking to [[Upminster_tube_station|Upminster]] was built by LTSR in 1885 and the District extended over the route in 1902. District withdrew between 1905 and 1932, when the route was quadrupled. Main-line trains ceased serving intermediate stations in 1962, and the District line today only uses the 1932 slow tracks.

District line: The westbound track between east of [[Ravenscourt_Park_tube_station|Ravenscourt Park]] and [[Turnham_Green_tube_station|Turnham Green]] and Turnham Green to Richmond (also used by [[London_Overground|London Overground]]) follows the alignment of a railway built by the [[London_&_South_Western_Railway|London & South Western Railway]] (LSWR) in 1869. The eastbound track between Turnham Green and east of Ravenscourt Park follows the alignment built in 1911; this was closed 1916 but was re-used when the Piccadilly line was extended in 1932.

District line: The line between [[East_Putney_tube_station|East Putney]] and [[Wimbledon_station|Wimbledon]] was built by the LSWR in 1889. The last scheduled main-line service ran in 1941 but it still sees a few through Waterloo passenger services at the start and end of the daily timetable. The route is also used for scheduled ECS movements to/from Wimbledon Park depot and for Waterloo services diverted during disruptions and track closures elsewhere.

Hammersmith & City: Between [[Paddington_tube_station_(Circle_and_Hammersmith_&_City_lines)|Paddington]] and [[Westbourne_Park_tube_station|Westbourne Park Underground station]], the line runs alongside the main line. The Great Western main line opened in 1838, serving a temporary terminus the other side of Bishop's Road. When the current Paddington station opened in 1854, the line passed to the south of the old station. On opening in 1864, the Hammersmith & City Railway (then part of the Metropolitan Railway) ran via the main line to a junction at Westbourne Park, until 1867 when two tracks opened to the south of the main line, with a crossing near Westbourne Bridge, Paddington. The current two tracks to the north of the main line and the subway east of Westbourne Park opened in 1878. The Hammersmith & City route is now completely segregated from the main line.

[[Jubilee_line|Jubilee line]]: The rail route between [[Canning_Town_station|Canning Town]] and [[Stratford_station|Stratford]] was built by the GER in 1846, with passenger services starting in 1847. The original alignment was quadrupled "in stages between 1860 and 1892" for freight services before the extra (western) tracks were lifted as traffic declined during the 20th century, and were re-laid for Jubilee line services that started in 1999. The current [[Docklands_Light_Railway|Docklands Light Railway]] (ex-North London line) uses the original eastern alignment and the Jubilee uses the western alignment.

Northern line: The line from [[East_Finchley_tube_station|East Finchley]] to [[Mill_Hill_East_tube_station|Mill Hill East]] was opened in 1867, and from [[Finchley_Central_tube_station|Finchley Central]] to [[High_Barnet_tube_station|High Barnet]] in 1872, both by the [[Great_Northern_Railway_(Great_Britain)|Great Northern Railway]].

Piccadilly line: The westbound track between east of Ravenscourt Park and Turnham Green was built by LSWR in 1869, and originally used for eastbound main-line and District services. The eastbound track was built in 1911; it closed in 1916 but was re-used when the Piccadilly line was extended in 1932.

sentence_128: Main article: [[London_Underground_rolling_stock|London Underground rolling stock]]
sentence_129: London Underground trains come in two sizes, larger sub-surface trains and smaller deep-tube trains.
sentence_130: Since the early 1960s all passenger trains have been electric multiple units with sliding doors and a train last ran with a guard in 2000.
sentence_131: All lines use fixed length trains with between six and eight cars, except for the Waterloo & City line that uses four cars.
sentence_132: New trains are designed for maximum number of [[Standing_passenger|standing passengers]] and for speed of access to the cars and have [[Regenerative_braking|regenerative braking]] and public address systems.
sentence_133: Since 1999 all new stock has had to comply with accessibility regulations that require such things as access and room for wheelchairs, and the size and location of door controls.
sentence_134: All underground trains are required to comply with [[Rail_Vehicle_Accessibility_Regulations|The Rail Vehicle Accessibility (Non Interoperable Rail System) Regulations 2010]] (RVAR 2010) by 2020.
sentence_135: Stock on sub-surface lines is identified by a letter (such as [[London_Underground_S7_and_S8_Stock|S Stock]], used on the [[Metropolitan_line|Metropolitan line]]), while tube stock is identified by the year of intended introduction (for example, 1996 Stock, used on the Jubilee line).
sentence_136: The Underground is served by the following depots:
sentence_137: Main article: [[List_of_former_and_unopened_London_Underground_stations|List of former and unopened London Underground stations]]
sentence_138: In the years since the first parts of the London Underground opened, many stations and routes have been closed.
sentence_139: Some stations were closed because of low passenger numbers rendering them uneconomical; some became redundant after lines were re-routed or replacements were constructed; and others are no longer served by the Underground but remain open to [[National_Rail|National Rail]] main line services.
sentence_140: In some cases, such as [[Aldwych_tube_station|Aldwych]], the buildings remain and are used for other purposes.
sentence_141: In others, such as [[British_Museum_tube_station|British Museum]], all evidence of the station has been lost through demolition.
sentence_142: See also: [[London_Underground_infrastructure#Ventilation_and_cooling|London Underground infrastructure: Ventilation and cooling]] and [[London_Underground_cooling|London Underground cooling]]
sentence_143: When the Bakerloo line opened in 1906 it was advertised with a maximum temperature of 60 °F (16 °C), but over time the tube tunnels have warmed up.
sentence_144: In 1938 approval was given for a ventilation improvement programme, and a refrigeration unit was installed in a lift shaft at Tottenham Court Road.
sentence_145: Temperatures of 47 °C (117 °F) were reported in the [[2006_European_heat_wave|2006 European heat wave]].
sentence_146: It was claimed in 2002 that, if animals were being transported, temperatures on the Tube would break European Commission animal welfare laws.
sentence_147: A 2000 study reported that air quality was seventy-three times worse than at street level, with a passenger breathing the same mass of particulates during a twenty-minute journey on the Northern line as when smoking a cigarette.
sentence_148: The main purpose of the London Underground's ventilation fans is to extract hot air from the tunnels, and fans across the network are being refurbished, although complaints of noise from local residents preclude their use at full power at night.
