sentence_149: In June 2006 a groundwater cooling system was installed at [[Victoria_station_(London)|Victoria station]].
sentence_150: In 2012, air-cooling units were installed on platforms at Green Park station using cool deep groundwater and at Oxford Circus using chiller units at the top of an adjacent building.
sentence_151: New air-conditioned trains are being introduced on the sub-surface lines, but space is limited on tube trains for air-conditioning units and these would heat the tunnels even more.
sentence_152: The Deep Tube Programme, investigating replacing the trains for the Bakerloo, Central, Waterloo and City and Piccadilly lines, is looking for trains with better energy conservation and regenerative braking, on which it might be possible to install a form of air conditioning.
sentence_153: In the original Tube design, trains passing through close fitting tunnels act as pistons to create air pressure gradients between stations.
sentence_154: This pressure difference drives ventilation between platforms and the surface exits through the passenger foot network.
sentence_155: This system depends on adequate cross sectional area of the airspace above the passengers' heads in the foot tunnels and escalators, where laminar airflow is proportional to the fourth power of the radius, the Hagen–Poiseuille equation.
sentence_156: It also depends on an absence of turbulence in the tunnel headspace.
sentence_157: In many stations the ventilation system is now ineffective because of alterations that reduce tunnel diameters and increase turbulence.
sentence_158: An example is Green Park tube station, where false ceiling panels attached to metal frames have been installed that reduce the above-head airspace diameter by more than half in many parts.
sentence_159: This has the effect of reducing laminar airflow by 94%.
sentence_160: Originally air turbulence was kept to a minimum by keeping all signage flat to the tunnel walls.
sentence_161: Now the ventilation space above head height is crowded with ducting, conduits, cameras, speakers and equipment acting as a baffle plates with predictable reductions in flow.
sentence_162: Often electronic signs have their flat surface at right angles to the main air flow, causing choked flow.
sentence_163: Temporary sign boards that stand at the top of escalators also maximise turbulence.
sentence_164: The alterations to the ventilation system are important, not only to heat exchange, but also the quality of the air at platform level, particularly given its asbestos content.
sentence_165: See also: [[London_Underground_infrastructure#Lifts_and_escalators|London Underground infrastructure: Lifts and escalators]]
sentence_166: Originally access to the deep-tube platforms was by a lift.
sentence_167: Each lift was staffed, and at some quiet stations in the 1920s the ticket office was moved into the lift, or it was arranged that the lift could be controlled from the ticket office.
sentence_168: The first escalator on the London Underground was installed in 1911 between the District and Piccadilly platforms at Earl's Court and from the following year new deep-level stations were provided with escalators instead of lifts.
sentence_169: The escalators had a diagonal shunt at the top landing.
sentence_170: In 1921 a recorded voice instructed passengers to stand on the right and signs followed in World War II.
sentence_171: Travellers were asked to stand on the right so that anyone wishing to overtake them would have a clear passage on the left side of the escalator.
sentence_172: The first 'comb' type escalator was installed in 1924 at Clapham Common.
sentence_173: In the 1920s and 1930s many lifts were replaced by escalators.
sentence_174: After the fatal 1987 [[King's_Cross_fire|King's Cross fire]], all wooden escalators were replaced with metal ones and the mechanisms are regularly degreased to lower the potential for fires.
sentence_175: The only wooden escalator not to be replaced was at [[Greenford_station|Greenford station]], which remained until March 2014 when TfL replaced it with the first incline lift on the UK transport network in October 2015.
sentence_176: There are 426 escalators on the London Underground system and the longest, at 60 metres (200 ft), is at [[Angel_tube_station|Angel]].
sentence_177: The shortest, at Stratford, gives a vertical rise of 4.1 metres (13 ft).
sentence_178: There are 184 lifts, and numbers have increased in recent years because of investment making tube stations accessible.
sentence_179: Over 28 stations will have lifts installed over the next 10 years, bring the total of step-free stations to over 100.
sentence_180: In mid-2012 London Underground, in partnership with [[Virgin_Media|Virgin Media]], tried out [[Wi-Fi|Wi-Fi]] hot spots in many stations, but not in the tunnels, that allowed passengers free internet access.
sentence_181: The free trial proved successful and was extended to the end of 2012 whereupon it switched to a service freely available to subscribers to Virgin Media and others, or as a paid-for service.
sentence_182: It was not previously possible to use mobile phones on most parts of the Underground (excluding services running overground or occasionally subsurface, depending on the phone and carrier) using native [[2G|2G]], 3G or [[4G|4G]] networks, and a project to extend coverage before the [[2012_Olympics|2012 Olympics]] was abandoned because of commercial and technical difficulties.
sentence_183: This partially changed in March 2020, when 4G signal was made available on parts of the Jubilee line, between Westminster and Canning Town, throughout the stations and tunnels.
sentence_184: UK subscribers to the Three mobile network can use the InTouch app to route their voice calls and texts messages via the Virgin Media Wifi network at 138 London Transport stations.
sentence_185: The [[EE_(telecommunications_company)|EE]] network also has recently released a WiFi calling feature available on the iPhone.

section_24.value: Northern line extension to Battersea Power Station

sentence_186: Main article: [[Northern_line_extension_to_Battersea|Northern line extension to Battersea]]
sentence_187: The [[Northern_Line|Northern Line]] is being extended from [[Kennington_tube_station|Kennington]] to [[Battersea_Power_Station_tube_station|Battersea Power Station]] via [[Nine_Elms_tube_station|Nine Elms]], serving the [[Battersea_Power_Station|Battersea Power Station]] and [[Nine_Elms|Nine Elms]] development areas.
sentence_188: In April 2013, Transport for London applied for the legal powers of a [[Transport_and_Works_Act_1992|Transport and Works Act Order]] to proceed with the extension.
sentence_189: Preparation works started in early 2015.
sentence_190: The main tunnelling was completed in November 2017, having started in April.
sentence_191: The extension is due to open in 2021.
sentence_192: Provision will be made for a possible future extension to [[Clapham_Junction_railway_station|Clapham Junction]] by notifying the [[London_Borough_of_Wandsworth|London Borough of Wandsworth]] of a reserved course under Battersea Park and subsequent streets.
sentence_193: Main article: [[Croxley_Rail_Link|Croxley Rail Link]]
sentence_194: The Croxley Rail Link involves re-routing the Metropolitan line's Watford branch from the current terminus at [[Watford_tube_station|Watford]] over part of the disused [[Watford_and_Rickmansworth_Railway|Croxley Green branch line]] to [[Watford_Junction_railway_station|Watford Junction]] with stations at [[Cassiobridge_tube_station|Cassiobridge]], [[Watford_Vicarage_Road_tube_station|Watford Vicarage Road]] and [[Watford_High_Street_railway_station|Watford High Street]] (which is currently only a part of London Overground).
sentence_195: Funding was agreed in December 2011, and the final approval for the extension was given on 24 July 2013, with the aim of completion by 2020.
sentence_196: In 2015, TfL took over responsibility for designing and building the extension from Hertfordshire County Council, and after further detailed design work concluded that an additional £50m would be needed.
sentence_197: As of November 2017, the project is on hold awaiting additional funding.
sentence_198: Main article: [[Bakerloo_line_extension|Bakerloo line extension]]
sentence_199: In 1931, the extension of the [[Bakerloo_line|Bakerloo line]] from Elephant & Castle to Camberwell was approved, with stations at Albany Road and an interchange at [[Denmark_Hill_railway_station|Denmark Hill]].
sentence_200: With post-war austerity, the plan was abandoned.
sentence_201: In 2006, [[Ken_Livingstone|Ken Livingstone]], the then [[Mayor_of_London|Mayor of London]], announced that within twenty years Camberwell would have a tube station.
sentence_202: Plans for an extension from [[Elephant_&_Castle_tube_station|Elephant & Castle]] to [[Lewisham_station|Lewisham]] via the [[Old_Kent_Road|Old Kent Road]] and [[New_Cross_Gate_railway_station|New Cross Gate]] are currently being developed by Transport for London, with possible completion by 2029.

section_28.value: Bakerloo line extension to Watford Junction

sentence_203: In 2007, as part of the planning for the transfer of the [[North_London_line|North London line]] to what became [[London_Overground|London Overground]], TfL proposed re-extending the Bakerloo line to [[Watford_Junction_railway_station|Watford Junction]].
sentence_204: In 2011, the [[London_Borough_of_Hillingdon|London Borough of Hillingdon]] has proposed that the Central line be extended from West Ruislip to Uxbridge via [[Ickenham|Ickenham]], claiming this would cut traffic on the [[A40_road|A40]] in the area.
sentence_205: According to the [[New_Civil_Engineer|New Civil Engineer]], the [[Canary_Wharf_Group|Canary Wharf Group]] has suggested the construction of a new rail line between [[Euston_tube_station|Euston]] and [[Canary_Wharf_tube_station|Canary Wharf]].
sentence_206: The proposal is being considered by the government.
sentence_207: Main article: [[New_Tube_for_London|New Tube for London]]
sentence_208: In mid-2014 Transport for London issued a tender for up to 18 trains for the Jubilee line and up to 50 trains for the Northern line.
sentence_209: These would be used to increase frequencies and cover the Battersea extension on the Northern line.
sentence_210: In early 2014 the Bakerloo, Central, Piccadilly and Waterloo & City line rolling-stock replacement project was renamed New Tube for London (NTfL) and moved from the feasibility stage to the design and specification stage.
sentence_211: The study had showed that, with new generation trains and re-signalling:

list.value: Piccadilly line capacity could be increased by 60% with 33 trains per hour (tph) at peak times by 2025.
Central line capacity increased by 25% with 33 tph at peak times by 2030.
Waterloo & City line capacity increased by 50% by 2032, after the track at Waterloo station is remodelled.
Bakerloo line capacity could be increased by 25% with 27 tph at peak times by 2033.

sentence_212: The project is estimated to cost £16.42 billon (£9.86 bn at 2013 prices).
sentence_213: A notice was published on 28 February 2014 in the [[Official_Journal_of_the_European_Union|Official Journal of the European Union]] asking for expressions of interest in building the trains.
sentence_214: On 9 October 2014 TFL published a shortlist of those ([[Alstom|Alstom]], Siemens, [[Hitachi|Hitachi]], [[Construcciones_y_Auxiliar_de_Ferrocarriles|CAF]] and [[Bombardier_Transportation|Bombardier]]) who had expressed an interest in supplying 250 trains for between £1.0 billion and £2.5 billion, and on the same day opened an exhibition with a design by PriestmanGoode.
sentence_215: The fully automated trains may be able to run without drivers, but the ASLEF and RMT trade unions that represent the drivers strongly oppose this, saying it would affect safety.
sentence_216: The [[Invitation_to_tender|invitation to tender]] for the trains was issued in January 2016; the specifications for the Piccadilly line infrastructure are expected in 2016, and the first train is due to run on the Piccadilly line in 2023.
sentence_217: Siemens Mobility's Inspiro design was selected in June 2018 in a £1.5 billion contract.
sentence_218: Main article: London Underground ticketing
sentence_219: The Underground received £2.669 billion in fares in 2016/17 and uses Transport for London's [[London_fare_zones|zonal fare system]] to calculate fares.
sentence_220: There are nine zones, zone 1 being the central zone, which includes the loop of the Circle line with a few stations to the south of River Thames.
sentence_221: The only London Underground stations in Zones 7 to 9 are on the Metropolitan line beyond [[Moor_Park_tube_station|Moor Park]], outside [[Greater_London|London region]].
sentence_222: Some stations are in two zones, and the cheapest fare applies.
sentence_223: Paper tickets, the contactless [[Oyster_cards|Oyster cards]], contactless debit or credit cards and [[Apple_Pay|Apple Pay]] and [[Android_Pay|Android Pay]] smartphones and watches can be used for travel.
sentence_224: Single and return tickets are available in either format, but [[Travelcards|Travelcards]] (season tickets) for longer than a day are available only on Oyster cards.
sentence_225: TfL introduced the Oyster card in 2003; this is a pre-payment [[Smartcard|smartcard]] with an embedded contactless [[RFID|RFID]] chip.
sentence_226: It can be loaded with Travelcards and used on the Underground, the Overground, buses, trams, the Docklands Light Railway, and National Rail services within London.
sentence_227: Fares for single journeys are cheaper than paper tickets, and a daily cap limits the total cost in a day to the price of a Day Travelcard.
sentence_228: The Oyster card must be 'touched in' at the start and end of a journey, otherwise it is regarded as 'incomplete' and the maximum fare is charged.
sentence_229: In March 2012 the cost of this in the previous year to travellers was £66.5 million.
sentence_230: In 2014, TfL became the first public transport provider in the world to accept payment from contactless bank cards.
sentence_231: The Underground first started accepting [[Contactless_payment|contactless]] [[Debit_card|debit]] and [[Credit_card|credit cards]] in September 2014.
sentence_232: This was followed by the adoption of [[Apple_Pay|Apple Pay]] in 2015 and [[Android_Pay|Android Pay]] in 2016, allowing payment using a contactless-enabled phone or smartwatch.
sentence_233: Over 500 million journeys have taken place using contactless, and TfL has become one of Europe's largest contactless merchants, with around 1 in 10 contactless transactions in the UK taking place on across the TfL network.
sentence_234: This technology, developed in-house by TfL, has been licensed to other major cities like [[New_York_City_Subway|New York City]] and [[Massachusetts_Bay_Transportation_Authority|Boston.]]
sentence_235: A concessionary fare scheme is operated by London Councils for residents who are disabled or meet certain age criteria.
sentence_236: Residents born before 1951 were eligible after their 60th birthday, whereas those born in 1955 will need to wait until they are 66.
sentence_237: Called a "[[Freedom_Pass|Freedom Pass]]" it allows free travel on TfL-operated routes at all times and is valid on some National Rail services within London at weekends and after 09:30 on Monday to Fridays.
sentence_238: Since 2010, the Freedom Pass has included an embedded holder's photograph; it lasts five years between renewals.
sentence_239: In addition to automatic and staffed faregates at stations, the Underground also operates on a [[Proof-of-payment|proof-of-payment]] system.
sentence_240: The system is patrolled by both uniformed and plain-clothes fare inspectors with hand-held Oyster-card readers.
sentence_241: Passengers travelling without a valid ticket must pay a penalty fare of £80 (£40 if paid within 21 days) and can be prosecuted for fare evasion under the [[Regulation_of_Railways_Act_1889|Regulation of Railways Act 1889]] and Transport for London Byelaws.
sentence_242: The tube closes overnight during the week, but since 2016, the [[Central_line_(London_Underground)|Central]], [[Jubilee_line|Jubilee]], [[Northern_line|Northern]], [[Piccadilly_line|Piccadilly]], and [[Victoria_line|Victoria]] lines, as well as a short section of the London Overground have operated all night on Friday and Saturday nights.
sentence_243: The first trains run from about 05:00 and the last trains until just after 01:00, with later starting times on Sunday mornings.
sentence_244: The nightly closures are used for maintenance, but some lines stay open on [[New_Year's_Eve|New Year's Eve]] and run for longer hours during major public events such as the [[2012_London_Olympics|2012 London Olympics]].
sentence_245: Some lines are occasionally closed for scheduled engineering work at weekends.
sentence_246: The Underground runs a limited service on Christmas Eve with some lines closing early, and does not operate on [[Christmas_Day|Christmas Day]].
sentence_247: Since 2010 a dispute between London Underground and [[Trade_union|trade unions]] over holiday pay has resulted in a limited service on [[Boxing_Day|Boxing Day]].
sentence_248: Main article: [[Night_Tube|Night Tube]]
sentence_249: On 19 August 2016, London Underground launched a 24-hour service on the Victoria and Central lines with plans in place to extend this to the Piccadilly, Northern and Jubilee lines starting on Friday morning and continuing right through until Sunday evening.
sentence_250: The Night Tube proposal was originally scheduled to start on 12 September 2015, following completion of upgrades, but in August 2015 it was announced that the start date for the Night Tube had been pushed back because of ongoing talks about contract terms between trade unions and London Underground.
sentence_251: On 23 May 2016 it was announced that the night service would launch on 19 August 2016 for the Central and Victoria lines.
sentence_252: The service operates on the:

list.value: Central line: between Ealing Broadway and Hainault via Newbury Park or Loughton. No service on the West Ruislip Branch, between Woodford and Hainault via Grange Hill or between Loughton and Epping.
Northern line: between Morden and Edgware / High Barnet via Charing Cross. No service on Mill Hill East or Bank branches.
Piccadilly line: between Cockfosters and Heathrow Terminals 1, 2, 3 and 5. No service to Terminal 4 or between Acton Town and Uxbridge.
Jubilee line: Full line – Stratford to Stanmore.
Victoria line: Full line – Walthamstow Central to Brixton.

sentence_253: The Jubilee, Piccadilly and Victoria lines, and the Central line between White City and Leytonstone, operate at 10-minute intervals.
sentence_254: The Central line operates at 20-minute intervals between Leytonstone and Hainault, between Leytonstone and Loughton, and between White City and Ealing Broadway.
sentence_255: The Northern line operates at roughly 8-minute intervals between Morden and Camden Town via Charing Cross, and at 15-minute intervals between Camden Town and Edgware and between Camden Town and High Barnet.
sentence_256: Accessibility for people with limited mobility was not considered when most of the system was built, and before 1993 fire regulations prohibited wheelchairs on the Underground.
sentence_257: The stations on the Jubilee Line Extension, opened in 1999, were the first stations on the system designed with accessibility in mind, but retrofitting accessibility features to the older stations is a major investment that is planned to take over twenty years.
sentence_258: A 2010 London Assembly report concluded that over 10% of people in London had reduced mobility and, with an aging population, numbers will increase in the future.
sentence_259: The standard issue tube map indicates stations that are step-free from street to platforms.
sentence_260: There can also be a step from platform to train as large as 12 inches (300 mm) and a gap between the train and curved platforms, and these distances are marked on the map.
sentence_261: Access from platform to train at some stations can be assisted using a boarding ramp operated by staff, and a section has been raised on some platforms to reduce the step.
sentence_262: As of October 2020, there are 80 stations with step-free access from platform to train, and there are plans to provide step-free access at another 19 stations by 2024.
sentence_263: By 2016 a third of stations had platform humps that reduce the step from platform to train.
sentence_264: New trains, such as those being introduced on the sub-surface network, have access and room for wheelchairs, improved audio and visual information systems and accessible door controls.
sentence_265: During peak hours, stations can get so crowded that they need to be closed.
sentence_266: Passengers may not get on the first train and the majority of passengers do not find a seat on their trains, some trains having more than four passengers every square metre.
sentence_267: When asked, passengers report overcrowding as the aspect of the network that they are least satisfied with, and overcrowding has been linked to poor productivity and potential poor heart health.
sentence_268: Capacity increases have been overtaken by increased demand, and peak overcrowding has increased by 16 percent since 2004/5.
sentence_269: Compared with 2003/4, the reliability of the network had increased in 2010/11, with lost customer hours reduced from 54 million to 40 million.
sentence_270: Passengers are entitled to a refund if their journey is delayed by 15 minutes or more due to circumstances within the control of TfL, and in 2010, 330,000 passengers of a potential 11 million Tube passengers claimed compensation for delays.
sentence_271: Mobile phone apps and services have been developed to help passengers claim their refund more efficiently.
sentence_272: See also: [[Safety_on_the_London_Underground|Safety on the London Underground]], [[Suicide_on_the_London_Underground|Suicide on the London Underground]], and [[List_of_London_Underground_accidents|List of London Underground accidents]]
sentence_273: London Underground is authorised to operate trains by the Office of Rail Regulation As at 19 March 2013 there had been 310 days since the last major incident, when a passenger had died after falling on the track.
sentence_274: As of 2015 there have been nine consecutive years in which no employee fatalities have occurred.
sentence_275: A special staff training facility was opened at [[West_Ashfield_tube_station|West Ashfield tube station]] in TFL's Ashfield House, [[West_Kensington|West Kensington]] in 2010 at a cost of £800,000.
sentence_276: Meanwhile, Mayor of London [[Boris_Johnson|Boris Johnson]] decided it should be demolished along with the [[Earls_Court_Exhibition_Centre|Earls Court Exhibition Centre]] as part of Europe's biggest regeneration scheme.
sentence_277: In November 2011 it was reported that 80 people had [[Suicide_in_the_United_Kingdom|died by suicide]] in the previous year on the London Underground, up from 46 in 2000.
sentence_278: Most platforms at deep tube stations have pits, often referred to as 'suicide pits', beneath the track.
sentence_279: These were constructed in 1926 to aid drainage of water from the platforms, but also halve the likelihood of a fatality when a passenger falls or jumps in front of a train.
sentence_280: The [[Tube_Challenge|Tube Challenge]] is the competition for the fastest time to travel to all London Underground stations, tracked by [[Guinness_World_Records|Guinness World Records]] since 1960.
sentence_281: The goal is to visit all the stations on the system, but not necessarily using all the lines; participants may connect between stations on foot, or by using other forms of public transport.
sentence_282: As of 2019, the record for fastest completion was held by Steve Wilson (UK) and AJ (nationality and full name unknown), who completed the challenge in 15 hours, 45 minutes and 38 seconds on 21 May 2015.
sentence_283: Main article: [[Tube_map|Tube map]]
sentence_284: Early maps of the Metropolitan and District railways were city maps with the lines superimposed, and the District published a pocket map in 1897.
sentence_285: A Central London Railway route diagram appears on a 1904 postcard and 1905 poster, similar maps appearing in District Railway cars in 1908.
sentence_286: In the same year, following a marketing agreement between the operators, a joint central area map that included all the lines was published.
sentence_287: A new map was published in 1921 without any background details, but the central area was squashed, requiring smaller letters and arrows.
sentence_288: Harry Beck had the idea of expanding this central area, distorting geography, and simplifying the map so that the railways appeared as straight lines with equally spaced stations.
sentence_289: He presented his original draft in 1931, and after initial rejection it was first printed in 1933.
sentence_290: Today's tube map is an evolution of that original design, and the ideas are used by many metro systems around the world.
sentence_291: The current standard tube map shows the Docklands Light Railway, London Overground, Emirates Air Line, London Tramlink and the London Underground; a more detailed map covering a larger area, published by National Rail and Transport for London, includes suburban railway services.
sentence_292: The tube map came second in a BBC and London Transport Museum poll asking for a favourite UK design icon of the 20th century and the underground's 150th anniversary was celebrated by a [[Google_Doodle|Google Doodle]] on the search engine.
sentence_293: While the first use of a [[Roundel|roundel]] in a London transport context was the trademark of the [[London_General_Omnibus_Company|London General Omnibus Company]] registered in 1905, it was first used on the Underground in 1908 when the UERL placed a solid red circle behind station nameboards on platforms to highlight the name.
sentence_294: The word "UNDERGROUND" was placed in a roundel instead of a station name on posters in 1912 by Charles Sharland and Alfred France, as well as on undated and possibly earlier posters from the same period.
sentence_295: [[Frank_Pick|Frank Pick]], impressed by the Paris Metro, thought the solid red disc cumbersome and took a version where the disc became a ring from a 1915 Sharland poster and gave it to Edward Johnston to develop, and registered the symbol as a trademark in 1917.
sentence_296: The roundel was first printed on a map cover using the Johnston typeface in June 1919, and printed in colour the following October.
sentence_297: After the UERL was absorbed into the London Passenger Transport Board in 1933, it used forms of the roundel for buses, trams and coaches, as well as the Underground.
sentence_298: The words "London Transport" were added inside the ring, above and below the bar.
sentence_299: The Carr-Edwards report, published in 1938 as possibly the first attempt at a graphics standards manual, introduced stricter guidelines.
sentence_300: Between 1948 and 1957 the word "Underground" in the bar was replaced by "London Transport".
sentence_301: As of 2013, forms of the roundel, with differing colours for the ring and bar, is used for other TfL services, such as London Buses, [[Tramlink|Tramlink]], [[London_Overground|London Overground]], [[London_River_Services|London River Services]] and [[Docklands_Light_Railway|Docklands Light Railway]].
sentence_302: [[Crossrail|Crossrail]] will also be identified with a roundel.
sentence_303: The 100th anniversary of the roundel was celebrated in 2008 by TfL commissioning 100 artists to produce works that celebrate the design.
sentence_304: See also: [[List_of_listed_London_Underground_stations|List of listed London Underground stations]]
sentence_305: Seventy of the 270 [[List_of_London_Underground_stations|London Underground stations]] use buildings that are on the [[Listed_building|Statutory List of Buildings of Special Architectural or Historic Interest]], and five have entrances in listed buildings.
sentence_306: The Metropolitan Railway's original seven stations were inspired by [[Italianate|Italianate]] designs, with the platforms lit by daylight from above and by [[Gas_lighting|gas lights]] in large glass globes.
sentence_307: Early District Railway stations were similar and on both railways the further from central London the station the simpler the construction.
sentence_308: The City & South London Railway opened with red-brick buildings, designed by [[T._P._Figgis|Thomas Phillips Figgis]], topped with a lead-covered dome that contained the lift mechanism and weather vane (still visible at many stations e.g. Clapham Common.
sentence_309: The Central London Railway appointed [[Harry_Bell_Measures|Harry Bell Measures]] as architect, who designed its pinkish-brown steel-framed buildings with larger entrances.
sentence_310: In the first decade of the 20th century [[Leslie_Green|Leslie Green]] established a house style for the tube stations built by the UERL, which were clad in [[Sang-de-boeuf_glaze|ox-blood]] [[Glazed_architectural_terra-cotta|faience]] blocks.
sentence_311: Green pioneered using building design to guide passengers with direction signs on tiled walls, with the stations given a unique identity with patterns on the platform walls.
sentence_312: Many of these tile patterns survive, though a significant number of these are now replicas.
sentence_313: Harry W. Ford was responsible for the design of at least 17 UERL and District Railway stations, including Barons Court and Embankment, and claimed to have first thought of enlarging the U and D in the UNDERGROUND wordmark.
sentence_314: The Met's architect [[Charles_Walter_Clark|Charles Walter Clark]] had used a neo-classical design for rebuilding Baker Street and [[Paddington_tube_station_(Bakerloo,_Circle_and_District_lines)|Paddington Praed Street]] stations before World War I and, although the fashion had changed, continued with Farringdon in 1923.
sentence_315: The buildings had metal lettering attached to pale walls.
sentence_316: Clark would later design "Chiltern Court", the large, luxurious block of apartments at Baker Street, that opened in 1929.
sentence_317: In the 1920s and 1930s, [[Charles_Holden|Charles Holden]] designed a series of [[Modern_architecture|modernist]] and [[Art-deco|art-deco]] stations some of which he described as his 'brick boxes with concrete lids'.
sentence_318: Holden's design for the Underground's headquarters building at [[55_Broadway|55 Broadway]] included avant-garde sculptures by [[Jacob_Epstein|Jacob Epstein]], [[Eric_Gill|Eric Gill]] and [[Henry_Moore|Henry Moore]].
sentence_319: When the Central line was extended east, the stations were simplified Holden proto-[[Brutalist|Brutalist]] designs, and a cavernous concourse built at [[Gants_Hill_tube_station|Gants Hill]] in honour of early [[Moscow_Metro|Moscow Metro]] stations.
sentence_320: Few new stations were built in the 50 years after 1948, but [[Misha_Black|Misha Black]] was appointed design consultant for the 1960s Victoria line, contributing to the line's uniform look, with each station having an individual tile motif.
sentence_321: Notable stations from this period include [[Moor_Park_station|Moor Park]], the stations of the Piccadilly line extension to Heathrow and [[Hillingdon_tube_station|Hillingdon]].
sentence_322: The stations of the 1990s extension of the Jubilee line were much larger than before and designed in a [[High-tech_architecture|high-tech style]] by architects such as [[Norman_Foster_(architect)|Norman Foster]] and [[Michael_Hopkins_(architect)|Michael Hopkins]], making extensive use of exposed metal plating.
sentence_323: [[West_Ham_station|West Ham station]] was built as a homage to the red brick tube stations of the 1930s, using brick, concrete and glass.
sentence_324: Many platforms have unique interior designs to help passenger identification.
sentence_325: The tiling at [[Baker_Street_tube_station|Baker Street]] incorporates repetitions of [[Sherlock_Holmes|Sherlock Holmes]]'s silhouette, at [[Tottenham_Court_Road_tube_station|Tottenham Court Road]] semi-abstract mosaics by [[Eduardo_Paolozzi|Eduardo Paolozzi]] feature musical instruments, tape machines and butterflies, and at [[Charing_Cross_tube_station|Charing Cross]], [[David_Gentleman|David Gentleman]] designed the mural depicting the construction of the [[Eleanor_cross|Eleanor Cross]].
sentence_326: [[Robyn_Denny|Robyn Denny]] designed the murals on the Northern line platforms at Embankment.
sentence_327: Main article: [[Johnston_(typeface)|Johnston (typeface)]]
sentence_328: The first posters used various type fonts, as was contemporary practice, and station signs used [[Sans_serif|sans serif]] block capitals.
sentence_329: The Johnston typeface was developed in upper and lower case in 1916, and a complete set of blocks, marked Johnston Sans, was made by the printers the following year.
sentence_330: A bold version of the capitals was developed by Johnston in 1929.
sentence_331: The Met changed to a serif letterform for its signs in the 1920s, used on the stations rebuilt by Clark.
sentence_332: Johnston was adopted systemwide after the formation of the LPTB in 1933 and the LT wordmark was applied to locomotives and carriages.
sentence_333: Johnston was redesigned, becoming New Johnston, for photo-typesetting in the early 1980s when Elichi Kono designed a range that included Light, Medium and Bold, each with its italic version.
sentence_334: The typesetters P22 developed today's electronic version, sometimes called TfL Johnston, in 1997.

section_46.value: Posters and patronage of the arts

sentence_335: Early advertising posters used various letter fonts.
sentence_336: Graphic posters first appeared in the 1890s, and it became possible to print colour images economically in the early 20th century.
sentence_337: The Central London Railway used colour illustrations in their 1905 poster, and from 1908 the Underground Group, under Pick's direction, used images of country scenes, shopping and major events on posters to encourage use of the tube.
sentence_338: Pick found he was limited by the commercial artists the printers used, and so commissioned work from artists and designers such as [[Dora_Batty|Dora Batty]], [[Edward_McKnight_Kauffer|Edward McKnight Kauffer]], the cartoonist [[George_Morrow_(illustrator)|George Morrow]], Herry (Heather) Perry, [[Graham_Sutherland|Graham Sutherland]], Charles Sharland and the sisters [[Anna_Zinkeisen|Anna]] and [[Doris_Zinkeisen|Doris Zinkeisen]].
sentence_339: According to Ruth Artmonsky, over 150 women artists were commissioned by Pick and latterly Christian Barman to design posters for London Underground, London Transport and London County Council Tramways.
sentence_340: The Johnston [[Sans-serif|Sans]] letter font began appearing on posters from 1917.
sentence_341: The Met, strongly independent, used images on timetables and on the cover of its Metro-land guide that promoted the country it served for the walker, visitor and later the house-hunter.
sentence_342: By the time London Transport was formed in 1933 the UERL was considered a patron of the arts and over 1000 works were commissioned in the 1930s, such as the cartoon images of Charles Burton and Kauffer's later abstract [[Cubist|cubist]] and [[Surrealist|surrealist]] images.
sentence_343: Harold Hutchison became London Transport publicity officer in 1947, after World War II and nationalisation, and introduced the "pair poster", where an image on a poster was paired with text on another.
sentence_344: Numbers of commissions dropped, to eight a year in the 1950s and just four a year in the 1970s, with images from artists such Harry Stevens and Tom Eckersley.
sentence_345: Art on the Underground was launched in 2000 to revive London Underground as a patron of the arts.
sentence_346: Today, commissions range from the pocket tube map cover, to temporary art pieces, to large scale permanent installations in stations.
sentence_347: Major commissions by Art on the Underground in recent years have included [[Labyrinth_(artwork)|Labyrinth]] by Turner prize winning artist [[Mark_Wallinger|Mark Wallinger]] to mark the 150th anniversary of the London Underground, "Diamonds and Circles" permanent works "in situ" by French artist [[Daniel_Buren|Daniel Buren]] at [[Tottenham_Court_Road_tube_station|Tottenham Court Road]] and "Beauty < Immortality", a memorial to [[Frank_Pick|Frank Pick]] by [[Langlands_&_Bell|Langlands & Bell]] at [[Piccadilly_Circus_tube_station|Piccadilly Circus]].
sentence_348: Similarly, Poems on the Underground has commissioned poetry since 1986 that are displayed in carriages.
sentence_349: Main article: London Underground in popular culture
sentence_350: The Underground (including several fictitious stations) has been featured in many movies and television shows, including [[Skyfall|Skyfall]], [[Die_Another_Day|Die Another Day]], [[Sliding_Doors|Sliding Doors]], [[An_American_Werewolf_in_London|An American Werewolf in London]], [[Creep_(2004_film)|Creep]], [[Tube_Tales|Tube Tales]], [[Sherlock_(TV_series)|Sherlock]] and [[Neverwhere|Neverwhere]].
sentence_351: The London Underground Film Office received over 200 requests to film in 2000.
sentence_352: The Underground has also featured in music such as [[The_Jam|The Jam]]'s "[[Down_in_the_Tube_Station_at_Midnight|Down in the Tube Station at Midnight]]" and in literature such as the graphic novel [[V_for_Vendetta|V for Vendetta]].
sentence_353: Popular legends about the Underground being haunted persist to this day.
sentence_354: In 2016, British composer [[Daniel_Liam_Glyn|Daniel Liam Glyn]] released his concept album Changing Stations based on the 11 main tube lines of the London Underground network.
sentence_355: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 3 has a single-player level named Mind The Gap where most of the level takes place between the dockyards and Westminster while the player and a team of [[Special_Air_Service|SAS]] attempt to take down terrorists attempting to escape using the London Underground via a hijacked train.
sentence_356: The game also features the multiplayer map "Underground", in which players are combating in a fictitious Underground station.
sentence_357: The London Underground map serves as a playing field for the conceptual game of [[Mornington_Crescent_(game)|Mornington Crescent]] (which is named after [[Mornington_Crescent_tube_station|a station]] on the [[Northern_line|Northern line]]) and the board game The London Game.
sentence_358: The London Underground is frequently studied by academics because it is one of the largest, oldest, and most widely used systems of public transit in the world.
sentence_359: Therefore, the transportation and [[Complex_network|complex network]] literatures include extensive information about the Tube system.
sentence_360: For London Underground passengers, research suggests that transfers are highly costly in terms of walk and wait times.
sentence_361: Because these costs are unevenly distributed across stations and platforms, path choice analyses may be helpful in guiding upgrades and choice of new stations.
sentence_362: Routes on the Underground can also be optimized using a global network optimization approach, akin to routing algorithms for [[Internet|Internet]] applications.
sentence_363: Analysis of the Underground as a network may also be helpful for setting safety priorities, since the stations targeted in the [[7_July_2005_London_bombings|2005 London bombings]] were amongst the most effective for disrupting the transportation system.
sentence_364: Since its beginnings in the 19th century, the Tube network has evolved greatly.

list.value: Harry Beck (1902–1974) designed the [[Tube_map|tube map]], named in 2006 as a British design icon.
[[Sir_John_Fowler,_1st_Baronet|John Fowler]] (1817–1898) was the railway engineer that designed the Metropolitan Railway.
[[MacDonald_Gill|MacDonald Gill]] (1884–1947), cartographer credited with drawing, in 1914, "the map that saved the London Underground".

[[James_Henry_Greathead|James Henry Greathead]] (1844–1896) was the engineer that dug the [[Tower_Subway|Tower Subway]] using a method using a wrought iron shield patented by [[Peter_W._Barlow|Peter W. Barlow]], and later used the same tunnelling shield to build the deep-tube City & South London and Central London railways.
Edward Johnston (1872–1944) developed the [[Johnston_(typeface)|Johnston Sans]] typeface, still in use today on the London Underground.
[[Charles_Pearson|Charles Pearson]] (1793–1862) suggested an underground railway in London in 1845 and from 1854 promoted a scheme that eventually became the Metropolitan Railway.

[[Frank_Pick|Frank Pick]] (1878–1941) was UERL publicity officer from 1908, commercial manager from 1912 and joint managing director from 1928. He was chief executive and vice chairman of the LPTB from 1933 to 1940. It was Pick that commissioned Edward Johnston to create the typeface and redesign the roundel, and established the Underground's reputation as patrons of the arts as users of the best in contemporary poster art and architecture.
[[Robert_Selbie|Robert Selbie]] (1868–1930) was manager of the Metropolitan Railway from 1908 until his death, marketing it using the [[Metro-land|Metro-land]] brand.
[[Edgar_Speyer|Edgar Speyer]] (1862–1932) Financial backer of Yerkes who served as UERL chairman from 1906 to 1915 during its formative years.
[[Albert_Stanley,_1st_Baron_Ashfield|Albert Stanley]] (1874–1948) was manager of the UERL from 1907, and became the first chairman of the London Passenger Transport Board (LPTB) in 1933.
[[Edward_Watkin|Edward Watkin]] (1819–1901) was chairman of the Metropolitan Railway from 1872 to 1894.

[[Charles_Yerkes|Charles Yerkes]] (1837–1905) was an American who founded the Underground Electric Railways Company of London (UERL) in 1902, which opened three tube lines and electrified the District Railway.

title: Limestone
sentence_0: For other uses, see [[Limestone_(disambiguation)|Limestone (disambiguation)]].
sentence_1: Limestone is a type of [[Carbonate_rock|carbonate]] [[Sedimentary_rock|sedimentary rock]].
sentence_2: It is composed mostly of the [[Minerals|minerals]] and [[Aragonite|aragonite]], which are different [[Polymorphism_(materials_science)|crystal forms]] of [[Calcium_carbonate|calcium carbonate]] (CaCO3).
sentence_3: A closely related rock is [[Dolomite_(rock)|dolomite]], which contains a high percentage of the mineral [[Dolomite_(mineral)|dolomite]], CaMg(CO3)2.
sentence_4: In old USGS publications, dolomite was referred to as magnesian limestone, a term now reserved for magnesium-deficient dolomites or magnesium-rich limestones.
sentence_5: About 10% of sedimentary rocks are limestones.
sentence_6: The [[Solubility|solubility]] of limestone in water and weak acid solutions leads to [[Karst|karst]] landscapes, in which water erodes the limestone over thousands to millions of years.
sentence_7: Most [[Cave|cave]] systems are found in limestone bedrock.
sentence_8: Limestone has numerous uses: as a building material, an essential component of [[Concrete|concrete]] ([[Portland_cement|Portland cement]]), as aggregate for the base of roads, as white pigment or filler in products such as [[Toothpaste|toothpaste]] or paints, as a chemical [[Feedstock|feedstock]] for the production of [[Lime_(material)|lime]], as a [[Soil_conditioner|soil conditioner]], and as a popular decorative addition to rock gardens.
sentence_9: Like most other sedimentary rocks, most limestone is composed of grains.
sentence_10: Most grains in limestone are skeletal fragments of marine organisms such as [[Coral|coral]] or [[Foraminiferal_Colouration_Index|foraminifera]].
sentence_11: These organisms secrete shells made of [[Aragonite|aragonite]] or , and leave these shells behind when they die.
sentence_12: Other [[Carbonate|carbonate]] grains composing limestones are ooids, [[Peloids|peloids]], and limeclasts ([[Intraclasts|intraclasts]] and extraclasts).
sentence_13: Limestone often contains variable amounts of [[Silica|silica]] in the form of [[Chert|chert]] ([[Chalcedony|chalcedony]], [[Flint|flint]], [[Jasper|jasper]], etc.) or siliceous skeletal fragment (sponge spicules, [[Diatoms|diatoms]], [[Radiolarians|radiolarians]]), and [[Travertine|travertine]] (a precipitate of calcite and aragonite).
sentence_14: Secondary calcite may be deposited by [[Supersaturation|supersaturated]] [[Meteoric_water|meteoric waters]] ([[Groundwater|groundwater]] that precipitates the material in caves).
sentence_15: This produces [[Speleothem|speleothems]], such as [[Stalagmite|stalagmites]] and [[Stalactite|stalactites]].
sentence_16: Another form taken by calcite is oolitic limestone, which can be recognized by its granular (oolite) appearance.
sentence_17: Other limestones are primarily composed of recrystalised lime mud, and are referred to as [[Micrite|micrite]].
sentence_18: The primary source of the calcite in limestone is most commonly [[Marine_biology|marine organisms]].
sentence_19: Some of these organisms can construct mounds of rock known as reefs, building upon past generations.
sentence_20: Below about 3,000 meters, water pressure and temperature conditions cause the dissolution of calcite to increase nonlinearly, so limestone typically does not form in deeper waters (see [[Lysocline|lysocline]]).
sentence_21: Limestones may also form in [[Lake|lacustrine]] and [[Evaporite|evaporite]] [[Sedimentary_depositional_environment|depositional environments]].
sentence_22: Calcite can be [[Solvation|dissolved]] or precipitated by groundwater, depending on several factors, including the water temperature, [[Acidity|pH]], and dissolved ion concentrations.
sentence_23: Calcite exhibits an unusual characteristic called [[Solubility#Temperature|retrograde solubility]], in which it becomes less soluble in water as the temperature increases.
sentence_24: Impurities (such as [[Clay|clay]], sand, organic remains, [[Iron_oxide|iron oxide]], and other materials) will cause limestones to exhibit different colors, especially with [[Weathering|weathered]] surfaces.
sentence_25: Limestone may be crystalline, [[Clastic_rock|clastic]], granular, or massive, depending on the method of formation.
sentence_26: Crystals of calcite, [[Quartz|quartz]], [[Dolomite_(mineral)|dolomite]] or [[Barite|barite]] may line small cavities in the rock.
sentence_27: When conditions are right for precipitation, calcite forms mineral coatings that cement the existing rock grains together, or it can fill fractures.
sentence_28: [[Travertine|Travertine]] is a banded, compact variety of limestone formed along streams, particularly where there are waterfalls and around hot or cold springs.
sentence_29: Calcium carbonate is deposited where evaporation of the water leaves a solution supersaturated with the chemical constituents of calcite.
sentence_30: [[Tufa|Tufa]], a porous or cellular variety of travertine, is found near waterfalls.
sentence_31: [[Coquina|Coquina]] is a poorly consolidated limestone composed of pieces of [[Coral|coral]] or [[Animal_shell|shells]].
sentence_32: During regional [[Metamorphism|metamorphism]] that occurs during the mountain building process ([[Orogeny|orogeny]]), limestone recrystallizes into [[Marble|marble]].
sentence_33: Limestone is a parent material of the [[Mollisol|Mollisol]] soil group.
sentence_34: See also: [[List_of_types_of_limestone|List of types of limestone]]
sentence_35: Two major classification schemes, the Folk and Dunham, are used for identifying the types of [[Carbonate_rocks|carbonate rocks]] collectively known as limestone.
sentence_36: Main article: [[Folk's_carbonate_classification|Folk's carbonate classification]]
sentence_37: Robert L. Folk developed a classification system that places primary emphasis on the detailed composition of grains and interstitial material in [[Carbonate_rocks|carbonate rocks]].
sentence_38: Based on composition, there are three main components: allochems (grains), matrix (mostly micrite), and cement (sparite).
sentence_39: The Folk system uses two-part names; the first refers to the grains and the second to the cement.
sentence_40: For example, a limestone consisting mainly of ooids, with a crystalline matrix, would be termed an oosparite.
sentence_41: It is helpful to have a petrographic microscope when using the Folk scheme, because it is easier to determine the components present in each sample.
sentence_42: Main article: [[Dunham_classification|Dunham classification]]
sentence_43: Robert J. Dunham published his system for limestone in 1962.
sentence_44: It focuses on the depositional fabric of carbonate rocks.
sentence_45: Dunham divides the rocks into four main groups based on relative proportions of coarser clastic particles, based on criteria such as whether the grains were originally in mutual contact, and therefore self-supporting, or whether the rock is characterized by the presence of frame builders and algal mats.
sentence_46: Unlike the Folk scheme, Dunham deals with the original porosity of the rock.
sentence_47: The Dunham scheme is more useful for hand samples because it is based on texture, not the grains in the sample.
sentence_48: A revised classification was proposed by Wright (1992).
sentence_49: It adds some diagenetic patterns to the classification scheme.
sentence_50: The solubility of calcium carbonate (CaCO3) is controlled largely by the partial pressure of [[Carbon_dioxide|carbon dioxide]] (CO2) in the water.
sentence_51: This is summarized in the reaction:
sentence_52: Increases in temperature or decreases in pressure tend to reduce the partial pressure of CO2 and precipitate CaCO3.
sentence_53: Reduction in salinity also reduces the solubility of CaCO3, by several orders of magnitude for fresh water versus seawater.
sentence_54: Near-surface water of the earth's oceans are oversaturated with CaCO3 by a factor of more than six.
sentence_55: The failure of CaCO3 to precipitate out of these waters is likely due to interference by dissolved [[Magnesium|magnesium]] ions with [[Nucleation|nucleation]] of calcite crystals, the necessary first step in precipitation.
sentence_56: Although ooids may form through purely inorganic processes, the bulk of CaCO3 precipitation in the oceans is the result of biological activity.
sentence_57: Much of this takes place on [[Carbonate_platform|carbonate platforms]].
sentence_58: Main article: [[Karst_topography|Karst topography]]
sentence_59: About 10% of all sedimentary rocks are limestones.
sentence_60: Limestone is partially soluble, especially in acid, and therefore forms many erosional landforms.
sentence_61: These include [[Limestone_pavement|limestone pavements]], [[Pot_hole|pot holes]], [[Cenote|cenotes]], caves and gorges.
sentence_62: Such erosion landscapes are known as [[Karsts|karsts]].
sentence_63: Limestone is less [[Resistance_(geology)|resistant]] than most [[Igneous|igneous]] rocks, but more resistant than most other [[Sedimentary_rock|sedimentary rocks]].
sentence_64: It is therefore usually associated with hills and [[Downland|downland]], and occurs in regions with other sedimentary rocks, typically clays.
sentence_65: Karst topography and caves develop in limestone rocks due to their [[Solubility|solubility]] in dilute [[Acid|acidic]] [[Groundwater|groundwater]].
sentence_66: The [[Solubility|solubility]] of limestone in water and weak acid solutions leads to [[Karst|karst]] landscapes.
sentence_67: Regions overlying limestone bedrock tend to have fewer visible above-ground sources (ponds and streams), as surface water easily drains downward through [[Joint_(geology)|joints]] in the limestone.
sentence_68: While draining, water and organic acid from the soil slowly (over thousands or millions of years) enlarges these cracks, dissolving the calcium carbonate and carrying it away in [[Solution|solution]].
sentence_69: Most [[Cave|cave]] systems are through limestone bedrock.
sentence_70: Cooling groundwater or mixing of different groundwaters will also create conditions suitable for cave formation.
sentence_71: Coastal limestones are often eroded by organisms which bore into the rock by various means.
sentence_72: This process is known as [[Bioerosion|bioerosion]].
sentence_73: It is most common in the tropics, and it is known throughout the [[Fossil_record|fossil record]] (see Taylor and Wilson, 2003).
sentence_74: Bands of limestone emerge from the Earth's surface in often spectacular rocky outcrops and islands.
sentence_75: Examples include the [[Rock_of_Gibraltar|Rock of Gibraltar]], the [[The_Burren|Burren]] in County Clare, Ireland; the [[Verdon_Gorge|Verdon Gorge]] in France; [[Malham_Cove|Malham Cove]] in [[North_Yorkshire|North Yorkshire]] and the [[Isle_of_Wight|Isle of Wight]], England; the [[Great_Orme|Great Orme]] in Wales; on [[Fårö|Fårö]] near the Swedish island of [[Gotland|Gotland]], the [[Niagara_Escarpment|Niagara Escarpment]] in Canada/United States, [[Notch_Peak|Notch Peak]] in Utah, the [[Ha_Long_Bay|Ha Long Bay]] National Park in Vietnam and the hills around the [[Lijiang_River|Lijiang River]] and Guilin city in China.
sentence_76: The [[Florida_Keys|Florida Keys]], islands off the south coast of [[Florida|Florida]], are composed mainly of [[Oolite|oolitic]] limestone (the Lower Keys) and the carbonate skeletons of [[Coral|coral]] reefs (the Upper Keys), which thrived in the area during interglacial periods when sea level was higher than at present.
sentence_77: Unique habitats are found on [[Alvar|alvars]], extremely level expanses of limestone with thin soil mantles.
sentence_78: The largest such expanse in Europe is the [[Stora_Alvaret|Stora Alvaret]] on the island of [[Öland|Öland]], Sweden.
sentence_79: Another area with large quantities of limestone is the island of Gotland, Sweden.
sentence_80: Huge quarries in northwestern Europe, such as those of Mount Saint Peter (Belgium/Netherlands), extend for more than a hundred kilometers.
sentence_81: The world's largest limestone quarry is at [[Michigan_Limestone_and_Chemical_Company|Michigan Limestone and Chemical Company]] in [[Rogers_City,_Michigan|Rogers City, Michigan]].
sentence_82: Limestone is very common in architecture, especially in Europe and North America.
sentence_83: Many landmarks across the world, including the [[Great_Pyramid_of_Giza|Great Pyramid]] and its associated [[Giza_pyramid_complex|complex]] in Giza, Egypt, were made of limestone.
sentence_84: So many buildings in [[Kingston,_Ontario|Kingston]], [[Ontario|Ontario]], Canada were, and continue to be, constructed from it that it is nicknamed the 'Limestone City'.
sentence_85: On the island of [[Malta|Malta]], a variety of limestone called Globigerina limestone was, for a long time, the only building material available, and is still very frequently used on all types of buildings and sculptures.
sentence_86: Limestone is readily available and relatively easy to cut into blocks or more elaborate carving.
sentence_87: Ancient American sculptors valued limestone because it was easy to work and good for fine detail.
sentence_88: Going back to the Late Preclassic period (by 200–100 BCE), the [[Maya_civilization|Maya civilization]] (Ancient Mexico) created refined sculpture using limestone because of these excellent carving properties.
sentence_89: The Maya would decorate the ceilings of their sacred buildings (known as [[Ancient_Maya_art|lintels]]) and cover the walls with carved limestone panels.
sentence_90: Carved on these sculptures were political and social stories, and this helped communicate messages of the king to his people.
sentence_91: Limestone is long-lasting and stands up well to exposure, which explains why many limestone ruins survive.
sentence_92: However, it is very heavy ([[Density|density]] 2.6), making it impractical for tall buildings, and relatively expensive as a building material.
sentence_93: Limestone was most popular in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
sentence_94: Train stations, banks and other structures from that era were normally made of limestone.
sentence_95: It is used as a facade on some skyscrapers, but only in thin plates for covering, rather than solid blocks.
sentence_96: In the United States, Indiana, most notably the Bloomington area, has long been a source of high-quality quarried limestone, called [[Indiana_limestone|Indiana limestone]].
sentence_97: Many famous buildings in London are built from [[Portland_limestone|Portland limestone]].
sentence_98: Houses built in [[Odessa|Odessa]] in [[Ukraine|Ukraine]] in the 19th century were mostly constructed from limestone and the extensive remains of the mines now form the [[Odessa_Catacombs|Odessa Catacombs]].
sentence_99: Limestone was also a very popular building block in the Middle Ages in the areas where it occurred, since it is hard, durable, and commonly occurs in easily accessible surface exposures.
sentence_100: Many medieval churches and castles in Europe are made of limestone.
sentence_101: [[Beer_stone|Beer stone]] was a popular kind of limestone for medieval buildings in southern England.
sentence_102: Limestone and (to a lesser extent) marble are reactive to acid solutions, making [[Acid_rain|acid rain]] a significant problem to the preservation of artifacts made from this stone.
sentence_103: Many limestone statues and building surfaces have suffered severe damage due to acid rain.
sentence_104: Likewise limestone gravel has been used to protect lakes vulnerable to acid rain, acting as a [[PH_buffer|pH buffering]] agent.
sentence_105: Acid-based cleaning chemicals can also etch limestone, which should only be cleaned with a neutral or mild alkali-based cleaner.
sentence_106: Other uses include:

list.value: It is the raw material for the manufacture of [[Quicklime|quicklime]] (calcium oxide), [[Slaked_lime|slaked lime]] (calcium hydroxide), [[Cement|cement]] and [[Mortar_(masonry)|mortar]].
Pulverized limestone is used as a soil conditioner to neutralize acidic soils ([[Agricultural_lime|agricultural lime]]).
Is crushed for use as aggregate—the solid base for many roads as well as in [[Asphalt_concrete|asphalt concrete]].
[[Geological_formation|Geological formations]] of limestone are important petroleum reservoirs;
As a [[Reagent|reagent]] in [[Flue-gas_desulfurization|flue-gas desulfurization]], it reacts with [[Sulfur_dioxide|sulfur dioxide]] for air pollution control.
[[Glass_making|Glass making]], in some circumstances, uses limestone.
It is added to toothpaste, paper, plastics, paint, tiles, and other materials as both white pigment and a cheap filler.
It can suppress methane explosions in underground coal mines.
Purified, it is added to bread and cereals as a source of calcium.
Calcium levels in livestock feed are supplemented with it, such as for poultry (when ground up).
It can be used for remineralizing and increasing the alkalinity of purified water to prevent pipe corrosion and to restore essential nutrient levels.
Used in [[Blast_furnace|blast furnaces]], limestone binds with silica and other impurities to remove them from the iron.

sentence_107: People can be exposed to limestone in the workplace by inhalation of and eye contact with the dust.
sentence_108: The [[Occupational_Safety_and_Health_Administration|Occupational Safety and Health Administration]] (OSHA) has set the legal limit ([[Permissible_exposure_limit|permissible exposure limit]]) for limestone exposure in the workplace as 15 mg/m total exposure and 5 mg/m respiratory exposure over an 8-hour workday.
sentence_109: The [[National_Institute_for_Occupational_Safety_and_Health|National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health]] (NIOSH) has set a recommended exposure limit (REL) of 10 mg/m total exposure and 5 mg/m respiratory exposure over an 8-hour workday.
sentence_110: Removing graffiti from weathered limestone is difficult because it is a porous and permeable material.
sentence_111: The surface is fragile so usual abrasion methods run the risk of "severe surface loss".
sentence_112: Because it is an acid-sensitive stone some cleaning agents cannot be used due to adverse effects.
sentence_113: The [[Cyanobacterium|cyanobacterium]] Hyella balani can bore through limestone; as can the [[Green_alga|green alga]] Eugamantia sacculata and the [[Fungus|fungus]] Ostracolaba implexa.

title: Kabul
sentence_0: For other places with the same name, see [[Kabul_(disambiguation)|Kabul (disambiguation)]].
sentence_1: Kabul ([[Pashto_language|Pashto]]: کابل‎, romanized: Kābəl; [[Dari_language|Dari]]: کابل‎, romanized: Kābol) is the [[Capital_city|capital]] and largest city of [[Afghanistan|Afghanistan]], located in the eastern section of the country.
sentence_2: It is also a [[Municipality|municipality]], forming part of the greater [[Kabul_Province|Kabul Province]], and divided into [[Neighborhoods_of_Kabul|22 districts]].
sentence_3: According to estimates in 2020, the population of Kabul is 4.222 million, which includes all the major [[Ethnic_groups_in_Afghanistan|ethnic groups]] of Afghanistan.
sentence_4: Afghanistan's only city with a population of over 1 million, Kabul serves as its political, cultural and economical center.
sentence_5: Rapid [[Urbanization|urbanization]] has made Kabul the world's 75th largest city.
sentence_6: Kabul is located high up in a narrow valley between the [[Hindu_Kush|Hindu Kush]] mountains, with an elevation of 1,790 metres (5,873 ft) making it one of the [[List_of_capital_cities_by_elevation|highest capitals in the world]].
sentence_7: The city is said to be over 3,500 years old, mentioned since at least the time of the [[Achaemenid_Empire|Achaemenid Empire]].
sentence_8: Located at crossroads in Asia - roughly halfway between [[Istanbul|Istanbul]] in the west and [[Hanoi|Hanoi]] in the east - it is in a strategic location along the trade routes of [[South_Asia|South]] and [[Central_Asia|Central Asia]], and a key location of the ancient [[Silk_Road|Silk Road]].
sentence_9: It has been part of the Achaemenids followed by the [[Seleucid_Empire|Seleucids]], [[Maurya_Empire|Mauryans]], [[Kushan_Empire|Kushans]], [[Kabul_Shahi|Kabul Shahis]], [[Saffarids|Saffarids]], [[Samanid_Empire|Samanids]], [[Ghaznavids|Ghaznavids]], [[Ghurids|Ghurids]], [[Khwarazmian_dynasty|Khwarazmians]], [[Qarlughids|Qarlughids]], [[Khalji_dynasty|Khaljis]], [[Timurid_Empire|Timurids]], [[Mughal_Empire|Mughals]], and [[Hotak_Empire|Hotaks]], until finally becoming part of the Durrani Empire (also known as the "Afghan Empire") in 1747.
sentence_10: Kabul became the capital of Afghanistan in 1776, during the reign of Timur Shah Durrani, the son of [[Ahmad_Shah_Durrani|Ahmad Shah Durrani]].
sentence_11: In the early 19th century, the [[British_Raj|British]] occupied the city, but after establishing [[Afghanistan–United_Kingdom_relations|foreign relations]], they were compelled to withdraw all forces from Afghanistan.
sentence_12: The city was occupied by the [[Soviet_Union|Soviets]] in 1979 but they too abandoned it after the 1988 [[Geneva_Accords_(1988)|Geneva Accords]] were signed.
sentence_13: [[Afghan_Civil_War_(1992–1996)|A civil war]] in the 1990s between various rebel groups destroyed much of the city, resulting in many casualties.
sentence_14: From late 2001 the city has been continuously rebuilt.
sentence_15: Kabul is known for its gardens, [[Bazaar|bazaars]], and palaces, well known examples being the [[Gardens_of_Babur|Gardens of Babur]] and [[Darul_Aman_Palace|Darul Aman Palace]].
sentence_16: It was also formerly a mecca for young western [[Hippie|hippies]].
sentence_17: Despite frequent terrorist attacks in the city, mainly by [[Taliban|Taliban]] insurgents, the city continues to develop and was the fifth fastest-growing city in the world as of 2012.
sentence_18: Kabul ([[English|/ˈkɑːbəl, ˈkɑːbuːl/]]; [[Pashto_language|Pashto]]: کابل‎ Kâbəl, IPA: [[Help:IPA|[kɑˈbəl]]; [[Persian_language|Persian]]: کابل‎ Kābol, IPA: [[Persian|[kɒːˈbol]]) is also spelled as Cabool, Cabol, Kabol, or Cabul.
sentence_19: Some believe the name Kabul to have derived from the ancient Israeli [[Kabul,_Israel|Kabul, Israel]].
sentence_20: See also: [[Timeline_of_Kabul|Timeline of Kabul]]
sentence_21: The origin of Kabul, who built it and when, is largely unknown.
sentence_22: The Hindu [[Rigveda|Rigveda]], composed between 1500–1200 BCE and one of the four canonical texts of Hinduism, and the [[Avesta|Avesta]], the primary cannon of texts of [[Zoroastrianism|Zoroastrianism]], refer to the [[Kabul_River|Kabul River]] and to a settlement called Kubha.
sentence_23: The Rigveda refers to Kubha as an "ideal city" and a vision of paradise set in the mountains.
sentence_24: The Kabul valley was part of the [[Medes|Median Empire]] (c. 678-549 BC).
sentence_25: In 549 BC, the Median Empire was annexed by [[Cyrus_the_Great|Cyrus The Great]] and Kabul became part the [[Achaemenid_Empire|Achaemenid Empire]] (c. 550–330 BC).
sentence_26: During that period, Kabul became a center of learning for [[Zoroastrianism|Zoroastrianism]], followed by [[Buddhism|Buddhism]] and [[Hinduism|Hinduism]].
sentence_27: An inscription on [[Darius_I|Darius the Great]]'s tombstone lists Kabul as one of the 29 countries of the Achaemenid Empire.
sentence_28: When [[Alexander_the_Great|Alexander]] annexed the Achaemenid Empire, the Kabul region came under his control.
sentence_29: After his death, his empire was seized by his general [[Seleucus_I_Nicator|Seleucus]], becoming part of the [[Seleucid_Empire|Seleucid Empire]].
sentence_30: In 305 BCE, the [[Seleucid_Empire|Seleucid Empire]] was extended to the [[Indus_river|Indus river]] which led to friction with the neighboring [[Mauryan_Empire|Mauryan Empire]], but it is widely believed that the two empires reached an alliance treaty.
sentence_31: During the Mauryan period, trade flourished because of uniform weights and measures.
sentence_32: Irrigation facilities for public use were developed leading to an increased harvest of crops.
sentence_33: People were also employed as artisans, jewelers, carpenters.
sentence_34: The [[Greco-Bactrian_Kingdom|Greco-Bactrians]] took control of Kabul from the Mauryans in the early 2nd century BC, then lost the city to their subordinates in the [[Indo-Greek_Kingdom|Indo-Greek Kingdom]] around the mid-2nd century BC.
sentence_35: Buddhism was greatly patronized by the rulers and majority of people of the city were adherents of the religion.
sentence_36: [[Indo-Scythians|Indo-Scythians]] expelled the Indo-Greeks by the mid 1st century BC, but lost the city to the [[Kushan_Empire|Kushan Empire]] about 100 years later.
sentence_37: Some historians ascribe Kabul the [[Sanskrit|Sanskrit]] name of Kamboja (Kamboj).
sentence_38: It is mentioned as Kophes or Kophene in some classical writings.
sentence_39: [[Xuanzang|Hsuan Tsang]] refers to the city as Kaofu in the 7th century AD, which is the [[Appellation|appellation]] of one of the five tribes of the [[Yuezhi|Yuezhi]] who had migrated from across the [[Hindu_Kush|Hindu Kush]] into the Kabul valley around the beginning of the [[Anno_Domini|Christian era]].
sentence_40: It was conquered by Kushan Emperor [[Kujula_Kadphises|Kujula Kadphises]] in about 45 AD and remained Kushan territory until at least the 3rd century AD.
sentence_41: The Kushans were [[Indo-European_languages|Indo-European-speaking]] peoples based in Bactria (northern Afghanistan).
sentence_42: Around 230 AD, the Kushans were defeated by the [[Sassanid_Empire|Sassanid Empire]] and replaced by Sassanid vassals known as the [[Indo-Sassanids|Indo-Sassanids]].
sentence_43: During the Sassanian period, the city was referred to as "Kapul" in [[Pahlavi_scripts|Pahlavi scripts]].
sentence_44: Kapol in the [[Persian_language|Persian language]] means Royal (ka) Bridge (pol), which is due to the main bridge on the Kabul River that connected the east and west of the city.
sentence_45: In 420 AD the Indo-Sassanids were driven out of Afghanistan by the [[Xionites|Xionite]] tribe known as the [[Kidarites|Kidarites]], who were then replaced in the 460s by the [[Hephthalite_Empire|Hephthalites]].
sentence_46: It became part of the surviving [[Ashina_tribe|Turk]] [[Kabul_Shahi|Shahi]] [[Kingdom_of_Kapisa|Kingdom of Kapisa]], also known as Kabul-Shahan.
sentence_47: According to Táríkhu-l Hind by [[Abu_Rayhan_Biruni|Al-Biruni]], Kabul was governed by princes of [[Turkic_peoples|Turkic]] lineage whose rule lasted for about 60 generations.
sentence_48: The Kabul rulers built a defensive wall around the city to protect it from enemy raids.
sentence_49: This wall has survived until today.
sentence_50: It was briefly held by the [[Tibetan_Empire|Tibetan Empire]] between 801 and 815.
sentence_51: Further information: [[Islamic_conquest_of_Afghanistan|Islamic conquest of Afghanistan]]
sentence_52: The [[Islamic_conquest_of_Afghanistan|Islamic conquest]] reached modern-day Afghanistan in 642 AD, at a time when Kabul was independent.
sentence_53: A number of failed expeditions were made to [[Islamization|Islamize]] the region.
sentence_54: In one of them, Abdur Rahman bin Samana arrived to Kabul from [[Zaranj|Zaranj]] in the late 600s and converted 12,000 inhabitants to [[Islam|Islam]] before abandoning the city.
sentence_55: [[Muslim|Muslims]] were a minority until [[Ya'qub_bin_Laith_as-Saffar|Ya'qub bin Laith as-Saffar]] of Zaranj conquered Kabul in 870 and established the first [[Saffarid_Dynasty|Islamic dynasty]] in the region.
sentence_56: It was reported that the rulers of Kabul were [[Muslim|Muslims]] with non-Muslims living close by.
sentence_57: Over the following centuries, the city was successively controlled by the [[Samanids|Samanids]], [[Ghaznavids|Ghaznavids]], [[Ghurids|Ghurids]], [[Khwarazmian_Empire|Khwarazmshahs]], [[Qarlughids|Qarlughids]], and [[Khalji_dynasty|Khaljis]].
sentence_58: In the 13th century, the invading [[Mongol_Empire|Mongols]] caused major destruction in the region.
sentence_59: Report of a [[Massacre|massacre]] in the close by [[Bamiyan|Bamiyan]] is recorded around this period, where the entire population of the valley was annihilated by the Mongol troops as a revenge for the death of Genghis Khan's grandson.
sentence_60: As a result, many natives of Afghanistan fled south toward the Indian subcontinent where some established [[Delhi_Sultanate|dynasties in Delhi]].
sentence_61: The [[Chagatai_Khanate|Chagatai Khanate]] and [[Kartids|Kartids]] were vassals of [[Ilkhanate|Ilkhanate]] till dissolution of latter in 1335.
sentence_62: Following the era of the Khalji dynasty in 1333, the famous [[Morocco|Moroccan]] scholar [[Ibn_Battuta|Ibn Battuta]] was visiting Kabul and wrote:
sentence_63: Further information: [[Timurid_Empire|Timurid Empire]] and [[Mughal_Empire|Mughal Empire]]
sentence_64: In the 14th century, Kabul became a major trading center under the kingdom of [[Timur|Timur]] (Tamerlane).
sentence_65: In 1504, the city fell to [[Babur|Babur]] from the north and made into his headquarters, which became one of the principal cities of his later [[Mughal_Empire|Mughal Empire]].
sentence_66: In 1525, Babur described [[Kabulistan|Kabulistan]] in [[Baburnama|his memoirs]] by writing that:
sentence_67: [[Mirza_Muhammad_Haidar_Dughlat|Mirza Muhammad Haidar Dughlat]], a poet from [[Hindustan|Hindustan]] who visited at the time wrote: "Dine and drink in Kabul: it is mountain, desert, city, river and all else."
sentence_68: It was from here that Babur began his 1526 conquest of Hindustan, which was ruled by the [[Pashtun_people|Afghan]] [[Lodi_dynasty|Lodi dynasty]] and began east of the [[Indus_River|Indus River]] in what is present-day [[Pakistan|Pakistan]].
sentence_69: [[Babur|Babur]] loved Kabul due to the fact that he lived in it for 20 years and the people were loyal to him, including its weather that he was used to.
sentence_70: His wish to be buried in Kabul was finally granted.
sentence_71: The inscription on his [[Gardens_of_Babur|tomb]] contains the famous Persian couplet, which states: اگرفردوس روی زمین است همین است و همین است و همین است (If there is a paradise on earth, it is this, it is this, it is this!)
sentence_72: Further information: [[Durrani_dynasty|Durrani dynasty]] and [[Barakzai_dynasty|Barakzai dynasty]]
sentence_73: Nine years after [[Nader_Shah|Nader Shah]] and his forces invaded and occupied the city as part of the more easternmost parts of his Empire, he was assassinated by his own officers, causing the rapid disintegration of it.
sentence_74: [[Ahmad_Shah_Durrani|Ahmad Shah Durrani]], commander of 4,000 [[Durrani|Abdali]] [[Afghan|Afghans]], asserted [[Pashtun_people|Pashtun]] rule in 1747 and further expanded his new Afghan Empire.
sentence_75: His ascension to power marked the beginning of Afghanistan.
sentence_76: His son Timur Shah Durrani, after inheriting power, transferred the capital of Afghanistan from [[Kandahar|Kandahar]] to Kabul in 1776, and used [[Peshawar|Peshawar]] in what is today Pakistan as the winter capital.
sentence_77: Timur Shah died in 1793 and was succeeded by his son Zaman Shah Durrani.
sentence_78: Kabul's first visitor from Europe was Englishman [[George_Forster_(traveller)|George Forster]], who described 18th-century Kabul as "the best and cleanest city in Asia".
sentence_79: In 1826, the kingdom was claimed by [[Dost_Mohammad_Khan|Dost Mohammad Khan]] but in 1839 [[Shah_Shujah_Durrani|Shujah Shah Durrani]] was re-installed with the help of [[British_Raj|British India]] during the [[First_Anglo-Afghan_War|First Anglo-Afghan War]].
sentence_80: In 1841 a local uprising resulted in the killing of the British resident and loss of mission in Kabul and the [[1842_retreat_from_Kabul|1842 retreat from Kabul]] to [[Jalalabad|Jalalabad]].
sentence_81: In 1842 the British returned to Kabul, plundering [[Bala_Hissar,_Kabul|Bala Hissar]] in revenge before fleeing back to [[British_Raj|British India]] (now Pakistan).
sentence_82: [[Wazir_Akbar_Khan|Akbar Khan]] took to the throne from 1842 to 1845 and was followed by Dost Mohammad Khan.
sentence_83: The [[Second_Anglo-Afghan_War|British-led Indian forces]] invaded in 1879 when Kabul was under [[Sher_Ali_Khan|Sher Ali Khan]]'s rule, as the Afghan king initially refused to accept British diplomatic mission and later the British residents were again massacred.
sentence_84: The British partially destroyed [[Bala_Hissar,_Kabul|Bala Hissar fortress]] before retreating to British India.
sentence_85: Having become an established [[Bazaar|bazaar]] city, leather and textile industries developed by 1916.
sentence_86: The majority of the population was concentrated on the south side of the river.
sentence_87: Kabul modernized throughout the regime of King [[Habibullah_Khan|Habibullah Khan]], with the introduction of electricity, telephone, and a postal service.
sentence_88: The first modern high school, [[Habibia_High_School|Habibia]], was established in 1903.
sentence_89: In 1919, after the [[Third_Anglo-Afghan_War|Third Anglo-Afghan War]], King [[Amanullah_Khan|Amanullah Khan]] announced Afghanistan's independence in [[Foreign_relations_of_Afghanistan|foreign affairs]] at [[Id_Gah_Mosque|Eidgah Mosque]] in Kabul.
sentence_90: Amanullah was reform-minded and he had a plan to build a new [[Capital_city|capital city]] on land about 6 km away from Kabul.
sentence_91: This area was named [[Darulaman|Darulaman]] and it consisted of the famous [[Darul_Aman_Palace|Darul Aman Palace]], where he later resided.
sentence_92: Many educational institutions were founded in Kabul during the 1920s.
sentence_93: In 1929 King Ammanullah left Kabul due to a local uprising orchestrated by [[Habibullah_Kalakani|Habibullah Kalakani]], but he himself was imprisoned and executed after nine months in power by King [[Mohammed_Nadir_Shah|Nader Khan]].
sentence_94: Three years later, in 1933, the new king was assassinated during an award ceremony inside a school in Kabul.
sentence_95: The throne was left to his 19-year-old son, [[Mohammad_Zahir_Shah|Zahir Shah]], who became the last [[King_of_Afghanistan|King of Afghanistan]].
sentence_96: Unlike Amanullah Khan, Nader Khan and Zahir Shah had no plans to create a new capital city, and thus Kabul remained the country's [[Seat_of_government|seat of government]].
sentence_97: During the [[Inter-war_period|inter-war period]] France and Germany helped develop the country and maintained high schools and lycees in the capital, providing education for the children of the city's elite families.
sentence_98: [[Kabul_University|Kabul University]] opened in 1932 and by the 1960s western educated Afghans made up the majority of teachers.
sentence_99: By the 1960s the majority of instructors at the university had degrees from Western universities.
sentence_100: When Zahir Shah took power in 1933 Kabul had the only 10 kilometers (6 miles) of rail in the country and the country had few internal telegraphs, phone lines or roads.
sentence_101: Zahir turned to the Japanese, Germans and Italians for help developing a modern transportation and communication network.
sentence_102: A radio tower built by the Germans in 1937 in Kabul allowing instant communication with outlying villages.
sentence_103: A national bank and state cartels were organized to allow for economic modernization.
sentence_104: Textile mills, power plants, carpet and furniture factories were also built in Kabul, providing much needed manufacturing and infrastructure.
sentence_105: During the 1940s and 1950s, [[Urbanization|urbanization]] accelerated and the [[Built-up_area|built-up area]] was increased to 68 km by 1962, an almost fourteen-fold increase compared to 1925.
sentence_106: Under the premiership of [[Mohammad_Daoud_Khan|Mohammad Daoud Khan]] in the 1950s, foreign investment and development increased.
sentence_107: In 1955, the Soviet Union forwarded $100 million in credit to Afghanistan, which financed public transportation, airports, a cement factory, mechanized bakery, a five-lane highway from Kabul to the Soviet border and dams, including the [[Salang_Pass|Salang Pass]] to the north of Kabul.
sentence_108: During the 1960s, Soviet-style [[Microrayon|microrayon]] housing estates were built, containing sixty blocks.
sentence_109: The government also built many ministry buildings in the [[Brutalist_architecture|brutalist architecture]] style.
sentence_110: In the 1960s the first [[Marks_&_Spencer|Marks & Spencer]] store in [[Central_Asia|Central Asia]] was built in the city.
sentence_111: [[Kabul_Zoo|Kabul Zoo]] was inaugurated in 1967, which was maintained with the help of visiting German [[Zoology|zoologists]].
sentence_112: Foreigners flocked to Kabul and the nation's tourism industry picked up speed.
sentence_113: Kabul experimented with liberalization, notably the loosening of restrictions on speech and assembly which led to student politics in the capital.
sentence_114: Socialist, Maoist and liberal factions demonstrated daily in Kabul while more traditional Islamic leaders spoke out against the failure to aid the Afghan countryside.
sentence_115: From the 1960s until the late 1970s, Kabul was a major stop on the famous [[Hippie_trail|Hippie trail]].
sentence_116: By the beginning of the 1970s, Kabul became known for its street sales of [[Hashish|hashish]] and became a major tourist attraction for western [[Hippies|hippies]].

section_7.value: Soviet occupation, civil war and Taliban rule

sentence_117: Further information: [[Soviet–Afghan_War|Soviet–Afghan War]] and [[Afghan_Civil_War_(1989–92)|Afghan Civil War (1989–92)]]
