sentence_118: On April 28, 1978, President Daoud and most of his family were assassinated in Kabul's [[Arg_(Kabul)|Presidential Palace]] in what is called the [[Saur_Revolution|Saur Revolution]].
sentence_119: Pro-Soviet PDPA under [[Nur_Muhammad_Taraki|Nur Muhammad Taraki]] seized power and slowly began to institute reforms.
sentence_120: Private businesses were nationalized in the Soviet manner.
sentence_121: Education was modified into the Soviet model, with lessons focusing on teaching [[Russian_language|Russian]], [[Marxism–Leninism|Marxism–Leninism]] and learning of other countries belonging to the Soviet bloc.
sentence_122: On December 24, 1979, the [[Soviet_Union|Soviet Union]] invaded Afghanistan and Kabul was heavily occupied by Soviet Armed Forces.
sentence_123: In Pakistan, [[Director-General|Director-General]] of the ISI Akhtar Abdur Rahman advocated for the idea of covert operation in Afghanistan by arming Islamic extremists who formed the mujahideen.
sentence_124: General Rahman was heard loudly saying: "Kabul must burn!
sentence_125: Kabul must burn!
sentence_126: ", and mastered the idea of [[Pakistan_and_state_terrorism|proxy war]] in Afghanistan.
sentence_127: Pakistani President [[Muhammad_Zia-ul-Haq|Zia-ul-Haq]] authorized this operation under General Rahman, which was later merged with [[Operation_Cyclone|Operation Cyclone]], a programme funded by the [[United_States|United States]] and carried out by the [[Central_Intelligence_Agency|Central Intelligence Agency]].
sentence_128: Large protests against the Soviet presence broke out in Kabul in 1980 in what is called the [[3_Hut_uprising|3 Hut uprising]].
sentence_129: The Soviets turned the city of Kabul into their command center during the [[Soviet–Afghan_War|Soviet–Afghan War]], though the city was considered moderately safe during that period since fighting was mostly taking place in the countryside.
sentence_130: However political crime such as assassinations of [[PDPA|PDPA]] party members or guerrilla attacks on military and government targets were quite common.
sentence_131: The Soviet Embassy, for example, was attacked four times with arms fire in the first five years of the war.
sentence_132: A Western correspondent revisiting Kabul in December 1983 after a year, said that the city was "converted into a fortress bristling with weapons".
sentence_133: Contrastingly, that same year American diplomat Charles Dunbar commented that the Soviet troops' presence was "surprisingly modest", and an author in a 1983 Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists article thought that the Soviet soldiers had a "friendly" atmosphere.
sentence_134: The city's population increased from around 500,000 in 1978 to 1.5 million in 1988.
sentence_135: The large influx were mostly internal refugees who fled other parts of the country for safety in Kabul.
sentence_136: During this time, women made up 40% of the workforce.
sentence_137: Soviet men and women were very common in the city's shopping roads, with the large availability of Western products.
sentence_138: Most Soviet civilians (numbering between 8,000 and 10,000) lived in the north eastern Soviet-style [[Mikrorayon|Mikrorayon]] ([[Microraion|microraion]]) housing complex that was surrounded by [[Barbed-wire|barbed-wire]] and armed tanks.
sentence_139: They sometimes received abuse from anti-Soviet civilians on the streets.
sentence_140: The mujahideen rebels managed to strike at the city a few times—on October 9, 1987, a car bomb planted by a mujahideen group killed 27 people, and on April 27, 1988 in celebrations of the 10th anniversary of the Saur Revolution, a truck bomb killed six people.
sentence_141: Main article: [[Afghan_Civil_War_(1992–96)|Afghan Civil War (1992–96)]]
sentence_142: After the fall of [[Mohammad_Najibullah|Mohammad Najibullah]]'s government in April 1992, different mujahideen factions entered the city and formed a government under the [[Peshawar_Accords|Peshawar Accords]], but [[Gulbuddin_Hekmatyar|Gulbuddin Hekmatyar]]'s party refused to sign the accords and started shelling the city for power, which soon escalated into a full-scale conflict.
sentence_143: This marked the start of a dark period of the city: at least 30,000 civilians were killed in a period known locally as the "Kabul Wars."
sentence_144: About 80 percent of the city was devastated and destroyed by 1996.
sentence_145: The old city and western areas were among the worst-hit.
sentence_146: A [[The_New_York_Times|The New York Times]] analyst said in 1996 that the city was more devastated than [[Sarajevo|Sarajevo]], which was similarly damaged during the [[Bosnian_War|Bosnian War]] at the time.
sentence_147: The city suffered heavily under a bombardment campaign between rival militias which intensified during the summer of 1992.
sentence_148: Its geographic location in a narrow valley made it an easy target from rockets fired by militias who based themselves in the surrounding mountains.
sentence_149: Within two years' time, the majority of infrastructure was destroyed, a massive exodus of the population left to the countryside or abroad, and electricity and water was completely out.
sentence_150: In late 1994, bombardment of the capital came to a temporary halt.
sentence_151: These forces took steps to restore law and order.
sentence_152: Courts started to work again, convicting individuals inside government troops who had committed crimes.
sentence_153: On September 27, 1996, the hardline [[Taliban|Taliban]] militia seized Kabul and established the [[Islamic_Emirate_of_Afghanistan|Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan]].
sentence_154: They imposed a strict form of [[Sharia|Sharia]] (Islamic law), restricting women from work and education, conducting amputations against common thieves, and hit-squads from the infamous "Ministry for Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice" watching public beatings of people.
sentence_155: Further information: [[Presidency_of_Hamid_Karzai|Presidency of Hamid Karzai]] and [[List_of_terrorist_attacks_in_Kabul_since_2008|List of terrorist attacks in Kabul since 2008]]
sentence_156: In November 2001, the [[Northern_Alliance|Northern Alliance]] captured Kabul after the Taliban had abandoned it following the [[US_invasion_of_Afghanistan|American invasion]].
sentence_157: A month later a [[Presidency_of_Hamid_Karzai|new government]] under President [[Hamid_Karzai|Hamid Karzai]] began to assemble.
sentence_158: In the meantime, a [[NATO|NATO]]-led International Security Assistance Force (ISAF) was deployed in Afghanistan.
sentence_159: The war-torn city began to see some positive development as many expatriate Afghans returned to the country.
sentence_160: The city's population grew from about 500,000 in 2001 to over 3 million in recent years.
sentence_161: Many foreign embassies re-opened, and the city has been recovering ever since.
sentence_162: In 2008 the process started to gradually hand over security responsibilities from NATO to Afghan forces.
sentence_163: As of 2014, the [[Afghan_National_Security_Forces|Afghan National Security Forces]] (ANSF) have been in charge of security in and around the city.
sentence_164: Kabul is periodically the scene of deadly bombings carried out mostly by the [[Taliban|Taliban]] but also by the [[Haqqani_network|Haqqani network]], [[Islamic_State_of_Iraq_and_the_Levant_–_Khorasan_Province|ISIL]], and other anti-state groups.
sentence_165: Government employees, soldiers and ordinary civilians have all been targets of attacks.
sentence_166: The Afghan government called the actions of the terrorists [[War_crime|war crimes]].
sentence_167: The deadliest attack yet was a [[May_2017_Kabul_attack|truck bombing in May 2017]].
sentence_168: Since 2010, a series of manned checkpoints called the [[Ring_of_Steel_(Kabul)|Ring of Steel]] operates in the city.
sentence_169: The city has experienced rapid urbanization with an increasing population.
sentence_170: Many informal settlements have been built.
sentence_171: Since the late 2000s, numerous modern housing complexes have been built, many of which are gated and secured, to serve a growing Afghan [[Middle_class|middle class]].
sentence_172: Some of these include the Aria City (in District 10) and Golden City (District 8).
sentence_173: Some complexes have been built out-of-town, such as the Omid-e-Sabz [[Township|township]] (District 13), Qasaba/Khwaja Rawash township (District 15), and Sayed Jamaludin township (District 12).
sentence_174: A major ambitious $80 billion project called "Kabul New City" aims to develop a large modern township of homes and businesses on 1,700 acres of land to the north of Kabul (Districts 18 and 19) and [[Bagram|Bagram]] in [[Parwan_Province|Parwan Province]].
sentence_175: The project was first conceptualized in 2007 and approved in 2009.
sentence_176: After years in planning and assistance from the Japanese government, construction started in 2015.
sentence_177: On [[May_2020_Afghanistan_attacks|12 May 2020]], three gunmen wearing police uniforms carried out a mass shooting in the maternity ward of [[Dashte_Barchi|Dashte Barchi]] hospital in Kabul, which is assisted by [[Médecins_Sans_Frontières|Médecins Sans Frontières]] (Doctors Without Borders) personnel.
sentence_178: The attackers killed 24 people and injured another 16.
sentence_179: The deaths included two newborn babies, one midwife, and 16 mothers, who were either pregnant [[Childbirth|giving birth]] or were with their newborns.
sentence_180: Three of the mothers were shot and killed in the delivery room along with their [[Fetus|unborn babies]].
sentence_181: The gunmen had walked straight past other wards closer to the hospital's entrance, and attacked only the maternity ward.
sentence_182: More than 80 women, infants, and staff, including three foreign nationals, were safely evacuated from the hospital, and all of the attackers were killed by the Afghan security forces.
sentence_183: No armed group claimed responsibility for the hospital shooting.
sentence_184: The U.S. government said that it had assessed that [[Islamic_State_of_Iraq_and_the_Levant_–_Khorasan_Province|ISIL–KP]] was responsible for the attack.
sentence_185: The Afghan government, however, claimed that the Taliban and the affiliated Haqqani network were behind the attack.
sentence_186: Further information: [[Geography_of_Afghanistan|Geography of Afghanistan]]
sentence_187: Kabul is situated in the eastern part of the country, 1,791 meters (5,876 feet) above sea level in a narrow valley, wedged between the [[Hindu_Kush|Hindu Kush]] mountains along the [[Kabul_River|Kabul River]].
sentence_188: Immediately to the south of the old city are the ancient city walls and the Sher Darwaza mountain, with the Shuhadayi Salihin [[Cemetery|cemetery]] behind it.
sentence_189: A bit further east is the ancient [[Bala_Hissar,_Kabul|Bala Hissar]] fortress with the Kol-e Hasmat Khan lake behind it.
sentence_190: Its location has been described as a "bowl surrounded by mountains".
sentence_191: Some of the mountains (which are called koh) include: Khair Khana-e Shamali, Khwaja Rawash, Shakhi Baran Tey, Chihil Sutun, Qurugh, Khwaja Razaq and Sher Darwaza.
sentence_192: There are also two mountains in between urban areas in western Kabul: [[Asamayi|Asamayi]] (also known as the Television hill) and Ali Abad.
sentence_193: Hills within the city (which are called tapa) include Bibi Mahro and Maranjan.
sentence_194: The city covers an area size of 1,023 square kilometres (395 sq mi), making it by far the largest in the country.
sentence_195: The closest foreign capital cities [[As_the_bird_flies|as the bird flies]] are [[Islamabad|Islamabad]], [[Dushanbe|Dushanbe]], [[Tashkent|Tashkent]], [[New_Delhi|New Delhi]] and [[Bishkek|Bishkek]].
sentence_196: Kabul is roughly equidistant between [[Istanbul|Istanbul]] (western Asia) and [[Hanoi|Hanoi]] (eastern Asia).
sentence_197: Kabul has a [[Cold_semi-arid_climate|cold semi-arid climate]] ([[Köppen_climate_classification|Köppen climate classification]] [[Cold_semi-arid_climate|BSk]]) with precipitation concentrated in the winter (almost exclusively falling as snow) and spring months.
sentence_198: Temperatures are cool compared to much of Southwest Asia, mainly due to the high elevation of the city.
sentence_199: Summer has very low humidity, providing relief from the heat.
sentence_200: Autumn features warm afternoons and sharply cooler evenings.
sentence_201: Winters are cold, with a January daily average of −2.3 °C (27.9 °F).
sentence_202: Spring is the wettest time of the year.
sentence_203: Sunny conditions dominate year-round.
sentence_204: The annual mean temperature is 12.1 °C (53.8 °F), much lower than the other large cities of Afghanistan.
sentence_205: The [[Kabul_River|Kabul River]] flows through the heart of the city, dividing the central bazaars.
sentence_206: There are several bridges (pul) crossing the river, the major ones being Pul-e Shah-Do Shamshira, Pul-e Bagh-e Omomi, Pul-e Khishti, and Pul-e Mahmoud.
sentence_207: Due to [[Climate_change|climate change]], since the 21st century, the river runs dry most of the year, only filling up in the wetter winter and spring seasons.
sentence_208: A large [[Lake|lake]] and [[Wetland|wetland]] is located just to the southeast from the old city called Kol-e Hashmat Khan.
sentence_209: The marsh provides a critical resting place to thousands of birds who fly between the [[Indian_subcontinent|Indian subcontinent]] and [[Siberia|Siberia]].
sentence_210: In 2017 the government declared the lake a [[Protected_area|protected area]].
sentence_211: Some rare species of birds have been spotted at the lake, such as the [[Eastern_imperial_eagle|Eastern imperial eagle]] and the [[Dalmatian_pelican|Dalmatian pelican]].
sentence_212: Kabul's other large lake is [[Qargha|Qargha]], located some 9 km northwest from the center.
sentence_213: It is a major attraction for locals as well as foreigners.
sentence_214: [[Air_pollution|Air pollution]] is a major problem in the city during the winter season, when many residents burn low-quality fuels.
sentence_215: The city of Kabul forms one of the 15 districts of [[Kabul_Province|Kabul Province]].
sentence_216: As the provincial capital, it forms a [[Municipality|municipality]] (shārwāli) which is further divided into 22 administrative districts called municipal districts or city districts (nāhia), which coincide with the official Police Districts (PD).
sentence_217: The number of city districts increased from 11 to 18 in 2005, and then to 22 by 2010 after the incorporation of Districts 14 and 19-22 which were annexed by Kabul Municipality from surrounding rural districts.
sentence_218: The city limits have thus substantially increased.
sentence_219: Due to demarcation disputes with the provincial administration, some of these new districts are more administered by the provincial districts than the municipality.
sentence_220: District 1 contains most of the old city.
sentence_221: Downtown Kabul mostly consist of Districts 2, 4 and 10.
sentence_222: In addition, Districts 3 and 6 house many commercial and governmental points of interests.
sentence_223: The city's north and west are the most urbanized, as opposed to the south and east.
sentence_224: The table below show the 22 city districts and their settlements, with information about its land size and usage, accurate as of 2011.
sentence_225: Each year about 20,000 foreign tourists visit Afghanistan.
sentence_226: Major hotels in Kabul include; the [[Kabul_Serena_Hotel|Serena Hotel]], the [[Hotel_Inter-Continental_Kabul|Inter-Continental]], and the [[Safi_Landmark_Hotel|Safi Landmark Hotel]] above the [[Kabul_City_Center|Kabul City Center]].
sentence_227: There are a number of other less-known hotels.
sentence_228: Most visitors prefer lodging at guest houses, which are found all over the city.
sentence_229: The better and safer ones are in the Wazir Akbar Khan neighborhood where the embassies are located.
sentence_230: The old part of Kabul is filled with [[Bazaar|bazaars]] nestled along its narrow, crooked streets.
sentence_231: Cultural sites include: the [[National_Museum_of_Afghanistan|National Museum of Afghanistan]], notably displaying an impressive statue of [[Surya|Surya]] excavated at [[Khair_Khana|Khair Khana]], the ruined [[Darul_Aman_Palace|Darul Aman Palace]], the tomb of Mughal Emperor [[Babur|Babur]] at [[Bagh-e_Babur|Bagh-e Babur]], and Chihil Sutun Park, the Minar-i-Istiqlal (Column of Independence) built in 1919 after the [[Third_Afghan_War|Third Afghan War]], the [[Tomb_of_Timur_Shah_Durrani|tomb of Timur Shah Durrani]], the [[Bagh-e_Bala_Palace|Bagh-e Bala Palace]] and the imposing [[Id_Gah_Mosque|Id Gah Mosque]] (founded 1893).
sentence_232: [[Bala_Hissar,_Kabul|Bala Hissar]] is a fort destroyed by the British in 1879, in retaliation for the death of their envoy, now restored as a military college.
sentence_233: There are also the Kolola Pushta fort, which is still garrisoned by the Afghan Army, and the nearby 19th-century Shahrara Tower fort, which was ruined in 1928.
sentence_234: The [[Chakari,_Afghanistan|Minaret of Chakari]], destroyed in 1998, had [[Buddhism|Buddhist]] [[Swastika|swastika]] and both [[Mahayana|Mahayana]] and [[Theravada|Theravada]] qualities.
sentence_235: Other places of interest include [[Kabul_City_Center|Kabul City Center]], which is Kabul's first shopping mall, the shops around Flower Street and Chicken Street, Wazir Akbar Khan district, [[Kabul_Golf_Club|Kabul Golf Club]], [[Kabul_Zoo|Kabul Zoo]], [[Abdul_Rahman_Mosque|Abdul Rahman Mosque]], [[Shah-Do_Shamshira_Mosque|Shah-Do Shamshira]] and other famous mosques, the National Gallery of Afghanistan, the [[National_Archives_of_Afghanistan|National Archives of Afghanistan]], Afghan Royal Family Mausoleum, the [[OMAR_Mine_Museum|OMAR Mine Museum]], Bibi Mahro Hill, Kabul Cemetery, and [[Paghman_Gardens|Paghman Gardens]].
sentence_236: The Aga Khan Development Network (AKDN) was also involved in the restoration of the [[Bagh-e_Babur|Bagh-e Babur]] (Babur Gardens).
sentence_237: Tappe-i-Maranjan is a nearby hill where Buddhist [[Statue|statues]] and Graeco-Bactrian [[Coin|coins]] from the 2nd century BC have been found.
sentence_238: Outside the city proper is a citadel and the royal palace.
sentence_239: [[Paghman|Paghman]] and [[Jalalabad|Jalalabad]] are interesting valleys west and east of the city.

sentence_240: Further information: [[Demographics_of_Afghanistan|Demographics of Afghanistan]] and [[Afghan_diaspora|Afghan diaspora]]
sentence_241: Kabul's population was estimated in 2020 at about 4.222 million.
sentence_242: Another 2015 estimate has put it at 3,678,034.
sentence_243: The city's population has long fluctuated due to the wars.
sentence_244: The lack of an up-to-date [[Census|census]] means that there are various estimates of the population.
sentence_245: Kabul's population is estimated to have been about 10,000 in 1700, 65,000 by 1878, and 120,000 by 1940.
sentence_246: More recently, the population was around 500,000 in 1979, whilst another source claims 337,715 as of 1976.
sentence_247: This figure rose to about 1.5 million by 1988, before dramatically dropping in the 1990s.
sentence_248: Kabul became one of the fastest growing cities in the world, with its population growing fourfold from 2001 to 2014.
sentence_249: This was partly due to the return of refugees after the fall of the [[Taliban|Taliban]] regime, and partly due to Afghans moving from other provinces mainly due to war between Taliban insurgents and Afghan government forces in their native areas as well as looking for labor.
sentence_250: This resulting rapid [[Urbanization|urbanization]] mean that many residents today live in informal settlements.
sentence_251: Shanty mud-brick homes on the mountainsides and steep hills have been built by them and these are usually poverty-stricken, not connected to the water and electricity grid.
sentence_252: Although the settlements are illegal, they have been tolerated by authorities.
sentence_253: In 2017 Kabul Municipality started a project to paint the homes in these settlements in bright colors in an effort to "cheer up" residents.
sentence_254: Kabul is the most ethnically diverse city in the country, with the population including Afghans from all over the country.
sentence_255: A 2009 report states that Kabul has large populations of all major ethnic groups, including [[Tajiks|Tajiks]] and [[Hazaras|Hazaras]] as well as [[Pashtuns|Pashtuns]] in pockets throughout, and smaller communities of [[Uzbeks|Uzbeks]] and other groups.
sentence_256: The [[Dari_language|Dari]] (Persian) and [[Pashto_language|Pashto]] languages are widely used in the region, although Dari serves as the [[Lingua_franca|lingua franca]].
sentence_257: [[Multilingualism|Multilingualism]] is common throughout the area, particularly among the Pashtun people.
sentence_258: The term "Kabuli" (کابلی) is referred to the urbanites of the city.
sentence_259: They are ethnic-neutral, typically speak Dari (Persian), are generally secularly educated, and favor Western fashion.
sentence_260: Many Kabulites (especially elites and the upper class) left the country during the civil war and are now outnumbered by rural people who moved in from the countryside, mostly refugees but also labor-seekers.
sentence_261: About 74% of the city's population follow [[Sunni_Islam|Sunni Islam]] while 25% are [[Shia_Islam_in_Afghanistan|Shiites]] (mainly the Hazaras and Qizilbash).
sentence_262: The remaining 1% are followers of Sikhism and [[Hinduism_in_Afghanistan|Hinduism]], as well as one known [[Christians|Christian]] resident (First Lady [[Rula_Ghani|Rula Ghani]]) and one [[Jewish|Jewish]] resident ([[Zablon_Simintov|Zablon Simintov]]); other known Christians and Jews exist though are not Afghan nationals and are generally workers at international organizations rather than permanent residents.
sentence_263: Kabul also has small [[Indians_in_Afghanistan|Indian]] (which the Sikhs and Hindus belong to) and [[Turks_in_Afghanistan|Turkish]] communities (mostly business-owners and investors), and in the 1980s had a sizable Russian community during the Soviet campaign in the country.
sentence_264: [[Cricket|Cricket]] is the dominant sport in Kabul with 2 of the 3 sports stadiums reserved for cricket.
sentence_265: Further information: [[Politics_of_Afghanistan|Politics of Afghanistan]]
sentence_266: The municipality's administrative structure consists of 17 departments under a [[Mayor|mayor]].
sentence_267: Like other provincial municipalities in Afghanistan, the municipality of Kabul deals with city affairs such as construction and infrastructure.
sentence_268: The city districts (nāhia) collect certain taxes and issue building licenses.
sentence_269: Each city district has a district head appointed by the mayor, and leads six major departments in the district office.
sentence_270: The neighborhood organization structure at the nahia level is called a gozar.
sentence_271: A wakil-e gozar is a person chosen to represent a community within a city district.
sentence_272: Kabul's Chief of Police is Lt. Gen. Abdul Rahman Rahimi.
sentence_273: The police are part of the [[Afghan_National_Police|Afghan National Police]] (ANP) under the [[Ministry_of_the_Interior_(Afghanistan)|Ministry of Interior]] and are arranged by city districts.
sentence_274: The Police Chief is selected by the Interior Minister and is responsible for all [[Law_enforcement|law enforcement]] activities throughout the Kabul province.
sentence_275: Further information: [[Economy_of_Afghanistan|Economy of Afghanistan]]
sentence_276: Kabul's main products include [[Fruit|fresh]] and dried fruit, [[Nut_(fruit)|nuts]], beverages, [[Afghan_rug|Afghan rugs]], [[Leather|leather]] and sheep skin products, furniture, antique [[Replica|replicas]], and domestic clothes.
sentence_277: The [[World_Bank|World Bank]] authorized [[United_States_dollar|US$]]25 million for the Kabul Urban Reconstruction Project which closed in 2011.
sentence_278: Over the last decade, the United States has invested approximately $9.1 billion into urban infrastructure in Afghanistan.
sentence_279: [[War_in_Afghanistan_(1978–present)|The wars since 1978]] have limited the city's economic productivity but after the establishment of the Karzai administration since late 2001, local economic developments have included a number of [[Indoor_shopping_mall|indoor shopping malls]].
sentence_280: The first of these was the [[Kabul_City_Center|Kabul City Center]], opened 2005.
sentence_281: Others have also opened in recent years including Gulbahar Center, City Walk Mall and Majid Mall.
sentence_282: Kabul's largest industrial hub is located in District 9, on the north banks of the River Kabul and near the airport.
sentence_283: About 6 km (4 mi) from downtown Kabul, in [[Bagrami_District|Bagrami]], a 9-hectare (22-acre) industrial complex has completed with modern facilities, which will allow companies to operate businesses there.
sentence_284: The park has professional management for the daily maintenance of public roads, internal streets, common areas, parking areas, 24 hours perimeter security, access control for vehicles and persons.
sentence_285: A number of factories operate there, including the $25 million Coca-Cola bottling plant and the Omaid Bahar juice factory.
sentence_286: According to [[Transparency_International|Transparency International]], the government of Afghanistan was the third most-[[Corruption|corrupt]] in the world, as of 2010.
sentence_287: Experts believe that the poor decisions of Afghan politicians contribute to the unrest in the region.
sentence_288: This also prevents foreign investment in Afghanistan, especially by Western countries.
sentence_289: In 2012, there were reportedly $3.9 billion paid to public officials in [[Bribery|bribes]] which contributed to these issues.
sentence_290: [[Da_Afghanistan_Bank|Da Afghanistan Bank]], the nation's [[Central_bank|central bank]], is headquartered in Kabul.
sentence_291: In addition, there are several commercial banks in the city.
sentence_292: A US$1 billion contract was signed in 2013 to commence work on the "New Kabul City", which is a major residential scheme that would accommodate 1.5 million people.
sentence_293: In the meantime, many high rise buildings are being constructed in order to control the overcrowding and also to modernize the city.
sentence_294: An initial concept design called the [[City_of_Light_Development|City of Light Development]], envisioned by Dr. Hisham N. Ashkouri, for the development and the implementation of a privately based investment enterprise has been proposed for multi-function commercial, historic and cultural development within the limits of the Old City of Kabul, along the southern side of the Kabul River and along Jade Meywand Avenue,
sentence_295: Further information: [[Communications_in_Afghanistan|Communications in Afghanistan]]
sentence_296: As of November 2015, there are more than 24 television stations based out of Kabul.
sentence_297: In Kabul, [[Amirzai_Sangin|Minister Amir Zai Sangin]] of the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology maintains statistics regarding telecommunications in the Islamic Republic of Afghanistan.
sentence_298: [[Afghanistan_Information_Management_Services|Afghanistan Information Management Services]] (AIMS) provides software development, capacity development, information management, and project management services to the Afghan Government and other NGOs, thereby supporting their on-the-ground activities.
sentence_299: [[GSM|GSM]]/[[GPRS|GPRS]] mobile phone services in the city are provided by [[Afghan_Wireless|Afghan Wireless]], [[Etisalat|Etisalat]], [[Roshan_(Telecom)|Roshan]], [[MTN_Group|MTN]] and Salaam.
sentence_300: As of 2012, all of them provide 3G services as well.
sentence_301: In November 2006, the [[Afghan_Ministry_of_Communications|Afghan Ministry of Communications]] signed a $64.5 million US dollar deal with [[ZTE|ZTE]] on the establishment of a countrywide fibre optical cable network to help improve telephone, internet, television and radio broadcast services not just in Kabul but throughout the country.
sentence_302: Internet cafes were introduced in 2002 and has been expanding throughout the country.
sentence_303: As of 2012, 3G services are also available.
sentence_304: There are a number of post offices throughout the city.
sentence_305: Package delivery services like FedEx, [[TNT_N.V.|TNT N.V.]], and [[DHL_Express|DHL]] are also available.
sentence_306: Further information: [[Transport_in_Afghanistan|Transport in Afghanistan]]
sentence_307: [[Hamid_Karzai_International_Airport|Hamid Karzai International Airport]] (Kabul International Airport) is located 25 km (16 mi) from the center of Kabul, which has always served as the country's main airport.
sentence_308: It is a hub to [[Ariana_Afghan_Airlines|Ariana Afghan Airlines]], the national carrier of Afghanistan, as well as private airlines such as [[Afghan_Jet_International|Afghan Jet International]], [[East_Horizon_Airlines|East Horizon Airlines]], [[Kam_Air|Kam Air]], [[Pamir_Airways|Pamir Airways]], and [[Safi_Airways|Safi Airways]].
sentence_309: Regional airlines such as [[Air_India|Air India]], [[SpiceJet|SpiceJet]], [[Flydubai|flydubai]], [[Emirates_(airline)|Emirates]], [[Gulf_Air|Gulf Air]], Mahan Air, Pakistan International Airlines, [[Turkish_Airlines|Turkish Airlines]] and others also have regularly scheduled flights to the airport.
sentence_310: A new international terminal was built by the government of Japan and began operation in 2008.
sentence_311: Kabul has no train service; its only railway service, the [[Kabul–Darulaman_Tramway|Kabul–Darulaman Tramway]], operated for six years from 1923 to 1929.
sentence_312: As part of the approved major [[Deh_Sabz|Deh Sabz]] "Kabul New City" development project that kicked off in 2015, a [[Light_rail|light rail]] service is being planned during the mid-term development period.
sentence_313: The [[AH76|AH76]] highway (or Kabul-Charikar Highway) connects Kabul north towards [[Charikar|Charikar]], [[Pol-e_Khomri|Pol-e Khomri]] and [[Mazar-i-Sharif|Mazar-i-Sharif]] (310 km (190 mi) away), with leading roads to [[Kunduz|Kunduz]] (250 km (160 mi) away).
sentence_314: The [[AH77|AH77]] highway goes west towards [[Bamiyan_Province|Bamiyan Province]] (150 km (93 mi) away) and [[Chaghcharan|Chaghcharan]] in the central mountains of Afghanistan.
sentence_315: To the south-west, the Kabul-Ghazni Highway goes to [[Ghazni|Ghazni]] (130 km (81 mi) away) and [[Kandahar|Kandahar]] (460 km (290 mi) away).
sentence_316: To the south, the Kabul-Gardez Highway connects it to [[Gardez|Gardez]] (100 km (62 mi) away) and [[Khost|Khost]].
sentence_317: To the east, the Kabul-Jalalabad Highway goes to [[Jalalabad|Jalalabad]] (120 km (75 mi) away) and across the border to [[Peshawar|Peshawar]].
sentence_318: Much of the road network in downtown Kabul consist of square or circle intersections (char-rahi).
sentence_319: The main square in the city is Pashtunistan Square (named after [[Pashtunistan|Pashtunistan]]), which has a large [[Fountain|fountain]] in it and is located adjacent to the presidential palace, the [[Da_Afghanistan_Bank|Central Bank]], and other landmarks.
sentence_320: The [[Massoud_Circle|Massoud Circle]] is located by the [[Embassy_of_the_United_States,_Kabul|U.S.
sentence_321: Embassy]] and has the road leading to the airport.
sentence_322: In the old city, Sar-e Chawk roundabout is at the center of Maiwand Road ([[Jadayi_Maiwand|Jadayi Maiwand]]).
sentence_323: Once all roads led to it, and in the 16th century was called the "navel of Kabul".
sentence_324: In the [[Shahr-e_Naw|Shahr-e Naw]] district there are several major intersections: Ansari, Haji Yaqub, Quwayi Markaz, Sedarat, and Turabaz Khan.
sentence_325: The latter, named after [[Turabaz_Khan|Turabaz Khan]], connect Flower Street and Chicken Street.
sentence_326: There are also two major intersections in western Kabul: the [[Deh_Mazang|Deh Mazang]] Circle and [[Kote_Sangi|Kote Sangi]].
sentence_327: Salang Watt is the main road to the north-west, whereas Asamayi Watt and Seh Aqrab (also called Sevom Aqrab) is the main road to western Kabul.
sentence_328: The steep population rise in the 21st century has caused major congestion problems for the city's roads.
sentence_329: In efforts to tackle this issue, a 95 km outer [[Ring_road|ring road]] costing $110 million was approved in 2017.
sentence_330: Construction will take five years and it will run from Char Asiab via Ahmad Shah Baba Mina, [[Deh_Sabz|Deh Sabz]] ("Kabul New City" development area), the AH76 highway, [[Paghman|Paghman]] and back to Char Asyab.
sentence_331: A new bus public transport service is also planned to be opened in 2018 (see below).
sentence_332: In September 2017, the head of the Kabul Municipality announced that 286 meters of pedestrian overpass [[Footbridge|footbridges]] will be built in eight busy areas "in the near future".
sentence_333: Under the Kabul Urban Transport Efficiency Improvement Project that was signed in 2014 and backed by the [[World_Bank|World Bank]], the city has seen widespread improvements in road conditions, including the building of new pedestrian sidewalks, drainage systems, lighting and [[Asphalt|asphalted]] road surfaces.
sentence_334: The project runs until December 31, 2019.
sentence_335: Private vehicles have been on the rise in Kabul since 2002, with about 700,000 cars registered as of 2013 and up to 80% of the cars reported to be [[Toyota_Corolla|Toyota Corollas]].
sentence_336: The number of dealerships have also increased from 77 in 2003 to over 550 by 2010.
sentence_337: Gas stations are mainly private-owned.
sentence_338: Bicycles on the road are a common sight in the city.
sentence_339: The [[Taxicab|taxicabs]] in Kabul are painted in a white and yellow livery.
sentence_340: The majority of these are older model Toyota Corollas.
sentence_341: A few Soviet-era Russian cabs are also still in operation.
sentence_342: Long-distance road journeys are made by private [[Mercedes-Benz_buses|Mercedes-Benz coach buses]] or vans, trucks and cars.
sentence_343: Although a nationwide bus service is available from Kabul, flying is safer, especially for foreigners.
sentence_344: The city's public bus service ([[Millie_Bus|Millie Bus]] / "National Bus") was established in the 1960s to take commuters on daily routes to many destinations.
sentence_345: The service has about 800 buses.
sentence_346: The Kabul bus system has discovered a new source of revenue in whole-bus advertising from [[MTN_Group|MTN]] similar to "bus wrap" advertising on public transit in more developed nations.
sentence_347: There is also an express bus that runs from downtown to Hamid Karzai International Airport for [[Safi_Airways|Safi Airways]] passengers.
sentence_348: An electric [[Trolleybus|trolleybus]] system operated in Kabul from February 1979 to 1992 using [[Å koda_Works|Å koda]] fleet built by a [[Czechoslovak|Czechoslovak]] company (see [[Trolleybuses_in_Kabul|Trolleybuses in Kabul]] for more).
sentence_349: The trolleybus service was highly popular mainly due to its low price compared to the Millie Bus conventional bus service.
sentence_350: The last trolleybus came to a halt in late 1992 due to warfare - much of the [[Copper|copper]] [[Overhead_line|overhead wires]] were later looted but a few of them, including the steel poles, can still be seen in Kabul today.
sentence_351: In June 2017 Kabul Municipality unveiled plans for a [[Kabul_bus_rapid_transit|new bus rapid transit]] system, the first major urban public transportation scheme.
sentence_352: It was expected to open by 2018, but its launch has been delayed.
sentence_353: Further information: [[List_of_schools_in_Kabul|List of schools in Kabul]] and [[Education_in_Afghanistan|Education in Afghanistan]]
sentence_354: The [[Ministry_of_Education_(Afghanistan)|Ministry of Education]] led by [[Ghulam_Farooq_Wardak|Ghulam Farooq Wardak]] is responsible for the education system in Afghanistan.
sentence_355: Public and [[Private_school|private schools]] in the city have reopened since 2002 after they were shut down or destroyed during fighting in the 1980s to the late 1990s.
sentence_356: Boys and girls are strongly encouraged to attend school under the [[Karzai_administration|Karzai administration]] but many more schools are needed not only in Kabul but throughout the country.
sentence_357: The [[Ministry_of_Education_(Afghanistan)|Afghan Ministry of Education]] has plans to build more schools in the coming years so that education is provided to all citizens of the country.
sentence_358: High schools in Kabul include:

title: J. K. Rowling
sentence_0: Joanne Rowling [[Companion_of_Honour|CH]], [[Officer_of_the_Order_of_the_British_Empire|OBE]], [[Honorary_Fellow_of_the_Royal_Society_of_Edinburgh|HonFRSE]], [[Fellow_of_the_Royal_College_of_Physicians_of_Edinburgh|FRCPE]], [[Fellow_of_the_Royal_Society_of_Literature|FRSL]] ([[English|/ˈroʊlɪŋ/]] ROH-ling; born 31 July 1965), better known by her [[Pen_name|pen name]] J. K. Rowling, is a British author, philanthropist, film producer, television producer and screenwriter.
sentence_1: She is best known for writing the [[Harry_Potter|Harry Potter]] fantasy series, which has won multiple awards and sold more than 500 million copies, becoming the [[List_of_best-selling_books|best-selling book series in history]].
sentence_2: The books are the basis of a [[Harry_Potter_(film_series)|popular film series]], over which Rowling had overall approval on the scripts and was a producer on the final films.
sentence_3: She also writes [[Crime_fiction|crime fiction]] under the pen name Robert Galbraith.
sentence_4: Born in [[Yate|Yate, Gloucestershire]], Rowling was working as a researcher and bilingual secretary for [[Amnesty_International|Amnesty International]] when she conceived the idea for the Harry Potter series while on a delayed train from [[Manchester|Manchester]] to [[London|London]] in 1990.
sentence_5: The seven-year period that followed saw the death of her mother, birth of her first child, divorce from her first husband, and relative poverty until the first novel in the series, [[Harry_Potter_and_the_Philosopher's_Stone|Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone]], was published in 1997.
sentence_6: There were six sequels, of which the last was released in 2007.
sentence_7: Since then, Rowling has written several books for adult readers: [[The_Casual_Vacancy|The Casual Vacancy]] (2012) and—under the pseudonym Robert Galbraith—the crime fiction Cormoran Strike series.
sentence_8: In 2020, her "political fairytale" for children, [[The_Ickabog|The Ickabog]], was released in instalments in an online version.
sentence_9: Rowling has lived a "[[Rags_to_riches|rags to riches]]" life in which she progressed from living on benefits to being named the world's first billionaire author by [[Forbes|Forbes]].
sentence_10: However, Rowling disputed the assertion, saying she was not a billionaire.
sentence_11: Forbes reported that she lost her billionaire status after giving away much of her earnings to charity.
sentence_12: Her UK sales total in excess of £238 million, making her the best-selling living author in Britain.
sentence_13: The [[Sunday_Times_Rich_List_2020|2020 Sunday Times Rich List]] estimated Rowling's fortune at £795 million, ranking her as the 178th richest person in the UK.
sentence_14: [[Time_(magazine)|Time]] named her a runner-up for its 2007 [[Time_Person_of_the_Year|Person of the Year]], noting the social, moral, and [[Politics_of_Harry_Potter|political]] inspiration she has given [[Harry_Potter_fandom|her fans]].
sentence_15: Rowling was appointed a [[Member_of_the_Order_of_the_Companions_of_Honour|Member of the Order of the Companions of Honour]] (CH) at the [[2017_Birthday_Honours|2017 Birthday Honours]] for services to literature and philanthropy.
sentence_16: In October 2010, she was named the "Most Influential Woman in Britain" by leading magazine editors.
sentence_17: Rowling has supported multiple charities, including [[Comic_Relief_(charity)|Comic Relief]], One Parent Families, and [[Multiple_Sclerosis_Society_of_Great_Britain|Multiple Sclerosis Society of Great Britain]], as well as launching her own charity, [[Lumos_(charity)|Lumos]].
sentence_18: Although she writes under the pen name J. K. Rowling, before her remarriage, her name was Joanne Rowling.
sentence_19: Her publishers asked that she use two initials rather than her full name, anticipating the possibility of the target audience of young boys not wanting to read a book written by a woman.
sentence_20: As she had no middle name, she chose K (for Kathleen) as the second initial of her pen name, from her paternal grandmother.
sentence_21: She calls herself Jo.
sentence_22: Following her remarriage, she has sometimes used the name Joanne Murray when conducting personal business.
sentence_23: During the [[Leveson_Inquiry|Leveson Inquiry]], she gave evidence under the name of Joanne Kathleen Rowling and her entry in [[Who's_Who_(UK)|Who's Who]] lists her name also as Joanne Kathleen Rowling.
sentence_24: Joanne Rowling was born on 31 July 1965 in [[Yate|Yate, Gloucestershire]], the daughter of science technician Anne (née Volant) and [[Rolls-Royce_Limited|Rolls-Royce]] aircraft engineer Peter James Rowling.
sentence_25: Her parents first met on a train departing from [[London_King's_Cross_railway_station|King's Cross Station]] bound for [[Arbroath|Arbroath]] in 1964.
sentence_26: They married on 14 March 1965.
sentence_27: One of Rowling's maternal great-grandfathers, Dugald Campbell, was a Scottish man from [[Lamlash|Lamlash]].
sentence_28: Her mother's French paternal grandfather, Louis Volant, was awarded the [[Croix_de_guerre_1914–1918_(France)|War Cross]] for exceptional bravery in defending the village of [[Courcelles-le-Comte|Courcelles-le-Comte]] during [[World_War_I|World War I]].
sentence_29: Rowling originally believed Volant had won the [[Legion_of_Honour|Legion of Honour]] during the war, as she said when she received it herself in 2009.
sentence_30: She later discovered the truth when featured in an episode of the UK genealogy series [[Who_Do_You_Think_You_Are?_(UK_TV_series)|Who Do You Think You Are?]]
sentence_31: in which she found out it was a different Louis Volant who won the Legion of Honour.
sentence_32: When she heard her grandfather's story of bravery and discovered that the War Cross was for "ordinary" soldiers like her grandfather, who had been a waiter, she stated the War Cross was "better" to her than the Legion of Honour.
sentence_33: Rowling's sister Dianne was born at their home when Rowling was 23 months old.
sentence_34: The family moved to the nearby village of [[Winterbourne,_Gloucestershire|Winterbourne]] when Rowling was four.
sentence_35: As a child, Rowling often wrote fantasy stories which she frequently read to her sister.
sentence_36: Aged nine, Rowling moved to [[Church_Cottage,_Tutshill|Church Cottage]] in the Gloucestershire village of [[Tutshill|Tutshill]], close to [[Chepstow|Chepstow]], Wales.
sentence_37: When she was a young teenager, her great-aunt gave her a copy of [[Jessica_Mitford|Jessica Mitford]]'s autobiography, [[Hons_and_Rebels|Hons and Rebels]].
sentence_38: Mitford became Rowling's heroine, and Rowling read all of her books.
sentence_39: Rowling has said that her teenage years were unhappy.
sentence_40: Her home life was complicated by her mother's diagnosis with [[Multiple_sclerosis|multiple sclerosis]] and a strained relationship with her father, with whom she is not on speaking terms.
sentence_41: Rowling later said that she based the character of [[Hermione_Granger|Hermione Granger]] on herself when she was eleven.
sentence_42: Sean Harris, her best friend in the Upper Sixth, owned a turquoise [[Ford_Anglia#Anglia_105E|Ford Anglia]] which she says inspired a flying version that appeared in [[Harry_Potter_and_the_Chamber_of_Secrets|Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets]].
sentence_43: Like many teenagers, she became interested in rock music, listening to [[The_Clash|the Clash]], [[The_Smiths|the Smiths]], and [[Siouxsie_Sioux|Siouxsie Sioux]], adopting the look of the latter with back-combed hair and black eyeliner, a look that she would still sport when beginning university.
sentence_44: As a child, Rowling attended [[St_Michael's_Primary_School|St Michael's Primary School]], a school founded by abolitionist [[William_Wilberforce|William Wilberforce]] and education reformer [[Hannah_More|Hannah More]].
sentence_45: Her headmaster at St Michael's, Alfred Dunn, has been suggested as the inspiration for the Harry Potter headmaster [[Albus_Dumbledore|Albus Dumbledore]].
sentence_46: She attended secondary school at Wyedean School and College, where her mother worked in the science department.
sentence_47: Steve Eddy, her first secondary school English teacher, remembers her as "not exceptional" but "one of a group of girls who were bright, and quite good at English".
sentence_48: Rowling took A-levels in English, French and German, achieving two As and a B and was head girl.
sentence_49: In 1982, Rowling took the entrance exams for [[Oxford_University|Oxford University]] but was not accepted and earned a [[Bachelor_of_Arts|BA]] in French and [[Classics|Classics]] at the [[University_of_Exeter|University of Exeter]].
sentence_50: Martin Sorrell, a French professor at Exeter, remembers "a quietly competent student, with a denim jacket and dark hair, who, in academic terms, gave the appearance of doing what was necessary".
sentence_51: Rowling recalls doing little work, preferring to read [[Charles_Dickens|Dickens]] and [[J._R._R._Tolkien|Tolkien]].
sentence_52: After a year of study in Paris, Rowling graduated from Exeter in 1986.
sentence_53: In 1988, Rowling wrote a short essay about her time studying Classics titled "What was the Name of that Nymph Again?
sentence_54: or Greek and Roman Studies Recalled"; it was published by the University of Exeter's journal Pegasus.
sentence_55: After working as a researcher and bilingual secretary in London for [[Amnesty_International|Amnesty International]], Rowling moved with her then-boyfriend to Manchester, where she worked at the Chamber of Commerce.
sentence_56: In 1990, while she was on a four-hour-delayed train trip from Manchester to London, the idea for a story of a young boy attending a school of wizardry "came fully formed" into her mind.
sentence_57: When she had reached her [[Clapham_Junction|Clapham Junction]] flat, she began to write immediately.
sentence_58: In December, Rowling's mother, Anne, died after ten years suffering from [[Multiple_sclerosis|multiple sclerosis]].
sentence_59: Rowling was writing Harry Potter at the time and had never told her mother about it.
sentence_60: Her mother's death heavily affected Rowling's writing, and she channelled her own feelings of loss by writing about Harry's own feelings of loss in greater detail in the first book.
sentence_61: An advertisement in [[The_Guardian|The Guardian]] led Rowling to move to [[Porto|Porto]], [[Portugal|Portugal]], to teach [[English_as_a_foreign_language|English as a foreign language]].
sentence_62: She taught at night and began writing in the day while listening to [[Pyotr_Ilyich_Tchaikovsky|Tchaikovsky's]] [[Violin_Concerto_(Tchaikovsky)|Violin Concerto]].
sentence_63: After 18 months in Porto, she met Portuguese television journalist Jorge Arantes in a bar and found they shared an interest in [[Jane_Austen|Jane Austen]].
sentence_64: They married on 16 October 1992 and their child, Jessica Isabel Rowling Arantes (named after [[Jessica_Mitford|Jessica Mitford]]), was born on 27 July 1993 in Portugal.
sentence_65: Rowling had previously suffered a [[Miscarriage|miscarriage]].
sentence_66: The couple separated on 17 November 1993.
sentence_67: Biographers have suggested that Rowling suffered [[Domestic_abuse|domestic abuse]] during her marriage, which was later confirmed by Rowling herself, and by her first husband, who, in an article for [[The_Sun_(United_Kingdom)|The Sun]] in June 2020, said he had slapped her and did not regret it.
sentence_68: The [[United_Kingdom|United Kingdom]]'s domestic abuse commissioner Nicole Jacobs formally advised [[The_Sun_(United_Kingdom)|The Sun]] that it was unacceptable "to repeat and magnify the voice of someone who openly admits to violence against a partner".
sentence_69: In December 1993, Rowling and her then infant daughter moved to [[Edinburgh|Edinburgh]], Scotland, to be near Rowling's sister with three chapters of what would become Harry Potter in her suitcase.
sentence_70: Seven years after graduating from university, Rowling saw herself as a failure.
sentence_71: Her marriage had failed, and she was jobless with a dependent child, but she described her failure as liberating and allowing her to focus on writing.
sentence_72: During this period, Rowling was diagnosed with clinical depression and contemplated suicide.
sentence_73: Her illness inspired the characters known as [[Dementors|Dementors]], soul-sucking creatures introduced in the third book.
sentence_74: Rowling signed up for [[Welfare_benefits|welfare benefits]], describing her economic status as being "poor as it is possible to be in modern Britain, without being homeless."
sentence_75: Rowling was left in despair after her estranged husband arrived in Scotland, seeking both her and their daughter.
sentence_76: She obtained an [[Restraining_order|Order of Restraint]], and Arantes returned to Portugal, with Rowling filing for divorce in August 1994.
sentence_77: She began a teacher training course in August 1995 at the [[Moray_House_School_of_Education|Moray House School of Education]], at [[University_of_Edinburgh|Edinburgh University]], after completing her first novel while living on state benefits.
sentence_78: She wrote in many cafés, especially Nicolson's Café (owned by her brother-in-law), and the Elephant House, wherever she could get Jessica to fall asleep.
sentence_79: In a 2001 [[BBC|BBC]] interview, Rowling denied the rumour that she wrote in local cafés to escape from her unheated flat, pointing out that it had heating.
sentence_80: Rowling stated that she wrote in cafés because coffee was available without her breaking the flow of writing, and that taking her baby out for a walk helped her to fall asleep.
sentence_81: Main article: [[Harry_Potter|Harry Potter]]
sentence_82: In 1995, Rowling finished her manuscript for [[Harry_Potter_and_the_Philosopher's_Stone|Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone]] which was typed on an old manual typewriter.
sentence_83: Upon the enthusiastic response of Bryony Evens, a reader who had been asked to review the book's first three chapters, the Fulham-based [[Christopher_Little_Literary_Agency|Christopher Little Literary Agency]] agreed to represent Rowling in her quest for a publisher.
sentence_84: The book was submitted to twelve publishing houses, all of which rejected the manuscript.
sentence_85: A year later, she was finally given the green light (and a £1,500 advance) by editor Barry Cunningham from [[Bloomsbury_Publishing|Bloomsbury]], a publishing house in London.
sentence_86: The decision to publish Rowling's book owes much to Alice Newton, the eight-year-old daughter of Bloomsbury's chairman, who was [[Publisher's_reader|given the first chapter to review]] by her father and immediately demanded the next.
sentence_87: Although Bloomsbury agreed to publish the book, Cunningham says that he advised Rowling to get a day job, since she had little chance of making money in children's books.
sentence_88: Soon after, in 1997, Rowling received an £8,000 grant from the [[Scottish_Arts_Council|Scottish Arts Council]] to enable her to continue writing.
sentence_89: In June 1997, Bloomsbury published Philosopher's Stone with an initial print run of 1,000 copies, 500 of which were distributed to libraries.
sentence_90: Today, such copies are valued between £16,000 and £25,000.
sentence_91: Five months later, the book won its first award, a Nestlé Smarties Book Prize.
sentence_92: In February 1998, the novel won the British Book Award for Children's Book of the Year and, later, the Children's Book Award.
sentence_93: In early 1998, an auction was held in the United States for the rights to publish the novel, and was won by Scholastic Inc., for US$105,000.
sentence_94: Rowling said that she "nearly died" when she heard the news.
sentence_95: In October 1998, Scholastic published Philosopher's Stone in the US under the title of Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone, a change Rowling says she now regrets and would have fought if she had been in a better position at the time.
sentence_96: Rowling moved from her flat with the money from the Scholastic sale, into 19 Hazelbank Terrace in Edinburgh.
sentence_97: Its sequel, [[Harry_Potter_and_the_Chamber_of_Secrets|Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets]], was published in July 1998 and again Rowling won the Smarties Prize.
sentence_98: In December 1999, the third novel, [[Harry_Potter_and_the_Prisoner_of_Azkaban|Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban]], won the Smarties Prize, making Rowling the first person to win the award three times running.
sentence_99: She later withdrew the fourth Harry Potter novel from contention to allow other books a fair chance.
sentence_100: In January 2000, Prisoner of Azkaban won the inaugural [[1999_Whitbread_Awards|Whitbread Children's Book of the Year award]], though it lost the Book of the Year prize to [[Seamus_Heaney|Seamus Heaney]]'s translation of [[Beowulf|Beowulf]].
sentence_101: The fourth book, [[Harry_Potter_and_the_Goblet_of_Fire|Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire]], was released simultaneously in the UK and the US on 8 July 2000 and broke sales records in both countries.
sentence_102: 372,775 copies of the book were sold in its first day in the UK, almost equalling the number Prisoner of Azkaban sold during its first year.
sentence_103: In the US, the book sold three million copies in its first 48 hours, smashing all records.
sentence_104: Rowling said that she had had a crisis while writing the novel and had to rewrite one chapter many times to fix a problem with the plot.
sentence_105: Rowling was named Author of the Year in the 2000 British Book Awards.
sentence_106: A wait of three years occurred between the release of Goblet of Fire and the fifth Harry Potter novel, [[Harry_Potter_and_the_Order_of_the_Phoenix|Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix]].
sentence_107: This gap led to press speculation that Rowling had developed [[Writer's_block|writer's block]], speculations she later denied.
sentence_108: Rowling later said that writing the book was a chore, that it could have been shorter, and that she ran out of time and energy as she tried to finish it.
sentence_109: The sixth book, [[Harry_Potter_and_the_Half-Blood_Prince|Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince]], was released on 16 July 2005.
sentence_110: It too broke all sales records, selling nine million copies in its first 24 hours of release.
sentence_111: In 2006, Half-Blood Prince received the Book of the Year prize at the British Book Awards.
sentence_112: The title of the seventh and final Harry Potter book was announced on 21 December 2006 as [[Harry_Potter_and_the_Deathly_Hallows|Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows]].
sentence_113: In February 2007, it was reported that Rowling wrote on a bust in her hotel room at the [[Balmoral_Hotel|Balmoral Hotel]] in Edinburgh that she had finished the seventh book in that room on 11 January 2007.
sentence_114: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows was released on 21 July 2007 (0:01 [[Western_European_Summer_Time|BST]]) and broke its predecessor's record as the fastest-selling book of all time.
sentence_115: It sold 11 million copies in the first day of release in the United Kingdom and United States.
sentence_116: The book's last chapter was one of the earliest things she wrote in the entire series.
sentence_117: Harry Potter is now a global brand worth an estimated US$15 billion, and the last four Harry Potter books have consecutively set records as the fastest-selling books in history.
sentence_118: The series, totalling 4,195 pages, has been translated, in whole or in part, into 65 languages.
sentence_119: The Harry Potter books have also gained recognition for sparking an interest in reading among the young at a time when children were thought to be abandoning books for computers, television and video games, although it is reported that despite the huge uptake of the books, adolescent reading has continued to decline.
sentence_120: Main article: [[Harry_Potter_(film_series)|Harry Potter (film series)]]
sentence_121: In October 1998, [[Warner_Bros.|Warner Bros.]] purchased the film rights to the first two novels for a seven-figure sum.
sentence_122: A film adaptation of [[Harry_Potter_and_the_Philosopher's_Stone_(film)|Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone]] was released on 16 November 2001, and [[Harry_Potter_and_the_Chamber_of_Secrets_(film)|Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets]] on 15 November 2002.
sentence_123: Both films were directed by [[Chris_Columbus_(filmmaker)|Chris Columbus]].
sentence_124: The film version of [[Harry_Potter_and_the_Prisoner_of_Azkaban_(film)|Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban]] was released on 4 June 2004, directed by [[Alfonso_Cuarón|Alfonso Cuarón]].
sentence_125: The fourth film, [[Harry_Potter_and_the_Goblet_of_Fire_(film)|Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire]], was directed by [[Mike_Newell_(director)|Mike Newell]], and released on 18 November 2005.
sentence_126: The film of [[Harry_Potter_and_the_Order_of_the_Phoenix_(film)|Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix]] was released on 11 July 2007.
sentence_127: [[David_Yates|David Yates]] directed, and [[Michael_Goldenberg|Michael Goldenberg]] wrote the screenplay, having taken over the position from [[Steve_Kloves|Steve Kloves]].
sentence_128: [[Harry_Potter_and_the_Half-Blood_Prince_(film)|Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince]] was released on 15 July 2009.
sentence_129: David Yates directed again, and Kloves returned to write the script.
sentence_130: Warner Bros. filmed the final instalment of the series, Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows, in two segments, with [[Harry_Potter_and_the_Deathly_Hallows_–_Part_1|part one]] being released on 19 November 2010 and [[Harry_Potter_and_the_Deathly_Hallows_–_Part_2|part two]] being released on 15 July 2011.
sentence_131: Yates directed both films.
sentence_132: Warner Bros. took considerable notice of Rowling's desires when drafting her contract.
sentence_133: One of her principal stipulations was the films be shot in Britain with an all-British cast, which has been generally adhered to.
sentence_134: Rowling also demanded that [[Coca-Cola|Coca-Cola]], the winner in the race to [[Tie-in|tie in]] their products to the film series, donate US$18 million to the American charity Reading Is Fundamental, as well as several community charity programs.
sentence_135: Steve Kloves wrote the screenplays for all but the fifth film; Rowling assisted him in the writing process, ensuring that his scripts did not contradict future books in the series.
sentence_136: She told [[Alan_Rickman|Alan Rickman]] ([[Severus_Snape|Severus Snape]]) and [[Robbie_Coltrane|Robbie Coltrane]] ([[Hagrid|Hagrid]]) certain secrets about their characters before they were revealed in the books.
sentence_137: [[Daniel_Radcliffe|Daniel Radcliffe]] ([[Harry_Potter_(character)|Harry Potter]]) asked her if Harry died at any point in the series; Rowling answered him by saying, "You have a death scene", thereby not explicitly answering the question.
sentence_138: Director [[Steven_Spielberg|Steven Spielberg]] was approached to direct the first film, but dropped out.
sentence_139: The press has repeatedly claimed that Rowling played a role in his departure, but Rowling stated that she had no say in who directed the films and would not have vetoed Spielberg.
sentence_140: Rowling's first choice for the director had been [[Monty_Python|Monty Python]] member [[Terry_Gilliam|Terry Gilliam]], but Warner Bros. wanted a family-friendly film and chose Columbus.

sentence_142: Rowling, producers [[David_Heyman|David Heyman]] and [[David_Barron_(film_producer)|David Barron]], along with directors [[David_Yates|David Yates]], [[Mike_Newell_(director)|Mike Newell]] and [[Alfonso_Cuarón|Alfonso Cuarón]] collected the Michael Balcon Award for Outstanding British Contribution to Cinema at the 2011 [[British_Academy_Film_Awards|British Academy Film Awards]] in honour of the Harry Potter film franchise.
sentence_143: In September 2013, Warner Bros. announced an "expanded creative partnership" with Rowling, based on a planned series of films about her character [[Newt_Scamander|Newt Scamander]], author of [[Fantastic_Beasts_and_Where_to_Find_Them|Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them]].
sentence_144: The [[Fantastic_Beasts_and_Where_to_Find_Them_(film)|first film]] was released in November 2016 and is set roughly 70 years before the events of the main series.

sentence_146: The second, Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes of Grindelwald, was released in November 2018.
sentence_147: In 2004, [[Forbes|Forbes]] named Rowling as the first person to become a US-dollar billionaire by writing books, the second-richest female entertainer and the 1,062nd richest person in the world.
sentence_148: Rowling disputed the calculations and said she had plenty of money, but was not a billionaire.
sentence_149: The 2020 [[Sunday_Times_Rich_List|Sunday Times Rich List]] estimated Rowling's fortune at £795 million, ranking her as the 178th richest person in the UK.
sentence_150: In 2012, Forbes removed Rowling from their rich list, claiming that her US$160 million in charitable donations and the high tax rate in the UK meant she was no longer a billionaire.
sentence_151: In February 2013, she was assessed as the 13th most powerful woman in the United Kingdom by [[Woman's_Hour|Woman's Hour]] on [[BBC_Radio_4|BBC Radio 4]].
sentence_152: Rowling acquired the [[Courtesy_titles_in_the_United_Kingdom|courtesy title]] of [[Laird|Laird]] of [[Killiechassie_House|Killiechassie]] in 2001 when she purchased the historic [[Killiechassie_House|Killiechassie House]], and its surrounding estate situated on the banks of the [[River_Tay|River Tay]], near [[Aberfeldy,_Scotland|Aberfeldy]], in [[Perth_and_Kinross|Perth and Kinross]].
sentence_153: Rowling also owns a £4.5 million [[Georgian_architecture|Georgian]] house in [[Kensington|Kensington]], west London, on a street with 24-hour security.
sentence_154: Rowling was named the most highly paid author in the world with earnings of £72 million ($95 million) a year by Forbes in 2017.
sentence_155: On 26 December 2001, Rowling married Neil Murray (born 30 June 1971), a Scottish doctor, in a private ceremony at her home, [[Killiechassie_House|Killiechassie House]], in Scotland.
sentence_156: Their son, David Gordon Rowling Murray, was born on 24 March 2003.
sentence_157: Shortly after Rowling began writing Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince, she ceased working on the novel to care for David in his early infancy.
sentence_158: Rowling is a friend of [[Sarah_Jane_Brown|Sarah Brown]], wife of former prime minister [[Gordon_Brown|Gordon Brown]], whom she met when they collaborated on a charitable project.

sentence_160: Rowling's youngest child, daughter Mackenzie Jean Rowling Murray, to whom she dedicated Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince, was born on 23 January 2005.
sentence_161: In October 2012, a [[The_New_Yorker|New Yorker]] magazine article stated that the Rowling family lived in a seventeenth-century Edinburgh house, concealed at the front by tall [[Conifer|conifer]] hedges.
sentence_162: Prior to October 2012, Rowling lived near the author [[Ian_Rankin|Ian Rankin]], who later said she was quiet and introspective, and that she seemed in her element with children.
sentence_163: As of June 2014, the family resides in Scotland.
sentence_164: In July 2011, Rowling parted company with her agent, Christopher Little, moving to a new agency founded by one of his staff, Neil Blair.
sentence_165: On 23 February 2012, his agency, the Blair Partnership, announced on its website that Rowling was set to publish a new book targeted at adults.
sentence_166: In a press release, Rowling said that her new book would be quite different from Harry Potter.

sentence_169: In its first three weeks of release, The Casual Vacancy sold over 1 million copies worldwide.
sentence_170: On 3 December 2012, it was announced that the [[BBC|BBC]] would be adapting The Casual Vacancy into [[The_Casual_Vacancy_(miniseries)|a television drama miniseries]].
sentence_171: Rowling's agent, Neil Blair acted as producer, through his independent production company and with Rick Senat serving as executive producer.
sentence_172: Rowling collaborated on the adaptation, serving as an executive producer for the series.

sentence_174: Main article: Cormoran Strike
sentence_175: In 2007, during the [[Edinburgh_Book_Festival|Edinburgh Book Festival]], author [[Ian_Rankin|Ian Rankin]] claimed that his wife spotted Rowling "scribbling away" at a detective novel in a café.
sentence_176: Rankin later retracted the story, claiming it was a joke, but the rumour persisted, with a report in 2012 in The Guardian speculating that Rowling's next book would be a crime novel.
sentence_177: In an interview with [[Stephen_Fry|Stephen Fry]] in 2005, Rowling had claimed that she would much prefer to write any subsequent books under a [[Pseudonym|pseudonym]], but had previously conceded to [[Jeremy_Paxman|Jeremy Paxman]] in 2003 that if she did, the press would probably "find out in seconds".
sentence_178: In April 2013, [[Little_Brown|Little Brown]] published [[The_Cuckoo's_Calling|The Cuckoo's Calling]], the purported [[Début_novel|début novel]] of author Robert Galbraith, whom the publisher described as "a former plainclothes [[Royal_Military_Police|Royal Military Police]] investigator who had left in 2003 to work in the civilian security industry".
sentence_179: The novel, a detective story in which [[Private_investigator|private investigator]] Cormoran Strike unravels the supposed suicide of a supermodel, sold 1,500 copies in hardback (although the matter was not resolved as of 21 July 2013; later reports stated that this number is the number of copies that were printed for the first run, while the sales total was closer to 500) and received acclaim from other crime writers and critics—a Publishers Weekly review called the book a "stellar debut", while the Library Journal's mystery section pronounced the novel "the debut of the month".
sentence_180: [[India_Knight|India Knight]], a novelist and columnist for [[The_Sunday_Times|The Sunday Times]], [[Twitter|tweeted]] on 9 July 2013 that she had been reading The Cuckoo's Calling and thought it was good for a [[Début_novel|début novel]].
sentence_181: In response, a tweeter called Jude Callegari said that the author was Rowling.
sentence_182: Knight queried this but got no further reply.
sentence_183: Knight notified Richard Brooks, arts editor of The Sunday Times, who began his own investigation.
sentence_184: After discovering that Rowling and Galbraith had the same agent and editor, he sent the books for linguistic analysis which found similarities, and subsequently contacted Rowling's agent who confirmed it was Rowling's pseudonym.
sentence_185: Within days of Rowling being revealed as the author, sales of the book rose by 4,000%, and Little Brown printed another 140,000 copies to meet the increase in demand.
sentence_186: As of 18 July 2013, a signed copy of the first edition sold for US$4,453 (£2,950), while an unsold signed first-edition copy was being offered for $6,188 (£3,950).
sentence_187: Rowling said that she had enjoyed working under a pseudonym.
sentence_188: On her Robert Galbraith website, Rowling explained that she took the name from one of her personal heroes, [[Robert_F._Kennedy|Robert F. Kennedy]], and a childhood fantasy name she had invented for herself, Ella Galbraith.
sentence_189: Soon after the revelation, Brooks pondered whether Jude Callegari could have been Rowling as part of wider speculation that the entire affair had been a publicity stunt.
sentence_190: Some also observed that many of the writers who had initially praised the book, such as [[Alex_Gray_(author)|Alex Gray]] or [[Val_McDermid|Val McDermid]], were within Rowling's circle of acquaintances; both vociferously denied any foreknowledge of Rowling's authorship.
sentence_191: Judith "Jude" Callegari was the best friend of the wife of Chris Gossage, a partner within Russells Solicitors, Rowling's legal representatives.
sentence_192: Rowling released a statement saying she was disappointed and angry; Russells apologised for the leak, confirming it was not part of a marketing stunt and that "the disclosure was made in confidence to someone he [Gossage] trusted implicitly".
sentence_193: Russells made a donation to the Soldiers' Charity on Rowling's behalf and reimbursed her for her legal fees.
sentence_194: On 26 November 2013, the Solicitors Regulation Authority (SRA) issued Gossage a written rebuke and £1,000 fine for breaching privacy rules.
sentence_195: On 17 February 2014, Rowling announced that the second Cormoran Strike novel, named [[The_Silkworm|The Silkworm]], would be released in June 2014.
sentence_196: It sees Strike investigating the disappearance of a writer hated by many of his old friends for insulting them in his new novel.
sentence_197: In 2015, Rowling stated on Galbraith's website that the third Cormoran Strike novel would include "an insane amount of planning, the most I have done for any book I have written so far.

sentence_199: On 24 April 2015, Rowling announced that work on the third book was completed.

sentence_201: In 2017, the [[BBC|BBC]] released a [[Cormoran_Strike_(TV_series)|Cormoran Strike]] television series, starring [[Tom_Burke_(actor)|Tom Burke]] as Cormoran Strike, it was picked up by [[HBO|HBO]] for distribution in the United States and Canada.

sentence_224: A print edition is scheduled for November 2020 and will contain illustrations selected from entries to a competition running concurrently with the online publication.
sentence_225: In 2000, Rowling established the Volant Charitable Trust, which uses its annual budget of £5.1 million to combat poverty and social inequality.

sentence_229: In 2001, the UK anti-poverty fundraiser [[Comic_Relief_(charity)|Comic Relief]] asked three best-selling British authors—cookery writer and TV presenter Delia Smith, [[Bridget_Jones|Bridget Jones]] creator [[Helen_Fielding|Helen Fielding]], and Rowling—to submit booklets related to their most famous works for publication.
sentence_230: Rowling's two booklets, [[Fantastic_Beasts_and_Where_to_Find_Them|Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them]] and [[Quidditch_Through_the_Ages|Quidditch Through the Ages]], are ostensibly facsimiles of books found in the Hogwarts library.

sentence_234: In 2005, Rowling and MEP [[Emma_Nicholson|Emma Nicholson]] founded the Children's High Level Group (now [[Lumos_(charity)|Lumos]]).

sentence_239: In 2008, Rowling agreed to publish the book with the proceeds going to Lumos.

sentence_243: M. Barrie]]'s [[Peter_Pan|Peter Pan]] as part of a tribute to [[Great_Ormond_Street_Hospital_for_Children|Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children]].
sentence_244: An inflatable representation of [[Lord_Voldemort|Lord Voldemort]] and other children's literary characters accompanied her reading.
sentence_245: Rowling has contributed money and support for research and treatment of [[Multiple_sclerosis|multiple sclerosis]], from which her mother suffered before her death in 1990.
sentence_246: In 2006, Rowling contributed a substantial sum toward the creation of a new Centre for Regenerative Medicine at [[Edinburgh_University|Edinburgh University]], later named the Anne Rowling Regenerative Neurology Clinic.
sentence_247: In 2010, she donated another £10 million to the centre, and in 2019 a further £15 million.
sentence_248: For unknown reasons, Scotland, Rowling's country of adoption, has the highest rate of multiple sclerosis in the world.
sentence_249: In 2003, Rowling took part in a campaign to establish a national standard of care for MS sufferers.
sentence_250: In April 2009, she announced that she was withdrawing her support for [[Multiple_Sclerosis_Society_of_Great_Britain|Multiple Sclerosis Society]] Scotland, citing her inability to resolve an ongoing feud between the organisation's northern and southern branches that had sapped morale and led to several resignations.
sentence_251: In May 2008, bookseller [[Waterstones|Waterstones]] asked Rowling and 12 other writers ([[Lisa_Appignanesi|Lisa Appignanesi]], [[Margaret_Atwood|Margaret Atwood]], Lauren Child, [[Sebastian_Faulks|Sebastian Faulks]], [[Richard_Ford|Richard Ford]], [[Neil_Gaiman|Neil Gaiman]], [[Nick_Hornby|Nick Hornby]], [[Doris_Lessing|Doris Lessing]], [[Michael_Rosen|Michael Rosen]], [[Axel_Scheffler|Axel Scheffler]], [[Tom_Stoppard|Tom Stoppard]] and Irvine Welsh) to compose a short piece of their own choosing on a single [[ISO_216|A5]] card, which would then be sold at auction in aid of the charities Dyslexia Action and English [[International_PEN|PEN]].
sentence_252: Rowling's contribution was an 800-word [[Harry_Potter_prequel|Harry Potter prequel]] that concerns Harry's father, [[James_Potter_(character)|James Potter]], and godfather, [[Sirius_Black|Sirius Black]], and takes place three years before Harry was born.
sentence_253: The cards were collated and sold for charity in book form in August 2008.
sentence_254: On 1 and 2 August 2006, she read alongside [[Stephen_King|Stephen King]] and [[John_Irving|John Irving]] at [[Radio_City_Music_Hall|Radio City Music Hall]] in New York City.
sentence_255: Profits from the event were donated to the Haven Foundation, a charity that aids artists and performers left uninsurable and unable to work, and the medical NGO [[Médecins_Sans_Frontières|Médecins Sans Frontières]].
sentence_256: In May 2007, Rowling pledged a donation reported as over £250,000 to a reward fund started by the tabloid [[News_of_the_World|News of the World]] for the safe return of a young British girl, [[Disappearance_of_Madeleine_McCann|Madeleine McCann]], who disappeared in Portugal.
sentence_257: Rowling, along with [[Nelson_Mandela|Nelson Mandela]], [[Al_Gore|Al Gore]], and [[Alan_Greenspan|Alan Greenspan]], wrote an introduction to a collection of Gordon Brown's speeches, the proceeds of which were donated to the Jennifer Brown Research Laboratory.
sentence_258: After her exposure as the true author of The Cuckoo's Calling led to a massive increase in sales, Rowling announced she would donate all her royalties to the Army Benevolent Fund, claiming she had always intended to but never expected the book to be a best-seller.
sentence_259: Rowling is a member of both English PEN and Scottish PEN.
sentence_260: She was one of 50 authors to contribute to First Editions, Second Thoughts, a charity auction for English PEN.

sentence_262: The book was the highest-selling lot of the event and fetched £150,000 ($228,600).
sentence_263: Rowling is a supporter of the [[The_Shannon_Trust|Shannon Trust]], which runs the Toe by Toe Reading Plan and the Shannon Reading Plan in prisons across Britain, helping and giving tutoring to prisoners who cannot read.
sentence_264: See also: [[Harry_Potter_influences_and_analogues|Harry Potter influences and analogues]]
sentence_265: Rowling has named [[Civil_rights|civil rights]] activist [[Jessica_Mitford|Jessica Mitford]] as her greatest influence.
sentence_266: She said "Jessica Mitford has been my heroine since I was 14 years old, when I overheard my formidable great-aunt discussing how Mitford had run away at the age of 19 to fight with the Reds in the [[Spanish_Civil_War|Spanish Civil War]]", and claims what inspired her about Mitford was that she was "incurably and instinctively rebellious, brave, adventurous, funny and irreverent, she liked nothing better than a good fight, preferably against a pompous and hypocritical target".
sentence_267: Rowling has described [[Jane_Austen|Jane Austen]] as her favourite author, calling [[Emma_(novel)|Emma]] her favourite book in [[O,_The_Oprah_Magazine|O, The Oprah Magazine]].
