sentence_270: See also: [[Politics_of_J._K._Rowling|Politics of J. K. Rowling]] and [[Politics_of_Harry_Potter|Politics of Harry Potter]]
sentence_271: To many, Rowling is known for her [[Centre-left_politics|centre-left]] political views.
sentence_272: In September 2008, on the eve of the [[Labour_Party_Conference|Labour Party Conference]], Rowling announced that she had donated £1 million to the [[Labour_Party_(UK)|Labour Party]], and publicly endorsed Labour Prime Minister [[Gordon_Brown|Gordon Brown]] over [[Conservative_Party_(UK)|Conservative]] challenger [[David_Cameron|David Cameron]], praising Labour's policies on child poverty.
sentence_273: Rowling is a close friend of [[Sarah_Brown_(spouse)|Sarah Brown]], wife of Gordon Brown, whom she met when they collaborated on a charitable project for One Parent Families.
sentence_274: Rowling has also commented on American politics, having discussed the [[2008_United_States_presidential_election|2008 United States presidential election]] in the Spanish-language newspaper [[El_País|El País]] in February 2008.
sentence_275: Rowling stating that the election would have a profound effect on the rest of the world, and commented that [[Barack_Obama|Barack Obama]] and [[Hillary_Clinton|Hillary Clinton]] would be "extraordinary" if elected into office.
sentence_276: In the same interview, Rowling identified [[Robert_F._Kennedy|Robert F. Kennedy]] as her hero.
sentence_277: In April 2010, an article by Rowling was published in [[The_Times|The Times]], in which she criticised then Conservative Prime Minister David Cameron's plan to encourage married couples to stay together by offering them a £150 annual tax credit: "Nobody who has ever experienced the reality of poverty could say 'it's not the money, it's the message'.
sentence_278: When your flat has been broken into, and you cannot afford a locksmith, it is the money.
sentence_279: When you are two pence short of a tin of baked beans, and your child is hungry, it is the money.
sentence_280: When you find yourself contemplating shoplifting to get nappies, it is the money."
sentence_281: Due to her residency in Scotland, Rowling was eligible to vote in the 2014 [[2014_Scottish_independence_referendum|referendum on Scottish independence]], during the run up to which she campaigned for the "No" vote.
sentence_282: She donated £1 million to the [[Better_Together_(campaign)|Better Together]] anti-independence campaign run by her former neighbour [[Alistair_Darling|Alistair Darling]], the largest donation it had received at the time.
sentence_283: In a blog post, Rowling explained that an open letter from Scottish medical professionals raised problems with First Minister [[Alex_Salmond|Alex Salmond]]'s plans for a common research funding.
sentence_284: Rowling compared some Scottish Nationalists with the [[Death_Eaters|Death Eaters]], characters from Harry Potter who are scornful of those without pure blood.
sentence_285: On 22 October 2015, a letter was published in [[The_Guardian|The Guardian]] signed by Rowling (along with over 150 other figures from arts and politics) opposing the cultural boycott of Israel, and announcing the creation of a network for dialogue, called Culture for Coexistence.
sentence_286: Rowling later explained her position in greater detail, stating that although she opposed most of [[Benjamin_Netanyahu|Benjamin Netanyahu]]'s actions, she did not believe the cultural boycott would bring about the removal of Israel's leader or the improvement of the situation in Israel and Palestine.
sentence_287: In June 2016, Rowling campaigned for the United Kingdom to stay in the [[European_Union|European Union]] in the run up to the [[2016_United_Kingdom_European_Union_membership_referendum|2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum]], stating on her website that, "I'm the mongrel product of this European continent and I'm an internationalist.
sentence_288: I was raised by a Francophile mother whose family was proud of their part-French heritage ... My values are not contained or proscribed by borders.
sentence_289: The absence of a visa when I cross the channel has symbolic value to me.
sentence_290: I might not be in my house, but I'm still in my hometown."
sentence_291: Rowling expressed concern that "racists and bigots" were directing parts of the Leave campaign.
sentence_292: In a blog post, she added: "How can a retreat into selfish and insecure individualism be the right response when Europe faces genuine threats, when the bonds that tie us are so powerful, when we have come so far together?
sentence_293: How can we hope to conquer the enormous challenges of terrorism and climate change without cooperation and collaboration?"
sentence_294: See also: [[Religious_debates_over_the_Harry_Potter_series|Religious debates over the Harry Potter series]]
sentence_295: Some religious people, figures and organisations have, over the years, objected to and decried Rowling's books for the perceived promotion of witchcraft.
sentence_296: Many objections have come from Christians in particular, though Rowling herself has stated that she identifies as a Christian, stating that "I believe in God, not magic."
sentence_297: Early on in writing the Harry Potter series of books and in response to criticism, Rowling disclosed her religious beliefs, feeling that if readers knew of her religious views, they would be able to predict plot lines of characters in her books.
sentence_298: In 2007, Rowling stated that she was the only person in her family who attended church regularly, and that she was an adherent of the Church of England.
sentence_299: As a student, she had previously been annoyed at the "smugness of religious people", and had attended less often.
sentence_300: Later, she began attending a [[Church_of_Scotland|Church of Scotland]] congregation around the time she was writing Harry Potter.
sentence_301: Her eldest daughter, Jessica, was baptised there.
sentence_302: In a 2006 interview with [[Tatler_(1901)|Tatler]], Rowling noted that, "like [[Graham_Greene|Graham Greene]], my faith is sometimes about if my faith will return.
sentence_303: It's important to me."
sentence_304: She has said that she has struggled with doubt, that she believes in an afterlife, and that her faith plays a part in her books.
sentence_305: In a 2012 radio interview, Rowling stated that she was a member of the [[Scottish_Episcopal_Church|Scottish Episcopal Church]], a province of the [[Anglican_Communion|Anglican Communion]].
sentence_306: In 2015, following the [[Same-sex_marriage_in_the_Republic_of_Ireland|referendum on same-sex marriage in Ireland]], Rowling joked that if Ireland legalised same-sex marriage, Dumbledore and [[Gandalf|Gandalf]] could get married there.
sentence_307: The [[Westboro_Baptist_Church|Westboro Baptist Church]], in response, stated that if the two got married, they would picket.

sentence_317: As one journalist noted, "Harry's [[Vernon_Dursley|Uncle Vernon]] is a grotesque philistine of violent tendencies and remarkably little brain.
sentence_318: It is not difficult to guess which newspaper Rowling gives him to read [in [[Harry_Potter_and_the_Goblet_of_Fire|Goblet of Fire]]."
sentence_319: In 2014, she successfully sued the Mail for libel over an article about her time as a single mother.
sentence_320: Some have speculated that Rowling's fraught relationship with the press was the inspiration behind the character [[Rita_Skeeter|Rita Skeeter]], a gossipy celebrity journalist who first appears in Goblet of Fire, but Rowling said in 2000 that the character's development predates her rise to fame.
sentence_321: In September 2011, Rowling was named as a "core participant" in the [[Leveson_Inquiry|Leveson Inquiry]] into the culture, practices and ethics of the British press, as one of dozens of celebrities who may have been the victim of [[Phone_hacking|phone hacking]].
sentence_322: On 24 November 2011, Rowling gave evidence before the inquiry; although she was not suspected to have been the victim of phone hacking, her testimony included accounts of photographers camping on her doorstep, her fiancé being duped into giving his home address to a journalist masquerading as a tax official, her chasing a journalist a week after giving birth, a journalist leaving a note inside her then-five year old daughter's schoolbag, and an attempt by [[The_Sun_(United_Kingdom)|The Sun]] to "blackmail" her into a photo opportunity in exchange for the return of a stolen manuscript.
sentence_323: Rowling claimed she had to leave her former home in Merchiston because of press intrusion.
sentence_324: In November 2012, Rowling wrote an article for [[The_Guardian|The Guardian]] in reaction to David Cameron's decision not to implement the full recommendations of the Leveson inquiry, saying she felt "duped and angry".
sentence_325: In 2014, Rowling reaffirmed her support for "Hacked Off", a campaign supporting the self-regulation of the press, by co-signing a declaration to "[safeguard] the press from political interference while also giving vital protection to the vulnerable" with other British celebrities.
sentence_326: See also: [[Politics_of_J._K._Rowling#Transgender_people|Politics of J. K. Rowling § Transgender people]]
sentence_327: In December 2019, Rowling [[Tweeting|tweeted]] her support for Maya Forstater, a British woman who lost her employment tribunal case against her former employer, the Center for Global Development, after her contract was not renewed due to her comments about [[Transgender|transgender]] people.
sentence_328: The tribunal ruled that Forstater's statements about transgender people, including the misgendering of a person, promoted "an intimidating, hostile, degrading, humiliating or offensive environment", and were not protected beliefs under the [[Equality_Act_2010|Equality Act 2010]].
sentence_329: As of February 2020, Forstater is appealing the judgment.
sentence_330: On 6 June 2020, Rowling tweeted criticism of the phrase "people who menstruate", and stated "If sex isn't real, the lived reality of women globally is erased.
sentence_331: I know and love trans people, but erasing the concept of sex removes the ability of many to meaningfully discuss their lives."
sentence_332: The term "people who menstruate" is used to include some trans men and non-binary people who also menstruate.
sentence_333: Rowling's tweets were criticised by [[GLAAD|GLAAD]], who called them "cruel" and "anti-trans".
sentence_334: Some members of the cast of the Harry Potter film series criticised Rowling's views or spoke out in support of trans rights, including [[Daniel_Radcliffe|Daniel Radcliffe]], [[Emma_Watson|Emma Watson]], [[Rupert_Grint|Rupert Grint]], [[Bonnie_Wright|Bonnie Wright]], and [[Katie_Leung|Katie Leung]], as did Fantastic Beasts lead actor [[Eddie_Redmayne|Eddie Redmayne]] and the fansites [[MuggleNet|MuggleNet]] and [[The_Leaky_Cauldron_(website)|The Leaky Cauldron]].
sentence_335: Actress [[Noma_Dumezweni|Noma Dumezweni]] (who played Hermione Granger in [[Harry_Potter_and_the_Cursed_Child|Harry Potter and the Cursed Child]]) initially expressed support for Rowling but backtracked following backlash.
sentence_336: On 10 June 2020, Rowling published a 3,600-word essay on her website in response to the criticism.
sentence_337: She said that she was a survivor of [[Domestic_violence|domestic abuse]] and [[Sexual_assault|sexual assault]], and stated that "When you throw open the doors of bathrooms and changing rooms to any man who believes or feels he's a woman ... then you open the door to any and all men who wish to come inside", while stating that most trans people were vulnerable and deserved protection.
sentence_338: She also wrote that many women consider terms like "people who menstruate" to be demeaning.
sentence_339: The essay was criticised by, among others, the children's charity [[Mermaids_(charity)|Mermaids]], who support transgender and gender non-conforming children and their parents.
sentence_340: Rowling has been referred to as a [[TERF|trans-exclusionary radical feminist (TERF)]] on multiple occasions, though she rejects the label.
sentence_341: Rowling has received support from actors [[Robbie_Coltrane|Robbie Coltrane]] and [[Brian_Cox_(actor)|Brian Cox]], and some feminists such as activist [[Ayaan_Hirsi_Ali|Ayaan Hirsi Ali]] and [[Radical_feminism|radical feminist]] [[Julie_Bindel|Julie Bindel]].
sentence_342: In August 2020, Rowling returned her [[Robert_F._Kennedy_Human_Rights_Award|Robert F. Kennedy Human Rights Award]] after [[Kerry_Kennedy|Kerry Kennedy]] released a statement expressing her "profound disappointment" in Rowling's "attacks upon the transgender community", which Kennedy called "inconsistent with the fundamental beliefs and values of RFK Human Rights and ... a repudiation of my father's vision".
sentence_343: Rowling stated that she was "deeply saddened" by Kennedy's statement, but maintained that no award would encourage her to "forfeit the right to follow the dictates" of her conscience.
sentence_344: Main article: [[Legal_disputes_over_the_Harry_Potter_series|Legal disputes over the Harry Potter series]]
sentence_345: Rowling, her publishers, and [[Time_Warner|Time Warner]], the owner of the rights to the [[Harry_Potter_(film_series)|Harry Potter films]], have taken numerous legal actions to protect their copyright.
sentence_346: The worldwide popularity of the Harry Potter series has led to the appearance of a number of locally produced, unauthorised sequels and other derivative works, sparking efforts to ban or contain them.
sentence_347: Another area of legal dispute involves a series of injunctions obtained by Rowling and her publishers to prohibit anyone from reading her books before their official release date.
sentence_348: The injunction drew fire from civil liberties and free speech campaigners and sparked debates over the "right to read".
sentence_349: Rowling has received honorary degrees from [[University_of_St_Andrews|St Andrews University]], the [[University_of_Edinburgh|University of Edinburgh]], [[Edinburgh_Napier_University|Edinburgh Napier University]], the [[University_of_Exeter|University of Exeter]] (which she attended), the [[University_of_Aberdeen|University of Aberdeen]], and [[Harvard_University|Harvard University]], where she spoke at the 2008 commencement ceremony.
sentence_350: In 2009, Rowling was made a Chevalier de la [[Légion_d'honneur|Légion d'honneur]] by French President [[Nicolas_Sarkozy|Nicolas Sarkozy]].
sentence_351: In 2002, Rowling became an [[Honorary_Fellow_of_the_Royal_Society_of_Edinburgh|Honorary Fellow of the Royal Society of Edinburgh]] (HonFRSE) as well a [[Fellow_of_the_Royal_Society_of_Literature|Fellow of the Royal Society of Literature]] (FRSL).
sentence_352: She was furthermore recognized as [[Fellow_of_the_Royal_College_of_Physicians_of_Edinburgh|Fellow of the Royal College of Physicians of Edinburgh]] (FRCPE) in 2011 for services to Literature and Philanthropy.
sentence_353: Other awards include:

sentence_0: The Kalmar Union ([[Danish_language|Danish]], [[Norwegian_language|Norwegian]], and [[Swedish_language|Swedish]]: Kalmarunionen; [[Latin_language|Latin]]: Unio Calmariensis) was a personal union in [[Scandinavia|Scandinavia]], agreed at [[Kalmar|Kalmar]] in Sweden, that from 1397 to 1523 joined under a single monarch the three kingdoms of [[Denmark|Denmark]], [[Sweden|Sweden]] (then including most of present-day [[Finland|Finland]]), and [[Norway|Norway]], together with [[List_of_possessions_of_Norway#Former_dependencies_and_homelands|Norway's overseas dependencies]] (then including [[Iceland|Iceland]], [[Greenland|Greenland]], the Faroe Islands, and the [[Northern_Isles|Northern Isles]] of [[Orkney|Orkney]] and [[Shetland|Shetland]]).
sentence_1: The union was not quite continuous; there were several short interruptions.
sentence_2: Legally, the countries remained separate sovereign states.
sentence_3: However, their domestic and foreign policies were directed by a common monarch.
sentence_4: [[Gustav_Vasa|Gustav Vasa]]'s election as king on 6 June 1523, and his triumphant entry into Stockholm eleven days later, marked Sweden's final secession from the Kalmar Union.
sentence_5: Formally, the Danish king acknowledged Sweden's independence 1524 at the [[Treaty_of_Malmö|Treaty of Malmö]].
sentence_6: The union was the work of Scandinavian aristocracy wishing to counter the influence of the [[Hanseatic_League|Hanseatic League]].
sentence_7: More personally, it was achieved by Queen [[Margaret_I_of_Denmark|Margaret I of Denmark]] (1353–1412).
sentence_8: She was a daughter of King Valdemar IV and had married King [[Haakon_VI_of_Norway|Haakon VI of Norway]] and Sweden, who was the son of King [[Magnus_IV_of_Sweden|Magnus IV of Sweden]], Norway and [[Scania|Scania]].
sentence_9: Margaret succeeded in having her son [[Olaf_II_of_Denmark|Olaf]] recognized as heir to the throne of Denmark.
sentence_10: In 1376 Olaf inherited the crown of Denmark from his maternal grandfather as King Olaf II, with his mother as guardian; when Haakon VI died in 1380, Olaf also inherited the crown of Norway.
sentence_11: Margaret became regent of Denmark and Norway when Olaf died in 1387, leaving her without an heir.
sentence_12: She adopted her great-nephew [[Eric_of_Pomerania|Eric of Pomerania]] the same year.
sentence_13: The following year, 1388, Swedish nobles called upon her help against King [[Albert,_King_of_Sweden|Albert]].
sentence_14: After Margaret defeated Albert in 1389, her heir Eric was proclaimed King of Norway.
sentence_15: Eric was subsequently elected King of Denmark and Sweden in 1396.
sentence_16: His coronation was held in [[Kalmar|Kalmar]] on 17 June 1397.
sentence_17: One main impetus for its formation was to block German expansion northward into the [[Baltic_region|Baltic region]].
sentence_18: The main reason for its failure to survive was the perpetual struggle between the monarch, who wanted a strong unified state, and the Swedish and Danish nobility, which did not.
sentence_19: Diverging interests (especially the [[Swedish_nobility|Swedish nobility]]'s dissatisfaction with the dominant role played by Denmark and [[Holstein|Holstein]]) gave rise to a conflict that would hamper the union in several intervals starting in the 1430s.
sentence_20: [[Charles_VIII_of_Sweden|Charles Bonde]], for example, was made king of Sweden three times by nationalists there, in 1440, 1464 and 1467.
sentence_21: The Union lost territory when the [[Northern_Isles|Northern Isles]] were [[Pledge_(law)|pledged]] by Christian I, in his capacity as King of Norway, as security against the payment of the [[Dowry|dowry]] of his daughter [[Margaret_of_Denmark,_Queen_of_Scotland|Margaret]], betrothed to [[James_III_of_Scotland|James III of Scotland]] in 1468.
sentence_22: The money was never paid, so in 1472 the islands were annexed by the [[Kingdom_of_Scotland|Kingdom of Scotland]].
sentence_23: In practice, the Kalmar Union fell apart when Sweden rebelled and became independent on 6 June 1523 and [[Gustav_I_of_Sweden|Gustav I of Sweden]] was elected as king there.
sentence_24: After the Northern Seven Years' War, the [[Treaty_of_Stettin_(1570)|Treaty of Stettin (1570)]] saw [[Frederick_II_of_Denmark|Frederick II]] renounce all claims to Sweden, officially dissolving the union.
sentence_25: One of the last structures of the Union remained until 1536/1537 when the Danish Privy Council, in the aftermath of the [[Count's_Feud|Count's Feud]], unilaterally declared Norway to be a Danish province: this did not happen; instead, Norway became a hereditary kingdom in a real union with Denmark.
sentence_26: Norway continued to remain a part of the realm of Denmark–Norway under the [[House_of_Oldenburg|Oldenburg dynasty]] for nearly three centuries, until it was [[Norway_in_1814|transferred to Sweden]] in 1814.
sentence_27: The ensuing [[Union_between_Sweden_and_Norway|union between Sweden and Norway]] lasted until 1905, when a grandson of both the [[Christian_IX_of_Denmark|incumbent king of Denmark]] and the [[Charles_XV_of_Sweden|late king of Sweden]] was elected king of Norway.

sentence_0: Toshiki Kaifu (海部 俊樹, Kaifu Toshiki, born 2 January 1931) is a Japanese politician who was [[Prime_Minister_of_Japan|Prime Minister of Japan]] from 1989 to 1991.
sentence_1: Kaifu was born in [[Nagoya_City|Nagoya City]], [[Aichi_Prefecture|Aichi Prefecture]], on 2 January 1931.
sentence_2: He was educated at Chuo University and [[Waseda_University|Waseda University]].
sentence_3: A member of the [[Liberal_Democratic_Party_(Japan)|Liberal Democratic Party]] (LDP), Kaifu ran successfully for the 1960 Japanese general election and took office as the youngest member of the [[National_Diet|National Diet]].
sentence_4: He served for sixteen terms, totaling 49 years.
sentence_5: Kaifu was education minister before rising to lead the party after the resignations of [[Takeshita_Noboru|Takeshita Noboru]] and [[Sōsuke_Uno|Sōsuke Uno]].
sentence_6: Facing [[Yoshiro_Hayashi_(politician)|Yoshiro Hayashi]] and [[Shintaro_Ishihara|Shintaro Ishihara]], Kaifu was elected on the platform of clean leadership.
sentence_7: He became the 76th [[Prime_Minister_of_Japan|Prime Minister of Japan]] in August 1989.
sentence_8: On 10 August 1991, Kaifu became the first leader of a major country to make an official visit to China and break China's diplomatic isolation after the [[1989_Tiananmen_Square_protests|Tiananmen Square Incident]] of June 4, 1989.
sentence_9: Kaifu ended Japan's participation in economic sanctions against China and offered $949.9 million in loans and an additional $1.5 million in emergency aid following flood damage in southern China in June and July.
sentence_10: Throughout his two Cabinets, Kaifu's faction was too small to push through the reforms he sought, and the continuing repercussions of the [[Sagawa_Express|Sagawa Express]] scandal caused problems.
sentence_11: He resigned in November 1991 and was replaced by [[Kiichi_Miyazawa|Kiichi Miyazawa]].
sentence_12: In 1994, he left the LDP to become head of the newly founded [[New_Frontier_Party_(Japan)|New Frontier Party]].
sentence_13: He supported Ichirō Ozawa's party until he returned to LDP in 2003.
sentence_14: He was defeated in the election of 2009 by DPJ candidate [[Mitsunori_Okamoto|Mitsunori Okamoto]], which witnessed the end of almost uninterrupted LDP dominance since 1955.
sentence_15: At the time of his defeat, he was the longest-serving member of the lower house of the [[Diet_of_Japan|Diet]], and he was also the first former prime minister to be defeated at a re-election since 1963.
sentence_16: From the corresponding article in the Japanese Wikipedia

sentence_17: Kaifu is one of several world leaders depicted on the cover of [[Megadeth|Megadeth]]'s 1990 album [[Rust_in_Peace|Rust in Peace]].

title: Longitude
sentence_0: For Dava Sobel's book about John Harrison, see [[Longitude_(book)|Longitude (book)]].
sentence_1: For the adaptation of Sobel's book, see [[Longitude_(TV_series)|Longitude (TV series)]].
sentence_2: For other uses, see [[Longitude_(disambiguation)|Longitude (disambiguation)]].
sentence_3: Longitude ([[English|/ˈlɒndʒɪtjuːd/]], AU and UK also [[English|/ˈlɒŋɡɪ-/]]), is a [[Geographic_coordinate_system|geographic coordinate]] that specifies the [[East|east]]–west position of a point on the Earth's surface, or the surface of a celestial body.
sentence_4: It is an angular measurement, usually expressed in [[Degree_(angle)|degrees]] and denoted by the [[Greek_alphabet|Greek letter]] lambda (λ).
sentence_5: [[Meridian_(geography)|Meridians]] (lines running from [[Geographical_pole|pole]] to pole) connect points with the same longitude.
sentence_6: The [[Prime_meridian|prime meridian]], which passes near the [[Royal_Observatory,_Greenwich|Royal Observatory, Greenwich]], England, is defined as 0° longitude by convention.
sentence_7: Positive longitudes are east of the prime meridian, and negative ones are west.
sentence_8: Because of the earth's rotation, there is a close connection between longitude and time.
sentence_9: Local time (for example from the position of the sun) varies with longitude, a difference of 15° longitude corresponding to a one-hour difference in local time.
sentence_10: Comparing local time to an absolute measure of time allows longitude to be determined.
sentence_11: Depending on the era, the absolute time might be obtained from a celestial event visible from both locations, such as a lunar eclipse, or from a time signal transmitted by telegraph or wireless.
sentence_12: The principle is straightforward, but in practice finding a reliable method of determining longitude took centuries and required the effort of some of the greatest scientific minds.
sentence_13: A location's [[North|north]]–[[South|south]] position along a meridian is given by its latitude, which is approximately the angle between the local vertical and the equatorial plane.
sentence_14: Longitude is generally given using the geometrical or astronomical vertical.
sentence_15: This can differ slightly from the gravitational vertical because of small variations in Earth's gravitational field.
sentence_16: Main article: [[History_of_longitude|History of longitude]]
sentence_17: The concept of longitude was first developed by ancient Greek astronomers.
sentence_18: [[Hipparchus|Hipparchus]] (2nd century BCE) used a coordinate system that assumed a spherical earth, and divided it into 360° as we still do today.
sentence_19: His [[Prime_meridian|prime meridian]] passed through [[Alexandria|Alexandria]].
sentence_20: He also proposed a method of determining longitude by comparing the local time of a [[Lunar_eclipse|lunar eclipse]] at two different places, thus demonstrating an understanding of the relationship between longitude and time.. [[Ptolemy|Claudius Ptolemy]] (2nd century CE) developed a mapping system using curved parallels that reduced distortion.
sentence_21: He also collected data for many locations, from Britain to the Middle East.
sentence_22: He used a prime meridian through the Canary Islands, so that all longitude values would be positive.
sentence_23: While Ptolemy's system was sound, the data he used were often poor, leading to a gross over-estimate (by about 70%) of the length of the Mediterranean.
sentence_24: After the fall of the Roman Empire, interest in geography greatly declined in Europe.
sentence_25: Hindu and Muslim astronomers continued to develop these ideas, adding many new locations and often improving on Ptolemy's data.
sentence_26: For example [[Al-Battani|al-Battānī]] used simultaneous observations of two lunar eclipses to determine the difference in longitude between [[Antakya|Antakya]] and [[Raqqa|Raqqa]] with an error of less than 1°.
sentence_27: This is considered to be the best that can be achieved with the methods then available - observation of the eclipse with the naked eye, and determination of local time using an [[Astrolabe|astrolabe]] to measure the altitude of a suitable "clock star".
sentence_28: In the later Middle Ages, interest in geography revived in the west, as travel increased, and Arab scholarship began to be known through contact with Spain and North Africa.
sentence_29: In the 12th Century, astronomical tables were prepared for a number of European cities, based on the work of [[Abū_Ishāq_Ibrāhīm_al-Zarqālī|al-Zarqālī]] in [[Toledo,_Spain|Toledo]].
sentence_30: The lunar eclipse of September 12, 1178 was used to establish the longitude differences between Toledo, [[Marseille|Marseilles]], and [[Hereford|Hereford]].
sentence_31: Christopher Columbus made two attempts to use lunar eclipses to discover his longitude, the first in Saona Island, on 14 September 1494 (second voyage), and the second in [[Jamaica|Jamaica]] on 29 February 1504 (fourth voyage).
sentence_32: It is assumed that he used astronomical tables for reference.
sentence_33: His determinations of longitude showed large errors of 13 and 38° W respectively.
sentence_34: Randles (1985) documents longitude measurement by the Portuguese and Spanish between 1514 and 1627 both in the Americas and Asia.
sentence_35: Errors ranged from 2-25°.
sentence_36: The telescope was invented in the early 17th-century.
sentence_37: Initially an observation device, developments over the next half century transformed it into an accurate measurement tool.
sentence_38: The [[Pendulum_clock|pendulum clock]] was patented by [[Christiaan_Huygens|Christiaan Huygens]] in 1657 and gave an increase in accuracy of about 30 fold over previous mechanical clocks.
sentence_39: These two inventions would revolutionize observational astronomy and cartography.
sentence_40: The main methods for dermining longitude are listed below.
sentence_41: With one exception (magnetic declination) they all depend on a common principle, which was to determine an absolute time from an event or measurement and to compare the corresponding local time at two different locations.

list.value: [[Lunar_distance_(navigation)|Lunar distances]]. In its orbit around the earth, the moon moves relative to the stars at a rate of just over 0.5°/hour. The angle between the moon and a suitable star is measured with a [[Sextant|sextant]], and (after consultation with tables and lengthy calculations) gives a value for absolute time.

Satellites of Jupiter. [[Galileo_Galilei|Galileo]] proposed that with sufficiently accurate knowledge of the orbits of the satellites, their positions could provide a measure of absolute time. The method requires a telescope, as the moons are not visible to the naked eye.

Appulses, occultations, and eclipses. An [[Appulse|appulse]] is the least apparent distance between two objects (the moon a star or a planet), an [[Occultation|occultation]] occurs when a star or planet passes behind the moon — essentially a type of eclipse. Lunar eclipses continued to be used. The times of any of these events can be used as the measure of absolute time.

[[Marine_chronometer|Chronometers]]. A clock is set to the local time of a starting point whose longitude is known, and the longitude of any other place can be determined by comparing its local time with the clock time.

Magnetic declination. A compass needle does not in general point exactly north. The [[Magnetic_declination|variation]] from true north varies with location, and it was suggested that this could provide a basis for determination of longitude.

sentence_42: With the exception of magnetic declination, all proved practicable methods.
sentence_43: Developments on land and sea, however, were very different.
sentence_44: On land, the period from the development of telescopes and pendulum clocks until the mid 18th-Century saw a steady increase in the number of places whose longitude had been determined with reasonable accuracy, often with errors of less than a degree, and nearly always within 2-3°.
sentence_45: By the 1720s errors were consistently less than 1°.
sentence_46: At sea during the same period, the situation was very different.
sentence_47: Two problems proved intractable.
sentence_48: The first was the need of a navigator for immediate results.
sentence_49: The second was the marine environment.
sentence_50: Making accurate observations in an ocean swell is much harder than on land, and pendulum clocks do not work well in these conditions.
sentence_51: In response to the problems of navigation, a number of European maritime powers offered prizes for a method to determine longitude at sea.
sentence_52: The best-known of these is the [[Longitude_Act|Longitude Act]] passed by the British parliament in 1714.
sentence_53: It offered two levels of rewards, for solutions within 1° and 0.5°.
sentence_54: Rewards were given for two solutions: lunar distances, made practicable by the tables of Tobias Mayer developed into an [[Nautical_almanac|nautical almanac]] by the Astronomer Royal [[Neville_Maskelyne|Neville Maskelyne]]; and for the chronometers developed by the Yorkshire carpenter and clock-maker John Harrison.
sentence_55: Harrison built five chronometers over more than three decades.
sentence_56: However, he was not awarded the prize by the Longitude Board and was forced to fight for his reward, finally receiving payment in 1773, after the intervention of parliament.
sentence_57: It was some while before either method became widely used in navigation.
sentence_58: In the early years, chronometers were very expensive, and the calculations required for lunar distances were still complex and time-consuming.
sentence_59: Lunar distances came into general use after 1790.
sentence_60: Chronometers had the advantages that both the observations and the calculations were simpler, and as they became cheaper in the early 19th-Century they started to replace lunars, which were seldom used after 1850.
sentence_61: The first working telegraphs were established in Britain by [[Charles_Wheatstone|Wheatstone]] and [[William_Fothergill_Cooke|Cooke]] in 1839, and in the US by [[Samuel_Morse|Morse]] in 1844.
sentence_62: It was quickly realised that the telegraph could be used to transmit a time signal for longitude determination.
sentence_63: The method was soon in practical use for longitude determination, especially in North America, and over longer and longer distances as the telegraph network expanded, including western Europe with the completion of transatlantic cables.
sentence_64: The [[U.S._National_Geodetic_Survey|US Coast Survey]] was particularly active in this development, and not just in the United States.
sentence_65: The Survey established chains of mapped locations through Central and South America, and the West Indies, and as far as Japan and China in the years 1874–90.
sentence_66: This contributed greatly to the accurate mapping of these areas.
sentence_67: While mariners benefited from the accurate charts, they could not receive telegraph signals while under way, and so could not use the method for navigation.
sentence_68: This changed when wireless telegraphy became available in the early 20th-Century.
sentence_69: Wireless time signals for the use of ships were transmitted from [[Halifax,_Nova_Scotia|Halifax, Nova Scotia]], starting in 1907 and from the [[Eiffel_Tower|Eiffel Tower]] in Paris from 1910.
sentence_70: These signals allowed navigators to check and adjust their chronometers on a frequent basis.
sentence_71: Radio navigation systems came into general use after [[World_War_II|World War II]].
sentence_72: The systems all depended on transmissions from fixed navigational beacons.
sentence_73: A ship-board receiver calculated the vessel's position from these transmissions.
sentence_74: They allowed accurate navigation when poor visibility prevented astronomical observations, and became the established method for commercial shipping until replaced by [[Global_Positioning_System|GPS]] in the early 1990s.
sentence_75: Longitude is given as an [[Angle|angular measurement]] ranging from 0° at the Prime Meridian to +180° eastward and −180° westward.
sentence_76: The Greek letter λ (lambda), is used to denote the location of a place on Earth east or west of the Prime Meridian.
sentence_77: Each degree of longitude is sub-divided into 60 [[Minute_of_arc|minutes]], each of which is divided into 60 [[Arcsecond|seconds]].
sentence_78: A longitude is thus specified in [[Sexagesimal|sexagesimal]] notation as 23° 27′ 30″ E. For higher precision, the seconds are specified with a [[Decimal#Decimal_fractions|decimal fraction]].
sentence_79: An alternative representation uses degrees and minutes, where parts of a minute are expressed in decimal notation with a fraction, thus: 23° 27.5′ E. Degrees may also be expressed as a decimal fraction: 23.45833° E. For calculations, the angular measure may be converted to [[Radian|radians]], so longitude may also be expressed in this manner as a signed fraction of π ([[Pi|pi]]), or an unsigned fraction of 2π.
sentence_80: For calculations, the West/East suffix is replaced by a negative sign in the [[Western_hemisphere|western hemisphere]].
sentence_81: The international standard convention (ISO 6709)—that East is positive—is consistent with a right-handed Cartesian coordinate system, with the North Pole up.
sentence_82: A specific longitude may then be combined with a specific latitude (positive in the northern hemisphere) to give a precise position on the Earth's surface.
sentence_83: Confusingly, the convention of negative for East is also sometimes seen, most commonly in the [[United_States|United States]]; the [[Earth_System_Research_Laboratory|Earth System Research Laboratory]] used it on an older version of one of their pages, in order "to make coordinate entry less awkward" for applications confined to the [[Western_Hemisphere|Western Hemisphere]].
sentence_84: They have since shifted to the standard approach.
sentence_85: There is no other physical principle determining longitude directly but with time.
sentence_86: Longitude at a point may be determined by calculating the time difference between that at its location and [[Coordinated_Universal_Time|Coordinated Universal Time]] (UTC).
sentence_87: Since there are 24 hours in a day and 360 degrees in a circle, the sun moves across the sky at a rate of 15 degrees per hour (360° ÷ 24 hours = 15° per hour).
sentence_88: So if the time zone a person is in is three hours ahead of UTC then that person is near 45° longitude (3 hours × 15° per hour = 45°).
sentence_89: The word near is used because the point might not be at the center of the time zone; also the time zones are defined politically, so their centers and boundaries often do not lie on meridians at multiples of 15°.
sentence_90: In order to perform this calculation, however, a person needs to have a [[Marine_chronometer|chronometer]] (watch) set to UTC and needs to determine local time by solar or astronomical observation.
sentence_91: The details are more complex than described here: see the articles on [[Universal_Time|Universal Time]] and on the [[Equation_of_time|equation of time]] for more details.
sentence_92: Note that the longitude is [[Mathematical_singularity|singular]] at the [[Geographical_pole|Poles]] and calculations that are sufficiently accurate for other positions may be inaccurate at or near the Poles.
sentence_93: Also the [[Discontinuity_(mathematics)|discontinuity]] at the ±[[180th_meridian|180° meridian]] must be handled with care in calculations.
sentence_94: An example is a calculation of east displacement by subtracting two longitudes, which gives the wrong answer if the two positions are on either side of this meridian.
sentence_95: To avoid these complexities, consider replacing latitude and longitude with another [[Horizontal_position_representation|horizontal position representation]] in calculation.
sentence_96: The Earth's [[Plate_tectonics|tectonic plates]] move relative to one another in different directions at speeds on the order of 50 to 100 mm (2.0 to 3.9 in) per year.
sentence_97: So points on the Earth's surface on different plates are always in motion relative to one another.
sentence_98: For example, the longitudinal difference between a point on the Equator in Uganda, on the [[African_Plate|African Plate]], and a point on the Equator in Ecuador, on the South American Plate, is increasing by about 0.0014 [[Minute_of_arc#Symbols_and_abbreviations|arcseconds]] per year.
sentence_99: These tectonic movements likewise affect latitude.
sentence_100: If a [[Geodetic_datum|global reference frame]] (such as WGS84, for example) is used, the longitude of a place on the surface will change from year to year.
sentence_101: To minimize this change, when dealing just with points on a single plate, a different reference frame can be used, whose coordinates are fixed to a particular plate, such as "NAD83" for North America or "[[ETRS89|ETRS89]]" for Europe.

sentence_107: Cos φ decreases from 1 at the equator to 0 at the poles, which measures how circles of latitude shrink from the equator to a point at the pole, so the length of a degree of longitude decreases likewise.
sentence_108: This contrasts with the small (1%) increase in the length of a degree of latitude (north–south distance), equator to pole.

Note that the distance between two points 1 degree apart on the same circle of latitude, measured along that circle of latitude, is slightly more than the shortest ([[Geodesic|geodesic]]) distance between those points (unless on the equator, where these are equal); the difference is less than 0.6 m (2 ft).
sentence_110: A [[Geographical_mile|geographical mile]] is defined to be the length of one [[Minute_of_arc|minute of arc]] along the equator (one equatorial minute of longitude), therefore a degree of longitude along the equator is exactly 60 geographical miles or 111.3 kilometers, as there are 60 minutes in a degree.
sentence_111: The length of 1 minute of longitude along the equator is 1 geographical mile or 1.855 km or 1.153 miles, while the length of 1 second of it is 0.016 geographical mile or 30.916 m or 101.43 feet.

title: Juventus F.C.
sentence_0: This article is about the men's association football club from Turin, Italy.
sentence_1: For the affiliated women's football club, see [[Juventus_F.C._Women|Juventus F.C. Women]].
sentence_2: For other uses, see [[Juventus_F.C._(disambiguation)|Juventus F.C. (disambiguation)]].
sentence_3: "Juventus" redirects here.
sentence_4: For other uses, see [[Juventus_(disambiguation)|Juventus (disambiguation)]].
sentence_5: Not to be confused with the ancient Roman goddess [[Juventas|Juventas]].
sentence_6: Juventus Football Club (from [[Latin_language|Latin]]: iuventūs, "youth"; Italian pronunciation: [[Italian|[juˈvɛntus]]), colloquially known as Juve (pronounced [[Italian|[ˈjuːve]]), is a professional [[Association_football|football]] club based in [[Turin|Turin]], Piedmont, Italy, that competes in the [[Serie_A|Serie A]], the top flight of Italian football.
sentence_7: Founded in 1897 by a group of Torinese students, the club has worn a black and white striped home kit since 1903 and has played home matches in different grounds around its city, the latest being the 41,507-capacity [[Juventus_Stadium|Juventus Stadium]].
sentence_8: Nicknamed Vecchia Signora ("the Old Lady"), the club has won 36 official [[List_of_Italian_football_champions|league titles]], 13 [[Coppa_Italia|Coppa Italia]] titles and eight [[Supercoppa_Italiana|Supercoppa Italiana]] titles, being the record holder for all these competitions; two [[Intercontinental_Cup_(football)|Intercontinental Cups]], two [[UEFA_Champions_League|European Cups / UEFA Champions Leagues]], one [[UEFA_Cup_Winners'_Cup|European Cup Winners' Cup]], a joint national record of three [[UEFA_Europa_League|UEFA Cups]], two [[UEFA_Super_Cup|UEFA Super Cups]] and a joint national record of one [[UEFA_Intertoto_Cup|UEFA Intertoto Cup]].
sentence_9: Consequently, the side leads the historical Federazione Italiana Giuoco Calcio (FIGC) ranking whilst on the international stage occupies the fifth position [[List_of_UEFA_club_competition_winners|in Europe]] and the eleventh in the world for most confederation titles won with eleven trophies, having led the [[UEFA_coefficient|UEFA ranking]] during seven seasons since its inception in 1979, [[UEFA_coefficient#Top_club_by_period|the most]] for an Italian team and joint second overall.
sentence_10: Founded with the name of Sport-Club Juventus, initially as an athletics club, it is the second oldest of its kind still active in the country after [[Genoa_C.F.C.|Genoa]]'s football section (1893) and has competed uninterruptedly in the [[Italian_football_league_system#Structure|top flight league]] (reformulated as [[Serie_A|Serie A]] from 1929) since its debut in 1900 after changing its name to Foot-Ball Club Juventus, with the exception of the [[2006–07_Serie_B|2006–07 season]], being managed by the [[Economy_of_Italy|industrial]] [[Agnelli_family|Agnelli family]] almost continuously since 1923.
sentence_11: The relationship between the club and that dynasty is the oldest and longest in national sports, making Juventus one of the first [[Professionalism_in_association_football|professional]] sporting clubs in the country, having established itself as a major force in the national stage since the 1930s and at [[UEFA_competitions|confederation level]] since the mid-1970s and becoming one of the first ten wealthiest in world football in terms of [[Forbes'_list_of_the_most_valuable_football_clubs|value]], [[Deloitte_Football_Money_League#Summary_table:_Some_teams_appearing_in_Top_10|revenue]] and [[Profit_(accounting)|profit]] since the mid-1990s, being listed on the [[Italian_Bourse|Borsa italiana]] since 2001.
sentence_12: Under the management of [[Giovanni_Trapattoni|Giovanni Trapattoni]], the club won 13 trophies in the ten years before 1986, including six league titles and five international titles, and became [[UEFA_club_competition_records_and_statistics#List_of_teams_to_have_won_the_three_main_European_club_competitions|the first]] to win all three seasonal competitions organised by the [[UEFA|Union of European Football Associations]]: the [[1976–77_UEFA_Cup|1976–77 UEFA Cup]] (first Southern European side to do so), the [[1983–84_European_Cup_Winners'_Cup|1983–84 Cup Winners' Cup]] and the [[1984–85_European_Cup|1984–85 European Champions' Cup]].
sentence_13: With successive triumphs in the [[1984_European_Super_Cup|1984 European Super Cup]] and [[1985_Intercontinental_Cup|1985 Intercontinental Cup]], it became [[Timeline_of_association_football#1980s|the first]] and thus far only in the world to complete a clean sweep of all confederation trophies; an achievement that they revalidated with the title won in the [[1999_UEFA_Intertoto_Cup|1999 UEFA Intertoto Cup]] after another successful era led by [[Marcello_Lippi|Marcello Lippi]], becoming in addition [[List_of_football_clubs_in_Italy_by_major_honours_won|the only professional Italian club]] to have won every ongoing honour available to the first team and organised by a national or international [[Football_association|football association]].
sentence_14: In December 2000, Juventus was ranked seventh in the [[FIFA_Club_of_the_Century|FIFA's historic ranking]] of the best clubs in the world and nine years later was ranked second best club in Europe during the 20th Century based on a statistical study series by the [[International_Federation_of_Football_History_&_Statistics|International Federation of Football History & Statistics]] (IFFHS), the highest for an Italian club in both.
sentence_15: The club's fan base is the largest at national level and one of the largest worldwide.
sentence_16: Unlike most European sporting supporters' groups, which are often concentrated around their own club's city of origin, it is widespread throughout the whole country and the [[Italian_diaspora|Italian diaspora]], making Juventus a symbol of ("anti-parochialism") and italianità ("Italianness").
sentence_17: Juventus players have won eight [[Ballon_d'Or|Ballon d'Or]] awards, four of these in consecutive years (1982–1985, an overall record), among these the first player representing Serie A, [[Omar_Sívori|Omar Sívori]], as well as [[Michel_Platini|Michel Platini]] and [[Ballon_d'Or#Winners|three of the five recipients with]] [[Italian_nationality_law|Italian nationality]] as the former member of the [[Juventus_F.C._Youth_Sector|youth sector]] [[Paolo_Rossi|Paolo Rossi]]; they have also won four [[FIFA_World_Player_of_the_Year|FIFA World Player of the Year]] awards, with winners as [[Roberto_Baggio|Roberto Baggio]] and [[Zinedine_Zidane|Zinedine Zidane]], a national record and third and joint second highest overall, respectively, in the cited prizes.
sentence_18: Additionally, players representing the club have won 11 [[Serie_A_Footballer_of_the_Year|Serie A Footballer of the Year]] awards including the only goalkeeper to win it, [[Gianluigi_Buffon|Gianluigi Buffon]], and 17 different players were inducted in the [[Serie_A_Team_of_the_Year|Serie A Team of the Year]], being both also a record.
sentence_19: Finally, the club has also provided the most [[Juventus_F.C._and_the_Italy_national_football_team|players to the Italy national team]]—mostly in official competitions in almost uninterrupted way since 1924—who often formed the group that led the [[Italy_national_football_team|Azzurri]] squad to international success, most importantly in the [[1934_FIFA_World_Cup|1934]], [[1982_FIFA_World_Cup|1982]] and [[2006_FIFA_World_Cup|2006 FIFA World Cups]].
sentence_20: Main article: [[History_of_Juventus_F.C.|History of Juventus F.C.]]
sentence_21: Juventus were founded as Sport-Club Juventus in late 1897 by pupils from the [[Massimo_D'Azeglio_Lyceum|Massimo D'Azeglio Lyceum]] school in Turin, among them the brothers [[Eugenio_Canfari|Eugenio]] and [[Enrico_Canfari|Enrico Canfari]], but were renamed as Foot-Ball Club Juventus two years later.
sentence_22: The club joined the [[Italian_Football_Championship|Italian Football Championship]] in [[1900_Italian_Football_Championship|1900]].
sentence_23: In 1904, the businessman [[Marco_Ajmone-Marsan|Ajmone-Marsan]] revived the finances of the football club Juventus, making it also possible to transfer the training field from piazza d'armi to the more appropriate Velodrome Umberto I.
sentence_24: During this period, the team wore a pink and black kit.
sentence_25: Juventus first won the league championship in [[1905_Italian_Football_Championship|1905]] while playing at their Velodrome Umberto I ground.
sentence_26: By this time the club colours had changed to black and white stripes, inspired by English side [[Notts_County_F.C.|Notts County]].
sentence_27: There was a split at the club in 1906, after some of the staff considered moving Juve out of Turin.
sentence_28: President [[Alfred_Dick_(entrepreneur)|Alfred Dick]] was unhappy with this and left with some prominent players to found [[Torino_F.C.|FBC Torino]] which in turn spawned the [[Derby_della_Mole|Derby della Mole]].
sentence_29: Juventus spent much of this period steadily rebuilding after the split, surviving the First World War.
sentence_30: [[Fiat_Automobiles|FIAT]] owner [[Edoardo_Agnelli_(industrialist)|Edoardo Agnelli]] gained control of the club in 1923 and built a new stadium.
sentence_31: This helped the club to its second [[Scudetto|scudetto]] (league championship) in the [[1925–26_Prima_Divisione|1925–26]] season, after beating [[S.S._Alba-Audace_Roma|Alba Roma]] with an aggregate score of 12–1 ([[Antonio_Vojak|Antonio Vojak]]'s goals were essential that season).
sentence_32: The club established itself as a major force in Italian football since the 1930s, becoming the country's first professional club and the first with a decentralised fan base, which led it to win a record of [[List_of_Italian_football_champions#Serie_A|five consecutive Italian championships]] (the first four under the management of [[Carlo_Carcano|Carlo Carcano]]) and form [[Nazio-Juve|the core]] of the [[Italy_national_football_team|Italy national team]] during the [[Vittorio_Pozzo|Vittorio Pozzo]]'s era, including the [[1934_FIFA_World_Cup|1934 world champion]] [[1934_FIFA_World_Cup_squads#Italy|squad]], with star players such as [[Raimundo_Orsi|Raimundo Orsi]], [[Luigi_Bertolini|Luigi Bertolini]], [[Giovanni_Ferrari|Giovanni Ferrari]] and [[Luis_Monti|Luis Monti]], among others.
sentence_33: Juventus moved to the [[Stadio_Olimpico_Grande_Torino|Stadio Comunale]], but for the rest of the 1930s and the majority of the 1940s they were unable to recapture championship dominance.
sentence_34: After the Second World War, [[Gianni_Agnelli|Gianni Agnelli]] was appointed honorary president.
sentence_35: The club added two more league championships to its name in the [[1949–50_Serie_A|1949–50]] and [[1951–52_Serie_A|1951–52]] seasons, the latter of which was under the management of Englishman Jesse Carver.
sentence_36: Two new strikers were signed during [[1957–58_Serie_A|1957–58]]: Welshman [[John_Charles|John Charles]] and Italian Argentine [[Omar_Sívori|Omar Sívori]], playing alongside longtime member [[Giampiero_Boniperti|Giampiero Boniperti]].
sentence_37: That season saw Juventus awarded with the [[Star_(football_badge)|Golden Star for Sport Excellence]] to wear on their shirts after becoming the first Italian side to win ten league titles.
sentence_38: In the same season, Sívori became the first ever player at the club to win the [[European_Footballer_of_the_Year|European Footballer of the Year]].
sentence_39: The following season, they beat [[ACF_Fiorentina|Fiorentina]] to complete their first league and cup double, winning [[1959–60_Serie_A|Serie A]] and Coppa Italia.
sentence_40: Boniperti retired in 1961 as the all-time top scorer at the club, with 182 goals in all competitions, a club record which stood for 45 years.
sentence_41: During the rest of the decade, the club won the league just once more in [[1966–67_Serie_A|1966–67]].
sentence_42: However, the 1970s saw Juventus further solidify their strong position in Italian football.
sentence_43: Under former player Čestmír Vycpálek, they won the scudetto in [[1971–72_Serie_A|1971–72]] and [[1972–73_Serie_A|1972–73]], with players such as [[Roberto_Bettega|Roberto Bettega]], [[Franco_Causio|Franco Causio]] and José Altafini breaking through.
sentence_44: During the rest of the decade, they won the league twice more, with defender [[Gaetano_Scirea|Gaetano Scirea]] contributing significantly.
sentence_45: The later win was under [[Giovanni_Trapattoni|Giovanni Trapattoni]], who also led the club to their first ever major European title (the [[UEFA_Europa_League|UEFA Cup]]) in [[1976–77_UEFA_Cup|1977]] and helped the club's domination continue on into the early part of the 1980s.
sentence_46: During Trapattoni's tenure, many Juventus players also formed the [[Blocco-Juve|backbone]] of the Italy national team during [[Enzo_Bearzot|Enzo Bearzot]]'s successful managerial era, including the [[1978_FIFA_World_Cup_squads#Italy|1978 World Cup]], [[UEFA_Euro_1980|UEFA Euro 1980]] and [[1982_FIFA_World_Cup|1982 world champion]] [[1982_FIFA_World_Cup_squads#Italy|squads]].
sentence_47: The Trapattoni era was highly successful in the 1980s and the club started the decade off well, winning the league title three more times by 1984.
sentence_48: This meant Juventus had won 20 Italian league titles and were allowed to add a second golden star to their shirt, thus becoming the only Italian club to achieve this.
sentence_49: Around this time, the club's players were attracting considerable attention and [[Paolo_Rossi|Paolo Rossi]] was named [[European_Footballer_of_the_Year|European Footballer of the Year]] following his contribution to Italy's victory in the 1982 World Cup, where he was named Player of the Tournament.
sentence_50: Frenchman [[Michel_Platini|Michel Platini]] was also awarded the European Footballer of the Year title for three years in a row in 1983, 1984 and 1985, which is a record.
sentence_51: Juventus are the first and one of the only two clubs to have players from their club winning the award in four consecutive years.
sentence_52: It was Platini who scored the winning goal in the [[1985_European_Cup_Final|1985 European Cup Final]] against [[Liverpool_F.C.|Liverpool]], but this was marred by a [[Heysel_Stadium_disaster|tragedy]] which changed European football.
sentence_53: That year, Juventus became the [[UEFA_club_competition_records_and_statistics#List_of_teams_to_have_won_the_three_main_European_club_competitions|first club in the history of European football]] to have won all three major [[UEFA_club_competition_records|UEFA competitions]] and, after their triumph in the [[1985_Intercontinental_Cup|Intercontinental Cup]], the club also became [[Timeline_of_association_football#1980s|the first]], and thus far, the only in association football history, to have won all possible confederation competitions,(:5) an achievement that it revalidated with the title won in the [[1999_UEFA_Intertoto_Cup|1999 UEFA Intertoto Cup]].
sentence_54: With the exception of winning the closely contested Italian Championship of [[1985–86_Serie_A|1985–86]], the rest of the 1980s were not very successful for the club.
sentence_55: As well as having to contend with [[Diego_Maradona|Diego Maradona]]'s [[S.S.C._Napoli|Napoli]], both of the Milanese clubs, [[A.C._Milan|Milan]] and [[Inter_Milan|Internazionale]], won Italian championships.
sentence_56: However, Juventus did win a [[1989–90_Coppa_Italia|Coppa Italia]]-UEFA Cup double in 1990 under the guidance of former club legend [[Dino_Zoff|Dino Zoff]].
sentence_57: In 1990, Juventus also moved into their new home, the [[Stadio_delle_Alpi|Stadio delle Alpi]], which was built for the [[1990_FIFA_World_Cup|1990 World Cup]].
sentence_58: Despite the arrival of Italian star [[Roberto_Baggio|Roberto Baggio]] later that year for a world record transfer fee, the early 1990s under Luigi Maifredi and subsequently Trapattoni once again also saw little success for Juventus, as they only managed to win the [[1993_UEFA_Cup_Final|UEFA Cup in 1993]].

section_4.value: Second Champions League and first Supercoppa Italiana titles (1994–2004)

sentence_59: [[Marcello_Lippi|Marcello Lippi]] took over as Juventus manager at the start of the [[1994–95_Serie_A|1994–95]] campaign.
sentence_60: His first season at the helm of the club was a successful one, as Juventus recorded their first Serie A championship title since the mid-1980s, as well as the [[1994–95_Coppa_Italia|Coppa Italia]].
sentence_61: The crop of players during this period featured [[Ciro_Ferrara|Ciro Ferrara]], [[Roberto_Baggio|Roberto Baggio]], [[Gianluca_Vialli|Gianluca Vialli]] and a young [[Alessandro_Del_Piero|Alessandro Del Piero]].
sentence_62: Lippi led Juventus to their first [[1995_Supercoppa_Italiana|Supercoppa Italiana]] and the [[1995–96_UEFA_Champions_League|Champions League]] the following season, beating [[AFC_Ajax|Ajax]] on penalties after a 1–1 draw in which [[Fabrizio_Ravanelli|Fabrizio Ravanelli]] scored for Juventus.
sentence_63: The club did not rest long after winning the European Cup: more highly regarded players were brought into the fold in the form of [[Zinedine_Zidane|Zinedine Zidane]], [[Filippo_Inzaghi|Filippo Inzaghi]] and [[Edgar_Davids|Edgar Davids]].
sentence_64: At home, Juventus won the [[1996–97_Serie_A|1996–97]] and [[1997–98_Serie_A|1997–98]] Serie A titles, as well as the [[1996_UEFA_Super_Cup|1996 UEFA Super Cup]] and the [[1996_Intercontinental_Cup|1996 Intercontinental Cup]].
sentence_65: Juventus reached the [[1997_UEFA_Champions_League_Final|1997]] and [[1998_UEFA_Champions_League_Final|1998]] Champions League finals during this period, but lost out to [[Borussia_Dortmund|Borussia Dortmund]] and [[Real_Madrid_C.F.|Real Madrid]] respectively.
sentence_66: After a two-and-a-half-season absence, Lippi returned to the club in 2001, following his replacement [[Carlo_Ancelotti|Carlo Ancelotti]]'s dismissal, signing big name players such as [[Gianluigi_Buffon|Gianluigi Buffon]], [[David_Trezeguet|David Trezeguet]], [[Pavel_Nedvěd|Pavel Nedvěd]] and [[Lilian_Thuram|Lilian Thuram]], helping the team to two more scudetto titles during the [[2001–02_Serie_A|2001–02]] and [[2002–03_Serie_A|2002–03]] seasons.
sentence_67: Juventus were also part of an all Italian Champions League final in [[2003_UEFA_Champions_League_Final|2003]], but lost out to Milan on penalties after the game ended in a 0–0 draw.
sentence_68: At the conclusion of the following season, Lippi was appointed as the Italy national team's head coach, bringing an end to one of the most fruitful managerial spells in Juventus' history.
sentence_69: [[Fabio_Capello|Fabio Capello]] was appointed as Juventus' coach in 2004 and led the club to two more consecutive Serie A first places.
sentence_70: In May 2006, Juventus became one of the five clubs linked to the Calciopoli scandal.
sentence_71: In July, Juventus was placed at the bottom of the league table and relegated to [[Serie_B|Serie B]] for the first time in its history.
sentence_72: The club was also stripped of the 2005 title won under Capello, while the 2006 title, after a period sub judice, was assigned to Inter Milan.
sentence_73: Many key players left following their relegation to Serie B, including Lillian Thuram, star striker [[Zlatan_Ibrahimović|Zlatan Ibrahimović]] and defensive stalwart [[Fabio_Cannavaro|Fabio Cannavaro]].
sentence_74: However, other big name players such as Alessandro Del Piero, Gianluigi Buffon, David Trezeguet and Pavel Nedvěd remained to help the club return to Serie A, while youngsters from the [[Campionato_Nazionale_Primavera|Primavera]] (youth team), such as [[Sebastian_Giovinco|Sebastian Giovinco]] and [[Claudio_Marchisio|Claudio Marchisio]], were integrated into the first team.
sentence_75: Juventus won the Cadetti (Serie B championship) despite starting with a points deduction and gained promotion straight back up to the top division as league winners after the [[2006–07_Serie_B|2006–07]] season, as captain Del Piero claimed the top scorer award with 21 goals.
sentence_76: As early as 2010, Juventus considered challenging the stripping of their scudetto from 2006 and the non-assignment of the 2005 title, dependent on the results of trials connected to the 2006 scandal.
sentence_77: When former general manager [[Luciano_Moggi|Luciano Moggi]]'s conviction in criminal court in connection with the scandal was partially written off by the Supreme Court on 23 March 2015, the club sued the Italian Football Federation (FIGC) for €443 million for damages caused by their 2006 relegation.
sentence_78: FIGC president [[Carlo_Tavecchio|Carlo Tavecchio]] offered to discuss reinstatement of the lost scudetti in exchange for Juventus dropping the lawsuit.
sentence_79: On 9 September 2015, the Supreme Court released a 150-page document that explained its final ruling of the case: despite that Moggi's remaining charges were cancelled without a new trial, due to statute of limitations, the court confirmed that Moggi was actively involved in the sporting fraud which was intended to favour Juventus and increase his own personal benefits.
sentence_80: Eventually, in 2016 the TAR tribunal rejected the request of compensation promoted by Juventus.
sentence_81: On 15 March 2017, Moggi's lifetime ban was definitively confirmed on final appeal.
sentence_82: After returning to Serie A in the [[2007–08_Serie_A|2007–08 season]], Juventus appointed [[Claudio_Ranieri|Claudio Ranieri]] as manager.
sentence_83: They finished in third place in their first season back in the top flight and qualified for the [[2008–09_UEFA_Champions_League|Champions League]] third qualifying round in the preliminary stages.
sentence_84: Juventus reached the group stages, where they beat Real Madrid in both home and away legs, before losing in the knockout round to [[Chelsea_F.C.|Chelsea]].
sentence_85: Ranieri was sacked following a string of unsuccessful results and [[Ciro_Ferrara|Ciro Ferrara]] was appointed as manager on a temporary basis for the last two games of the [[2008–09_Serie_A|2008–09 season]], before being subsequently appointed as the manager for the [[2009–10_Serie_A|2009–10 season]].
sentence_86: Ferrara's stint as Juventus manager, however, proved to be unsuccessful, with Juventus knocked out of [[2009–10_UEFA_Champions_League|Champions League]] and [[2009–10_Coppa_Italia|Coppa Italia]], as well as just lying on the sixth place in the league table at the end of January 2010, leading to the dismissal of Ferrara and the naming of [[Alberto_Zaccheroni|Alberto Zaccheroni]] as caretaker manager.
sentence_87: Zaccheroni could not help the side improve, as Juventus finished the season in seventh place in Serie A.
sentence_88: For the [[2010–11_Serie_A|2010–11 season]], [[Jean-Claude_Blanc|Jean-Claude Blanc]] was replaced by [[Andrea_Agnelli|Andrea Agnelli]] as the club's president.
sentence_89: Agnelli's first action was to replace Zaccheroni and director of sport Alessio Secco with [[U.C._Sampdoria|Sampdoria]] manager [[Luigi_Delneri|Luigi Delneri]] and director of sport [[Giuseppe_Marotta|Giuseppe Marotta]].
sentence_90: However, Delneri failed to improve their fortunes and was dismissed.
sentence_91: Former player and fan favourite [[Antonio_Conte|Antonio Conte]], fresh after winning promotion with [[S.S._Robur_Siena|Siena]], was named as Delneri's replacement.
sentence_92: In September 2011, Juventus relocated to the new [[Juventus_Stadium|Juventus Stadium]].

section_7.value: Historic four consecutive doubles and nine consecutive league titles (2011–present)

sentence_93: With Conte as manager, Juventus went unbeaten for the entire [[2011–12_Serie_A|2011–12 Serie A]] season.
sentence_94: Towards the second half of the season, the team was mostly competing with northern rivals Milan for first place in a tight contest.
sentence_95: Juventus won the title on the 37th matchday after beating [[Cagliari_Calcio|Cagliari]] 2–0 and Milan losing to Internazionale 4–2.
sentence_96: After a 3–1 win in the final matchday against [[Atalanta_B.C.|Atalanta]], Juventus became the first team to go the season unbeaten in the current 38-game format.
sentence_97: Other noteworthy achievements included the biggest away win (5–0 at Fiorentina), best defensive record (20 goals conceded, fewest ever in the current league format) in Serie A and second best in the top six European leagues that year.
sentence_98: In [[2013–14_Serie_A|2013–14]], Juventus won a third consecutive scudetto with a [[Football_records_in_Italy|record]] 102 points and 33 wins.
sentence_99: The title was the 30th official league championship in the club's history.
sentence_100: They also achieved the semi-finals of [[2013–14_UEFA_Europa_League|Europa League]], where they were eliminated at home against ten-man [[S.L._Benfica|Benfica]]'s [[Catenaccio|catenaccio]], missing the [[2014_UEFA_Europa_League_Final|final]] at the Juventus Stadium.
sentence_101: In [[2014–15_Serie_A|2014–15]], [[Massimiliano_Allegri|Massimiliano Allegri]] was appointed as manager, with whom Juventus won their 31st official title, making it a fourth-straight, as well as achieving a record tenth [[2015_Coppa_Italia_Final|Coppa Italia]] for the [[Double_(association_football)|double]].
sentence_102: The club also beat Real Madrid in the semi-finals of the [[2014–15_UEFA_Champions_League|Champions League]] 3–2 on aggregate to face [[FC_Barcelona|Barcelona]] in the [[2015_UEFA_Champions_League_Final|final]] in Berlin for the first time since the [[2002–03_UEFA_Champions_League|2002–03 Champions League]].
sentence_103: Juventus lost the final to Barcelona 3–1 after an early fourth-minute goal from [[Ivan_Rakitić|Ivan Rakitić]], followed by an [[Álvaro_Morata|Álvaro Morata]] equalizer in the 55th minute.
sentence_104: Then Barcelona took the lead again with a goal from [[Luis_Suárez|Luis Suárez]] in the 70th minute, followed by a final minute goal by [[Neymar|Neymar]] as Juventus were caught out on the counterattack.
sentence_105: On 14 December 2015, Juventus won the [[Serie_A_Football_Club_of_the_Year|Serie A Football Club of the Year]] award for the 2014–15 season, the fourth time in succession.
sentence_106: On 25 April 2016, the club won their fifth-straight title (and 32nd overall) since last winning five straight between 1930–31 and 1934–35, after second place Napoli lost to Roma to give Juventus mathematical certainty of the title with three games to spare; last losing to [[U.S._Sassuolo_Calcio|Sassuolo]] on 25 October 2015, which left them in 12th place, before taking 73 points of a possible 75.
sentence_107: On 21 May, the club then won the [[2016_Coppa_Italia_Final|Coppa Italia]] for the 11th time and their second straight title, becoming the first team in Italy's history to win Serie A and Coppa Italia [[Double_(association_football)|doubles]] in back-to-back seasons.
sentence_108: On 17 May 2017, Juventus won their [[2016–17_Coppa_Italia|12th Coppa Italia title]] in a 2–0 win over Lazio (the first team to win three consecutive championships).
sentence_109: Four days later on 21 May, Juventus became the first team to win six consecutive Serie A titles.
sentence_110: On 3 June 2017, Juventus reached a [[2017_UEFA_Champions_League_Final|second Champions League Final]] in three years, but were defeated 1–4 by defending champions Real Madrid—a [[2017_Turin_stampede|stampede]] in Turin happened ten minutes before the end of the match.
sentence_111: On 9 May 2018, Juventus won their [[2018_Coppa_Italia_Final|13th Coppa Italia title]], and fourth in a row, in a 4–0 win over Milan, extending the all-time record of successive Coppa Italia titles.
sentence_112: Four days later on 13 May, Juventus secured their seventh consecutive Serie A title, extending the all-time record of successive triumphs in the competition.
sentence_113: In July 2018, Juventus broke the record for a fee paid for a player over 30 years old and the record for a fee paid by an Italian club by purchasing the 33-year-old [[Cristiano_Ronaldo|Cristiano Ronaldo]] from [[Real_Madrid_C.F.|Real Madrid]] for €112 million, or £99.2 million.
sentence_114: On 20 April 2019, Juventus secured their eighth consecutive Serie A title, further extending the all-time record of successive triumphs in the competition.
sentence_115: Following Allegri's dismissal, [[Maurizio_Sarri|Maurizio Sarri]] was appointed manager of the club ahead of the [[2019–20_Juventus_F.C._season|2019–20 season]].
sentence_116: On 26 July 2020, Juventus were confirmed [[2019–20_Serie_A|2019–20 Serie A]] champions, reaching an unprecedented milestone of nine consecutive league titles.
sentence_117: On 8 August 2020, Sarri was sacked by the club, one day after Juventus were eliminated from the Champions league by [[Olympique_Lyonnais|Lyon]].
sentence_118: On the same day, former player [[Andrea_Pirlo|Andrea Pirlo]] was announced as the new coach, signing a two year contract.
sentence_119: Juventus have played in black and white striped shirts, with white shorts, sometimes black shorts since 1903.
sentence_120: Originally, they played in pink shirts with a black tie.
sentence_121: The father of one of the players made the earliest shirts, but continual washing faded the colour so much that in 1903 the club sought to replace them.
sentence_122: Juventus asked one of their team members, Englishman John Savage, if he had any contacts in England who could supply new shirts in a colour that would better withstand the elements.
sentence_123: He had a friend who lived in Nottingham, who being a [[Notts_County_F.C.|Notts County]] supporter, shipped out the black and white striped shirts to Turin.
sentence_124: Juventus have worn the shirts ever since, considering the colours to be aggressive and powerful.
sentence_125: Juventus's official emblem has undergone different and small modifications since the 1920s.
sentence_126: The previous modification of the Juventus badge took place in 2004, when the emblem of the team changed to a black-and-white [[Shield_(heraldry)|oval shield]] of a type used by Italian ecclesiastics.
sentence_127: It is divided in five vertical stripes: two white stripes and three black stripes, inside which are the following elements, while in its upper section the name of the society superimposed on a white [[Convex_set|convex section]], over golden curvature (gold for honour).
sentence_128: The white silhouette of a [[Cattle|charging bull]] is in the lower section of the oval shield, superimposed on a black [[Shield_(heraldry)|old French shield]] and the charging bull is a symbol of the comune of Turin.
sentence_129: There is also a black silhouette of a [[Mural_crown|mural crown]] above the black spherical triangle's base.
sentence_130: This is a reminiscence to Augusta Tourinorum, the old city of the [[Roman_Empire|Roman era]] which the present capital of Piedmont region is its cultural heiress.
sentence_131: In January 2017, president Andrea Agnelli announced the most recent change to the Juventus badge, revealing a video showing the introduction of the new badge.
sentence_132: The badge shows the word Juventus on top, with two capital Js shown together in different fonts with a small opening between them to almost make a bigger J. Agnelli said that the badge reflects "the Juventus way of living".
sentence_133: Juventus was the first team in association football history to adopt a [[Star_(football_badge)|star]], who added one above their badge in 1958 to represent their tenth Italian Football Championship and Serie A title, and has since become popularized with other clubs as well.
sentence_134: In the past, the convex section of the emblem had a blue colour (another symbol of Turin) and it was [[Concave_polygon|concave]] in shape.
sentence_135: The old French shield and the mural crown, also in the lower section of the emblem, had a considerably greater size.
sentence_136: The two "Golden Stars for Sport Excellence" were located above the convex and concave section of Juventus' emblem.
sentence_137: During the 1980s, the club emblem was the blurred silhouette of a zebra, alongside the two golden stars with the club's name forming an arc above.
sentence_138: Juventus unofficially won their 30th league title in 2011–12, but a dispute with the FIGC, which stripped Juventus of their 2004–05 title and did not assign them the 2005–06 title due to their involvement in the Calciopoli, left their official total at 28.
sentence_139: They elected to wear no stars at all the [[2012–13_Serie_A|following season]].
sentence_140: Juventus won their 30th title in 2013–14 and thus earned the right to wear their third star, but club president Andrea Agnelli stated that the club suspended the use of the stars until another team wins their 20th championship, thus having the right to wear two stars, "to emphasise Juventus' superiority".
sentence_141: However, for the [[2015–16_Juventus_F.C._season|2015–16 season]], Juventus reintroduced the stars and added the third star to their jersey as well with new kit manufacturers [[Adidas|Adidas]], in addition to the Coppa Italia badge for winning their tenth [[2014–15_Coppa_Italia|Coppa Italia]] the [[2014–15_Juventus_F.C._season|previous season]].
sentence_142: For the [[2016–17_Juventus_F.C._season|2016–17 season]], Juventus re-designed their kit with a different take on the trademark black and white stripes.
sentence_143: For the [[2017–18_Juventus_F.C._season|2017–18 season]], Juventus introduced the J shaped logo onto the kits.
sentence_144: In September 2015, Juventus officially announced a new project called JKids for its junior supporters on its website.
sentence_145: Along with this project, Juventus also introduced a new mascot to all its fans which is called J. J is a cartoon-designed zebra, black and white stripes with golden edge piping on its body, golden shining eyes, and three golden stars on the front of its neck.
sentence_146: J made its debut at [[Juventus_Stadium|Juventus Stadium]] on 12 September 2015.
sentence_147: During its history, the club has acquired a number of nicknames, la Vecchia Signora (the Old Lady) being the best example.
sentence_148: The "old" part of the nickname is a pun on Juventus which means "youth" in Latin.
sentence_149: It was derived from the age of the Juventus star players towards the middle of the 1930s.
sentence_150: The "lady" part of the nickname is how fans of the club affectionately referred to it before the 1930s.
sentence_151: The club is also nicknamed la Fidanzata d'Italia (the Girlfriend of Italy), because over the years it has received a high level of support from [[Southern_Italy|Southern Italian]] immigrant workers (particularly from Naples and [[Palermo|Palermo]]), who arrived in Turin to work for FIAT since the 1930s.
sentence_152: Other nicknames include; [La] Madama ([[Piedmontese_language|Piedmontese]] for Madam), i bianconeri (the black-and-whites), le zebre (the zebras) in reference to Juventus' colours.
sentence_153: I gobbi (the hunchbacks) is the nickname that is used to define Juventus supporters, but is also used sometimes for team's players.
sentence_154: The most widely accepted origin of gobbi dates to the fifties, when the bianconeri wore a large jersey.
sentence_155: When players ran on the field, the jersey, which had a laced opening at the chest, generated a bulge over the back (a sort of parachute effect), making the players look hunchbacked.
sentence_156: The official anthem of Juventus is Juve (storia di un grande amore), or Juve (story of a great love) in English, written by Alessandra Torre and Claudio Guidetti, in the version of the singer and musician [[Paolo_Belli|Paolo Belli]] composed in 2007.
sentence_157: In 2016, a documentary film called Black and White Stripes: The Juventus Story was produced by the [[La_Villa_brothers|La Villa brothers]] about Juventus.
sentence_158: On 16 February 2018, the first three episodes of a [[Docu-series|docu-series]] called First Team: Juventus, which followed the club throughout the [[2017–18_Juventus_F.C._season|season]], by spending time with the players behind the scenes both on and off the field, was released on [[Netflix|Netflix]]; the other three episodes were released on 6 July 2018.
