sentence_159: Main articles: [[Juventus_Stadium|Juventus Stadium]], [[Stadio_Olimpico_di_Torino|Stadio Olimpico di Torino]], [[Stadio_delle_Alpi|Stadio delle Alpi]], [[Stadio_di_Corso_Marsiglia|Stadio di Corso Marsiglia]], and Stadio Motovelodromo Umberto I
sentence_160: After the first two years (1897 and 1898), during which Juventus played in the Parco del Valentino and Parco Cittadella, their matches were held in the Piazza d'Armi Stadium until 1908, except in 1905 (the first year of the scudetto) and in 1906, years in which it played at the Corso Re Umberto.
sentence_161: From 1909 to 1922, Juventus played their internal competitions at Corso Sebastopoli Camp before moving the following year to Corso Marsiglia Camp, where they remained until 1933, winning four league titles.
sentence_162: At the end of 1933, they began to play at the new [[Stadio_Olimpico_Grande_Torino|Stadio Benito Mussolini]] inaugurated for the [[1934_FIFA_World_Cup|1934 World Championships]].
sentence_163: After the Second World War, the stadium was renamed as Stadio Comunale [[Vittorio_Pozzo|Vittorio Pozzo]].
sentence_164: Juventus played home matches at the ground for 57 years, a total of 890 league matches.
sentence_165: The team continued to host training sessions at the stadium until July 2003.
sentence_166: From 1990 until the 2005–06 season, the Torinese side contested their home matches at Stadio delle Alpi, built for the 1990 FIFA World Cup, although in very rare circumstances the club played some home games in other stadia such as [[Stadio_Renzo_Barbera|Renzo Barbera]] at Palermo, Dino Manuzzi at [[Cesena|Cesena]] and the [[Stadio_Giuseppe_Meazza|Stadio Giuseppe Meazza]] at [[Milan|Milan]].
sentence_167: In August 2006, Juventus returned to play in the Stadio Comunale, then known as [[Stadio_Olimpico_Grande_Torino|Stadio Olimpico]], after the restructuring of the stadium for the [[2006_Winter_Olympics|2006 Winter Olympics]] onward.
sentence_168: In November 2008, Juventus announced that they would invest around €120 million to build a new ground, the Juventus Stadium, on the site of delle Alpi.
sentence_169: Unlike the old ground, there is not a running track and instead the pitch is only 7.5 metres away from the stands.
sentence_170: The capacity is 41,507.
sentence_171: Work began during spring 2009 and the stadium was opened on 8 September 2011, ahead of the start of the 2011–12 season.
sentence_172: Since 1 July 2017, the Juventus Stadium is known commercially as the [[Allianz|Allianz]] Stadium of Turin until 30 June 2030.
sentence_173: See also: Juventus F.C. ultras
sentence_174: Juventus is the best-supported football club in Italy, with over 12 million fans or tifosi, which represent approximately 34% of the total Italian football fans according to a research published in September 2016 by Italian research agency Demos & Pi, as well as one of the most supported football clubs in the world, with over 300 million supporters (41 million in Europe alone), particularly in the Mediterranean countries to which a large number of [[Italian_diaspora|Italian diaspora]] have emigrated.
sentence_175: The Torinese side has fan clubs branches across the globe.
sentence_176: Demand for Juventus tickets in occasional home games held away from Turin is high, suggesting that Juventus have stronger support in other parts of the country.
sentence_177: Juventus is widely and especially popular throughout mainland Southern Italy, [[Sicily|Sicily]] and [[Malta|Malta]], leading the team to have one of the largest followings in its away matches, more than in Turin itself.
sentence_178: Main articles: [[Derby_della_Mole|Derby della Mole]], [[Derby_d'Italia|Derby d'Italia]], [[Juventus_F.C.–A.C._Milan_rivalry|Juventus F.C.–A.C.
sentence_179: Milan rivalry]], [[ACF_Fiorentina–Juventus_F.C._rivalry|ACF Fiorentina–Juventus F.C. rivalry]], and [[Juventus_F.C.–S.S.C._Napoli_rivalry|Juventus F.C.–S.S.C.
sentence_180: Napoli rivalry]]
sentence_181: Juventus have significant rivalries with two main clubs.
sentence_182: Their traditional rivals are fellow Turin club Torino; matches between the two sides are known as the Derby della Mole (Turin Derby).
sentence_183: The rivalry dates back to 1906 as Torino was founded by break-away Juventus players and staff.
sentence_184: Their most high-profile rivalry is with Internazionale, another big Serie A club located in [[Milan|Milan]], the capital of the neighbouring region of [[Lombardy|Lombardy]].
sentence_185: Matches between these two clubs are referred to as the [[Derby_d'Italia|Derby d'Italia]] (Derby of Italy) and the two regularly challenge each other at the top of the league table, hence the intense rivalry.
sentence_186: Until the Calciopoli scandal which saw Juventus forcibly relegated, the two were the only Italian clubs to have never played below Serie A.
sentence_187: Notably, the two sides are the first and the second most supported clubs in Italy and the rivalry has intensified since the later part of the 1990s; reaching its highest levels ever post-Calciopoli, with the return of Juventus to Serie A.
sentence_188: The rivalry with [[A.C._Milan|A.C.
sentence_189: Milan]] is a rivalry between the two most titled teams in Italy.
sentence_190: The challenge confronts also two of the clubs with greater basin of supporters as well as those with the greatest turnover and stock market value in the country.
sentence_191: The match-ups between Milan and Juventus, is regarded as the championship of Serie A, and both teams were often fighting for the top positions of the standings, sometimes even decisive for the award of the title.
sentence_192: They also have rivalries with [[A.S._Roma|Roma]], [[ACF_Fiorentina|Fiorentina]] and [[S.S.C._Napoli|Napoli]].
sentence_193: Main article: [[Juventus_F.C._Youth_Sector|Juventus F.C.
sentence_194: Youth Sector]]
sentence_195: The Juventus youth set-up has been recognised as one of the best in Italy for producing young talents.
sentence_196: While not all graduates made it to the first team, many have enjoyed successful careers in the Italian top flight.
sentence_197: Under long-time coach [[Vincenzo_Chiarenza|Vincenzo Chiarenza]], the Primavera (Under-20) squad enjoyed one of its successful periods, winning all age-group competitions from 2004 to 2006.
sentence_198: Like Dutch club Ajax and many [[Premier_League|Premier League]] clubs, Juventus operates several satellite clubs and football schools outside of the country (i.e. United States, Canada, [[Greece|Greece]], [[Saudi_Arabia|Saudi Arabia]], Australia and [[Switzerland|Switzerland]]) and numerous camps in the local region to expand talent scouting.
sentence_199: The youth system is also notable for its contribution to the Italian national senior and youth teams.
sentence_200: 1934 World Cup winner [[Gianpiero_Combi|Gianpiero Combi]], [[Football_at_the_1936_Summer_Olympics|1936 Gold Medal]] and [[1938_FIFA_World_Cup|1938 World Cup]] winner [[Pietro_Rava|Pietro Rava]], [[Giampiero_Boniperti|Giampiero Boniperti]], Roberto Bettega, 1982 World Cup hero Paolo Rossi and more recently Claudio Marchisio and Sebastian Giovinco are a number of former graduates who have gone on to make the first team and full Italy squad.

sentence_218: Below is a list of Juventus managers from 1923, when the [[Agnelli_family|Agnelli family]] took over and the club became more structured and organised, until the present day.
sentence_219: Main articles: [[List_of_Juventus_F.C._honours|List of Juventus F.C. honours]] and [[List_of_Juventus_F.C._seasons|List of Juventus F.C. seasons]]
sentence_220: Italy's most successful club of the 20th century and the [[Football_records_in_Italy#Most_successful_clubs_overall_(1898–present)|most successful club]] in the history of [[Football_in_Italy|Italian football]], Juventus have won the [[Serie_A|Italian League Championship]], the country's premier football club competition and organised by [[Lega_Serie_A|Lega Nazionale Professionisti Serie A]] (LNPA), a record 36 times and have the [[Football_records_in_Italy#Consecutives|record of consecutive triumphs]] in that tournament (nine, between [[2011–12_Serie_A|2011–12]] and [[2019–20_Serie_A|2019–20]]).
sentence_221: They have also won the [[Coppa_Italia|Coppa Italia]], the country's primary single-elimination competition, a record 13 times, becoming the first team to retain the trophy successfully with their triumph in the 1959–60 season, and the first to win it in three consecutive seasons from the 2014–15 season to the 2016–17 season, and went on to win it a fourth consecutive time in 2017–18.
sentence_222: In addition, the club holds the record for [[Supercoppa_Italiana|Supercoppa Italiana]] wins with eight, the most recent coming in [[2018_Supercoppa_Italiana|2018]].
sentence_223: Overall, Juventus have won 68 official competitions, [[Football_records_in_Italy#Most_successful_clubs_overall_(1898–present)|more than any other Italian club]]: 57 domestic trophies (which is also a record) and 11 official international competitions, making them, in the latter case, the second most successful Italian club in [[List_of_UEFA_club_competition_winners#By_club|European competition]].
sentence_224: The club is fifth in Europe and eleventh in the world with the most international titles won officially recognised by their respective [[FIFA#Structure|association football confederation]] and [[FIFA|Fédération Internationale de Football Association]] (FIFA).
sentence_225: In [[1976–77_UEFA_Cup|1977]], the Torinese side become the first in Southern Europe to have won the [[UEFA_Europa_League|UEFA Cup]] and the first—and only to date—in Italian football history to achieve an international title with a squad composed by national footballers.
sentence_226: In [[1992–93_UEFA_Cup|1993]], the club won its third competition's trophy, an unprecedented feat in the continent until then and the most for an Italian club.
sentence_227: Juventus was also the first Italian club to achieve the title in the [[UEFA_Super_Cup|European Super Cup]], having won the competition in [[1984_European_Super_Cup|1984]] and the first European club to win the [[Intercontinental_Cup_(football)|Intercontinental Cup]] in [[1985_Intercontinental_Cup|1985]], since it was restructured by [[UEFA|Union of European Football Associations]] (UEFA) and [[CONMEBOL|Confederación Sudamericana de Fútbol]] (CONMEBOL)'s organizing committee five years beforehand.
sentence_228: The club has earned the distinction of being allowed to wear three Golden Stars ([[Italian_language|Italian]]: stelle d'oro) on its shirts representing its league victories, the tenth of which was achieved during the 1957–58 season, the 20th in the [[1981–82_Serie_A|1981–82 season]] and the 30th in the [[2013–14_Serie_A|2013–14 season]].
sentence_229: Juventus were the first Italian team to have achieved [[Double_(association_football)|the national double]] four times (winning the Italian [[Serie_A|top tier division]] and the [[Coppa_Italia|national cup]] competition in the same season), in the 1959–60, 1994–95, 2014–15 and 2015–16 seasons.
sentence_230: In the 2015–16 season, Juventus won the [[2016_Coppa_Italia_Final|Coppa Italia]] for the 11th time and their second-straight title, becoming the first team in Italy's history to complete Serie A and Coppa Italia [[Double_(association_football)|doubles]] in back-to-back seasons; Juventus would go on to win another two consecutive doubles in 2016–17 and 2017–18.
sentence_231: The club is unique in the world in having won all official confederation competitions and they have received, in recognition to winning [[UEFA_club_competition_records_and_statistics#List_of_teams_to_have_won_the_three_main_European_club_competitions|the three major]] [[UEFA_club_competition_records|UEFA competitions]]—[[Timeline_of_association_football#1980s|first case]] in the history of the [[European_football|European football]] and the only one to be reached with the same coach— [[The_UEFA_Plaque|The UEFA Plaque]] by the [[UEFA|Union of European Football Associations]] (UEFA) on 12 July 1988.
sentence_232: The Torinese side was placed seventh—but the top Italian club—in the [[FIFA_Club_of_the_Century|FIFA's century ranking]] of the best clubs in the world on 23 December 2000 and nine years later was ranked second best club in Europe during the 20th Century based on a statistical study series by [[International_Federation_of_Football_History_&_Statistics|International Federation of Football History & Statistics]], the highest for an Italian club in both.
sentence_233: Juventus have been proclaimed [[International_Federation_of_Football_History_&_Statistics#The_World's_Club_Team_of_the_Year|World's Club Team of the Year]] twice (1993 and 1996) and was ranked in 3rd place—the highest ranking of any Italian club—in the [[International_Federation_of_Football_History_&_Statistics#Club_World_Ranking|All-Time Club World Ranking]] (1991–2009 period) by the IFFHS.
sentence_234: Main article: [[List_of_Juventus_F.C._records_and_statistics|List of Juventus F.C. records and statistics]]
sentence_235: Alessandro Del Piero holds Juventus' official appearance record of 705 appearances.
sentence_236: He took over from Gaetano Scirea on 6 April 2008 against [[U.S._Città_di_Palermo|Palermo]].
sentence_237: He also holds the record for Serie A appearances with 478.
sentence_238: Including all official competitions, Del Piero is the all-time leading goalscorer for Juventus, with 290—since joining the club in 1993.
sentence_239: Giampiero Boniperti, who was the all-time topscorer since 1961 comes in second in all competitions with 182.
sentence_240: In the [[1933–34_Serie_A|1933–34 season]], [[Felice_Borel|Felice Borel]] scored 31 goals in 34 appearances, setting the club record for Serie A goals in a single season.
sentence_241: Ferenc Hirzer is the club's highest scorer in a single season with 35 goals in 26 appearances in the 1925–26 season (record of Italian football).
sentence_242: The most goals scored by a player in a single match is 6, which is also an Italian record.
sentence_243: This was achieved by Omar Sívori in a game against Internazionale in the [[1960–61_Serie_A|1960–61 season]].
sentence_244: The first ever official game participated in by Juventus was in the [[1900_Italian_Football_Championship|Third Federal Football Championship]], the predecessor of Serie A, against [[F.B.C._Torinese|Torinese]] in a Juventus loss 0–1.
sentence_245: The biggest victory recorded by Juventus was 15–0 against Cento, in the second round of the Coppa Italia in the 1926–27 season.
sentence_246: In the league, Fiorentina and Fiumana were famously on the end of Juventus' biggest championship wins, with both beaten 11–0 in the 1928–29 season.
sentence_247: Juventus' heaviest championship defeats came during the 1911–12 and 1912–13 seasons: they were against Milan in 1912 (1–8) and Torino in 1913 (0–8).
sentence_248: The signing of [[Gianluigi_Buffon|Gianluigi Buffon]] in 2001 from [[S.S.D._Parma_Calcio_1913|Parma]] cost Juventus €52 million (100 billion lire), making it the then-most expensive transfer for a goalkeeper of all-time until 2018.
sentence_249: On 20 March 2016, Buffon set a new Serie A record for the longest period without conceding a goal (974 minutes) in the Derby della Mole during the 2015–16 season.
sentence_250: On 26 July 2016, Argentine forward [[Gonzalo_Higuaín|Gonzalo Higuaín]] became the third highest football transfer of all-time and highest ever transfer for an Italian club, at the time, when he was signed by Juventus for €90 million from Napoli.
sentence_251: On 8 August 2016, [[Paul_Pogba|Paul Pogba]] returned to his first club, [[Manchester_United_F.C.|Manchester United]], for an all-time record for highest football transfer fee of €105 million, surpassing the former record holder [[Gareth_Bale|Gareth Bale]].
sentence_252: The sale of [[Zinedine_Zidane|Zinedine Zidane]] from Juventus to Real Madrid of Spain in 2001 was the world football transfer record at the time, costing the Spanish club around €77.5 million (150 billion lire).
sentence_253: On 10 July 2018, [[Cristiano_Ronaldo|Cristiano Ronaldo]] became the highest ever transfer for an Italian club with his €100 million transfer from Real Madrid.

section_23.value: Contribution to the Italy national team

sentence_254: Main article: [[Juventus_F.C._and_the_Italy_national_football_team|Juventus F.C. and the Italy national football team]]
sentence_255: Overall, Juventus are the club [[Juventus_F.C._and_the_Italy_national_football_team#List_of_call-ups_of_Juventus_F.C._players_to_the_Italy_national_major_teams|that has contributed the most players]] to the [[Italy_national_football_team|Italy national team]] in history, being the only Italian club that has contributed players to every Italy national team since the [[1934_FIFA_World_Cup|2nd FIFA World Cup]].
sentence_256: Juventus have contributed numerous players to Italy's [[FIFA_World_Cup|World Cup]] campaigns, these successful periods principally have coincided with two golden ages of the Turin club's history, referred as Quinquennio d'Oro (The Golden Quinquennium), from 1931 until 1935, and Ciclo Leggendario (The Legendary Cycle), from 1972 to 1986.
sentence_257: Below are a list of Juventus players who represented the Italy national team during World Cup winning tournaments.

list.value: [[1934_FIFA_World_Cup|1934 FIFA World Cup]] (9): [[Gianpiero_Combi|Gianpiero Combi]], [[Virginio_Rosetta|Virginio Rosetta]], [[Luigi_Bertolini|Luigi Bertolini]], [[Felice_Borel|Felice Borel]] IIº, [[Umberto_Caligaris|Umberto Caligaris]], [[Giovanni_Ferrari|Giovanni Ferrari]], [[Luis_Monti|Luis Monti]], [[Raimundo_Orsi|Raimundo Orsi]] and [[Mario_Varglien|Mario Varglien]] Iº
[[1938_FIFA_World_Cup|1938 FIFA World Cup]] (2): [[Alfredo_Foni|Alfredo Foni]] and [[Pietro_Rava|Pietro Rava]]

[[2006_FIFA_World_Cup|2006 FIFA World Cup]] (5): [[Fabio_Cannavaro|Fabio Cannavaro]], [[Gianluigi_Buffon|Gianluigi Buffon]], [[Mauro_Camoranesi|Mauro Camoranesi]], [[Alessandro_Del_Piero|Alessandro Del Piero]] and [[Gianluca_Zambrotta|Gianluca Zambrotta]]

sentence_258: Two Juventus players have won the [[FIFA_World_Cup_awards|golden boot]] award at the World Cup with Italy, Paolo Rossi in 1982 and [[Salvatore_Schillaci|Salvatore Schillaci]] in [[1990_FIFA_World_Cup|1990]].
sentence_259: As well as contributing to Italy's World Cup winning sides, two Juventus players Alfredo Foni and Pietro Rava, represented Italy in the gold medal winning squad at the [[Football_at_the_1936_Summer_Olympics|1936 Summer Olympics]].
sentence_260: Three Juventus players represented their nation during the [[1968_European_Football_Championship|1968 European Football Championship]] win for Italy: [[Sandro_Salvadore|Sandro Salvadore]], [[Ernesto_Castano|Ernesto Càstano]] and [[Giancarlo_Bercellino|Giancarlo Bercellino]].
sentence_261: The Torinese club has also contributed to a lesser degree to the national sides of other nations.
sentence_262: [[Zinedine_Zidane|Zinedine Zidane]] and captain [[Didier_Deschamps|Didier Deschamps]] were Juventus players when they won the [[1998_FIFA_World_Cup|1998 World Cup]] with [[French_national_football_team|France]], as well as [[Blaise_Matuidi|Blaise Matuidi]] in the [[2018_FIFA_World_Cup|2018 World Cup]], making it as the association football club which supplied the most FIFA World Cup winners globally (25).
sentence_263: Three Juventus players have also won the [[UEFA_European_Football_Championship|European Football Championship]] with a nation other than Italy, [[Luis_del_Sol|Luis del Sol]] won it in [[1964_European_Football_Championship|1964]] with [[Spanish_national_football_team|Spain]], while the Frenchmen Michel Platini and Zidane won the competition in [[1984_UEFA_European_Football_Championship|1984]] and [[2000_UEFA_European_Football_Championship|2000]] respectively.
sentence_264: Since 27 June 1967, Juventus Football Club has been a società per azioni (S.p.A.) and since 3 December 2001 the Torinese side is listed on the [[Borsa_Italiana|Borsa Italiana]].
sentence_265: As of 31 December 2015, the Juventus' [[Share_(finance)|shares]] are distributed between 63.8% to [[Exor_(company)|EXOR N.V.]], the Agnelli family's [[Holding_company|holding]] (a company of the Giovanni Agnelli and C.S.a.p.a Group), 5.0% to Lindsell Train Ltd. and 31.2% to other shareholders.
sentence_266: (<2.0%) As of 5 July 2016, Lindsell Train Ltd. increased its holding to 10% and then Exor S.P.A decreased to 60.0%.
sentence_267: Since 2012, [[Jeep|Jeep]] became the new sponsor of Juventus, a car brand acquired by FIAT after the 2000s global financial crisis.
sentence_268: Along with [[S.S._Lazio|Lazio]] and Roma, Juventus is one of only three Italian clubs quoted on [[Borsa_Italiana|Borsa Italiana]] (Italian stock exchange); it also has a secondary listing on Borsa Italiana's sister stock exchange, the [[London_Stock_Exchange|London Stock Exchange]].
sentence_269: Juventus was also the only association football club in the country member of STAR (Segment of Stocks conforming to High Requirements, Italian: Segmento Titoli con Alti Requisiti), one of the main [[Market_segmentation|market segment]] in the world.
sentence_270: However, Juventus had to move from the STAR segment to MTA market due to 2011 financial results.
sentence_271: The club's [[Juventus_Training_Center_(Vinovo)|training ground]] was owned by Campi di Vinovo S.p.A, controlled by Juventus Football Club S.p.A. to 71.3%.
sentence_272: In 2003, the club bought the lands from the subsidiary and later the company was dissolved.
sentence_273: Since then, Juventus has not had any subsidiary.
sentence_274: From 1 July 2008, the club has implemented a safety management system for employees and athletes in compliance with the requirements of international OHSAS 18001:2007 regulation and a Safety Management System in the medical sector according to the international [[ISO_9000#2000_version|ISO 9001:2000]] resolution.
sentence_275: The club is one of the founders of the [[European_Club_Association|European Club Association]] (ECA), which was formed after the dissolution of the [[G-14|G-14]], an international group of Europe's most elite clubs of which Juventus were also a founding member.
sentence_276: According to the [[Deloitte_Football_Money_League|Deloitte Football Money League]], a research published by consultants [[Deloitte|Deloitte]] Touche Tohmatsu on 17 January 2014, Juventus are the ninth-highest earning football club in the world with an estimated revenue of €272.4 million, the most for an Italian club.
sentence_277: The club is also ranked ninth on [[Forbes'_list_of_the_most_valuable_football_clubs|Forbes' list of the most valuable football clubs]] in the world with an estimate value of US$850 million (€654 million), making them the second richest association football club in Italy.
sentence_278: Juventus re-capitalized on 28 June 2007, increasing €104,807,731.60 of share capital.
sentence_279: The team made an aggregate net loss in the following seasons (2006 to date): –€927,569 (2006–07), –€20,787,469 (2007–08), net income €6,582,489 (2008–09) and net loss €10,967,944 (2009–10).
sentence_280: After an unaudited €43,411,481 net loss was recorded in the first nine months of 2010–11 season, the board of directors announced that a capital increase of €120 million was planned, scheduled to submit to the extraordinary shareholder's meeting in October.
sentence_281: Eventually, the 2010–11 season net loss was €95,414,019.
sentence_282: In the 2012–13 season, Juventus continued to recover from recent seasons' net losses thanks to the biggest payment in UEFA's Champions League 2012–13 revenue distribution, earning €65.3 million.
sentence_283: Despite being knocked out in the quarterfinal stage, Juventus took the lion's share thanks to the largesse of the Italian national TV market and the division of revenues with the only other Italian team making the competition's final phase, Milan.
sentence_284: Confirming the trend of marked improvement in net result, the 2013–14 financial year closed with a loss of €6.7 million, but with the first positive operating income since 2006.
sentence_285: In the 2014–15 season, by the excellent sports results achieved (the fourth year in a row of Serie A titles, the tenth Coppa Italia title and playing the Champions League final), net income reached €2.3 million.
sentence_286: Compared to the loss of €6.7 million last year, 2014–15 showed a positive change of €9 million and returned to a profit after six years since 2008–09.
sentence_287: As Italy's famous pink sports newspaper, [[La_Gazzetta_dello_Sport|La Gazzetta dello Sport]], produced its annual list of salaries in Serie A, there was one headline that stuck out above all the rest .CR7 that has elevated Juve's total spend.
sentence_288: The Old Lady has no less than nine players earning €6 million or more per season compared to just three who take home more than that figure in the entirety of the rest of the league.
sentence_289: Their struggles in selling players during the previous transfer window has also served to increase their overall spend on wages.
sentence_290: Juve tried and failed to sell Paulo Dybala, Sami Khedira, Gonzalo Higuain and Mario Mandzukic in the summer, players who cost the club €26.8 million per season in salaries.

title: Literacy
sentence_0: "Illiterate" redirects here.
sentence_1: For the 2013 film, see [[Illiterate_(film)|Illiterate (film)]].
sentence_2: "Reading and writing" redirects here.
sentence_3: For the journal, see [[Reading_and_Writing_(journal)|Reading and Writing (journal)]].
sentence_4: Literacy is popularly understood as an ability to [[Reading_(process)|read]], [[Writing|write]] and use [[Numeracy|numeracy]] in at least one method of writing, an understanding reflected by mainstream dictionary and handbook definitions.
sentence_5: Starting in the 1980s, however, literacy researchers have maintained that defining literacy as an ability apart from any actual event of reading and writing ignores the complex ways reading and writing always happen in a specific context and in tandem with the values associated with that context.
sentence_6: The view that literacy always involves social and cultural elements is reflected in [[UNESCO|UNESCO]]'s stipulation that literacy is an "ability to identify, understand, interpret, create, communicate and compute, using printed and written materials associated with varying contexts."
sentence_7: Modern attention to literacy as a "context-dependent assemblage of social practices" reflects the understanding that individuals' reading and writing practices develop and change over the lifespan as their cultural, political, and historical contexts change.
sentence_8: For example, in [[Scotland|Scotland]], literacy has been defined as: "The ability to read, write and use numeracy, to handle information, to express ideas and opinions, to make decisions and solve problems, as family members, workers, citizens and lifelong learners."
sentence_9: Such expanded definitions have altered long-standing "[[Rule_of_thumb|rule of thumb]]" measures of literacy, e.g., the ability to read the newspaper, in part because the increasing involvement of computers and other digital technologies in communication necessitates additional skills (e.g. interfacing with [[Web_browser|web browsers]] and [[Word_processing|word processing]] programs; organizing and altering the configuration of files, etc.).
sentence_10: By extension, the expansion of these necessary skill-sets became known, variously, as [[Computer_literacy|computer literacy]], information literacy, and [[Technological_literacy|technological literacy]].
sentence_11: Elsewhere definitions of literacy extend the original notion of "acquired ability" into concepts like "arts literacy," [[Visual_literacy|visual literacy]] (the ability to understand visual forms of communication such as [[Body_language|body language]], pictures, maps, and video), [[Statistical_literacy|statistical literacy]], [[Critical_literacy|critical literacy]], [[Media_literacy|media literacy]], [[Ecological_literacy|ecological literacy]], disaster literacy, and [[Health_literacy|health literacy]].
sentence_12: See also: [[History_of_writing|History of writing]] and [[History_of_education|History of education]]
sentence_13: Literacy emerged with the development of [[Numeracy|numeracy]] and computational devices as early as 8000 BCE.
sentence_14: Script developed independently at least five times in human history Mesopotamia, [[Egypt|Egypt]], the [[Indus_civilization|Indus civilization]], lowland [[Mesoamerica|Mesoamerica]], and [[China|China]].
sentence_15: The earliest forms of [[Written_communication|written communication]] originated in Sumer, located in southern Mesopotamia about 3500-3000 BCE.
sentence_16: During this era, literacy was "a largely functional matter, propelled by the need to manage the new quantities of information and the new type of governance created by trade and large scale production".
sentence_17: Writing systems in Mesopotamia first emerged from a recording system in which people used impressed token markings to manage trade and agricultural production.
sentence_18: The token system served as a precursor to early [[Cuneiform|cuneiform]] writing once people began recording information on clay tablets.
sentence_19: [[Proto-cuneiform|Proto-cuneiform]] texts exhibit not only numerical signs, but also [[Ideograms|ideograms]] depicting objects being counted.
sentence_20: [[Egyptian_hieroglyphs|Egyptian hieroglyphs]] emerged from 3300-3100 BCE and depicted royal iconography that emphasized power amongst other elites.
sentence_21: The Egyptian hieroglyphic writing system was the first notation system to have [[Phonetic|phonetic]] values.
sentence_22: Writing in lowland Mesoamerica was first put into practice by the [[Olmec|Olmec]] and [[Zapotec_civilization|Zapotec]] civilizations in 900-400 BCE.
sentence_23: These civilizations used glyphic writing and bar-and-dot numerical notation systems for purposes related to royal iconography and calendar systems.
sentence_24: The earliest written notations in China date back to the [[Shang_Dynasty|Shang Dynasty]] in 1200 BCE.
sentence_25: These systematic notations were found inscribed on bones and recorded sacrifices made, tributes received, and animals hunted, which were activities of the elite.
sentence_26: These oracle-bone inscriptions were the early ancestors of modern Chinese script and contained [[Logosyllabic|logosyllabic]] script and numerals.
sentence_27: [[Indus_script|Indus script]] is largely pictorial and has not been deciphered yet.
sentence_28: It may or may not include abstract signs.
sentence_29: It is thought that they wrote from right to left and that the script is thought to be [[Logographic|logographic]].
sentence_30: Because it has not been deciphered, linguists disagree on whether it is a complete and independent writing system; however, it is genuinely thought to be an independent writing system that emerged in the [[Harappa|Harappa]] culture.
sentence_31: These examples indicate that early acts of literacy were closely tied to power and chiefly used for management practices, and probably less than 1% of the population was literate, as it was confined to a very small ruling elite.
sentence_32: According to [[Social_anthropologist|social anthropologist]] [[Jack_Goody|Jack Goody]], there are two interpretations that regard the origin of the alphabet.
sentence_33: Many classical scholars, such as historian [[Ignace_Gelb|Ignace Gelb]], credit the Ancient Greeks for creating the first alphabetic system (c. 750 BCE) that used distinctive signs for consonants and vowels.
sentence_34: But Goody contests, "The importance of Greek culture of the subsequent history of Western Europe has led to an over-emphasis, by [[Classics|classicists]] and others, on the addition of specific [[Vowel|vowel]] signs to the set of [[Consonant|consonantal]] ones that had been developed earlier in Western Asia".
sentence_35: Thus, many scholars argue that the [[Ancient_Semitic-speaking_peoples|ancient Semitic-speaking peoples]] of northern [[Canaan|Canaan]] (modern-day [[Syria|Syria]]) invented the consonantal alphabet as early as 1500 BCE.
sentence_36: Much of this theory's development is credited to English archeologist [[Flinders_Petrie|Flinders Petrie]], who, in 1905, came across a series of Canaanite inscriptions located in the turquoise mines of [[Serabit_el-Khadem|Serabit el-Khadem]].
sentence_37: Ten years later, English Egyptologist Alan Gardiner reasoned that these letters contain an alphabet, as well as references to the Canaanite goddess [[Asherah|Asherah]].
sentence_38: In 1948, [[William_F._Albright|William F. Albright]] deciphered the text using additional evidence that had been discovered subsequent to Goody's findings.
sentence_39: This included a series of inscriptions from [[Ugarit|Ugarit]], discovered in 1929 by French archaeologist [[Claude_F._A._Schaeffer|Claude F. A. Schaeffer]].
sentence_40: Some of these inscriptions were mythological texts (written in an early Canaanite dialect) that consisted of a 32-letter [[Cuneiform|cuneiform]] consonantal alphabet.
sentence_41: Another significant discovery was made in 1953 when three arrowheads were uncovered, each containing identical Canaanite inscriptions from twelfth century BCE.
sentence_42: According to [[Frank_Moore_Cross|Frank Moore Cross]], these inscriptions consisted of alphabetic signs that originated during the transitional development from pictographic script to a linear alphabet.
sentence_43: Moreover, he asserts, "These inscriptions also provided clues to extend the decipherment of earlier and later alphabetic texts".
sentence_44: The consonantal system of the Canaanite script inspired alphabetical developments in subsequent systems.
sentence_45: During the Late [[Bronze_Age|Bronze Age]], successor alphabets appeared throughout the Mediterranean region and were employed for [[Phoenician_language|Phoenician]], [[Hebrew|Hebrew]] and [[Aramaic|Aramaic]].
sentence_46: According to Goody, these cuneiform scripts may have influenced the development of the Greek alphabet several centuries later.
sentence_47: Historically, the Greeks contended that their writing system was modeled after the Phoenicians.
sentence_48: However, many Semitic scholars now believe that Ancient Greek is more consistent with an early form Canaanite that was used c. 1100 BCE.
sentence_49: While the earliest Greek inscriptions are dated c. eighth century BCE, epigraphical comparisons to [[Proto-Canaanite|Proto-Canaanite]] suggest that the Greeks may have adopted the consonantal alphabet as early as 1100 BCE, and later "added in five characters to represent vowels".
sentence_50: Phoenician, which is considered to contain the first [[List_of_writing_systems|"linear alphabet"]], rapidly spread to the Mediterranean port cities in northern [[Canaan|Canaan]].
sentence_51: Some archeologists believe that Phoenician scripture had some influence on the developments of the Hebrew and Aramaic alphabets based on the fact that these languages evolved during the same time period, share similar features, and are commonly categorized into the same language group.
sentence_52: When the Israelites migrated to Canaan between 1200 and 1001 BCE, they also adopted a variation of the Canaanite alphabet.
sentence_53: [[Baruch_ben_Neriah|Baruch ben Neriah]], Jeremiah's scribe, used this alphabet to create the later scripts of the [[Old_Testament|Old Testament]].
sentence_54: The early Hebrew alphabet was prominent in the Mediterranean region until [[Neo-Babylonian|Chaldean Babylonian]] rulers exiled the Jews to [[Babylon|Babylon]] in the sixth century BCE.
sentence_55: It was then that the new script ("Square Hebrew") emerged and the older one rapidly died out.
sentence_56: The [[Aramaic_alphabet|Aramaic alphabet]] also emerged sometime between 1200 and 1000 BCE.
sentence_57: As the [[Bronze_Age_collapse|Bronze Age collapsed]], the [[Aramaeans|Aramaeans]] moved into Canaan and Phoenician territories and adopted their scripts.
sentence_58: Although early evidence of this writing is scarce, archeologists have uncovered a wide range of later Aramaic texts, written as early as the seventh century BCE.
sentence_59: Due to its longevity and prevalence in the region, Achaemenid rulers would come to adopt it as a "diplomatic language".
sentence_60: The modern Aramaic alphabet rapidly spread east to the Kingdom of Nabataea, then to [[Sinai_Peninsula|Sinai]] and the [[Arabian_Peninsula|Arabian Peninsula]], eventually making its way to [[Africa|Africa]].
sentence_61: Aramaean merchants carried older variations of Aramaic as far as [[India|India]], where it later influenced the development of the [[Brahmi_script|Brahmi script]].
sentence_62: It also led to the developments of [[Arabic_alphabet|Arabic]] and [[Pahlavi_scripts|Pahlavi]] (an Iranian adaptation), "as well as for a range of alphabets used by early [[Turkish_peoples|Turkish]] and [[Mongol|Mongol]] tribes in [[Siberia|Siberia]], [[Mongolia|Mongolia]] and [[Turkestan|Turkestan]]".

section_7.value: Spread of literacy since the mid-twentieth century

sentence_97: Literacy data published by [[UNESCO|UNESCO]] displays that since 1950, the adult literacy rate at the world level has increased by 5 percentage points every decade on average, from 55.7 per cent in 1950 to 86.2 per cent in 2015.
sentence_98: However, for four decades, the population growth was so rapid that the number of illiterate adults kept increasing, rising from 700 million in 1950 to 878 million in 1990.
sentence_99: Since then, the number has fallen markedly to 745 million in 2015, although it remains higher than in 1950 despite decades of universal education policies, literacy interventions and the spread of print material and information and communications technology (ICT).
sentence_100: However, these trends have been far from uniform across regions.
sentence_101: Available global data indicates significant variations in literacy rates between world regions.
sentence_102: [[North_America|North America]], [[Europe|Europe]], [[West_Asia|West Asia]], and [[Central_Asia|Central Asia]] have achieved almost full adult literacy (individuals at or over the age of 15) for both men and women.
sentence_103: Most countries in [[East_Asia_and_the_Pacific|East Asia and the Pacific]], as well as [[Latin_America_and_the_Caribbean|Latin America and the Caribbean]], are above a 90% literacy rate for adults.
sentence_104: Illiteracy persists to a greater extent in other regions: 2013 UNESCO Institute for Statistics (UIS) data indicates adult literacy rates of only 67.55% in [[South_Asia|South Asia]] and [[North_Africa|North Africa]], 59.76% in [[Sub-Saharan_Africa|Sub-Saharan Africa]].
sentence_105: In much of the world, high youth literacy rates suggest that illiteracy will become less and less common as younger generations with higher educational attainment levels replace older ones.
sentence_106: However, in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, where the vast majority of the world's illiterate youth live, lower school enrollment implies that illiteracy will persist to a greater degree.
sentence_107: According to 2013 UIS data, the youth literacy rate (individuals ages 15 to 24) is 84.03% in South Asia and North Africa, and 70.06% in Sub-Saharan Africa.
sentence_108: Yet the literate/illiterate distinction is not clear-cut: for example, given that a large part of the benefits of literacy can be obtained by having access to a literate person in the household, some recent literature in economics, starting with the work of Kaushik Basu and James Foster, distinguishes between a "proximate illiterate" and an "isolated illiterate".
sentence_109: The former refers to an illiterate person who lives in a household with literates and the latter to an illiterate who lives in a household of all illiterates.
sentence_110: What is of concern is that many people in poor nations are not proximate illiterates but rather isolated illiterates.
sentence_111: That being said, literacy has rapidly spread in several regions in the last twenty-five years (see image).
sentence_112: The global initiative of the United Nations to actualize the [[Sustainable_Development_Goal_4|Sustainable Development Goal 4]] is also gaining momentum.
sentence_113: According to 2015 UIS data collected by the UNESCO Institute for Statistics, about two-thirds (63%) of the world's illiterate adults are women.
sentence_114: This disparity was even starker in previous decades: from 1970 to 2000, the global gender gap in literacy would decrease by roughly 50%.
sentence_115: In recent years, however, this progress has stagnated, with the remaining gender gap holding almost constant over the last two decades.
sentence_116: In general, the gender gap in literacy is not as pronounced as the regional gap; that is, differences between countries in overall literacy are often larger than gender differences within countries.
sentence_117: However, the gap between men and women would narrow from 1990 onwards, after the increase of male adult literacy rates at 80 per cent (see image).
sentence_118: [[Sub-Saharan_Africa|Sub-Saharan Africa]], the region with the lowest overall literacy rates, also features the widest gender gap: just 52% of adult females are literate, and 68% among adult men.
sentence_119: Similar gender disparity persists in two other regions, [[North_Africa|North Africa]] (86% adult male literacy, 70% adult female literacy) and South Asia (77% adult male literacy, 58% adult female literacy).
sentence_120: The 1990 World Conference on [[Education_For_All|Education for All]], held in Jomtien, Thailand, would bring attention to the literacy gender gap and prompt many developing countries to prioritize women's literacy.
sentence_121: In many contexts, female illiteracy co-exists with other aspects of gender inequality.
sentence_122: [[Martha_Nussbaum|Martha Nussbaum]] suggests illiterate women are more vulnerable to becoming trapped in an abusive marriage, given that illiteracy limits their employment opportunities and worsens their [[Intra-household_bargaining|intra-household bargaining]] position.
sentence_123: Moreover, Nussbaum links literacy to the potential for women to effectively communicate and collaborate with one another in order "to participate in a larger movement for political change."
sentence_124: Social barriers prevent expanding literacy skills among women and girls.
sentence_125: Making literacy classes available can be ineffective when it conflicts with the use of the valuable limited time of women and girls.
sentence_126: School age girls, in many contexts, face stronger expectations than their male counterparts to perform household work and care after younger siblings.
sentence_127: Generational dynamics can also perpetuate these disparities: illiterate parents may not readily appreciate the value of literacy for their daughters, particularly in traditional, rural societies with expectations that girls will remain at home.
sentence_128: A 2015 [[World_Bank|World Bank]] and the International Center for Research on Women review of academic literature would conclude that [[Child_marriage|child marriage]], which predominantly impacts girls, tends to reduce literacy levels.
sentence_129: A 2008 analysis of the issue in Bangladesh found that for every additional year of delay in a girl's marriage, her likelihood of literacy would increase by 5.6 percent.
sentence_130: Similarly, a 2014 study found that in sub-Saharan Africa, marrying early would significantly decrease a girl's probability of literacy, holding other variables constant.
sentence_131: A 2015 review of the [[Child_marriage|child marriage]] literature therefore would recommend marriage postponement as part of a strategy to increase educational attainment levels, including female literacy in particular.

sentence_155: Efforts to increase adult literacy often encompass other development priorities as well; for example, initiatives in [[Ethiopia|Ethiopia]], [[Morocco|Morocco]], and [[India|India]] have combined adult literacy programs with vocational skills trainings in order to encourage enrollment and address the complex needs of women and other marginalized groups who lack economic opportunity.

sentence_160: The [[Human_Development_Index|Human Development Index]], produced by the [[United_Nations_Development_Programme|United Nations Development Programme]] (UNDP), uses education as one of its three indicators; originally, adult literacy represented two-thirds of this education index weight.

sentence_207: Main article: [[Learning_to_read|Learning to read]]
sentence_208: Critiques of autonomous models of literacy notwithstanding, the belief that [[Reading_(process)|reading]] development is key to literacy remains dominant, at least in the United States, where it is understood as progression of skills that begins with the ability to understand spoken words and decode written words, and that culminates in the deep understanding of text.
sentence_209: Reading development involves a range of complex language-underpinnings including awareness of speech sounds ([[Phonology|phonology]]), spelling patterns (orthography), word meaning ([[Semantics|semantics]]), grammar, ([[Syntax|syntax]]) and patterns of word formation ([[Morphology_(linguistics)|morphology]]), all of which provide a necessary platform for reading [[Fluency|fluency]] and comprehension.
sentence_210: Once these skills are acquired, it is maintained, a reader can attain full language literacy, which includes the abilities to apply to printed material critical analysis, inference and synthesis; to write with accuracy and coherence; and to use information and insights from text as the basis for informed decisions and creative thought.
sentence_211: For this reason, teaching English literacy in the [[United_States|United States]] is dominated by a focus on a set of discrete decoding skills.
sentence_212: From this perspective, literacy—or, rather, reading—comprises a number of subskills that can be taught to students.
sentence_213: These skill sets include [[Phonological_awareness|phonological awareness]], [[Phonics|phonics (decoding)]], [[Fluency|fluency]], [[Reading_comprehension|comprehension]], and [[Vocabulary|vocabulary]].
sentence_214: Mastering each of these subskills is necessary for students to become proficient readers.
sentence_215: From this same perspective, readers of [[Alphabetic_language|alphabetic languages]] must understand the alphabetic principle to master basic reading skills.
sentence_216: For this purpose a writing system is "alphabetic" if it uses symbols to represent individual language sounds, though the degree of correspondence between letters and sounds varies between alphabetic languages.
sentence_217: [[Syllabary|Syllabic writing systems]] (such as [[Japanese_writing_system|Japanese]] [[Kana|kana]]) use a symbol to represent a single syllable, and [[Logogram|logographic writing systems]] (such as [[Written_Chinese|Chinese]]) use a symbol to represent a [[Morpheme|morpheme]].
sentence_218: There are any number of approaches to teaching literacy; each is shaped by its informing assumptions about what literacy is and how it is best learned by students.
sentence_219: [[Phonics|Phonics]] instruction, for example, focuses on reading at the level of the word.
sentence_220: It teaches readers to observe and interpret the letters or groups of letters that make up words.
sentence_221: A common method of teaching phonics is [[Synthetic_phonics|synthetic phonics]], in which a novice reader pronounces each individual sound and "blends" them to pronounce the whole word.
sentence_222: Another approach is embedded phonics instruction, used more often in [[Whole_language|whole language]] reading instruction, in which novice readers learn about the individual letters in words on a just-in-time, just-in-place basis that is tailored to meet each student's reading and writing learning needs.
sentence_223: That is, teachers provide phonics instruction opportunistically, within the context of stories or student writing that feature many instances of a particular letter or group of letters.
sentence_224: Embedded instruction combines letter-sound knowledge with the use of meaningful context to read new and difficult words.
sentence_225: Techniques such as [[Directed_listening_and_thinking_activity|directed listening and thinking activities]] can be used to aid children in learning how to read and [[Reading_comprehension|reading comprehension]].
sentence_226: In a 2012 proposal, it has been claimed that reading can be acquired naturally if print is constantly available at an early age in the same manner as spoken language.
sentence_227: If an appropriate form of written text is made available before formal schooling begins, reading should be learned inductively, emerge naturally, and with no significant negative consequences.
sentence_228: This proposal challenges the commonly held belief that written language requires formal instruction and schooling.
sentence_229: Its success would change current views of literacy and schooling.
sentence_230: Using developments in behavioral science and technology, an interactive system (Technology Assisted Reading Acquisition, TARA) would enable young pre-literate children to accurately perceive and learn properties of written language by simple exposure to the written form.

title: Los Angeles Dodgers
sentence_0: "Dodgers" redirects here.
sentence_1: For any other use, see [[Dodger_(disambiguation)|Dodger (disambiguation)]].
sentence_2: The Los Angeles Dodgers are an American professional [[Baseball|baseball]] team based in [[Los_Angeles|Los Angeles, California]].
sentence_3: The Dodgers compete in [[Major_League_Baseball|Major League Baseball]] (MLB) as a member club of the [[National_League|National League]] (NL) [[National_League_West|West]] division.
sentence_4: Established in 1883 in the city of [[Brooklyn|Brooklyn]], which later became a borough of [[City_of_Greater_New_York|New York City]], the team joined the NL in 1890 as the Brooklyn Bridegrooms and assumed several different monikers thereafter before finally settling on the name Dodgers in 1932.
sentence_5: From the 1940s through the mid-1950s, the Dodgers developed a fierce cross-town [[Dodgers-Yankees_rivalry|rivalry]] with the [[New_York_Yankees|New York Yankees]] as the two clubs faced each other in the [[World_Series|World Series]] seven times, with the Dodgers losing the first five matchups before defeating them to win the franchise's first title in [[1955_World_Series|1955]].
sentence_6: It was also during this period that the Dodgers made history by breaking the [[Baseball_color_line|baseball color line]] in 1947 with the debut of [[Jackie_Robinson|Jackie Robinson]], the first African-American to ever play in the Major Leagues.
sentence_7: Another major milestone was reached in 1956 when [[Don_Newcombe|Don Newcombe]] became the first player ever to win both the [[Cy_Young_Award|Cy Young Award]] and the [[Major_League_Baseball_Most_Valuable_Player_Award|NL MVP]] in the same season.
sentence_8: After 68 seasons in Brooklyn, Dodgers owner and president Walter O'Malley [[Major_League_Baseball_relocation_of_1950s–1960s|relocated the franchise]] to Los Angeles before the 1958 season.
sentence_9: The team played their first four seasons at the [[Los_Angeles_Memorial_Coliseum|Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum]] before moving to their current home of Dodger Stadium in 1962.
sentence_10: The Dodgers found immediate success in Los Angeles by winning the [[1959_World_Series|1959 World Series]], representing the franchise's first championship since moving to Los Angeles.
sentence_11: Success continued into the 1960s with their one-two punch ace pitchers [[Sandy_Koufax|Sandy Koufax]] and [[Don_Drysdale|Don Drysdale]] being the cornerstones of two more titles in [[1963_World_Series|1963]] and [[1965_World_Series|1965]].
sentence_12: During the 1980s, Mexican phenom pitcher [[Fernando_Valenzuela|Fernando Valenzuela]] quickly became a sensation—affectionately referred to as "Fernandomania"—when he led the team as a rookie to another championship in [[1981_World_Series|1981]].
sentence_13: Valenzuela became the first and, to date, the only player to ever win the Cy Young and [[Major_League_Baseball_Rookie_of_the_Year_Award|Rookie of the Year]] awards in the same season.
sentence_14: The Dodgers were once again victorious in [[1988_World_Series|1988]], upsetting their heavily favored opponent in each series and becoming the first and only franchise to win multiple titles in the 80s.
sentence_15: After a 32-year drought, which included 12 postseason appearances in a 17-year span and eight consecutive division titles from 2013 to 2020, the Dodgers won the [[2020_World_Series|2020]] World Series.
sentence_16: One of the most successful and storied franchises in MLB, the Dodgers have won seven [[List_of_World_Series_champions|World Series]] championships and a record 24 [[List_of_National_League_pennant_winners|National League pennants]].
sentence_17: Eleven NL MVP award winners have played for the Dodgers, winning a total of 14.
sentence_18: Eight Cy Young Award winners have pitched for the club, winning a total of 12—by far the most of any Major League franchise.
sentence_19: Additionally, the Dodgers boast 18 Rookie of the Year Award winners, twice as many as the next club.
sentence_20: This includes four consecutive Rookies of the Year from 1979 to 1982 and five consecutive from 1992 to 1996.
sentence_21: Today, the Dodgers are among the most popular MLB teams, enjoying large fan support both at home and on the road.
sentence_22: They maintain a fierce [[Dodgers-Giants_rivalry|rivalry]] with the [[San_Francisco_Giants|San Francisco Giants]] dating back to when the two clubs were based in New York City.
sentence_23: As of 2020, [[Forbes|Forbes]] ranks the Dodgers second in MLB franchise valuation at $3.4 billion.
sentence_24: In the early 20th century, the team, then sometimes called the Brooklyn Robins after manager [[Wilbert_Robinson|Wilbert Robinson]], won league pennants in [[1916_Major_League_Baseball_season|1916]] and [[1920_Major_League_Baseball_season|1920]], losing the World Series both times, first to [[Boston_Red_Sox|Boston]] and then [[Cleveland_Indians|Cleveland]].
sentence_25: In the 1930s, the team officially adopted the Dodgers nickname, which had been in use since the 1890s, named after the Brooklyn pedestrians who dodged the streetcars in the city.
sentence_26: In 1941, the Dodgers captured their third [[National_League_pennant|National League pennant]], only to lose to the [[New_York_Yankees|New York Yankees]].
sentence_27: This marked the onset of the [[Dodgers–Yankees_rivalry|Dodgers–Yankees rivalry]], as the Dodgers would face them in their next six [[World_Series|World Series]] appearances.
sentence_28: Led by [[Jackie_Robinson|Jackie Robinson]], the first black Major League Baseball player of the modern era; and three-time National League Most Valuable Player [[Roy_Campanella|Roy Campanella]], also signed out of the Negro Leagues, the Dodgers captured their first [[1955_World_Series|World Series title in 1955]] by defeating the Yankees for the first time, a story notably described in the 1972 book [[The_Boys_of_Summer_(book)|The Boys of Summer]].
sentence_29: Following the [[1957_Brooklyn_Dodgers_season|1957 season]] the team left Brooklyn.
sentence_30: In just their second season in Los Angeles, the Dodgers won their second World Series title, beating the Chicago White Sox in six games in 1959.
sentence_31: Spearheaded by the dominant pitching style of [[Sandy_Koufax|Sandy Koufax]] and [[Don_Drysdale|Don Drysdale]], the Dodgers captured three pennants in the 1960s and won two more World Series titles, sweeping the Yankees in four games in 1963, and edging the Minnesota Twins in seven in 1965.
sentence_32: The 1963 sweep was their second victory against the Yankees, and their first against them as a Los Angeles team.
sentence_33: The Dodgers won four more pennants in 1966, 1974, 1977 and 1978, but lost in each World Series appearance.
sentence_34: They went on to win the World Series again in 1981, thanks in part to pitching sensation [[Fernando_Valenzuela|Fernando Valenzuela]].
sentence_35: The early 1980s were affectionately dubbed "[[Fernandomania|Fernandomania]]."
sentence_36: In 1988, another pitching hero, [[Orel_Hershiser|Orel Hershiser]], again led them to a World Series victory, aided by one of the most memorable home runs of all time, by their injured star outfielder [[Kirk_Gibson|Kirk Gibson]] coming off the bench to pinch hit with two outs in the bottom of the ninth inning of game 1, in his only appearance of the series.
sentence_37: The Dodgers won the pennant in 2017 and 2018, but lost the World Series to the Houston Astros and Boston Red Sox respectively.
sentence_38: They went on to win the World Series again in 2020.
sentence_39: The Dodgers share a fierce [[Dodgers–Giants_rivalry|rivalry]] with the [[San_Francisco_Giants|San Francisco Giants]], dating back to when the two franchises played in New York City.
sentence_40: Both teams moved west for the 1958 season.
sentence_41: The Brooklyn/Los Angeles Dodgers have appeared in the World Series 21 times, while the New York/San Francisco Giants have appeared in the World Series 20 times.

sentence_43: After the move to California, the Dodgers have won six World Series while the Giants have won three.
sentence_44: Main article: [[History_of_the_Brooklyn_Dodgers|History of the Brooklyn Dodgers]]
sentence_45: The Dodgers were founded in 1883 as the Brooklyn Atlantics, borrowing the name of a defunct team that had played in Brooklyn before them.

sentence_48: The team was known alternatively as the Bridegrooms, Grooms, Superbas, Robins, and Trolley Dodgers before officially becoming the Brooklyn Dodgers in the 1930s.
sentence_49: In Brooklyn, the Dodgers won the NL pennant twelve times ([[1890_Brooklyn_Bridegrooms_season|1890]], [[1899_Brooklyn_Superbas_season|1899]], [[1900_Brooklyn_Superbas_season|1900]], [[1916_Brooklyn_Robins_season|1916]], [[1920_Brooklyn_Robins_season|1920]], [[1941_Brooklyn_Dodgers_season|1941]], [[1947_Brooklyn_Dodgers_season|1947]], [[1949_Brooklyn_Dodgers_season|1949]], [[1952_Brooklyn_Dodgers_season|1952]], [[1953_Brooklyn_Dodgers_season|1953]], [[1955_Brooklyn_Dodgers_season|1955]], [[1956_Brooklyn_Dodgers_season|1956]]) and the [[World_Series|World Series]] in [[1955_World_Series|1955]].
sentence_50: After moving to Los Angeles, the team won National League pennants in [[1959_Los_Angeles_Dodgers_season|1959]], [[1963_Los_Angeles_Dodgers_season|1963]], [[1965_Los_Angeles_Dodgers_season|1965]], [[1966_Los_Angeles_Dodgers_season|1966]], [[1974_Los_Angeles_Dodgers_season|1974]], [[1977_Los_Angeles_Dodgers_season|1977]], [[1978_Los_Angeles_Dodgers_season|1978]], [[1981_Los_Angeles_Dodgers_season|1981]], [[1988_Los_Angeles_Dodgers_season|1988]], [[2017_Los_Angeles_Dodgers_season|2017]], [[2018_Los_Angeles_Dodgers_season|2018]], and [[2020_Los_Angeles_Dodgers_season|2020]], with World Series championships in [[1959_World_Series|1959]], [[1963_World_Series|1963]], [[1965_World_Series|1965]], [[1981_World_Series|1981]], [[1988_World_Series|1988]], and [[2020_World_Series|2020]].
sentence_51: In all, the Dodgers have appeared in 21 World Series: 9 in Brooklyn and 12 in Los Angeles.
sentence_52: Main article: [[Jackie_Robinson|Jackie Robinson]]
sentence_53: For most of the first half of the 20th century, no Major League Baseball team employed an African American player.

sentence_55: This was mainly due to general manager [[Branch_Rickey|Branch Rickey]]'s efforts.

sentence_57: Rickey was a member of [[The_Methodist_Church_(USA)|The Methodist Church]], the antecedent denomination to [[The_United_Methodist_Church|The United Methodist Church]] of today, which was a strong advocate for [[Social_justice|social justice]] and active later in the [[American_Civil_Rights_Movement|American Civil Rights Movement]].
sentence_58: This event was the harbinger of the integration of professional sports in the United States, the concomitant demise of the [[Negro_league_baseball|Negro Leagues]], and is regarded as a key moment in the history of the American Civil Rights Movement.
