sentence_91: The Dodgers' official history reports that the term "Trolley Dodgers" was attached to the Brooklyn ballclub due to the complex maze of trolley cars that weaved its way through the borough of Brooklyn.
sentence_92: In 1892, the city of Brooklyn (Brooklyn was an independent city until annexed by New York City in 1898) began replacing its slow-moving, horse-drawn trolley lines with the faster, more powerful electric trolley lines.
sentence_93: Within less than three years, by the end of 1895, electric trolley accidents in Brooklyn had resulted in more than 130 deaths and maimed well over 500 people.
sentence_94: Brooklyn's high profile, the significant number of widely reported accidents, and a trolley strike in early 1895, combined to create a strong association in the public's mind between Brooklyn and trolley dodging.
sentence_95: Sportswriters started using the name "Trolley Dodgers" to refer to the Brooklyn team early in the 1895 season.
sentence_96: The name was shortened to, on occasion, the "Brooklyn Dodgers" as early as 1898.
sentence_97: Sportswriters in the early 20th century began referring to the Dodgers as the "Bums", in reference to the team's fans and possibly because of the "street character" nature of Jack Dawkins, the "Artful Dodger" in Charles Dickens' Oliver Twist.
sentence_98: Newspaper cartoonist [[Willard_Mullin|Willard Mullin]] used a drawing of famous clown [[Emmett_Kelly|Emmett Kelly]] to depict "Dem Bums": the team would later use "Weary Willie" in promotional images, and Kelly himself was a club mascot during the 1950s.
sentence_99: Other team names used by the franchise were the Atlantics, Grays, Grooms, Bridegrooms, Superbas and Robins.
sentence_100: All of these nicknames were used by fans and sportswriters to describe the team, but not in any official capacity.
sentence_101: The team's legal name was the Brooklyn Base Ball Club.
sentence_102: However, the Trolley Dodger nickname was used throughout this period, simultaneously with these other nicknames, by fans and sportswriters of the day.
sentence_103: The team did not use the name in any formal sense until 1932, when the word "Dodgers" appeared on team jerseys.
sentence_104: The "conclusive shift" came in 1933, when both home and road jerseys for the team bore the name "Dodgers".
sentence_105: Examples of how the many popularized names of the team were used are available from newspaper articles before 1932.
sentence_106: A New York Times article describing a game in 1916 starts out: "Jimmy Callahan, pilot of the Pirates, did his best to wreck the hopes the Dodgers have of gaining the National League pennant", but then goes on to comment: "the only thing that saved the Superbas from being toppled from first place was that the Phillies lost one of the two games played".
sentence_107: What is interesting about the use of these two nicknames is that most baseball statistics sites and baseball historians generally now refer to the pennant-winning 1916 Brooklyn team as the Robins.
sentence_108: A 1918 New York Times article uses the nickname in its title: "Buccaneers Take Last From Robins", but the subtitle of the article reads: "Subdue The Superbas By 11 To 4, Making Series An Even Break".
sentence_109: Another example of the use of the many nicknames is found on the program issued at Ebbets Field for the [[1920_World_Series|1920 World Series]], which identifies the matchup in the series as "Dodgers vs. Indians" despite the fact that the Robins nickname had been in consistent use for around six years.
sentence_110: The "Robins" nickname was derived from the name of their Hall of Fame manager, Wilbert Robinson, who led the team from 1914 to 1931.
sentence_111: The Dodgers' uniform has remained relatively unchanged since the 1930s.
sentence_112: The home jersey is white with "Dodgers" written in script across the chest in royal.
sentence_113: The road jersey is gray with "Los Angeles" written in script across the chest in royal.
sentence_114: The word "Dodgers" was first used on the front of the team's home jersey in 1933; the uniform was then white with red pinstripes and a stylized "B" on the left shoulder.
sentence_115: The Dodgers also wore green outlined uniforms and green caps throughout the 1937 season but reverted to blue the following year.
sentence_116: The current design was created in 1939, and has remained the same ever since with only cosmetic changes.
sentence_117: Originally intended for the [[1951_World_Series|1951 World Series]] for which the ballclub failed to qualify, red numbers under the "Dodgers" script were added to the home uniform in [[1952_Brooklyn_Dodgers_season|1952]].
sentence_118: The road jersey also has a red uniform number under the script.
sentence_119: When the franchise moved from Brooklyn to Los Angeles, the city name on the road jersey changed, and the stylized "B" was replaced with the interlocking "LA" on the caps in 1958.
sentence_120: In 1970, the Dodgers removed the city name from the road jerseys and had "Dodgers" on both the home and away uniforms.
sentence_121: The city script returned to the road jerseys in 1999, and the tradition-rich Dodgers flirted with an alternate uniform for the first time since 1944 (when all-blue satin uniforms were introduced).
sentence_122: These 1999 alternate jerseys had a royal top with the "Dodgers" script in white across the chest, and the red number on the front.
sentence_123: These were worn with white pants and a new cap with silver brim, top button and Dodger logo.
sentence_124: These alternates proved unpopular and the team abandoned them after only one season.
sentence_125: In 2014, the Dodgers introduced an alternate road jersey: a gray version with the "Dodgers" script instead of the city name.
sentence_126: In 2018, the Dodgers wore their 60th anniversary patch to honor the 60 years of being in Los Angeles.
sentence_127: The Dodgers have been groundbreaking in their signing of players from Asia; mainly [[Japan|Japan]], [[South_Korea|South Korea]], and [[Taiwan|Taiwan]].
sentence_128: Former owner [[Peter_O'Malley|Peter O'Malley]] began reaching out in 1980 by starting clinics in China and South Korea, building baseball fields in two Chinese cities, and in 1998 becoming the first major league team to open an office in Asia.
sentence_129: The Dodgers were the second team to start a Japanese player in recent history, pitcher [[Hideo_Nomo|Hideo Nomo]], the first team to start a South Korean player, pitcher [[Chan_Ho_Park|Chan Ho Park]], and the first Taiwanese player, [[Chin-Feng_Chen|Chin-Feng Chen]].
sentence_130: In addition, they were the first team to send out three Asian pitchers, from different Asian countries, in one game: Park, [[Hong-Chih_Kuo|Hong-Chih Kuo]] of Taiwan, and [[Takashi_Saito_(baseball)|Takashi Saito]] of Japan.
sentence_131: In the 2008 season, the Dodgers had the most Asian players on its roster of any major league team with five.
sentence_132: They included Japanese pitchers [[Takashi_Saito_(baseball)|Takashi Saito]] and [[Hiroki_Kuroda|Hiroki Kuroda]]; South Korean pitcher [[Chan_Ho_Park|Chan Ho Park]]; and Taiwanese pitcher [[Hong-Chih_Kuo|Hong-Chih Kuo]] and infielder [[Chin-Lung_Hu|Chin-Lung Hu]].
sentence_133: In 2005, the Dodgers' [[Hee_Seop_Choi|Hee Seop Choi]] became the first Asian player to compete in the [[Home_Run_Derby|Home Run Derby]].
sentence_134: For the 2013 season, the Dodgers signed starting pitcher [[Hyun-Jin_Ryu|Hyun-Jin Ryu]] with a six-year, $36 million contract, after posting a bid of nearly $27 million to acquire him from the [[Korea_Baseball_Championship|KBO]]'s [[Hanhwa_Eagles|Hanhwa Eagles]].
sentence_135: For the 2016 season, the Dodgers signed starting pitcher [[Kenta_Maeda|Kenta Maeda]] with an eight-year, $25 million contract, after posting a bid of $20 million to acquire him from the NPB's [[Hiroshima_Toyo_Carp|Hiroshima Toyo Carp]].
sentence_136: The Dodgers' rivalry with the [[San_Francisco_Giants|San Francisco Giants]] dates back to the 19th century, when the two teams were based in New York; the rivalry with the [[New_York_Yankees|New York Yankees]] took place when the Dodgers were based in New York, but was revived with their East Coast/West Coast World Series battles in 1963, 1977, 1978, and 1981.
sentence_137: The Dodgers rivalry with the [[Philadelphia_Phillies|Philadelphia Phillies]] also dates back to their days in New York, but was most fierce during the 1970s, 1980s, and 2000s.
sentence_138: The Dodgers also had a heated rivalry with the [[Cincinnati_Reds|Cincinnati Reds]] during the 1970s, 1980s and early 1990s.
sentence_139: The intra-city rivalry with the [[Los_Angeles_Angels|Los Angeles Angels]] dates back to the Angels' inaugural season in 1961.
sentence_140: Main article: [[Dodgers–Giants_rivalry|Dodgers–Giants rivalry]]
sentence_141: The Dodgers–Giants rivalry is one of the longest-standing rivalries in U.S. baseball.
sentence_142: The feud between the Dodgers and the [[San_Francisco_Giants|San Francisco Giants]] began in the late 19th century when both clubs were based in New York City, with the Dodgers playing in [[Brooklyn|Brooklyn]] and the Giants playing at the [[Polo_Grounds|Polo Grounds]] in [[Manhattan|Manhattan]].
sentence_143: After the 1957 season, Dodgers owner [[Walter_O'Malley|Walter O'Malley]] moved the team to Los Angeles for financial and other reasons.
sentence_144: Along the way, he managed to convince Giants owner Horace Stoneham—who was considering moving his team to [[Minnesota|Minnesota]]—to preserve the rivalry by bringing his team to California as well.
sentence_145: [[Sports_in_New_York_City|New York]] baseball fans were stunned and heartbroken by the move.
sentence_146: Given that the cities of Los Angeles and San Francisco have been bitter rivals in economic, cultural, and political arenas for over a century and a half, the new venue in California became fertile ground for its transplantation.
sentence_147: Each team's ability to endure for over a century while moving across an entire continent, as well as the rivalry's leap from a cross-city to a cross-state engagement, have led to the rivalry being considered one of the greatest in American sports history.
sentence_148: Unlike many other historic baseball match-ups in which one team remains dominant for most of their history, the Dodgers–Giants rivalry has exhibited a persistent balance in the respective successes of the two teams.
sentence_149: While the Giants have more wins in franchise history, the Dodgers have the most National League pennants at 24, with the Giants following close behind at 23.
sentence_150: The Giants have won eight [[World_Series|World Series]] titles, while the Dodgers have won seven.
sentence_151: The [[2010_World_Series|2010 World Series]] was the Giants' first championship since moving to California, while the Dodgers had won six World Series titles since their move, their last title coming in the [[2020_World_Series|2020 World Series]].
sentence_152: Main article: [[Freeway_Series|Freeway Series]]
sentence_153: This rivalry refers to a series of games played with the [[Los_Angeles_Angels|Los Angeles Angels]].
sentence_154: The Freeway Series takes its name from the massive freeway system in the [[Greater_Los_Angeles_Area|greater Los Angeles metropolitan area]], the home of both teams; one could travel from one team's stadium to the other simply by traveling along [[Interstate_5|Interstate 5]].
sentence_155: The term is akin to [[Subway_Series|Subway Series]] which refers to meetings between New York City baseball teams.
sentence_156: The term "Freeway Series" also inspired the official name of the region's [[National_Hockey_League|NHL]] rivalry: the [[Freeway_Face-Off|Freeway Face-Off]].
sentence_157: Animosity between the team's fanbases grew stronger in 2005, when the Angel's new team owner Arte Moreno changed the name of his ball club from the 'Anaheim Angels', to the 'Los Angeles Angels of Anaheim'.
sentence_158: Since the city of Anaheim is located roughly 30 miles from Downtown Los Angeles, the Angels franchise was ridiculed throughout the league for the contradictory nature surrounding the name, especially by Dodgers owner [[Frank_McCourt_(executive)|Frank McCourt]], who filed a formal complaint to commissioner [[Bud_Selig|Bud Selig]].
sentence_159: Once the complaint was denied, McCourt devised a t-shirt mocking the crosstown rivals reading 'The Los Angeles Dodgers of Los Angeles', which remains popular amongst the fanbase to this day.
sentence_160: Main articles: [[Dodgers–Yankees_rivalry|Dodgers–Yankees rivalry]] and [[Subway_Series|Subway Series]]
sentence_161: The Dodgers–[[New_York_Yankees|Yankees]] rivalry is one of the most well-known rivalries in Major League Baseball.
sentence_162: The two teams have met eleven times in the [[World_Series|World Series]], more times than any other pair from the [[American_League|American]] and [[National_League|National Leagues]].
sentence_163: The initial significance was embodied in the two teams' proximity in New York City, when the Dodgers initially played in [[Brooklyn|Brooklyn]].
sentence_164: After the Dodgers moved to Los Angeles in 1958, the rivalry retained its significance as the two teams represented the dominant cities on each coast of the United States, and [[Largest_cities_in_the_United_States_by_population_by_decade|since the 1980s]], the two largest cities in the United States.
sentence_165: Although the rivalry's significance arose from the two teams' numerous World Series meetings, the Yankees and Dodgers have not met in the World Series since [[1981_World_Series|1981]].
sentence_166: They would not play each other in a non-exhibition game until 2004, when they played a three-game [[Interleague_play|interleague]] series.
sentence_167: Their last meeting was in August 2019, when the Yankees won two out of three games in Los Angeles.
sentence_168: The Dodgers have a loyal fanbase, evidenced by the fact that the Dodgers were the first MLB team to attract more than 3 million fans in a season (in 1978), and accomplished that feat six more times before any other franchise did it once.
sentence_169: The Dodgers drew at least 3 million fans for 15 consecutive seasons from 1996 to 2010, the longest such streak among all MLB teams.
sentence_170: The team's largest fan club, Pantone 294 (a reference to the [[Pantone|Pantone]] code of [[Dodger_blue|Dodger blue]]), regularly travel to away games to cheer for the Dodgers.
sentence_171: On July 3, 2007, Dodgers management announced that total franchise attendance, dating back to 1901, had reached 175 million, a record for all professional sports.
sentence_172: In 2007, the Dodgers set a franchise record for single-season attendance, attracting over 3.8 million fans.
sentence_173: On March 28, 2008, the Dodgers set the world record for the largest attendance for a single baseball game during an exhibition game against the [[2008_Boston_Red_Sox_season|Boston Red Sox]] at the [[Los_Angeles_Memorial_Coliseum|Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum]] in honor of the Dodgers' 50th anniversary, with 115,300 fans in attendance.
sentence_174: In 2009, the Dodgers led the MLB in total attendance.
sentence_175: The Dodger baseball cap is consistently in the top three in sales.
sentence_176: Given the team's proximity to Hollywood, numerous celebrities can often be seen attending home games at Dodger Stadium.
sentence_177: Celebrities such as co-owner [[Magic_Johnson|Magic Johnson]], [[Mary_Hart|Mary Hart]], [[Larry_King|Larry King]], [[Tiger_Woods|Tiger Woods]], [[Alyssa_Milano|Alyssa Milano]], [[Shia_LaBeouf|Shia LaBeouf]], [[Lana_Del_Rey|Lana Del Rey]], [[Mila_Kunis|Mila Kunis]] and [[Ashton_Kutcher|Ashton Kutcher]] are known to frequently attend Dodger games, with some sitting at field box seats behind home plate where they sign autographs for fellow Dodger fans.
sentence_178: Actor [[Bryan_Cranston|Bryan Cranston]] is a lifelong Dodger fan.
sentence_179: Primarily, Dodgers fans are from their own location in southern California and also parts of southern [[Nevada|Nevada]].
sentence_180: However, there are also strong pockets of supporters in Mexico and throughout Asia, and their away games throughout the US will usually attract substantial numbers of expats and traveling fans.
sentence_181: Main article: [[List_of_Los_Angeles_Dodgers_broadcasters|List of Los Angeles Dodgers broadcasters]]
sentence_182: [[Vin_Scully|Vin Scully]] called Dodgers games from 1950 to 2016.
sentence_183: His longtime partners were [[Jerry_Doggett|Jerry Doggett]] (1956–1987) and [[Ross_Porter_(American_broadcaster)|Ross Porter]] (1977–2004).
sentence_184: In 1976, he was selected by Dodgers fans as the Most Memorable Personality (on the field or off) in the team's history.
sentence_185: He is also a recipient of the [[National_Baseball_Hall_of_Fame_and_Museum|Baseball Hall of Fame]]'s [[Ford_C._Frick_Award|Ford C. Frick Award]] for broadcasters (inducted in 1982).
sentence_186: Unlike the modern style in which multiple sportscasters have an on-air conversation (usually with one functioning as [[Play-by-play|play-by-play announcer]] and the other[s] as [[Color_commentator|color commentator]]), Scully, Doggett and Porter generally called games solo, trading with each other inning-by-inning.
sentence_187: In the 1980s and 1990s, Scully would call the entire radio broadcast except for the third and seventh inning, allowing the other Dodger commentators to broadcast an inning.
sentence_188: When Doggett retired after the 1987 season, he was replaced by Hall-of-Fame Dodgers pitcher [[Don_Drysdale|Don Drysdale]], who previously broadcast games for the [[Los_Angeles_Angels_of_Anaheim|California Angels]] and [[Chicago_White_Sox|Chicago White Sox]].
sentence_189: Drysdale died in his hotel room following a heart attack before a game in [[Montreal|Montreal]] in 1993.
sentence_190: This was a difficult broadcast for Scully and Porter who could not mention it on-air until Drysdale's family had been notified and the official announcement made.
sentence_191: He was replaced by former Dodgers outfielder [[Rick_Monday|Rick Monday]].
sentence_192: Porter's tenure ended after the 2004 season, after which the format of play-by-play announcers and color commentators was installed, led by Monday and newcomer [[Charley_Steiner|Charley Steiner]].
sentence_193: Scully, however, continued to announce solo.
sentence_194: Scully called roughly 100 games per season (all home games and road games in California and Arizona) for both [[Flagship|flagship]] radio station [[KLAC_(AM)|KLAC]] and on television for [[SportsNet_LA|SportsNet LA]].
sentence_195: Scully was simulcast for the first three innings of each of his appearances, then announced only for the TV audience.
sentence_196: If Scully was calling the game, Steiner took over play-by-play on radio beginning with the fourth inning, with Monday as color commentator.
sentence_197: If Scully was not calling the game, Steiner and [[Orel_Hershiser|Orel Hershiser]] called the entire game on television while Monday and Kevin Kennedy did the same on radio.
sentence_198: In the event the Dodgers were in post-season play, Scully called the first three and last three innings of the radio broadcast alone and Steiner and Monday handled the middle innings.
sentence_199: Vin Scully retired from calling games in 2016.
sentence_200: His tenure with the Dodgers was the longest with any single sports team at 67 years.
sentence_201: Youthful announcer [[Joe_Davis_(sportscaster)|Joe Davis]] was selected in 2017 by Dodgers management to handle play by play on television with Orel Hershiser as his colorman; Steiner continues to substitute for Davis during the latter's [[Fox_Sports_(United_States)|Fox Sports]] [[Major_League_Baseball_on_Fox|MLB]] and [[NFL_on_Fox|NFL]] assignments, with [[Tim_Neverett|Tim Neverett]] taking Steiner's place on radio.
sentence_202: The Dodgers also broadcast on radio in two other languages, Spanish and Korean.
sentence_203: In Spanish, the play-by-play is voiced by another Frick Award winner, [[Jaime_Jarrín|Jaime Jarrín]], who has been with the Dodgers since 1959.
sentence_204: The color analyst for some games is former Dodger pitcher [[Fernando_Valenzuela|Fernando Valenzuela]], for whom Jarrin once translated post-game interviews.
sentence_205: The Spanish-language radio flagship station is [[KTNQ_(AM)|KTNQ]].
sentence_206: Meanwhile, the Dodgers' Korean broadcast began in 2013 through [[KMPC|KMPC]].
sentence_207: Main article: [[List_of_Los_Angeles_Dodgers_owners_and_executives|List of Los Angeles Dodgers owners and executives]]
sentence_208: See also: [[List_of_Major_League_Baseball_retired_numbers|List of Major League Baseball retired numbers]]
sentence_209: Koufax, Campanella, and Robinson were the first Dodgers to have their numbers retired, in a ceremony at Dodger Stadium on June 4, 1972.
sentence_210: This was the year in which Koufax was inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame; Robinson and Campanella were already Hall-of-Famers.
sentence_211: Alston's number was retired in the year following his retirement as the Dodgers manager, six years before he was inducted into the Hall of Fame.
sentence_212: Gilliam died suddenly in 1978 after a 28-year career with the Dodgers organization.
sentence_213: The Dodgers retired his number two days after his death, prior to Game 1 of the [[1978_World_Series|1978 World Series]].
sentence_214: As of 2018, he is the only non-Hall-of-Famer to have his number retired by the Dodgers (Alston's number was retired before he was elected to the Hall of Fame).
sentence_215: Beginning in 1980, the Dodgers have retired the numbers of longtime Dodgers (Snider, Reese, Drysdale, Lasorda, and Sutton) during the seasons in which each was inducted into the Hall of Fame.
sentence_216: In 1997, 50 years after he broke the [[Baseball_color_line|color barrier]] and 25 years after the Dodgers retired his number, Robinson's No.
sentence_217: 42 was retired throughout Major League Baseball.
sentence_218: Robinson is the only major league baseball player to have this honor bestowed upon him.
sentence_219: Starting in the 2007 season, [[Jackie_Robinson_Day|Jackie Robinson Day]] (April 15, commemorating Opening Day of Robinson's rookie season of 1947) has featured many or all players and coaches wearing the number 42 as a tribute to Robinson.
sentence_220: The Dodgers have not issued the number 34 since the departure of [[Fernando_Valenzuela|Fernando Valenzuela]] in 1991, although it has not been officially retired.
sentence_221: Main article: [[Los_Angeles_Dodgers_award_winners_and_league_leaders|Los Angeles Dodgers award winners and league leaders]]
sentence_222: Main article: [[Los_Angeles_Dodgers_team_records|Los Angeles Dodgers team records]]
sentence_223: Main article: [[List_of_Los_Angeles_Dodgers_owners_and_executives|List of Los Angeles Dodgers owners and executives]]
sentence_224: Main article: [[List_of_Los_Angeles_Dodgers_managers|List of Los Angeles Dodgers managers]]
sentence_225: Since 1884, the Dodgers have used a total of 31 Managers, the most current being [[Dave_Roberts_(outfielder)|Dave Roberts]], who was appointed following the 2015 postseason, after the departure of [[Don_Mattingly|Don Mattingly]].
sentence_226: Over the nearly 43 years from 1954 to mid-1996, the Dodgers employed only two managers, [[Walter_Alston|Walter Alston]] and [[Tommy_Lasorda|Tommy Lasorda]], both of whom are in the [[National_Baseball_Hall_of_Fame_and_Museum|Hall of Fame]].
sentence_227: During this entire time period of extraordinary stability, the Dodgers were family owned by [[Walter_O'Malley|Walter O'Malley]] and then his son [[Peter_O'Malley|Peter O'Malley]].
sentence_228: It was during this era that the Dodgers won 11 of their 24 pennants, and all six of their World Series championships.
sentence_229: The managers of the Los Angeles Dodgers (1958–present) are as follows:
sentence_230: From the Dodgers' move to Los Angeles from Brooklyn in 1958, the Dodgers employed a handful of well-known public address announcers; the most famous of which was [[John_Ramsey_(announcer)|John Ramsey]], who served as the PA voice of the Dodgers from 1958 until his retirement in 1982; he was also well known for announcing at other venerable Los Angeles venues, including the [[Los_Angeles_Memorial_Coliseum|Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum]] and [[Los_Angeles_Memorial_Sports_Arena|Sports Arena]], and the [[The_Forum_(Inglewood,_California)|Forum]].
sentence_231: Ramsey died in 1990.
sentence_232: From 1958 to 1982, Doug Moore, Philip Petty, and Dennis Packer served as back-up voices for John Ramsey for the Dodgers, California Angels, Los Angeles Chargers, USC football and Los Angeles Rams.
sentence_233: Packer was Ramsey's primary backup for the Los Angeles Lakers and Los Angeles Kings until Ramsey's retirement from the Forum in 1978.
sentence_234: Thereafter, Packer became the public address announcer for the Lakers, Kings, indoor soccer and indoor tennis events at the Forum.
sentence_235: [[Nick_Nickson|Nick Nickson]], a radio broadcaster for the [[Los_Angeles_Kings|Los Angeles Kings]], replaced John Ramsey as the Dodger Stadium public address announcer in 1983 and served in that capacity through the 1989 season to work with the Kings full-time.
sentence_236: Dennis Packer and Pete Arbogast were emulators of John Ramsey, using the same stentorian style of announcing Ramsey was famous for.
sentence_237: Packer and Arbogast shared the stadium announcing chores for the [[1994_FIFA_World_Cup|1994 FIFA World Cup]] matches at the [[Rose_Bowl_(stadium)|Rose Bowl]].
sentence_238: Arbogast won the Dodgers job on the day that Ramsey died on January 25, 1990, by doing a verbatim imitation of Ramsey's opening and closing remarks that were standard at each game.
sentence_239: His replacement, in 1994 was Mike Carlucci, who remained as the Dodgers' PA voice announcer until he resigned in 2002 to concentrate on his voiceover and acting career along with his Olympics announcing duties.
sentence_240: From 2003 to 2014, the Dodgers public address announcer was Eric Smith, who also announces for the [[Los_Angeles_Clippers|Los Angeles Clippers]] and [[USC_Trojans|USC Trojans]].
sentence_241: On April 3, 2015 the Dodgers announced that former radio broadcaster Todd Leitz was hired to become their new public address announcer.
sentence_242: Leitz was an anchor and news reporter in Los Angeles at [[KNX_(AM)|KNX]] 1070 [[AM_radio|AM]] for 10 years, and a news reporter at [[KABC_(AM)|KABC]] 790 for two years.
sentence_243: From 1988 to 2015, Nancy Bea enjoyed popularity behind the Dodger Stadium keyboard similar to Gladys Goodding.
sentence_244: Since retirement in 2015, Beal's replacement and current organist is [[Dieter_Ruehle|Dieter Ruehle]], who also plays at [[Staples_Center|Staples Center]] for [[Los_Angeles_Kings|Los Angeles Kings]] games.
sentence_245: [[Vin_Scully|Vin Scully]] is permanently honored in the Baseball Hall of Fame's "Scribes & Mikemen" exhibit as a result of winning the [[Ford_C._Frick_Award|Ford C. Frick Award]] in 1982.
sentence_246: Frick Award recipients are not official members of the Hall.
sentence_247: [[Sue_Falsone|Sue Falsone]], was the first female physical therapist in Major League baseball, and from 2012 to 2013, was the first female head [[Athletic_trainer|athletic trainer]].

sentence_249: The Los Angeles Dodgers farm system consists of nine minor league affiliates.

title: Left-wing politics
sentence_0: "Leftism" redirects here.
sentence_1: For the political position that combines centrist and left-wing policies, see [[Centre-left_politics|Centre-left politics]].
sentence_2: For the album by the group Leftfield, see [[Leftism_(album)|Leftism (album)]].
sentence_3: "Left wing" redirects here.
sentence_4: For the sports position, see [[Winger_(sports)|Winger (sports)]].
sentence_5: Left-wing politics supports [[Social_equality|social equality]] and egalitarianism, often in opposition to [[Social_hierarchy|social hierarchy]].
sentence_6: Left-wing politics typically involves a concern for those in society whom its adherents perceive as disadvantaged relative to others as well as a belief that there are unjustified inequalities that need to be reduced or abolished.
sentence_7: According to emeritus professor of economics Barry Clark, left-wing supporters "claim that human development flourishes when individuals engage in cooperative, mutually respectful relations that can thrive only when excessive differences in status, power, and wealth are eliminated."
sentence_8: Within the [[Left–right_political_spectrum|left–right political spectrum]], Left and Right were coined during the [[French_Revolution|French Revolution]], referring to the seating arrangement in the French [[Estates_General_(France)|Estates General]].
sentence_9: Those who sat on the left generally opposed the [[Ancien_Régime|Ancien Régime]] and the [[House_of_Bourbon|Bourbon]] monarchy and supported the French Revolution, the creation of a [[Democracy|democratic]] [[Republic|republic]] and the [[Secularisation|secularisation]] of society while those on the right were supportive of the traditional institutions of the [[Ancien_Régime|Old Regime]].
sentence_10: Usage of the term Left became more prominent after the restoration of the French monarchy in 1815, when it was applied to the Independents.
sentence_11: The word wing was first appended to Left and Right in the late 19th century, usually with disparaging intent, and left-wing was applied to those who were unorthodox in their religious or political views.
sentence_12: The term Left was later applied to a number of movements, especially [[Republicanism|republicanism]] in France during the 18th century, followed by [[Socialism|socialism]], including [[Anarchism|anarchism]], [[Communism|communism]], the [[Labour_movement|labour movement]], [[Marxism|Marxism]], [[Social_democracy|social democracy]] and [[Syndicalism|syndicalism]] in the 19th and 20th centuries.
sentence_13: Since then, the term left-wing has been applied to a broad range of movements, including the [[Civil_rights_movement|civil rights movement]], [[Feminist_movement|feminist movement]], [[LGBT_rights_movement|LGBT rights movement]], [[Anti-war_movement|anti-war movement]] and [[Environmental_movement|environmental movement]] as well as a wide range of [[Political_parties|political parties]].
sentence_14: See also: [[American_Left|American Left]], [[French_Left|French Left]], [[Left–right_political_spectrum|Left–right political spectrum]], and History of political thought
sentence_15: In politics, the term Left derives from the [[French_Revolution|French Revolution]] as the political groups opposed to the royal veto privilege ([[The_Mountain|Montagnard]] and [[Jacobin_(politics)|Jacobin]] deputies from the [[Estates-General_of_1789|Third Estate]]) generally sat to the left of the presiding member's chair in parliament while the ones in favour of the royal veto privilege sat on its right.
sentence_16: That habit began in the French [[Estates_General_of_1789|Estates General of 1789]].
sentence_17: Throughout the 19th century, the main line dividing [[Politics_of_France|Left and Right]] was between supporters of the French [[Republic|republic]] and those of the monarchy's privileges.
sentence_18: The [[June_Days_uprising|June Days uprising]] during the [[French_Second_Republic|Second Republic]] was an attempt by the Left to re-assert itself after the [[1848_Revolution_(France)|1848 Revolution]], but only a small portion of the population supported this.
sentence_19: In the mid-19th century, [[Nationalism|nationalism]], [[Socialism|socialism]], [[Democracy|democracy]] and [[Anti-clericalism|anti-clericalism]] became key features of the French Left.
sentence_20: After [[Napoleon_III|Napoleon III]]'s 1851 coup and the subsequent establishment of the [[Second_French_Empire|Second Empire]], [[Marxism|Marxism]] began to rival radical republicanism and [[Utopian_socialism|utopian socialism]] as a force within left-wing politics.
sentence_21: The influential Communist Manifesto by [[Karl_Marx|Karl Marx]] and [[Friedrich_Engels|Friedrich Engels]], published amidst the wave of [[Revolutions_of_1848|revolutions of 1848]] across Europe, asserted that all of human history is defined by [[Class_struggle|class struggle]].
sentence_22: They predicted that a [[Proletarian|proletarian]] revolution would eventually overthrow [[Bourgeois|bourgeois]] [[Capitalism|capitalism]] and create a [[Stateless_society|stateless]], moneyless and [[Classless|classless]] [[Communist_society|communist society]].
sentence_23: It was in this period that the word wing was appended to both Left and Right.
sentence_24: The [[International_Workingmen's_Association|International Workingmen's Association]] (1864–1876), sometimes called the First International, brought together delegates from many different countries, with many different views about how to reach a classless and stateless society.
sentence_25: Following a split between supporters of Marx and [[Mikhail_Bakunin|Mikhail Bakunin]], anarchists formed the [[International_Workers'_Association|International Workers' Association]].
sentence_26: The [[Second_International|Second International]] (1888–1916) became divided over the issue of [[World_War_I|World War I]].
sentence_27: Those who opposed the war, among them [[Vladimir_Lenin|Vladimir Lenin]] and [[Rosa_Luxemburg|Rosa Luxemburg]], saw themselves as further to the left.
sentence_28: In the United States, leftists such as [[Social_liberals|social liberals]], [[Progressivism_in_the_United_States|progressives]] and [[Trade_unionists|trade unionists]] were influenced by the works of [[Thomas_Paine|Thomas Paine]], who introduced the concept of [[Asset-based_egalitarianism|asset-based egalitarianism]] which theorises that [[Social_equality|social equality]] is possible by a redistribution of resources.
sentence_29: After the [[Reconstruction_era_of_the_United_States|Reconstruction]] era in the aftermath of the [[American_Civil_War|American Civil War]], the phrase "the Left" was used to describe those who supported trade unions, the [[Civil_rights_movement|civil rights movement]] and the [[Anti-war_movement|anti-war movement]].
sentence_30: More recently, left-wing and right-wing have often been used as synonyms for the [[Democratic_Party_(United_States)|Democratic]] and [[Republican_Party_(United_States)|Republican]] parties, or as synonyms for [[Modern_liberalism_in_the_United_States|liberalism]] and [[Conservatism_in_the_United_States|conservatism]], respectively.
sentence_31: Since the Right was populist, both in the Western and the [[Eastern_Bloc|Eastern Bloc]] anything viewed as avant-garde art was called leftist across Europe, thus the identification of Picasso's [[Guernica_(Picasso)|Guernica]] as "leftist" in Europe and the condemnation of the Russian composer [[Shostakovich|Shostakovich]]'s opera (The Lady Macbeth of Mtsensk District) in [[Pravda|Pravda]] as follows: "Here we have 'leftist' confusion instead of natural, human music".
sentence_32: The following positions are typically associated with left-wing politics.
sentence_33: See also: [[Anarchist_economics|Anarchist economics]], [[Marxism_and_Keynesianism|Marxism and Keynesianism]], and [[Socialist_economics|Socialist economics]]
sentence_34: Leftist economic beliefs range from Keynesian economics and the [[Welfare_state|welfare state]] through [[Industrial_democracy|industrial democracy]] and the [[Social_market|social market]] to the [[Nationalization|nationalization]] of the economy and [[Planned_economy|central planning]], to the [[Anarcho-syndicalist|anarcho-syndicalist]] advocacy of a council- and assembly-based self-managed [[Anarchist_communism|anarchist communism]].
sentence_35: During the [[Industrial_Revolution|Industrial Revolution]], leftists supported [[Trade_union|trade unions]].
sentence_36: At the beginning of the 20th century, many leftists advocated strong government intervention in the economy.
sentence_37: Leftists continue to criticize the perceived exploitative nature of [[Globalization|globalization]], the "race to the bottom" and unjust lay-offs and exploitation of workers.
sentence_38: In the last quarter of the 20th century, the belief that the government (ruling in accordance with the interests of the people) ought to be directly involved in the day-to-day workings of an economy declined in popularity amongst the [[Centre-left|centre-left]], especially [[Social_democrats|social democrats]] who adopted the [[Third_Way|Third Way]].
sentence_39: Other leftists believe in [[Marxian_economics|Marxian economics]], named after the economic theories of [[Karl_Marx|Karl Marx]].
sentence_40: Some distinguish Marx's economic theories from his political philosophy, arguing that Marx's approach to understanding the economy is independent of his advocacy of revolutionary socialism or his belief in the inevitability of a proletarian revolution.
sentence_41: Marxian economics do not exclusively rely on Marx and draw from a range of Marxist and non-Marxist sources.
sentence_42: The [[Dictatorship_of_the_proletariat|dictatorship of the proletariat]] and [[Workers'_state|workers' state]] are terms used by some Marxists, particularly [[Leninists|Leninists]] and [[Marxist–Leninists|Marxist–Leninists]], to describe what they see as a temporary state between the [[Capitalist|capitalist]] [[State_of_affairs_(sociology)|state of affairs]] and a [[Communist_society|communist society]].
sentence_43: Marx defined the proletariat as salaried workers, in contrast to the [[Lumpenproletariat|lumpenproletariat]], who he defined as the outcasts of society such as beggars, tricksters, entertainers, buskers, criminals and prostitutes.
sentence_44: The political relevance of farmers has divided the left.
sentence_45: In Das Kapital, Marx scarcely mentioned the subject.
sentence_46: [[Mikhail_Bakunin|Mikhail Bakunin]] thought the lumpenproletariat was a revolutionary class while [[Mao_Zedong|Mao Zedong]] believed that it would be rural peasants, not urban workers, who would bring about the proletarian revolution.
sentence_47: [[Left-libertarians|Left-libertarians]], [[Libertarian_socialists|libertarian socialists]] and [[Anarchists|anarchists]] believe in a [[Decentralized|decentralized]] economy run by [[Trade_unions|trade unions]], [[Workers'_councils|workers' councils]], [[Cooperatives|cooperatives]], [[Municipalities|municipalities]] and [[Commune_(model_of_government)|communes]], opposing both [[State_ownership|state]] and [[Private_property|private]] control of the economy, preferring [[Social_ownership|social ownership]] and local control in which a nation of decentralized regions is united in a [[Confederation|confederation]].
sentence_48: The [[Global_justice_movement|global justice movement]], also known as the [[Anti-globalisation_movement|anti-globalisation movement]] and the [[Alter-globalisation|alter-globalisation]] movement, protests against [[Corporate|corporate]] [[Economic_globalisation|economic globalisation]] due to its negative consequences for the poor, workers, the environment, and small businesses.
sentence_49: See also: [[Eco-socialism|Eco-socialism]], [[Green_anarchism|Green anarchism]], and [[Green_politics|Green politics]]
sentence_50: One of the foremost left-wing advocates was Thomas Paine, one of the first individuals since left and right became political terms to describe the collective human ownership of the world which he speaks of in Agrarian Justice.
sentence_51: As such, most of left-wing thought and literature regarding environmentalism stems from this duty of ownership and the aforementioned form of cooperative ownership means that humanity must take care of the Earth.
sentence_52: This principle is reflected in much of the historical left-wing thought and literature that came afterwards, although there were disagreements about what this entailed.
sentence_53: Both Karl Marx and the early socialist philosopher and scholar [[William_Morris|William Morris]] arguably had a concern for environmental matters.
sentence_54: According to Marx, "[e]ven an entire society, a nation, or all simultaneously existing societies taken together, are not the owners of the earth.
sentence_55: They are simply its possessors, its beneficiaries, and have to bequeath it in an improved state to succeeding generations".
sentence_56: Following the Russian Revolution, environmental scientists such as revolutionary [[Alexander_Bogdanov|Alexander Bogdanov]] and the [[Proletkult|Proletkult]] organisation made efforts to incorporate environmentalism into Bolshevism and "integrate production with natural laws and limits" in the first decade of [[Soviet_Union|Soviet]] rule, before [[Joseph_Stalin|Joseph Stalin]] attacked ecologists and the science of ecology, purged environmentalists and promoted the [[Pseudoscience|pseudoscience]] of [[Trofim_Lysenko|Trofim Lysenko]] during his rule up until his death in 1953.
sentence_57: Similarly, [[Mao_Zedong|Mao Zedong]] rejected environmentalism and believed that based on the laws of historical materialism, all of nature must be put into the service of revolution.
sentence_58: From the 1970s onwards, environmentalism became an increasing concern of the left, with social movements and several unions campaigning on environmental issues and causes.
sentence_59: In Australia, the left-wing [[Builders_Labourers_Federation|Builders Labourers Federation]], led by the communist Jack Mundy, united with environmentalists to place [[Green_ban|green bans]] on environmentally destructive development projects.
sentence_60: Several segments of the socialist and Marxist left consciously merged environmentalism and anti-capitalism into an [[Eco-socialist|eco-socialist]] ideology.
sentence_61: [[Barry_Commoner|Barry Commoner]] articulated a left-wing response to [[The_Limits_to_Growth|The Limits to Growth]] model that predicted catastrophic resource depletion and spurred environmentalism, postulating that capitalist technologies were the key cause responsible for environmental degradation, as opposed to human population pressures.
sentence_62: Environmental degradation can be seen as a class or equity issue, as environmental destruction disproportionately affects poorer communities and countries.
sentence_63: Several left-wing or socialist groupings have an overt environmental concern and several green parties contain a strong socialist presence.
sentence_64: The [[Green_Party_of_England_and_Wales|Green Party of England and Wales]] features an eco-socialist group, the [[Green_Left_(UK)|Green Left]], which was founded in June 2005.
sentence_65: Its members held several influential positions within the party, including both the former Principal Speakers [[Siân_Berry|Siân Berry]] and [[Derek_Wall|Derek Wall]], himself an eco-socialist and Marxist academic.
sentence_66: In Europe, several green left political parties such as the [[European_United_Left–Nordic_Green_Left|European United Left–Nordic Green Left]] combine traditional social-democratic values such as a desire for greater economic equality and workers rights with demands for environmental protection.
sentence_67: Democratic socialist [[Bolivian_president|Bolivian president]] [[Evo_Morales|Evo Morales]] has traced [[Environmental_degradation|environmental degradation]] to capitalist [[Consumerism|consumerism]], stating that "[t]he Earth does not have enough for the North to live better and better, but it does have enough for all of us to live well".
sentence_68: [[James_Hansen|James Hansen]], [[Noam_Chomsky|Noam Chomsky]], [[Raj_Patel|Raj Patel]], [[Naomi_Klein|Naomi Klein]], [[The_Yes_Men|The Yes Men]] and [[Dennis_Kucinich|Dennis Kucinich]] hold similar views.
sentence_69: In the 21st century, questions about the environment have become increasingly politicized as the Left almost unanimously accepted the findings and consensus of environmental scientists and climatologists about [[Anthropogenic_global_warming|anthropogenic global warming]], while the Right has disputed or outright rejected the scientific consensus that modern-day global warming is caused by human activity.
sentence_70: However, the Left is also divided over how to effectively and equitably reduce [[Carbon_emissions|carbon emissions]] as the center-left often advocates a reliance on market measures such as [[Emissions_trading|emissions trading]] and a [[Carbon_tax|carbon tax]] while those further to the left support direct government regulation and intervention in the form of a [[Green_New_Deal|Green New Deal]], either alongside or instead of market mechanisms.
sentence_71: See also: [[Anarchism_and_nationalism|Anarchism and nationalism]], [[Anti-imperialism|Anti-imperialism]], [[Internationalism_(politics)|Internationalism (politics)]], [[Left-wing_nationalism|Left-wing nationalism]], and [[Proletarian_internationalism|Proletarian internationalism]]
sentence_72: The question of [[Nationality|nationality]], [[Imperialism|imperialism]] and [[Nationalism|nationalism]] has been a central feature of political debates on the Left.
sentence_73: During the French Revolution, nationalism was a key policy of the Republican Left.
sentence_74: The Republican Left advocated for [[Civic_nationalism|civic nationalism]] and argued that the nation is a "daily plebiscite" formed by the subjective "will to live together".
sentence_75: Related to [[Revanchism|revanchism]], the belligerent will to take revenge against Germany and retake control of [[Alsace-Lorraine|Alsace-Lorraine]], nationalism was sometimes opposed to [[Imperialism|imperialism]].
sentence_76: In the 1880s, there was a debate between leftists such as the [[Radical_Party_(France)|Radical]] [[Georges_Clemenceau|Georges Clemenceau]], the [[French_Section_of_the_Workers'_International|Socialist]] [[Jean_Jaurès|Jean Jaurès]] and the nationalist [[Maurice_Barrès|Maurice Barrès]], who argued that colonialism diverted France from liberating the "blue line of the Vosges", in reference to Alsace-Lorraine; and the "[[French_colonial_empire|colonial lobby]]" such as [[Jules_Ferry|Jules Ferry]] of the [[Moderate_Republicans_(France)|Moderate Republicans]], [[Léon_Gambetta|Léon Gambetta]] of the [[Republican_Union_(France)|Republicans]] and [[Eugène_Etienne|Eugène Etienne]], the president of the Parliamentary Colonial Group.
sentence_77: After the [[Antisemitic|antisemitic]] [[Dreyfus_Affair|Dreyfus Affair]] in which officer [[Alfred_Dreyfus|Alfred Dreyfus]] was falsely convicted of sedition and exiled to a penal colony in 1894 before being exonerated in 1906, nationalism in the form of [[Boulangism|Boulangism]] increasingly became associated with the far-right.
sentence_78: The [[Marxist|Marxist]] social class theory of [[Proletarian_internationalism|proletarian internationalism]] asserts that members of the working class should act in solidarity with working people in other countries in pursuit of a common class interest, rather than only focusing on their own countries.
sentence_79: Proletarian internationalism is summed up in the slogan: "[[Workers_of_the_world,_unite!|Workers of the world, unite!
sentence_80: ]]", the last line of The Communist Manifesto.
sentence_81: Union members had learned that more members meant more bargaining power.
sentence_82: Taken to an international level, leftists argued that workers should act in solidarity with the international proletariat in order to further increase the power of the working class.
sentence_83: Proletarian internationalism saw itself as a deterrent against war and international conflicts, because people with a common interest are less likely to take up arms against one another, instead focusing on fighting the [[Bourgeoisie|bourgeoisie]] as the ruling class.
sentence_84: According to Marxist theory, the [[Antonym|antonym]] of proletarian internationalism is [[Bourgeois_nationalism|bourgeois nationalism]].
sentence_85: Some Marxists, together with others on the left, view [[Nationalism|nationalism]], [[Racism|racism]] (including antisemitism) and [[Religion|religion]] as divide and conquer tactics used by the ruling classes to prevent the working class from uniting against them in solidarity with one another.
sentence_86: Left-wing movements have often taken up anti-imperialist positions.
sentence_87: Anarchism has developed a critique of nationalism that focuses on nationalism's role in justifying and consolidating state power and domination.
sentence_88: Through its unifying goal, nationalism strives for centralisation (both in specific territories and in a ruling elite of individuals) while it prepares a population for capitalist exploitation.
sentence_89: Within anarchism, this subject has been extensively discussed by [[Rudolf_Rocker|Rudolf Rocker]] in his book titled [[Nationalism_and_Culture|Nationalism and Culture]] and by the works of Fredy Perlman such as [[Against_His-Story,_Against_Leviathan|Against His-Story, Against Leviathan]] and The Continuing Appeal of Nationalism.
sentence_90: The failure of revolutions in [[German_Revolution|Germany]] and [[Hungarian_Soviet_Republic|Hungary]] in the 1918–1920 years ended [[Bolshevik|Bolshevik]] hopes for an imminent [[World_revolution|world revolution]] and led to the promotion of the doctrine of [[Socialism_in_one_country|socialism in one country]] by [[Joseph_Stalin|Joseph Stalin]].
sentence_91: In the first edition of his book titled Osnovy Leninizma (Foundations of Leninism, 1924), Stalin argued that revolution in one country is insufficient.
sentence_92: By the end of that year in the second edition of the book, he argued that the "[[Proletariat|proletariat]] can and must build the socialist society in one country".
sentence_93: In April 1925, [[Nikolai_Bukharin|Nikolai Bukharin]] elaborated on the issue in his brochure titled Can We Build Socialism in One Country in the Absence of the Victory of the West-European Proletariat?, whose position was adopted as state policy after Stalin's January 1926 article titled On the Issues of Leninism (К вопросам ленинизма) was published.
sentence_94: This idea was opposed by [[Leon_Trotsky|Leon Trotsky]] and his supporters, who declared the need for an international "[[Permanent_revolution|permanent revolution]]" and condemned Stalin for betraying the goals and ideals of the socialist revolution.
sentence_95: Various [[Fourth_International|Fourth Internationalist]] groups around the world who describe themselves as [[Trotskyist|Trotskyist]] see themselves as standing in this tradition while Maoist China formally supported the theory of socialism in one country.
sentence_96: European social democrats strongly support [[Europeanism|Europeanism]] and supranational integration within the [[European_Union|European Union]], although there is a minority of nationalists and [[Eurosceptics|Eurosceptics]] on the left.
sentence_97: Several scholars have linked this form of left-wing nationalism to the pressure generated by economic integration with other countries, often encouraged by [[Neoliberal|neoliberal]] [[Free_trade|free trade]] agreements.
sentence_98: This view is sometimes used to justify hostility towards supranational organizations.
sentence_99: Left-wing nationalism can also refer to any form of nationalism which emphasizes a leftist working-class populist agenda that seeks to overcome exploitation or oppression by other nations.
sentence_100: Many Third World [[Decolonization|anti-colonialist movements]] have adopted leftist and socialist ideas.
sentence_101: Third-Worldism is a tendency within leftist thought that regards the division between [[First_World|First World]] and [[Second_World|Second World]] [[Developed_country|developed countries]] and [[Third_World|Third World]] [[Developing_countries|developing countries]] as being of high political importance.
sentence_102: This tendency supports [[Decolonization|decolonization]] and [[National_liberation_movements|national liberation movements]] against imperialism by capitalists.
sentence_103: Third-Worldism is closely connected with [[African_socialism|African socialism]], [[Latin_American_socialism|Latin American socialism]], [[Maoism|Maoism]], [[Pan-Africanism|pan-Africanism]] and [[Pan-Arabism|pan-Arabism]].
sentence_104: Several left-wing groups in the developing world such as the [[Zapatista_Army_of_National_Liberation|Zapatista Army of National Liberation]] in Mexico, the [[Abahlali_baseMjondolo|Abahlali baseMjondolo]] in [[South_Africa|South Africa]] and the [[Naxalites|Naxalites]] in India have argued that the First World and the Second World Left takes a racist and paternalistic attitude towards liberation movements in the Third World.
sentence_105: See also: [[Anarchism_and_religion|Anarchism and religion]], [[Buddhist_socialism|Buddhist socialism]], [[Christian_anarchism|Christian anarchism]], [[Christian_communism|Christian communism]], [[Christian_left|Christian left]], [[Christian_socialism|Christian socialism]], [[Jewish_left|Jewish left]], and [[Islamic_socialism|Islamic socialism]]
sentence_106: The original [[French_Left|French Left]] was firmly [[Anti-clerical|anti-clerical]], strongly opposing the influence of the [[Roman_Catholic_Church|Roman Catholic Church]] and supporting [[Atheism|atheism]] and the [[Separation_of_church_and_state|separation of church and state]], ushering in a policy known as [[Laïcité|laïcité]].
sentence_107: [[Karl_Marx|Karl Marx]] asserted that "[r]eligion is the sigh of the oppressed creature, the heart of a heartless world, and the soul of soulless conditions.
sentence_108: It is the [[Opium_of_the_people|opium of the people]]".
sentence_109: In Soviet Russia, the [[Bolsheviks|Bolsheviks]] under [[Vladimir_Lenin|Vladimir Lenin]] originally embraced an ideological principle which professed that all religion would eventually atrophy and resolved to eradicate organized [[Christianity|Christianity]] and other religious institutions.
sentence_110: In 1918, 10 [[Russian_Orthodox|Russian Orthodox]] hierarchs were summarily executed by a firing squad, and children were deprived of any religious education outside of the home.
sentence_111: Today in the [[Western_world|Western world]], those on the Left generally support [[Secularization|secularization]] and the separation of church and state.
sentence_112: However, religious beliefs have also been associated with many left-wing movements such as the [[Progressive_movement|progressive movement]], the [[Social_Gospel|Social Gospel]] movement, the [[Civil_rights_movement|civil rights movement]], the [[Anti-war_movement|anti-war movement]], the anti-[[Capital_punishment|capital punishment]] movement and [[Liberation_Theology|Liberation Theology]].
sentence_113: Early [[Utopian_socialist|utopian socialist]] thinkers such as [[Robert_Owen|Robert Owen]], [[Charles_Fourier|Charles Fourier]] and the [[Comte_de_Saint-Simon|Comte de Saint-Simon]] based their theories of socialism upon Christian principles.
sentence_114: From [[St._Augustine_of_Hippo|St.
sentence_115: Augustine of Hippo]]'s [[City_of_God_(book)|City of God]] through [[St._Thomas_More|St.
sentence_116: Thomas More]]'s [[Utopia_(book)|Utopia]], major Christian writers defended ideas that socialists found agreeable and advocated for.
sentence_117: Other common leftist concerns such as [[Pacifism|pacifism]], [[Social_justice|social justice]], racial equality, [[Human_rights|human rights]] and the rejection of capitalism and excessive wealth can be found in the [[Holy_Bible|Holy Bible]].
sentence_118: In the late 19th century, the Social Gospel movement arose, particularly among [[Anglicans|Anglicans]], [[Lutherans|Lutherans]], [[Methodists|Methodists]] and [[Baptists|Baptists]] in North America and Britain which integrated [[Progressivism|progressive]] and [[Socialist|socialist]] thought with [[Christianity|Christianity]] through faith-based social activism, promoted by movements such as Christian anarchism, Christian socialism and Christian communism.
sentence_119: In the 20th century, the theology of liberation and [[Creation_Spirituality|Creation Spirituality]] was championed by several scholars and priests, such as [[Gustavo_Gutierrez|Gustavo Gutierrez]] and [[Matthew_Fox_(priest)|Matthew Fox]].
sentence_120: Other left-wing religious movements include Buddhist socialism, Jewish socialism and Islamic socialism.
sentence_121: There have been alliances between the left and anti-war [[Muslims|Muslims]], such as the [[Respect_Party|Respect Party]] and the [[Stop_the_War_Coalition|Stop the War Coalition]] in Britain.
sentence_122: In France, the left has been divided over moves to ban the [[Hijab|hijab]] from schools, with some leftists supporting a ban based on the separation of church and state in accordance with the principle of [[Laïcité|laïcité]] and other leftists opposing the prohibition based on personal and religious freedom.
sentence_123: See also: [[Counterculture|Counterculture]], [[New_Left|New Left]], [[Socialism_and_LGBT_rights|Socialism and LGBT rights]], and [[Socialist_feminism|Socialist feminism]]
sentence_124: [[Social_progress|Social progressivism]] is another common feature of modern leftism, particularly in the United States, where social progressives played an important role in the [[Abolitionism_in_the_United_States|abolition of slavery]], the enshrinement of [[Women's_suffrage|women's suffrage]] in the [[United_States_Constitution|United States Constitution]], and the protection of [[Civil_rights|civil rights]], [[LGBTQ_rights|LGBTQ rights]], [[Women's_rights|women's rights]] and multiculturalism.
sentence_125: Progressives have both advocated for [[Alcohol_prohibition|alcohol prohibition]] legislation and worked towards its repeal in the mid to late 1920s and early 1930s.
sentence_126: Current positions associated with social progressivism in the [[Western_world|Western world]] include strong opposition to the [[Death_penalty|death penalty]], [[Torture|torture]], [[Mass_surveillance|mass surveillance]], and the war on drugs, and support for [[Abortion|abortion]] rights, [[Cognitive_liberty|cognitive liberty]], [[LGBTQ_rights|LGBTQ rights]] including legal recognition of [[Same-sex_marriage|same-sex marriage]], [[Same-sex_adoption|same-sex adoption]] of children, the [[Gender_reassignment|right to change one's legal gender]], distribution of [[Contraceptives|contraceptives]], and public funding of embryonic [[Stem-cell_research|stem-cell research]].
sentence_127: The desire for an expansion of social and civil liberties often overlaps that of the [[Libertarian|libertarian]] movement.
sentence_128: Public education was a subject of great interest to groundbreaking social progressives such as [[Lester_Frank_Ward|Lester Frank Ward]] and [[John_Dewey|John Dewey]], who believed that a democratic society and system of government was practically impossible without a universal and comprehensive nationwide system of education.
sentence_129: Various counterculture and anti-war movements in the 1960s and 1970s were associated with the New Left.
sentence_130: Unlike the earlier leftist focus on [[Labour_union|labour union]] activism and a proletarian revolution, the New Left instead adopted a broader definition of political activism commonly called [[Social_activism|social activism]].
sentence_131: The New Left in the United States is associated with the [[Hippie_movement|hippie movement]], mass protest movements on school campuses and a broadening of focus from protesting class-based oppression to include issues such as [[Gender|gender]], [[Race_(classification_of_human_beings)|race]] and [[Sexual_orientation|sexual orientation]].
sentence_132: The British New Left was an intellectually driven movement which attempted to correct the perceived errors of the [[Old_Left|Old Left]].
sentence_133: The New Left opposed prevailing authoritarian structures in society which it designated as "[[The_Establishment|The Establishment]]" and became known as the "Anti-Establishment".
sentence_134: The New Left did not seek to recruit industrial workers en masse, but instead concentrated on a social activist approach to organization, convinced that they could be the source for a better kind of [[Social_revolution|social revolution]].
sentence_135: This view has been criticized by several [[Marxists|Marxists]], especially [[Trotskyists|Trotskyists]], who characterized this approach as "substitutionism" which they described as a misguided and non-Marxist belief that other groups in society could "substitute" for and "replace" the revolutionary agency of the working class.
sentence_136: Many early [[Feminists|feminists]] and advocates of [[Women's_rights|women's rights]] were considered a part of the Left by their contemporaries.
sentence_137: Feminist pioneer [[Mary_Wollstonecraft|Mary Wollstonecraft]] was influenced by [[Thomas_Paine|Thomas Paine]].
sentence_138: Many notable leftists have been strong supporters of gender equality such as [[Marxist|Marxist]] philosophers and activists [[Rosa_Luxemburg|Rosa Luxemburg]], [[Clara_Zetkin|Clara Zetkin]] and [[Alexandra_Kollontai|Alexandra Kollontai]], [[Anarchist|anarchist]] philosophers and activists such as [[Virginia_Bolten|Virginia Bolten]], [[Emma_Goldman|Emma Goldman]] and Lucía Sánchez Saornil and [[Democratic_socialist|democratic socialist]] philosophers and activists such as [[Helen_Keller|Helen Keller]] and [[Annie_Besant|Annie Besant]].
sentence_139: However, Marxists such as Rosa Luxemburg, Clara Zetkin, and Alexandra Kollontai, who are supporters of radical social equality for women and have rejected and opposed liberal Western feminism because they considered it to be a capitalist [[Bourgeois|bourgeois]] ideology.
sentence_140: Marxists were responsible for organizing the first [[International_Working_Women's_Day|International Working Women's Day]] events.
sentence_141: The [[Women's_liberation_movement|women's liberation movement]] is closely connected to the New Left and other [[New_social_movements|new social movements]] which openly challenged the orthodoxies of the Old Left.
sentence_142: Socialist feminism as exemplified by the [[Freedom_Socialist_Party|Freedom Socialist Party]] and Radical Women and [[Marxist_feminism|Marxist feminism]], spearheaded by [[Selma_James|Selma James]], saw themselves as a part of the Left that challenges male-dominated and [[Sexist|sexist]] structures within the Left.
sentence_143: [[Liberal_feminism|Liberal feminism]] is closely connected with [[Social_liberalism|social liberalism]] and feminism in the United States is closely associated with the left-wing of mainstream politics, being mainly represented by the [[National_Organization_for_Women|National Organization for Women]].
sentence_144: The connection between left-wing ideologies and the struggle for [[LGBTQ_rights|LGBTQ rights]] also has an important history.
sentence_145: Prominent socialists who were involved in early struggles for LGBTQ rights include [[Edward_Carpenter|Edward Carpenter]], [[Oscar_Wilde|Oscar Wilde]], Harry Hay, [[Bayard_Rustin|Bayard Rustin]] and [[Daniel_Guérin|Daniel Guérin]], among others.
sentence_146: The New Left is also strongly supportive of LGBTQ rights and liberation, having been instrumental in the founding of the [[LGBTQ_rights_movement|LGBTQ rights movement]] in the aftermath of the [[Stonewall_Uprising|Stonewall Uprising]] of 1969 and contemporary leftist activists and socialist countries such as Cuba are actively supportive of LGBTQ+ people and are involved in the struggle for LGBTQ+ rights and equality.
sentence_147: The spectrum of left-wing politics ranges from [[Centre-left|centre-left]] to [[Far-left|far-left]] or ultra-left.
sentence_148: The term centre-left describes a position within the political mainstream that accepts capitalism and a market economy.
sentence_149: The terms far-left and ultra-left are used for positions that are more [[Radical_politics|radical]], more strongly rejecting [[Capitalism|capitalism]] and mainstream [[Representative_democracy|representative democracy]], instead advocating for a socialist society based on [[Economic_democracy|economic democracy]] and [[Direct_democracy|direct democracy]], representing economic, political and social democracy.
sentence_150: The centre-left includes [[Social_democrats|social democrats]], [[Social_liberals|social liberals]], [[Progressivism|progressives]] and [[Green_politics|greens]].
sentence_151: Centre-left supporters accept market allocation of resources in a [[Mixed_economy|mixed economy]] with an empowered [[Public_sector|public sector]] and a thriving [[Private_sector|private sector]].
sentence_152: Centre-left policies tend to favour limited [[State_intervention|state intervention]] in matters pertaining to the public interest.
sentence_153: In several countries, the terms far-left and radical left have been associated with many varieties of [[Anarchism|anarchism]], [[Autonomism|autonomism]] and [[Communism|communism]].
sentence_154: They have been used to describe groups that advocate [[Anti-capitalism|anti-capitalism]] and [[Eco-terrorism|eco-terrorism]].
sentence_155: In France, a distinction is made between the centre-left and the left represented by the [[Socialist_Party_(France)|Socialist Party]] and the [[French_Communist_Party|French Communist Party]] and the far-left as represented by [[Anarcho-communists|anarcho-communists]], [[Maoists|Maoists]] and [[Trotskyists|Trotskyists]].
sentence_156: The [[United_States_Department_of_Homeland_Security|United States Department of Homeland Security]] defines "left-wing extremism" as groups that "seek to bring about change through violent revolution, rather than through established political processes".
sentence_157: In China, the term [[Chinese_New_Left|Chinese New Left]] denotes those who oppose the [[Economic_reform_in_the_People's_Republic_of_China|economic reforms]] enacted by [[Deng_Xiaoping|Deng Xiaoping]] in the 1980s and 1990s, favour instead the restoration of Maoist policies and the immediate transition to a socialist economy.
sentence_158: In the [[Western_world|Western world]], the term New Left is used for social and cultural politics.
sentence_159: In the United Kingdom during the 1980s, the term [[Hard_left|hard left]] was applied to supporters of [[Tony_Benn|Tony Benn]] such as the [[Campaign_Group|Campaign Group]] and those involved in the London Labour Briefing newspaper as well as Trotskyist groups such as [[Militant_(Trotskyist_group)|Militant]] and the [[Alliance_for_Workers'_Liberty|Alliance for Workers' Liberty]].
sentence_160: In the same period, the term soft left was applied to supporters of the British [[Labour_Party_(UK)|Labour Party]] who were perceived to be more moderate and closer to the centre, accepting Keynesianism.
sentence_161: Under the leadership of [[Tony_Blair|Tony Blair]] and [[Gordon_Brown|Gordon Brown]], the Labour Party adopted the [[Third_Way|Third Way]] and rebranded itself as [[New_Labour|New Labour]] in order to promote the notion that it was less left-wing than it had been in the past to accommodate the [[Neoliberal|neoliberal]] trend arising since the 1970s with the [[Displacement_of_Keynesianism|displacement of Keynesianism]] and [[Post-war_social_democracy|post-war social democracy]].
sentence_162: One of the first actions of [[Ed_Miliband|Ed Miliband]], the Labour Party leader who succeeded Blair and Brown, was the rejection of the New Labour label and a promise to abandon the Third Way and turn back to the left.
sentence_163: However, Labour's voting record in the House of Commons from 2010 to 2015 indicated that the Labour Party under Miliband had maintained the same distance from the left as it did under Blair.
sentence_164: In contrast, the election of [[Jeremy_Corbyn|Jeremy Corbyn]] as the Labour Party leader was viewed by scholars and political commentators as Labour turning back toward its more classical socialist roots, rejecting neoliberalism and the Third Way whilst supporting a [[Democratic_socialist|democratic socialist]] society and an end to [[Austerity|austerity]] measures.
sentence_165: Leftist post-modernism and [[Post-modern_philosophy|post-modern philosophy]] oppose attempts to supply universal explanatory theories, including Marxism, deriding them as grand [[Meta-narrative|meta-narratives]].
sentence_166: Post-modernism views culture as a contested space and seeks to undermine all pretenses of absolute truth through [[Deconstruction|deconstruction]].
sentence_167: Left-wing critics of post-modernism assert that [[Cultural_studies|cultural studies]] inflates the importance of culture by denying the existence of an independent reality.
