sentence_67: In March 2009, [[Lions_Gate_Entertainment|Lions Gate Entertainment]] (known as Lionsgate) entered into a co-production agreement for The Hunger Games with [[Nina_Jacobson|Nina Jacobson]]'s production company [[Color_Force_(film_company)|Color Force]], which had acquired worldwide distribution rights to the novel a few weeks earlier, reportedly for $200,000.
sentence_68: Alli Shearmur and Jim Miller, president and senior vice president of motion picture production at Lionsgate, took charge of overseeing the production of the film, which they described as "an incredible property... a thrill to bring home to Lionsgate".
sentence_69: The studio, which had not made a profit for five years, raided the budgets of other productions and sold assets to secure a budget of $88,000,000—one of its largest ever—for the film.
sentence_70: Collins' agent Jason Dravis remarked that "they [Lionsgate] had everyone but the valet call us" to help secure the franchise.
sentence_71: Lionsgate subsequently acquired [[Movie_production_incentives_in_the_United_States|tax breaks]] of $8 million for shooting the film in [[North_Carolina|North Carolina]].
sentence_72: Collins adapted the novel for film herself, in collaboration with screenwriter Billy Ray and director Gary Ross.
sentence_73: The screenplay remains extremely faithful to the original novel, with Ross saying he "felt the only way to make the film really successful was to be totally subjective", echoing Collins' presentation of the novel in the first person [[Present_tense|present]].
sentence_74: Instead of Katniss' [[Internal_monologue|internal monologue]] about the Capitol's machinations, the screenplay expanded the character of Seneca Crane, the Head Gamemaker, to allow several developments to be shown directly to the audience.
sentence_75: Ross explained, "In the book, Katniss speculates about the game-makers' manipulations... in the film, we can't get inside Katniss's head, but we do have the ability to cut away and actually show the machinations of the Capitol behind the scenes.
sentence_76: I created the game centre and also expanded the role of Seneca Crane for those reasons.
sentence_77: I thought it was totally important."
sentence_78: Ross also added several scenes between Crane and Coriolanus Snow, the elderly President of Panem, noting that "I thought that it was very interesting that there would be one generation [of Panem citizens] who knew that [the Games] were actually an instrument of political control, and there would be a successive generation who was so enamoured with the ratings and the showbiz and the sensations and the spectacle that was subsuming the actual political intention, and that's really where the tension is".
sentence_79: The Gamemakers' control center, about which Katniss can only speculate in the novel, was also developed as a location, helping to remind the audience of the artificial nature of the arena.
sentence_80: Ross commented, "so much of the film happens in the woods that it's easy to forget this is a futuristic society, manipulating these events for the sake of an audience.
sentence_81: The look of the control center, the antiseptic feeling of it and the use of holograms were all intended to make the arena feel 'constructed' even when you weren't seeing the control room."
sentence_82: Ross and visual effects supervisor Sheena Duggal were keen to use the omniscient view that the setting provided to justify the literal [[Dei_ex_machina|dei ex machina]] Katniss experiences in the arena; Duggal explained that "we really didn't want to have to explain things... how do you get compelled by these [animals] that just appear at the end of the movie?
sentence_83: We wanted to find a way to introduce them without having to explain specifically and exactly what they were and the game room was a really great opportunity for us to be able to do that."
sentence_84: Lionsgate confirmed in March 2011 that about 30 actresses auditioned or read for the role of Katniss Everdeen, including [[Hailee_Steinfeld|Hailee Steinfeld]], [[Abigail_Breslin|Abigail Breslin]], [[Emma_Roberts|Emma Roberts]], [[Saoirse_Ronan|Saoirse Ronan]], [[Chloë_Grace_Moretz|Chloë Grace Moretz]], Jodelle Ferland, [[Lyndsy_Fonseca|Lyndsy Fonseca]], [[Emily_Browning|Emily Browning]], [[Shailene_Woodley|Shailene Woodley]], [[Kaya_Scodelario|Kaya Scodelario]] and Troian Bellisario.
sentence_85: On March 16, 2011, it was announced that Jennifer Lawrence (who was at the time filming for X-Men: First Class) had landed the coveted role.
sentence_86: Ross described Lawrence as having "an incredible amount of self-assuredness, you got the sense that this girl knew exactly who she was.
sentence_87: And then she came in and read for me and just knocked me out; I'd never seen an audition like that before in my life.
sentence_88: It was one of those things where you just glimpse your whole movie in front of you."
sentence_89: Though Lawrence was 20 when filming began, four years older than the character, Collins said that the role demanded "a certain maturity and power" and said she would rather the actress be older than younger.
sentence_90: She added that Lawrence was the "only one who truly captured the character I wrote in the book" and that she had "every essential quality necessary to play Katniss".
sentence_91: Lawrence, a fan of the books, took three days to accept the role, initially intimidated by the size of the production.
sentence_92: Contenders for the role of Peeta other than Hutcherson included [[Alexander_Ludwig|Alexander Ludwig]] (who was later cast as Cato), [[Hunter_Parrish|Hunter Parrish]], [[Lucas_Till|Lucas Till]], and [[Evan_Peters|Evan Peters]].
sentence_93: Other actors considered for the role of Gale included [[David_Henrie|David Henrie]], [[Drew_Roy|Drew Roy]], and [[Robbie_Amell|Robbie Amell]].
sentence_94: In April 2011, [[John_C._Reilly|John C. Reilly]] was in talks with Lionsgate to portray Haymitch Abernathy.
sentence_95: The following month Lionsgate announced that the role had gone to Oscar nominee [[Woody_Harrelson|Woody Harrelson]].
sentence_96: The casting of Grammy winner [[Lenny_Kravitz|Lenny Kravitz]] as Cinna, Oscar nominee [[Stanley_Tucci|Stanley Tucci]] as Caesar Flickerman, and [[Toby_Jones|Toby Jones]] as Claudius Templesmith, soon followed.
sentence_97: Both got the role at the time they were promoting Captain America: The First Avenger.
sentence_98: Multiple-[[Golden_Globe_Award|Golden Globe Award]] winner [[Donald_Sutherland|Donald Sutherland]] was cast as President Coriolanus Snow in late May 2011.
sentence_99: [[Gary_Ross|Gary Ross]], [[Sam_Mendes|Sam Mendes]], [[David_Slade|David Slade]], [[Andrew_Adamson|Andrew Adamson]], [[Susanna_White|Susanna White]], [[Rupert_Sanders|Rupert Sanders]], and Francis Lawrence were listed as possible directing candidates, but in the end Ross was announced as the film's director in November 2010.
sentence_100: Fireman's Fund Insurance Company insured the production, but as part of the underwriting process insisted on a thorough risk analysis of hazards as diverse as wayward arrows, poison ivy, bears, bugs, and a chase across fast-running water.
sentence_101: Lawrence dyed her blond hair dark for the part of Katniss.
sentence_102: She also underwent extensive training to get in shape for the role, including [[Archery|archery]], rock and tree climbing, combat, running, [[Parkour|parkour]], and [[Yoga|yoga]], and had an accident on the last day of her six-week training phase, in which she hit a wall while running at full speed, but was not seriously injured.
sentence_103: Other stars who dyed their hair for the movie include [[Josh_Hutcherson|Josh Hutcherson]] as Peeta and [[Liam_Hemsworth|Liam Hemsworth]] as Gale.
sentence_104: Lionsgate hired Olympic bronze medal-winning archer [[Khatuna_Lorig|Khatuna Lorig]] to teach Lawrence how to shoot.
sentence_105: With an initial budget of $75 million, principal photography began near [[Brevard,_North_Carolina|Brevard]] in [[Transylvania_County,_North_Carolina|Transylvania County]] in [[Western_North_Carolina|Western North Carolina]] in May 2011 and concluded on September 15, 2011, with a final budget reported as between $90 and $100 million, reduced to $78 million after subsidies.
sentence_106: [[Steven_Soderbergh|Steven Soderbergh]] served as a second unit director, and filmed much of the District 11 riot scene.
sentence_107: The movie was shot on film as opposed to digital due (in part) to the tightness of the schedule; as Ross said in an interview with The New York Times, "I didn't want to run the risk of the technical issues that often come with shooting digitally—we simply couldn't afford any delays."
sentence_108: Virtually all production photography took place in [[North_Carolina|North Carolina]], with Lionsgate receiving tax credits of around $8 million from the state government to do so.
sentence_109: It was estimated that the state economy gained up to $60 million from the production, with over 5,000 people employed as extras, crew and support staff.
sentence_110: Most outdoor scenes, both from the arena and from the outskirts of District 12, were filmed in DuPont State Forest; the [[Little_River_(North_Carolina)|Little River]], with its multiple waterfalls, provided several locations for shooting the river running through the arena.
sentence_111: To run across [[Triple_Falls_(DuPont_State_Forest)|Triple Falls]], Lawrence was attached to wires and ran on a board.
sentence_112: Many of the urban and interior locations, in the Capitol and elsewhere, were filmed in [[Shelby,_North_Carolina|Shelby]] and [[Charlotte,_North_Carolina|Charlotte]]; other scenes also took place and was filmed in the [[Asheville,_North_Carolina|Asheville]] area.
sentence_113: Ross and production designer Phil Messina drew on the buildings of the [[1939_New_York_World's_Fair|1939 New York World's Fair]] and symbols of political power including [[Tiananmen_Square|Tiananmen Square]] and Red Square, when designing the Capitol architecture, which they wanted "to be set in the future but have a sense of its own past... it's festive and alluring and indulgent and decadent but it also has to have the kind of might and power behind it".
sentence_114: For Katniss' neighborhood in District 12, the production team found [[Henry_River_Mill_Village,_North_Carolina|Henry River Mill Village]], an abandoned mill town which Ross said "just worked perfectly for the movie to evoke the scene"; Messina explained that "originally we talked about maybe building one house and the facade of the house next door and redressing it, and maybe doing some CG extensions... we ended up finding a whole abandoned mill town... it was absolutely perfect".
sentence_115: For the costume design, [[Judianna_Makovsky|Judianna Makovsky]] and her crew looked at a lot of photographs of coal mining districts from the 1950s in the search of a very American feel.
sentence_116: The idea was to create clothing unique for every character and to differentiate strongly the people in Capitol and in districts Grey and blue prevailed in the color palette for the district, while the people in Capitol were chosen to look bright in theatrical hats, flowers, ruffles, with powdered and eyebrowless faces.
sentence_117: Main article: The Hunger Games: Songs from District 12 and Beyond
sentence_118: The soundtrack album for The Hunger Games contains songs inspired by the film; only three of them ("Abraham's Daughter", "Safe & Sound", and "Kingdom Come", respectively) appear in the film itself, during the closing credits.
sentence_119: The first single from the film's companion album, "[[Safe_&_Sound_(Taylor_Swift_song)|Safe & Sound]]" by [[Taylor_Swift|Taylor Swift]] featuring [[The_Civil_Wars|The Civil Wars]], was released on December 23, 2011.
sentence_120: It reached number one on the [[ITunes|iTunes]] overall charts in 12 hours.
sentence_121: The music video for "[[Safe_&_Sound_(Taylor_Swift_song)|Safe & Sound]]" was released on February 13, 2012.
sentence_122: Along with separate songs from Swift and The Civil Wars, the soundtrack also features songs by [[The_Decemberists|The Decemberists]], [[Arcade_Fire|Arcade Fire]], [[The_Secret_Sisters|The Secret Sisters]], [[Miranda_Lambert|Miranda Lambert]] featuring The [[Pistol_Annies|Pistol Annies]], Neko Case, [[Kid_Cudi|Kid Cudi]] [[Academy_Award|Academy Award]] winner Glen Hansard, [[The_Low_Anthem|The Low Anthem]], [[Punch_Brothers|Punch Brothers]], [[Birdy_(musician)|Birdy]], [[Maroon_5|Maroon 5]], Jayme Dee, and [[Carolina_Chocolate_Drops|Carolina Chocolate Drops]].
sentence_123: The soundtrack was released on March 20, 2012.
sentence_124: The soundtrack track list was revealed on iTunes on February 13, 2012, and on the 14th "One Engine" was released as the second single.
sentence_125: Jennifer Lawrence singing "Rue's Lullaby" was not included on the soundtrack.
sentence_126: The album debuted at No.
sentence_127: 1 on the Billboard Top 200 chart, having sold 175,000 copies in its first week.
sentence_128: It is one of just 16 soundtracks to grace the top slot in the history of the Top 200 and the first since Michael Jackson's This Is It to debut at #1.
sentence_129: Lionsgate originally announced that [[Danny_Elfman|Danny Elfman]] and T-Bone Burnett would score The Hunger Games, with Burnett also acting as the film's executive music producer to produce songs for the soundtrack.
sentence_130: Due to scheduling conflicts, Elfman was replaced by James Newton Howard.
sentence_131: The score album was released on March 26, 2012.
sentence_132: Arcade Fire also contributed to the movie's original score.
sentence_133: The group composed the fascistic-inspired Panem national anthem, entitled "Horn of Plenty", an important and signature leitmotif appearing throughout the film.
sentence_134: "We were interested in making music that would be more integral in the movie, just as a mental exercise," Butler, who co-wrote the song with Chassagne, explained.
sentence_135: "And there's an anthem that runs throughout the books, the national anthem of the fascist Capitol.
sentence_136: So as a thought experiment, we tried to write what that might sound like.
sentence_137: It's like the Capitol's idea of itself, basically."
sentence_138: He further added that "it's not a pop song or anything.
sentence_139: More of an anthem that could be playing at a big sporting event like the [Hunger] Games.
sentence_140: So we did a structure for that, and then James Newton Howard made a movie-score version of it that happens in several places in the film."
sentence_141: Arcade Fire's Panem national anthem has received strong reviews.
sentence_142: According to [[Spin_(magazine)|Spin]], "'Horn of Plenty' pulls off the neat feat of sounding both exactly like Arcade Fire and exactly like a futuristic anthem.
sentence_143: It still has one foot in the band's uncorrupted neighborhoods, but another is up on the podium at the end of Star Wars accepting an Olympic gold medal or something.
sentence_144: Horns blare, a choir booms, strings swell, the martial percussion steals the show, and we just realized how much we love Big Brother."
sentence_145: The film also features a rather obscure analog track from the 1970s composed by [[Laurie_Spiegel|Laurie Spiegel]] for its "cornucopia scene", as well as music by Steve Reich, [[Ólafur_Arnalds|Ólafur Arnalds]], and the [[Hypnotic_Brass_Ensemble|Hypnotic Brass Ensemble]].
sentence_146: These do not appear on the soundtrack or score releases.
sentence_147: The Hunger Games received mostly positive reviews from critics.
sentence_148: [[Rotten_Tomatoes|Rotten Tomatoes]] gives the film an 84% approval rating, based on 309 reviews, and an average rating of 7.27/10.
sentence_149: The site's consensus states, "Thrilling and superbly acted, The Hunger Games captures the dramatic violence, raw emotion, and ambitious scope of its source novel."
sentence_150: On [[Metacritic|Metacritic]], the film has a score of 68 out of 100 score, based on reviews from 49 critics, indicating "generally favorable reviews".
sentence_151: Audiences polled by CinemaScore gave the film a grade A.
sentence_152: Many critics praised Jennifer Lawrence for her portrayal as Katniss Everdeen, as well as most of the main cast.
sentence_153: According to The Hollywood Reporter, Lawrence embodies Katniss, "just as one might imagine her from the novel".
sentence_154: [[Empire_(magazine)|Empire]] magazine said "Lawrence is perfect as Katniss, there's very little softness about her, more a melancholy determination that good must be done even if that requires bad things."
sentence_155: Several critics have reviewed the film favorably and compared it with other [[Young_adult_fiction|young adult fiction]] adaptations such as [[Harry_Potter_(film_series)|Harry Potter]] and [[The_Twilight_Saga_(film_series)|Twilight]].
sentence_156: Justin Craig of [[Fox_News|Fox News]] rated the film as "[e]xcellent" and stated: "Move over Harry Potter.
sentence_157: A darker, more mature franchise has come to claim your throne."
sentence_158: Rafer Guzman of [[Newsday|Newsday]] referred to The Hunger Games as being "darker than 'Harry Potter,' more sophisticated than 'Twilight'."
sentence_159: David Sexton of [[The_Evening_Standard|The Evening Standard]] stated that The Hunger Games "is well cast and pretty well acted, certainly when compared with Harry Potter's juvenile leads".
sentence_160: [[Roger_Ebert|Roger Ebert]] of the [[Chicago_Sun-Times|Chicago Sun-Times]] gave the film three stars out of four, praising the movie as "effective entertainment" and Lawrence's performance.
sentence_161: Despite a largely positive review, he criticized the film for being too long and noted that the film misses opportunities for social criticism.
sentence_162: Simon Reynolds of [[Digital_Spy|Digital Spy]] gave the film four stars out of five, calling it "enthralling from beginning to end, science fiction that has depth and intelligence to match its pulse-racing entertainment value".
sentence_163: Reynolds also spoke highly of Lawrence's performance and director Gary Ross, whose "rough and ready handheld camerawork" meant that viewers were "with Katniss for every blood-flecked moment of her ordeal in the combat arena".
sentence_164: However, film critic David Thomson of the magazine [[The_New_Republic|The New Republic]] called it a "terrible movie", criticizing it for a lack of character development and unclear presentation of the violence, describing the latter as "un-American".
sentence_165: Eric Goldman of [[IGN|IGN]] awarded the film four out of five stars, stating that director Gary Ross "gets the tone of The Hunger Games right.
sentence_166: This is a grounded, thoughtful and sometimes quite emotional film, with its dark scenario given due weight.
sentence_167: Ross doesn't give the film a glossy, romanticized 'Hollywood' feel, but rather plays everything very realistically and stark, as Katniss must endure these outrageous and horrible scenarios."
sentence_168: The film received some criticism for its [[Shaky_camera|shaky camera]] style, but it was said to "add to the film in certain ways".
sentence_169: The violence drew commentary as well.
sentence_170: Time critic Mary Pols considered that the film was too violent for young children, even though the violence had been toned down compared with the novel, while critic Théoden Janes of the Charlotte Observer found that "[...] the violence is so bland it dilutes the message".
sentence_171: Also writing in Time, psychologist Christopher J. Ferguson argued that parents' fears of the effect of the film's violent content on their children were unnecessary, and that children are capable of viewing violent content without being psychologically harmed.
sentence_172: The Hunger Games earned $408 million in the US & Canada, and $286.4 million in other countries, for a worldwide total of $694.4 million.
sentence_173: It made the largest worldwide opening weekend for a film not released during the summer or the holiday period, earning $211.8 million, which was just ahead of [[Alice_in_Wonderland_(2010_film)|Alice in Wonderland]]'s previous record ($210.1 million).
sentence_174: In North America, The Hunger Games is the 22nd-highest-grossing film, the highest-grossing film released outside the summer or holiday period, and the highest-grossing film distributed by Lionsgate.
sentence_175: [[Box_Office_Mojo|Box Office Mojo]] estimates that the film sold more than 50 million tickets in the US.
sentence_176: The film set a midnight-gross record for a non-sequel ($19.7 million), which is also the tenth-highest midnight gross overall.
sentence_177: On its opening day, it topped the box office at $67.3 million (including midnight showings), setting opening-day and single-day records for a non-sequel.
sentence_178: The film also achieved the sixteenth-highest opening-day and nineteenth-highest single-day grosses of all time.
sentence_179: For its opening weekend, the movie retained the No.
sentence_180: 1 spot and grossed $152.5 million, breaking Alice in Wonderland's opening-weekend records for a film released in March, for any spring release, and for a non-sequel.
sentence_181: Its opening weekend gross was the third highest of 2012 behind [[The_Avengers_(2012_film)|The Avengers]] ($207.4 million) and [[The_Dark_Knight_Rises|The Dark Knight Rises]] ($160.8 million) as well as the largest for any film released outside the summer season and the eighth-largest overall.
sentence_182: The film held the March and spring opening weekend records for four years until they were broken by Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice.
sentence_183: It remained in first place at the North American box office for four consecutive weekends, becoming the first film since [[Avatar_(2009_film)|Avatar]] to achieve this.
sentence_184: On June 10, 2012 (its 80th day in theaters), it became the 14th movie to pass the $400-million-mark.
sentence_185: On April 20, 2012, Lionsgate and [[IMAX_Corporation|IMAX Corporation]] announced that due to "overwhelming demand", The Hunger Games would return to North American IMAX cinemas on April 27 for a further one-week engagement.
sentence_186: Outside North America, the film was released in most countries during March and April 2012, with the exception of China, where it was released in June 2012.
sentence_187: On its first weekend ( March 23–25, 2012), the film topped the box office outside North America with $59.25 million from 67 markets, finishing at first place in most of them.
sentence_188: The largest opening weekends were recorded in China ($9.6 million), Australia ($9.48 million), and the UK, Ireland and Malta ($7.78 million).
sentence_189: In total earnings, its highest-grossing markets after North America are the UK ($37.3 million), Australia ($31.1 million) and China ($27.0 million).
sentence_190: With regard to ticket sales, The Hunger Games broke the record for first-day advance ticket sales on [[Fandango_(ticket_service)|Fandango]] on February 22, 2012, topping the previous record of The Twilight Saga: Eclipse.
sentence_191: The sales were reported to be 83 percent of the site's totals for the day.
sentence_192: According to first tracking, unaided awareness for The Hunger Games was 11%, definite interest was 54%, first choice was 23% and total awareness was 74%.
sentence_193: In the week leading up to its release, the film sold-out over 4,300 showings via Fandango and MovieTickets.com On Fandango alone it ranks as the third-highest advance ticket seller ever behind The Twilight Saga: New Moon and [[Harry_Potter_and_the_Deathly_Hallows_–_Part_2|Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows – Part 2]].
sentence_194: Finally, according to Fandango it broke the site's single-day sales record (March 23), the mobile sales record for a weekend ( March 23–25, 2012) and the site's highest share of a film's opening weekend (Fandango sold 22% of the film's opening weekend tickets).
sentence_195: Interpretations of the film's themes and messages have been widely discussed among critics and general commentators.
sentence_196: In his review for [[The_Washington_Times|The Washington Times]], Peter Suderman expressed that "[m]aybe it's a liberal story about inequality and the class divide.
sentence_197: Maybe it's a libertarian epic about the evils of authoritarian government.
sentence_198: Maybe it's a feminist revision on the sci-fi action blockbuster.
sentence_199: Maybe it's a bloody satire of reality television", but concludes the film only proposes these theories and brings none of them to a reasonable conclusion.
sentence_200: Reviewers and critics have differing views on whether the film represents feminist issues.
sentence_201: Historically, among the "top 200 worldwide box-office hits ever ($350 million and up), not one has been built around a female action star".
sentence_202: Manohla Dargis sees Katniss Everdeen as a female hero following in the lineage of "archetypal figures in the literature of the American West" such as [[Natty_Bumppo|Natty Bumppo]], as well as characters portrayed by American actors such as [[John_Wayne|John Wayne]] and [[Clint_Eastwood|Clint Eastwood]].
sentence_203: Katniss is also seen as defying normative gender roles: she exhibits both "masculine" and "feminine" traits equally.
sentence_204: Dargis also notes that Katniss is a female character with significant agency: "Katniss is a fantasy figure, but partly what makes her powerful—and, I suspect, what makes her so important to a lot of girls and women—is that she's one of the truest feeling, most complex female characters to hit American movies in a while.
sentence_205: She isn't passive, she isn't weak, and she isn't some random girl.
sentence_206: She's active, she's strong and she's the girl who motivates the story."
sentence_207: Similarly, Shelley Bridgeman of [[The_New_Zealand_Herald|The New Zealand Herald]] wrote that because the characteristics of "athleticism, strength, courageousness and prowess at hunting" are not given to a male protagonist, but to Katniss, her character is an abrupt departure from the stereotypical depiction of women as being innately passive or helpless.
sentence_208: Mahvesh Murad of [[The_Express_Tribune|The Express Tribune]] said that the film's triumph is "a young female protagonist with agency", comparing her with [[Joss_Whedon|Joss Whedon]]'s [[Buffy_Summers|Buffy Summers]].
sentence_209: The film has drawn varying interpretations for its political overtones, including arguments in favor of [[Left-wing_politics|left-wing]], [[Right-wing_politics|right-wing]], and [[Libertarianism|libertarian]] viewpoints.
sentence_210: Bob Burnett of The Huffington Post observed the film displays a general distrust of government, regardless of the audience's political party affiliation.
sentence_211: Steven Zeitchik and Emily Rome, in the [[Dallas_Morning_News|Dallas Morning News]], also stated that some viewers formed an opinion about The Hunger Games as a [[Parable|parable]] of the [[Occupy_Wall_Street|Occupy Wall Street]] activity.
sentence_212: The Huffington Post reported that [[Penn_Badgley|Penn Badgley]], a supporter of Occupy Wall Street, saw the film as a social commentary on the movement.
sentence_213: Burnett also states that "Collins doesn't use the terms 1 percent and 99 percent, but it's clear that those in the Capitol are members of the 1 percent and everyone in the Panem districts is part of the 99 percent".
sentence_214: Steven Zeitchik and Emily Rome, in the [[Los_Angeles_Times|Los Angeles Times]] and the Dallas Morning News reported that, among other disparate interpretations, some viewers saw The Hunger Games as a Christian [[Allegory|allegory]].
sentence_215: Jeffrey Weiss of Real Clear Religion, published in the [[Star_Tribune|Star Tribune]] has remarked on what he saw as the intentional absence of religion in The Hunger Games universe, and has commented that while the stories contain no actual religion, people are "find[ing] aspects that represent their own religious values" within it.
sentence_216: Further information: Battle royale genre
sentence_217: David Sexton of The Evening Standard compared The Hunger Games unfavourably to [[Kinji_Fukasaku|Kinji Fukasaku]]'s [[Cinema_of_Japan|Japanese film]] [[Battle_Royale_(film)|Battle Royale]], as did several other critics; the novel had earlier faced criticism for its similarities to the novel [[Battle_Royale_(novel)|Battle Royale]] by Koushun Takami.
sentence_218: Jonathan Looms of The Oxford Student argues that it is "unfair that the film is only drawing comparisons with Battle Royale" but that it "is a veritable pastiche of other movies" as well, comparing it to [[The_Truman_Show|The Truman Show]], [[Death_Race_(film)|Death Race]], the [[Bourne_(film_series)|Bourne]] films, and [[Zoolander|Zoolander]], and that it is common for artists to borrow from and "improve on many sources.
sentence_219: [[Quentin_Tarantino|Quentin Tarantino]] has built his career on this principle."
sentence_220: The Hunger Games is considered to be part of a wider battle royale genre, which had earlier been defined by Battle Royale.
sentence_221: Prior to The Hunger Games, the battle royale genre was largely limited to Japan, where Battle Royale had inspired a wave of [[Manga|manga]], [[Anime|anime]] and [[Visual_novel|visual novel]] works, such as [[Gantz|Gantz]] (2000), [[Higurashi:_When_They_Cry|Higurashi: When They Cry]] (2002), [[Future_Diary|Future Diary]] (2006), [[Btooom!|Btooom!]]
sentence_222: (2009), [[Zero_Escape|Zero Escape]] (2009) and [[Danganronpa|Danganronpa]] (2010).
sentence_223: [[Wheeler_Winston_Dixon|Wheeler Winston Dixon]], a film professor at the [[University_of_Nebraska-Lincoln|University of Nebraska-Lincoln]], listed several precedents: Battle Royale, Jackson's "The Lottery", [[William_Golding|William Golding]]'s [[Lord_of_the_Flies|Lord of the Flies]], [[Metropolis_(2001_film)|Metropolis]], [[Blade_Runner|Blade Runner]], [[Death_Race_2000|Death Race 2000]], and [[George_Orwell|George Orwell]]'s [[Nineteen_Eighty-Four|Nineteen Eighty-Four]].
sentence_224: [[Manohla_Dargis|Manohla Dargis]] in The New York Times compares it to Battle Royale, [[Ender's_Game|Ender's Game]], and Twilight, but contrasts The Hunger Games in terms of how its "exciting" female protagonist Katniss "rescues herself with resourcefulness, guts and true aim".
sentence_225: Steve Rose of [[The_Guardian|The Guardian]] refers to the film as "think Battle Royale meets [[The_Running_Man_(1987_film)|The Running Man]] meets [[Survivor_(TV_series)|Survivor]]".
sentence_226: Charles McGrath, writing for [[The_New_York_Times|The New York Times]], said that the film will remind viewers of the television series [[Survivor_(TV_series)|Survivor]], a little of [[The_Bachelorette|The Bachelorette]], and of the short story "[[The_Lottery|The Lottery]]" by [[Shirley_Jackson|Shirley Jackson]] published in 1948 by [[The_New_Yorker|The New Yorker]].
sentence_227: It reminded an author at [[Salon_(website)|Salon]] of the 1932 film [[The_Most_Dangerous_Game_(film)|The Most Dangerous Game]].
sentence_228: The Hunger Games has also been conceptually compared to [[Robert_Sheckley|Robert Sheckley]]'s 1953 short story "[[Seventh_Victim|Seventh Victim]]" and its 1965 [[Cinema_of_Italy|Italian film]] adaptation by [[Elio_Petri|Elio Petri]], [[The_10th_Victim|The 10th Victim]], as the story and film feature a government-endorsed, televised (in the film's case) "Big Hunt", featuring contestants from around the world acting as "hunters" and "victims".
sentence_229: Writing in The Atlantic, [[Govindini_Murty|Govindini Murty]] made a list of touchstones the film alludes to, from the [[Ancient_Greece|ancient Greek]], [[Roman_Empire|Roman]] and [[Ancient_Egypt|Egyptian civilizations]] to modern references such as the [[Great_Depression|Great Depression]], the Vietnam and [[Iraq_War|Iraq Wars]], and reality television.
sentence_230: For her part, author Collins cites the myth of [[Theseus|Theseus]], reality television and [[Media_coverage_of_the_Iraq_War|coverage of the Iraq War]] as her inspiration.
sentence_231: During the film's opening weekend, controversial statements about various members of the cast arose, sparking open dialogue about issues of racism, sexism and unrealistic [[Body_image|body image]].
sentence_232: Comparisons were also made between The Hunger Games premise of children killing each other, and the child soldiers of the [[Lord's_Resistance_Army|Lord's Resistance Army]] led by [[Joseph_Kony|Joseph Kony]].
sentence_233: In a [[Jezebel_(website)|Jezebel]] article published March 26, 2012, Dodai Stewart reported that several users on Twitter posted racist tweets, criticizing the portrayals of Rue, Thresh and Cinna by African American actors.
sentence_234: In a 2011 interview with Entertainment Weekly, Collins stated that while she did not have any ethnic background in mind for lead characters Katniss and Gale because the book is written in "a time period where hundreds of years have passed" and there would be "a lot of ethnic mixing", she explains "there are some characters in the book who are more specifically described", and states that both Rue and Thresh are African American.
sentence_235: Lyneka Little of [[The_Wall_Street_Journal|The Wall Street Journal]] states that although it is easy to find bigoted or offensive postings online, "the racist 'Hunger Games' tweets, because they are so shockingly ignorant even by the standards of the fringes of the internet, have kicked up a storm".
sentence_236: Fahima Haque of [[The_Washington_Post|The Washington Post]], [[Bim_Adewunmi|Bim Adewunmi]] of The Guardian, and Christopher Rosen of [[The_Huffington_Post|The Huffington Post]] all reiterate the fact that Rue and Thresh are described in The Hunger Games as having dark brown skin, as well as Collins's assertion that they were intended to be depicted as African Americans.
sentence_237: Adewunmi remarked that "it comes to this: if the casting of Rue, Thresh and Cinna has left you bewildered and upset, consider two things.
sentence_238: One: you may be a racist—congrats!
sentence_239: Two: you definitely lack basic reading comprehension.
sentence_240: Mazel tov!"
sentence_241: Erik Kain of [[Forbes|Forbes]] saw the controversy as a way to appreciate the value of free speech.
sentence_242: He states that while society may never be free of racism, "racist comments made on Facebook and Twitter quickly become public record.
sentence_243: Aggregations of these comments, like the Jezebel piece, expose people for what they are.
sentence_244: Sure, many hide under the cloak of anonymity, but many others cannot or choose not to.
sentence_245: And as the internet becomes more civilized and its denizens more accountable, this sort of thing carries more and more weight."
sentence_246: Amandla Stenberg responded to the controversy with the following statement: "As a fan of the books, I feel fortunate to be part of The Hunger Games family...
sentence_247: It was an amazing experience; I am proud of the film and my performance.
sentence_248: I want to thank all of my fans and the entire Hunger Games community for their support and loyalty."
sentence_249: Dayo Okeniyi was quoted saying "I think this is a lesson for people to think before they tweet" and "It's sad... We could now see where society is today.
sentence_250: But I try not to think about stuff like that."
sentence_251: A number of critics expressed disappointment in Lawrence's casting as Katniss because her weight was not representative of a character who has suffered a life of starvation.
sentence_252: Manohla Dargis, in her review of the film for The New York Times stated "[a] few years ago Ms. Lawrence might have looked hungry enough to play Katniss, but now, at 21, her seductive, womanly figure makes a bad fit for a dystopian fantasy about a people starved into submission".
sentence_253: Todd McCarthy of The Hollywood Reporter said that in certain scenes, Lawrence displays "lingering baby fat".
sentence_254: These remarks have been rebuked by a number of journalists for pushing unrealistic body image expectations for women.
sentence_255: L.V.
sentence_256: Anderson of [[Slate_(magazine)|Slate]] states that "[j]ust as living in a world with abundant calories does not automatically make everyone fat, living in a dystopian world like Panem with sporadic food access would not automatically make everyone skinny.
sentence_257: Some bodies, I daresay, would be even bigger than Lawrence's."
sentence_258: Since none of Lawrence's male co-stars have come under the same scrutiny, Anderson concludes complaints about Lawrence's weight are inherently sexist.
sentence_259: [[MTV|MTV]] asked for responses from audiences on the controversy and reported that most found criticism of Lawrence's weight "misguided".
sentence_260: One response pointed to Collins's physical description of Katniss in The Hunger Games novel which reads: "I stand straight, and while I'm thin, I'm strong.
sentence_261: The meat and plants from the woods combined with the exertion it took to get them have given me a healthier body than most of those I see around me."
sentence_262: Los Angeles Times writer Alexandra Le Tellier commented that "[t]he sexist commentary along with the racist barbs made by so-called fans are as stomach-churning as the film's cultural commentary, which, in part, shines a light on the court of public opinion and its sometimes destructive power to determine someone else's fate".
sentence_263: The film has been rated 12A by the British Board of Film Classification (BBFC) in the UK for "intense threat, moderate violence and occasional gory moments".
sentence_264: To achieve that rating, Lionsgate had to cut or substitute seven seconds of film by "digitally removing blood splashes and the sight of blood on wounds and weapons."
sentence_265: The uncut version was ultimately released on Blu-ray in the UK with a 15 certificate.
sentence_266: In the United States, the film was granted a PG-13 rating from the [[Motion_Picture_Association_of_America|Motion Picture Association of America]] (MPAA) for "intense violent thematic material and disturbing images—all involving teens"; as Collins had originally anticipated.
sentence_267: Screening of The Hunger Games was delayed indefinitely in Vietnam.
sentence_268: The film was to be released on March 30, 2012, but, according to a member of the Vietnamese National Film Board, the Board considers the film to be too violent and unanimously voted for the indefinite delay.
sentence_269: It was later banned.

sentence_272: Extras include The World is Watching: Making The Hunger Games, numerous featurettes, the propaganda video in its entire form, a talk with the director Gary Ross and also Elvis Mitchell and a marketing archive.
sentence_273: In its first weekend on sale, Lionsgate reported that 3.8 million DVD/Blu-ray Disc copies of the movie were sold, with more than one-third in the Blu-ray Disc format.

sentence_278: On August 8, 2011, while still shooting the film, Lionsgate announced that a film adaptation of the second novel in The Hunger Games trilogy, The Hunger Games: Catching Fire, was scheduled to be released on November 22, 2013.
sentence_279: In November 2011, Lionsgate entered negotiations with screenwriter [[Simon_Beaufoy|Simon Beaufoy]] to adapt the novel for screen, since the post-production schedule for The Hunger Games was too crowded for Ross and Collins to adapt the next film as originally planned.
sentence_280: The Hunger Games: Catching Fire began production in the summer of 2012.

sentence_0: .বাংলা ([[Romanization_of_Bengali|romanized]] as .bangla) is a secondary [[Internet|Internet]] [[Country_code_top-level_domain|country code top-level domain]] ([[CcTLD|ccTLD]]) for [[Bangladesh|Bangladesh]].
sentence_1: This domain is meant for web addresses in the [[Bengali_language|Bengali language]].
sentence_2: বাংলা is transliterated to bangla, but the web addresses will end in বাংলা.
sentence_3: It is administered by the [[Ministry_of_Posts,_Telecommunications_and_Information_Technology|Ministry of Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology]].
sentence_4: [[.bd|.bd]] is the primary Internet country code top-level domain (ccTLD) for Bangladesh.
sentence_5: .বাংলা was introduced in 2011 but delegated to the Bangladesh Telecommunications Company in 2016, meaning that the process of defining sub domains could start.
sentence_6: .বাংলা is available for registration for all since December 16, 2016.
